In total, more than 2 million infants are represented in this database, providing a rich resource for information on the care and hospital outcomes of high-risk infants. National and international quality collaboratives are filling an important role in neonatology by providing a platform to gather information on maternal child health as well as improving the care delivered to newborns. Although the scope and direction of the quality initiatives vary, several perinatal state collaboratives, such as California Perinatal Quality Care Collaborative, the Ohio Perinatal Quality Collaborative, the Perinatal Quality Collaborative of North Carolina, and Tennessee Initiative for Perinatal Quality Care, have contributed ## PDF page 41 valuable data on rates of late onset sepsis, nonindicated cesarean section, antenatal corticosteroid use, and narcotic abstinence syndrome.8,9 ### Birth Data There were 3,613,647 births in the United States in 2020, a number that has consistently decreased over the past decade (Fig. 2.1).10 The mean age of a mother at first birth has risen to 27.1 years in the United States and 30.7 in the United Kingdom.10–12 The increase in maternal age at first birth is reflected in a steady rise in birth rate for women age 30 and older. However, the teenage birth rate (ages 15–19) has continued to decline to 15.4 per 1,000 live births—a greater than 75% reduction from its peak in 1991 (Fig. 2.2).10 In the United States, the overwhelming majority of births occur in a hospital, approximately 98%, and are attended by an allopathic doctor of medicine (84%) or nurse midwife (8%).13 In 2020, 45,646 deliveries occurred at home, a relative increase of 22%; this change is believed to be related to the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. Of the births occurring in the hospital setting in 2020, the rate of delivery by cesarean section is 31.8% overall, with increasing rates among all age groups as compared with 2019. Significant disparities exist in rates of cesarean section, with non-Hispanic Black women having the highest rate at 36.3% as compared with non-Hispanic White women at 30.8%.10,14 In 2020, 112,437 infants were born as twins in the United States, a rate of 31.15 per 1000 births—the lowest 5 4 Number of births (millions) 3 1970 1975 1980 0 1985 1990 1995 • Fig. 2.1 Number of live births and general fertility rates, 1970–2020. (Source: NCHS. National Vital Statistics System. Natl Vital Stat Rep. February 7, 2022;70[17] [cdc.gov].) rate in nearly 20 years. The twin birth rate increased steadily by 76% between 1980 and 2009. The increase has slowed since the mid-2000s; however, the peak rate was in 2014, at 33.9 per 1000 births.10,15 The increases in twinning rates have been associated with increased use of assistive reproductive therapies (ARTs) such as fertility-enhancing drugs and are reflected by the increasing mean maternal age. In contrast, the rate of higher-order multiples has decreased dramatically (79.6/100,000) since the 1998 peak of 193.5 per 100,000 births. The reduction in higher-order births has been associated with more conservative use of ART, such as limiting the numbers of implanted embryos during in vitro fertilization. ### Fetal Deaths Rates of fetal death are the most difficult-to-interpret statistic because of inconsistencies in reporting. For statistical purposes, the fetal period is defined as the in utero period from 8 weeks after conception until term. A fetal death is commonly referred to as a miscarriage if it occurs at less than 20 weeks’ gestation and a stillbirth if it occurs after 20 weeks’ gestation.5 ### Infant Deaths Infant mortality (IM) is a critical measure of the health and welfare of a population. In 2019, 20,927 infants died before reaching age 1 year, resulting in an IM rate of 5.8 deaths per 1000 live births (Fig. 2.3).15 This rate achieved the Healthy 100 Rate per 1000 women aged 15–44 Number 80 Rate 60 0 2000 2010 2005 2020 2015 ## PDF page 42 | printed page 23 200 25–29 years 100 30–34 years Rate per 1000 women 35–39 years 10 40–44 years 5 1990 1995 1 2000 2005 • Fig. 2.2 Birth rates by age of mother, 1990–2020. The impact of these social determinants of health can be seen in the marked health disparities that exist in IM rates by race. The rate of IM among non-Hispanic Black infants is more than two times the rate of that for non-Hispanic White infants (10.62 vs. 4.49) (Fig. 2.4).15 ### Pregnancy-Related Deaths Pregnancy-related deaths, also known as maternal mortality, is defined as death of a woman either during pregnancy or in the 1 year following the end of pregnancy and is related to pregnancy or its management, excluding those caused by accidents or incidental causes. In 1983, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) began surveillance of pregnancy-related deaths, using death certificates voluntarily submitted by the 50 states, New York City, and the District of Columbia.17 From 1987 to 2017, the rate of pregnancyrelated deaths has increased from 7.2 to 17.3 per 100,000 live births.17 The reasons for the increased rates of mortality are unclear, although they may be due in part to increased reporting. However, it is well recognized that there has been an increase in the number of pregnant women with chronic health conditions such as obesity, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and cardiovascular disease.17,18 These conditions place a pregnant woman at a higher risk of adverse outcomes. Non-Hispanic Black women experience pregnancyrelated mortality rates three times higher than those of non-Hispanic White women (41.7 vs. 13.4 per 100,000 live births) (Fig. 2.5).17 ### Maternal Morbidity Severe maternal morbidity is any unexpected outcome of the pregnancy or labor and delivery process that results in short- and long-term impacts on a woman’s health. title: Big Data for the Smallest Patients—What We Can Learn From Neonatal Database Research

paragraphs.text: 3 Big Data for the Smallest Patients—What We Can Learn From Neonatal Database Research
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: A recent systematic review identified more than 82 neonatal clinical databases.1 These databases, which include both regional and national sources and originate in many different countries, are a rich source of data for observational research and have resulted in more than 2000 publications.
paragraphs.heading: Introduction: Neonatal Database Research

paragraphs.text: Important insights can be made using observational studies from these sources of “big data.” Big data describes large, complex data that are both structured and unstructured. Structured data are captured in predefined methods such as pick list (e.g., International Classification of Diseases codes, gestational age, and birth weight). Unstructured data are not predefined and not coded (e.g., free text comments, pictures, and audio messages). With overwhelming amounts of data stored in electronic medical records, electronic bedside patient monitors, ventilators, laboratory equipment, and smartphones, data scientists spend 50% to 80% of their time curating and preparing data before they can be analyzed. Big data should be organized and easily retrievable and should inform the care we provide to our current and future patients. Big data are valuable only if they are explored and validated.
paragraphs.heading: Introduction: Neonatal Database Research

paragraphs.text: In neonatology, we are fortunate to have many highquality datasets, including (but not limited to) the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention National Vital Statistics System,2 National Institute of Child Health and Development Generic Database,3 Canadian Neonatal Network,4 Children’s Hospitals Neonatal Consortium,5 Vermont Oxford Network (VON),6 California Perinatal Quality Care Collaborative,7 UK National Neonatal Research Database,8 Neonatal Research Network of Japan,9 and Pediatrix Clinical Data Warehouse (CDW),10 and others. Although database studies cannot replace prospective randomized trials,
paragraphs.heading: Introduction: Neonatal Database Research

paragraphs.text: they have become an essential tool to incorporate real-world clinical data and observations toward expanding our knowledge in neonatal medicine.
paragraphs.heading: Introduction: Neonatal Database Research

paragraphs.text: Research studies from neonatal databases have been critical in defining the incidence of neonatal disease, such as reporting important neonatal morbidities among extremely premature infants.3 They have also been used to identify emerging diseases and the associated health care cost, such as in the rapid rise in neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome.11,12 Database research also can provide important benchmarks for care, such as the data provided by the VON.13
paragraphs.heading: Defining Neonatal Diseases

paragraphs.text: Sometimes, database research can help elucidate differences between similar diseases, especially when the incidence is uncommon. For example, factors to help distinguish spontaneous intestinal perforation (SIP) from necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) have come from comparing these uncommon diseases using large clinical data sets.14 Compared with infants with NEC, patients with SIP are smaller and less mature and required more support.15 Database queries can be used to discriminate between the severities of a single disease, such as distinguishing surgical NEC from other forms.16 In addition, database queries can isolate outcomes related to multiple definitions of disease in circumstances where clinical definitions are changing or imprecise.17
paragraphs.heading: Defining Neonatal Diseases

paragraphs.text: Neonatal databases have been critical in the development of standards for assigning small and large for gestational age
paragraphs.heading: Defining Neonatal Diseases

paragraphs.text: at birth and monitoring growth following birth in preterm infants.18–20 Data on anthropomorphic measurements have increased our understanding of the limitations of those standards and challenged the validity of specific growth standards.21 Indeed, disease-specific standards can also be explored—fetal growth curves for infants with gastroschisis have been developed and described.22
paragraphs.heading: Defining Neonatal Diseases

paragraphs.text: One of the most important contributions of neonatal database research is that it allows a detailed look at current medical management. For example, there is significant intercenter variability in the initiation and active treatment of infants born at 22, 23, and 24 weeks of gestation.23 This particular example has shifted the thresholds around clinical and ethical principles used in shared decision making at the limits of perinatal viability. This type of research can also highlight important observations about general variation in neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) use.24
paragraphs.heading: Understanding Variations in Care

paragraphs.text: Many database studies focus on the epidemiology of individual therapies; for example, the reported changes in management of the patent ductus arteriosus have been described using multiple different datasets.4,7 Other times, database studies have been used to describe the impact of national guidance changes, such as the change in steroid use and subsequent rates of bronchopulmonary dysplasia after the American Academy of Pediatrics consensus statement on postnatal steroids.25
paragraphs.heading: Understanding Variations in Care

paragraphs.text: Database research can also inform us about therapeutic creep and unintended consequences of specific therapies.26 For therapeutic hypothermia, there has been an increase in
paragraphs.heading: Understanding Variations in Care

paragraphs.text: use and emerging use in populations which are distinctively different from the population in which it was studied.27
paragraphs.heading: Understanding Variations in Care

paragraphs.text: Neonatal databases can play an important role in identifying health care practices associated with harm. Using data from the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD) Neonatal Research Network’s very low birth weight registry, Guillet et al.28 showed the antecedent use of H2-receptor blocker treatment was associated with an increased incidence of NEC. Subsequent studies have produced similar findings and add the concerning finding of increased late-onset sepsis and mortality.29,30 Based partially on these associations, the American Academy of Pediatrics has discouraged the use of these medications in premature infants.31
paragraphs.heading: Detecting Adverse Events

paragraphs.text: Research in the Pediatrix CDW found cefotaxime was associated with an increased risk of mortality, including infants across all gestational age groups.32 With quality improvement and educational efforts, cefotaxime use decreased, survival improved, and fungal sepsis decreased.33,34 This change in antibiotic use is described in Fig. 3.1.
paragraphs.heading: Detecting Adverse Events

paragraphs.text: Mohamed et al.35 used the Pediatric Hospital Information System database to evaluate the use of 37 nephrotoxic medications and their relationship with acute kidney injury. Of 192,229 neonates, 74% were treated with at least one nephrotoxic medication. Kidney disease was significantly higher in the treated group, highlighting the importance of acute kidney injury in the context of these medications.35
paragraphs.heading: Detecting Adverse Events

paragraphs.text: Case-control studies can also efficiently define risk factors of adverse events and inform both clinical risk prediction
paragraphs.heading: Detecting Adverse Events

paragraphs.text: and the construction of future prospective trials. In a recent example, risk factors for neonatal thromboses were identified which can lead to targeted surveillance and controlled testing of potential anticoagulating interventions.36
paragraphs.heading: Detecting Adverse Events

paragraphs.text: Neonatal database research has been used to develop risk of mortality and morbidity calculators. One important example is the NICHD outcome estimator—which calculates potential risks for both in-hospital and 2-year outcomes based on a few clinical variables. The developers of this calculator leveraged the large number of included patients to offer insights to clinicians and families.37,38 These types of calculators have also been used to define risk of future development of chronic lung disease and can be used to make sample size calculations for prospective clinical studies.39
paragraphs.heading: Development of Risk Estimators

paragraphs.text: Another widely used calculator was developed and tested using data from hospitals managed by Kaiser Permanente in Northern California.40 The authors studied 200,000 newborns born at 35 weeks’ gestation or later to understand factors associated with early-onset sepsis. They demonstrated that clinical care algorithms developed using multivariable risk prediction modeling could safely reduce the proportion of newborns undergoing laboratory testing and empiric antibiotic treatment.
paragraphs.heading: Development of Risk Estimators

paragraphs.text: Database research can be a useful tool for hypothesis generation in cases where a randomized trial would be challenging to perform. In such cases, enrolling a large enough sample size to be able to identify possible harms and benefits might preclude a full trial. In a recent study, several dosing amounts of hydrocortisone were evaluated, and higher dosages were associated with a greater risk of death.41
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Questions Not Suited for Randomized Trials

paragraphs.text: There are other instances where a randomized trial is not feasible. One example is examining models of care and the effects related to how the medical system(s) administer provisions of neonatal intensive care. In one study, short-term in-hospital outcomes were examined as a function of the duration of neonatology rotations.42 Although this study found few differences, large clinical datasets were important to examine the intersection of a clinical-administrative question that is pervasively discussed, and varied, in our field. Another recent study found important risk factors that were associated with attendance at high-risk follow-up clinic visits.43
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Questions Not Suited for Randomized Trials

paragraphs.text: Database research permits the examination of how changes in care impact patient outcomes in the context of natural experiments where lack of equipoise may preclude a clinical trial. With the national supply shortage of vitamin A in 2011, rates of BPD remained unchanged despite marked reductions in vitamin A use.44 Database research can also be helpful in elucidating factors that cannot be randomly
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Questions Not Suited for Randomized Trials

paragraphs.text: assigned—particularly important when describing ongoing concerns of the differences in equity of care.45
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Questions Not Suited for Randomized Trials

paragraphs.text: Generating real-world evidence on the effectiveness and safety of preventive and therapeutic interventions can be done using neonatal databases. Neonatal databases reflect routine care delivery and provide timely, generalizable evidence from a large, diverse group of patients. For example, understanding the outcome of infants with congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) who are treated with inhaled nitric oxide is limited by the rare nature of this anomaly. Meta-analysis is helpful, but the sample size for assessing important outcomes in CDH infants is small.46 Using the administrative Pediatric Health Information System database, 1713 neonates with CDH admitted to 33 US pediatric hospitals were examined. More than half received nitric oxide during their inpatient stay, and use varied dramatically between hospitals. Neonates treated with nitric oxide accumulated greater than $81 million in pharmacy charges. Although the proportion of infants receiving nitric oxide and their duration of therapy increased significantly, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) utilization and mortality did not change significantly. Likewise, hospitalspecific mortality rates did not correlate with nitric oxide therapy, ECMO utilization, or case volume.47
paragraphs.heading: Comparative Effectiveness Research

paragraphs.text: Understanding the comparative effectiveness of specific surfactant preparations is important. However, randomized trials comparing the efficacy of different surfactant preparations often demonstrated equivocal results or were terminated early due to lack of enrollment. There are no clinical trials that compare the three surfactant preparations used in the United States, and it is unlikely a head-to-head randomized trial of different surfactant preparations will be done, because of cost and recruitment issues. In this setting, comparative effectiveness analyses or meta-analyses are justified to determine the differences in safety and efficacy, if any, between surfactant preparations.48
paragraphs.heading: Comparative Effectiveness Research

paragraphs.text: Linking databases can be used to overcome each individual dataset’s limitations and provide novel questions to be asked and answered. Some clinical databases can offer strengths in disease definitions and clinical outcomes, whereas some administrative datasets offer measures in charges/costs and resource utilizations. Combining these at the patient level can offer insights into both variation and “value” or some metric of outcomes relative to costs. For example, 29% of the total variations in costs were noted between centers for infants with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, and sources of these variations could be identified using the combined strengths of both linked datasets.49
paragraphs.heading: Linkage Analyses

paragraphs.text: Database research can also inform about the real-world effectiveness of interventions that are based in prospective research. Large randomized clinical trials suggested a need
paragraphs.heading: Linkage Analyses

paragraphs.text: for changes in pulse oximetry alarm policies, but changing the polices was unrelated to both mortality and severe retinopathy among infants born very preterm.50
paragraphs.heading: Linkage Analyses

paragraphs.text: Large databases in neonatal medicine have transformed the creation, execution, and implementation of quality improvement initiatives. With pre-existing definitions of process and outcome measures, databases can be used to follow change and improve health care delivery and services with the implementation of new approaches. Moreover, these databases can serve to underpin improvements in patient-centered clinical outcomes and foster collaborations within and across institutions to support novel and future improvements to babies’ care and outcomes.
paragraphs.heading: Supporting Quality Improvement Initiatives

paragraphs.text: Unit-level quality improvement has been successfully implemented at a large scale to increase compliance with predetermined best practices and outcomes, including both survival and multiple prematurity-associated morbidities.33 Databases and their associated networks can be used to increase compliance and alignment with external recommendations such as a large reduction in antibiotic use achieved across 146 NICUs participating in an antibiotic stewardship quality initiative.51 In parallel endeavors, multidisciplinary collaborations were used to reduce postoperative health care adverse events.52,53
paragraphs.heading: Supporting Quality Improvement Initiatives

paragraphs.text: There are several points to consider when analyzing and interpreting research findings from large neonatal databases. Database studies are inherently different from randomized trials. Randomized controlled trials are prospectively defined to mitigate biases. Each data element of the electronic case report form is designed to insure precise reporting of demographic, laboratory, treatment, and outcome data. Randomization is used to create unbiased groups for comparison. Using this approach, cause and effect can be established. However, generalizability is often a concern in randomized studies to determine whether the studied group of patients is similar to other real-world cohorts.
paragraphs.heading: Interpretation of Neonatal Database Studies

paragraphs.text: Neonatal database research incorporates real-world data and is infrequently subject to the biases that occur with soliciting consent to participate. Two of the biggest limitations of database research are that the population was not randomly selected and that the data collection was not necessarily designed to assess the investigative question. This becomes particularly problematic if the tested hypothesis was subject to confounding by indication or there are covariates that remained unmeasured or unknown. Limitations in data capture become limitations in the extent to which the analyses can be performed. As such, results from observation studies from databases can only report associations between exposure and outcome variables and
paragraphs.heading: Interpretation of Neonatal Database Studies

paragraphs.text: are best used as hypothesis-generating tools. These studies can inform sample size calculations and identify safe ways to change care to improve outcomes. Although investigators may include factors to account for severity of illness and/or proxies used to account for selection bias, they can be incomplete and may not reflect adequately the true severity of illness. Missing data can prevent us from capturing important confounding variables that may strengthen or even nullify the observed associations. Care is variable across sites, and site variations in the process of care influence outcome. Evaluating the interactions between treatment approaches is difficult. Understanding these limitations is critical to thoughtful evaluation of database research studies. Use of the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines may provide a more complete view of the strengths and weaknesses of observation studies.54 Directed acyclic graphs may be useful in study design and interpretation when causal pathways are complex.55
paragraphs.heading: Interpretation of Neonatal Database Studies

paragraphs.text: Intent is another variable difficult to discern in database research, often because intent is difficult to isolate in clinical bedside care and challenging to code for specifically in datasets. Although later administration of systemic corticosteroids was associated with developing more severe forms of BPD, preventive measures of BPD or treatment of inflammatory changes associated with evolving BPD cannot be easily discerned. Thus confounding by indication must be considered in these complex interpretations.56
paragraphs.heading: Interpretation of Neonatal Database Studies

paragraphs.text: The biggest challenge for data analysis of neonatal databases is the ability to detect and account for bias. Bias in the analysis can lead to underestimating or overestimating the primary outcome signal. There are many different types of bias, but four of the most important are ascertainment bias, referral bias, selection bias, and survivor bias.
paragraphs.heading: Common Types of Bias in Database Research

paragraphs.text: Ascertainment bias occurs where there are systematic differences in subject definition such that the identification and inclusion of subjects create bias. In database research, this often results from how infants are classified with a disease state. For example, SIP was poorly defined in the late 1980s, but NEC was well defined. As the clinical distinction was reported, reporting of SIPs became more commonly used and this led to an (apparent) increased incidence of the disease. This change was driven by education and not by an underlying change in the disease or therapies/interventions. Ascertainment bias can also occur retrospectively if changes in data collection occurred prior to when the research query is being asked and answered. Knowledge and management of these changes are essential to creating and executing an accurate analysis.
paragraphs.heading: Common Types of Bias in Database Research

paragraphs.text: Selection bias is introduced by the selection of infants such that there are measured or unmeasured differences between the groups of infants that are being compared. For example, we know from prospective clinical trials that inhaled nitric oxide is unrelated to risks of mortality in term infants who meet criteria for treatment with ECMO.
paragraphs.heading: Common Types of Bias in Database Research

paragraphs.text: However, in most database studies, it will appear that infants treated with inhaled nitric oxide are more likely to die—particularly when data analyses of infants are not corrected for severity of illness. What drives this finding is that nitric oxide is generally reserved for infants who deteriorate even with mechanical ventilation and have significant lung disease with pulmonary hypertension. Without clear, reproducible, and measured markers of pulmonary hypertension, the use of nitric oxide in this population becomes a surrogate marker for severity of illness, rather than a possible cause of harm.
paragraphs.heading: Common Types of Bias in Database Research

paragraphs.text: Referral bias occurs where the sample of infants in the study does not accurately reflect the general population of infants who are being studied and is a subset of selection bias. This bias clusters in infants hospitalized in quaternary, referral-based NICUs. Infants admitted to these facilities are typically outborn and are referred for complex management and highly specialized care (e.g., pediatric subspecialty care/ services). The proportion of infants with genetic diseases and major congenital anomalies is higher in these types of hospitals than in a similar level of care hospital with a delivery service. Given the complexities of disease(s)—and their interactions—the anticipated morbidities are greater.57 For example, infants with suspected NEC or NEC that can be managed medically are often managed in perinatal centers without pediatric surgical support; conversely, infants with severe NEC and/or pneumoperitoneum require access to surgical services and require transfer to a quaternary center. Referral biases would invalidate comparisons in outcomes related to NEC between NICUs offering pediatric surgical services and NICUs that did not. Furthermore, the outcomes of infants with NEC who were cared for at NICUs with pediatric services will be different than those reported from NICUs without surgical support. Correcting for referral bias requires careful reporting of the study cohort and the severity of illness.
paragraphs.heading: Common Types of Bias in Database Research

paragraphs.text: In contrast, a NICU with an internal delivery service that refers complex infants to a quaternary center will have fewer complex patients and likely have fewer patients with morbidities and/or risks for adverse events. For these reasons, many neonatal databases used in quality improvement stratify results by carefully defined levels of care. These distinctions are not standardized, and the level of care offered at a single institution can change over time. Even within the same hospital, complex infants are referred for subspecialty care in units outside of the NICU, which further reduces the complexity of the population remaining in the NICU. This leads to systematic and differential biases in the populations that are cared for in each unit that is not always accounted for in the definitions or classifications of NICUs.
paragraphs.heading: Common Types of Bias in Database Research

paragraphs.text: Survivor bias is another form of selection bias that is caused by differential inclusion or exclusion of infants who have died in comparison groups. For example, if we are comparing mortality of infants who received a specific medication early in life to other infants treated later in age with the same drug, we may see that the “early use” is associated with a higher mortality. This is the distortion introduced
paragraphs.heading: Common Types of Bias in Database Research

paragraphs.text: by survivor bias. When comparing these two infants, we have artificially exclusively selected survivors to the group of infants who were treated late. Dobson et al.58 found this scenario in a study of early caffeine use in premature infants. Infants receiving early caffeine, particularly those at younger than 24 weeks’ gestational age, had a higher incidence of death. Although this finding is of potential concern, the lower mortality observed in the late caffeine group is more likely a result of survival bias. Mortality at this gestation is high, and most deaths occur early after birth. In this study, an infant who received early caffeine (shortly after birth) remained at higher risk of dying through day of life 4. In contrast, an infant in late caffeine cohort (who received caffeine on day of life 5) had already survived this period.58
paragraphs.heading: Common Types of Bias in Database Research

paragraphs.text: The data in neonatal databases are typically derived data from two broad groups—first, patient registries that are designed to support quality improvement and/or research efforts. These data are typically extracted into structured data from a medical record by trained personnel. They offer benefits: abstraction permit adherence to prespecific definitions in a standard method, the ability to conduct interrater and intra-rater reliability testing and even validation of inter-rater coding that can augment the validity and accuracy of data collected. Although very resource intensive, this time-honored method of data collection permits reliable, accurate, and reproducible data collection.
paragraphs.heading: Understanding Data Sources

paragraphs.text: The second broad group is data captured as part of electronic documentation of the medical record. These data are typically considered administrative, are less structured, and generally need more curation and coding. A subset of these ascertain data from the nonclinical parts of the medical record, even the billing record (e.g., Pediatric Health Information Systems) that can be used to glean what types of clinical interventions were performed in relationship to the outcomes achieved. A clear strength is the amount of data types, structured and unstructured, as well as the volume of data that can be harnessed. Because each neonatal database has its own unique set of limitations with regards to data source, it is important to be thoughtful when evaluating how each study chose to define the denominator and the numerator. A schematic representing data capture in the Children’s Hospitals Neonatal Consortium’s Database in Fig. 3.2 describes the complex relationship of data capture.
paragraphs.heading: Understanding Data Sources

paragraphs.text: Choices made in defining the study cohort are important—how was the denominator defined? Inclusion and exclusion factors meaningfully influence the denominator in cohort studies. Examples include: if outborn infant referrals are included; if infants with congenital anomalies are excluded; and if infants transferred to another service or higher level of care institution are included in the study cohort. A key consideration is often whether the infants included in the study were eligible to achieve the outcome. Outborn infants are generally referred to a higher level of
paragraphs.heading: Understanding Data Sources

paragraphs.text: care for critical illness. Although this may be a small proportion of all admissions to a NICU, it can represent a large part of the denominator for a given study cohort. For example, many infants admitted for therapeutic hypothermia are outborn. In evaluating event rates among infants treated with therapeutic hypothermia, it is important to include outborn infants.
paragraphs.heading: Understanding Data Sources

paragraphs.text: Invariably, all databases will have missing data. Whether these data were unmeasured at the clinical level, errors are present (e.g., 3500 kg), or records have an uncertain outcome or exposure, some data will be omitted. Consideration of biases in omission is an essential step toward classifying the denominator of infants eligible for the study. One way to evaluate biases associated with omitting database records is to analyze characteristics of the included and omitted groups and report how the groups are similar and how they may be different. For example, when reporting on readmission rates of infants with severe BPD and at risk for pulmonary hypertension, the basis for the diagnosis was echocardiography. However, not all infants with severe BPD had an echocardiogram. Thus comparing the study cohort of infants with an echocardiogram to infants without can help mitigate this bias.59
paragraphs.heading: Understanding Data Sources

paragraphs.text: The challenge with defining diseases—how was the numerator defined? Some diseases are hard to diagnose and may even have imprecise definitions. Distinguishing between NEC and SIP is difficult clinically, and the reported rate of NEC is different depending on how well the confounding diagnosis of SIP is made.15 How diagnoses are recorded in medical databases can also change over time. This is further complicated by changes between the ICD-9 compared with the ICD-10 designations. Even the use of a diagnosis changes over time. In a Pediatrix CDW report on patent ductus arteriosus, Bixler et al.60 found a 25% reduction in the diagnosis of patent ductus arteriosus during the study period. Because it is extremely unlikely that the underlying physiology of the ductus arteriosis has changed, we favor that this change in disease coding was more likely related to clinicians’ changing preferences in diagnostic coding.
paragraphs.heading: Understanding Data Sources

paragraphs.text: Some important diseases have no consistent coding. Suspected sepsis is a true disease entity but very difficult to track. Similarly, clinical sepsis is also not standardized in neonatal medicine and is not included in the ICD-10 code list. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia ICD coding may not reflect actual respiratory disease.61 Diagnoses or interventions that remain challenging to accurately and precisely
paragraphs.heading: Understanding Data Sources

paragraphs.text: define in the clinical arena become predictable pitfalls when analyzing as secondary data.
paragraphs.heading: Understanding Data Sources

paragraphs.text: The data source for each database is unique. For example, the Pediatrix CDW only captures infants who are admitted to NICUs. It does not include infants cared for in the normal newborn nursery or infants who die in the delivery room and are never admitted to a NICU. In contrast, the Children’s Hospitals Neonatal Consortium captures structured data from participating quaternary NICUs/institutions with few deliveries and with most patients referred from other NICUs and institutions. Other participants include birth weight and age criteria, and even within certain registries, different amounts/level of data collection may be elected by an individual hospital. Thus care to understand the difference in data collection over time, and the requisite changes in cohorts and infants, must be taken prior to any analyses. Datasets that are more inclusive may produce different results.10
paragraphs.heading: Understanding Data Sources

paragraphs.text: In addition, infants transferred out of the birth hospital often are lost to follow-up, and data on morbidities that occur or are diagnosed later in life (NEC, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and periventricular leukoencephalomalacia, or retinopathy) are not reported. Some databases specifically capture morbidity-specific outcomes, but no database can be comprehensive and exhaustive enough to capture all relevant disease-related outcomes. Study cohorts that include transferred patients in the denominator may report artificially low rates of morbidities that occur later in hospitalization (e.g., BPD and retinopathy of prematurity [ROP]) because transferred patients contribute to the denominator but not the numerator.
paragraphs.heading: Understanding Data Sources

paragraphs.text: There are several common statistical approaches that are commonly used in studies of large neonatal databases. Each study type drives the statistical approach.
paragraphs.heading: Statistical Methods

paragraphs.text: Monitoring epidemiologic trends in changes in disease, management strategies, and outcomes is primarily descriptive.62 Deciding the groupings, and specifically the definitions of disease which frequently can be not standardized, and timing events is critical. There are two commonly applied statistical approaches. The Cochran-Armitage test evaluates how the reported rate is changing over time, using a chi-square approach that tests the linearity between the response variable and experimental variables and detects trends that would not be noticed by more crude methods. Linear regression tools evaluate the slope of the regression line over time. The significance level is dependent on how different the slope over time is different from zero. Challenges are that not all changes are linear and many are not consistent over time.63 In such cases, alternative nonlinear model may be applied to describe temporal trends. In studies designed to evaluate changes in therapies based on new evidence, it may be preferable to graphically represent the
paragraphs.heading: Changes Over Time

paragraphs.text: unadjusted results and annotate rather than apply a specific statistical test.
paragraphs.heading: Changes Over Time

paragraphs.text: After descriptions of cohorts, the most common statistical method used in database research is multivariate logistic regression. Multiple logistic regression evaluates the association between confounding variables and an outcome variable that is dichotomous (e.g., lived or died). In general, the goal is to define the best-fitting, most parsimonious (smallest or most efficient), and biologically reasonable equation to describe the relationship between an outcome and a set of predictors. The confounding or predictor variables may be of any type of data (categorical, ordinal, or continuous). How variables are selected to be included in the statistical model influences the degree of independent association between each variable and the outcome, and it has become common to report results based on several different models.64 Clinicians must be careful to avoid misinterpretation of effects estimates for reported covariates that were not the main exposure—the so-called Table 2 Fallacy.65
paragraphs.heading: Logistic Regression

paragraphs.text: With large sample sizes common in neonatal registries, validation of these equations is becoming common to test whether a developed equation/model can predict outcomes in other infants with fidelity.66,67 Typically this is accomplished by segregating cohorts of studied, eligible infants into a development and validation cohort. Such analyses are the foundation for risk adjustment in comparing differing cohorts of infants to minimize selection biases.68
paragraphs.heading: Logistic Regression

paragraphs.text: In case-control studies, an additional technique to logistic modeling is matched pairs analysis. Infants in a study (treatment) group are matched with a comparison (control) group based on important confounding variables (e.g., gestational age, birth weight, gender, mode of delivery, exposure to antenatal steroids, and a surrogate marker for severity of illness). The goal is to minimize the measured, unmeasured, and unknown differences between the treatment and control groups so that differences in the main exposure can be isolated and tested for observed differences.36
paragraphs.heading: Matching

paragraphs.text: Propensity score matching is similar to matched pairs analysis but uses a different matching strategy. First, a regression analysis is completed that uses patient characteristics to calculate the probability that each infant will be offered a specific therapy. This probability is labeled as the propensity score and can be used in various matching approaches. The goal of matching is to mimic randomization and reduce selection bias. Matching tools are particularly helpful when randomized trials would be difficult to perform69 or to establish equipoise for a prospective trial.70
paragraphs.heading: Matching

paragraphs.text: A constant concern in prospective clinical trials is whether the study was sufficiently powered to detect a meaningful
paragraphs.heading: Interpretation of Statistical Significance

paragraphs.text: difference between the intervention and control groups. Factors that drive this analysis are the occurrence rate for the primary outcome, the magnitude of the expected difference between the two groups, and the achievable sample size. It requires a larger sample to evaluate the differences between outcomes if the effect size is small or the event rate is rare. This becomes problematic in randomized controlled trials if the a priori estimates overestimate the primary outcome rate and/or the difference between intervention and control groups. Single center trials are oftentimes underpowered to detect a difference.71
paragraphs.heading: Interpretation of Statistical Significance

paragraphs.text: When using big data, the opposite is true. Because the sample sizes are large, it is much easier for investigators to detect differences that are statistically significant. These may not be clinically important. For example, in a recent NICHD study evaluating extremely preterm infants, maternal age differed significantly across gestational age.3 Although this difference was statistically significant, the clinical significance of some gestational age infants having a maternal age that was 1 year greater is probably marginal. Similarly, Bloom et al.72 found a difference in head circumference at the time of hospital discharge in a continuous quality improvement project aimed at improving growth of very low birth weight infants during the first 28 days. The difference after the intervention was an increase in the mean of 0.2 cm. Although statistically significant, the difference is within the error of the measurement and it is unlikely that the difference was clinically meaningful.
paragraphs.heading: Interpretation of Statistical Significance

paragraphs.text: In the NICU, there remain many opportunities for additional data collection. Nursing assessments include vital signs, pain/comfort assessments, and the interventions that infants require (e.g., suction, repositioning, titration of FiO2). Respiratory therapists and rehabilitation specialists provide insights on other critical functions to assess
paragraphs.heading: The Future of Big Data in Neonatology

paragraphs.text: Key Points
paragraphs.heading: The Future of Big Data in Neonatology

paragraphs.text: • Neonatal database research is increasing and has the
paragraphs.heading: The Future of Big Data in Neonatology

paragraphs.text: potential to add meaningful clinical evidence. • Database research has been used to describe disease
paragraphs.heading: The Future of Big Data in Neonatology

paragraphs.text: incidence and variations in care, identify adverse
paragraphs.heading: The Future of Big Data in Neonatology

paragraphs.text: swallowing, tone, responses to therapy, and even whether cardiorespiratory support can be sufficient to promote an acceptable neurodevelopmental trajectory. Patient electronic monitors routinely display real-time trends in heart rate, pulse oximetry, respiratory rate measure by impedance changes, and, when arterial access is present, blood pressure. In infants with respiratory failure, mechanical ventilation devices have evolved to display, track, and store trends in numerous markers of pulmonary function/physiology. Ancillary monitors for indirect markers of cardiac output (e.g., near-infrared spectroscopy) and the up-and-coming generation of wearable devices73 will continue to expand the trend of incorporating large data sources into neonatology’s clinical practice, research, and quality improvement.
paragraphs.heading: References

paragraphs.text: Creating real-time dashboards that allow monitoring of changes in care and associated changes in outcome may allow us to identify important associations.74 If we carefully document the diagnoses we make and the care we provide in a structured way, there is much we can learn from the patterns that accumulate. Changes in the way that data are analyzed, using techniques such as machine learning75 and target trials,76 may also offer greater insights into neonatal care. Database research might also be used to augment future clinical trials by identifying high-risk populations, decreasing sample sizes, and gaining efficiency in time and costs of these trials.
paragraphs.heading: References

paragraphs.text: There is a difference between knowledge and wisdom. Knowledge is the accumulation of meaningful facts. Wisdom is integration of knowledge in a way that offers benefits. In health care, we may know the precisely correct diagnosis and the treatment, but it takes wisdom to apply that knowledge to plans that takes into account the clinical context of the patient and the impact of the diagnosis and treatment on our patients. Neonatal database research can be instrumental in increasing both diagnostic precision and therapeutic effectiveness to minimize burdens and improve outcomes for children and their families.

figures.caption: • Fig. 3.1 Change in the use of ampicillin, gentamicin, and cefotaxime over time from the Pediatrix Clinical Data Warehouse based on NICU discharges. Cefotaxime decreased in the early 2000s after reports of an association between cephalosporins and fungal sepsis and increased mortality32 and following Pediatrixinitiated quality improvement efforts to reduce use of cefotaxime.33 Use of ampicillin and gentamicin decreased after 2016 as there was an increased use of an early-onset sepsis calculator.40 Antibiotic stewardship was associated with decline in antibiotic use, especially cephalosporins and related complications. NICU, Neonatal intensive care unit.

figures.caption: • Fig. 3.2 Schematic of entity relationship diagram for Children’s Hospitals Neonatal Consortium’s Database (CHND). Patient- and maternal-related data are recorded once per patient. One-to-one relationships describe measures related to admission to the NICU (e.g., transport, admission, and hospital course, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation [ECMO] support). One-to-multiple relationships denote those events that can occur more than once per NICU admission (e.g., diagnoses, central venous access devices (CVADs), surgeries, infections, and respiratory support periods). Disposition of each patient from the NICU can be home, intRA-facility, intER-facility, or mortality. Specific data fields are collected based on disposition from the NICU through 1 year of age. 3 Big Data for the Smallest Patients—What We Can Learn From Neonatal Database Research

### VEERAL NALIN TOLIA, REESE H. CLARK, AND KARNA MURTHY

### Introduction: Neonatal Database Research

A recent systematic review identified more than 82 neonatal clinical databases.1 These databases, which include both regional and national sources and originate in many different countries, are a rich source of data for observational research and have resulted in more than 2000 publications.

Important insights can be made using observational studies from these sources of “big data.” Big data describes large, complex data that are both structured and unstructured. Structured data are captured in predefined methods such as pick list (e.g., International Classification of Diseases codes, gestational age, and birth weight). Unstructured data are not predefined and not coded (e.g., free text comments, pictures, and audio messages). With overwhelming amounts of data stored in electronic medical records, electronic bedside patient monitors, ventilators, laboratory equipment, and smartphones, data scientists spend 50% to 80% of their time curating and preparing data before they can be analyzed. Big data should be organized and easily retrievable and should inform the care we provide to our current and future patients. Big data are valuable only if they are explored and validated.

In neonatology, we are fortunate to have many highquality datasets, including (but not limited to) the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention National Vital Statistics System,2 National Institute of Child Health and Development Generic Database,3 Canadian Neonatal Network,4 Children’s Hospitals Neonatal Consortium,5 Vermont Oxford Network (VON),6 California Perinatal Quality Care Collaborative,7 UK National Neonatal Research Database,8 Neonatal Research Network of Japan,9 and Pediatrix Clinical Data Warehouse (CDW),10 and others. Although database studies cannot replace prospective randomized trials,

28

they have become an essential tool to incorporate real-world clinical data and observations toward expanding our knowledge in neonatal medicine.

### The Scope of Research Using Neonatal

### Databases

### Defining Neonatal Diseases

Research studies from neonatal databases have been critical in defining the incidence of neonatal disease, such as reporting important neonatal morbidities among extremely premature infants.3 They have also been used to identify emerging diseases and the associated health care cost, such as in the rapid rise in neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome.11,12 Database research also can provide important benchmarks for care, such as the data provided by the VON.13

Sometimes, database research can help elucidate differences between similar diseases, especially when the incidence is uncommon. For example, factors to help distinguish spontaneous intestinal perforation (SIP) from necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) have come from comparing these uncommon diseases using large clinical data sets.14 Compared with infants with NEC, patients with SIP are smaller and less mature and required more support.15 Database queries can be used to discriminate between the severities of a single disease, such as distinguishing surgical NEC from other forms.16 In addition, database queries can isolate outcomes related to multiple definitions of disease in circumstances where clinical definitions are changing or imprecise.17

Neonatal databases have been critical in the development of standards for assigning small and large for gestational age


## PDF page 48 | printed page 29

at birth and monitoring growth following birth in preterm infants.18–20 Data on anthropomorphic measurements have increased our understanding of the limitations of those standards and challenged the validity of specific growth standards.21 Indeed, disease-specific standards can also be explored—fetal growth curves for infants with gastroschisis have been developed and described.22

### Understanding Variations in Care

One of the most important contributions of neonatal database research is that it allows a detailed look at current medical management. For example, there is significant intercenter variability in the initiation and active treatment of infants born at 22, 23, and 24 weeks of gestation.23 This particular example has shifted the thresholds around clinical and ethical principles used in shared decision making at the limits of perinatal viability. This type of research can also highlight important observations about general variation in neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) use.24

Many database studies focus on the epidemiology of individual therapies; for example, the reported changes in management of the patent ductus arteriosus have been described using multiple different datasets.4,7 Other times, database studies have been used to describe the impact of national guidance changes, such as the change in steroid use and subsequent rates of bronchopulmonary dysplasia after the American Academy of Pediatrics consensus statement on postnatal steroids.25

Database research can also inform us about therapeutic creep and unintended consequences of specific therapies.26 For therapeutic hypothermia, there has been an increase in

### Detecting Adverse Events

Neonatal databases can play an important role in identifying health care practices associated with harm. Using data from the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD) Neonatal Research Network’s very low birth weight registry, Guillet et al.28 showed the antecedent use of H2-receptor blocker treatment was associated with an increased incidence of NEC. Subsequent studies have produced similar findings and add the concerning finding of increased late-onset sepsis and mortality.29,30 Based partially on these associations, the American Academy of Pediatrics has discouraged the use of these medications in premature infants.31

Research in the Pediatrix CDW found cefotaxime was associated with an increased risk of mortality, including infants across all gestational age groups.32 With quality improvement and educational efforts, cefotaxime use decreased, survival improved, and fungal sepsis decreased.33,34 This change in antibiotic use is described in Fig. 3.1.

Mohamed et al.35 used the Pediatric Hospital Information System database to evaluate the use of 37 nephrotoxic medications and their relationship with acute kidney injury. Of 192,229 neonates, 74% were treated with at least one nephrotoxic medication. Kidney disease was significantly higher in the treated group, highlighting the importance of acute kidney injury in the context of these medications.35

Case-control studies can also efficiently define risk factors of adverse events and inform both clinical risk prediction

Cefotaxime

2010 2011 2012 2013 2014 2015 2016 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021


## PDF page 49

and the construction of future prospective trials. In a recent example, risk factors for neonatal thromboses were identified which can lead to targeted surveillance and controlled testing of potential anticoagulating interventions.36

### Development of Risk Estimators

Neonatal database research has been used to develop risk of mortality and morbidity calculators. One important example is the NICHD outcome estimator—which calculates potential risks for both in-hospital and 2-year outcomes based on a few clinical variables. The developers of this calculator leveraged the large number of included patients to offer insights to clinicians and families.37,38 These types of calculators have also been used to define risk of future development of chronic lung disease and can be used to make sample size calculations for prospective clinical studies.39

Another widely used calculator was developed and tested using data from hospitals managed by Kaiser Permanente in Northern California.40 The authors studied 200,000 newborns born at 35 weeks’ gestation or later to understand factors associated with early-onset sepsis. They demonstrated that clinical care algorithms developed using multivariable risk prediction modeling could safely reduce the proportion of newborns undergoing laboratory testing and empiric antibiotic treatment.

### Clinical Questions Not Suited for Randomized Trials

Database research can be a useful tool for hypothesis generation in cases where a randomized trial would be challenging to perform. In such cases, enrolling a large enough sample size to be able to identify possible harms and benefits might preclude a full trial. In a recent study, several dosing amounts of hydrocortisone were evaluated, and higher dosages were associated with a greater risk of death.41

There are other instances where a randomized trial is not feasible. One example is examining models of care and the effects related to how the medical system(s) administer provisions of neonatal intensive care. In one study, short-term in-hospital outcomes were examined as a function of the duration of neonatology rotations.42 Although this study found few differences, large clinical datasets were important to examine the intersection of a clinical-administrative question that is pervasively discussed, and varied, in our field. Another recent study found important risk factors that were associated with attendance at high-risk follow-up clinic visits.43

Database research permits the examination of how changes in care impact patient outcomes in the context of natural experiments where lack of equipoise may preclude a clinical trial. With the national supply shortage of vitamin A in 2011, rates of BPD remained unchanged despite marked reductions in vitamin A use.44 Database research can also be helpful in elucidating factors that cannot be randomly

assigned—particularly important when describing ongoing concerns of the differences in equity of care.45

### Comparative Effectiveness Research

Generating real-world evidence on the effectiveness and safety of preventive and therapeutic interventions can be done using neonatal databases. Neonatal databases reflect routine care delivery and provide timely, generalizable evidence from a large, diverse group of patients. For example, understanding the outcome of infants with congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) who are treated with inhaled nitric oxide is limited by the rare nature of this anomaly. Meta-analysis is helpful, but the sample size for assessing important outcomes in CDH infants is small.46 Using the administrative Pediatric Health Information System database, 1713 neonates with CDH admitted to 33 US pediatric hospitals were examined. More than half received nitric oxide during their inpatient stay, and use varied dramatically between hospitals. Neonates treated with nitric oxide accumulated greater than $81 million in pharmacy charges. Although the proportion of infants receiving nitric oxide and their duration of therapy increased significantly, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) utilization and mortality did not change significantly. Likewise, hospitalspecific mortality rates did not correlate with nitric oxide therapy, ECMO utilization, or case volume.47

Understanding the comparative effectiveness of specific surfactant preparations is important. However, randomized trials comparing the efficacy of different surfactant preparations often demonstrated equivocal results or were terminated early due to lack of enrollment. There are no clinical trials that compare the three surfactant preparations used in the United States, and it is unlikely a head-to-head randomized trial of different surfactant preparations will be done, because of cost and recruitment issues. In this setting, comparative effectiveness analyses or meta-analyses are justified to determine the differences in safety and efficacy, if any, between surfactant preparations.48

### Linkage Analyses

Linking databases can be used to overcome each individual dataset’s limitations and provide novel questions to be asked and answered. Some clinical databases can offer strengths in disease definitions and clinical outcomes, whereas some administrative datasets offer measures in charges/costs and resource utilizations. Combining these at the patient level can offer insights into both variation and “value” or some metric of outcomes relative to costs. For example, 29% of the total variations in costs were noted between centers for infants with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, and sources of these variations could be identified using the combined strengths of both linked datasets.49

Database research can also inform about the real-world effectiveness of interventions that are based in prospective research. Large randomized clinical trials suggested a need


## PDF page 50 | printed page 31

for changes in pulse oximetry alarm policies, but changing the polices was unrelated to both mortality and severe retinopathy among infants born very preterm.50

### Supporting Quality Improvement Initiatives

Large databases in neonatal medicine have transformed the creation, execution, and implementation of quality improvement initiatives. With pre-existing definitions of process and outcome measures, databases can be used to follow change and improve health care delivery and services with the implementation of new approaches. Moreover, these databases can serve to underpin improvements in patient-centered clinical outcomes and foster collaborations within and across institutions to support novel and future improvements to babies’ care and outcomes.

Unit-level quality improvement has been successfully implemented at a large scale to increase compliance with predetermined best practices and outcomes, including both survival and multiple prematurity-associated morbidities.33 Databases and their associated networks can be used to increase compliance and alignment with external recommendations such as a large reduction in antibiotic use achieved across 146 NICUs participating in an antibiotic stewardship quality initiative.51 In parallel endeavors, multidisciplinary collaborations were used to reduce postoperative health care adverse events.52,53

### Interpretation of Neonatal Database Studies

There are several points to consider when analyzing and interpreting research findings from large neonatal databases. Database studies are inherently different from randomized trials. Randomized controlled trials are prospectively defined to mitigate biases. Each data element of the electronic case report form is designed to insure precise reporting of demographic, laboratory, treatment, and outcome data. Randomization is used to create unbiased groups for comparison. Using this approach, cause and effect can be established. However, generalizability is often a concern in randomized studies to determine whether the studied group of patients is similar to other real-world cohorts.

Neonatal database research incorporates real-world data and is infrequently subject to the biases that occur with soliciting consent to participate. Two of the biggest limitations of database research are that the population was not randomly selected and that the data collection was not necessarily designed to assess the investigative question. This becomes particularly problematic if the tested hypothesis was subject to confounding by indication or there are covariates that remained unmeasured or unknown. Limitations in data capture become limitations in the extent to which the analyses can be performed. As such, results from observation studies from databases can only report associations between exposure and outcome variables and

are best used as hypothesis-generating tools. These studies can inform sample size calculations and identify safe ways to change care to improve outcomes. Although investigators may include factors to account for severity of illness and/or proxies used to account for selection bias, they can be incomplete and may not reflect adequately the true severity of illness. Missing data can prevent us from capturing important confounding variables that may strengthen or even nullify the observed associations. Care is variable across sites, and site variations in the process of care influence outcome. Evaluating the interactions between treatment approaches is difficult. Understanding these limitations is critical to thoughtful evaluation of database research studies. Use of the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines may provide a more complete view of the strengths and weaknesses of observation studies.54 Directed acyclic graphs may be useful in study design and interpretation when causal pathways are complex.55

Intent is another variable difficult to discern in database research, often because intent is difficult to isolate in clinical bedside care and challenging to code for specifically in datasets. Although later administration of systemic corticosteroids was associated with developing more severe forms of BPD, preventive measures of BPD or treatment of inflammatory changes associated with evolving BPD cannot be easily discerned. Thus confounding by indication must be considered in these complex interpretations.56

### Common Types of Bias in Database Research

The biggest challenge for data analysis of neonatal databases is the ability to detect and account for bias. Bias in the analysis can lead to underestimating or overestimating the primary outcome signal. There are many different types of bias, but four of the most important are ascertainment bias, referral bias, selection bias, and survivor bias.

Ascertainment bias occurs where there are systematic differences in subject definition such that the identification and inclusion of subjects create bias. In database research, this often results from how infants are classified with a disease state. For example, SIP was poorly defined in the late 1980s, but NEC was well defined. As the clinical distinction was reported, reporting of SIPs became more commonly used and this led to an (apparent) increased incidence of the disease. This change was driven by education and not by an underlying change in the disease or therapies/interventions. Ascertainment bias can also occur retrospectively if changes in data collection occurred prior to when the research query is being asked and answered. Knowledge and management of these changes are essential to creating and executing an accurate analysis.

Selection bias is introduced by the selection of infants such that there are measured or unmeasured differences between the groups of infants that are being compared. For example, we know from prospective clinical trials that inhaled nitric oxide is unrelated to risks of mortality in term infants who meet criteria for treatment with ECMO.


## PDF page 51

However, in most database studies, it will appear that infants treated with inhaled nitric oxide are more likely to die—particularly when data analyses of infants are not corrected for severity of illness. What drives this finding is that nitric oxide is generally reserved for infants who deteriorate even with mechanical ventilation and have significant lung disease with pulmonary hypertension. Without clear, reproducible, and measured markers of pulmonary hypertension, the use of nitric oxide in this population becomes a surrogate marker for severity of illness, rather than a possible cause of harm.

Referral bias occurs where the sample of infants in the study does not accurately reflect the general population of infants who are being studied and is a subset of selection bias. This bias clusters in infants hospitalized in quaternary, referral-based NICUs. Infants admitted to these facilities are typically outborn and are referred for complex management and highly specialized care (e.g., pediatric subspecialty care/ services). The proportion of infants with genetic diseases and major congenital anomalies is higher in these types of hospitals than in a similar level of care hospital with a delivery service. Given the complexities of disease(s)—and their interactions—the anticipated morbidities are greater.57 For example, infants with suspected NEC or NEC that can be managed medically are often managed in perinatal centers without pediatric surgical support; conversely, infants with severe NEC and/or pneumoperitoneum require access to surgical services and require transfer to a quaternary center. Referral biases would invalidate comparisons in outcomes related to NEC between NICUs offering pediatric surgical services and NICUs that did not. Furthermore, the outcomes of infants with NEC who were cared for at NICUs with pediatric services will be different than those reported from NICUs without surgical support. Correcting for referral bias requires careful reporting of the study cohort and the severity of illness.

In contrast, a NICU with an internal delivery service that refers complex infants to a quaternary center will have fewer complex patients and likely have fewer patients with morbidities and/or risks for adverse events. For these reasons, many neonatal databases used in quality improvement stratify results by carefully defined levels of care. These distinctions are not standardized, and the level of care offered at a single institution can change over time. Even within the same hospital, complex infants are referred for subspecialty care in units outside of the NICU, which further reduces the complexity of the population remaining in the NICU. This leads to systematic and differential biases in the populations that are cared for in each unit that is not always accounted for in the definitions or classifications of NICUs.

Survivor bias is another form of selection bias that is caused by differential inclusion or exclusion of infants who have died in comparison groups. For example, if we are comparing mortality of infants who received a specific medication early in life to other infants treated later in age with the same drug, we may see that the “early use” is associated with a higher mortality. This is the distortion introduced

by survivor bias. When comparing these two infants, we have artificially exclusively selected survivors to the group of infants who were treated late. Dobson et al.58 found this scenario in a study of early caffeine use in premature infants. Infants receiving early caffeine, particularly those at younger than 24 weeks’ gestational age, had a higher incidence of death. Although this finding is of potential concern, the lower mortality observed in the late caffeine group is more likely a result of survival bias. Mortality at this gestation is high, and most deaths occur early after birth. In this study, an infant who received early caffeine (shortly after birth) remained at higher risk of dying through day of life 4. In contrast, an infant in late caffeine cohort (who received caffeine on day of life 5) had already survived this period.58

### Understanding Data Sources

The data in neonatal databases are typically derived data from two broad groups—first, patient registries that are designed to support quality improvement and/or research efforts. These data are typically extracted into structured data from a medical record by trained personnel. They offer benefits: abstraction permit adherence to prespecific definitions in a standard method, the ability to conduct interrater and intra-rater reliability testing and even validation of inter-rater coding that can augment the validity and accuracy of data collected. Although very resource intensive, this time-honored method of data collection permits reliable, accurate, and reproducible data collection.

The second broad group is data captured as part of electronic documentation of the medical record. These data are typically considered administrative, are less structured, and generally need more curation and coding. A subset of these ascertain data from the nonclinical parts of the medical record, even the billing record (e.g., Pediatric Health Information Systems) that can be used to glean what types of clinical interventions were performed in relationship to the outcomes achieved. A clear strength is the amount of data types, structured and unstructured, as well as the volume of data that can be harnessed. Because each neonatal database has its own unique set of limitations with regards to data source, it is important to be thoughtful when evaluating how each study chose to define the denominator and the numerator. A schematic representing data capture in the Children’s Hospitals Neonatal Consortium’s Database in Fig. 3.2 describes the complex relationship of data capture.

Choices made in defining the study cohort are important—how was the denominator defined? Inclusion and exclusion factors meaningfully influence the denominator in cohort studies. Examples include: if outborn infant referrals are included; if infants with congenital anomalies are excluded; and if infants transferred to another service or higher level of care institution are included in the study cohort. A key consideration is often whether the infants included in the study were eligible to achieve the outcome. Outborn infants are generally referred to a higher level of
