The challenge with defining diseases—how was the numerator defined? Some diseases are hard to diagnose and may even have imprecise definitions. Distinguishing between NEC and SIP is difficult clinically, and the reported rate of NEC is different depending on how well the confounding diagnosis of SIP is made.15 How diagnoses are recorded in medical databases can also change over time. This is further complicated by changes between the ICD-9 compared with the ICD-10 designations. Even the use of a diagnosis changes over time. In a Pediatrix CDW report on patent ductus arteriosus, Bixler et al.60 found a 25% reduction in the diagnosis of patent ductus arteriosus during the study period. Because it is extremely unlikely that the underlying physiology of the ductus arteriosis has changed, we favor that this change in disease coding was more likely related to clinicians’ changing preferences in diagnostic coding.

Some important diseases have no consistent coding. Suspected sepsis is a true disease entity but very difficult to track. Similarly, clinical sepsis is also not standardized in neonatal medicine and is not included in the ICD-10 code list. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia ICD coding may not reflect actual respiratory disease.61 Diagnoses or interventions that remain challenging to accurately and precisely


## PDF page 53

define in the clinical arena become predictable pitfalls when analyzing as secondary data.

The data source for each database is unique. For example, the Pediatrix CDW only captures infants who are admitted to NICUs. It does not include infants cared for in the normal newborn nursery or infants who die in the delivery room and are never admitted to a NICU. In contrast, the Children’s Hospitals Neonatal Consortium captures structured data from participating quaternary NICUs/institutions with few deliveries and with most patients referred from other NICUs and institutions. Other participants include birth weight and age criteria, and even within certain registries, different amounts/level of data collection may be elected by an individual hospital. Thus care to understand the difference in data collection over time, and the requisite changes in cohorts and infants, must be taken prior to any analyses. Datasets that are more inclusive may produce different results.10

In addition, infants transferred out of the birth hospital often are lost to follow-up, and data on morbidities that occur or are diagnosed later in life (NEC, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and periventricular leukoencephalomalacia, or retinopathy) are not reported. Some databases specifically capture morbidity-specific outcomes, but no database can be comprehensive and exhaustive enough to capture all relevant disease-related outcomes. Study cohorts that include transferred patients in the denominator may report artificially low rates of morbidities that occur later in hospitalization (e.g., BPD and retinopathy of prematurity [ROP]) because transferred patients contribute to the denominator but not the numerator.

### Statistical Methods

There are several common statistical approaches that are commonly used in studies of large neonatal databases. Each study type drives the statistical approach.

### Changes Over Time

Monitoring epidemiologic trends in changes in disease, management strategies, and outcomes is primarily descriptive.62 Deciding the groupings, and specifically the definitions of disease which frequently can be not standardized, and timing events is critical. There are two commonly applied statistical approaches. The Cochran-Armitage test evaluates how the reported rate is changing over time, using a chi-square approach that tests the linearity between the response variable and experimental variables and detects trends that would not be noticed by more crude methods. Linear regression tools evaluate the slope of the regression line over time. The significance level is dependent on how different the slope over time is different from zero. Challenges are that not all changes are linear and many are not consistent over time.63 In such cases, alternative nonlinear model may be applied to describe temporal trends. In studies designed to evaluate changes in therapies based on new evidence, it may be preferable to graphically represent the

unadjusted results and annotate rather than apply a specific statistical test.

### Logistic Regression

After descriptions of cohorts, the most common statistical method used in database research is multivariate logistic regression. Multiple logistic regression evaluates the association between confounding variables and an outcome variable that is dichotomous (e.g., lived or died). In general, the goal is to define the best-fitting, most parsimonious (smallest or most efficient), and biologically reasonable equation to describe the relationship between an outcome and a set of predictors. The confounding or predictor variables may be of any type of data (categorical, ordinal, or continuous). How variables are selected to be included in the statistical model influences the degree of independent association between each variable and the outcome, and it has become common to report results based on several different models.64 Clinicians must be careful to avoid misinterpretation of effects estimates for reported covariates that were not the main exposure—the so-called Table 2 Fallacy.65

With large sample sizes common in neonatal registries, validation of these equations is becoming common to test whether a developed equation/model can predict outcomes in other infants with fidelity.66,67 Typically this is accomplished by segregating cohorts of studied, eligible infants into a development and validation cohort. Such analyses are the foundation for risk adjustment in comparing differing cohorts of infants to minimize selection biases.68

### Matching

In case-control studies, an additional technique to logistic modeling is matched pairs analysis. Infants in a study (treatment) group are matched with a comparison (control) group based on important confounding variables (e.g., gestational age, birth weight, gender, mode of delivery, exposure to antenatal steroids, and a surrogate marker for severity of illness). The goal is to minimize the measured, unmeasured, and unknown differences between the treatment and control groups so that differences in the main exposure can be isolated and tested for observed differences.36

Propensity score matching is similar to matched pairs analysis but uses a different matching strategy. First, a regression analysis is completed that uses patient characteristics to calculate the probability that each infant will be offered a specific therapy. This probability is labeled as the propensity score and can be used in various matching approaches. The goal of matching is to mimic randomization and reduce selection bias. Matching tools are particularly helpful when randomized trials would be difficult to perform69 or to establish equipoise for a prospective trial.70

### Interpretation of Statistical Significance

A constant concern in prospective clinical trials is whether the study was sufficiently powered to detect a meaningful


## PDF page 54 | printed page 35

difference between the intervention and control groups. Factors that drive this analysis are the occurrence rate for the primary outcome, the magnitude of the expected difference between the two groups, and the achievable sample size. It requires a larger sample to evaluate the differences between outcomes if the effect size is small or the event rate is rare. This becomes problematic in randomized controlled trials if the a priori estimates overestimate the primary outcome rate and/or the difference between intervention and control groups. Single center trials are oftentimes underpowered to detect a difference.71

When using big data, the opposite is true. Because the sample sizes are large, it is much easier for investigators to detect differences that are statistically significant. These may not be clinically important. For example, in a recent NICHD study evaluating extremely preterm infants, maternal age differed significantly across gestational age.3 Although this difference was statistically significant, the clinical significance of some gestational age infants having a maternal age that was 1 year greater is probably marginal. Similarly, Bloom et al.72 found a difference in head circumference at the time of hospital discharge in a continuous quality improvement project aimed at improving growth of very low birth weight infants during the first 28 days. The difference after the intervention was an increase in the mean of 0.2 cm. Although statistically significant, the difference is within the error of the measurement and it is unlikely that the difference was clinically meaningful.

### The Future of Big Data in Neonatology

In the NICU, there remain many opportunities for additional data collection. Nursing assessments include vital signs, pain/comfort assessments, and the interventions that infants require (e.g., suction, repositioning, titration of FiO2). Respiratory therapists and rehabilitation specialists provide insights on other critical functions to assess

• Neonatal database research is increasing and has the

potential to add meaningful clinical evidence. • Database research has been used to describe disease

Patient electronic monitors routinely display real-time trends in heart rate, pulse oximetry, respiratory rate measure by impedance changes, and, when arterial access is present, blood pressure. In infants with respiratory failure, mechanical ventilation devices have evolved to display, track, and store trends in numerous markers of pulmonary function/physiology. Ancillary monitors for indirect markers of cardiac output (e.g., near-infrared spectroscopy) and the up-and-coming generation of wearable devices73 will continue to expand the trend of incorporating large data sources into neonatology’s clinical practice, research, and quality improvement.

Creating real-time dashboards that allow monitoring of changes in care and associated changes in outcome may allow us to identify important associations.74 If we carefully document the diagnoses we make and the care we provide in a structured way, there is much we can learn from the patterns that accumulate. Changes in the way that data are analyzed, using techniques such as machine learning75 and target trials,76 may also offer greater insights into neonatal care. Database research might also be used to augment future clinical trials by identifying high-risk populations, decreasing sample sizes, and gaining efficiency in time and costs of these trials.

There is a difference between knowledge and wisdom. Knowledge is the accumulation of meaningful facts. Wisdom is integration of knowledge in a way that offers benefits. In health care, we may know the precisely correct diagnosis and the treatment, but it takes wisdom to apply that knowledge to plans that takes into account the clinical context of the patient and the impact of the diagnosis and treatment on our patients. Neonatal database research can be instrumental in increasing both diagnostic precision and therapeutic effectiveness to minimize burdens and improve outcomes for children and their families.

title: Medical Ethics in Neonatal Care

paragraphs.text: 4 Medical Ethics in Neonatal Care
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: This chapter explores the complexity of moral problem solving in neonatal medicine. First, principles of medical ethics and key terms and concepts are reviewed, followed by the application of these concepts in specific moral problems that arise (1) in the prenatal consultation at the limits of gestational viability, (2) when withholding and withdrawing life-sustaining medical treatment in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) is undertaken, and (3) in defining brain death and exploring organ donation. Ethical responsibilities and approaches for collaborative end-of-life decision making and conflict resolution, including impact on parents and team members, use of analgesic agents, and the conduct of clinical research will be presented. This chapter emphasizes the importance of the clinician-parent relationship for effective communication supporting affective and cognitive needs of parents while appreciating diversity in perspectives and values. This list is not an exhaustive representation of ethical challenges facing NICU clinicians but rather highlights some that are frequently encountered. The principles offered to address them are applicable to many other situations.
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: Three elements characterize the practice of medicine that are timeless, universal, and irrefutably true: (1) the fact of illness and the vulnerability it creates, (2) the act of the profession (the use of medical skills for the benefit of the patient), and (3) the practice of medicine itself—that which clinicians and patients do together in the clinical encounter, characterized by mutual intentionality.1 These three elements are well exemplified in the care of sick neonates, in which the vulnerability of anxious parents is manifest, the clinical competence and moral discretion of health professionals are used for the benefit of newborn patients and their parents, and the practice is carried out in a patient-parent-physician relationship characterized by mutual trust and pursuit of the neonatal patient’s and parents’ good.
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: Medical ethics involves the systematic, reasoned evaluation and justification of the “right” action in pursuit of human good or well-being in the context of medical practice. In the practice of neonatal intensive care, medical ethics has become a central focus because it contains all the elements of moral discourse but without clear-cut “right” answers expected in routine clinical practice. Numerous ethical issues arise as clinicians attempt to determine how best to use technology in pursuit of what benefits the patient, in consideration of the values parents place on different outcomes.
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: These issues are compounded by several limitations on NICU clinicians’ ability to elicit and understand parents’ values; these can be pragmatic, related to patient and professional time restrictions, or may result from limitations in the provider’s knowledge and expertise of how best to have these difficult conversations.2,3 Care is also complicated by the medical uncertainty surrounding accurate outcome prediction of potentially adverse findings and by the very nature of many decisions in which quality of life and life itself may be under consideration.4 All these issues make the NICU a challenging, highly scrutinized environment in how ethical issues are examined, reasoned, and justified, and raise fundamental questions about what the responsibilities of clinicians should be.
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: Ethical issues may be experienced as moral dilemmas, or moral distress. A moral dilemma is present when the clinician believes there is an obligation to pursue two (or more) conflicting courses of action. Because only one of these courses can be pursued, the clinician must make a valuebased choice that compromises one of these obligations. Conflict between respect for parental authority and professional duty to provide recommended medical care is a frequently encountered example of a moral dilemma.
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: Moral dilemmas may also arise when there is uncertainty in whether a course of action or resultant outcome is ethical. This is commonly manifest as uncertainty on the part
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: of parents who might struggle with a concomitant desire to prolong the life of their infant but wish to avoid burdensome procedures or a quality of life deemed worse than death. On the part of clinicians, moral uncertainty might appear when treatments are readily available, but with a low likelihood of success.
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: Moral distress arises when the decision maker feels certain about the morally right thing to do, but this perceived “right” course of action is constrained for numerous reasons, including the clinician’s lack of decision-making authority or institutional or financial constraints. This phenomenon was initially described among nurses5 but is also experienced by other NICU providers, including physicians, and involves a sense of powerlessness, frustration, physical symptoms, and ultimately professional “burnout.”6 Although unprocessed moral distress can result in maladaptive “moral residue,”7,8 contemporary explorations of this topic have focused on constructive approaches to building moral resilience8 and directing moral distress toward positive actions to improve patient care.9
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: Ethical reasoning requires an understanding of the fundamental principles that define a domain (Box 4.1). Beauchamp and Childress10 have described four core bioethical principles: autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice. Consideration of a real-time ethical conflict or dilemma in the context of these principles can be a useful starting point and can be particularly helpful in articulating the ethical questions, uniting a struggling team by use of commonly held, noninflammatory language. However, a principles-based approach is less helpful when the problem revolves around a conflict between the principles themselves, as is often the case in the NICU. In many cases, a “principalis” paradigm may not do justice to the nature or complexity of the moral problem. In addition, in a purely principle-based approach, the role of the neonatal clinician as moral agent (i.e., someone with personal virtues and values and the opportunity to take action that comports with that judgment of morality) is de-emphasized. This chapter does not prescribe adherence to any particular ethical framework but aims to enhance appreciation of the language of ethical discourse to enable nuanced reflection, reasoning, and ethical decision making, and to underline the role of the clinician in these situations.
paragraphs.heading: Principles in Medical Ethics

paragraphs.text: The principle of autonomy supports the right of competent patients to make their own health care choices. An individual who makes an autonomous choice acts intentionally, with understanding and without external controlling influences.10 An idealized expression of autonomy occurs when a competent adult chooses voluntarily and intelligently from among various options whose relative risks and benefits have been fully explained to them by the clinicians (i.e., via a truly informed consent process).
paragraphs.heading: Parental Authority

paragraphs.text: The term parental autonomy is often used interchangeably with parental authority, although most argue that autonomy can strictly be used only when making decisions for oneself. Parental authority is the more correct term when referring to the role of parents in decision making for their newborn infants.
paragraphs.heading: Parental Authority

paragraphs.text: Neonatal clinicians should show respect for parental authority: 1. because of the presumption that parents will make deci-
paragraphs.heading: Parental Authority

paragraphs.text: sions that are in their child’s best interests (parents are often described as the “natural surrogate decision makers” for children)10 2. as a means of promoting shared decision making
paragraphs.heading: Parental Authority

paragraphs.text: Parents are not uniform in their desire to direct or even participate in medical decision making for their children.11,12 Clinicians must be conscious of the impact of their authority, the power that derives from expertise and confidence, as well as limitations in their own ability to determine how directive parents wish for them to be in preference-sensitive decisions.13
paragraphs.heading: Parental Authority

paragraphs.text: In the second half of the 20th century, there was a major shift away from a paternalistic “doctor knows best” approach of information sharing and medical decision making toward empowerment of the patient to make autonomous choices.14,15 This condemnation of paternalism has more recently been viewed as excessively burdening some patients with weighty decisions that they do not wish to make alone.16 There is a body of evidence that the prevailing bioethics emphasis on autonomy and self-determination can be overwhelming to parents.17 A more nuanced application of respect for parental authority can be satisfactorily achieved by including parents in decision making as true partners and team members, recognizing that decision making can exist on a continuum.15,18
paragraphs.heading: Parental Authority

paragraphs.text: Too rigid or simplistic an interpretation and application of respect for parental authority by clinicians is also problematic, such as when agreeing to a parental statement that “we want everything done.” Without exploring what underlies this declaration, clinicians may neglect the complexity of the situation and the underlying parental fear of “abandonment.” Finding the right balance between respect for
paragraphs.heading: Parental Authority

paragraphs.text: parental authority and the clinician’s role and responsibility in any decision-making process requires insight, empathy, and great analytical and communication skills.
paragraphs.heading: Parental Authority

paragraphs.text: Beneficence is the obligation to “do good,” that is, to promote patients’ best interests.10 In newborns, this obligation is embodied in the concept of the “best interests of the newborn.” This is a moral and legal standard of judgment that helps to establish the primacy of duties to infants, ensuring they be regarded as fully human individuals with interests, even when clearly unable to express their own value system. Pursuing a course of action in the best interests of an infant implies determining what treatment course has a more favorable benefit-to-harm ratio than other possible options. Interpretation of the meaning of “benefit” can vary between infants and between stakeholders (parents, relatives, clinicians) for the same infant. Interpretations of what it means for a treatment to be beneficial include improvement in the infant’s condition, stabilization of the infant’s condition, or delaying the onset of clinical deterioration. Amelioration of clinical symptoms, or avoidance of complications of treatment, might also be construed as benefit. Benefit can also be achieved by identifying a less restrictive or intrusive treatment.
paragraphs.heading: Beneficence

paragraphs.text: Determination of best interests may involve discussions of the child’s potential quality of life. Quality-of-life considerations encompass the predicted cognitive and neurodevelopmental outcome, the potential for motor disability or other physical handicap (e.g., vision, hearing), and longerterm concerns such as behavioral and learning difficulties or school problems. It also considers the requirements for repeated or prolonged hospitalization, surgery, or medication; technology dependence; and the potential for pain and suffering to be endured. Quality-of-life considerations may also include less concrete medical states, such as the capacity for meaningful and potentially enjoyable interaction with other people and the environment. Some of the most ferocious disagreements between and within NICU teams relate to the inherently subjective nature of quality of life. Contemporary clinical ethicists have moved away from seemingly quantifiable assessments of quality of life, related to measurable outcomes, toward a more subjective interpretation, informed largely by the parents’ expressed values.2 Although well-intentioned clinicians might seek to “correct” parents’ interpretation of the quality of an anticipated outcome, recognition that some families might see more value in survival with neurodevelopmental disability or technology dependence than others is crucial to familycentered care and shared decision making. In addition, clinicians must be very cautious about judging the quality of life of others, viewing disability as a “harm,” and underestimating the ability of those with disabilities to have a wonderful, fulfilled, and meaningful life.19
paragraphs.heading: Beneficence

paragraphs.text: The standard of best interests of the newborn acts as a threshold for judgment, yet the subjective nature of this
paragraphs.heading: Beneficence

paragraphs.text: assessment and the fact that the assessment is being done by surrogate decision makers must always be recognized. In addition, it is imperative for clinicians to be aware of their limited powers of prognostication. Repeated studies by Meadow and colleagues have shown that when health care professionals predict that an infant will not survive to discharge, they are incorrect relatively frequently.20 However, there are circumstances in which the best interest standard can be very helpful to medical teams, such as when urgent decisions must be made in the absence of parental input or when parents refuse clearly life-saving interventions. For the latter, best interest serves as a standard for overriding parental decisions.
paragraphs.heading: Beneficence

paragraphs.text: Diekema has suggested that the more conservative “harm” principle be applied in overriding parental wishes. By this principle, rather than determine the “best interests,” a harm threshold will be determined below which the parents’ decision will be overruled.21 Although invocation of the harm principle can be quite helpful, stakeholders for sick neonates must be careful to apply it in the context of illness severity, urgency, and maintenance of professional standards and integrity.16,22
paragraphs.heading: Beneficence

paragraphs.text: Despite these definitional difficulties and suggested alternative standards such as the “harm” principle, “best interests of the newborn” is accepted as a guiding principle for decision makers because it unites different meanings under one standard and exhibits reasonableness, given the prevailing conditions.23 Properly understood, the concept can serve as a powerful tool in settling disputes about how to make good decisions for individuals who cannot decide for themselves.
paragraphs.heading: Beneficence

paragraphs.text: The principle of nonmaleficence implies an obligation not to inflict harm on others. It has been closely associated with the maxim primum non nocere (first do no harm).10 Although beneficence incorporates preventing and removing harm as part of promoting “the good” of a patient, the injunction not to inflict harm remains a distinct principle and requires intentionally refraining from actions that cause harm. Such harm is generally interpreted as physical harm, especially pain, disability, or death. Nonmaleficence requires that no initiation or continuation of treatment be considered without consideration of whether the treatment is overly burdensome or harmful. This is especially relevant given a historical context in which attention to pain in neonates has been sorely disregarded, to the degree in which surgeries were performed without anesthesia. However, as for benefit, defining events and interventions that are harmful to the infant can be subjective. For some, harm is narrowly defined as pain or anxiety related to the condition or its treatment; assessment of this kind of harm can be aided by using bedside pain scores and other objective measures. For others, any intervention that does not change the ultimate outcome for the infant imparts undue burden. Clinicians and parents may differ about whether hospitalization in an
paragraphs.heading: Nonmaleficence

paragraphs.text: intensive care unit (ICU), without the promise of recovery or discharge home, is harmful to the infant.
paragraphs.heading: Nonmaleficence

paragraphs.text: Justice is the dominant principle relating to social cooperation. Justice is the framework by which we determine how social benefits, such as health care, and burdens, such as research risks, are distributed. Although justice is regarded as a guiding principle for any health care system, no single, simple, ideal implementation adequately addresses the priorities of all relevant stakeholders. Generally, concepts of justice range from the broader utilitarian calculus to promote the greatest good for the greatest number in underwriting the distribution of resources (macroallocation) to a more narrowly focused equality of opportunity for each individual (microallocation). Justice in the distribution of resources requires that: 1. patients in similar situations have access to the same
paragraphs.heading: Justice

paragraphs.text: health care 2. the level of health care available for one set of patients
paragraphs.heading: Justice

paragraphs.text: considers the effect of such a use of resources on other patients Contemporary interpretations of resource allocation have focused on disparities,24 both on equality in access to care, upstream from provision of the medical intervention itself, and emphasized the principle of equity over equality. This distinction is important in emphasizing the equality of health outcome rather than equality in provision of any specific resource.
paragraphs.heading: Justice

paragraphs.text: There is increasing attention paid to health care disparities in the NICU, along with improvements that must be made in the areas of diversity, equity, and inclusion. Unfortunately, there is significant evidence of “complex racial inequities and/or disparities in structure, process, and outcome measures, most often disadvantaging infants of color, especially African American infants.”25 In the United States, this involves evidence that infants of color are both more likely to receive care in quality-challenged hospitals as well as to face disparities within NICUs.25 Barfield, Cox, and Henderson have suggested five key actions that may begin to address NICU care for traditionally vulnerable neonates:26 1. Dispelling the myth of an inherent advantage by Black
paragraphs.heading: Justice

paragraphs.text: premature infants 2. Approach quality improvement with a lens toward health
paragraphs.heading: Justice

paragraphs.text: equity 3. Identify measures that provide a better understanding of
paragraphs.heading: Justice

paragraphs.text: both the type and quality of care 4. To reduce mortality and disparities, ensure that all infants
paragraphs.heading: Justice

paragraphs.text: receive care in risk-appropriate facilities 5. Use research to identify the drivers of disparities, as well
paragraphs.heading: Justice

paragraphs.text: as solutions, to ensure health equity These are justice issues that must be addressed. As Barfield, Cox, and Henderson conclude, “[w]e owe the infants of this country consistent high-quality care, no matter their skin color, and...there is work to be done.”26
paragraphs.heading: Justice

paragraphs.text: Although fairness in allocation of resources for the individual patient is an important consideration, it is not the
paragraphs.heading: Justice

paragraphs.text: fundamental standard in this interaction. Microallocation issues are very rarely appropriate at the bedside; individual clinicians caring for individual patients are poorly suited to make decisions about whether one patient, or another, is more deserving of a limited resource, or to make ad hoc institutional-level decisions about how limited resources will be distributed. First, there is an inherent conflict of interest, in which the clinician might rightly prioritize the immediate needs of the patient she is caring for over larger, systems-level considerations. Second, rationing and allocation schemes depend on economic and public health expertise beyond that possessed by most clinicians. However, individual clinicians do have a moral obligation to judiciously use medical resources for individual patients and ought not use unnecessarily expensive treatments or treatments that will not effectively promote the patient’s health. The conventional ethical prohibition of bedside rationing is also complicated by daily realities of medical care in which time, ICU beds, and limited-quantity equipment are tacitly managed as a matter of routine.27
paragraphs.heading: Justice

paragraphs.text: The COVID-19 pandemic required society as well as health care systems to rapidly consider the appropriate triage framework to use in the face of an overwhelming demand for care while constrained with a limited supply of ventilators, medications, equipment, and personnel. When supplies are scarce, the primary ethical considerations discussed in this chapter such as autonomy and best interests may be outweighed by utilitarian/justice considerations.27 Indeed, tensions during the pandemic highlighted conflicts between “public health ethics,” where the goal is to promote greater societal good, and “duty to care,” where clinician obligations focus on maximizing individual patient outcomes. Triage decision-makers, who should not be bedside clinicians, may have to allocate resources between a premature infant and a geriatric adult. Scoring systems, such as the Sequential Organ Failure System (SOFA) in adults and the National Institutes of Health Extremely Preterm Birth Outcomes Tool in premature neonates, have been proposed as a transparent and objective means for decision making.28 Some survey literature, however, suggests that newborn infants, particularly premature infants, may be “undervalued” compared to other age groups.29 Consequently, it is essential that advocates for neonatal patients are involved in both the development and implementation of any resource allocation strategies.
paragraphs.heading: Justice

paragraphs.text: In every system and under non-pandemic “normal” circumstances, the provision of neonatal services requires guidelines to be developed for determining appropriate use of these costly and often limited resources. Priorities must be set and justified by organizational leaders. Any change in the way neonatal care is delivered needs to be fair and accessible, as well as open and challengeable. Disputes should be addressed based on the acceptance of objective measures and trust in the integrity and fairness of the process and the individuals responsible for management of the process. With greater attention being paid to escalating health care costs, there is little question that how resources for sick
paragraphs.heading: Justice

paragraphs.text: newborns are used and justified may become more critically and ethically questioned. However, neonatal intensive care has been shown via a number of approaches to be remarkably cost effective,30 particularly relative to the care of other patient populations.31
paragraphs.heading: Justice

paragraphs.text: Shared decision-making paradigms encourage partnerships between clinicians and parents in making care decisions through mutual consent, balancing parental authority with professional obligations of beneficence toward the infant. Benefits of shared decision making for parents include decreased decisional conflict and regret, and improved long-term mental health.32–35 Although various models for shared decision making exist, in adult patient-physician relationships, the deliberative-interactive model is the ideal, wherein clinicians not only help the patient with clarification of their values, but also strive to make their own reasoning transparent for the patient to appreciate the many factors that inform their professional opinion.14 In neonatal care, despite intentions to follow similar interactive exchanges, practices often resemble informative models of shared decision making, wherein clinicians believe parents can make choices independently if provided sufficient information.36
paragraphs.heading: Shared Decision Making and Personalized Decision Making

paragraphs.text: Informative models assume parents follow rational, or cognitive-based deliberations in which they know and can apply their values to interpret complicated medical information without the influence of strong emotions. These models encourage clinicians to focus largely on communicating objective facts to equalize knowledge imbalances. Although this approach may work for some parents, for others, contextual features such as emotions or personal-lived experiences influence and guide deliberations, leading toward more heuristic approaches in decision making.37
paragraphs.heading: Shared Decision Making and Personalized Decision Making

paragraphs.text: Heuristic decision-making approaches (also known as “mental shortcuts” or “gut instincts”) are strategies to simplify complex information or decisions by using “nonrational” processes to guide choices and deliberations.38 For example, associations are made between related facts and similar, but not exact, past experiences. Some of these associations lead to imperfect assumptions, or cognitive biases, whereas others, such as emotions or sacred values, highlight salient features of the decision or outcome.38,39 For parents who follow heuristic decisional processes, a personalized approach rather than a standardized, informative model may be preferable.
paragraphs.heading: Shared Decision Making and Personalized Decision Making

paragraphs.text: Personalized decision making acknowledges parents’ variability in tolerance for risk, desire for decisional responsibility, and affective and cognitive needs.40 It allows flexibility for those parents who may want to assume decisional responsibility and for those who delegate decision making to clinicians. Some scholars have recommended nudges as a potential strategy for those who prefer to delegate
paragraphs.heading: Shared Decision Making and Personalized Decision Making

paragraphs.text: decisions.41 Nudges treat one option as appropriate, without making an explicit suggestion, allowing parents to overrule that assumption if they notice or feel that they want that authority.42 In these instances, clinicians adjust options based on knowledge of parental values, hopes, and beliefs. Although these approaches have been criticized as paternalistic, decreasing parental authority, scholars question whether how choices are presented, or choice architecture, can ever truly be neutral.41 Relational autonomy, another conceptualization of parental authority, unites emotions with reason, by recognizing that relationships can guide or influence decisions.43 For neonatal decision making, adhering to relational autonomy “establishes the beginnings of a trusting relationship with the health care team, which may last throughout the baby’s hospitalization and care, benefitting all parties involved.”44
paragraphs.heading: Shared Decision Making and Personalized Decision Making

paragraphs.text: Regardless of the decision-making model followed or the ultimate decision maker, clinicians should always support parents after choices have been made. As stated, “ ...support for surrogate decision makers is focused far too much on the details of medical intervention options and not nearly enough on assisting with the confusions, dilemmas, and self-recriminations inherent in trying to formulate a guiding personal duty to serve in the role of surrogate decision maker.”45 This can be accomplished by building strong parent-clinician relationships through personalized communication, empathy, and trust.
paragraphs.heading: Shared Decision Making and Personalized Decision Making

paragraphs.text: A sound patient-physician relationship is a sine qua non of good medicine, for it is within this relationship that physicians exercise their humanity, understanding, and respect for the values of others. In neonatal medicine, the physician’s communication relationship is with the parents (or legal guardians) of the newborn, respecting parental authority and fulfilling the dual role of caring for the infant and the parents. Every communication interaction with parents, whether formal or informal, is an opportunity for relationship building—the core of risk communication and bioethics. Failures in communication often stem from inadequate parent-clinician relationships and can lead to bioethical conflict, emotional distress, and even undermine autonomy.3,46,47
paragraphs.heading: Communication With Parents and the Clinician-Parent Relationship (Box 4.2)

paragraphs.text: Recent trends in communication approaches parallel those in neonatal bioethical decision making, away from outcomes toward process-driven analyses emphasizing therapeutic alliances.40,41,48 Overarching goals of communication for critically ill patients or their surrogates include establishing trusting relationships, providing emotional support and information, value exploration, and supporting personalized decision making (when applicable).49,50 This aligns with American Academy of Pediatrics recommendations, reaffirmed in 2017, that effective communication address both affective and cognitive needs.51 It is also supported by research in risk communication, where precise
paragraphs.heading: Communication With Parents and the Clinician-Parent Relationship (Box 4.2)

paragraphs.text: numbers and lists of detailed facts do not necessarily correlate with an adequate understanding of risk, unless parents also have mental models that give intuitive meaning to their situation.52 Finding a balance between information that is sufficient to promote competence but not irrelevant to be burdensome requires insight into what outcomes matter most to parents.53 Some parents may need help understanding their thoughts, some may need coaching on how to parent, and some may want information to participate in decision making. This can be achieved through personalized communication and strong clinician-parent partnerships.
paragraphs.heading: Communication With Parents and the Clinician-Parent Relationship (Box 4.2)

paragraphs.text: Patient-centered communication, characterized by active listening, expressions of empathy, statements reaffirming non-abandonment, and support for decision making, has been associated with increased family satisfaction, a qualityof-care metric.50,54 Personalized communication, within a patient-centered approach, seeks to individualize cognitive
paragraphs.heading: Patient-Centered, Personalized Communication

paragraphs.text: information while taking the time to understand the affective and psychosocial context of the parents’ experience.40,48 Parents’ lived experiences, psychological make-up, risk tolerance, and values reflect the multiple sociocultural facets that can influence perspectives.40 Personalized communications are not “one size fits all,” but rather seek to afford parents latitude in determining how they prefer to receive, absorb, and engage with complex information while building rapport with the parent. These approaches “titrate clinicians’ interactions with the parents’” reality, supporting them in ways they need it, at the time when they need it.48
paragraphs.heading: Patient-Centered, Personalized Communication

paragraphs.text: Several frameworks exist to guide personalized communications with parents, consistent with best practice.50,55–57 Each framework begins with clinician self-reflection, and situational and environmental awareness. Physician-related factors, such as implicit biases58 which are subconscious, unintentional assumptions that shape perspectives or attitudes, or external pressures, such as time constraints from competing clinical, administrative, or academic obligations, can inadvertently impact how communication is delivered and received by parents. Parental concerns, emotions, and baseline understanding should be explored early during an interaction to understand parents’ perceptions of the clinical situation and/or correct misunderstandings that may anchor impressions. For example, cognitive biases such as the anchoring adjustment bias can lead parents to adjust insufficiently for the expected difference in outcomes with weeks of prematurity;38,59 addressing the parents’ emotional experience decreases parental stress more effectively than providing information alone.60
paragraphs.heading: Patient-Centered, Personalized Communication

paragraphs.text: Any personalized communication with parents requires flexibility; some parents may prefer detailed information, whereas others prefer the general gist. Even when faced with decisions, the desired level of involvement and disclosure of medical versus non-medical information may vary based on the nature of the decision and the parents’ decisionmaking preferences, and may evolve with time during the infant’s hospitalization.12,48 How information is communicated influences not only parents’ understanding of the situation61 and their comfort in addressing moral issues and values openly, but also their ability to engage effectively in a decision-making process. Likewise, supplemental information should be guided by individualized preferences allowing parents to check their understanding of critical information. Decision aids can improve comprehension for some parents; however, aids may also increase, rather than lessen, decisional conflict by showing the options in sharp relief. Therefore they should not be used in lieu of a strong clinician-parent relationship.
paragraphs.heading: Patient-Centered, Personalized Communication

paragraphs.text: At a minimum, communication should always seek to empower parenthood, a key component in family integrated care.18,62 Feeling safe and respected in the clinician-parent relationship can promote parental characteristics, such as
paragraphs.heading: Empowering Parenthood and Good Parenting Beliefs

paragraphs.text: resilience, which have been linked to favorable projections of future quality of life for neurologically impaired infants regardless of illness severity.63 Remaining sensitive to barriers affecting daytime parental presence at the bedside, such as responsibilities to other children and family members, costs of transportation to and from the hospital, and the need for one or both parents to return to work, are important when offering care opportunities. Language such as “some parents want to be present on rounds, other parents prefer to speak with clinicians later” permits choices without pressuring parents to adhere to standards they may not be able to or want to achieve.62
paragraphs.heading: Empowering Parenthood and Good Parenting Beliefs

paragraphs.text: Good parenting beliefs, described initially in the pediatric intensive care literature, represents approaches and ideas that parents use to help them cope with, define, and fulfill their roles as parents of critically ill children.64 For parents of neonates, developing good parenting beliefs and feeling empowered takes time: they must overcome feelings of guilt, feel like parents, and eventually feel like good parents as they begin their parenthood journey under surreal experiences in an intensive care unit.65 Communication strategies such as verbal statements of praise within the constructs of effective partnerships can encourage positive transformations.66
paragraphs.heading: Empowering Parenthood and Good Parenting Beliefs

paragraphs.text: Communication pitfalls can also hinder empowerment. Medical jargon, terminology that implies value judgments (“poor prognosis”), or impersonal labels (“the hypoplast”) impact perceptions of quality of life.67 Dominating conversations with too much medical information can overwhelm a parent’s ability to absorb information.46 Studies of family conferences show correlation between the frequency of family speech and satisfaction.68 When given opportunities to talk, parents share emotions, hopes, and beliefs which can drive medical decision making and facilitate patient-centered communications.46,69,70 Barriers to communication become especially pronounced when cultural differences in beliefs, decisional roles, language, and communication preferences strain clinician-parent relationships.
paragraphs.heading: Empowering Parenthood and Good Parenting Beliefs

paragraphs.text: Culture represents a complex multifaceted entity inclusive of a variety of elements related to socioeconomic, racial, ethnic identification, sexual orientation, gender, spirituality, educational attainment, and physical abilities. Cultural sensitivity has been described in the literature using various terminology (cultural humility, cross-cultural efficacy, cultural sensibility, cultural care, cultural safety, and critical cultural competence).71 Common to all is a consciousness of reflection and behavior on the part of the clinician in delivering patient care. Cultural sensitivity extends beyond an acknowledgement of different cultural norms and considers system-wide contributions to promote structural competence. Cultural sensitivity is central to patient-centered communication and has been shown to ameliorate (or perpetuate when absent) maternal morbidity and neonatal outcome disparities.24,72 Recognition of the child’s place within the family highlights the cultural, religious, and spiritual
paragraphs.heading: Cultural Sensitivity

paragraphs.text: dimensions of families’ lives and may bring to light significant diversity within these domains. In a pluralistic society, parents and physicians are unlikely to share the same values, cultural systems, personal histories, and experiences, and at times of stress these differences may present health care providers with significant challenges. Clinicians should recognize the dynamic nature of how families’ interests are shaped by these contexts; therefore it is important not to stereotype the members of specific social, cultural, ethnic, or religious groups. Individuals’ affiliations may not be predictive of their beliefs and values in the care of their infant, and the health care team should regard each patient and family as unique and attend carefully to their specific views and values.
paragraphs.heading: Cultural Sensitivity

paragraphs.text: When attentiveness to the views and values of families is difficult because of language barriers, professional interpreters should be used. Use of an interpreter is advisable for three reasons: 1. It ensures that parents’ views are available to the health
paragraphs.heading: Cultural Sensitivity

paragraphs.text: care team 2. It removes the burden on family members or friends for
paragraphs.heading: Cultural Sensitivity

paragraphs.text: the transfer of information 3. It limits the potential for miscommunication
paragraphs.heading: Cultural Sensitivity

paragraphs.text: In certain situations, a cultural interpreter not only can facilitate language comprehension but can also provide useful information about cultural norms and traditions that are unfamiliar to the health care team. Access to high-quality interpretation services is an essential component of ethically and culturally sensitive care that also satisfies a regulatory requirement and decreases medicolegal risk.
paragraphs.heading: Cultural Sensitivity

paragraphs.text: Religion and the more general concept of spirituality as a major determinant of culture, tradition, and family values often needs to be addressed with parents, particularly when end-of-life decision making is undertaken. A qualitative questionnaire study completed by parents after their child’s death revealed the emergence of four explicitly spiritual/religious themes: prayer, faith, access to and care from clergy, and belief in the transcendent quality of the parent-child relationship that endures beyond death.73 Other significant themes with a religious/spiritual dynamic include finding meaning, hope, trust, and love. In another study focused on the delivery room consultation, mothers stated that religion, spirituality, and hope were the major factors that guided their decision making.69 The implication of these studies is that health care teams need to consider whether they have or need to create an environment that is hospitable to, and supportive of, religious or spiritual practice; that clinical staff recognize parents’ spiritual needs and provide access to hospital chaplains and community clergy, and, on a deeper level, appreciate parents’ religious and spiritual perspectives in prenatal consultations and end-of-life discussions.
paragraphs.heading: Cultural Sensitivity

paragraphs.text: As medicine advances, physicians and parents must sometimes struggle with information that is at the limits of medical knowledge and in which the implications of findings are
paragraphs.heading: Conditions of Uncertainty

paragraphs.text: uncertain. The way medical uncertainty, specifically prognostic uncertainty, is (or is not) communicated is extremely important and influences subsequent decision making. “Message framing,” for example, whether the reported outcome is mortality or survival, has a major impact on decision making.74 Parents may also struggle with value uncertainty, as they try to infer preferences without previous experiential learning.
paragraphs.heading: Conditions of Uncertainty

paragraphs.text: Neonatologists communicate uncertainty in different ways: some provide additional information, some acknowledge uncertainty to illustrate boundaries of medical evidence, and some use uncertainty to foster hope and humanize their relationship with parents.75 Experts recommend that clinicians should: 1. normalize uncertainty: “... we can never be certain about
paragraphs.heading: Conditions of Uncertainty

paragraphs.text: the future. I wish I could be more certain” 2. address emotions: “it is tough not knowing what the
paragraphs.heading: Conditions of Uncertainty

paragraphs.text: future will bring” 3. help parents refocus on the present: “what can we do to
paragraphs.heading: Conditions of Uncertainty

paragraphs.text: help you now, since we are unsure of what the future will bring”76 For parents, hope, spirituality, and affective elements play a central role in mitigating uncertainty69—hope that clinicians are wrong or hope that favorable outcomes are still possible.75
paragraphs.heading: Conditions of Uncertainty

paragraphs.text: Neonatology groups may use different strategies to operationalize prognostic uncertainty. Some examine outcome data and identify thresholds below which intensive care will not be offered because of unacceptably poor outcomes and thresholds above which intensive care is obligatory because of reasonably good outcomes. In isolation, this strategy has been criticized because: 1. one or more stakeholders cannot accept the possibility of
paragraphs.heading: Conditions of Uncertainty

paragraphs.text: forgoing a chance of survival for statistical outliers 2. of limitations to available outcome data 3. statistical information is not viewed as helpful to deci-
paragraphs.heading: Conditions of Uncertainty

paragraphs.text: sion making2,77 A wait-until-certainty approach78 initiates life-sustaining interventions for almost every infant with any chance of survival. Treatment continues unless severe, adverse medical findings become unequivocally evident. A problem with this strategy is the false promise that certainty will at some point exist, and it potentially relegates parents and other members of the health care team to the role of bystanders as the medical course unfolds.
paragraphs.heading: Conditions of Uncertainty

paragraphs.text: A trial of therapy approach79 focuses on individualization within consistently and fairly applied institutional guidelines, in which available population-based epidemiology, individual factors not accounted for by large studies, and parental values are considered. This approach emphasizes remaining prognostic uncertainty, even for families who request full intervention, using moral responsibility as a guide for the continuation of life sustaining treatment.
paragraphs.heading: Conditions of Uncertainty

paragraphs.text: As prognoses become more unfavorable, disclosures are sometimes delayed because of worry that poor prognostic
paragraphs.heading: Delivering Bad News: Hope and Urgency

paragraphs.text: information may extinguish hope. However, multiple hopes may coexist, and new hopes emerge after realistic and truthful information is shared.80 “I wish” statements can help acknowledge the parents’ primary hope while communicating realistic expectations: “I also wish the treatment would have worked,” or can be used as warning shots to prepare parents for difficult news to come: “I wish I had better news. What I have to share will be difficult to hear.”81 Emotive phrases such as “I’m worried” or “I’m concerned” can help open discussions describing outcomes and reinforce the clinician’s commitment to the physician-parent relationship.
paragraphs.heading: Delivering Bad News: Hope and Urgency

paragraphs.text: Lizotte et al.82 recommended a stepwise approach for communication under urgent situations where a pre-existing clinician-parent relationship or a designated person for communication is absent. Preparation includes introductions and conveying the urgency and intensity of the pending clinical situation. During the event, managing expectations with brief updates regarding next steps and potential outcomes (“we will try this medication but if it does not work, he will die”) can prepare parents if interventions fail. Simple, straightforward language when death occurs (“he is dead”) is more helpful than metaphors. Meeting with parents after death can help validate decisions or experiences, answer questions, and support parents through grief.
paragraphs.heading: Delivering Bad News: Hope and Urgency

paragraphs.text: Ideally parents’ readiness to receive information and their coping resources should be ascertained so that appropriate information is shared with consideration of their adaptation to the medical setting. Follow-up conversations provide opportunities to support parents and give them time to absorb new information. Especially when bad news is shared, it is important to provide specific information about when a follow-up conversation will occur.81 In acute situations, if an urgent decision is required, the physician needs to move the relationship rapidly, however, from one of “moral strangers” to one in which moral issues can be openly discussed.
paragraphs.heading: Follow-up Conversations

paragraphs.text: In some units, neonatal intensive care is provided by many clinicians with expertise in different fields and, though the nature of intensive care may require teams to change, ways to maintain continuity have been developed. Some NICUs identify a primary clinician to integrate all the important information and maintain a consistent relationship and pattern of communication with parents. However, minimizing fragmented or inconsistent information is the responsibility of all who care for the parents and the patient. This requires an understanding among the team members of different responsibilities in communication with parents, such as when conveying day-to-day quantifiable, objective information; when to communicate severe diagnoses; or when to be more speculative about prognostic significance of specific findings. Inter-specialty meetings, in which all the clinicians involved with the patient share their findings and perspectives, are crucial to ensuring consistent and coherent messaging. Peer-to-peer support programs can
paragraphs.heading: Follow-up Conversations

paragraphs.text: provide an additional and informal way to establish continuity and support parenting in the NICU.
paragraphs.heading: Follow-up Conversations

paragraphs.text: Informed consent is enshrined as a foundational cornerstone of the ethical practice. Tenets of informed consent include (1) disclosure of information, (2) understanding, (3) competence or capacity, and (4) voluntariness or freedom to choose.10 Some authorities posit that obtaining formal, informed consent is necessary from parents for virtually every neonatal test or procedure as a means of maintaining a high standard of ethical care. Ensuring that parents are kept up to date and advised of treatment plans is important; however, information gathered from an ethnographic study showed that parents did not want to be asked to consent to every procedure.83 They often felt overwhelmed when asked to consent for routine and minor procedures and felt they were given the illusion that they could or should say stop when there was no real choice and no time to learn more about each procedure. Parents found it was easier to discuss questions and dilemmas when communication occurred remote from consent processes. When consent was required, parents emphasized the need for a two-way informed agreement between partners with established mutual trust and respect.
paragraphs.heading: Informed Consent

paragraphs.text: When a pregnant patient acts in such a way as potentially to create a serious risk of harm for the developing fetus, either by declining a recommended intervention or by actively engaging in a behavior that is harmful to the fetus, some authorities argue that state intervention is morally justified to promote fetal health and well-being. However, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) maintains that such intervention not only violates the pregnant person’s autonomy, integrity, and privacy, but also undermines the principle of reproductive freedom.84
paragraphs.heading: Refusal of Treatment During Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: Authorities who advocate for state intervention place some limits on the principle of reproductive freedom: whatever rights a pregnant woman may have to direct the course of the pregnancy, they do not include an unlimited right to harm the fetus. In practice, which parental behaviors lead to state intervention is generally determined by the legality rather than the inherent harmfulness of the intervention, leading, for example, to paradoxically harsher repercussions for occasional marijuana use than for heavy alcohol consumption, even though the harms to the fetus from the former are not nearly as well described as those from the latter.
paragraphs.heading: Refusal of Treatment During Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: Significantly, professional bodies have commonly resolved the moral dilemma between the pregnant person’s autonomy and the fetus’s well-being in favor of respecting the principle of autonomy. An ACOG Committee Opinion
paragraphs.heading: Refusal of Treatment During Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: on “Refusal of Medically Recommended Treatment During Pregnancy” states that “it is never acceptable for obstetrician-gynecologists to attempt to influence patients toward a clinical decision using coercion.”84 They note that this can include “threats” to involve the courts or child protective services to coerce a person to choose a particular medical decision. During these difficult situations, clinicians are encouraged to promote shared decision making, promote a team approach, and utilize ethics consultation.
paragraphs.heading: Refusal of Treatment During Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: Viability can have a physiologic definition, such as the point at which life can be maintained outside of the uterus, or be based on quality-of-life considerations in which there is an explicit value judgment regarding the degree of morbidity that is acceptable if such a life were to be maintained. Although no universally accepted definition of a viable fetus exists in clinical practice, guidelines from professional societies in several countries have defined gestational age ranges at which the benefit-to-burden ratio of aggressive obstetric or neonatal care becomes questionable.85,86 These gestational ages are also known as the “gray zone,” where prognostic uncertainty and moral ambiguity permit parental discretion for delivery room management.
paragraphs.heading: Gestational Viability and Clinical Guideline

paragraphs.text: Recently, neonatology teams have developed the capacity to maintain physiologic signs of life at extremely low gestational ages, resulting in survival possible after a gestation of 22 weeks with some neurologically intact survivors, shifting the lower border of marginal gestational viability from 23 to 22 weeks.86–88 Similarly, examination of the outcomes of infants born at or after 24 weeks suggests that the majority of these infants survive, and the majority of NICU graduates survive without moderate or severe neurodevelopmental impairment.88 Although some intensive care units continue to allow parents to forgo resuscitation until 26 weeks, resuscitation of infants born at or after 24 weeks should be pursued in the absence of major co-morbidities, such as extreme intrauterine growth restriction or major congenital anomalies.
paragraphs.heading: Gestational Viability and Clinical Guideline

paragraphs.text: Yet, using gestational age alone to guide decisions warrants caution. Gestational age decision thresholds can generate self-fulfilling prophecies: if life-sustaining care is not offered at a gestational age, there will be no survivors at that gestational age.89 Estimations of gestational age are also inherently flawed; first trimester ultrasounds used for dating can be imprecise ± 1 week and daily growth toward the end of the second trimester is exponential.85,89 In addition, factors other than gestational age impact prognoses.85,90 An “outcomes estimator” developed by Tyson and coworkers accounts for five factors (gestational age, estimated birth weight, singleton status, antenatal steroids, and gender) that impact prognosis and provides the likelihood of death or adverse neurodevelopmental outcome.90 The estimator is available without charge on the Internet,91 and although not perfect, it does seem to “promote treatment decisions that are less arbitrary, more individualized, more
paragraphs.heading: Gestational Viability and Clinical Guideline

paragraphs.text: transparent, and better justified than decisions based solely on gestational age thresholds.”90
paragraphs.heading: Gestational Viability and Clinical Guideline

paragraphs.text: The challenge facing the life-defining “resuscitate or not” issue for parents and the neonatal team in the “gray zone” is compounded by the “moral strangeness” between the participants, the vulnerability and unfamiliar physical and emotional context for parents, constraints of time, and the great degree of medical uncertainty in prognosticating outcome for individual infants. Nevertheless, the urgent context exerts its own demands, and the opportunity for prenatal consultation must be optimized, because it is considered more conducive to an exploration of parental and physician/team views than if this conversation occurs in the delivery room or in the NICU in the first few hours of the infant’s life.
paragraphs.heading: Gestational Viability and Clinical Guideline

paragraphs.text: The antenatal consultation at the margin of gestational viability has three primary aims: 1. To develop a relationship with parents to provide affec-
paragraphs.heading: Antenatal Consultation at the Margin of Viability

paragraphs.text: tive support and explore values 2. To provide individualized information on which deci-
paragraphs.heading: Antenatal Consultation at the Margin of Viability

paragraphs.text: sions can be based 3. To support personalized parental decision-making pro-
paragraphs.heading: Antenatal Consultation at the Margin of Viability

paragraphs.text: cesses about whether a trial of therapy will be undertaken in the delivery room Recent trends in antenatal consultation have highlighted personalized approaches which rely on strong clinicianparent relationships, the hallmark of communication and compassionate care. These consultations focus equally on the process of deliberation, attending to emotions and fostering trust, as on the outcomes, recognizing that parents differ in their experiences, preferences, and approaches to decision making.40,41,92
paragraphs.heading: Antenatal Consultation at the Margin of Viability

paragraphs.text: Consistent with practices to support effective communication, preparation for the consultation begins with a thorough medical record review, communication with the obstetrical team, and history taking. If possible, joint consultation with obstetrical colleagues is recommended by professional societies.93,94 After introductions and addressing the parents’ emotional crisis, next steps explore values and fears. Helping parents not only identify but also prioritize pertinent, and at times conflicting, values is an essential component of antenatal consultation which can help empower them when making decisions.
paragraphs.heading: Antenatal Consultation at the Margin of Viability

paragraphs.text: Recognizing that many parents want information from the antenatal consultation, the burden rests with the clinician to strike a balance between sufficiently informing parents without overwhelming them. Information can be used to guide decision making and/or prepare for potential futures, depending on the parents’ values and preferred approach to decision making. Parents who rely on emotions instead of data-driven risk assessments, or who prioritize quality of life over sanctity of life, may differ in their cognitive and affective needs.
paragraphs.heading: Antenatal Consultation at the Margin of Viability

paragraphs.text: Regardless of the exact content or intent, any data shared should be current, individualized to the baby, personalized to parental concerns and needs, and germane to the unit in which the patient is being cared for. Parents often desire information pertaining to chances of survival and information about the long-term outcomes—including quantitative and qualitative measures when available (functional abilities, learning, behavior, impact on family)—with recognition that parents may differ in their previous experiences with disability and chronic disease and the value they place on these outcomes. Even in the setting of a value-exploration approach, a standardized form (Fig. 4.1) may provide a reminder to the clinician of topics that could be covered while remaining mindful that some parents prefer details and others the general gist.95
paragraphs.heading: Antenatal Consultation at the Margin of Viability

paragraphs.text: Several scholars have called for increased parental participation in research to identify and investigate outcomes that matter most to parents, because the disability categories generated by experts may not align with parents’ perspectives.53 For example, the composite outcome of death and severe disability may represent two outcomes that are not valued equivalently by parents, whereas a behavioral disability may be extremely stressful for parents yet is not classified as a “severe disability” in research studies.53 Disability categories may also not adequately capture “big picture views” without considering the impact of societal accommodations or family environment on the child’s adaptation. Kukora and Boss have offered a conceptual model of parental characterization of a “good” or “bad” outcome (Fig. 4.2), which offers an explanation for why some parents pursue interventions in the face of a poor prognosis.2
paragraphs.heading: Antenatal Consultation at the Margin of Viability

paragraphs.text: However, irrespective of the consultative model and decision-making approach pursued, parents should never feel abandoned to make decisions without support, nor should they feel intimidated to make choices they believe are not in the best interests of their infant or inconsistent with their values. Both retrospective data11,33 and hypothetical survey data12,96 reveal that parents want involvement with resuscitation decisions, and those who perceive some level of participation in the process experience less decisional regret and conflict, and improved long-term mental health.32,34 Although joint decision making for infants is preferred by most parents, some delegate decision making to clinicians, emphasizing “one size does not fit all.”96 These delegations must be accepted as appropriate expressions of parental authority. An evolving body of science has focused on use of decision support tools and enhanced information to improve processes and support parents with sensitive decision making.97 However, it must be remembered that these tools should only be used within the constructs of a strong clinician-parent relationship.
paragraphs.heading: Antenatal Consultation at the Margin of Viability

paragraphs.text: Lastly, descriptions of gestational viability should always be sensitive to the parents’ identification of personhood of the fetus. Reduction of a future child, whose sex might be known, whose name is picked out, and whose bedroom is already decorated, to the status of a “nonviable fetus” has the potential to antagonize parents and present an obstacle
paragraphs.heading: Antenatal Consultation at the Margin of Viability

paragraphs.text: immunodeficiency virus; HR, heart rate; IUGR, intrauterine growth restriction; LMP, last menstrual period; NICU, neonatal intensive care unit; PROM, premature rupture of membranes; RDS, respiratory distress syndrome; UAC / UVC, umbilical arterial and venous catheter; VDRL, Venereal Disease Research Laboratory.
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 4.1 Standardized form for the prenatal consultation. GBS, Group B Streptococcus; HIV, human

paragraphs.text: to productive prenatal decision making. Counselors must also be cognizant of, and attuned to, the many beliefs and perspectives that inform parental decisions. Parents often use views such as “giving the baby a chance,” hope, faith, or “good parenting beliefs” when navigating decisions.64,69
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 4.1 Standardized form for the prenatal consultation. GBS, Group B Streptococcus; HIV, human

paragraphs.text: Two studies highlight the importance of and validate collaborative consultative approaches at the margin of gestational viability. In one study, Payot describes two models used by neonatologists when counseling parents regarding resuscitation decisions.98 In the neutral information model, parents made their decision independently after receiving comprehensive information, whereas in an assent model, the neonatologists expressed their preferences, and a decision was sought during the consultation. Neither model fully addressed parental expectations; parents expressed the need for a more individualized relationship in the neutral information model but felt abandoned if recommendations did not fit their expectations in the assent model.
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 4.1 Standardized form for the prenatal consultation. GBS, Group B Streptococcus; HIV, human

paragraphs.text: In another study, Leuthner describes the different approaches taken to incorporate parental views, assessing how much moral weight should be ascribed to their views of the infant’s best interests in delivery room management decisions.99 In one approach, the infant’s best interests are based on physician judgment, the medical expertise model. In another model, the infant’s best interests are driven by parental input reflecting on physician and parent values, the negotiated model. Leuthner concludes that the negotiated model is more ethically appropriate, which is consistent with current trends in personalized decision making and recommendations for parental involvement in decision making under
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 4.1 Standardized form for the prenatal consultation. GBS, Group B Streptococcus; HIV, human

paragraphs.text: conditions of prognostic uncertainty and moral ambiguity. These studies highlight the critical importance of relationships between the decision makers to allow exploration of the facts, expectations, and values and reinforces the validity of parental involvement in decision making at the margins of viability.
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 4.1 Standardized form for the prenatal consultation. GBS, Group B Streptococcus; HIV, human

paragraphs.text: Treatment considerations for extremely premature infants must be viewed in context against other areas of medicine in which difficult decisions must be made. There is evidence that, without clear justification, premature infants are considered “morally different” from older children and adults,29 which may be attributed to biases in which neonatologists feel more responsibility toward the potential of creating disability than of saving lives, the “saving vs. creating” bias.100
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 4.1 Standardized form for the prenatal consultation. GBS, Group B Streptococcus; HIV, human

paragraphs.text: It is worth reflecting on the reasons for the lack of congruency in decisions that can occur between physicians and parents, where differences seem to arise from three sources:98 1. Starting points. Physician’s intent is to give the facts,
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 4.1 Standardized form for the prenatal consultation. GBS, Group B Streptococcus; HIV, human

paragraphs.text: whereas the family’s reaction is to the premature interruption and fracture of the family narrative and a threat to their anticipated parenthood. 2. How information is used. Physicians attempt to be as
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 4.1 Standardized form for the prenatal consultation. GBS, Group B Streptococcus; HIV, human

paragraphs.text: objective as possible with facts and figures, whereas parents reformulate those chances or may rely on emotions and use information to prepare for the future rather than deliberate about a decision. 3. What constitutes the “right” decision or “right” process. For
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 4.1 Standardized form for the prenatal consultation. GBS, Group B Streptococcus; HIV, human

paragraphs.text: physicians, a good decision follows full parental comprehension of provided information. For parents, it is after they have had their own experience considered, and their
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 4.1 Standardized form for the prenatal consultation. GBS, Group B Streptococcus; HIV, human

paragraphs.text: decision is supported by a scientifically competent and humane medical team. Some parents will follow a rational choice model, whereas others use emotions or heuristic decision-making styles. Although populations of infants born with congenital anomalies and genetic disorders have not been as extensively studied, either in terms of short- and long-term outcomes or in terms of approaches to counseling and decision making, many of the principles that apply to antenatal consultation at the margin of gestational viability are also applicable to these other maternal and fetal complications. One notable exception is for infants with trisomies 13 and 18, where extensive literature has demonstrated variability in individual patient outcomes and parental perceptions of a meaningful life leading to an evolution in counseling and management options offered to parents.101
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 4.1 Standardized form for the prenatal consultation. GBS, Group B Streptococcus; HIV, human
