paragraphs.text: Withholding life-sustaining medical treatment involves a decision not to provide a form of treatment that is not considered beneficial, whereas withdrawal involves a decision to remove treatment that has not achieved its goal.102 Morally, there is no difference between these two acts: If it is morally right (or wrong) to withhold treatment deemed to be ineffective, it is equally right (or wrong) to withdraw this same treatment after it is started, should it later become clear that the treatment is ineffective. However, this concept is emotionally difficult to accept for many parents and for many health care providers. Supporting stakeholders struggling with the moral weight of withdrawing an ongoing therapy with reinforcement of the ethical equivalence of withdrawing and withholding is crucial to provision of endof-life care, particularly as many neonates die with stable physiology after decisions to discontinue life-prolonging care rather than with unstable physiology after a code.103 It is also important to avoid using phrases such as “withdraw support” or “withdraw care,” because these may reinforce fears that families may have of being abandoned by their medical providers once a decision has been made to prioritize palliative goals, or that they themselves have made a decision to abandon or “give up on” their baby. Withdrawal of life-sustaining medical treatment and redirection of care are more appropriate terms for these activities.
paragraphs.heading: Withholding and Withdrawing Life-Sustaining Medical Treatment in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: Criteria for decisions to withhold or withdraw life-sustaining medical treatment are usually based on one of three general criteria: 1. Inevitability of death. When infants are very likely to die
paragraphs.heading: Withholding and Withdrawing Life-Sustaining Medical Treatment in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: in the NICU, regardless of whether life-sustaining treatment is continued, life-sustaining treatments that serve only to delay the moment of death need not and, in fact, ought not be continued beyond the time necessary to support the parents as they assimilate information and prepare for the infant’s death. However, clinicians must
paragraphs.heading: Withholding and Withdrawing Life-Sustaining Medical Treatment in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: recognize the difficulty in predicting outcomes with certainty, because studies suggest that in many circumstances neither clinical intuition nor objective scoring systems are reliably able to predict mortality in critically ill neonates.104 In addition, although additional hours or days of survival might not ultimately change the outcome for the infant, this time might be highly valued by the family, either as a good unto itself or as an opportunity to gather friends and loved ones in anticipation of the infant’s death. 2. Ineffective treatment. Treatment that has not or is not
paragraphs.heading: Withholding and Withdrawing Life-Sustaining Medical Treatment in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: expected to meet the intended goals, particularly when the treatment that imparts pain and suffering to the infant without appreciable benefit is considered ineffective. 3. Poor quality of life. As previously described in this chap-
paragraphs.heading: Withholding and Withdrawing Life-Sustaining Medical Treatment in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: ter, despite the difficulty in determining the quality of a life with limited cognitive or relational capacity, mobility, or self-awareness, or a life of continued pain and suffering, poor quality of life is a valid consideration and ethically permissible reason to withdraw or withhold lifesustaining interventions. Some authors cite futility of medical treatment as a criterion for withholding or withdrawing medical treatment. It is difficult to know what follows from such claims, however, because there is considerable debate and diversity of opinion as to the meaning of futility.105 A strong and certain prediction that death is inevitable or exceedingly likely should not be conflated with risk of a poor neurologic outcome. In addition to the debate about the meaning of the term futility, arguments have emerged about the authority of the physician to determine when an intervention is futile. Some authors contend that futility is a medical decision to be made by the physician alone, whereas others believe that the decision is value-laden and that parents should be involved in this determination. When futility is determined solely on medical or physiologic factors (a rare occurrence unless death is imminent), unilateral decision making by the physician based on sound medical knowledge and expertise may be appropriate. When subjective elements form part of the determination, however, the physician has no unique claim to moral expertise. In consideration of these more value-laden and subjective determinations of futility, the term “potentially inappropriate” has been put forth as more encompassing of the complexities of these situations.106 The Society for Critical Care Medicine has published a seven-step process for an organizational approach to conflict resolution in consideration of potentially inappropriate treatments.107 These guidelines, which are not specific to neonates, do take into account the value of neurologic recovery to the point of being able to “perceive the benefits of treatment” and emphasize the role of individualization, time-limited trials of interventions, and careful attention to pain and suffering. The American Academy of Pediatrics offers specific guidance on forgoing life-sustaining medical treatment for children, which recognizes the role of parents
paragraphs.heading: Withholding and Withdrawing Life-Sustaining Medical Treatment in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: in decision making, communication, iterative examination of the child’s condition and prognosis, and reliance on other supportive hospital services, such as ethics committees, pastoral care, palliative care, and others.108
paragraphs.heading: Withholding and Withdrawing Life-Sustaining Medical Treatment in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: Following a structured approach and decision-making process helps to ensure that appropriate views and preferences are made explicit. As described previously, the clinician-parent relationship is central to ensuring collaborative decision making, as all the participants in the process may come to understand the reasons and values underlying a particular choice. The following procedural framework is an example of one approach emphasizing three phases: preparation, delivery, and follow up.81 1. Prepare for the meeting. Discussions with clinical team
paragraphs.heading: End-of-Life Conversations

paragraphs.text: members can share insights about coping strategies or concerns parents have communicated. Ensuring all team members are updated on the infant’s medical condition, prognosis, and care options can help deliver a coherent message in a supportive and sensitive manner to parents. Frameworks such as those proposed by Racine and colleagues for infants with neurologic injury considers potential differences in perceptions of disability among stakeholders, through the practice of reflective, self-examination using the mnemonic “ouR- HOPE”: Reflection, Humility, Open-mindedness, Partnership, and Engagement.56 2. Create an optimal environment for discussion. It is impor-
paragraphs.heading: End-of-Life Conversations

paragraphs.text: tant to create a quiet and uninterrupted environment in which ethical issues and values can be thoroughly explored, despite the demands on the time and energy of parents and staff. In the setting of a teaching hospital, the value of educational opportunities for students and trainees should be balanced with parent-centered goals of creating a comfortable and nonintimidating environment for parents. It is generally advisable to meet away from the infant’s bedside to help focus attention on the discussion, and to consider which other stakeholders should participate. The patient’s nurse should be given the opportunity to participate, and in NICUs that use a primary nurse model for continuity, the primary nurse’s availability should be considered. The parents should be given the opportunity to identify other individuals they wish to include, including family members, spiritual leaders, and medical staff. Whenever possible, participating clinicians should be relieved of other responsibilities to limit interruptions. 3. Address emotions and check in. After introductions are
paragraphs.heading: End-of-Life Conversations

paragraphs.text: made, addressing emotions helps to reinforce the clinical team’s role in supporting parents and sets the tone for a collaboration. Emotive phrases such as “I am concerned,” or “I wish” statements such as “I wish I had better news,” can help warn parents of forthcoming difficult news while conveying empathy.
paragraphs.heading: End-of-Life Conversations

paragraphs.text: 4. Identify any ethical problems in which moral values con-
paragraphs.heading: End-of-Life Conversations

paragraphs.text: flict or moral uncertainty exists. Ethical deliberation is often complicated by communication problems and psychological issues. Approaches such as those described earlier in the chapter include exploring their perceptions and understanding of the clinical situation, at the same time remaining sensitive to the parents’ emotional crisis. These need to be disentangled from the ethical issues. Consultation with hospital ethics committees, or in some cases palliative care or clinical mediation services, can be helpful in supporting constructive, nonconfrontational dialogue and use of a common, respectful vocabulary. In most hospitals, ethics committees will offer nonbinding recommendations or delineate whether the proposed course of action is ethically permissible. Clinical ethics consultants should not interpret medical facts or supplant the responsible clinicians as the arbiter of medical decisions. 5. Identify the rightful decision makers. Many individuals
paragraphs.heading: End-of-Life Conversations

paragraphs.text: may be legitimately involved in the decision-making process, including, at least, the parents, the physician with primary responsibility, and other members of the health care team directly involved in the care of the patient. Individuals who bear the greatest burden of care and conscience; individuals with special knowledge; and nurses and other health care professionals with the most continuous, committed, and trusting relationship with the patient or parents should be included at the meeting.109 Thorough documentation of family meetings, medical decision making, and ethical rationale can be helpful to unify the team and minimize miscommunication, particularly when shift work and irregular schedules preclude participation of important clinician stakeholders. Disagreements about the rightful surrogate decision makers for neonates are rare, as in most cases, parents assume this role by default. Scenarios in which parents disagree with each other, are incapacitated and unable to participate in decision making, or in which biologic or legal parenthood is in dispute may call for consultation with the hospital ethics committee, along with other ancillary hospital services. There are also occasions where parents are identified as surrogate decision makers but do not want to assume the primary responsibility. Indeed, few parents want to feel that they are deciding the time and place of their infant’s death. Reinforcing tools from collaborative decision making and communication strategies in which the health care team guides the parents with phrases such as “we now face a difficult decision” or assumes final responsibility can help provide support while adhering to patient wishes and safeguarding their mental health. 6. Establish the relevant facts. “Good ethics begins with
paragraphs.heading: End-of-Life Conversations

paragraphs.text: good facts.” Medical facts include the diagnosis, the prognosis (and the estimated certainty of outcomes), relevant institutional policies, and available professional
paragraphs.heading: End-of-Life Conversations

paragraphs.text: guidelines. Nonmedical facts include information about family relationships, language barriers, cultural and religious beliefs, and past experiences with the health care system. Exploring the parents’ understanding of the medical facts, their expectations of the technology involved, the quality of communication between the parents themselves, and the degree of trust in physicians and the medical system can help correct misperceptions and build trust. The willingness of the clinician to discuss parents’ personal views and beliefs may enhance gathering of such information. 7. Explore the options. Explicit discussion of treatment
paragraphs.heading: End-of-Life Conversations

paragraphs.text: options and their known potential short-term and long-term consequences should occur, while keeping in mind outcomes that matter most to the parents may or may not align with categories chosen by experts. To encourage informed decision making, parents should be presented with the risks, benefits, and alternatives of each option. However, although most parents desire involvement in value-laden decisions,12 given the emotional nature of these discussions, they may not want or be able to absorb detailed descriptions of statistical risks. In addition, how the information is presented can strongly influence parents, and clinicians must be careful to avoid coercion.74,110 Close attention should be paid to the format in which pertinent information is delivered, allowing parents time and support to absorb critical information.61 8. Develop consensus. Open, honest discussion of the goals
paragraphs.heading: End-of-Life Conversations

paragraphs.text: and consequences of treatment allows parents, physicians, and other legitimate decision makers to carefully consider a range of professional and personal beliefs, values, and preferences, and to explore reasoned arguments for and against various options meaningfully. This process holds the promise of harmonious, collaborative decision making. Although care must be taken to ensure that parents do not feel abandoned or overburdened by these high-stakes decisions, a decision to withdraw or withhold life-sustaining treatment unilaterally against parental wishes should occur only after all avenues of reconciliation, including transfer of care to another institution for a second opinion, have been exhausted. 9. Implement the decision. When a consensual decision has
paragraphs.heading: End-of-Life Conversations

paragraphs.text: been reached, additional issues may need to be addressed with parents to ensure effective implementation. Clinicians always have a duty to care for their patients, even when the goals have shifted from aggressive measures to comfort and palliation, and to support the decisions they have asked parents to make.45,111 Parents should not be faced with continued doubts from staff, even if well intentioned. Once a decision is made to withhold or withdraw life-sustaining treatment, there should be an open discussion about the manner of death, the option for parents to be present, the performance of religious rituals, the anticipated grieving process, and the supports available for bereaved parents.112
paragraphs.heading: End-of-Life Conversations

paragraphs.text: 10. Follow-up care. Care for the family and parent does not
paragraphs.heading: End-of-Life Conversations

paragraphs.text: end with the death of the infant. Follow-up conversations should be considered part of the process. They serve to validate the parents’ experience and decisions while reinforcing the impact their child had on the lives of those who cared for them.81 Debriefings for the health care team members are also crucial because unattended moral distress can lead to burnout and have other negative consequences.
paragraphs.heading: End-of-Life Conversations

paragraphs.text: In most instances, decision makers can arrive at a morally sound decision regarding the best course of action in a particular situation. Clinicians and families sometimes fail to reach consensus, resulting in intractable conflict. Intractable conflict between parents is rare and is usually the result of divergent beliefs about what is in the infant’s best interest.
paragraphs.heading: Conflict Resolution When Consensus Cannot Be Reached

paragraphs.text: The following guidelines are proposed to promote continuing negotiation and resolution of conflict in the NICU: 1. Allow time for further clinical observation. In the specific
paragraphs.heading: Conflict Resolution When Consensus Cannot Be Reached

paragraphs.text: case of parental objections to forgoing treatment that the physician believes is not beneficial, it may be unrealistic to expect agreement from the parents the first time this recommendation is made. Prudence suggests moving as fast as the slowest member of the decision-making group, provided the infant’s condition is not rapidly changing and pain and agitation can be alleviated. 2. Ensure full parental comprehension of the medical infor-
paragraphs.heading: Conflict Resolution When Consensus Cannot Be Reached

paragraphs.text: mation. Early expressions of treatment preference by parents, such as “do everything possible,” need to be examined carefully. There is a tendency for busy medical teams to reduce parental expressions into simple one-line statements and not to explore their meaning. Such statements may be an expression of parental love or an expression of frustration with the medical team and not really an informed choice about what is in the best interests of the newborn. In addition, in view of parents’ potential ability to accept (or frank denial of) the severity of their infant’s condition, it is important to check parents’ understanding repeatedly. If it seems that inconsistent information has been provided by different individuals or teams, it may be advisable to convene a formal interdisciplinary case conference to explicate these differing viewpoints. 3. Continue to discuss, explore, and acknowledge the underly-
paragraphs.heading: Conflict Resolution When Consensus Cannot Be Reached

paragraphs.text: ing reasons for the differences in choice. It is important for health care providers to try to understand the parents’ views, beliefs, and preferences. Physicians must recognize that the parents’ beliefs and values are informed by ethnic and cultural traditions, customs, and institutions, and that these influences may be significantly divergent from their own. 4. Continue to work toward consensus. Parents may have great
paragraphs.heading: Conflict Resolution When Consensus Cannot Be Reached

paragraphs.text: difficulty in making an unassisted decision. The burden and potential guilt of decision making experienced by
paragraphs.heading: Conflict Resolution When Consensus Cannot Be Reached

paragraphs.text: parents is often immense and may be underappreciated by the medical team. The collaborative nature of a joint decision-making process and the shared burden of the decision must be reinforced. In addition, there may be medically imposed obstacles to achieving consensus, such as frequent changes in the responsible clinician from one neonatologist to the next, the failure of a clinician to establish a therapeutic alliance with the parents, the persistence of communication barriers between the medical team and the parents, or the development of a “contest of wills” between stakeholders as to who will sway the other. 5. Broaden the parents’ moral community. Identifying the
paragraphs.heading: Conflict Resolution When Consensus Cannot Be Reached

paragraphs.text: locus of decision-making authority within each family’s moral community may involve the inclusion of additional family members, grandparents, significant others, and religious or spiritual advisors in meetings with parents and the physician/team or in less structured communication opportunities. Families might differ in terms of who drives decision making, how internal disagreements are resolved, and how information is shared. Inclusive care requires medical teams to recognize and honor differences balancing respect for preferred hierarchical and gender roles within a family, helping all parents fully express their values and preferences, and the need to screen for coercive or abusive relationships. 6. Share the attending physician’s moral load by actively seeking
paragraphs.heading: Conflict Resolution When Consensus Cannot Be Reached

paragraphs.text: opinions from colleagues. Although the attending physician responsible for the infant bears the final responsibility for the approach taken with the parents, for personal and legal reasons, it is often helpful to obtain a second opinion from a colleague. 7. Involve a bioethicist or ethics consultation team, as appro-
paragraphs.heading: Conflict Resolution When Consensus Cannot Be Reached

paragraphs.text: priate. It may be beneficial to involve an institutional ethics committee with experience in case consultation and review, a clinical ethics consultation team, or a clinical ethicist, depending on available resources. Many hospital ethics committees are interprofessional in nature and include experts in medicine, nursing, philosophy, law, religion, and social services. The function of these committees varies widely. In some institutions, the whole ethics committee reviews cases; more commonly, a smaller subcommittee, an infant care review team, or an individual ethics consultant undertakes this responsibility. Ethics consultants can be very helpful in working to clarify values and build consensus (i.e., a process to ensure that facts are confirmed, relevant parties are involved, and decision makers are empowered, but not to be the decision-making group per se). 8. Consider transferring responsibility of care for the infant to
paragraphs.heading: Conflict Resolution When Consensus Cannot Be Reached

paragraphs.text: another accepting service or institution. In some situations, the therapeutic alliance between the medical team and an infant’s parents can be fractured beyond repair, and transfer to another unit or another hospital becomes a reasonable option. Although this can be procedurally difficult and require an adjustment for the parents as well as the infant, transfer to a different institution is generally
paragraphs.heading: Conflict Resolution When Consensus Cannot Be Reached

paragraphs.text: preferable to allowing parents to “fire” specific neonatologists (or other clinicians). Allowing parents to choose their care team is difficult to carry out without significant disruptions to NICU team function and structure, and it is unlikely that removal of a single member of the medical team will result in sustained resolution of a contentious relationship and is not generally advisable, as it is potentially harmful to the functioning of the medical team. Despite these efforts, the moral problem may not be amenable to consensual resolution. Rational people of good will may hold views that are irreconcilable. Individuals involved in a failed attempt at deriving consensus may experience what Webster and Baylis113 term moral residue, “that which each of us carries with us from those times in our lives when in the face of moral distress we have seriously compromised ourselves or allowed ourselves to be compromised.” There is growing attention on the deleterious effects of unresolved moral distress and resultant and moral residue, which over time and repeated instances, results in a “crescendo effect” in which caregiver reactions are amplified in subsequent encounters.114 Ethical conflict has been shown to contribute to moral distress and moral injury, poor professional and personal outcomes for clinicians, and worse individual and system performance.115
paragraphs.heading: Conflict Resolution When Consensus Cannot Be Reached

paragraphs.text: Withdrawal of life-sustaining medical treatment should generally not be undertaken until the therapeutic relationship is mended and interaction between the family and the medical team is less fraught. Rarely, physicians seek authority to make unilateral decisions via institutional or legal redress. When ethical conflict seems intractable, an institutional decision may be made to seek legal recourse. This course of action, although sometimes necessary, is generally unsatisfactory; it increases the anguish for patients and families, it destroys the parent-physician relationship, it creates (or increases) conflict between members of the health care team, and it invariably results in a significant drain on staff time and morale. It can also be extremely costly and time consuming for all parties involved. Ideally, institutional policies developed by the hospital ethics committee and staff should be in place to minimize the need for judicial intervention.
paragraphs.heading: Conflict Resolution When Consensus Cannot Be Reached

paragraphs.text: Organs for transplantation remain a scarce resource with a higher demand than supply. Although infants historically have been excluded from consideration, explorations have revealed that in fact, they could qualify as eligible donors.116,117 In their review, “Neonatal organ donation: Ethical insights and policy implications,” Ahmad, Raffell, and Weise identified eight considerations associated with neonatal donation: 1. The preservation of dignity and the ethicality of premor-
paragraphs.heading: Brain Death, Donation After Cardiac Death, and Organ Donation Organ Donation After Death in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: tem interventions
paragraphs.heading: Brain Death, Donation After Cardiac Death, and Organ Donation Organ Donation After Death in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: 2. The difficulty in determining brain death and the contro-
paragraphs.heading: Brain Death, Donation After Cardiac Death, and Organ Donation Organ Donation After Death in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: versy surrounding circulatory determination of death in neonates 3. Issues pertaining to surrogate decision making for neo-
paragraphs.heading: Brain Death, Donation After Cardiac Death, and Organ Donation Organ Donation After Death in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: nates 4. Respecting parental wishes and donor interests while bal-
paragraphs.heading: Brain Death, Donation After Cardiac Death, and Organ Donation Organ Donation After Death in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: ancing the needs for donor organs 5. Ensuring utmost attention to pain relief and palliation
paragraphs.heading: Brain Death, Donation After Cardiac Death, and Organ Donation Organ Donation After Death in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: for the dying neonate 6. Donation to provide meaning to the parents’ loss and
paragraphs.heading: Brain Death, Donation After Cardiac Death, and Organ Donation Organ Donation After Death in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: provision of emotional support for parents during the donation process 7. Resource allocation and transplant ethics considerations 8. Dilemmas of intrapartum care for mothers in cases of
paragraphs.heading: Brain Death, Donation After Cardiac Death, and Organ Donation Organ Donation After Death in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: terminal diagnosis in the fetus118 In the joint consensus statement “Management of the Potential Organ Donor in the ICU,” the Society of Critical Care Medicine, American College of Chest Physicians, and the Association of Organ Procurement Organizations advocate that the organ procurement organization should be notified: 1. at the initial indication that a patient has suffered a non-
paragraphs.heading: Brain Death, Donation After Cardiac Death, and Organ Donation Organ Donation After Death in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: recoverable neurologic injury 2. as soon as a “brain death” examination is contemplated 3. before initiating a discussion that may lead to withdrawal
paragraphs.heading: Brain Death, Donation After Cardiac Death, and Organ Donation Organ Donation After Death in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: of life-sustaining therapy119 In any situation that organ donation is being considered after the anticipated death of an infant, whether by neurologic or circulatory criteria, avoidance of real and perceived conflict of interest is essential. Based on the principle that no human’s life should be used as a means to an end, medical care of the living must be done with the intent of benefiting that patient in some way—it is categorically impermissible to knowingly harm a patient with the goal of preservation of organ function, prioritizing future donation over the patient’s own interests.120 Initiation of interventions aimed at organ preservation for future donation require parental informed consent.120 Specific interventions targeted at preserving organ function for future transplantation after determination of death by neurologic criteria are deliniated.119 Firm separation between the patient’s care team and the organ recovery team is also essential,120 even though it is appropriate for the medical team to discuss potential organ donation.119
paragraphs.heading: Brain Death, Donation After Cardiac Death, and Organ Donation Organ Donation After Death in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: Although brain death is well-defined for children and adolescents and has been accepted in most jurisdictions for decades as the threshold criterion for the removal of organs from heart-beating donors (without violating the dead donor rule), controversies persist about the determination of death by neurologic criteria for infants. Historically, infants have been excluded from clinical determination of death by neurologic criteria because of speculations that the neonatal brain pathophysiology and response to increased intracranial pressure differs from older children.121 The American Academy of Pediatrics and The Pediatric Section
paragraphs.heading: Brain Death

paragraphs.text: of the Society of Critical Care Medicine jointly published “Guidelines for the Determination of Death in Infants and Children” (reaffirmed in 2015), which defines brain death as the “irreversible cessation of all functions of the entire brain including the brainstem.”121 This guideline includes infants born at or after 37 and 0/7 weeks gestation and contains detailed algorithms, tables, and examination checklists to aid the clinician. Determination of brain death in a term neonate is based on the absence of neurologic function as determined clinically with a known cause of irreversible coma119 and requires two examinations performed at least 24 hours apart (12 hours for infants >30 days old). However, because of insufficient data and difficulty in assessing level of consciousness in a preterm infant, complicated by the developmental immaturity of neurologic reflexes at the time of injury, no criteria exist to diagnose brain death in premature infants. Anencephaly is not equivalent to brain death, as infants with anencephaly can retain brainstem function and therefore they are not by de facto candidates for organ donation.119 Some have hypothesized that therapeutic hypothermia treatment for infants with hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy might support organ function and facilitate organ donation following determination of death by neurologic criteria; however, this has yet to be confirmed.122
paragraphs.heading: Brain Death

paragraphs.text: Despite these advances, brain death as a concept, the process for its evaluation, and declaration of brain death remains a subject of considerable controversy. Certain religious groups have sought exception from neurologic criteria for brain death: “all religions distinguish between the living and the dead, but not all religions accept death by neurologic criteria as death.”123 As noted in a New England Journal of Medicine editorial from 2001, “one subject [that] can be said to be at once well settled and persistently unresolved...[is]...how to determine that death has occurred.”124 This was most notably demonstrated by the highly publicized pediatric case of a 13-year-old who was declared brain dead following a postoperative hemorrhage from a tonsillectomy in 2013.125 In addition, some families have contended that an explicit informed consent process should be required before a brain death evaluation on the basis that the apnea test, a component of the exam, carries risks of cardiorespiratory decompensation.121 This is especially salient for neonates, who often present with bradycardias before apneic events; however, the question of surrogate consent remains debated by bioethicists.126,127
paragraphs.heading: Brain Death

paragraphs.text: Although some parents reject brain death examinations or declarations by neurologic criteria, other parents find solace in opportunities to give meaning in the face of tragic death.128 It is, however, recommended that clinical teams consult hospital policies and national guidelines before initiating examinations. Once a declaration of death has been made, parental permission is not required to discontinue mechanical ventilation, medications, and monitoring. However, it is often reasonable to continue interventions that prolong cardiorespiratory function for a time-limited
paragraphs.heading: Brain Death

paragraphs.text: period to permit the family to conduct religious and/or memory-making rituals.
paragraphs.heading: Brain Death

paragraphs.text: Cardiac death occurs when an individual has sustained “irreversible cessation of circulatory and respiratory function.”129 This definition has been endorsed for neonates, specifically.130 However, after cardiac death, the time required to mobilize resources necessary for organ retrieval results in excessive warm ischemia time, excluding the possibility of organ donation. Attempts to improve retrieval of viable organs from non-heart-beating donors have focused on trying to control the circumstances of withdrawal of life support, thereby allowing “donation after cardiac death” (DCD) as a reasonable alternative to determination of death by neurologic criteria. DCD protocols are considerably different from traditional end-of-life situations: patients are brought to the operating room before withdrawal of life support, and after there has been circulatory arrest for a specific length of time, organ recovery efforts are begun immediately. The Canadian guideline statement for pediatric DCD endorses a 5-minute “handsoff observation of arrest of circulation prior to determination of death,” supported by the use of a “well-functioning arterial catheter” to “confirm arrest of anterograde arterial circulation.”130
paragraphs.heading: Donation After Cardiac Death

paragraphs.text: Successful transplantation following “donation after cardiac death” of neonatal organs includes heart131 and kidney132 transplants. Neonatal hepatocyte donation has also been explored to treat infants and children with inborn errors of metabolism, and as a potential source of healthy liver cells for transplant. Early studies suggest this is possible following “donation after cardiac death” procedures, including in preterm infants.133 In principle, preterm infants ought to be candidates for DCD, provided their absolute size or weight do not exclude the possibility of organ procurement and transplantation.
paragraphs.heading: Donation After Cardiac Death

paragraphs.text: Whether donation occurs after cardiac death or based on neurologic criteria, there must be a unified approach that continues to focus on humane and compassionate care of the patient and family. Many NICUs have well-established bereavement and end-of-life care protocols that encourage families to gather, participate in religious and cultural traditions, and spend hours to days with their baby after death has occurred. Donation after cardiac death policies may disrupt the flow of this care and families need to be informed about the changes. It is also essential that DCD protocols provide families “a clear understanding of the DCD donation process and a realistic understanding of all possible outcomes of donation, including successful transplant or an inability to recover or transplant for medical reasons.”128
paragraphs.heading: Donation After Cardiac Death

paragraphs.text: Both the American Academy of Pediatrics policy statement “Ethical Controversies in Organ Donation After Circulatory Death”120 and the “Canadian Guidelines for Controlled Pediatric Donation of Circulatory
paragraphs.heading: Donation After Cardiac Death

paragraphs.text: Determination of Death”130 permit clinicians to declare conscience-based refusal to participate in a DCD process. The potential impact on families to have opportunities to explore DCD in light of heterogeneity between hospitals in the ability to provide DCD to infants and children raises concerns related to justice which are incompletely mediated by transfer to another hospital, given the emotional and economic burdens of family separation.130
paragraphs.heading: Donation After Cardiac Death

paragraphs.text: Both physicians and nurses have an ethical obligation to relieve pain and suffering, and this applies to infants at the end of life.134 Partridge and Wall demonstrated that in most cases of withholding or withdrawing life support from critically ill infants, neonatologists provided opioid analgesia to these infants, despite the potential respiratory depression of these agents, the so-called double effect.135 The intent of the action—to alleviate pain and promote comfort—distinguishes the use of analgesics from the use of other agents, such as paralyzing agents, whose intent is to ensure death. The introduction of neuromuscular blocking agents at the time of withdrawal of life-sustaining medical treatment is considered ethically inappropriate, as is any form of active euthanasia.136
paragraphs.heading: Use of Analgesic Agents at the Time of Withdrawing Life-Sustaining Medical Treatment

paragraphs.text: Although the expressed intention of alleviating suffering and discomfort is usually cited as justification for the “double effect” of analgesics and sedatives, the distinction from hastening death is sometimes difficult. To some authors, such as April and Parker,137 the ban on active euthanasia (i.e., the use of drugs with the specific intent to end life) exists largely because professional guidelines in most jurisdictions call for the distinction and as such is a reflection of current consensus. They contend that relief of symptoms and concern for a newborn’s suffering should be the primary goal, and the ban on physicians’ role in active euthanasia is in their view not a moral argument but an appeal to public opinion and the moral primacy of the status quo.
paragraphs.heading: Use of Analgesic Agents at the Time of Withdrawing Life-Sustaining Medical Treatment

paragraphs.text: This issue has been stirred by the Groningen protocol in the Netherlands where, in rare cases, in a newborn with an extremely poor prognosis and intractable suffering, and after all measures to alleviate the suffering have been unsuccessful, the deliberate ending of life may be considered legal.138,139 Many, but not all, authorities consider such active neonatal euthanasia to be unsupportable and believe that the Groningen protocol should be abandoned.7,140 Most authorities believe, similar to Costeloe,141 that despite the conceptual difficulty in defining the difference between drugs used to alleviate pain and drugs given with the intention of ending life, in practice, “experienced neonatologists and neonatal nurses feel comfortable with this distinction.” They can discuss it openly with families and help them understand the acceptability of infusing opiates at a dose that controls pain
paragraphs.heading: Use of Analgesic Agents at the Time of Withdrawing Life-Sustaining Medical Treatment

paragraphs.text: and distress but the unacceptability of increasing the dose further with the primary intention of hastening death.27
paragraphs.heading: Use of Analgesic Agents at the Time of Withdrawing Life-Sustaining Medical Treatment

paragraphs.text: Research is essential to advance clinical care for sick newborns; improvements in the practice of clinical neonatology would not occur without such research. Because of their inherent vulnerability and potential for exploitation, inability to provide informed consent, and, for infants and young children, inability to engage meaningfully in assent, enrolling minors in clinical research has historically been difficult. Until recently, a protectionist view prevailed, such that studies in children were justified only if they were unsuitable in adults, resulting in adaptation of treatments from other groups applied to neonates without sufficient evidence. This perspective has changed, reflecting a shift from the dominance of beneficence or protectionism toward vulnerable groups, such as infants, to a stance based on the principle of justice. According to the principle of justice, individuals who are the subject of a treatment should have an equal opportunity to share the benefits of human research.
paragraphs.heading: Ethics of Research in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: Despite this ethical imperative, many challenges exist in conducting neonatal research.142 It is difficult to obtain “authentic,” morally valid, informed consent from parents, because this requires surrogate decision making by anxious and stressed decision makers, often following an unanticipated, acute emergency. Language, cultural, and religious diversity add further complexity, and the act of soliciting consent itself can exacerbate parental stress. “Therapeutic misconception,” first described in the 1980s, is the erroneous attribution of therapeutic intent to clinical research.143 The research team should use accessible language and documents that clearly explain what the research activities have to do with the infant’s clinical care, and carefully explain concepts such as randomization.
paragraphs.heading: Ethics of Research in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: In some cases, the person approaching families or enrolling infants to participate in clinical research studies also provides clinical care for that infant—this introduces the possibility for real or perceived conflict of interest for the clinician. Parents may feel beholden to their infant’s care team and therefore obligated to agree or they may fear that their infant’s care will suffer if they decline. Whenever possible, it is advisable to separate clinical care from research recruitment, such that the person obtaining parental consent is not also providing clinical care to the infant. A central tenet of voluntary research participation is the ability to withdraw from a study at any time, thus informed consent for research should be viewed as a continuous process, with iterative points of contact between the family and the research team.
paragraphs.heading: Ethics of Research in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: It may be disturbing for parents to learn there exists uncertainty about neonatal practice, which in turn could potentially diminish their confidence in NICU care. Before discussing neonatal research with parents, general issues
paragraphs.heading: Ethics of Research in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: facing the ethical conduct of research need to be ensured, including the scientific value and validity of the study proposal, the existence of clinical equipoise in randomized trials, the distinction between therapeutic and nontherapeutic research (where the study would not lead to direct benefit for that infant), the existence of any potential conflicts of interest or financial incentives, and the overall risk/benefit analysis of the research proposal. Clinical equipoise, when there is insufficient clinical evidence and genuine uncertainty to recommend one course of action over another, is a moral requirement to justify human subjects research.144
paragraphs.heading: Ethics of Research in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: Informed consent for clinical research can follow different models depending on the level of risk resulting from the research and emergent or nonemergent circumstances. Categories of potential risk exist guiding whether one or both parents are required to provide consent based on recommendations from the Health and Human Services142,145: 1. Research not involving greater than minimal risk—
paragraphs.heading: Ethics of Research in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: requires consent from one parent 2. Research posing greater than minimal risk with potential
paragraphs.heading: Ethics of Research in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: of direct benefit to the infant—requires consent from one parent 3. Research posing greater than minimum risk without
paragraphs.heading: Ethics of Research in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: direct benefit to the infant but may improve knowledge about the condition—requires consent from both parents 4. Research not otherwise approvable which presents an
paragraphs.heading: Ethics of Research in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: opportunity to understand, prevent, or alleviate a serious problem affecting the health or welfare of children— requires consent from both parents Exceptions to requirement for consent from both parents only exists when one parent is deceased, unknown, incompetent, or not reasonably available or in custody arrangements whereby only one parent is the legal guardian.145 In a standard model, parents are solicited when their infant becomes eligible for a study, given written and verbal information, encouraged to ask questions, and required to sign a consent form. Other proposed models include a steplike process of consent;146 an advanced consent, in which parents are approached in anticipation that their infant may meet inclusion criteria at a later date; emergency consent; and randomization without consent, in which randomization occurs before potential participants are approached, and only participants allocated to experimental therapies are informed of the trial and invited to give or withhold consent (Zelen randomization).147,148 The individuals allocated to continue with standard therapies are not informed that they are trial participants at that stage.
paragraphs.heading: Ethics of Research in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: Research involving the procurement of genetic or other information with potential long-term implications, indefinite storage of specimens, and/or information for future use introduces a series of ethical concerns. These include how to manage genetic findings of unclear clinical significance, diagnosing adult-onset genetic diseases, questions about who “owns” the specimen, and whether study participants should be given the opportunity to continue or
paragraphs.heading: Ethics of Research in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: withdraw participation when they reach the age of majority.149 For example, studies involving institutional biobanks, newborn blood spots obtained for newborn screening, and blood or tissue specimens obtained for therapeutic purposes raise concerns about the moral validity of “broad consent.” Although a “broad consent” process may promote more diverse heterogenous data sets, the risk of unknown future use and preserving the sanctity of voluntariness is problematic.150 One proposed solution has been following an “opt out” research consent, in which the default option is enrollment, unless the parents actively refuse (as opposed to the conventional approach of “opt in,” in which the default state is not to be enrolled).151
paragraphs.heading: Ethics of Research in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: Significant controversy involving consent and neonatal research issues surrounded the National Institutes of Health– funded Surfactant, Positive Pressure, and Oxygenation Randomized Trial (SUPPORT). The study was designed to determine the appropriate range of oxygen saturation in extremely premature infants by using two target saturation ranges, one low and one high. Consumer advocacy group Public Citizen accused the investigators of deceiving parents with “egregious” deficiencies in the informed consent process.152 Although the consent documents varied by institution, they were approved by 23 institutional review boards; whereas there were certainly ethicists criticizing the study, most leading pediatric ethicists vigorously defended the ethics of the study.153,154 Ultimately, the most positive outcome of the controversy has been a renewed focus to optimize the consent process in neonatal research, including “deliberative democratic discussions with a broad array of societal representatives (parents, clinicians, researchers, and ethicists).”155
paragraphs.heading: Ethics of Research in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: The optimal model for consent for neonatal research is one that protects and promotes parental authority, is sensitive to the vulnerability and stress of parents, and is beneficent to the infants. Golec and colleagues148 suggested that a “morally optimizing approach to research recruitment” is one in which: 1. parents are approached one study at a time 2. studies have relevance to the current clinical status of the
paragraphs.heading: Ethics of Research in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: neonate 3. researchers minimize information overload 4. researchers promote respect for parental autonomy 5. researchers inform parents about research in a continuing
paragraphs.heading: Ethics of Research in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: process, not as an event 6. adequate time is allowed to make decisions 7. there are limits on subsequent solicitation approaches
paragraphs.heading: Ethics of Research in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: No model of soliciting parental permission is perfect, and the concept of informed consent cannot be the sole safeguard protecting the welfare of the neonate in research studies. The integrity of the researcher, the role of the institutional review board, and safety and monitoring by all individuals involved help to ensure the safety and protection of neonates. Another important resource to ensure ethical conduct of neonatal research is the role of the NICU nurse. Not only are nurses in a strategic position to promote parental understanding and improve the likelihood that the conditions of informed consent are met, but nurses also can
paragraphs.heading: Ethics of Research in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: help set priorities in neonatal research by playing an active role in the formulation of research policy and being “at the table” where priorities are set.156
paragraphs.heading: Ethics of Research in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: How neonatal medicine is practiced will certainly change, but the fundamental ethical obligations of neonatal clinicians will remain unchanged (Box 4.3). The clinician’s responsibility to the competent pregnant patient is defined and well established—to respect the patient’s wishes regarding treatment even when this may be contrary to fetal best interests. So too is the clinician’s responsibility to the neonatal patient—right and good action within the best interests standard of judgment. In the broadest terms, these responsibilities are best discharged in the context of a constructive and mutually respectful parent-clinician relationship that recognizes that patient and family values and beliefs are integral to the decision-making process.
paragraphs.heading: Ethical Responsibilities of Neonatal Physicians

paragraphs.text: In the context of team medicine, the attending neonatologist is responsible for developing and maintaining positive relationships with all members of the health care team to promote better, open discussion of moral problems and to work toward consensus among the individuals directly involved in the patient’s care. The attending also has an obligation to foster the ethical experience and education of the interdisciplinary team and that of junior staff and trainees. The perinatal high-risk unit or NICU team should be more than a group of physicians, nurses, and other professionals working in an isolated area of the hospital trying to master new technology and break new ground. Ideally, it should be an open, analytic, self-critical, and responsive group providing ethically responsible care to pregnant women, newborn infants, and their families.
paragraphs.heading: Ethical Responsibilities of Neonatal Physicians

paragraphs.text: By setting a standard of moral responsibility for the care of newborns and families, clinicians working in neonatal care send a message to society that promotes public confidence and trust in their professional practice and responsible use of expensive resources. Finally, all health care professionals in neonatal care need to consider their own moral conscience and agency. Ethical deliberation is essentially a reflective task that requires participants to be explicit about what they believe and why, as well as what they value and on what grounds.

figures.caption: • Fig. 4.1 Standardized form for the prenatal consultation. GBS, Group B Streptococcus; HIV, human immunodeficiency virus; HR, heart rate; IUGR, intrauterine growth restriction; LMP, last menstrual period; NICU, neonatal intensive care unit; PROM, premature rupture of membranes; RDS, respiratory distress syndrome; UAC / UVC, umbilical arterial and venous catheter; VDRL, Venereal Disease Research Laboratory.

• Fig. 4.2 Values-based shared decision making in the antenatal period. (A) A neonatologist may perceive a high likelihood of nonsurvival paired with a high chance of moderate-to-severe impairment among survivors as dismal, with a very low chance of the “desired” outcome of intact survival. Because of the statistical probabilities, the burdens of infant suffering and societal cost may appear to outweigh benefit of therapy, and comfort care may logically be recommended. (B) A parent, however, may view these outcomes very differently. If any survival, even with significant impairment, is seen as a desirable outcome, the probability of a “good” outcome rises. If having a surviving, very impaired, child is considered the most undesirable outcome, the risk of this is quite low, because many of the sickest infants die. Finally, if dying following intensive care is perceived as more favorable than possibly missing an opportunity to have an intact survivor, the risk of the unfavorable outcome falls to zero if an attempt at resuscitation is made. (From Kukora SK, Boss RD. Values-based shared decision-making in the antenatal period. Semin Fetal Neonatal Med. 2017;23:17–24.)

# 4. Medical Ethics in Neonatal Care

## PDF page 58 | printed page 39

4 Medical Ethics in Neonatal Care

### MARLYSE F. HAWARD, JONATHAN M. FANAROFF, AND NAOMI T. LAVENTHAL

### Introduction

This chapter explores the complexity of moral problem solving in neonatal medicine. First, principles of medical ethics and key terms and concepts are reviewed, followed by the application of these concepts in specific moral problems that arise (1) in the prenatal consultation at the limits of gestational viability, (2) when withholding and withdrawing life-sustaining medical treatment in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) is undertaken, and (3) in defining brain death and exploring organ donation. Ethical responsibilities and approaches for collaborative end-of-life decision making and conflict resolution, including impact on parents and team members, use of analgesic agents, and the conduct of clinical research will be presented. This chapter emphasizes the importance of the clinician-parent relationship for effective communication supporting affective and cognitive needs of parents while appreciating diversity in perspectives and values. This list is not an exhaustive representation of ethical challenges facing NICU clinicians but rather highlights some that are frequently encountered. The principles offered to address them are applicable to many other situations.

Three elements characterize the practice of medicine that are timeless, universal, and irrefutably true: (1) the fact of illness and the vulnerability it creates, (2) the act of the profession (the use of medical skills for the benefit of the patient), and (3) the practice of medicine itself—that which clinicians and patients do together in the clinical encounter, characterized by mutual intentionality.1 These three elements are well exemplified in the care of sick neonates, in which the vulnerability of anxious parents is manifest, the clinical competence and moral discretion of health professionals are used for the benefit of newborn patients and their parents, and the practice is carried out in a patient-parent-physician relationship characterized by mutual trust and pursuit of the neonatal patient’s and parents’ good.

Medical ethics involves the systematic, reasoned evaluation and justification of the “right” action in pursuit of human good or well-being in the context of medical practice. In the practice of neonatal intensive care, medical ethics has become a central focus because it contains all the elements of moral discourse but without clear-cut “right” answers expected in routine clinical practice. Numerous ethical issues arise as clinicians attempt to determine how best to use technology in pursuit of what benefits the patient, in consideration of the values parents place on different outcomes.

These issues are compounded by several limitations on NICU clinicians’ ability to elicit and understand parents’ values; these can be pragmatic, related to patient and professional time restrictions, or may result from limitations in the provider’s knowledge and expertise of how best to have these difficult conversations.2,3 Care is also complicated by the medical uncertainty surrounding accurate outcome prediction of potentially adverse findings and by the very nature of many decisions in which quality of life and life itself may be under consideration.4 All these issues make the NICU a challenging, highly scrutinized environment in how ethical issues are examined, reasoned, and justified, and raise fundamental questions about what the responsibilities of clinicians should be.

Ethical issues may be experienced as moral dilemmas, or moral distress. A moral dilemma is present when the clinician believes there is an obligation to pursue two (or more) conflicting courses of action. Because only one of these courses can be pursued, the clinician must make a valuebased choice that compromises one of these obligations. Conflict between respect for parental authority and professional duty to provide recommended medical care is a frequently encountered example of a moral dilemma.

Moral dilemmas may also arise when there is uncertainty in whether a course of action or resultant outcome is ethical. This is commonly manifest as uncertainty on the part

of parents who might struggle with a concomitant desire to prolong the life of their infant but wish to avoid burdensome procedures or a quality of life deemed worse than death. On the part of clinicians, moral uncertainty might appear when treatments are readily available, but with a low likelihood of success.

Moral distress arises when the decision maker feels certain about the morally right thing to do, but this perceived “right” course of action is constrained for numerous reasons, including the clinician’s lack of decision-making authority or institutional or financial constraints. This phenomenon was initially described among nurses5 but is also experienced by other NICU providers, including physicians, and involves a sense of powerlessness, frustration, physical symptoms, and ultimately professional “burnout.”6 Although unprocessed moral distress can result in maladaptive “moral residue,”7,8 contemporary explorations of this topic have focused on constructive approaches to building moral resilience8 and directing moral distress toward positive actions to improve patient care.9

### Principles in Medical Ethics

Ethical reasoning requires an understanding of the fundamental principles that define a domain (Box 4.1). Beauchamp and Childress10 have described four core bioethical principles: autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice. Consideration of a real-time ethical conflict or dilemma in the context of these principles can be a useful starting point and can be particularly helpful in articulating the ethical questions, uniting a struggling team by use of commonly held, noninflammatory language. However, a principles-based approach is less helpful when the problem revolves around a conflict between the principles themselves, as is often the case in the NICU. In many cases, a “principalis” paradigm may not do justice to the nature or complexity of the moral problem. In addition, in a purely principle-based approach, the role of the neonatal clinician as moral agent (i.e., someone with personal virtues and values and the opportunity to take action that comports with that judgment of morality) is de-emphasized. This chapter does not prescribe adherence to any particular ethical framework but aims to enhance appreciation of the language of ethical discourse to enable nuanced reflection, reasoning, and ethical decision making, and to underline the role of the clinician in these situations.

### Parental Authority

The principle of autonomy supports the right of competent patients to make their own health care choices. An individual who makes an autonomous choice acts intentionally, with understanding and without external controlling influences.10 An idealized expression of autonomy occurs when a competent adult chooses voluntarily and intelligently from among various options whose relative risks and benefits have been fully explained to them by the clinicians (i.e., via a truly informed consent process).

The term parental autonomy is often used interchangeably with parental authority, although most argue that autonomy can strictly be used only when making decisions for oneself. Parental authority is the more correct term when referring to the role of parents in decision making for their newborn infants.

Neonatal clinicians should show respect for parental authority: 1. because of the presumption that parents will make deci-

sions that are in their child’s best interests (parents are often described as the “natural surrogate decision makers” for children)10 2. as a means of promoting shared decision making

Parents are not uniform in their desire to direct or even participate in medical decision making for their children.11,12 Clinicians must be conscious of the impact of their authority, the power that derives from expertise and confidence, as well as limitations in their own ability to determine how directive parents wish for them to be in preference-sensitive decisions.13

In the second half of the 20th century, there was a major shift away from a paternalistic “doctor knows best” approach of information sharing and medical decision making toward empowerment of the patient to make autonomous choices.14,15 This condemnation of paternalism has more recently been viewed as excessively burdening some patients with weighty decisions that they do not wish to make alone.16 There is a body of evidence that the prevailing bioethics emphasis on autonomy and self-determination can be overwhelming to parents.17 A more nuanced application of respect for parental authority can be satisfactorily achieved by including parents in decision making as true partners and team members, recognizing that decision making can exist on a continuum.15,18

Too rigid or simplistic an interpretation and application of respect for parental authority by clinicians is also problematic, such as when agreeing to a parental statement that “we want everything done.” Without exploring what underlies this declaration, clinicians may neglect the complexity of the situation and the underlying parental fear of “abandonment.” Finding the right balance between respect for

### Beneficence

Beneficence is the obligation to “do good,” that is, to promote patients’ best interests.10 In newborns, this obligation is embodied in the concept of the “best interests of the newborn.” This is a moral and legal standard of judgment that helps to establish the primacy of duties to infants, ensuring they be regarded as fully human individuals with interests, even when clearly unable to express their own value system. Pursuing a course of action in the best interests of an infant implies determining what treatment course has a more favorable benefit-to-harm ratio than other possible options. Interpretation of the meaning of “benefit” can vary between infants and between stakeholders (parents, relatives, clinicians) for the same infant. Interpretations of what it means for a treatment to be beneficial include improvement in the infant’s condition, stabilization of the infant’s condition, or delaying the onset of clinical deterioration. Amelioration of clinical symptoms, or avoidance of complications of treatment, might also be construed as benefit. Benefit can also be achieved by identifying a less restrictive or intrusive treatment.

Determination of best interests may involve discussions of the child’s potential quality of life. Quality-of-life considerations encompass the predicted cognitive and neurodevelopmental outcome, the potential for motor disability or other physical handicap (e.g., vision, hearing), and longerterm concerns such as behavioral and learning difficulties or school problems. It also considers the requirements for repeated or prolonged hospitalization, surgery, or medication; technology dependence; and the potential for pain and suffering to be endured. Quality-of-life considerations may also include less concrete medical states, such as the capacity for meaningful and potentially enjoyable interaction with other people and the environment. Some of the most ferocious disagreements between and within NICU teams relate to the inherently subjective nature of quality of life. Contemporary clinical ethicists have moved away from seemingly quantifiable assessments of quality of life, related to measurable outcomes, toward a more subjective interpretation, informed largely by the parents’ expressed values.2 Although well-intentioned clinicians might seek to “correct” parents’ interpretation of the quality of an anticipated outcome, recognition that some families might see more value in survival with neurodevelopmental disability or technology dependence than others is crucial to familycentered care and shared decision making. In addition, clinicians must be very cautious about judging the quality of life of others, viewing disability as a “harm,” and underestimating the ability of those with disabilities to have a wonderful, fulfilled, and meaningful life.19

The standard of best interests of the newborn acts as a threshold for judgment, yet the subjective nature of this

assessment and the fact that the assessment is being done by surrogate decision makers must always be recognized. In addition, it is imperative for clinicians to be aware of their limited powers of prognostication. Repeated studies by Meadow and colleagues have shown that when health care professionals predict that an infant will not survive to discharge, they are incorrect relatively frequently.20 However, there are circumstances in which the best interest standard can be very helpful to medical teams, such as when urgent decisions must be made in the absence of parental input or when parents refuse clearly life-saving interventions. For the latter, best interest serves as a standard for overriding parental decisions.

Diekema has suggested that the more conservative “harm” principle be applied in overriding parental wishes. By this principle, rather than determine the “best interests,” a harm threshold will be determined below which the parents’ decision will be overruled.21 Although invocation of the harm principle can be quite helpful, stakeholders for sick neonates must be careful to apply it in the context of illness severity, urgency, and maintenance of professional standards and integrity.16,22

Despite these definitional difficulties and suggested alternative standards such as the “harm” principle, “best interests of the newborn” is accepted as a guiding principle for decision makers because it unites different meanings under one standard and exhibits reasonableness, given the prevailing conditions.23 Properly understood, the concept can serve as a powerful tool in settling disputes about how to make good decisions for individuals who cannot decide for themselves.

### Nonmaleficence

The principle of nonmaleficence implies an obligation not to inflict harm on others. It has been closely associated with the maxim primum non nocere (first do no harm).10 Although beneficence incorporates preventing and removing harm as part of promoting “the good” of a patient, the injunction not to inflict harm remains a distinct principle and requires intentionally refraining from actions that cause harm. Such harm is generally interpreted as physical harm, especially pain, disability, or death. Nonmaleficence requires that no initiation or continuation of treatment be considered without consideration of whether the treatment is overly burdensome or harmful. This is especially relevant given a historical context in which attention to pain in neonates has been sorely disregarded, to the degree in which surgeries were performed without anesthesia. However, as for benefit, defining events and interventions that are harmful to the infant can be subjective. For some, harm is narrowly defined as pain or anxiety related to the condition or its treatment; assessment of this kind of harm can be aided by using bedside pain scores and other objective measures. For others, any intervention that does not change the ultimate outcome for the infant imparts undue burden. Clinicians and parents may differ about whether hospitalization in an

intensive care unit (ICU), without the promise of recovery or discharge home, is harmful to the infant.

### Justice

Justice is the dominant principle relating to social cooperation. Justice is the framework by which we determine how social benefits, such as health care, and burdens, such as research risks, are distributed. Although justice is regarded as a guiding principle for any health care system, no single, simple, ideal implementation adequately addresses the priorities of all relevant stakeholders. Generally, concepts of justice range from the broader utilitarian calculus to promote the greatest good for the greatest number in underwriting the distribution of resources (macroallocation) to a more narrowly focused equality of opportunity for each individual (microallocation). Justice in the distribution of resources requires that: 1. patients in similar situations have access to the same

health care 2. the level of health care available for one set of patients

considers the effect of such a use of resources on other patients Contemporary interpretations of resource allocation have focused on disparities,24 both on equality in access to care, upstream from provision of the medical intervention itself, and emphasized the principle of equity over equality. This distinction is important in emphasizing the equality of health outcome rather than equality in provision of any specific resource.

There is increasing attention paid to health care disparities in the NICU, along with improvements that must be made in the areas of diversity, equity, and inclusion. Unfortunately, there is significant evidence of “complex racial inequities and/or disparities in structure, process, and outcome measures, most often disadvantaging infants of color, especially African American infants.”25 In the United States, this involves evidence that infants of color are both more likely to receive care in quality-challenged hospitals as well as to face disparities within NICUs.25 Barfield, Cox, and Henderson have suggested five key actions that may begin to address NICU care for traditionally vulnerable neonates:26 1. Dispelling the myth of an inherent advantage by Black

premature infants 2. Approach quality improvement with a lens toward health

equity 3. Identify measures that provide a better understanding of

both the type and quality of care 4. To reduce mortality and disparities, ensure that all infants

receive care in risk-appropriate facilities 5. Use research to identify the drivers of disparities, as well

as solutions, to ensure health equity These are justice issues that must be addressed. As Barfield, Cox, and Henderson conclude, “[w]e owe the infants of this country consistent high-quality care, no matter their skin color, and...there is work to be done.”26

Although fairness in allocation of resources for the individual patient is an important consideration, it is not the

fundamental standard in this interaction. Microallocation issues are very rarely appropriate at the bedside; individual clinicians caring for individual patients are poorly suited to make decisions about whether one patient, or another, is more deserving of a limited resource, or to make ad hoc institutional-level decisions about how limited resources will be distributed. First, there is an inherent conflict of interest, in which the clinician might rightly prioritize the immediate needs of the patient she is caring for over larger, systems-level considerations. Second, rationing and allocation schemes depend on economic and public health expertise beyond that possessed by most clinicians. However, individual clinicians do have a moral obligation to judiciously use medical resources for individual patients and ought not use unnecessarily expensive treatments or treatments that will not effectively promote the patient’s health. The conventional ethical prohibition of bedside rationing is also complicated by daily realities of medical care in which time, ICU beds, and limited-quantity equipment are tacitly managed as a matter of routine.27

The COVID-19 pandemic required society as well as health care systems to rapidly consider the appropriate triage framework to use in the face of an overwhelming demand for care while constrained with a limited supply of ventilators, medications, equipment, and personnel. When supplies are scarce, the primary ethical considerations discussed in this chapter such as autonomy and best interests may be outweighed by utilitarian/justice considerations.27 Indeed, tensions during the pandemic highlighted conflicts between “public health ethics,” where the goal is to promote greater societal good, and “duty to care,” where clinician obligations focus on maximizing individual patient outcomes. Triage decision-makers, who should not be bedside clinicians, may have to allocate resources between a premature infant and a geriatric adult. Scoring systems, such as the Sequential Organ Failure System (SOFA) in adults and the National Institutes of Health Extremely Preterm Birth Outcomes Tool in premature neonates, have been proposed as a transparent and objective means for decision making.28 Some survey literature, however, suggests that newborn infants, particularly premature infants, may be “undervalued” compared to other age groups.29 Consequently, it is essential that advocates for neonatal patients are involved in both the development and implementation of any resource allocation strategies.

In every system and under non-pandemic “normal” circumstances, the provision of neonatal services requires guidelines to be developed for determining appropriate use of these costly and often limited resources. Priorities must be set and justified by organizational leaders. Any change in the way neonatal care is delivered needs to be fair and accessible, as well as open and challengeable. Disputes should be addressed based on the acceptance of objective measures and trust in the integrity and fairness of the process and the individuals responsible for management of the process. With greater attention being paid to escalating health care costs, there is little question that how resources for sick
