In addition, dramatic variation in the processes and outcomes of care has been documented that cannot be explained by differences in case mix, suggesting differences in the quality-of-care delivery.15–20 For example, in a study of over 400,000 infants with birth weights of 401 to 1500 grams born from 2005 to 2014 and cared for at 756 Vermont Oxford Network (VON) member NICUs in the United States, NICUs in the worst decile had rates nearly twice as high as those in the best decile for several major morbidities (late-onset infection, severe retinopathy of prematurity, severe intraventricular hemorrhage, and necrotizing enterocolitis) of very low birth weight (VLBW) infants.
paragraphs.heading: The Case for Improvement

paragraphs.text: Despite the variation, improvements in NICU care over the past decade have heralded dramatic improvement in mortality and morbidities for VLBW infants.19 Health care–associated infection rates provide a striking example. At the 756 US NICUs in the study described above, the rate of late bacterial (including coagulase-negative Staphylococcus) or fungal infection significantly decreased from 2005, when 21.9% of infants had infections, to 2014 when 10.1%
paragraphs.heading: The Case for Improvement

paragraphs.text: of the infants had infections. Remarkably, 75% of NICUs achieved rates of performance as good as or better than what the best 25% of units had achieved only 8 years earlier. Over the last decade, reduction of health care–associated infection has been at the center of national health policy efforts to improve the value of health care delivery, including aligning hospital payments with quality-of-care delivery. Widespread efforts in the neonatal community have proved successful in facilitating broad-based and sustained reductions in health care–associated infection rates and represent an encouraging blueprint for improvements in care in other areas.7 Such improvements have also resulted in improved survival without major morbidity. In a study of 49,333 VLBW infants (<1500 grams) across 142 NICUs in the California Perinatal Quality Care Collaborative (CPQCC) from 2008 to 2017, survival with more than three and four major morbidities decreased by more than 40% each.21 Nevertheless, persistent wide variation across NICUs indicates continued opportunities for improvement.
paragraphs.heading: The Case for Improvement

paragraphs.text: Another indicator for quality deficits in the neonatal intensive care setting is the widespread delivery of inappropriate care—defined as underuse, overuse, and misuse of interventions.22,23 Examples include the underuse of hand hygiene by NICU personnel,24 the overuse of antibiotics, and the misuse of medications because of medical errors. An example of an effort to address overuse and misuse is Choosing Wisely (www.choosingwisely.org).25 Choosing Wisely, an initiative of the American Board of Internal Medicine, has challenged national medical specialty societies to identify “Top Five” lists of commonly used tests or procedures whose necessity should be questioned and discussed with patients. The American Academy of Pediatrics Section of Neonatal Perinatal Medicine (SONPM) developed a Top Five list for neonatology using a multistep process that included expert input via a modified Delphi experiment and formal evidence assessment. These final Top Five items are shown in Box 5.1.
paragraphs.heading: The Case for Improvement

paragraphs.text: Medical errors represent another example of misuse. Current health care operations produce unacceptable rates of medical errors that result in patient injury or death. In
paragraphs.heading: The Case for Improvement

paragraphs.text: To Err Is Human, the Institute of Medicine concluded that between 44,000 and 98,000 Americans die annually from hospital errors, which kill more Americans than breast cancer, traffic accidents, or AIDS.12
paragraphs.heading: The Case for Improvement

paragraphs.text: Preterm infants in the NICU are particularly vulnerable to medical errors, due to their small size, physiologic immaturity, and limited compensatory abilities.26,27 Medication errors are a common problem in sick newborns due to breakdowns in patient identification28 and rapid changes in physiologic maturity, body weight, and volumes of distribution that require frequent dose adjustments. NICU patients are more likely to experience a medication error than other hospital patients.29 For example, a study at two Boston hospitals documented that errors in the process of ordering, dispensing, or monitoring medications occurred for more than 90% of the infants cared for in the NICU.30 Another study, using a trigger tool in the electronic health record, identified 0.74 adverse events per patient,29 and 56% of these were deemed preventable. These estimates are likely only the tip of the iceberg.
paragraphs.heading: The Case for Improvement

paragraphs.text: Medication errors are not the only safety challenges preterm infants face. Using a voluntary, anonymous, errorreporting system established by the VON, Suresh et al.31 documented a broad range of errors at 54 NICUs. Only about half involved medications; the remainder involved a wide variety of errors, including errors in administration or method of using a treatment (14%), patient misidentification (11%), other system failure (9%), error or delay in diagnosis (7%), and error in the performance of an operation, procedure, or test (4%). A study from eight Dutch NICUs found that incidents concerning mechanical ventilation, blood products, intravascular lines, parenteral nutrition, and medication dosing errors posed the highest risk to patients in the NICU.32
paragraphs.heading: The Case for Improvement

paragraphs.text: The necessary engagement of parents or other primary caregivers for delivery of high-quality care for hospitalized children is now well recognized.33,34 Families contribute to the quality and safety of health care through their direct involvement in caregiving and decision-making for their loved ones and through engagement in clinical unit and hospital-wide quality and safety initiatives.35 In neonatal care, the critical role of parents as essential caregivers for preterm and ill newborns is undisputed. For example, active parent involvement in preterm infant caregiving leads to higher breastfeeding rates, earlier discharge, and improved long-term neurodevelopment.36 Conversely, untreated NICU-related parent stress and depression adversely affect preterm children’s long-term social, behavioral, and functional development.37 Despite strong evidence, family involvement in care and decision-making and in quality and safety initiatives is often lacking or variably implemented within and across neonatal care settings.
paragraphs.heading: The Case for Improvement

paragraphs.text: Furthermore, our health care delivery system has not reliably delivered many interventions that are deemed to be effective. McGlynn et al.38 in adults and later Mangione- Smith et al.39 in children demonstrated that Americans receive guideline-recommended care only about half the
paragraphs.heading: The Case for Improvement

paragraphs.text: time. In the newborn setting, antenatal steroids are an example where opportunities for improvement in administration have been documented.40–42
paragraphs.heading: The Case for Improvement

paragraphs.text: Finally, evidence is building that the care we provide and the outcomes of patients are not equitably distributed.43 Reasons for this include historical injustices, structural and institutional racism, social determinants of health, and uneven access to care. It is important to understand that these conditions can have downstream effects that span generations. Such inequities are not unique to the United States and are global issues. At the level of NICU care, important contributors to inequities include between-NICU and within-NICU variation in care.37,44 Between-NICU variation implies the segregation of groups into resource-limited hospitals.45 Within-NICU variation is the result of implicit or explicit bias by health care workers impacting the care of infants and their families.46 Quality improvement has been posited as a tool to address inequities but may improve, perpetuate, or even worsen them. Therefore all such activities should explicitly consider equity implications.
paragraphs.heading: The Case for Improvement

paragraphs.text: The inability of the health care system to consistently deliver the highest quality of care results in an enormous waste of human lives and valuable resources. Berwick and Hackbarth47 showed that “in just six categories of waste— overtreatment, failures of care coordination, failures in execution of care processes, administrative complexity, pricing failures, and fraud and abuse—the sum of the lowest available estimates exceeds 20% of total health care expenditures.” In the United States, the care of preterm infants consumes about $40 billion annually (adjusted for inflation).11 These health expenditures directly affect families and patients. More than half a million households file for bankruptcy annually due to medical reasons.48
paragraphs.heading: The Case for Improvement

paragraphs.text: With the recognition of the extent of the opportunities for improvement have come efforts by providers, provider networks, payers, nongovernmental organizations, and governmental agencies to improve the value of health care expenditures. At the provider network and health system level, efforts have focused on quality assurance and alignment of financial incentives. For example, quality assurance has been pursued through benchmarking of performance by provider networks such as the CPQCC49 or the VON,50 as well as other statewide neonatal collaborative organizations, including those in Massachusetts, Ohio, Tennessee, North Carolina, Florida, Wisconsin, and Michigan. Significant efforts have been made to develop, evaluate, and harmonize quality measures through organizations such as the National Quality Forum. Public reporting51–53 of quality measures and realignment of financial incentives away from a fee-forservice system toward a pay-for-quality system are becoming more widespread.54,55 We provide more detail on these issues later in this chapter.
paragraphs.heading: The Case for Improvement

paragraphs.text: At the hospital level, health care professionals have engaged in quality improvement efforts to meet the expectations of this changing marketplace. Several institutions have undergone fundamental reengineering of their health care delivery systems. This transformation has been the consequence of a
paragraphs.heading: The Case for Improvement

paragraphs.text: growing recognition that the current model of health care delivery is in many ways outmoded and has failed to incorporate many of the lessons that propelled other sectors of the economy to large gains in quality and productivity. When health care professionals work together in teams and include families, they can harness the joint wisdom of their respective expertise. Crowdsourcing of expertise is important because the expert health care professional mind is fallible and divergent,56 prone to systematic bias,57–59 limited in its ability to process complex information (maximally 7 ± 2 simultaneous variables),60 and unable to stay current on medical knowledge (doubling time of 8 years).22,61 Thus a hierarchical physician-centric approach to care results in clinical variability that is driven by provider rather than patient factors, and this ultimately degrades care. For all of these reasons, a new approach must be pursued that is based on flat team hierarchies, standardization and systematic use of clinical data, and evidence. Other industries have grappled with similar transitions and have provided a blueprint for improvement that is now actively pursued by many high-performing health systems. We briefly examine some of the historical foundations of these developments.
paragraphs.heading: The Case for Improvement

paragraphs.text: A thorough description of the history of quality improvement is beyond the scope of this chapter. Instead, we provide a brief overview of strategic stages of progress that are particularly salient for medicine (Fig. 5.1). Before the late 19th and early 20th centuries, quality was largely conceived of as quality assurance (oversight) and the result of personal excellence and training. For example, craftsmen organized in guilds chose their trainees selectively, often based on
paragraphs.heading: Brief History of Industrial Quality Improvement

paragraphs.text: heritage, and provided formal apprenticeships. Mastery of the craft was achieved through training, supervision, and ongoing practice. The guilds secured a livelihood for their members through a combination of trade secrecy, price collusion, and monopolistic behaviors. The quality of labor and goods was the result of limited competition, quality controls by the authorities, and peer review. This approach is still prevalent in medicine today.
paragraphs.heading: Brief History of Industrial Quality Improvement

paragraphs.text: With the advent of industrialization and mass production of goods, a new field referred to as “scientific management” emerged, a field that combined lessons from statistics, management, and economics. The goal of this movement was to increase productivity, reduce scrap, and reduce cost. Frederick Taylor (1856–1915) was one of the main innovators during this era. A mechanic and pattern maker by training,62 Taylor became a consultant for the Ford Motor Company and played an important role in the success of the famous Model T. Gains in factory efficiency lowered the overall cost of each car. Taylor harbored negative views about the motivations of frontline workers, and efforts to maximize their efficiency not infrequently resulted in social unrest. In transferring power to management and engineers, frontline workers with the most detailed knowledge of production processes were largely excluded from participating in quality improvement.
paragraphs.heading: Brief History of Industrial Quality Improvement

paragraphs.text: The next leap in industrial management was achieved through the work of Walter Shewhart (1891–1967). An engineer, physicist, and statistician, Shewhart is known as the “father of statistical quality control.” Before Shewhart, industrial quality mostly involved inspection and removal of defective products. Working at Bell Telephone Laboratories, he noted the importance of reducing variation in manufacturing processes. Shewhart highlighted that continual process adjustment (tampering) in reaction to process nonconformance actually increases variation and degrades
paragraphs.heading: Brief History of Industrial Quality Improvement

paragraphs.text: quality, a process common in the NICU. Shewhart framed the problem of process variation in terms of assignable and chance variation (Deming later referred to these as special and common cause variation) and developed the “control chart” to operationalize these concepts. A control chart or the related run chart, described later in the chapter, allows for simple tracking of process variation by displaying the extent to which a process varies over time, the idea being that excessive common cause variation indicates a poorly controlled process that is not being addressed in a standardized way. It also identifies special cause variation according to a variety of patterns. Both excessive common cause and special cause variation are indications of opportunities for quality improvement. Shewhart emphasized the importance of bringing and keeping a production process into statistical control so as to predict and manage future output, another critical idea for medicine, where little can be learned from large variation but where process standardization allows for testing of novel approaches.63
paragraphs.heading: Brief History of Industrial Quality Improvement

paragraphs.text: William Edwards Deming (1900–1993) was perhaps the most influential thinker on quality during the last century. Inspired by Shewhart’s teachings on statistical process control, Deming realized that these principles could be applied not only to manufacturing processes but also to the management of companies. Deming is most famous for his
paragraphs.heading: Brief History of Industrial Quality Improvement

paragraphs.text: contributions after World War II to the economic revival of Japan, where he famously taught statistical process control methods to Japanese business leaders. Previously known for low-quality products, Japan applied Deming’s teachings, which are widely credited with jump-starting the Japanese postwar revival and its ascent as an economic superpower.
paragraphs.heading: Brief History of Industrial Quality Improvement

paragraphs.text: Deming’s philosophy taught that, by adopting appropriate principles of management, organizations can increase quality and simultaneously reduce costs (by reducing waste, rework, staff attrition, and litigation while increasing customer loyalty). When organizations focus on quality by improving their work processes, costs will fall. In contrast, when organizations focus on costs, then quality will fall and costs will rise. Deming developed the Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycle, which he called the Shewhart cycle, a staple in modern quality improvement. He also developed 14 Key Points in Management and 7 Deadly Diseases (Box 5.2). For Deming, the key to success was to practice continual improvement in the quality of products, uniformity of processes, and qualifications of employees. He taught that all processes yield three parallel outcomes that must be measured: a work product (medical outcome), cost outcome, and service outcome (patient satisfaction). All processes contain built-in variation (common cause), but they are also affected by external factors (special cause). Management,
paragraphs.heading: Brief History of Industrial Quality Improvement

paragraphs.text: not frontline workers, controls common cause variation through systems design. In opposition to Taylor’s view of frontline workers, Deming cherished their contributions and felt that involving them in improving care processes would instill meaning and pride in their work.
paragraphs.heading: Brief History of Industrial Quality Improvement

paragraphs.text: Kiichiro Toyoda, the founder of Toyota Motor Company, was among Deming’s audience in 1950. Based on Deming’s lectures, Toyoda developed the Toyota Production System (TPS), an integrated sociotechnical system comprised of its management philosophy and practices. The system is a precursor of the more generic lean manufacturing. At the core of TPS is elimination of waste (muda) and total focus on reliable, high quality through continuous improvement (kaizen). Lean production focuses on just-in-time use of materials and optimization of production flow (mura) in response to customer demand. Toyota’s success derived from its innovative production engineering, which puts quality control in the hands of the frontline workers who can stop the production line and call for help when something goes wrong. However, production engineering is only part of story. An equally important contributor to Toyota’s success has been coined the “Toyota Way,” principles that embody a relentless focus on the needs and desires of customers.
paragraphs.heading: Brief History of Industrial Quality Improvement

paragraphs.text: Another variant of statistical process control originally developed by Motorola in 1985 is Six Sigma, which is a set of process improvement tools and strategies that seek to improve quality by minimizing defects and variability. In Six Sigma, a defect is defined as any process output that does not meet customer specifications or that could lead to creating an output that does not meet customer specifications. The term “Six Sigma process” means that, if one has 6 standard deviations between the process mean and the nearest specification limit, then only 3.4 out of 1 million outputs will fail to meet specifications. To illustrate, a 1-sigma process produces 69%, a 2-sigma process produces 31%, and a 6-sigma process produces 0.00034% defective outputs. Current evidence suggests that much of health care operates at the 1- or 2-sigma level.38,39 Six Sigma includes methodologies that lean on Deming’s PDSA cycle, such as DMAIC for reengineering existing processes: Define the problem. Measure key aspects. Analyze data for key relationships. Improve the current process (using a set of specific techniques). Control the future process.
paragraphs.heading: Brief History of Industrial Quality Improvement

paragraphs.text: Industrial quality improvement methods have been applied to health care for more than 30 years. In Curing Health Care: New Strategies for Quality Improvement, Berwick and co-workers64 provided the initial evidence that the tools of modern quality improvement, with which other industries have achieved breakthroughs in performance, can help in health care as well. Since then, the core ideas of quality improvement have been adapted to the needs of health care and implemented by health care organizations around the world. In neonatology, multidisciplinary teams from NICUs across the United States have applied quality improvement tools and methods to address the quality
paragraphs.heading: Brief History of Industrial Quality Improvement

paragraphs.text: and safety of medical care for newborn infants and their families.49,65–69
paragraphs.heading: Brief History of Industrial Quality Improvement

paragraphs.text: Successful adaptation of these industrial methods to the NICU setting requires recognition that health care is a process and that quality improvement requires process management. However, a focus on care delivery processes is not sufficient. Rather, process management needs to be accompanied by efforts to optimize the organizational environment in ways that promote continual learning, teamwork, and adherence to the mission of serving patients and families. Several theoretical frameworks exist to further our understanding of the complex interplay among the organizational environment, process, and outcomes.
paragraphs.heading: Brief History of Industrial Quality Improvement

paragraphs.text: The Institute of Medicine defines quality-of-care delivery as the extent to which health services provided to individuals and patient populations improve desired health outcomes. In Crossing the Quality Chasm,13 it developed the following six domains of quality of delivery of care:
paragraphs.heading: Definitions

paragraphs.text: Safety—Avoiding preventable injuries, reducing medical er-
paragraphs.heading: Definitions

paragraphs.text: rors Effectiveness—Providing services based on scientific knowl-
paragraphs.heading: Definitions

paragraphs.text: edge (clinical guidelines) Patient-centeredness—Care that is respectful and responsive
paragraphs.heading: Definitions

paragraphs.text: to individuals Efficiency—Avoiding the wasting of time and other resources Timeliness—Reducing wait times and improving the prac-
paragraphs.heading: Definitions

paragraphs.text: tice flow Equity—Care that should be tailored to address the unique
paragraphs.heading: Definitions

paragraphs.text: social and medical needs faced by patients and families from minoritized communities
paragraphs.heading: Definitions

paragraphs.text: We have added being socially and environmentally responsible to this list.50 Together, these domains are useful guideposts for practitioners in developing comprehensive quality programs and measurement systems.70
paragraphs.heading: Definitions

paragraphs.text: Various authors have developed conceptual or explanatory models that provide users with a systematic understanding of the components and facilitators of high-quality health care delivery. These frameworks are often adapted from other sciences, including manufacturing, engineering, organizational theory, and psychology. They share a common premise that high quality-of-care delivery is the result of efforts to create a work environment in which people work together to reliably execute processes that are known to work or thought to work, and to avoid care that is known to be unhelpful. We mention a few commonly applied ones here.
paragraphs.heading: Conceptual Frameworks for Quality

paragraphs.text: Maybe the best-known framework for quality improvement was developed by Avedis Donabedian (1919–2000). Donabedian was the first to collate evidence on the quality of health care delivery; he developed a simple structure, process, and outcome model of quality that has been the mainstay of quality research.71 Structure traditionally has been interpreted as the physical facilities and the training and education of staff. This notion has been expanded to include executive leadership, organizational culture, organizational design, incentive structure, and information systems and technology.72 Processes include the activities that clinicians and support staff undertake as part of or in support of care delivery. Outcomes are the results of these activities.
paragraphs.heading: Donabedian: Structure, Processes, Outcomes

paragraphs.text: Realistic evaluation goes beyond the traditional cause-andeffect paradigm and poses that program effectiveness also depends on many interrelated contextual variables.73 This concept is formalized by the following formula: Context + Mechanism = Outcome, or C + M = O. A given intervention does not necessarily work for the group, but may be quite useful to some individuals, depending on their specific circumstances.
paragraphs.heading: Pawson and Tilley: Realistic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Frontline application of quality improvement efforts draws from the various theoretical frameworks presented in the preceding section. In the following, we highlight a few approaches that are commonly applied in neonatology. For practitioners, the practical application of quality improvement work may be more effective if supported by a formal approach, such as those provided by the Model for Improvement, Deming’s integrated management model, lean manufacturing, and Six Sigma. Each of these models makes use of various management tools to assist with project planning and execution, including team organization, process mapping, problem identification, problem resolution, task prioritization, and execution. We briefly mention several of these in the section titled Quality and Safety Applied. However, a full description of these tools is beyond the scope of this chapter. For more details on these, we refer to the extant literature.74 We now turn our attention to the Model for Improvement, which has been widely adopted as a strategy for collaborative quality improvement in the neonatal community.75
paragraphs.heading: Translation of Frameworks into Action

paragraphs.text: The Model for Improvement is based on The Improvement Guide: A Practical Approach to Enhancing Organizational Performance by Langley et al.76 The model identifies four strategic elements of successful process improvement: (1) specific and measurable aims, (2) measures of improvement that are tracked over time, (3) strategic changes that will result in the desired improvement, and (4) a series of PDSA cycles during which teams learn how to apply crucial
paragraphs.heading: Model for Improvement

paragraphs.text: change ideas.75 These principles correspond to three questions asked of collaborative teams (Fig. 5.2).
paragraphs.heading: Model for Improvement

paragraphs.text: The first question, which refers to the aim(s) of the project, is “What are we trying to accomplish?” In other words, what are the main outcomes that the team is trying to change or improve. There are several considerations when considering the aim of a prospective project. Are there historical and/or peer benchmark data to suggest that there is a problem in the local NICU? Is there a variation in outcomes among NICUs to suggest that variations in practices can lead to differences in outcomes? Are there evidence-based practices that have been shown to improve the outcome of interest? The aim should be well defined and realistic. It should also be quantifiable and encompass a defined time period.77
paragraphs.heading: Model for Improvement

paragraphs.text: One helpful technique for crafting a well-designed aim statement is the SMART Aim approach (Table 5.1). An example of a suboptimal aim statement may be, “Reduce infection rates in our NICU.” Although a worthy goal, that statement is vague, and it will be difficult to assess if it has been accomplished. In contrast, the following aim statement is more specific and follows the SMART Aim approach: “Reduce by 50% the number of central lineassociated bloodstream infections as defined by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in infants born at 24 to 30 weeks’ gestational age in the NICU by using an insertion and maintenance bundle over a 12-month time period.”
paragraphs.heading: Model for Improvement

paragraphs.text: The second question, corresponding to the measures of the project, is “How will we know that a change is an improvement?” As a team embarks on a quality improvement project, one can consider three main groups of measurements: outcomes, processes, and balancing measures. The outcome measure is typically a clinical outcome, such as nosocomial infection or bronchopulmonary dysplasia. A process measure related to reduction of nosocomial infection could be the use of an insertion checklist. In some instances, a process measure can serve as the main outcome of a quality improvement project when that process measure has been clearly linked to a benefit in clinical outcomes. Examples are a focus on improving the rate of antenatal steroid administration for premature birth or on increasing breast milk provision for premature infants. A balancing
paragraphs.heading: Model for Improvement

paragraphs.text: measure for increased breast milk provision for premature infants may be growth velocity, which may have a negative correlation.78 The idea behind a balancing measure is to ensure that the quality improvement intervention does not generate unwanted secondary effects.
paragraphs.heading: Model for Improvement

paragraphs.text: The third question, which corresponds to the strategic changes that will lead to improvement, is “What changes can we make that will result in improvement?” These changes should be evidence based but must also account for local cultural and organizational characteristics. Plsek79 coined the term “potentially better practices” rather than “better” or “best” practices to stress that no change idea is truly better or best until it has been adapted, implemented, and tested in the local context in which it will be applied. This is consistent with the ideas surrounding “context” described by Pawson and Tilley73 noted in the previous section on Frameworks for Quality. The PDSA cycles in the Model for Improvement can be conceptualized as an application of the scientific method (see Fig.
paragraphs.heading: Model for Improvement

paragraphs.text: 5.2). Each PDSA cycle is a test of a hypothesis of how a specific change will affect the system.
paragraphs.heading: Model for Improvement

paragraphs.text: Another model for quality improvement in health care focuses on the elimination of process variation. This approach derives from Deming’s work and has been adapted with success for health care by several organizations. For example, Intermountain Healthcare helped refocus the health system’s quality improvement efforts on process standardization, active management, and ongoing organizational learning. Work units identify high-value clinical processes and set up multidisciplinary provider teams to develop evidence-based, detailed care pathways (shared baselines) to execute these processes in a consistent, reliable manner. Use of the term shared baseline, rather than protocol or guideline, highlights its development and ongoing refinement by the local work unit. Control rests with frontline care providers, not managers. The purpose of these shared baselines is to minimize the variation that is driven by providers and not accounted for by patient need. Providers are encouraged to deviate from the shared baseline as warranted by the needs of individual patients. This approach allows providers to bring their expertise to bear on the clinical situations that truly warrant an alternative treatment approach. It also effectively ameliorates concerns regarding “cookbook” medicine, given an explicit expectation that no guideline perfectly fits any patient. On the contrary, providers are asked to assess situations where they have deviated from the shared baseline. This information is then used to modify the shared baseline when appropriate. Overall, the use of shared baselines makes the workflow more predictable, efficient, safer for patients, and less stressful for nursing staff.80–83
paragraphs.heading: Integrated Quality Management

paragraphs.text: Similar to the Model for Improvement, the modified Deming approach uses key measures to track cornerstones of the process, clinical outcomes, service outcomes (such as patient satisfaction), and cost. The key to promote organizational learning and standardization is tracking process deviations and systems to modify the shared baselines according to ongoing provider input. To facilitate the success of local projects, strategic staff from clinical work units receive training and technical support for their improvement work from a centralized quality improvement institute. Institutional commitment is foundational to achieving excellence in care delivery.81
paragraphs.heading: Integrated Quality Management

paragraphs.text: Lean is a quality improvement model that focuses on reducing process waste and improving process flow.84 The seven forms of waste in Lean are overproduction, inventory, waiting, transportation, defects, staff movement, and unnecessary processing. Lean focuses on customers, patients, and families and encourages users to examine their process steps and eliminate those that do not provide value to customers. Attention to “flow” attempts to optimize the use of time and resources.
paragraphs.heading: Lean

paragraphs.text: These approaches and others are guiding practical and theoretical improvement work. Although meaningful in their differences, their common thread lies in the centrality of managing work processes while optimizing the care delivery environment. Organizational goals for high-quality care delivery and patient safety are undergirded by strategies that encourage continuous monitoring of processes and outcomes, facilitate continuous learning, and minimize unwarranted waste and process variation.
paragraphs.heading: Lean

paragraphs.text: Not everything that can be counted counts. Not everything that counts can be counted.
paragraphs.heading: Data and Methods for Quality Improvement

paragraphs.text: It is essential that quality improvement be data driven. First, to identify opportunities for quality improvement, data are necessary to determine performance relative to historical performance or peer-derived benchmarks. Second, essential to the Plan-Do-Study-Act approach, when quality improvement has been undertaken, data are used to assess the extent to which each specific intervention has or has not been effective, as well as to identify unintended negative consequences. Although we use the term data, what we are really collecting is information that we can use to guide the course of our quality improvement. To lower the burden of collection, we should only select the minimal amount of data that can guide our progress, and, if possible, we should use data that can be derived from or efficiently incorporated into the workflow.
paragraphs.heading: —ATTRIBUTED TO ALBERT EINSTEIN

paragraphs.text: In following Donabedian’s framework, the main data types can be categorized as structural or contextual measures, process measures, and outcome measures (including medical outcomes, cost, and service outcomes such as family satisfaction with care). The three most important considerations for any data element are its clarity of definition, the ease with which it can be identified and extracted from the medical record or its administrative source, and its universality across time and location. Stable definitions across time are important to assess the extent to which a morbidity has decreased or increased over time. Agreed-upon definitions are essential to compare outcomes across NICUs both within and across countries. The widespread adoption of the definitions developed by the VON has made both national and international comparisons possible.
paragraphs.heading: Data Elements for Assessment

paragraphs.text: Although the focus of quality improvement has largely been on changing processes of care, there is an increasing awareness of the importance of the context in which improvement activities occur. In addition to changing the behavior
paragraphs.heading: Structure and Institutional Context

paragraphs.text: of members of the health care team, quality improvement often relies on changing systems of care and with it the organizational environment. Efforts at measuring care structure and context have been motivated by numerous studies linking these aspects to clinical and organizational outcomes.
paragraphs.heading: Structure and Institutional Context

paragraphs.text: Maybe the best-examined aspect of structure is the patient-to-nurse ratio. In adult and pediatric intensive care unit settings,85,86 rising patient-to-nurse ratios have been linked to worse clinical outcomes and higher mortality. In neonatology, this link is less well understood.87 Although most studies imply a benefit of greater staffing ratios, this finding is not uniform.88 Nurse staffing ratios may be suboptimal in general and associated with nosocomial infection rates.89 Other examples of structural measures that can impact the quality of care include academic teaching status, 24-hour coverage by an in-house intensivist, patient volume, and level of care.
paragraphs.heading: Structure and Institutional Context

paragraphs.text: Contextual measures are different from traditional measures in that they attempt to assess the links between how care delivery is organized and supported by the institution and quality of care. Kaplan and colleagues90 developed a framework for examining these linkages and coined it Model for Understanding Success in Quality (MUSIQ). This model includes different components that support improvements in the processes and outcomes of care delivery at various levels of the institution, including characteristics of the improvement team (diversity, physician involvement, leadership) and the NICU, as well as higher-level organizational functions (quality improvement leadership and administrative support).91
paragraphs.heading: Structure and Institutional Context

paragraphs.text: One well-researched aspect of care context is safety culture. The NICU safety culture describes the shared norms of leadership, staff, and the organization with regard to patient safety, or, simply, the “way we do things around here.” Culture influences quality of care in important ways. Whether a process is failure proof depends on how reliably it is implemented. Non-adherence to care standards may reflect a clinical need, but also lack of a standard or willful disregard. Safety culture assessments attempt to capture safety context through surveys that ask about health care worker perceptions. The measured domains are referred to as climates (e.g., teamwork climate, safety climate). The term “climate” reflects that perceptions are shared among health workers; that is, they cluster more strongly within a work unit (e.g., the NICU) than between work units.
paragraphs.heading: Structure and Institutional Context

paragraphs.text: Ongoing assessment of safety culture is a requirement for hospital accreditation by the Joint Commission, an accreditation agency that assesses safety and quality of care. There are several validated survey tools to measure safety culture.26,92–94 The Safety Attitudes Questionnaire (SAQ) reflects caregiver attitudes on safety culture, is psychometrically sound, and has demonstrated wide interinstitutional variation across NICUs.95 Safety culture, as measured by the SAQ, has been linked to a variety of clinical and organizational outcomes. Most famously, this instrument was used by Pronovost and co-workers96 in their implementation of the Comprehensive Unit-based Safety Program
paragraphs.heading: Structure and Institutional Context

paragraphs.text: (CUSP) in 103 adult ICUs in Michigan, where, through implementation of a checklist and a focus on teamwork and safety, median catheter-related bloodstream infection rates were reduced to zero. This program has been endorsed for implementation in all ICUs by the US government. In a study of 44 NICUs and over 2000 respondents, teamwork was negatively correlated with health care–associated infections among VLBW infants.97 Of note, physicians tend to rate safety culture significantly higher than do nurses and other personnel, highlighting an apparent disconnect in perceptions.
paragraphs.heading: Structure and Institutional Context

paragraphs.text: Various approaches to improving safety culture have been described. Among them are leadership engagement via Leadership WalkRounds98 and a teamwork training curriculum developed by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, called Team Strategies and Tools to Enhance Performance and Patient Safety (TeamSTEPPS). The TeamSTEPPS intervention includes assessment, training, and sustainment phases focused on four core competencies: (1) team leadership, (2) situation monitoring, (3) mutual support, and (4) communication.99 This approach has been used in multiple health care settings,100,101 including one reported intervention that included NICU providers and demonstrated an improvement in perceptions of teamwork.102
paragraphs.heading: Structure and Institutional Context

paragraphs.text: Another emerging aspect of care context is health care worker resilience, operationally often defined as the absence of burnout. Burnout describes a condition of fatigue, detachment, and cynicism resulting from prolonged high levels of stress.103 In the critical care setting, burnout rates may be consequent to high workload, frequent changes in technology and guidelines, and the emotional challenges of dealing with critically ill patients and their families. Severe burnout affects between a quarter and half of health care workers,103,104 and the COVID-19 pandemic has resulted in a substantial increase.105 Burnout has negative consequences for health care providers, organizations, and patient care (Box 5.3).
paragraphs.heading: Structure and Institutional Context

paragraphs.text: A systematic review identified that both organizational as well as individually focused interventions are effective in reducing physician burnout.106 A randomized controlled trial of an individual intervention program (WISER) using positive psychology tools delivered via cell phone to NICU health care workers demonstrated lasting benefits with regard to burnout, work-life balance, and depression among participants.107 Overall, context provides the soil in which quality improvement thrives or withers. Leadership recognition of these factors is critical; to provide high quality of care to our patients, we must also care for ourselves and our colleagues.
paragraphs.heading: Structure and Institutional Context

paragraphs.text: Outcomes are the result of specific actions termed processes. Although process measures are an essential element of quality assessment, it is important that the process being measured is linked to the outcome. A key role of the PDSA approach is to assess if the change in process felt to be related to the
paragraphs.heading: Processes

paragraphs.text: outcome, when executed as specified, brings about change in that outcome. If there is no change in outcome, and careful review indicates that the new or modified process has been implemented as specified, then it is unlikely that this process is linked to the outcome. From a quality improvement perspective, this should not be viewed as a failure but should serve as an indicator that the process should be abandoned. In essence, it keeps one from going down a dead-end road. The study of how certain process measures relate to outcomes can also contribute to the broader evidence base for best clinical practices. An example of processes and practices that could relate to the reduction of line infections in the NICU is shown in Table 5.2.
paragraphs.heading: Processes

paragraphs.text: Reducing process variation (i.e., reducing the many ways we might act in a specific situation) has been a strategic component of quality improvement, going back to Shewhart. On a control chart, the width of the control boundaries (the upper and lower rates that capture the majority of all the rates) are an indication of process variation. When quality improvement is successful, one will see both an increase (or decrease) in rate and a tightening of the control boundaries.
paragraphs.heading: Processes

paragraphs.text: Outcomes are the end results of the clinical care delivery process and represent what patients, families, and providers truly care about. Pragmatically, outcomes can be a reduction in negative events such as a decrease in the rates of death and morbidity or an increase in the rates of positive events such as breast milk on discharge or antenatal steroid use. For an outcome to serve as an effective quality indicator, it must be malleable; that is, there must be strong evidence that variations in process or structure can change its occurrence. A widely used outcome measure is health care–associated infections or their more specific cousin,
paragraphs.heading: Outcomes

paragraphs.text: central line–associated bloodstream infections. These outcomes are important quality indicators because they cause significant morbidity and have been shown to be sensitive to specific processes (e.g., hand hygiene, intravenous line care) to reduce their occurrence.108
paragraphs.heading: Outcomes

paragraphs.text: Infection-related efforts have served as a success story and model for other quality improvement activities. Studies of the rates of health care–associated infections in the NICU have shown wide risk-adjusted variation by hospital. The observation that a significant number of hospitals are able to achieve very low infection rates indicates opportunities for improvement and has led to highly successful efforts to reduce infections at collaborative levels.109–114
paragraphs.heading: Outcomes

paragraphs.text: When teams work on improving one aspect of care, it is possible that related outcomes suffer; for example, a decrease in growth velocity may be observed with a focus on improving breast milk feeding rates. Balancing measures may include clinical, service, or cost outcomes. These balancing measures should be collected in or close to real time to detect any unintended consequences of quality improvement projects. Although traditionally balancing measures were developed to assess potential adverse effects of improvement activities, they can also show that the new way of doing things is safe.
paragraphs.heading: Balancing Measures

paragraphs.text: For performance assessment within an organization whose patient demographics are stable over time, tracking a process or outcome measure over time may be sufficient to
paragraphs.heading: Risk Adjustment/Fair Comparisons

paragraphs.text: spur quality improvement activities and assess their impact. However, for comparative performance assessments between organizations, as currently applied for purposes such as setting benchmarks, pay-for-performance, or public reporting, further statistical and methodological considerations are required to ensure fair comparisons.
paragraphs.heading: Risk Adjustment/Fair Comparisons

paragraphs.text: The use of risk adjustment levels the playing field by accounting for expected rates of positive or negative outcomes based on the risk profiles (case mix) seen at each institution. Expectation is pivotal to the notion of quality, which can be operationally defined as the degree to which the observed rate of an outcome or process is higher, lower, or equal to its expected rate.23 An observed rate of morbidity that is higher than the expected rate indicates that there is an opportunity for quality improvement. Does hospital A with an observed neonatal mortality rate (NMR) of 5 provide better care than hospital B with an observed NMR of 10? Without knowing the expected rate of mortality at these two hospitals, it is impossible to assess their relative quality of care. For example, hospital B might be a tertiary care center, in which an observed NMR of 10 is much lower than its expected NMR of 18. Hospital A could be a primary care hospital, in which an observed NMR of 5 is much higher than its expected NMR of 3.
paragraphs.heading: Risk Adjustment/Fair Comparisons

paragraphs.text: Mathematically, risk-adjustment methods level the playing field using one of the variants of multivariate regression. Typically based on data on risks and outcomes from multiple institutions, an estimate of the impact of each of the risk factors considered to be important to the outcome is used to create an expectation model. The model can then generate the expected outcome of a NICU based on its specific case mix.
paragraphs.heading: Risk Adjustment/Fair Comparisons

paragraphs.text: The factors used in risk adjustment for neonatal quality assessment will encompass both maternal sociodemographic and clinical factors, as well as infant factors. Two essential requirements guide variable selection: (1) the variable should be a risk factor for the outcome of interest, and (2) the variable should not be under the control of the entity being evaluated. Mother’s age, education, payer for delivery, and perinatal complications, as well as the infant’s birth weight, gestational age, plurality, intrauterine growth, birth defects, and gender, are risk factors that are commonly used as risk adjusters to control for institutional differences in case mix so as to make fair comparisons across NICUs.23,91 They are highly predictive of morbidity and mortality and are not under the control of clinicians in the NICU. Using this approach to quality assessment, the ratio of the observed number of deaths (or adverse outcomes) to the expected number of deaths (or adverse outcomes), the standardized mortality (or morbidity) ratio (SMR), can then be calculated.
paragraphs.heading: Risk Adjustment/Fair Comparisons

paragraphs.text: In addition to reporting the SMR as a measure of performance, an alternative approach is to calculate the difference between the observed and expected number of cases (O– E), where the expected number can be determined using the same regression approach described earlier. The VON routinely reports the O–E values for mortality and major
paragraphs.heading: Risk Adjustment/Fair Comparisons

paragraphs.text: morbidities to its members using a method that accounts for risk using regression models and accounts for chance variation using an empirical Bayesian shrinkage method.115,116 These data are reported with 95% confidence intervals in table and graphic form to give an individual center an estimate of its performance in relationship to the overall group (Fig. 5.3). It is important to recognize that all estimates of risk-adjusted performance must be interpreted carefully and that these estimates are only the first step in assessing the quality of care.117,118
paragraphs.heading: Risk Adjustment/Fair Comparisons

paragraphs.text: Because the statistical power to detect quality-of-care outliers using multivariate risk-adjustment methods based on a single year may be low due to a small number of births or cases, it may be useful to consider performing analyses on data combined from several years.119 Even employing very accurate predictive models and combining several years of data might not be able to overcome the problem of a small sample size in some NICUs.120 In this case, multivariate risk models may be useful for identifying individual infants with adverse outcomes despite a favorable case mix. The medical records of such infants can then be chosen for detailed review and audit.
paragraphs.heading: Risk Adjustment/Fair Comparisons

paragraphs.text: Although all NICUs can be mathematically assessed based on the standard risk factors listed above, one might argue that, even with risk adjustment, comparing a small community NICU with a large regional referral NICU is like comparing apples to oranges. In addition to reporting standardized ratios of observed-to-predicted rates for mortality, the VON and the CPQCC provide their members with the opportunity to compare important morbidities with similar centers, with the goal of using these data to identify opportunities for improvement. The Committee on the Fetus and Newborn of the American Academy
paragraphs.heading: Risk Adjustment/Fair Comparisons

paragraphs.text: of Pediatrics has proposed a NICU classification system that may be useful for this purpose.121 However, there is a caveat to this approach. For example, although a small NICU’s mortality may be superior in comparison to other small NICUs within its network, the overall rate of mortality across the small network may be much higher than in higher-level NICUs. In most cases, this is due to the birth of infants whose needs exceed the technical capacity of the small NICU. Studies have shown that lower levels of care and patient volume are associated with increased neonatal mortality for preterm infants.122,123 In this situation, if quality was only based on NICU level–specific data, it would mask that many of the high-risk mothers delivering should have been referred to a higher level of care.
paragraphs.heading: Risk Adjustment/Fair Comparisons

paragraphs.text: Several physiology-based severity scores have been developed for use in neonatal intensive care: Clinical Risk Index for Babies (CRIB), which uses infant characteristics within the first hour after birth124; CRIB II score (a five-item version of the CRIB score)125; Score for Neonatal Acute Physiology (SNAP), a physiology-based illness severity score based on measurements of 26 routine clinical tests and vital signs; and its derivatives, SNAP-PE (an additive score based on birth weight, 5-minute Apgar score, size for gestational age, and SNAP) and SNAP II (a six-item score based on variables collected during the first 12 hours after admission).126,127 Zupancic et al.128 found that models based on perinatal descriptors perform similarly to those based on physiologic measures.
paragraphs.heading: Risk Adjustment/Fair Comparisons

paragraphs.text: The Transport Risk Index of Physiologic Stability (TRIPS) is a scoring system that was developed to assess infant transport care. Based on the collection of only four variables (temperature, respiratory status, systolic blood pressure, and response to noxious stimuli), this approach
paragraphs.heading: Risk Adjustment/Fair Comparisons

paragraphs.text: predicts 7-day survival and severe intraventricular hemorrhage,129 particularly after accounting for the use of cardiac pressor medications and the level of oxygen in intubated infants (calculator available at http://www.health-infosolutions.com/CPQCC-CPeTS/tripsmobile/tripsmobile. html).
paragraphs.heading: Risk Adjustment/Fair Comparisons

paragraphs.text: Tyson and colleagues130 used the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development Neonatal Research Network database to develop a multivariable model to predict survival and neurodevelopmental outcome for preterm infants of 22 to 25 weeks’ gestation based on birth weight, gestational age, gender, multiplicity, and antenatal steroid status. This estimation has been validated in a populationbased cohort that includes a diverse group of community and academic NICUs.131 An online calculator is available to estimate survival and survival free of disability for specific values of the five variables in the model (https://www.nichd .nih.gov/research/supported/EPBO). Hospital-specific predictions based on this approach are available on the VON online reporting site, Nightingale.
paragraphs.heading: Risk Adjustment/Fair Comparisons

paragraphs.text: In addition to data collected specifically for the purpose of quality improvement, the use of currently available data such as hospital administrative data and vital records data may allow for increased data capture and efficiency. We refer to this repurposed data as green data. Secondary datasets that have been used to evaluate quality of care include the uniform hospital discharge database (which captures diagnostic, procedural, and costs data), birth certificate files, and death certificates files. Although these administrative databases were not primarily designed for evaluating perinatal care, they contain data elements that have made it possible to examine risk-adjusted perinatal complication rates,132 maternal morbidities,133 cesarean delivery,134 and neonatal readmission rates.135 However, secondary data sources do have several disadvantages. They may not have all of the desired data items, and definitions might not be the same as those used in NICU databases. Underreporting may be significant.136 For example, congenital anomalies are markedly underreported on both birth and death certificates.137
paragraphs.heading: Data Sources Administrative Data

paragraphs.text: Because both clinical and administrative databases vary with respect to the extent of their maternal, neonatal, morbidity, and mortality, as well as important sociodemographic data, the linkage of multiple datasets is a strategy to obtain a more comprehensive picture of perinatal risks and outcomes at the regional, community, and hospital level.136,138 Examples of population-based studies using a linked database include the relationship between discharge timing after birth and infant readmission,135 risk factors and neonatal outcomes,132 neonatal outcomes in childbearing beyond the age of 40,139 factors associated with the birth of infants with very low birth weight at non-NICU hospitals,140 trends in cesarean delivery for various conditions,141,142 and quality assessment of perinatal regionalization.143
paragraphs.heading: Data Sources Administrative Data

paragraphs.text: The use of secondary data can also provide a highly efficient approach to building a complete quality improvement reporting system. The California Maternal Quality Care Collaborative (CMQCC, www.cmqcc.org) provides hospitals close to real-time (within 45 days from discharge) data based on linking the infant’s birth certificate to the mother’s and the infant’s discharge ICD-10 codes. In addition to perinatal quality metrics, the CMQCC also provides a near real-time assessment of data quality as part of an ongoing initiative to improve its administrative data sources. The reports also contain confidential drill-down analyses in order to identify ways to improve performance. For example, if there was an increase in early-term elective delivery for a hospital (Fig. 5.4), then one could examine cases over a period of time to check if there are certain diagnoses that may be contributing to an increase in the elective delivery rate. The rate of elective delivery can also be calculated by a provider to see if there are opportunities to work with individuals who may be contributing most to an increased rate. A demonstration site with artificial data is available at https ://demo.datacenter.cmqcc.org.
paragraphs.heading: Data Sources Administrative Data

paragraphs.text: When data are collected primarily for the purpose of quality assessment, computer-based data entry systems using local or web-based data entry interfaces allow for efficiency in checking for errors such as missing fields or out-of-range entries. An advantage of these systems is that they detect errors in completeness, range, and consistency as the data are being abstracted and entered. The result is a clean record at the point of data entry that avoids costly offsite error detection and correction cycles.144
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Data

paragraphs.text: However, in carrying out a quality improvement initiative, it is often necessary to collect your own primary process, balancing, and outcome measures, as well as patient characteristics (if risk adjustment is needed). Data collection is always time consuming, so it is important to collect the minimal number of data elements needed to assess whether or not interventions are working. Incorporating data collection into the workflow can also lessen the burden. Data elements should be clearly and systematically defined, using universal or published definitions to enable comparison with other hospitals working on the same quality issue or published results.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Data

paragraphs.text: Obtaining data from the electronic health record is an extremely efficient technique; however, it is crucial that the definitions that your hospital use in the electronic record are standardized across everyone who enters data and are based on widely recognized criteria. Unless all entities use the same definition, an objective and consistent assessment within and across NICUs may not be possible from electronic medical record data. For example, if the diagnosis of patent ductus arteriosus differs across individual NICUs, then comparisons of the incidence or the effects of treatment will be meaningless.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Data

paragraphs.text: In addition to its potential to provide data to inform quality improvement, the electronic health record can also
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Data

paragraphs.text: be used to facilitate standardized practice. Examples include prompts and/or requirements to perform and report retinopathy of prematurity eye examinations in preterm infants and notification that an infant with a central line has reached sufficient enteral intake and requires justification for continued use. Such systems will allow for the close alignment of clinical care and quality assessment.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Data

paragraphs.text: Because not everything that counts can be counted, qualitative techniques are an important set of tools that can provide practitioners with valuable insights regarding the design, execution, and outcome of quality improvement interventions. These techniques may include strategic informant interviews, focus groups, written evaluations, and observations directly or by video.145 These tools may unearth aspects of care that may not be readily collected in the medical record by capturing the “voice of the customer,” such as a parent’s ability to speak up in order to promote safety for their child in the NICU.146
paragraphs.heading: Qualitative Data

paragraphs.text: During a quality improvement initiative or in the evaluation phase, qualitative research can help to discern which aspects of a project were the key drivers of change and what steps might be taken for similar subsequent projects.
paragraphs.heading: Qualitative Data

paragraphs.text: Although the subject matter and aim of the project may differ, there may be common barriers and facilitators for implementation in quality improvement projects. A summary of such findings undertaken in three different projects (maternal hemorrhage, breast milk nutrition for preterm infants, delivery room management) is shown in Table 5.3.147–149
paragraphs.heading: Qualitative Data

paragraphs.text: Evaluation of these data can be labor intensive in a research environment, but quality improvement teams can often rapidly extract meaningful and useable information. When there is a deficiency in care or perhaps when things are going well from a quality perspective, these approaches may help us to better understand the reasons underlying the results. When planning a quality improvement initiative, searching out and learning from similar studies that also describe the qualitative aspects of their journey can contribute greatly to the planning and success of your initiative. These tools also offer a great opportunity to involve family partners along the improvement journey.
paragraphs.heading: Qualitative Data

paragraphs.text: Now that we have reviewed the different types of data that may be available to improve quality-of-care delivery, we need to consider what data are needed for what purpose and how
paragraphs.heading: Quality Measurement and Improvement

paragraphs.text: best to present the data for each of those purposes. Quality measurement is necessary for improvement but not sufficient. Although all stakeholders, such as providers, consumers, payers, or policymakers, have an interest in improving qualityof-care delivery, they have different information needs and different levers to motivate or effect improvement.
paragraphs.heading: Quality Measurement and Improvement

paragraphs.text: Berwick, James, and Coye developed a framework that divides quality measurement according to purpose into two pathways (Fig. 5.5).150 Pathway 1 highlights the purpose of selection. One of the main interests of stakeholders in this pathway is to gain knowledge about provider performance and to seek out care for either themselves or their constituents accordingly. Stakeholders have the ability to “motivate” providers by either forgoing care or paying less to low-performance
paragraphs.heading: Quality Measurement and Improvement

paragraphs.text: providers. Pathway 2 highlights the pathway of change. The stakeholders here are the organization and the frontline care providers themselves. Motivation for measurement is derived from an internal desire to optimize care delivery for organizational improvement. In the following sections, we provide practical and theoretical considerations regarding quality measurement in these different pathways, including what types of measures may be appropriate for each.
paragraphs.heading: Quality Measurement and Improvement

paragraphs.text: In general, the information need regarding the process of care delivery is highest for frontline providers (pathway 2), whereas stakeholders who are further removed from the organization are more interested in outcomes of care (pathway 1). This is not to say that frontline providers do not care about outcomes of care but rather that the process of care executed in the local care context is what delivers the outcome. Because local contexts differ, a focus on outcomes by external stakeholders and consumers sets guideposts for quality expectations and provides NICUs space for experimentation and innovation to meet them. External stakeholders should avoid a proscriptive focus on process measurement, unless the supporting scientific evidence is strong (e.g., antenatal steroid administration for preterm infants <34 weeks’ gestational age).
paragraphs.heading: Quality Measurement and Improvement

paragraphs.text: It is important to recognize that the data collection costs of individual institutions are significant, potentially diverting resources from other care priorities. Possibly with the advent of functional electronic health records, these collection costs will drop. However, until then, it is necessary for external stakeholders and quality improvement practitioners to be parsimonious in their measurement activities.
paragraphs.heading: Quality Measurement and Improvement

paragraphs.text: A rising demand exists for transparency and public reporting of quality in health care with the goal to spur consumer choice, allow for performance-based reimbursement, and motivate better care. In other areas of medicine, public release of information on quality has been on the rise (http:// www.cms.gov/Medicare/Quality-Initiatives-Patient-Assessment-Instruments/HospitalQualityInits/OutcomeMeasure s.html), and this can be expected in neonatology as well.
paragraphs.heading: Data for Selection

paragraphs.text: U.S. News & World Report releases annual rankings of children’s hospitals and subspecialties, including neonatology. The ranking methodology is based on Donabedian’s structure, process, outcomes model, with points assigned for meeting each criterion (https://health.usnews.com/besthospitals/pediatric-rankings/neonatal-care). Expert opinion traditionally also represented an additional component, but its influence has decreased with the advent of quantitative data. Little is known regarding the validity of these rankings. Many variables have only face validity to support their use. Nevertheless, these rankings are important to hospital administrators who use them for advertising. The focus on optimizing these rankings may have positive and negative effects. Positive aspects include hospitals dedicating resources to support care structure and quality improvement activities based on measured priorities. Negative aspects include a potential misalignment between hospital leadership focus and NICU priorities. Furthermore, one can expect that hospitals will game their data given the reputational value.
paragraphs.heading: Data for Selection

paragraphs.text: The Leapfrog Group (http://www.leapfroggroup.org/), a consortium of Fortune 500 companies, provides hospitalspecific performance data to the public. Although measurement of perinatal care is limited, the group does provide a rating of quality of care for high-risk deliveries, defined as the care provided for VLBW infants. Neonatal teams must understand the strengths and weaknesses of different methods for making risk-adjusted comparisons of neonatal outcomes as they attempt to assist the public in understanding these data and to use the data themselves to monitor, evaluate, and improve the quality of care that they provide.
paragraphs.heading: Data for Selection

paragraphs.text: One of the rationales for public reporting of health care quality is the concept that the existence of such reports motivates and influences providers and organizations to improve their quality of care. The Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (http://www.talkingquality.ahrq.gov/about. htm) has promoted the use of public reporting and guided its implementation for many organizations. Although there needs to be continued research on the impact of public reporting on health care quality, thus far results are mixed. Public reports do not appear to inform consumer choice significantly, and improvements in quality measures are moderate at best.151 Consumer Reports (www.consumerre ports.org) is another consumer-oriented organization that presents hospital quality assessments.
paragraphs.heading: Data for Selection

paragraphs.text: These sources have not been well validated and have shown results that conflict with other measurement tools.152 These publications generally use league tables (rank ordering of institutions) and can provide an idea of how one
paragraphs.heading: Data for Selection

paragraphs.text: center might compare with other similar centers for specific measures. However, the interpretation of league tables must be informed by the context of reliability of measurements, adequate risk adjustment, and consistency of results, as what may appear to be an orderly ranking may not ultimately denote significant differences among NICUs.153 For example, in a league table, the difference between a top and middle performer may not be clinically or statistically significant. Nevertheless, hospitals feature such ratings prominently in marketing their services, and substantial intramural efforts are devoted to maximizing ratings.
paragraphs.heading: Data for Selection

paragraphs.text: The use of public reporting for perinatal care is relatively underdeveloped; however, it may be an untapped strategy for improving quality. Women of childbearing age are among the most frequent users of the Internet, and pregnancy is the featured topic of many websites geared toward this group.154–157 Studies have shown that women in general, and specifically expectant and current mothers, view the Internet as a way to connect to other women having similar experiences and to share information with one another,158–163 so that each woman who finds a public reporting website useful may communicate that experience to others. Some providers may feel that the development of well-designed public reporting websites that provide quality data on maternal and neonatal measures ensures their consumer relevance, accuracy, and fairness, and some rating websites are beginning to include these measures already in their hospital portals. For example, Yelp is now showing several perinatal indicators as a standard feature (Fig. 5.6).
paragraphs.heading: Data for Selection

paragraphs.text: Interest in quality assessment continues to increase for perinatal medicine. An important development in ensuring that proposed measures can actually reflect the quality of care has been the work of the National Quality Forum (NQF; www.qualityforum.org), a multi-stakeholder group that evaluates proposed quality measures. In considering measures, several important areas are assessed, including the importance of the measure to making significant gains in health care quality, the reliability and validity of the measure, the extent to which the results can be understood and be useful for decision making, and the feasibility of collection. The Joint Commission published a list of core perinatal measures in 2007. A list of current measures from the NQF is noted in Table 5.4. When considering a potential measure for widespread use, it is important to have evidence that the aspect of care that the measure reflects has been shown to be malleable—that is, shown to be improvable in at least one multi-institutional quality improvement initiative.
paragraphs.heading: National Quality Measures

paragraphs.text: As the list of quality measures continues to grow, it may become overwhelming for stakeholders, including clinicians, payers, and consumers, to extract a meaningful global picture of quality-of-care delivery at a given NICU. In addition, Profit demonstrated that correlations between quality measures of the care provided to VLBW infants are generally weak, meaning that it is difficult to infer overall qualityof-care delivery based on a small subset of clinical measures. Strategies for global assessments of quality may provide a more comprehensive assessment.164 We explore two of these in the next section.
paragraphs.heading: National Quality Measures

paragraphs.text: Although we have so far discussed the collection and presentation of data for provider selection, the active work of quality improvement requires different considerations. First, as the purpose of data collection for quality improvement is geared toward identifying potential areas of need and tracking change as soon as possible, there may be a lower threshold for identifying what might be considered an outlying value. In other words, data that are “good enough” to expose areas sorely in need for improvement may be better than waiting for “perfect” data. Second, there may be additional demands for data collection. Although some of the data sources noted in the preceding may allow for facilitation of quality improvement activities to some extent, there are several other aspects of data necessary for active quality improvement or data collections that may allow a specific question in quality improvement to be answered.
paragraphs.heading: Data for Improvement

paragraphs.text: When data are analyzed for the purposes of benchmarking and comparisons, historical data that are collected over a stable period of time may be optimal. However, amid an effort to improve quality for specific processes or outcomes, data will need to be collected and presented in or close to real time.
paragraphs.heading: Data for Improvement

paragraphs.text: A strategic aspect of data collection for quality improvement may be the need for additional process measures to be collected. For example, in an effort to increase temperature
paragraphs.heading: Data for Improvement

paragraphs.text: of very preterm infants at delivery, several important variables could contribute to this effort, including delivery room temperature, use of devices such as plastic wrap or a chemical warming mattress, and use of a checklist or noting of adequate team communication before delivery. Another example could be a project to reduce central line infections, in which the team may want to collect data on whether a line insertion or maintenance checklist is being followed, number of line days, and whether the line necessity is being assessed regularly. Although temperature and the presence of an infection may already be part of real-time data collection, the other data elements may not be typically collected or even noted in the medical record in a systematic fashion. During the quality improvement project, the additional data may be collected to facilitate the quality improvement cycle and identify areas for improvement.
paragraphs.heading: Data for Improvement

paragraphs.text: When several groups participate together in a collaborative to improve quality, a database program may serve as a common data repository and serve several useful purposes. First, it allows for the systematic collection of data in real time and for the specific purpose of the quality improvement project. Second, it allows each center to assess how it is doing compared with other groups and therefore to identify areas for improvement. Third, it can give insight into what processes may be most important to the main outcome of interest for the quality improvement project.
paragraphs.heading: Data for Improvement

paragraphs.text: An essential purpose of data assessment of provider performance is to serve as an agent for change. To fulfill this purpose, data must be available in a timely manner. Data that are too old cannot inform decision-making reliably. To meet this need, data reports have been evolving from fixed, periodic (e.g., annual) reports to more flexible reporting that also allows for user choice in measures presented, time period, comparison groups, and type of presentation. Both the VON and the CPQCC provide users with secure real-time access to customizable data queries that allow for monitoring of trends over time and benchmarking against peer groups. Although the user can take advantage of the multiple features for selection of data presentation, there is also the option of monitoring performance across multiple measures on interactive dashboards (Fig. 5.7A–F). This dashboard shows case mix–adjusted individual NICU performance in comparison to its peers. CPQCC now also displays a health equity dashboard that allows users to view performance on multiple equity-sensitive process and outcome measures by race/ethnicity (Fig. 5.7F). Each metric is shown with regard to the performance difference between the best and worst performing subgroups.
paragraphs.heading: Data for Improvement

paragraphs.text: Run charts and standardized process control (SPC) charts (Fig. 5.7E) are powerful tools for quality improvement.165 A run chart displays a series of data according to a criterion, usually time. Time is recorded on the x-axis, and the quality indicator is shown on the y-axis.
