This simple run chart can provide important insights regarding trends and variation in the process that results in the quality indicator. A Shewhart (or SPC) chart similarly tracks a quality indicator
paragraphs.heading: Data for Improvement

paragraphs.text: Another method to cut through the thicket of individual quality measures is to combine them meaningfully into a composite indicator. To simplify the presentation of quality assessment, a composite quality rating may ultimately serve as a simple way to quickly assess quality. Composite indicators of quality are aggregates of individual measures of quality. Numerous choices have to be made by developers with regard to measure selection, definition, weighting, and aggregation phases. These choices require that development of composite indicators proceeds in an explicit, systematic, and transparent manner, and that the impact of the developers’ choices on NICU performance ratings is subjected to sensitivity analysis.
paragraphs.heading: Global Assessments of Perinatal Quality: The Baby-MONITOR

paragraphs.text: The Baby-MONITOR is an attempt at providing such a simplified global assessment tool. The composite is an aggregate of nine measures of quality routinely collected by members of the VON and the CPQCC. The nine measures were selected by an expert panel and validated by a sample of clinicians.166,167 Quality measures are risk adjusted, standardized by calculating an observed minus expected event difference, and equally weighted and averaged. The measure has been robust to sensitivity analyses invoking different aggregation and weighting schemes. Subsequent use has shown large variation across California NICUs by level of care168 and by race/ethnicity.43 National use of the Baby- MONITOR in VON data similarly revealed disparities,
paragraphs.heading: Global Assessments of Perinatal Quality: The Baby-MONITOR

paragraphs.text: particularly among process measures for Black and Native American populations (Fig. 5.8).169
paragraphs.heading: Global Assessments of Perinatal Quality: The Baby-MONITOR

paragraphs.text: Another composite measure of NICU outcomes, developed by Kaempf et al.,170 aggregates eight measures in a “benefit” measure and divides these by length of stay in a “value” measure. These first formal iterations of composite indicators provide a yardstick for the future development of multidimensional quality measures.
paragraphs.heading: Global Assessments of Perinatal Quality: The Baby-MONITOR

paragraphs.text: Although composite measurement is still in its early days, such tools may prove useful in a variety of ways. They may allow users to monitor overall progress on key quality measures and to summarily assess the effect of quality interventions on performance. Through a more holistic focus, composite measurement may provide an incentive for NICUs to engage in systems-based quality improvement efforts that have the potential to affect multiple aspects of quality simultaneously. In addition, it may facilitate discussions with other stakeholder groups on quality of care. Without a comprehensive quality assessment tool, external stakeholders may increasingly subject NICUs to piecemeal appraisals that may not do justice to their overall performance.
paragraphs.heading: Global Assessments of Perinatal Quality: The Baby-MONITOR

paragraphs.text: The previous sections have focused on the history, theoretical frameworks, models, and data necessities that underpin quality improvement work, at either the individual unit or the health system level. Neonatology has been at the vanguard of the quality improvement field. Experimentation and refinement of applied methods occur in a large variety of formats. Neonatal providers undertake improvement work at the individual unit level and in collaboration with
paragraphs.heading: Quality and Safety Applied

paragraphs.text: vast networks. Formats include in-person or web-based collaboration, and methods for improvement use quantitative as well as qualitative techniques. For improvement work to be effective, a few principles deserve explicit recognition.
paragraphs.heading: Quality and Safety Applied

paragraphs.text: NICU care is rarely the sole purview of any one discipline, and most care is complex, requiring a multidisciplinary approach. Nursing, the therapies (respiratory therapy, physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy), pharmacy, and social work are the most common disciplines in addition to medicine that provide direct care to neonates. Nursing provides the majority of direct care to infants, so their involvement in quality improvement is essential. Efforts to address common quality improvement problems in neonatal care such as thermoregulation, unplanned extubation, nosocomial infection, medication errors, or skin breakdown are considered nurse-sensitive indicators of quality; thus neonatal quality improvement work should include partnerships with nursing to identify the problem, gather data, and trial solutions.171
paragraphs.heading: Interdisciplinary Collaboration

paragraphs.text: Another key partnership in quality improvement work that is not explicit in the frameworks and models described above involves the parents/guardians and other primary caregivers. Not only do families contribute to the quality and safety of their individual infants by contributing key observations and participating in daily care, but they can also contribute at a unit and institutional level to the quality improvement program, providing the perspective of “lived experience,” along with the patients. The Agency for Healthcare Quality (AHRQ; https://www.ahrq.gov/patientsafety/patients-families/engagingfamilies/index.html) published evidence-based guidelines and a toolkit to enable patients, families, and health professionals to work together as partners to promote improvements in care. Over the past decades, the NICU has become a leader in engaging families in improvement work (Box 5.4).172
paragraphs.heading: Families as Quality Improvement Partners

paragraphs.text: In addition, the most valuable neonatal quality improvement endeavor that a hospital can embark on is the implementation or expansion of family-centered care (FCC) initiatives. In the NICU, parents should be regarded as essential care providers and significant members of their baby’s medical team. Because of the symbiotic nature of the parent-child relationship, parental involvement has been shown to improve overall health outcomes for both parents and babies, a priority and natural outcome of successful FCC. Moreover, FCC has been proven to facilitate bonding and cognitive development and to positively impact the mental health of the mother-baby dyad. When adopted consistently, FCC can empower and encourage patient families on their NICU journeys.173
paragraphs.heading: Families as Quality Improvement Partners

paragraphs.text: FCC empowers parents in their role as their baby’s primary caregiver, welcoming them as an integral part of the
paragraphs.heading: Families as Quality Improvement Partners

paragraphs.text: medical team, answering their questions, and including them in rounds and in shared decision-making. In addition, FCC encourages parents to fulfill caregiving tasks such as skin-to-skin or kangaroo care, breastfeeding, diapering, reading, etc., to create a sense of intimacy, love, and protection in a challenging environment. Amid uncertainty, families find a sense of purpose and support when their holistic health care needs are met. It is worth noting that physical needs within the hospital facility are only half the equation. Whenever possible, hospitals must engage with communitybased organizations that prioritize the social and emotional needs of patient families. By doing so, they are investing in FCC and, ultimately, health equity (Box 5.5).
paragraphs.heading: Families as Quality Improvement Partners

paragraphs.text: Over time, there has been a transition from the efforts of individuals to NICU-wide efforts to network-based efforts. Increasingly, these efforts engage multiple stakeholders, including families, providers, payers, purchasers, and regulators. In the next section, we provide an example of a practical real-world quality improvement project and highlight some of the successes and failures that have beset many similar projects. This example also makes use of a small subset of management tools used in such projects.74
paragraphs.heading: Families as Quality Improvement Partners

paragraphs.text: The example NICU experienced an unexpected string of inadvertent extubations after introduction of a new
paragraphs.heading: Local Quality Improvement Applied: An Example

paragraphs.text: endotracheal tube securement device, prompting an effort to reduce such events. A multidisciplinary team composed of a physician champion, a neonatal nurse practitioner, a nurse, a respiratory therapist, and a parent advisor was formed.74 The team developed the following aim statement: “To reduce the inadvertent extubation rate in infants in the Newborn Center by 50% within 12 months.” Inadvertent extubations were defined as those not ordered by a physician or nurse practitioner.
paragraphs.heading: Local Quality Improvement Applied: An Example

paragraphs.text: The team began with a brainstorming session, in which members considered factors that contributed to inadvertent extubations. All ideas were collected and grouped in themes, such as baby, device, method, caregiver, and procedure. These themes were then graphed in a fishbone diagram (Fig. 5.9) for clarity. Factors were then assessed with regard to whether they were amenable to intervention and with regard to their likely importance as contributors to inadvertent extubations. A resulting small set of factors was extracted, and over the course of the next several weeks the team followed up each inadvertent extubation with a key informant interview (usually the bedside nurse present during the extubation). Results were tallied and graphed in
paragraphs.heading: Local Quality Improvement Applied: An Example

paragraphs.text: a Pareto chart (Fig. 5.10). Based on this information, the team developed a driver diagram (Fig. 5.11), a version of a cause-and-effect diagram, which clarified the team’s perceived linkages among the overall aim, key change strategies for achieving the aim, and change hypotheses. The change strategies were introduced in successive PDSA cycles.
paragraphs.heading: Local Quality Improvement Applied: An Example

paragraphs.text: The primary outcome measure was the number of inadvertent extubations per 100 ventilator days. The team recognized several barriers to change, including staff resistance to the new securement method and concern regarding increased mobility of the endotracheal tube with this device, as well as its cost. Because of the recognition of potential risks of fewer inadvertent extubations, such as prolonged intubation, several balancing measures, including the number of days on nasal continuous positive airway pressure and the rate of chronic lung disease, were followed. These measures were already being collected as part of the NICU’s membership in the VON.
paragraphs.heading: Local Quality Improvement Applied: An Example

paragraphs.text: The planned interventions were presented to the service, revised as needed, and approved for implementation. A staff education plan was devised and implemented. Small cycles of change were used to further refine process details. A process control chart was set up (Fig. 5.12), and caregivers received intermittent project updates. As can be gleaned from Fig. 5.12, introduction of the securement device led to a further spike in extubation rates beyond the control limit, indicating special cause variation. The new baseline is displayed. After successive implementation of the change ideas, extubation rates dropped substantially (again, special cause variation), prompting another resetting of the baseline. After these initial successes, a renewed deterioration in inadvertent extubation rates occurred when caregiver attention was diverted by the introduction of a new electronic health record. This period spotlights a common concern for quality improvement practitioners—the difficulty of holding the gains, which brings us to our next section.
paragraphs.heading: Local Quality Improvement Applied: An Example

paragraphs.text: Although there are now many examples of successful quality improvement projects, less is known about sustainability, particularly after resource-intensive projects. The goal to sustain improvement may rely on two potential strategies. One is to design an intervention such that new processes are seamlessly integrated into unit workflows and do not rely on extra effort by staff. Another approach may be to create a culture of improvement rather than just focusing on the intervention itself, where improvement becomes “the way we do things around here.” Quality improvement, as with many other skills, may benefit from practice and experience. Indeed, hospitals participating in a CMQCC project had greater improvement if they had experience participating in a previous quality improvement project.174

paragraphs.text: Sustainable quality improvement requires a genuine investment in a culture of improvement but also in the team members that do the work on the front lines, especially quality improvement leaders who require time and resources to thoughtfully plan and carry out initiatives. Key to sustainability is also codesigning initiatives (e.g., https://www.pointofcarefoundation.org.uk/resource/experience-based-co-design-ebcdtoolkit/step-by-step-guide/1-experience-based-co-design/) impacting patients and families with paid family stakeholders and paid community advisors, ideally from the start. The process of identifying and creating relationships with family and community partners equally requires time and resources. Funding for such work can be attained locally at the division or hospital level, citywide, or through local and national grant mechanisms.

paragraphs.text: The Institute for Healthcare Improvement has published a White Paper on “Sustaining Improvement,” which provides further theoretical frameworks for sustainability and some practical suggestions.176 This resource focuses primarily on organizational structure and management and how that context can provide optimal opportunities for sustained improvement.

One may be to “wean down” from a complete intervention to a lighter version, such as reducing the set of measurements to a minimal set needed to track progress. Another strategy could be to keep motivation going by holding periodic staff gettogethers in order to celebrate accomplishments. Building quality improvement capacity is critical to sustaining a culture of ongoing improvement, engagement, and sustainability. Allowing staff to channel their frontline expertise into improvement promotes Deming’s vision of the improvement journey. Sustainability is an active topic of quality improvement research, bringing us to our next section.

paragraphs.text: Despite striving for improvement for all patients, unconscious bias and structural racism permeate all aspects of society, including our health care system; thus quality improvement initiatives have the potential to perpetuate or widen health disparities.177 However, with an explicit focus on improving outcomes for groups experiencing a disparity, quality improvement initiatives may reduce these disparities. Equity-focused quality improvement offers an actionoriented, inclusive framework whereby equity is integrated throughout the design and implementation of a quality improvement initiative, from the development of a SMART Aim approach to designing and testing change ideas.178
paragraphs.heading: Quality Improvement as a Tool to Address Health Disparities

paragraphs.text: Stratifying local data by sociodemographic variables, such as race, ethnicity, preferred language, or insurance status, is a critical first step to identify a disparity. When interpreting stratified data, teams explicitly discuss what the specific sociodemographic variable represents. For example, if data are stratified by race/ethnicity, discussions should focus on how race is a social construct and a proxy for racism and social determinants of health. Comparator groups are then selected based on specific criteria, such as population size or performance on a specific metric. Data can be compared within a NICU or between NICUs using local, regional, or national data.
paragraphs.heading: Quality Improvement as a Tool to Address Health Disparities

paragraphs.text: Stakeholder mapping is inclusive and centers around patients, families, and community voices. Eliciting the “voice of the customer” through informal interviews and surveys informs initiative design, planning, and implementation. Stakeholders brainstorm root causes, specifically examining modifiable systems and processes, including racism and bias in health care systems and policies. Interventions are selected, prioritized, designed, and tested, targeting specific barriers and needs of the groups experiencing disparities. Data visualization tools are adapted to display and monitor disparity trends over time. Results are made easily accessible and disseminated to all stakeholders, including patients and community stakeholders. A case example can be found in Box 5.6.
paragraphs.heading: Quality Improvement as a Tool to Address Health Disparities

paragraphs.text: The evidence-based movement in medicine has been a hallmark of our time, and the randomized controlled trial has
paragraphs.heading: Quality Improvement Research

paragraphs.text: emerged as the gold standard by which research studies are judged and whereby clinicians adopt certain practices. However, the dissemination and implementation of evidence-based practices are not always easy. It has been noted that the time required for new knowledge generated by clinical trials to be incorporated into general practice may be 17 years.179 Therefore one could argue that the study of the translation of evidence into practice is a crucial subsequent step in maximizing and expediting the impact of the discoveries made in clinical trials.180 The study of quality improvement activities may sometimes not be amenable to a traditional trial, and such a trial may not be the optimal approach. Nevertheless, rigorous research is needed to avoid the adoption of inferior or ineffective practices in the name of quality improvement.
paragraphs.heading: Quality Improvement Research

paragraphs.text: Quality improvement research and implementation science share related aims and methods but are in some ways quite distinct. Both approaches aim to improve health care quality; however, quality improvement has usually focused on a specific problem of poor performance in relation to existing standards, addressing safety issues, or reducing adverse outcomes in a specific health care clinical setting. In contrast, implementation science has usually been focused more upstream to explore and explain underutilization of evidence-based practices or technologies or overutilization/misutilization of ineffective practices (e.g., de-implementation). Implementation science has an explicit aim of developing generalizable knowledge beyond the individual unit, institution, or system. Quality improvement research is often aimed at informing local or within-region or system practices. Implementation science and quality improvement research approaches are effective when applied synergistically. For example, quality improvement research may identify that there is underutilization of neonatal interventions. Implementation science research will explore the potential barriers and enablers to uptake and sustainment of the practices and lead to a series of further
paragraphs.heading: Quality Improvement Research

paragraphs.text: studies to test interventions based on theories of behavior or systems change. When the research has demonstrated an effective implementation strategy, ongoing quality improvement monitoring will inform the sustained impact of the practices.181
paragraphs.heading: Quality Improvement Research

paragraphs.text: The importance of publishing and therefore disseminating the results of quality improvement projects has been recognized by the pediatric community, and several journals publish such reports. Another recognition by the broader medical community of the importance of quality improvement research has been the formation of the Standards for Quality Improvement Reporting Excellence (SQUIRE) guidelines (Table 5.5). These guidelines and their 2.0 iteration were established to promote rigor in designing and reporting quality improvement research.182 Although the usual conventions for publishing scientific papers largely apply, the SQUIRE guidelines recognize several relatively unique aspects of quality improvement research. First, although a rigorous clinical trial requires prespecification of patient groups and interventions, the course of a quality improvement study may be somewhat dynamic. Improvement strategies may be modified in response to feedback from the ongoing project. The results of a clinical trial are “hidden” until the end of the study to avoid bias and change of behavior from the investigators. On the other hand, the clinicians involved in a quality improvement project may continuously try to learn from the contextual environment and ongoing results and subsequently modify their behavior to increase the impact of the intervention.
paragraphs.heading: Quality Improvement Research

paragraphs.text: For the mentioned reasons, Berwick183 has referred to randomized controlled trials as being “an impoverished way to learn” in the context of quality improvement, suggesting that learning from experience “while doing” can be an important part of improving the quality of care. In a simulation study comparing “learning” and putting into practice findings from significant randomized trials only versus quality improvement collaborative projects, the quality improvement model was found to be a potentially superior approach.184
paragraphs.heading: Quality Improvement Research

paragraphs.text: In addition to the aspect of learning while doing, a patient-level randomization study for quality improvement may not be feasible, as improvement activities on intervention subjects in a single NICU are likely to contaminate the control group. Approaches such as cluster randomization or stepped wedge designs may be better suited for experimental studies of quality improvement.185,186 The Canadian Neonatal Network conducted a cluster randomized trial of 12 NICUs in which half of the units focused on nosocomial infections and the other half focused on reducing bronchopulmonary dysplasia rates.187 Although bronchopulmonary dysplasia was reduced only in the corresponding group, nosocomial infections decreased in both groups. Their findings may suggest that quality improvement activities in one area may also influence quality in other areas, making the interpretation of such trials challenging. Walsh et al.186 led a cluster randomized controlled trial on the effect of benchmarking and multimodal quality improvement at
paragraphs.heading: Quality Improvement Research

paragraphs.text: 17 NICUs that were members of the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development on bronchopulmonary dysplasia rates. Three NICUs were selected as best performers, and the remaining 14 NICUs were randomized to intervention or control. Changes in rates of survival free of bronchopulmonary dysplasia were compared between study year 1 and year 3. Intervention NICUs did change practices related to bronchopulmonary dysplasia, but no statistically significant difference in the primary outcome was found. Horbar et al.185 conducted a cluster randomized controlled trial in 114 NICUs alongside a quality improvement collaborative of surfactant timing at delivery. Eligible infants in the intervention NICUs received surfactant in a more timely manner (median of 21 minutes vs. 78 minutes; P < .001).
paragraphs.heading: Quality Improvement Research

paragraphs.text: The literature surrounding the effectiveness of quality improvement collaborative activities is still in its infancy. However, relative to other specialties, neonatal-perinatal medicine is at a relatively advanced stage. In a systematic review of the impact of quality improvement collaborative studies by Schouten and co-workers,188 four of the nine studies considered in the main analysis concerned neonatal outcomes. There are still many opportunities for studying many aspects of quality improvement: its effectiveness as well as optimal designs for broader implementation. Little is known regarding what works and what does not in furthering health equity. Substantial efforts have been dedicated toward education on health equity topics, but educational interventions by themselves do not have a good track record of changing patient outcomes.

paragraphs.text: Experimentation to link education with applied quality improvement efforts may hold more promise. Equity efforts should address segregation of minoritized populations into safety net NICUs, where, due to challenges with resources, the quality of care may differ. In addition, they should focus on disparate treatment within NICUs, where interpersonal racism may lead to suboptimal care. Much work also remains to be done to diversify the neonatology personnel workforce. Finally, equity efforts will need to strengthen the bridge into the community setting, recognizing that our care and responsibility do not end at the exit door of the NICU. Appropriate funding should be provided to support these endeavors.
paragraphs.heading: SQUIRE 2.0 Guidelines

paragraphs.text: Although this chapter has focused on some of the quality work done in the United States, similarly sophisticated regional and national collaborative networks, as well as quality efforts by individual NICUs, are underway throughout the world. The quality improvement aims in many high- and upper-middle-income countries are reductions in neonatal morbidities and improving the value and experience of care, such as those outlined in the United States. However, the quality improvement aims in many low- and lower-middle-income countries (LMICs) remain focused on reducing neonatal mortality rates. Although access to care, including delivery in a health facility, remains a challenge in many LMIC settings, access to care is no longer viewed as a priority competing with quality of care by those implementing newborn health programs globally.189 The international community is focused on improving care and inequities in health outcomes for infants and their families, by targeting Sustainable Development Goal 3.2 to end preventable deaths of newborns and to reduce the global neonatal mortality rate to 12 or fewer per 1000 live births in all countries by 2030.190 However, based on progress to date, it is predicted that many countries in Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa will not reach these goals without an enhanced focus on equity, quality of perinatal and essential newborn care, and improved institutional care for small or sick newborns and their families.191
paragraphs.heading: Quality and Safety in the International Context

paragraphs.text: The World Health Organization (WHO) recognizes their key position in establishing standards for improving the quality of maternal and newborn care in health facilities,192 the care for small and sick newborns in health facilities,193 communicating human resource strategies to improve newborn care in health facilities in LMICs,194 and recommending maternal and newborn care for a positive postnatal experience.195 The second edition of the WHO Essential Newborn Care Course is included in WHO resources that integrate quality improvement discussion points and reflection questions into WHO’s foundational materials for the essential care of every newborn used by health care providers worldwide (https://www.w ho.int/tools/essential-newborn-care-training-course).196 These standards and seminal documents are necessary for a culture change in neonatal care, embracing the notion that daily improvements in care are at the core of our work as health care professionals. However, in order to operationalize standards and identify and quantify gaps in care, we must also establish systems that allow interrogation of the “Know-Do gap,” the difference between providers’ knowledge of appropriate care and the care they actually provide in a clinical encounter.197,198 Without data, health care providers and the systems they work in are powerless to improve the care they provide, learn from their own practice, collaborate effectively with peer facilities, or advocate successfully for the resources they need.199,200
paragraphs.heading: Quality and Safety in the International Context

paragraphs.text: The power and excitement of collaborative quality improvement, key ingredients to maximize sustainability, often come from the development of community. Many neonatal units have found value in joining international neonatal networks or peer learning communities, such as VON. Recognizing that the trajectory to reach global neonatal improvement targets in resource-limited settings will be dependent on initiatives led by LMIC clinicians and experts, VON has proudly worked with Ethiopian leaders to co-develop quality improvement education and tools to serve as the foundation for the Ethiopian Neonatal Network.201 Building on these efforts and momentum, VON is partnering with the African Neonatal Association to develop an African peer learning community with a foundation of a co-designed data system and quality improvement strategy, harmonizing when possible and collaborating with
paragraphs.heading: Quality and Safety in the International Context

paragraphs.text: additional key academic groups, non-governmental organizations, and research initiatives.202
paragraphs.heading: Quality and Safety in the International Context

paragraphs.text: Although there are many barriers along the path to facility-level data in an LMIC setting, much progress has been made, and future projects can build upon these successes and lessons learned. Indeed, a systematic accounting of improvement efforts that work and those that do not is necessary to leverage and spread existing knowledge, contributing to the community’s understanding of potentially better practices and the diverse environments in which they are implemented.
paragraphs.heading: Quality and Safety in the International Context

paragraphs.text: Neonatal teams have been at the forefront of adapting and evolving industrial quality improvement methods.203 These efforts have yielded great benefits to infants requiring neonatal intensive care and their families. Quality and safety are emerging fields, and the supporting science is being developed. At its core, quality improvement endeavors are founded in experiential learning, but as rigor in methods advances, so does generalizability. Despite its relative youth, it is quality improvement that may hold the greatest hope for solving one of the most important issues of our time: health equity. We think the field will make a meaningful contribution in this area. Indeed, although more work needs to be done, the indication is that quality improvement work is, in fact, health equity work, as over the past decade disparity gaps have narrowed in many areas.204–207

paragraphs.heading: Conclusion

paragraphs.text: Since the first version of this chapter appeared in 2001, quality improvement methods have been adopted by newborn care teams around the world. Improvement and implementation sciences have become rigorous academic disciplines. The American Board of Pediatrics requires participation in quality improvement projects for maintenance of certification by neonatologists. Quality improvement research is recognized as satisfying the research requirement for fellows training in neonatal-perinatal medicine. Trainees in pediatrics frequently spend elective time working on quality improvement projects. Importantly, the scope of quality improvement has expanded, as evidenced by the addition of new co-authors for this chapter with expertise in family-centered care (KN, LF), health equity (MP), global health (DE), and implementation science (LF). These developments move us closer to realizing the ideal that each of us has two jobs, providing care and improving it for the infants and families we serve.

# 5. Improving the Quality, Safety, and Equity of Neonatal Intensive Care for Infants and Families
> Source attribution: [Source credits](../../SOURCE_CREDITS.md).


## PDF page 84 | printed page 65

5 Improving the Quality, Safety, and Equity of Neonatal Intensive Care for Infants and Families

### JOCHEN PROFIT, JEFFREY B. GOULD, MICHELLE-MARIE PEÑA, KIMBERLY NOVOD, LINDA S. FRANCK, DANIELLE E.Y. EHRET, AND JEFFREY D. HORBAR

### Overview

Over the last decades, neonatology has achieved dramatic decreases in neonatal mortality and morbidity globally. Unfortunately, wide variation persists across neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) with respect to the quality of care and outcomes, as well as the extent of medical errors. Racial and ethnic disparities are also a consideration with regard to quality of care and outcomes. An important goal of quality improvement is to reduce variation in outcomes and errors and to address disparities in order to ensure the best possible outcomes for infants and their families. In neonatal quality improvement, we assess the need for action based on quantitative outcomes data and qualitative input from NICU staff and families. The location and type of intervention are determined by an analysis of the context and processes believed to drive desired change. The run chart displays data over time and indicates if those interventions have been successful. This chapter presents the historical development of neonatology quality improvement and provides an overview of models, methods, and measures of NICU-based quality improvement. We review the ways data can be collected, evaluated, and applied to improve the quality, safety, and equity of medical care for newborn infants and their families.

Making improvements happen also requires ... unshakeable belief in the idea that everyone in healthcare really has two jobs when they come to work every day: to do their work and to improve it.1

Systematic evaluation of the quality, safety, and efficiency of clinical care has become an integral part of medical practice. Health professionals, hospitals, and large health

care organizations are required to monitor, report on, and continuously improve their services. Public release of hospital performance data is becoming increasingly common. Health professionals in neonatology must learn how to evaluate themselves and learn how they will be evaluated by others, including policy makers, hospital administrators, regulators, payers, and the families and public they serve.

Evaluation is not an end in itself. Health professionals must learn how to use available information to improve the quality and safety of health care continuously. This is not just an option. It is a requirement set forth by regulatory licensing bodies (www.ABP.org) and a responsibility we have to patients and their families.

### The Case for Improvement

Public health and health care delivery systems in highincome nations have much to be proud of. Over the past century, they have combined to reduce infant and maternal mortality, as well as to prolong life expectancy to unsurpassed levels in human history. During the 20th century, infant mortality dropped from more than 100 per 1000 live births to about 5 per 1000 live births; maternal deaths dropped by 99% to about 10 per 100,000 live births.2–4

During the first half of the 20th century, these improvements were driven largely by advances in public health, especially access to clean water, which dramatically reduced infection-related morbidity and mortality.5 However, although health care delivery conferred little benefit to population-based health during the first half of the century, there have since been demonstrable contributions to added life expectancy.6 Neonatal intensive care is a case in point. Although relatively few interventions (e.g., heated incubator

65


## PDF page 85

care, intravenous nutrition, oxygen) were available to support sick newborns until the 1960s, technical and scientific advances in nutrition, physiologic monitoring, mechanical ventilation, pharmaceuticals, and the inclusion of parents in delivering care (e.g., kangaroo care, skin-to-skin care) have made it possible for infants to survive previously fatal degrees of prematurity or genetic or other newborn disease.7–9

On the other hand, new medical treatments in combination with greater access and demand for care and a rise in the prevalence of chronic disease conditions have resulted in rising health expenditures, which have outpaced national incomes.10,11 As a consequence, in the United States, health care consumes an ever-greater proportion of gross domestic product. In 2020, national health expenditures accounted for 18% of gross domestic product, which severely strains the budgets of those paying for health care: consumers, through taxes, co-pays, deductibles, insurance, and reduced wage growth; companies, through insurance; and state and federal governments, through obligations under Medicaid and Medicare.

Further, health care access and resources are not distributed equally among populations, creating disparate health and financial burdens for minoritized groups. In light of these constraints, a commitment to population health requires optimization of the value of each dollar expended for health care equitably. However, a sequence of sentinel Institute of Medicine of the National Academy of Sciences reports have highlighted that health care delivery, including neonatal intensive care, falls short of its value and equity potential,12 and they have provided a blueprint toward optimization using quality improvement and safety tools.13

In neonatology, as in other clinical fields, opportunities for improving the quality, safety, and equity of care are substantial. A compelling body of literature suggests that neonatal intensive care is supply-side sensitive14; that is, the more NICUs there are, the more patients will be admitted to them, potentially indicating waste. In addition, dramatic variation in the processes and outcomes of care has been documented that cannot be explained by differences in case mix, suggesting differences in the quality-of-care delivery.15–20 For example, in a study of over 400,000 infants with birth weights of 401 to 1500 grams born from 2005 to 2014 and cared for at 756 Vermont Oxford Network (VON) member NICUs in the United States, NICUs in the worst decile had rates nearly twice as high as those in the best decile for several major morbidities (late-onset infection, severe retinopathy of prematurity, severe intraventricular hemorrhage, and necrotizing enterocolitis) of very low birth weight (VLBW) infants.

Despite the variation, improvements in NICU care over the past decade have heralded dramatic improvement in mortality and morbidities for VLBW infants.19 Health care–associated infection rates provide a striking example. At the 756 US NICUs in the study described above, the rate of late bacterial (including coagulase-negative Staphylococcus) or fungal infection significantly decreased from 2005, when 21.9% of infants had infections, to 2014 when 10.1%

of the infants had infections. Remarkably, 75% of NICUs achieved rates of performance as good as or better than what the best 25% of units had achieved only 8 years earlier. Over the last decade, reduction of health care–associated infection has been at the center of national health policy efforts to improve the value of health care delivery, including aligning hospital payments with quality-of-care delivery. Widespread efforts in the neonatal community have proved successful in facilitating broad-based and sustained reductions in health care–associated infection rates and represent an encouraging blueprint for improvements in care in other areas.7 Such improvements have also resulted in improved survival without major morbidity. In a study of 49,333 VLBW infants (<1500 grams) across 142 NICUs in the California Perinatal Quality Care Collaborative (CPQCC) from 2008 to 2017, survival with more than three and four major morbidities decreased by more than 40% each.21 Nevertheless, persistent wide variation across NICUs indicates continued opportunities for improvement.

Another indicator for quality deficits in the neonatal intensive care setting is the widespread delivery of inappropriate care—defined as underuse, overuse, and misuse of interventions.22,23 Examples include the underuse of hand hygiene by NICU personnel,24 the overuse of antibiotics, and the misuse of medications because of medical errors. An example of an effort to address overuse and misuse is Choosing Wisely (www.choosingwisely.org).25 Choosing Wisely, an initiative of the American Board of Internal Medicine, has challenged national medical specialty societies to identify “Top Five” lists of commonly used tests or procedures whose necessity should be questioned and discussed with patients. The American Academy of Pediatrics Section of Neonatal Perinatal Medicine (SONPM) developed a Top Five list for neonatology using a multistep process that included expert input via a modified Delphi experiment and formal evidence assessment. These final Top Five items are shown in Box 5.1.

Medical errors represent another example of misuse. Current health care operations produce unacceptable rates of medical errors that result in patient injury or death. In

• BOX 5.1 Choosing Wisely Top Five List for

Newborn Medicine

1. Avoid routine use of antireflux medications for treatment

of symptomatic gastroesophageal reflux disease or for treatment of apnea and desaturation in preterm infants. 2. Avoid routine continuation of antibiotic therapy beyond 48

hours for initially asymptomatic infants without evidence of bacterial infection. 3. Avoid routine use of pneumograms for predischarge

assessment of ongoing and/or prolonged apnea of prematurity. 4. Avoid routine daily chest radiographs without an indication

for intubated infants. 5. Avoid routine screening term-equivalent or discharge brain

MRIs in preterm infants.


## PDF page 86 | printed page 67

To Err Is Human, the Institute of Medicine concluded that between 44,000 and 98,000 Americans die annually from hospital errors, which kill more Americans than breast cancer, traffic accidents, or AIDS.12

Preterm infants in the NICU are particularly vulnerable to medical errors, due to their small size, physiologic immaturity, and limited compensatory abilities.26,27 Medication errors are a common problem in sick newborns due to breakdowns in patient identification28 and rapid changes in physiologic maturity, body weight, and volumes of distribution that require frequent dose adjustments. NICU patients are more likely to experience a medication error than other hospital patients.29 For example, a study at two Boston hospitals documented that errors in the process of ordering, dispensing, or monitoring medications occurred for more than 90% of the infants cared for in the NICU.30 Another study, using a trigger tool in the electronic health record, identified 0.74 adverse events per patient,29 and 56% of these were deemed preventable. These estimates are likely only the tip of the iceberg.

Medication errors are not the only safety challenges preterm infants face. Using a voluntary, anonymous, errorreporting system established by the VON, Suresh et al.31 documented a broad range of errors at 54 NICUs. Only about half involved medications; the remainder involved a wide variety of errors, including errors in administration or method of using a treatment (14%), patient misidentification (11%), other system failure (9%), error or delay in diagnosis (7%), and error in the performance of an operation, procedure, or test (4%). A study from eight Dutch NICUs found that incidents concerning mechanical ventilation, blood products, intravascular lines, parenteral nutrition, and medication dosing errors posed the highest risk to patients in the NICU.32

The necessary engagement of parents or other primary caregivers for delivery of high-quality care for hospitalized children is now well recognized.33,34 Families contribute to the quality and safety of health care through their direct involvement in caregiving and decision-making for their loved ones and through engagement in clinical unit and hospital-wide quality and safety initiatives.35 In neonatal care, the critical role of parents as essential caregivers for preterm and ill newborns is undisputed. For example, active parent involvement in preterm infant caregiving leads to higher breastfeeding rates, earlier discharge, and improved long-term neurodevelopment.36 Conversely, untreated NICU-related parent stress and depression adversely affect preterm children’s long-term social, behavioral, and functional development.37 Despite strong evidence, family involvement in care and decision-making and in quality and safety initiatives is often lacking or variably implemented within and across neonatal care settings.

Furthermore, our health care delivery system has not reliably delivered many interventions that are deemed to be effective. McGlynn et al.38 in adults and later Mangione- Smith et al.39 in children demonstrated that Americans receive guideline-recommended care only about half the

time. In the newborn setting, antenatal steroids are an example where opportunities for improvement in administration have been documented.40–42

Finally, evidence is building that the care we provide and the outcomes of patients are not equitably distributed.43 Reasons for this include historical injustices, structural and institutional racism, social determinants of health, and uneven access to care. It is important to understand that these conditions can have downstream effects that span generations. Such inequities are not unique to the United States and are global issues. At the level of NICU care, important contributors to inequities include between-NICU and within-NICU variation in care.37,44 Between-NICU variation implies the segregation of groups into resource-limited hospitals.45 Within-NICU variation is the result of implicit or explicit bias by health care workers impacting the care of infants and their families.46 Quality improvement has been posited as a tool to address inequities but may improve, perpetuate, or even worsen them. Therefore all such activities should explicitly consider equity implications.

The inability of the health care system to consistently deliver the highest quality of care results in an enormous waste of human lives and valuable resources. Berwick and Hackbarth47 showed that “in just six categories of waste— overtreatment, failures of care coordination, failures in execution of care processes, administrative complexity, pricing failures, and fraud and abuse—the sum of the lowest available estimates exceeds 20% of total health care expenditures.” In the United States, the care of preterm infants consumes about $40 billion annually (adjusted for inflation).11 These health expenditures directly affect families and patients. More than half a million households file for bankruptcy annually due to medical reasons.48

With the recognition of the extent of the opportunities for improvement have come efforts by providers, provider networks, payers, nongovernmental organizations, and governmental agencies to improve the value of health care expenditures. At the provider network and health system level, efforts have focused on quality assurance and alignment of financial incentives. For example, quality assurance has been pursued through benchmarking of performance by provider networks such as the CPQCC49 or the VON,50 as well as other statewide neonatal collaborative organizations, including those in Massachusetts, Ohio, Tennessee, North Carolina, Florida, Wisconsin, and Michigan. Significant efforts have been made to develop, evaluate, and harmonize quality measures through organizations such as the National Quality Forum. Public reporting51–53 of quality measures and realignment of financial incentives away from a fee-forservice system toward a pay-for-quality system are becoming more widespread.54,55 We provide more detail on these issues later in this chapter.

At the hospital level, health care professionals have engaged in quality improvement efforts to meet the expectations of this changing marketplace. Several institutions have undergone fundamental reengineering of their health care delivery systems. This transformation has been the consequence of a


## PDF page 87

growing recognition that the current model of health care delivery is in many ways outmoded and has failed to incorporate many of the lessons that propelled other sectors of the economy to large gains in quality and productivity. When health care professionals work together in teams and include families, they can harness the joint wisdom of their respective expertise. Crowdsourcing of expertise is important because the expert health care professional mind is fallible and divergent,56 prone to systematic bias,57–59 limited in its ability to process complex information (maximally 7 ± 2 simultaneous variables),60 and unable to stay current on medical knowledge (doubling time of 8 years).22,61 Thus a hierarchical physician-centric approach to care results in clinical variability that is driven by provider rather than patient factors, and this ultimately degrades care. For all of these reasons, a new approach must be pursued that is based on flat team hierarchies, standardization and systematic use of clinical data, and evidence. Other industries have grappled with similar transitions and have provided a blueprint for improvement that is now actively pursued by many high-performing health systems. We briefly examine some of the historical foundations of these developments.

### Brief History of Industrial Quality Improvement

A thorough description of the history of quality improvement is beyond the scope of this chapter. Instead, we provide a brief overview of strategic stages of progress that are particularly salient for medicine (Fig. 5.1). Before the late 19th and early 20th centuries, quality was largely conceived of as quality assurance (oversight) and the result of personal excellence and training. For example, craftsmen organized in guilds chose their trainees selectively, often based on

The goal of this movement was to increase productivity, reduce scrap, and reduce cost. Frederick Taylor (1856–1915) was one of the main innovators during this era. The next leap in industrial management was achieved through the work of Walter Shewhart (1891–1967). An engineer, physicist, and statistician, Shewhart is known as the “father of statistical quality control.” Before Shewhart, industrial quality mostly involved inspection and removal of defective products. Working at Bell Telephone Laboratories, he noted the importance of reducing variation in manufacturing processes. Kiichiro Toyoda, the founder of Toyota Motor Company, was among Deming’s audience in 1950. Based on Deming’s lectures, Toyoda developed the Toyota Production System (TPS), an integrated sociotechnical system comprised of its management philosophy and practices. The system is a precursor of the more generic lean manufacturing. At the core of TPS is elimination of waste (muda) and total focus on reliable, high quality through continuous improvement (kaizen). Lean production focuses on just-in-time use of materials and optimization of production flow (mura) in response to customer demand. Toyota’s success derived from its innovative production engineering, which puts quality control in the hands of the frontline workers who can stop the production line and call for help when something goes wrong. However, production engineering is only part of story. An equally important contributor to Toyota’s success has been coined the “Toyota Way,” principles that embody a relentless focus on the needs and desires of customers.

Another variant of statistical process control originally developed by Motorola in 1985 is Six Sigma, which is a set of process improvement tools and strategies that seek to improve quality by minimizing defects and variability. In Six Sigma, a defect is defined as any process output that does not meet customer specifications or that could lead to creating an output that does not meet customer specifications. The term “Six Sigma process” means that, if one has 6 standard deviations between the process mean and the nearest specification limit, then only 3.4 out of 1 million outputs will fail to meet specifications. To illustrate, a 1-sigma process produces 69%, a 2-sigma process produces 31%, and a 6-sigma process produces 0.00034% defective outputs. Current evidence suggests that much of health care operates at the 1- or 2-sigma level.38,39 Six Sigma includes methodologies that lean on Deming’s PDSA cycle, such as DMAIC for reengineering existing processes: Define the problem. Measure key aspects. Analyze data for key relationships. Improve the current process (using a set of specific techniques). Control the future process.

Industrial quality improvement methods have been applied to health care for more than 30 years. In Curing Health Care: New Strategies for Quality Improvement, Berwick and co-workers64 provided the initial evidence that the tools of modern quality improvement, with which other industries have achieved breakthroughs in performance, can help in health care as well. Since then, the core ideas of quality improvement have been adapted to the needs of health care and implemented by health care organizations around the world. In neonatology, multidisciplinary teams from NICUs across the United States have applied quality improvement tools and methods to address the quality

and safety of medical care for newborn infants and their families.49,65–69

Successful adaptation of these industrial methods to the NICU setting requires recognition that health care is a process and that quality improvement requires process management. However, a focus on care delivery processes is not sufficient. Rather, process management needs to be accompanied by efforts to optimize the organizational environment in ways that promote continual learning, teamwork, and adherence to the mission of serving patients and families. Several theoretical frameworks exist to further our understanding of the complex interplay among the organizational environment, process, and outcomes.

### Definitions and Conceptual Frameworks for Quality

### Definitions

The Institute of Medicine defines quality-of-care delivery as the extent to which health services provided to individuals and patient populations improve desired health outcomes. In Crossing the Quality Chasm,13 it developed the following six domains of quality of delivery of care:



Safety—Avoiding preventable injuries, reducing medical er-

rors Effectiveness—Providing services based on scientific knowl-

edge (clinical guidelines) Patient-centeredness—Care that is respectful and responsive

to individuals Efficiency—Avoiding the wasting of time and other resources Timeliness—Reducing wait times and improving the prac-

tice flow Equity—Care that should be tailored to address the unique

social and medical needs faced by patients and families from minoritized communities

We have added being socially and environmentally responsible to this list.50 Together, these domains are useful guideposts for practitioners in developing comprehensive quality programs and measurement systems.70

### Conceptual Frameworks for Quality

Various authors have developed conceptual or explanatory models that provide users with a systematic understanding of the components and facilitators of high-quality health care delivery. These frameworks are often adapted from other sciences, including manufacturing, engineering, organizational theory, and psychology. They share a common premise that high quality-of-care delivery is the result of efforts to create a work environment in which people work together to reliably execute processes that are known to work or thought to work, and to avoid care that is known to be unhelpful. We mention a few commonly applied ones here.


## PDF page 90 | printed page 71

### Donabedian: Structure, Processes, Outcomes

Maybe the best-known framework for quality improvement was developed by Avedis Donabedian (1919–2000). Donabedian was the first to collate evidence on the quality of health care delivery; he developed a simple structure, process, and outcome model of quality that has been the mainstay of quality research.71 Structure traditionally has been interpreted as the physical facilities and the training and education of staff. This notion has been expanded to include executive leadership, organizational culture, organizational design, incentive structure, and information systems and technology.72 Processes include the activities that clinicians and support staff undertake as part of or in support of care delivery. Outcomes are the results of these activities.

### Pawson and Tilley: Realistic Evaluation

Realistic evaluation goes beyond the traditional cause-andeffect paradigm and poses that program effectiveness also depends on many interrelated contextual variables.73 This concept is formalized by the following formula: Context + Mechanism = Outcome, or C + M = O. A given intervention does not necessarily work for the group, but may be quite useful to some individuals, depending on their specific circumstances.

### Translation of Frameworks into Action

Frontline application of quality improvement efforts draws from the various theoretical frameworks presented in the preceding section. In the following, we highlight a few approaches that are commonly applied in neonatology. For practitioners, the practical application of quality improvement work may be more effective if supported by a formal approach, such as those provided by the Model for Improvement, Deming’s integrated management model, lean manufacturing, and Six Sigma. Each of these models makes use of various management tools to assist with project planning and execution, including team organization, process mapping, problem identification, problem resolution, task prioritization, and execution. We briefly mention several of these in the section titled Quality and Safety Applied. However, a full description of these tools is beyond the scope of this chapter. For more details on these, we refer to the extant literature.74 We now turn our attention to the Model for Improvement, which has been widely adopted as a strategy for collaborative quality improvement in the neonatal community.75

### Model for Improvement

The Model for Improvement is based on The Improvement Guide: A Practical Approach to Enhancing Organizational Performance by Langley et al.76 The model identifies four strategic elements of successful process improvement: (1) specific and measurable aims, (2) measures of improvement that are tracked over time, (3) strategic changes that will result in the desired improvement, and (4) a series of PDSA cycles during which teams learn how to apply crucial

The first question, which refers to the aim(s) of the project, is “What are we trying to accomplish?” In other words, what are the main outcomes that the team is trying to change or improve. There are several considerations when considering the aim of a prospective project. Are there historical and/or peer benchmark data to suggest that there is a problem in the local NICU? Is there a variation in outcomes among NICUs to suggest that variations in practices can lead to differences in outcomes? Are there evidence-based practices that have been shown to improve the outcome of interest? The aim should be well defined and realistic. It should also be quantifiable and encompass a defined time period.77

One helpful technique for crafting a well-designed aim statement is the SMART Aim approach (Table 5.1). An example of a suboptimal aim statement may be, “Reduce infection rates in our NICU.” Although a worthy goal, that statement is vague, and it will be difficult to assess if it has been accomplished. In contrast, the following aim statement is more specific and follows the SMART Aim approach: “Reduce by 50% the number of central lineassociated bloodstream infections as defined by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in infants born at 24 to 30 weeks’ gestational age in the NICU by using an insertion and maintenance bundle over a 12-month time period.”

The second question, corresponding to the measures of the project, is “How will we know that a change is an improvement?” As a team embarks on a quality improvement project, one can consider three main groups of measurements: outcomes, processes, and balancing measures. The outcome measure is typically a clinical outcome, such as nosocomial infection or bronchopulmonary dysplasia. A process measure related to reduction of nosocomial infection could be the use of an insertion checklist. In some instances, a process measure can serve as the main outcome of a quality improvement project when that process measure has been clearly linked to a benefit in clinical outcomes. Examples are a focus on improving the rate of antenatal steroid administration for premature birth or on increasing breast milk provision for premature infants. A balancing

The third question, which corresponds to the strategic changes that will lead to improvement, is “What changes can we make that will result in improvement?” These changes should be evidence based but must also account for local cultural and organizational characteristics. ### Integrated Quality Management

Another model for quality improvement in health care focuses on the elimination of process variation. This approach derives from Deming’s work and has been adapted with success for health care by several organizations. For example, Intermountain Healthcare helped refocus the health system’s quality improvement efforts on process standardization, active management, and ongoing organizational learning. Work units identify high-value clinical processes and set up multidisciplinary provider teams to develop evidence-based, detailed care pathways (shared baselines) to execute these processes in a consistent, reliable manner. Use of the term shared baseline, rather than protocol or guideline, highlights its development and ongoing refinement by the local work unit. Control rests with frontline care providers, not managers. The purpose of these shared baselines is to minimize the variation that is driven by providers and not accounted for by patient need. Providers are encouraged to deviate from the shared baseline as warranted by the needs of individual patients. This approach allows providers to bring their expertise to bear on the clinical situations that truly warrant an alternative treatment approach. It also effectively ameliorates concerns regarding “cookbook” medicine, given an explicit expectation that no guideline perfectly fits any patient. On the contrary, providers are asked to assess situations where they have deviated from the shared baseline. This information is then used to modify the shared baseline when appropriate. Overall, the use of shared baselines makes the workflow more predictable, efficient, safer for patients, and less stressful for nursing staff.80–83

Similar to the Model for Improvement, the modified Deming approach uses key measures to track cornerstones of the process, clinical outcomes, service outcomes (such as patient satisfaction), and cost. The key to promote organizational learning and standardization is tracking process deviations and systems to modify the shared baselines according to ongoing provider input. To facilitate the success of local projects, strategic staff from clinical work units receive training and technical support for their improvement work from a centralized quality improvement institute. Institutional commitment is foundational to achieving excellence in care delivery.81

### Lean

Lean is a quality improvement model that focuses on reducing process waste and improving process flow.84 The seven forms of waste in Lean are overproduction, inventory, waiting, transportation, defects, staff movement, and unnecessary processing. Lean focuses on customers, patients, and families and encourages users to examine their process steps and eliminate those that do not provide value to customers. Attention to “flow” attempts to optimize the use of time and resources.

Although meaningful in their differences, their common thread lies in the centrality of managing work processes while optimizing the care delivery environment. Organizational goals for high-quality care delivery and patient safety are undergirded by strategies that encourage continuous monitoring of processes and outcomes, facilitate continuous learning, and minimize unwarranted waste and process variation.

### Data and Methods for Quality Improvement

Not everything that can be counted counts. Not everything that counts can be counted.

### —ATTRIBUTED TO ALBERT EINSTEIN

It is essential that quality improvement be data driven. First, to identify opportunities for quality improvement, data are necessary to determine performance relative to historical performance or peer-derived benchmarks. Second, essential to the Plan-Do-Study-Act approach, when quality improvement has been undertaken, data are used to assess the extent to which each specific intervention has or has not been effective, as well as to identify unintended negative consequences. Although we use the term data, what we are really collecting is information that we can use to guide the course of our quality improvement. To lower the burden of collection, we should only select the minimal amount of data that can guide our progress, and, if possible, we should use data that can be derived from or efficiently incorporated into the workflow.

### Data Elements for Assessment

In following Donabedian’s framework, the main data types can be categorized as structural or contextual measures, process measures, and outcome measures (including medical outcomes, cost, and service outcomes such as family satisfaction with care). The three most important considerations for any data element are its clarity of definition, the ease with which it can be identified and extracted from the medical record or its administrative source, and its universality across time and location. Stable definitions across time are important to assess the extent to which a morbidity has decreased or increased over time. Agreed-upon definitions are essential to compare outcomes across NICUs both within and across countries. The widespread adoption of the definitions developed by the VON has made both national and international comparisons possible.

### Structure and Institutional Context

Although the focus of quality improvement has largely been on changing processes of care, there is an increasing awareness of the importance of the context in which improvement activities occur. In addition to changing the behavior

of members of the health care team, quality improvement often relies on changing systems of care and with it the organizational environment. Efforts at measuring care structure and context have been motivated by numerous studies linking these aspects to clinical and organizational outcomes.

Maybe the best-examined aspect of structure is the patient-to-nurse ratio. In adult and pediatric intensive care unit settings,85,86 rising patient-to-nurse ratios have been linked to worse clinical outcomes and higher mortality. In neonatology, this link is less well understood.87 Although most studies imply a benefit of greater staffing ratios, this finding is not uniform.88 Nurse staffing ratios may be suboptimal in general and associated with nosocomial infection rates.89 Other examples of structural measures that can impact the quality of care include academic teaching status, 24-hour coverage by an in-house intensivist, patient volume, and level of care.

Contextual measures are different from traditional measures in that they attempt to assess the links between how care delivery is organized and supported by the institution and quality of care. Kaplan and colleagues90 developed a framework for examining these linkages and coined it Model for Understanding Success in Quality (MUSIQ). This model includes different components that support improvements in the processes and outcomes of care delivery at various levels of the institution, including characteristics of the improvement team (diversity, physician involvement, leadership) and the NICU, as well as higher-level organizational functions (quality improvement leadership and administrative support).91

One well-researched aspect of care context is safety culture. The NICU safety culture describes the shared norms of leadership, staff, and the organization with regard to patient safety, or, simply, the “way we do things around here.” Culture influences quality of care in important ways. Whether a process is failure proof depends on how reliably it is implemented. Non-adherence to care standards may reflect a clinical need, but also lack of a standard or willful disregard. Safety culture assessments attempt to capture safety context through surveys that ask about health care worker perceptions. The measured domains are referred to as climates (e.g., teamwork climate, safety climate). The term “climate” reflects that perceptions are shared among health workers; that is, they cluster more strongly within a work unit (e.g., the NICU) than between work units.

Ongoing assessment of safety culture is a requirement for hospital accreditation by the Joint Commission, an accreditation agency that assesses safety and quality of care. There are several validated survey tools to measure safety culture.26,92–94 The Safety Attitudes Questionnaire (SAQ) reflects caregiver attitudes on safety culture, is psychometrically sound, and has demonstrated wide interinstitutional variation across NICUs.95 Safety culture, as measured by the SAQ, has been linked to a variety of clinical and organizational outcomes. Most famously, this instrument was used by Pronovost and co-workers96 in their implementation of the Comprehensive Unit-based Safety Program


## PDF page 93

(CUSP) in 103 adult ICUs in Michigan, where, through implementation of a checklist and a focus on teamwork and safety, median catheter-related bloodstream infection rates were reduced to zero. This program has been endorsed for implementation in all ICUs by the US government. In a study of 44 NICUs and over 2000 respondents, teamwork was negatively correlated with health care–associated infections among VLBW infants.97 Of note, physicians tend to rate safety culture significantly higher than do nurses and other personnel, highlighting an apparent disconnect in perceptions.

Various approaches to improving safety culture have been described. Among them are leadership engagement via Leadership WalkRounds98 and a teamwork training curriculum developed by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, called Team Strategies and Tools to Enhance Performance and Patient Safety (TeamSTEPPS). The TeamSTEPPS intervention includes assessment, training, and sustainment phases focused on four core competencies: (1) team leadership, (2) situation monitoring, (3) mutual support, and (4) communication.99 This approach has been used in multiple health care settings,100,101 including one reported intervention that included NICU providers and demonstrated an improvement in perceptions of teamwork.102

Another emerging aspect of care context is health care worker resilience, operationally often defined as the absence of burnout. Burnout describes a condition of fatigue, detachment, and cynicism resulting from prolonged high levels of stress.103 In the critical care setting, burnout rates may be consequent to high workload, frequent changes in technology and guidelines, and the emotional challenges of dealing with critically ill patients and their families. Severe burnout affects between a quarter and half of health care workers,103,104 and the COVID-19 pandemic has resulted in a substantial increase.105 Burnout has negative consequences for health care providers, organizations, and patient care (Box 5.3).

A systematic review identified that both organizational as well as individually focused interventions are effective in reducing physician burnout.106 A randomized controlled trial of an individual intervention program (WISER) using positive psychology tools delivered via cell phone to NICU health care workers demonstrated lasting benefits with regard to burnout, work-life balance, and depression among participants.107 Overall, context provides the soil in which quality improvement thrives or withers. Leadership recognition of these factors is critical; to provide high quality of care to our patients, we must also care for ourselves and our colleagues.

Reducing process variation (i.e., reducing the many ways we might act in a specific situation) has been a strategic component of quality improvement, going back to Shewhart. On a control chart, the width of the control boundaries (the upper and lower rates that capture the majority of all the rates) are an indication of process variation. When quality improvement is successful, one will see both an increase (or decrease) in rate and a tightening of the control boundaries.

### Outcomes

Outcomes are the end results of the clinical care delivery process and represent what patients, families, and providers truly care about. Pragmatically, outcomes can be a reduction in negative events such as a decrease in the rates of death and morbidity or an increase in the rates of positive events such as breast milk on discharge or antenatal steroid use. For an outcome to serve as an effective quality indicator, it must be malleable; that is, there must be strong evidence that variations in process or structure can change its occurrence. A widely used outcome measure is health care–associated infections or their more specific cousin,

### Balancing Measures

When teams work on improving one aspect of care, it is possible that related outcomes suffer; for example, a decrease in growth velocity may be observed with a focus on improving breast milk feeding rates. Balancing measures may include clinical, service, or cost outcomes. These balancing measures should be collected in or close to real time to detect any unintended consequences of quality improvement projects. Although traditionally balancing measures were developed to assess potential adverse effects of improvement activities, they can also show that the new way of doing things is safe.

### Risk Adjustment/Fair Comparisons

For performance assessment within an organization whose patient demographics are stable over time, tracking a process or outcome measure over time may be sufficient to

spur quality improvement activities and assess their impact. However, for comparative performance assessments between organizations, as currently applied for purposes such as setting benchmarks, pay-for-performance, or public reporting, further statistical and methodological considerations are required to ensure fair comparisons.

The use of risk adjustment levels the playing field by accounting for expected rates of positive or negative outcomes based on the risk profiles (case mix) seen at each institution. Expectation is pivotal to the notion of quality, which can be operationally defined as the degree to which the observed rate of an outcome or process is higher, lower, or equal to its expected rate.23 An observed rate of morbidity that is higher than the expected rate indicates that there is an opportunity for quality improvement. Does hospital A with an observed neonatal mortality rate (NMR) of 5 provide better care than hospital B with an observed NMR of 10? Without knowing the expected rate of mortality at these two hospitals, it is impossible to assess their relative quality of care. For example, hospital B might be a tertiary care center, in which an observed NMR of 10 is much lower than its expected NMR of 18. Hospital A could be a primary care hospital, in which an observed NMR of 5 is much higher than its expected NMR of 3.

Mathematically, risk-adjustment methods level the playing field using one of the variants of multivariate regression. Typically based on data on risks and outcomes from multiple institutions, an estimate of the impact of each of the risk factors considered to be important to the outcome is used to create an expectation model. The model can then generate the expected outcome of a NICU based on its specific case mix.

The factors used in risk adjustment for neonatal quality assessment will encompass both maternal sociodemographic and clinical factors, as well as infant factors. Two essential requirements guide variable selection: (1) the variable should be a risk factor for the outcome of interest, and (2) the variable should not be under the control of the entity being evaluated. Mother’s age, education, payer for delivery, and perinatal complications, as well as the infant’s birth weight, gestational age, plurality, intrauterine growth, birth defects, and gender, are risk factors that are commonly used as risk adjusters to control for institutional differences in case mix so as to make fair comparisons across NICUs.23,91 They are highly predictive of morbidity and mortality and are not under the control of clinicians in the NICU. Using this approach to quality assessment, the ratio of the observed number of deaths (or adverse outcomes) to the expected number of deaths (or adverse outcomes), the standardized mortality (or morbidity) ratio (SMR), can then be calculated.

In addition to reporting the SMR as a measure of performance, an alternative approach is to calculate the difference between the observed and expected number of cases (O– E), where the expected number can be determined using the same regression approach described earlier.
