### Data Sources Administrative Data

In addition to data collected specifically for the purpose of quality improvement, the use of currently available data such as hospital administrative data and vital records data may allow for increased data capture and efficiency. We refer to this repurposed data as green data. Secondary datasets that have been used to evaluate quality of care include the uniform hospital discharge database (which captures diagnostic, procedural, and costs data), birth certificate files, and death certificates files. Although these administrative databases were not primarily designed for evaluating perinatal care, they contain data elements that have made it possible to examine risk-adjusted perinatal complication rates,132 maternal morbidities,133 cesarean delivery,134 and neonatal readmission rates.135 However, secondary data sources do have several disadvantages. They may not have all of the desired data items, and definitions might not be the same as those used in NICU databases. Underreporting may be significant.136 For example, congenital anomalies are markedly underreported on both birth and death certificates.137

Because both clinical and administrative databases vary with respect to the extent of their maternal, neonatal, morbidity, and mortality, as well as important sociodemographic data, the linkage of multiple datasets is a strategy to obtain a more comprehensive picture of perinatal risks and outcomes at the regional, community, and hospital level.136,138 Examples of population-based studies using a linked database include the relationship between discharge timing after birth and infant readmission,135 risk factors and neonatal outcomes,132 neonatal outcomes in childbearing beyond the age of 40,139 factors associated with the birth of infants with very low birth weight at non-NICU hospitals,140 trends in cesarean delivery for various conditions,141,142 and quality assessment of perinatal regionalization.143

The use of secondary data can also provide a highly efficient approach to building a complete quality improvement reporting system. The California Maternal Quality Care Collaborative (CMQCC, www.cmqcc.org) provides hospitals close to real-time (within 45 days from discharge) data based on linking the infant’s birth certificate to the mother’s and the infant’s discharge ICD-10 codes. In addition to perinatal quality metrics, the CMQCC also provides a near real-time assessment of data quality as part of an ongoing initiative to improve its administrative data sources. The reports also contain confidential drill-down analyses in order to identify ways to improve performance. For example, if there was an increase in early-term elective delivery for a hospital (Fig. 5.4), then one could examine cases over a period of time to check if there are certain diagnoses that may be contributing to an increase in the elective delivery rate. The rate of elective delivery can also be calculated by a provider to see if there are opportunities to work with individuals who may be contributing most to an increased rate. A demonstration site with artificial data is available at https ://demo.datacenter.cmqcc.org.

### Clinical Data

When data are collected primarily for the purpose of quality assessment, computer-based data entry systems using local or web-based data entry interfaces allow for efficiency in checking for errors such as missing fields or out-of-range entries. An advantage of these systems is that they detect errors in completeness, range, and consistency as the data are being abstracted and entered. The result is a clean record at the point of data entry that avoids costly offsite error detection and correction cycles.144

However, in carrying out a quality improvement initiative, it is often necessary to collect your own primary process, balancing, and outcome measures, as well as patient characteristics (if risk adjustment is needed). Data collection is always time consuming, so it is important to collect the minimal number of data elements needed to assess whether or not interventions are working. Incorporating data collection into the workflow can also lessen the burden. Data elements should be clearly and systematically defined, using universal or published definitions to enable comparison with other hospitals working on the same quality issue or published results.

Obtaining data from the electronic health record is an extremely efficient technique; however, it is crucial that the definitions that your hospital use in the electronic record are standardized across everyone who enters data and are based on widely recognized criteria. Unless all entities use the same definition, an objective and consistent assessment within and across NICUs may not be possible from electronic medical record data. For example, if the diagnosis of patent ductus arteriosus differs across individual NICUs, then comparisons of the incidence or the effects of treatment will be meaningless.

In addition to its potential to provide data to inform quality improvement, the electronic health record can also

### Qualitative Data

Because not everything that counts can be counted, qualitative techniques are an important set of tools that can provide practitioners with valuable insights regarding the design, execution, and outcome of quality improvement interventions. These techniques may include strategic informant interviews, focus groups, written evaluations, and observations directly or by video.145 These tools may unearth aspects of care that may not be readily collected in the medical record by capturing the “voice of the customer,” such as a parent’s ability to speak up in order to promote safety for their child in the NICU.146

During a quality improvement initiative or in the evaluation phase, qualitative research can help to discern which aspects of a project were the key drivers of change and what steps might be taken for similar subsequent projects.

Although the subject matter and aim of the project may differ, there may be common barriers and facilitators for implementation in quality improvement projects. A summary of such findings undertaken in three different projects (maternal hemorrhage, breast milk nutrition for preterm infants, delivery room management) is shown in Table 5.3.147–149

Evaluation of these data can be labor intensive in a research environment, but quality improvement teams can often rapidly extract meaningful and useable information. When there is a deficiency in care or perhaps when things are going well from a quality perspective, these approaches may help us to better understand the reasons underlying the results. When planning a quality improvement initiative, searching out and learning from similar studies that also describe the qualitative aspects of their journey can contribute greatly to the planning and success of your initiative. These tools also offer a great opportunity to involve family partners along the improvement journey.

### Data for Selection

A rising demand exists for transparency and public reporting of quality in health care with the goal to spur consumer choice, allow for performance-based reimbursement, and motivate better care. In other areas of medicine, public release of information on quality has been on the rise (http:// www.cms.gov/Medicare/Quality-Initiatives-Patient-Assessment-Instruments/HospitalQualityInits/OutcomeMeasure s.html), and this can be expected in neonatology as well.

U.S. News & World Report releases annual rankings of children’s hospitals and subspecialties, including neonatology. The ranking methodology is based on Donabedian’s structure, process, outcomes model, with points assigned for meeting each criterion (https://health.usnews.com/besthospitals/pediatric-rankings/neonatal-care). Expert opinion traditionally also represented an additional component, but its influence has decreased with the advent of quantitative data. Little is known regarding the validity of these rankings. Many variables have only face validity to support their use. Nevertheless, these rankings are important to hospital administrators who use them for advertising. The focus on optimizing these rankings may have positive and negative effects. Positive aspects include hospitals dedicating resources to support care structure and quality improvement activities based on measured priorities. Negative aspects include a potential misalignment between hospital leadership focus and NICU priorities. Furthermore, one can expect that hospitals will game their data given the reputational value.

The Leapfrog Group (http://www.leapfroggroup.org/), a consortium of Fortune 500 companies, provides hospitalspecific performance data to the public. Although measurement of perinatal care is limited, the group does provide a rating of quality of care for high-risk deliveries, defined as the care provided for VLBW infants. Neonatal teams must understand the strengths and weaknesses of different methods for making risk-adjusted comparisons of neonatal outcomes as they attempt to assist the public in understanding these data and to use the data themselves to monitor, evaluate, and improve the quality of care that they provide.

One of the rationales for public reporting of health care quality is the concept that the existence of such reports motivates and influences providers and organizations to improve their quality of care. The Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (http://www.talkingquality.ahrq.gov/about. htm) has promoted the use of public reporting and guided its implementation for many organizations. Although there needs to be continued research on the impact of public reporting on health care quality, thus far results are mixed. Public reports do not appear to inform consumer choice significantly, and improvements in quality measures are moderate at best.151 Consumer Reports (www.consumerre ports.org) is another consumer-oriented organization that presents hospital quality assessments.

These sources have not been well validated and have shown results that conflict with other measurement tools.152 These publications generally use league tables (rank ordering of institutions) and can provide an idea of how one

center might compare with other similar centers for specific measures. However, the interpretation of league tables must be informed by the context of reliability of measurements, adequate risk adjustment, and consistency of results, as what may appear to be an orderly ranking may not ultimately denote significant differences among NICUs.153 For example, in a league table, the difference between a top and middle performer may not be clinically or statistically significant. Nevertheless, hospitals feature such ratings prominently in marketing their services, and substantial intramural efforts are devoted to maximizing ratings.

The use of public reporting for perinatal care is relatively underdeveloped; however, it may be an untapped strategy for improving quality. Women of childbearing age are among the most frequent users of the Internet, and pregnancy is the featured topic of many websites geared toward this group.154–157 Studies have shown that women in general, and specifically expectant and current mothers, view the Internet as a way to connect to other women having similar experiences and to share information with one another,158–163 so that each woman who finds a public reporting website useful may communicate that experience to others. Some providers may feel that the development of well-designed public reporting websites that provide quality data on maternal and neonatal measures ensures their consumer relevance, accuracy, and fairness, and some rating websites are beginning to include these measures already in their hospital portals. For example, Yelp is now showing several perinatal indicators as a standard feature (Fig. 5.6).

### National Quality Measures

Interest in quality assessment continues to increase for perinatal medicine. An important development in ensuring that proposed measures can actually reflect the quality of care has been the work of the National Quality Forum (NQF; www.qualityforum.org), a multi-stakeholder group that evaluates proposed quality measures. In considering measures, several important areas are assessed, including the importance of the measure to making significant gains in health care quality, the reliability and validity of the measure, the extent to which the results can be understood and be useful for decision making, and the feasibility of collection. The Joint Commission published a list of core perinatal measures in 2007. A list of current measures from the NQF is noted in Table 5.4. When considering a potential measure for widespread use, it is important to have evidence that the aspect of care that the measure reflects has been shown to be malleable—that is, shown to be improvable in at least one multi-institutional quality improvement initiative.

As the list of quality measures continues to grow, it may become overwhelming for stakeholders, including clinicians, payers, and consumers, to extract a meaningful global picture of quality-of-care delivery at a given NICU. In addition, Profit demonstrated that correlations between quality measures of the care provided to VLBW infants are generally weak, meaning that it is difficult to infer overall qualityof-care delivery based on a small subset of clinical measures. Strategies for global assessments of quality may provide a more comprehensive assessment.164 We explore two of these in the next section.

### Data for Improvement

Although we have so far discussed the collection and presentation of data for provider selection, the active work of quality improvement requires different considerations. First, as the purpose of data collection for quality improvement is geared toward identifying potential areas of need and tracking change as soon as possible, there may be a lower threshold for identifying what might be considered an outlying value. In other words, data that are “good enough” to expose areas sorely in need for improvement may be better than waiting for “perfect” data. Second, there may be additional demands for data collection. Although some of the data sources noted in the preceding may allow for facilitation of quality improvement activities to some extent, there are several other aspects of data necessary for active quality improvement or data collections that may allow a specific question in quality improvement to be answered.

When data are analyzed for the purposes of benchmarking and comparisons, historical data that are collected over a stable period of time may be optimal. However, amid an effort to improve quality for specific processes or outcomes, data will need to be collected and presented in or close to real time.

A strategic aspect of data collection for quality improvement may be the need for additional process measures to be collected. For example, in an effort to increase temperature

of very preterm infants at delivery, several important variables could contribute to this effort, including delivery room temperature, use of devices such as plastic wrap or a chemical warming mattress, and use of a checklist or noting of adequate team communication before delivery. Another example could be a project to reduce central line infections, in which the team may want to collect data on whether a line insertion or maintenance checklist is being followed, number of line days, and whether the line necessity is being assessed regularly. Although temperature and the presence of an infection may already be part of real-time data collection, the other data elements may not be typically collected or even noted in the medical record in a systematic fashion. During the quality improvement project, the additional data may be collected to facilitate the quality improvement cycle and identify areas for improvement.

When several groups participate together in a collaborative to improve quality, a database program may serve as a common data repository and serve several useful purposes. First, it allows for the systematic collection of data in real time and for the specific purpose of the quality improvement project. Second, it allows each center to assess how it is doing compared with other groups and therefore to identify areas for improvement. Third, it can give insight into what processes may be most important to the main outcome of interest for the quality improvement project.

An essential purpose of data assessment of provider performance is to serve as an agent for change. To fulfill this purpose, data must be available in a timely manner. Data that are too old cannot inform decision-making reliably. To meet this need, data reports have been evolving from fixed, periodic (e.g., annual) reports to more flexible reporting that also allows for user choice in measures presented, time period, comparison groups, and type of presentation. Both the VON and the CPQCC provide users with secure real-time access to customizable data queries that allow for monitoring of trends over time and benchmarking against peer groups. Although the user can take advantage of the multiple features for selection of data presentation, there is also the option of monitoring performance across multiple measures on interactive dashboards (Fig. 5.7A–F). This dashboard shows case mix–adjusted individual NICU performance in comparison to its peers. CPQCC now also displays a health equity dashboard that allows users to view performance on multiple equity-sensitive process and outcome measures by race/ethnicity (Fig. 5.7F). Each metric is shown with regard to the performance difference between the best and worst performing subgroups.

Run charts and standardized process control (SPC) charts (Fig. 5.7E) are powerful tools for quality improvement.165 A run chart displays a series of data according to a criterion, usually time. Time is recorded on the x-axis, and the quality indicator is shown on the y-axis. This simple run chart can provide important insights regarding trends and variation in the process that results in the quality indicator. ### Global Assessments of Perinatal Quality: The Baby-MONITOR

Another method to cut through the thicket of individual quality measures is to combine them meaningfully into a composite indicator. To simplify the presentation of quality assessment, a composite quality rating may ultimately serve as a simple way to quickly assess quality. Composite indicators of quality are aggregates of individual measures of quality. Numerous choices have to be made by developers with regard to measure selection, definition, weighting, and aggregation phases. These choices require that development of composite indicators proceeds in an explicit, systematic, and transparent manner, and that the impact of the developers’ choices on NICU performance ratings is subjected to sensitivity analysis.

The Baby-MONITOR is an attempt at providing such a simplified global assessment tool. The composite is an aggregate of nine measures of quality routinely collected by members of the VON and the CPQCC. The nine measures were selected by an expert panel and validated by a sample of clinicians.166,167 Quality measures are risk adjusted, standardized by calculating an observed minus expected event difference, and equally weighted and averaged. The measure has been robust to sensitivity analyses invoking different aggregation and weighting schemes. Subsequent use has shown large variation across California NICUs by level of care168 and by race/ethnicity.43 National use of the Baby- MONITOR in VON data similarly revealed disparities,

Through a more holistic focus, composite measurement may provide an incentive for NICUs to engage in systems-based quality improvement efforts that have the potential to affect multiple aspects of quality simultaneously. In addition, it may facilitate discussions with other stakeholder groups on quality of care. Without a comprehensive quality assessment tool, external stakeholders may increasingly subject NICUs to piecemeal appraisals that may not do justice to their overall performance.

### Quality and Safety Applied

The previous sections have focused on the history, theoretical frameworks, models, and data necessities that underpin quality improvement work, at either the individual unit or the health system level. Neonatology has been at the vanguard of the quality improvement field. Experimentation and refinement of applied methods occur in a large variety of formats. Neonatal providers undertake improvement work at the individual unit level and in collaboration with

vast networks. Formats include in-person or web-based collaboration, and methods for improvement use quantitative as well as qualitative techniques. For improvement work to be effective, a few principles deserve explicit recognition.

### Interdisciplinary Collaboration

NICU care is rarely the sole purview of any one discipline, and most care is complex, requiring a multidisciplinary approach. Nursing, the therapies (respiratory therapy, physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy), pharmacy, and social work are the most common disciplines in addition to medicine that provide direct care to neonates. Nursing provides the majority of direct care to infants, so their involvement in quality improvement is essential. Efforts to address common quality improvement problems in neonatal care such as thermoregulation, unplanned extubation, nosocomial infection, medication errors, or skin breakdown are considered nurse-sensitive indicators of quality; thus neonatal quality improvement work should include partnerships with nursing to identify the problem, gather data, and trial solutions.171

### Families as Quality Improvement Partners

Another key partnership in quality improvement work that is not explicit in the frameworks and models described above involves the parents/guardians and other primary caregivers. Not only do families contribute to the quality and safety of their individual infants by contributing key observations and participating in daily care, but they can also contribute at a unit and institutional level to the quality improvement program, providing the perspective of “lived experience,” along with the patients. The Agency for Healthcare Quality (AHRQ; https://www.ahrq.gov/patientsafety/patients-families/engagingfamilies/index.html) published evidence-based guidelines and a toolkit to enable patients, families, and health professionals to work together as partners to promote improvements in care. Over the past decades, the NICU has become a leader in engaging families in improvement work (Box 5.4).172

In addition, the most valuable neonatal quality improvement endeavor that a hospital can embark on is the implementation or expansion of family-centered care (FCC) initiatives. In the NICU, parents should be regarded as essential care providers and significant members of their baby’s medical team. Because of the symbiotic nature of the parent-child relationship, parental involvement has been shown to improve overall health outcomes for both parents and babies, a priority and natural outcome of successful FCC. Moreover, FCC has been proven to facilitate bonding and cognitive development and to positively impact the mental health of the mother-baby dyad. When adopted consistently, FCC can empower and encourage patient families on their NICU journeys.173

A multidisciplinary team composed of a physician champion, a neonatal nurse practitioner, a nurse, a respiratory therapist, and a parent advisor was formed.74 The team developed the following aim statement: “To reduce the inadvertent extubation rate in infants in the Newborn Center by 50% within 12 months.” Inadvertent extubations were defined as those not ordered by a physician or nurse practitioner.

The team began with a brainstorming session, in which members considered factors that contributed to inadvertent extubations. All ideas were collected and grouped in themes, such as baby, device, method, caregiver, and procedure. These themes were then graphed in a fishbone diagram (Fig. 5.9) for clarity. Factors were then assessed with regard to whether they were amenable to intervention and with regard to their likely importance as contributors to inadvertent extubations. A resulting small set of factors was extracted, and over the course of the next several weeks the team followed up each inadvertent extubation with a key informant interview (usually the bedside nurse present during the extubation). Results were tallied and graphed in

a Pareto chart (Fig. 5.10). Based on this information, the team developed a driver diagram (Fig. 5.11), a version of a cause-and-effect diagram, which clarified the team’s perceived linkages among the overall aim, key change strategies for achieving the aim, and change hypotheses. The change strategies were introduced in successive PDSA cycles.

The primary outcome measure was the number of inadvertent extubations per 100 ventilator days. The team recognized several barriers to change, including staff resistance to the new securement method and concern regarding increased mobility of the endotracheal tube with this device, as well as its cost. Because of the recognition of potential risks of fewer inadvertent extubations, such as prolonged intubation, several balancing measures, including the number of days on nasal continuous positive airway pressure and the rate of chronic lung disease, were followed. These measures were already being collected as part of the NICU’s membership in the VON.

The planned interventions were presented to the service, revised as needed, and approved for implementation. A staff education plan was devised and implemented. Small cycles of change were used to further refine process details. A process control chart was set up (Fig. 5.12), and caregivers received intermittent project updates. As can be gleaned from Fig. 5.12, introduction of the securement device led to a further spike in extubation rates beyond the control limit, indicating special cause variation. The new baseline is displayed. After successive implementation of the change ideas, extubation rates dropped substantially (again, special cause variation), prompting another resetting of the baseline. After these initial successes, a renewed deterioration in inadvertent extubation rates occurred when caregiver attention was diverted by the introduction of a new electronic health record. This period spotlights a common concern for quality improvement practitioners—the difficulty of holding the gains, which brings us to our next section.

### Sustainability

Although there are now many examples of successful quality improvement projects, less is known about sustainability, particularly after resource-intensive projects. The goal to sustain improvement may rely on two potential strategies. One is to design an intervention such that new processes are seamlessly integrated into unit workflows and do not rely on extra effort by staff. Another approach may be to create a culture of improvement rather than just focusing on the intervention itself, where improvement becomes “the way we do things around here.” Quality improvement, as with many other skills, may benefit from practice and experience. Indeed, hospitals participating in a CMQCC project had greater improvement if they had experience participating in a previous quality improvement project.174

a few potential strategies that could be tested. One may be to “wean down” from a complete intervention to a lighter version, such as reducing the set of measurements to a minimal set needed to track progress. Another strategy could be to keep motivation going by holding periodic staff gettogethers in order to celebrate accomplishments. Building quality improvement capacity is critical to sustaining a culture of ongoing improvement, engagement, and sustainability. Allowing staff to channel their frontline expertise into improvement promotes Deming’s vision of the improvement journey. Sustainability is an active topic of quality improvement research, bringing us to our next section.

### Quality Improvement as a Tool to Address Health Disparities

Despite striving for improvement for all patients, unconscious bias and structural racism permeate all aspects of society, including our health care system; thus quality improvement initiatives have the potential to perpetuate or widen health disparities.177 However, with an explicit focus on improving outcomes for groups experiencing a disparity, quality improvement initiatives may reduce these disparities. Equity-focused quality improvement offers an actionoriented, inclusive framework whereby equity is integrated throughout the design and implementation of a quality improvement initiative, from the development of a SMART Aim approach to designing and testing change ideas.178

Stratifying local data by sociodemographic variables, such as race, ethnicity, preferred language, or insurance status, is a critical first step to identify a disparity. When interpreting stratified data, teams explicitly discuss what the specific sociodemographic variable represents. For example, if data are stratified by race/ethnicity, discussions should focus on how race is a social construct and a proxy for racism and social determinants of health. Comparator groups are then selected based on specific criteria, such as population size or performance on a specific metric. Data can be compared within a NICU or between NICUs using local, regional, or national data.

Stakeholder mapping is inclusive and centers around patients, families, and community voices. Eliciting the “voice of the customer” through informal interviews and surveys informs initiative design, planning, and implementation. Stakeholders brainstorm root causes, specifically examining modifiable systems and processes, including racism and bias in health care systems and policies. Interventions are selected, prioritized, designed, and tested, targeting specific barriers and needs of the groups experiencing disparities. Data visualization tools are adapted to display and monitor disparity trends over time. Results are made easily accessible and disseminated to all stakeholders, including patients and community stakeholders. A case example can be found in Box 5.6.

However, the dissemination and implementation of evidence-based practices are not always easy. It has been noted that the time required for new knowledge generated by clinical trials to be incorporated into general practice may be 17 years.179 Therefore one could argue that the study of the translation of evidence into practice is a crucial subsequent step in maximizing and expediting the impact of the discoveries made in clinical trials.180 The study of quality improvement activities may sometimes not be amenable to a traditional trial, and such a trial may not be the optimal approach. Nevertheless, rigorous research is needed to avoid the adoption of inferior or ineffective practices in the name of quality improvement.

Quality improvement research and implementation science share related aims and methods but are in some ways quite distinct. Both approaches aim to improve health care quality; however, quality improvement has usually focused on a specific problem of poor performance in relation to existing standards, addressing safety issues, or reducing adverse outcomes in a specific health care clinical setting. In contrast, implementation science has usually been focused more upstream to explore and explain underutilization of evidence-based practices or technologies or overutilization/misutilization of ineffective practices (e.g., de-implementation). Implementation science has an explicit aim of developing generalizable knowledge beyond the individual unit, institution, or system. Quality improvement research is often aimed at informing local or within-region or system practices. Implementation science and quality improvement research approaches are effective when applied synergistically. For example, quality improvement research may identify that there is underutilization of neonatal interventions. Implementation science research will explore the potential barriers and enablers to uptake and sustainment of the practices and lead to a series of further

studies to test interventions based on theories of behavior or systems change. When the research has demonstrated an effective implementation strategy, ongoing quality improvement monitoring will inform the sustained impact of the practices.181

The importance of publishing and therefore disseminating the results of quality improvement projects has been recognized by the pediatric community, and several journals publish such reports. Another recognition by the broader medical community of the importance of quality improvement research has been the formation of the Standards for Quality Improvement Reporting Excellence (SQUIRE) guidelines (Table 5.5). These guidelines and their 2.0 iteration were established to promote rigor in designing and reporting quality improvement research.182 Although the usual conventions for publishing scientific papers largely apply, the SQUIRE guidelines recognize several relatively unique aspects of quality improvement research. First, although a rigorous clinical trial requires prespecification of patient groups and interventions, the course of a quality improvement study may be somewhat dynamic. Improvement strategies may be modified in response to feedback from the ongoing project. The results of a clinical trial are “hidden” until the end of the study to avoid bias and change of behavior from the investigators. On the other hand, the clinicians involved in a quality improvement project may continuously try to learn from the contextual environment and ongoing results and subsequently modify their behavior to increase the impact of the intervention.

For the mentioned reasons, Berwick183 has referred to randomized controlled trials as being “an impoverished way to learn” in the context of quality improvement, suggesting that learning from experience “while doing” can be an important part of improving the quality of care. In a simulation study comparing “learning” and putting into practice findings from significant randomized trials only versus quality improvement collaborative projects, the quality improvement model was found to be a potentially superior approach.184

In addition to the aspect of learning while doing, a patient-level randomization study for quality improvement may not be feasible, as improvement activities on intervention subjects in a single NICU are likely to contaminate the control group. Approaches such as cluster randomization or stepped wedge designs may be better suited for experimental studies of quality improvement.185,186 The Canadian Neonatal Network conducted a cluster randomized trial of 12 NICUs in which half of the units focused on nosocomial infections and the other half focused on reducing bronchopulmonary dysplasia rates.187 Although bronchopulmonary dysplasia was reduced only in the corresponding group, nosocomial infections decreased in both groups. Their findings may suggest that quality improvement activities in one area may also influence quality in other areas, making the interpretation of such trials challenging. ### Quality and Safety in the International Context

Although this chapter has focused on some of the quality work done in the United States, similarly sophisticated regional and national collaborative networks, as well as quality efforts by individual NICUs, are underway throughout the world. The quality improvement aims in many high- and upper-middle-income countries are reductions in neonatal morbidities and improving the value and experience of care, such as those outlined in the United States. However, the quality improvement aims in many low- and lower-middle-income countries (LMICs) remain focused on reducing neonatal mortality rates. Although access to care, including delivery in a health facility, remains a challenge in many LMIC settings, access to care is no longer viewed as a priority competing with quality of care by those implementing newborn health programs globally.189 The international community is focused on improving care and inequities in health outcomes for infants and their families, by targeting Sustainable Development Goal 3.2 to end preventable deaths of newborns and to reduce the global neonatal mortality rate to 12 or fewer per 1000 live births in all countries by 2030.190 However, based on progress to date, it is predicted that many countries in Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa will not reach these goals without an enhanced focus on equity, quality of perinatal and essential newborn care, and improved institutional care for small or sick newborns and their families.191

The World Health Organization (WHO) recognizes their key position in establishing standards for improving the quality of maternal and newborn care in health facilities,192 the care for small and sick newborns in health facilities,193 communicating human resource strategies to improve newborn care in health facilities in LMICs,194 and recommending maternal and newborn care for a positive postnatal experience.195 The second edition of the WHO Essential Newborn Care Course is included in WHO resources that integrate quality improvement discussion points and reflection questions into WHO’s foundational materials for the essential care of every newborn used by health care providers worldwide (https://www.w ho.int/tools/essential-newborn-care-training-course).196 These standards and seminal documents are necessary for a culture change in neonatal care, embracing the notion that daily improvements in care are at the core of our work as health care professionals. However, in order to operationalize standards and identify and quantify gaps in care, we must also establish systems that allow interrogation of the “Know-Do gap,” the difference between providers’ knowledge of appropriate care and the care they actually provide in a clinical encounter.197,198 Without data, health care providers and the systems they work in are powerless to improve the care they provide, learn from their own practice, collaborate effectively with peer facilities, or advocate successfully for the resources they need.199,200

The power and excitement of collaborative quality improvement, key ingredients to maximize sustainability, often come from the development of community. Many neonatal units have found value in joining international neonatal networks or peer learning communities, such as VON. Recognizing that the trajectory to reach global neonatal improvement targets in resource-limited settings will be dependent on initiatives led by LMIC clinicians and experts, VON has proudly worked with Ethiopian leaders to co-develop quality improvement education and tools to serve as the foundation for the Ethiopian Neonatal Network.201 Building on these efforts and momentum, VON is partnering with the African Neonatal Association to develop an African peer learning community with a foundation of a co-designed data system and quality improvement strategy, harmonizing when possible and collaborating with

Although there are many barriers along the path to facility-level data in an LMIC setting, much progress has been made, and future projects can build upon these successes and lessons learned. Indeed, a systematic accounting of improvement efforts that work and those that do not is necessary to leverage and spread existing knowledge, contributing to the community’s understanding of potentially better practices and the diverse environments in which they are implemented.

### Conclusion

Neonatal teams have been at the forefront of adapting and evolving industrial quality improvement methods.203 These efforts have yielded great benefits to infants requiring neonatal intensive care and their families. Quality and safety are emerging fields, and the supporting science is being developed. At its core, quality improvement endeavors are founded in experiential learning, but as rigor in methods advances, so does generalizability. Despite its relative youth, it is quality improvement that may hold the greatest hope for solving one of the most important issues of our time: health equity. We think the field will make a meaningful contribution in this area. Indeed, although more work needs to be done, the indication is that quality improvement work is, in fact, health equity work, as over the past decade disparity gaps have narrowed in many areas.204–207

title: Importance of Simulation in Neonatology

paragraphs.text: 6 Importance of Simulation in Neonatology
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Simulation has become a cornerstone of medical education and has its roots in the fundamental principles of “first do no harm” and “never the first time on a patient.” With the introduction of work hour rules, exposure to medical procedures and acute clinical situations has decreased significantly for trainees. Medical simulation provides a safe environment to practice repeatedly on mannequins and to master a technique before performing it for the first time on a patient. In the United States, there are approximately 400,000 preventable deaths and 3.5 million iatrogenic injuries causing disabilities every year.1 It has become ethically imperative to incorporate simulation into medical education.2 Simulation has become a reliable and proven tool to decrease errors in high reliability organizations and is now being enthusiastically embraced by the medical community. Simulation has become not just an effective tool but also an essential tool to mitigate errors and enhance safety. Learning is best facilitated when the learning opportunities are tailored to meet the needs of the learners. Training models that offer the same content in the same fashion to all learners (thus implying that competency can be attained and maintained simply by spending a particular, often arbitrary, amount of time at a task) fail to recognize that adults have different strengths, weaknesses, and life experiences and acquire and maintain different skills at different rates. Some characteristics of effective adult learning strategies include the following: • Focus on active rather than passive learning activities. • Integrate skill sets while performing under realistic
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: conditions. • Emphasize competency/proficiency (the ability to per-
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: form successfully) rather than compliance (adherence to rules, such as participation in an activity for a predetermined period of time). Simulation may be defined broadly as any exercise that allows an individual to experience a situation that, although not real, nevertheless generates authentic responses on his or her part.3 The best simulations realistically recreate the key
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: visual, auditory, and tactile cues of actual situations to provide experiences that closely mimic the conditions encountered when working in the real environment. Provision of these key cues creates a high level of fidelity to the real environment. Because of this degree of realism, those participating in the simulation respond as they would to a real-life situation; thus their performance during a simulated situation can be hypothesized to resemble what it would be in the real world. In general, the term simulation is typically reserved to describe comprehensive learning, assessment, and research/quality improvement activities that occur in realistic physical and virtual environments. Activities conducted in less pragmatic environments (case studies, roleplaying, and practice of one particular skill in isolation from other elements associated with that skill) may be better labeled as task training. By suspending their knowledge that they are working in a contrived situation, participants display knowledge, skills, and behaviors similar or identical to those manifest when working in the real environment. The closer the simulation mimics real life, the more likely the participant will be able to identify and address any weaknesses that become apparent. Identification and remediation of weaknesses is the raison d’être of simulation.
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: Even though medical simulation has existed in a very elemental form for centuries, other high reliability organizations have incorporated simulation in some form or another to increase operational safety in the past century. Edwin Link was the inventor of the first flight simulator in 1929; the “blue box” flight trainer was developed as a less expensive and safer method to learn to fly a plane.4 The army used these trainers after several aviation accidents in 1934. World War II saw an exponential increase in the use of these “blue boxes” and inspired other Link innovations. This simulation technology was adopted by civil aviation in 1955 and was required as an essential tool for recertification of commercial pilots’ licenses
paragraphs.heading: Nonmedical Simulation

paragraphs.text: by the Federal Aviation Administration. The 1950s were characterized by the birth of analog computers and alliance with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) in the 1960s, after the development of digital computers. This eventually led to the development of Apollo simulators that were the first to be fully digital. In the 1970s, the simulation technology was adopted by the field of power plants. The high number of reported deaths during flight training in the 1980s was the major impetus for extension of simulators to military aircrafts and naval submarines. By the 1990s, simulation was a standard form of training not just for the cockpit personnel but also for all the crew in the commercial airline industry. Despite the high cost of simulators, they have proven very cost-effective in terms of lives saved and flight equipment spared.4,5
paragraphs.heading: Nonmedical Simulation

paragraphs.text: The 1990s heralded the advent of high-resolution graphics in the gaming industry and creation of high-quality simulators, which became standard of training in high reliability organizations.
paragraphs.heading: Nonmedical Simulation

paragraphs.text: Medical simulation was first described as early as 800 BCE, when an Indian surgeon, Sushruta, had his students practice incisions, ligation, and suturing on pieces of leather, tissue, or lotus leaves.
paragraphs.heading: Medical Simulation

paragraphs.text: Prior to the advent of high-quality mannequins, actors were used to facilitate education in 1963. These actors were trained to portray different medical conditions. This eventually progressed to using “patient instructors,” where a patient with chronic stable findings was used to teach physical examination and diagnostic skills. This terminology was changed to standardized patients (SPs) and became an essential part of clinical examination in the 1990s.4
paragraphs.heading: Medical Simulation

paragraphs.text: The present-day mannequins have their origins in the 1960s, when plastic human torso models were used for mouth-to-mouth resuscitation and chest compressions. Over the years, these have now evolved into varying degrees of high-fidelity simulators from initially being task trainers.
paragraphs.heading: Medical Simulation

paragraphs.text: Much has been made of the importance of the concept of fidelity in simulation-based training in health care. Simulation fidelity is typically thought of in terms of its physical, biologic, and psychological elements. Physical fidelity refers to the realism of the physical space in which training occurs; this space is made to look real by including appropriate working medical equipment, fluids, pharmacologic agents, beds, and the other elements necessary for patient care. Biologic fidelity includes the patient simulators and SPs as well as human beings acting as confederates during the simulation, playing roles designed to assist the evolution of the scenario. Patient simulators have been described as high, medium, and low fidelity, but there is no standardized definition of simulator fidelity. In reality, no physical patient simulator currently in use bears close resemblance to
paragraphs.heading: Simulation-Based Training in Health Care

paragraphs.text: a human being, either in terms of anatomy or physiology. The use of the term high fidelity when describing the current generation of patient simulators more likely refers to high complexity or high cost rather than any intrinsic similarity to a living human being. Finally, all of the previously mentioned elements interact with the mindset brought into the scenario by the trainees to create a sense of realism or “psychological” fidelity. The overall goal of simulation-based training is to provide experiences that closely mimic the conditions encountered when working in the actual clinical environment. The major difference between the simulated environment and the real environment is the absence of live human patients. Although debate continues in the health care simulation community as to how much fidelity is necessary, some may argue that the higher the fidelity of the scenario to real life, the better the learning opportunity. It should be understood that as long as sufficient attention is paid to providing the key (not all) visual, auditory, and tactile cues for trainees, allowing them to form a shared mental model of the nature of the situation that they are facing, they will have the opportunity to work effectively to resolve the clinical problems that become manifest during the scenario and therefore achieve the learning objectives.6 This has been endorsed by the use of “low fidelity” mannequins in low-resource countries with improved early neonatal outcomes after delivery.7
paragraphs.heading: Simulation-Based Training in Health Care

paragraphs.text: This change in the learning paradigm incorporates the key skills of adult learning KSA philosophy (Knowledge, Skills, Attitude) • (K) Cognitive skills—What we know in our brains (con-
paragraphs.heading: Simulation-Based Training in Health Care

paragraphs.text: tent knowledge and decision making) • (S) Technical skills—What we do with our hands • (A) Behavioral skills—How we use the first two skill sets
paragraphs.heading: Simulation-Based Training in Health Care

paragraphs.text: while caring for patients and working under realistic time pressure with our colleagues
paragraphs.heading: Simulation-Based Training in Health Care

paragraphs.text: A simulation center has become an essential part of almost all medical and nursing schools; however, these centers are not easily accessible to trainees at the hospital. Nonacademic and smaller community hospitals have almost no access to large simulation centers yet are committed to providing education and high-quality medical care. It has become an expectation for all hospitals to provide some level of training to all medical personnel to enhance safety and teamwork. It is highly recommended that every team responding to deliveries and providing emergency care to newborns has some degree of ongoing simulation training. This could even be in the form of low-fidelity simulation.8,9
paragraphs.heading: Neonatal Simulation

paragraphs.text: Every residency and neonatology fellowship program should make every attempt to incorporate simulation in all aspects of training.10
paragraphs.heading: Neonatal Simulation

paragraphs.text: Approximately 4 million babies are born in the United States every year; only approximately 10% require some
paragraphs.heading: Simulation in the Delivery Room

paragraphs.text: degree of resuscitation, with 1% needing extensive resuscitative efforts such as chest compressions, intubation, or delivery of medication. The Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP) was established by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) in 1987 to standardize the care of the newborns in the delivery room. The initial paradigm of a didactic program evolved into one with emphasis on technical skills using suitable task trainers. Dr. Louis Halamek et al. can be credited for establishing and disseminating the realistic technique of learning via simulation in the field of neonatology.3 In 2010, the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation (ILCOR) noted that a number of studies had demonstrated that the use of simulation-based learning methodologies enhances performance during simulated resuscitations.
paragraphs.heading: Simulation in the Delivery Room

paragraphs.text: ILCOR recommends that simulation, briefing, and debriefing techniques should be used during training when caring for simulated patients and in the course of clinical activities involving real patients to facilitate the acquisition and maintenance of the skills necessary for effective neonatal resuscitation. This recommendation continues to remain in effect with the publication of the 2020 ILCOR guidelines.11
paragraphs.heading: Simulation in the Delivery Room

paragraphs.text: In the past 20 years, the NRP has undergone a major shift in learning methodology. Instructors are now required to shift their role from that of a teacher responsible for imparting knowledge to trainees, to that of a facilitator who fosters acquisition of skills by trainees as they accept primary responsibility for their own learning. The NRP Steering Committee also developed a list of the characteristics desired in a cost-effective human neonatal patient simulator and published this online in 2005 as a request for proposals to industry. This marked the first time in the history of health care simulation that a professional body, rather than industry, drove development of a realistic patient simulator based on established learning objectives. Since that time, a number of full-term and preterm neonatal patient simulators have been developed by several commercial companies, indicative of the growth of the simulator industry at large and the field of neonatal simulation in particular.
paragraphs.heading: Simulation in the Delivery Room

paragraphs.text: In 2004, The Joint Commission (JC) published in a Sentinel Event Alert that ineffective communication was a major cause in almost 75% of the 47 cases of neonatal mortality or severe neonatal morbidity (lifelong serious neurologic compromise) reported to that agency; since then, an additional 62 cases have been added.12 In response to these root cause analyses, The JC recommended that all health care organizations responsible for delivering newborns “conduct team training in perinatal areas to teach staff to work together and communicate more effectively” and “for high-risk events, such as shoulder dystocia, emergency cesarean delivery, maternal hemorrhage, and neonatal resuscitation, conduct clinical drills to help staff prepare for when such events actually occur, and conduct debriefings to evaluate team performance and identify areas for improvement.” This recommendation laid the foundation for emphasis on key behavioral skills during neonatal resuscitation (Box 6.1).
paragraphs.heading: Simulation in the Delivery Room

paragraphs.text: Inclusion of the obstetric team is essential for building teamwork. Although very limited data of combined obstetrics and neonatal (OB-NEO) simulation are available regarding neonatal outcomes, there are some emerging data from Southeast Asia which demonstrate a decrease in morbidity with this OB-NEO collaboration.13
paragraphs.heading: Simulation in the Delivery Room

paragraphs.text: There is unequivocal evidence in the obstetric literature that simulation lab training translates to improved outcome at the bedside.14 Some of the most convincing work published to date regarding the value of simulationbased training involves the reduction in the incidence of serious sequelae of shoulder dystocia after implementation of comprehensive simulation-based training. In the Obstetrics Emergency Training Program at Southmead Hospital, Bristol, United Kingdom, Draycott and colleagues used a variety of patient simulators in several simulated environments to show that simulation-based learning resulted in enhanced content knowledge and improved technical management of shoulder dystocia.15–18 In a retrospective multicenter cohort observational study of 19,460 infants, (1) the incidence of infants born with 5-minute Apgar scores of 6 or less decreased from 86.6 to 44.6 per 10,000 births (P < .001), and (2) encephalopathy decreased from 27.3 to 13.6 per 10,000 births (P < .032) over a 5-year period following the introduction of a training program consisting of a review of fetal heart rate tracings and hands-on drills in the management of shoulder dystocia, postpartum hemorrhage, eclampsia, twin delivery, breech presentation, and maternal and neonatal resuscitation. This work has been replicated and shown to produce similar improvements in clinically relevant outcomes, serving to document the value of rigorous immersive training.19
paragraphs.heading: Simulation in the Delivery Room

paragraphs.text: There is a growing body of evidence for improved teamwork, confidence of providers, and improved procedural skills in the delivery room during resuscitation; however, none of these has shown long-term retention of skills, which demonstrates the need for high-frequency simulations even if they are of short duration and even for experienced providers.20,21
paragraphs.heading: Simulation in the Delivery Room

paragraphs.text: Simulation has now moved from the delivery room to all aspects of neonatal care and medical care in general.22
paragraphs.heading: Simulation in Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: It is common practice to use simulation in varying degrees for all procedures, be they intubation, use of laryngeal mask airway, umbilical line placement, other central line placement, intraosseous needle placement, chest tube placement, paracentesis, or pericardiocentesis, among others. Opportunities to do actual procedures are extremely limited because of low frequency of most of these procedures and the added effect of work hour rules for the physician trainees.
paragraphs.heading: Simulation in Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: “Just in time” procedural practice (reviewing and practicing the procedure on a mannequin) is gaining popularity because it helps refresh the technique just prior to the procedure and helps boost the confidence of the learner. Readily available task trainers in the work areas are being used to review certain procedures (intubation, spinal tap, umbilical lines) during a planned procedure.23–25
paragraphs.heading: Simulation in Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: With the advent of single-room NICUs, new nurses have lost some of the continued mentorship of experienced nurses for bedside care. It has now become a growing practice for new nurses to perform intensive training through simulation, and there is a growing body of evidence in the nursing literature of its utility and effectiveness.26–29 Simulation continues to be used for improvement of skills and teamwork (e.g., extracorporeal membrane oxygenation [ECMO],34,36 reduction of central line infections, golden hour, and “small baby protocols”). It has also become an important part of education and is used in all aspects of patient safety and quality improvement endeavors as well as in neonatal transport.30–32,35 Simulation has also shown to be an effective tool to identify latent safety threats as demonstrated by Wong et al. during magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in neonatal patients.33
paragraphs.heading: Simulation in Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: Simulation techniques have also permeated the world of communication and are being used for antenatal consults and even for training fellows and residents for “difficult conversations” with patients and families. There is a growing trend toward also incorporating this technology for education of home caregivers for technology-dependent patients.22,37,38
paragraphs.heading: Simulation in Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

paragraphs.text: Helping Babies Breathe (HBB) is an educational program that was developed by the AAP in 2010 designed to decrease neonatal mortality in low-resourced countries and has proven to be a powerful model for simulation success, despite the fact that it is low fidelity. Since its implementation in more than 80 countries, meta-analysis has demonstrated an average consistent reduction in fresh stillbirths of 34% (odds ratio [OR] 0.66; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.52–0.85) and very early neonatal mortality an average of 30% (OR 0.70; 95% CI 0.51–0.98).39,40
paragraphs.heading: Simulation in Low-Resourced Areas

paragraphs.text: Innovative virtual trainings are now being proven effective in retaining knowledge when in-person training is not feasible.
paragraphs.heading: Simulation in Low-Resourced Areas

paragraphs.text: A debriefing is defined as a discussion of events that have already occurred and can be led by an individual or a group.
paragraphs.heading: Debriefing

paragraphs.text: This is in contrast to a briefing, which is held to discuss planned or future events. In debriefing of a health care team, the flow of information happens between the leader(s) and the members of the team, as well as among the members of the team. In contrast, feedback is the provision of information (from a person or a device) to a person in which the flow of that information is one way. Although not as interactive as a debriefing, it is important to note that not all learning requires the type of interaction typically ascribed to debriefing. For example, the acquisition and maintenance of a technical skill such as intubation do not require debriefing; rather, the provision of feedback as to appropriate finger and hand position on the laryngoscope and other aspects of intubation technique can be provided by an instructor experienced in intubation without the extensive interaction with trainees ascribed to debriefing.
paragraphs.heading: Debriefing

paragraphs.text: Much of the health care literature has been devoted to the theoretical underpinnings of debriefing, rather than actual practical strategies and techniques, and it has focused on relatively inexperienced trainees rather than experienced health care professionals. Most of the models described in the literature use a very similar approach consisting of three primary phases: 1. An individual trained in debriefing who is not a member
paragraphs.heading: Debriefing

paragraphs.text: of the team leads the discussion; 2. the discussion typically includes reaction, description,
paragraphs.heading: Debriefing

paragraphs.text: analysis, and summary phases; and 3. patient outcome is not routinely emphasized (and may
paragraphs.heading: Debriefing

paragraphs.text: actually be avoided if felt to potentially produce negative reactions in team members). This stands in contrast to how debriefing is conducted in other industries in which the risk to human life is high. In these industries, the emphasis of debriefing is on facts, not feelings, and objective outcomes, not subjective interpretations.3,41–45
paragraphs.heading: Debriefing

paragraphs.text: There are several techniques for debriefing, including Promoting Excellence and Reflective Learning in Simulation (PEARLS), the three-dimensional (3D) model, and the diamond method, to name just a few.46,47 It is not uncommon for experienced debriefers to use a blended model of the various techniques. The debriefing model adopted by the NRP originated at the Center for Advanced Pediatric and Perinatal Education (CAPE), located at Packard Children’s Hospital in California. The CAPE debriefing model focuses on the actions of the individual, how those actions contribute to the performance of the team, and ultimately how team performance influences the care of the patient, therefore aligning closely with debriefing methods used by aerospace, commercial aviation, and the military. In this model, the person(s) leading the debriefing draws the assessment of individual and team performance from the team members themselves as they evaluate patient outcome in response to their actions and objectively analyze those actions. Upon the conclusion of the debriefing, team members must understand how actions beneficial to the patient can be replicated and how any actions that were nonproductive or harmful can be avoided. The guiding principles
paragraphs.heading: Debriefing

paragraphs.text: and specific strategies that facilitate delivery of this model of debriefing are listed in Boxes 6.2 and 6.3, respectively.
paragraphs.heading: Debriefing

paragraphs.text: It is very important to understand the difference between a technical performance debriefing (used to assess human and system performance) and a critical incident stress debriefing (conducted to provide emotional/psychological support). A critical incident is defined as “an event that has the potential for people to experience significant physical, cognitive, emotional, and behavioral reactions immediately after the incident or days, weeks, months, and even sometimes years later.”48 If simulated clinical scenarios are welldesigned and the associated debriefings are conducted in an appropriate manner, a critical incident stress debriefing should very rarely be required; if it is, appropriate professional counseling should be arranged.
paragraphs.heading: Debriefing

paragraphs.text: Although several studies have not consistently shown clear benefits to the use of video during debriefing, it must be acknowledged that, for the cognitive, technical, and behavioral skills of the team members to be effectively debriefed, an accurate record of the display of those skills must be available.49–54 Reliance on memory alone to provide such an accurate record is dubious at best. The ability to display a video stream illustrating key viewing angles coupled with an audio stream that picks up communication among team members provides an objective record of events that is capable of effectively bridging any gap between team members’ memories and the actual facts of the scenario. Incorporating debriefing into significant clinical events/ resuscitations will help learners accept this methodology as a “routine” learning and reflective tool without the fear of any negative judgment or repercussions.55,56
paragraphs.heading: Debriefing

paragraphs.text: In situ simulations conducted in the actual clinical space are gaining popularity in the medical field, with definite benefits in terms of an authentic environment, readily available clinical staff who are actually present, easy availability of
paragraphs.heading: Simulation-Based Research and In Situ Simulation

paragraphs.text: multidisciplinary team, and minimal costs. It is particularly time efficient because the learners do not need to travel and the scenario and debriefing can be performed in minimal time. In situ simulation also comes with the added potential of identifying latent safety threats,57,58 be it availability of essential equipment, personnel, and communication, all the way to major issues such as the inability to operate critical equipment such as a defibrillator.
paragraphs.heading: Simulation-Based Research and In Situ Simulation

paragraphs.text: However, clinical space simulation has certain limitations for success, especially in the case of a high census and acuity and understandable reluctance of staff participation during
paragraphs.heading: Simulation-Based Research and In Situ Simulation

paragraphs.text: busy clinical times. The potential effect that these may have on families and visitors and the inability to video record because of privacy issues can also be a major deterrent.57–61
paragraphs.heading: Simulation-Based Research and In Situ Simulation

paragraphs.text: The key to successful in situ simulation lies in careful planning with well-established learning objectives and acceptance from multidisciplinary teams (nurses, physicians, nurse practitioners, and respiratory therapists). It may also be prudent to notify families and visitors of this educational session. There is evidence for improved interdisciplinary performance during in situ simulation in the delivery room.62–64
paragraphs.heading: Simulation-Based Research and In Situ Simulation

paragraphs.text: Simulation-based research in health care has focused on two major areas—assessing task trainers and using mannequins, and validating simulation-based training methodology and duration of persistence of this knowledge and skills. Unfortunately, because of the inherent nature of simulation, it is not easy to perform a prospective, randomized, controlled, sufficiently powered study because it would need a very large sample size to control for all the variances and multiple factors, including objective markers of cognitive, technical, and behavioral performances. It would also need long-term follow-up to evaluate the effect on patient outcomes.65 Most of the research is concentrated on validation of the various simulators as teaching tools. Regardless, because simulation is expensive, better-designed and larger
paragraphs.heading: Simulation-Based Research and In Situ Simulation

paragraphs.text: Key Points
paragraphs.heading: Simulation-Based Research and In Situ Simulation

paragraphs.text: • Simulation-based training is practicing doing the right
paragraphs.heading: Simulation-Based Research and In Situ Simulation

paragraphs.text: thing under realistic conditions. • Simulation should be incorporated into every aspect of
paragraphs.heading: Simulation-Based Research and In Situ Simulation

paragraphs.text: clinical care and quality improvement. • Standardized simulated clinical environments allow the
paragraphs.heading: Simulation-Based Research and In Situ Simulation

paragraphs.text: investigation of issues that are difficult to study in the real health care environment.
paragraphs.heading: Simulation-Based Research and In Situ Simulation

paragraphs.text: studies are needed to demonstrate the critical advantages of simulation. There are minimal data on cost-effectiveness of simulation and the outcomes related to cost. Innovations incorporating low-cost 3D-printed human models may prove to be fiscally relevant in the future.66–69 As of now, there is a dearth of evidence in neonatal literature demonstrating improved long-term patient outcomes as a result of simulation, although there are data demonstrating improved mortality in pediatric trauma patients in centers using simulation.70
paragraphs.heading: References

paragraphs.text: Research networks are traditional in every specialty but still in their infancy in neonatal simulation. Simulation research networks (SRN) have their foundation in the medical education network. There is promising potential for developing a neonatal SRN based on the blueprint of a very successful pediatric simulation network—International Network for Simulation-based Pediatric Innovation, Research, and Education (INSPIRE).71,72
