6 Importance of Simulation in Neonatology

### MONIKA BHOLA

### Introduction

Simulation has become a cornerstone of medical education and has its roots in the fundamental principles of “first do no harm” and “never the first time on a patient.” With the introduction of work hour rules, exposure to medical procedures and acute clinical situations has decreased significantly for trainees. Medical simulation provides a safe environment to practice repeatedly on mannequins and to master a technique before performing it for the first time on a patient. In the United States, there are approximately 400,000 preventable deaths and 3.5 million iatrogenic injuries causing disabilities every year.1 It has become ethically imperative to incorporate simulation into medical education.2 Simulation has become a reliable and proven tool to decrease errors in high reliability organizations and is now being enthusiastically embraced by the medical community. Simulation has become not just an effective tool but also an essential tool to mitigate errors and enhance safety. Learning is best facilitated when the learning opportunities are tailored to meet the needs of the learners. Training models that offer the same content in the same fashion to all learners (thus implying that competency can be attained and maintained simply by spending a particular, often arbitrary, amount of time at a task) fail to recognize that adults have different strengths, weaknesses, and life experiences and acquire and maintain different skills at different rates. Some characteristics of effective adult learning strategies include the following: • Focus on active rather than passive learning activities. • Integrate skill sets while performing under realistic

conditions. • Emphasize competency/proficiency (the ability to per-

form successfully) rather than compliance (adherence to rules, such as participation in an activity for a predetermined period of time). Simulation may be defined broadly as any exercise that allows an individual to experience a situation that, although not real, nevertheless generates authentic responses on his or her part.3 The best simulations realistically recreate the key

100

visual, auditory, and tactile cues of actual situations to provide experiences that closely mimic the conditions encountered when working in the real environment. Provision of these key cues creates a high level of fidelity to the real environment. Because of this degree of realism, those participating in the simulation respond as they would to a real-life situation; thus their performance during a simulated situation can be hypothesized to resemble what it would be in the real world. In general, the term simulation is typically reserved to describe comprehensive learning, assessment, and research/quality improvement activities that occur in realistic physical and virtual environments. Activities conducted in less pragmatic environments (case studies, roleplaying, and practice of one particular skill in isolation from other elements associated with that skill) may be better labeled as task training. By suspending their knowledge that they are working in a contrived situation, participants display knowledge, skills, and behaviors similar or identical to those manifest when working in the real environment. The closer the simulation mimics real life, the more likely the participant will be able to identify and address any weaknesses that become apparent. Identification and remediation of weaknesses is the raison d’être of simulation.

### History of Simulation

### Nonmedical Simulation

Even though medical simulation has existed in a very elemental form for centuries, other high reliability organizations have incorporated simulation in some form or another to increase operational safety in the past century. Edwin Link was the inventor of the first flight simulator in 1929; the “blue box” flight trainer was developed as a less expensive and safer method to learn to fly a plane.4 The army used these trainers after several aviation accidents in 1934. World War II saw an exponential increase in the use of these “blue boxes” and inspired other Link innovations. This simulation technology was adopted by civil aviation in 1955 and was required as an essential tool for recertification of commercial pilots’ licenses


## PDF page 120 | printed page 101

by the Federal Aviation Administration. The 1950s were characterized by the birth of analog computers and alliance with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) in the 1960s, after the development of digital computers. This eventually led to the development of Apollo simulators that were the first to be fully digital. In the 1970s, the simulation technology was adopted by the field of power plants. The high number of reported deaths during flight training in the 1980s was the major impetus for extension of simulators to military aircrafts and naval submarines. By the 1990s, simulation was a standard form of training not just for the cockpit personnel but also for all the crew in the commercial airline industry. Despite the high cost of simulators, they have proven very cost-effective in terms of lives saved and flight equipment spared.4,5

The 1990s heralded the advent of high-resolution graphics in the gaming industry and creation of high-quality simulators, which became standard of training in high reliability organizations.

### Medical Simulation

Medical simulation was first described as early as 800 BCE, when an Indian surgeon, Sushruta, had his students practice incisions, ligation, and suturing on pieces of leather, tissue, or lotus leaves.

Prior to the advent of high-quality mannequins, actors were used to facilitate education in 1963. These actors were trained to portray different medical conditions. This eventually progressed to using “patient instructors,” where a patient with chronic stable findings was used to teach physical examination and diagnostic skills. This terminology was changed to standardized patients (SPs) and became an essential part of clinical examination in the 1990s.4

The present-day mannequins have their origins in the 1960s, when plastic human torso models were used for mouth-to-mouth resuscitation and chest compressions. Over the years, these have now evolved into varying degrees of high-fidelity simulators from initially being task trainers.

### Simulation-Based Training in Health Care

Much has been made of the importance of the concept of fidelity in simulation-based training in health care. Simulation fidelity is typically thought of in terms of its physical, biologic, and psychological elements. Physical fidelity refers to the realism of the physical space in which training occurs; this space is made to look real by including appropriate working medical equipment, fluids, pharmacologic agents, beds, and the other elements necessary for patient care. Biologic fidelity includes the patient simulators and SPs as well as human beings acting as confederates during the simulation, playing roles designed to assist the evolution of the scenario. Patient simulators have been described as high, medium, and low fidelity, but there is no standardized definition of simulator fidelity. In reality, no physical patient simulator currently in use bears close resemblance to

a human being, either in terms of anatomy or physiology. The use of the term high fidelity when describing the current generation of patient simulators more likely refers to high complexity or high cost rather than any intrinsic similarity to a living human being. Finally, all of the previously mentioned elements interact with the mindset brought into the scenario by the trainees to create a sense of realism or “psychological” fidelity. The overall goal of simulation-based training is to provide experiences that closely mimic the conditions encountered when working in the actual clinical environment. The major difference between the simulated environment and the real environment is the absence of live human patients. Although debate continues in the health care simulation community as to how much fidelity is necessary, some may argue that the higher the fidelity of the scenario to real life, the better the learning opportunity. It should be understood that as long as sufficient attention is paid to providing the key (not all) visual, auditory, and tactile cues for trainees, allowing them to form a shared mental model of the nature of the situation that they are facing, they will have the opportunity to work effectively to resolve the clinical problems that become manifest during the scenario and therefore achieve the learning objectives.6 This has been endorsed by the use of “low fidelity” mannequins in low-resource countries with improved early neonatal outcomes after delivery.7

This change in the learning paradigm incorporates the key skills of adult learning KSA philosophy (Knowledge, Skills, Attitude) • (K) Cognitive skills—What we know in our brains (con-

tent knowledge and decision making) • (S) Technical skills—What we do with our hands • (A) Behavioral skills—How we use the first two skill sets

while caring for patients and working under realistic time pressure with our colleagues

### Neonatal Simulation

A simulation center has become an essential part of almost all medical and nursing schools; however, these centers are not easily accessible to trainees at the hospital. Nonacademic and smaller community hospitals have almost no access to large simulation centers yet are committed to providing education and high-quality medical care. It has become an expectation for all hospitals to provide some level of training to all medical personnel to enhance safety and teamwork. It is highly recommended that every team responding to deliveries and providing emergency care to newborns has some degree of ongoing simulation training. This could even be in the form of low-fidelity simulation.8,9

Every residency and neonatology fellowship program should make every attempt to incorporate simulation in all aspects of training.10

### Simulation in the Delivery Room

Approximately 4 million babies are born in the United States every year; only approximately 10% require some


## PDF page 121

degree of resuscitation, with 1% needing extensive resuscitative efforts such as chest compressions, intubation, or delivery of medication. The Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP) was established by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) in 1987 to standardize the care of the newborns in the delivery room. The initial paradigm of a didactic program evolved into one with emphasis on technical skills using suitable task trainers. Dr. Louis Halamek et al. can be credited for establishing and disseminating the realistic technique of learning via simulation in the field of neonatology.3 In 2010, the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation (ILCOR) noted that a number of studies had demonstrated that the use of simulation-based learning methodologies enhances performance during simulated resuscitations.

ILCOR recommends that simulation, briefing, and debriefing techniques should be used during training when caring for simulated patients and in the course of clinical activities involving real patients to facilitate the acquisition and maintenance of the skills necessary for effective neonatal resuscitation. This recommendation continues to remain in effect with the publication of the 2020 ILCOR guidelines.11

In the past 20 years, the NRP has undergone a major shift in learning methodology. Instructors are now required to shift their role from that of a teacher responsible for imparting knowledge to trainees, to that of a facilitator who fosters acquisition of skills by trainees as they accept primary responsibility for their own learning. The NRP Steering Committee also developed a list of the characteristics desired in a cost-effective human neonatal patient simulator and published this online in 2005 as a request for proposals to industry. This marked the first time in the history of health care simulation that a professional body, rather than industry, drove development of a realistic patient simulator based on established learning objectives. Since that time, a number of full-term and preterm neonatal patient simulators have been developed by several commercial companies, indicative of the growth of the simulator industry at large and the field of neonatal simulation in particular.

In 2004, The Joint Commission (JC) published in a Sentinel Event Alert that ineffective communication was a major cause in almost 75% of the 47 cases of neonatal mortality or severe neonatal morbidity (lifelong serious neurologic compromise) reported to that agency; since then, an additional 62 cases have been added.12 In response to these root cause analyses, The JC recommended that all health care organizations responsible for delivering newborns “conduct team training in perinatal areas to teach staff to work together and communicate more effectively” and “for high-risk events, such as shoulder dystocia, emergency cesarean delivery, maternal hemorrhage, and neonatal resuscitation, conduct clinical drills to help staff prepare for when such events actually occur, and conduct debriefings to evaluate team performance and identify areas for improvement.” This recommendation laid the foundation for emphasis on key behavioral skills during neonatal resuscitation (Box 6.1).

• BOX 6.1 Key Behavioral Skills

• Know your environment • Anticipate and plan • Assume the leadership role • Communicate effectively • Delegate workload optimally • Allocate attention wisely • Use all available information • Use all available resources • Call for help when needed • Maintain professionalism

Inclusion of the obstetric team is essential for building teamwork. Although very limited data of combined obstetrics and neonatal (OB-NEO) simulation are available regarding neonatal outcomes, there are some emerging data from Southeast Asia which demonstrate a decrease in morbidity with this OB-NEO collaboration.13

There is unequivocal evidence in the obstetric literature that simulation lab training translates to improved outcome at the bedside.14 Some of the most convincing work published to date regarding the value of simulationbased training involves the reduction in the incidence of serious sequelae of shoulder dystocia after implementation of comprehensive simulation-based training. In the Obstetrics Emergency Training Program at Southmead Hospital, Bristol, United Kingdom, Draycott and colleagues used a variety of patient simulators in several simulated environments to show that simulation-based learning resulted in enhanced content knowledge and improved technical management of shoulder dystocia.15–18 In a retrospective multicenter cohort observational study of 19,460 infants, (1) the incidence of infants born with 5-minute Apgar scores of 6 or less decreased from 86.6 to 44.6 per 10,000 births (P < .001), and (2) encephalopathy decreased from 27.3 to 13.6 per 10,000 births (P < .032) over a 5-year period following the introduction of a training program consisting of a review of fetal heart rate tracings and hands-on drills in the management of shoulder dystocia, postpartum hemorrhage, eclampsia, twin delivery, breech presentation, and maternal and neonatal resuscitation. This work has been replicated and shown to produce similar improvements in clinically relevant outcomes, serving to document the value of rigorous immersive training.19

There is a growing body of evidence for improved teamwork, confidence of providers, and improved procedural skills in the delivery room during resuscitation; however, none of these has shown long-term retention of skills, which demonstrates the need for high-frequency simulations even if they are of short duration and even for experienced providers.20,21

### Simulation in Neonatal Intensive Care Unit

Simulation has now moved from the delivery room to all aspects of neonatal care and medical care in general.22


## PDF page 122 | printed page 103

It is common practice to use simulation in varying degrees for all procedures, be they intubation, use of laryngeal mask airway, umbilical line placement, other central line placement, intraosseous needle placement, chest tube placement, paracentesis, or pericardiocentesis, among others. Opportunities to do actual procedures are extremely limited because of low frequency of most of these procedures and the added effect of work hour rules for the physician trainees.

“Just in time” procedural practice (reviewing and practicing the procedure on a mannequin) is gaining popularity because it helps refresh the technique just prior to the procedure and helps boost the confidence of the learner. Readily available task trainers in the work areas are being used to review certain procedures (intubation, spinal tap, umbilical lines) during a planned procedure.23–25

With the advent of single-room NICUs, new nurses have lost some of the continued mentorship of experienced nurses for bedside care. It has now become a growing practice for new nurses to perform intensive training through simulation, and there is a growing body of evidence in the nursing literature of its utility and effectiveness.26–29 Simulation continues to be used for improvement of skills and teamwork (e.g., extracorporeal membrane oxygenation [ECMO],34,36 reduction of central line infections, golden hour, and “small baby protocols”). It has also become an important part of education and is used in all aspects of patient safety and quality improvement endeavors as well as in neonatal transport.30–32,35 Simulation has also shown to be an effective tool to identify latent safety threats as demonstrated by Wong et al. during magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in neonatal patients.33

Simulation techniques have also permeated the world of communication and are being used for antenatal consults and even for training fellows and residents for “difficult conversations” with patients and families. There is a growing trend toward also incorporating this technology for education of home caregivers for technology-dependent patients.22,37,38

### Simulation in Low-Resourced Areas

Helping Babies Breathe (HBB) is an educational program that was developed by the AAP in 2010 designed to decrease neonatal mortality in low-resourced countries and has proven to be a powerful model for simulation success, despite the fact that it is low fidelity. Since its implementation in more than 80 countries, meta-analysis has demonstrated an average consistent reduction in fresh stillbirths of 34% (odds ratio [OR] 0.66; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.52–0.85) and very early neonatal mortality an average of 30% (OR 0.70; 95% CI 0.51–0.98).39,40

Innovative virtual trainings are now being proven effective in retaining knowledge when in-person training is not feasible.

### Debriefing

A debriefing is defined as a discussion of events that have already occurred and can be led by an individual or a group.

This is in contrast to a briefing, which is held to discuss planned or future events. In debriefing of a health care team, the flow of information happens between the leader(s) and the members of the team, as well as among the members of the team. In contrast, feedback is the provision of information (from a person or a device) to a person in which the flow of that information is one way. Although not as interactive as a debriefing, it is important to note that not all learning requires the type of interaction typically ascribed to debriefing. For example, the acquisition and maintenance of a technical skill such as intubation do not require debriefing; rather, the provision of feedback as to appropriate finger and hand position on the laryngoscope and other aspects of intubation technique can be provided by an instructor experienced in intubation without the extensive interaction with trainees ascribed to debriefing.

Much of the health care literature has been devoted to the theoretical underpinnings of debriefing, rather than actual practical strategies and techniques, and it has focused on relatively inexperienced trainees rather than experienced health care professionals. Most of the models described in the literature use a very similar approach consisting of three primary phases: 1. An individual trained in debriefing who is not a member

of the team leads the discussion; 2. the discussion typically includes reaction, description,

analysis, and summary phases; and 3. patient outcome is not routinely emphasized (and may

actually be avoided if felt to potentially produce negative reactions in team members). This stands in contrast to how debriefing is conducted in other industries in which the risk to human life is high. In these industries, the emphasis of debriefing is on facts, not feelings, and objective outcomes, not subjective interpretations.3,41–45

There are several techniques for debriefing, including Promoting Excellence and Reflective Learning in Simulation (PEARLS), the three-dimensional (3D) model, and the diamond method, to name just a few.46,47 It is not uncommon for experienced debriefers to use a blended model of the various techniques. The debriefing model adopted by the NRP originated at the Center for Advanced Pediatric and Perinatal Education (CAPE), located at Packard Children’s Hospital in California. The CAPE debriefing model focuses on the actions of the individual, how those actions contribute to the performance of the team, and ultimately how team performance influences the care of the patient, therefore aligning closely with debriefing methods used by aerospace, commercial aviation, and the military. In this model, the person(s) leading the debriefing draws the assessment of individual and team performance from the team members themselves as they evaluate patient outcome in response to their actions and objectively analyze those actions. Upon the conclusion of the debriefing, team members must understand how actions beneficial to the patient can be replicated and how any actions that were nonproductive or harmful can be avoided. The guiding principles

• Debriefers should set a professional, business-like,

dominate, discussion among team members. • Debriefings should be focused on the actions of

It is very important to understand the difference between a technical performance debriefing (used to assess human and system performance) and a critical incident stress debriefing (conducted to provide emotional/psychological support). A critical incident is defined as “an event that has the potential for people to experience significant physical, cognitive, emotional, and behavioral reactions immediately after the incident or days, weeks, months, and even sometimes years later.”48 If simulated clinical scenarios are welldesigned and the associated debriefings are conducted in an appropriate manner, a critical incident stress debriefing should very rarely be required; if it is, appropriate professional counseling should be arranged.

Although several studies have not consistently shown clear benefits to the use of video during debriefing, it must be acknowledged that, for the cognitive, technical, and behavioral skills of the team members to be effectively debriefed, an accurate record of the display of those skills must be available.49–54 Reliance on memory alone to provide such an accurate record is dubious at best. The ability to display a video stream illustrating key viewing angles coupled with an audio stream that picks up communication among team members provides an objective record of events that is capable of effectively bridging any gap between team members’ memories and the actual facts of the scenario. Incorporating debriefing into significant clinical events/ resuscitations will help learners accept this methodology as a “routine” learning and reflective tool without the fear of any negative judgment or repercussions.55,56

### Simulation-Based Research and In Situ Simulation

In situ simulations conducted in the actual clinical space are gaining popularity in the medical field, with definite benefits in terms of an authentic environment, readily available clinical staff who are actually present, easy availability of

In situ simulation also comes with the added potential of identifying latent safety threats,57,58 be it availability of essential equipment, personnel, and communication, all the way to major issues such as the inability to operate critical equipment such as a defibrillator.

However, clinical space simulation has certain limitations for success, especially in the case of a high census and acuity and understandable reluctance of staff participation during

busy clinical times. The potential effect that these may have on families and visitors and the inability to video record because of privacy issues can also be a major deterrent.57–61

The key to successful in situ simulation lies in careful planning with well-established learning objectives and acceptance from multidisciplinary teams (nurses, physicians, nurse practitioners, and respiratory therapists). It may also be prudent to notify families and visitors of this educational session. There is evidence for improved interdisciplinary performance during in situ simulation in the delivery room.62–64

Simulation-based research in health care has focused on two major areas—assessing task trainers and using mannequins, and validating simulation-based training methodology and duration of persistence of this knowledge and skills. It would also need long-term follow-up to evaluate the effect on patient outcomes.65 Most of the research is concentrated on validation of the various simulators as teaching tools. title: Perinatal and Neonatal Care in Developing Countries

paragraphs.text: 7 Perinatal and Neonatal Care in Developing Countries
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: The science and practice of modern neonatology evolved as a medical specialty in the United States and the Western world over the past 70 years. Neonatology as a specialty in developing countries is still evolving. The increased attention to improving newborn care at a global level can be traced to the recognition by the World Health Organization (WHO) of unacceptably high infant mortality in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).1,2 The Alma-Ata Declaration was the first serious effort by the WHO to address the problem of high infant mortality rate (IMR) among developing countries. Since then, several policies have been proposed and implemented to decrease the IMR and neonatal mortality rate (NMR) across the globe. There has been steady improvement in overall global newborn care resulting in the reduction of NMR and IMR in LMICs since the latter part of the 20th century. The major factors responsible for overall improvements in maternal and child care in LMICs probably include: (1) improved access to medical and technical information, (2) rapid transfer of technology, (3) largescale studies in LMICs especially packages of care focused on reduction in neonatal mortality, (4), increased awareness of health and change in health care–seeking behavior among women, and (5) international campaigns such as the advocacy of the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs)3 and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).4 Several large controlled trials have demonstrated the benefits of selected interventions, including packages of care such as the Mother-Baby Package5 and the neonatal resuscitation and Essential Newborn Care programs.1,2,6–8 Considerable progress is being made in reducing maternal and child mortality in developing countries; however, many challenges remain. This chapter provides an overview of global neonatal and perinatal problems, presents data on the changing trends in IMR and NMR, and discusses strategies to decrease the IMR and NMR in developing countries.
paragraphs.heading: WALDEMAR A. CARLO

paragraphs.text: Because of concerns of high global IMR and NMR, numerous interventions have been proposed and implemented by world organizations over the past four decades (Table 7.1). The Alma-Ata Declaration of 1978 by the WHO and the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) set a goal to achieve “Health for all by the year 2000.” The declaration included a goal for the reduction of maternal and infant mortality through primary care. In 1987, the International Conference on Safe Motherhood drew attention to high maternal mortality rates (MMRs) in developing countries and encouraged policymakers to develop new strategies to reduce maternal mortality. This action led to the worldwide program of Safe Motherhood, placing an emphasis on antenatal care. A similar resolution, the Bamako Initiative, was instituted at the annual meeting of the African Ministries of Health in 1987. The objective was the achievement of universal maternal-child health coverage at the periphery by 2000. In 1988, the Task Force for Child Survival set objectives for a reduction in under-5 mortality and MMR by at least half.
paragraphs.heading: Historical Perspective

paragraphs.text: In 1994, the WHO developed the Mother-Baby Package to help reduce MMR and NMR further.5 At the WHO 48th World Health Assembly, the concept of integrated management of childhood illness was adopted to improve the well-being of the whole child younger than 5 years old.9 This concept included an emphasis on improved care of newborns. By the end of the 20th century, a significant decrease in MMR and IMR was reported as one of the top 10 achievements of the century.10 However, the high IMR and NMR in the LMICs

paragraphs.text: continued to be a major concern to global policymakers. The World Bank initiated the Global Burden of Disease study, which showed that perinatal conditions, including infant mortality, form a significant portion (39%) of the global burden of disease. It showed that developing countries are the major contributors to global perinatal and neonatal mortality. Perinatal mortality constitutes one of the 10 leading causes of death in developing countries. Neonatal mortality is the major part of perinatal mortality. These findings underscore the importance of improving perinatal and neonatal care in developing countries, as declared in the MDGs in 2000.3
paragraphs.heading: Global Initiatives to Decrease Neonatal, Child, and Maternal Mortality

paragraphs.text: In 2000, the United Nations developed eight MDGs to be achieved by 2015.3 The targets were measured by preset quantifiable measures. The MDGs focus on some specific health issues but also emphasize social, economic, and public health and health-policy matters that affect the “health” of the people and addressed specific indicator goals for perinatal care (Table 7.2).
paragraphs.heading: The Millennium Development Goals

paragraphs.text: In addition to these developments, the series of landmark scientific publications in The Lancet provided evidence-based scalable interventions that could reduce NMR and IMR in resource-poor countries.11,12 These publications generated great interest among researchers and health policymakers around the globe. The Child Survival series examined the potential impact of scaling up 43 interventions that could reduce child mortality by 2015. In 2005, the series on newborn survival provided the first systematic estimates of neonatal deaths by cause and identified simple and cost-effective scalable interventions that could reduce neonatal deaths globally. The impact of some
paragraphs.heading: The Millennium Development Goals

paragraphs.text: of the suggested interventions is described later in this chapter.
paragraphs.heading: The Millennium Development Goals

paragraphs.text: In 2015, the United Nations proposed the SDGs to be achieved by 2030.4,13 These goals were adopted to end poverty, protect the planet, and ensure prosperity for all as part of a new sustainable development agenda. Each goal has specific targets to be achieved over the next 15 years. There are 17 goals (Fig. 7.1).4 Goal 3 is focused on health and aims to ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all at all ages. This goal includes specific targets for perinatal and childhood health outcomes. The maternal and childhood targets aim to reduce global maternal mortality ratios to less than 70 per 100,000 live births and end preventable deaths of newborns and children younger than 5 years of age, with all countries aiming to reduce neonatal mortality to at least 12 per 1000 live births and under-5 mortality to at least 25 per 1000 live births. These aspiring goals are ambitious and will require commitment from all stakeholders to achieve them.
paragraphs.heading: The Sustainable Development Goals

paragraphs.text: Worldwide efforts are taking place to implement SDGs and track their impact. There is a need for accurate birth and death data from all participating countries. Unfortunately, collecting accurate NMR, IMR, and under-5 mortality data on a global scale remains a major problem. There are several hurdles to collect these data accurately. High-income countries (HICs) have well-established vital statistics of births and deaths, whereas the LMICs do not. Only 60 of the 193 countries studied had fully functioning sources of mortality
paragraphs.heading: Tracking the Global Progress of the Sustainable Development Goals

paragraphs.text: data14; the rest of the countries depend on annual or periodic surveys. There is a need for improvement in accurate vital statistics to establish the true burden of MMR, NMR, and IMR and to develop appropriate strategies to monitor progress.
paragraphs.heading: Tracking the Global Progress of the Sustainable Development Goals

paragraphs.text: Maternal mortality has been a major global burden of disease. More than 99% of the yearly maternal deaths occur in LMICs. The causes of maternal death include maternal hemorrhage (25%), sepsis (15%), abortion (13%), hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (12%), and obstructed labor (8%). More than 50% of the deaths related to pregnancy and childbirth were estimated to be preventable using simple, well-accepted interventions. The MDG #5 aimed at reducing the MMR by 75% between 1990 and 2015, but this was not accomplished. Global MMR in 2015 had decreased by 44% (from 385/100,000 in 1990 to 216/100,000).15 The highest regional rate of decline for 1990 to 2015 occurred in eastern Asia (5.0% annual decline). Sub-Saharan Africa continues to have the highest MMR, with 546/100,000 live births (Fig. 7.2). Sub-Saharan Africa contributed more than 66% of the maternal deaths worldwide in 2015.
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Mortality

paragraphs.text: More than 98% of neonatal deaths occur in LMICs; the majority of these deaths occur in South Asia and
paragraphs.heading: Neonatal and Infant Mortality

paragraphs.text: sub-Saharan Africa. There are limited data on NMR or IMR that go back to the early 20th century, but there were major reductions in mortality. Fig. 7.3 shows global trends in IMR during 1950 to 2000.16 In the 1950s, there were wide variations in IMR among different regions of the world. IMR was lowest in industrialized Western countries (33 per 1000). It decreased to around 5 per 1000 by 2000, a reduction of 85%. In 1950, sub-Saharan Africa had the highest IMR (157 per 1000) and showed the least reduction (only 32%) among all the regions of the world during the next 50 years. South Asia, the Middle East/North Africa, and Latin America/Caribbean showed 53%, 70%, and 74% decreases, respectively. At the end of the 20th century, IMR continued to remain significantly high: 70 per 1000 in South Asia, 45 per 1000 in the Middle East, and 27 per 1000 in Latin America.
paragraphs.heading: Neonatal and Infant Mortality

paragraphs.text: The global NMR decreased by 51% from 36.6 per 1000 live births in 1990 to 18.0 deaths per 1000 live births in 2017.17 The estimated number of neonatal deaths during the same period decreased from 5.0 to 2.5 million. The NMR is the highest (30.2 per 1000 live births) in West and Central Africa and in South Asia (26.9). Countries with the highest NMRs were concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, accounting for 79% of the total burden of global neonatal deaths (see Fig. 7.3). The under-5 mortality is decreasing faster than those in neonatal mortality, and now neonatal mortality accounts for 47% of the global under-5 deaths compared with 40% in 1990. In spite of these decreases in NMR across the LMICs, the annual rate of NMR reduction was still well below the MDG #4 goal of 4.4% and below the IMR and under-5 mortality rate

paragraphs.text: Factors that influence MMR and NMR include commonly known maternal and neonatal medical problems, socioeconomic conditions, gender inequality, environmental factors, and economic and political instability. Socioeconomic factors greatly influence the health of mother and baby, in particular, in LMICs, as discussed in the following section.
paragraphs.heading: Causes of Global Maternal and Neonatal Mortality

paragraphs.text: The socioeconomic factors adversely influencing IMR include gender bias against women, maternal education, and economic dependence. SDG #5 is aimed at eliminating gender inequity. Gender bias against women has a negative effect on every phase of a woman’s life, interfering with her education, economic power, and health. Gender-biased discrimination begins its influence early in life, leading to poorer nutrition and health in girls compared with boys. Gender inequalities persist worldwide, depriving women and girls of their basic rights and opportunities. SDG #1 aims to end poverty in
paragraphs.heading: Socioeconomic and Cultural Factors

paragraphs.text: all its forms everywhere. SDG #4 aims to ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all. Evidence shows that a woman with more education has fewer children, better economic status, lower fertility rate, lower IMR, and improved quality of life. Maternal education is associated with lower mortality rates at all ages. Education increases earning potential, and higher income is associated with lower mortality. Earning power provides women with economic, social, and political empowerment. In short, education is seen as a means of ensuring health. Health-seeking behavior during pregnancy, childbirth, and the neonatal period is influenced by regional, religious, and ethnic differences and by cultural beliefs. Understanding the cultural beliefs and their influences on care of the mother and infant is crucial to providing appropriate counseling to mothers. Health strategies to improve MMR and IMR in LMICs include implementation of programs that eliminate gender inequities, end poverty, and ensure equitable education to enable women to improve their health and that of their children. In addition, increasing awareness of maintaining health, improving health-seeking behavior, and improving access to health care will improve health outcomes.
paragraphs.heading: Socioeconomic and Cultural Factors

paragraphs.text: Economic stability alone does not guarantee better health of the mother and child. For example, many oil- and
paragraphs.heading: Influence of Political Instability, War, and Conflict

paragraphs.text: mineral-rich countries in Middle East, Africa, and Latin America with a sizeable global income are a unique group with wide disparities of wealth and health.24 Despite high gross national product, some of these countries have high IMR, high under-5 mortality rate, high MMR, and low life expectancy.16 Although the overall IMR has decreased substantially, IMRs continue to be high in many countries in these regions, particularly in Africa.
paragraphs.heading: Influence of Political Instability, War, and Conflict

paragraphs.text: Women and children account for a disproportionate morbidity burden among conflict-affected populations. Political instability and wars have adversely affected perinatal and neonatal outcome. For example, IMR and under-5 mortality rate increased during the conflict in Syria.25 Similarly, natural disasters such as Hurricane Katrina and tsunamis call for preparedness to care for pregnant women, parturient mothers, and neonates.14,26 Pediatricians and neonatologists serving in areas of war conflicts and those working in the armed forces should be well-prepared to manage these situations. Personnel from government, nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), academics, care providers, and media need to develop, organize, and strengthen their health systems in disaster preparedness and enable effective and efficient processes to handle national and global emergencies.27
paragraphs.heading: Influence of Political Instability, War, and Conflict

paragraphs.text: In developing countries, prematurity, birth asphyxia, and sepsis/pneumonia continue to constitute a major portion of
paragraphs.heading: Medical Causes of Neonatal Mortality

paragraphs.text: the global causes of childhood deaths (see Fig. 7.5).19 About 47% of the under-5 mortality rate is because of NMR. Neonatal death caused by prematurity is the number one cause of under-5 mortality rate. Birth asphyxia and sepsis/pneumonia are the other major causes of neonatal mortality.28 The WHO estimates that 40% to 60% of neonatal deaths are preventable. The time of death is dependent on these causes of death (Fig. 7.8).29 Furthermore, specific causes of death vary substantially by regions of the world (Fig. 7.9).28 In contrast to the major contributions of prematurity, birth asphyxia, and sepsis/pneumonia in LMIC settings, congenital malformations and prematurity are the dominant causes of neonatal mortality in HICs. The major causes of neonatal mortality are discussed in detail in the following section.
paragraphs.heading: Medical Causes of Neonatal Mortality

paragraphs.text: Although prematurity is the most frequent cause of death in neonates, the specific cause of death in premature babies worldwide is not known. Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) is the most common cause of death in HICs, but in LMICs it is likely that lack of neonatal intensive care accounts for most of the deaths from prematurity. A metaanalysis conclusively demonstrates that surfactant administration reduces mortality in LMIC settings with neonatal intensive care units (NICUs).30 There are many other effective therapies, such as thermoregulation, nutrition, and prevention and treatment of sepsis, that may have a large impact in LMIC settings. It is likely that most interventions that reduce neonatal mortality in NICUs in HICs will reduce neonatal mortality in similar settings in LMICs also.
paragraphs.heading: Prematurity

paragraphs.text: Failure to achieve a smooth postnatal transition may lead to various degrees of birth asphyxia. Death caused by birth
paragraphs.heading: Birth Asphyxia

paragraphs.text: asphyxia is defined as death caused by the inability to breathe or sustain breathing soon after birth. Of the 136 million births per year globally, almost 1 million babies die of birth asphyxia. Most of these deaths occur in LMICs, where an estimated 4 to 10 million infants per year experience birth asphyxia. Birth asphyxia contributes to 20% to 40% of all neonatal deaths, depending on the setting.
paragraphs.heading: Birth Asphyxia

paragraphs.text: The burden of birth asphyxia and the number of babies requiring resuscitation at birth at a global level are shown in Fig. 7.10.31 It is estimated that, of the 136 million annual births, about 10 million (5%–10%) respond to simple stimulation to initiate breathing efforts, 3% to 6% require basic resuscitation with bag and mask (6 million), and only less than 1% (<1 million) require advanced resuscitation (0.1% chest compression and 0.05% require drugs). Causes of birth asphyxia include poor maternal health, inadequate antenatal care, high-risk pregnancies, intrapartum complications, and inadequate care during labor and delivery. Prematurity also contributes to the problem of birth asphyxia. Lack of skilled birth attendants and lack of availability of proper equipment at the time of delivery are the major contributing factors for higher birth asphyxia–related morbidity and mortality in developing countries. It is heartening to note that in recent years, great strides have been made to overcome these deficiencies. Many countries have initiated training programs to improve resuscitation skills at the grass-roots level. In addition to the earlier efforts of WHO and UNICEF, the Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP), developed by the American Academy of Pediatrics and American Heart Association, has been introduced in its full or modified form in almost 100 countries, including India and China. Helping Babies Breathe (HBB) is a simplified version of neonatal resuscitation that advocates proper assessment of baby at birth, stimulation to breathe,

paragraphs.text: The main life-saving skill is ventilation with a bag and mask. Because of the simplicity of the skill training, it is easily adoptable to train health care workers attending deliveries at a health facility in rural settings. Two largescale trials that enrolled almost 200,000 deliveries showed that Essential Newborn Care (now simplified as Essential Care for Every Baby and Essential Care for Small Babies) and resuscitation programs reduced early neonatal mortality by more than 60%7 and fresh stillbirth by more than 30%,6 markedly reducing perinatal mortality. These programs are being implemented by many global partners, including UNICEF, WHO, and United States Agency for International Development (USAID) in many LMICs.33 In India, the NRP became a standard skill-training module and reduced deaths related to birth asphyxia.34 Almost 100 countries have introduced resuscitation programs, including HBB, which will help to further reduce birth asphyxia– related mortality among LMICs. In a review of 24 studies, 20 observational, two quasi-experimental, and two cluster randomized controlled trials, neonatal resuscitation at birth was associated with significant reduction in overall neonatal mortality (relative risk [RR] = 0.70, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.59–0.84), especially early NMR (see Fig. 7.11).31 It was estimated that immediate newborn assessment and stimulation would reduce both intrapartum-related and preterm deaths by 10%. Facility-based resuscitation would prevent a further 10% of preterm deaths, and communitybased resuscitation would prevent a further 20% of intrapartum-related deaths and 5% of preterm deaths. Many
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 7.10 The global burden of neonatal resuscitation demonstrating the potential number of babies who

paragraphs.text: intrapartum deaths are classified as stillbirths who are not included in vital statistics in some countries. Many stillbirths are preventable, including with postnatal resuscitation.6,35 Stillbirths are very prevalent worldwide and need to be given a higher priority on the global health agenda.36,37 These encouraging projections regarding the benefits of training health professionals in neonatal resuscitation are supported by the large-scale trials (Fig. 7.11).6,7 The overwhelming majority of survivors following birth asphyxia in low-resource settings have been found to have normal neurodevelopment.38 This is likely caused by the difficulty in keeping alive the most severely asphyxiated newborns. Therapeutic hypothermia reduces mortality and morbidity from hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) in HICs.39 Using innovative inexpensive methods, body cooling in HIE is showing promise even in LMICs,40 but a large multicenter randomized controlled trial in LMICs did not show benefits and increased the risk of death.41
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 7.10 The global burden of neonatal resuscitation demonstrating the potential number of babies who

paragraphs.text: Neonatal hypothermia is a common and important potentially life-threatening condition. Neonatal hypothermia occurs in 30% to 80% of newborn infants.42,43 The incidence of neonatal hypothermia is substantially higher in LMICs compared with HICs. Neonatal hypothermia (core body temperature <97.7° F or 36.5° C) is common in LMICs even during summer months. In Nepal, more than 80% of infants became hypothermic at birth and 50% remained hypothermic at 24 hours after birth.44 Hypothermia is associated with higher risk of neonatal mortality.44 When adequate warmth is not provided, both preterm and term infants are at risk of developing hypothermia.
paragraphs.heading: Hypothermia

paragraphs.text: The causes of neonatal hypothermia in LMICs are many, starting from low ambient temperature of delivery rooms. Inadequate clothing and giving routine baths soon after birth are causes of neonatal hypothermia. Newborns may also experience heat losses within the hospital during transport from delivery room to the postnatal ward and during transport home from the hospital or from hospital to hospital. Neonatal hypothermia increases metabolic demand, oxygen consumption, and neonatal mortality. In the absence of sophisticated and expensive incubators, simple techniques can be adopted to abate hypothermia.45
paragraphs.heading: Hypothermia

paragraphs.text: To reduce neonatal hypothermia, the WHO recommends the “warm chain,” a thermoregulation protocol that should be implemented in every nursery and with every newborn during the first several days and weeks after birth. The warm chain includes warm delivery rooms, immediate drying, uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact as much as possible, early breastfeeding, delayed bathing and weighing, appropriate bundling, mother and baby together, warm transportation, warm resuscitation, and training and awareness raising.46 However, not all the elements recommended in the WHO thermoregulation protocol are practiced routinely in many birth facilities around the world.47 Plastic bags and wrapping with plastic wrap at birth are effective in decreasing hypothermia in term and preterm infants.48 This is a very inexpensive and effective method of providing thermal protection to the newborn in the immediate neonatal period. Kangaroo mother care (KMC) is becoming a universal practice,49 and in addition to keeping the baby warm, the immediate initiation of breastfeeding provides early provision of calories. A Cochrane meta-analysis showed that KMC in preterm and low birth weight (LBW) infants also reduces mortality at the time of discharge.50 A large multicenter randomized controlled trial of early (day 1) KMC in 3211 preterm infants (birth weight 1.2–1.8 kg) markedly reduced neonatal deaths from 15.7% to 12.0% and reduced hypothermia.51
paragraphs.heading: Hypothermia

paragraphs.text: It is estimated that worldwide, 15% to 20% of newborns die of neonatal infection. The incidence of sepsis is estimated to be 5 to 6 per 1000 live births (600,000–750,000) among hospitalized patients. Meningitis accounts for 0.7 to 1 per 1000 live births (88,000–126,000 cases per year), and acute respiratory infections account for 800,000 deaths in neonates. Among these deaths are cases of pneumonia, bronchiolitis, and laryngotracheitis. Cord infections and neonatal tetanus are preventable causes of acquired infection. The maternal transmission of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) to the newborn was a major factor contributing to neonatal deaths in some countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, but effective prevention is largely available.52
paragraphs.heading: Infections

paragraphs.text: Infections in the neonatal period can manifest at birth but most often occur within the first few days, peaking at 2 weeks
paragraphs.heading: Burden of Neonatal Sepsis

paragraphs.text: after birth (see Fig. 7.8).29 Estimating the burden (incidence) of neonatal infections in developing countries is challenging because of several factors: (1) most births take place at home, and those newborns with sepsis rarely seek medical attention. (2) Hospital-derived information does not represent true incidence of sepsis in the community. (3) Laboratory facilities for cultures are inadequate or nonexistent. Population-based studies from developing countries have reported clinical sepsis rates ranging from 49 to 170 per 1000 live births.53 Among 18 studies from developing countries, the median incidence of blood culture–confirmed sepsis was 16 per 1000 live births. A study from Bangladesh found the incidence of clinically suspected neonatal sepsis to be 50 per 1000 live births, and the incidence of culture-confirmed sepsis was 3 per 1000 live births.54 The incidence of culture-confirmed neonatal sepsis was 5.5 per 1000 live births among neonates presenting to a first-level health facility in rural Kenya.55 However, the absence of active community surveillance suggests that the true burden is probably higher. A review of early-onset neonatal sepsis in developing countries found only five studies.56 The incidence of clinical sepsis ranged from 20.7 to 50 per 1000 live births, and the incidence of culture-confirmed early-onset neonatal sepsis ranged from 2.2 to 9.8 per 1000 live births. Only two of these studies reported case fatality rates, of 18% and 19%, respectively. These observations contrast with neonatal culture-confirmed sepsis rates of 1 to 3 per 1000 live births reported from industrialized countries,57 indicating the huge preventable burden of neonatal infections in LMICs.
paragraphs.heading: Burden of Neonatal Sepsis

paragraphs.text: As noted, although blood culture is the gold standard for diagnosis of neonatal sepsis, lack of laboratory facilities is a major barrier to diagnosis and treatment of neonatal sepsis in LMICs. Therefore clinicians and health care workers depend on clinical signs of sepsis for diagnosis and treatment. Several clinical scores have been described to facilitate the diagnosis by health care workers in the field. Bang and co-workers have described a simple set of clinical criteria to recognize sepsis in a rural setting.58 The Young Infants Clinical Signs Study Group conducted a large multicountry study to identify clinical signs with high sensitivity and specificity for predicting sepsis.59 They identified seven common clinical signs that could be identified easily by health care workers in primary care settings. Other investigators have used slight modifications of these signs for clinical diagnosis of neonatal sepsis in community-based neonatal programs. The WHO also has developed guidelines for the Integrated Management of Childhood Illnesses for resource-limited countries.60 Using the aforementioned background information, an algorithm may be used by health care workers in LMICs to assess infants at home or in health facilities, initiate treatment for sepsis, and triage infants to higher levels of care.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis of Neonatal Sepsis

paragraphs.text: Infographics can be used to assist clinicians and identify possible maternal61 (Fig. 7.12) and neonatal62 sepsis.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis of Neonatal Sepsis

paragraphs.text: Danger signs include chest indrawing or fast breathing, not feeding, too hot or too cold, convulsions, no movement, yellow palms or soles of feet. Fig. 7.13 shows an algorithm of the elements of observation and action based on common clinical findings: feeding, crying, variations in skin temperature on touch, activity, breathing pattern, and condition of the cord. These findings can be graded from mild to severe. Any two milder forms of distress can be treated and managed at home by the health care worker. Infants showing more severe forms of distress must be treated and transferred to a referral health center. Recent randomized controlled trials by the African Neonatal Sepsis trial group showed feasibility of community-based diagnosis of clinical signs of possible serious bacterial infection and simplified antibiotic regimens, including injectable and oral combinations.63,64
paragraphs.heading: STOP SEPSIS!

paragraphs.text: Although the global health policies described in the beginning of this chapter are being adopted by many countries,
paragraphs.heading: Evidence-Based Interventions to Reduce Maternal Mortality Rates, Neonatal Mortality Rates, and Infant Mortality Rates

paragraphs.text: researchers are also actively investigating the causes of high global maternal and neonatal mortality and gathering information for evidence-based effective interventions that are adoptable and scalable in reducing MMR, NMR, and IMR in LMICs. Three series of landmark publications, popularly known as The Lancet series (described earlier), provided evidence-based, scalable interventions that reduced MMR, NMR, and IMR in resource-poor countries.11,12,65 The Lancet Child Survival Series conducted comprehensive reviews of 23 interventions with a focus on under-5 child survival. Interventions were introduced in preconception, antenatal, intrapartum, and postpartum periods. Sixteen major community-based interventions were analyzed for their efficacy in reducing NMR.66 Increasing coverage of these 16 interventions to 90% of the population could save 590,000 to 1.08 million lives in South Asia annually at an additional cost of US $900 million to $1.76 billion. In sub-Saharan Africa, it could save up to 450,000 to 800,000 lives at a cost of US $680 million to $1.32 billion.
paragraphs.heading: Evidence-Based Interventions to Reduce Maternal Mortality Rates, Neonatal Mortality Rates, and Infant Mortality Rates

paragraphs.text: Many antenatal, intrapartum, and neonatal interventions may be very effective in reducing NMR.67 The 11 major evidence-based effective antenatal and neonatal interventions are listed in Box 7.1. These include two major antenatal
paragraphs.heading: Evidence-Based Interventions to Reduce Maternal Mortality Rates, Neonatal Mortality Rates, and Infant Mortality Rates

paragraphs.text: interventions, antenatal steroids and antibiotic therapy for premature rupture of membranes (PROM). Also described are nine neonatal interventions, including late cord clamping68 and neonatal resuscitation.6,7 After birth, surfactant therapy and application of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) reduce mortality in infants with RDS. Probiotics decrease necrotizing enterocolitis, sepsis, and all-cause mortality in LMICs.69 These findings are of great clinical importance to practitioners as well as health policymakers because they provide a basis for adoption of new cost-effective interventions in saving many high-risk newborns.
paragraphs.heading: Evidence-Based Interventions to Reduce Maternal Mortality Rates, Neonatal Mortality Rates, and Infant Mortality Rates

paragraphs.text: Prematurity is a major cause of neonatal deaths in developing countries, and RDS is the leading cause of neonatal
paragraphs.heading: Evidence-Based Interventions to Reduce Maternal Mortality Rates, Neonatal Mortality Rates, and Infant Mortality Rates

paragraphs.text: death in this population in HICs. The goal should be to consider preventive antenatal care and proven interventions, such as antenatal steroid therapy in preterm labor,70 implementation of delivery room neonatal resuscitation, early use of CPAP, and surfactant therapy.71 In a multicenter placebo-controlled trial of 2852 women at risk for preterm delivery, antenatal dexamethasone decreased neonatal deaths from 23.5% to 19.6%.70 Using antenatal steroids as a preventative measure will be the least expensive. Antenatal steroid treatment of mothers in premature labor has been estimated to save 500,000 lives a year.72 Infants with RDS can be best managed with inexpensive nasal CPAP devices. Evidence suggests that in LMICs, postnatal CPAP followed
paragraphs.heading: Evidence-Based Interventions to Reduce Maternal Mortality Rates, Neonatal Mortality Rates, and Infant Mortality Rates

paragraphs.text: by surfactant therapy can significantly reduce mortality and morbidity from RDS.21 Use of nasal CPAP as a first choice of treatment decreases the need for surfactant replacement therapy and reduces mortality and bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) compared with early surfactant.73 Appropriate CPAP devices, supplies, and training are essential for successful implementation.74 Therefore outcomes can be improved by using early CPAP and reducing the use of surfactant for infants who respond to CPAP as is done now in HICs.75
paragraphs.heading: Evidence-Based Interventions to Reduce Maternal Mortality Rates, Neonatal Mortality Rates, and Infant Mortality Rates

paragraphs.text: With the increased access to neonatal intensive care and improved survival of preterm and very LBW infants, there is a financial burden on families and risk of associated morbidities among survivors. Three major neonatal emerging challenges in developing countries are of great concern. They include (1) BPD, also known as chronic lung disease (CLD)76; (2) retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)77,78; and (3) neurodevelopmental delays.79,80 All three conditions are related to prematurity, and as survival of preterm infants increases, so does the incidence of CLD, ROP, and neurodevelopmental delays. Data regarding the prevalence of these morbidities in LMICs are lacking. Interventions can be delivered throughout the life span from before conception until adolescence to help infants and children not only survive into adulthood but also develop optimally, support their well-being, and help them reach their full developmental potential.81
paragraphs.heading: The Impact of Progress

paragraphs.text: BPD is a newly emerging disease in LMICs.76 LMICs contemplating the development of modern NICUs should be well-prepared to recognize these complications and associated costs. Strategies need to be developed to minimize the overall burden of disease on the community. In this regard, the application of CPAP as the first approach to managing RDS is to be encouraged in LMICs.21
paragraphs.heading: The Impact of Progress

paragraphs.text: ROP was first encountered in the early 1950s in HICs, with the introduction of high oxygen therapy and again with the introduction of ventilator care and increasing survival of extremely premature infants. Although the rate and severity of ROP are decreasing in HICs, they are beginning to increase in LMICs. A multicenter survey of oxygen practices in Africa showed that there are opportunities to improve oxygen supplementation and monitoring.82 As NMR is steadily decreasing, it is estimated that globally at least 50,000 children are blind from ROP. This observed large number of ROP worldwide has come to be known as the third epidemic.77 Fig. 7.14 shows estimates of ROP and visual impairment at regional and global levels. ROP is increasing worldwide including in middle- and low-income countries where oxygen availability is increasing but continuous oxygen saturation monitoring may not be universally used. About 3% of survivors of prematurity born at <32 weeks have visual impairment.19 ROP is being increasingly reported from India and China, home to more than one-sixth of the world’s population. Blindness caused by ROP begins to rise as the IMR of a country continues to decrease. These data suggest the influence of increased survival of preterm infants with the introduction of NICU care, oxygen therapy,83,84 and ventilation: the lower the IMR, the higher the rate of ROP-related blindness. ROP will soon become a public health issue in these countries unless control activities keep pace with the increased survival of premature babies at risk.
paragraphs.heading: The Impact of Progress

paragraphs.text: There is a need to develop and implement educational programs to avoid the potentially hazardous practices of high oxygen therapy, to promote early detection of ROP, and to pursue a multidisciplinary approach to prevent ROP. LMICs also have the additional problem of lack of awareness of ROP among pediatricians, whereas ophthalmologists may be inadequately trained in the recognition and management of ROP.78
paragraphs.heading: The Impact of Progress

paragraphs.text: The overall cost of neonatal intensive care at the tertiary level in developing countries is relatively high and sometimes affordable only to middle- and upper-income groups. Infants with RDS can be successfully managed with ventilator support85 at an average cost of US $1391 per survivor. The per-day cost of NICU care of neonates in a government teaching hospital was estimated to be US $125/day.86 NICU care for infants born at 24 to 26, 27 to 29, and 30 to 33 weeks’ gestational age in Mexico prolonged life expectancy by 28, 43, and 34 years and averted 9, 15, and 12 disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) at incremental costs per infant of US $11,400, US $9500, and US $3000, respectively, compared with infants with no intensive care.87 These data provide evidence that even in LMICs, provision of NICU care is costeffective in improving survival and decreasing morbidity. Unfortunately, in many LMICs, parents have to bear 80%
paragraphs.heading: The Burden of the High Cost of Advanced Neonatal Care

paragraphs.text: of hospital costs out of pocket, which may exceed their resources.88
paragraphs.heading: The Burden of the High Cost of Advanced Neonatal Care

paragraphs.text: Data on long-term outcomes in LMICs are limited. Lack of a uniform database of surviving infants, lack of expertise in assessing developmental disabilities, and the lack of a support system for needy families and children are the major barriers to develop meaningful information regarding the morbidity of surviving infants. Mwaniki and co-workers reviewed 153 studies from around the world suitable for inclusion for analysis of developmental outcome of high-risk newborns.79 Altogether, there were 22,161 survivors of intrauterine or neonatal insults. The overall median risk of at least one sequela in any domain was 39% (interquartile range [IQR] 20%–55%), with a risk of at least one severe impairment in any insult domain of 18% (8%–33%), at least one moderate impairment of 5% (0%–13%), and at least one mild impairment of 10% (1%–18%).
paragraphs.heading: Long-Term Neurodevelopmental Outcome

paragraphs.text: The pooled risk estimate of at least one sequela associated with one or more of the insults studied (excluding HIV) was 37% (95% CI 27%–48%). The most common deficits were learning difficulties, cognition, or developmental delay (N = 4032; 59%); cerebral palsy (N = 1472; 21%); hearing
paragraphs.heading: Long-Term Neurodevelopmental Outcome

paragraphs.text: impairment (N = 1340; 20%); and visual impairment (N = 1228; 18%). Only 40 studies included data for multidomain impairments. These studies (26%) included 2815 individuals, of whom 1048 (37%) had impairments, with 334 (32%) having multiple impairments. These findings show that in developing countries, perinatal adverse insults have a high risk of causing substantial long-term neurologic morbidity.
paragraphs.heading: Long-Term Neurodevelopmental Outcome

paragraphs.text: Shillcutt and co-workers80 studied the estimates of long-term disabilities following neonatal illness in a district of Bangladesh. They found that “a significant burden of disability results from neonatal conditions.” They also projected that their national newborn project might have averted several years lost to disability.
paragraphs.heading: Long-Term Neurodevelopmental Outcome

paragraphs.text: The preceding two studies provide important information on the impact of advanced care and increasing survival of at-risk infants in LMICs. Comparable cohort studies in other resource-poor regions should be done to assess the burden of long-term outcome effects of improved neonatal survival.
paragraphs.heading: Long-Term Neurodevelopmental Outcome

paragraphs.text: The issues of the high cost of hospital care and uncertain outcomes of LBW and critically ill newborns pose ethical dilemmas to practicing neonatologists in LMICs. Most
paragraphs.heading: Ethical Dilemmas

paragraphs.text: poor populations cannot afford the high cost of care. In these countries, although public sector health care caters to the care of the poor, the private sector is rapidly expanding services to selected families able to afford the cost of NICU care.
paragraphs.heading: Ethical Dilemmas

paragraphs.text: Because of changing economic demographics among LMICs, there will be two divergent situations regarding the care of the sick newborn in the NICU, with one group of families who cannot afford the high cost of NICU care. As stated by Singh, undue emphasis may be placed on saving an individual infant with an uncertain outcome at any cost to the family.89 He suggests that to ensure the principle of cost-effectiveness in resource-poor countries, the narrow principle of the “best interests” of the child should be replaced by the concept of a broader benefit to the family, society, and state. In recent years, rapid demographic and economic transitions have changed the expectations of middle-class and upper-middle-class families in countries such as India, China, and other LMICs. When the families and parents with adequate economic resources are
paragraphs.heading: Ethical Dilemmas

paragraphs.text: willing to avail themselves of such care in spite of the high cost, the care cannot be denied. Therefore the neonatologist has the responsibility to prepare parents with prenatal counseling and provide realistic evidence-based treatment options to parents.90 There is a need for a larger debate and development of ethical guidelines for practitioners among LMICs.
paragraphs.heading: Ethical Dilemmas

paragraphs.text: Evidence-based interventions from preconception to the neonatal period to improve perinatal and neonatal outcomes have been reviewed (Table 7.3). Implementation of these strategies will substantially decrease adverse perinatal and neonatal outcomes. Strategies to reduce perinatal mortality in LMICs should include social and medical programs that are integrated into national plans. Box 7.2 outlines the

paragraphs.text: Schiffman and Sultana noted that the factors that led to national advocacy for newborn health in Bangladesh were both a strong commitment of the government to achieving the MDG targets and donor resources.91 They noted that the emergence of successful policy to improve newborn survival involved interactions between global and national agencies rather than either alone. To quote
paragraphs.heading: Middle-Income Countries

paragraphs.text: the authors, “In Bangladesh, newborn survival emerged from obscurity to relative prominence on the government’s health policy agenda.” These observations are applicable to other LMICs. Many LMICs are developing similar programs to scale up maternal and neonatal services.
paragraphs.heading: Middle-Income Countries

paragraphs.text: Developing countries continue to share the major burden of neonatal and infant mortality. The major causes responsible for such disparity between HICs and LMICs are a lack of health facilities, lack of skilled personnel, and lack of access to health care. The SDGs declared in 2015 are the single most influential program bringing the world community, governments, scientists, and policymakers together to address the issues of high neonatal and infant
paragraphs.heading: Summary

paragraphs.text: Key Points
paragraphs.heading: Summary

paragraphs.text: • More than 98% of the neonatal deaths worldwide occur
paragraphs.heading: Summary

paragraphs.text: in low- and middle-income countries. The majority of these deaths occur in South Asia and Africa. • Neonatal deaths constitute approximately 40% of
paragraphs.heading: Summary

paragraphs.text: global under-5 childhood mortality, of which the highest proportion is related to complications of preterm birth, intrapartum-related complications, and sepsis. • Preterm birth complications (14% of under-5
paragraphs.heading: Summary

paragraphs.text: deaths), birth asphyxia (also called intrapartumrelated) complications (9%), and sepsis/meningitis (5%) were the most frequent causes of death in the neonatal period. • The increased attention to improving newborn care at a
paragraphs.heading: Summary

paragraphs.text: global level can be traced to the recognition by the World
paragraphs.heading: Summary

paragraphs.text: mortality in LMICs. The publication of The Lancet series also evoked great interest among researchers to explore the causes of high NMR and find evidence-based costeffective interventions to reduce MMR, NMR, and IMR in LMICs. A review of the literature clearly identified several evidence-based effective antenatal, intrapartum, and neonatal interventions. It remains to be seen how well these interventions will be implemented in LMICs. It is recognized that successful implementation of the MDGs requires both commitment of national governments and collaboration of international agencies. It is encouraging to note that some LMICs have reached their targets of MDGs #4 and #5, but many countries have not reached their MDGs. There is lot more to be done in a large number of LMICs. Neonatology is a work in progress in LMICs.

7 Perinatal and Neonatal Care in Developing Countries

### WALDEMAR A. CARLO

The science and practice of modern neonatology evolved as a medical specialty in the United States and the Western world over the past 70 years. Neonatology as a specialty in developing countries is still evolving. The increased attention to improving newborn care at a global level can be traced to the recognition by the World Health Organization (WHO) of unacceptably high infant mortality in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).1,2 The Alma-Ata Declaration was the first serious effort by the WHO to address the problem of high infant mortality rate (IMR) among developing countries. Since then, several policies have been proposed and implemented to decrease the IMR and neonatal mortality rate (NMR) across the globe. There has been steady improvement in overall global newborn care resulting in the reduction of NMR and IMR in LMICs since the latter part of the 20th century. The major factors responsible for overall improvements in maternal and child care in LMICs probably include: (1) improved access to medical and technical information, (2) rapid transfer of technology, (3) largescale studies in LMICs especially packages of care focused on reduction in neonatal mortality, (4), increased awareness of health and change in health care–seeking behavior among women, and (5) international campaigns such as the advocacy of the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs)3 and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).4 Several large controlled trials have demonstrated the benefits of selected interventions, including packages of care such as the Mother-Baby Package5 and the neonatal resuscitation and Essential Newborn Care programs.1,2,6–8 Considerable progress is being made in reducing maternal and child mortality in developing countries; however, many challenges remain. This chapter provides an overview of global neonatal and perinatal problems, presents data on the changing trends in IMR and NMR, and discusses strategies to decrease the IMR and NMR in developing countries.

108

### Global Initiatives to Reduce Infant Mortality Rate and Neonatal Mortality Rate

### Historical Perspective

Because of concerns of high global IMR and NMR, numerous interventions have been proposed and implemented by world organizations over the past four decades (Table 7.1). The Alma-Ata Declaration of 1978 by the WHO and the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) set a goal to achieve “Health for all by the year 2000.” The declaration included a goal for the reduction of maternal and infant mortality through primary care. In 1987, the International Conference on Safe Motherhood drew attention to high maternal mortality rates (MMRs) in developing countries and encouraged policymakers to develop new strategies to reduce maternal mortality. This action led to the worldwide program of Safe Motherhood, placing an emphasis on antenatal care. A similar resolution, the Bamako Initiative, was instituted at the annual meeting of the African Ministries of Health in 1987. The objective was the achievement of universal maternal-child health coverage at the periphery by 2000. In 1988, the Task Force for Child Survival set objectives for a reduction in under-5 mortality and MMR by at least half.

In 1994, the WHO developed the Mother-Baby Package to help reduce MMR and NMR further.5 At the WHO 48th World Health Assembly, the concept of integrated management of childhood illness was adopted to improve the well-being of the whole child younger than 5 years old.9 This concept included an emphasis on improved care of newborns. By the end of the 20th century, a significant decrease in MMR and IMR was reported as one of the top 10 achievements of the century.10 However, the high IMR and NMR in the LMICs

The World Bank initiated the Global Burden of Disease study, which showed that perinatal conditions, including infant mortality, form a significant portion (39%) of the global burden of disease. It showed that developing countries are the major contributors to global perinatal and neonatal mortality. Perinatal mortality constitutes one of the 10 leading causes of death in developing countries. Neonatal mortality is the major part of perinatal mortality. These findings underscore the importance of improving perinatal and neonatal care in developing countries, as declared in the MDGs in 2000.3

### The Millennium Development Goals

In 2000, the United Nations developed eight MDGs to be achieved by 2015.3 The targets were measured by preset quantifiable measures. The MDGs focus on some specific health issues but also emphasize social, economic, and public health and health-policy matters that affect the “health” of the people and addressed specific indicator goals for perinatal care (Table 7.2).

In addition to these developments, the series of landmark scientific publications in The Lancet provided evidence-based scalable interventions that could reduce NMR and IMR in resource-poor countries.11,12 These publications generated great interest among researchers and health policymakers around the globe. The Child Survival series examined the potential impact of scaling up 43 interventions that could reduce child mortality by 2015. In 2005, the series on newborn survival provided the first systematic estimates of neonatal deaths by cause and identified simple and cost-effective scalable interventions that could reduce neonatal deaths globally.
