### The Sustainable Development Goals

In 2015, the United Nations proposed the SDGs to be achieved by 2030.4,13 These goals were adopted to end poverty, protect the planet, and ensure prosperity for all as part of a new sustainable development agenda. Each goal has specific targets to be achieved over the next 15 years. There are 17 goals (Fig. 7.1).4 Goal 3 is focused on health and aims to ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all at all ages. This goal includes specific targets for perinatal and childhood health outcomes. The maternal and childhood targets aim to reduce global maternal mortality ratios to less than 70 per 100,000 live births and end preventable deaths of newborns and children younger than 5 years of age, with all countries aiming to reduce neonatal mortality to at least 12 per 1000 live births and under-5 mortality to at least 25 per 1000 live births. These aspiring goals are ambitious and will require commitment from all stakeholders to achieve them.

### Tracking the Global Progress of the Sustainable Development Goals

Worldwide efforts are taking place to implement SDGs and track their impact. There is a need for accurate birth and death data from all participating countries. Unfortunately, collecting accurate NMR, IMR, and under-5 mortality data on a global scale remains a major problem. There are several hurdles to collect these data accurately. High-income countries (HICs) have well-established vital statistics of births and deaths, whereas the LMICs do not. Only 60 of the 193 countries studied had fully functioning sources of mortality

### Global Burden of Maternal and Neonatal Deaths

### Maternal Mortality

Maternal mortality has been a major global burden of disease. More than 99% of the yearly maternal deaths occur in LMICs. The causes of maternal death include maternal hemorrhage (25%), sepsis (15%), abortion (13%), hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (12%), and obstructed labor (8%). More than 50% of the deaths related to pregnancy and childbirth were estimated to be preventable using simple, well-accepted interventions. The MDG #5 aimed at reducing the MMR by 75% between 1990 and 2015, but this was not accomplished. Global MMR in 2015 had decreased by 44% (from 385/100,000 in 1990 to 216/100,000).15 The highest regional rate of decline for 1990 to 2015 occurred in eastern Asia (5.0% annual decline). Sub-Saharan Africa continues to have the highest MMR, with 546/100,000 live births (Fig. 7.2). Sub-Saharan Africa contributed more than 66% of the maternal deaths worldwide in 2015.

### Neonatal and Infant Mortality

More than 98% of neonatal deaths occur in LMICs; the majority of these deaths occur in South Asia and

sub-Saharan Africa. There are limited data on NMR or IMR that go back to the early 20th century, but there were major reductions in mortality. Fig. 7.3 shows global trends in IMR during 1950 to 2000.16 In the 1950s, there were wide variations in IMR among different regions of the world. IMR was lowest in industrialized Western countries (33 per 1000). It decreased to around 5 per 1000 by 2000, a reduction of 85%. In 1950, sub-Saharan Africa had the highest IMR (157 per 1000) and showed the least reduction (only 32%) among all the regions of the world during the next 50 years. South Asia, the Middle East/North Africa, and Latin America/Caribbean showed 53%, 70%, and 74% decreases, respectively. At the end of the 20th century, IMR continued to remain significantly high: 70 per 1000 in South Asia, 45 per 1000 in the Middle East, and 27 per 1000 in Latin America.

The global NMR decreased by 51% from 36.6 per 1000 live births in 1990 to 18.0 deaths per 1000 live births in 2017.17 The estimated number of neonatal deaths during the same period decreased from 5.0 to 2.5 million. The NMR is the highest (30.2 per 1000 live births) in West and Central Africa and in South Asia (26.9). Countries with the highest NMRs were concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, accounting for 79% of the total burden of global neonatal deaths (see Fig. 7.3). The under-5 mortality is decreasing faster than those in neonatal mortality, and now neonatal mortality accounts for 47% of the global under-5 deaths compared with 40% in 1990. ### Causes of Global Maternal and Neonatal Mortality

Factors that influence MMR and NMR include commonly known maternal and neonatal medical problems, socioeconomic conditions, gender inequality, environmental factors, and economic and political instability. Socioeconomic factors greatly influence the health of mother and baby, in particular, in LMICs, as discussed in the following section.

### Socioeconomic and Cultural Factors

The socioeconomic factors adversely influencing IMR include gender bias against women, maternal education, and economic dependence. SDG #5 is aimed at eliminating gender inequity. Gender bias against women has a negative effect on every phase of a woman’s life, interfering with her education, economic power, and health. Gender-biased discrimination begins its influence early in life, leading to poorer nutrition and health in girls compared with boys. Gender inequalities persist worldwide, depriving women and girls of their basic rights and opportunities. SDG #1 aims to end poverty in

### Medical Causes of Neonatal Mortality

In developing countries, prematurity, birth asphyxia, and sepsis/pneumonia continue to constitute a major portion of

Neonatal death caused by prematurity is the number one cause of under-5 mortality rate. Birth asphyxia and sepsis/pneumonia are the other major causes of neonatal mortality.28 The WHO estimates that 40% to 60% of neonatal deaths are preventable. The major causes of neonatal mortality are discussed in detail in the following section.

### Prematurity

Although prematurity is the most frequent cause of death in neonates, the specific cause of death in premature babies worldwide is not known. Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) is the most common cause of death in HICs, but in LMICs it is likely that lack of neonatal intensive care accounts for most of the deaths from prematurity. A metaanalysis conclusively demonstrates that surfactant administration reduces mortality in LMIC settings with neonatal intensive care units (NICUs).30 There are many other effective therapies, such as thermoregulation, nutrition, and prevention and treatment of sepsis, that may have a large impact in LMIC settings. It is likely that most interventions that reduce neonatal mortality in NICUs in HICs will reduce neonatal mortality in similar settings in LMICs also.

### Hypothermia

Neonatal hypothermia is a common and important potentially life-threatening condition. Neonatal hypothermia occurs in 30% to 80% of newborn infants.42,43 The incidence of neonatal hypothermia is substantially higher in LMICs compared with HICs. The causes of neonatal hypothermia in LMICs are many, starting from low ambient temperature of delivery rooms. Inadequate clothing and giving routine baths soon after birth are causes of neonatal hypothermia. Newborns may also experience heat losses within the hospital during transport from delivery room to the postnatal ward and during transport home from the hospital or from hospital to hospital. Neonatal hypothermia increases metabolic demand, oxygen consumption, and neonatal mortality. In the absence of sophisticated and expensive incubators, simple techniques can be adopted to abate hypothermia.45

To reduce neonatal hypothermia, the WHO recommends the “warm chain,” a thermoregulation protocol that should be implemented in every nursery and with every newborn during the first several days and weeks after birth. The warm chain includes warm delivery rooms, immediate drying, uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact as much as possible, early breastfeeding, delayed bathing and weighing, appropriate bundling, mother and baby together, warm transportation, warm resuscitation, and training and awareness raising.46 However, not all the elements recommended in the WHO thermoregulation protocol are practiced routinely in many birth facilities around the world.47 Plastic bags and wrapping with plastic wrap at birth are effective in decreasing hypothermia in term and preterm infants.48 This is a very inexpensive and effective method of providing thermal protection to the newborn in the immediate neonatal period. Kangaroo mother care (KMC) is becoming a universal practice,49 and in addition to keeping the baby warm, the immediate initiation of breastfeeding provides early provision of calories. A Cochrane meta-analysis showed that KMC in preterm and low birth weight (LBW) infants also reduces mortality at the time of discharge.50 A large multicenter randomized controlled trial of early (day 1) KMC in 3211 preterm infants (birth weight 1.2–1.8 kg) markedly reduced neonatal deaths from 15.7% to 12.0% and reduced hypothermia.51

### Infections

It is estimated that worldwide, 15% to 20% of newborns die of neonatal infection. The incidence of sepsis is estimated to be 5 to 6 per 1000 live births (600,000–750,000) among hospitalized patients. Meningitis accounts for 0.7 to 1 per 1000 live births (88,000–126,000 cases per year), and acute respiratory infections account for 800,000 deaths in neonates. Among these deaths are cases of pneumonia, bronchiolitis, and laryngotracheitis. Cord infections and neonatal tetanus are preventable causes of acquired infection. The maternal transmission of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) to the newborn was a major factor contributing to neonatal deaths in some countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, but effective prevention is largely available.52

### Burden of Neonatal Sepsis

Infections in the neonatal period can manifest at birth but most often occur within the first few days, peaking at 2 weeks

after birth (see Fig. 7.8).29 Estimating the burden (incidence) of neonatal infections in developing countries is challenging because of several factors: (1) most births take place at home, and those newborns with sepsis rarely seek medical attention. (2) Hospital-derived information does not represent true incidence of sepsis in the community. (3) Laboratory facilities for cultures are inadequate or nonexistent. Population-based studies from developing countries have reported clinical sepsis rates ranging from 49 to 170 per 1000 live births.53 Among 18 studies from developing countries, the median incidence of blood culture–confirmed sepsis was 16 per 1000 live births. A study from Bangladesh found the incidence of clinically suspected neonatal sepsis to be 50 per 1000 live births, and the incidence of culture-confirmed sepsis was 3 per 1000 live births.54 The incidence of culture-confirmed neonatal sepsis was 5.5 per 1000 live births among neonates presenting to a first-level health facility in rural Kenya.55 However, the absence of active community surveillance suggests that the true burden is probably higher. A review of early-onset neonatal sepsis in developing countries found only five studies.56 The incidence of clinical sepsis ranged from 20.7 to 50 per 1000 live births, and the incidence of culture-confirmed early-onset neonatal sepsis ranged from 2.2 to 9.8 per 1000 live births. Only two of these studies reported case fatality rates, of 18% and 19%, respectively. These observations contrast with neonatal culture-confirmed sepsis rates of 1 to 3 per 1000 live births reported from industrialized countries,57 indicating the huge preventable burden of neonatal infections in LMICs.

### Diagnosis of Neonatal Sepsis

As noted, although blood culture is the gold standard for diagnosis of neonatal sepsis, lack of laboratory facilities is a major barrier to diagnosis and treatment of neonatal sepsis in LMICs. Therefore clinicians and health care workers depend on clinical signs of sepsis for diagnosis and treatment. Several clinical scores have been described to facilitate the diagnosis by health care workers in the field. Bang and co-workers have described a simple set of clinical criteria to recognize sepsis in a rural setting.58 The Young Infants Clinical Signs Study Group conducted a large multicountry study to identify clinical signs with high sensitivity and specificity for predicting sepsis.59 They identified seven common clinical signs that could be identified easily by health care workers in primary care settings. Other investigators have used slight modifications of these signs for clinical diagnosis of neonatal sepsis in community-based neonatal programs. The WHO also has developed guidelines for the Integrated Management of Childhood Illnesses for resource-limited countries.60 Using the aforementioned background information, an algorithm may be used by health care workers in LMICs to assess infants at home or in health facilities, initiate treatment for sepsis, and triage infants to higher levels of care.

Infographics can be used to assist clinicians and identify possible maternal61 (Fig. 7.12) and neonatal62 sepsis.

### The Impact of Progress

With the increased access to neonatal intensive care and improved survival of preterm and very LBW infants, there is a financial burden on families and risk of associated morbidities among survivors. Three major neonatal emerging challenges in developing countries are of great concern. They include (1) BPD, also known as chronic lung disease (CLD)76; (2) retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)77,78; and (3) neurodevelopmental delays.79,80 All three conditions are related to prematurity, and as survival of preterm infants increases, so does the incidence of CLD, ROP, and neurodevelopmental delays. Data regarding the prevalence of these morbidities in LMICs are lacking. Interventions can be delivered throughout the life span from before conception until adolescence to help infants and children not only survive into adulthood but also develop optimally, support their well-being, and help them reach their full developmental potential.81

BPD is a newly emerging disease in LMICs.76 LMICs contemplating the development of modern NICUs should be well-prepared to recognize these complications and associated costs. Strategies need to be developed to minimize the overall burden of disease on the community. In this regard, the application of CPAP as the first approach to managing RDS is to be encouraged in LMICs.21

ROP was first encountered in the early 1950s in HICs, with the introduction of high oxygen therapy and again with the introduction of ventilator care and increasing survival of extremely premature infants. Although the rate and severity of ROP are decreasing in HICs, they are beginning to increase in LMICs. A multicenter survey of oxygen practices in Africa showed that there are opportunities to improve oxygen supplementation and monitoring.82 As NMR is steadily decreasing, it is estimated that globally at least 50,000 children are blind from ROP. This observed large number of ROP worldwide has come to be known as the third epidemic.77 Fig. 7.14 shows estimates of ROP and visual impairment at regional and global levels. ROP is increasing worldwide including in middle- and low-income countries where oxygen availability is increasing but continuous oxygen saturation monitoring may not be universally used. About 3% of survivors of prematurity born at <32 weeks have visual impairment.19 ROP is being increasingly reported from India and China, home to more than one-sixth of the world’s population. Blindness caused by ROP begins to rise as the IMR of a country continues to decrease. These data suggest the influence of increased survival of preterm infants with the introduction of NICU care, oxygen therapy,83,84 and ventilation: the lower the IMR, the higher the rate of ROP-related blindness. ROP will soon become a public health issue in these countries unless control activities keep pace with the increased survival of premature babies at risk.

There is a need to develop and implement educational programs to avoid the potentially hazardous practices of high oxygen therapy, to promote early detection of ROP, and to pursue a multidisciplinary approach to prevent ROP. LMICs also have the additional problem of lack of awareness of ROP among pediatricians, whereas ophthalmologists may be inadequately trained in the recognition and management of ROP.78

### The Burden of the High Cost of Advanced Neonatal Care

The overall cost of neonatal intensive care at the tertiary level in developing countries is relatively high and sometimes affordable only to middle- and upper-income groups. Infants with RDS can be successfully managed with ventilator support85 at an average cost of US $1391 per survivor. The per-day cost of NICU care of neonates in a government teaching hospital was estimated to be US $125/day.86 NICU care for infants born at 24 to 26, 27 to 29, and 30 to 33 weeks’ gestational age in Mexico prolonged life expectancy by 28, 43, and 34 years and averted 9, 15, and 12 disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) at incremental costs per infant of US $11,400, US $9500, and US $3000, respectively, compared with infants with no intensive care.87 These data provide evidence that even in LMICs, provision of NICU care is costeffective in improving survival and decreasing morbidity. ### Long-Term Neurodevelopmental Outcome

Data on long-term outcomes in LMICs are limited. Lack of a uniform database of surviving infants, lack of expertise in assessing developmental disabilities, and the lack of a support system for needy families and children are the major barriers to develop meaningful information regarding the morbidity of surviving infants. Mwaniki and co-workers reviewed 153 studies from around the world suitable for inclusion for analysis of developmental outcome of high-risk newborns.79 Altogether, there were 22,161 survivors of intrauterine or neonatal insults. The overall median risk of at least one sequela in any domain was 39% (interquartile range [IQR] 20%–55%), with a risk of at least one severe impairment in any insult domain of 18% (8%–33%), at least one moderate impairment of 5% (0%–13%), and at least one mild impairment of 10% (1%–18%).

The pooled risk estimate of at least one sequela associated with one or more of the insults studied (excluding HIV) was 37% (95% CI 27%–48%). The most common deficits were learning difficulties, cognition, or developmental delay (N = 4032; 59%); cerebral palsy (N = 1472; 21%); hearing

impairment (N = 1340; 20%); and visual impairment (N = 1228; 18%). Only 40 studies included data for multidomain impairments. These studies (26%) included 2815 individuals, of whom 1048 (37%) had impairments, with 334 (32%) having multiple impairments. These findings show that in developing countries, perinatal adverse insults have a high risk of causing substantial long-term neurologic morbidity.

Shillcutt and co-workers80 studied the estimates of long-term disabilities following neonatal illness in a district of Bangladesh. They found that “a significant burden of disability results from neonatal conditions.” They also projected that their national newborn project might have averted several years lost to disability.

The preceding two studies provide important information on the impact of advanced care and increasing survival of at-risk infants in LMICs. Comparable cohort studies in other resource-poor regions should be done to assess the burden of long-term outcome effects of improved neonatal survival.

title: Social and Economic Contributors to Neonatal Outcome in the United States

paragraphs.text: 8 Social and Economic Contributors to Neonatal Outcome in the United States
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Although there have been significant improvements in infant mortality (death within 1 year of life) and neonatal mortality (death within 28 days of life) in the United States over the past 50 years, compared with other highincome countries in the world, the United States alarmingly lags behind these other countries in infant mortality rates.1 Infant mortality and morbidity rates are commonly used as an important indicator worldwide of overall population health. Recent research has focused on why the United States has not seen continued improvements in these public health indices as have other countries, and indeed several markers of US infant health have worsened in recent years. It is important to understand recent US trends and contributing factors to provide optimal care and public health planning in the prenatal, perinatal, neonatal, and postneonatal periods to improve these outcomes. One major factor contributing to these poor perinatal and infant outcomes in the United States is the significant health disparities seen among women and infants related to race and ethnicity. Other disparities in health outcomes in the perinatal and infant period in the United States are related to poverty, poor maternal health, lack of health care access and health insurance, and other overall indicators of poor socioeconomic status.
paragraphs.heading: Epidemiology of Health Disparities in Neonatal and Perinatal Medicine

paragraphs.text: Although the United States had a steady decline in infant mortality over the past decades, declining 19% from 6.89 deaths per 1000 live births in 2000 to 5.58 per 1000 in 2019
paragraphs.heading: Infant Mortality

paragraphs.text: (Fig. 8.1),2 this rate is still almost twice that of other comparable countries in the world. Recent data comparing infant mortality indicated that the United States had two to three times the infant mortality rate of countries such as Japan, Italy, and Sweden1 in spite of significantly larger health care expenditures in the United States per capita compared with these other countries.3 Multiple studies have attempted to delineate the factors unique to the United States that might explain this discrepancy. The United States has made continued progress in decreasing the neonatal mortality rate as well, with a rate of 3.69 per 1000 births in 2019, a significant decrease from 4.62 per 1000 births documented in 2000.2 However, this rate is also significantly higher than the neonatal mortality rates seen in comparable countries.
paragraphs.heading: Infant Mortality

paragraphs.text: Prematurity (infants born at less than 37 weeks) overall in the United States has a major impact on the high infant mortality rates. Previous studies show that the United States has rates of prematurity two to three times that of other developed countries.4 Clearly this is a significant contributor to the high infant mortality seen in the United States. During the 1990s and early 2000s, the US preterm birth rate steadily increased by 20% from 10.6% in 1990 to 12.8% in 2006.5 At that time, after widespread public health efforts, it seemed the United States was making significant progress in decreasing the rate of prematurity. The United States initially saw a steady decrease in the prematurity rate over the next decade, with a decrease to 9.57% in 2014, the lowest rate the United States has ever experienced (Fig. 8.2).6 Disturbingly, this trend in the prematurity rate has reversed in recent years, with a significant increase in the younger than 37 weeks’ birthrate to 10.23% in 2019 and 10.09% in 2020, primarily because of an increase in late preterm births (34–36 weeks’ completed gestation).6,7 It is unclear

paragraphs.text: Given that the percentage overall of preterm births in the United States is twice that of comparable countries, addressing the causes of prematurity are critical to reducing the US infant mortality rate. However, a higher rate of prematurity alone does not explain the higher US infant mortality rate because the gestational age specific infant mortality rates are also increased above other countries at gestational ages 32 weeks and greater, the category with the highest number of preterm births as well as term births.4,6 Addressing prematurity is a significant financial priority as well as public health priority. Recent estimates from a large commercially insured population (763,566 infants) reveal that the cost for the median term birth for the first 6 months of life was $3787, whereas for a premature infant born at 24 weeks, the median cost for the first 6 months is $548,865.8 It was estimated that in recent years, more than $25 billion is spent each year on premature births.9

paragraphs.text: It is now well established that a major contributor to the concerning infant mortality rates in the United States is the significant health disparities seen in the country. The major health disparity is related to racial and ethnic differences seen in numerous aspects of infant and perinatal health outcomes in all states in the United States, with wide variation state to state. Epidemiologists have carefully tracked infant mortality rates by race and ethnicity in the United States for many years and have documented significant differences in neonatal and infant mortality by race and ethnicity, worsening in recent years. Indeed, over the past 100 years in the United States, while the neonatal and post-neonatal mortality rates for both non-Hispanic White and non-Hispanic
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 8.2 Preterm birth rates: United States, final 2007 to 2019 and provisional 2020. (From National

paragraphs.text: Black have improved, the Black/White ratios of mortality have steadily worsened and remained high over the past 100 years.1 Studies have generally gathered data according to the following racial and ethnic distinctions with a variation in naming in multiple references: non-Hispanic White, non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic, American Indian or Alaska Native, and Asian or Pacific Islander. More recent data have separated Pacific Islanders from the Asian outcomes, with the realization that these are actually very different groups with different outcomes.2,6 In addition, Hispanic groups are often further subcategorized by Hispanic origin: Puerto Rican, Mexican, Central and South American, and Cuban.2 Several studies have also investigated if race and ethnicity are impacted by whether the mother is US or foreign born.10 These studies have shown a worse outcome for the same racial groups if born in the United States compared with being foreign born, both for Hispanics and non- Hispanic Blacks.

paragraphs.text: Recent epidemiologic studies have consistently shown that non-Hispanic Black infants have an infant mortality rate greater than two times that of non-Hispanic White infants (10.62 deaths per 1000 live births in 2019 vs. 4.49 per 1000 live births) (Fig. 8.3).2 American Indian or Alaskan Native and Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander infants also exhibit substantially higher infant mortality rates than non-Hispanic Whites.2 Past infant mortality data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) grouped Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander infants with Asian infants and indicated low infant mortality rates,11 but recent studies separating these groups from Asian infants indicate that Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander outcomes for infant mortality are much more similar to American Indian
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 8.2 Preterm birth rates: United States, final 2007 to 2019 and provisional 2020. (From National

paragraphs.text: or Alaska Native outcomes.2 Interestingly, Asian infants have consistently exhibited the lowest neonatal and infant mortality rates for many years, whereas Hispanic infant mortality rates track close to non-Hispanic White infant mortality rates, in spite of economic disadvantages and poor health care access for many Hispanic women and infants.2

paragraphs.text: As noted, overall infant mortality rates in total and for each race or ethnic group have decreased each year.2,11 It appeared that the United States was making great strides in reducing the discrepancies in infant mortality rates related to race with a 20% decline from 2005 to 2014 seen in non-Hispanic Black rates compared to the overall US decline of 16% during those years. However, recent US infant mortality data show disturbingly that in 2019, only non-Hispanic Whites had a significant decrease; other groups did not show a statistically significant improvement.2 Of concern, the 2019 data indicate that for non-Hispanic Black infants compared to non-Hispanic White infants, the infant mortality rate disparity increased from 2.24 in 2014 to 2.37 in 2019. The disparity in neonatal mortality for non-Hispanic Black infants compared to non-Hispanic White infants also is disturbingly high at 2.35. However, a different picture emerges for neonatal and infant mortality rates of Native American/Alaska Natives and Native Hawaiian/ Pacific Islanders. These two groups have also had higher infant mortality rates compared to non-Hispanic White infants (see Fig. 8.3). However, for both non-Hispanic White and Black infants the contribution to infant mortality of deaths for the postneonatal period is similar at about 35%, while for Pacific Islanders it is increased to almost 40% of infant mortality and for American Indian or Alaska Native infants, the contribution to infant mortality in the postneonatal period is almost 50%.2 Thus it is likely that there are differences in each of these racial groups for the higher infant mortality rates compared to non-Hispanic White infants and it appears that in the United States, these disparities by race are worsening in recent years. As noted, infant mortality rates for Hispanics track closely with those of non-Hispanic White infants. Interestingly, when looking closely at the infant and neonatal mortality rates in Hispanics by ethnicity, wide ranges exist, with Cuban Hispanic infants having a much lower infant mortality rate compared to Puerto Rican Hispanic infants in 2019 (4.14 per 1,000 live births compared to 6.17 per 1,000 live births.2 In addition, there are significant differences in infant mortality by state in the United States, with the southern states having the highest infant mortality. These are also the states with the highest percentage of non-Hispanic Black women in their population (Fig. 8.4). In addition, those states with the greatest increase in level of income inequality in recent years have higher risks of infant and neonatal mortality.12

paragraphs.text: It is also important to evaluate perinatal mortality rates (late fetal deaths at 28 completed weeks of gestation or more and early neonatal deaths less than age 7 days) because this can be an indicator of the quality of health care before, during, and after delivery and also of the health status of the nation. In addition, late fetal deaths are not accounted for in neonatal and infant mortality and may skew infant mortality rates when evaluating by race. Similar to infant mortality in
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 8.2 Preterm birth rates: United States, final 2007 to 2019 and provisional 2020. (From National

paragraphs.text: the United States, there was a significant decrease in perinatal mortality in the United States from 1990 to 2011, which did not improve over the next 5 years. Encouragingly, there has been a small but significant decrease in perinatal mortality since 2017 in both late fetal and early neonatal deaths.13 However, mirroring the infant mortality rate disparities, fetal deaths and perinatal mortality rates show wide ranges when looking closely at race and ethnicity. Non-Hispanic Black fetal mortality rates are twice as high as non-Hispanic White rates.13 Poorer maternal health and decreased access to prenatal care may have an impact on this outcome.

paragraphs.text: To understand the impact of race and ethnicity on neonatal and infant mortality in the United States, we must first understand whether differences exist in maternal and prenatal factors that would impact mortality. Similar to the significant racial disparities seen in infant mortality, the incidence of prematurity (babies less than 37 weeks) varies greatly by race and ethnicity. Non-Hispanic Black women consistently have the highest rate of overall prematurity, and it was almost 60% higher than the prematurity rates of non-Hispanic White women in 2020.6 The disparities in the incidence of severe prematurity also increase greatly by race and ethnicity, with the percentage of births less than 28 weeks (the risk of highest mortality) in 2020 for non-Hispanic Blacks being more than three times the percent of non-Hispanic Whites in 2020 (1.47% vs. 0.44%).6 When evaluating the impact of prematurity on mortality, those born at the lowest gestational ages have the highest mortality. Similar to infant mortality outcomes, the highest prematurity rate of infants born less than 34 weeks occurs for non-Hispanic Black infants (4.82 %) compared with non-Hispanic Whites (2.21%). The lowest prematurity rate of infants less than 34 weeks is seen in Asian infants (2.08%), with Hispanic infants (2.52%) slightly greater than those of non-Hispanic Whites (Table 8.1). American Indian/Alaskan Native infants and Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander infants show a more favorable less than 34-week percentage at 3.05% and 3.08% of births, respectively, in 2020 compared with the rate for non-Hispanic Black infants.6 As noted previously, overall US prematurity rates for less than 37 weeks’ gestation are increased in recent years compared with the lowest rate in 2014, and we will need to carefully investigate the contribution of racial disparities to this recent increase in prematurity.6,7 Similar to the wide variation in infant mortality by state in the United States, there are vast differences state by state in the rate of prematurity in the United States, with Southern states having the highest preterm rates (see Fig. 8.4).

Congenital malformations are the leading cause of death for non-Hispanic White infants,2 whereas death because of low birth weight/preterm-related causes is the leading cause of death for non-Hispanic Blacks compared with non-Hispanic

paragraphs.text: Whites at almost four times the rate. Compared with non-Hispanic White infants, non-Hispanic Black infants also die at a disproportionate rate because of congenital malformations and newborns affected by maternal complications of pregnancy. In contrast, Native Americans and Alaska Natives have a much lower infant mortality because of prematurity compared with other groups but have the highest rate of infant deaths because of SIDS of all racial and ethnic groups examined. There are also differences in mortality noted within certain ethnic groups. For Puerto Rican infants, the rate of infant mortality because of preterm causes is almost twofold that of non-Hispanic Whites and is the highest among the Hispanic subgroups, with Central (Mexico) and South Americans having much lower rates of prematurity and infant mortality.2 This could reflect the longerterm presence of the Puerto Rican population in the United States compared with more recent Hispanic immigrants and the cumulative toxic effect in the United States of low socioeconomic status over time on adverse pregnancy outcomes.

paragraphs.text: Congenital anomalies and subsequent infant mortality are also impacted by health disparities. Bassil et al. found that
paragraphs.heading: Selected Maternal and Birth Characteristics by Race and Hispanic Origin of Mother, 2020 Final Data. National Center for Health Statistics

paragraphs.text: socioeconomic inequities lead to a significant increase in major congenital anomalies in babies born to mothers in areas of highest deprivation.14 Further analysis revealed that there were higher odds of chromosomal and multiple systems anomalies in the highest deprivation areas. These findings could be explained by higher exposure to teratogens or to poor health of these disadvantaged mothers. A more recent study from California found that increased social deprivation and exposures to environmental pollutants are associated with a higher incidence of congenital heart disease.15 Minorities in the United States are often the racial groups living in the poorest neighborhoods, with increased exposure to pollution and environmental toxins.

paragraphs.text: Postneonatal mortality in SIDS and SUID, leading and increasing causes of infant mortality, also exhibit racial and ethnic disparities. Sharp declines in the rates of SIDS in the 1990s have been associated with national efforts to promote infant safe sleep, mainly through the Back-to-Sleep campaign.16 In addition, cases previously diagnosed as SIDS deaths are now being classified as unknown or accidental strangulation in bed. Therefore the encompassing term of SUID captures the true
paragraphs.heading: Selected Maternal and Birth Characteristics by Race and Hispanic Origin of Mother, 2020 Final Data. National Center for Health Statistics

paragraphs.text: trend of these deaths more accurately. However, racial disparities in SIDS/SUID have persisted. For American Indian or Alaska Natives, the largest difference in infant mortality outcomes when compared with non-Hispanic Whites is the almost threefold increase in mortality rate in 2020 caused by SIDS from recent data (American Indian: 84.4 per 100,000 live births, non-Hispanic White: 28.9 per 100,000 live births)2 compared with a slight increase in mortality rate because of prematurity for American Indian or Alaska Natives when compared with White infants.2 Similar to overall infant mortality, non-Hispanic Black infants also have a very high rate of death caused by SIDS seen in 2020, only slightly less than that of American Indian or Alaska Natives. Similar racial disparities for American Indian or Alaska Natives are seen in SUID. For American Indian or Alaska Natives, the largest difference in mortality outcomes when compared with non- Hispanic Whites is the twofold increase in deaths caused by SUID (American Indian: 177.6 per 100,000 live births, non-Hispanic White: 84.5 per 100,000 live births).17 Non- Hispanic Blacks also have an extremely high rate of mortality from SUID (172.4 per 100,000 live births), only slightly lower than the rate for Native American infants.17 The lowest rate of SUID is seen in Hispanic and Asian/Pacific Islander infants (Hispanic: 49.3 per 100,000 live births, Asian/Pacific Islanders: 28.3 per 100,000 live births), even lower than the non-Hispanic White rate. A significant impact on SUID is decreasing gestational age at birth, with infants born at 24 to 27 weeks having a 3.5- to 5-fold increase in the rate of SIDS compared with term infants.18 Again, racial disparities are seen here, with a SUID rate in non-Hispanic Blacks at less than 28 weeks of 382.3 per 100,000 live births compared with the lowest group Asian/Pacific Islanders: 126.6 per 100,000 live births at less than 28 weeks.17 Given that the highest rate of prematurity is seen in non-Hispanic Blacks, this contribution to SIDS/SUID also negatively impacts this population and infant mortality. It is unclear what impact genetic versus cultural factors may play in mortality caused by SUID and SIDS. Finally, there has been a distressing increase in infant mortality because of accidental suffocation and strangulation in bed (ASSB) over more than 20 years.19 A recent study has shown that ASSB mortality continues to increase significantly: for 1999 to 2016, 4.4-fold for non-Hispanic Black girls (45.8 per 100,000 in 2016), 3.5-fold for non-Hispanic Black boys (53.8), 2.7-fold for non-Hispanic White girls (15.8), and 4.0-fold for non-Hispanic White boys (25.9). As for many other factors impacting the racial inequities impacting infant mortality, the overall rates were much higher for non-Hispanic Black infants. The authors also noted factors previously associated with ASSB (unmarried mothers and mothers with low educational attainment, low infant birth weight, low gestational age, lack of prenatal care) continue to be associated with both overall ASSB and racial inequalities adversely affecting non-Hispanic Black infants.
