### Maternal Mortality

Maternal mortality related to pregnancy has been steadily increasing in the United States over the past 20 years and

continues to increase20,21 despite significant decreases seen in other high-income countries during this same time period.

A maternal death is defined by the World Health Organization as “the death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, irrespective of the duration and the site of the pregnancy, from any cause related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management, but not from accidental or incidental causes.” Again, alarming racial and ethnic disparities are seen in pregnancy-related mortality in the United States, with non-Hispanic Black women dying at a rate almost three times that of non-Hispanic White women (55.3/100,000 live births vs. 19.1/100,000).20 This is especially concerning for pregnant non-Hispanic Black women over the age of 40, with a rate of 263.1 per 100,000 live births.20 The higher maternal mortality rates for Black women are consistent regardless of education level.22 For Native American and Alaska Natives mothers, similar to the high infant mortality rates, the maternal mortality rates are more than twice that of non-Hispanic White mothers.22 Maternal mortality rates have also increased over the past years for Hispanic mothers, but their rates are similar to, and even slightly lower than, non-Hispanic White mothers.22 Although the reasons for the dramatic increase in US pregnancy related mortality and morbidity are not clearly understood, underlying poorer maternal health, obesity, lack of prenatal care, poor access to medical care, inadequate or no health insurance, teen pregnancies, and single mothers without support systems all are likely contributors to this high mortality rate. Maternal morbidities and other indicators of poor health care during pregnancy are significantly higher in non-Hispanic Black women and American Indian and Alaskan Native women compared with Non-Hispanic White women.6,23,24 Maternal deaths caused by hemorrhage, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, emboli, and anesthesia complications have declined because of state initiatives and focused educational and obstetric interventions; however, contributions to maternal death from cardiovascular conditions, cardiomyopathy, stroke, and noncardiovascular medical conditions have significantly increased in recent years.24 Looking more closely at severe maternal morbidity during the delivery period and post delivery in the Medicaid population, non- Hispanic Black women (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.53), Hispanic women (aOR, 1.46), and women of other races or ethnicities (aOR, 1.40) had higher rates of morbidity during delivery hospitalization than non-Hispanic White women; however, only the disparity between Black and White women (aOR, 1.69; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.57–1.81) persisted into the postdischarge period.23 Racial disparities impact a variety of maternal morbidities, with non-Hispanic Black and American Indian and Alaska Native women having the highest rates of blood transfusion, heart failure, shock, eclampsia, and renal failure in the perinatal period, as well as an overall rate of severe maternal morbidity more than twice that of non- Hispanic White women during delivery hospitalization.24 Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are particularly dangerous conditions leading to maternal morbidity and death, as well as several neonatal complications, especially preterm birth and its associated complications for the neonate. The rates of


## PDF page 157

hypertensive disorders of pregnancy as well as chronic hypertension in women during their pregnancies have dramatically increased in the past 30 years.25 Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are highest in non-Hispanic Black mothers and American Indians/Alaska Natives but lower in Hispanics and Asians compared with non-Hispanic White women.26 However, in a study looking at more than 11 million deliveries in the United States from 2016 to 2018, although Black women were the most likely to experience preeclampsia, Asian/Pacific women were the most at risk for acute cardiovascular complications during delivery hospitalization.26 In addition, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and subsequent elective deliveries because of maternal risks are a leading cause of prematurity.

As noted, the worsening health of many women before and during pregnancy has been a leading cause of poor maternal and infant outcomes.25 The massive rise in obesity in the US population over the past years has been well documented. Of significant concern to those in the public health arena is how this has negatively impacted women of productive age and their future children. Maternal obesity is another aspect of health disparities in that those races and ethnicities exhibiting worse perinatal and neonatal outcomes also have significantly higher rates of obesity than the general population. Recent data indicate that in the past decade, non-Hispanic Black women older than the ages of 20 have an extremely high incidence of obesity at 56.9% compared with non-Hispanic White women at 39.8%.27 Hispanic women also suffer from this epidemic of increased weight with a recent obesity incidence of 43.7%. In recent years, the rate of prepregnancy obesity has increased significantly in spite of the known health risks during pregnancy. Disparities in the incidence of obesity during pregnancy also are seen in non-Hispanic Black women who have the highest rates of obesity before and during pregnancy in the general population, especially at the highest categories of obesity. From 2016 to 2019, the percentage of non-Hispanic White women with prepregnancy obesity rose 10% (from 24.1% to 26.6%), 7% for non-Hispanic Black women (36.4%–39.1%), and 12% for Hispanic women (28.9%–32.4%).28 Obesity is known to increase the risk of gestational diabetes from a baseline of 2.8% to a high of 14.6% in pregnant women with class III obesity.29 Other morbidities of pregnancy such as gestational hypertensive disorders (increasing fourfold at highest obesity classes), infection, cesarean section rates, and cardiovascular events are all higher in obese pregnant women. Although obesity has its own risks of increased morbidity in pregnant women, obesity is also associated with increased neonatal/infant mortality and morbidity, as well as preterm delivery and congenital malformations.28 Infant mortality increases with each increase in obesity category. Declercq et al. found that with a normal prepregnancy weight as a reference, the odds ratio (OR) for an infant death rose from 1.32 for mothers in the obese I category up to 1.73 for obese III category pregnant mothers.30 Lemon et al. reported that compared with non-Hispanic White women, non-Hispanic Black women were more likely to have obesity and experienced a higher rate of stillbirth (8.3 vs. 3.6 stillbirths per 1000 liveborn and stillborn infants) and infant death (8.5 vs. 3.0 infant deaths per 1000 live births).31

In addition, obesity during pregnancy also is associated with increased neonatal morbidities such as increased prematurity, sepsis, large for gestational age infants, and neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission.29 Increasing obesity also results in an increased risk of major malformations in the neonate and were the highest as the severity of obesity increased.32 Congenital malformations were seen in the cardiovascular system, malformations of the nervous system, and limb defects. Clearly, the obesity epidemic is adversely affecting minority women during pregnancy and their babies disproportionately. It is also likely that an impact to reduce these adverse outcomes must be implemented before conception to impact these events which develop even before most mothers realize they are pregnant.

Separate from its relation to obesity, there has also been a significant increase in diabetes during pregnancy, both for type I and II diabetes before pregnancy and gestational diabetes during pregnancy.25,33 Diabetes during pregnancy leads to significant poor outcomes for the mother, as well as for the fetus and infant. Severe maternal diabetes at the time of conception can result in major congenital anomalies. Diabetes during the pregnancy can result in cardiac anomalies, birth asphyxia, and severe hypoglycemia in the neonate. However, there are known racial and ethnic differences in gestational diabetes. A recent study of gestational diabetes by Shah et al. found that, among individuals with a singleton first live birth in the United States from 2011 to 2019, rates of gestational diabetes increased across all racial and ethnic subgroups, overall by 3.7% per year. Gestational diabetes rates were highest in Asian Indian mothers, and among Hispanic/Latina participants, gestational diabetes rates were highest among Puerto Rican individuals.33 However, this study did not include American Indians/Alaska Natives, a group known to have extremely high rates of both pre-existing diabetes and gestational diabetes.34 In addition, this study also found that non- Hispanic Black mothers had the highest rate of pregestational diabetes, more than 50% higher than non-Hispanic White mothers (14.2 per 1000 live births compared with 7.9).33

A significant body of research has focused on the high teen pregnancy rate in the United States compared with other high-income countries. In the United States, babies born to mothers younger than the age of 20 have the highest infant mortality rates,2,35 with those mothers at the lowest ages having even higher infant mortality rates.36 Encouragingly, rates of teen pregnancies have significantly decreased in recent years for all races and ethnicities in the United States.6,37 However, several groups with high teen pregnancy rates, (non-Hispanic Black women, American Indian/Alaska Native, and Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander women) also have the highest infant mortality rates, and prematurity rate and teen pregnancies are likely to play a factor in these outcomes. There are also significant regional differences in the United States in teen birth rates, with the Southern states having much higher rates of teen pregnancies.6,37

There has been great interest in the comparatively good infant mortality outcomes seen in Hispanics in the United States, despite many poor indicators of health care and overall health and high poverty. Interestingly, although teen pregnancies (ages

### Determinants of Prematurity and Adverse Outcomes Social Determinants of Health

As defined by the World Health Organization, the social determinants of health (SDOH) are the nonmedical factors that influence health outcomes. They are the conditions in which people are born, grow, work, live, and age and the wider set of forces and systems shaping the conditions of daily life. These forces and systems include economic policies and systems, development agendas, social norms, social policies, and political systems.43 Health is determined in part by access to social and economic opportunities; the resources and supports available in homes, neighborhoods, and communities; the quality of schooling; the safety of workplaces; the cleanliness of water, food, and air; and the nature of social interactions and relationships. These circumstances are shaped by the distribution of money, power, and resources at global, national, and local levels. Health care disparities are important contributors to overall health disparities along with SDOH. These health care disparities adversely affect members of racial and ethnic minority groups and other socially disadvantaged populations. However, it is important to stress that “race” is not a biological entity but a socially defined group based on skin color or appearance. Thus it has become increasingly clear that there is no biologic predisposition to overall poor outcomes based on race but rather because of the inequities that are evident in the United States based on race and ethnicity.44 A discussion of maternal and infant health disparities would be incomplete without an exploration of these factors associated with health disparities.

These social determinants also greatly impact perinatal outcomes.45 SDOH have been described as largely responsible for the preventable differences in health status (health inequities). Poverty limits access to healthy foods and safe neighborhoods, and it is also known that increased education is a predictor of better health. A recent study found that a decrease in maternal education could explain persistent socioeconomic disparities in infant, neonatal, and postneonatal mortality rates in the United States.1 Examples of SDOH include: • Availability of resources to meet daily needs (e.g., safe

housing and local food markets) • Access to educational, economic, job opportunities, health

care services, and quality of education and job training • Availability of community-based resources in support of

community living and opportunities for recreational and leisure-time activities • Transportation options and public safety • Social support, social norms and attitudes (e.g., discrimi-

nation, racism, and distrust of government)

• Exposure to crime, violence, and social disorder (e.g.,

presence of trash and lack of cooperation in a community) • Socioeconomic conditions (e.g., concentrated poverty

and the stressful conditions that accompany it) • Residential segregation, language/literacy, and culture • Access to mass media and emerging technologies (e.g.,

cell phones, the Internet, and social media) A “place-based” organizing framework, reflecting five key areas of SDOH, was developed by Healthy People 2030.46 These five key areas (determinants) include: (1) economic stability, (2) education access and quality, (3) health care access and quality, (4) neighborhood and built environment, and (5) social and community context.46 Each of these five areas reflect several critical components/key issues that make up the underlying factors.

Recent emphasis has been placed on screening patients for the social determinants of health in the medical setting to improve health outcomes.47 Health literacy is considered an important social determinant of health that may underlie many health disparities, but it is possible that inadequate health literacy among pregnant individuals is associated with adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes. Inadequate maternal health literacy is associated with a variety of adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes including a greater risk of cesarean delivery, small for gestational age, low birth weight, and a 5-minute Apgar score less than 4.48

The complex history of race and ethnicity in the United States may affect individual responses to medical recommendations for screening tests and adherence to treatment plans, contributing to disparate outcomes along racial lines. Numerous examples exist of racial and ethnic groups being targeted for forced medical procedures or experimentation. These past atrocities in the United States have left a lasting mistrust in minority communities. Although distrust of the health care system has not been well studied in the prenatal/obstetric/ neonatal context, it may be an important additional mediator in the relationship between utilization and outcomes for those at risk of disparities. Experiences of racism, segregation, and discrimination likely play a role in health system engagement and prenatal care utilization, as well as affecting the outcomes of premature infants.49 In a survey of mothers, non-Hispanic Black or Hispanic race/ethnicity was associated with almost three times higher odds of discrimination because of race, language, or culture, and uninsured women had nearly twice the odds of experiencing any perceived discrimination.50

Adequacy of prenatal care has been found to be significantly associated with improved infant outcomes, particularly gestational age at delivery and birth weight.50,51 Race6 and living in a distressed neighborhood are associated with late presentation to prenatal care. Proximity to the hospital is a key mediator in prenatal care utilization, and transportation to appointments and affordability of transportation are key factors in adherence to prenatal care. The impact of the neighborhood of residence on prenatal care disparities has not been explained by provider or physician supply alone. Racial segregation is likely to be an important factor in poorer outcomes seen by races and ethnicity. Mehra, investigating racial segregation based on maternal


## PDF page 160 | printed page 141

residence at birth, found greater Black-White and Hispanic- White disparities in preterm birth in racially isolated counties (exposure) relative to nonisolated counties.52 However, they also found reduced Hispanic-White disparities in term low birth weight in racially concentrated and centralized counties relative to nonsegregated counties. Area-level poverty explained most of the moderating effect of segregation on disparities in adverse birth outcomes, suggesting that area-level poverty is a mediator of these associations. Segregation appears to modify racial/ethnic disparities in adverse birth outcomes.

Social determinants such as insurance status, availability of social support in the form of childcare and adequate housing, neighborhood, and transportation likely play some role in prenatal care utilization and ultimately neonatal outcomes.50 Not surprisingly, a previous study investigating SDOH during a previous economic downturn in the United States indicated that individual and community indicators of need increased at these times.53 Providing adequate nutrition to mothers and infants via the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children (WIC) program is an important assistance program in the United States. In this study, WIC may have been more effective at reducing late/no prenatal care utilization than the other maternal and child health safety net programs.53 Community-based research has shown that bundling prenatal care with other services such as child care that specifically aimed to reduce known disparities in social determinants improves outcomes.53 Homelessness in the United States has increased in recent years, also impacting those women of childbearing age. Non-Hispanic Black women are more likely to be homeless during their pregnancy or preconception period, and prenatal homelessness is associated with higher odds of low birth weight and preterm delivery. A recent study found homelessness in pregnancy was associated with adverse perinatal outcomes, including increased odds of preterm delivery across all gestational ages, and increased risk of NICU admission and low birth weight independent of preterm delivery.54

Access to health care is central to the delivery of health care services. In the health care context, it is defined as access to a service, a provider, or an institution, thus defined as the opportunity or ease with which consumers or communities are able to use appropriate services in proportion to their needs. Levesque et al.55 conceptualize five dimensions of accessibility of services: Approachability, Acceptability, Availability and Accommodation, Affordability, and Appropriateness. Five corresponding abilities of persons interact with these dimensions of accessibility to generate access; these dimensions of abilities include: Ability to perceive; Ability to seek; Ability to reach; Ability to pay; and Ability to engage. The various dimensions of access identified are not completely independent constructs.

Although the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) has increased the number of US children with coverage, insurance coverage alone does not guarantee access to needed health care. Angier et al. found affordability and lack of availability to be the most commonly reported barriers to health care access in a cohort of parents with incomes less than 133% of the federal poverty level; despite their child having health insurance, parents were unable to receive necessary health

care services.56 This is similar to reports from other studies highlighting lack of affordable and available care as major access barriers. Low socioeconomic status is associated with poor health status before, during, and after pregnancy.

The disturbing increases in racial and ethnic disparities in infant and neonatal mortality may be related to additional inequities in the provision of health care. Although the United States has always been a nation of immigrants, recent statelevel immigrant policies have made it much more difficult to address health inequities seen by race and ethnicity. Several states are seeking to criminalize immigrants, even those who are pregnant.57 A recent study analyzed birth record data from all 50 states and the District of Columbia in 2018, as well as state-level indicators of inclusive and criminalizing immigrant policies. More inclusive policies led to a reduction in preterm birth for those mothers born outside of the United States; in contrast, each additional criminalizing policy was associated with a 5% increase in preterm birth among Black women born outside the United States.57

Before the Affordable Care Act (ACA) spurred major expansions in health insurance coverage, non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic working-age adults were far more likely than non-Hispanic Whites to be uninsured.58 Uninsured women are 77% less likely to use obstetric services, have higher rates of severe morbidity, and are more likely to have inadequate prenatal care.50 Having health insurance makes it easier to gain access to and afford care, but insurance alone is unlikely to eliminate differences in access among all groups. Increased state-level Medicaid reimbursement for care increases adequate prenatal care utilization.

A recent systematic review by Sigurdson was performed to document racial/ethnic disparities in quality of care for infants in the NICU setting. Their review of more than 40 articles revealed complex racial and/or ethnic disparities in structure, process, and outcome measures, most often disadvantaging infants of color, especially non-Hispanic Black infants.59 Another study using the data from the Vermont Oxford Network (VON) found that infants were segregated among the 743 NICUs by race and ethnicity.60 Compared with non-Hispanic White infants, non-Hispanic Black infants were concentrated at NICUs with lower-quality scores, and Hispanic and Asian infants were concentrated at NICUs with higher-quality scores. Region of residence explained the observed inequality for Hispanic infants but not for non-Hispanic Black or Asian infants. There were large differences between geographic regions in NICU quality. Another study using the VON NICUs database examined care practices and outcomes, and relation to race and ethnicity over a 10-year period.61 Improvements in outcomes did occur, and compared with non-Hispanic White infants, non-Hispanic Black infants had a faster decline for mortality, hypothermia, necrotizing enterocolitis, and lateonset sepsis, whereas Hispanic infants had a faster decline for mortality, respiratory distress syndrome, and pneumothorax. However, despite the improvements, rate differences in outcomes including hypothermia, mortality, necrotizing enterocolitis, late onset sepsis, and severe intraventricular hemorrhage remained elevated by the end of the study period, especially


## PDF page 161

among non-Hispanic Black infants. Another study investigating unexpected newborn complication in New York City hospitals found non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic women were more likely to deliver in hospitals with high complication rates than were non-Hispanic White or Asian American women.62 The authors concluded these findings implicate hospital quality in contributing to preventable newborn health disparities among low-risk, term births. Nurse staffing and shortages may explain some of these continued disparities in NICUs. Survey data from a Multi-State Nursing Care and Patient Safety Study were analyzed and found nurses in high-Black NICUs missed nearly 50% more nursing care than in low-Black NICUs.63 Lower nurse staffing (an additional patient per nurse) significantly increased the odds of missed care, whereas better practice environments decreased the odds. Nurses in high-Black NICUs face inadequate staffing and they are more likely to miss required nursing care.

Racism, chronic stress, and worry by disadvantaged mothers likely have a significant impact on poor perinatal and neonatal outcomes. Braveman et al. found that non-Hispanic Black women reported significantly higher chronic worry about racial discrimination compared with non-Hispanic White women.64 Surprisingly, rates of worry for non-Hispanic Black women were highest in those with higher income and education levels. Those with the highest rates of worry also had the highest rates of preterm birth. Even more intriguing is the evidence for continued generational effects of racial disparities with non-Hispanic Black mothers who were small for gestational age or preterm themselves having a higher risk than non-Hispanic White mothers to deliver a subsequent small for gestational age or preterm infant.64a More recent studies have shown that pregnant women who are Hispanic or non-Hispanic Blacks experience frequent and pervasive discrimination and mistreatment during their pregnancy.65,66

### Interventions to Reduce Neonatal Health Outcome Disparities

It is unlikely that improving care in the NICU alone will have a dramatic impact on reducing the US neonatal and infant mortality rates. However, by addressing and improving the significant health disparities and racial and ethnic differences seen in outcomes, there can be marked improvements in this indicator of US population health. It is important to investigate the areas of greatest impact that will result in improving maternal and neonatal health, as well as which local, state, and national initiatives can result in significant improvements in outcomes. First, all women, but especially those at highest risk such as non-Hispanic Black women and Native American/Alaska women and Pacific Islanders, must have improved health status even before conception. Programs that can screen and identify women at risk must be implemented. Maternal and child health care must be easily accessible, affordable, and equitable for all. This is certainly a challenge in very rural/ remote areas where health care access is limited or nonexistent and mortality rates are higher compared with urban areas.67

Access to adequate health care is also a challenge on most of the reservations and pueblos where many Native Americans reside. In addition, many urban settings have a maldistribution of health care providers and poor access to affordable transportation, making access difficult to those most in need.

The causes of poor maternal health, including obesity, diabetes, and hypertension, are multifactorial, but chronic maternal stress related to racial and ethnic disparities seen in the United States may also play a significant role. Screening and health promotion for obesity, diabetes, and hypertension are critical to improving the health of the mother. Current models of physician reimbursement discourage the significant time needed for such interventions. Innovative models, such as mobile clinics, group counseling, and specially trained health care workers have all shown to improve health outcomes in women of childbearing age. Chronic conditions, such as hypertension and diabetes must be well controlled over time, with continued and affordable access to medications that are known to be effective. The current dramatic increase in obesity, especially in the South and among non-Hispanic Blacks, Native Americans, and Hispanics in the United States, is a particular challenge. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) has recently published Clinical Management Guidelines for the management of obesity in pregnancy.68 This guideline offers an integrated approach to the management of obesity in women of reproductive age who are planning a pregnancy because of the concern for adverse outcomes. It also acknowledges the difficulty in successfully treating obesity in this population. Not often recognized is the lack of healthy food available in underserved and rural areas, as well as urban food deserts, which contributes to this problem. Similar to obesity management, mothers must be screened and treated for diabetes, hypertension, and renal disease before and during pregnancy. This will reduce many of the adverse outcomes seen in neonates and infants.

Other modifiable factors must be addressed for women at risk of becoming pregnant. Tobacco, alcohol, narcotics, and illicit substance use/abuse all have negative impacts on pregnancy outcomes and are often disproportionately used by those at highest risk of adverse outcomes. Culturally specific and appropriate educational materials and interventions must be available in a variety of settings, including schools. Tobacco cessation programs specifically during pregnancy, especially quitting early in pregnancy, have been shown to decrease the risk of preterm birth, especially if cessation occurs prior to conception.69 Alcohol use and abuse is particularly high among Native American and Alaska Natives and results in high rates of fetal alcohol syndrome.70 Fetal alcohol syndrome/fetal alcohol spectrum disorder is the largest cause of preventable long-term neurodevelopmental disability in children. Treatment of those ingesting alcohol during pregnancy is particularly difficult. However, intensive interventions have made some impact.71 Finally, the current opioid epidemic has been well publicized, as has the impact on those at the lowest socioeconomic populations. Pregnant women are often the least likely to get medical help given the highly punitive


## PDF page 162 | printed page 143

nature of some state programs, even to the point of arresting and incarcerating pregnant women, especially those women of minorities. However, programs that deal with multiple aspects of maternal drug use with known effective interventions and a less punitive approach have been shown to significantly improve neonatal and maternal outcomes, including more controlled or even cessation of drug use.72 Other innovative prenatal care programs such as group-based centering, easier access to care during pregnancy, and culturally centered care models also have been shown to have a significant impact on avoiding adverse outcomes of pregnancy.73

Renewed efforts must be made to improve the prepregnancy health of the mother. An important factor is access to health care and health insurance. Medicaid provides health insurance to those poorest Americans including the “working poor,” but this coverage is still woefully inadequate. Recent efforts have been made by the federal government to expand Medicaid coverage, but many states with significant minority populations, as well as eligible non-Hispanic Whites, have declined to expand eligibility for their Medicaid programs. Recent federal initiatives to provide even greater incentives to states have been only partially successful. Adults in Medicaid expansion states reported better coverage and access rates, narrower disparities between groups, and greater improvements across nearly every measure between 2013 and 2019.74 Interestingly, Hispanic adults continue to have the highest percentage of uninsured population, perhaps a reflection of concerns about immigration status/noncitizenship and subsequent adverse consequences of accessing the medical system. The most recent years since 2016 have seen a further deterioration in Medicaid coverage for all those in the United States, especially for Hispanics and non-Hispanic Blacks.

Access to insurance coverage before, during, and after pregnancy is also a vital piece of health care and improving maternal and infant outcomes. Having health insurance reduces racial and ethnic disparities in key measures of pregnancy for health care access and affordability, even after adjusting for income and other factors. Medicaid is currently the largest payor for maternity care in the United States. Implementation of the ACA and Medicaid expansion has decreased racial and ethnic disparities in insurance and access, and more quality-of-care measures are improving than worsening for racial and ethnic minority groups. However, many disparities have not changed, and overall progress is modest.75 Based on data from 2011 to 2016, state Medicaid expansion was not significantly associated with differences in rates of low birth weight or preterm birth outcomes overall, although there were significant improvements in relative disparities for non-Hispanic Black infants compared with for non-Hispanic White infants in states that expanded Medicaid versus those that did not.75 In contrast, a study by Bhatt did show that overall infant mortality rate decline was greater in Medicaid expansion states, with greater declines among non-Hispanic Black infants.76 Recent data indicate that insurance source can impact neonatal outcomes. A study by Kim et al. looked at infant mortality by payment source for delivery in the United States. They found overall infant mortality was lower in mothers who paid with private

insurance than in those who paid with Medicaid insurance (relative risk [RR] = 0.91 in 2017), but it was higher in self-paid women than in Medicaid-insured women at delivery (RR = 1.16, in 2017). Non-Hispanic Black (RR = 1.16 in 2017) and Hispanic (RR = 1.22 in 2017) mothers with self-payment had a higher risk for infant mortality than those with Medicaid at delivery. They found newborns whose mothers have no health insurance are more vulnerable to infant mortality than Medicaid beneficiaries, and non-Hispanic White ethnic groups with self-payment have an elevated risk of infant mortality among other racial and ethnic groups.77

As noted earlier, the ACA has significantly decreased the uninsured in the United States, with varying improvements based on states’ Medicaid expansion. This program has also mandated insurance coverage by all health plans for prenatal, postnatal, and infant care. Nonetheless, minority women and children in the United States are still less likely to be insured. The CHIP funded by the United States has increased coverage of uninsured children. Survey-based research shows positive associations between CHIP expansions and children’s health care utilization. Thus continued access to insurance for women and children is likely to have a significant impact on reducing the disparities seen in health outcomes in the United States. Unlike other developed countries, the United States has no universal health care, and the ACA has been a significant, albeit controversial, improvement in this area. Those in health care, both providers and insurers, must advocate for the most vulnerable in the population to maintain and expand this coverage.

Women often qualify for Medicaid coverage once the pregnancy is identified but cannot access the health care system before the pregnancy to improve their health, thus putting them at greater risk. Medicaid coverage increases during pregnancy for those mothers that are noninsured or underinsured. Recent federal efforts have also focused on increasing current postpartum coverage from 6 weeks to 12 months to improve the care of the mother while her child is young and for the next pregnancy. Data for new mothers with Medicaidcovered prenatal care in 2015 to 2018 from 43 states participating in the Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System (PRAMS) found that 26.8% of new mothers with Medicaid-covered prenatal care were uninsured before pregnancy, 21.9% became uninsured 2 to 6 months postpartum, and 34.5% were uninsured in either period, with higher perinatal uninsurance rates in nonexpansion states and for Hispanic women who completed the PRAMS survey in Spanish.78 Together, these findings indicate that, despite recent coverage gains, further policy change is needed to help women maintain health insurance coverage before and after pregnancy and to allow them to address ongoing health issues including obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and depression. Again, many states have been resistant to implementing this expanded coverage despite federal support. Only half of the states have implemented or plan to implement expanded postpartum coverage. Of concern is that some of the states with the greatest racial perinatal disparities or worst perinatal outcomes are those that have resisted expanded postpartum coverage for up


## PDF page 163

to 12 months.79 However, studies have shown that mothers at greatest health inequities may still have significant medical issues such as hypertension at 6 weeks postpartum, at which time they may no longer be eligible for Medicaid coverage.80

In addition, improving nutrition for women and infants can have a significant impact on outcome. A recent study examined the association between race and ethnicity, participation in WIC, and a series of infant health outcomes including infant mortality, low birth weight, preterm birth, extended infant hospitalization, and stays in the NICU.81 In this study, using the PRAMS from 2009 to 2017, infants born to non-Hispanic Black women, and to a lesser extent Hispanic women, were in worse health than those born to non-Hispanic White mothers in the United States. However, participation in WIC was associated with reductions in the gap in infant health experienced by racial and ethnic minorities. They concluded prenatal WIC participation was associated with improvements in the health of non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic infants and reduced racial and ethnic disparities in infant health outcomes.

Another public health initiative which will have a significant impact on health care disparities in the perinatal and neonatal period is in pregnancy delay, short interpregnancy intervals, and prevention of unintended pregnancies. Improved education about pregnancy prevention, including in the schools, as well as easier access to contraception, is critical. In addition, long-acting reproductive contraception (LARC) has been shown to be particularly effective and is reversible at the time of desired pregnancy. Contraception for those who desire it must be more readily available, especially immediately after delivery of a baby. Contraceptive counseling is rarely done during postpartum care or while a baby is in the NICU, but these are valuable missed opportunities to improve the health of the mother and her future children. Improved access to contraception will also increase interpregnancy intervals. Short interpregnancy intervals less than 6 months are more common in non-Hispanic Black mothers (7.1%) compared with non-Hispanic White mothers (4.1%) and Hispanic mothers (5.0%).82 The shortest interval of interpregnancy conception (<6 months) has been shown to have the highest adverse outcomes, especially in teen mothers.83 Access to contraception, especially for teen pregnancies, of which three-fourths are unintended, is critical to lengthen interpregnancy intervals and prevent adverse outcomes associated with teen pregnancy. Local legislation will be important to this public health intervention. For unwanted pregnancies, or for women that feel they cannot support having another child, abortion is an option. However, many states are considering or have implemented restrictions on abortion, especially those states with high minority populations. In addition, there are racial disparities in abortion rates for women of lower socioeconomic status and women of color. Hispanic women and non-Hispanic Black women have an up to fourfold higher rate of abortion than non-Hispanic White women.84 Recent efforts to decrease access to abortion for these women may only widen the health disparities for future generations.

As noted earlier, there are significant disparities in rates of prenatal care related to race and ethnicity, with non- Hispanic Blacks overall having the lowest rates of adequate

prenatal care and the highest rates of no prenatal care (see Table 8.1). Innovative models must be investigated and implemented. Statewide Medicaid-enhanced prenatal care programs have been shown to reduce infant mortality risk.85 Implementation of such a program in Michigan reduced the odds of infant death by 27%, with the highest reduction in Black infant mortality (29%). The greatest reduction was seen in those women who fully participated in the program using a population-based home visitation program to improve outcomes. For non-Hispanic Black women, this program further resulted in lower odds of low birth weight (0.76), very low birth weight (0.42), and very preterm birth (0.41) compared with matched nonparticipants.86

Although the underlying cause of prematurity is multifactorial and not clearly understood, certain interventions have been shown to reduce preterm birth. For those women identified with a singleton pregnancy and a previous history of spontaneous preterm birth, 17 alpha-hydroxyprogesterone caproate (17P) has been shown to reduce the risk of subsequent preterm delivery by up to 30%.87 However, access to this medication requires weekly injections, and the current drug delivery and reimbursement model is problematic for both physicians and women at risk. Many state Medicaid plans are investigating novel methods to deliver this drug to mothers at risk, given its known effectiveness.

Breastfeeding has been shown to have important benefits to both the mother and infant, including decreased breast and ovarian cancer rates and less postpartum depression and osteoporosis in the mother, as well as fewer infections, less risk of diabetes, heart disease, and asthma in the infant. Breastfeeding also has a significant impact on infant mortality. More importantly, breastfeeding initiation is significantly associated with reduced odds of post-perinatal infant death in multiple racial and ethnic groups within the US population.88 However, significant disparities exist in the rates of breastfeeding among different races and ethnicities.89 Non-Hispanic Black women have the lowest rates of initiation of breastfeeding, exclusive breastfeeding at 6 months, and any breastfeeding at 12 months. The disparities in adjusted breastfeeding rates have also become larger between non-Hispanic Black and non-Hispanic White infants in recent years. In addition, certain areas of the United States with the highest poverty levels, such as the Deep South and Appalachian states, have the lowest rates of breastfeeding. However, targeted interventions can be successful in improving breastfeeding rates in this part of the United States. After implementing the Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding program in delivery hospitals in four Southern states, the disparity in breastfeeding initiation between non-Hispanic Black and non-Hispanic White infants decreased by 9.6% over the course of 31 months.90 Breastfeeding initiation increased from 66% to 75% for all races combined, and exclusivity increased from 34% to 39%. Initiation and exclusive breastfeeding among non-Hispanic Black infants increased from 46% to 63% and from 19% to 31%, respectively. Successful implementation of breastfeeding must begin before delivery with targeted and appropriate education. Baby-friendly initiatives in the United States have resulted in increased awareness of the importance of this public health


## PDF page 164 | printed page 145

measure, but more must be done. Lactation specialists must be available to all mothers immediately after delivery and during the postnatal period to improve initiation of and adherence to breastfeeding. Finally, the United States has no national policy guaranteeing paid leave to employed women who give birth, one of only three countries worldwide.91 Paid maternity leave significantly predicts lower odds of maternal and infant rehospitalization and higher odds of doing well with exercise and stress management. Paid maternity leave also promotes breastfeeding for a longer period of time with increased benefit to the infant and mother.

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and March of Dimes (MOD) have initiated the Safe Sleep campaign in an effort to reduce SIDS.92 Of concern is the current increase in SUID/SIDS and accidental strangulation in bed in the United States noted in some states. Although the Safe Sleep program is effective, other measures must be addressed, such as the lack of separate sleeping spaces for the infant and cobedding in minority populations. It is often difficult to intervene in those families with limited finances. Programs such as Back to Sleep and Baby Sleeping Boxes are simple and effective interventions. However, continued local and state educational efforts must be maintained and supported.

title: Genetic Aspects of Perinatal Disease and Prenatal Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: 9 Genetic Aspects of Perinatal Disease and Prenatal Diagnosis
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: The genetic basis of human disorders is a fundamental cornerstone of modern medicine. Recent advances in our understanding of complex genetic disorders coupled with technical developments have allowed genetics to become an invaluable part of clinical practice. This chapter highlights essential concepts regarding the genetic basis of disease and issues surrounding prenatal evaluation and diagnosis. Principles of inheritance, teratogens, genetic screening, and diagnostic modalities are discussed.
paragraphs.heading: SUSAN J. GROSS AND CIPRIAN P. GHEORGHE

paragraphs.text: In humans, normal gametes are composed of 23 chromosomes each. A normal human somatic cell contains 46 chromosomes. In both genders, 22 pairs of chromosomes, also known as autosomes, are identical. Women have a homologous pair of sex chromosomes known as the X chromosome. Men have a nonhomologous pair, an X and a Y chromosome.
paragraphs.heading: Chromosomal Disorders

paragraphs.text: A chromosome is composed of a linear DNA molecule that is complexed with structural proteins known as histones to form chromatin. Each chromosome has a centromere which divides the chromosome into a short arm (the p arm) and a long arm (the q arm). Where the centromere is located helps describe chromosomes as metacentric, submetacentric, and acrocentric. In metacentric chromosomes, the arm length is equal, whereas in submetacentric chromosomes, one arm is larger than the other. If the p arm contains such small amounts of genetic material that it is almost negligible, the chromosome is considered acrocentric. In humans, the acrocentric chromosomes are 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22. The ends of each chromosome are known as telomeres. During cell division, the chromosomes condense more than 10,000-fold, resulting in compact structures that can segregate.
paragraphs.heading: Chromosomal Disorders

paragraphs.text: To analyze chromosomes, a karyotype is produced (Fig. 9.1). The chromosomes are paired and organized according to size. The overall structure and banding pattern are evaluated and are reported according to the International System for Cytogenetic Nomenclature. According to this nomenclature, a karyotype designation includes the total chromosome number followed by the sex chromosome constitution. Genetically assigned females are 46,XX and males are 46,XY. If there are any variants or abnormalities, this is reported after the sex chromosomes (Table 9.1).1 Chromosome disorders can be either structural or numeric. The consequence of the abnormality depends on the amount of genomic imbalance and the genes involved.
paragraphs.heading: Chromosomal Disorders

paragraphs.text: Epidemiologic studies suggest that women are having fewer children, often later in life. World Bank data show the fertility rate (births per woman) worldwide has declined to 2.406 in 2020 (down from 2.7 in 2000). The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) reported that from 2000 to 2014, the proportion of first births to women aged 30 to 34 increased 28% (from 16.5% to 21.1%), and first births to women aged 35 and older increased 23% (from 7.4% to 9.1%).2 Chromosomal analysis of samples from spontaneous abortions, prenatal diagnosis, and live births reveals that there is a steady increase in aneuploidy as a woman ages (Fig. 9.2).
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Age Considerations

paragraphs.text: The mere presence of additional genetic material, albeit of normal makeup, can result in clinically significant phenotypes. Following is a discussion of the various types of numeric abnormalities.
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities of Chromosome Number

paragraphs.text: Triploid fetuses have three sets of chromosomes for a total number of 69. Triploid fetuses are rarely born alive; when
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities of Chromosome Number

paragraphs.text: they are, survival is poor. Most triploidy is the result of fertilization by two sperm. Tetraploids, fetuses with 96 chromosomes, are usually miscarried in the first trimester. Partial molar pregnancies will exhibit triploidy with the extra set of chromosomes being of paternal origin.3
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities of Chromosome Number

paragraphs.text: In humans, the term aneuploid is used to describe any genotype in which the total chromosome number is not a
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities of Chromosome Number

paragraphs.text: multiple of 23. Most aneuploid patients have either a monosomy (only one representative of a particular chromosome) or a trisomy (three copies of a particular chromosome). As a rule, monosomies tend to be more deleterious than trisomies. Complete monosomies are generally not viable except for monosomy X (Turner syndrome). Trisomies for chromosomes 13, 18, 21, X, and Y are compatible with life, with trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) being the most common trisomy in live-born infants.
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities of Chromosome Number

paragraphs.text: The most common mechanism for aneuploidy is meiotic nondisjunction, in which a pair of chromosomes fails to separate during either of the meiotic divisions (Fig. 9.3). Nondisjunction can rarely occur during a mitotic division after the formation of the zygote. If this happens early in cleavage, mosaicism may occur. In this situation, two or more different chromosome complements are present in one individual. The clinical significance of mosaicism is difficult to evaluate and depends on the developmental timing when the mosaicism occurred, the tissues affected, and the proportion of tissue affected.
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities of Chromosome Number

paragraphs.text: Chromosomal structural abnormalities are the result of chromosome breakage followed by anomalous reconstitution. Rearrangements result spontaneously or are caused
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities of Chromosome Structure

paragraphs.text: by inducing agents, such as ionizing radiation. Structural abnormalities can be divided into two categories—balanced and unbalanced. Balanced rearrangements have the normal complement of chromosomal material. In addition, a balanced rearranged chromosome must have a functional centromere and two functional telomeres. Unbalanced rearrangements are either missing or have additional genetic information.
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities of Chromosome Structure

paragraphs.text: Structural rearrangements include deletions, insertions, ring chromosomes, isochromosomes, and translocations (Fig. 9.4). One unique type of translocation is the Robertsonian translocation, in which two acrocentric chromosomes lose their short arms and fuse near the centromeric region. The acrocentric chromosomes are 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22. Because the short arms of acrocentric chromosomes contain only genes for ribosomal RNAs, loss of the short arm is rarely deleterious. The result is a balanced karyotype with only 45 chromosomes, including the translocated chromosome, which comprises the long arms of two chromosomes. Carriers of Robertsonian translocations are phenotypically normal but have the risk of producing unbalanced gametes. The main clinical relevance of a Robertsonian translocation is that one involving chromosome 21 could result in a child with Down syndrome. About 4% of cases of Down syndrome have 46 chromosomes, one of which is a Robertsonian translocation between chromosome 21 and another chromosome. Similarly, trisomy 18 and trisomy 13 can also occur as a result of balanced Robertsonian translocations. Carriers of balanced translocations involving other chromosomes are also at risk for chromosomal anomalies in offspring. Thanks to breakthroughs involving newer technologies such as genome sequencing, we are learning that these “balanced” translocations may not be benign and may actually be unbalanced at a molecular level. Gene disruptions may occur at the relevant translocation breakpoints and significantly impact health.4
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities of Chromosome Structure

paragraphs.text: Mendel studied the offspring characteristics of garden peas and observed that certain phenotypic characteristics occurred in fixed proportions. Single-gene traits for which mutations cause predictable disease are described as exhibiting Mendelian inheritance, because they follow the rules that he originally described. Currently, several thousand diseases are known to exhibit Mendelian patterns of inheritance. New sequencing technologies have expanded
paragraphs.heading: Single-Gene Disorders

paragraphs.text: our understanding of the contribution of these disorders among ill infants admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU).5
paragraphs.heading: Single-Gene Disorders

paragraphs.text: Variants of a gene are called alleles. For many genes, there is one prevailing allele, which is referred to as the wild-type allele. The other versions of the gene are mutations, not all of which may cause disease. Mutations can be inherited or de novo, meaning that neither parent possessed the mutation. Instead, the mutation occurred as a random error
paragraphs.heading: Single-Gene Disorders

paragraphs.text: during gametogenesis. To distinguish between benign and deleterious mutations, the professional genetics community now calls the latter pathogenic variants.
paragraphs.heading: Single-Gene Disorders

paragraphs.text: Approximately half of Mendelian disorders are inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. Inheritance usually exhibits a vertical pattern of transmission, meaning that the phenotype appears in every generation, with each affected person having an affected parent (Fig. 9.5). For each offspring of an affected parent, the risk of inheriting the mutated allele is 50%. An example of a disorder inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion is osteogenesis imperfecta. Biochemical defects in either the amount or the structure of
paragraphs.heading: Autosomal Dominant Disorders

paragraphs.text: collagen result in various clinical phenotypes depending on the mutation.
paragraphs.heading: Autosomal Dominant Disorders

paragraphs.text: The link between advanced maternal age and genetic abnormalities has been well established. The role of advanced paternal age, defined as 40 or older, is not as clear. It has been established that the rate of base substitution mutations during spermatogenesis increases as a man ages. The risk of de novo autosomal dominant disorders in offspring of fathers 40 years old or older is estimated at 0.3% or lower.6 Some evidence has suggested that advanced paternal age is associated with an increased risk for complex disorders such as schizophrenia, autism, and congenital anomalies. The relative risk for these conditions is 2% or less. Although there may be slightly increased risk for a range of disorders associated with advanced paternal age, the overall risk remains low. No screening or diagnostic tests target conditions associated with advanced paternal age. Pregnancies that are fathered by men 40 years old or older should be treated according to standard guidelines established by the American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG) and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG).7
paragraphs.heading: Autosomal Dominant Disorders

paragraphs.text: An autosomal recessive condition occurs when an individual possesses two mutant alleles that were inherited from heterozygous parents. For autosomal recessive diseases, an individual with one normal allele does not manifest the disease because the normal gene copy is able to compensate. Autosomal recessive disorders exhibit horizontal transmission, meaning that if the phenotype appears in more than one family member, it is typically in the siblings of the proband, not in parents, offspring, or other relatives (Fig. 9.6). If both parents are carriers of a mutated
paragraphs.heading: Autosomal Recessive Disorders

paragraphs.text: allele, 25% of offspring have the autosomal recessive disease. Consanguineous unions (mating between individuals who are second cousins or closer) are at increased risk for an autosomal recessive disorder because there is a higher likelihood that both individuals carry the same recessive mutation. A common autosomal recessive disease is cystic fibrosis. Carrier screening and prenatal implications are discussed in a later section.
paragraphs.heading: Autosomal Recessive Disorders

paragraphs.text: X chromosome inactivation is a normal process in females in which one X chromosome is randomly inactivated early in development. Females are normally mosaic with respect to X-linked gene expression. Disorders of genes located on the X chromosome have a characteristic pattern of inheritance that is affected by gender. Males with an X-linked mutant allele are described as being hemizygous for that allele. Males have a 50% chance of inheriting a mutant allele if the mother is a carrier. Females can be homozygous wild-type allele, homozygous mutant allele, or a heterozygote.
paragraphs.heading: Sex-Linked Disorders

paragraphs.text: An X-linked recessive mutation is phenotypically expressed in all males but is expressed only in females who are homozygous for the mutation. As a result, X-linked recessive disorders are generally seen in males and rarely seen in females. An example of such a condition is hemophilia A. X-linked dominant disorders may manifest differently among heterozygous females in the same family because of different patterns of X chromosome inactivation. X-linked inheritance is classically characterized by the lack of male-to-male transmission because males transmit their Y chromosome to their sons, not their X chromosome (Fig. 9.7).
paragraphs.heading: Sex-Linked Disorders

paragraphs.text: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is organized as a 16.5-kb circular chromosome located in the mitochondrial organelles of a cell, not the cell nucleus. mtDNA contains 37 genes that encode for important proteins, including proteins involved in oxidative phosphorylation.
paragraphs.heading: Non-Mendelian Patterns of Inheritance Mitochondrial Inheritance

paragraphs.text: Mitochondrial inheritance has a few distinct features that differ from Mendelian inheritance: maternal inheritance, replicative segregation, and heteroplasmy. Because sperm mitochondria are eliminated from the forming embryo, mtDNA is inherited entirely from the maternal side, with very rare exception. At cell division, the mitochondria sort randomly between two daughter cells, a process known as replicative segregation. A cell containing a mix of mutant and wild-type mtDNA can distribute variable proportions of mutant or wild-type DNA to daughter cells. By chance, a daughter cell may receive all wild-type or all mutant mtDNA, a state known as homoplasmy. Heteroplasmic daughter cells can result in variable penetrance and expression depending on the amount of mutant mtDNA present.
paragraphs.heading: Non-Mendelian Patterns of Inheritance Mitochondrial Inheritance

paragraphs.text: More than 100 different mutations in mtDNA have been identified to cause disease in humans, and with new technologies, that number is growing.8 Most of these involve the central nervous system or musculoskeletal system (Table 9.2).
paragraphs.heading: Non-Mendelian Patterns of Inheritance Mitochondrial Inheritance

paragraphs.text: Mitochondrial disease typically manifests as dysfunction in high energy-consuming organs such as the brain, muscle, heart, and kidneys. Poor growth, muscle weakness, loss of coordination, or developmental delay not explained by more common causes should alert a neonatologist or pediatrician to the possibility of a mitochondrial disease. When a mitochondrial disease is suspected, the child should be referred to a specialized medical center wherein comprehensive evaluation, including genetic studies, can be performed.
paragraphs.heading: Non-Mendelian Patterns of Inheritance Mitochondrial Inheritance

paragraphs.text: Epigenetics refers to modification of genes that determines whether a gene is expressed or not (see Chapter 15). These modifications, an example of which is methylation, affect the expression of a gene but not the primary DNA sequence itself. Imprinting refers to a phenomenon in which genetic material is differentially expressed depending on whether it was inherited from the father or the mother. A different phenotype can result depending on the parent of origin because, for certain genes, only the allele from one parent is transcriptionally active.
paragraphs.heading: Epigenetics and Uniparental Disomy

paragraphs.text: Uniparental disomy is the inheritance of a pair of homologous chromosomes from one parent rather than the normal scenario in which one chromosome is inherited from each parent. This situation is thought to arise most commonly by a process called trisomy rescue, during which a trisomic cell is converted into a disomic cell. It is a matter of chance as to which chromosome drops out. When trisomy rescue occurs, both chromosomes are from one parent a third of the time.
paragraphs.heading: Epigenetics and Uniparental Disomy

paragraphs.text: Classic examples of disorders related to genomic imprinting are Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes. Both these syndromes involve the long arm of chromosome 15 (15q11- 15q13). At birth, Prader-Willi syndrome is characterized by hypotonia, low birth weight, and almond-shaped eyes. During childhood, other features such as short stature, obesity, indiscriminate eating habits, small hands and feet, intellectual disability, and hypogonadism develop. In most of these cases, there is paternally derived deletion, which means
paragraphs.heading: Epigenetics and Uniparental Disomy

paragraphs.text: that all the genetic information in the region is maternal in origin. Angelman syndrome, characterized by intellectual disability, short stature, abnormal facies, and seizures, is the opposite situation, in which the deletion is maternally derived, and the genetic information in the region is paternal only in origin. Approximately 30% of Prader-Willi cases and 5% of Angelman cases are the result of uniparental disomy. In this scenario, there is no cytogenetically detectable deletion. Because of imprinting, Prader-Willi syndrome results from uniparental disomy in which both chromosomes derive from the mother. The loss of the paternal contribution results in Prader-Willi syndrome. Paternal uniparental disomy in the same region results in Angelman syndrome because of the loss of maternal contribution of genes in the 15q11-q13 region.
paragraphs.heading: Epigenetics and Uniparental Disomy

paragraphs.text: Another aspect of epigenetics that has become an exciting avenue for research is the fetal origin of adult disease hypothesis. This is also known as the Barker hypothesis, named after British epidemiologist David Barker, who proposed that intrauterine stress in the form of growth restriction and prematurity can predispose the individual to hypertension, cardiac disease, and diabetes. The initial evidence was provided by epidemiologic data that correlated low birth weight with poor health outcomes in adulthood.9 Since then, several animal and human studies have shown that a harsh intrauterine environment can lead to a host of changes in DNA methylation and ultimately influence gene expression and metabolic dysregulation in adulthood.10
paragraphs.heading: Epigenetics and Uniparental Disomy

paragraphs.text: Most mutations, when they occur, remain unchanged as they get passed from one generation to the next. However, there is a subset of disorders for which an expansion of an area of DNA containing repeating units results in disease. In this case, as the gene is passed on, the number of repeats (usually consisting of three nucleotides each) can increase to beyond polymorphic range and begin to affect gene
paragraphs.heading: Trinucleotide Repeat Expansion

paragraphs.text: function. Although the mechanism of how this expansion occurs is not completely elucidated, it is thought to be the result of a slipped mispairing mechanism in which an insertion occurs when a newly synthesized strand temporarily dissociates from the template strand. A dozen or so diseases, including congenital myotonic dystrophy, Huntington disease, Friedreich ataxia, and fragile X syndrome, are the result of unstable repeat expansions.
paragraphs.heading: Trinucleotide Repeat Expansion

paragraphs.text: Fragile X syndrome, the most common hereditary form of mental retardation, has an incidence of approximately 1 in 4000 births. The normal number of triplet repeats in the Xq27.3 region (FMR1 gene) is less than 45; a full mutation is considered to be greater than 200 repeats. Individuals with 45 to 54 repeats are referred to as intermediate carriers—these individuals are not at risk for any phenotypic abnormalities and are not at risk for expansion to a full mutation in their offspring. Individuals with 55 to 200 repeats are known as premutation carriers. Besides the risk of having an offspring with the full mutation, these premutation carriers are also at risk for adult-onset cerebellar dysfunction (known as fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome) and premature ovarian failure.11
paragraphs.heading: Trinucleotide Repeat Expansion

paragraphs.text: Individuals who have any family or personal history of developmental delay, mental retardation, ovarian dysfunction, or tremor should be offered screening for fragile X syndrome. There has been increasing adoption of prenatal screening for fragile X in the general population, despite not being recommended by professional bodies.12
paragraphs.heading: Trinucleotide Repeat Expansion

paragraphs.text: There are disorders that affect certain families more than others but do not follow Mendelian patterns of inheritance or fit into the non-Mendelian inheritance phenomenon. These disorders are thought to be the result of interplay between genetic and environmental factors and gene-gene
paragraphs.heading: Multifactorial Inheritance

paragraphs.text: interactions. Known as multifactorial or complex inheritance, these disorders have a greater incidence than disorders secondary to chromosomal or single-gene mutations. These disorders provide unique genetic counseling dilemmas regarding recurrence risks because, although genotypes predisposing to disease may aggregate in families, the phenotypic expression is discordant, owing to differences in nongenetic exposures.
paragraphs.heading: Multifactorial Inheritance

paragraphs.text: An illustrative example of multifactorial inheritance is the occurrence of neural tube defects (NTDs). Spina bifida and anencephaly are NTDs that cluster in families and are a leading cause of fetal loss and handicap. Spina bifida is the result of incomplete fusion of vertebral arches and manifests in various degrees of severity. Anencephaly is a devastating condition in which the forebrain, overlying meninges, bone, and skin are absent. Most fetuses with anencephaly are stillborn. Although some NTDs can be explained by teratogens, amniotic bands, or chromosomal disorders, most are multifactorial. Decreased levels of maternal folic acid have been inversely correlated with the risk of NTDs. Folic acid levels are affected by two factors—dietary intake and enzymatic processing. Folic acid levels are detrimentally affected by a mutation in the enzyme 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR). Fifteen percent of the population is homozygous for the mutation. It has been shown that the mothers of infants with NTDs were twice as likely to have MTHFR mutations than controls. Preconceptual supplementation of folic acid has been shown to decrease the risk of NTDs.13 All reproductive-age women should consume 0.4 mg of folic acid daily. Prenatal screening for NTDs is discussed later in this chapter.
paragraphs.heading: Multifactorial Inheritance

paragraphs.text: Environmental exposures—medications, maternal conditions, or infections—are the etiology of malformations in 10% of cases. The impact of the agent relates to the timing and amount of exposure (duration and dosage). The susceptibility of a fetus depends on its stage of development when an exposure takes place (Fig. 9.8).14
paragraphs.heading: Teratogens

paragraphs.text: Exposure during the first 2 weeks after conception usually either is lethal to the embryo or has no adverse effect. This window is known as the “all-or-none” period. During organogenesis, teratogenic exposure may result in major morphologic abnormalities because of disruption of the forming organ systems.
paragraphs.heading: Teratogens

paragraphs.text: Most commonly prescribed medications can be used with relative safety during pregnancy. For the medications that are suspected or known teratogens, genetic counseling should emphasize relative risk. That is, risk increases should be presented in relation to a woman’s baseline risk of a birth defect, which is 2% to 3%. The possibility that certain medical conditions if left untreated pose greater threat to the fetus than the medications used to treat the condition should be addressed. In 2014, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) removed the letter categories for drugs in pregnancy, and labeling now includes information on whether a drug
paragraphs.heading: Teratogens

paragraphs.text: is absorbed systemically and relevant information to help providers manage and counsel patients.15
paragraphs.heading: Teratogens

paragraphs.text: Use of these drugs in pregnancy ultimately requires expertise and access to up-to-date databases specializing in teratogenesis, available through a prenatal genetics service. Certain drugs may be a significant risk but only during a particular trimester. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole should be avoided in the third trimester to avoid kernicterus in the newborn but may be used in the first and second trimesters. Likewise, a certain drug may be a genuine teratogen, but the risk of stopping the drug would be of even greater consequence. Lithium use during the first trimester of pregnancy has been associated with cardiac malformations, including Ebstein anomaly.16 Although efforts should be made to avoid lithium during the first trimester, if an alternative therapy is inappropriate, the lowest possible lithium dose should be used. Finally, certain drugs are known teratogens, but the underlying disorder may contribute to birth defects independently. Women with epilepsy are at increased risk of fetal malformations such as orofacial clefts, independent of whether or not they are taking anticonvulsant therapy.
paragraphs.heading: Teratogens

paragraphs.text: Reflex discontinuation of medications upon the diagnosis of pregnancy is discouraged, and prompt consultation with a perinatologist should be obtained to discuss an individual risk benefit assessment for each patient. Ideally, these discussions should be undertaken before conception in all childbearing age women, and either effective long-term contraception should be offered or medications should be adjusted for those planning an upcoming pregnancy.
paragraphs.heading: Teratogens

paragraphs.text: Radiographic imaging modalities are widely used in inpatient and outpatient settings. Safety of ionizing radiation exposure in pregnancy is an important concern because of the association of ionizing radiation with prenatal death, malformation, and carcinogenesis. It is necessary to weigh the risk of exposure versus the risk to the mother and fetus of a delayed diagnosis. With proper test selection, shielding, and procedure modifications, fetal risk can be significantly reduced or eliminated.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Imaging

paragraphs.text: Exposure greater than 10 to 20 mGy has been associated with an increased risk of malformations. However, diagnostic imaging rarely, if ever, exposes the fetus to this level of radiation. Iodinated contrast materials can cross the placenta and produce transient effects in the developing fetal thyroid. Although not contraindicated, iodinated contrast material should be used with great care.17 Approximate levels of diagnostic imaging are as follows: • Chest x-ray, two views generally: 0.0005 to 0.01 mGy • Abdominal radiography: 0.1 to 3 mGy • Intravenous pyelogram (IVP): 5 to 10 mGy • Double contrast barium enema: 1.0 to 20 mGy • Head or neck computed tomography (CT): 1.0 to 10 mGy • Chest CT or CT pulmonary angiography: 0.01 to
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Imaging

paragraphs.text: 0.66 mGy • Abdominal CT: 1.3 to 35 mGy

Of note, data from survivors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki showed no increase in birth defects in the offspring of pregnant mothers who were exposed to radiation in the aftermath of the explosions.18 In light of this, diagnostic imaging should not be routinely denied to pregnant patients, but an effort should be made to minimize exposure whenever possible.

paragraphs.text: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which uses electromagnetic radio waves to generate images, has not been associated with any harmful effects to the developing fetus and is considered a first-line imaging modality. Of note, although MRI is considered safe, gadolinium, the contrast agent most commonly used in MRI, crosses the placenta. There has been limited evaluation of its safety, and it is not recommended for use in pregnancy. Its use should be limited to situations in which there is a significant need for specific diagnostic performance.
