It has been shown that a fixed error of about 8% (plus or minus) can be anticipated when determining gestational age by ultrasound, consistent with the observation that the earlier gestational age is determined, the lower the margin of error in days. If accelerated or restricted growth supervenes, however, biometric markers are generally compromised accordingly.
paragraphs.heading: Pregnancy Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Selection of the most useful single parameter depends on the timing and purpose of measurement and is influenced by specific limitations. Commercial equipment has a variety of preinstalled normograms, biometry-based dating, and weight estimation formulae. Embryonic pole and crownrump lengths are considered most precise for early dating of pregnancy, becoming more variable with fetal flexion effects at the end of the first trimester. Biparietal diameter (BPD), obtainable after parietal bone calcification in week 12, maintains the closest correlation with gestational age in the second trimester. BPD is measured from the outer to the inner table of the skull, perpendicular to the parietal bones and central falx cerebri. The proper plane contains the cavum septum pellucidum, thalami, third ventricle, and tentorial hiatus, within the bony table of a complete head circumference (HC) (Fig. 10.24). In cases of variation in the shape of the skull, an HC measurement obtained in the same plane may be an effective alternative. Microcephaly may be suspected when the HC measurement is more than 3
paragraphs.heading: Pregnancy Evaluation

paragraphs.text: standard deviations (SDs) below the mean but is rarely diagnosed prenatally. Additionally, antenatal sonographic estimation of HC is associated with significant underestimation compared with the actual postnatal HC. This discrepancy may have important clinical implications and should be taken into account in the interpretation of sonographically
paragraphs.heading: Pregnancy Evaluation

paragraphs.text: measured HC.21 BPD and HC are relatively spared in nutritional and perfusional disorders of growth, although cranial measurements may also be distorted by compression effects. The abdominal circumference (AC), measured along the outer margin of the abdominal skin line at the level of the gastric bubble and the intrahepatic portion of the umbilical vein (UV) at the bifurcation of the portal veins, is the best single predictor of growth aberrations but is less helpful for dating (Fig. 10.25). Femoral length (FL) is the fourth measurement commonly included in biometric formulae, less affected by hypoperfusion but potentially influenced by familial stature. Extraocular and transcerebellar diameters and humeral and pedal lengths are common additional dating parameters. Special curves are available for non- Caucasian ethnicity and multiple gestations, although not universally accepted as essential.
paragraphs.heading: AC

paragraphs.text: Use of multiple predictors improves the accuracy of estimates, and an individualized approach is recommended for fetal growth assessment. The various epidemiologic factors influencing fetal growth should be considered. Clinical application of fetal biometry is of utmost importance in recognizing dating errors, growth abnormalities, chromosomal anomalies, and skeletal dysplasias.
paragraphs.heading: AC

paragraphs.text: Serial measurements over time are the best way to judge fetal growth. The sac and embryo grow perceptibly each day; by the second trimester, intervals of 2 or 3 weeks between studies are more reliable. Problems arise when attempting simultaneously to assign age and weight percentiles without reliable dating. The AC is a better indicator of decreased perfusion or increased glycogen storage than the cranial measures; ratios of AC to the HC and FL amplify differences but have poor sensitivity and specificity. Strategies to identify small-for-dates fetuses have included risk panels, Doppler ratios, amniotic fluid volume, placental scores, and biometry-based weights; none has had completely satisfactory results, although outcomes appear to have improved.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Growth

paragraphs.text: Correctly identifying fetal growth abnormalities remains an elusive goal despite their major contribution to adverse perinatal outcomes and stillbirth. Current clinical screening relies on the symphyseal-fundal height measurement, but fewer than 25% of small-for-gestational-age infants will be identified using this methodology in a low-risk population. Routine third-trimester ultrasound study for growth assessment has a better detection rate, ranging from 50% to 80%, but the impact on perinatal outcome is unclear.22
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Growth

paragraphs.text: Several common findings, in addition to risk panels, underlying maternal diseases (particularly with vascular components) and prior stillbirth or growth-restricted outcomes may raise concern for fetal growth restriction (FGR).23 These include a modest size-dates discrepancy (within-method error) on a first-trimester study, abnormal maternal serum levels of pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A (PAPP-A), and free β-human chorionic gonadotropin at 9 to 13 weeks, usually obtained as part of genetic screens. Other findings include early elevation of maternal blood pressure and abnormal uterine artery resistance by Doppler at 11 0/7 to 13 6/7 weeks, and a hypoglycemic response to glucose testing may be an early third-trimester observation. By combining uterine artery Doppler findings and baseline maternal characteristics, detection rates for early-onset FGR have reached clinically acceptable levels. Unfortunately, FGR developing later in pregnancy still goes largely undetected.24
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Growth

paragraphs.text: Placental conditions affecting the mother and/or fetus include gestational trophoblastic diseases, placental hematoma, chorangioma, abruption, placenta previa, placenta accreta/increta/ percreta, vasa previa, choriocarcinoma, chorioamnionitis, viral
paragraphs.heading: Placental Abnormalities

paragraphs.text: and parasitic villitis and placentitis, decidual and thrombotic vasculopathies, infarction, polyps, and retained products of conception. Although gross inspection and histopathology provide the ultimate diagnosis, ultrasonography is the definitive prenatal modality for evaluating the majority of these conditions. MRI and computed tomography (CT) are infrequent adjunctive measures, and the latter is occasionally helpful in tumor staging or trauma cases.25
paragraphs.heading: Placental Abnormalities

paragraphs.text: Placental location can be confidently established by abdominal and transvaginal ultrasound studies. Low-lying placentation, present in up to 60% of early second-trimester studies, persists as placenta previa in only 1% to 2% of patients at term (Fig. 10.26). Fetal vessels near the cervix can be visualized using color Doppler, facilitating the diagnosis of funic (umbilical cord) presentation and vasa previa (fetal vessels overlying the os) (Fig. 10.27). Normally inserted centrally in the placenta, the umbilical cord may later, as a result of asymmetric placental growth, be located marginally or even on the membranes; in the latter situation, traumatic
paragraphs.heading: Placental Location

paragraphs.text: lacerations, hemorrhage, and compression-linked heart rate changes are potential consequences.
paragraphs.heading: Placental Location

paragraphs.text: Morbidly adherent placenta (MAP) or placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) encompasses the histopathological diagnoses of placenta accreta (a small focus or more generalized muscular invasion), placenta increta (deeper myometrial invasion up to the uterine serosal layer), and placenta percreta (invasion through the serosa to adjacent visceral or vascular structures).26 It is potentially life threatening, as forced removal of an abnormally invasive placenta can lead to catastrophic maternal hemorrhage; management of all but the most circumscribed lesions usually requires hysterectomy (Figs. 10.28A and B).
paragraphs.heading: Placental Location

paragraphs.text: PAS was previously diagnosed only when failed attempts to remove the placenta were followed by massive bleeding. Improvements in antenatal diagnosis enabled reductions in maternal mortality and morbidity by allowing planned cesarean delivery at 34 to 35 weeks by experienced multidisciplinary teams.27 Placental accretion is significantly more likely in women with the combination of placenta previa and a history of one or more cesarean sections, after myomectomy or curettage, and with high parity.28 The
paragraphs.heading: Placental Location

paragraphs.text: frequency of accretion, now complicating 1 in 2500 deliveries, has increased more than 10-fold in the past 25 years, echoing rising cesarean rates.28
paragraphs.heading: Placental Location

paragraphs.text: Sonographic criteria for placenta accreta were developed using conventional gray-scale, 2D and 3D color and power Doppler transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasonography in high-risk women.29 In the early first trimester between 6 and 9 weeks, ultrasound markers of PAS include low implantation of the gestational sac and cesarean scar pregnancy. Studies show that most PAS cases have a low implantation in the early first trimester scans; however, low implantation is noted in only 28% in the late first trimester.30 A cesarean scar pregnancy is diagnosed if the chorionic sac is adjacent to or embedded in the scar of a previous cesarean delivery, in close proximity to the bladder, wedged in a niche, and demonstrates extensive vascularization or an arteriovenous malformation. Cesarean scar pregnancy is considered to be a precursor of PAS, as histopathology of both appear indistinguishable.31 The implantation in the niche rather than the scar and a thin remaining myometrium may be helpful to define cases that will evolve into the most severe types of PAS. In the late first, second, and third trimester, the sonographic characteristics of PAS are lacunae (multiple large sonolucent spaces in the placenta), abnormal uteroplacental interface (described as loss/irregularity of the echo-free “clear space” between the uterus and the placental basal plate, myometrial thinning, or increased vascularity on Doppler), abnormal uterovesical interface (bridging vessels extending from the placenta across the myometrium and/or beyond the serosa, increased vascularity between the uterus and bladder, and interruption of the bladder wall), placental bulge, and exophytic mass (diagnostic for placenta percreta).32 Among these markers, loss of the clear zone performs best with a sensitivity of 84% and a specificity of 82%, with a diagnostic odds ratio of 24 in the late first trimester (i.e., at 11–14 weeks).33 Coexisting markers such
paragraphs.heading: Placental Location

paragraphs.text: as lacunae or bladder wall interruption improve the diagnostic performance.31,34
paragraphs.heading: Placental Location

paragraphs.text: In the second and third trimester, the presence of large multiple lacunae (>3) with irregular borders and high turbulent flow is the most sensitive marker with a negative predictive value of 88% to 100%. The presence of an exophytic mass or placental bulge increases the risk for deep invasion (i.e., increta or percreta).30,35
paragraphs.heading: Placental Location

paragraphs.text: Antepartum diagnosis of abnormal attachment permits multidisciplinary planning for prematurity management, anesthesia, transfusion, hemostatic and uterotonic medications, balloon tamponade, arterial embolization, or scheduled preterm (around 34–35 weeks) cesarean hysterectomy prior to the onset of labor (Fig. 10.29). MRI mapping is most helpful when there is posterior placentation or suspected lateral extension, after myomectomies, for evaluation of adjacent viscera with percreta, or when ultrasound findings are ambiguous.36
paragraphs.heading: Placental Location

paragraphs.text: Placental abruption is defined as complete or partial separation of the placenta that presents with hemorrhage in the retroplacental, subchorionic, or placental chorionic
paragraphs.heading: Placental Location

paragraphs.text: space on ultrasound. Most patients have pain and bleeding except for rare cases of concealed abruption. The diagnosis of placental abruption remains a clinical one due to low sensitivity of ultrasound. The role of imaging in this disorder is to exclude placenta previa and other sources of bleeding. One series reported 24% sensitivity and 53% negative predictive value for ultrasound diagnosis of abruption. Subchorionic hematomas are often noted on transvaginal scans early in gestation. Size and persistence have been traditionally linked to poorer outcomes such as abortion, stillbirth, preterm delivery, and preterm rupture of the membrane. In contrast, a recent study reported that subchorionic hematomas were not independent risk factors for adverse outcome when controlled for other maternal risk factors, vaginal bleeding, and gestational age.37 Later abruptions are more difficult to visualize; acute bleeding is isoechoic with placenta and can be mistaken for placentomegaly. Hypoechoic fluid collections and hyperechoic infarcted areas appear in more chronic presentations.
paragraphs.heading: Placental Location

paragraphs.text: Placenta previa is defined as placenta overlying the internal os. In the second trimester, placenta previa or a low-lying placenta with the inferior edge 2 cm from the internal os is seen frequently, in approximately in 5% to 20% of ultrasound studies. The prevalence decreases to 0.3% to 0.5% at term. A posterior low-positioned placenta is more likely to persist into the third trimester.38 Transvaginal ultrasound is superior to the transabdominal approach and is safe for the evaluation of placenta previa. A persistent low-lying placenta or placenta previa is an indication for cesarean delivery, and follow-up scans are recommended at 32 weeks and 36 weeks for delivery planning.39
paragraphs.heading: Placental Location

paragraphs.text: Vasa previa is characterized by the presence of unprotected fetal blood vessels by the umbilical cord or placenta over the cervical os or within 2 cm from the cervical os. It complicates 1 in 2500 deliveries. Membrane rupture prior to labor can lead to fetal hemorrhage, exsanguination, death, and bad long-term sequelae in survivors. Prenatal identification prior to the onset of labor or rupture of membranes improves survival to 98.6% from 72% and intact survival to 96.7% from 28.1%.40 An ultrasound study typically shows fetal vessels over the cervical os that appear like bubbles or lines on gray scale (Fig. 10.27). Fetal arterial waveforms can be confirmed by Doppler. Vessels with venous flow should be followed to their origin if possible to differentiate maternal vessels. Low-lying placenta, resolved placenta previa, velamentous cord insertion, accessory lobes, bilobed placenta, multiple pregnancies, and artificial reproductive therapy increase the risk of vasa previa. In these cases, consideration should be given to rule out vasa previa, preferably by transvaginal imaging.41
paragraphs.heading: Placental Location

paragraphs.text: Grading placental appearance to detect disturbed growth or maturation is of limited benefit. Persistent immaturity is linked to hydrops fetalis, although not as often as increased echogenicity and thickening (Fig. 10.30). Placental lakes are hypoechoic spaces with slow venous flow and are benign findings; however, they must be differentiated from retroplacental or subchorionic hemorrhage. Partial or complete
paragraphs.heading: Placental Location

paragraphs.text: mole in the first trimester, PAS, mesenchymal dysplasia, chorioangioma, and confined placental mosaicism can present with cystic spaces in the placenta.42
paragraphs.heading: Placental Location

paragraphs.text: Amniotic fluid is initially secreted by the amnion; by the 16th week of pregnancy, fetal renal production accounts for the majority, with nearly complete turnover during a 24-hour period. Malformations of the esophagus and upper gastrointestinal tract, inhibited fetal swallowing, aneuploidy, intermittent renal obstruction, maternal diabetes, TTTS, some forms of dwarfism, and fetal hydrops are associated with marked polyhydramnios. Severe growth restriction with polyhydramnios carries a poor prognosis. Polyhydramnios is idiopathic in almost half of the cases; associated complications include maternal respiratory compromise, premature membrane rupture, preterm labor and delivery, malposition, abruption, cord prolapse, preeclampsia, amniotic fluid embolism, and puerperal hemorrhage. Maximum vertical pocket or summed depths across quadrants conveniently serve as proxies for volume calculation in clinical settings (Fig. 10.31). Oligohydramnios may occur after membrane rupture, after fetal renal compensation for placental hypoperfusion, due to functional or obstructive urogenital anomalies, with maternal dehydration, or following exposure to some medications, including indomethacin and angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors. Maternal obesity is associated with underestimation of amniotic volumes. Amniotic fluid measurements may be combined with non-stress and fetal biophysical testing to provide reassurance of fetal well-being.
paragraphs.heading: Amniotic Fluid Volume

paragraphs.text: Cervical length and appearance are frequently assessed during routine antenatal ultrasound; transvaginal measurements (Fig. 10.32) are more reliable and reproducible than transabdominal views. The closed endocervical canal length is positively correlated with duration of gestation in
paragraphs.heading: Cervical Length and Pelvic Structures

paragraphs.text: a continuous fashion. Moreover, when values fall below 25 mm, preterm deliveries increase. In patients with prematurity risks, shorter cervical length is strongly predictive of delivery before 36 weeks; in combination with fetal fibronectin and other biomarker assays, ultrasound aids in identifying those at highest risk for imminent delivery.43
paragraphs.heading: Q2

paragraphs.text: Attempts to prevent premature births by tocolysis have been ineffective; postponing delivery for 48 hours to permit steroid enhancement of lung maturity has proven more feasible. First-trimester ultrasound prediction of the need for cervical cerclage has not been reliable. Specific candidates may benefit from elective cerclage based on previous pregnancy history, ultrasound-indicated cerclage with shortened cervical length, and prior history of spontaneous
paragraphs.heading: Q2

paragraphs.text: preterm delivery, or “rescue” cerclage with an open cervix on physical examination. Progesterone prophylaxis against prematurity by intramuscular injection or vaginal preparation has increased in recent years; the former has supporting evidence for effectiveness in women with a previous history of preterm delivery, whereas the latter is shown to be effective when a short cervix is noted by ultrasound.43
paragraphs.heading: Q4

paragraphs.text: The gravid uterus is conveniently studied by ultrasound. Congenital Müllerian anomalies, including duplications and septations, occur in about 0.5% of the population (Fig. 10.33). Patients with bicornuate uteri may experience irregular bleeding in early pregnancy, altered cervical competency, and, rarely, torsions or ruptures of the horn in which the gestational sac is located. Poorly vascularized septations are etiologically
paragraphs.heading: Q4

paragraphs.text: associated with abruption and pregnancy failure. Myomas complicate 1% to 2% of pregnancies with more frequent cesareans and prematurity, abruption, degeneration, and fetal malpresentation; less common complications include fetal deformation, dystocia (7.5%), puerperal hemorrhage, and hysterectomy.44 Adverse obstetric outcomes are rare; studies are confounded by age, ethnicity, and other differences in those who develop myomas. Generally, good maternal and neonatal outcomes are expected in most pregnancies with uterine fibroids.44
paragraphs.heading: Q4

paragraphs.text: Normal adnexal structures are not palpable after the first trimester; ultrasound is the first choice for ovarian evaluation during pregnancy, although often augmented by MRI and CT. Ovarian torsion is a rare but acute surgical emergency; it is more likely with ART, ovarian cysts, and adnexal masses, favoring first-trimester or puerperal onset. When an adnexal mass has been discovered by ultrasound, better characterization by MRI may be essential to avoiding unnecessary surgery during pregnancy. Asymptomatic lesions, even when quite large, are now generally expectantly managed until delivery or the postpartum period if malignancy is not suspected. Ultrasound is frequently sufficient for a secure diagnosis of corpus luteal cysts, benign cystic teratomas, and endometriomas. Use of MRI for atypical lesions can confirm the presence of fat, key to the diagnosis of teratoma and the exclusion of endometrioma. MRI aids in the identification of hydrosalpinges and nongynecological lesions. Expectant management of many adnexal masses past delivery is now more common, based on benign ultrasound, Doppler, and MRI characteristics.45
paragraphs.heading: Q4

paragraphs.text: During second-trimester studies, a number of normal fetal structures are routinely identified, and anomalies excluded.
paragraphs.heading: Second-Trimester Ultrasound Study of the Fetus

paragraphs.text: Basic anatomic surveys usually include documentation of fetal cranial integrity and central nervous system anatomy: midline brain structures, cavum septum pellucidum and thalami, lateral and third ventricles, choroid plexus, cerebellum, and posterior fossa.
paragraphs.heading: Second-Trimester Ultrasound Study of the Fetus

paragraphs.text: Views confirming facial symmetry, intact orbits, clear lenses, paired nares, intact lips and hard palate, and normal profile are part of comprehensive studies. Fetal swallowing, respiratory movements, and nuchal structures may be noted. The spinal column is normally imaged in the longaxis, transverse, and coronal views. Distinct advantages for the visualization of the facial features, small parts, and spine are provided by 3D imaging (Fig. 10.34). Views of the thorax, including the axis, site, and relative proportions of cardiac and mediastinal structures with respect to the lungs and pulmonary vessels, yield indirect support for the integrity of the diaphragm. Over time, the basic cardiac examination has expanded from obtaining the axis, laterality, and rate to requiring symmetric four-chamber apical views and, as feasible, images of normal outflows, ductal and aortic arches, and additional arterial and venous tracts (Fig. 10.35). Prenatal echocardiography adds M-mode rhythm, color flow Doppler, and structural studies capable of details and diagnostic accuracy approaching those of postnatal examinations, subject to predictable limitations.46 Fetal abdominal views confirm the closure of the ventral wall; presence, normal size, and site of hepatic, gastric, splenic, pancreatic, vascular, and choledochal structures; renal and adrenal contours; normal bowel dimensions and echogenicity; bladder filling; and umbilical cord appearance. Accuracy of fetal sex assignment exceeds 99% by the midtrimester (Figs. 10.12 and 10.36). Fetal digits, small parts, cerebellar vermis, and palatal components are often imaged by a combination of 2D and 3D. As gestation progresses, neurosonography may identify additional features of intracranial architecture and cerebral maturation.
paragraphs.heading: Second-Trimester Ultrasound Study of the Fetus

paragraphs.text: Initially considered revolutionary, obstetric Doppler has been hampered by costs, time constraints, safety concerns, and lack of clear utility for most patients. Currently accepted applications, originally employed in research and referral centers, commonly include identification and localization of blood flow, resistance to flow, vessel patterns, and directionality and velocity in cardiopulmonary structures and in a wide range of additional vessels, most commonly the uterine arteries, umbilical vessels, DV, and middle cerebral artery.
paragraphs.heading: Doppler Ultrasound

paragraphs.text: Uterine blood flow patterns reflect both maternal vascular resistance and placental site. Abnormal Doppler results in these and other vessels precede growth restriction and maternal hypertensive complications. Paired umbilical cord arteries are readily shown by color Doppler to bifurcate around the bladder (Fig. 10.5). Absence of one umbilical cord artery may have associated cardiac and renal anomalies, aneuploidies, or growth restriction. Abnormally high UA resistance is more often characteristic of uteroplacental constraints on fetal growth than of anomalies or aneuploidy. Doppler findings may suggest the origin of a size/date discrepancy, but weight estimation more reliably identifies the small-for-gestational-age fetus. Persistent absence or reversal of end-diastolic flow, albeit rare, is associated with severe growth restriction, and increased perinatal morbidity and mortality.47 Decreased middle cerebral artery resistance indices indicating brain sparing and increased DV resistance indices usually develop later in the course of compromised perfusion; paradoxical DV and umbilical venous patterns are considered premorbid. Schemes combining clinical risks, gestational age, biometry, Doppler measurements of the umbilical and middle cerebral vessels, and biophysical testing appear to have improved outcomes for growthrestricted fetuses while reducing the frequency of iatrogenic prematurity.13
paragraphs.heading: Doppler Ultrasound

paragraphs.text: Doppler measurement of peak systolic velocity in the middle cerebral artery has become integral to detection of fetal anemia and management of isoimmunization (Fig. 10.37). Previously, isoimmunization and related fetal anemia were screened for invasively by serial amniocentesis to detect hemoglobin products in the amniotic fluid, but such screening was complicated by technical challenges,
paragraphs.heading: B

paragraphs.text: prematurity, and fetal losses. Furthermore, hemoglobin products have low screening sensitivity in Kell antibodyrelated anemia, which causes bone marrow suppression in addition to red blood cell destruction. Peak systolic velocity of the middle cerebral artery by noninvasive Doppler, relatively easily obtained, is inversely correlated with fetal hemoglobin values.48 At a cutoff of 1.5 multiples of the median, the sensitivity for clinically significant anemia approaches 100%, with a false-positive rate from 0% to 28%. The false-positive rate may increase starting at 34 to 35 weeks; however, the false-negative rate remains similar to that at 34 to 35 weeks.48 Severe growth restriction may contribute to false-positive results but is usually distinguished by clinical context. Color flow Doppler distinguishes between cystic and vascular lesions, confirms the presence or site of organs, and aids in evaluating brain, cardiac, and pulmonary vasculature. When combined with 3D, color flow generates dramatic virtual vascular casts, although with more limited prenatal applications.
paragraphs.heading: B

paragraphs.text: Placental dysfunction leading to FGR is an important risk factor for neurodevelopmental delay. Observations clarify that FGR evolves prenatally from a preclinical phase of abnormal vascular, nutrient, and endocrine milieu to a clinical phase differing in characteristics in preterm versus term pregnancies. Relating childhood neurodevelopment to prenatal characteristics may aid in identifying mechanisms and timing of critical insults. Based on available studies, lagging HC, degree of FGR, gestational age, umbilical artery (UA), aortic, and cerebral Doppler parameters may be independent prenatal predictors of infant and childhood neurodevelopment. HC is meaningful independent of gestational age, but a generalized growth delay has greater impact in early-onset FGR. Gestational age at
paragraphs.heading: Doppler Studies of the Growth-Restricted Fetus

paragraphs.text: delivery becomes the chief determinant of neurodevelopment before 32 to 34 weeks’ gestation. Doppler evidence of placental resistance to flow is increasingly important after 27 weeks, with maximum concern when flow reversals are noted in the UA, aorta, ductus venosus (DV), or the UV. These findings predominate in early-onset FGR; cerebral vascular impedance changes, sometimes expressed as a ratio between the pulsatility indices of the middle cerebral and umbilical arteries, are important in later FGR. Abnormal motor and neurologic delays occurring in preterm FGR give way to cognitive effects and abnormalities related to specific brain areas as gestation advances, suggesting different pathophysiologies or evolving vulnerabilities of the fetal brain. Current studies do not suggest that fetal deterioration has an independent effect on neurodevelopment in early-onset FGR. The role of intervention in late FGR requires more research, as risks for damage and patterns of deterioration may differ in the third trimester.49
paragraphs.heading: Doppler Studies of the Growth-Restricted Fetus

paragraphs.text: Elucidation of normal venous anatomy and its roles in normal fetal development and in the evaluation and management of intrauterine growth restriction and other cardiovascular disorders, as well as its association as a part of complex structural anomalies, are being researched extensively. In the fetus, oxygen- and nutrient-rich blood from the placenta is delivered through the UV and the DV to the fetal heart. The DV connects to the inferior vena cava (IVC) distally, together with the left hepatic vein (LHV) and the middle hepatic vein (MHV), proximal to the entrance into the right atrium (Fig. 10.38). The UV and DV atrophy after birth.49
paragraphs.heading: Doppler Studies of the Fetal Venous System

paragraphs.text: Within the developing fetal liver, two apposed venous systems develop, the afferent and efferent. The afferent venous system, composed of the fetal liver, UV, portal vein, portal system, and DV, and the efferent venous system (the hepatic veins [HVs]) form two systems positioned in the caudal and cranial portions of the liver, respectively.50 The main function of the fetal venous system is to deliver blood rich with oxygen and nutrients from the placenta. The DV plays a critical role in this important function. The venous system represents one component of the four that comprise the fetomaternal vascular system, the others being the heart, the placenta, and the arterial system. In order to provide a normal amount of blood flow toward the heart, low placental resistance and improved cardiac contraction must work in synergy. A pressure gradient is created between the atria and ventricles which reduces the preload in the venous circulatory system and allows blood to flow toward the heart. This pressure gradient is further accentuated by the physiologic stenosis of the DV.
paragraphs.heading: Doppler Studies of the Fetal Venous System

paragraphs.text: Doppler waveforms of the fetal precordial veins mirror the heart cycle. Their typical three-peak form represents the ventricular systolic phase (S), passive diastolic phase (D), and active diastolic phase (A). As opposed to the IVC and HVs, DV blood flows forward throughout the entire heart
paragraphs.heading: Doppler Studies of the Fetal Venous System

paragraphs.text: cycle, assuring a constant high-quality blood supply to the heart. The DV is sampled at its inlet with a large sample volume in a near-sagittal scan at a low angle of insonation (Fig. 10.38). Alternatively, DV flow can be sampled in an oblique transverse section of the fetal abdomen. Changes in DV flow are seen in fetal hypoxia and hypovolemia in experimental animal models and in human fetuses.51
paragraphs.heading: Doppler Studies of the Fetal Venous System

paragraphs.text: Real-time ultrasound is well suited by virtue of safety, economy, and convenience for guiding placement of needles, cannulae, catheters, and other devices used in fetal diagnosis and therapy. The range of procedures includes oocyte retrieval and embryo transfers, embryonic and fetal reduction, selective termination in multiple gestations, chorionic villus sampling, placental and skin biopsies, amniocentesis and amnioreduction, cord blood sampling, intrauterine transfusion, aspiration of fluid from various fetal and maternal sites, bladder and thoracic shunts, intrauterine surgical procedures such as neural tube defect repair, and an adjunct to fetoscopy and vascular ablation. The effectiveness of and complications from procedures are often apparent in real time. Important accepted applications include determinations of fetal status; relative fetal and umbilical cord positions during external version for malpresentations, labors, and immediately before transfusions; surgical interventions; and the ex utero intrapartum treatment (EXIT) procedure.
paragraphs.heading: Ultrasound-Guided Procedures

paragraphs.text: A tenet of antepartum testing is that more accurate predictions of fetal wellness are achieved in proportion to the number of variables considered. The biophysical profile (BPP) is a noninvasive, ultrasound-based clinical tool that integrates levels of dynamic biophysical activities into a useable standard. The BPP attempts to predict the presence or absence of fetal asphyxia to prevent progression to
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Well-Being Assessment

paragraphs.text: metabolic acidosis and fetal death. The BPP seeks to identify four parameters in a 30-minute period, each of which is assigned two points: (1) observation of continuous tidal fetal breathing for 30 seconds, (2) a vertical amniotic fluid pocket of at least 2 cm (or 2 cm in two planes), (3) three obvious fetal movements, and (4) fetal tone, manifested by brisk flexion of small parts or hands. Death or injury within 1 week is more likely with scores below six, with loss of tone considered a late finding. Conversely, scores of eight are considered highly reassuring for well-being during the same period. A fetal non-stress test, sometimes included for an additional two points (total score of 10), does not usually affect the predictive value of the BPP.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Well-Being Assessment

paragraphs.text: Antepartum testing by BPP should not be performed prior to viability or when fetal or maternal conditions preclude successful intervention. Cautious interpretation is appropriate for extreme fetal prematurity, in the presence of anomalies, for maternal metabolic abnormalities, during labor, and with some drugs, including opiates, sedatives, and antenatal corticosteroids.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Well-Being Assessment

paragraphs.text: Doppler investigation is the only noninvasive in utero method for assessing fetoplacental hemodynamic status. Each component of the fetomaternal circulation has a different role in placental function and fetal well-being. Doppler evaluation of the venous system aims to assess fetal cardiac function, which in severe cases may deteriorate to an acute event of congestive heart failure. Cardiac events are apparent in the DV waveform. Reversed or zero flow in the A-wave is a simple sign of disordered cardiac function. There is reduced velocity in the A-wave in intrauterine growth restriction, and as the situation worsens it is further deflected due to increased afterload and preload, as well as increased end-diastolic pressure, the direct effects of hypoxia, and increased adrenergic drive.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Well-Being Assessment

paragraphs.text: The evolution of fetoplacental Doppler abnormalities is dependent on the gestational age at onset and the severity of the placental disease. Mild cases present with UA and middle cerebral artery Doppler abnormalities at 32 weeks.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Well-Being Assessment

paragraphs.text: Severe cases establish abnormal UA Doppler values at 27 weeks, followed by rapid progression to severe arterial and venous Doppler abnormalities, such as absent/reversed UA diastolic velocity, absent/reversed DV A-wave, and UV pulsation.52
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Well-Being Assessment

paragraphs.text: Late first-trimester ultrasound study without an established protocol on low-risk populations can detect approximately 30% of the major fetal anomalies after exclusion of chromosomal aberrations.11,12 The detection rate increases to 61% in high-risk populations.11 Use of a standard protocol increases the yield for fetal anomalies. As such, the American Institute of Ultrasound in Medicine published detailed first-trimester scanning guidelines for high-risk pregnancies in 2021.53 Other factors improving performance include adequate examination time, the experience and training of the performing sonographer, the quality of the ultrasound equipment, maternal body mass index, use of transvaginal ultrasound study for cases with suboptimal transabdominal imaging, and the presence of an easily detectable marker for an underlying abnormality.54–56 In some cases, late first-trimester scans may not be diagnostic; however, they may demonstrate findings suggestive of a structural anomaly (Fig. 10.39). In these patients, secondtrimester ultrasound studies before 18 weeks can lead to earlier prenatal diagnoses. To decrease false positivity, the natural history of abnormal findings should be known. Two such examples are the resolution of isolated bowel herniation (physiologic omphalocele) and isolated megacystis in euploid fetuses with longitudinal bladder length less than 15 mm with advancing gestation.57 The detection
paragraphs.heading: Ultrasound Examination for Fetal Abnormalities in the Late First Trimester

paragraphs.text: rate of fetal anomalies during late first trimester scan varies for different types of major anomalies in the various organ systems as summarized below.53
paragraphs.heading: Ultrasound Examination for Fetal Abnormalities in the Late First Trimester

paragraphs.text: Most cases of acrania, alobar holoprosencephaly, and encephalocele can be accurately diagnosed. Posterior fossa malformations (Fig. 10.19B), callosal agenesis, ventriculomegaly, destructive lesions, cortical development abnormalities, hemorrhage, thrombosis, and tumors are usually diagnosed in the second and third trimester as they develop or become more prominent with advancing pregnancy. It is feasible to correctly diagnose more than half of fetuses with open spina bifida (OSB) in the first trimester. There are many suggestive markers of OSB in the late first-trimester scan, including obliterated fourth ventricle (intracranial translucency) and cisterna magna (Fig. 10.19B), increased brainstem distance, peduncles and aqueduct of Sylvius, increased choroid plexus/frontooccipital diameter ratio, an abnormal frontomaxillary facial angle, and the dry brain sign.58
paragraphs.heading: Central Nervous System

paragraphs.text: Up to one-third of cases with cleft lip and palate are detectable in the first trimester. Isolated cleft lip and palate, unilateral cleft lip, and micrognathia, unless severe, are usually diagnosed in the second trimester.56 Suggestive signs of facial abnormalities shown to be helpful include absent mandibular gap for micrognathia, maxillary gap for cleft palate, and retronasal view abnormalities for cleft lip and palate.58
paragraphs.heading: Face

paragraphs.text: Conditions such as hyper- and hypotelorism, anophthalmia, and microphthalmia have been diagnosed from 12 weeks to 16 weeks by measuring the interocular distance, ocular diameter, and biocular distance. Isolated anomalies are rare, and most of the anomalies are associated with other malformations, especially those of the developing brain (alobar holoprosencephaly), as well as with aneuploidy (trisomy 13) and nonchromosomal syndromes.
paragraphs.heading: Ocular Anomalies

paragraphs.text: Approximately 29% of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) cases can be detected in the first trimester. Mediastinal shift and upturned superior mesenteric artery sign can be suggestive of CDH.58 Most chest masses were diagnosed after the first trimester in one large case series.56,58
paragraphs.heading: Chest

paragraphs.text: Most cases of tricuspid atresia, hypoplastic left heart, atrioventricular septal defects, and more than half of complex heart defects and left atrial isomerism can be detected in the first trimester.56 For other defects, detection rate remains lower than 50%. Increased nuchal translucency, abnormal DV blood flow pattern as demonstrated by a Doppler study, tricuspid regurgitation, and abnormal cardiac axis in the
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac

paragraphs.text: first trimester are associated with an increased risk for congenital cardiac disease.58,59–61
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac

paragraphs.text: Most cases with omphalocele, gastroschisis, or limb-body wall complex and more than 70% of lower urinary tract obstructions are detected in the first trimester.58 When the enlarged hyperechogenic kidneys are noted in the first trimester, polycystic kidney disease should be suspected. Though autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease also has been diagnosed in the first trimester, follow-up examination in the second trimester is needed to confirm the diagnosis. Abdominal cysts, bowel atresia, abnormal genitalia, and renal anomalies are not usually detected in the first trimester.58
paragraphs.heading: Gastrointestinal and Genitourinary

paragraphs.text: More than 70% of absent extremities, fetal akinesia deformation sequence, and lethal skeletal dysplasias are detected in the first trimester.58 Most cases with talipes anomaly and nonlethal skeletal dysplasias and approximately more than 60% of abnormal digits and hemivertebrae of the spine are detected after the first trimester.58
paragraphs.heading: Skeleton

paragraphs.text: Although the 11+0 to 13+6-week scan is effective in identifying a large variety of fetal defects, there are some important possible disadvantages compared with secondtrimester ultrasound examination. First, due to the small size of anomalous organs, the number of major anomalies that can be detected through a systematic scan is limited, and the scan can be done only in highly experienced hands. Second, undetectable anomalies mostly relate to structures not yet fully developed prior to 14 weeks—for example, cerebellar anomalies and echogenic lung cysts. In addition, some anomalies, such as aortic and pulmonary stenosis, can progress into more severe malformations with advancing gestation, so there may not be an obvious abnormality at this period. Finally, some defects may resolve in utero, such as ventricular septal defects.61
paragraphs.heading: Disadvantages Compared With Second-Trimester Ultrasound

paragraphs.text: Neonatal outcomes can be optimized by forewarning and timely preparation when fetal abnormalities are present. Unfortunately, more than one-third of birth defects remain unrecognized prenatally. False-positive diagnoses are less frequent, but the up to 10% discordancy with autopsy findings highlights the inherent uncertainties of prenatal diagnosis. Familiarity with imaging pitfalls associated with common anomalies is imperative to avoid misdiagnosis. Suspected structural defects should always be visualized in the correct plane with attempted confirmation in other planes. Precise
paragraphs.heading: Ultrasound Examination for Fetal Abnormalities in the Second or Third Trimester

paragraphs.text: measurements using specific criteria, appropriate gain settings, and additional modalities may be required for correct interpretation and management. Expert second opinions by patient referral or image review are available for most findings. Despite acknowledged limitations, prenatal ultrasound is the standard method for recognition of fetal anomalies.
paragraphs.heading: Ultrasound Examination for Fetal Abnormalities in the Second or Third Trimester

paragraphs.text: Hydrocephalus and ventriculomegaly are not strictly synonymous. Hydrocephalus connotes raised intracranial pressure, a functional observation not directly amenable to ultrasound. Prenatal enlargement of the lateral ventricles (Fig. 10.40) may occur without altered pressure because of developmental abnormalities. Enlargement of the atria and posterior horns of the lateral cerebral ventricles (colpocephaly) may be associated with agenesis of the corpus callosum or type II Chiari malformations.62 Dilated lateral ventricles may also result from obstructed cerebrospinal fluid flow by hemorrhage or from brain destruction by a variety of causes, including ischemia and infection (e.g., cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, Zika virus). A single measurement over 10 mm at the level of the posterior atria of the lateral ventricles defines ventriculomegaly between 16 and 40 weeks of gestational age.
paragraphs.heading: Central Nervous System Fetal Ventriculomegaly

paragraphs.text: Atrial widths tend to decrease slightly during pregnancy. Choroid plexus positioning is gravity dependent; on axial views, the choroid, attached at the level of the foramen of Monro, rests on the dependent wall of the lateral ventricle, marking the limit of the lateral ventricle, even when the wall cannot be visualized. A “dangling” choroid plexus
paragraphs.heading: Central Nervous System Fetal Ventriculomegaly

paragraphs.text: conveys the extent and severity of ventricular enlargement (Fig. 10.41).
paragraphs.heading: Central Nervous System Fetal Ventriculomegaly

paragraphs.text: Clinical outcomes of severe ventriculomegaly (atrial size greater than 15 mm) are discouraging; survivors are often mentally and physically impaired. Hydrocephalus associated with arachnoid cyst, atresia of Monro, absence of the corpus callosum, or minor intracranial hemorrhage may have a better prognosis. By contrast, hydrocephaly seen with holoprosencephaly, encephalocele, congenital syndromes, or infection generally leads to loss or greater disability. Formal diagnostic and management algorithms, combining ultrasound, MRI, genetic diagnosis, and infectious disease screening, play an essential role in counseling and care when hydrocephaly is identified.63
paragraphs.heading: Central Nervous System Fetal Ventriculomegaly

paragraphs.text: In utero shunting has no current role in the treatment of prenatal ventriculomegaly. Asymmetric or rounded lateral ventricles and mild ventriculomegaly (widths between 10 and 12 mm) convey an uncertain prognosis, as most infants are normal, particularly when resolution occurs; slightly wider dimensions (12–15 mm) carry an intermediate prognosis.
paragraphs.heading: Central Nervous System Fetal Ventriculomegaly

paragraphs.text: Agenesis of the corpus callosum can be isolated but is commonly associated with other anomalies of abnormal neuronal migration. Midtrimester diagnosis of many brain lesions is hampered by ongoing differentiation and growth of the central nervous system; third-trimester transvaginal cranial ultrasound and MRI are particularly helpful in assessing the progressive development of gyri and sulci of the brain (Fig. 10.42).
paragraphs.heading: Central Nervous System Fetal Ventriculomegaly

paragraphs.text: Meningomyelocele (Fig. 10.43) may be associated with a Chiari II malformation (that is, downward displacement of the hindbrain), as well as with other brain anomalies,
paragraphs.heading: Meningomyelocele and (Type II) Chiari Malformation

paragraphs.text: including ventriculomegaly (Fig. 10.44). Progressive hydrocephalus can develop requiring shunting early after delivery. Open neural tube defect (Fig. 10.45) is usually accompanied by markedly elevated alpha-fetoprotein levels in both maternal serum and amniotic fluid. A meningomyelocele appears on ultrasound as splaying or divergence of the posterior ossification centers, best appreciated on axial spinal views. A fluid-filled sac may be seen and the integrity of the overlying skin can be visibly disrupted on axial and sagittal images. The level of the meningomyelocele can be ascertained more accurately with 3D ultrasound and MRI (Figs. 10.34 and 10.43), helpful for predicting the outcome in affected children. Severe cases may be associated with kyphoscoliotic spinal deformity or clubbing of one or both feet. Prenatally, extremity movement may seem to be preserved; however, absence of normal activity better correlates with postnatal motor function.
paragraphs.heading: Meningomyelocele and (Type II) Chiari Malformation

paragraphs.text: The “lemon sign” refers to the altered appearance of the calvarium, similar in shape to a lemon, on an axial view of the skull and brain (Fig. 10.41). Biconcave frontal bones produce the calvarial distortion. The sign is best demonstrated between 18 and 24 weeks but is not specific, appearing sometimes in otherwise normal children. The “banana sign” refers to abnormal cerebellar positioning, curled in a crescent (banana-like) around the brainstem (Fig. 10.45). Obliteration of the cisterna magna and cerebellar distortion are secondary to type II Chiari malformation. One or both signs are seen in the majority of spina
paragraphs.heading: The Skull and Brain in Spina Bifida

paragraphs.text: bifida cases during the midtrimester and should prompt a more detailed examination of the spine. Prenatal surgical closure of defects may improve outcomes in appropriate candidates, particularly with respect to preservation of motor function, to decrease the need for shunting in the early newborn period, and for the prevention of hindbrain displacement.
paragraphs.heading: The Skull and Brain in Spina Bifida

paragraphs.text: Anencephaly, the absence of normal brain and calvarium superior to the orbits, can be detected as early as 10 weeks but is recognizable throughout gestation (Fig. 10.46). Maternal serum alpha fetoprotein is usually very elevated. About half of cases have associated anomalies, such as meningomyelocele, cleft palate, or clubfoot. Occasionally, the typical appearance is altered by the presence of echogenic material superior to the orbits, identified pathologically as angiomatous stroma (“area cerebrovasculosa”). Polyhydramnios and malpresentation are common later findings. Abnormal prolongation of pregnancy may occur, presumably secondary to lack of fetal neurohormonal cues for labor. Anencephaly is considered incompatible with meaningful survival; most affected liveborn infants succumb in the immediate neonatal period. Intervention for purely fetal indications is futile and is not recommended.
paragraphs.heading: Anencephaly

paragraphs.text: Extracranial protrusion of brain tissue within a meningeal sac is a straightforward ultrasound diagnosis, although dependent on site and size of lesion and appropriate visualization. Most encephaloceles in the Western world are occipital and midline and should be distinguished from soft tissue edema, hemangioma, or lymphangioma of the neck. The identification of a calvarial defect allows a specific diagnosis (Fig. 10.47). Encephaloceles may be isolated or associated with amniotic band syndrome (when off midline) and genetic syndromes such as Meckel-Gruber. Prognosis is affected by the site, size, and amount of extruded tissue and is adversely affected by ventriculomegaly, microcephaly, and syndromic etiology. Anterior sites
paragraphs.heading: Encephalocele

paragraphs.text: is absent above the orbits.
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 10.46 Three-dimensional orthogonal image of anencephaly at 17 weeks’ gestation. The cranial vault

paragraphs.text: Lower images: Posterior encephalocele with meninges and neuronal tissue.
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 10.47 Upper image: Occipital encephalocele with herniation of meninges through the defect (arrow).

paragraphs.text: are more common in Asian populations; small nasal or frontoethmoidal encephaloceles may initially elude even postnatal detection.
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 10.47 Upper image: Occipital encephalocele with herniation of meninges through the defect (arrow).

paragraphs.text: Holoprosencephaly, a malformation resulting from early failure of division of the embryologic prosencephalon or forebrain, is frequently associated with facial abnormalities (Fig. 10.48A). Its incidence ranges from 0.6 to 1.9 per 10,000 live births, although this is likely an underestimate because many cases spontaneously abort and milder variants can be unrecognized. In cases without chromosomal abnormalities, recurrence risk is estimated to be 6%. The etiology of holoprosencephaly is heterogeneous and not fully known, as most cases are sporadic. Environmental, mechanical, and genetic factors have all been implicated. Several chromosomal disorders are linked to this anomaly, most notably trisomy 13, with 70% exhibiting holoprosencephaly.
paragraphs.heading: Holoprosencephaly

paragraphs.text: Holoprosencephaly in association with extra-cephalic malformations strongly suggests aneuploidy; there are also autosomal dominant and recessive familial forms. The condition has been induced by a variety of teratogenic agents in animal models. In alobar holoprosencephaly, the most severe form, there is a complete failure of cleavage of the forebrain into two hemispheres. The cerebral hemispheres are fused and enclose a single prosencephalic ventricle. In addition to a single ventricular cavity, the thalami are fused, and the cavum septum pellucidum, corpus callosum, falx cerebri, optic tracts, and olfactory bulbs are all absent. The alobar condition is often associated with fetal loss; the vast majority of liveborn infants experience severe neurologic dysfunction or death in early infancy; less severe variants have a wider, less predictable range of outcomes. Partial cleavage results in semilobar holoprosencephaly, with posterior separation of the cerebral hemispheres, variable degrees of thalamic fusion, and absent olfactory bulbs and corpus callosum. In lobar
paragraphs.heading: Holoprosencephaly

paragraphs.text: holoprosencephaly, the abnormalities may be confined to absence of the cavum septum pellucidum and corpus callosum with fusion of the lateral ventricles and cingulate gyrus; hemispheres are separated anteriorly and posteriorly. The mildest form, septal optic dysplasia, lacks only the cavum septum pellucidum. Severe forms of holoprosencephaly may exhibit cyclopia (median mono-ophthalmia) with or without proboscis, cebocephaly (ocular hypotelorism and a blind single nostril), ethmocephaly (ocular hypotelorism with proboscis) (Fig. 10.48B), and median facial clefts. The diagnosis of holoprosencephaly was typically made during the midtrimester anatomic survey by noting fused lateral ventricles and thalami and the absence of normal midline structures. Early prenatal detection of holoprosencephaly can occur between 11 and 14 weeks’ gestation by obtaining transverse cranial images in which the normal “butterfly sign” of choroid and ventricles is absent (Fig. 10.48C).
paragraphs.heading: Holoprosencephaly

paragraphs.text: The Dandy-Walker malformation is a fluid-filled posterior fossa cyst, with variable occurrence of lateral ventriculomegaly; the posterior fossa is always enlarged and the tentorium uplifted.62 The cerebellar hemispheres, separated by the cyst, are rudimentary. Agenesis of the cerebellar vermis is difficult to confirm before 20 weeks because wide variations in developmental timing mean that full formation may not yet be present. The Dandy-Walker variant consists of direct communication between the fourth ventricle and cisterna magna, without posterior fossa enlargement and with only mild hypoplasia of the inferior vermis. The subtle ultrasound findings can be associated with serious abnormalities of neuronal migration; confirmation from MRI is helpful (Fig. 10.49). The fetal brainstem-vermis (BV) and
paragraphs.heading: Dandy-Walker Malformation

paragraphs.text: brainstem-tentorium (BT) angles are of great help in the differential diagnosis of upward rotation of the fetal cerebellar vermis. These simple and reproducible measurements provide valuable additional information for the categorization of upward rotation of the fetal cerebellar vermis and posterior fossa cyst. A BV angle >45 degrees is strongly suggestive of a Dandy-Walker malformation, whereas a measurement of <30 degrees favors the diagnosis of a Blake’s pouch cyst.62
paragraphs.heading: Dandy-Walker Malformation

paragraphs.text: Cysts in the choroid plexus, noted in 1% to 2% of normal second-trimester pregnancies, usually resolve by the early third trimester (Fig. 10.17). Cyst number, size, or persistence imparts no additional clinical significance. Isolated choroid plexus cysts are generally associated with normal karyotype, do not require follow-up to confirm resolution, and do not affect postnatal development.64 Choroid cysts have been associated with trisomy 18.
paragraphs.heading: Choroid Plexus Cyst

paragraphs.text: 3D imaging is extremely useful for studying fetal spine, vertebrae, ribs, pelvic bones, and spinal cord. Operators can simultaneously visualize three orthogonal planes, scroll through volumes along any given orientation, and precisely locate abnormalities by use of stable anatomic reference points (Fig. 10.50). Sacrococcygeal teratomas (SCTs) are congenital germ cell tumors, usually benign but often large, arising posteriorly at the medial spinal base. Posterior bony elements of the lumbosacral spine are typically intact. Often SCT is associated with polyhydramnios and prematurity, and more rarely with anemia, high-output cardiac failure, and hydrops. Maternal serum alpha fetoprotein is usually elevated. Generally, SCTs are not related to aneuploidy, although rare cases of chromosomal abnormalities have been reported. The typical teratoma is a complex cystic and solid mass protruding from the fetal rump, with arterial and venous flow seen by color Doppler. Uncommonly,
paragraphs.heading: Spine

paragraphs.text: it may be entirely cystic or solid, extend into the fetal pelvis (Fig. 10.51) and abdomen, or undergo malignant degeneration. Some SCTs have unique characteristics, including those found in Currarino syndrome (presacral SCT, sacral malformation, and anorectal anomalies, with or without associated Hirschsprung disease and cloacal anomalies). Prenatal diagnosis is extremely important in planning the timing and route of delivery, given tumor size and potential for hemorrhage, and in anticipation of postnatal surgery. Critically ill fetuses distant from term may benefit from referral to a fetal surgery center for early delivery for signs of fetal heart failure. Emergency delivery may be precipitated by tumor hemorrhage, mass effects, or by obstetric mirror syndrome, a rare maternal complication simulating severe preeclampsia. The prognosis for uncomplicated SCT is generally excellent, although anterior extension and high levels of circulating alpha-fetoprotein and other markers, particularly in immature teratomas, convey elevated risks for recurrence or malignancy.65,66
paragraphs.heading: Spine

paragraphs.text: After 14 weeks, visualization of the nose, nares, orbits, forehead, lips, eyes, and ears is feasible. Orbits are clearly seen axially; the ocular diameters and interocular and binocular distances (defining hypertelorism and hypotelorism) are measurable. The profile reveals the forehead, nose, and jaw sagittally (contrast Fig. 10.1 with Fig. 10.52). The coronal view, best for facial structures, includes the orbits (and lenses), eyelids, nose, and lips. Coronal and 3D views identify facial clefting, including cleft lip and palate; clefts may be central or lateral, unilateral or bilateral, involving nasal structures or, more subtly, the soft palate. Sagittal views should include the nasal bones; nasal bone hypoplasia or absence is associated with an increased risk for Down syndrome. The complex anatomy of the fetal face is shown exquisitely by 3D sonography. The distinction between
paragraphs.heading: Head and Neck

paragraphs.text: normal and abnormal facial features can be seen clearly by comparing Figure 10.8 with Figure 10.53.
paragraphs.heading: Head and Neck

paragraphs.text: Cystic hygroma is a septate, cystic mass arising from the neck and occipital region secondary to lymphatic malformation; it may extend over the entire trunk (Fig. 10.54A). Posterior septation of the nuchal ligament and bony integrity distinguish this lesion from neural tube defects. Associated aneuploidies, particularly monosomy X (45,X), are common. When associated with generalized edema, cystic hygromas carry a grim prognosis; when small, isolated, and with normal karyotype, more favorable outcomes, including regression, are well documented. Less common neck lesions include teratomas, hemangiomas, branchial cleft cysts, and, anteriorly, thyroid goiters and thymic absence.
paragraphs.heading: Head and Neck

paragraphs.text: Increased nuchal translucency (Fig. 10.11) and nuchal fold thickness (Fig. 10.16) are associated with aneuploidies, including trisomies 21 and 18, cardiac malformations, diaphragmatic herniation, skeletal dysplasias, a wide range of other anomalies and genetically inherited disorders (Noonan syndrome), lymphatic obstruction sequence, and
paragraphs.heading: Head and Neck

paragraphs.text: fetal loss. With normal karyotypes and reassuring midtrimester surveys with resolved edema and normal anatomical examination, outcomes are generally good.67
paragraphs.heading: Head and Neck

paragraphs.text: Optimal timing of the fetal heart study is a compromise between finding defects as soon as possible and accurately assessing complex anatomy, recognizing that some lesions manifest late in pregnancy. Basic heart evaluation is now an integral part of anatomic surveys at 18 to 22 weeks’ gestation. Initial appreciation of first-trimester cardiac anatomy is feasible by either a transvaginal or a transabdominal approach, augmented by color Doppler; however, the best timing for early imaging of the four chambers and great arteries is usually at 13 to 14 weeks. In experienced hands, first-trimester fetal echocardiography is quite sensitive for the detection of major structural cardiac abnormalities. Some features useful in combination with nuchal measurements for aneuploidy screening include abnormal flow patterns in the DV and tricuspid valve; these are also early markers for cardiac abnormalities and should prompt more detailed assessment. A focused cardiac examination should be performed for known medical or historical risks, with teratogen exposures, and when any significant extra-cardiac anomaly or chromosomal defect has been identified. Cardiac defects should also be excluded in the presence of an aberrant right subclavian artery or other vascular anomalies.67
paragraphs.heading: Heart

paragraphs.text: Screening for fetal cardiac abnormalities was introduced more than 35 years ago, yet prenatal detection remains challenging. Most major congenital heart defects are amenable to prenatal identification, with tertiary centers reporting high diagnostic accuracy; however, overall detection rates remain low and highly operator dependent. Pregnancies with predisposing factors are usually referred for echocardiogram, but most cases of congenital heart disease occur
paragraphs.heading: Heart

paragraphs.text: in low-risk pregnancies. Prenatal diagnosis, particularly for babies at risk for acute cardiovascular collapse (for example, with ductal-dependent or restrictive lesions), could reduce both morbidity and mortality.46
paragraphs.heading: Heart

paragraphs.text: Basic cardiac studies attempt to obtain symmetric, appropriately oriented four-chamber views of the fetal heart (Fig. 10.35), showing pulmonary veins, atrioventricular valves, intra-atrial and intraventricular septa, as well as aortic and ductal arches and normal outflow views that link the aorta and neck vessels with the left ventricle and the bifurcating pulmonary artery with the right. The echocardiographic three-vessel view (Fig. 10.54B) allows assessment of the superior vena cava, ascending aorta, and main pulmonary artery. These views aid in identification of transposition of the great arteries, tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus, and some aortic abnormalities. Fetal arrhythmias may also be analyzed (Fig. 10.55). Sensitivity for complex cardiac lesions exceeds that for isolated septal defects; accurate diagnosis remains dependent on experience and the absence of obstacles posed by poor resolution or unfavorable fetal position.
paragraphs.heading: Heart

paragraphs.text: Physiologic migration of the gut into the proximal umbilical cord occurs between gestational weeks 7 and 10 and may be seen on first-trimester scans (Fig. 10.56) up to 12 weeks. The normal liver always remains intra-abdominal; bowel migration should not be mistaken for a ventral abdominal wall defect. The fetal stomach, seen transvaginally by 9 to 10 weeks of gestation, is an echo-free structure in the upper left abdomen, varying in size as it empties and fills.
paragraphs.heading: Gastrointestinal Tract Normal Bowel Appearance

paragraphs.text: Fetal small bowel is not differentiated in appearance early in gestation but appears as central abdominal fluid-filled loops by the late second trimester (Fig. 10.57). Fetal colon is clearly evident by the third trimester as a hypoechoic, haustrated tube at the abdominal periphery. Meconium in
paragraphs.heading: Gastrointestinal Tract Normal Bowel Appearance

paragraphs.text: the large bowel is normal in the third trimester; second-trimester meconium normally may have transiently increased echogenicity. Hyperechogenic bowel, bright as adjacent osseous structures, is a concerning but nonspecific finding associated with trisomy 21, cystic fibrosis, bowel atresia, congenital infections (e.g., cytomegalovirus), growth restriction, placental abruption, and poor outcome.68
paragraphs.heading: Gastrointestinal Tract Normal Bowel Appearance

paragraphs.text: Gastrointestinal tract obstruction can often be diagnosed by ultrasound. Blockage of the proximal alimentary canal interferes with normal amniotic fluid regulation by fetal swallowing and gut absorption. In complete proximal obstructions, assuming intact membranes and normal renal production, polyhydramnios is noted in the majority, although this may develop in late gestation.
paragraphs.heading: Gastrointestinal Tract Normal Bowel Appearance

paragraphs.text: A nonvisualized fetal stomach combined with polyhydramnios should alert the examiner to the possibility of esophageal atresia. Unfortunately, these signs coincide in only 40% of cases. Nonvisualization of the stomach is not specific for esophageal atresia; proximal esophageal pouches are rarely
paragraphs.heading: Esophageal Atresia and Tracheoesophageal Fistula

paragraphs.text: visualized. Polyhydramnios, although present in two-thirds of cases, may not develop until the third trimester. The VACTERL complex consists of three or more components of vertebral, anal, cardiovascular, tracheal, esophageal, renal, and limb malformations; these systems should be scrutinized if tracheoesophageal fistula is suspected. The stomach may also fail to fill when there is little fluid to swallow (e.g., as in oligohydramnios, or secondary to neuromuscular conditions such as Pena-Shokeir syndrome that interfere with swallowing).
paragraphs.heading: Esophageal Atresia and Tracheoesophageal Fistula

paragraphs.text: In duodenal atresia, the distended stomach and proximal duodenum produce a “double-bubble” sign akin to the neonatal radiologic finding (Fig. 10.14). A strong (25%) association with trisomy 21 warrants genetic testing when duodenal atresia is suspected. Other etiologies include annular pancreas, duodenal web, malrotation, and severe duodenal stenosis. Ileal and jejunal atresias usually cause multiple distended bowel loops, often exhibiting exaggerated peristalsis (Fig. 10.58). More distal obstruction, as seen in meconium ileus, Hirschsprung disease, and anal
paragraphs.heading: Small Bowel Obstruction

paragraphs.text: atresia, may not result in visible bowel dilation until the third trimester or postpartum. Meconium peritonitis, a sterile but morbid chemical response to intrauterine bowel perforation, is characterized by echogenic peritoneal calcifications and free intraperitoneal fluid (Fig. 10.59); some cases progress to echogenic pseudocysts. An Australian study noted the increased prevalence of aneuploidy, cytomegalovirus, cystic fibrosis, and FGR in pregnancies complicated by the midtrimester sonographic finding of fetal echogenic bowel. However, reassuringly, 67% of cases with ultrasound-detected echogenic bowel in the second trimester had a normal short-term neonatal outcome.68
paragraphs.heading: Small Bowel Obstruction

paragraphs.text: A midline ventral abdominal wall defect involving the base of the umbilical cord is characteristic of omphalocele (Fig. 10.60). A sac of amnion and peritoneum surrounds the herniated viscera and may include the liver and bowel (Figs. 10.61 and 10.62). Omphaloceles are often associated with other anomalies (Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, pentalogy of Cantrell) and aneuploidies (trisomies 13 and 18). In contrast, in cases with gastroschisis, herniated bowel loops float freely in the amniotic cavity without a covering membrane (Fig. 10.63). Defects are usually to the right of the umbilical insertion; aneuploidy, extraintestinal abnormalities, familial forms, and recurrence are not customary with gastroschisis. Gastroschisis is thought to be caused by a vascular accident with wall infarction; young maternal age, and the use of vasoactive substances or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) have been related to increased risk for this lesion.
paragraphs.heading: Anterior Abdominal Wall Defects

paragraphs.text: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (Fig. 10.64) is a defect in the formation of the diaphragm. Most cases are left sided
paragraphs.heading: Diaphragmatic Hernia and Thoracic Lesions

paragraphs.text: and are diagnosed when abdominal organs (usually stomach and bowel) are seen in the thorax. Fluid-filled intrathoracic bowel loops with visible peristalsis and stomach seen at the level of the four-chamber view help confirm the diagnosis. The liver is in the thorax in almost all cases with right-sided herniation. Associated congenital heart disease, other structural defects, prematurity, and chromosomal abnormalities worsen a guarded prognosis. Hernia contents produce a mass effect, shifting the mediastinum and compressing the lungs (Fig. 10.65); the resulting pulmonary hypoplasia and
paragraphs.heading: Diaphragmatic Hernia and Thoracic Lesions

paragraphs.text: secondary pulmonary hypertension are major determinants of mortality. Polyhydramnios and lagging abdominal circumference (AC) are common associations. Estimation of survival with ultrasound is based on contralateral lung measurements at the level of the four-chamber heart normalized for gestational age (expressed as observed to expected lung area/HC). Calculated 3D lung volumes by ultrasound study and MRI provide more precise measurements of the lungs but with only minor impact on prognostic accuracy. Liver herniation into the chest (Fig. 10.66) indicates a worse
paragraphs.heading: ACI

paragraphs.text: prognosis in left-sided hernias. Right-sided hernias are more difficult to recognize and may also increase mortality. Bilateral herniation is generally lethal with few documented exceptions.
paragraphs.heading: ACI

paragraphs.text: Congenital pulmonary adenomatoid malformations (CPAMs) (Fig. 10.67) may have cysts with an appearance similar to that of the bowel but lack peristalsis and displacement of identified abdominal organs. Microcystic forms are echogenic and resemble sequestrations; the latter usually have systemic arterial feeding vessels (Fig. 10.68), although blended forms have been described. Growth is variable, with spontaneous regression during pregnancy commonly reported. “Vanishing” lesions, not identified by postnatal x-rays, are always present on chest CT. Fetal hydrops may develop,69 and fetal surgery may be indicated to avert this
paragraphs.heading: ACI

paragraphs.text: potentially fatal complication. The cystic adenomatoid malformation volume ratio (CPAM volume/HC) is a marker used for prediction of hydrops and the need for shunting in macrocystic CPAM, in addition to identifying the need for fetal intervention in early gestation in severe cases. In predominantly microcystic lesions, maternal betamethasone therapy has been reported to lower risks for polyhydramnios and fetal hydrops.69
paragraphs.heading: ACI

paragraphs.text: A choledochal cyst is a localized circular dilation of the biliary system, often involving the common bile duct and located in the upper right abdominal quadrant, separate from the gallbladder. Echogenic gallstones and sludge are noted in the gallbladder lumen on third-trimester scans (Fig. 10.69) in one out of every 200 fetuses. The prognosis of fetal gallstones and biliary sludge is favorable. Followup studies in neonates generally confirm resolution when separated from the maternal hormonal milieu; infants are usually asymptomatic. The fetal gallbladder can often be seen after 14 weeks’ gestation. Persistent nonvisualization is associated with a variety of abnormal conditions, most notably biliary atresia and cystic fibrosis.70
paragraphs.heading: Gallbladder and Bile Ducts

paragraphs.text: The kidneys, readily visible by 12 to 14 weeks’ gestation, are located lateral to the fetal spine (Fig. 10.70) below the
paragraphs.heading: Genitourinary Tract

paragraphs.text: diaphragm and prominent fetal adrenal glands. Normal renal size and volume can be plotted against gestational age. By the late third trimester, fat deposition creates an echogenic border, enhancing visualization. The bladder may be seen by 11 weeks of gestation, flanked by paired umbilical arteries (Fig. 10.71). Normal fetal ureters are not visible by ultrasound. Fetal adrenal glands are usually identifiable because of a relatively large cortex and unique, contrasting echo textures.
paragraphs.heading: B

paragraphs.text: Lethal renal malfunctions, including bilateral multicystic dysplasia, bilateral agenesis, and some cases of congenital autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease result in failure of fetal urine production. After 16 weeks, amniotic fluid is almost entirely fetal urine, but oligohydramnios may not become apparent until 18 to 20 weeks of gestation. Infants born after prolonged oligohydramnios have a characteristic facial appearance, limb deformities, and pulmonary hypoplasia, termed Potter syndrome (or sequence). The finding of oligohydramnios should direct attention to the fetal urinary tract with rescanning at 30-minute intervals for confirmation if the fetal bladder is not initially visualized. Anhydramnios (no measurable fluid), a persistently empty bladder, and an inability to identify fetal kidneys or renal arteries are strongly suggestive of bilateral renal agenesis. Unfortunately, absence of amniotic fluid may impede making a secure diagnosis with its associated implications for management, particularly because fetal adrenal glands, losing their normal angulation in renal agenesis, may be mistaken for kidneys. Fetal MRI can be ideal in establishing this lethal diagnosis. Care must be exercised when suspecting unilateral renal agenesis to exclude renal ectopy (pelvic kidney); color Doppler may reveal the aberrant course of the renal artery (Fig. 10.4).
paragraphs.heading: B

paragraphs.text: Pyelectasis (dilation of the renal pelvis) occurs in up to 5% of pregnancies and is a variant that should not be misinterpreted as hydronephrosis. Pyelectasis is considered a minor marker for trisomy 21 but when isolated is not usually an indication for amniocentesis; transient urinary reflux is a common underlying cause.71 Measurements of
paragraphs.heading: B

paragraphs.text: anteroposterior views of the kidneys and renal pelves in the transverse plane are used to identify both pyelectasis and hydronephrosis. Upper limits of 4 mm and 7 mm in the second and third trimesters, respectively, define pyelectasis, with normalization routinely anticipated by the third trimester. Pelvic dilation above 1 cm is suspicious for hydronephrosis, particularly with calyceal involvement. Vague correlation exists between the magnitude of fetal renal pyelectasis and renal abnormalities. Persistent pyelectasis should be confirmed neonatally and followed until either resolved or an etiology is established.71
paragraphs.heading: B

paragraphs.text: Urinary tract obstruction may have a variable sonographic appearance, depending mainly on timing of onset. Renal dysplasia, sometimes with cyst formation, is the consequence of early obstruction; obstruction occurring later in gestation is more likely to result in dilation of the collecting system (Fig. 10.72). Hydronephrosis may be unilateral, resulting from obstruction of the ureteropelvic or ureterocystic junctions, or bilateral, secondary to lower tract obstruction by posterior urethral valves or urethral agenesis. A distended, thick-walled bladder may be seen in males with a posterior urethral valve along with hydroureters; urinary ascites may occur as a result of calyceal or bladder rupture with intraperitoneal accumulation of urine. “Keyhole” dilation of the posterior urethra helps in distinguishing this lesion from Eagle-Barrett (prune belly) syndrome (Fig. 10.73).
paragraphs.heading: B

paragraphs.text: Multicystic dysplastic kidney disease (MCDKD) is commonly an incidental unilateral finding on prenatal examination. Bilaterality is less frequent but lethal. In unilateral cases, abnormalities of the contralateral kidney
paragraphs.heading: B

paragraphs.text: are common.72 Associated nonrenal abnormalities occur frequently with both unilateral and bilateral MCDKD, increasing risks for chromosomal abnormality. Males predominate in unilateral MCDKD (ratio of 2.4:1), but females are four times more likely to have chromosomal abnormalities and twice as likely to have nonrenal anomalies or lethal bilateral disease.72 The option of chromosomal analysis should be discussed whenever there are extrarenal abnormalities or bilaterality. Unilateral isolated MCDKD with normal amniotic fluid is not associated with abnormal genetic studies and usually has a favorable outcome; however, a neonatal work-up to exclude reflux in the unaffected kidney should be performed.72
paragraphs.heading: B

paragraphs.text: Severe hydronephrosis, in contrast to MCDKD, is an orderly arrangement of the enlarged renal pelvis with connecting, dilated calyces. Bilateral renal anomalies including bilateral secondary multicystic renal dysplasia are common (4%) in the fetus (Fig. 10.74). Dilated ureters occur in ureterovesical junction obstruction, in primary megaureter, or secondary to reflux. Infantile autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease causes bilaterally enlarged, echogenic reniform kidneys (Fig. 10.75). Other renal and urogenital anomalies identified prenatally include cysts, masses, duplicated collecting systems, and bladder exstrophy; in the last, a nonvisualized bladder coincides with normal amniotic fluid and renal appearance, as well as a short or bifid male phallus.
paragraphs.heading: B
