title: Adverse Exposures to the Fetus

paragraphs.text: 13 Adverse Exposures to the Fetus
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Exposure to environmental toxicants during pregnancy may have a significant impact on the developing fetus. Fetal adverse exposures are growing in importance as our population expands and the number of women participating in the workforce continues to rise. In 2020, women comprised 48% of the workforce in the United States, and 63.4 million women 16 years of age and over were employed. Approximately 78% worked full time.1 In addition, more pregnant women are staying in the workforce and continuing to work until later into pregnancy. According to the US Census Bureau, 66.4% of women worked during their first pregnancy from 2016 to 2019, and 88% continued into the third trimester.2
paragraphs.heading: MARGARET KUPER-SASSÉ, DINA E. EL-METWALLY, AND CYNTHIA F. BEARER

paragraphs.text: Environmental exposures increase as the world’s population and economic needs expand. In 1900, there were 1.25 billion people on Earth. This number doubled by 1950 and doubled again in 1987 to 5 billion. The world population was estimated at 7.7 billion in 2019; it is projected to increase to 9.7 billion by 2050, and 11 billion by 2100.3 Pressures of population growth are reflected in increasing need for land, water, food, and fuel. With population expansion, economic growth, and technologic advances comes increasing interaction with chemicals in our environment that are developed to support our society. The growth of industry, commerce, and agriculture brings overuse of land, changes to the environment such as global warming, and contamination of air, water, food, and soil. It is inevitable that all humans are exposed to environmental toxicants, including the developing fetus.
paragraphs.heading: MARGARET KUPER-SASSÉ, DINA E. EL-METWALLY, AND CYNTHIA F. BEARER

paragraphs.text: The Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD) is a field of study that explores the relationship between exposure to environmental stressors during critical periods of fetal development and adverse health outcomes that occur across a lifetime (see also Chapter 15). This paradigm suggests that the developing fetus exhibits significant genetic plasticity that may be impacted by the intrauterine environment. Thus genetic “reprogramming” that occurs prenatally can alter phenotypic expression, both following birth and in generations to come. The DOHaD is based on work originally published in 1990 by the British
paragraphs.heading: MARGARET KUPER-SASSÉ, DINA E. EL-METWALLY, AND CYNTHIA F. BEARER

paragraphs.text: epidemiologist David Barker. The Barker hypothesis (or fetal origins hypothesis) describes fetal nutritional and metabolic programming as the mechanism linking intrauterine growth restriction to the development of coronary artery disease as an adult. Fetal exposure to toxicants is a stressor that has also been implicated in the DOHaD and is the subject of this chapter.4 Toxic environmental exposures may be nonconcurrent or concurrent with pregnancy. This chapter describes the role of epigenetics and developmental plasticity, pathways of fetal exposure to environmental toxicants, unique pharmacokinetics of the fetus, and the spectrum of adverse outcomes associated with fetal exposure to specific environmental toxicants (Fig. 13.1).
paragraphs.heading: MARGARET KUPER-SASSÉ, DINA E. EL-METWALLY, AND CYNTHIA F. BEARER

paragraphs.text: Environmental exposures that affect the fetus may occur long before conception and possibly in an earlier generation than the parents. Commonly, the exposure impacts the ovum or sperm. In addition, there are chemicals that bioaccumulate prior to pregnancy and impact the fetus by enhanced elimination during pregnancy. Lipid-soluble toxins and heavy metals such as lead are stored in adipose tissue and bone and mobilized during pregnancy. Some chemicals, such as organohalogens, can affect the fetus by both nonconcurrent and concurrent exposure.5
paragraphs.heading: Exposures Not Concurrent With Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: Epigenetics is the study of phenotypic changes occurring in the absence of modification of DNA sequence. Environmental epigenetics describes the relationship between endogenous and exogenous factors (such as chemical exposure) and the epigenome. Changes to the epigenome are stable, heritable, and a target for environmental toxicants. The term epimutation refers to a heritable change in gene expression that does not affect DNA base-pair structure.4
paragraphs.heading: Preconceptual Effects The Epigenome

paragraphs.text: The epigenome is susceptible to dysregulation at any time but is highly vulnerable during fetal life when the rate of DNA synthesis is high. Epigenetic mechanisms include
paragraphs.heading: Preconceptual Effects The Epigenome

paragraphs.text: alterations in expression patterns of microRNAs, modifications of histone proteins, and DNA methylation.6 Micro RNAs are small segments of noncoding RNA that regulate post-transcriptional expression of mRNA.4,6 Histones are a group of eight nuclear proteins that package and tightly compact DNA chromatin into smaller, coiled segments referred to as nucleosomes, which contain 146 base pairs. Histone modifications such as acetylation and phosphorylation alter the histone protein at the N-terminal tail, changing nucleosome structure and activating or repressing transcription.6 DNA methylation is a well-described epigenetic modification involving the addition of a methyl group to the nucleotide cytosine when it precedes guanine, frequently at the promoter region. Methylated segments of DNA are more tightly coiled, hiding the promoter region and limiting gene expression. In less methylated areas, the promoter is open, allowing for DNA transcription. Although DNA methylation is not entirely static across a lifetime, much of the epigenome is established during fetal development.4,6
paragraphs.heading: Preconceptual Effects The Epigenome

paragraphs.text: One of the best-described epigenetic processes is genomic imprinting. Genomic imprinting occurs during early development and involves silencing of one parental allele leading to monoallelic gene expression. Dysregulation of genomic imprinting, potentially due to aberrant methylation of DNA, leads to disorders such as Angelman syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome, and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and has been linked to autism and cancer later in life. Imprinted genes are ideal models to study epigenetic modifications. As imprinting occurs early in fetal development, epigenetic adaptations are likely to have a significant effect. For example, adults who were conceived during the Dutch famine of World War II (1944–1945) demonstrate widespread and persistent changes in DNA methylation of imprinted insulin-like growth factor-2 (IGF-2) loci, with diverse biologic functions. These genes are known to be important modulators of growth, and epigenetic modifications are implicated in the development of metabolic and
paragraphs.heading: Preconceptual Effects The Epigenome

paragraphs.text: cardiovascular disease in adults. Offspring conceived during the famine have developed these metabolic and cardiovascular conditions more frequently as adults.6,9
paragraphs.heading: Preconceptual Effects The Epigenome

paragraphs.text: Prenatal exposure to maternal smoking has been shown to affect DNA methylation in the fetus that persists to adolescence and adulthood. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are neurotoxic and carcinogenic chemicals found in fumes from vehicle exhaust, coal, charbroiled foods, and cigarette smoke. They are lipophilic and cross the placenta and fetal blood-brain barrier. Byproducts of PAH metabolism have the capacity to bind DNA, forming PAH-DNA adducts. The fetus is highly susceptible to formation of PAH-DNA adducts and associated genetic mutations, a known cancer risk.7 A meta-analysis of prospective cohorts studies of offspring of smoking mothers found 69 separate sites in 36 genomic regions that express variable methylation, consistent with previously described newborn methylation studies.10
paragraphs.heading: Preconceptual Effects The Epigenome

paragraphs.text: In early fetal life, oogonia are formed by meiotic division. Before birth, oogonia develop into primary oocytes and complete the prophase stage of the first meiotic division.11 Oocytes remain in this state until puberty. As cells are highly susceptible to environmental toxicants while in active phases of division, fetal life represents a critical period of vulnerability. This hypothesis is supported by the increasing incidence of nondisjunction events with advancing maternal age and prolonged environmental exposures. Exposures impacting regulatory and endocrine functions of the ovum can influence ovarian competence throughout life. Fig. 13.3 shows critical windows of exposures that may impact the male and female reproductive system.11
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Exposures

paragraphs.text: Active smoking during pregnancy is associated with decreased fertility in female fetuses later in life, likely related to loss of number of ova.12,13 Endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) are compounds that act as agonists or antagonists to the endocrine system. As of 2020, there are 1482 of these human-made compounds and they are hypothesized to have made a major contribution to the falling human fertility rates in the last 50 years. Bisphenol A (BPA) is an EDC found in plastic products. An inverse relationship has
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Exposures

paragraphs.text: been found between the number of eggs recovered during in vitro fertilization and urinary BPA levels.14
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Exposures

paragraphs.text: Developmental exposure to environmental toxicants can have an impact on fertility that may be transmitted to future generations. Inheritance of epigenetic information between generations that leads to phenotypic variation in the absence of direct environmental influence is termed epigenetic transgenerational inheritance. Epigenetic transgenerational inheritance requires epimutations to be present in the germline, as only sperm and eggs pass this information to the next generation.7 Epigenetic transgenerational inheritance has been proposed as a mechanism for phenotypic aberrations that have occurred following fetal exposure to the EDC diethylstilbestrol (DES). DES is an estrogenic drug that was prescribed to 5 to 10 million women worldwide from the 1940s to the 1970s to prevent miscarriage. Although vaginal clear cell adenocarcinoma has occurred infrequently in daughters of women exposed to DES, infertility and poor pregnancy outcomes are extremely prevalent. The female grandchildren of the women who were exposed in utero to DES (or the “DES-exposed third generation”) have a statistically higher risk of reproductive abnormalities including irregular menses, amenorrhea, and preterm delivery, indicating that DES altered the gametes of the fetuses who were exposed.15
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Exposures

paragraphs.text: Similar to women, men also have experienced a decrease in fertility over the last 50 years that is associated with both lower sperm counts and lower quality of sperm. Environmental toxicants that impact spermatogenesis have been identified. Spermatogonia are highly sensitive to apoptosis after exposure to cytotoxic agents. Toxicants may also impact male fertility by limiting sperm production. Unlike the female, cell divisions in the male that produce mature spermatozoa occur after puberty, and mature spermatozoa are incapable of DNA repair, making them susceptible to mutagen exposures that occur throughout life.16
paragraphs.heading: Paternal Exposures

paragraphs.text: A gradual decline in sperm concentration has been reported in reproductive-age males, and human male infertility is currently approaching 10%. Increased exposure to environmental toxicants has been postulated as a contributing factor. For many of these exposures, findings have been reproduced for several generations, and epigenetic transgenerational inheritance is a proposed mechanism.16 In the rat model, exposure of the pregnant female to two EDCs (vinclozolin, a fungicide used in the wine industry, and the pesticide methoxychlor) led to impaired spermatogenesis and infertility in males in four subsequent generations. Phthalates are plasticizers and known EDCs that are now ubiquitous in our environment. Bis(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) is found in polyvinyl compounds, and dibutyl phthalate (DBP) is used primarily to add flexibility to plastics. Both compounds can adversely affect male reproductive function. In animal studies, prenatal exposure has been linked to spermatogenic cell apoptosis, seminiferous tubule atrophy, and testicular dysfunction. Phenotypic alterations following exposure prenatally include cryptorchidism,
paragraphs.heading: Paternal Exposures

paragraphs.text: hypospadias, ambiguous genitalia, reduced sperm production, and decreased anogenital distance.17
paragraphs.heading: Paternal Exposures

paragraphs.text: The relationship between paternal occupation and cancer in offspring has been extensively studied. Studies in cohorts in different countries around the world have suggested an increased risk of childhood leukemias and solid tumors related to paternal exposure to toxicants. The international Childhood Cancer Cohort Consortium analyzed pooled data from five birth cohorts and included over 320,000 pregnancies. An increased risk of acute myeloid leukemia was found after paternal occupational exposure to pesticides (hazard ratio [HR] = 2.62; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.91–7.55), fungicides (HR = 2.59; 95% CI, 0.78–8.56), animals (HR = 3.89; 95% CI, 1.18–12.90), and organic dust (HR = 2.12; 95% CI, 0.88–5.12), but there was not an increased risk of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) or solid tumors.18
paragraphs.heading: Paternal Exposures

paragraphs.text: Maternal exposures have long been recognized as having the potential to cause birth defects. The National Birth Defects Prevention Study collected data related to infants born between 1997 and 2004, including infants with birth defects and normal controls. Increased prevalence of birth defects in offspring of fathers employed as janitors, painters, printers, agricultural workers, groundskeepers, welders, electrical industry workers, and firefighters have been reported, suggesting an association with occupational exposures and birth defects.19
paragraphs.heading: Paternal Exposures

paragraphs.text: Male fertility diminishes and sperm DNA mutations increase with advancing paternal age. Advanced paternal age is associated with pregnancy loss, birth defects, and autosomal dominant genetic disorders such as Marfan syndrome and achondroplasia. Congenital malformations seen more frequently in fetuses of older fathers include cleft lip and palate, hydrocephalus, neural tube defects, limb reduction defects, tracheoesophageal fistula, congenital cataracts,
paragraphs.heading: Paternal Exposures

paragraphs.text: and congenital heart disease (CHD).20 In Prader-Willi syndrome, there is a functional mutation in paternal 15q, resulting in inactivation of the genes in that region of the chromosome. Environmental factors may play a role in uniparental disomy and lead to paternally mediated effects on the fetus. Studies have shown association between paternal exposure to hydrocarbons and Prader-Willi syndrome. Seasonal increases in the incidence of Prader-Willi syndrome also have been observed. This likely is due to seasonal changes in occupational exposures (e.g., farming, painting, landscaping), as significant association with seasonal viruses has not been established.21
paragraphs.heading: Paternal Exposures

paragraphs.text: The developing fetus may be exposed to xenobiotics (chemicals not naturally produced by the organism) after increased mobilization from maternal storage compartments during pregnancy. Adipose tissue is a storage site for hydrophobic chemicals, and both lead and fluoride are stored in bone.
paragraphs.heading: Secondary Fetal Exposure: Maternal Body Burden

paragraphs.text: Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) are EDCs that are mobilized from adipose tissue during pregnancy and readily cross the placenta. They are lipophilic organochlorine chemicals that bioaccumulate in the environment, enter the food chain, and are stored in adipose tissue.22 Exposure occurs primarily through ingestion of dairy, animal fat, and fish. PCBs were used as liquid insulators for transformers and capacitors in the 1970s. Because PCBs remain stable in the environment and are resistant to biologic breakdown, they are classified as persistent organic pollutants (POPs).22 Although the use of PCBs has been banned or limited in many countries, exposure remains a public health concern. The presence of PCBs has been documented in blood samples from pregnant women and in breast milk.22
paragraphs.heading: Polychlorinated Biphenyls

paragraphs.text: Prenatal exposure to PCBs has been correlated with neurodevelopmental impairment and autism.22 Maternal occupational exposure is linked to low birth weight and prematurity.23 Human poisonings have occurred through dietary consumption of PCBs. In 1979, an epidemic of PCB poisoning from contaminated rice oil occurred in Taiwan, termed yu-cheng disease. Adults who were exposed developed hyperpigmentation, acne, and peripheral neuropathy. Of the first 39 hyperpigmented children born to poisoned women, 8 died. Children born up to 6 years after the outbreak of yu-cheng disease had ectodermal defects and developmental delay. Children born 6 years after maternal exposure were as developmentally impaired as those born within 1 year of the epidemic, indicating significant maternal body burden.24 Cognitive defects seen in Taiwanese children with yu-cheng disease are comparable to those observed in American children prenatally exposed to PCBs. Studies in Michigan and North Carolina showed neurodevelopmental impairment in children prenatally exposed to
paragraphs.heading: Polychlorinated Biphenyls

paragraphs.text: PCBs through maternal body burden. In Michigan, cognitive deficits were seen in children who had elevated cord blood levels of PCBs and whose mothers had regularly consumed contaminated sport fish.23
paragraphs.heading: Polychlorinated Biphenyls

paragraphs.text: The major repository for lead is bone, and chronic exposure results in significant accumulation of lead in the skeleton. Lead stores are mobilized from bone during pregnancy, potentially exposing the fetus during critical stages of brain development. It is postulated that enhanced calcium turnover during pregnancy increases lead mobilization. Maternal tibial and patellar bone lead levels are correlated with low birth weight and decreased head circumference. One study established maternal trabecular bone lead level as an independent risk factor for cognitive delay at 24 months of age. Lead is readily transported across the placenta and blood-brain barrier. Lead is a potent neurotoxin. Developmental exposure is linked to learning disability, cognitive and language deficits, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Treatment of pregnant women with calcium supplementation may limit lead mobilization from bone and could decrease circulating maternal lead levels and placental transfer to the fetus.25
paragraphs.heading: Lead

paragraphs.text: Biomarkers of fetal exposure have been developed using cord blood and meconium.26,27 In 2007, the Environmental Working Group measured cord blood levels of 413 chemicals from 10 US newborns. They found 287 toxicants, with an average of 200 chemicals in cord blood of each infant. Chemicals included pesticides, PCBs, and heavy metals such as mercury.26 Meconium analysis is a sensitive tool utilized to determine antenatal exposure to environmental toxicants. In a study of 426 infants born in the Philippines, the exposure rates were 26.5% for lead, 83.9% for mercury, and 53% for the organophosphate pesticide (OP) malathion.27
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Exposures Concurrent With Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: Specific congenital anomalies have been linked to maternal occupations. For example, cleft lip and palate occur more frequently in offspring of leather workers, hairdressers, housekeepers, and transport and communication workers. Limb anomalies have been reported in children of agricultural workers, and neural tube defects in children of cleaners and health care providers working with anesthesia and radiation.28 In a large population-based case control study that examined the relationship between various maternal occupations and 45 birth defects, jobs with the highest number of associated anomalies were janitors/cleaners, scientists, and electronic equipment operators. Teachers and
paragraphs.heading: Occupation and Paraoccupation

paragraphs.text: health care workers had the lowest risk of delivering a child with congenital anomalies.28
paragraphs.heading: Occupation and Paraoccupation

paragraphs.text: Paraoccupational exposures occur when others living in the home come in contact with an occupationally exposed individual, or occupational chemicals are brought into the home on clothing or other materials. Paraoccupational exposure to pesticides remains an occupational hazard today. An important route of exposure to neurotoxic OPs occurs in families of farm workers. A systematic review of 10 studies assessing prenatal exposure to OPs reported neurocognitive impairment involving working memory and attention in toddlers and children at school age.29
paragraphs.heading: Occupation and Paraoccupation

paragraphs.text: Although climate change has been widely accepted as the largest public health threat in the modern world, attention to its effects on the fetus and neonate has only recently increased. Climate change has caused increasing frequency and severity of heat waves, wildfires, and extreme weather events, causing flooding, drought, pollution, power outages, and physical displacement. The direct and indirect effects of these exposures are associated with adverse effects on fetal growth and birth weight, preterm birth, spontaneous abortion, and neonatal death. Fig. 13.4 illustrates the impacts of climate change on pregnancy outcomes.30
paragraphs.heading: Climate Change

paragraphs.text: Many chemicals found in outdoor air pollution are neurotoxic. Exposure is associated with disruption of the blood-brain barrier, chronic central nervous system (CNS) inflammation, microglia activation, and white matter injury.31 The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) established air-quality standards in 1971. Although some progress has been achieved, outdoor air pollution continues to carry significant health risks. Particulate matter, ground-level ozone, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide, and airborne lead are examples of outdoor air pollutants with known adverse health outcomes. These air pollutants are the focus of air quality standards, such as the EPA’s Clean Air Act. The Air Quality Index is an indicator of daily air quality calculated by the EPA for these six major air pollutants that are regulated by the Clean Air Act. Both carbon monoxide and airborne lead are typically meeting safety standards.32
paragraphs.heading: Air Pollution

paragraphs.text: Particulate matter pollution consists of fine inhalable particles comprised of many different chemicals found in outdoor air (PM2.5 and PM10, which are 2.5 μm and 10 μm in diameter, respectively). Particles less than 10 μm are readily inhaled into the lungs, interact with the immune system, and are absorbed systemically. Ground-level ozone (the primary component of smog) is formed in the atmosphere by photochemical reactions between sunlight, nitrogen
paragraphs.heading: Air Pollution

paragraphs.text: oxide species, and volatile organic compounds, which are photochemically reactive hydrocarbons. Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide are also components of smog. Emissions from industrial facilities, motor vehicle exhaust, gasoline vapors, and chemical solvents are common sources of these toxicants.32
paragraphs.heading: Air Pollution

paragraphs.text: Exposure to outdoor air pollution is difficult to avoid during pregnancy, especially in highly polluted areas. There is strong evidence relating exposure to air pollution to both increased infant mortality and respiratory morbidities such as asthma in early childhood. In addition, there is evidence from epidemiologic studies linking prenatal exposure to air pollution and prematurity, low birth weight, impaired lung and immune function, autism spectrum disorders, and neuromotor impairment in early childhood.31
paragraphs.heading: Air Pollution

paragraphs.text: The drinking water supply is obtained from a variety of sources that include groundwater and surface water from rivers, lakes, reservoirs, and aquifers. Environmental toxicants that contaminate drinking water are associated with adverse health outcomes. Common drinking water contaminants include the heavy metals lead and arsenic, inorganic compounds such as nitrates and nitrites found in fertilizers and livestock manure, pesticides such as atrazine and glyphosate, disinfection byproducts such as chloroform, and organic solvents such as trichloroethylene. Congenital anomalies, specifically cardiac defects, and low birth weight were found in studies evaluating trichloroethylene-contaminated drinking water. The EPA and the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) monitor the safety of drinking water; the EPA is responsible for drinking water standards for public water systems.33
paragraphs.heading: Drinking Water

paragraphs.text: Arsenic enters the water supply naturally and is also found in agricultural and industrial chemicals. Arsenic readily crosses the placenta; prenatal exposure is associated with fetal growth restriction and increased infant mortality in animal models. Population studies of health outcomes associated with arsenic exposure have been conducted primarily in countries such as Bangladesh, Taiwan, and Chile, where naturally occurring arsenic levels in groundwater are elevated. A systematic review and meta-analysis of these studies noted an association between prenatal arsenic exposure and spontaneous abortion, stillbirth, low birth weight, and neonatal mortality. Although the studies on dose-response were limited, the strongest correlation was between prenatal arsenic exposure and spontaneous abortion.34
paragraphs.heading: Drinking Water

paragraphs.text: Maternal diet during pregnancy appears to impact the fetal epigenome. The Dutch famine of 1944–1945 showed a correlation between maternal undernutrition/starvation and low birth weight, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic diseases in the offspring. Similarly, the study of seasonal diets in Gambia, an African country with alternating seasons of
paragraphs.heading: Diet

paragraphs.text: abundance and famine, has shown increased DNA methylation and increased risk of premature death and the development of noncommunicable diseases and cardiovascular disease in offspring who were conceived during the hungry season (time of undernutrition). Several studies have documented the relationship among maternal obesity, gestational diabetes mellitus, and altered epigenome methylation in the placenta and cord blood; findings may potentially correlate with the risk for metabolic conditions in offspring.4
paragraphs.heading: Diet

paragraphs.text: Many animal studies have produced results similar to those observed in humans and provide an avenue for study of the contributing epigenetic mechanisms. Studies in pigs and rats have shown a positive correlation between low protein maternal diet, epigenetic modifications, and increased insulin tolerance and metabolic syndrome in offspring. Studies of high-fat maternal diets in rodents and primates have shown similar results, as well as changes in the rat brain that correlate with depression-like behavior.4
paragraphs.heading: Diet

paragraphs.text: Similarly, vitamin B12 and folate deficiency during pregnancy has been proposed to impact the fetal methionine-homocysteine cycle via epigenetic alterations in DNA methylation. The methionine-homocysteine pathway is an important regulator of methylation and is dependent on vitamin B12 and folate as cofactors. Deficiency in vitamin B12 or folate leads to high levels of homocysteine, a well-established risk factor for adult cardiovascular disease. Pregnant sheep exposed to diets restricted in vitamin B12, folate, and methionine delivered offspring who developed increased body mass, impaired immune function, insulin resistance, and hypertension as adults.35
paragraphs.heading: Diet

paragraphs.text: Inorganic mercury (methylmercury) is an example of a xenobiotic that contaminates our food supply. Methylmercury is a lipid-soluble and potent neurotoxin found in fish and seafood. Methylmercury readily crosses both the placenta and blood-brain barrier.36 The EPA has set an oral reference dose of mercury at 0.1 μg/kg/day. Approximately 8% of women have body burdens exceeding this reference dose. The fetus is very susceptible to the neurotoxic effects of methylmercury. Prenatal exposure has been associated with microcephaly, seizures, and cognitive and sensory impairment.36
paragraphs.heading: Diet

paragraphs.text: Two routes of fetal exposure to environmental toxins are placenta-dependent pathways and placenta-independent pathways. Placenta-dependent pathways require chemicals to enter the mother’s bloodstream by inhalation, ingestion, or transdermal absorption and to cross the placenta in significant amounts. Placental transfer of many environmental chemicals has been studied using perfusion studies of the term placenta. After a term human birth, the placenta is used immediately; the substance of interest is perfused through the maternal side, transfer to the fetal side is measured, and the placenta is histologically examined to characterize the transfer of the chemical.37 Substances can
paragraphs.heading: Placenta-Dependent Pathways

paragraphs.text: cross the maternal-fetal interface of the placenta by simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion, transport-mediated diffusion, and endocytosis. Most xenobiotics cross the placenta by passive diffusion, making the concentration gradient between maternal and fetal circulation and placental blood flow the primary determinants of fetal exposure.37 Properties enabling chemicals to cross the placenta more readily are low molecular weight, protein binding, lipid solubility, ionization, and resemblance to nutrients with specific transport mechanisms. An example of a low-molecular-weight compound is carbon monoxide, a constituent of environmental tobacco smoke (ETS). Carbon monoxide has a very high affinity for hemoglobin and displaces oxygen. Accumulation of carboxyhemoglobin leads to hypoxia and impaired cellular metabolism.37 Examples of lipid-soluble chemicals that readily cross the placenta are PCBs, ethanol, and polycyclic hydrocarbons such as benzo[a]pyrene, a carcinogen in ETS. Lead is actively transported across the placenta via calcium-specific channels; calcium supplementation may reduce the transfer of lead to the fetus.37
paragraphs.heading: Placenta-Dependent Pathways

paragraphs.text: Ionizing radiation is a well-characterized teratogen that is most harmful to the fetus in the first trimester during organogenesis. Prenatal exposure is associated with infertility, microcephaly, and increased incidence of childhood cancer in offspring.38 Children of survivors of the atomic bombs in Hiroshima and Nagasaki exposed in utero at <18 weeks’ gestation developed microcephaly, with the lowest observable effect at a dose of 1 to 9 rad (Fig. 13.5).39 An excess of cancer among Japanese individuals exposed in utero has also been reported (Fig. 13.6).41 Not all forms of radiation are hazardous to the fetus. Ultraviolet light does not penetrate to the fetus and does not constitute a future cancer risk.38 The brain of a neonate undergoing cranial computed tomography (CT) with settings of 400 mA, 125 kV (peak), and a standard slice
paragraphs.heading: Placenta-Independent Pathways Radiation

paragraphs.text: thickness of 4 mm receives a dose of 10.5 rad. Therefore it has been recommended that CT be used sparingly for infants, particularly when other imaging techniques are available.40
paragraphs.heading: Placenta-Independent Pathways Radiation

paragraphs.text: Excessive heat exposure to the fetus can cause birth defects, especially cardiac defects, as well as increasing risk of miscarriage. Animal studies demonstrate that both maternal core temperature 2° C above baseline and duration of hyperthermia are important risk factors and have caused the obstetrical recommendation to avoid excessive heat and humidity and caution against vigorous exercise. Emerging evidence has shown that the increased temperature-regulating mechanisms associated with pregnancy likely are protective against heat injury to the fetus. Heat transfer to the fetus occurs through the placenta and maternal blood flow and thus relies on the mother’s ability to regulate her body temperature. This indicates that the risk to the fetus is likely less than previously thought with maternal environmental exposure or exercise and limited to increases in maternal core temperature, as with fever or heat exhaustion.42
paragraphs.heading: Heat

paragraphs.text: Sound exposure is an important form of sensory stimulation in the developing fetus. At 23 to 25 weeks, sound begins to produce physiologic changes in fetal state; by 25 to 29 weeks’ gestation, the auditory system is functional.43 At 27 weeks, the fetus primarily hears low-frequency sounds below 500 Hz; frequencies above 500 Hz are not perceived until closer to 29 weeks due to filtering by the maternal tissues and uterus.43,44 Both low- and high-frequency noise can be detrimental and produce physiologic changes in the fetus. Applying vibroacoustic stimulation directly to the maternal abdomen leads to increases in fetal heart rate and movement.44 Intense and sustained noise exposure during the prenatal period is associated with congenital anomalies, prematurity, and low birth weight.43 In addition, noiseinduced hearing loss may be evident after in utero exposure. The cochlear hair cells are sensitive to low-frequency sound. Animal studies have shown that intense low-frequency
paragraphs.heading: Noise

paragraphs.text: sound can damage the cochlear hair cells; effects are determined by gestational age and the intensity and duration of sound exposure.44 The Sound Study Group recommends that pregnant women should avoid extended exposure to low-frequency sound levels (<250 Hz) greater than 65 dB and that sources of sound applied directly to the mother’s abdomen (headphones) should be avoided because of no clear benefit and potential risks to fetal hearing.44
paragraphs.heading: Noise

paragraphs.text: Physiologic changes during pregnancy influence maternal absorption and distribution of toxicants to the fetus. Increases in maternal progesterone concentration prolong gastric emptying time and slow intestinal motility, impacting enterohepatic circulation and absorption of xenobiotics. This results in reduced peak maternal levels of xenobiotics but increased overall exposure.45 Distribution of xenobiotics in the maternal compartment is impacted by increases in fat stores, extracellular fluid volume, and plasma volume during pregnancy. In addition, amniotic fluid represents a third potential compartment for the distribution of water-soluble chemicals. This amniotic fluid compartment is characterized by low protein concentration and delayed elimination, resulting in a potential source for prolonged exposure to unbound chemicals that may be harmful to both mother and fetus. As the fetal kidney matures, higher concentrations of xenobiotics may be stored in this compartment.45
paragraphs.heading: Absorption and Distribution

paragraphs.text: During pregnancy, plasma volume increases by 50%. Dilutional hypoalbuminemia is a result of plasma volume expansion that surpasses albumin production. Dilutional hypoalbuminemia alters the ratio of protein-bound chemicals and the volume of distribution in maternal blood, facilitating both clearance of free fractions of xenobiotics in the liver and placental transport to the fetal compartment. The fraction that is protein bound is not active and cannot affect the mother nor be transported across the placenta, but the increasing unbound fraction is biologically active and requires elimination to protect the mother and fetus.46 Changes in maternal plasma volume also impact excretion of toxicants. Increased renal blood flow, glomerular filtration rate, and tubular transport result in maternal excretion of toxicants before reaching the fetus.45
paragraphs.heading: Absorption and Distribution

paragraphs.text: Distribution of xenobiotics in the fetal compartment is also influenced by acid-base status and protein binding. As fetal pH is more acidic than maternal pH, weak bases that are nonionized in the maternal compartment are readily transported across the placenta. In the fetal compartment, weak bases become ionized, resulting in higher concentration and “ion trapping.” Although maternal serum albumin gradually declines during pregnancy relative to plasma volume, fetal albumin concentration progressively increases. Thus unbound xenobiotics that easily cross the placenta become protein-bound in the fetus and accumulate in the fetal compartment.46
paragraphs.heading: Absorption and Distribution

paragraphs.text: Although maternal fat stores serve as a reservoir for lipophilic compounds, there is minimal fetal adipose tissue development until after 29 weeks’ gestation. Before that time, lipid-soluble toxicants accumulate in tissues containing adipose, such as the developing brain. An example is shown in Fig. 13.7. The pesticide dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) was administered orally to mice at ages corresponding to the human brain growth spurt. Radioactivity was measured in brain tissue after 24 hours and 7 days. At 24 hours, 20-day-old mice accumulated more DDT in their brains than at other ages. DDT persisted in the brain longest in the animals given DDT at 10 days. Mice treated at 10 days had more behavioral abnormalities than those treated on other days, suggesting that the persistence was more important than initial accumulation. These results reflect the complexities of chemical distribution in the developing fetus.47
paragraphs.heading: Absorption and Distribution

paragraphs.text: The maternal basal metabolic rate increases during pregnancy, facilitating hepatic metabolism of xenobiotics. The most widely described hepatic metabolizing enzyme systems are phase I (cytochrome P450 enzymatic oxidation, dehydrogenation, reduction, and hydrolysis) and phase II (enzymatic glucuronidation, sulfation, methylation, and glutathione conjugation) processes. Approximately 75% of chemicals are toxic in their original state, and the remaining 25% are metabolized to toxic intermediates in the liver. Certain phase I and phase II enzymatic processes have been shown to be activated as a direct response to pregnancyinduced circulating estrogen levels, impacting metabolism and excretion of xenobiotics. Maternal metabolism and clearance of xenobiotics may additionally be reduced by estrogen-induced cholestasis that occurs physiologically during pregnancy.45,46
paragraphs.heading: Metabolism

paragraphs.text: Prior to reaching the fetal compartment, some degree of first-pass metabolism by phase I and phase II processes occurs in the placenta. In the fetus, expression of metabolic enzymes in the liver matures with advancing gestational age. Metabolism can lead to detoxification and facilitate excretion or activation of a xenobiotic to a more potent toxin.45,46 The fetus may be protected if the active form of a toxin is its metabolite. An example is acetaminophen, a common drug used in suicide attempts during pregnancy. Acetaminophen is metabolized by phase I enzymes to hepatotoxic and nontoxic intermediates. Expression of the phase I enzymes is developmentally regulated. Because many of these enzymes are poorly expressed in fetal tissues, the fetus may be protected.48
paragraphs.heading: Metabolism

paragraphs.text: Polymorphisms in human drug-metabolizing enzymes have been described that impact the susceptibility of the fetus to environmental toxicants. For example, risk of fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) is impacted by genetic polymorphisms in the expression of the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH). If the high-activity variant of ADH is inherited, ethanol oxidation and elimination are enhanced, decreasing the teratogenic effects of alcohol on the developing fetus.49 A second example involves deactivation of organophosphate pesticides (OPs) by the antioxidant enzyme paraoxonase 1 (PON1). In the liver, certain organophosphates are converted to a biologically active toxic form by cytochrome P450 enzymes. PON1 is responsible for hydrolyzing this toxic intermediate to an inactive metabolite that can be excreted. Genetic polymorphisms in PON1 have been described that impact both expression and catalytic capability of PON1, thus providing enhanced protection or greater susceptibility to toxic effects of these pesticides. When four birth cohorts were pooled (n = 936), negative associations were found between organophosphate metabolites in maternal urine and the Bayley Mental Developmental Index at 24 months in carriers of a particular PON1 allele.50
paragraphs.heading: Metabolism

paragraphs.text: In utero exposure to cigarette smoke has been shown to cause decreased fertility in female and male fetuses later in life, delayed embryonal and fetal development as early as during the first trimester of pregnancy, congenital anomalies, preterm birth, miscarriage, stillbirth, sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS), growth restriction and low birth weight, and childhood obesity in offspring.12,13,52 The effect of delayed early growth is more pronounced when combined with conception using assisted reproductive technology and when exposure is to ≥10 cigarettes/day.12
paragraphs.heading: Cigarette Smoke

paragraphs.text: Despite the known consequences of smoking, over 2.3 million women worldwide per year smoke during pregnancy.12 Both active maternal smoking during pregnancy and passive exposure to ETS are harmful to the fetus and are associated with lower birth weight.52 ETS consists of
paragraphs.heading: Cigarette Smoke

paragraphs.text: smoke coming from the end of a burning cigarette (sidestream smoke) and from smoker’s exhalation (mainstream smoke); it is also known as secondhand smoke. ETS contains over 250 harmful chemicals, including carbon monoxide, cyanide, benzene, ethylene oxide, nitrogen oxides, arsenic, formaldehyde, vinyl chloride, toluene, and PAHs such as benzo[a]pyrene. At least 69 are known carcinogens; the amount of each chemical varies with each cigarette. Cotinine is a metabolite of nicotine that has a long half-life (∼20 hours) and is the biologic marker used to measure exposure to ETS. There is no safe level of exposure to ETS.51
paragraphs.heading: Cigarette Smoke

paragraphs.text: Vaping products have been used as a nicotine replacement therapy since the early 2010s. They consist of a heating device that aerosolizes a mixture of nicotine, propylene glycol, vegetable oil, and flavorings for inhalation. Although initially intended as a smoking cessation aid, they also have become widely used on their own, in the absence of a prior addiction to nicotine. Although not all potential harm from vaping is currently understood, especially in pregnancy, it is generally accepted as a less harmful mode of nicotine delivery than cigarette smoking. Recent studies have not shown a relationship between vaping during pregnancy and lower birth weight (in contrast to smoking). Further studies will have to be conducted to evaluate whether toxic exposures from additives in the vaping liquid, which may include organic solvents and heavy metals, can be harmful to the fetus.52 Vaping also releases particles when the users exhale and subject those around them to secondhand aerosol exposure, which may contain nicotine, heavy metals, volatile organic compounds, or other harmful substances.51
paragraphs.heading: Cigarette Smoke

paragraphs.text: Because smoking in public and the workplace has become restricted, the most common source of ETS exposure is at home. Paternal smoking is the most frequently reported source of environmental exposure.51
paragraphs.heading: Sources of Exposure

paragraphs.text: Active smoking is associated with infertility, reduction in successful in vitro fertilization, and early onset of menopause. Impaired female fertility may be secondary to hormonal imbalance, direct impact on follicular growth and ovulation, or reduced motility in the female reproductive tract. Cotinine and benzo[a]pyrene, a carcinogen and endocrine disruptor, have been found in follicular fluid and ovarian granulosa cells; levels correlate with the degree of active and passive exposure. Active paternal smoking is linked to decreased production, impaired motility, and altered sperm morphology.13 Active smoking also impacts the developing fetus. Nicotine leads to vasoconstriction of the uteroplacental blood vessels, reducing the delivery of oxygen and nutrients. Additionally, carboxyhemoglobin production from carbon monoxide contributes to fetal hypoxia and chronic hypoxic stress.12 Fetal exposure to active maternal smoking is associated with placental dysfunction, spontaneous
paragraphs.heading: Toxic Effects

paragraphs.text: abortion, intrauterine growth restriction, preterm delivery, and congenital anomalies such as cleft lip and palate. Active maternal smoking during pregnancy is an important risk factor for SIDS.12,13,51,53 A direct dose-response relationship has been noted between maternal smoking and intrauterine growth restriction; one study suggested a 5% reduction in relative fetal weight per pack of cigarettes smoked daily.53 Nicotine is toxic to the developing nervous system, impacting neuronal proliferation and differentiation. Maternal active smoking during pregnancy is associated with impaired cognitive functioning, auditory processing deficits, impulsivity, anxiety, depression, ADHD, obesity, and conduct disorders in offspring.53 Maternal smoking also appears to impact infant stress response via epigenetic mechanisms. DNA hypomethylation of the placental glucocorticoid receptor promotor region was found in one study to correlate with infant salivary cortisol levels over the first month of life.54 Epidemiologic studies show a relationship between prenatal maternal active smoking and both reduced lung function and asthma in offspring.53 At present, there is insufficient evidence to decisively link ETS with infertility, spontaneous abortion, or congenital anomalies; however, prenatal exposure to ETS has been associated with increased incidence of both SIDS and low birth weight.13,53 Evidence is suggestive of a relationship between ETS and preterm delivery. The literature also suggests a relationship between prenatal exposure to both active maternal smoking and ETS and the incidence of childhood cancers; further evidence is necessary to support this relationship.12,51
paragraphs.heading: Toxic Effects

paragraphs.text: Smoking prevention programs should focus on education and treatment of preteens, adolescents, and women of childbearing age. As nicotine is a neurotoxin, nicotine replacement should be avoided as a means to quit smoking during pregnancy. Smoking during pregnancy and common sequelae such as preterm birth and low birth weight have been diminished using behavioral therapy programs. Some programs have shown success in promoting nicotine abstinence during pregnancy but none has been identified to successfully prevent relapse to smoking after delivery.52
paragraphs.heading: Prevention Strategies

paragraphs.text: Effects of alcohol on the fetus are extensive, devastating, and often permanent. Approximately 10% of women report drinking alcohol at some time during their pregnancy.55 The incidence of fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) in the United States is estimated as 0.2 to 1.5 per 1000 live births, and 1% to 5% of school-aged children in the United States and Western Europe may have a fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD), a larger group of disabilities caused by fetal alcohol exposure but not meeting criteria for FAS.56 FAS is estimated to incur a lifetime cost for one person of $2 million, and the cost to the United States is estimated to be over $4 billion per year.56 Because the full spectrum of FASD is
paragraphs.heading: Ethanol

paragraphs.text: more prevalent, this is bound to be an underestimate of the total cost of FASD.
paragraphs.heading: Ethanol

paragraphs.text: Although most ethanol exposure is the result of deliberate ingestion by pregnant mothers, measurable levels of ethanol in the blood after the use of hand sanitizers has been documented, although not in pharmacologically significant amounts. Much higher amounts are found secondary to inhalation after use of hand sanitizer in enclosed spaces. Measurable levels of ethanol in air in neonatal intensive care unit incubators following the use of hand sanitizers has been shown.58 Patients are also exposed to ethanol as an excipient in medications, as well as benzyl alcohol and propylene glycol.59 In a cohort of 106 very low birth weight infants over the period of 1 year, it was found that 98% of the infants were exposed to excipients and 5% to 9% of them received doses higher than acceptable recommended doses for adults.59
paragraphs.heading: Sources of Exposure

paragraphs.text: FAS was identified more than 50 years ago. It is defined by craniofacial abnormalities (including smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, and short palpebral fissures), growth deficiency (at or below the 10th percentile), and CNS dysfunction (structural, neurologic, and/or functional). FAS is generally considered to be the extreme end of the spectrum of negative outcomes that result from alcohol exposure during pregnancy.56
paragraphs.heading: Toxic Effects

paragraphs.text: FASD is an umbrella term that covers all diagnoses that pertain to children who were exposed to alcohol in utero. This includes FAS, as well as partial FAS, alcoholrelated neurodevelopmental disorder, and alcohol-related birth defects. Children exposed to alcohol in utero tend to have poor outcomes. They can have lower IQ scores, poor reasoning skills, hyperactivity, poor memory, learning difficulties, speech and language delay, intellectual disability, and/or problems with attention, sleep, vision, or hearing or with heart, kidney, or bone. Prenatal exposure to ethanol is still the leading known cause of intellectual delay.56 Among the numerous comorbid conditions that have been identified in people with FASD, the top five are abnormal results of function studies of peripheral nervous system and special senses, conduct disorder, receptive language disorder, chronic serous otitis media, and expressive language disorder. People prenatally exposed to alcohol are also at risk for epilepsy; one study showed that 17.7% of a prenatally alcohol-exposed population have at least one documented seizure60 and depression and anxiety disorders.56
paragraphs.heading: Toxic Effects

paragraphs.text: Although much of the work examining outcomes after exposure to ethanol is focused on brain development and behavior, other organ systems are also at risk. For example, prenatal alcohol exposure results in smaller, immature lungs, as well as disruption of both innate and adaptive immunity in the lung, which increases risk of infection. There is an increased risk of congenital heart disease (CHD). The growth deficiency is part of the diagnosis of
paragraphs.heading: Toxic Effects

paragraphs.text: FAS that points to skeletal abnormalities; this deficiency continues at least through early adolescence and is associated with abnormal bone growth. There are also reports of abnormalities in other systems, including kidney, liver, and gastrointestinal.61
paragraphs.heading: Toxic Effects

paragraphs.text: Heavy alcohol consumption increases the risk of miscarriage from ∼15% to 45%55 and increases stillbirths sixfold.62 Typically, FAS and FASD are associated with moderate to high levels of alcohol consumption, but lower levels of exposure are associated with more subtle changes. There even have been associations between one alcoholic drink per day in any trimester and increased risk of behavioral disturbances in young adults. It is widely agreed upon between obstetric and pediatric organizations that there is no safe level of alcohol exposure at any time during pregnancy, and complete abstinence is recommended.63
paragraphs.heading: Toxic Effects

paragraphs.text: Certainly, the cause of FAS and FASD is known and has been for many years; however, the rate of alcohol consumption by pregnant women is remarkably stable over time.55 Other sources of alcohol such as gasoline and hand sanitizer have not been well studied. Although the human literature can be inconsistent regarding outcomes following exposure to alcohol, the best advice remains to abstain from alcohol exposure during pregnancy. Women planning to become pregnant should also consider abstaining, as the effects of preconception exposure are not well understood at this time and critical exposure can occur before the first missed
paragraphs.heading: Prevention Strategies

paragraphs.text: period. Treatments for FASD have always focused on treatment of the symptoms and comorbid conditions, but recent animal and human studies have suggested a benefit to choline after prenatal alcohol exposure.63
paragraphs.heading: Prevention Strategies

paragraphs.text: Pesticides are applied in agriculture and both in and around homes. More than 2 million metric tons of pesticides are used throughout the world every year. Pesticides are defined as any chemical utilized to eradicate insects (insecticides), plants and weeds (herbicides), microorganisms (disinfectants, bactericides, fungicides, and algaecides), and other pests.64,65,67 Pesticides are classified by the function of their active ingredient and the intended target organism. Some of the more common classifications of pesticides, mechanisms of action, and examples are shown in Table 13.1. In addition to their active ingredient, pesticides contain other chemicals that are not required to be readily available for consumers.64
paragraphs.heading: Pesticides

paragraphs.text: Organochlorines (DDT, methoxychlor, chlordane, aldrin, dieldrin, and lindane) and organophosphates (chloropyrifos, diazinon, and parathion) are neurotoxic insecticides that were historically applied commercially in agriculture. Both classes of insecticides have been restricted because of toxic effects in animals and humans.50,67 Organochlorines are lipid soluble and bioaccumulate in the environment. Although the organochlorine DDT was banned by the EPA in 1972, use continues in some parts of the world for control of diseases such as malaria and for agriculture.
paragraphs.heading: Pesticides

paragraphs.text: Organophosphates are water soluble and exert their neurotoxic effects via irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase. Residential application of most organophosphates has been restricted or banned due to toxicities in humans.50,65 Pyrethoids, pyrethrins, and piperonyls are insecticides primarily marketed for residential use. Generally, they are less toxic, but health effects have been reported.66 The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention conducts a biomonitoring program for many common pesticides. In 2005, 29 of 45 pesticides were identified in samples from random subjects; the most prevalent were organochlorine and organophosphate insecticides.67
paragraphs.heading: Pesticides

paragraphs.text: Important sources of exposure include direct inhalation after application and ingestion of contaminated food. Organochlorine pesticides have a long half-life and bioaccumulate in our food supply.66 Frequent sources of the organochlorine DDT include meat, dairy products, and fish. DDT and its metabolites have been found in breast milk. The organochlorines aldrin and dieldrin are found in fish, shellfish, root crops, dairy products, and meats. Plants absorb these chemicals directly from the soil; even organic vegetables may contain high levels if grown in contaminated areas.67 The EPA sets acceptable standards for pesticide residue, which are regulated by the FDA. In 2019, human food testing found pesticide residues in 57.6% of 1258 domestic and 50.6% of 3069 imported samples, and violations of EPA standards (residue for which there is no tolerance or residues above the tolerance level) were found in 1.3% of domestic and 10.9% of imported samples. The majority of domestic samples were fruits and vegetables (71.1%), with the highest violation rate found in vegetables at 2.2%. The overall violation rate was greatest for imported grains at 18.9%. Imidacloprid (neonicotinoid insecticide used in agriculture), pyraclostrobin (fungicide used in agriculture), acetamiprid (another neonicotinoid insecticide used in agriculture), and thiabendazole (an antifungal and antiparasitic which also is used medicinally as a chelating agent for metal toxicity) were the most frequently reported pesticide residues.68
paragraphs.heading: Sources of Exposure

paragraphs.text: Pregnant women may be exposed in the home environment via indoor use of disinfectants, insecticides, and rodenticides and outdoor application of herbicides, insecticides, and fungicides. Certain products such as sprays and foggers may lead to prolonged exposure in the home. Another potential source of exposure in the home is drinking water. Herbicides are a frequent contaminant of drinking water in agricultural areas; in urban areas, both insecticides and herbicides are known contaminants.67 Occupational or paraoccupational exposure to pesticides and living in close proximity to pesticide-treated agricultural areas represent other important sources for pregnant women or women of childbearing age.50,70
paragraphs.heading: Sources of Exposure

paragraphs.text: Biomarkers have been identified to evaluate fetal pesticide exposure. In 2004, the Environmental Working Group found 21 of 28 organochlorine pesticides in cord blood of
paragraphs.heading: Sources of Exposure

paragraphs.text: 10 babies. Amniotic fluid from amniocentesis samples has been used to characterize early fetal exposure; meconium samples have been utilized to determine exposure during the second and third trimester. Organophosphates have been identified in amniotic fluid, and both organophosphates and pyrethroid pesticides have been found in meconium samples.69
paragraphs.heading: Sources of Exposure

paragraphs.text: Although most pesticides are neurotoxins, the degree of toxicity varies between classes. Pesticides also can function as endocrine disruptors, immunotoxicants, and carcinogens in animals and humans.50,70 Epidemiologic data suggest a link between parental pesticide exposure and infertility, spontaneous abortion, fetal demise, preterm birth, intrauterine growth restriction, and congenital anomalies.67,70 One study demonstrated a relationship between exposure to chloropyrifos and DDE (a metabolite of DDT) and both low birth weight and microcephaly.69 Additionally, biomarkers for organophosphates found in maternal urine, blood, or umbilical cord samples are associated with low birth weight and preterm birth.70 A relationship between exposure to organochlorines such as DDT and both cryptorchidism and hypospadias has been reported, suggesting endocrine disruption as a mechanism of toxicity.67
paragraphs.heading: Toxic Effects

paragraphs.text: Evidence supports a relationship between prenatal exposure to organochlorine and organophosphate pesticides (OPs) and adverse neurodevelopmental and behavioral outcomes that persist into childhood. Findings include increased incidence of cognitive delays and intellectual disability that persist into childhood and increased incidence of both ADHD and autism spectrum disorders.50,67 There is increasing epidemiologic evidence correlating parental pesticide exposure and childhood cancers. Multiple studies report a correlation between maternal pesticide use (both occupational and household) before and during pregnancy and childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia. There is stronger evidence linking maternal exposure to pesticides and leukemia than paternal exposure. Similarly, more than 25 studies have described a relationship between prenatal pesticide exposure and brain tumors. The most consistent risk factors identified are maternal and paternal prenatal exposures to pesticides at home or at work.67
paragraphs.heading: Toxic Effects

paragraphs.text: Dietary changes may decrease contact, and exposure to pesticide residues may be limited by the ingestion of organic foods. One study showed that urinary excretion of organophosphate metabolites significantly decreased when children were placed on an organic diet for 5 days.5,67 Washing produce may remove pesticide residue, and avoiding animal fat and certain fish can limit exposure to lipid-soluble pesticides such as organochlorines. The EPA recommends integrated pest management as a strategy to avoid environmental exposure to pesticides. Maternal occupational and household exposures should be avoided during pregnancy.5
paragraphs.heading: Prevention Strategies

paragraphs.text: Bisphenol A (BPA) is a chemical plasticizer that is added to plastic resins to enhance rigidity. It has been used since the 1960s in the production of polycarbonate plastic bottles and in epoxy resins utilized as protective coating inside metal food and beverage cans. It is also used in water supply pipes, medical devices, dental sealants and composites, and many other products that are part of our daily lives.5,71,73 BPA is in widespread use worldwide and is pervasive in our environment, with more than 6 billion pounds manufactured annually.71
paragraphs.heading: Bisphenols A, S, and F

paragraphs.text: As concerns for the health effects of BPA have been identified and have become widely recognized by the public, alternative products that are “BPA-free” are being sought by both consumers and industry. Two BPA analogs, bisphenol S (BPS) and bisphenol F (BPF), are utilized as alternatives to BPA with similar physical properties. BPS is used as a coating for thermal paper that allows for inkless printing. Rolled thermal paper with BPS (“BPA-free” paper) is found in cash registers and ATM terminal receipts and paper products such as boarding passes and currency. BPF is used in epoxy resins and coatings of industrial and consumer materials to increase thickness and durability. Use of BPS and BPF is currently not regulated.72
paragraphs.heading: Bisphenols A, S, and F

paragraphs.text: Human exposure to BPA is significant and nearly ubiquitous in developed countries and has become one of the most extensively studied EDCs. BPA leaches from plastic bottles and the epoxy resin coating metallic cans and other products; contamination of the food supply and routine ingestion by humans is presumed. Leaching also occurs from dental sealants. Heat and both acidic and basic conditions lead to hydrolysis of BPA polymers and leaching into the food supply. It is a widespread environmental contaminant, since it is present in so many products, and was found in 2003 to provide nearly all of the estrogenic effects of landfill leachates71,73 Due to the emerging evidence of harmful effects of BPA and public knowledge of its danger, BPA analogs BPS and BPF are now being used in increasing quantities. Because fewer studies have examined their risk and they are unregulated, products containing BPS or BPF can be advertised as “BPA free” without evidence of decreased risk from exposure.73,75
paragraphs.heading: Sources of Exposure

paragraphs.text: BPA is a known estrogenic EDC. BPA binds to estrogen receptors and acts as an agonist with estrogenic properties at very low concentrations; it also has been shown to be a thyroid receptor antagonist and to have antiandrogenic properties in vitro.73 BPA is primarily unbound to plasma proteins; in this active form, BPA may exert estrogenic effects during critical stages of fetal development. BPA may significantly impact fetal neurodevelopment, as estrogen plays an important role in the developing brain. Prenatal and neonatal exposure to low doses of BPA may result in
paragraphs.heading: Toxic Effects

paragraphs.text: organizational changes in the prostate, breast, testis, mammary glands, body size, brain structure and chemistry, and behavior of laboratory animals, as well as potential disruptions in sexual differentiation of various organs including the brain.71,73,74
paragraphs.heading: Toxic Effects

paragraphs.text: Numerous studies have documented adverse effects in vivo, many at doses below acceptable reference levels for human daily intake (50 μg/kg). Animals exposed to BPA during gestation develop a wide range of endocrine pathology. In the rodent, low-dose perinatal effects of BPA include urogenital anomalies, accelerated pubertal development, and predisposition to prostate cancer in the male and breast cancer in the female.71,73,74 Additionally, animal studies have shown that prenatal exposure impacts neurodevelopment and increases behaviors such as aggression and anxiety.73 In the mouse model, perinatal BPA exposure modifies estrogen sensitivity later in life.74
paragraphs.heading: Toxic Effects

paragraphs.text: The body of literature documenting BPA exposure in humans is increasing with >100 published epidemiological studies and dozens of prospective studies. Maternal exposure during pregnancy is associated with anxiety, depression, hyperactivity, and aggression in offspring. In women, BPA exposure has been associated with infertility, recurrent miscarriages, preterm delivery, polycystic ovarian syndrome, breast cancer, and chromosomal anomalies in offspring.71,73,74 In men, elevated urinary BPA levels have been correlated with low sperm count, poor motility and quality, and increased sperm DNA breakage.71,75 Decreased anogenital distance has been documented in male infants whose fathers were occupationally exposed to BPA.75
paragraphs.heading: Toxic Effects

paragraphs.text: Prenatal and childhood exposure is associated with hypospadias, precocious puberty, neurodevelopmental and behavioral impairment, increased adipokine levels, and obesity. Adipokines are a diverse group of secretory proteins that modulate lipid and glucose metabolism.73,74,75 In one study of 244 mothers and their 3-year-old children, a 10-fold increase in urinary BPA levels during pregnancy was associated with higher scores for anxiety, depression, hyperactivity, and poor emotional regulation in offspring.73
paragraphs.heading: Toxic Effects

paragraphs.text: BPS and BPF are also estrogenic endocrine disruptors. Although the literature documenting the estrogenic effects of these BPA analogs in vivo is limited, in vitro studies indicate toxicity and potency similar to those of BPA. In a study in which BPF was administered to pregnant rats via a feeding tube, the active form was found in the placenta, amniotic fluid, and fetal tissue.75
paragraphs.heading: Toxic Effects

paragraphs.text: To avoid exposure to BPA and its structural analogs, pregnant women can refrain from using plastic materials that contain BPA. Reducing contact with thermal paper receipts can also limit exposure to these chemicals. Resin identification codes are identified by symbols appearing on plastic products that identify the plastic resin out of which the product is made. Many products that contain BPA contain the resin identification code 7. As heat may
paragraphs.heading: Prevention Strategies

paragraphs.text: lead to release of BPA, plastic materials containing BPA should not be boiled, washed in the dishwasher, or placed in the microwave.38,73,74
paragraphs.heading: Prevention Strategies

paragraphs.text: Phthalates are a class of chemical plasticizers that are present in multiple common products in outdoor and household use. High molecular weight phthalates provide flexibility to plastics such as polyvinyl chloride (PVC), and low molecular weight phthalates are solvents. They can be found in household materials such as hoses, flooring, roofing, shoes, children’s toys, plastic bags, and many more common objects. They also are found in adhesives, lubricants, paint, cosmetics, shampoo, and many other personal care products. Like BPA, phthalates are ubiquitous in our environment and have become significant environmental pollutants.76,77 Certain phthalates are considered toxic chemicals, and their release into the environment is monitored by the EPA’s Toxic Release Inventory database (available at www.epa.gov/tri).
paragraphs.heading: Phthalates

paragraphs.text: Like BPA, exposure to phthalates is substantial. Diet is the main source of exposure; phthalates leach from plastic containers and plastic wrap, particularly after heating, and can be ingested. They are found in infant formula, baby food, and plastic dishes and utensils. Transdermal absorption from cosmetics, fragrances, lotions, and insect repellents has been reported. In particular, usage of fragrance, nail polish, and eye shadow has been correlated with concentrations
paragraphs.heading: Sources of Exposure

paragraphs.text: of phthalate metabolites in the urine of pregnant women. Dibutyl phthalate (DBP) is commonly used in deodorant, cosmetics, and nail polish. DBP levels are significantly higher in women of reproductive age than in men. Inhalation is another potential route of exposure. Phthalates have been found in ambient air, household dust, and fumes from new paint or vinyl flooring.77,78 There is potential for direct intravascular exposure via intravenous (IV) tubing, blood product or IV bags, and ECMO tubing, with additional exposure occurring through plastic tubing used with ventilators.78 Because phthalate esters are not covalently bound to the products that contain them, they are easily released and transferred and pass freely across the placenta.77
paragraphs.heading: Sources of Exposure

paragraphs.text: Phthalates are antiandrogenic endocrine disruptors. Phthalate exposure during pregnancy has been associated with pregnancy loss, preterm delivery, and adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes.76 It appears that the most sensitive tissue to phthalates is the male reproductive tract.76,77 Phthalate metabolite concentration in maternal urine is significantly associated with decreased anogenital distance in offspring, which also is significantly correlated with small scrotum, reduced penile length, and testicular maldescent.76,78 Fig. 13.8 outlines the effects of prenatal exposure to phthalates.76
paragraphs.heading: Toxic Effects

paragraphs.text: Food and products made from PVC plastics represent the most common sources of exposure. PVC plastics are labeled with the resin identification code 3.78 Processed foods and
paragraphs.heading: Prevention Strategies

paragraphs.text: those individually wrapped in plastic tend to contain the highest concentrations. The FDA recommends careful use of plastic containers, avoidance of reheating plastic containers in the microwave, and using only plastics in the microwave that are labeled for microwave oven use. One-time-use containers (such as carry-out containers) should not be used in microwave ovens. Plastic wrap should not touch foods during microwaving. Avoidance of long-term storage of foods in plastic, heating plastic containers, and consumption of processed foods may decrease exposure.5 Until more information is available, limiting exposure to phthalates during pregnancy is a reasonable approach.
paragraphs.heading: Prevention Strategies

paragraphs.text: Organic solvents are a large, diverse group of volatile carbon-based chemicals used to dissolve lipids and other high molecular weight compounds in solution. Organic solvents are found in volatile anesthetics, paint and paint thinners, cleaning supplies, dry cleaning solutions, dyes, office supplies such as copier fluid and printer ink, cosmetics, nail polish remover, glues, adhesives, spot removers, and detergents.19 They can be classified into three families of chemicals: oxygenated solvents, petroleum solvents, and chlorinated solvents.79 Organic solvents are well established as neurotoxic to adults based on studies surrounding occupational exposure. They are small, lipophilic molecules and thus pass freely across the placenta to the fetus.79
paragraphs.heading: Organic Solvents

paragraphs.text: Organic solvents are ubiquitous in our environment, and concentrations are much greater indoors than outdoors. Many of these chemicals persist in ambient air long after their use. Organic solvents are commonly found in household products such as cleaning supplies, and occupational exposure is significant.79,80 As many women continue to work throughout pregnancy, exposure to organic solvents poses a risk to the fetus. Because organic solvents are volatile, inhalation represents the most common route of exposure. Recreational inhalation of toluene found in spray paint and glue has resulted in multiple congenital anomalies and neurodevelopmental delay. Oral ingestion and transdermal exposure also occurs.80
paragraphs.heading: Sources of Exposure

paragraphs.text: Organic solvents cross the placenta and, as with other lipophilic chemicals, concentrate in organs with higher lipid content, such as the brain.79 In animals, organic solvents are teratogenic. Spontaneous abortion, congenital anomalies, and male infertility are seen in animals prenatally exposed.81 Animal studies also have demonstrated neurotoxicity in vivo in offspring following prenatal exposure. A prospective cohort study conducted in France followed mothers with occupational exposure to organic solvents during pregnancy and found a significant association between exposure during pregnancy and behavioral
paragraphs.heading: Toxic Effects

paragraphs.text: problems in offspring at 2 years of age. Interestingly, the change did not persist and was less severe at 6 years of age.79 Epidemiologic studies in humans link maternal occupational exposure to organic solvents with risk of spontaneous abortion and congenital anomalies. Congenital malformations include cleft lip and palate, neural tube defects, and congenital heart disease (CHD).80,81 The National Birth Defects Prevention Study 1997–2002 was a case control study that enrolled 2951 control mothers and 2047 mothers of infants with CHD. The study demonstrated an association between occupational organic solvent exposure during the month prior to conception through the first trimester and CHD—specifically, left ventricular and right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, conotruncal defects, and septal defects.80 Toluene (methyl benzene) is an aromatic hydrocarbon utilized in industry in paint, glue, and other organic compounds. Toluene embryopathy has been described after maternal abuse of these organic solvents as inhalants, termed “solvent sniffing.” Findings include intrauterine growth restriction, microcephaly, facial features similar to fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS), and neurodevelopmental impairment.82
paragraphs.heading: Toxic Effects

paragraphs.text: Organic solvents should be used in a well-ventilated area, and partially used containers should be discarded after use. Pregnant women should avoid paint fumes to reduce exposure in both home and occupational settings. Cleaning supplies should be used in well-ventilated areas while wearing protective gloves. There are specific recommendations for nail salon workers and hairdressers that include limiting work hours, wearing gloves and masks when appropriate, ensuring optimal ventilation, covering containers and garbage, and separating areas to handle food and to eat.5
paragraphs.heading: Prevention Strategies

paragraphs.text: In 2014, the leading causes of infant death were congenital malformations and chromosomal abnormalities, short gestation and low birth weight, newborns affected by maternal complications of pregnancy, and SIDS.71 All have been associated with environmental exposures discussed in this chapter. This chapter has described the many different sources of exposure and the timing of exposure to occupational and environmental chemicals. The complexity of maternal-fetal pharmacokinetics has been outlined, and many of the various types of outcomes have been discussed. The science of environmental medicine continues to evolve. More recently, literature has begun to focus on the impact of co-exposure to environmental toxicants; a growing body of evidence supports the deleterious effect of simultaneous exposure at concentrations lower than those known to cause toxicity individually.57 Genome-wide association studies and epigenome-wide association studies are novel methodologies being utilized to better understand the molecular basis for exposure risk.55
paragraphs.heading: Conclusion

paragraphs.text: When caring for a patient with a diagnosis that may be secondary to an environmental exposure, it can be difficult to demonstrate a causal relationship. Hotlines for teratology information are part of the Organization of Teratology Information Services and are listed online at
paragraphs.heading: Conclusion

paragraphs.heading: Conclusion

paragraphs.heading: Conclusion

paragraphs.heading: Conclusion

Mechanisms include histone modifications, altered DNA methylation, and expression of microRNA. • Epigenetic transgenerational inheritance refers to epimuta-
paragraphs.heading: Conclusion

paragraphs.text: tions in the germline (egg or sperm) that are passed to future generations and leads to variation in phenotypic expression. • Exposure to environmental toxicants that impact the

Certain toxicants, such as lead and polychlorinated biphenyls, are stored in maternal compartments and mobilized during pregnancy. Air pollution and diet (food and water) represent common sources of exposure during pregnancy. • Toxicants reach the fetus via placenta-dependent and
paragraphs.heading: Conclusion

Certain chemical properties promote transport across the placenta, such as low molecular weight, lipid solubility, protein binding, and ability to utilize nutrient transport mechanisms. Examples of placenta-independent environmental exposures that are potentially hazardous to the fetus include ionizing radiation, heat, and noise.
