Preterm birth prior to 34 weeks was also significantly lower in the progesterone group when compared with the placebo group (2.7% vs. 18.5%, respectively, P < .05). Meis and colleagues66 from the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD) Maternal-Fetal Medicine Units (MFMU) Network reported similar results from a large randomized clinical trial designed to evaluate the efficacy of 17α-hydroxyprogesterone caproate (17-OHPC) for the prevention of preterm birth in high-risk women. Among women receiving weekly intramuscular progesterone therapy from 16 to 36 weeks’ gestation, the incidence of preterm birth prior to 37 weeks’ gestation was 36.3%, compared with an incidence of 54.9% in the placebo group (RR = 0.66; 95% CI, 0.54–0.81). The incidence of preterm birth at less than 35 weeks (RR = 0.67; 95% CI, 0.48–0.93) and at less than 32 weeks (RR = 0.58; 95% CI, 0.37–0.91) was also significantly decreased in women treated with progesterone when compared with placebo. Fonseca et al.67 screened more than 24,000 women and enrolled 1.7% of them whose cervical length was less than 15 mm (less than third percentile). Women randomized to 200 mg vaginal progesterone suppositories had a lower preterm birth rate (19% vs. 44%; RR = 0.56; 95% CI, 0.36–0.86) compared with those randomized to placebo. Hassan and colleagues68 screened more than 32,000 women worldwide and enrolled those with cervical lengths of 10 to 20 mm. Four hundred sixty-five women were randomized to 90 mg vaginal progesterone gel (daily until 36 weeks) and had lower rates of preterm birth before 28, 33, and 35 weeks compared with placebo. Neonatal morbidity and mortality were also lower in treated women (7.7% vs. 13.5%; RR = 0.57; 95% CI, 0.33–0.99).
paragraphs.heading: Progesterone

paragraphs.text: However, as the number and size of such trials have increased, the role of progesterone in preventing prematurity has become less clear. O’Brien and colleagues69 conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multinational trial evaluating whether prophylactic administration
paragraphs.heading: Progesterone

paragraphs.text: of vaginal progesterone would reduce the risk of preterm birth in high-risk women with a history of spontaneous preterm birth. Therapy with either progesterone vaginal gel or placebo was initiated between 18 weeks and 0 days and 22 weeks and 6 days of gestation, and patients were asked to continue once-daily treatment until delivery, 37 weeks’ gestation, or development of preterm rupture of the membranes. In this trial, progesterone did not decrease the frequency of preterm birth at less than or equal to 32 weeks, and there was no difference between the groups with respect to the mean gestational age at delivery, infant morbidity or mortality, or other maternal or neonatal outcome measures.69 However, examination of a subset of this cohort in a planned secondary analysis revealed that vaginal progesterone may reduce the rate of early preterm birth and improve neonatal outcomes in women with a short sonographic cervical length in addition to a history of a prior spontaneous preterm birth.70 Moreover, the use of vaginal progesterone in high-risk women was investigated in the OPPTIMUM study, published in 2016. This was a large (1228 subjects), multicenter, double-masked, randomized trial comparing 200 mg of vaginal progesterone per day to placebo in women at high risk for preterm birth, including those with previous spontaneous birth at less than or equal to 34 weeks’ gestation, or a cervical length less than or equal to 25 mm, or those with positive fetal fibronectin test combined with other clinical risk factors for preterm birth. Progesterone supplementation did not reduce the risk of preterm birth or composite neonatal outcomes and had no long-term benefit on outcomes of children at 2 years of age. In addition, in a subgroup of women with a history of a prior spontaneous preterm birth (n = 903), there were no significant differences in the rate of preterm birth less than 34 weeks of gestation between those receiving vaginal progesterone and placebo (15.9% vs. 18.8%).71
paragraphs.heading: Progesterone

paragraphs.text: Recently, the Progestin’s Role in Optimizing Neonatal Gestation (PROLONG) trial, a double-blind, placebocontrolled, international trial in which women with a prior spontaneous preterm birth in a singleton gestation were randomized to weekly intramuscular injections of 250 mg of 17-OHPC from 16 to 36 weeks or placebo. The trial found no benefit of 17-OHPC compared with placebo in reducing the rate of preterm births at <35 weeks (11% vs. 11.5%; RR = 0.95; 95% CI, 0.71–1.26) or neonatal composite outcome (5.4% vs. 5.2%; RR = 1.05; 95% CI, 0.68–1.61).72
paragraphs.heading: Progesterone

paragraphs.text: An individual participant data meta-analysis (EPPPIC) of 30 randomized trials evaluating progestins for preterm birth prevention (>11,600 participants) was recently published.73 The review included trials comparing vaginal progesterone, intramuscular 17-OHPC, or oral progesterone with control, or with each other, in asymptomatic women at risk of preterm birth. In the analysis of data in singleton pregnancies with either a previous spontaneous preterm birth or short cervix (≤25 mm) at 16 to 24 weeks in the current pregnancy, the preterm birth rate <34 weeks was reduced by 20% in patients who received either vaginal progesterone (RR = 0.78; 95% CI 0.68–0.90; nine trials; N = 3769) or
paragraphs.heading: Progesterone

paragraphs.text: 17-OHPC (RR = 0.83; 95% CI, 0.68–1.01; five trials; N = 3053). The authors could not dependably establish whether preterm births were spontaneous or not. Serious composite neonatal complications were reduced for vaginal progesterone, with an RR of 0.82 (95% CI, 0.65–1.04), and for 17-OHPC, with an RR of 0.81 (95% CI, 0.60–1.09) but the difference was not statistically significant. Treatment in multifetal pregnancies was not supported by the evidence. Of note, a network analysis comparing vaginal progesterone and 17-OHPC found no difference in benefit when the analysis was restricted to women with short cervical length or history of a previous preterm birth.74
paragraphs.heading: Progesterone

paragraphs.text: Subsequently, the ACOG and SMFM endorsed offering progesterone supplementation (either vaginal progesterone or intramuscular 17-OHPC) to patients with a singleton pregnancy and a prior spontaneous preterm birth and offering vaginal progesterone to asymptomatic patients with a singleton pregnancy with a short cervix (<2.5 cm) between 20 and 36+6 weeks of gestation.75,76
paragraphs.heading: Progesterone

paragraphs.text: Use of progesterone has also been investigated in other populations. Rozenberg and colleagues77 performed an open-label, multicenter, RCT enrolling women presenting with preterm labor symptoms and a cervical length measurement less than 25 mm. After successful tocolysis, women were assigned to receive either intramuscular progesterone injections or placebo until 36 weeks’ gestation, with no benefit seen in the prevention of preterm birth in the group assigned to the progesterone arm of the trial.77
paragraphs.heading: Progesterone

paragraphs.text: Progesterone has also been evaluated in the setting of multiple gestations, with studies showing no reduction in rates of preterm birth in women with twin and triplet gestations.58,78 Progesterone use has been examined in otherwise low-risk patients with cervical shortening. In a large, multicenter RCT enrolling nulliparous women with cervical shortening (<30 mm), Grobman and associates79 within the MFMU network showed no benefit with regard to prevention of spontaneous preterm birth in women assigned to weekly 17-OHPC as compared with placebo.
paragraphs.heading: Progesterone

paragraphs.text: Currently, the SMFM and ACOG recommend that women with a singleton gestation and a history of prior preterm birth receive progesterone prophylaxis until term and undergo transvaginal serial cervical surveillance starting at 16 weeks to determine which patients are candidates for cerclage placement (cervical length <25 mm). Women without a history of prior spontaneous preterm birth and a cervical length of 25 mm or less before 24 weeks are recommended to start on vaginal progesterone.3
paragraphs.heading: Progesterone

paragraphs.text: Cerclage is a procedure in which a nonresorbable suture is placed in a simple purse-string fashion at the level of the internal os. It can be placed either transvaginally or transabdominally. The transvaginal approach consists mainly of the McDonald (suture placed at the cervicovaginal junction) and the Shirodkar (the suture is placed as close to the internal cervical os by dissecting the vesicocervical mucosa)
paragraphs.heading: Cerclage

paragraphs.text: methods. The transabdominal approach is usually performed due to anatomic limitations (prior trachelectomy) or a history of previous failed transvaginal approaches. Indications for cervical cerclage include history of secondtrimester painless cervical dilation one or more times that resulted in pregnancy loss in the absence of abruption or labor; second-trimester findings on physical exam consistent with painless dilated cervix; or history of preterm less than 34 weeks and with cervical length less than 25 mm before 24 weeks’ gestation.
paragraphs.heading: Cerclage

paragraphs.text: Cerclage is most beneficial in women with prior cervical insufficiency when placed electively before any cervical change. This case scenario leads to low rates of complication and high cerclage success rates. The optimal time for cerclage placement is the early second trimester (12–14 weeks), as miscarriage rates are more likely to occur before this interval, and major anatomic anomalies (e.g., anencephaly) can be detected by this period.80 In addition, this period allows obstetricians to perform early aneuploidy testing by chorionic villus sampling. The upper limit of the gestational age for which cerclage placement is contraindicated remains controversial. It is generally accepted that after fetal viability (23–24 weeks’ gestation), complication risks outweigh the potential benefits of the intervention, and cerclage should not be attempted. Moreover, interventional trials that elucidated the efficacy of cerclage limited gestational age at 24 weeks for screening and initiation of therapies. It is not recommended to place a cerclage after 24 weeks; above this gestational age, there should be extensive counseling about the benefits and risks of the procedure when the patient desires cerclage placement.
paragraphs.heading: Cerclage

paragraphs.text: Contraindications to cerclage placement include rupture of membranes, fetal demise, evidence of intrauterine infection, fetal anomalies incompatible with life, active vaginal bleeding of unknown cause, and active labor. Potential morbidities associated with cerclage placement include bleeding, infection, rupture of membranes, maternal soft tissue injury, spontaneous suture displacement, and the risks of anesthesia. Additional complications may be seen in association with delivery, including cervical laceration in up to 13% of cases. Rare reports of uterine rupture have also been reported in patients in whom labor occurred before suture removal. Scarring of the cervix from the procedure may also contribute to an increased incidence of cesarean delivery.
paragraphs.heading: Cerclage

paragraphs.text: Adverse outcomes are increased in patients with prolapsed membranes or an extensively dilated cervix, particularly when dilation exceeds 4 cm.81 A recently published study reported reasonable neonatal outcomes with cerclage placement in patients with dilated cervixes, 0 mm cervical length, and/or prolapsed membranes.82 Perioperative complications within 2 weeks after the procedure, such as rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis, preterm delivery, bleeding, and complications of anesthesia, were reported to be significantly different between the different indications for cerclage (history indicated: 7.9%; ultrasound indicated: 10.4%; physical examination indicated: 27.6%).83
paragraphs.heading: Cerclage

paragraphs.text: Peripartum complications such as difficult suture removal or cervical lacerations were not different and varied between 11% and 18%.
paragraphs.heading: Cerclage

paragraphs.text: Cerclage success rates were first reported to be greater than 75%. These initial findings may have been misleading. Because pregnancy outcomes in the intervention group were compared to prior pregnancies, the trials did not account for patients who may have a successful pregnancy even after repeated mid-trimester losses. Several trials that followed evaluated the efficacy of cerclage in women with a history of preterm birth rather than with a classical history of cervical insufficiency. The majority of these studies showed no advantage of cerclage in reducing the rates of preterm birth, PPROM, or perinatal mortality, despite being associated with higher administration rates of tocolytic agents and hospitalization. In a large study conducted by the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, 1292 patients with a history of either an early delivery or a prior cervical surgery were randomly assigned to cerclage placement or expectant management.84 Significantly fewer deliveries occurred before 33 weeks in the cerclage group (13% vs. 17%), but a higher incidence of puerperal pyrexia was also demonstrated in this treatment group.84 Limitations of all of these studies included the ill-defined subjective enrollment criteria and the lack of statistical power to adequately address neonatal morbidity outcomes.
paragraphs.heading: Cerclage

paragraphs.text: As discussed, the use of transvaginal cervical sonography has greatly altered current recommendations regarding cerclage placement for singleton gestations. Cerclage placement has been shown to be beneficial in women with a history of preterm birth and a short cervix. Several prospective studies have been conducted using cervical length shortening as a marker to determine the patient population that may best benefit from cerclage placement for the prevention of recurrent preterm birth.85–89 Althuisius and colleagues85 reported findings from a small randomized trial comparing the efficacy of therapeutic cerclage plus bed rest with bed rest alone for the prevention of subsequent preterm birth in women with an ultrasonographically determined short cervix (less than 25 mm) before 27 weeks’ gestation. Use of cerclage in this study was associated with a significant reduction in the incidence of preterm birth prior to 34 weeks when compared with women treated with bed rest alone (0% vs. 44%; P < .002).85 In contrast, To and colleagues,89 in a large, multicenter randomized trial of cervical cerclage for women with an ultrasound-detected short cervix (less than 15 mm) between 22 and 24 weeks’ gestation, reported that the use of prophylactic Shirodkar cerclage did not significantly reduce the incidence of preterm birth at less than 33 weeks’ gestation when compared with expectant management (22% vs. 26%; P < .44). A meta-analysis by Belej- Rak and colleagues86 evaluated the literature relating to the effectiveness of cervical cerclage in women with a sonographically detected shortened cervix.86 Based on this systematic analysis of six pertinent trials, the authors reported that there was no statistically significant effect of cerclage on the rates of preterm birth (<37, <34, <32, and <28 weeks).
paragraphs.heading: Cerclage

paragraphs.text: Singleton pregnancies with a history of prior preterm birth have been shown to have a greater than 30% risk of developing a short cervix (<25 mm) before 24 weeks.87,90 Owen et al.90 randomized 302 women with a history of preterm birth and cervix length of <25 mm to either have or not have cerclage placed. In this large multicenter trial, women with cerclage had reduced perinatal death by almost 50% (8% vs. 16%), and reduced births before 24 weeks (6.1% vs. 14%) and before 37 weeks (45% vs. 60%). In the same high-risk population, Berghella et al.91 performed a metaanalysis review that showed a 30% reduction in preterm birth rate at less than 35 weeks’ gestation (28% vs. 41%; RR = 0.70; 95% CI, 0.55–0.89). The composite perinatal morbidity and mortality was also reduced by 36% (16 vs. 25%; RR = 0.64; 95% CI, 0.45–0.95) in the cerclage group. A later meta-analysis by Alfirevic et al.92 showed a 6% reduction in preterm birth less than 34 weeks (18% vs. 24%; RR = 0.77; 95% CI, 0.66–0.89; nine RCTs; 2415 subjects).
paragraphs.heading: Cerclage

paragraphs.text: Early evidence concerning cerclage placement in women with multiple gestations and short cervix (cervical length < 25 mm) showed a twofold increase in preterm birth (RR = 2.15; 95% CI, 1.15–4.01).91 Since then, two meta-analyses have shown the benefit of cerclage placement in twin gestation with a cervical length of <15 mm or dilated cervix >10 mm.93,94 In light of these results, cerclage placement may be an option on a case-by-case basis when the cervix is very short or dilated in the setting of multiple gestation.
paragraphs.heading: Cerclage

paragraphs.text: Removal of the cerclage is usually performed at about 36 to 37 weeks’ gestation unless active preterm labor begins before that time. There are no prospective studies to guide the management of women with a cerclage in PPROM. Retrospective studies report conflicting results but have generally concluded that retaining the cerclage for 24 hours after PPROM was associated with pregnancy prolongation95 without significant adverse neonatal, maternal, or obstetric outcomes.96 Due to their retrospective nature, the results of the studies may have been biased due to other confounders such as preterm labor or infection. Other studies have reported that cerclage retention after PPROM was associated with increased neonatal deaths due to infection, sepsis, chorioamnionitis, and RDS.95,97 Whereas cerclage retention may certainly be reasonable to permit completion of a course of antenatal corticosteroids (ACS), prolonged retention should be undertaken only with extreme caution with close observation for signs or symptoms of intra-amniotic infection. ACOG does not recommend antibiotic prophylaxis beyond 7 days if the cerclage remains in place.
paragraphs.heading: Cerclage

paragraphs.text: The use of pessaries for the prevention of preterm birth in women at risk for preterm birth has been evaluated and was first proposed in the 1950s. Although several different pessary types have been used, the Arabin pessary, a flexible ringlike silicone device, has been most effective in published trials. This pessary is designed such that the smaller inner diameter should fit around the cervix while the wider
paragraphs.heading: Pessaries

paragraphs.text: outside diameter stays in the vaginal canal, thereby holding the cervix closed in an effort to prevent exposure of fetal membranes to the vaginal flora and maintaining the angle of the cervical canal, directing it posteriorly, so that the weight of the pregnancy centers on the anterior lower segment.
paragraphs.heading: Pessaries

paragraphs.text: The PECEP trial, the largest trial to date, was an RCT that enrolled women with cervical shortening (cervical length ≤25 mm). Among the participants, 192 were assigned to receive an Arabin pessary, and 193 were assigned to expectant management.98 Twelve women (6%) delivered before 34 weeks’ gestation in the pessary arm compared with 51 women (27%) in the expectant management arm, an 82% reduction.98 Despite these encouraging positive results, evidence from two other RCTs did not show such benefit.99,100 Data from two large clinical trials showed no benefit in asymptomatic women with twins with no other risk factors (not screened for short cervical length) that received pessaries.101,102
paragraphs.heading: Pessaries

paragraphs.text: Three prospective studies elaborated the role of pessaries in preventing preterm birth in women with multiple gestations and with a short cervix (cervical length ≤25 mm before 25 weeks’ gestation).101–103 The Arabin pessary was used in all the trials. Only two out of the three RCTs supported the use of pessaries in this population by significantly reducing rates of preterm birth.101,103 One review pooled the above-referenced RCTs and reported no significant differences in preterm birth rates or neonatal outcomes among the group that received pessary versus the no pessary group.104
paragraphs.heading: Pessaries

paragraphs.text: A recent Cochrane review compared cervical pessary to standard of care or no pessary in asymptomatic patients at high risk of preterm birth (12 studies; 4687 women and 7167 fetuses/infants). Cervical pessaries were not beneficial in singleton gestations with short cervix, unselected twin gestations, or twin gestation with a cervical length of <38 mm or ≤25 mm.105 The role of pessaries in preventing preterm birth remains questionable. We are still awaiting several RCTs to be completed. The use of pessaries for the prevention of preterm birth should be reserved for research purposes.
paragraphs.heading: Pessaries

paragraphs.text: In the United States, up to one in eight children are born before 37 weeks.31 Despite being poorly understood, the impact of preterm birth on neonatal morbidity and mortality is detrimental, with skyrocketing health care costs,106 emphasizing the importance of identifying an efficacious treatment for this burden. The optimal tocolytic agent remains to be determined, and various obstacles have hindered RCTs evaluating their efficacy. Designing clinical trials to test tocolytics is complicated in that the health of two patients must be considered. These trials also face problems related to the fact that the nature of preterm birth and its outcomes are different in the setting of early preterm labor (less than 28 weeks) compared with late preterm labor (34–36 weeks). Maintenance tocolysis is not
paragraphs.heading: Tocolytics

paragraphs.text: effective in improving neonatal outcomes or preventing preterm birth,107,108 whereas short-term tocolysis is superior to placebo.109 Given the difficulty in predicting and preventing preterm birth, management has been focused on patients admitted for preterm labor. In the latter case, the most critical intervention to date is the administration of ACS.110 Hence, the primary objective of tocolytic administration has been shifted to preserve pregnancy for at least 48 hours to allow steroid administration, magnesium for neuroprotection, or transportation to a higher level of care facility.
paragraphs.heading: Tocolytics

paragraphs.text: In general, β-sympathomimetic tocolytic agents are β2 selective agents. β2 receptors are located in the uterus, blood vessels, bronchioles, and liver. These agents bind to β2 receptors as agonists and activate the cyclic AMP pathway (increasing adenyl cyclase), leading to intracellular depletion of free calcium, decrease in myometrial contractility, and ultimately smooth muscle relaxation. Despite being β2 selective, when administered in vivo at the dosages used pharmacologically, these agents stimulate nonselective β-receptors throughout the body, leading to many adverse effects, thus limiting their clinical use. In the United States, terbutaline is the most common β2-adrenergic agonist used in obstetrics. Ritodrine is no longer available in the US market despite being the most studied and the only US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved tocolytic agent.
paragraphs.heading: β-Sympathomimetic Agents

paragraphs.text: Initial studies supported the use of ritodrine as an efficient tocolytic agent with minimal side effects.111 In addition, these studies showed a statistically significant effect on pregnancy prolongation, with a reduction in neonatal morbidity and mortality. Subsequent reports have not been as positive with respect to neonatal morbidity and mortality, as well as maternal side effects. Ritodrine treatment was still shown to delay delivery but without significant improvement in perinatal outcomes. Relative contraindications to ritodrine use include poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, underlying cardiac disease, use of digitalis, poorly controlled hyperthyroidism, severe anemia, and hypertension. Many of the maternal side effects result from stimulation of beta receptors throughout the body. These side effects include tachycardia, hypotension, tremulousness, headache, fever, apprehension, chest tightness or pain, and shortness of breath.
paragraphs.heading: β-Sympathomimetic Agents

paragraphs.text: Terbutaline was initially studied by Ingemarsson,112 who randomly assigned 30 patients with preterm labor to either intravenous terbutaline therapy or placebo. Ingemarsson demonstrated an 80% success rate in comparison to only 20% for the placebo. Unfortunately, as with other tocolytic agents, subsequent studies did not show such positive results.
paragraphs.heading: β-Sympathomimetic Agents

paragraphs.text: Terbutaline can be administered via oral, subcutaneous, and intravenous routes. Clinicians must carefully monitor the fetus, fluid balance, cardiac status, and electrolytes when administered intravenously. Orally administered terbutaline undergoes significant first-pass metabolism in the intestinal tract, resulting in a bioavailability ranging from only 10% to 15%. The mean half-life of oral terbutaline is 3.7 hours, with increased clearance noted in pregnant patients. A subcutaneous regimen is the most common route of administration, and it usually involves 250-μg doses every 20 to 30 minutes (up to three doses with careful monitoring of maternal response and heart rate). Although subcutaneous terbutaline administration is one of the first-line tocolytic agents for preterm contractions it does not affect actual preterm birth rates.
paragraphs.heading: β-Sympathomimetic Agents

paragraphs.text: One possible explanation for the failure of long-term treatment with β-sympathomimetics is a phenomenon involving desensitization or downregulation of responsiveness to these agents. The use of a low-dose subcutaneous infusion pump attempts to overcome this problem. Lam and colleagues113 compared the use of the terbutaline pump with oral terbutaline therapy. The average duration of treatment before breakthrough of preterm labor was 9 weeks with the pump and 2 weeks with oral administration of terbutaline. The total daily drug dosage was also considerably lower (3 mg vs. 30 mg/day) with the pump.113 Guinn and associates114 conducted a prospective, doubleblind RCT comparing terbutaline pump maintenance therapy with placebo and demonstrated no significant differences in the preterm delivery rate or neonatal outcomes. A Cochrane review of 12 RCTs (1367 women) showed that β2 agonists compared to placebo were associated with decreased risk of delivery within 48 hours (RR = 0.68; 95% CI, 0.53–0.88) and within 7 days (RR = 0.8; 95% CI, 0.65–0.98), but no effect on delivery before 37 weeks (RR = 0.95; 95% CI, 0.88–1.03) and no significant effect on perinatal morbidity or mortality.115 Another review of 95 RCTs demonstrated similar results; the probability of delaying delivery within 48 hours was higher in women that received β2 agonists (OR = 2.41; 95% CI, 1.27– 4.55). β2 agonists had higher rates of adverse effects that required physicians to opt for another alternative agent (OR = 22.68; 95% CI, 7.51–73.67).109
paragraphs.heading: β-Sympathomimetic Agents

paragraphs.text: Maternal side effects and complications are similar to those stated for ritodrine. Terbutaline seems to affect the maternal heart rate less than ritodrine when administered intravenously. However, both oral and intravenous forms of terbutaline are more diabetogenic than ritodrine. Interestingly, subcutaneous administration of terbutaline via pump does not appear to increase the risk of gestational diabetes but does cause elevations in blood glucose levels in patients with diabetes. Neonatal effects of maternally administered terbutaline are similar to those of ritodrine.
paragraphs.heading: β-Sympathomimetic Agents

paragraphs.text: In 2011, a warning was released by the FDA concerning terbutaline administration to treat preterm labor secondary to serious maternal side effects.116 Another study reported an association between antenatal exposure of the drug and offspring adverse behavioral effects.117 Based on the above
paragraphs.heading: β-Sympathomimetic Agents

paragraphs.text: evidence, it is recommended to limit the use of terbutaline for only inpatient short-term tocolysis or the acute management of uterine tachysystole.
paragraphs.heading: β-Sympathomimetic Agents

paragraphs.text: Magnesium sulfate has been one of the most commonly used tocolytic agents, especially as it has been shown to have fetal neuroprotective effects. Magnesium appears to have similar efficacy with fewer side effects than terbutaline. Magnesium has tocolytic properties by acting as a calcium competitor in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, diminishing the interaction of calcium with the actin-myosin complex and interfering with myometrial repolarization.118,119 Magnesium may also block extracellular calcium influx and disrupt intracellular calcium release via inositol triphosphate pathways. Ultimately, the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction is decreased, leading to reduced amplitude of motor endplate potential and decreased sensitivity.
paragraphs.heading: Magnesium Sulfate

paragraphs.text: Magnesium sulfate is administered intravenously and is usually given as an initial bolus of 4 to 6 g over 30 minutes, followed by a maintenance infusion of 2 g/h. In contrast to intravenous magnesium sulfate for tocolysis, oral magnesium therapy is ineffective for treating preterm labor.
paragraphs.heading: Magnesium Sulfate

paragraphs.text: Magnesium is a bivalent cation, and it is the second most common intracellular cation.120 Less than 1% is found extracellularly. It is most commonly found in bone (53%), followed by myocytes (27%).121 Most extracellular magnesium is in ionized form, and its serum level drops in pregnancy secondary to hemodilution of pregnancy.122,123 It is transported across the cell membrane through a sodium adenosine triphosphate-dependent transporter.
paragraphs.heading: Magnesium Sulfate

paragraphs.text: Magnesium is almost exclusively excreted by the kidneys. Approximately 75% of the infused dose of magnesium is excreted during the actual infusion, with 90% excretion by 24 hours. Magnesium is reabsorbed at the renal level by a transport-limited mechanism; therefore the glomerular filtration rate significantly affects excretion. Serum magnesium levels of 5 to 8 mg/dL are considered therapeutic for inhibiting myometrial activity on the basis of in vitro studies. When cessation of uterine activity has been achieved, the patient is maintained at the lowest possible rate for 12 to 24 hours and then weaned off as tolerated.
paragraphs.heading: Magnesium Sulfate

paragraphs.text: Maternal side effects caused by magnesium sulfate are typically dose related. Common side effects include flushing, heat intolerance, nausea, headache, drowsiness, and blurry vision. Constant monitoring of deep tendon reflexes is mandatory to avoid toxicity. Diminished deep tendon reflexes occur when serum magnesium levels reach or exceed 12 mg/dL (10 mEq/L). Significant respiratory depression can occur as serum levels reach 14 to 18 mg/dL (12–14 mEq/L), and cardiac arrest may occur with levels greater than 18 mg/dL (15 mEq/L). In general, respiratory depression does not occur before the loss of deep tendon reflexes. The toxic effects of high magnesium levels can be rapidly reversed with the infusion of 1 g of calcium gluconate.
paragraphs.heading: Magnesium Sulfate

paragraphs.text: Magnesium sulfate is absolutely contraindicated in patients with myasthenia gravis or heart block. It is relatively
paragraphs.heading: Magnesium Sulfate

paragraphs.text: contraindicated in patients with underlying renal disease or a history of a recent myocardial infarction. It is also relatively contraindicated in women who are receiving calcium channel blockers.
paragraphs.heading: Magnesium Sulfate

paragraphs.text: Pulmonary edema has been reported to have an incidence of approximately 1%. The risk for pulmonary edema is increased in patients with multifetal gestations and in those receiving combined tocolytic therapy. Because of the potential risk of fluid overload and the subsequent development of pulmonary edema, periodic assessment of fluid balance is essential.
paragraphs.heading: Magnesium Sulfate

paragraphs.text: Magnesium readily crosses the placenta, achieving steady-state fetal levels within hours after the start of treatment. No significant alterations in neurologic status or Apgar scores have been reported with mean umbilical cord concentrations of 3.6 mg/dL. At a cord concentration between 4 and 11 mg/dL, though, apnea, hypotension, refractory bradycardia, respiratory depression, hypotonia, and motor depression have been reported. Long-term use of magnesium (greater than 7 days) has been shown to cause fetal bone loss in the proximal humerus, a finding of unclear significance as these cases were based on unsolicited reports to the FDA’s Adverse Event Reporting System (18 cases) and epidemiologic analysis with design concerns.124–129
paragraphs.heading: Magnesium Sulfate

paragraphs.text: Consequently, the FDA released a warning against using magnesium sulfate for more than 5 to 7 days for the sole purpose of preventing or treating preterm labor. As a result, the safety drug classification for magnesium was changed from class A to class D.130 The ACOG and SMFM followed with a statement advising obstetricians to continue using magnesium for the following indications131: • Seizure prophylaxis in preeclampsia or treatment of
paragraphs.heading: Magnesium Sulfate

paragraphs.text: eclampsia • Fetal neuroprotection before anticipated early preterm
paragraphs.heading: Magnesium Sulfate

paragraphs.text: (less than 32 weeks of gestation) delivery • Short-term prolongation of pregnancy (up to 48 hours)
paragraphs.heading: Magnesium Sulfate

paragraphs.text: to allow for the administration of ACS in pregnant women who are at risk of preterm delivery within 7 days Mercer et al.132 reviewed the role of magnesium sulfate as a tocolytic agent. Only three out of the four RCTs comparing magnesium sulfate as control or placebo evaluated its effect on delivery within 48 hours or 7 days.133–136 Magnesium did not affect preterm delivery within 48 hours (RR = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.54–1.03). The same results were noted for delivery before 37 weeks or within 7 days. There was also no improvement in neonatal morbidities. Compared to magnesium, alternative tocolytic agents (total of 16 RCTs: beta mimetics, calcium channel blockers, and cyclooxygenase inhibitors) did not show any additional improvements in delivery at 48 hours, 7 days, preterm delivery, or LBW. These findings were supported in a meta-analysis of 37 trials, a total of 3571 women and over 3600 babies.137 Compared to no treatment or placebo, magnesium sulfate did not reduce birth within 48 hours (RR = 0.56; 95% CI, 0.27–1.14; three trials; N = 182) nor did it improve neonatal outcomes. When compared to
paragraphs.heading: Magnesium Sulfate

paragraphs.text: other tocolytics (33 trials), magnesium sulfate was neither less nor more effective.
paragraphs.heading: Magnesium Sulfate

paragraphs.text: Initial observational studies suggesting the beneficial role of magnesium in decreasing neonatal neurologic morbidities occurred in the early 1990s.138–140 Since then, several RCTs have been performed to elucidate this role.141–146 Mittendorf et al.144,145 included women in preterm labor before 34 weeks and cervical dilation greater than 4 cm (N = 57) that were randomized to either magnesium or placebo. Infant death was not increased in the neuroprotection group, but when performing a secondary analysis of magnesium sulfate versus other tocolytic agents, infant death was significantly increased in the former group. This led to the early termination of the trial. This was followed by a multicenter placebo-controlled trial that included women with planned or expected delivery within 24 hours at less than 30 weeks’ gestation. Infant death, cerebral palsy, or both by 2 years of age did not differ in the women who received magnesium.141 Secondary analysis showed that infants exposed to magnesium had less frequent inability to walk without assistance. Another placebo-controlled trial included 564 gravid women less than 33 weeks’ gestation, with planned or expected delivery within 24 hours.143 There was no significant difference between infant death, severe white matter injury, or both before discharge or in a 2-year follow-up among groups. Although there was no decrease in cerebral palsy in the long-term follow-up, the authors reported a reduction in “gross motor dysfunction” or “motor” or “cognitive dysfunction” in the magnesium group. This was followed by a large multicenter trial that included 2241 gravid women at less than 32 weeks’ gestation with imminent risk of delivery before 32 weeks’ gestation.146 Subjects were randomized to receive either magnesium or a placebo. The magnesium treatment group had a significant reduction in moderate to severe cerebral palsy. When performing a prespecified secondary analysis, magnesium reduced cerebral palsy by greater than 30% (4.2 vs. 7.3%; P = .004). Pooling the results from the above RCTs, Doyle et al.147 suggested that antenatal administration of magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection decreased the incidence of cerebral palsy (RR = 0.71; 95% CI, 0.74–0.98). These results were confirmed in two other metanalyses.148,149 Based on the above evidence, magnesium sulfate, when given before early preterm delivery, reduces the risk of cerebral palsy in surviving infants.
paragraphs.heading: Magnesium Sulfate

paragraphs.text: Because prostaglandins appear to play a pivotal role in the pathway leading to preterm labor and delivery, attempts to interrupt this cascade of events are of utmost importance. Prostaglandins are 20-carbon cyclopentane carboxylic acids derived from membrane phospholipids (primarily arachidonic acid) via the enzymatic action of phospholipase A and cyclooxygenase (prostaglandin synthetase). Because several drugs are available that inhibit the activity of prostaglandin synthetase (e.g., aspirin, ibuprofen, indomethacin, sulindac), this pathway represents a key target for pharmacologic intervention. Of these drugs, indomethacin has been the
paragraphs.heading: Prostaglandin Synthetase Inhibitors

paragraphs.text: most extensively studied. It is a reversible, nonspecific cyclooxygenase inhibitor.
paragraphs.heading: Prostaglandin Synthetase Inhibitors

paragraphs.text: Haas and colleagues150 sought to determine the optimal first-line tocolytic agent for the treatment of premature labor. They performed a quantitative analysis that included 58 RCTs. They evaluated outcomes of delay of delivery for 48 hours and 7 days, term deliveries, adverse effects causing discontinuation of therapy, RDS, and neonatal survival. A random-effects meta-analysis showed that all tocolytic agents were superior to placebo or control groups in delaying delivery for at least 48 hours (53% for placebo compared with 75%–93% for the tocolytics) and 7 days (39% for placebo compared with 61%–78% for the tocolytics). No statistically significant differences were found for the other outcomes, including the incidence of respiratory distress and rates of neonatal survival. Importantly, this decision model demonstrated that prostaglandin inhibitors provided the best balance between tolerance and delay of delivery, concluding that these agents may be considered the optimal first-line agent for tocolysis prior to 32 weeks of gestation.
paragraphs.heading: Prostaglandin Synthetase Inhibitors

paragraphs.text: A meta-analysis showed that out of 1000 gravid women receiving prostaglandin inhibitors, only 80 would deliver within 48 hours versus 182 for the subsequent best treatment. The authors concluded that prostaglandin inhibitors should be considered first-line for preterm labor before 37 weeks.150 In a network meta-analysis, prostaglandin inhibitors were shown to be more efficacious than placebo in delaying delivery by 48 hours (OR = 5.94; 95% CI, 2.14–12.34).109 In this analysis, the authors suggested that this class of tocolytics was more efficient than any other agent and ranked prostaglandin inhibitors in the top three most efficacious tocolytics (96% probability).
paragraphs.heading: Prostaglandin Synthetase Inhibitors

paragraphs.text: A 2015 Cochrane review identified two trials comparing prostaglandin inhibitors to placebo in treating preterm labor.151,152 The authors reported a nonsignificant trend toward a lower risk of delivery before 37 weeks’ gestation within 48 hours (RR = 0.20; 95% CI, 0.03–1.28) or within 7 days of receiving the tocolytic agent (RR = 0.41; CI, 0.1– 1.66). Compared with any beta-agonists, indomethacin showed a significantly lower rate of preterm deliveries earlier than 37 weeks’ gestation within 48 hours of administration (RR = 0.27; 95% CI, 0.08–0.9; two trials; N = 100) and was as effective as nifedipine (RR = 1.08; 95% CI, 0.58–2.01; two trials; N = 230).
paragraphs.heading: Prostaglandin Synthetase Inhibitors

paragraphs.text: Indomethacin is usually administered orally or rectally in divided doses. A 50-mg loading dose is followed by 25 mg orally every 6 hours for up to 48 hours. Indomethacin blood concentrations usually peak 1 to 2 hours after oral administration, whereas rectal administration is associated with levels that peak slightly earlier. Approximately 90% of the drug is protein bound, undergoing excretion by the kidneys unchanged. Indomethacin readily crosses the placenta, equilibrating with maternal concentrations 5 hours after
paragraphs.heading: Prostaglandin Synthetase Inhibitors

paragraphs.text: administration. The half-life is approximately 15 hours in term neonates and somewhat shorter in preterm neonates.
paragraphs.heading: Prostaglandin Synthetase Inhibitors

paragraphs.text: Most studies have limited the use of indomethacin to 24 to 48 hours’ duration because of concerns regarding the development of oligohydramnios and constriction of the ductus arteriosus. These effects may lead to fetal pulmonary hypertension and neonatal persistent pulmonary hypertension.153 If more extended therapy is required, close fetal monitoring is indicated, including weekly amniotic fluid indexes to evaluate for oligohydramnios and ductal velocity assessment to examine for ductal constriction or closure. If the amniotic fluid volume (measured as the fluid depth in the four quadrants of the uterus) falls below 5 cm or if the pulsatility index of the ductus arteriosus decreases to less than 2 cm/s, discontinuation of therapy should be considered. Several long-term studies have evaluated the efficacy and safety of this drug.
paragraphs.heading: Prostaglandin Synthetase Inhibitors

paragraphs.text: Maternal contraindications to indomethacin use include peptic ulcer disease, allergies to indomethacin or related compounds, significant hematologic disease, hepatic or renal dysfunction, and drug-induced asthma. Significant maternal side effects are minimal and infrequent. Gastrointestinal upset may occur but can be relieved by either taking the medication with meals or using an antacid.
paragraphs.heading: Prostaglandin Synthetase Inhibitors

paragraphs.text: Fetal contraindications include pre-existing oligohydramnios, gestational age greater than 32 weeks, and congenital fetal heart disease in which the fetus is dependent on the ductus arteriosus for circulation. Several fetal side effects have been reported with the use of indomethacin. It has been associated with oligohydramnios. Although indomethacin has been shown to reduce fetal urine output, these levels return to baseline within 24 hours after discontinuation. Examining the effect on renal artery blood flow, Mari and colleagues154 found no change in the pulsatility index in 17 fetuses during the first 24 hours of indomethacin therapy, suggesting that renal artery constriction and a decrease in renal blood flow are responsible for the reduction in urine output. Regardless, oligohydramnios is usually seen with long-term therapy of more than 7 days, although this onset seems to vary from one patient to another and is somewhat unpredictable. Therefore the amniotic fluid index should be followed while the patient is receiving therapy. Resolution of oligohydramnios usually occurs within 48 hours of discontinuation of treatment. Although persistent anuria, neonatal death, and microcystic renal lesions have been reported with prenatal indomethacin exposure, most infants were exposed to doses greater than 200 mg/d for up to 36 weeks of gestation with inadequate amniotic fluid volume assessment.
paragraphs.heading: Prostaglandin Synthetase Inhibitors

paragraphs.text: Another significant potential complication of prenatal indomethacin exposure is the development of ductus arteriosus constriction or closure. It is theorized that ductal constriction or closure leads to diverging right ventricular blood flow into the pulmonary vasculature. With time, this causes pulmonary arterial hypertrophy. After birth, relative pulmonary hypertension can cause right-to-left blood shunting through the foramen ovale and away from the lungs,
paragraphs.heading: Prostaglandin Synthetase Inhibitors

paragraphs.text: resulting in persistent pulmonary hypertension. This complication has been described with long-term indomethacin therapy but not in fetuses exposed to the drug for less than 48 hours.155 Development of ductus arteriosus constriction can be identified by Doppler echocardiography. Moise and colleagues153 detected ductal constriction in 7 of 14 fetuses exposed to indomethacin in utero, with these changes seen up to 72 hours after initiation of treatment. There was no correlation with maternal drug levels, and the constriction resolved within 24 hours after treatment was stopped. No cases of persistent pulmonary hypertension were reported in this case series. The observed effects on ductal constriction have been shown to increase with advancing gestational age, with 50% of fetuses demonstrating constriction when exposed at 32 weeks’ gestation. Based on these data, indomethacin therapy should be discontinued by 32 weeks at the latest.
paragraphs.heading: Prostaglandin Synthetase Inhibitors

paragraphs.text: Yet another reported complication is an increased risk of necrotizing enterocolitis in infants exposed to indomethacin prenatally. This complication is seen explicitly in neonates born at less than 30 weeks’ gestation. Norton and coworkers156 performed a retrospective case-control study of 57 neonates delivered at less than 30 weeks’ gestation after recent antenatal exposure to indomethacin, comparing them to 57 matched control fetuses. In this study, the incidence of necrotizing enterocolitis was 29% in the indomethacin group versus 8% in the control group. Additionally, a statistically higher incidence of grade II to IV intraventricular hemorrhage and patent ductus arteriosus was noted in the indomethacin treatment group.156 No correlations were made regarding duration of treatment or the time frame between exposure and delivery. Although these results are of concern, indomethacin appears to be a relatively safe and effective tocolytic agent when used with the appropriate caution (less than 48 hours’ duration of therapy in pregnancies only at less than 32 weeks’ gestation).
paragraphs.heading: Prostaglandin Synthetase Inhibitors

paragraphs.text: Sulindac is another nonselective prostaglandin synthetase inhibitor closely related to indomethacin in structure. Although this agent has been reported to have fewer side effects than indomethacin when used for tocolysis, preliminary experiences also indicate that oral sulindac therapy may not be very useful in preventing preterm birth. Kramer and colleagues156a conducted a randomized, double-blind study to evaluate the comparative effects of sulindac and terbutaline on fetal urine production and amniotic fluid volume. Sulindac administration also resulted in a significant decrease in fetal urine flow and amniotic fluid volume. Additionally, two fetuses developed severe ductus arteriosus constriction. These data suggest that sulindac shares many fetal side effects associated with indomethacin.
paragraphs.heading: Prostaglandin Synthetase Inhibitors

paragraphs.text: In the setting of inflammation, cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) is preferentially upregulated. Given that many early preterm labor and delivery cases are likely related to underlying
paragraphs.heading: Prostaglandin Synthetase Inhibitors

paragraphs.text: occult infection or inflammation of the upper genital tract, specific targeting of COX-2 represents a logical target for tocolytic therapy. In addition, by explicitly targeting COX- 2, there is a theoretical potential for reducing some of the untoward renal, gastrointestinal, and cardiac side effects that are relatively common with the nonselective COX inhibitors.
paragraphs.heading: Prostaglandin Synthetase Inhibitors

paragraphs.text: The emergence of several selective COX-2 inhibitors (e.g., celecoxib, nimesulide) led to several investigations designed to evaluate the efficacy of these agents for the treatment of preterm labor.157–159 For example, Stika and colleagues159 reported findings from a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of celecoxib versus indomethacin to treat preterm labor. In this small study of 24 women, no difference between the two agents was noted with regard to the length of prolongation of pregnancy. Although a transient decrease in amniotic fluid volume was noted with both agents, mean maximal ductus arteriosus blood flow velocity, which was increased with indomethacin, was not significantly altered in women receiving celecoxib. Sawdy and colleagues157,158 conducted a similar randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of nimesulide versus indomethacin versus sulindac to treat preterm labor. Similar reductions were noted among the three treatment groups with regard to amniotic fluid volume, fetal urine production, and ductus arteriosus Doppler pulsatility index over the initial 48-hour treatment period. To date, no large trials have been reported that have critically evaluated the therapeutic efficacy of the COX-2 inhibitors to prevent preterm birth or reduce neonatal morbidity in women presenting with preterm labor.
paragraphs.heading: Prostaglandin Synthetase Inhibitors

paragraphs.text: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (nifedipine and nicardipine) act on L-type calcium channels blocking transmembrane calcium influx into myometrial cells; other mechanisms include an increase in the efflux of intracellular calcium and hindering its release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Low intracellular calcium levels counteract myosin light chain kinase activation, preventing myometrial contraction. Most clinical investigations evaluating calcium channel blockers for treating preterm labor have used nifedipine. Ulmsten and associates160 first reported using nifedipine to treat preterm labor in a study involving 10 patients, with resultant cessation of uterine activity for 3 days in all patients receiving treatment. In a subsequent three-armed randomized control study, Read and colleagues161 reported that the nifedipine group had a significantly longer time interval from presentation to delivery than either ritodrine or placebo. These results suggest that nifedipine is as effective as ritodrine in prolonging pregnancy, with far fewer side effects causing discontinuation of therapy.
paragraphs.heading: Calcium Channel Blockers

paragraphs.text: Nifedipine can be administered orally or in a sublingual form. The gastrointestinal tract rapidly absorbs it, with detectable blood levels attained within 5 minutes of sublingual administration. Duration of action is up to 6 hours, and its half-life is 2 to 3 hours. Nifedipine readily crosses
paragraphs.heading: Calcium Channel Blockers

paragraphs.text: the placenta, and serum concentrations of the fetus and the mother are comparable. Most studies used an initial loading dose of 10 to 30 mg orally, followed by 10 to 20 mg every 4 to 8 hours.162 Up to 30 mg can be administered per dose, but such high amounts may result in more side effects. Maximum daily dose is 180 mg. The sublingual form should be avoided to treat preterm labor because it acts more rapidly than the oral form, resulting in an increased risk of acute hypotension.
paragraphs.heading: Calcium Channel Blockers

paragraphs.text: Contraindications to nifedipine, or any of the calcium channel blockers, include hypersensitivity to the drug, hypotension, preload-dependent cardiac lesions (e.g., aortic stenosis), and decompensated congestive heart failure. Concurrent use of calcium channel blockers and magnesium sulfate can result in profound hypotension and should be avoided. Maternal side effects, including dizziness, lightheadedness, flushing, headache, palpitations, and peripheral edema, result from the potent vasodilatory effects of these agents. These side effects occur in approximately 17% of patients and are severe enough to warrant discontinuation of therapy in only 2% to 5% of women.
paragraphs.heading: Calcium Channel Blockers

paragraphs.text: Studies evaluating the fetal effects of calcium channel blocker therapy have been limited. One obstacle that limits the performance of large trials is the potentially adverse effects that calcium channel blockers may have on uteroplacental blood flow. Although uteroplacental blood flow appears to be reduced in animal models, studies examining blood flow in humans have yet to demonstrate any significant adverse effects on fetal or uteroplacental blood flow during treatment with nifedipine. Additional studies are needed to thoroughly evaluate the potential fetal effects of calcium channel blocker therapy.
paragraphs.heading: Calcium Channel Blockers

paragraphs.text: Several meta-analyses support the use of nifedipine as an effective acute tocolytic agent. A Cochrane review elaborating the role of calcium channel blockers in acute tocolysis included 38 RCTs (N = 3550 patients). A review included 26 RCTs (N = 2179 patients); nifedipine was not superior to other tocolytic agents in preventing birth within 48 hours. However, compared to β2-adrenergic agonists, it delayed delivery within 7 days and prolonged gestation past 37 weeks.162 Minimal adverse effects were noted in the nifedipine group. Network meta-analysis and decision analysis suggested that nifedipine be considered a first-line tocolytic with regard to various important outcomes.109,150 A subsequent review compared the use of calcium channel blockers with no treatment or placebo for preterm labor and found that calcium channel blockers decreased the risk of delivery within 48 hours (RR = 0.30; 95% CI, 0.21–0.43; two trials; N = 173).163 This was not noted compared to other tocolytic agents (for β2-adrenergic agonists, RR = 0.86; 95% CI, 0.67–1.10; 19 trials; N = 1505). With regard to pregnancy prolongation (mean difference, 4.38 days; 95% CI, 0.25–8.52), neonatal severe adverse events (intraventricular hemorrhage, RDS, jaundice, and necrotizing enterocolitis) and adverse maternal outcomes (RR = 0.36; 95% CI, 0.24–0.53), calcium channel blockers were more beneficial
paragraphs.heading: Calcium Channel Blockers

paragraphs.text: over β2-adrenergic agonists. The authors concluded that these agents effectively delayed delivery, permitting time for administration of ACS and transportation to higher level care.163
paragraphs.heading: Calcium Channel Blockers

paragraphs.text: Other investigators regard nifedipine as a cost-effective option, with cost taking into account both the drug’s price and the costs of treating adverse events. Hayes and associates164 determined the optimal tocolytic based on a costdecision analysis. A PubMed search of commonly used tocolytics was performed to assess the probability of adverse events. The cost for an agent was determined by acquisition cost and the likelihood and cost of adverse events. Nineteen clinical trials yielded a cohort of 1073 patients (indomethacin, 176; magnesium sulfate, 451; nifedipine, 176; terbutaline, 270). The probability of adverse events was 58% for terbutaline, 22% for magnesium sulfate, 27% for nifedipine, and 11% for indomethacin. Nifedipine and indomethacin were the least expensive treatment options at less than $20 each, compared with $200 for magnesium sulfate and $400 for terbutaline, primarily related to the cost of monitoring and treating adverse events. They concluded that if one elects to proceed with tocolysis, either nifedipine or indomethacin should be the agent of choice based on this cost-decision analysis. These findings essentially agree with the recommendations by Haas and coworkers,150 who recommended prostaglandin inhibitors as the top three most efficacious tocolytic agents.
paragraphs.heading: Calcium Channel Blockers

paragraphs.text: Oxytocin antagonists are a novel category of agents that may be useful for treating preterm labor. Based on the theory that preterm labor may result from early gap junction formation coupled with a rise in oxytocin receptor concentration, oxytocin may be an essential hormone in the evolution of parturition. Oxytocin is intimately involved in the physiologic pathways leading to both term and preterm labor. Whereas the role of oxytocin may represent the terminal event for various pathophysiology pathways leading to preterm delivery, it represents an essential central pathway that may be amenable to therapeutic intervention. Because the primary cellular targets for oxytocin are the myometrium and decidua, oxytocin antagonists have the theoretical benefit of being highly organ specific with minimal potential for adverse side effects.
paragraphs.heading: Oxytocin Antagonists

paragraphs.text: Oxytocin antagonists have been shown to effectively inhibit oxytocin-induced uterine contractions in both in vitro and in vivo animal models. The initial human experience with oxytocin antagonist therapy came from several small uncontrolled studies performed in the late 1980s.165,166 Akerlund and colleagues165 reported on a series of 13 patients who received a short-term infusion of an oxytocin antagonist. This therapy inhibited premature labor in all patients, but 10 subsequently required treatment with β-agonists. Similarly, Anderson and associates166 reported their experience with 12 patients between 27 and 33 weeks of gestation treated with a competitive oxytocin receptor antagonist for 1.5 to 13 hours. Of these 12 patients, 9 had
paragraphs.heading: Oxytocin Antagonists

paragraphs.text: an arrest of contractions and the remaining 3 had no change in contraction frequency.
paragraphs.heading: Oxytocin Antagonists

paragraphs.text: The most studied oxytocin antagonist is atosiban. Atosiban is a nonapeptide oxytocin analog that competitively antagonizes the oxytocin-vasopressin receptor and can thus inhibit oxytocin-induced uterine contractions. Atosiban is typically administered intravenously. Standard dosing recommendations are for a single initial intravenous bolus of 6.75 mg of atosiban followed by an intravenous infusion of 300 μg/min for the first 3 hours and then 100 μg/min for up to 45 hours. Maintenance therapy can be implemented at a rate of 30 μg/ min via continuous infusion. The total duration of treatment should not exceed 48 hours, and the total atosiban dose should not exceed 330 mg. It appears to have an excellent maternal safety profile, with rare and non-life-threatening side effects (hypersensitivity and injection site–related reactions).
paragraphs.heading: Oxytocin Antagonists

paragraphs.text: Several prospective, randomized, masked clinical trials have demonstrated that atosiban effectively diminishes uterine contractions in women with threatened preterm birth without causing significant maternal, fetal, or neonatal adverse effects. In a prospective, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter investigation of 501 women with documented preterm labor, Romero and coworkers167 demonstrated that atosiban was significantly more effective than placebo in delaying delivery for 24 hours, 48 hours, and 7 days. Importantly, however, the median from the start of therapy to delivery or treatment failure was not significantly different between the study groups, nor were perinatal outcomes. In this trial, extremely premature fetal death rates were higher in the atosiban group, despite not reaching statistical significance. The lack of stratification may explain these concerns by gestation in the randomization method of the trial (the atosiban group had significantly higher numbers of women less than 26 weeks’ gestation) and the presence of other significant confounders. Moutquin and colleagues168 compared atosiban to ritodrine for the treatment of preterm labor. In this multicenter, double-blind RCT of 212 women, the investigators demonstrated that the tocolytic efficacy of atosiban was comparable to that of conventional ritodrine therapy in terms of the cessation of preterm labor and neonatal outcomes, with fewer adverse side effects reported with atosiban. The potential use of atosiban for maintenance therapy in patients with arrested preterm labor has also been evaluated. Valenzuela and associates169 reported experience from a multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 513 women with arrested preterm labor. Median time from the start of maintenance therapy to the first recurrence of labor was significantly longer for women treated with atosiban (32.6 days) than those treated with placebo (27.6 days). Another trial by Salim and colleagues170 compared atosiban to nifedipine, showing that more women undergoing tocolysis with atosiban remained pregnant after 48 hours, but nifedipine had longer lasting effects (i.e., patients more likely to stay pregnant after 7 days). These data suggest that atosiban may help delay delivery 24 to 48 hours in the setting of preterm labor, but this delay appears to have minimal impact on neonatal outcomes.
paragraphs.heading: Oxytocin Antagonists

paragraphs.text: In the Haas network meta-analysis, atosiban was superior to placebo in postponing delivery within 48 hours (OR = 2.02; 95% CI, 1.1–3.8), but compared to other tocolytics, its efficacy was not better.109 In an updated Cochrane review (14 studies, N = 2485), atosiban was not superior to β2agonists, placebo, or calcium channel blockers in neonatal outcomes nor in tocolytic efficacy.171 Compared to placebo, atosiban did not decrease the birth rate within 48 hours of initiation of treatment (RR = 1.05; 95% CI, 0.15–7.43; two trials; N = 152), the preterm birth rate at <28 weeks of gestation (RR = 3.11; 95% CI, 1.02–9.51; one trial; N = 501), or preterm birth rate at <37 weeks (RR = 1.17; 95% CI, 0.99–1.37; two trials; N = 664). Lower infant birth weight and higher drug adverse effects were noted in the atosiban group (weighted mean difference, –138.86 g; 95% CI, –250.53 to –27.18; RR = 4.02; 95% CI, 2.05–7.85, respectively). In the same review, the rates of birth at <48 hours were not different when compared to beta-agonists (RR = 0.89; 95% CI, 0.66–1.22; eight trials; N = 1389) and calcium channel blockers (RR = 1.09; 95% CI, 0.44–2.73; two trials; N = 225).
paragraphs.heading: Oxytocin Antagonists

paragraphs.text: Further well-designed, randomized, placebo-controlled trials are needed to more clearly elucidate the role, if any, of oxytocin antagonists in the therapeutic armamentarium for preterm labor.
paragraphs.heading: Oxytocin Antagonists

paragraphs.text: Nitric oxide is a potent endogenous hormone that facilitates smooth muscle relaxation in the vasculature, gastrointestinal tract, and uterus. Interest has arisen in the potential use of nitric oxide donors (e.g., nitroglycerin, glycerol trinitrate) as tocolytic agents. Lees and colleagues172 compared transdermal glycerol trinitrate to ritodrine for tocolysis in a randomized investigation of 245 women with documented preterm labor between 24 and 36 weeks’ gestation. These investigators found no significant differences in either tocolytic effect or neonatal outcomes, but glycerol trinitrate was associated with fewer maternal side effects.
paragraphs.heading: Nitric Oxide Donors

paragraphs.text: El-Sayed and colleagues173 evaluated 31 women with documented preterm labor before 35 weeks’ gestation in a randomized comparison of intravenous nitroglycerin and magnesium sulfate. Tocolytic failure (continued need for tocolysis after 12 hours of treatment) was significantly more common in patients treated with nitroglycerin than in women treated with magnesium sulfate. Notably, 25% of the patients treated with nitroglycerin experienced significant hypotension, requiring treatment discontinuation.
paragraphs.heading: Nitric Oxide Donors

paragraphs.text: An updated Cochrane review on this topic included 12 RCTs (N = 1227 women).174 Three trials compared this class of drugs to a placebo. Delaying delivery for 48 hours was not different among groups (RR = 1.19; 95% CI, 0.74–1.9; two trials; N = 186). The same observation was noted compared to other tocolytic agents. The network meta-analysis by Haas et al.109 suggested that these agents will have at best a 4% probability of delaying delivery for 48 hours and 10% probability of being the best agent based on maternal side effects.
paragraphs.heading: Nitric Oxide Donors

paragraphs.text: Given the small number of trials available, the data are not sufficient to determine whether nitric oxide donors are effective tocolytics. Therefore clinical use of these agents for the treatment of preterm labor should only be investigational.
paragraphs.heading: Nitric Oxide Donors

paragraphs.text: Before 37 weeks of gestation, PPROM complicates approximately 3% of pregnancies and accounts for one-third of all preterm births. Also, PPROM is associated with significant maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality related to infection, umbilical cord compression, placental abruption, and preterm birth. Preterm labor, especially at less than 30 weeks’ gestation, has been associated with occult upper genital tract infection. Many of the bacterial species involved in this occult infection are capable of inciting an inflammatory response, which ultimately may culminate in preterm labor and delivery. On this basis, antibiotics have been suggested as a potential therapy for the treatment or prevention of spontaneous preterm birth.
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: Elder and associates175 provided the first insights into the potential use of antibiotics to prevent preterm birth, demonstrating that treating asymptomatic pregnant patients with daily tetracycline therapy resulted in fewer preterm deliveries. Despite these promising results, subsequent prospective trials using antibiotics in women colonized with Chlamydia, Ureaplasma, and group B streptococci have shown no significant decrease in preterm birth. The association of bacterial vaginosis (BV) with preterm birth prompted renewed interest in the potential use of antibiotics to prevent preterm birth in asymptomatic women. Several prospective trials have demonstrated that antenatal treatment of BV in asymptomatic women at high risk for spontaneous preterm delivery may reduce the subsequent spontaneous preterm delivery rate. For example, Hauth and colleagues42,176 conducted a prospective, randomized, double-blind, placebocontrolled study of 624 women who were at risk for preterm delivery (e.g., history of previous preterm birth or prepregnancy weight of less than 50 kg). These women were randomized to metronidazole (250 mg three times a day for 7 days) and erythromycin (333 mg three times a day for 14 days) therapy or placebo. The investigators observed a significant reduction in the rate of preterm birth (49% vs. 31%) in women with BV who received antibiotic treatment. In women without BV, antibacterial treatment was associated with a significant increase in the preterm birth rate (13.4% vs. 4.8%, P < .02). Carey and coworkers41 further evaluated the use of metronidazole to prevent preterm birth. In a prospective, randomized, placebo-controlled study of 1704 low-risk asymptomatic women with BV, treatment with metronidazole was not found to reduce the risk for preterm delivery or adverse perinatal outcomes. Based on these data, screening and treatment of BV in women at high risk for preterm delivery may be an effective treatment to prevent preterm birth. Still, nondiscriminative screening and treatment of asymptomatic low-risk women do not appear to offer any clear benefit.
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: Several investigations have explored targeted antibiotic therapy using fetal fibronectin as a screening tool to identify asymptomatic women at the greatest risk for early preterm birth induced by infection or inflammation.176–178 Goldenberg and colleagues178 first explored this interesting theory. In a subgroup analysis of women enrolled in a trial of antibiotic therapy for the prevention of preterm birth, 70 women with BV and a positive fetal fibronectin test were randomized to receive either two courses of metronidazole treatment or placebo. Patients who received metronidazole treatment had a lower incidence of preterm birth (8%) than the placebo group (16%), but this difference did not reach statistical significance (P = .311).178 Despite the lack of statistical significance, this trend was compelling enough to lead to several randomized clinical trials designed to further evaluate the efficacy of antibiotic therapy in women with a positive fetal fibronectin test.176–178
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: In the largest of these trials, Andrews and colleagues177 screened 16,317 women between 21 and 25 gestational weeks with cervical or vaginal swabs for fetal fibronectin. Of the screened women, 1079 (6.6%) had a positive fetal fibronectin test (50 ng/mL or greater), 759 of whom consented to randomization to receive a 10-day course of metronidazole (250 mg orally three times per day) and erythromycin (250 mg orally four times per day) or identical placebo pills. The primary outcome of this investigation was spontaneous delivery before 37 weeks’ gestation. No difference was observed in the incidence of spontaneous preterm birth prior to 37 weeks’ (14.4% vs. 12.4%; P = .43), 35 weeks’ (6.9% vs. 7.5%; P = .76), or 32 weeks’ (4.3% vs. 2.2%; P = .12) gestation between the antibiotic-treated women and the placebo-treated women. Interestingly, among women with a prior spontaneous preterm delivery, the rate of recurrent spontaneous preterm birth before 37 weeks was significantly higher in the metronidazole plus erythromycin group than in the placebo group (46.7% vs. 23.9%; RR = 1.95; 95% CI, 1.03–3.71; P = .04).179
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: The findings of the MFMU Network trial were consistent with those of two similar studies.176 It is clear from these investigations that the use of antibiotic therapy in asymptomatic women with a positive cervical or vaginal fetal fibronectin test in the late mid-trimester does not decrease the incidence of spontaneous preterm delivery.
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: In contrast, the use of antibiotics for the treatment of acute preterm labor has had mixed results.180 More than 15 investigations have been reported that evaluate the efficacy of different antibiotic regimens (i.e., ampicillin, erythromycin, clindamycin, ceftizoxime, amoxicillin-clavulanate, ampicillin plus erythromycin, ampicillin plus sulbactam, ampicillin plus metronidazole, amoxicillin-clavulanate plus erythromycin, and mezlocillin plus erythromycin) for the prevention of spontaneous preterm birth in women presenting with preterm labor and intact membranes.181 These studies have yielded inconsistent results about the benefits of antibiotics in prolonging pregnancy or improving short- and long-term neonatal outcomes.180 The ORACLE II trial, the largest such study to date, was a multicenter,
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: prospective, randomized study of antibiotics (erythromycin alone, amoxicillin-clavulanate alone, or a combination of both agents) versus placebo in 6295 women with preterm labor and intact membranes.182 This study failed to demonstrate significant prolongation of pregnancy or an improvement in a predefined composite neonatal outcome among women receiving any of the antibiotic regimens. An updated Cochrane review further evaluated the use of antibiotics in this population of women (14 trials; N = 7837).183 The reviewers concluded as follows: (1) antibiotic use was associated with a significant prolongation of pregnancy (5.59 days; 95% CI, 0.31–10.87), but birth rates within 48 hours (RR = 1.04; 95% CI 0.89– 1.23) or 7 days from randomization (RR = 0.98; 95% CI, 0.87–1.10) were not different; (2) maternal infection was decreased in women receiving antibiotic treatment (OR = 0.74; 95% CI, 0.63–0.86); (3) the rate of birth prior to 36 or 37 weeks’ gestation was not significantly reduced with maternal treatment using antibiotics (OR = 0.98; 95% CI, 0.92–1.05); and (4) there was a trend toward a decreased risk of neonatal sepsis in the setting of maternal treatment with antibiotics (OR = 0.86; 95% CI, 0.64–1.17). Surprisingly, the meta-analysis also demonstrated an increased perinatal mortality rate associated with maternal antibiotic treatment (OR = 1.57; 95% CI, 1.03–2.40). The authors therefore concluded that despite the prolongation in time to delivery, antibiotic treatment for women in preterm labor with intact membranes in the absence of signs of infection should not be given. Antibiotics do play a clear role in the prevention of neonatal sepsis caused by group B streptococci. In women perceived to be at an acute risk for preterm delivery, antibiotic therapy with appropriate agents against group B streptococci should be continued until either negative cultures are obtained or imminent delivery is no longer anticipated.
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: In the setting of preterm delivery caused by PPROM, antibiotic therapy remains a mainstay of treatment. Numerous investigations have shown that the use of a variety of antibiotics in this setting can result in an increased latency period from the time of membrane rupture to the time of delivery. A large, prospective, randomized clinical investigation by Mercer and coworkers184 conducted through the NICHD MFMU Network was designed to more clearly address the neonatal benefits of antenatal antibiotic use in women with PPROM. In this trial, 614 women with PPROM were randomized to treatment with either intravenous ampicillin (2 g every 6 hours) plus erythromycin (250 mg every 6 hours) for 48 hours followed by oral amoxicillin (250 mg every 8 hours) and erythromycin base (333 mg every 8 hours) for 5 days or to a matched placebo treatment regimen. In addition to significantly increasing the latency period, the use of antibiotics in this investigation resulted in significant reductions in the incidences of RDS, necrotizing enterocolitis, and composite neonatal morbidity (defined as any of the following: fetal or infant death, respiratory distress, severe intraventricular hemorrhage, stage 2 or 3 necrotizing enterocolitis, or
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: sepsis within 72 hours of birth).184 In contrast, Kenyon and colleagues185 reported that antibiotic use in the setting of PPROM did not result in a reduction in neonatal morbidity. These investigators conducted a large, multicenter, multinational investigation of 4809 women with PPROM at less than 37 weeks’ gestation. Women were randomized to one of four treatment regimens for 10 days: placebo, amoxicillin-clavulanate, erythromycin, or a combination of amoxicillin-clavulanate plus erythromycin. Significant prolongation of pregnancy was noted among all antibiotic treatment groups when compared with placebo therapy. The investigators, however, noted no significant differences among the four treatment groups with regard to composite neonatal morbidity (defined as neonatal death, chronic lung disease, or major cerebral abnormality on ultrasound): placebo, 15%; amoxicillin-clavulanate, 14%; erythromycin, 13%; and amoxicillin-clavulanate plus erythromycin, 14%.185
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: Altogether, the use of antibiotics in the setting of PPROM appears to result in significant prolongation of pregnancy, with a potential reduction of neonatal shortterm morbidity in certain subsets of patients (i.e., early PPROM at less than 32 weeks’ gestation). On the basis of a meta-analysis, Hutzal and colleagues186 confirmed these conclusions, showing that antibiotics prolong pregnancy and reduce neonatal morbidity in women with PPROM at a gestation of 34 weeks or less, an effect that is not seen in women in preterm labor.
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: A 2013 Cochrane metanalysis187 (22 placebo controlled trials, N = 6872 women and babies) showed that antibiotic administration following PPROM significantly reduced chorioamnionitis (RR = 0.66; 95% CI, 0.46–0.96), neonatal infection (RR = 0.67; 95% CI, 0.52–0.85), use of surfactant (RR = 0.83; 95% CI, 0.72–0.96), neonatal oxygen therapy (RR = 0.88; 95% CI, 0.81–0.96), and abnormal cerebral ultrasound scan prior to hospital discharge (RR = 0.81; 95% CI, 0.68–0.98).
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: Secondary to shortages of erythromycin, azithromycin use has been on the rise as an alternative despite the absence of randomized clinical trials. A 2022 meta-analysis (five observational studies; N = 1289 women with PPROM) comparing azithromycin with erythromycin for prophylaxis found that azithromycin was associated with a lower rate of clinical chorioamnionitis (14.5% vs. 24.4%; OR = 0.53; 95% CI, 0.39–0.71), and the mean length of latency was similar between both antibiotic regimens: 6.6 days versus 6.7 days (mean difference, 0.07 days; 95% CI, –0.45 to 0.60; I2 = 0%).188
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: Care must therefore be taken with the administration of antenatal and intrapartum antibiotics. Although they prolong pregnancy in the setting of PPROM, eradicate group B streptococci, and are effective in reducing the incidence of early-onset neonatal sepsis and other neonatal outcomes, this benefit may come at the cost of favoring the emergence of ampicillin-resistant organisms that may cause severe neonatal infections. In circumstances where erythromycin is not available, azithromycin seems to be a good alternative;
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: further randomized clinical trials are needed to support such a regimen.
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: The use of antenatal corticosteroids (ACS) to prevent neonatal RDS stems from original animal work performed by Liggins and Howie189 in the late 1960s. They initially observed that, in gravid sheep given glucocorticoids to induce preterm labor, lambs demonstrated accelerated fetal lung maturity and decreased respiratory problems at birth.
