title: Multiple Gestation-Fetal and Maternal Considerations

paragraphs.text: 20 Multiple Gestation: Fetal and Maternal Considerations
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Twins account for 3% of all births and triplets for 0.08%. There is a worldwide increase in the rate of multiple gestation since the 1980s.1 Some studies report an increase in twin and triplet pregnancies despite a decrease in total live births.2 This increase is attributed partly to advanced maternal age,3 but it is the use of assisted reproductive technology (ART) that has had the major impact on increasing the rate of multiple pregnancies. Recently, ART guidelines in many countries include single embryo transfer in in vitro fertilization (IVF), to reduce the rates of twin and triplet pregnancies. However, procedures such as preimplantation genetic testing increase the odds of embryo splitting, resulting in monozygotic (MZ) twins.1,4 Spontaneous twin rates vary worldwide, from 8 per 1000 live births in Asia up to over 17 per 1000 births in Africa.5,6
paragraphs.heading: Epidemiology

paragraphs.text: Multifetal pregnancies have a major contribution to neonatal morbidity and mortality, including 60% and greater than 95% preterm delivery (prior to 37 weeks’ gestation) for twins and triplets, respectively, versus approximately 8% for singleton. Compared with less than 1.5% singleton infants born with a very low birth weight (VLBW) of less than 1500 g, the rate is 9% and greater than 30% for twins and triplets, respectively.7 In 2018, the US twin birth rate was 32.6 twins per 1000 births. This rate increased by 76% (from 18.9 to 33.2 per 1000 births) from 1980 to 2009, was generally stable from 2009 to 2012, and then increased to 33.9 per 1000 births in 2014, the highest rate ever reported. The rate of triplet and higher-order multiple births in 2018 was 93 per 100,000 births, which was 8% less than in 2017 and less than 50% of the 1998 peak of 193.5 births per 100,000.7
paragraphs.heading: Epidemiology

paragraphs.text: Acknowledgment of the higher risk for maternal and neonatal perinatal morbidity and mortality associated with higher-order pregnancies led to advanced changes in infertility treatment practices, contributing to a steady decline of around 0.1% per year in multiple gestation rates.7
paragraphs.heading: Epidemiology

paragraphs.text: Twin pregnancy may be the result of two sperms fertilizing two ova, generating dizygotic (DZ) twins, or one sperm fertilizing one ovum, which undergoes an early cleavage to create MZ twins.8 Rates of DZ twins are affected by genetic predisposition, maternal age, parity, body mass index, and more.8 Multiple embryo transfer during ART has increased substantially the rate of DZ twins.9
paragraphs.heading: Classification of Twin Pregnancies

paragraphs.text: MZ twinning occurs in around 30% of twin pregnancies,6,10 with a largely uniform and stable rate worldwide.8 Interestingly, their incidence increased twofold to fivefold in ART pregnancies, possibly because of IVF techniques, culture media, or infertility-associated abnormalities.11
paragraphs.heading: Classification of Twin Pregnancies

paragraphs.text: Beyond zygosity, which defines the genetic makeup multifetal pregnancies, chorionicity and amnionicity should be defined for multifetal pregnancies. Chorionicity refers to the number of outer membranes and placentas, whereas amnionicity refers to the number of separate amniotic fluid sacs. All DZ pregnancies are dichorionic and diamniotic (DCDA).
paragraphs.heading: Classification of Twin Pregnancies

paragraphs.text: MZ twins may be DCDA or monochorionic (MC). The MC can be diamniotic (MCDA) or monoamniotic (MCMA), depending on the timing of division or cleavage of the zygote. DCDA twins have fewer perinatal and neonatal complications compared with MCDA twins (Table 20.1).
paragraphs.heading: Classification of Twin Pregnancies

paragraphs.text: In one-third of the cases, early cleavage (days 1–4 post fertilization) will create DCDA. In two-thirds of the cases, later cleavage of the zygote (days 3–8) gives rise to an MCDA pregnancy; and less frequently, in 1%, cleavage at 8 to 12 days post fertilization creates MCMA twins. Delayed cleavage, beyond the 13th day, is very rare and may result in a conjoined twin pregnancy (Fig. 20.1).8,10
paragraphs.heading: Classification of Twin Pregnancies

paragraphs.text: The well-known paradigm regarding zygosity and chorionicity has been enriched with rare reports of various atypical cases which open the door for additional pathways and
paragraphs.heading: Unusual Twinning

paragraphs.text: definitions in twinning. Atypical twins include chimeric twins, phenotypically discordant MZ twins, mirror-image twins, polar body twins, complete hydatidiform mole with a coexistent twin, vanishing twins, fetus papyraceus, fetus in fetus, superfetation, and superfecundation.11
paragraphs.heading: Unusual Twinning

paragraphs.text: Chimerism in monochorionic dizygotic twins (MCDZ) refers to a few case reports that have found MC twins that are DZ. This condition is probably because of partial early fusion of two embryos. The chimerism could be confined to the blood (blood chimerism) or could be more extensive and include chimerism in other tissues.12
paragraphs.heading: Unusual Twinning

paragraphs.text: For many decades, fetal assessment during pregnancy follow-up began during midgestation when many of the complications of multiple gestation are already in process; therefore prevention and therapeutic strategies were very limited. A new concept for pregnancy follow-up was developed by Kypros Nicolaides, with the paradigm of the “inverted pyramid,” elaborating the idea that intensive assessment should be implemented in the first trimester, to screen for pregnancy complications and to enable early diagnosis and treatment and to plan the pregnancy’s specific follow-up accordingly. Many of these new modalities have become the standard of care.13
paragraphs.heading: First Trimester Assessment of Multiple Gestations (11+0 to 13+6 Weeks Scans)

paragraphs.text: Early pregnancy assessment is even more essential in multiple gestation. Accurate determination of the chronicity is crucial and paves the way for planning antenatal follow-up. Very early anatomy scans may detect fetal anomalies and may enable a discussion regarding selective fetal reduction. Screening for fetal genetic abnormalities may be performed successfully on the first trimester scan at 11 to 13 weeks’ gestation, and a chorionic villus sampling (CVS) may be offered as needed. It has been shown that about half the major anatomical anomalies may be detected at this stage.14,15 Early assessment for preterm delivery is important to provide better antenatal care. Evaluating the risk for preeclampsia (PE) is an ongoing goal, and randomized trials for its prevention in twins are being conducted nowadays.
paragraphs.heading: First Trimester Assessment of Multiple Gestations (11+0 to 13+6 Weeks Scans)

paragraphs.text: In the past, first-trimester scanning was mainly used to measure the nuchal translucency (NT) to assess the risk for trisomy 21. However, because of extensive progress in fetal medicine research, the NT scan may be used for extensive evaluation of the pregnancy and provide early detection and prediction of complications. This may allow prevention and treatment strategies that can reduce morbidity and mortality.
paragraphs.heading: First Trimester Assessment of Multiple Gestations (11+0 to 13+6 Weeks Scans)

paragraphs.text: Once multiple gestation is discovered, a thorough ultrasound scan examination is needed to diagnose the chorionicity. For example, if two fetuses are detected, one should look for the interfetal membrane which separates them. In DC twins, the membrane is thick and in the junction between the interfetal membrane and the placenta, there is a triangular projection of the placental tissue from the base of the placenta into the membranes (lambda sign, twin peak sign). In MC twins, the interfetal membrane is thin and there is no placental tissue projection from the base of the membrane (T-sign). In MCMA twins, there is no membrane separating them (Fig. 20.2).16
paragraphs.heading: Determining the Chronicity

paragraphs.text: One of the most important tasks in twin pregnancies is to label the twins early in the pregnancy course in a way that enables identifying which is which in future examinations. Fetus 1 is the twin above the internal os of the cervix, whereas fetus 2 is the adjacent one. It is important to also include all the additional information required for identification of each twin. Such identifiers include placenta location (anterior, posterior, fundal, left, right), cord insertion position (central, velamentous insertion, etc.), fetal gender, and position of the amniotic sac in relation to the mother (left or right side). It is critical to keep the name of each fetus as initially determined, and even if they change their position with regard to the cervix, the fetus that was labeled as fetus 1 will maintain its name. Before delivery, it is important to know which is the presenting twin (the one that will come first). Usually it will be fetus 1. However, there are condition in which fetus 2 is the presenting fetus.
paragraphs.heading: Labeling Twins

paragraphs.text: Accurate determination of gestational age is important for pregnancy follow-up. Wrong dating can cause misdiagnosis of intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), wrong delivery time, etc. Traditionally, dating is based on the last menstrual period. However, in many cases it is inaccurate, and therefore in spontaneous conception the crown-rump length of the longest fetus is used for dating when scanned at 11 to 13 weeks. In IVF conception, the day of conception determines the dating of the pregnancy.
paragraphs.heading: Pregnancy Dating

paragraphs.text: Traditionally, an anatomy scan is performed between 19 and 23 weeks of gestation to detect fetal anomalies. Because of improved ultrasound accuracy and resolution, along with
paragraphs.heading: Anatomy Assessment

paragraphs.text: extended knowledge in fetal medicine, it is now possible to perform an elaborate anatomy scan in the first trimester, as described. Still, some anomalies may only be detected at a later stage, and therefore it is still necessary to perform the late anatomy scan. Early detection of fetal anomalies is important in multiple pregnancies because, if selective termination is required, there is evidence of improved pregnancy outcome (reduced rate of pregnancy loss, reduced rate of early preterm delivery) when performed early.17
paragraphs.heading: Anatomy Assessment

paragraphs.text: Combination of maternal age, ultrasound of NT measurement, and biochemical markers constitutes the first-trimester screening test for trisomy 21, with a detection rate of
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Fetal Genetic Abnormalities

paragraphs.text: 96% in singleton and 90% in twins.18 Cell-free fetal deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) testing (cffDNA testing) may be performed as early as 10 weeks of gestation and has a detection rate of 99% for trisomy 21 in both singletons and in twins.19 In pregnancies at high risk for genetic abnormality, CVS may be performed safely both in DC and MC twins.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Fetal Genetic Abnormalities

paragraphs.text: Multiple gestations are at a 10-fold increased risk for preterm delivery compared with the 1% rate in singleton pregnancies.20 Shortening of the cervix is a warning flag for preterm birth. As in singleton pregnancies, a new powerful tool for prediction of preterm delivery is cervical length, which is measured by the ultrasound scan. It is recommended to
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Preterm Delivery

paragraphs.text: measure the cervix starting from the 11 to 13 weeks’ scan and from 16 weeks every 2 weeks. In case of shortening of the cervix, cervical cerclage and vaginal progesterone were found to be useful in singleton pregnancies but have a limited effect in twin pregnancies.21
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Preterm Delivery

paragraphs.text: PE is a serious complication of pregnancy and a major cause of short- and long-term maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality. Extensive research in the past decade has resulted in effective first-trimester screening for early PE, allowing prediction of about 90% of early PE with delivery at less than 32 weeks’ gestation. In twin pregnancies, the rate of PE is about 9%, which is 3 times higher than in singleton pregnancies. This is an underestimation because twins are usually delivered prematurely, and the rate is most increased ninefold compared with singleton pregnancies. Therefore all twin pregnancies should be regarded as high-risk of preterm PE. An ongoing multicenter study is investigating the role of prophylactic lowdose aspirin early in multiple-gestation pregnancies.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Preeclampsia

paragraphs.text: Significant associations between twinning and birth defects have been observed for a wide range of birth defects in large, registry-based studies.22,23 Twins are at an increased risk of congenital anomalies, and this risk differs depending on zygosity and chorionicity.24 MZ twins are at an increased risk of birth defects compared with both singletons and DZ twins.23
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Malformations

paragraphs.text: Several studies have reported that rates of congenital anomalies in DZ twins are similar to those of singletons, whereas the rate in MZ twins is up to fivefold higher.25 Anomalies in multiple gestations have been reported in all organ systems, but the most common involve the cardiovascular and central nervous systems.26
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Malformations

paragraphs.text: Compared with singletons, DC twins and MC twins are at increased risk for developing cardiac anomalies.27,28 Increased incidence of structural anomalies in MCMA twins, with up to 16% structural anomalies, may be explained by a two-hit theory, with the twinning process being the first hit and a second insult causing unequal development. Another explanation may be an unequal division of the embryonic cell mass.29 In a large retrospective study of more than 3500 twin pairs, concordance rate between MZ twins was higher compared with DZ twins only for malformation of the nervous system, circulatory system, cleft lip/palate, and urinary system.30
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Malformations

paragraphs.text: The risk for at least one of an MCDA twin pair having some form of congenital heart defect (CHD) is approximately 7%. The most frequently seen malformation is a ventricular septal defect, but all types of CHD are represented in this group.31
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Malformations

paragraphs.text: The spectrum of brain malformations in twins includes polymicrogyria, subcortical heterotopia, periventricular nodular heterotopia, cerebellar hypoplasia, and classic Dandy-Walker malformation. Twinning-associated brain
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Malformations

paragraphs.text: disruptions include hydranencephaly, porencephaly, multicystic encephalomalacia, and less specific loss of white matter volume.
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Malformations

paragraphs.text: Twinning-associated brain malformations and disruptions occur in both MZ and DZ twins, which supports a prenatal vascular pathogenesis, including defects in vasculogenesis, defects in vascular perfusion, and intracranial hemorrhage.32
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Malformations

paragraphs.text: In a survey of more than 20,000 pairs of twins, using parental report for assessing the rate of clubfoot, oral cleft, deafness, cerebral palsy (CP), muscular dystrophy, spina bifida, strabismus, and CHD, the authors reported the prevalence of clubfoot (2.9 per 1000 live births) was found to be about twofold higher than that of the general population, and there was a substantially greater risk for spina bifida (1.3 vs. 0.35 per 1000 live births, respectively).33 Twins were not found to have an increased risk for chromosomal anomalies.34
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Malformations

paragraphs.text: Overall, rates of congenital malformations are increased in MZ twins when compared with singletons. Etiology is most probably multifactorial and involves genetic, epigenetic, vascular, and other factors.
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Malformations

paragraphs.text: MC pregnancies have a shared blood system because of communicating vessels over their single placenta and may develop unique complications (Table 20.2). The most important complications are twin-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS), selective intrauterine growth restriction (sIUGR), twin anemia polycythemia sequence (TAPS), twin reversed arterial perfusion syndrome (TRAP), discordance for fetal abnormality (anomalies in one), and single intrauterine death in monoamniotic twins (MCMA). Half of complicated MC pregnancies require intrauterine interventions.35 Some MC pregnancies may develop more than one complication (e.g., TTTS with sIUGR), and therefore the management becomes more challenging.
paragraphs.heading: Complications of Monochorionic Twins

paragraphs.text: TTTS is identified in 10% to 20% of MC pregnancies usually between 16 and 26 weeks. In this condition, there is an unbalanced passage of blood through the placental anastomosis between the twins, and extra blood volume is transferred from one twin to the other. The twin that receives the excessive blood volume is defined as the “recipient twin,” while the contributing twin is addressed as the “donor twin.” The donor will present with symptoms of hypovolemia leading to oliguria and oligohydramnios, whereas the recipient will have characteristics of volume overload, hypervolemia, polyuria, and polyhydramnios. These signs are detected by an ultrasound scan and are the basis for the Quintero classification of TTTS (Table 20.3).36 It is important to clarify that there is no discordance in the hemoglobin/hematocrit levels and no size difference between the twins in TTTS. MC pregnancies complicated with TTTS have an increased risk for ischemic brain lesions; therefore it is recommended to conduct a detailed brain ultrasound
paragraphs.heading: Twin-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS)

paragraphs.text: scan or brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) a few weeks after the detection of TTTS. TTTS is a major cause of death and handicap in an MC twin pregnancy because of a combination of factors, including the blood volume imbalance (which affects different organs including the brain, heart, kidneys), the increased risk for preterm delivery of two sick infants, and as a consequence of intrauterine demise of one twin. In the past, fetal therapy for TTTS was started with serial reductions of amniotic fluid from the recipient twin, or septostomy which perforates the amniotic membranes between the twins, to equalize the amniotic fluid level. These were found to have limited value because
paragraphs.heading: Twin-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS)

paragraphs.text: they failed to treat the underlying problem (i.e., the placental anastomoses). Nowadays, fetal surgery, using fetoscopic laser coagulation of all anastomoses along the equator, is the accepted treatment. This is currently the best treatment option regardless of disease severity. In this procedure (Fig. 20.3), a 3-mm port is inserted through the maternal abdomen, usually into the amniotic sac of the recipient. Through the port, a fetoscope is inserted and the blood anastomosis are easily visualized; using a laser fiber that is introduced into the fetoscope channel, the anastomoses are ablated.37
paragraphs.heading: Twin-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS)

paragraphs.text: Laser therapy aims to cure the disease by disconnecting the two fetal circulations. After laser therapy, there is a 50% to 60% survival of both twins and an 80% survival at least one twin. Of surviving infants, 11% have some form of developmental impairment. CP is the most common impairment, affecting 5%. Both donor and recipient are at equal risk of long-term impairments. The single most important risk factor of adverse long-term outcome is prematurity.35
paragraphs.heading: Twin-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS)

paragraphs.text: Another approach to TTTS treatment is selective feticide of one of the twins. This is required if one twin is severely injured or when laser coagulation cannot be performed technically. Because selective feticide by KCl injection is not an option in MC twins caused by the risk of KCl leakage to the other twin through the placental anastomoses, feticide is therefore performed in these cases by ultrasound-guided bipolar forceps.37
paragraphs.heading: Twin-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS)

paragraphs.text: sIUGR affects 10% to 20% of MC pregnancies. The definition of sIUGR in MC twins is not universally established, and it is often defined as an estimated fetal weight less than the 10th percentile in one twin, while the second twin has a normal estimated fetal weight. sIUGR is an important complication of MC pregnancies, with a high risk of intrauterine demise and neurologic adverse outcome for both twins. This condition is usually derived from unequal division of the placenta: one fetus has very few blood vessels emerging from the umbilical cord and therefore dominates only a small portion of the placenta, leading to growth restriction, whereas the other usually has many blood vessels that emerge from the umbilical cord and dominate large parts of the placenta.
paragraphs.heading: Selective Intrauterine Growth Restriction (sIUGR)

paragraphs.text: The condition is subdivided into three types according to the Doppler finding of the end-diastolic flow (EDF) in the umbilical artery of the small fetus—type I: EDF positive, associated with good prognosis; type II: EDF absent or reversed, associated with predicated early deterioration of the small twin; and type III: EDF cyclical change from positive to absent and reversed, associated with unexpected fetal demise (around 15%) or neurologic injury in one or both twins (around 20%) along with increased risk of ischemic brain lesions in the larger twin (Fig. 20.4).38 Therapeutic strategies are related to the sIUGR type and the gestational age. These include conservative management with close observation, fetoscope laser coagulation of all anastomoses along the equator, thus protecting the larger twin in case of smaller twin fetal demise (30% mortality or severe morbidity from brain

paragraphs.text: damage caused by the drop in blood pressure following blood leakage), or selective feticide of the small twin.39
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 20.3 Fetoscopic laser ablation of communicating blood vessels in monochorionic diamniotic twins

paragraphs.text: TAPS is characterized by large intertwin hemoglobin differences that occur because of red blood cells’ passage from one fetus (donor/anemic) to the other (recipient/polycythemic) through tiny placental blood anastomoses. It is important to differentiate TAPS from TTTS. In TAPS there is change in the hemoglobin level, whereas in TTTS there is difference in blood volume. TAPS may occur spontaneously in about 5% of MC twin pregnancies (usually after 26 weeks). In addition, TAPS may develop after laser surgery for TTTS in about 2% to 13% of post laser cases. Antenatal diagnosis of TAPS can be reached based on Doppler ultrasound abnormalities showing an increased peak systolic velocity in the middle cerebral artery in the donor twin suggestive of fetal anemia, and a decreased velocity in the recipient twin suggestive of polycythemia (Table 20.4). Postnatal diagnosis of TAPS is based on the presence of chronic anemia in the donor and polycythemia in the recipient, defined as intertwin hemoglobin difference greater than 8.0 g/dL and at least one of the following: reticulocyte count ratio greater than 1.7 and placenta with only small (diameter <1 mm) vascular anastomoses. TAPS severity is assessed by the TAPS staging system (Fig. 20.5).40 Fetal anemia is associated with a decreased blood viscosity leading to an increase in blood speed. Fetal polycythemia is associated with an increased blood viscosity leading to a decrease in blood speed. The blood speed is measured in centimeters per second and converted to multiples of the median (MoM), which represents how far the measurement is from the average for the specific gestational week. The average is 1 MoM. Measurements greater than 1 will be considered as increased velocity (anemia), whereas measurements less than 1 will be considered as low velocity (polycythemia).
paragraphs.heading: Twin Anemia Polycythemia Sequence (TAPS)

paragraphs.text: The management of TAPS depends on the gestational age, the stage, and the accessibility of the equator and includes intrauterine blood transfusion to the anemic fetus (although this may deteriorate the condition of the polycythemic fetus because of blood leakage through the anastomoses), fetoscopy and laser ablation of the placental anastomosis, selective termination of one of the twins, and, in cases identified after 30 weeks’ gestation, delivery (considered because of the increased risk for intrauterine fetal demise [IUFD]).35
paragraphs.heading: Twin Anemia Polycythemia Sequence (TAPS)

paragraphs.text: TRAP is a rare condition affecting less than 1% of MC pregnancies, in which there is normal development of one twin (pump twin) while the other twin lacks a heart/not fully formed (acardiac twin). In DC twins, a failure of one twin to develop a heart will end up as fetal demise, while the other twin is not affected. However, in MC twins, blood supply from the normal fetus can keep the acardiac twin “alive” through the placental anastomoses. The acardiac twin usually has a poorly developed body and may be missing a head, limbs, or torso. Because the heart of the “pump twin” supplies blood to both fetuses, congestive heart failure may develop, and if untreated, perinatal mortality rate is up to 55%. The outcome may be improved by interventions to disconnect the circulation of the acardiac twin, usually performed after 16 weeks of gestation, with survival of the pump twin rising up to 80%. In the past decade, widespread introduction of a routine first-trimester ultrasound examination has led to early
paragraphs.heading: Twin Reversed Arterial Perfusion Syndrome (TRAP)

paragraphs.text: detection of the TRAP sequence. Preliminary data have demonstrated the feasibility, effectiveness, and safety of intrafetal laser performed at 12 to 14 weeks; hence survival may be improved by elective intervention at this stage.41
paragraphs.heading: Twin Reversed Arterial Perfusion Syndrome (TRAP)

paragraphs.text: Uterine demise of one twin has unique aspects in MC pregnancies. Because of the shared circulation, one twin’s death may lead to double demise in 15% of the cases or to severe brain injury in 25% of the cases caused by exsanguination of the surviving co-twin into its demised twin’s circulation.42 Single fetal demise, which may occur after successful laser coagulation for TTTS, does not affect the surviving twin, since anastomoses are ablated and the surviving twin is protected from exsanguination. In cases with recent single intrauterine death it is important to measure the middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) to predict fetal anemia, and consider intrauterine blood transfusion if anemia exists. Careful follow-up, including detailed brain scans as well as brain MRI, is indicated to reveal brain injury.
paragraphs.heading: Single Intrauterine Fetal Death

paragraphs.text: Because both twins are in the same amniotic sac, cord entanglement is usually demonstrable as early as in the first trimester.
paragraphs.heading: Monoamniotic Twin (MCMA) Complications

paragraphs.text: The cords typically insert close to one another on the placenta, with very large anastomoses connecting the stem vessels of both twins. MA twins are at increased risk of adverse outcome: discordant structural anomalies affecting 20% of MA twins and increased risk of unexpected and usually double intrauterine demise, mostly caused by acute fetofetal
paragraphs.heading: Monoamniotic Twin (MCMA) Complications

paragraphs.text: hemorrhage across the large-caliber anastomoses triggered by cord compression.35
paragraphs.heading: Monoamniotic Twin (MCMA) Complications

paragraphs.text: Careful surveillance (inpatient monitoring starting at 28 weeks) and planned preterm birth (elective cesarean section at 32-33 weeks) seem to improve survival rates of MCMA twins up to 80%.
paragraphs.heading: Monoamniotic Twin (MCMA) Complications

paragraphs.text: MC twin pregnancies carry an increased risk of perinatal death compared with DC twins.34,43 This is mainly because of higher prematurity rates, selective fetal growth restriction, congenital anomalies, and TTTS.44 MCMA twins carry an additional risk for perinatal death because of twin-related congenital anomalies and cord-related complications.45,46
paragraphs.heading: Delivery Considerations

paragraphs.text: A systematic review by D’Antonio et al. showed 6% fetal loss in MCMA pregnancies,46a most of which occurred before 30 weeks of gestation. At 31 to 32 and 33 to 34 weeks of gestation, fetal loss rate was 1% and 2%, respectively. In addition, these authors have reported fetal loss of 3% in twins of pregnancies managed as inpatients, compared with 7% in those followed up as outpatients.47 Thus MCMA pregnancies are usually delivered between 32+0 and 34+6 weeks of gestation in view of the reported high risk of unexpected fetal loss with advancing gestation.43,48 In practice, in many leading fetal medicine units, hospital MCMA are delivered at 32+0 weeks.34
paragraphs.heading: Delivery Considerations

paragraphs.text: For uncomplicated DCDA twins, the recommended time of birth is between 38 and 39 weeks of gestation. Uncomplicated MCDA twins should most probably be delivered at 34+0 to 37+6 weeks in uncomplicated pregnancies, although in many fetal units these are delivered at 36+0 weeks.46,49,50 There is some evidence for increased
paragraphs.heading: Delivery Considerations

paragraphs.text: fetal death in twin pregnancies continued beyond 38 weeks of gestation,51 although other studies found no short- or long-term risks for twins delivered beyond 38 weeks.52 For an uncomplicated trichorionic triamniotic pregnancy, the recommended time of birth is 35 weeks’ gestation, via cesarean section.51 Chorionicity does not play a role regarding the mode of delivery. Uncomplicated diamniotic twins, whether DC or MC, may be delivered vaginally or via cesarean section, given that the first twin is in a cephalic position.53–57 Current recommendation for delivery of MCMA twins is by cesarean section.51
paragraphs.heading: Delivery Considerations

paragraphs.text: Multifetal gestation carries a significantly increased risk of preterm delivery, with nearly 60% of twins being born preterm at less than 37 weeks’ gestation and 12% to 14% born prior to 34 weeks.58 Over the years, there was a debate regarding the favorable effects of antenatal corticosteroids (ACSs) in multifetal pregnancies.59 Several studies reported that administration of ACSs up until 7 days prior to birth was associated with a significant decrease in neonatal mortality and morbidity in twin pregnancies, comparable with the effect on singleton infants.60
paragraphs.heading: Antenatal Steroids in Twin Pregnancies

paragraphs.text: The EPIPAGE-2 study showed administration of a single complete course of ACSs reduced the incidence of severe neurologic morbidities and composite outcome in twins born between 24 and 31 completed weeks of gestation. In that study, in-hospital mortality was reduced only when the interval between ACS administration and delivery was 7 days or fewer.61
paragraphs.heading: Antenatal Steroids in Twin Pregnancies

paragraphs.text: Some studies suggested suboptimal benefits of ACS treatment in twin pregnancies may be attributable to different maternal physiologic changes in twin pregnancies, such as greater maternal blood volume expansion and differences in betamethasone clearance.62 Other studies have established that there is no difference in pharmacokinetics, maternal serum, or cord blood betamethasone between multiple and singleton pregnancies.63 Studies comparing twin and singleton pregnancies reported that optimal ACS administration led to comparably improved outcomes64 and that the number of fetuses is not a determinant of the effect of ACSs in neonatal outcomes.65 However, twin pregnancy imposes an independent risk factor for suboptimal ACS administration timing because twin preterm labor is harder to predict, and therefore women are often treated too early or too late in regard to the ideal therapeutic window.66
paragraphs.heading: Antenatal Steroids in Twin Pregnancies

paragraphs.text: Given the increased risk of maternal and fetal complications during multiple gestation, the overall outcome for multiples is worse when compared with the outcome of singletons. This is mostly because approximately half of twins are born preterm. However, advancements in antenatal and neonatal
paragraphs.heading: Outcome

paragraphs.text: care have resulted a significant decrease in perinatal and early neonatal mortality rates for both the first (8.6-fold reduction) and the second (6.8-fold reduction) twin.67
paragraphs.heading: Outcome

paragraphs.text: Multiples remain at higher risk for CP. However, this risk has been decreasing steadily since the 1990s, a decrease attributed to advances in perinatal care.
paragraphs.heading: Outcome

paragraphs.text: Recent studies from worldwide CP registries indicate the overall prevalence of CP is greater in triplets and quadruplets than in twins. This is most probably related to higher risk of preterm birth in higher-order multiples. Singleton and multiple births with CP display similar severity of motor impairment.68,69
paragraphs.heading: Outcome

paragraphs.text: When evaluating the impact of perinatal factors (i.e., IVF, growth restriction, prematurity) in DCDA twin pregnancies on main neurodevelopmental sequelae, similar risk for neurologic sequelae were observed in IVF DZ twins in comparison with their naturally conceived peers and singletons from assisted conception. Moreover, overall development and health status at 4 years of age in IVF twins was found comparable with that of 4-year-old IVF singletons, after adjusting for mediators and confounders. However, for twins born following fetal growth restriction, there was a fourfold risk for neurologic sequelae (motor development, speech and language development, and internalizing difficulties) versus normal growth twins. Significantly worse results regarding cognition, language, and motor skills were found in the smaller twin of a discordant pair at 2.5 to 3 years of age. Risk of death and neurologic impairments in twins with birth weight less than 1000 g was higher compared with singletons with similar birth weights. A high rate of mild to moderate cognitive impairment and severe neurodevelopmental impairment (NDI) at age 5 years was not identified at age 2 years. These data highlight the importance of longitudinal follow-up of survivors of TTTS beyond age 2 years and emphasize the precautions that should be taken when diagnosing an absence of impairment before school age.70 However, twins versus singletons born at less than 34 weeks of age had comparable motor and cognitive outcomes at 2 years of age.71
paragraphs.heading: Outcome

paragraphs.text: Follow-up of 66 twins and 157 singletons at 5 years of age in Turku, Finland revealed no major neurodevelopmental risks in twins compared with singletons. These data should be interpreted in light of the advanced perinatal care in Finland.72
paragraphs.heading: Outcome

paragraphs.text: In MC twins with sIUGR, evidence suggests that patients treated with laser therapy, considering the potential risks and complications of the procedure, may have an improved outcome over those managed expectantly, mainly because of postponing gestational age at delivery. Results show improvement of fetal growth in more than 50% of growth-restricted twins, while protecting the well-growing twin from the adverse consequences that could result from the fetal demise of the growthrestricted twin.73
paragraphs.heading: Outcome

paragraphs.text: Outcome at school age of MC twins treated with fetoscopic laser surgery for TTTS was found comparable with that of DC twins without invasive treatment. The long-term neurodevelopment was mainly dependent on gestational age
paragraphs.heading: Outcome

paragraphs.text: at birth.74 A recent systematic review demonstrated a 14% incidence of neurologic impairments after laser therapy at 2 years of age. CP was described in about 6% of the children treated with laser therapy.75
paragraphs.heading: Outcome

paragraphs.text: Overall, data reflect an increased risk for increased adverse perinatal outcome for the second twin, independent of chorionicity, sex, and presentation.76
paragraphs.heading: Outcome

paragraphs.text: In summary, multiple gestations are challenging and carry an increased risk for complications. Advances in fetal
paragraphs.heading: Outcome

20 Multiple Gestation: Fetal and Maternal Considerations

### NOA OFEK SHLOMAI, SMADAR EVENTOV FRIEDMAN, AND YUVAL GIELCHINSKY

### Epidemiology

Twins account for 3% of all births and triplets for 0.08%. There is a worldwide increase in the rate of multiple gestation since the 1980s.1 Some studies report an increase in twin and triplet pregnancies despite a decrease in total live births.2 This increase is attributed partly to advanced maternal age,3 but it is the use of assisted reproductive technology (ART) that has had the major impact on increasing the rate of multiple pregnancies. Recently, ART guidelines in many countries include single embryo transfer in in vitro fertilization (IVF), to reduce the rates of twin and triplet pregnancies. However, procedures such as preimplantation genetic testing increase the odds of embryo splitting, resulting in monozygotic (MZ) twins.1,4 Spontaneous twin rates vary worldwide, from 8 per 1000 live births in Asia up to over 17 per 1000 births in Africa.5,6

Multifetal pregnancies have a major contribution to neonatal morbidity and mortality, including 60% and greater than 95% preterm delivery (prior to 37 weeks’ gestation) for twins and triplets, respectively, versus approximately 8% for singleton. Compared with less than 1.5% singleton infants born with a very low birth weight (VLBW) of less than 1500 g, the rate is 9% and greater than 30% for twins and triplets, respectively.7 In 2018, the US twin birth rate was 32.6 twins per 1000 births. This rate increased by 76% (from 18.9 to 33.2 per 1000 births) from 1980 to 2009, was generally stable from 2009 to 2012, and then increased to 33.9 per 1000 births in 2014, the highest rate ever reported. The rate of triplet and higher-order multiple births in 2018 was 93 per 100,000 births, which was 8% less than in 2017 and less than 50% of the 1998 peak of 193.5 births per 100,000.7

Acknowledgment of the higher risk for maternal and neonatal perinatal morbidity and mortality associated with higher-order pregnancies led to advanced changes in infertility treatment practices, contributing to a steady decline of around 0.1% per year in multiple gestation rates.7

### Classification of Twin Pregnancies

Twin pregnancy may be the result of two sperms fertilizing two ova, generating dizygotic (DZ) twins, or one sperm fertilizing one ovum, which undergoes an early cleavage to create MZ twins.8 Rates of DZ twins are affected by genetic predisposition, maternal age, parity, body mass index, and more.8 Multiple embryo transfer during ART has increased substantially the rate of DZ twins.9

MZ twinning occurs in around 30% of twin pregnancies,6,10 with a largely uniform and stable rate worldwide.8 Interestingly, their incidence increased twofold to fivefold in ART pregnancies, possibly because of IVF techniques, culture media, or infertility-associated abnormalities.11

Beyond zygosity, which defines the genetic makeup multifetal pregnancies, chorionicity and amnionicity should be defined for multifetal pregnancies. Chorionicity refers to the number of outer membranes and placentas, whereas amnionicity refers to the number of separate amniotic fluid sacs. All DZ pregnancies are dichorionic and diamniotic (DCDA).

MZ twins may be DCDA or monochorionic (MC). The MC can be diamniotic (MCDA) or monoamniotic (MCMA), depending on the timing of division or cleavage of the zygote. DCDA twins have fewer perinatal and neonatal complications compared with MCDA twins (Table 20.1).

In one-third of the cases, early cleavage (days 1–4 post fertilization) will create DCDA. In two-thirds of the cases, later cleavage of the zygote (days 3–8) gives rise to an MCDA pregnancy; and less frequently, in 1%, cleavage at 8 to 12 days post fertilization creates MCMA twins. Delayed cleavage, beyond the 13th day, is very rare and may result in a conjoined twin pregnancy (Fig. 20.1).8,10

### Unusual Twinning

The well-known paradigm regarding zygosity and chorionicity has been enriched with rare reports of various atypical cases which open the door for additional pathways and

Chimerism in monochorionic dizygotic twins (MCDZ) refers to a few case reports that have found MC twins that are DZ. This condition is probably because of partial early fusion of two embryos. The chimerism could be confined to the blood (blood chimerism) or could be more extensive and include chimerism in other tissues.12

### First Trimester Assessment of Multiple Gestations (11+0 to 13+6 Weeks Scans)

For many decades, fetal assessment during pregnancy follow-up began during midgestation when many of the complications of multiple gestation are already in process; therefore prevention and therapeutic strategies were very limited. A new concept for pregnancy follow-up was developed by Kypros Nicolaides, with the paradigm of the “inverted pyramid,” elaborating the idea that intensive assessment should be implemented in the first trimester, to screen for pregnancy complications and to enable early diagnosis and treatment and to plan the pregnancy’s specific follow-up accordingly. Many of these new modalities have become the standard of care.13

Early pregnancy assessment is even more essential in multiple gestation. Accurate determination of the chronicity is crucial and paves the way for planning antenatal follow-up. Very early anatomy scans may detect fetal anomalies and may enable a discussion regarding selective fetal reduction. Screening for fetal genetic abnormalities may be performed successfully on the first trimester scan at 11 to 13 weeks’ gestation, and a chorionic villus sampling (CVS) may be offered as needed. It has been shown that about half the major anatomical anomalies may be detected at this stage.14,15 Early assessment for preterm delivery is important to provide better antenatal care. Evaluating the risk for preeclampsia (PE) is an ongoing goal, and randomized trials for its prevention in twins are being conducted nowadays.

In the past, first-trimester scanning was mainly used to measure the nuchal translucency (NT) to assess the risk for trisomy 21. However, because of extensive progress in fetal medicine research, the NT scan may be used for extensive evaluation of the pregnancy and provide early detection and prediction of complications. This may allow prevention and treatment strategies that can reduce morbidity and mortality.

### Determining the Chronicity

Once multiple gestation is discovered, a thorough ultrasound scan examination is needed to diagnose the chorionicity. For example, if two fetuses are detected, one should look for the interfetal membrane which separates them. In DC twins, the membrane is thick and in the junction between the interfetal membrane and the placenta, there is a triangular projection of the placental tissue from the base of the placenta into the membranes (lambda sign, twin peak sign). In MC twins, the interfetal membrane is thin and there is no placental tissue projection from the base of the membrane (T-sign). In MCMA twins, there is no membrane separating them (Fig. 20.2).16

### Labeling Twins

One of the most important tasks in twin pregnancies is to label the twins early in the pregnancy course in a way that enables identifying which is which in future examinations. Fetus 1 is the twin above the internal os of the cervix, whereas fetus 2 is the adjacent one. It is important to also include all the additional information required for identification of each twin. Such identifiers include placenta location (anterior, posterior, fundal, left, right), cord insertion position (central, velamentous insertion, etc.), fetal gender, and position of the amniotic sac in relation to the mother (left or right side). It is critical to keep the name of each fetus as initially determined, and even if they change their position with regard to the cervix, the fetus that was labeled as fetus 1 will maintain its name. Before delivery, it is important to know which is the presenting twin (the one that will come first). Usually it will be fetus 1. However, there are condition in which fetus 2 is the presenting fetus.

### Pregnancy Dating

Accurate determination of gestational age is important for pregnancy follow-up. Wrong dating can cause misdiagnosis of intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), wrong delivery time, etc. Traditionally, dating is based on the last menstrual period. However, in many cases it is inaccurate, and therefore in spontaneous conception the crown-rump length of the longest fetus is used for dating when scanned at 11 to 13 weeks. In IVF conception, the day of conception determines the dating of the pregnancy.

### Screening for Preeclampsia

PE is a serious complication of pregnancy and a major cause of short- and long-term maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality. Extensive research in the past decade has resulted in effective first-trimester screening for early PE, allowing prediction of about 90% of early PE with delivery at less than 32 weeks’ gestation. In twin pregnancies, the rate of PE is about 9%, which is 3 times higher than in singleton pregnancies. This is an underestimation because twins are usually delivered prematurely, and the rate is most increased ninefold compared with singleton pregnancies. Therefore all twin pregnancies should be regarded as high-risk of preterm PE. An ongoing multicenter study is investigating the role of prophylactic lowdose aspirin early in multiple-gestation pregnancies.

### Congenital Malformations

Significant associations between twinning and birth defects have been observed for a wide range of birth defects in large, registry-based studies.22,23 Twins are at an increased risk of congenital anomalies, and this risk differs depending on zygosity and chorionicity.24 MZ twins are at an increased risk of birth defects compared with both singletons and DZ twins.23

Several studies have reported that rates of congenital anomalies in DZ twins are similar to those of singletons, whereas the rate in MZ twins is up to fivefold higher.25 Anomalies in multiple gestations have been reported in all organ systems, but the most common involve the cardiovascular and central nervous systems.26

Compared with singletons, DC twins and MC twins are at increased risk for developing cardiac anomalies.27,28 Increased incidence of structural anomalies in MCMA twins, with up to 16% structural anomalies, may be explained by a two-hit theory, with the twinning process being the first hit and a second insult causing unequal development. Another explanation may be an unequal division of the embryonic cell mass.29 In a large retrospective study of more than 3500 twin pairs, concordance rate between MZ twins was higher compared with DZ twins only for malformation of the nervous system, circulatory system, cleft lip/palate, and urinary system.30

The risk for at least one of an MCDA twin pair having some form of congenital heart defect (CHD) is approximately 7%. The most frequently seen malformation is a ventricular septal defect, but all types of CHD are represented in this group.31

The spectrum of brain malformations in twins includes polymicrogyria, subcortical heterotopia, periventricular nodular heterotopia, cerebellar hypoplasia, and classic Dandy-Walker malformation. Twinning-associated brain

disruptions include hydranencephaly, porencephaly, multicystic encephalomalacia, and less specific loss of white matter volume.

Twinning-associated brain malformations and disruptions occur in both MZ and DZ twins, which supports a prenatal vascular pathogenesis, including defects in vasculogenesis, defects in vascular perfusion, and intracranial hemorrhage.32

In a survey of more than 20,000 pairs of twins, using parental report for assessing the rate of clubfoot, oral cleft, deafness, cerebral palsy (CP), muscular dystrophy, spina bifida, strabismus, and CHD, the authors reported the prevalence of clubfoot (2.9 per 1000 live births) was found to be about twofold higher than that of the general population, and there was a substantially greater risk for spina bifida (1.3 vs. 0.35 per 1000 live births, respectively).33 Twins were not found to have an increased risk for chromosomal anomalies.34

Overall, rates of congenital malformations are increased in MZ twins when compared with singletons. Etiology is most probably multifactorial and involves genetic, epigenetic, vascular, and other factors.

### Complications of Monochorionic Twins

MC pregnancies have a shared blood system because of communicating vessels over their single placenta and may develop unique complications (Table 20.2). The most important complications are twin-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS), selective intrauterine growth restriction (sIUGR), twin anemia polycythemia sequence (TAPS), twin reversed arterial perfusion syndrome (TRAP), discordance for fetal abnormality (anomalies in one), and single intrauterine death in monoamniotic twins (MCMA). Half of complicated MC pregnancies require intrauterine interventions.35 Some MC pregnancies may develop more than one complication (e.g., TTTS with sIUGR), and therefore the management becomes more challenging.

### Twin-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS)

TTTS is identified in 10% to 20% of MC pregnancies usually between 16 and 26 weeks. In this condition, there is an unbalanced passage of blood through the placental anastomosis between the twins, and extra blood volume is transferred from one twin to the other. The twin that receives the excessive blood volume is defined as the “recipient twin,” while the contributing twin is addressed as the “donor twin.” The donor will present with symptoms of hypovolemia leading to oliguria and oligohydramnios, whereas the recipient will have characteristics of volume overload, hypervolemia, polyuria, and polyhydramnios. These signs are detected by an ultrasound scan and are the basis for the Quintero classification of TTTS (Table 20.3).36 It is important to clarify that there is no discordance in the hemoglobin/hematocrit levels and no size difference between the twins in TTTS. MC pregnancies complicated with TTTS have an increased risk for ischemic brain lesions; therefore it is recommended to conduct a detailed brain ultrasound

These were found to have limited value because

they failed to treat the underlying problem (i.e., the placental anastomoses). Nowadays, fetal surgery, using fetoscopic laser coagulation of all anastomoses along the equator, is the accepted treatment. This is currently the best treatment option regardless of disease severity. In this procedure (Fig. 20.3), a 3-mm port is inserted through the maternal abdomen, usually into the amniotic sac of the recipient. Through the port, a fetoscope is inserted and the blood anastomosis are easily visualized; using a laser fiber that is introduced into the fetoscope channel, the anastomoses are ablated.37

Laser therapy aims to cure the disease by disconnecting the two fetal circulations. After laser therapy, there is a 50% to 60% survival of both twins and an 80% survival at least one twin. Of surviving infants, 11% have some form of developmental impairment. CP is the most common impairment, affecting 5%. Both donor and recipient are at equal risk of long-term impairments. The single most important risk factor of adverse long-term outcome is prematurity.35

Another approach to TTTS treatment is selective feticide of one of the twins. This is required if one twin is severely injured or when laser coagulation cannot be performed technically. Because selective feticide by KCl injection is not an option in MC twins caused by the risk of KCl leakage to the other twin through the placental anastomoses, feticide is therefore performed in these cases by ultrasound-guided bipolar forceps.37

### Selective Intrauterine Growth Restriction (sIUGR)

sIUGR affects 10% to 20% of MC pregnancies. The definition of sIUGR in MC twins is not universally established, and it is often defined as an estimated fetal weight less than the 10th percentile in one twin, while the second twin has a normal estimated fetal weight. sIUGR is an important complication of MC pregnancies, with a high risk of intrauterine demise and neurologic adverse outcome for both twins. This condition is usually derived from unequal division of the placenta: one fetus has very few blood vessels emerging from the umbilical cord and therefore dominates only a small portion of the placenta, leading to growth restriction, whereas the other usually has many blood vessels that emerge from the umbilical cord and dominate large parts of the placenta.

The condition is subdivided into three types according to the Doppler finding of the end-diastolic flow (EDF) in the umbilical artery of the small fetus—type I: EDF positive, associated with good prognosis; type II: EDF absent or reversed, associated with predicated early deterioration of the small twin; and type III: EDF cyclical change from positive to absent and reversed, associated with unexpected fetal demise (around 15%) or neurologic injury in one or both twins (around 20%) along with increased risk of ischemic brain lesions in the larger twin (Fig. 20.4).38 Therapeutic strategies are related to the sIUGR type and the gestational age. ### Twin Anemia Polycythemia Sequence (TAPS)

TAPS is characterized by large intertwin hemoglobin differences that occur because of red blood cells’ passage from one fetus (donor/anemic) to the other (recipient/polycythemic) through tiny placental blood anastomoses. It is important to differentiate TAPS from TTTS. In TAPS there is change in the hemoglobin level, whereas in TTTS there is difference in blood volume. TAPS may occur spontaneously in about 5% of MC twin pregnancies (usually after 26 weeks). In addition, TAPS may develop after laser surgery for TTTS in about 2% to 13% of post laser cases. Antenatal diagnosis of TAPS can be reached based on Doppler ultrasound abnormalities showing an increased peak systolic velocity in the middle cerebral artery in the donor twin suggestive of fetal anemia, and a decreased velocity in the recipient twin suggestive of polycythemia (Table 20.4). Postnatal diagnosis of TAPS is based on the presence of chronic anemia in the donor and polycythemia in the recipient, defined as intertwin hemoglobin difference greater than 8.0 g/dL and at least one of the following: reticulocyte count ratio greater than 1.7 and placenta with only small (diameter <1 mm) vascular anastomoses. TAPS severity is assessed by the TAPS staging system (Fig. 20.5).40 Fetal anemia is associated with a decreased blood viscosity leading to an increase in blood speed. Fetal polycythemia is associated with an increased blood viscosity leading to a decrease in blood speed. The blood speed is measured in centimeters per second and converted to multiples of the median (MoM), which represents how far the measurement is from the average for the specific gestational week. The average is 1 MoM. Measurements greater than 1 will be considered as increased velocity (anemia), whereas measurements less than 1 will be considered as low velocity (polycythemia).

### Twin Reversed Arterial Perfusion Syndrome (TRAP)

TRAP is a rare condition affecting less than 1% of MC pregnancies, in which there is normal development of one twin (pump twin) while the other twin lacks a heart/not fully formed (acardiac twin). In DC twins, a failure of one twin to develop a heart will end up as fetal demise, while the other twin is not affected. However, in MC twins, blood supply from the normal fetus can keep the acardiac twin “alive” through the placental anastomoses. The acardiac twin usually has a poorly developed body and may be missing a head, limbs, or torso. Because the heart of the “pump twin” supplies blood to both fetuses, congestive heart failure may develop, and if untreated, perinatal mortality rate is up to 55%. The outcome may be improved by interventions to disconnect the circulation of the acardiac twin, usually performed after 16 weeks of gestation, with survival of the pump twin rising up to 80%. ### Single Intrauterine Fetal Death

Uterine demise of one twin has unique aspects in MC pregnancies. Because of the shared circulation, one twin’s death may lead to double demise in 15% of the cases or to severe brain injury in 25% of the cases caused by exsanguination of the surviving co-twin into its demised twin’s circulation.42 Single fetal demise, which may occur after successful laser coagulation for TTTS, does not affect the surviving twin, since anastomoses are ablated and the surviving twin is protected from exsanguination. In cases with recent single intrauterine death it is important to measure the middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) to predict fetal anemia, and consider intrauterine blood transfusion if anemia exists. Careful follow-up, including detailed brain scans as well as brain MRI, is indicated to reveal brain injury.

The cords typically insert close to one another on the placenta, with very large anastomoses connecting the stem vessels of both twins. ### Delivery Considerations

MC twin pregnancies carry an increased risk of perinatal death compared with DC twins.34,43 This is mainly because of higher prematurity rates, selective fetal growth restriction, congenital anomalies, and TTTS.44 MCMA twins carry an additional risk for perinatal death because of twin-related congenital anomalies and cord-related complications.45,46

A systematic review by D’Antonio et al. showed 6% fetal loss in MCMA pregnancies,46a most of which occurred before 30 weeks of gestation. At 31 to 32 and 33 to 34 weeks of gestation, fetal loss rate was 1% and 2%, respectively. In addition, these authors have reported fetal loss of 3% in twins of pregnancies managed as inpatients, compared with 7% in those followed up as outpatients.47 Thus MCMA pregnancies are usually delivered between 32+0 and 34+6 weeks of gestation in view of the reported high risk of unexpected fetal loss with advancing gestation.43,48 In practice, in many leading fetal medicine units, hospital MCMA are delivered at 32+0 weeks.34

For uncomplicated DCDA twins, the recommended time of birth is between 38 and 39 weeks of gestation. ### Antenatal Steroids in Twin Pregnancies

Multifetal gestation carries a significantly increased risk of preterm delivery, with nearly 60% of twins being born preterm at less than 37 weeks’ gestation and 12% to 14% born prior to 34 weeks.58 Over the years, there was a debate regarding the favorable effects of antenatal corticosteroids (ACSs) in multifetal pregnancies.59 Several studies reported that administration of ACSs up until 7 days prior to birth was associated with a significant decrease in neonatal mortality and morbidity in twin pregnancies, comparable with the effect on singleton infants.60

The EPIPAGE-2 study showed administration of a single complete course of ACSs reduced the incidence of severe neurologic morbidities and composite outcome in twins born between 24 and 31 completed weeks of gestation. In that study, in-hospital mortality was reduced only when the interval between ACS administration and delivery was 7 days or fewer.61

Some studies suggested suboptimal benefits of ACS treatment in twin pregnancies may be attributable to different maternal physiologic changes in twin pregnancies, such as greater maternal blood volume expansion and differences in betamethasone clearance.62 Other studies have established that there is no difference in pharmacokinetics, maternal serum, or cord blood betamethasone between multiple and singleton pregnancies.63 Studies comparing twin and singleton pregnancies reported that optimal ACS administration led to comparably improved outcomes64 and that the number of fetuses is not a determinant of the effect of ACSs in neonatal outcomes.65 However, twin pregnancy imposes an independent risk factor for suboptimal ACS administration timing because twin preterm labor is harder to predict, and therefore women are often treated too early or too late in regard to the ideal therapeutic window.66

### Outcome

Given the increased risk of maternal and fetal complications during multiple gestation, the overall outcome for multiples is worse when compared with the outcome of singletons. This is mostly because approximately half of twins are born preterm. However, advancements in antenatal and neonatal

care have resulted a significant decrease in perinatal and early neonatal mortality rates for both the first (8.6-fold reduction) and the second (6.8-fold reduction) twin.67

Multiples remain at higher risk for CP. However, this risk has been decreasing steadily since the 1990s, a decrease attributed to advances in perinatal care.

Recent studies from worldwide CP registries indicate the overall prevalence of CP is greater in triplets and quadruplets than in twins. This is most probably related to higher risk of preterm birth in higher-order multiples. Singleton and multiple births with CP display similar severity of motor impairment.68,69

When evaluating the impact of perinatal factors (i.e., IVF, growth restriction, prematurity) in DCDA twin pregnancies on main neurodevelopmental sequelae, similar risk for neurologic sequelae were observed in IVF DZ twins in comparison with their naturally conceived peers and singletons from assisted conception. Moreover, overall development and health status at 4 years of age in IVF twins was found comparable with that of 4-year-old IVF singletons, after adjusting for mediators and confounders. However, for twins born following fetal growth restriction, there was a fourfold risk for neurologic sequelae (motor development, speech and language development, and internalizing difficulties) versus normal growth twins. Significantly worse results regarding cognition, language, and motor skills were found in the smaller twin of a discordant pair at 2.5 to 3 years of age. Risk of death and neurologic impairments in twins with birth weight less than 1000 g was higher compared with singletons with similar birth weights. A high rate of mild to moderate cognitive impairment and severe neurodevelopmental impairment (NDI) at age 5 years was not identified at age 2 years. These data highlight the importance of longitudinal follow-up of survivors of TTTS beyond age 2 years and emphasize the precautions that should be taken when diagnosing an absence of impairment before school age.70 However, twins versus singletons born at less than 34 weeks of age had comparable motor and cognitive outcomes at 2 years of age.71

Follow-up of 66 twins and 157 singletons at 5 years of age in Turku, Finland revealed no major neurodevelopmental risks in twins compared with singletons. These data should be interpreted in light of the advanced perinatal care in Finland.72

In MC twins with sIUGR, evidence suggests that patients treated with laser therapy, considering the potential risks and complications of the procedure, may have an improved outcome over those managed expectantly, mainly because of postponing gestational age at delivery. Results show improvement of fetal growth in more than 50% of growth-restricted twins, while protecting the well-growing twin from the adverse consequences that could result from the fetal demise of the growthrestricted twin.73

Outcome at school age of MC twins treated with fetoscopic laser surgery for TTTS was found comparable with that of DC twins without invasive treatment. The long-term neurodevelopment was mainly dependent on gestational age

with a steady increase since the 1980s, an increase that is attributed mostly to assisted reproductive technology. Multifetal pregnancies have a major contribution to neonatal morbidity and mortality, including preterm delivery, low birth weight, and more.

### • Twin pregnancies are classified into dizygotic twins, in

which two sperms fertilize two ova, and to monozygotic twins, in which an ovum fertilized by sperm has undergone early cleavage. Chorionicity is determined by the timing of the cleavage.
