title: Post-Term Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: 21 Post-Term Pregnancy
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Post-term pregnancy defines a gestation that has completed or gone beyond 294 days or 42 weeks from the last menstrual period (LMP). The prevalence of this condition varies across countries and is dependent on an accurate evaluation of pregnancy dating. There has been a decline in post-term pregnancies in recent years due to early interventions and labor inductions. The etiologies are varied and include parity, genetic, and environmental factors. It is associated with complications for both mother and baby, such as an increased risk of preeclampsia, oligohydramnios, macrosomia, fetal distress, and perinatal death. There is also an increase in the need for obstetrical interventions and cesarean deliveries. Long-term complications such as obesity and behavioral problems have been reported. Close monitoring and consideration of labor induction are recommended for women in or approaching the post-term period. This chapter discusses the etiologies, risks, and complications associated with post-term pregnancy and reviews ways of accurately estimating gestational age, methods of monitoring fetus well-being, and the different ways of inducing labor.
paragraphs.heading: DAVID PELEG AND YAEL SIMPSON-LAVY

paragraphs.text: The human gestation for singleton pregnancies lasts an average of 266 days from fertilization or 280 days (40 weeks) from the first day of the LMP. In the past, the period between 37 and 42 weeks was considered “term,” as this was the interval during which most women delivered and newborns had the fewest complications. However, this has been shown to be inaccurate, as research has reported that the frequency of adverse outcomes is lowest between 39 weeks, 0 days and 40 weeks, 6 days.1 This interval has now been designated “full term.” The American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine have proposed that the terminology for deliveries after 37 weeks be changed (Box 21.1).2 “Post-term” is still defined as a gestation that has completed or gone beyond 294 days or 42 weeks from the LMP. Although the gestational age known as 42 “completed” weeks has been shown to be at increased risk for perinatal and neonatal mortality, as well as other adverse perinatal outcomes, some consider 41 weeks as the beginning of increased risk. In order to
paragraphs.heading: Defining Post-Term

paragraphs.text: minimize confusion when describing post-term, the use of the terms “postdates,” “prolonged,” or “postmature” should be discouraged. Table 21.1 lists the potential complications experienced by the mother and infant during the post-term period.3 Before proceeding with a discussion of these complications, we need to understand the importance of accurate pregnancy dating.
paragraphs.heading: Defining Post-Term

paragraphs.text: An accurate gestational age and estimated due date (EDD) are important for appropriate prenatal care. Using the LMP for establishing gestational age is based on the assumption that a woman’s cycle is regular and that ovulation occurs after 14 days. This method is notably inaccurate for several reasons, as it is dependent on the mother’s recall, regular cycle length, and timing of ovulation. First-trimester ultrasound has been shown to be more accurate to establish and/ or confirm gestational age, as well as to improve the EDD. It is now common practice to adjust the LMP and EDD if there is a discrepancy of 6 or more days as demonstrated on first-trimester ultrasound. Between 6% and 40% of women will have their LMP adjusted after a first-trimester ultrasound.4,5 However, the accuracy of dating a pregnancy by using a second or third trimester is suboptimal, with discrepancies of 7 to 14 days or more.6
paragraphs.heading: Estimated Gestational Age

paragraphs.text: The incidence of post-term pregnancy varies widely, as it is dependent on methodology and the population studied.
paragraphs.heading: Incidence of Post-Term Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: The incidence of post-term pregnancy in the United States was 7.2% in 2000, 5.6% in 2006, and 0.35% in 2016,7 and the rate is continuing to decrease because early intervention is becoming common practice. The incidence varies by country due to different approaches to dating, recording, and management, as well as the multiple sociodemographic and obstetric factors involved. These include cultural differences, attitudes and education of women, and the availability of medical care. As an example, the reported incidence in China was 0.70% in 2016,8 but among European countries there is great variation, with rates reported as high as 7% to 8% in Denmark and Sweden and as low as 0.4% in Austria in the year 2000.9 Post-term applies to singleton pregnancies. There is no consensus as to what gestational age is considered post-term for twin pregnancies, although it is rare for twins to continue beyond 40 gestational weeks.
paragraphs.heading: Incidence of Post-Term Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: There are several identifiable risk factors, which include nulliparity, male fetus, fetal anencephaly, prior post-term pregnancy, obesity, and X-linked placental sulfatase deficiency and adrenal hypoplasia.10
paragraphs.heading: Etiology

paragraphs.text: The familial and genetic factors predisposing for post-term pregnancy are not well understood. One study of close to half a million Swedish births demonstrated familial clustering of post-term pregnancies and estimated that nearly half of the variation could be attributed to genetic (maternal and fetal) factors.11 Sisters of women with a post-term birth were also at increased risk of delivering post-term. Little is known about the genes and genetic influences involved in post-term labor. One report investigated 9141 individuals from two Northern Finland cohorts, among whom 1167 were born post-term, and the authors reported an association between post-term pregnancy and intronic genetic variant within the ADAMTS13 gene.12 Other gene variants
paragraphs.heading: Genetic Factors

paragraphs.text: were identified as well. The effect of these variants on postterm pregnancy is under investigation.
paragraphs.heading: Genetic Factors

paragraphs.text: As many as 25% of routine inductions in low-risk women are performed due to post-term pregnancy.13 It has been suggested that some of the risks of post-term delivery, especially long term, are associated with shared underlying genetic factors rather than due to the prolonged gestation per se.14 Use of the term “post-term potential” has been suggested to describe those individuals genetically predisposed to post-term labor that were born term due to induction of labor and hence might still be prone to long-term “post-term” complications.
paragraphs.heading: Genetic Factors

paragraphs.text: Stress is associated with post-term pregnancy, which may represent an adaptive strategy to a stressful, suboptimal environment. Using the September 11, 2001, terror attack in the United States as the stressor, it was found that the odds of post-term delivery among gestations at 33 to 36 weeks in September 2001 exceeded what was statistically expected for all race, ethnic, and sex groups.15 It was proposed that stress later in gestation may operate to prolong delivery until conditions improve, the fetus is hardier, or the risks associated with prolonged gestation and post-term delivery outweigh the risks of giving birth to a baby in a suboptimal environment. Maternal obesity has also been found to be associated with post-term pregnancy. There is a direct correlation between obesity category and absolute post-term birth risk.16
paragraphs.heading: Environmental Factors

paragraphs.text: Pregnancies that have progressed to late term or post-term are at increased risk of macrosomia.17 In one study of over 50,000 births, macrosomia (defined as a birth weight of over 4000 g) increased from 8% at 40 weeks’ to 12% at 41 weeks’ and 15% at 42 weeks’ gestation.18 This obviously contributed to the rise in cesarean delivery, which increased from 7% to 14%. Similarly, post-term pregnancy is a known risk factor for shoulder dystocia.19
paragraphs.heading: Macrosomia, Cesarean Delivery, Shoulder Dystocia

paragraphs.text: It is believed by many that the placenta has a preprogrammed lifespan, and function begins to deteriorate after term. Syncytiotrophabast dysfunction and placental apoptosis have been demonstrated in the post-term period.20 This has been associated with reduced functionality of the placenta and reduced oxygenation of the fetus. This was demonstrated by a 67% increase in umbilical cord erythropoietin concentration in post-term pregnancies.21 The post-term period is also associated with decreased amniotic fluid, although the exact mechanism of this reduction is still being debated. The two common methods of defining oligohydramnios are a deepest
paragraphs.heading: Placental Dysfunction

paragraphs.text: vertical pocket that is <2 cm or an amniotic fluid index of <5 cm. Because of oligohydramnios, there is increased risk of fetal heart rate abnormalities (“fetal distress”) as a result of cord compression.22,23 The association between a reduced amniotic fluid volume and variable decelerations has been well documented. The risk of developing preeclampsia also increases with gestational age. In one study of over 3000 low-risk nulliparous women, the incidence of preeclampsia increased from 5.0% in those delivering at 39 weeks to 6.9% in those delivering at 40 weeks and beyond.24
paragraphs.heading: Placental Dysfunction

paragraphs.text: In 1954, Clifford25 described the post-maturity syndrome, which included the absence of vernix, dry and crackled skin, and an “old and worried” appearance, with infants having open eyes and being alert. The syndrome was related to in utero meconium release, meconium aspiration syndrome, placental dysfunction, intrauterine hypoxia, intrauterine mortality, and increased risk of neonatal death. This description is still valid today. Post-term delivery is associated with higher rates of meconium-stained amniotic fluid, increased risk for meconium aspiration syndrome, low 5-minute Apgar scores, asphyxia,26–28 and neonatal convulsions. There are also higher admission rates to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) and shoulder dystocia.29-31,18,32
paragraphs.heading: Neonatal Risks of Post-Term Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: Po’ at el.33 suggested that the perinatal mortality rate remains rather constant between 38 and 41 weeks’ gestation but begins to climb from 42 weeks onward; for example, Figure 21.1 shows the perinatal mortality of 12 million births for the 3-year period from 2014 to 2016 in the United States. However, there remains conflicting data regarding perinatal death in the post-term period. Earlier studies reported a significant increase in stillborn and neonatal death, whereas later studies, mainly on well-monitored, low-risk pregnancies, showed no such increase.27,32 Some of the confusion is due to research based on live-born registries, which do not include cases of intrauterine fetal death.
paragraphs.heading: Neonatal Risks of Post-Term Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: One study investigated the association of post-term pregnancy with neonatal outcomes in low-risk singleton newborns.32 Infants in the post-term group had more NICU admissions, greater respiratory morbidity, and more infections, but not more meconium aspiration syndrome, than term babies. They also observed more hypoglycemia in postterm babies. They did not find any increase in birth trauma or neurological morbidity.
paragraphs.heading: Neonatal Risks of Post-Term Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: Post-term delivery is associated with a decrease in IQ compared with term babies.27,34,35 Although consistent and statistically significant, the reported effect is relatively small (approximately 2 IQ points) and of unknown clinical significance. This slight reduction of IQ scores might be influenced by the small group of post-term infants that are severely impaired due to birth trauma and asphyxia. A large register-based study also demonstrated increased risk for intellectual disability, whereas risks for cerebral palsy, epilepsy, and sensorineural defects were not increased.27 However, another study did find a statistically significant increase in cerebral palsy among children born after 42 weeks of gestation, with a relative risk of 1.44.36
paragraphs.heading: Long-Term Complications of Post-Term Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: There is evidence for increased behavioral and emotional problems in children born post-term, as well as increased risk for mental disorders as adults. Overall, behavioral problems and attention deficit or hyperactivity problems were reported to be twice as high in post-term children (1.5 and 3 years, respectively) than in full-term children.37 There was a significant increase in the risk of any mental disorder in general, particularly of substance use and anxiety disorders, especially in men.38 Post-term birth is also associated with greater risk of being overweight or obese in boys, with higher body mass index (BMI) at 3 years of age and older compared to term infants. This difference continues to increase as they age.39
paragraphs.heading: Long-Term Complications of Post-Term Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: Given the overall increased risks to the mother and fetus during the post-term period, intervention is warranted, although the method and timing are still debated. Intervention may take the form of either fetal surveillance or labor induction (delivery). Although there is no consensus, it is suggested that induction should be considered sometime during the 41st week of gestation and certainly by the 42nd week. One retrospective study compared expectant management versus induction beyond 41 weeks and found no difference in the cesarean or operative vaginal delivery rate.40 Another randomized trial compared induction versus fetal surveillance starting at 41 weeks.41 Fetal testing included non-stress testing and amniotic fluid volume assessment. In this trial, 901 women were managed by fetal surveillance and 900 women by induction of labor. There was one fetal death (0.1%) in the induction group and two (0.2%) in the expectant management group. There were no neonatal deaths. The composite adverse perinatal outcome was 1.7% in the induction group versus 3.1% in the expectant management group, which was marginally significant. The cesarean delivery rate was similar in both groups (10.7%).
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: Several tests are available to assess fetal well-being. These include fetal kick counts, non-stress test (NST), biophysical profile (BPP), oxytocin contraction test, and the modified BPP, which combines the NST with amniotic fluid assessment (Table 21.2). There is no consensus as to which type, frequency, or combination of testing is optimal. One randomized study compared testing after 42 weeks using the
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Surveillance

paragraphs.text: BPP versus the modified BPP.42 There were more abnormal results with the BPP. The authors suggested this may be the result of using the amniotic fluid index rather than the deepest vertical pocket to evaluate amniotic fluid volume. There are no randomized controlled trials showing that antepartum fetal testing decreases morbidity or mortality; however, based on the increased fetal morbidity and mortality, it seems prudent to begin fetal testing no later than 41 weeks. By performing testing, the provider and mother should agree that induction and delivery are indicated if testing is abnormal.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Surveillance

paragraphs.text: Once it has been agreed upon, induction of labor can be initiated. One survey from 2006 of obstetricians in the United States reported that 73% of them would routinely induce low-risk women at 41 weeks.43 Methods for induction are listed in Table 21.3.
paragraphs.heading: Induction of Labor

paragraphs.text: Successful induction is defined as placing a nonlaboring woman into active labor. There are several factors that increase the success rate of induction. These include a “favorable” cervix, engaged presenting part, and parity. Most agree that a diagnosis of failed induction cannot be made in the absence of rupture of membranes. A favorable cervix suggests that induction of labor is more likely to be successful. There is no exact definition of favorable, although it is agreed that the more the cervix is dilated and effaced, the more favorable it is.

21 Post-Term Pregnancy

### DAVID PELEG AND YAEL SIMPSON-LAVY

Post-term pregnancy defines a gestation that has completed or gone beyond 294 days or 42 weeks from the last menstrual period (LMP). The prevalence of this condition varies across countries and is dependent on an accurate evaluation of pregnancy dating. There has been a decline in post-term pregnancies in recent years due to early interventions and labor inductions. The etiologies are varied and include parity, genetic, and environmental factors. It is associated with complications for both mother and baby, such as an increased risk of preeclampsia, oligohydramnios, macrosomia, fetal distress, and perinatal death. There is also an increase in the need for obstetrical interventions and cesarean deliveries. Long-term complications such as obesity and behavioral problems have been reported. Close monitoring and consideration of labor induction are recommended for women in or approaching the post-term period. This chapter discusses the etiologies, risks, and complications associated with post-term pregnancy and reviews ways of accurately estimating gestational age, methods of monitoring fetus well-being, and the different ways of inducing labor.

### Defining Post-Term

The human gestation for singleton pregnancies lasts an average of 266 days from fertilization or 280 days (40 weeks) from the first day of the LMP. In the past, the period between 37 and 42 weeks was considered “term,” as this was the interval during which most women delivered and newborns had the fewest complications. However, this has been shown to be inaccurate, as research has reported that the frequency of adverse outcomes is lowest between 39 weeks, 0 days and 40 weeks, 6 days.1 This interval has now been designated “full term.” The American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine have proposed that the terminology for deliveries after 37 weeks be changed (Box 21.1).2 “Post-term” is still defined as a gestation that has completed or gone beyond 294 days or 42 weeks from the LMP. Although the gestational age known as 42 “completed” weeks has been shown to be at increased risk for perinatal and neonatal mortality, as well as other adverse perinatal outcomes, some consider 41 weeks as the beginning of increased risk. In order to

minimize confusion when describing post-term, the use of the terms “postdates,” “prolonged,” or “postmature” should be discouraged. Table 21.1 lists the potential complications experienced by the mother and infant during the post-term period.3 Before proceeding with a discussion of these complications, we need to understand the importance of accurate pregnancy dating.

### Estimated Gestational Age

An accurate gestational age and estimated due date (EDD) are important for appropriate prenatal care. Using the LMP for establishing gestational age is based on the assumption that a woman’s cycle is regular and that ovulation occurs after 14 days. This method is notably inaccurate for several reasons, as it is dependent on the mother’s recall, regular cycle length, and timing of ovulation. First-trimester ultrasound has been shown to be more accurate to establish and/ or confirm gestational age, as well as to improve the EDD. It is now common practice to adjust the LMP and EDD if there is a discrepancy of 6 or more days as demonstrated on first-trimester ultrasound. Between 6% and 40% of women will have their LMP adjusted after a first-trimester ultrasound.4,5 However, the accuracy of dating a pregnancy by using a second or third trimester is suboptimal, with discrepancies of 7 to 14 days or more.6

### Incidence of Post-Term Pregnancy

The incidence of post-term pregnancy varies widely, as it is dependent on methodology and the population studied.

The incidence of post-term pregnancy in the United States was 7.2% in 2000, 5.6% in 2006, and 0.35% in 2016,7 and the rate is continuing to decrease because early intervention is becoming common practice. The incidence varies by country due to different approaches to dating, recording, and management, as well as the multiple sociodemographic and obstetric factors involved. These include cultural differences, attitudes and education of women, and the availability of medical care. As an example, the reported incidence in China was 0.70% in 2016,8 but among European countries there is great variation, with rates reported as high as 7% to 8% in Denmark and Sweden and as low as 0.4% in Austria in the year 2000.9 Post-term applies to singleton pregnancies. There is no consensus as to what gestational age is considered post-term for twin pregnancies, although it is rare for twins to continue beyond 40 gestational weeks.

### Etiology

There are several identifiable risk factors, which include nulliparity, male fetus, fetal anencephaly, prior post-term pregnancy, obesity, and X-linked placental sulfatase deficiency and adrenal hypoplasia.10

### Genetic Factors

The familial and genetic factors predisposing for post-term pregnancy are not well understood. One study of close to half a million Swedish births demonstrated familial clustering of post-term pregnancies and estimated that nearly half of the variation could be attributed to genetic (maternal and fetal) factors.11 Sisters of women with a post-term birth were also at increased risk of delivering post-term. Little is known about the genes and genetic influences involved in post-term labor. One report investigated 9141 individuals from two Northern Finland cohorts, among whom 1167 were born post-term, and the authors reported an association between post-term pregnancy and intronic genetic variant within the ADAMTS13 gene.12 Other gene variants

were identified as well. The effect of these variants on postterm pregnancy is under investigation.

As many as 25% of routine inductions in low-risk women are performed due to post-term pregnancy.13 It has been suggested that some of the risks of post-term delivery, especially long term, are associated with shared underlying genetic factors rather than due to the prolonged gestation per se.14 Use of the term “post-term potential” has been suggested to describe those individuals genetically predisposed to post-term labor that were born term due to induction of labor and hence might still be prone to long-term “post-term” complications.

### Environmental Factors

Stress is associated with post-term pregnancy, which may represent an adaptive strategy to a stressful, suboptimal environment. Using the September 11, 2001, terror attack in the United States as the stressor, it was found that the odds of post-term delivery among gestations at 33 to 36 weeks in September 2001 exceeded what was statistically expected for all race, ethnic, and sex groups.15 It was proposed that stress later in gestation may operate to prolong delivery until conditions improve, the fetus is hardier, or the risks associated with prolonged gestation and post-term delivery outweigh the risks of giving birth to a baby in a suboptimal environment. Maternal obesity has also been found to be associated with post-term pregnancy. There is a direct correlation between obesity category and absolute post-term birth risk.16

### Maternal Complications

### Macrosomia, Cesarean Delivery, Shoulder Dystocia

Pregnancies that have progressed to late term or post-term are at increased risk of macrosomia.17 In one study of over 50,000 births, macrosomia (defined as a birth weight of over 4000 g) increased from 8% at 40 weeks’ to 12% at 41 weeks’ and 15% at 42 weeks’ gestation.18 This obviously contributed to the rise in cesarean delivery, which increased from 7% to 14%. Similarly, post-term pregnancy is a known risk factor for shoulder dystocia.19

### Placental Dysfunction

It is believed by many that the placenta has a preprogrammed lifespan, and function begins to deteriorate after term. Syncytiotrophabast dysfunction and placental apoptosis have been demonstrated in the post-term period.20 This has been associated with reduced functionality of the placenta and reduced oxygenation of the fetus. This was demonstrated by a 67% increase in umbilical cord erythropoietin concentration in post-term pregnancies.21 The post-term period is also associated with decreased amniotic fluid, although the exact mechanism of this reduction is still being debated. The two common methods of defining oligohydramnios are a deepest


## PDF page 390 | printed page 375

vertical pocket that is <2 cm or an amniotic fluid index of <5 cm. Because of oligohydramnios, there is increased risk of fetal heart rate abnormalities (“fetal distress”) as a result of cord compression.22,23 The association between a reduced amniotic fluid volume and variable decelerations has been well documented. The risk of developing preeclampsia also increases with gestational age. In one study of over 3000 low-risk nulliparous women, the incidence of preeclampsia increased from 5.0% in those delivering at 39 weeks to 6.9% in those delivering at 40 weeks and beyond.24

### Neonatal Risks of Post-Term Pregnancy

In 1954, Clifford25 described the post-maturity syndrome, which included the absence of vernix, dry and crackled skin, and an “old and worried” appearance, with infants having open eyes and being alert. The syndrome was related to in utero meconium release, meconium aspiration syndrome, placental dysfunction, intrauterine hypoxia, intrauterine mortality, and increased risk of neonatal death. This description is still valid today. Post-term delivery is associated with higher rates of meconium-stained amniotic fluid, increased risk for meconium aspiration syndrome, low 5-minute Apgar scores, asphyxia,26–28 and neonatal convulsions. There are also higher admission rates to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) and shoulder dystocia.29-31,18,32

Po’ at el.33 suggested that the perinatal mortality rate remains rather constant between 38 and 41 weeks’ gestation but begins to climb from 42 weeks onward; for example, Figure 21.1 shows the perinatal mortality of 12 million births for the 3-year period from 2014 to 2016 in the United States. However, there remains conflicting data regarding perinatal death in the post-term period. Earlier studies reported a significant increase in stillborn and neonatal death, whereas later studies, mainly on well-monitored, low-risk pregnancies, showed no such increase.27,32 Some of the confusion is due to research based on live-born registries, which do not include cases of intrauterine fetal death.

One study investigated the association of post-term pregnancy with neonatal outcomes in low-risk singleton newborns.32 Infants in the post-term group had more NICU admissions, greater respiratory morbidity, and more infections, but not more meconium aspiration syndrome, than term babies. They also observed more hypoglycemia in postterm babies. They did not find any increase in birth trauma or neurological morbidity.

### Long-Term Complications of Post-Term Pregnancy

Post-term delivery is associated with a decrease in IQ compared with term babies.27,34,35 Although consistent and statistically significant, the reported effect is relatively small (approximately 2 IQ points) and of unknown clinical significance. This slight reduction of IQ scores might be influenced by the small group of post-term infants that are severely impaired due to birth trauma and asphyxia. A large register-based study also demonstrated increased risk for intellectual disability, whereas risks for cerebral palsy, epilepsy, and sensorineural defects were not increased.27 However, another study did find a statistically significant increase in cerebral palsy among children born after 42 weeks of gestation, with a relative risk of 1.44.36

There is evidence for increased behavioral and emotional problems in children born post-term, as well as increased risk for mental disorders as adults. Overall, behavioral problems and attention deficit or hyperactivity problems were reported to be twice as high in post-term children (1.5 and 3 years, respectively) than in full-term children.37 There was a significant increase in the risk of any mental disorder in general, particularly of substance use and anxiety disorders, especially in men.38 Post-term birth is also associated with greater risk of being overweight or obese in boys, with higher body mass index (BMI) at 3 years of age and older compared to term infants. This difference continues to increase as they age.39

### Management

Given the overall increased risks to the mother and fetus during the post-term period, intervention is warranted, although the method and timing are still debated. Intervention may take the form of either fetal surveillance or labor induction (delivery). Although there is no consensus, it is suggested that induction should be considered sometime during the 41st week of gestation and certainly by the 42nd week. One retrospective study compared expectant management versus induction beyond 41 weeks and found no difference in the cesarean or operative vaginal delivery rate.40 Another randomized trial compared induction versus fetal surveillance starting at 41 weeks.41 Fetal testing included non-stress testing and amniotic fluid volume assessment. In this trial, 901 women were managed by fetal surveillance and 900 women by induction of labor. There was one fetal death (0.1%) in the induction group and two (0.2%) in the expectant management group. There were no neonatal deaths. The composite adverse perinatal outcome was 1.7% in the induction group versus 3.1% in the expectant management group, which was marginally significant. The cesarean delivery rate was similar in both groups (10.7%).

### Fetal Surveillance

Several tests are available to assess fetal well-being. These include fetal kick counts, non-stress test (NST), biophysical profile (BPP), oxytocin contraction test, and the modified BPP, which combines the NST with amniotic fluid assessment (Table 21.2). There is no consensus as to which type, frequency, or combination of testing is optimal. One randomized study compared testing after 42 weeks using the

### Induction of Labor

Once it has been agreed upon, induction of labor can be initiated. One survey from 2006 of obstetricians in the United States reported that 73% of them would routinely induce low-risk women at 41 weeks.43 Methods for induction are listed in Table 21.3.

### Factors Associated With Successful Induction

Successful induction is defined as placing a nonlaboring woman into active labor. There are several factors that increase the success rate of induction. These include a “favorable” cervix, engaged presenting part, and parity. Most agree that a diagnosis of failed induction cannot be made in the absence of rupture of membranes. A favorable cervix suggests that induction of labor is more likely to be successful. There is no exact definition of favorable, although it is agreed that the more the cervix is dilated and effaced, the more favorable it is.

title: Immune and Nonimmune Hydrops Fetalis

paragraphs.text: 22 Immune and Nonimmune Hydrops Fetalis
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Hydrops fetalis (HF) is defined as the presence of excessive fetal fluid in two or more of the following spaces: abdominal ascites, pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, skin edema, polyhydramnios, or placentomegaly. The diagnosis is made by ultrasound imaging evaluating body cavities, the placenta, and the amniotic fluid volume. Classically, HF has been classified into two categories based on etiology: Immune HF accounts for an estimated 10% to 24%, and nonimmune HF accounts for 76% to 90% of cases and is becoming increasingly the main cause of HF (Table 22.1).
paragraphs.heading: KAITLYN HEBERT TAYLOR, PAMELA M. SIMMONS, AND EVERETT F. MAGANN

paragraphs.text: Immune hydrops fetalis (IHF) was initially recognized as the combination of neonatal hydrops, anemia, and jaundice along with erythroblastosis and red blood cell (RBC) hemolysis by Diamond and coinvestigators in 1932.1 The pathophysiology of the IHF was explained by the work of Karl Landsteiner and associates, who discovered the rhesus (Rh) antigen in 1940. In 1941, Levine and coworkers2 observed that, if an Rh-negative woman is exposed to RBCs that are Rh positive, she will form antibodies that may result in transplacental passage of the antibodies to fetal RBCs and may result in fetal hemolysis. The resultant maternal alloimmunization was initially documented by Chown and coworkers.3
paragraphs.heading: Immune Hydrops Fetalis

paragraphs.text: Anti-D antibodies were proposed as a method to prevent the nonimmunized Rh-negative mother from becoming sensitized after birth. Freda and coworkers studied the efficacy of specific anti-D immune globulin in Rh-negative male prison volunteers who were given Rh-D-positive blood and observed that sensitization could be prevented.4 A subsequent investigation confirmed that if prisoners were given Rh-D-positive blood and received anti-D immune globulin within 72 hours, alloimmunization did not occur.5
paragraphs.heading: Immune Hydrops Fetalis

paragraphs.text: Blood group antigens were among the first discoveries of genetic polymorphisms in human proteins.6 Of these, the
paragraphs.heading: Genetics of the Rh System

paragraphs.text: Rh factor (the largest of all of the blood groups) has more than 50 different described antigens, with additional discoveries likely to continue. Most of these are quantitative antigens (affecting the amounts of Rh factors expressed), although some are qualitative in nature. Not all antigens have clinical significance in pregnancy. Three of the most concerning antigens in pregnancy, the Rh(D), Rh(Cc), and Rh(Ee) antigens, are encoded at two human loci, found on chromosome #1 (1p36.1).7 They can cause antibody formation in pregnancy and lead to significant hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN) in future pregnancies. Although there are multiple nomenclature systems for maternal rhesus (DCE) status, the Fisher and Race method has clinical advantages, such as ease of use and remembering, and was also proved genetically correct.8 In this system, each parent contributes an allele from the Rh(D), Rh(C), and Rh(E) gene loci. In broad terms, these alleles are called D or d, C or c, and E or e. A person can be homozygous or heterozygous for each of these alleles. The genes are so closely linked on chromosome #1 that crossover between the alleles is not thought to occur.
paragraphs.heading: Genetics of the Rh System

paragraphs.text: The D antigen is a transmembrane protein with several extracellular loops located on erythrocytes and their immediate progenitors. Most alleles of the Rh(D) gene (∼170 identified) are caused by nonsense or missense mutations, although frameshift and splice-site mutations have also been reported.9 Alleles that cause strongly reduced or complete absence of the Rh-D antigen are often referred to as DEL or negative alleles, respectively. These include the most common European d (Rh-negative) phenotype. The Rh-negative phenotype is most common in individuals of European and North American descent (15%–17%) followed by African and Indian (3%–8%), with the rarest in Asia (0.1%–0.3%).10,11 Thirty percent of Rh-negative Asians actually carry a DEL allele, whereas this phenotype is rare in Europeans. Other alleles may result in “partial D” antigens (qualitative). There are also alleles that produce a “weak” Rh(D) antigen. DEL, negative, partial D, and weak D alleles can be clinically significant in pregnancy and increase the risk for HDN.
paragraphs.heading: Genetics of the Rh System

paragraphs.text: The D alleles are dominant over the d alleles. It is important to note that d is simply the absence of D antigen; there has been no identification of an actual d antigen. Thus it is the presence or absence (and the extent) of the D antigen that will determine if an individual is Rh positive or Rh negative. There are significantly fewer alleles identified at the Rh(CcEe) gene. Unlike the Rh(D) alleles, the Cc and Ee alleles are codominant; both are expressed in a heterozygote state. The mutations/changes between the alleles are limited and result in amino acid changes at only five locations.12 Partial C, c, E, and e antigens can be present, but the clinical significance of these in pregnancy is undetermined.
paragraphs.heading: Genetics of the Rh System

paragraphs.text: The Kell blood group gene, located on chromosome #7 (7q33),7 has many polymorphisms, and its alleles encode for approximately 20 to 25 antigens. Behind the Rh and ABO blood group antigens, Kell antigens carry the most risk for HDN in human pregnancy. The two most common alleles are K and k. The Kell protein transverses the RBC membrane only once, unlike D and CcEe. Kell antibodies work differently in the lysing of fetal RBCs than Rh and CcEe antibodies; Kell antibodies actually destroy early precursors of erythrocytes in the fetal liver and affect early proliferation of RBCs, instead of only attacking mature RBCs in fetal circulation.13
paragraphs.heading: Genetics of the Rh System

paragraphs.text: Because each of these antigens can lead to HDN, knowing ethnicity may be helpful in predicting risks for fetal status in a broad sense or if the father of a fetus is unavailable. Of course, when possible, it is advisable to obtain paternal DCE antigen and/or Kell antigen genotyping in at-risk pregnancies. Certainly other antigens have been linked to
paragraphs.heading: Genetics of the Rh System

paragraphs.text: HDN, but genotyping is not available for all of these blood groups. These results are of great importance in delineating the best courses of action during gestation for monitoring an at-risk fetus.
paragraphs.heading: Genetics of the Rh System

paragraphs.text: Typical methods of monitoring at-risk fetuses have included monitoring of maternal antibody titers; targeted ultrasounds to obtain serial middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) values and exclude the presence of hydrops, amniocentesis, or chorionic villus sampling for fetal antigen genotyping; and/or amniocentesis to determine ΔOD450, whereas the latter is rarely used clinically anymore. Traditionally, fetal genotyping has been performed using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) on amniocytes or chorionic villi. New technology now allows for noninvasive determination of fetal Rh-D antigen status through the use of cell-free fetal DNA collection from a maternal blood sample. Although this technology is relatively new, this method of testing has proved to be very accurate (94%– 97%), with high sensitivity and specificity.14,15 Because fetal DNA is directly tested from maternal serum, it reduces the need for invasive testing, Rh-D prophylaxis, and paternal antigen genotyping in most cases.
paragraphs.heading: Genetics of the Rh System

paragraphs.text: Alloimmunization, which was formerly known as isoimmunization, occurs when a mother develops antibodies to a paternally derived RBC antigen that is inherited by the fetus or from a transfusion of unmatched or mismatched blood. If this occurs, hemolytic disease of the fetus or neonate in subsequent pregnancies can occur. In Rh alloimmunization, an Rh-D-negative mother is exposed to Rh-D-positive blood. A quantifiable amount of hemorrhage occurs between the fetus and the mother in up to 75% of all pregnancies. This may range from less than 0.1 mL of blood in 60% of pregnancies to an excess of 5 mL in less than 1% of pregnancies. In an analysis of maternal fetal hemorrhage, 0.01 mL of fetal blood was detected in the maternal circulation in 3%, 12%, and 46% in the first, second, and third trimesters of pregnancy, respectively.16 The risk of sensitization is related to the amount of blood that passes between the fetus and mother. For 0.1 mL of blood, the risk of sensitization is 3%; for 0.4 mL, the risk rises to 22%. Rh sensitization has been reported as early as 38 days, and fetal maternal hemorrhage has been demonstrated as early as 5 to 6 weeks (mean maternal fetal transfusion at 8 weeks is 0.3 mL). The minimal amount of fetal blood needed to cause alloimmunization is estimated to be 0.25 mL. The greatest risk occurs at the time of delivery, when that risk is approximately 17%. ABO incompatibility of the mother and fetus in pregnancy with Rh sensitization (mother O; father A, B, or AB) will reduce the sensitization risk to 2%. Additionally, 30% of Rh-negative individuals are nonresponders and will not become sensitized. Box 22.1 summarizes the numerous risk factors for maternal fetal hemorrhage during pregnancy.
paragraphs.heading: Pathophysiology of Rh-D Isoimmunization

paragraphs.text: IHF is the end result of progressive RBC destruction, in which even with the recruitment of extramedullary tissue
paragraphs.heading: Pathophysiology of Rh-D Isoimmunization

paragraphs.text: (liver and spleen) the severity of the hemolysis results in severe fetal anemia, HF, and often fetal death. Although the fetus is able to compensate for progressive anemia, one study determined that, when the hemoglobin deficit has exceeded 7 g/dL, this compensatory ability of the fetus may become exhausted and IHF will ensue.17 The concept of a fixed hemoglobin level for IHF likely should be adjusted for gestational age, because with advancing gestational age the mean hemoglobin value increases, going from 10.6 g/dL at 18 weeks to 13.8 g/dL at 40 weeks. It has been suggested that a hemoglobin value of less than 0.5 times the median for gestational age might be a more appropriate predictor for fetuses at significant risk for HF.
paragraphs.heading: Pathophysiology of Rh-D Isoimmunization

paragraphs.text: Progressive ultrasound findings of IHF include the early findings of polyhydramnios and placentomegaly, followed
paragraphs.heading: Pathophysiology of Rh-D Isoimmunization

paragraphs.text: by hepatomegaly and pericardial effusions and late findings of ascites, scalp edema, pleural effusions, and, finally, oligohydramnios.18 Severe fetal anemia (fetal hemoglobin of ≤5 g/dL) associated with the development of HF19 has implications on fetal survival. In a study with intravascular transfusions, the survival rate for nonhydropic fetuses was 94% compared with 74% in fetuses with hydrops.20 The exact mechanism that causes IHF is unknown. Proposed mechanisms include high output cardiac failure, liver dysfunction, and fetal hypoxemia from fetal anemia. It is likely that a combination of all three is responsible for fetal hydrops.
paragraphs.heading: Pathophysiology of Rh-D Isoimmunization

paragraphs.text: Prevention of Rh alloimmunization begins at the first prenatal visit. A careful history should be taken of any problems associated with previous pregnancies or deliveries, prior blood transfusions, or blood disorders. Initial laboratory work should include ABO typing, Rh-D status, and an antibody screen. If the mother is Rh-D negative, this should be carefully documented in the chart. If the antibody screen is positive, the antibody test and a titer of the antibody should be repeated and a determination should be made for antibodies, Rh-D, and others that are not Rh-D to ascertain if the antibody is known to cause HDN (Fig. 22.1). If the antibody is positive Rh-D, then the patient should be questioned about a prior injection of anti-D immune globulin, as this could be the reason for the positive antibody titer.
paragraphs.heading: Management Prevention

paragraphs.text: Anti-D immune globulin is a passive immunoglobulin that, when given to Rh-D-negative women, will prevent the
paragraphs.heading: Rh-Immunoglobulin Prophylaxis

paragraphs.text: vast majority of cases of alloimmunization. Unfortunately, there are no other immune globulins specific for the other RBC antigens. After the initial screen at the first prenatal visit, a repeat Rh-D antibody screen is done at 24 to 28 weeks. If the antibody screen is negative, 300 μg of anti- D immune globulin is administered at that gestational age and then again within 72 hours of delivery if the neonate is Rh-D positive. Other accepted regimens are 100 μg at 28 and 34 weeks and following delivery if the neonate is Rh-D positive. Suggested doses of anti-D immune globulin for a first-trimester induced or spontaneous abortion, amniocentesis, or chorionic villus sampling and first-trimester ectopic pregnancy are 50–120 μg of anti-D immune globulin up to 12 weeks’ gestation. After 12 weeks’ gestation, it is recommended to use 300 μg of anti-D immune globulin.21–23 Three hundred micrograms of anti-D immune globulin will suppress the immune response of 30 mL of fetal blood or 15 mL of packed D-positive RBCs. Women should be screened at delivery and when maternal fetal hemorrhage is suspected to prevent an inadequate dose of anti-D immune globulin being administered and subsequent alloimmunization (Table 22.2).
paragraphs.heading: Rh-Immunoglobulin Prophylaxis

paragraphs.text: Techniques using molecular genetics have permitted the preimplantation diagnosis of Rh-D status.24 This technology has the potential to prevent Rh isoimmunization through selective transfer of Rh-D-negative embryos. In the
paragraphs.heading: Preimplantation Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: case of severe maternal alloimmunization, the approach can prevent fetal hemolytic disease with its associated morbidity and mortality. In the first use of this technology in 2005, an unaffected Rh-negative neonate was born to an Rh-D alloimmunized mother.25 Following intracytoplasmic sperm injection, 12 embryos were obtained, and on day 3 biopsies were performed followed by PCR. Two Rh-D-negative embryos that were subsequently transferred resulted in the delivery of a healthy Rh-D-negative infant at 39 weeks of gestation. Notwithstanding the emotional, psychological, and financial burdens of in vitro fertilization, this represents a potentially lifesaving approach for selected couples with maternal Rh alloimmunization.
paragraphs.heading: Preimplantation Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Detection of Rh alloimmunization begins with the initial laboratory work. Pregnant women who are Rh negative are screened for antibodies by the indirect Coombs test. This allows detection of Rh-D antibodies, as well as antibodies to other atypical antigens known to cause alloimmunization. If Rh-negative women are alloimmunized to Rh-D, they need to have their anti-D titer determined, because that titer is known to roughly correlate with the severity of the disease and the need for Doppler flow studies. Although each lab sets its own standards based on experience, anti-D titers of 1:16 or greater require further assessment. If the titer is less than 1:16, the patient can be followed with monthly titers.
paragraphs.heading: Rh Alloimmunization

paragraphs.text: In sensitized Rh-D-negative women where the father is Rh-D positive, paternal genotyping may help clarify the fetal risk. PCR determination of paternal Rh-D status can facilitate counseling and dictate the need for intervention, because paternal heterozygosity is associated with a 50% risk of fetal Rh-D negativity, whereas homozygosity always produces an Rh-D-positive fetus, assuming correct paternity. Fetal Rh-D typing can also be done with amniocytes in the second trimester or with villi in the first trimester (Fig. 22.2). More recently, fetal Rh-D genotyping has been achieved through isolation of cell-free fetal DNA from the maternal circulation and provides a noninvasive way to directly assess fetal blood type and antibody status.
paragraphs.heading: Rh Alloimmunization

paragraphs.text: Cordocentesis and sampling of fetal blood is the most accurate method to determine if fetal anemia is present; however, this technique is invasive and carries a fetal loss risk of up to 3%. This has led to the use of other techniques to evaluate when the risk for fetal anemia is present so that fetal blood sampling can be undertaken. Fetal anemia had been determined previously by amniocentesis and determination of risk for fetal anemia using optical density of amniotic fluid (ΔOD450). This method used an assessment of the bilirubin content of amniotic fluid to determine the estimated level of fetal anemia. Often, a series of amniocenteses was necessary to monitor the pregnancy and determine when a more invasive cordocentesis was undertaken. With improvements
paragraphs.heading: Prediction of Anemia

paragraphs.text: in ultrasound technology, this method has been replaced by serial assessments of the peak systolic velocity (PSV) of the middle cerebral artery (MCA) in the detection of fetal anemia.26
paragraphs.heading: Prediction of Anemia

paragraphs.text: The objective of Doppler flow studies is to detect physiologic compensatory changes in the fetal circulation that would be associated with mild to moderate anemia. As anemia progresses, both right and left ventricular outputs increase up to 45% with the heart rate remaining unchanged. This increases stroke volume. Progressive anemia leads to decreased blood viscosity. If the given fetal blood vessel cross-sectional area also remains unchanged and applying Poiseuille’s law (blood velocity is directly proportional to flow), increased stroke volume results in increased flow (flow being the product of velocity and the cross-sectional area).
paragraphs.heading: Prediction of Anemia

paragraphs.text: A number of fetal vessels were evaluated by Doppler flow studies to determine which vessel would be the most predictive of fetal anemia. The MCA was selected because it is well known that the cerebral arteries respond rapidly to hypoxemia by increasing blood flow velocity to maintain cerebral perfusion. Additionally, the MCA is easy to identify with low interobserver and intraobserver variability. Mari and the Collaborative Group for Doppler Assessment of the Blood Velocity in Anemic Fetuses measured the hemoglobin concentrations in blood obtained by cordocentesis and correlated those concentrations with MCA-PSV in 111 fetuses at risk for anemia secondary to RBC alloimmunization.27 The group used a hemoglobin
paragraphs.heading: Prediction of Anemia

paragraphs.text: concentration of 5 g/dL as a threshold to calculate degrees of anemia, because fetal hydrops is rare with a hemoglobin concentration greater than 5 g/dL.28 Strict cutoffs using receiver operating characteristic curves were determined to detect 100% of those fetuses with moderate to severe anemia. They found that the optimal threshold was 1.29 times the median for mild anemia, 1.5 times the median for moderate anemia, and 1.55 times the median for severe anemia, with a false-positive rate of 12%. These thresholds were chosen so as not to miss any fetus with moderate or severe anemia that might result in either fetal hydrops or death (Table 22.3). Measurements of the MCA-PSV can be started as early as 16 to 18 weeks and should be repeated at 1- to 2-week intervals.
paragraphs.heading: Prediction of Anemia

paragraphs.text: Although most fetuses with severe Rh alloimmunization can be treated with in utero intravascular transfusions, some cannot because of gestational age (<18 weeks); they may be difficult to transfuse because of small vessels or other technical issues that may make the intravascular transfusion impractical or impossible. Maternal administration of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) has been proposed as an alternative therapy until an intravascular transfusion is possible. The proposed mechanism of action is feedback inhibition of maternal antibody synthesis, blockade of reticuloendothelial Fc receptors, or blockade of placental antibody transport. There is some literature that suggests that, in pregnancies with severe Rh alloimmunization before 20 weeks, treatment with high-dose IVIG followed by an intrauterine transfusion after 20 weeks compared with pregnancies treated only with an intrauterine transfusion after 20 weeks had improved fetal survival rates.29 In another series of four pregnancies with severe Rh alloimmunization treated with high-dose IVIG, there appeared to be no effect on the total number of transfusions or the amount of blood transfused or progression to fetal hydrops.30 In one study of Rh-sensitized pregnancies with mild anemia treated with high-dose IVIG, benefit was observed only if treatment was started before the development of severe anemia.31 In another, a combination of plasmapheresis and IVIG had been reported to be successful in the treatment of severe maternal RBC alloimmunization.32 Despite the high cost of treatment with IVIG, there may be a role in pregnancies less than 18 to 20 weeks with severe fetal anemia caused by Rh alloimmunization, either with IVIG alone or in combination with other therapies, to prolong the pregnancy so that an intrauterine transfusion can be done at a later gestational age. Unfortunately, the cost of treatment with IVIG is a limiting factor in the treatment of Rh alloimmunization.
paragraphs.heading: Suppressive Therapy Intravenous Immunoglobulin

paragraphs.text: The first direct intravascular fetal blood transfusion for Rh alloimmunization was done by fetoscopy and described in 1984.33 Since that time, fetoscopy is no longer used, and needle placement is done by ultrasound. When screening Rh alloimmunized pregnancies, if the MCA-PSV exceeds 1.5 multiples of the median (MoM), then sampling of the fetal blood is necessary to determine if fetal anemia is present. Fetal transfusions are typically done between 18 and 35 weeks. If fetal anemia is confirmed, then an intrauterine fetal transfusion will be necessary. The blood transfused is type O, Rh(D)-negative, cytomegalovirus-negative, irradiated packed RBCs crossmatched against maternal blood. The usual hematocrit of the blood is around 75%, which allows for minimal blood volume to be transfused.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Transfusion Intravascular Transfusion

paragraphs.text: The procedure should be performed by a trained surgeon in an operating room or in close proximity to an operating
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Transfusion Intravascular Transfusion

paragraphs.text: room, in case there is a complication that would require an urgent delivery.34 For this reason, an anesthetist should see the patient before the procedure and be immediately available if there is an urgent need for an abdominal delivery. The administration of corticosteroids to accelerate fetal lung maturity should also be considered in those pregnancies starting at viability. Depending on the institution, this can be between 22 5/7 weeks and up to 34 weeks of gestation. The administration of antibiotics and/or tocolytics before the procedure is not supported by any randomized trials. The tubing and syringes used in the procedure are heparinized. The maternal abdomen is prepped, and sterile towels and sheets are used to create a sterile field. A 20- to 22-gauge echogenic tip needle is used to puncture the umbilical vein, with the most desirable site being near the cord insertion site into the placenta. A free loop of cord, the intrahepatic portion of the hepatic vein, or the umbilical artery may be considered as alternatives but are less desirable sites because of fetal bradycardia and procedure-related complications that may accompany cord puncture at those sites.33,35–37 Some surgeons prefer a fetal paralytic agent (vecuronium 0.1 mg/kg), which may then be injected intramuscularly or intravascularly at the time of cordocentesis to prevent fetal movements. A system should be in place to report the fetal hematocrit as soon as possible. The blood sample can be confirmed using the mean corpuscular volume, which is greater than 110 μm3 in fetal blood. The volume of blood to be transfused depends on the estimated weight of the fetus, the fetal hematocrit, and the hematocrit of the RBCs to be transfused and the gestational age. This can be calculated using a variety of techniques, with a common calculator available online.38 Following the blood transfusion, hematocrit assessment should be obtained. A post-transfusion hematocrit should be approximately 40% unless the gestational age is less than 24 weeks. If the gestational age is less than 24 weeks, the post-transfusion hematocrit should be 25%, with a repeat procedure in 48 hours.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Transfusion Intravascular Transfusion

paragraphs.text: The overall procedure-related fetal loss rate is approximately 1%, and the emergency delivery rate within 24 hours for procedure-related complications and subsequent perinatal demise is 1.8%.39 Following the procedure, the fetus is continuously monitored for up to 4 to 6 hours, but that time may be extended if there are complications during the procedure or if uterine contractions develop following the procedure. Typically, the fetal hematocrit will fall approximately 1 percentage point per day, and a follow-up transfusion is likely to be necessary in approximately 2 weeks. Ultrasound evaluation of the MCA-PSV after the procedure may have to use a higher MoM cutoff of 1.69.40
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Transfusion Intravascular Transfusion

paragraphs.text: Intraperitoneal transfusions are rarely performed in modern practice except when the caliber of the umbilical vessels does not permit placement of the needle for the transfusion (generally <18 weeks) or when an intravascular transfusion is technically impossible because of fetal position or the location of the umbilical cord. The infused RBCs are absorbed
paragraphs.heading: Intraperitoneal Transfusion

paragraphs.text: into the circulation via the subdiaphragmatic lymphatic lacunae and the right lymphatic duct, making fetal respiration important for absorption to occur. Early work in sheep suggests that the time to complete absorption is about 150 hours and that the absorption rate is directly related to the transfusion volume: the higher the volume, the faster the absorption.41 Generally, fetal intraperitoneal transfusions are less effective when fetal hydrops is present. In an assessment of intraperitoneal transfusions covering 154 fetuses treated by 270 intraperitoneal transfusions, the survival rate in the nonhydropic group increased from 35% to 83% over the 22 years of the study compared with the hydropic group, in whom the survival increased from 24% to 42% over those same 22 years.42
paragraphs.heading: Intraperitoneal Transfusion

paragraphs.text: In the literature, the size of the needle used for the transfusion has varied from a 16- to 20-gauge Tuohy needle, with the smaller needle being more commonly used when the rarely needed intraperitoneal transfusion is undertaken. The fetal abdomen is usually entered between the umbilicus and the fetal bladder to avoid the liver. The catheter tip should be free in the abdominal cavity, which can be confirmed with injected saline. Calculation of the amount of blood to transfuse is important, because if the intraperitoneal pressure exceeds the pressure of blood in the umbilical vein, there will be no blood flow and fetal demise will result.43 This should not occur using the formula of Bowman for infused blood volume [volume = (weeks’ gestation − 20) × 10 mL]. Generally, not enough blood can be given with the first transfusion, and a second transfusion may be necessary 9 or 10 days later. Before fetal intravascular transfusions, the transfusions were repeated every 4 weeks with delivery at 34 to 35 weeks. In modern practice, intraperitoneal transfusion often can be abandoned as soon as vascular access can be achieved.
paragraphs.heading: Intraperitoneal Transfusion

paragraphs.text: The overall timing of the delivery is somewhat controversial but is generally calculated based on the severity of alloimmunization and degree of HF. If antenatal testing suggests that the fetal hemolysis is determined to be mild, then a reasonable approach would be to induce labor between 37 and 38 weeks or sooner if the fetal lung studies document lung maturity at an earlier gestational age. If the studies suggest severe alloimmunization, with fetal/neonatal survival greater than 95% in most tertiary neonatal intensive care units, the last transfusion should be given at around 30 to 32 weeks, with delivery between 32 and 34 weeks and corticosteroids given to accelerate fetal lung maturity and to decrease the morbidity linked with preterm deliveries. Other experts have advocated that intrauterine transfusions continue up through the 35th week when there is a reasonable chance of fetal lung maturity with delivery at 37 weeks. The fetus should have continuous electronic fetal monitoring during labor, and a cord blood sample should be sent immediately to the laboratory following delivery for neonatal blood group, Rh typing, direct Coombs, bilirubin, hemoglobin, and hematocrit. Delivery should occur at
paragraphs.heading: Timing of Delivery

paragraphs.text: a tertiary care facility that has adequate neonatal intensive care, blood banking, and laboratory services.
paragraphs.heading: Timing of Delivery

paragraphs.text: With improvements in ultrasound technology, improved echogenic tip needles, and level of care offered in tertiary neonatal intensive care units, perinatal survival following an intrauterine fetal transfusion has increased dramatically. These improvements were well demonstrated in two large retrospective studies from The Netherlands and Scotland.44,45 A retrospective review of survival in fetuses treated for anemia caused by Rh alloimmunization with intrauterine transfusions between 1988 and 1999 in The Netherlands was performed in 208 pregnant women treated with 593 blood transfusions.45 The overall survival rate was 86%. Survival of the hydropic fetuses (78%) was significantly less than the survival of those pregnancies without hydrops (92%). Low survival rates were also observed if the first transfusion took place at less than 20 weeks and the fetus was hydropic (55%). Survival was much greater in Rh alloimmunized pregnancies (89%) compared with Kell alloimmunized pregnancies (58%). Overall fetal loss rate linked to the procedure was 4.8%.
paragraphs.heading: Outcome Short Term

paragraphs.text: In a retrospective review of the short-term outcomes of 116 pregnancies that underwent 457 transfusions in Scotland from 1993 to 2004, the rate of intrauterine death as a complication of the procedure was 2.3% for 1993 to 1998 and 0.8% for 1999 to 2004.44 Eight infants (6.9%) were delivered by emergency cesarean as a result of a complication during the intrauterine transfusion. The survival rate of neonates from birth to discharge was 97.4%. The majority of the neonates were delivered by cesarean or vaginally at 35 weeks. Roughly 33% of neonates required some type of respiratory support following delivery. Sixteen of the neonates had an exchange transfusion following delivery, with the number of exchanges ranging from one to four. At least one top-up transfusion was required in 54% of the neonates, with one infant requiring nine transfusions.
paragraphs.heading: Outcome Short Term

paragraphs.text: A more recent retrospective cohort study of the outcomes of 6650 cordocentesis in Thailand from 1992 to 2018 reported that the rate of fetal loss following cordocentesis was 1.8% (123/6650),34 although the rate of fetal loss secondary to the procedure is likely around 0.8%, as the rate of fetal loss among the control group was 1%. The study also identified specific procedural risk factors associated with fetal loss after cordocentesis. Prolonged bleeding from the puncture site, presence of fetal bradycardia, and penetration of the placenta were all identified as significant procedural risk factors for fetal loss. The professional level of the operator, difficulty of the procedure, gestational age, and puncture site (free loop vs. cord insert) were not significantly associated with increased rate of fetal loss.
paragraphs.heading: Outcome Short Term

paragraphs.text: The short-term neonatal outcomes of intrauterine transfusion are generally very good. In the The Netherlands study, pregnancies complicated by hydrops, pregnancies in which the first transfusion was undertaken at less than 20
paragraphs.heading: Outcome Short Term

paragraphs.text: weeks, and alloimmunization secondary to Kell had poorer outcomes. In the cohort from Scotland, there was minimal procedural loss, a low rate of emergency cesarean deliveries because of procedural complications, and no more than the expected rate of respiratory support needed secondary to gestational age of delivery at 35 weeks. All neonates were treated with phototherapy, and 16 needed exchange transfusions, primarily those who underwent an emergency delivery because of procedural problems with the intrauterine transfusions.
paragraphs.heading: Outcome Short Term

paragraphs.text: More information is now becoming available on the longterm outcome of fetuses who receive intrauterine transfusions. Previously, this information had been very limited because of the small size of the studies, length of follow-up, lack of controls, and unclear criteria used to evaluate development of the child. The publication of the LOTUS study provided much-needed additional information on longterm effects of fetuses undergoing this procedure.46 The LOTUS study evaluated the neurodevelopment of children with hemolytic disease treated with an intrauterine transfusion. Two hundred and ninety-one children were evaluated at a median age of 8.2 years. Cerebral palsy was detected in 2.1%, severe developmental delay in 3.1%, and bilateral deafness in 1%. The overall incidence of neurodevelopmental impairment was 4.8% (14/291). The only risk factor that could be linked with neurodevelopmental delay was severe fetal HF. The very high rate of intact survival in these atrisk pregnancies complicated by severe anemia is reassuring and confirms the relative safety of the treatment with intrauterine transfusions even in the fetus with severe hemolytic disease, including HF.
paragraphs.heading: Long Term

paragraphs.text: As the incidence of Rh disease has decreased with the administration of anti-D immune globulin, the incidence of alloimmunization caused by other RBC antigens has increased. This rise is because there are no screening programs for women who are negative for these other atypical antigens that have the potential for causing hemolytic disease. The greatest risk factor for isoimmunization of the other RBC antigens is a prior blood transfusion, but it can also occur after a maternal-fetal hemorrhage during pregnancy. Fortunately, most of the antibodies produced against these antigens are of the IgM type, do not cross the placenta, and therefore do not result in HDN. Because of the rarity of many of these atypical antigens, there is a paucity of evidence supporting specific management algorithms. Critical titers at which time additional surveillance should be undertaken are also not well established. Box 22.2 outlines a partial list of antibodies associated with HDN.
paragraphs.heading: Atypical Antigens

paragraphs.text: The most troublesome of the atypical antigens is the Kell antigen, which is highly immunogenic. After the reactions that occur with ABO and Rh blood groups, the Kell antigen is the most immunogenic. There are 25 Kell antigens
paragraphs.heading: Atypical Antigens

paragraphs.text: encoded by a single gene on chromosome 7, with the “K” antigen being the most clinically significant. The pathophysiology of the HDN is different from that seen with ABO and Rh sensitization. The Kell IgG antibodies cause destruction of erythroid precursors by macrophages in the fetal liver and can result in severe fetal anemia.47
paragraphs.heading: Atypical Antigens

paragraphs.text: Fortunately, 91% of the population is Kell negative and only 5% of the population will form Kell antibodies after a transfusion, making the disorder relatively rare. Assessment of the father’s genotype, if paternity is certain, is initially undertaken because if he is Kell negative, then the pregnancy is not affected and no further workup is needed. In Kell alloimmunization, early suppression of fetal RBC synthesis results in less bilirubin being released during hemolysis. Because of this, serial amniocentesis for ΔOD450 titers is not reliable or could even be misleading and should not be used. Results have suggested that MCA-PSV with a cutoff greater than 1.5 is highly predictive of severe fetal anemia, as it is in the prediction of fetal anemia in Rh-D-negative mothers, and it should be routinely used in management.48 Other antibodies that have been infrequently linked with severe disease include Colton, Diego, Duffy, and MNS. Those associated with mild disease include Dombrock, Duffy, Kidd, and Gerbich. Surveillance is done with MCA- PSV using the threshold of greater than 1.5 for the diagnosis of fetal anemia.
paragraphs.heading: Atypical Antigens

paragraphs.text: Although the incidence of HF has remained stable in the range of 1/1500 to 1/3800 births since the development of Rh immunoglobulin, up to 90% of cases of HF are now the result of nonimmune etiologies. Nonimmune hydrops fetalis (NIHF) defines hydrops in those fetuses whose mothers are Rh positive or that results from a nonimmune cause.49–
paragraphs.heading: Nonimmune Hydrops Fetalis

paragraphs.text: 51 Although improvements in ultrasound technology have allowed earlier diagnosis and improved understanding of underlying conditions, unfortunately the prognosis for NIHF neonates remains poor, with perinatal mortality rates ranging from 50% to 90%.49 Maternal complications associated with NIHF include preeclampsia, mirror syndrome, and increased cesarean rates when NIHF is diagnosed in the antepartum period.42,52
paragraphs.heading: Nonimmune Hydrops Fetalis

paragraphs.text: After ruling out fetal hydrops due to RBC alloimmunization, NIHF is defined by the same ultrasonographic presence of excessive fetal fluid in two or more of the following spaces: abdominal ascites, pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, skin edema, polyhydramnios, or placentomegaly (see Table 22.1). Unlike alloimmunization, there is not a specific screening test for the multiple etiologies of NIHF, and often this diagnosis is made incidentally after a mother undergoes an ultrasound for another indication (e.g., polyhydramnios, standard fetal evaluations).
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Hydrops occurs when interstitial fluid production and lymphatic return become imbalanced, leading to fluid accumulation in interstitial spaces within the fetus. This can result from a myriad of conditions, including those that cause reduced lymphatic flow (e.g., pulmonary masses, lymphatic malformations), lower plasma oncotic pressure (e.g., gastrointestinal anomalies, inborn errors of metabolism, liver failure), or increased central venous pressure (e.g., chromosomal abnormalities, heart failure caused by volume overload or anemia, compensatory hypoxia) (Fig. 22.3). NIHF rarely resolves spontaneously and, in general, carries a worse prognosis the earlier in pregnancy it is diagnosed.53
paragraphs.heading: Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: Just as the pathophysiology of NIHF can result from several different pathways, the conditions or anomalies that lead to these pathophysiologic changes are vast. Fig. 22.4 summarizes 14 separate etiologies most commonly associated with NIHF and the respective percentage for which a cause is identified.53 Within each of these categories, specific diagnoses or anomalies are further summarized in Table 22.4. In sum, more than 100 conditions, although many are very rare, have been associated with the ultimate finding and diagnosis of NIHF.
paragraphs.heading: Differential Diagnosis/Etiology

paragraphs.text: The clinical presentation of fetuses can vary depending on the underlying condition and the gestational age at which it is identified. A common finding in NIHF diagnosed before 20 weeks is a cystic hygroma, often associated with chromosomal anomalies. Common chromosomal abnormalities include Turner syndrome (45 XO) as well as trisomies 21, 18, and 13.54 In intrathoracic masses, restrictive fetal swallowing often causes polyhydramnios, resulting in uterine size measuring larger than gestational age and prompting ultrasound evaluation.55 Once identified, antepartum evaluation focusing on identification of the
paragraphs.heading: Antepartum Evaluation

paragraphs.text: underlying cause includes a detailed history (personal and family), often with the assistance of a genetics counselor, targeted ultrasound, fetal echocardiography, MCA-PSV analysis, laboratory testing including evaluation of recent viral exposures, and sometimes diagnostic invasive testing. Table 22.5 summarizes the components of a full antenatal evaluation of NIHF.
paragraphs.heading: Antepartum Evaluation

paragraphs.text: More recent studies of prenatal genetic testing show promise in aiding in evaluation of NIHF. In a case series from 2018 to 2020, 127 fetuses with unexplained NIHF underwent exome sequencing.56 Of these 127 cases, 37 (29%) had an identifiable genetic disorder as a result of exome sequencing. paragraphs.text: Depending on gestational age at the time of diagnosis and whether a cause for NIHF can be identified, various management options may include termination of pregnancy, invasive therapeutic intervention, or conservative management, including supportive care and monitoring of the mother and fetus. Fetal surveillance may include frequent non-stress
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: testing or biophysical profiles on a weekly or twice-weekly basis. Because early delivery and neonatal compromise often occur, early consultation with relevant subspecialists (e.g., neonatologists, pediatric surgeons, pediatric cardiologists) is often warranted. If delivery is thought to be imminent, inpatient surveillance with the administration of antenatal corticosteroids may be indicated.
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: Maternal risks of conservative management include a condition known as mirror syndrome (Ballantyne syndrome).58 If this occurs, the mother begins to demonstrate similar findings of the fetus, including generalized maternal edema, often with pulmonary involvement, thus “mirroring” the edema of the hydropic fetus and placenta. Although the pathogenesis of this condition is unknown, it is thought that the hydropic placenta causes a systemic inflammatory response as a result of increased shedding of trophoblastic debris into maternal blood.59
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: In some cases, invasive fetal therapeutic interventions may be considered. Conditions such as diaphragmatic hernia, congenital pulmonary adenomatoid malformations, or extralobar pulmonary sequestration may benefit from in utero surgery. Although paracentesis or thoracentesis may be informative for diagnostic purposes, the fluid removed from the fetal body cavity often reaccumulates in a short period of time. In these cases, shunt placement is sometimes considered, with some notable improvement in survival.
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: Delivery may be indicated if there is evidence of maternal mirror syndrome. Other indications for delivery include gestational age greater than 34 weeks, mature fetal lung profile, or persistent biophysical profiles of less than 6. Cesarean delivery should be reserved for routine obstetrical indications (Table 22.6). Traumatic delivery because of severe soft
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: tissue edema often occurs; however, this risk is not negated by cesarean delivery. Given the increased frequency of nonreassuring fetal testing and labor dystocia, however, the likelihood of cesarean delivery in NIHF is increased.
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: Overall survival of a fetus diagnosed with NIHF remains poor. This is largely related to the underlying etiology of the condition. If a structural defect is identified or if no
paragraphs.heading: Prognosis

paragraphs.text: underlying cause is identified, then the perinatal mortality rate approaches 100%. In general, perinatal mortality rates are worse when NIHF is identified early in pregnancy (<24 weeks) and, conversely, when identified, delivery and neonatal treatments may be beneficial and improve mortality. Certainly the risks associated with prematurity compound the already tenuous status of a fetus with NIHF. Given the rareness of this entity, the risk of recurrence is also rare, especially when the cause is something other than a hereditary factor.

paragraphs.text: fetus. Given the seriousness of many of the underlying conditions, perinatal morbidity and mortality remain exceedingly high. Although the prognosis of IHF remains positive in those fetuses who receive intrauterine blood transfusions, treatment in NIHF is often conservative, with increased surveillance of fetal well-being but minimal improvement in short- or long-term neonatal outcomes. Invasive fetal treatment, however, is associated with improved survival in select conditions causing NIHF. All pregnancies should undergo screening for Rh alloimmunization with maternal blood typing and antibody screening. Despite improvements in technology and testing, a certain diagnosis of NIHF occurs only in approximately 67% of cases. Minimizing maternal complications such as mirror syndrome and determining the most appropriate timing for delivery remain challenging in this high-risk pregnancy population.
