title: Perinatal Infections and Chorioamnionitis

paragraphs.text: 24 Perinatal Infections and Chorioamnionitis
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Chorioamnionitis (or intra-amniotic infection) is typically defined as an infection with resultant inflammation of the amniotic fluid, placenta, fetus, fetal membranes, or decidua.1 Chorioamnionitis most commonly results from ascension of bacteria colonizing the lower maternal genital tract, although it may rarely occur after invasive procedures or by a hematogenous route secondary to maternal systemic infection. There are strong associations between chorioamnionitis and maternal morbidity, preterm birth, and several adverse neonatal outcomes. However, the literature supporting these associations has been inconsistent, largely because of a lack of precision in both the definition and diagnosis of chorioamnionitis.
paragraphs.heading: Definitions and Epidemiology

paragraphs.text: When characteristic clinical signs of inflammation are present, the condition is usually termed clinical chorioamnionitis (see Diagnosis section below). Clinical chorioamnionitis complicates 2% to 10% of all pregnancies2,3; however, the reported incidence varies widely based upon gestational age and diagnostic criteria used. Two main varieties of chorioamnionitis can be identified: acute chorioamnionitis and subclinical chorioamnionitis. They differ in their clinical manifestations, microbiology, and risk to the fetus (Fig. 24.1).
paragraphs.heading: Definitions and Epidemiology

paragraphs.text: Histologic chorioamnionitis refers to inflammation of the chorion and amnion as seen on pathologic examination and is three times as common as clinical chorioamnionitis confirmed by amniotic fluid culture.4 The prevalence of histologic chorioamnionitis ranges from 50% to 70% in very low birth weight infants to 10% to 15% for infants born at term gestation. Approximately 30% of women with preterm labor and intact membranes exhibit histologic chorioamnionitis, as do 80% of women with preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM). Histologic acute chorioamnionitis, which represents the inflammatory response of the mother and fetus, cannot occur before the fusion of the amnion and chorion (≈11 weeks’ gestation) and is rare before 20 weeks of gestation. Before that time, a chronic chorio deciduitis can develop, which is subclinical and has been linked to an increased incidence of preterm birth, chronic lung disease, and periventricular leukomalacia. It is controversial whether chorio deciduitis represents an infectious process or a maternal immune response to fetal antigens.5 Histologic chorioamnionitis has been associated with intra-amniotic infection in 72% of cases of preterm birth. However, the likelihood of neonatal sepsis in women with histologic or clinical chorioamnionitis varies dramatically with gestational age (Table 24.1).6
paragraphs.heading: Definitions and Epidemiology

paragraphs.text: Part of the difficulty of identifying women with chorioamnionitis is that microbial invasion of the amniotic cavity can be chronic and clinically silent. Furthermore, histologic chorioamnionitis can occur with negative cultures from amniotic fluid. Some of these “negative cultures” can be explained by the fastidiousness of the microorganisms found in amniotic fluid and the difficulty in recovering them using standard culture techniques. Others are the result of sterile intra-amniotic inflammation, a poorly understood yet clinically important entity associated with preterm delivery and neonatal morbidity.7 The precise stimuli for sterile intra-amniotic inflammation in patients have not been identified, although damage-associated molecular patterns are thought to play a major role in its pathogenesis.7
paragraphs.heading: Definitions and Epidemiology

paragraphs.text: Epidemiologic investigations have demonstrated several factors associated with the development of clinical chorioamnionitis, including maternal colonization with group B streptococcus (GBS), GBS bacteriuria, nulliparity, the use of internal monitoring devices, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, serial vaginal digital examinations, duration of active labor, and duration of membrane rupture.8 Importantly, meconium-stained amniotic fluid is not only a risk factor for chorioamnionitis but also may be a consequence of fetal stress secondary to intra-amniotic infection. There are some data to suggest that women diagnosed with chorioamnionitis during their first pregnancy are at increased risk for developing chorioamnionitis in subsequent pregnancies, indicating a persistent predisposing condition or underlying host susceptibility. Gene association studies have identified single nucleotide polymorphisms in immunoregulatory genes that may influence susceptibility to chorioamnionitis.9 The presence of abnormal cervicovaginal flora (e.g., bacterial vaginosis, aerobic vaginitis) during the first trimester is associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes, including early preterm birth, miscarriage, and microbial invasion of the amniotic cavity,10 although discrete evidence linking the presence of abnormal flora of the lower genital tract with the development of acute clinical chorioamnionitis is lacking. Rather, it is hypothesized that these vaginal microbes ascend into the intrauterine cavity and induce a subclinical, chronic inflammatory response that, in turn, predisposes to preterm rupture of membranes and/or the onset of preterm labor.
paragraphs.heading: Risk Factors

paragraphs.text: Chorioamnionitis is almost always polymicrobial. However, many of the species that cause chorioamnionitis are difficult to grow under microbiological laboratory conditions and therefore may not be identified through standard culture techniques. Broad-range polymerase chain reaction (PCR) with bacterial probes followed by metagenomic sequencing11 or mass spectrometry12 analysis allows superior detection of uncultivatable organisms but is rarely used in clinical practice. A summary of data from multiple studies—using both standard culture and molecular detection techniques—shows that Ureaplasma, Streptococcus, Escherichia coli, and Mycoplasma hominis are among the most commonly identified organisms in chorioamnionitis, but a
paragraphs.heading: Microbiology

paragraphs.text: diverse assortment of other microbes is also commonly found (Fig. 24.2).13
paragraphs.heading: Microbiology

paragraphs.text: Broad-range PCR has been used to identify the kinds of microorganisms found in the amniotic fluid of women with preterm labor or PPROM. These studies reveal that the patterns of microorganisms in amniotic fluid in women with preterm labor and intact membranes are different from those found in amniotic fluid samples from women with PPROM (Figs. 24.3 and 24.4).14 However, given the high sensitivity of PCR, the increased likelihood of detecting DNA from nonviable or environmental contaminants makes the clinical significance of this microbial diversity somewhat uncertain. Studies of the association of microbial invasion of the amniotic cavity (using PCR-based techniques) with fetal inflammation or perinatal outcomes noted statistically significant associations with elevated concentrations of inflammatory mediators in amniotic fluid and increased rates of histologic chorioamnionitis and preterm delivery.12 These studies lend support to an increasingly accepted theory that molecular identification of uncultivatable organisms from intrauterine sampling—in the absence of significant maternofetal inflammation—likely reflects environmental or procedural contamination rather than true infection.
paragraphs.heading: Microbiology

paragraphs.text: Confirmation of intrauterine infection and/or inflammation requires amniotic fluid sampling and/or placental pathology. Therefore, in the vast majority of cases, the diagnosis is made using clinical criteria. The classic definition required maternal fever (≥100.4° F or 38° C) plus two other findings, including maternal leukocytosis, maternal and fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, and foul-smelling or purulent amniotic fluid.15 Individual clinical criteria have variable sensitivity and generally low specificity for chorioamnionitis, with little improvement in diagnostic accuracy when used in combination (Table 24.2).16
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: There have been several attempts to refine these diagnostic criteria in recent years. In 2016, a new descriptive term, intrauterine inflammation, or infection, or both (triple I), was proposed by an expert panel to reflect the current understanding of pathophysiology, whereby inflammation does not always equal infection.17 Suspected triple I was defined as the presence of maternal intrapartum fever without a clear source, plus one or more of the following: maternal

paragraphs.text: leukocytosis, purulent cervical drainage, or fetal tachycardia. The most recent recommendation from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists defines suspected intra-amniotic infection as a maternal temperature ≥39.0° C or when the maternal temperature is 38.0° to 38.9° C and one additional clinical criterion is present.
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 24.3 Phylum-level distribution of bacterial taxa identified in amniotic fluid. Data obtained from studies

paragraphs.text: It is noteworthy that both of the above definitions recognize isolated maternal fever as a distinct entity. Maternal fever may be caused by intrauterine or extrauterine etiologies. For example, epidural anesthesia is associated with an increased risk of fever during labor and, in most instances, it is thought to be noninfectious in origin. However, fever may be more likely to occur when placental inflammation is present. Fever can occur within 1 hour of epidural placement, but it almost always occurs within 4 to 6 hours.
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 24.3 Phylum-level distribution of bacterial taxa identified in amniotic fluid. Data obtained from studies

paragraphs.text: Laboratory testing may be helpful in confirming or excluding the diagnosis of chorioamnionitis, particularly when the diagnosis is uncertain. Leukocytosis has been described in the majority of patients with clinical chorioamnionitis. However, in the absence of other signs and symptoms, isolated leukocytosis is of limited value. A number of amniotic fluid markers have been studied for the diagnosis of chorioamnionitis.
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 24.3 Phylum-level distribution of bacterial taxa identified in amniotic fluid. Data obtained from studies

paragraphs.text: These include culture, Gram stain, glucose levels, white blood cell counts, leukocyte esterase, damage-associated molecular patterns, soluble Toll-like receptors (TLRs), matrix metalloproteinase, cytokines (e.g., TNF-alpha, interleukins-6 and -8, matrix metalloproteinase-8), and qualitative assessment of amniotic proteins (proteomics). Proteomic analysis of amniotic fluid has led to the discovery of several novel biomarkers associated with the degree of intra-amniotic inflammation and time to delivery.18 The development of rapid, noninvasive assays to measure biomarkers associated with microbial invasion of the amniotic cavity in cervicovaginal fluid specimens holds promise for future diagnostics.19
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 24.3 Phylum-level distribution of bacterial taxa identified in amniotic fluid. Data obtained from studies

paragraphs.text: The histopathologic findings of chorioamnionitis are well characterized and involve both maternal and fetal immune systems.20 The initial inflammatory response occurs within 6 to 12 hours, is maternal in origin, and is manifested by an infiltration of neutrophils on the undersurface of the chorionic plate (acute subchorionitis). The next site of involvement occurs at the trophoblast layer of the membranous chorion (acute chorionitis). Over the next 12 to 36 hours, the infection spreads to the adjacent chorion and amnion (chorioamnionitis). If the infectious process is prolonged (36–48

paragraphs.text: hours), necrotizing chorioamnionitis (stage 3 acute chorioamnionitis) can result. Fetal vasculitis is an indication of a fetal inflammatory response and represents diapedesis and transmigration of fetal cells across the vessel wall in response to chemotactic agents. In preterm pregnancies, the fetal responses first appear in the chorionic plate (chorionic vasculitis), whereas in term pregnancies they are first evident in the umbilical vein (umbilical phlebitis). Stage 1 fetal inflammatory responses are characterized by neutrophils in the chorionic vessels and/or umbilical vein vasculitis; stage 2 is reached when neutrophils enter the wall of the umbilical artery (umbilical arteritis). With increasing duration of inflammation, neutrophils migrate out of the umbilical artery and vein and enter Wharton jelly to assume an arc-like distribution (stage 3). Funisitis is a general term signifying inflammation of the umbilical artery and vein. It is important to distinguish umbilical arteritis from umbilical phlebitis because the former is associated with increased concentrations of circulating fetal cytokines, whereas the latter is not. It is noteworthy that most neutrophils in both the amniotic fluid and airspaces of the newborn’s lungs are fetal in origin.
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 24.3 Phylum-level distribution of bacterial taxa identified in amniotic fluid. Data obtained from studies

paragraphs.text: Microorganisms typically invade the intrauterine space by ascending through the cervix from the lower genital tract. Retrograde migration from the abdominal cavity through the fallopian tubes, hematogenous spread through the
paragraphs.heading: Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: placenta, and iatrogenic introduction via amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling are additional mechanisms by which organisms gain access to the uterine cavity.21
paragraphs.heading: Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: During pregnancy, the cervical mucus plug, fetal membranes, and placenta function to protect the developing fetus from invading bacteria. The cervical mucus plug is particularly important because it is not only an anatomic barrier but it also contains numerous antibacterial peptides with bactericidal activity against potential pathogens that commonly colonize the vaginal tissues.22 It is generally believed that once organisms gain access to the intrauterine space, they reside and replicate in the choriodecidual space before entering the amniotic fluid.23 However, data suggest an initial intra-amniotic entry of bacteria through a restricted cervical region of membranes.24 After replication in the amniotic cavity, microorganisms then invade the amnion and its connective tissue and progress into the chorion and decidua.
paragraphs.heading: Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: Stimulation of the innate immune response first occurs when the pathogen-associated molecular patterns of invading microorganisms are recognized by pattern recognition receptors (TLRs, nucleotide oligomerization domain [NOD]-like receptors [NLRs]) expressed by host epithelial cells, circulating immune cells, and perhaps most important, placental trophoblast cells.25,26 Once stimulated, these receptors induce a cascade of proinflammatory signaling, including stimulation of Myd88 (TLRs) and inflammasome (NLRs) pathways. Subsequent production of various
paragraphs.heading: Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: cytokines, chemokines, matrix-degrading enzymes, prostaglandins, and other mediators leads to an inflammatory cell infiltrate, membrane rupture, cervical ripening, and in some cases, the onset of labor. Experimental evidence from animal models of intrauterine infection suggests that the specific inflammatory pathway leading to the induction of preterm labor is dependent on the particular TLR activated (determined by the nature of infecting agent) as well as the route of infection (ascending versus systemic). Recent investigations using human placental explant models have identified the NLRP3 inflammasome as a central mediator of proinflammatory interleukin-1β elaboration, which, in turn, promotes neutrophil infiltration of pregnancy tissues and initiation of labor.27
paragraphs.heading: Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: As mentioned, bacterial invasion of the amniotic cavity may be chronic, existing for several weeks without clinical symptoms. This is particularly true in infections with Ureaplasma spp.28 Several investigators have found amniotic fluid cultures positive for Ureaplasma in asymptomatic women undergoing genetic amniocenteses at 16 to 20 weeks’ gestation.29 Despite a lack of overt symptomatology, a significant portion of these women exhibited a robust inflammatory response as measured by expression of inflammatory cytokines in the amniotic fluid and subsequently went on to experience adverse pregnancy outcomes (fetal loss, preterm birth) compared with those women with sterile cultures. In fact, there is ample evidence to suggest that Ureaplasma spp., traditionally considered to be of relatively low virulence, may evoke a more intense host inflammatory response as compared with other pathogens associated with chorioamnionitis.
paragraphs.heading: Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: Recent practice guidelines from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists emphasize the distinction between isolated intrapartum maternal fever and clinically diagnosed chorioamnionitis. Although obstetricians often administer antibiotics in the setting of isolated maternal fever, this practice is of uncertain benefit, and additional research is needed to understand both the mechanism and appropriate management of isolated maternal fever. Whether or not antibiotics are administered for isolated intrapartum maternal fever, the diagnosis and rationale behind its obstetric management should be conveyed to the neonatology team for consideration in planning care of the newborn.
paragraphs.heading: Obstetric Management

paragraphs.text: In the setting of true clinical chorioamnionitis, administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics and prompt delivery of the fetus reduce both fetal and maternal morbidity. Chorioamnionitis alone is not a sufficient indication for cesarean delivery because there is no evidence it improves neonatal outcomes and may increase maternal complications such as wound infection.30 However, findings consistent with fetal
paragraphs.heading: Obstetric Management

paragraphs.text: or maternal instability in the setting of chorioamnionitis can be indications for cesarean delivery.
paragraphs.heading: Obstetric Management

paragraphs.text: Ampicillin and gentamicin are the most commonly prescribed antimicrobials for intra-amniotic infection, although there are no randomized trials comparing the efficacy of various antibiotic regimens. It is worth noting that standard antibiotic regimens used to treat chorioamnionitis do not provide coverage against Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma spp., two of the most common organisms associated with intra-amniotic infection. Several authors and expert panels have proposed alternative antibiotic protocols to cover these organisms, but these proposals have not been subjected to clinical trials.31 If cesarean delivery is performed, clindamycin (or metronidazole) is often added for anaerobic coverage.
paragraphs.heading: Obstetric Management

paragraphs.text: The administration of antenatal corticosteroids to enhance fetal lung maturity in the setting of chorioamnionitis is controversial because it is believed that the immunosuppressive effects of steroids may exacerbate maternal or neonatal infectious complications. Although randomized clinical trials addressing this issue are lacking, there are observational data to suggest that antenatal steroids may actually reduce neonatal morbidity, including severe intraventricular hemorrhage and periventricular leukomalacia in the presence of chorioamnionitis.32,33
paragraphs.heading: Obstetric Management

paragraphs.text: PPROM is associated with intra-amniotic infection, and evidence supports routine administration of antibiotics to women presenting with PPROM with the intention of reducing progression to chorioamnionitis, prolonging pregnancy, and decreasing neonatal morbidities (early-onset sepsis, need for supplemental oxygen, brain injury).34 In a 2020 update to practice guidelines, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommended 48 hours of intravenous ampicillin and erythromycin, followed by oral amoxicillin and erythromycin, to complete a 7-day course in uncomplicated PPROM.35
paragraphs.heading: Obstetric Management

paragraphs.text: Despite the benefits listed above, there is not strong evidence to show that antibiotic administration for PPROM reduces infant mortality. Furthermore, the use of antenatal antibiotics in particular circumstances may be harmful. The administration of co-amoxiclav (ampicillin/clavulanic acid) in women with PPROM or preterm labor with intact membranes was associated with an increased risk for necrotizing enterocolitis in neonates. In addition, the use of both erythromycin and co-amoxiclav antibiotics for women with preterm labor and intact membranes was associated with an unexpected increase in the incidence of cerebral palsy at a 7-year follow-up evaluation.36
paragraphs.heading: Obstetric Management

paragraphs.text: Guidelines for the management of infants with suspected or proven sepsis from the Committee on the Fetus and Newborn of the American Academy of Pediatrics were revised in 2018.37,38 The two clinical reports were divided into
paragraphs.heading: Management of the Exposed Infant

paragraphs.text: recommendations for infants ≥350/7 weeks’ gestation38 and infants ≤346/7 weeks’ gestation.37 Although chorioamnionitis is still considered a risk factor for early-onset sepsis in infants ≥350/7 weeks’ gestation, the specificity of this diagnosis is poor, and relatively few infants born to women with chorioamnionitis in that gestational age strata develop earlyonset sepsis. Additionally, the diagnosis of clinical chorioamnionitis is often made when fever is the sole manifestation of an intrauterine infection. Therefore many infants may be unnecessarily exposed to broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy. Complicating this issue is the increased incidence of fever in women receiving epidural anesthesia. Therefore, if fever is the sole manifestation of suspected chorioamnionitis, consultation with the obstetric provider is recommended to determine the level of clinical suspicion before routinely treating asymptomatic infants.
paragraphs.heading: Management of the Exposed Infant

paragraphs.text: The Committee on the Fetus and Newborn recommends selecting from three different approaches for infants ≥350/7 weeks’ gestation with a history of chorioamnionitis. The first, termed the categorical risk factor assessment, recommends laboratory testing and empirical antibiotics for all infants born to women with chorioamnionitis and any infant who is ill appearing. This strategy will likely lead to considerable overtreatment of uninfected infants. The second approach, termed multivariate risk assessment, uses established risk factors and the infant’s clinical condition in the first 6 to 12 hours of life to estimate the risk of sepsis. These variables can be entered into a web-based early-onset sepsis calculator (https://neonatalsepsiscalculator.kaiserpermanente.org). (See also Chapter 50.) Blood culture and enhanced clinical observations are recommended for an estimated risk of early-onset sepsis ≥1 per 1000 live births, and empirical antibiotics are recommended for an estimated risk of sepsis ≥3 per 1000 live births. The third strategy relies on identification of clinical signs of illness regardless of any estimation of neonatal or maternal risk factors. Infants who develop signs of illness in the first 48 hours of life are either empirically treated with antibiotics or further evaluated with laboratory testing. Both the multivariate risk approach and serial examination strategy have reduced the number of sepsis evaluations, but the use of either approach will still lead to overtreatment of a substantial number of infants who are uninfected. There is growing evidence to suggest that close observation, rather than empiric antibiotic therapy, is the preferred strategy for the management of asymptomatic full-term infants exposed to chorioamnionitis.39,40 The risk of sepsis in this population is exceedingly low given that the incidence of early-onset sepsis has declined dramatically over the past two decades (because of widespread implementation of intrapartum prophylaxis for mothers colonized with GBS and the treatment of women with chorioamnionitis with antibiotics during labor). This substantially increases the number of healthy term newborns who would require antibiotics to prevent a single case of sepsis.41 Because the risk of early-onset sepsis in infants born to women with chorioamnionitis is strongly dependent on gestational age,
paragraphs.heading: Management of the Exposed Infant

paragraphs.text: it remains prudent to empirically treat chorioamnionitisexposed preterm infants ≤346/7 weeks’ gestation.
paragraphs.heading: Management of the Exposed Infant

paragraphs.text: Chorioamnionitis can adversely affect the mother and her unborn infant. The associations between chorioamnionitis and adverse outcomes are not straightforward given the multiple causes of maternal fever and a lack of concordance between maternal intra-amniotic infection, histologic chorioamnionitis, and clinical chorioamnionitis. In pregnant women, chorioamnionitis is associated with a two-fold increase in abnormal progression of labor, an increased risk of cesarean section,30 postpartum hemorrhage, poor cervical dilation, placental abruption, and intensive care admission.42 Surgical complications after cesarean section, such as endometritis, pelvic abscess, wound infection, thromboembolism, and bacteremia, are also more common in women with chorioamnionitis. The effects of intrauterine infection on the fetus depend on the duration and timing of the inflammatory process. Acute chorioamnionitis is an important risk factor for early-onset neonatal sepsis. Chronic infections, however, are often subclinical and have been associated with a wide variety of organ injury, including the brain (periventricular leukomalacia), lung (bronchopulmonary dysplasia [BPD]), eye (retinopathy of prematurity), intestine (necrotizing enterocolitis), and thymus (involution and a change in cellular composition).43 Chorioamnionitis, especially with a fetal inflammatory component, has also been associated with hemodynamic instability in the preterm newborn infant.
paragraphs.heading: Outcomes

paragraphs.text: Chorioamnionitis is thought to initiate 40% to 70% of preterm births; the incidence may even be higher at lower gestational ages. The evidence linking infection and preterm labor is as follows: (1) intrauterine infection (or exposure to microbial products) in experimental animals results in preterm delivery; (2) extrauterine maternal infections (e.g., pyelonephritis) are associated with preterm labor; (3) subclinical intrauterine infections are associated with preterm labor and birth; (4) patients with evidence of intrauterine inflammation (e.g., increased amniotic fluid cytokines or matrix metalloproteinases) in the mid-third trimester are at increased risk for preterm delivery; (5) in experimental animal models, antibiotic treatment of intrauterine infections can prevent prematurity; (6) treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria prevents prematurity; (7) administration of antibiotics to women with PPROM prolongs gestation; (8) microorganisms can be cultured from the placenta in a high percentage of women presenting with preterm labor; and (9) polymorphonuclear infiltrations in the placenta are associated with spontaneous preterm birth. A possible mechanism for infection-associated preterm birth is shown in Fig. 24.5.16 It is important to note that although microorganisms are associated with preterm birth, sterile inflammation is more frequently associated
paragraphs.heading: Outcomes

paragraphs.text: with preterm labor and intact membranes, PPROM, and asymptomatic short cervix than microbe-associated intraamniotic infection.44
paragraphs.heading: Outcomes

paragraphs.text: Acute chorioamnionitis is a risk factor for neonatal sepsis.41 Both histologic chorioamnionitis and clinical chorioamnionitis are associated with early-onset neonatal sepsis.45,46 Among infants of ≥37 weeks’ gestation with proven early-onset sepsis owing to E. coli or GBS, clinical chorioamnionitis was documented in the medical record about one-third of the time, and histologic chorioamnionitis was documented in 90% of the cases.6 Importantly, the risk of early-onset sepsis in infants born to women with chorioamnionitis is inversely correlated with gestational age. Reported rates of confirmed sepsis in infants born at ≥35 weeks’ gestation to mothers with clinical chorioamnionitis range from 0.47% to 1.24%.47,48 In contrast, rates in moderate and extremely preterm infants exposed to chorioamnionitis are 5 to 10 times higher.49,50
paragraphs.heading: Outcomes

paragraphs.text: Despite extensive study, the relationship between intrauterine infection, brain injury, and respiratory outcomes remains uncertain. Some of the controversy likely results from a lack of precision in the definition of chorioamnionitis and whether a fetal inflammatory response is also present. It is worth emphasizing that chorioamnionitis without
paragraphs.heading: Outcomes

paragraphs.text: evidence of fetal inflammation is unlikely to cause fetal or neonatal injury. Furthermore, the adverse effects on the newborn infant may simply be the result of preterm birth and the host of postnatal complications that affect preterm infants (e.g., respiratory distress syndrome, necrotizing enterocolitis, or intraventricular hemorrhage).
paragraphs.heading: Outcomes

paragraphs.text: The association with antenatal inflammation and chronic lung disease is indirect and based on a number of experimental observations. In 1996 Watterberg concluded that chorioamnionitis decreased the risk of respiratory distress syndrome but increased the likelihood of BPD.51 However, those data came from an era when antenatal steroids were used infrequently. In contrast, Van Marter et al. demonstrated a reduced risk of BPD in infants born to women with chorioamnionitis, but an increased risk of BPD in infants born from an infected intrauterine environment who were mechanically ventilated.52 A meta-analysis of 244,000 infants concluded that chorioamnionitis increased the risk of BPD.53 This association was significant for clinical and histologic chorioamnionitis. Chorioamnionitis did not affect the incidence of respiratory distress syndrome. Multivariate regression analysis found that 64% of chorioamnionitis-associated BPD risk was explained by differences in gestational age and rate of respiratory distress syndrome. However, when adjusted for gestational age, other studies have not confirmed the association of chorioamnionitis with an increased risk of BPD.53 There appears to be a protective effect of antenatal inflammation on the incidence of respiratory distress syndrome, which is consistent with animal data demonstrating that both bacterial cell wall products (e.g., lipopolysaccharide) and inflammatory mediators (IL-6) accelerate surfactant production.54,55 Intra-amniotic injection of endotoxin in fetal sheep inhibited alveolar septation and decreased alveolar number by 20% but increased alveolar volume by almost 30%.56 This suggests that any improvement in lung function may be at the expense of impaired alveolar development. Been et al. demonstrated that infants born to women with histologic chorioamnionitis and a fetal vasculitis weaned from oxygen and mechanical ventilation more slowly and exhibited a decreased response to exogenous surfactant.57 That group of infants was more likely to develop BPD. This study supports the importance of the additive effects of inflammation and mechanical ventilation on the risk of BPD. This “multiple hit model,” in which both antenatal (chorioamnionitis) and postnatal factors (sepsis, surfactant production and function, mechanical ventilation) modulate the risk for BPD, is supported by most recent epidemiologic studies and data from experimental animal models (Fig. 24.6).58–60
paragraphs.heading: Outcomes

paragraphs.text: The relationship between clinical chorioamnionitis and white matter disease is also controversial.61,62 In many studies, but not all, cytokine levels are increased in the cord blood of infants who develop periventricular leukomalacia.63 Postmortem immunohistochemical studies on the brains of preterm infants noted an increased expression of cytokines in the periventricular region of infants with
paragraphs.heading: Outcomes

paragraphs.text: periventricular leukomalacia compared with those without evidence of brain injury. More recent meta-analyses’ data have noted significant associations between histologic and clinical chorioamnionitis with the risk of cerebral palsy.64 However, individual studies have not been consistent in those findings.65,66 Data most supportive of that relationship have come from the Extremely Low Gestational Age Newborns (ELGAN) study, in which nearly 900 placentas were cultured and biopsied following the delivery of extremely low–birth weight infants.67 Histologic chorioamnionitis was associated with ventriculomegaly and diparetic cerebral palsy. The recovery of any aerobic or anaerobic organism from the placenta significantly increased the odds ratios for both these outcomes, as well as the presence of echolucent lesions on head ultrasound. Furthermore, the investigators were able to demonstrate a dose-response relationship between the number of species recovered and the risk of these morbidities.
paragraphs.heading: Outcomes

paragraphs.text: Despite improved understanding of the pathogenic mechanism by which intrauterine infection leads to adverse
paragraphs.heading: Areas for Future Investigation

paragraphs.text: Key Points
paragraphs.heading: Areas for Future Investigation

paragraphs.text: • Intra-amniotic infection most frequently results from ascen-
paragraphs.heading: Areas for Future Investigation

paragraphs.text: sion of pathogens from the lower genital tract, eliciting variable inflammatory responses in both the mother and fetus. • Exposure to intrauterine inflammation increases the risk
paragraphs.heading: Areas for Future Investigation

paragraphs.text: of preterm birth and increases the risk of long-term morbidities, including cerebral palsy, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and retinopathy of prematurity.
paragraphs.heading: Areas for Future Investigation

paragraphs.text: pregnancy outcomes, research efforts over the past few decades have yielded little in the way of effective clinical strategies for the prevention and management of intrauterine infection. The development of more rigorous diagnostic criteria may better identify those women and fetuses most likely to benefit from antimicrobial treatment and reduce unnecessary, potentially harmful antibiotic exposure. The development of sepsis calculators that combine a rigorous assessment of intrapartum risk factors together with clinical presentation, like the one introduced by Puopolo and Escobar, may better identify neonates most at risk for early-onset sepsis and reduce the number of healthy infants exposed to unnecessary antimicrobial therapy.68 Continued exploration of the protective role of a healthy vaginal microbiome, mechanisms of abnormal colonization of the lower genital tract, and characterization of maternal/fetal immune responses to specific pathogens may help to identify those women most at risk for infectious complications of pregnancy and open the door for novel preventive strategies. Finally, exploration of potential anti-inflammatory therapies to reduce infection-related morbidities in both the mother and infant is warranted.
paragraphs.heading: Areas for Future Investigation

paragraphs.text: • Administration of intrapartum antibiotics to mothers
paragraphs.heading: Areas for Future Investigation

paragraphs.text: with chorioamnionitis decreases the risk of neonatal sepsis and postpartum maternal infections. However, novel interventions to disrupt inflammatory signaling cascades in utero are greatly needed.

Perinatal Infections and Chorioamnionitis > Source attribution: [Source credits](../../SOURCE_CREDITS.md). ## PDF page 429 | printed page 414 24 Perinatal Infections and Chorioamnionitis ### RICHARD ALAN POLIN, THOMAS ALEXANDER HOOVEN, AND TARA M. RANDIS ### Definitions and Epidemiology Chorioamnionitis (or intra-amniotic infection) is typically defined as an infection with resultant inflammation of the amniotic fluid, placenta, fetus, fetal membranes, or decidua.1 Chorioamnionitis most commonly results from ascension of bacteria colonizing the lower maternal genital tract, although it may rarely occur after invasive procedures or by a hematogenous route secondary to maternal systemic infection. There are strong associations between chorioamnionitis and maternal morbidity, preterm birth, and several adverse neonatal outcomes. However, the literature supporting these associations has been inconsistent, largely because of a lack of precision in both the definition and diagnosis of chorioamnionitis. When characteristic clinical signs of inflammation are present, the condition is usually termed clinical chorioamnionitis (see Diagnosis section below). Clinical chorioamnionitis complicates 2% to 10% of all pregnancies2,3; however, the reported incidence varies widely based upon gestational age and diagnostic criteria used. Two main varieties of chorioamnionitis can be identified: acute chorioamnionitis and subclinical chorioamnionitis. They differ in their clinical manifestations, microbiology, and risk to the fetus (Fig. 24.1). Approximately 30% of women with preterm labor and intact membranes exhibit histologic chorioamnionitis, as do 80% of women with preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM). Histologic acute chorioamnionitis, which represents the inflammatory response of the mother and fetus, cannot occur before the fusion of the amnion and chorion (≈11 weeks’ gestation) and is rare before 20 weeks of gestation. Before that time, a chronic chorio deciduitis can develop, which is subclinical and has been linked to an increased incidence of preterm birth, chronic lung disease, and periventricular leukomalacia. It is controversial whether chorio deciduitis represents an infectious process or a maternal immune response to fetal antigens.5 Histologic chorioamnionitis has been associated with intra-amniotic infection in 72% of cases of preterm birth. However, the likelihood of neonatal sepsis in women with histologic or clinical chorioamnionitis varies dramatically with gestational age (Table 24.1).6 Part of the difficulty of identifying women with chorioamnionitis is that microbial invasion of the amniotic cavity can be chronic and clinically silent. Furthermore, histologic chorioamnionitis can occur with negative cultures from amniotic fluid. Some of these “negative cultures” can be explained by the fastidiousness of the microorganisms found in amniotic fluid and the difficulty in recovering them using standard culture techniques. Others are the result of sterile intra-amniotic inflammation, a poorly understood yet clinically important entity associated with preterm delivery and neonatal morbidity.7 The precise stimuli for sterile intra-amniotic inflammation in patients have not been identified, although damage-associated molecular patterns are thought to play a major role in its pathogenesis.7 ### Automatic table extraction — verify rendered original |Group B Streptococcus

There are some data to suggest that women diagnosed with chorioamnionitis during their first pregnancy are at increased risk for developing chorioamnionitis in subsequent pregnancies, indicating a persistent predisposing condition or underlying host susceptibility. Gene association studies have identified single nucleotide polymorphisms in immunoregulatory genes that may influence susceptibility to chorioamnionitis.9 The presence of abnormal cervicovaginal flora (e.g., bacterial vaginosis, aerobic vaginitis) during the first trimester is associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes, including early preterm birth, miscarriage, and microbial invasion of the amniotic cavity,10 although discrete evidence linking the presence of abnormal flora of the lower genital tract with the development of acute clinical chorioamnionitis is lacking. Rather, it is hypothesized that these vaginal microbes ascend into the intrauterine cavity and induce a subclinical, chronic inflammatory response that, in turn, predisposes to preterm rupture of membranes and/or the onset of preterm labor. ### Microbiology Chorioamnionitis is almost always polymicrobial. However, many of the species that cause chorioamnionitis are difficult to grow under microbiological laboratory conditions and therefore may not be identified through standard culture techniques. Broad-range polymerase chain reaction (PCR) with bacterial probes followed by metagenomic sequencing11 or mass spectrometry12 analysis allows superior detection of uncultivatable organisms but is rarely used in clinical practice. A summary of data from multiple studies—using both standard culture and molecular detection techniques—shows that Ureaplasma, Streptococcus, Escherichia coli, and Mycoplasma hominis are among the most commonly identified organisms in chorioamnionitis, but a 25 Weeks 26 Weeks 27 Weeks 28 Weeks 51% 48% 41% 34% 19% 19% 15% 14% 2% 2% 2% 1% diverse assortment of other microbes is also commonly found (Fig. 24.2).13 Broad-range PCR has been used to identify the kinds of microorganisms found in the amniotic fluid of women with preterm labor or PPROM. These studies reveal that the patterns of microorganisms in amniotic fluid in women with preterm labor and intact membranes are different from those found in amniotic fluid samples from women with PPROM (Figs. 24.3 and 24.4).14 However, given the high sensitivity of PCR, the increased likelihood of detecting DNA from nonviable or environmental contaminants makes the clinical significance of this microbial diversity somewhat uncertain. Studies of the association of microbial invasion of the amniotic cavity (using PCR-based techniques) with fetal inflammation or perinatal outcomes noted statistically significant associations with elevated concentrations of inflammatory mediators in amniotic fluid and increased rates of histologic chorioamnionitis and preterm delivery.12 These studies lend support to an increasingly accepted theory that molecular identification of uncultivatable organisms from intrauterine sampling—in the absence of significant maternofetal inflammation—likely reflects environmental or procedural contamination rather than true infection. ### Diagnosis Confirmation of intrauterine infection and/or inflammation requires amniotic fluid sampling and/or placental pathology. Therefore, in the vast majority of cases, the diagnosis is made using clinical criteria. The classic definition required maternal fever (≥100.4° F or 38° C) plus two other findings, including maternal leukocytosis, maternal and fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, and foul-smelling or purulent amniotic fluid.15 Individual clinical criteria have variable sensitivity and generally low specificity for chorioamnionitis, with little improvement in diagnostic accuracy when used in combination (Table 24.2).16 There have been several attempts to refine these diagnostic criteria in recent years. In 2016, a new descriptive term, intrauterine inflammation, or infection, or both (triple I), was proposed by an expert panel to reflect the current understanding of pathophysiology, whereby inflammation does not always equal infection.17 Suspected triple I was defined as the presence of maternal intrapartum fever without a clear source, plus one or more of the following: maternal ## PDF page 431 Others 14.1% Enterococcus 1.9% Staphylococcus 2.2% Prevotella 2.2% Peptostreptococcus 2.2% Bacteroides 2.6% Pseudomonas 3.1% Gardnerella vaginalis 3.6% Lactobacillus 4.0% Candida 4.0% Fusobacterium 6.0% Mycoplasma hominis 6.4% ### • Fig. 24.2 Frequencies of microbes recovered from amniotic fluid or placental samples collected in the setting of clinical chorioamnionitis. The most recent recommendation from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists defines suspected intra-amniotic infection as a maternal temperature ≥39.0° C or when the maternal temperature is 38.0° to 38.9° C and one additional clinical criterion is present. It is noteworthy that both of the above definitions recognize isolated maternal fever as a distinct entity. Maternal fever may be caused by intrauterine or extrauterine etiologies. For example, epidural anesthesia is associated with an increased risk of fever during labor and, in most instances, it is thought to be noninfectious in origin. However, fever may be more likely to occur when placental inflammation is present. Fever can occur within 1 hour of epidural placement, but it almost always occurs within 4 to 6 hours. Laboratory testing may be helpful in confirming or excluding the diagnosis of chorioamnionitis, particularly when the diagnosis is uncertain. Leukocytosis has been described in the majority of patients with clinical chorioamnionitis. However, in the absence of other signs and symptoms, isolated leukocytosis is of limited value. A number of amniotic fluid markers have been studied for the diagnosis of chorioamnionitis. unc. Bacteroidetesb Lactobacillus Gardnerella Peptoniphilus Bifidobacterium Enterococcus Listeria Peptostreptococcus Propionibacterium These include culture, Gram stain, glucose levels, white blood cell counts, leukocyte esterase, damage-associated molecular patterns, soluble Toll-like receptors (TLRs), matrix metalloproteinase, cytokines (e.g., TNF-alpha, interleukins-6 and -8, matrix metalloproteinase-8), and qualitative assessment of amniotic proteins (proteomics). Proteomic analysis of amniotic fluid has led to the discovery of several novel biomarkers associated with the degree of intra-amniotic inflammation and time to delivery.18 The development of rapid, noninvasive assays to measure biomarkers associated with microbial invasion of the amniotic cavity in cervicovaginal fluid specimens holds promise for future diagnostics.19 The histopathologic findings of chorioamnionitis are well characterized and involve both maternal and fetal immune systems.20 The initial inflammatory response occurs within 6 to 12 hours, is maternal in origin, and is manifested by an infiltration of neutrophils on the undersurface of the chorionic plate (acute subchorionitis). The next site of involvement occurs at the trophoblast layer of the membranous chorion (acute chorionitis). Over the next 12 to 36 hours, the infection spreads to the adjacent chorion and amnion (chorioamnionitis). If the infectious process is prolonged (36–48 ## PDF page 433 TABLE Clinical and Amniotic Fluid Laboratory Diagnosis of Chorioamnionitis 24.2 Test Result Suggesting Chorioamnionitis Clinical Parameters Fever Temperature >100.4° F twice or >101° F once Maternal tachycardia >100/min Fetal tachycardia >160/min Fundal tenderness Tenderness on palpation Vaginal discharge Foul-smelling discharge Amniotic Fluid Parameters Culture Microbial growth Gram stain Bacteria or white blood cells (>6 per high power field) Glucose level <15 mg/dL IL-6 >7.9 ng/mL Matrix metalloproteinase Positive result White blood cell count >30/cubic mm Leukocyte esterase Positive (dipsticks) Data from Tita AT, Andrews WW. Diagnosis and management of clinical chorioamnionitis. Clin Perinatol. 2010;37:339–354. hours), necrotizing chorioamnionitis (stage 3 acute chorioamnionitis) can result. Fetal vasculitis is an indication of a fetal inflammatory response and represents diapedesis and transmigration of fetal cells across the vessel wall in response to chemotactic agents. In preterm pregnancies, the fetal responses first appear in the chorionic plate (chorionic vasculitis), whereas in term pregnancies they are first evident in the umbilical vein (umbilical phlebitis). Stage 1 fetal inflammatory responses are characterized by neutrophils in the chorionic vessels and/or umbilical vein vasculitis; stage 2 is reached when neutrophils enter the wall of the umbilical artery (umbilical arteritis). With increasing duration of inflammation, neutrophils migrate out of the umbilical artery and vein and enter Wharton jelly to assume an arc-like distribution (stage 3). Funisitis is a general term signifying inflammation of the umbilical artery and vein. It is important to distinguish umbilical arteritis from umbilical phlebitis because the former is associated with increased concentrations of circulating fetal cytokines, whereas the latter is not. It is noteworthy that most neutrophils in both the amniotic fluid and airspaces of the newborn’s lungs are fetal in origin. ### Pathogenesis Microorganisms typically invade the intrauterine space by ascending through the cervix from the lower genital tract. Retrograde migration from the abdominal cavity through the fallopian tubes, hematogenous spread through the Comments Generally Nonspecific 95%–100% sensitive 50%–80% sensitive 40%–70% sensitive 4%–25% sensitive 5%–22% sensitive Diagnostic gold standard 24% sensitive, 99% specific Affected by maternal hyperglycemia 57% sensitive, 74% specific 81% sensitive, 75% specific 90% sensitive, 80% specific 57% sensitive, 78% specific 85%–91% sensitive, 95%–100% specific placenta, and iatrogenic introduction via amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling are additional mechanisms by which organisms gain access to the uterine cavity.21 During pregnancy, the cervical mucus plug, fetal membranes, and placenta function to protect the developing fetus from invading bacteria. The cervical mucus plug is particularly important because it is not only an anatomic barrier but it also contains numerous antibacterial peptides with bactericidal activity against potential pathogens that commonly colonize the vaginal tissues.22 It is generally believed that once organisms gain access to the intrauterine space, they reside and replicate in the choriodecidual space before entering the amniotic fluid.23 However, data suggest an initial intra-amniotic entry of bacteria through a restricted cervical region of membranes.24 After replication in the amniotic cavity, microorganisms then invade the amnion and its connective tissue and progress into the chorion and decidua. Stimulation of the innate immune response first occurs when the pathogen-associated molecular patterns of invading microorganisms are recognized by pattern recognition receptors (TLRs, nucleotide oligomerization domain [NOD]-like receptors [NLRs]) expressed by host epithelial cells, circulating immune cells, and perhaps most important, placental trophoblast cells.25,26 Once stimulated, these receptors induce a cascade of proinflammatory signaling, including stimulation of Myd88 (TLRs) and inflammasome (NLRs) pathways. Subsequent production of various ## PDF page 434 | printed page 419 cytokines, chemokines, matrix-degrading enzymes, prostaglandins, and other mediators leads to an inflammatory cell infiltrate, membrane rupture, cervical ripening, and in some cases, the onset of labor. Experimental evidence from animal models of intrauterine infection suggests that the specific inflammatory pathway leading to the induction of preterm labor is dependent on the particular TLR activated (determined by the nature of infecting agent) as well as the route of infection (ascending versus systemic). Recent investigations using human placental explant models have identified the NLRP3 inflammasome as a central mediator of proinflammatory interleukin-1β elaboration, which, in turn, promotes neutrophil infiltration of pregnancy tissues and initiation of labor.27 As mentioned, bacterial invasion of the amniotic cavity may be chronic, existing for several weeks without clinical symptoms. This is particularly true in infections with Ureaplasma spp.28 Several investigators have found amniotic fluid cultures positive for Ureaplasma in asymptomatic women undergoing genetic amniocenteses at 16 to 20 weeks’ gestation.29 Despite a lack of overt symptomatology, a significant portion of these women exhibited a robust inflammatory response as measured by expression of inflammatory cytokines in the amniotic fluid and subsequently went on to experience adverse pregnancy outcomes (fetal loss, preterm birth) compared with those women with sterile cultures. In fact, there is ample evidence to suggest that Ureaplasma spp., traditionally considered to be of relatively low virulence, may evoke a more intense host inflammatory response as compared with other pathogens associated with chorioamnionitis. ### Treatment ### Obstetric Management Recent practice guidelines from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists emphasize the distinction between isolated intrapartum maternal fever and clinically diagnosed chorioamnionitis. Although obstetricians often administer antibiotics in the setting of isolated maternal fever, this practice is of uncertain benefit, and additional research is needed to understand both the mechanism and appropriate management of isolated maternal fever. Whether or not antibiotics are administered for isolated intrapartum maternal fever, the diagnosis and rationale behind its obstetric management should be conveyed to the neonatology team for consideration in planning care of the newborn. In the setting of true clinical chorioamnionitis, administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics and prompt delivery of the fetus reduce both fetal and maternal morbidity. Chorioamnionitis alone is not a sufficient indication for cesarean delivery because there is no evidence it improves neonatal outcomes and may increase maternal complications such as wound infection.30 However, findings consistent with fetal or maternal instability in the setting of chorioamnionitis can be indications for cesarean delivery. Ampicillin and gentamicin are the most commonly prescribed antimicrobials for intra-amniotic infection, although there are no randomized trials comparing the efficacy of various antibiotic regimens. It is worth noting that standard antibiotic regimens used to treat chorioamnionitis do not provide coverage against Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma spp., two of the most common organisms associated with intra-amniotic infection. Several authors and expert panels have proposed alternative antibiotic protocols to cover these organisms, but these proposals have not been subjected to clinical trials.31 If cesarean delivery is performed, clindamycin (or metronidazole) is often added for anaerobic coverage. The administration of antenatal corticosteroids to enhance fetal lung maturity in the setting of chorioamnionitis is controversial because it is believed that the immunosuppressive effects of steroids may exacerbate maternal or neonatal infectious complications. Although randomized clinical trials addressing this issue are lacking, there are observational data to suggest that antenatal steroids may actually reduce neonatal morbidity, including severe intraventricular hemorrhage and periventricular leukomalacia in the presence of chorioamnionitis.32,33 PPROM is associated with intra-amniotic infection, and evidence supports routine administration of antibiotics to women presenting with PPROM with the intention of reducing progression to chorioamnionitis, prolonging pregnancy, and decreasing neonatal morbidities (early-onset sepsis, need for supplemental oxygen, brain injury).34 In a 2020 update to practice guidelines, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommended 48 hours of intravenous ampicillin and erythromycin, followed by oral amoxicillin and erythromycin, to complete a 7-day course in uncomplicated PPROM.35 Despite the benefits listed above, there is not strong evidence to show that antibiotic administration for PPROM reduces infant mortality. Furthermore, the use of antenatal antibiotics in particular circumstances may be harmful. The administration of co-amoxiclav (ampicillin/clavulanic acid) in women with PPROM or preterm labor with intact membranes was associated with an increased risk for necrotizing enterocolitis in neonates. In addition, the use of both erythromycin and co-amoxiclav antibiotics for women with preterm labor and intact membranes was associated with an unexpected increase in the incidence of cerebral palsy at a 7-year follow-up evaluation.36 ### Management of the Exposed Infant Guidelines for the management of infants with suspected or proven sepsis from the Committee on the Fetus and Newborn of the American Academy of Pediatrics were revised in 2018.37,38 The two clinical reports were divided into ## PDF page 435 recommendations for infants ≥350/7 weeks’ gestation38 and infants ≤346/7 weeks’ gestation.37 Although chorioamnionitis is still considered a risk factor for early-onset sepsis in infants ≥350/7 weeks’ gestation, the specificity of this diagnosis is poor, and relatively few infants born to women with chorioamnionitis in that gestational age strata develop earlyonset sepsis. Additionally, the diagnosis of clinical chorioamnionitis is often made when fever is the sole manifestation of an intrauterine infection. Therefore many infants may be unnecessarily exposed to broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy. Complicating this issue is the increased incidence of fever in women receiving epidural anesthesia. Therefore, if fever is the sole manifestation of suspected chorioamnionitis, consultation with the obstetric provider is recommended to determine the level of clinical suspicion before routinely treating asymptomatic infants. The Committee on the Fetus and Newborn recommends selecting from three different approaches for infants ≥350/7 weeks’ gestation with a history of chorioamnionitis. The first, termed the categorical risk factor assessment, recommends laboratory testing and empirical antibiotics for all infants born to women with chorioamnionitis and any infant who is ill appearing. This strategy will likely lead to considerable overtreatment of uninfected infants. The second approach, termed multivariate risk assessment, uses established risk factors and the infant’s clinical condition in the first 6 to 12 hours of life to estimate the risk of sepsis. These variables can be entered into a web-based early-onset sepsis calculator (https://neonatalsepsiscalculator.kaiserpermanente.org). (See also Chapter 50.) Blood culture and enhanced clinical observations are recommended for an estimated risk of early-onset sepsis ≥1 per 1000 live births, and empirical antibiotics are recommended for an estimated risk of sepsis ≥3 per 1000 live births. The third strategy relies on identification of clinical signs of illness regardless of any estimation of neonatal or maternal risk factors. Infants who develop signs of illness in the first 48 hours of life are either empirically treated with antibiotics or further evaluated with laboratory testing. Both the multivariate risk approach and serial examination strategy have reduced the number of sepsis evaluations, but the use of either approach will still lead to overtreatment of a substantial number of infants who are uninfected. There is growing evidence to suggest that close observation, rather than empiric antibiotic therapy, is the preferred strategy for the management of asymptomatic full-term infants exposed to chorioamnionitis.39,40 The risk of sepsis in this population is exceedingly low given that the incidence of early-onset sepsis has declined dramatically over the past two decades (because of widespread implementation of intrapartum prophylaxis for mothers colonized with GBS and the treatment of women with chorioamnionitis with antibiotics during labor). This substantially increases the number of healthy term newborns who would require antibiotics to prevent a single case of sepsis.41 Because the risk of early-onset sepsis in infants born to women with chorioamnionitis is strongly dependent on gestational age, it remains prudent to empirically treat chorioamnionitisexposed preterm infants ≤346/7 weeks’ gestation. ### Outcomes Chorioamnionitis can adversely affect the mother and her unborn infant. The associations between chorioamnionitis and adverse outcomes are not straightforward given the multiple causes of maternal fever and a lack of concordance between maternal intra-amniotic infection, histologic chorioamnionitis, and clinical chorioamnionitis. In pregnant women, chorioamnionitis is associated with a two-fold increase in abnormal progression of labor, an increased risk of cesarean section,30 postpartum hemorrhage, poor cervical dilation, placental abruption, and intensive care admission.42 Surgical complications after cesarean section, such as endometritis, pelvic abscess, wound infection, thromboembolism, and bacteremia, are also more common in women with chorioamnionitis. The effects of intrauterine infection on the fetus depend on the duration and timing of the inflammatory process. Acute chorioamnionitis is an important risk factor for early-onset neonatal sepsis. Chronic infections, however, are often subclinical and have been associated with a wide variety of organ injury, including the brain (periventricular leukomalacia), lung (bronchopulmonary dysplasia [BPD]), eye (retinopathy of prematurity), intestine (necrotizing enterocolitis), and thymus (involution and a change in cellular composition).43 Chorioamnionitis, especially with a fetal inflammatory component, has also been associated with hemodynamic instability in the preterm newborn infant. Chorioamnionitis is thought to initiate 40% to 70% of preterm births; the incidence may even be higher at lower gestational ages. The evidence linking infection and preterm labor is as follows: (1) intrauterine infection (or exposure to microbial products) in experimental animals results in preterm delivery; (2) extrauterine maternal infections (e.g., pyelonephritis) are associated with preterm labor; (3) subclinical intrauterine infections are associated with preterm labor and birth; (4) patients with evidence of intrauterine inflammation (e.g., increased amniotic fluid cytokines or matrix metalloproteinases) in the mid-third trimester are at increased risk for preterm delivery; (5) in experimental animal models, antibiotic treatment of intrauterine infections can prevent prematurity; (6) treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria prevents prematurity; (7) administration of antibiotics to women with PPROM prolongs gestation; (8) microorganisms can be cultured from the placenta in a high percentage of women presenting with preterm labor; and (9) polymorphonuclear infiltrations in the placenta are associated with spontaneous preterm birth. A possible mechanism for infection-associated preterm birth is shown in Fig. 24.5.16 It is important to note that although microorganisms are associated with preterm birth, sterile inflammation is more frequently associated ## PDF page 436 | printed page 421 Chorioamnionitis/funisitis Maternal and neonatal sepsis, morbidity, death Maternal inflammation Fetal inflammation/FIRS Cytokines and chemokines IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α, MMP • Prostaglandin release • Cervical changes • Weakened membranes Fetal/neonatal brain and multi-organ injury Preterm labor PPROM Perinatal death and long-term morbidities including cerebral palsy PTB • Fig. 24.5 Pathogenesis of chorioamnionitis: maternal and fetal response and complications. Clin Perinatol. 2010;37:339–354.) with preterm labor and intact membranes, PPROM, and asymptomatic short cervix than microbe-associated intraamniotic infection.44 Acute chorioamnionitis is a risk factor for neonatal sepsis.41 Both histologic chorioamnionitis and clinical chorioamnionitis are associated with early-onset neonatal sepsis.45,46 Among infants of ≥37 weeks’ gestation with proven early-onset sepsis owing to E. coli or GBS, clinical chorioamnionitis was documented in the medical record about one-third of the time, and histologic chorioamnionitis was documented in 90% of the cases.6 Importantly, the risk of early-onset sepsis in infants born to women with chorioamnionitis is inversely correlated with gestational age. Reported rates of confirmed sepsis in infants born at ≥35 weeks’ gestation to mothers with clinical chorioamnionitis range from 0.47% to 1.24%.47,48 In contrast, rates in moderate and extremely preterm infants exposed to chorioamnionitis are 5 to 10 times higher.49,50 Despite extensive study, the relationship between intrauterine infection, brain injury, and respiratory outcomes remains uncertain. Some of the controversy likely results from a lack of precision in the definition of chorioamnionitis and whether a fetal inflammatory response is also present. It is worth emphasizing that chorioamnionitis without evidence of fetal inflammation is unlikely to cause fetal or neonatal injury. Furthermore, the adverse effects on the newborn infant may simply be the result of preterm birth and the host of postnatal complications that affect preterm infants (e.g., respiratory distress syndrome, necrotizing enterocolitis, or intraventricular hemorrhage). The association with antenatal inflammation and chronic lung disease is indirect and based on a number of experimental observations. In 1996 Watterberg concluded that chorioamnionitis decreased the risk of respiratory distress syndrome but increased the likelihood of BPD.51 However, those data came from an era when antenatal steroids were used infrequently. In contrast, Van Marter et al. demonstrated a reduced risk of BPD in infants born to women with chorioamnionitis, but an increased risk of BPD in infants born from an infected intrauterine environment who were mechanically ventilated.52 A meta-analysis of 244,000 infants concluded that chorioamnionitis increased the risk of BPD.53 This association was significant for clinical and histologic chorioamnionitis. Chorioamnionitis did not affect the incidence of respiratory distress syndrome. Multivariate regression analysis found that 64% of chorioamnionitis-associated BPD risk was explained by differences in gestational age and rate of respiratory distress syndrome. However, when adjusted for gestational age, other studies have not confirmed the association of chorioamnionitis with an increased risk of BPD.53 There appears to be a protective effect of antenatal inflammation on the incidence of respiratory distress syndrome, which is consistent with animal data demonstrating that both bacterial cell wall products (e.g., lipopolysaccharide) and inflammatory mediators (IL-6) accelerate surfactant production.54,55 Intra-amniotic injection of endotoxin in fetal sheep inhibited alveolar septation and decreased alveolar number by 20% but increased alveolar volume by almost 30%.56 This suggests that any improvement in lung function may be at the expense of impaired alveolar development. Been et al. demonstrated that infants born to women with histologic chorioamnionitis and a fetal vasculitis weaned from oxygen and mechanical ventilation more slowly and exhibited a decreased response to exogenous surfactant.57 That group of infants was more likely to develop BPD. This study supports the importance of the additive effects of inflammation and mechanical ventilation on the risk of BPD. This “multiple hit model,” in which both antenatal (chorioamnionitis) and postnatal factors (sepsis, surfactant production and function, mechanical ventilation) modulate the risk for BPD, is supported by most recent epidemiologic studies and data from experimental animal models (Fig. 24.6).58–60 The relationship between clinical chorioamnionitis and white matter disease is also controversial.61,62 In many studies, but not all, cytokine levels are increased in the cord blood of infants who develop periventricular leukomalacia.63 Postmortem immunohistochemical studies on the brains of preterm infants noted an increased expression of cytokines in the periventricular region of infants with ## PDF page 437 Inflammation during resuscitation Antenatal inflammation Immaturity Immaturity Steroids Chorioamnionitis Resuscitation First hit Second hit • Fig. 24.6 The role of chorioamnionitis in the development of bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD). Elsevier; 2021:748–756.) periventricular leukomalacia compared with those without evidence of brain injury. More recent meta-analyses’ data have noted significant associations between histologic and clinical chorioamnionitis with the risk of cerebral palsy.64 However, individual studies have not been consistent in those findings.65,66 Data most supportive of that relationship have come from the Extremely Low Gestational Age Newborns (ELGAN) study, in which nearly 900 placentas were cultured and biopsied following the delivery of extremely low–birth weight infants.67 Histologic chorioamnionitis was associated with ventriculomegaly and diparetic cerebral palsy. The recovery of any aerobic or anaerobic organism from the placenta significantly increased the odds ratios for both these outcomes, as well as the presence of echolucent lesions on head ultrasound. Furthermore, the investigators were able to demonstrate a dose-response relationship between the number of species recovered and the risk of these morbidities. ### Areas for Future Investigation Despite improved understanding of the pathogenic mechanism by which intrauterine infection leads to adverse Key Points • Intra-amniotic infection most frequently results from ascen- sion of pathogens from the lower genital tract, eliciting variable inflammatory responses in both the mother and fetus. • Exposure to intrauterine inflammation increases the risk of preterm birth and increases the risk of long-term morbidities, including cerebral palsy, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and retinopathy of prematurity. Postnatal inflammation BPD O2 Immaturity Infections Mechanical ventilation Third hit pregnancy outcomes, research efforts over the past few decades have yielded little in the way of effective clinical strategies for the prevention and management of intrauterine infection. The development of more rigorous diagnostic criteria may better identify those women and fetuses most likely to benefit from antimicrobial treatment and reduce unnecessary, potentially harmful antibiotic exposure. The development of sepsis calculators that combine a rigorous assessment of intrapartum risk factors together with clinical presentation, like the one introduced by Puopolo and Escobar, may better identify neonates most at risk for early-onset sepsis and reduce the number of healthy infants exposed to unnecessary antimicrobial therapy.68 Continued exploration of the protective role of a healthy vaginal microbiome, mechanisms of abnormal colonization of the lower genital tract, and characterization of maternal/fetal immune responses to specific pathogens may help to identify those women most at risk for infectious complications of pregnancy and open the door for novel preventive strategies. Finally, exploration of potential anti-inflammatory therapies to reduce infection-related morbidities in both the mother and infant is warranted. • Administration of intrapartum antibiotics to mothers with chorioamnionitis decreases the risk of neonatal sepsis and postpartum maternal infections. However, novel interventions to disrupt inflammatory signaling cascades in utero are greatly needed. ## PDF page 438 | printed page 423 ### References 1.
