Communication between the obstetric and neonatal teams is essential to the graded response needed for neonatal resuscitation. In some situations, a single competent person is appropriate to the clinical situation. At other times, a full resuscitation team of three or more skilled providers may be necessary. Identifying a high-risk situation before delivery of the infant provides time for adequate preparation and gathering the appropriate personnel in the delivery room. Because of modern obstetric techniques and anesthesia, it is no longer necessary to consider a repeat cesarean section as a high-risk delivery because this form of delivery carries no greater risk than a vertex vaginal delivery at term.38 Only if the cesarean section involves a premature infant, fetal distress, or other complications is there any cause for added concern. It is impossible to identify every infant who may need assistance. At every delivery, equipment and personnel should be available in case of unanticipated neonatal depression.

### Ethical and Legal Aspects of Delivery Room Resuscitation

The American Medical Association code of medical ethics may be applied to neonatal resuscitation situations.39 This code provides guidance on how providers should act, taking into account the chance that therapy will succeed; the risk involved in treatment and nontreatment; the degree to which the therapy, if successful, will extend life; the pain and discomfort associated with the therapy; and the anticipated quality of life for the newborn with and without treatment. State and federal laws prescribe how providers must act in resuscitation scenarios within their jurisdictions. In 1984, a Federal Child Abuse Amendment required physicians to provide care except if the child is clinically and irreversibly comatose, if treatment would only prolong dying, or if treatment would be deemed “futile.”40 In 1989, a civil rights law mandated medical care for every child. As time progressed, issues arose regarding criminal as well as civil liability in cases where newborns were not resuscitated and in other cases where newborns were successfully resuscitated against their parents’ wishes and survived with significant handicaps. There is no law mandating delivery room resuscitation in all circumstances. Local and state laws differ in various regions of the country, and the resuscitation team should be aware of laws in their locale. Moreover, the parents should be part of the decision-making process, especially when there is a question of whether or not to begin resuscitation in the periviable baby and sufficient time to give adequate information prior to birth.1,41 However, when parental direction is unclear, the provider must always be the advocate for the child.

### Adequate Equipment

Whenever an infant is delivered, appropriate equipment must be close at hand and in good working order. An area in or near the delivery room should be designated as the resuscitation area, and provisions should be made for adequate space, heat (radiant warmer), blended oxygen, and suction. Supplies and drugs as specified in the resuscitation guidelines should be placed in a code cart or bag or attached to a wall board for easy access.1 These supplies should be routinely checked by hospital personnel and rechecked for completeness and effectiveness (e.g., laryngoscope light works) before an anticipated resuscitation. A delay in effective resuscitation may occur if someone needs to leave the delivery room during the procedure to obtain an essential piece of equipment. When expecting an extremely depressed infant (e.g., terminal bradycardia resulting in an emergency cesarean section), it may be appropriate to prepare the umbilical catheter and draw up epinephrine before delivery.

### Adequate Personnel

Individuals vested with the responsibility of resuscitating infants should be adequately trained, readily available, and capable of working together as a team. Having trained personnel readily available means having someone present at every delivery who has the skill required to initiate resuscitation, with other available staff close at hand in case they are needed. This person does not have to be a physician but should be able to recognize the need for resuscitation and perform the initial steps, including the initiation of PPV. The hospital is responsible for ensuring the competence of these personnel in the same way a surgeon is credentialed to perform certain operations.4 At least two, if not three, people are needed to carry out a full resuscitation. Adequate training involves more than simply going through a course and receiving a certificate of completion. The NRP of the AHA/AAP and similar courses are simply starting points.1 These programs do not ensure competence or qualify one to assume independent responsibility.

Finally, the personnel available to the delivery room should be capable of working together as a team. If staff are skilled at carrying out their responsibilities and can anticipate each other’s needs, the tension inherent in any resuscitation can be reduced, and the process will go much more smoothly. The use of simulation training using manikins, holding mock code drills on an ongoing basis, and reviewing video recordings of resuscitations may help to maintain skills and develop coordination among staff.33,34,37,42

### Umbilical Cord Blood Gases

Umbilical cord blood analysis for high-risk deliveries (i.e., low 5-minute Apgar score, severe intrauterine growth restriction, fetal heart rate tracing abnormalities, intrapartum fever, multiple gestation pregnancies, and cesarean deliveries for fetal distress) is currently recommended by ACOG.4 The arterial cord gas can be a valuable representation of the fetal acid-base state prior to delivery.45–48 Adverse neurologic sequelae have been associated with a low arterial cord pH.49 Using both the arterial and venous cord values, the clinician may be able to determine the intrapartum events leading to neonatal depression.46,50 Severe acidosis in a cord blood gas may inform the resuscitation and determine triage of the newborn to the appropriate postresuscitation care.51,52 An arterial cord pH less than 7.0 and a base excess greater than –16 in association with signs of neonatal encephalopathy have been used as criteria for therapeutic hypothermia in the treatment of intrapartum asphyxia.53,54 If only one cord blood gas is reported, it may be from the umbilical vein, as this vessel is larger and more easily sampled.46,51 One clue that a single gas sample is of venous origin is the PaO2 value. If the reported PaO2 is >31 mm Hg, it is highly likely to be a venous sample.46

In the ideal situation, both arterial and venous umbilical cord blood will be sampled for blood gas analysis.4,45,52 The umbilical artery pH should be at least 0.02 units lower than that of the vein.51 The normal umbilical arterial pCO2 is usually more than 4 mm Hg greater than that of the vein.

### Elements of a Resuscitation

A resuscitation can be viewed as a series of elements. The process is not a linear set of steps in which one marches inexorably from one point to another; rather, it involves an evaluation of the infant’s condition, a decision based on that evaluation, and action.55 These steps are repeated until the process is concluded. Fig. 30.6 provides an overview of the resuscitation process.1

Virtually all infants undergo the initial steps. Most infants requiring active resuscitation respond to appropriately administered PPV.1,3 Adequate ventilation is the most important aspect of a successful neonatal resuscitation. Unfortunately, the administration of mask ventilation is subjective with very little feedback to the provider, and the technique may be unsatisfactory, resulting in inadequate alveolar ventilation (see Chapter 31). All infants, whether they require only the initial steps or a complete resuscitation, are entitled to a skilled and timely response, regardless of who is performing the resuscitation. Parents may be present while perinatal care is being provided to neonates, including procedures, resuscitation, and stabilization. Parents should be informed about and involved in the care of their infants within the principles of family-centered care.1,41

### Initial Quick Overview

Most infants are vigorous, cry at birth, and breathe easily thereafter; however, there may be a delay of 30 seconds or more before a healthy baby takes a first breath. Many times parents prefer that the infant go to the mother immediately after birth rather than be placed on a warmer and put through the “initial steps” in resuscitation. In most circumstances, a healthy and vigorous infant does not require suctioning after delivery. With appropriate triaging and oversight, most newborns can be given directly to the mother immediately after birth without compromising their care.

When positioning, the infant is placed in a “sniffing” position, which will facilitate opening the airway. If needed, secretions can be cleared with a bulb syringe and the infant is dried, unless very preterm, in which case a plastic wrap is used to maintain temperature. ### Thermal Management

The fetus maintains a body temperature about 0.5° higher than maternal temperature. Through the accumulation of brown fat late in gestation, the term newborn is able to activate thermogenesis by stimuli of oxygenation, ventilation, and oxidative metabolism via various hormonal intermediaries. The lack of brown fat accumulation in preterm infants and the sequelae of asphyxia in term infants put these newborns at significant disadvantage in thermoregulation postdelivery.20 Delivery rooms are kept at a level of thermal comfort for the adults working in them. The neonate with a very large ratio of surface area to mass is susceptible to cold stress; this is especially true for depressed infants with poor perfusion and extremely low birth weight infants. Unintentional hypothermia in neonates has been associated with metabolic acidosis, increased oxygen consumption, and increased mortality, especially in very preterm infants.58 For very low birth weight infants, one large cohort study revealed a 28% increase in mortality for each 1 °C decrease in neonatal intensive care unit admission temperature.59

Studies have shown that >30% of infants with extremely low birth weight (<1000 g) become hypothermic with standard warming techniques in the delivery room.58,60 Because this population makes up less than 1% of all deliveries, special preparations should be made for these infants by prewarming the delivery room or an adjacent resuscitation area to 75° to 78 °F and using a radiant warmer and food-grade plastic wrap to keep the infant warm after birth.1,58,61 Other strategies may include prewarmed blankets, hats, exothermic mattresses, and the use of warmed, humidified air/oxygen for ventilation.24 Care must be taken not to overheat an infant, as animal studies have shown that hyperthermia is synergistic with asphyxia in worsening cerebral injury.2

For a term nondistressed newborn, the infant should be placed skin-to-skin with the mother or in the microenvironment of a preheated radiant warmer immediately after birth. Newborns who do not qualify for routine care should be placed in warm blankets and quickly moved to a preheated radiant warmer set at 100% power. The infant should be thoroughly dried, and the wet blankets should be promptly removed to avoid evaporative heat loss. These simple measures can minimize the decrease in core temperature that the term infant experiences at birth.62 Preventing excessive

heat loss can become especially important with a preterm infant or an infant who is asphyxiated and hypoxic. Because hypoxia blunts the normal response to cold, a hypoxic infant undergoes a greater than normal decline in core temperature if not thermally protected.63 Recovery from acidosis also is delayed by hypothermia (see Chapter 35).64

### Clearing the Airway

Previously, it was recommended that the airway should be cleared with the use of a bulb syringe or a suction catheter. However, if the newborn is vigorous and born through clear amniotic fluid, this procedure is not necessary,65,66 and stimulation of the posterior portion of the pharynx may induce bradycardia.67 If the infant has excessive secretions, a bulb syringe may be used to clear first the mouth and then the nose (“m” before “n”). An infant exposed to meconium in the amniotic fluid represents a special circumstance (discussed in Chapter 33).

### Monitoring

Heart rate may be evaluated by palpation of a peripheral pulse or the umbilical cord; however, studies have shown that these measurements are not reliable.68 If the resuscitation team is expecting a significantly depressed baby or a very low birth weight infant who probably needs help in transition, attaching electrocardiogram (ECG) leads to monitor heart rate should be done early in the resuscitation process. Use of a pulse oximeter to guide treatment is also suggested by the NRP.1 There may be a delay of 1 to 2 minutes after attaching the pulse oximeter until accurate readings of both heart rate and oxygen saturation are obtained. If the baby has poor perfusion or a very low heart rate, the pulse oximeter may not give accurate readings.

### Tactile Stimulation and Assessment

Usually the act of drying the infant is enough tactile stimulation to initiate respiration. An infant in primary apnea will generally respond to these gentle measures. All babies will be cyanotic at birth, and blow-by oxygen is not indicated. If the infant does not breathe after tactile stimulation, gently flicking the soles of the feet or rubbing the infant’s back may be enough additional stimulation to elicit regular respirations. After initial steps, if stimulation fails to elicit a vigorous response, the baby should be assumed to be in secondary apnea, and PPV should be quickly initiated. PPV may be given initially to infants ≥35 weeks with air (21% FiO2). Continued and more vigorous tactile stimulation is not useful and may be harmful if ineffective maneuvers allow the baby to remain hypoxic and acidotic. The decisions from this point revolve around the response of the infant—primarily heart rate and respirations.

### Preparing for Oxygen Administration

Over the past several years, there has been considerable discussion and research on the use of oxygen in neonatal resuscitation (see Chapter 32).69–72 Previously, the Textbook of Neonatal Resuscitation recommended that free-flow oxygen be used if the newborn remained cyanotic after


## PDF page 555

30 seconds of initial steps (drying, warmth) and evaluation, or if PPV was needed. This recommendation has been revised based on numerous studies. The current recommendation is to use pulse oximetry if resuscitation is anticipated, when PPV is given, and if central cyanosis persists after 5 to 10 minutes. Resuscitation for infants ≥35 weeks should begin with room air (21% oxygen at sea level), and oxygen should be given if necessary and titrated according to the interquartile range of healthy term newborns after vaginal birth at sea level (Fig. 30.6). If the newborn is <35 weeks’ gestation, the initial oxygen concentration should be 21% to 30% FiO2. If chest compressions, medication, or both are needed, 100% oxygen is recommended (Fig. 30.6).1,2 Current recommendations advise against the routine use of oxygen for transient cyanosis and the avoidance of high concentrations of oxygen whenever possible.2,71

If the infant is spontaneously breathing and the heart rate is greater than 100 bpm, but the infant remains cyanotic for >5 minutes after birth, oxygen may be administered through a free-flow system until it can be shown that the oxygen concentration can be reduced (arterial oxygen saturation [SaO2] > 85%) or that lowering the concentration makes no difference (cyanotic heart disease). title: Role of Positive Pressure Ventilation in Neonatal Resuscitation

paragraphs.text: 31 Role of Positive Pressure Ventilation in Neonatal Resuscitation
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Newborn babies who do not spontaneously breathe at birth require support to safely make the transition to extrauterine life. Over the past 20 years, guidelines for those providing care to these infants have been developed.1 However, the evidence available to guide initial respiratory support remains limited, reflecting the challenges associated with conducting research in the delivery room.
paragraphs.heading: LOUISE S. OWEN AND PETER G. DAVIS

paragraphs.text: The crucial steps in the adaption to extrauterine life involve the transition from liquid-filled to air-filled lungs, and the establishment of functional residual capacity (FRC). These changes normally occur in the first minutes after birth and include an increase in pulmonary blood flow and the onset of regular respiration. Lung aeration and the development of an FRC facilitate gas exchange. Deferring cord clamping until these are achieved ensures a smooth transition to extrauterine life. If an infant does not quickly establish effective respiration, assistance is immediately required. Typically, this is a brief need for basic respiratory support only,2 unless there is abnormal anatomy or significant fetal acidemia or ineffective respiratory support is provided. Preterm infants have additional requirements at birth; although most preterm infants breathe and cry,3 very preterm infants are still likely to need support to effectively establish and maintain FRC. Preterm lungs are delicate, and lung injury can occur with just a few high-volume positive pressure inflations.4 This has led to a shift in emphasis in preterm stabilization toward a gentle, supportive approach to augment rather than override their efforts, and to minimize lung injury.
paragraphs.heading: LOUISE S. OWEN AND PETER G. DAVIS

paragraphs.text: In healthy, newborn, term infants, normal transition is characterized by repeated, short, deep inspirations, each followed by a prolonged expiratory phase through a partially
paragraphs.heading: Normal Transition and Initial Spontaneous Breathing

paragraphs.text: closed glottis (crying). The inspiratory efforts generate large negative transpulmonary pressures, typically −50 cm H2O to −100 cm H2O, such that the high-resistance liquid filling the infant’s airways is driven distally, moving the air-liquid interface toward the distal airways.
paragraphs.heading: Normal Transition and Initial Spontaneous Breathing

paragraphs.text: Detailed imaging of rabbit lungs demonstrates that initial lung aeration depends on the generation of this transpulmonary pressure, with consequent stepwise increases in FRC over three to five repeated inspiratory efforts. More volume is inspired than expired with each breath, which overcomes small losses in FRC between inspiratory efforts as lung liquid moves back into the airways.5 The lung liquid then moves into the interstitial tissue and is cleared over the following hours.
paragraphs.heading: Normal Transition and Initial Spontaneous Breathing

paragraphs.text: Prolonged expiration through a partially closed glottis, with simultaneous abdominal muscle contraction pressurizes the chest, further pushing the air-liquid interface distally; this is called expiratory braking (Fig. 31.1). Flow recordings of the first breaths in preterm infants have shown that they use crying and expiratory braking to facilitate lung recruitment and development of FRC (Fig. 31.2).6 These observations have been supported by electrical impedance tomography (EIT) recordings, which demonstrate that newborn infants generate unique flow and volume patterns during this process (Fig. 31.3).7
paragraphs.heading: Normal Transition and Initial Spontaneous Breathing

paragraphs.text: Some infants do not breathe or have ineffective breathing at birth. Guidelines recommend initial steps of stimulating, drying, and wrapping the baby, followed by clamping the cord and then opening, and in some cases clearing, the airway.1 They stipulate that positive pressure support should be commenced by 60 seconds of age if the baby remains apneic, has irregular or gasping respirations, or has a heart rate less
paragraphs.heading: Delayed Transition and Need for Respiratory Support

paragraphs.text: than 100 beats per minute (bpm).1 However, following these recommendations may not always be straightforward. • Healthy babies may not take their first breath immedi-
paragraphs.heading: Delayed Transition and Need for Respiratory Support

paragraphs.text: ately after birth; there may be a delay of 30 seconds or longer. • In practice, initial evaluation often takes longer than 60
paragraphs.heading: Delayed Transition and Need for Respiratory Support

paragraphs.text: seconds,8 particularly in light of current recommendations for greater than 30 or 60 seconds of delayed cord clamping in preterm and term infants, respectively. • Clinical assessment of heart rate at birth, either by palpa-
paragraphs.heading: Delayed Transition and Need for Respiratory Support

paragraphs.text: tion or auscultation, is intermittent and inaccurate.9 • Assessment of a newborn’s color is subjective and unreli-
paragraphs.heading: Delayed Transition and Need for Respiratory Support

paragraphs.text: able.10 Although assessment of color is not used in the most recent resuscitation guidelines, it remains part of the Apgar assessment. These factors make assessment at birth, and the decision whether to intervene, more complex. If decisions are made too early, unnecessary interventions may be applied, whereas if decisions are delayed, there may be further cardiorespiratory compromise. It may be helpful to be aware that: • Accurate measurements of oxygen saturation (SpO2) and
paragraphs.heading: Delayed Transition and Need for Respiratory Support

paragraphs.text: heart rate can be obtained by about 90 seconds using pulse oximetry,11 and heart rate values may be seen within 1 minute using electrocardiography.12
paragraphs.heading: Delayed Transition and Need for Respiratory Support

paragraphs.text: • The key sign of an infant’s condition in the minutes after
paragraphs.heading: Delayed Transition and Need for Respiratory Support

paragraphs.text: birth, and response during stabilization, is the heart rate. • An infant who has good tone is unlikely to be severely
paragraphs.heading: Delayed Transition and Need for Respiratory Support

paragraphs.text: hypoxic.
paragraphs.heading: Delayed Transition and Need for Respiratory Support

paragraphs.text: When an infant fails to establish spontaneous breathing after birth, the caregiver must commence positive pressure support. Typically, this is initially applied using a face mask and a pressure-generating device. If the infant is breathing irregularly or with difficulty, continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) may aid inflation of the lungs and establishment of FRC. CPAP helps to establish and maintain end expiratory lung volume, reduce alveolar collapse, and decrease the work of breathing. It aids lung expansion and helps to conserve surfactant. CPAP also improves oxygenation, lung compliance, and ventilation-perfusion mismatch.13 However, an infant who has no respiratory effort, or who is bradycardic, will require positive pressure ventilation (PPV). Ideally, PPV should be given along with positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), although not all resuscitation devices are capable of delivering PEEP
paragraphs.heading: Basics of Positive Pressure Support

paragraphs.text: (Table 31.1). Studies in intubated preterm animals have demonstrated that the addition of PEEP to PPV results in more rapid acquisition of FRC, improved oxygenation and lung compliance, and decreased lung injury.14 PEEP is recommended for the resuscitation of preterm infants,1 although clinical trials have failed to show a significant difference in the proportion of infants requiring intubation in the delivery room15 or in SpO2 at 5 minutes of age16 when PEEP was added. Use of PEEP during stabilization of preterm infants in the delivery room in major units in the United Kingdom and Canada was higher than 75% 10 years ago17,18 and is currently reported to be 90% to 99% in Australia, New Zealand,19 and Italy.20
paragraphs.heading: Basics of Positive Pressure Support

paragraphs.text: Endotracheal intubation should be considered for infants who have an ongoing need for PPV and those who remain bradycardic and/or hypoxic despite adequate mask PPV. The management of preterm infants who require
paragraphs.heading: Basics of Positive Pressure Support

paragraphs.text: ongoing respiratory support has evolved over the past decade, moving away from immediate intubation and surfactant administration toward continuing CPAP support with either rescue intubation and surfactant treatment if certain criteria are met, or rescue surfactant administration with ongoing noninvasive respiratory support, without endotracheal intubation.21 Meta-analysis of trials that assessed immediate intubation versus initial CPAP found a reduction in the combined outcome of death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) in the CPAP group, without any difference in pneumothorax risk.22 Both strategies may be appropriate; however, international guidelines currently recommend initial CPAP for spontaneously breathing preterm infants with respiratory distress, rather than routine intubation.23 As a gentler approach to early respiratory support has become more popular, more preterm infants are likely to be supported by CPAP in the delivery room.
paragraphs.heading: Basics of Positive Pressure Support

paragraphs.text: Various devices are available for generating positive pressure in the delivery room. The choice of device may be made based on availability of a gas supply, the skills of the resuscitator, the desire to deliver PEEP and CPAP, and local preferences. A 2010 European survey reported that centers typically use more than one device. At the time, selfinflating bags (SIBs) were most commonly used (85%),24 whereas a 2015 Japanese survey reported flow-inflating bags (FIBs) to be most commonly used (63%),25 and a 2019 Australian/New Zealand survey reported the T-piece to be most frequently used (92%).19
paragraphs.heading: How to Generate Positive Pressure

paragraphs.text: SIBs (Fig. 31.4A and B) re-expand after compression. These are the only devices that can be used without a gas supply; they have been shown to be an effective method for reducing mortality from birth asphyxia in resource-limited areas.26 Their use is an integral part of the international Helping Babies Breathe program.27
paragraphs.heading: Self-Inflating Bags

paragraphs.text: Several types and sizes of SIBs exist. The smallest sizes, approximately 240 mL, are most appropriate for newborns. The peak pressure delivered by an SIB depends on how hard and fast the bag is squeezed. SIBs usually incorporate a valve, which limits the maximum deliverable pressure. The valve can be manually overridden to deliver higher pressures
paragraphs.heading: Self-Inflating Bags

paragraphs.text: but can be inadvertently overridden if the SIB is squeezed hard and fast. Pressures greater than 100 cm H2O have been reported, resulting in very high delivered volumes, greater than 20 mL/kg. The more fingers that are used to squeeze the bag, the more pressure is generated28; for most resuscitations, a gentle squeeze with a finger and thumb is all that is required. Many studies, including Bassani et al., have shown that it is difficult to deliver consistent peak pressures when using an SIB, particularly if an operator is inexperienced.29 Manometers attached to the SIB help to improve the consistency of peak pressure delivery,30 and newer “upright” designs of SIB have been shown to provide more consistent volume and pressure delivery,31 even with novice operators.32 If a PEEP valve is attached to an SIB, some PEEP can be delivered. However, it is difficult to achieve the desired PEEP, and delivered PEEP is dependent on the inflation rate.33 PEEP levels decay quickly between inflations,34 although newer valve models are better.35 Different brands of SIB have different capacities to deliver inflations of differing duration36; closing the pressure relief valve can increase the ability to lengthen inflation duration.37 It is not possible to deliver CPAP using an SIB; therefore it may not be the optimal device for stabilizing preterm infants.
paragraphs.heading: Self-Inflating Bags

paragraphs.text: An FIB needs a continuous gas supply, something which may not always be readily available. The delivered pressure and tidal volume depend on how hard the bag is squeezed. A pressure-limiting valve can be attached to prevent high pressure being inadvertently delivered. PEEP can be delivered
paragraphs.heading: Flow-Inflating Bags

paragraphs.text: with an FIB by manually controlling the rate of gas escaping from the back of the bag during expiration. This technique requires experience because it can inadvertently lead to dangerously high PEEP. It is difficult to consistently deliver both the desired PEEP and peak pressures with an FIB,38,39 and many operators find the FIB more difficult to use than the SIB. Prolonged inflations can be delivered by a skilled operator, but the pressure achieved is more variable than that delivered using a T-piece.40 It is very difficult to deliver CPAP with an FIB.
paragraphs.heading: Flow-Inflating Bags

paragraphs.text: T-piece devices (see Fig. 31.4C) also require a continuous gas supply, again something that may not be available in resource-limited settings. The gas flow and an internal valve generate the set peak pressure and set PEEP. The peak pressure is achieved by occluding the hole in the top/side of the T-piece with a finger. When the hole is open, PEEP or CPAP is delivered. Inflation time depends on how long the hole is occluded.
paragraphs.heading: T-Piece Devices

paragraphs.text: T-pieces are easy to use and are preferred by both experienced and inexperienced operators.41 In manikin studies, the T-piece device delivers peak and PEEP pressures more accurately and consistently than other devices, resulting in more stable tidal volume delivery,42 even with inexperienced operators.29
paragraphs.heading: T-Piece Devices

paragraphs.text: Although face mask leak is common during PPV, leak has less detrimental effect on pressure and volume delivery when using a T-piece, compared with an SIB.43 Randomized studies of infants requiring PPV at birth have shown less need for intubation,44,45 less supplemental oxygen, and shorter duration of PPV when using a T-piece compared with an SIB,45 but no difference in proportion of infants with heart rate greater than 100 bpm at 2 minutes of life44 or other longer-term outcomes.
paragraphs.heading: T-Piece Devices

paragraphs.text: Occlusion of the hole on the T-piece allows delivery of a consistent, sustained inflation of any duration or pressure.40 Likewise, the T-piece is capable of delivering consistent CPAP42 and therefore may be the optimal device for
paragraphs.heading: T-Piece Devices

paragraphs.text: providing respiratory support for preterm infants at birth.41 However, care needs to be taken if gas flow is increased during T-piece PPV, because increased flow increases the delivered pressures, particularly PEEP.46 In addition, as set PEEP is increased in some T-piece systems, the resistance and imposed work of breathing can increase.47 Recent work using a test lung suggests that during PPV, some T-pieces inadvertently deliver PEEP (and in some cases peak inspiratory pressure) levels well above those set by the clinician.48
paragraphs.heading: T-Piece Devices

paragraphs.text: Positive pressure support can be delivered using a neonatal ventilator; this delivers accurate peak and PEEP pressures and may allow both synchronization of inflations with the infant’s own efforts, and tidal volume measurement.49 CPAP can also be continuously delivered through a ventilator. Other methods of providing noninvasive CPAP support in the delivery room have been used, although they do not include the capacity to deliver PPV. These methods include nasal high-flow support,50,51 and CPAP generated using a Benveniste gas-jet valve that uses the Venturi effect to entrain and pressurize gas. Delivered pressure is not monitored with either device, and there are no blow-off valves or alarms to avoid delivery of excessive pressure.
paragraphs.heading: Other Options for Providing Positive Pressure

paragraphs.text: In the resource-limited setting, no devices may be available to generate positive pressure support, so mouth-tomask52 and mouth-to-tube53 ventilation may be used. Both are preferable to mouth-to-mouth resuscitation, but both still carry some risk of infection.
paragraphs.heading: Other Options for Providing Positive Pressure

paragraphs.text: In summary, there are advantages and pitfalls with all these devices (see Table 31.1). A systematic review of the topic identified four eligible randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Resuscitation with a T-piece resuscitator was associated with a reduced duration of PPV and reduced risk of BPD than an SIB.54 However, the authors concluded that the evidence was of low certainty, and therefore a strong recommendation could not be made. With the possible exception of a ventilator, no device provides information
paragraphs.heading: Other Options for Providing Positive Pressure

paragraphs.text: on perhaps the most important parameter—the tidal volume being delivered. Novel resuscitation devices and simple delivery room monitors that accurately measure and display delivered tidal volume are currently being developed and tested but are not in general clinical use. Whichever pressure delivery device is used, providers need to be trained in how to set up, use, and troubleshoot the equipment.
paragraphs.heading: Other Options for Providing Positive Pressure

paragraphs.text: Positive pressure may be delivered via face mask, nasal tube, nasal mask, nasal cannulae, laryngeal masks, and endotracheal tubes (ETTs).
paragraphs.heading: Choosing an Interface to Deliver Positive Pressure

paragraphs.text: Use of a face mask requires a good seal between the mask and the infant’s face,55 but this is difficult to achieve and maintain; leak and pressure loss leading to reduced tidal volume delivery are common. Round, cushion-rimmed masks are used more commonly than anatomically shaped, triangular masks,56 and there is conflicting evidence as to whether leak is greater with one type or the other. Newer masks being tested may help to overcome this.57,58 However, it is clear that mask leak is common in the delivery room and is frequently large and troublesome.59
paragraphs.heading: Face Masks

paragraphs.text: A face mask should seal around the mouth and nose but not cover the eyes or overlap the chin. Several makes and sizes of round face masks are available, but many commonly used brands may be too large for very preterm infants.60 Accurate positioning and mask hold are required to minimize mask leak. An accurate position can be obtained when the correctly sized mask is rolled upward onto the face from a finger placed on the chin tip
paragraphs.heading: Face Masks

paragraphs.text: (Fig. 31.5); this technique reduces leak.61 The optimal hold for a mask varies with the brand of mask being used; for example, two commonly used brands are shown to have similar leak in the delivery room.62 With the Laerdal mask (Laerdal Medical, Stavanger, Norway), equal pressure should be applied to either side of the top flat portion of the mask, with the thumb and index finger where the silicone is thickest around the stem, to obtain the best seal (Fig. 31.6A).61 The operator’s fingers should not encroach onto the “skirt” of the mask, because this distorts the rim, causing kinking and gas leakage.63 In contrast, when using the Fisher & Paykel round masks (Fisher & Paykel Healthcare, Auckland, New Zealand), the thumb and index finger should form a “C” shape (as in the “OK” hand gesture) placed around the top flat portion of the mask, applying an even distribution of pressure to the outer edge of the mask to provide the best seal (see Fig. 31.6B).61 Initial education and regular retraining are important for the maintenance of this important skill.61
paragraphs.heading: Face Masks

paragraphs.text: Typically, operators using a T-piece and face mask with a neonatal manikin have 40% to 60% mask leak, although this can be reduced with training61 and by using a two-handed mask hold technique.64 Despite large and variable mask leaks, the desired pressure may still be achieved.43 Unfortunately, neither the delivered pressure nor the amount of chest rise seen correlates well with the delivered tidal volume.65 Variable leaks may result in some tidal volumes that are too low and others that are dangerously large.59,66 Concern over large face mask leak may lead the provider to apply excessive pressure to the mask67 and therefore to the face and head of the infant.68 This pressure may obstruct the airway69 by distorting the nose and altering the position of the mouth and chin; obstruction occurs in 25% to 75% of preterm mask resuscitations.69,70 Although inefficient mask ventilation may not achieve adequate pressure and tidal volume, there may still be some benefit because of stimulation of Head’s paradoxical reflex. This reflex generates a large inspiratory effort in response to a small inflation. The response may assist with the first effective inspiratory volume during newborn transition, even if mask ventilation fails to adequately inflate the lungs.
paragraphs.heading: Face Masks

paragraphs.text: Alternative interfaces include a single nasal tube (Fig. 31.7A), binasal prongs, nasal masks, and nasal cannulae. To ensure minimal leak when the nasal route is used, it may be necessary to close the mouth, and when a single nasal tube
paragraphs.heading: Single Nasal Tube and Binasal Prongs

paragraphs.text: is used, it may also be necessary to occlude the contralateral nostril.
paragraphs.heading: Single Nasal Tube and Binasal Prongs

paragraphs.text: An RCT comparing a single nasal tube with a round cushion-rimmed face mask showed no difference in measures of effectiveness of resuscitation of preterm infants, including intubation in the delivery room, or in short- or long-term respiratory outcomes.71 The authors subsequently reported more leak and obstruction with the nasal prong and less overall tidal volume delivery.72 Therefore a nasal tube may be a useful alternative to a face mask, but there is no evidence for its superiority. Retrospective reports exist of delivery room CPAP application via nasal cannulae73 (e.g., with RAM cannulae); however, higher pressures are required to achieve lung inflation with this device,74 and no randomized data regarding efficacy exist. Nasal cannulae have also been used to deliver high-flow support to stabilize preterm infants in the delivery room; one randomized trial in infants 28 to 34 weeks’ gestation did not demonstrate any short-term differences between high flow and CPAP.50
paragraphs.heading: Single Nasal Tube and Binasal Prongs

paragraphs.text: It is important to be able to accurately assess whether the support being given is effective. However, clinical assessments of color change10 and heart rate9 are imprecise and
paragraphs.heading: Assessing the Effectiveness of Noninvasive Positive Pressure Ventilation

paragraphs.text: inaccurate. Pulse oximeters provide rapid, continuous, accurate displays of heart rate and oxygenation and are now recommended for use in babies requiring assistance in the delivery room. In addition, clinicians are poor at assessing mask leak, chest rise, and delivered tidal volume.65 A respiratory function monitor can assist with assessment of leak and adequate tidal volume delivery.71,75 O’Currain et al. conducted an RCT which demonstrated that the use of a respiratory function monitor during newborn resuscitation training improved tidal volume delivery and reduced leak.76 A systematic review identified three RCTs evaluating the use of respiratory function monitors in the delivery room.77 Pooled analysis showed no effect on mortality but a significant reduction in rates of intraventricular hemorrhage in infants managed with a respiratory function monitor.
paragraphs.heading: Assessing the Effectiveness of Noninvasive Positive Pressure Ventilation

paragraphs.text: A colorimetric carbon dioxide (CO2) detector or quantitative end-tidal carbon dioxide monitor may help to determine whether there is gas exchange occurring during mask ventilation,78 but neither has been shown to improve short-term clinical outcomes.79 Most recently, cerebral oxygenation using near-infrared spectroscopy has been used in the delivery room to give additional information on the effectiveness of resuscitation.80 Normal values have been ascertained,81 but targeting cerebral oxygenation levels has not been shown to alter short-term outcomes in preterm infants.82
paragraphs.heading: Assessing the Effectiveness of Noninvasive Positive Pressure Ventilation

paragraphs.text: Laryngeal mask airways are supraglottic airways (SGAs) commonly used during anesthesia. SGAs consist of a soft elliptical mask with an inflatable, or gel rim, and a flexible airway tube (see Fig. 31.7B and C). The mask is inserted into the infant’s mouth using the index finger, such that the mask covers the laryngeal opening and the rim conforms to the contours of the hypopharynx, occluding the esophagus. The inflatable rim can be expanded via a small balloon. The airway tube can be attached to any resuscitation device. Various sizes and reusable and disposable versions are commercially available. An SGA may be helpful for infants with congenital anomalies involving the mouth, lip, palate, or other upper airway anomalies where endotracheal intubation is difficult. It may also be a useful technique where resources, training, and clinical experience are lacking. Almost all SGA insertions are successful at the first attempt and within 10 seconds.83 Several studies have assessed the effectiveness of PPV delivered by SGA in term and nearterm infants, and international guidelines now recommend that an SGA be used in these infants if mask ventilation is unsuccessful and endotracheal intubation is not possible.23 A large RCT conducted in Uganda enrolled infants requiring PPV and compared the use of SGA with face mask.84 There were no important differences in rates of mortality or neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission between the groups. Studies have assessed SGA use in more immature preterm infants for the delivery of surfactant, with promising results.85,86 However, there are currently no SGA devices small enough for infants less than 1500 g.
paragraphs.heading: Laryngeal Mask Airway

paragraphs.text: There are no absolute criteria for tracheal intubation after birth. Indications vary depending on gestational age, degree of respiratory effort, response to noninvasive ventilation, and the skill and experience of the resuscitator. International guidelines suggest intubation is considered at several stages: • if the heart rate is less than 100 bpm after 30 seconds of
paragraphs.heading: Endotracheal Tube

paragraphs.text: effective PPV,87 • if noninvasive ventilation does not increase the heart
paragraphs.heading: Endotracheal Tube

paragraphs.text: rate, or • if the infant continues to be apneic despite adequate
paragraphs.heading: Endotracheal Tube

paragraphs.text: ventilation. It is also recommended if mask ventilation is prolonged or ineffective or if there are congenital anomalies affecting transition. Infants without a detectable heartbeat and who are very hypotonic should be intubated and ventilated as soon as possible. For infants less than 29 weeks who are spontaneously breathing and who have respiratory distress requiring respiratory support in the delivery room, international guidelines now suggest initial use of CPAP in preference to routine intubation.23
paragraphs.heading: Endotracheal Tube

paragraphs.text: Neonatal intubation is a difficult skill to acquire and maintain. Fewer infants are now intubated, and skills are declining. Although experienced operators are successful more than 85% of the time, junior trainees are successful in less than half of attempts.88 Success can be increased by techniques such as use of videolaryngoscopy,89,90 but less experienced operators still take longer to perform intubations. Successful intubations frequently take longer than the recommended 30 seconds, and infants often become bradycardic and deteriorate during intubation attempts.88
paragraphs.heading: Endotracheal Tube

paragraphs.text: Nasal high-flow therapy has been used in older children and adults to facilitate safe intubation using a technique known as transnasal humidified rapid insufflation ventilatory exchange (THRIVE).91 When applied to neonates in both the delivery room and NICU, this technique improved the likelihood of successful intubation on the first attempt without physiologic instability.92 By providing more time before the infant’s saturations decrease to unacceptable levels, this technique appears to be most beneficial when junior trainees are attempting intubation.
paragraphs.heading: Endotracheal Tube

paragraphs.text: Neonatal ETTs are uncuffed and usually straight. Some providers use a stylet inside the ETT, although there is no evidence that this reduces the duration or improves the rate of successful intubation.93
paragraphs.heading: Endotracheal Tube

paragraphs.text: Prior to endotracheal intubation, all necessary equipment should be assembled, a team and team leader identified, their roles delineated, and an escalation plan made for the possibility of intubation not initially being successful. The suggested items are outlined in Box 31.1. The infant should be placed supine in a “sniffing position” (Fig. 31.8A), avoiding both flexion and hyperextension of the neck, which make the glottis hard to visualize. The tip of the laryngoscope blade should be advanced over the tongue to the vallecula, or over the top of the epiglottis, and elevated gently
paragraphs.heading: Intubation Procedure

paragraphs.text: to reveal the vocal cords (see Fig. 31.8B). The laryngoscope should support the tongue toward the left side of the mouth to have adequate space to see the larynx and pass the ETT. If the laryngoscope blade is advanced too far, the tip will be in the lower pharynx and the larynx will not be visible. Gentle cricoid pressure may be helpful in bringing the larynx into view.
paragraphs.heading: Intubation Procedure

paragraphs.text: The ETT should be inserted to the level of the tube marker, so that it is visible just above the larynx (Fig. 31.9). The ETT should be secured with the appropriate centimeter side mark located at the upper lip (Table 31.2). This level is estimated as 6.0 cm plus the infant’s weight in kilograms. If a stylet is used to assist with ETT insertion, care must be taken not to allow the stylet to protrude beyond the tip of the ETT and damage the trachea. When removing a stylet from a correctly placed ETT, care must be taken not to dislodge the tube. If a nasal intubation is being performed, McGill forceps may be required to advance the ETT through the vocal cords.
paragraphs.heading: Intubation Procedure

paragraphs.text: The position of the ETT in the trachea must always be verified. The best clinical indicator of correct placement is a prompt increase in heart rate. Correct positioning can be verified by visualizing the tube passing through the vocal cords, listening to both axillae with a stethoscope, observing misting inside the ETT during expiration, and observing chest movements during inflations. However, none of these methods are absolute confirmation. Use of an end-tidal CO2 detector on the ETT connector is currently recommended to verify correct tube placement quickly.87 Colorimetric CO2 detectors can rapidly demonstrate CO2 in the expired ETT gas more quickly than changes in heart rate and oxygen saturations are seen.94 However, they can give a false-negative result when very
paragraphs.heading: Intubation Procedure

paragraphs.text: low tidal volumes are being delivered95 and false-positive results when contaminated by adrenaline or surfactant.96 Respiratory function monitors can provide a quicker indication of correct ETT placement than clinical assessment and expired CO2 detectors.97 When insertion is verified, correct depth of ETT insertion should be assessed by checking the measurement on the tube at the lips, by assessing symmetric chest movement, and with chest radiography.
paragraphs.heading: Intubation Procedure

paragraphs.text: When delivering PPV, the clinician aims to provide effective ventilation for adequate gas exchange, without causing lung injury. It has been well documented that lung injury can be caused by lung overdistention (volutrauma),98 excessive pressure (barotrauma), and repeated alveolar collapse and re-expansion (atelectrauma). Studies in preterm animals have shown that lung injury can occur within the first few positive pressure inflations, resulting in an inflammatory response within a few minutes.99 Therefore knowledge about the causes and prevention of lung injury during ventilation of preterm infants should be applied from birth. Actions to prevent lung injury include facilitating formation and maintenance of FRC, avoiding large tidal volumes that can easily and inadvertently be delivered with currently available resuscitation equipment,66 and avoiding repeated lung collapse and re-expansion.
paragraphs.heading: Applying Positive Pressure Support

paragraphs.text: Very premature infants are especially vulnerable to the interventions applied in the first minutes after birth.100 Therefore, as most preterm infants spontaneously breathe soon after birth, they may manage with CPAP alone, which is likely to cause less lung damage than routinely intubating them and applying PPV.101 For infants who do not breathe or who require more than CPAP support, a gentle ventilatory strategy needs to be applied.
paragraphs.heading: Applying Positive Pressure Support

paragraphs.text: The long initial inspirations, followed by prolonged expirations through a partially closed glottis that are seen in spontaneously breathing infants at birth, led researchers to question whether longer initial positive pressure inflations would be beneficial in infants without adequate spontaneous breathing. In anesthetized, intubated, preterm animal models, sustained inflation at modest pressure leads to rapid lung aeration without overexpansion, immediate development of appropriate FRC, and uniformly aerated lungs102 without serious side effects.103 Alternative strategies such as serial increases in applied PEEP may also have similar benefits.104
paragraphs.heading: The First Breaths

paragraphs.text: The optimal pressure and duration of a sustained inflation in preterm infants are unknown, and the effects of variable face mask leak, intermittent spontaneous breathing, and potential closure of the glottis make the standardization of applying a sustained inflation difficult. The Sustained Aeration for Infant Lungs (SAIL) trial did not reduce the combined primary outcome of death or BPD. Rates of early mortality were higher in the sustained inflation arm, leading to the early closure of the trial.105 Systematic review of the topic identified nine studies including 1406 infants. Pooled analysis was consistent with the findings of the SAIL trial, with no effect on death or BPD and higher early mortality in infants managed with sustained inflation.106 The International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation (ILCOR) currently suggests against the routine use of sustained inflation and to limit its use to randomized clinical trials.1
paragraphs.heading: The First Breaths

paragraphs.text: Tidal volumes are not usually measured in the delivery room; therefore clinicians must use peak pressure and clinical judgment of chest rise as a proxy for volume delivery. Neither of these provides reliable guidance regarding volume delivery.59,107 However, they remain the most practical methods of targeting delivered volume given the equipment currently available. The actual delivered volume depends on multiple factors—the infant’s spontaneous breathing effort, lung compliance, mask leak, obstruction at the mouth and nose, and the resuscitation device used. This means that tidal volumes delivered during PPV are variable and usually much higher than those generated during spontaneous breathing.108 Animal studies have shown that high tidal volumes given soon after birth result in reduced oxygenation, increased need for ventilatory support, and instability of cerebral blood flow that increases the risk of brain injury.109 The ideal target volumes for ventilation of term and preterm infants remain uncertain. Avoidance of tidal volumes greater than 8 mL/kg appears reasonable.110 Development and testing of inexpensive, reliable, and accurate techniques to measure and display tidal volume is an important priority in neonatal resuscitation.
paragraphs.heading: Peak Inflation Pressures and Tidal Volumes

paragraphs.text: In the absence of tidal volume monitoring devices, clinicians rely on set peak pressure and clinical signs to deliver safe and effective ventilation. Typically, pressures in the range of 20 to 30 cm H2O are suggested as initial settings87,111 and have been shown to produce reasonable tidal volumes. Infants who make no respiratory effort may require higher pressures initially. As the lungs aerate and become more compliant, pressure may need to be reduced.112 A rising heart rate is a good sign that effective ventilation is being delivered.87
paragraphs.heading: Peak Inflation Pressures and Tidal Volumes

paragraphs.text: The lungs of preterm infants are immature, surfactant deficient, partially liquid filled, and prone to collapse at end expiration. PEEP provides many beneficial effects (Box 31.2).
paragraphs.heading: Positive End-Expiratory Pressure

paragraphs.text: PEEP protects against lung injury and distal airway collapse at end expiration, while improving lung compliance, oxygenation, and accumulation of FRC. Whether or not an initial sustained inflation is given, animal studies have shown that without PEEP, no FRC is established14 or maintained.102 After an inflation without PEEP, lung volume is lost, airways collapse, and the infant becomes at risk of atelectrauma during subsequent inflations.113
paragraphs.heading: Positive End-Expiratory Pressure

paragraphs.text: There are few randomized studies in premature infants examining the use of PEEP at birth. Those that have been published failed to show a significant benefit over PPV without PEEP in terms of short-term respiratory outcomes.15,16
paragraphs.heading: Positive End-Expiratory Pressure

paragraphs.text: Key Points
paragraphs.heading: Positive End-Expiratory Pressure

paragraphs.text: • Most full-term and late preterm infants breathe at birth
paragraphs.heading: Positive End-Expiratory Pressure

paragraphs.text: and need no assistance to transition to extrauterine life. • Infants who do not establish regular respiration require
paragraphs.heading: Positive End-Expiratory Pressure

paragraphs.text: prompt respiratory support. • Effective mask ventilation should result in a rapid
paragraphs.heading: Positive End-Expiratory Pressure

paragraphs.text: increase in heart rate.
paragraphs.heading: Positive End-Expiratory Pressure

paragraphs.text: International guidelines suggest that PEEP is likely to be beneficial during positive pressure support of preterm infants and that if it is available, it should be used.87
paragraphs.heading: References

paragraphs.text: It is not possible to predict a single optimal PEEP level for all infants; however, infants with the highest oxygen requirements usually have the smallest FRC and may benefit from higher PEEP. Guidelines currently suggest the use of PEEP of 5 cm H2O in the delivery room.1 Trials of different levels of PEEP during resuscitation of human infants at birth are underway.
paragraphs.heading: References

paragraphs.text: There is little evidence on which to base the optimal inflation rate. Rates of 40 to 60 per minute are recommended and match the typical respiratory rates of healthy newborns. In an infant who has some respiratory effort, it is likely that manual inflations will sometimes be asynchronous with spontaneous breaths. This may lead to ineffective resuscitation, inadvertent high pressures, and increased risk of injury such as pneumothorax.114 The duration of each inflation may, following the initial inflations, be best timed to reflect spontaneous inspiratory times of newborn infants to last approximately 0.3 seconds.
paragraphs.heading: Inflation Rate and Duration

paragraphs.text: It is rarely necessary to change the gas flow to greater than the standard 8 to 10 L/min during a resuscitation. Alteration of gas flow may not affect pressure or volume delivery when using an SIB or FIB. Increasing gas flow to greater than recommended rates during T-piece ventilation increases leak; it also increases the PEEP without increasing the peak pressure, resulting in lower delivered tidal volumes.46,115

31 Role of Positive Pressure Ventilation in Neonatal Resuscitation

### LOUISE S. OWEN AND PETER G. DAVIS

Newborn babies who do not spontaneously breathe at birth require support to safely make the transition to extrauterine life. Over the past 20 years, guidelines for those providing care to these infants have been developed.1 However, the evidence available to guide initial respiratory support remains limited, reflecting the challenges associated with conducting research in the delivery room.

The crucial steps in the adaption to extrauterine life involve the transition from liquid-filled to air-filled lungs, and the establishment of functional residual capacity (FRC). These changes normally occur in the first minutes after birth and include an increase in pulmonary blood flow and the onset of regular respiration. Lung aeration and the development of an FRC facilitate gas exchange. Deferring cord clamping until these are achieved ensures a smooth transition to extrauterine life. If an infant does not quickly establish effective respiration, assistance is immediately required. Typically, this is a brief need for basic respiratory support only,2 unless there is abnormal anatomy or significant fetal acidemia or ineffective respiratory support is provided. Preterm infants have additional requirements at birth; although most preterm infants breathe and cry,3 very preterm infants are still likely to need support to effectively establish and maintain FRC. Preterm lungs are delicate, and lung injury can occur with just a few high-volume positive pressure inflations.4 This has led to a shift in emphasis in preterm stabilization toward a gentle, supportive approach to augment rather than override their efforts, and to minimize lung injury.

### Normal Transition and Initial Spontaneous Breathing

In healthy, newborn, term infants, normal transition is characterized by repeated, short, deep inspirations, each followed by a prolonged expiratory phase through a partially

closed glottis (crying). The inspiratory efforts generate large negative transpulmonary pressures, typically −50 cm H2O to −100 cm H2O, such that the high-resistance liquid filling the infant’s airways is driven distally, moving the air-liquid interface toward the distal airways.

Detailed imaging of rabbit lungs demonstrates that initial lung aeration depends on the generation of this transpulmonary pressure, with consequent stepwise increases in FRC over three to five repeated inspiratory efforts. More volume is inspired than expired with each breath, which overcomes small losses in FRC between inspiratory efforts as lung liquid moves back into the airways.5 The lung liquid then moves into the interstitial tissue and is cleared over the following hours.

Prolonged expiration through a partially closed glottis, with simultaneous abdominal muscle contraction pressurizes the chest, further pushing the air-liquid interface distally; this is called expiratory braking (Fig. 31.1). Flow recordings of the first breaths in preterm infants have shown that they use crying and expiratory braking to facilitate lung recruitment and development of FRC (Fig. 31.2).6 These observations have been supported by electrical impedance tomography (EIT) recordings, which demonstrate that newborn infants generate unique flow and volume patterns during this process (Fig. 31.3).7

### Delayed Transition and Need for Respiratory Support

Some infants do not breathe or have ineffective breathing at birth. Guidelines recommend initial steps of stimulating, drying, and wrapping the baby, followed by clamping the cord and then opening, and in some cases clearing, the airway.1 They stipulate that positive pressure support should be commenced by 60 seconds of age if the baby remains apneic, has irregular or gasping respirations, or has a heart rate less

### Basics of Positive Pressure Support

When an infant fails to establish spontaneous breathing after birth, the caregiver must commence positive pressure support. Typically, this is initially applied using a face mask and a pressure-generating device. If the infant is breathing irregularly or with difficulty, continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) may aid inflation of the lungs and establishment of FRC. CPAP helps to establish and maintain end expiratory lung volume, reduce alveolar collapse, and decrease the work of breathing. It aids lung expansion and helps to conserve surfactant. CPAP also improves oxygenation, lung compliance, and ventilation-perfusion mismatch.13 However, an infant who has no respiratory effort, or who is bradycardic, will require positive pressure ventilation (PPV). Ideally, PPV should be given along with positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), although not all resuscitation devices are capable of delivering PEEP

### Application of Noninvasive Positive Pressure Support

### How to Generate Positive Pressure

Various devices are available for generating positive pressure in the delivery room. The choice of device may be made based on availability of a gas supply, the skills of the resuscitator, the desire to deliver PEEP and CPAP, and local preferences. A 2010 European survey reported that centers typically use more than one device. At the time, selfinflating bags (SIBs) were most commonly used (85%),24 whereas a 2015 Japanese survey reported flow-inflating bags (FIBs) to be most commonly used (63%),25 and a 2019 Australian/New Zealand survey reported the T-piece to be most frequently used (92%).19

### Self-Inflating Bags

SIBs (Fig. 31.4A and B) re-expand after compression. These are the only devices that can be used without a gas supply; they have been shown to be an effective method for reducing mortality from birth asphyxia in resource-limited areas.26 Their use is an integral part of the international Helping Babies Breathe program.27

Several types and sizes of SIBs exist. The smallest sizes, approximately 240 mL, are most appropriate for newborns. The peak pressure delivered by an SIB depends on how hard and fast the bag is squeezed. SIBs usually incorporate a valve, which limits the maximum deliverable pressure. The valve can be manually overridden to deliver higher pressures

The more fingers that are used to squeeze the bag, the more pressure is generated28; for most resuscitations, a gentle squeeze with a finger and thumb is all that is required. Many studies, including Bassani et al., have shown that it is difficult to deliver consistent peak pressures when using an SIB, particularly if an operator is inexperienced.29 Manometers attached to the SIB help to improve the consistency of peak pressure delivery,30 and newer “upright” designs of SIB have been shown to provide more consistent volume and pressure delivery,31 even with novice operators.32 If a PEEP valve is attached to an SIB, some PEEP can be delivered. However, it is difficult to achieve the desired PEEP, and delivered PEEP is dependent on the inflation rate.33 PEEP levels decay quickly between inflations,34 although newer valve models are better.35 Different brands of SIB have different capacities to deliver inflations of differing duration36; closing the pressure relief valve can increase the ability to lengthen inflation duration.37 It is not possible to deliver CPAP using an SIB; therefore it may not be the optimal device for stabilizing preterm infants.

### T-Piece Devices

T-piece devices (see Fig. 31.4C) also require a continuous gas supply, again something that may not be available in resource-limited settings. The gas flow and an internal valve generate the set peak pressure and set PEEP. The peak pressure is achieved by occluding the hole in the top/side of the T-piece with a finger. When the hole is open, PEEP or CPAP is delivered. Inflation time depends on how long the hole is occluded.

T-pieces are easy to use and are preferred by both experienced and inexperienced operators.41 In manikin studies, the T-piece device delivers peak and PEEP pressures more accurately and consistently than other devices, resulting in more stable tidal volume delivery,42 even with inexperienced operators.29

Although face mask leak is common during PPV, leak has less detrimental effect on pressure and volume delivery when using a T-piece, compared with an SIB.43 Randomized studies of infants requiring PPV at birth have shown less need for intubation,44,45 less supplemental oxygen, and shorter duration of PPV when using a T-piece compared with an SIB,45 but no difference in proportion of infants with heart rate greater than 100 bpm at 2 minutes of life44 or other longer-term outcomes.

Occlusion of the hole on the T-piece allows delivery of a consistent, sustained inflation of any duration or pressure.40 Likewise, the T-piece is capable of delivering consistent CPAP42 and therefore may be the optimal device for

Cproviding respiratory support for preterm infants at birth.41 However, care needs to be taken if gas flow is increased during T-piece PPV, because increased flow increases the delivered pressures, particularly PEEP.46 In addition, as set PEEP is increased in some T-piece systems, the resistance and imposed work of breathing can increase.47 Recent work using a test lung suggests that during PPV, some T-pieces inadvertently deliver PEEP (and in some cases peak inspiratory pressure) levels well above those set by the clinician.48

### Other Options for Providing Positive Pressure

Positive pressure support can be delivered using a neonatal ventilator; this delivers accurate peak and PEEP pressures and may allow both synchronization of inflations with the infant’s own efforts, and tidal volume measurement.49 CPAP can also be continuously delivered through a ventilator. Other methods of providing noninvasive CPAP support in the delivery room have been used, although they do not include the capacity to deliver PPV. These methods include nasal high-flow support,50,51 and CPAP generated using a Benveniste gas-jet valve that uses the Venturi effect to entrain and pressurize gas. Delivered pressure is not monitored with either device, and there are no blow-off valves or alarms to avoid delivery of excessive pressure.

In the resource-limited setting, no devices may be available to generate positive pressure support, so mouth-tomask52 and mouth-to-tube53 ventilation may be used. Both are preferable to mouth-to-mouth resuscitation, but both still carry some risk of infection.

In summary, there are advantages and pitfalls with all these devices (see Table 31.1). A systematic review of the topic identified four eligible randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Resuscitation with a T-piece resuscitator was associated with a reduced duration of PPV and reduced risk of BPD than an SIB.54 However, the authors concluded that the evidence was of low certainty, and therefore a strong recommendation could not be made. ### Choosing an Interface to Deliver Positive Pressure

Positive pressure may be delivered via face mask, nasal tube, nasal mask, nasal cannulae, laryngeal masks, and endotracheal tubes (ETTs).

### Face Masks

Use of a face mask requires a good seal between the mask and the infant’s face,55 but this is difficult to achieve and maintain; leak and pressure loss leading to reduced tidal volume delivery are common. Round, cushion-rimmed masks are used more commonly than anatomically shaped, triangular masks,56 and there is conflicting evidence as to whether leak is greater with one type or the other. Newer masks being tested may help to overcome this.57,58 However, it is clear that mask leak is common in the delivery room and is frequently large and troublesome.59

A face mask should seal around the mouth and nose but not cover the eyes or overlap the chin. Several makes and sizes of round face masks are available, but many commonly used brands may be too large for very preterm infants.60 Accurate positioning and mask hold are required to minimize mask leak. An accurate position can be obtained when the correctly sized mask is rolled upward onto the face from a finger placed on the chin tip

D C

(Fig. 31.5); this technique reduces leak.61 The optimal hold for a mask varies with the brand of mask being used; for example, two commonly used brands are shown to have similar leak in the delivery room.62 With the Laerdal mask (Laerdal Medical, Stavanger, Norway), equal pressure should be applied to either side of the top flat portion of the mask, with the thumb and index finger where the silicone is thickest around the stem, to obtain the best seal (Fig. 31.6A).61 The operator’s fingers should not encroach onto the “skirt” of the mask, because this distorts the rim, causing kinking and gas leakage.63 In contrast, when using the Fisher & Paykel round masks (Fisher & Paykel Healthcare, Auckland, New Zealand), the thumb and index finger should form a “C” shape (as in the “OK” hand gesture) placed around the top flat portion of the mask, applying an even distribution of pressure to the outer edge of the mask to provide the best seal (see Fig. 31.6B).61 Initial education and regular retraining are important for the maintenance of this important skill.61

Typically, operators using a T-piece and face mask with a neonatal manikin have 40% to 60% mask leak, although this can be reduced with training61 and by using a two-handed mask hold technique.64 Despite large and variable mask leaks, the desired pressure may still be achieved.43 Unfortunately, neither the delivered pressure nor the amount of chest rise seen correlates well with the delivered tidal volume.65 Variable leaks may result in some tidal volumes that are too low and others that are dangerously large.59,66 Concern over large face mask leak may lead the provider to apply excessive pressure to the mask67 and therefore to the face and head of the infant.68 This pressure may obstruct the airway69 by distorting the nose and altering the position of the mouth and chin; obstruction occurs in 25% to 75% of preterm mask resuscitations.69,70 Although inefficient mask ventilation may not achieve adequate pressure and tidal volume, there may still be some benefit because of stimulation of Head’s paradoxical reflex. This reflex generates a large inspiratory effort in response to a small inflation. The response may assist with the first effective inspiratory volume during newborn transition, even if mask ventilation fails to adequately inflate the lungs.

### Assessing the Effectiveness of Noninvasive Positive Pressure Ventilation

It is important to be able to accurately assess whether the support being given is effective. However, clinical assessments of color change10 and heart rate9 are imprecise and

inaccurate. Pulse oximeters provide rapid, continuous, accurate displays of heart rate and oxygenation and are now recommended for use in babies requiring assistance in the delivery room. In addition, clinicians are poor at assessing mask leak, chest rise, and delivered tidal volume.65 A respiratory function monitor can assist with assessment of leak and adequate tidal volume delivery.71,75 O’Currain et al. conducted an RCT which demonstrated that the use of a respiratory function monitor during newborn resuscitation training improved tidal volume delivery and reduced leak.76 A systematic review identified three RCTs evaluating the use of respiratory function monitors in the delivery room.77 Pooled analysis showed no effect on mortality but a significant reduction in rates of intraventricular hemorrhage in infants managed with a respiratory function monitor.

A colorimetric carbon dioxide (CO2) detector or quantitative end-tidal carbon dioxide monitor may help to determine whether there is gas exchange occurring during mask ventilation,78 but neither has been shown to improve short-term clinical outcomes.79 Most recently, cerebral oxygenation using near-infrared spectroscopy has been used in the delivery room to give additional information on the effectiveness of resuscitation.80 Normal values have been ascertained,81 but targeting cerebral oxygenation levels has not been shown to alter short-term outcomes in preterm infants.82

### Laryngeal Mask Airway

Laryngeal mask airways are supraglottic airways (SGAs) commonly used during anesthesia. SGAs consist of a soft elliptical mask with an inflatable, or gel rim, and a flexible airway tube (see Fig. 31.7B and C). The mask is inserted into the infant’s mouth using the index finger, such that the mask covers the laryngeal opening and the rim conforms to the contours of the hypopharynx, occluding the esophagus. The inflatable rim can be expanded via a small balloon. The airway tube can be attached to any resuscitation device. Various sizes and reusable and disposable versions are commercially available. An SGA may be helpful for infants with congenital anomalies involving the mouth, lip, palate, or other upper airway anomalies where endotracheal intubation is difficult. It may also be a useful technique where resources, training, and clinical experience are lacking. Almost all SGA insertions are successful at the first attempt and within 10 seconds.83 Several studies have assessed the effectiveness of PPV delivered by SGA in term and nearterm infants, and international guidelines now recommend that an SGA be used in these infants if mask ventilation is unsuccessful and endotracheal intubation is not possible.23 A large RCT conducted in Uganda enrolled infants requiring PPV and compared the use of SGA with face mask.84 There were no important differences in rates of mortality or neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission between the groups. Studies have assessed SGA use in more immature preterm infants for the delivery of surfactant, with promising results.85,86 However, there are currently no SGA devices small enough for infants less than 1500 g.

### Endotracheal Tube

There are no absolute criteria for tracheal intubation after birth. Indications vary depending on gestational age, degree of respiratory effort, response to noninvasive ventilation, and the skill and experience of the resuscitator. International guidelines suggest intubation is considered at several stages: • if the heart rate is less than 100 bpm after 30 seconds of

effective PPV,87 • if noninvasive ventilation does not increase the heart

rate, or • if the infant continues to be apneic despite adequate

ventilation. It is also recommended if mask ventilation is prolonged or ineffective or if there are congenital anomalies affecting transition. Infants without a detectable heartbeat and who are very hypotonic should be intubated and ventilated as soon as possible. For infants less than 29 weeks who are spontaneously breathing and who have respiratory distress requiring respiratory support in the delivery room, international guidelines now suggest initial use of CPAP in preference to routine intubation.23

Neonatal intubation is a difficult skill to acquire and maintain. Fewer infants are now intubated, and skills are declining. Although experienced operators are successful more than 85% of the time, junior trainees are successful in less than half of attempts.88 Success can be increased by techniques such as use of videolaryngoscopy,89,90 but less experienced operators still take longer to perform intubations. Successful intubations frequently take longer than the recommended 30 seconds, and infants often become bradycardic and deteriorate during intubation attempts.88

Nasal high-flow therapy has been used in older children and adults to facilitate safe intubation using a technique known as transnasal humidified rapid insufflation ventilatory exchange (THRIVE).91 When applied to neonates in both the delivery room and NICU, this technique improved the likelihood of successful intubation on the first attempt without physiologic instability.92 By providing more time before the infant’s saturations decrease to unacceptable levels, this technique appears to be most beneficial when junior trainees are attempting intubation.

Neonatal ETTs are uncuffed and usually straight. Some providers use a stylet inside the ETT, although there is no evidence that this reduces the duration or improves the rate of successful intubation.93

### Intubation Procedure

Prior to endotracheal intubation, all necessary equipment should be assembled, a team and team leader identified, their roles delineated, and an escalation plan made for the possibility of intubation not initially being successful. The suggested items are outlined in Box 31.1. The infant should be placed supine in a “sniffing position” (Fig. 31.8A), avoiding both flexion and hyperextension of the neck, which make the glottis hard to visualize. The tip of the laryngoscope blade should be advanced over the tongue to the vallecula, or over the top of the epiglottis, and elevated gently

### Applying Positive Pressure Support

When delivering PPV, the clinician aims to provide effective ventilation for adequate gas exchange, without causing lung injury. It has been well documented that lung injury can be caused by lung overdistention (volutrauma),98 excessive pressure (barotrauma), and repeated alveolar collapse and re-expansion (atelectrauma). Studies in preterm animals have shown that lung injury can occur within the first few positive pressure inflations, resulting in an inflammatory response within a few minutes.99 Therefore knowledge about the causes and prevention of lung injury during ventilation of preterm infants should be applied from birth. Actions to prevent lung injury include facilitating formation and maintenance of FRC, avoiding large tidal volumes that can easily and inadvertently be delivered with currently available resuscitation equipment,66 and avoiding repeated lung collapse and re-expansion.
