title: Neonatal Cardiorespiratory Monitoring

paragraphs.text: 37 Neonatal Cardiorespiratory Monitoring
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Maintaining stable respiration and adequate oxygenation is a fundamental aspect of newborn care. This can be challenging in premature infants, as preterm birth is marked by immature respiratory control regions of the brain superimposed on an underdeveloped lung. As a result, preterm infants exhibit a high incidence of apnea, bradycardia, and intermittent hypoxemia events during early postnatal life.1,2 Pharmacotherapy and respiratory support (e.g., supplemental oxygen, continuous positive airway pressure [CPAP], and mechanical ventilation) are used to stabilize respiration and maintain adequate oxygenation, with a goal of decreasing duration and level of support to minimize the incidence of chronic lung disease and associated adverse respiratory and neurodevelopmental outcomes. These treatment decisions are most often based on medical chart documentation of apnea, heart rate, and desaturation alarms, making bedside cardiorespiratory monitoring an integral part of clinical care in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU).
paragraphs.heading: Summary

paragraphs.text: The challenges of cardiorespiratory monitoring in the NICU include continuous, accurate, artifact-free recordings obtained in a safe and noninvasive manner accounting for the small stature and fragile skin of the extremely low birth weight (ELBW) infant. Monitors and accompanying sensors are often developed for adult patients or older children, followed by application in newborns with minimal data demonstrating accuracy and safety. Nevertheless, even a well-designed monitor is only as good as the end user. Therefore a thorough understanding of individual monitor functionality is also needed to reduce both nuisance alarms and signal distortion of real events. This chapter includes a description of the principles of operation of cardiorespiratory monitoring modalities, including current and future directions of hemodynamic, blood gas, and respiratory waveform acquisition in the NICU setting.
paragraphs.heading: Summary

paragraphs.text: During each heartbeat, an electrical impulse originates in the sinoatrial node and is propagated among the muscles
paragraphs.heading: Electrocardiogram

paragraphs.text: of the atrium, through the atrioventricular node, followed by dispersion throughout the ventricles. The small alterations in voltage generated by the heart can be measured at the body surface with electrocardiogram (ECG) electrodes placed on the chest, the most common types being the silver-silver chloride, foil-based, recessed, or floating electrode. Each electrode contains a highly conductive electrolyte gel with a composition that varies by manufacturer. Electrode location is important in acquiring a signal of adequate resolution, especially in neonates with a limited surface area. Multiple probe applications should be avoided to optimize adhesiveness of the electrodes and ECG signal integrity and decrease the chance of skin damage, including high trans epidermal water losses,3 in extremely preterm infants with fragile skin. Under investigation are next-generation ultrathin epidermal electronic systems that provide wireless ECG measurements that only require water to adhere to the skin.4
paragraphs.heading: Electrocardiogram

paragraphs.text: The ability of traditional electrodes to detect small electrical changes with each heartbeat requires the application of a current to the chest wall. The recommendations of acceptable current limits by the American Heart Association (AHA) cover two aspects of electrical safety. The first entails the amount of current allowable in a patient-connected lead that can flow through the myocardium without inducing ventricular fibrillation. The second aspect pertains to the allowable chassis leakage current that flows through the patient to ground. The AHA recommends that currents be limited to 10 μA through patient leads and less than 100 μA, with an optimal level of 10 μA, for chassis leakage current.
paragraphs.heading: Electrocardiogram

paragraphs.text: The initial goal of simple heart rate measurements has expanded to include identification of specific arrhythmias and more complex algorithms of heart rate variability. Longitudinal regression-based models of abnormal heart rate characteristics associated with systemic infection and inflammation have been shown to reduce infant mortality in very low birth weight (VLBW) infants,5 leading to the development of the commercially available HeRO System, providing early warning of patient distress days before patient deterioration. Additional sophisticated mathematical analyses such as cross-correlation of heart rate and other vital signs,6 currently
paragraphs.heading: Electrocardiogram

paragraphs.text: limited to the research arena, may expand the ability to detect subtle high-risk alterations in heart rate variability, assisting in early interventions and improved patient outcomes such as late-onset sepsis and necrotizing enterocolitis.
paragraphs.heading: Electrocardiogram

paragraphs.text: Application of the Fick principle is considered the gold standard of cardiac output monitoring in a research setting. This method states
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac Output

paragraphs.text: CO = VO2/ (Ca −Cv)
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac Output

paragraphs.text: where VO2 = oxygen consumption, Ca = oxygen concentration of arterial blood, and Cv = oxygen concentration of mixed venous blood. Although the Fick principle may be accurate, especially in low flow states, precision may be limited by air leakage, cardiopulmonary disease, and enhanced pulmonary oxygen consumption.7
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac Output

paragraphs.text: Noninvasive methods that are validated in neonates include transcutaneous Doppler, transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), and thoracic electrical impedance. Doppler ultrasound uses an ultrasound beam to measure blood flow velocity. A velocity-time waveform is then produced from spectral analysis of Doppler shifts, caused by moving erythrocytes. The stroke distance can be calculated by the area under the velocity-time waveform. If the cross-sectional area of the vessel is known, cardiac output can be calculated by:
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac Output

paragraphs.text: Cardiac output
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac Output

paragraphs.text: = stroke distance × cross-sectional area of the vessel
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac Output

paragraphs.text: × heart rate
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac Output

paragraphs.text: Doppler-based cardiac output measurements can vary widely and should be limited to trend monitoring.7
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac Output

paragraphs.text: During TTE, measures of left ventricular output, right ventricular output, or superior vena cava (SVC) flow can be obtained. Validation data with TTE have been limited to transthoracic left ventricular output measures, which have been shown to be comparable with pulmonary artery thermodilution and O2-Fick methods.7 A variation of thoracic electrical impedance, electrical velocimetry, includes surface ECG electrodes placed on the forehead, left side of the neck, left mid-axillary line at the level of xiphoid process, and left thigh. During application of a small alternating electrical current through the thorax, changes in voltage are measured during periods of systole and diastole. Stroke volume (SV) is then determined using the following equation:
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac Output

paragraphs.text: SV = Vept × νLVET × LVET
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac Output

paragraphs.text: where Vept (mL) = volume of electrically participating tissue derived from body mass and height, νLVET (s−1) I = ohmic equivalent of mean aortic blood velocity during left ventricular ejection, and LVET (s) = left ventricular ejection time. Data have shown electrical velocimetry as a comparable mode of measuring left ventricular output in neonates when compared with echocardiography,8 although variation among individuals was seen using both techniques.
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac Output

paragraphs.text: Additional bedside TTE techniques have been reported in emerging literature on bedside evaluation of neonatal shock, including SVC flow and descending aortic flow.7 Doppler flow and SVC diameter measured at the entrance of the SVC into the right atrium reflects the blood returning from the brain and upper body, which may be a surrogate measure for cerebral blood flow.9 Various modifications of TTE calculations of SVC flow have been investigated, with high error percentage and considerable variation in reference ranges potentially limiting its clinical application.10 Doppler flow and diameter of the descending aorta when measured below the level of the ductus arteriosus would correspond with the systemic blood flow to the lower body, including the abdomen.9 Absence of end-diastolic flow or flow reversal may indicate a hemodynamically significant left-to-right shunt from a patent ductus arteriosus.11
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac Output

paragraphs.text: Direct continuous readings from an indwelling arterial line are considered the gold standard for blood pressure monitoring in the neonate. Arterial and potentially venous pressures are accessed by a catheter placed in the umbilical vessels and attached to a domed transducer. The transducer works on the principle that fluid exerts a force on the diaphragm. This force can be converted to a change in voltage and calibrated to a given pressure. The dome must be flushed, making sure there are no bubbles in the circuit; the transducer must be placed at the level of the distal tip of the catheter; and a zero pressure should be established before patient data are acquired. If the transducer is higher than the heart, readings will be erroneously low.
paragraphs.heading: Blood Pressure

paragraphs.text: Indirect blood pressure readings can be acquired through a cuff or inflatable bladder placed around the upper arm, preferably the right upper arm, or calf. The cuff is inflated to a pressure adequate to cause occlusion of the arterial flow. During deflation of the cuff, measurements of diastolic and systolic blood pressure can be obtained. Mean blood pressure is then defined as the integrated area under the arterial pressure waveform.
paragraphs.heading: Blood Pressure

paragraphs.text: The size and placement of the cuff can affect accurate measurements of blood pressure. A cuff that is too narrow or applied loosely may result in falsely high readings. The AHA recommends a cuff width of approximately 40% of the limb circumference. The two modes of indirect blood pressure monitoring include the auscultatory and oscillometry methods. The auscultatory method entails rapid inflation of the cuff, followed by slow deflation while listening for distal Korotkoff sounds with a stethoscope. This method, commonly used in adults, is limited by the inaudible frequency range of arterial sounds in neonates, intra-observer variability, and disturbance to the patient. The oscillometry method is more often used in NICUs. In this method, cuff pressure is rapidly inflated to above systolic pressure. As the pressure is slowly released, small pulsations can be detected as the cuff approaches systolic pressure. When the cuff pressure decreases to below systolic pressure the oscillations
paragraphs.heading: Blood Pressure

paragraphs.text: increase in magnitude because of blood flowing into the artery. Ultimately a maximum oscillation point will be reached, corresponding to mean arterial pressure, followed by a decline as the cuff pressure decreases to baseline (Fig. 37.1). In critically ill premature infants, oscillometric blood pressure measurements have been shown to have good agreement with arterial catheter values, although accuracy is greatly diminished in infants with a mean arterial pressure less than or equal to 30 mm Hg.12 Accordingly, noninvasive measurements tend to overestimate invasive blood pressure measurements, particularly in smaller infants at lower blood pressure measurements.13,14 Although the use of a cuff does not allow for continuous monitoring of blood pressure, many systems provide automated transient readings. Additionally, new wireless devices are being developed that use binodal epidermal pulse arrival time algorithms as a surrogate of systolic blood pressure.4
paragraphs.heading: Blood Pressure

paragraphs.text: Arterial blood gas sample measurements provide the most accurate estimate of arterial oxygen and carbon dioxide status. An arterial blood gas measures (1) the percentage of available heme sites on hemoglobin molecules occupied by oxygen within the arterial red blood cell as a percent oxygen saturation (SaO2) by spectrophotometry, (2) the partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2) by the current produced when oxygen from the blood sample diffuses across a semipermeable membrane and is reduced at the cathode of a polarographic electrode (Clark electrode), and (3) the partial pressure of carbon dioxide (Paco2) by indirectly sensing a change in pH (Severinghaus electrode) wherein carbon dioxide in the blood sample equilibrates across a gas-permeable membrane with a bicarbonate solution in a reaction that generates hydrogen ions. However, blood gases are limited by painful and time-consuming procedures, inherent risks including infection and vascular events, and intermittent short-term monitoring of PaO2 and Paco2. Continuous monitoring of oxygenation and carbon dioxide modalities offer an
paragraphs.heading: Blood Gas Monitoring

paragraphs.text: improved alternative by providing noninvasive, easy-to-use, portable, high-resolution, and fast-response options to alert the clinician to rapid decompensations that often occur in this high-risk infant cohort. Ideally, implementation of these devices in the NICU setting would lead to the “ultimate goal” of ventilation of the neonate—to stabilize respiration and oxygenation and minimize the use of supplemental oxygen and invasive respiratory support.
paragraphs.heading: Blood Gas Monitoring

paragraphs.text: Immature respiratory control superimposed on an underdeveloped lung, with or without confounding acute illness, often leads to respiratory instability and periods of hypoxemia. Blood gas measurements are useful for reporting prolonged baseline levels of oxygenation but cannot capture short desaturation events that commonly occur in this patient population.15 As a result, intermittent blood gas sampling is often accompanied by noninvasive continuous pulse oximetry or transcutaneous monitoring.
paragraphs.heading: Oxygenation

paragraphs.text: The principle of pulse oximetry is based on the Beer-Lambert law, which states that the concentration of an absorbing substance in solution can be determined by the intensity of the light transmitted through the solution. Applying this concept, pulse oximetry relies on the light absorption characteristics of deoxygenated and oxygenated hemoglobin in the red (600–750 nm wavelength) and infrared (IR) (850–1000 nm wavelength) light spectrum ranges, respectively (Fig. 37.2). The oximeter probe comprises two lightemitting diodes (LEDs), each emitting light of a specified wavelength (660 and 940 nm) through the capillary bed of the infant’s extremity. A photodiode detector on the opposing side of the electrode measures the intensity of the light passing through the extremity at each wavelength, which is equivalent to the amount absorbed by tissue, and venous and arterial blood. Oxygen saturation values can be extrapolated from this measurement by exploiting the relatively small
paragraphs.heading: Pulse Oximetry

paragraphs.text: arterial pulsatile changes, also known as the plethysmogram waveform, with each heartbeat. This is accomplished by measuring the ratio of the transmitted light owing to the arterial pulsatile component (pulsatile) to the transmitted light owing to the constant component of the signal (constant); that is, tissue and baseline blood in tissue (Fig. 37.3). This ratio is calculated separately for both the red and IR waveform signals. The ratio of the red (pulsatile/constant component at 660 nm) to the IR signal (pulsatile/constant component at 940 nm) can then be converted to a measure representing the proportion of hemoglobin molecules in the arterial blood that are loaded with oxygen.
paragraphs.heading: Pulse Oximetry

paragraphs.text: The probe requires no heating or calibration by the user and is routinely placed on the palm of the hand or sole of the foot. In sick infants, with intravenous lines or heparin locks precluding access to these extremities, the wrist or ankle has been suggested as an adequate alternate site. The
paragraphs.heading: Pulse Oximetry

paragraphs.text: rapid response time of 3 to 4 seconds (the time it takes for blood to travel from the lung to the peripheral sensor), lack of heating at the skin, and continuous measurement capabilities make pulse oximetry the ideal low-risk modality for detection of intermittent hypoxemia, especially in preterm infants.
paragraphs.heading: Pulse Oximetry

paragraphs.text: Accuracy of pulse oximetry is dependent on multiple factors including range of oxygenation, probe position, motion and ambient light interference, and low perfusion, among others. Many companies report SpO2 accuracy of ±2% full scale, but error is increased with manufacturerspecific calibration extrapolations at low ranges of SpO2. For example, in a study of 1664 preterm infants, overall mean differences between SaO2 and SpO2 were −1.84 ± 2.93%, but less than 40% of infants were within 3% of the corresponding SaO2 when SpO2 fell below 88%.16 Under conditions of excessive ambient light interference, the SpO2 will trend toward a value of 85%, the SpO2 value at which the ratio of red to IR light absorption equals 1, or 0% when complete failure to detect SpO2 occurs.17 Direct opposition of the emitter and detector and covering of the extremity can minimize an optical shunt and reduce ambient light interference. Signal quality indicators and improved adaptive noise-canceling algorithms (Fig. 37.4) have minimized underestimation of oxygenation or loss of signal with the perfusion index, if available, further alerting the user to periods of low peripheral perfusion caused by movement or changes in physiology (i.e., periods of hypothermia, low cardiac output, or vasoconstriction). Differences in SpO2 values between manufacturers can be attributed to multiple factors including functional versus fractional SpO2 values that typically differ by 2%, the value equivalent to the levels of COHb, MetHb, and other dysfunctional hemoglobins in healthy, nonsmoking adults. Melanin is a secondary absorber of near-infrared light but, in contrast to adults, during infancy it does not
paragraphs.heading: Pulse Oximetry

paragraphs.text: play a strong role in SpO2 accuracy with either no difference18 or a modest bias towards SpO2 overestimation in Black infants.19 Lastly, fetal hemoglobin can contribute to deviations in both the displayed value of SpO2 and the clinical interpretation of oxygen content delivery. In the presence of fetal hemoglobin, a normally clinically acceptable level of SpO2 may not translate to adequate oxygen delivery to the tissue because of its high affinity to oxygen. This effect is noted by a left shift in the oxygen dissociation curve. Blood transfusions during the first week of life will reduce the proportion of fetal hemoglobin and should be taken into consideration when oxygen therapy is being regulated.
paragraphs.heading: Pulse Oximetry

paragraphs.text: It is important to note that clinical interpretation and intervention based on SpO2 values can be significantly altered by the oximeter software and settings. Users of early generation oximeters relied on visual documentation of a stable plethysmographic waveform to identify periods of motion associated with artificial falls in SpO2 that immediately returned to baseline indicating lapses in signal integrity. More recent new generation oximeters have implemented noise reduction filters with vast improvements in signal quality but potentially at the expense of missed hypoxemia and bradycardia, with the number of missed events dependent on the individual manufacturer. Alarm settings can vary by NICU, but a high oximeter alarm of 95% to 96% is commonly used for infants receiving supplemental oxygen to comply with the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommended oxygen saturation target of 90% to 95%20 and avoid excessive oxygen exposure. Low alarm thresholds of 87% to 89%, combined with a plan to increase FiO2 in small increments, can be used to reduce periods of hypoxemia while avoiding periods of “hyperoxia overshoot.” Alarm delays range from 0 to 15 seconds depending on the manufacturer and individual NICU guidelines to reduce nuisance alarms and allow for spontaneous recovery (thereby preventing unnecessary supplemental oxygen exposure) with the cost of increasing response time. The longest delay of 15 seconds has been shown to reduce the number of alarms by as much as 67%.21 In contrast, increasing the averaging time from 2 to 16 seconds decreased the number of alarms by ∼50% but also doubled the alarm duration with overall no effect on the proportion of time in alarm conditions.
paragraphs.heading: Pulse Oximetry

paragraphs.text: Averaging time is probably the most misunderstood parameter on the pulse oximeter display. Conceptually, a longer averaging time will minimize oscillations in the SpO2 waveform and reduce nuisance alarms by averaging the current data point with previous values within a specified window (2–16 seconds). However, prolonged averaging times (>10 seconds) can distort the SpO2 waveform by eliminating true short events, reducing actual event severity (nadir), and merging closely occurring events into fewer events but of longer duration,22 which is concerning as longer events are more likely to be treated with supplemental oxygen. Although there is no official standard, the commonly used averaging time of 8 seconds has been shown to reduce alarms due to short (<20 seconds) self-resolving hypoxemia events while minimizing the creation of falsely prolonged events.22
paragraphs.heading: Pulse Oximetry

paragraphs.text: SpO2 values are displayed on the monitor and updated approximately every second. Many oximeters also provide histogram distributions of the percent time the infant spent in user-defined oxygen saturation ranges. This can provide the clinician with the overall time spent in hyper/ hypoxia but cannot distinguish multiple prolonged events from one prolonged event. Recent improvements in commercial software (Trace, Masimo) can inform the clinician with the number, duration, and time of each hypoxemic event. Future research expanding on models encompassing the entire oxygen saturation waveform, as opposed to falls below an arbitrarily chosen threshold, is sorely needed to identify subtle, high-risk patterns of oxygenation linked to poor outcomes. For example, preliminary data using wavelet models have revealed that lower frequency spectral components by 3 weeks of life were associated with the future progression of severe retinopathy of prematurity.23 These types of time series models can inform the next generation of pulse oximetry by providing an early warning of patients that can most benefit from interventional therapeutics.
paragraphs.heading: Pulse Oximetry

paragraphs.text: Lastly, smartphone vital sign monitoring has become prevalent and pulse oximetry has been no exception. Pulse oximetry-based home baby monitors are popular among parents but are not regulated by the US Food and Drug Administration. Concerning findings have revealed large inconsistencies in hypoxemia and bradycardia detection on smartphone-based oximeters when compared to standard hospital bedside monitors (Masimo, Radical 7).24 In fact, this study reported that two marketed home monitors had sensitivities of 0% to 88.8% and 0% for hypoxemia and bradycardia, respectively; caution should be exercised when discussing these home monitors with patient families.
paragraphs.heading: Pulse Oximetry

paragraphs.text: Transcutaneous oxygen tension (PtcO2) provides an estimate of the concentration of oxygen dissolved in the plasma and is based on the principle of oxygen diffusion through the skin. The electrode consists of a platinum cathode and silver reference anode encased in an electrolyte solution that is then separated from the skin by a membrane permeable to oxygen. The electrode is heated, which arterializes the blood in the capillaries underneath the skin and breaks down the stratum corneum barrier, allowing diffusion across the skin surface. The oxygen from the skin sensor reacts with the platinumsilver chloride sensor to create an electrical current, which is converted to partial pressure measurements of oxygen.
paragraphs.heading: Transcutaneous Monitoring of Oxygen

paragraphs.text: Agreement between PtcO2 measured at the skin surface and arterial PaO2 is influenced by multiple factors, including decreased solubility of oxygen in blood owing to heating of the skin, oxygen consumption in the heated skin and inside the electrode, air bubbles under the sensor, insecure seal with the skin, and excessive contact gel. The sensor must be placed in a well-perfused area and properly heated before reliable values can be attained, which may take as long as 15 minutes. A goal temperature of 44.0° C has been suggested, as lower temperatures will underestimate arterial values,25 and the sensor location should be altered every 2 to 4 hours to correct for transient electrode drift and avoid heat-related
paragraphs.heading: Transcutaneous Monitoring of Oxygen

paragraphs.text: skin complications. However, even shorter durations of 2 hours have been associated with hyperpigmented macules and prolonged erythema in preterm infants with fragile skin. Multiple studies have shown a linear relationship between PtcO2 and PaO2, but accuracy may differ at low and high levels of PaO2, with about 15% of hypoxemic and hyperoxemic events missed by PtcO2 monitors25 and overall sensitivity ranging from 68% to 100% for hypoxemia (<50 mm Hg) and 71% to 92% for hyperoxemia (>80 mm Hg).25 Given this wide variability in sensitivity, PtcO2 should be used in conjunction with intermittent blood gas sampling to confirm levels of oxygenation and minimize unnecessary supplemental oxygen exposure.
paragraphs.heading: Transcutaneous Monitoring of Oxygen

paragraphs.text: Although PtcO2 monitoring offers the advantages of continuous oxygenation monitoring and increased stability during motion, it is limited by a slow response time and a reduced period in which reliable data can be acquired.25 In contrast to pulse oximetry, which can detect immediate arterial changes at the sensor site of the percentage of oxygen-bound heme, PtcO2 monitoring must account for a 16- to 30-second time delay, the time needed for oxygen to diffuse through the capillaries and across the sensor membrane. During SpO2 probe placement, oxygen saturation measurements can be immediately acquired after detection of an adequate plethysmograph waveform with no need for relocation of the probe. In contrast, a delay of approximately 15 minutes needed to heat the transcutaneous probe compounded with multiple site locations to reduce the risk of burns can lead to a large percentage of the monitoring period without measurements of oxygenation. Given these limitations, pulse oximetry is considered the most widely accepted modality for continuous measures of oxygenation in the neonatal intensive care setting.
paragraphs.heading: Transcutaneous Monitoring of Oxygen

paragraphs.text: In contrast to pulse oximetry, which measures arterial oxygenation, near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) measures oxygen uptake in the tissue. This technology has been used in a variety of organ systems, with a particular interest in cerebral oxygenation in the preterm infant population. NIRS relies on the presence of chromophores, compounds whose absorption of NIR light is dependent on oxygen status, in the tissue. These chromophores include cytochrome aa3, myoglobin, and the most often studied, hemoglobin. Using light absorption properties of oxyhemoglobin (HbO2) and deoxyhemoglobin (HHb) in the IR range (700–1300 nm), NIRS measures the difference between the oxygen delivered and the oxygen extracted by the tissue. This measurement is also known as regional oxygen saturation (rSO2), where
paragraphs.heading: Near-Infrared Spectroscopy

paragraphs.text: rSO2 = HbO2/ (HbO2 + HHb)
paragraphs.heading: Near-Infrared Spectroscopy

paragraphs.text: Cerebral NIRS entails a probe placed on one temple of the infant’s head with a laser or LED probe as a source of NIR wavelength transmission. The lasers/LEDs are pulsed in sequential order where multiple photodetectors, attached to the opposite temple, collect the transmitted light photons
paragraphs.heading: Near-Infrared Spectroscopy

paragraphs.text: that are not absorbed in the tissue. An additional reference signal is used to correct for light reflected from the skin, laser drift, and skin coloration. By measuring the difference between the amount of light transmitted through the deep tissue and the surface path, NIRS values can estimate the amount of spectral absorption that occurs in the tissue bed. Spatial resolution is currently limited to approximately 1 cm2 with several layers of tissue, including skin, skull surface vasculature, and gray matter in one two-dimensional sample. The current primary target area is restricted to the surface of the cortex, because access to deeper brain structures would require lasers of increased intensity and risk of damage to brain tissue. Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) values have been shown to correlate with cerebral venous saturation with improved precision with increased tissue homogeneity.26 However, overall comparability and reproducibility of different NIRS devices remain poor. This may be because of manufacturer-specific variations in design that include the source of monochromatic light, the number and specific wavelengths used, the frequency of light cycling, and the frequency at which the signals are updated for digital display. Modifications in sensor geometry27 and adjustments for the variability in arterial blood pressure28 may have promise in improving precision.
paragraphs.heading: Near-Infrared Spectroscopy

paragraphs.text: An international standard has been recently issued by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) that should improve differences between manufacturers.29 Nevertheless, interpretation of absolute measurements of rSO2 is still the subject of ongoing research. Average cerebral oxygen saturation values of 77.9% ± 8.5% have been recorded in healthy term newborns30 with a normative range of 55% to 85% in extremely preterm infants,31 but rSO2 can be influenced by gestational age,32 body position,33 and age at the time of study.32,34 There has been some suggestion that alterations in neonatal cerebral oxygenation may be associated with clinical outcomes such as intraventricular hemorrhage, cognitive impairment, and mortality, whereas others have shown no relationship with any clinical characteristics.32 This is further complicated by improvements in oxygen saturation stability and time in target not always translating into improved cerebral oxygen tissue saturation.35 Given these findings, the role of NIRS in identifying etiologies of brain injury has yet to be determined, and more extensive research is needed before NIRS can be routinely used in the clinical neonatal setting. In extremely preterm infants, treatment guided by cerebral oximetry monitoring for the first 72 hours after birth was not associated with a lower incidence of death or severe brain injury at 36 weeks’ postmenstrual age than usual care.
paragraphs.heading: Near-Infrared Spectroscopy

paragraphs.text: The presence of hypocarbia, hypercarbia, and fluctuations between states has been implicated with a wide range of neonatal morbidities, including chronic lung disease, intraventricular hemorrhage, and neurodevelopmental impairment,36,37 although optimal ranges require further investigation.38 For this reason, maintenance of normocarbia and avoidance
paragraphs.heading: Carbon Dioxide

paragraphs.text: of extreme levels of arterial CO2 are imperative in preterm infants. As discussed, an arterial blood gas is the gold standard for assessing gas exchange, but it is intermittent, invasive, and may cause complications. During periods of respiratory instability in which oscillations in Paco2 are known to occur,39 arterial sampling or indwelling catheters may not be adequate. Under these conditions, continuous measurements of end-tidal or transcutaneous CO2 monitoring have become increasingly popular in the intensive care unit.
paragraphs.heading: Carbon Dioxide

paragraphs.text: End-tidal CO2 monitoring originally used mass spectroscopy to estimate CO2 from samples of exhaled gas. Because of improvements in technology allowing for portable devices, IR spectroscopy is now the method of choice. IR spectroscopy is based on the principle that CO2 molecules absorb light in the IR wavelength of 4.26 μm. Light is transmitted through the sample using an IR emitter with light absorption measured with photodetectors. The amount of light absorbed in the given IR spectrum is then proportional to the concentration of CO2.
paragraphs.heading: End-Tidal Carbon Dioxide Monitoring

paragraphs.text: Capnography sensor designs fall into two categories: sidestream and mainstream. Sidestream systems require constant aspiration of expired gas, which may result in underestimation of CO2 readings in preterm infants with low tidal volumes. This incidence may be reduced with the development of microstream technology, which uses a refined spectrum of discrete wavelengths, allowing for extremely small sample volumes (15 μL) and a correspondingly lower sample rate of 50 mL/min.40 The advantage of the sidestream system is that it can be used on both spontaneously breathing and intubated patients. During intubation, sampling of gas at the distal end of the endotracheal tube is recommended to improve accuracy, although both proximal and distal measurements of the end-tidal pressure of carbon dioxide (Petco2) have been shown to provide acceptable estimates of Paco2 in relatively healthy infants with diminished performance in infants with more severe respiratory disease.41 Accuracy may be affected by water vapor or secretions occluding the adapter or condensation on the photo detector. This is eliminated by vertical positioning or the use of Nafion tubing, a semipermeable polymer that allows water to pass through and evaporate. Mainstream systems rely on gas passing through a wide chamber, or cuvette, placed in line with the patient circuit. As opposed to a remote device with sidestream systems, a miniature IR optical system is placed directly over the chamber. This allows for nearinstantaneous measurements in less than 500 ms. However, it is limited to intubated patients or patients with a closed circuit, that is, a sealed nasal/oral mask. Erroneous values caused by water condensation are reduced by slight heating of the cuvette. Additional factors that can contribute to measurement error for both sidestream and mainstream systems include temperature dependence, miscalibration, drift, noise, and pressure effects from the sampling system.
paragraphs.heading: End-Tidal Carbon Dioxide Monitoring

paragraphs.text: In addition to instrumental design, the accuracy of end-tidal CO2 monitoring is dependent on patient
paragraphs.heading: End-Tidal Carbon Dioxide Monitoring

paragraphs.text: characteristics. Petco2 has been shown to accurately estimate alveolar CO2 in healthy newborns,42 but the agreement is poor and negatively influenced by the presence and severity of pulmonary disease43 and inadequate gas exchange caused by atelectasis, V/Q mismatch, and chronic lung disease in bronchopulmonary dysplasia.44 Neonates have small tidal volumes and high respiratory rates, which often result in wide variations in end-tidal CO2 values and underestimation of true alveolar gas, also making it a prohibitive modality for estimating CO2 during high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV). Microstream capnography through a double-lumen endotracheal tube with specially designed software for HFOV has been introduced.45 Despite its limitations, the ability to detect extreme low and high CO2 levels may be of use for trending or screening patients for abnormal arterial CO2 values. End-tidal CO2 monitoring may also be used to guide respiratory support in the delivery room.46
paragraphs.heading: End-Tidal Carbon Dioxide Monitoring

paragraphs.text: Disposable colorimetric end-tidal CO2 detectors are an efficient method of verifying correct endotracheal tube placement in the newborn.47 When placed between the ventilator and endotracheal tube, the pH-sensitive chemical indicator (metacresol purple) changes from purple to yellow when exposed to expired CO2. The minimum and maximum CO2 concentrations needed to establish a color change are 0.54% (0.5 kPa) and 2% to 5% (2–5 kPa), respectively. Because neonatal extubation failure can have devastating consequences, calorimetric detectors can play a significant role in the intensive care unit. However, this device cannot detect hypocarbia, hypercarbia, right mainstem bronchus intubation, or oropharyngeal placement in spontaneous breathing patients.
paragraphs.heading: End-Tidal Carbon Dioxide Monitoring

paragraphs.text: Transcutaneous carbon dioxide tension measurements are based on the principle of CO2 diffusion through the skin. The sensor consists of a pH-sensitive glass electrode with an adjacent silver chloride reference anode covered by a hydrophobic membrane permeable to carbon dioxide and separated by a sodium bicarbonate electrolyte solution. Changes in pH are measured as carbon dioxide from the skin diffuses through the electrode membrane. These changes are then converted to corresponding Paco2 values.
paragraphs.heading: Transcutaneous Monitoring of Carbon Dioxide

paragraphs.text: Data assessing the relationship between Paco2 and transcutaneously measured partial pressure of CO2 (Ptcco2) in preterm infants have shown a wide variation in both slope and intercept values.48,49 Additional data by Martin et al. demonstrated a progressive increase in the difference between tcPco2 and Paco2 as Paco2 increased (tcPco2 − Paco2, 5 ± 4 mm Hg and 9 ± 6 mm Hg in normocapnia and hypercapnia, respectively).50 These data suggest that as Paco2 increases, there may be an imbalance between CO2 production and removal. This can be attributed to multiple factors, including metabolic events in the skin, circulatory disturbances that permit gas to accumulate in the tissues, the anaerobic heating coefficient of blood, and increased CO2 tension with higher electrode temperature.
paragraphs.heading: Transcutaneous Monitoring of Carbon Dioxide

paragraphs.text: The determination of Ptcco2 or end-tidal CO2 monitoring should include considerations of the risk/benefit ratio for each patient. The use of heated Ptcco2 electrodes entails a risk of skin damage caused by burns that require repeated repositioning of the sensor. This can be a serious limitation when considering low birth weight infants with fragile skin, although newer devices that have used lower local temperatures show only modest discrepancies in performance.51,52 Additionally, transcutaneous CO2 detectors have been shown to be accurate during HFOV51,53 and useful during neonatal transport.54 This alternative mode of noninvasive CO2 monitoring may be a reasonable screening tool for preterm infants with small tidal volumes and during periods of rapid breathing where end-tidal CO2 may underestimate Paco2. Regardless of the modality chosen, clinical care should include comparisons with blood gas values, especially during periods of relative hypercapnia.
paragraphs.heading: Transcutaneous Monitoring of Carbon Dioxide

paragraphs.text: Respiratory instability in the preterm infant can be attributed to immaturity of the central nervous system and a highly compliant chest wall, resulting in both central and obstructive apnea. During normal respiration, the diaphragm contracts, expanding the thorax in conjunction with activation of accessory muscles that stabilize the rib cage and maintain upper airway patency. Because of the highly compliant chest wall of the preterm infant, any loss of accessory muscle tone, including intercostals stabilizing the rib cage or hypoglossus maintaining upper airway patency, may result in instability and retraction of the rib cage in response to negative pressure generated by the diaphragm during inspiration. As a result, asynchronous or paradoxical chest wall movements will occur with partial airway obstruction, which is a common respiratory pattern in the preterm infant, particularly during rapid eye movement sleep. During extreme occasions, total airway obstruction may occur, presenting as asynchronous chest wall and abdominal efforts and no corresponding airflow. Respiratory pauses may also arise because of decreased central respiratory drive, as can occur during periods of periodic breathing and spontaneous central apnea. Therefore ideal respiratory monitoring should have the ability to detect both central and obstructive apnea.
paragraphs.heading: Respiratory Monitoring

paragraphs.text: The pneumotachometer is considered the gold standard for measuring flow and volume and is most often used during mechanical ventilation and calculations of respiratory mechanics. There are two types of pneumotachometers: fixed orifice and laminar flow. The fixed orifice design consists of a fixed orifice placed within the tubular attachment placed in the airway. The differential pressure is measured across the fixed orifice, which is proportional to the square of the flow rate. This mathematical relationship can then be used to calculate a given flow. The laminar flow design consists of a simple compartment containing a resistive element, usually
paragraphs.heading: Flow Sensors

paragraphs.text: consisting of a mesh screen or capillary network. The pressure drop across the resistive element is linearly related to the flow passing through the compartment and can be calibrated accordingly. The range in which there is a linear relationship between pressure and flow will be dependent on the design of the device, including the length, width, and type of resistive element used. To maintain precision, all flow must pass through the device, which may be problematic during mechanical ventilation in preterm infants with a high occurrence of endotracheal tube leaks. During spontaneous respiration, the pneumotachometer must be incorporated into a nasal/oral mask. To minimize the effect of the mask on the respiratory pattern, the mask design should include minimal dead space, the ability to flush the mask to reduce CO2 retention, and low resistance to minimize work of breathing.
paragraphs.heading: Flow Sensors

paragraphs.text: Pneumotachometer use in the clinical setting has been limited to pulmonary function measurements in spontaneously breathing patients, incorporated into a sealed nasal/ oral mask, or tidal volume measurements when attached to the endotracheal tube in mechanically ventilated patients. During these periods, the device may add a significant resistive load, especially in severely ill ELBW infants. As a result, many companies have replaced the pneumotachometer with the hot-wire anemometer for volume measurements during mechanical ventilation. The hot-wire anemometer includes a heated element placed in the airway circuit. As flow passes, the sensor is cooled. The system delivers an electrical current to maintain the default sensor temperature. The amount of current needed to maintain the sensor temperature can be calibrated to a given flow. If bidirectional flow is desired, a second wire can be placed in the system. Accurate measurements of flow may be compromised if secretions accumulate on the heated element. However, because of its high-frequency response, proven accuracy, and minimal resistive load, the hot-wire anemometer is a promising modality for measurements of respiration in the preterm infant, including periods of high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV).55
paragraphs.heading: Flow Sensors

paragraphs.text: Although the pneumotachometer and hot-wire anemometer give quantifiable measurements of flow and volume, additional devices, such as thermistor/thermocouple sensors and end-tidal CO2, can display qualitative estimates. The relationship between peak-to-peak amplitude of the thermistor signal and actual measures of flow has been shown to be nonlinear and frequency dependent.56 There is also minimal correlation between Petco2 and actual measures of volume. Therefore the implementation of thermistor or Petco2 monitoring is limited to the sleep lab, where, used in conjunction with chest wall motion sensors, it can be used to identify the presence or absence of flow associated with central and obstructive apnea.
paragraphs.heading: Flow Sensors

paragraphs.text: Despite concerns regarding the accuracy of impedance-based apnea monitoring,57 impedance technology continues to be the most widely used modality for measuring respiration in
paragraphs.heading: Other Respiratory Monitoring Devices

paragraphs.text: the hospital setting. With two electrodes placed on either side of the chest above and below the insertion of the diaphragm, impedance monitoring measures changes in electrical impedance across the thorax during a breath. Specific placement of electrodes for optimal signal quality can vary between infants. This modality is based on the principle that air has a much higher level of impedance than tissue. During inspiration, there is a decrease in conductivity (and corresponding increase in impedance), owing to both an increase in gas volume of the chest in relation to the fluid volume and increased length of the conductance path with chest wall expansion. Using a high-frequency current of greater than 25 kHz, the same electrodes used for measuring ECG can be used for detection of respiratory efforts. The ECG waveform is filtered out by manufacturer-based signal processing algorithms, thus eliminating this potential source of noise artifact. However, changes in thoracic blood volume may be falsely identified as a breath. In addition, proprietary algorithms cannot distinguish obstructive efforts from normal respiration with no monitor alarm during obstructive apnea as air moves from one compartment to the other.
paragraphs.heading: Other Respiratory Monitoring Devices

paragraphs.text: Impedance-based apnea detection is both poorly sensitive and predictive in preterm infants,57 but there are advancements in machine learning methods and application of impedance technology. For example, recent developments using hidden Markov-based models have identified robust algorithms that can identify or predict apnea with accompanying bradycardia and/or hypoxemia58,59 and may be a first step toward personalized risk assessment for severe clinical events during hospitalization and after NICU discharge. Ongoing advances in impedance technology, notably electrical impedance tomography (EIT), also show great promise in identifying continuous high-resolution images of gas distribution throughout the lung. Small alternating currents applied sequentially through 8 to 32 electrodes placed circumferentially around the thorax are reconstructed into one image. Sequential images are compared to a baseline, and variations over a given time interval represent alterations in ventilation distribution across the region. EIT is currently used as a noninvasive and radiation-free imaging tool providing data on lung collapse, overdistension, and air distribution in mechanically ventilated patients60 but may have a future role in bedside impedance monitoring by identifying obstructive apnea in spontaneously breathing infants.
paragraphs.heading: Other Respiratory Monitoring Devices

paragraphs.text: Respiratory inductance plethysmography (RIP) has been used extensively in both clinical research and pulmonary function lab settings. It is currently not used at the bedside but could be a promising alternative for respiratory monitoring. As with impedance, it is a noninvasive method of measuring respiration with two bands wrapped around the chest and abdomen, respectively. Each band contains a sinusoidal inductance coil with a small AC current that travels through the coil, as opposed to through the chest wall, as occurs with impedance. RIP relies on the principle that a current applied through a loop of wire generates a magnetic field (Faraday’s law) and that a change in the area enclosed by the loop generates an opposing current directly proportional to the change in area (Lenz’s
paragraphs.heading: Other Respiratory Monitoring Devices

paragraphs.text: law). Thus, as the chest wall expands, the coil in the band elongates, altering the magnetic properties, or inductance, of the band. The strength of this modality is the representation of respiration as a two-dimensional model. Thus obstructive apnea will present as asynchronous, 180-degree out-of-phase movements between the rib cage and abdomen as air flows from one compartment to the other. With the addition of a software algorithm to calibrate the rib cage and abdominal waveforms, a semiquantitative volume waveform can be acquired, giving RIP the ability to identify obstructive apnea without the need for an oral/nasal flow sensor (Fig. 37.5).
paragraphs.heading: Other Respiratory Monitoring Devices

paragraphs.text: A small cohort study of moderately preterm infants has shown that transcutaneous diaphragm electromyogram (dEMG) activity is feasible in the delivery room as a useful indicator of respiratory rate, heart rate, and diaphragm activity. Heart rate (dEMG) measures showed high to moderate agreement with ECG and pulse oximeter values, respectively, with modest agreement between respiratory rate (dEMG) and direct measures of airflow.61 Neural measures of electrical diaphragmatic activity (Edi) using an orogastric catheter provide another EMG-based alternative to respiratory monitoring and are part of the standard procedure during noninvasive ventilation with neurally adjusted ventilatory assist support (NIV-NAVA).62 Further investigations of the addition of respiratory efforts, as denoted by EMG amplitude, could lead to a better understanding of respiratory physiology and optimization of respiratory support.
paragraphs.heading: Other Respiratory Monitoring Devices

paragraphs.text: Overall, the current technology for respiratory monitoring contains many obstacles for newborn infants, including cumbersome sensors and wiring that compromise clinical care, skin integrity, and overall infant comfort. Ongoing developments in wireless and inexpensive polyvinylidenefluoride sensors with complementary metal-oxide semiconductors integrated circuitry use both pyroelectric and piezoelectric properties and are small enough to be incorporated into a nasal cannula or patient mattress.63 Acoustic sensors placed on the neck region, carotid vessel complex, and nasal region and contactless ultrawideband pulse radar sensors are also being investigated as alternative modes for measuring respiration. Preliminary data suggest that these prototypes can detect respiration in an ideal, experimental environment, but many challenges need to be overcome before they can be implemented in the NICU setting.
paragraphs.heading: Other Respiratory Monitoring Devices

paragraphs.text: The need for advanced diagnostic systems, including cardiorespiratory monitors, in neonatal care continues to expand. This growth should incorporate the development of safe and effective devices for use in the NICU and a collaborative research and testing effort among the biomedical engineering disciplines. Areas in which improvements are needed include the development of “smart alarms” for cardiorespiratory monitoring, education of personnel pertaining to the use of equipment, automated signal quality assessment, wireless technology, and electronic storage of longitudinal waveforms. The implementation of more
paragraphs.heading: Future Directions

paragraphs.text: sophisticated algorithms should be countered by a less complex user interface.
paragraphs.heading: HR

paragraphs.text: As physicians continue to be bombarded with physiologic data from bedside monitors, current clinical practice uses only a fraction of the information available for patient care. For instance, pulse oximetry waveform extrapolation is limited to simple values of baseline oxygen saturation and time in various target ranges. Future exploitation of these various waveforms may include identification of subtle pathologic heart rate cross-correlation factors6 and SpO2 waveform patterns,64 maintaining normocapnia,65 and the use of automated feedback controllers66 to avoid or alert caregivers of high-risk patterns associated with adverse outcomes. Implementation of electronic servers for storage of

paragraphs.heading: HR

paragraphs.text: continuous cardiorespiratory waveforms and application of sophisticated mathematical algorithms (e.g., stochastic modeling, spectral and wavelet analysis) to longitudinal datasets to identify early patterns of cardiorespiratory instability58,67 associated with morbidity,23,68,69 is currently limited to research protocols. The major challenge for development and application of high-risk predictive models to the clinical setting requires large-scale centralized and automated storage of waveforms and development of integrated systems incorporating multiple physiologic parameters from electronic patient database records while protecting patient confidentiality. Current trials are attempting to meet this challenge by reducing this vast amount of data into a comprehensible parameter that is useful for clinical practice.

# 37. Neonatal Cardiorespiratory Monitoring
> Source attribution: [Source credits](../../SOURCE_CREDITS.md).


## PDF page 631 | printed page 622

37 Neonatal Cardiorespiratory Monitoring

### JULIANN M. DI FIORE AND THOMAS M. RAFFAY

### Summary

Maintaining stable respiration and adequate oxygenation is a fundamental aspect of newborn care. This can be challenging in premature infants, as preterm birth is marked by immature respiratory control regions of the brain superimposed on an underdeveloped lung. As a result, preterm infants exhibit a high incidence of apnea, bradycardia, and intermittent hypoxemia events during early postnatal life.1,2 Pharmacotherapy and respiratory support (e.g., supplemental oxygen, continuous positive airway pressure [CPAP], and mechanical ventilation) are used to stabilize respiration and maintain adequate oxygenation, with a goal of decreasing duration and level of support to minimize the incidence of chronic lung disease and associated adverse respiratory and neurodevelopmental outcomes. These treatment decisions are most often based on medical chart documentation of apnea, heart rate, and desaturation alarms, making bedside cardiorespiratory monitoring an integral part of clinical care in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU).

The challenges of cardiorespiratory monitoring in the NICU include continuous, accurate, artifact-free recordings obtained in a safe and noninvasive manner accounting for the small stature and fragile skin of the extremely low birth weight (ELBW) infant. Monitors and accompanying sensors are often developed for adult patients or older children, followed by application in newborns with minimal data demonstrating accuracy and safety. Nevertheless, even a well-designed monitor is only as good as the end user. Therefore a thorough understanding of individual monitor functionality is also needed to reduce both nuisance alarms and signal distortion of real events. This chapter includes a description of the principles of operation of cardiorespiratory monitoring modalities, including current and future directions of hemodynamic, blood gas, and respiratory waveform acquisition in the NICU setting.

### Hemodynamic Monitoring

### Electrocardiogram

During each heartbeat, an electrical impulse originates in the sinoatrial node and is propagated among the muscles

622

of the atrium, through the atrioventricular node, followed by dispersion throughout the ventricles. The small alterations in voltage generated by the heart can be measured at the body surface with electrocardiogram (ECG) electrodes placed on the chest, the most common types being the silver-silver chloride, foil-based, recessed, or floating electrode. Each electrode contains a highly conductive electrolyte gel with a composition that varies by manufacturer. Electrode location is important in acquiring a signal of adequate resolution, especially in neonates with a limited surface area. Multiple probe applications should be avoided to optimize adhesiveness of the electrodes and ECG signal integrity and decrease the chance of skin damage, including high trans epidermal water losses,3 in extremely preterm infants with fragile skin. Under investigation are next-generation ultrathin epidermal electronic systems that provide wireless ECG measurements that only require water to adhere to the skin.4

The ability of traditional electrodes to detect small electrical changes with each heartbeat requires the application of a current to the chest wall. The recommendations of acceptable current limits by the American Heart Association (AHA) cover two aspects of electrical safety. The first entails the amount of current allowable in a patient-connected lead that can flow through the myocardium without inducing ventricular fibrillation. The second aspect pertains to the allowable chassis leakage current that flows through the patient to ground. The AHA recommends that currents be limited to 10 μA through patient leads and less than 100 μA, with an optimal level of 10 μA, for chassis leakage current.

The initial goal of simple heart rate measurements has expanded to include identification of specific arrhythmias and more complex algorithms of heart rate variability. Longitudinal regression-based models of abnormal heart rate characteristics associated with systemic infection and inflammation have been shown to reduce infant mortality in very low birth weight (VLBW) infants,5 leading to the development of the commercially available HeRO System, providing early warning of patient distress days before patient deterioration. Additional sophisticated mathematical analyses such as cross-correlation of heart rate and other vital signs,6 currently


## PDF page 632 | printed page 623

limited to the research arena, may expand the ability to detect subtle high-risk alterations in heart rate variability, assisting in early interventions and improved patient outcomes such as late-onset sepsis and necrotizing enterocolitis.

### Cardiac Output

Application of the Fick principle is considered the gold standard of cardiac output monitoring in a research setting. This method states

CO = VO2/ (Ca −Cv)

where VO2 = oxygen consumption, Ca = oxygen concentration of arterial blood, and Cv = oxygen concentration of mixed venous blood. Although the Fick principle may be accurate, especially in low flow states, precision may be limited by air leakage, cardiopulmonary disease, and enhanced pulmonary oxygen consumption.7

Noninvasive methods that are validated in neonates include transcutaneous Doppler, transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), and thoracic electrical impedance. Doppler ultrasound uses an ultrasound beam to measure blood flow velocity. A velocity-time waveform is then produced from spectral analysis of Doppler shifts, caused by moving erythrocytes. The stroke distance can be calculated by the area under the velocity-time waveform. If the cross-sectional area of the vessel is known, cardiac output can be calculated by:

Cardiac output

= stroke distance × cross-sectional area of the vessel

× heart rate

Doppler-based cardiac output measurements can vary widely and should be limited to trend monitoring.7

During TTE, measures of left ventricular output, right ventricular output, or superior vena cava (SVC) flow can be obtained. Validation data with TTE have been limited to transthoracic left ventricular output measures, which have been shown to be comparable with pulmonary artery thermodilution and O2-Fick methods.7 A variation of thoracic electrical impedance, electrical velocimetry, includes surface ECG electrodes placed on the forehead, left side of the neck, left mid-axillary line at the level of xiphoid process, and left thigh. During application of a small alternating electrical current through the thorax, changes in voltage are measured during periods of systole and diastole. Stroke volume (SV) is then determined using the following equation:

SV = Vept × νLVET × LVET

where Vept (mL) = volume of electrically participating tissue derived from body mass and height, νLVET (s−1) I = ohmic equivalent of mean aortic blood velocity during left ventricular ejection, and LVET (s) = left ventricular ejection time. Data have shown electrical velocimetry as a comparable mode of measuring left ventricular output in neonates when compared with echocardiography,8 although variation among individuals was seen using both techniques.

Additional bedside TTE techniques have been reported in emerging literature on bedside evaluation of neonatal shock, including SVC flow and descending aortic flow.7 Doppler flow and SVC diameter measured at the entrance of the SVC into the right atrium reflects the blood returning from the brain and upper body, which may be a surrogate measure for cerebral blood flow.9 Various modifications of TTE calculations of SVC flow have been investigated, with high error percentage and considerable variation in reference ranges potentially limiting its clinical application.10 Doppler flow and diameter of the descending aorta when measured below the level of the ductus arteriosus would correspond with the systemic blood flow to the lower body, including the abdomen.9 Absence of end-diastolic flow or flow reversal may indicate a hemodynamically significant left-to-right shunt from a patent ductus arteriosus.11

### Blood Pressure

Direct continuous readings from an indwelling arterial line are considered the gold standard for blood pressure monitoring in the neonate. Arterial and potentially venous pressures are accessed by a catheter placed in the umbilical vessels and attached to a domed transducer. The transducer works on the principle that fluid exerts a force on the diaphragm. This force can be converted to a change in voltage and calibrated to a given pressure. The dome must be flushed, making sure there are no bubbles in the circuit; the transducer must be placed at the level of the distal tip of the catheter; and a zero pressure should be established before patient data are acquired. If the transducer is higher than the heart, readings will be erroneously low.

Indirect blood pressure readings can be acquired through a cuff or inflatable bladder placed around the upper arm, preferably the right upper arm, or calf. The cuff is inflated to a pressure adequate to cause occlusion of the arterial flow. During deflation of the cuff, measurements of diastolic and systolic blood pressure can be obtained. Mean blood pressure is then defined as the integrated area under the arterial pressure waveform.

The size and placement of the cuff can affect accurate measurements of blood pressure. A cuff that is too narrow or applied loosely may result in falsely high readings. The AHA recommends a cuff width of approximately 40% of the limb circumference. The two modes of indirect blood pressure monitoring include the auscultatory and oscillometry methods. The auscultatory method entails rapid inflation of the cuff, followed by slow deflation while listening for distal Korotkoff sounds with a stethoscope. This method, commonly used in adults, is limited by the inaudible frequency range of arterial sounds in neonates, intra-observer variability, and disturbance to the patient. The oscillometry method is more often used in NICUs. In this method, cuff pressure is rapidly inflated to above systolic pressure. As the pressure is slowly released, small pulsations can be detected as the cuff approaches systolic pressure. When the cuff pressure decreases to below systolic pressure the oscillations

Ultimately a maximum oscillation point will be reached, corresponding to mean arterial pressure, followed by a decline as the cuff pressure decreases to baseline (Fig. 37.1). In critically ill premature infants, oscillometric blood pressure measurements have been shown to have good agreement with arterial catheter values, although accuracy is greatly diminished in infants with a mean arterial pressure less than or equal to 30 mm Hg.12 Accordingly, noninvasive measurements tend to overestimate invasive blood pressure measurements, particularly in smaller infants at lower blood pressure measurements.13,14 Although the use of a cuff does not allow for continuous monitoring of blood pressure, many systems provide automated transient readings. Additionally, new wireless devices are being developed that use binodal epidermal pulse arrival time algorithms as a surrogate of systolic blood pressure.4

### Blood Gas Monitoring

Arterial blood gas sample measurements provide the most accurate estimate of arterial oxygen and carbon dioxide status. An arterial blood gas measures (1) the percentage of available heme sites on hemoglobin molecules occupied by oxygen within the arterial red blood cell as a percent oxygen saturation (SaO2) by spectrophotometry, (2) the partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2) by the current produced when oxygen from the blood sample diffuses across a semipermeable membrane and is reduced at the cathode of a polarographic electrode (Clark electrode), and (3) the partial pressure of carbon dioxide (Paco2) by indirectly sensing a change in pH (Severinghaus electrode) wherein carbon dioxide in the blood sample equilibrates across a gas-permeable membrane with a bicarbonate solution in a reaction that generates hydrogen ions. However, blood gases are limited by painful and time-consuming procedures, inherent risks including infection and vascular events, and intermittent short-term monitoring of PaO2 and Paco2. Continuous monitoring of oxygenation and carbon dioxide modalities offer an

Ideally, implementation of these devices in the NICU setting would lead to the “ultimate goal” of ventilation of the neonate—to stabilize respiration and oxygenation and minimize the use of supplemental oxygen and invasive respiratory support.

### Oxygenation

Immature respiratory control superimposed on an underdeveloped lung, with or without confounding acute illness, often leads to respiratory instability and periods of hypoxemia. Blood gas measurements are useful for reporting prolonged baseline levels of oxygenation but cannot capture short desaturation events that commonly occur in this patient population.15 As a result, intermittent blood gas sampling is often accompanied by noninvasive continuous pulse oximetry or transcutaneous monitoring.

### Pulse Oximetry

The principle of pulse oximetry is based on the Beer-Lambert law, which states that the concentration of an absorbing substance in solution can be determined by the intensity of the light transmitted through the solution. Applying this concept, pulse oximetry relies on the light absorption characteristics of deoxygenated and oxygenated hemoglobin in the red (600–750 nm wavelength) and infrared (IR) (850–1000 nm wavelength) light spectrum ranges, respectively (Fig. 37.2). The oximeter probe comprises two lightemitting diodes (LEDs), each emitting light of a specified wavelength (660 and 940 nm) through the capillary bed of the infant’s extremity. A photodiode detector on the opposing side of the electrode measures the intensity of the light passing through the extremity at each wavelength, which is equivalent to the amount absorbed by tissue, and venous and arterial blood. Oxygen saturation values can be extrapolated from this measurement by exploiting the relatively small

This is accomplished by measuring the ratio of the transmitted light owing to the arterial pulsatile component (pulsatile) to the transmitted light owing to the constant component of the signal (constant); that is, tissue and baseline blood in tissue (Fig. 37.3). This ratio is calculated separately for both the red and IR waveform signals. The ratio of the red (pulsatile/constant component at 660 nm) to the IR signal (pulsatile/constant component at 940 nm) can then be converted to a measure representing the proportion of hemoglobin molecules in the arterial blood that are loaded with oxygen.

The probe requires no heating or calibration by the user and is routinely placed on the palm of the hand or sole of the foot. In sick infants, with intravenous lines or heparin locks precluding access to these extremities, the wrist or ankle has been suggested as an adequate alternate site. The

Accuracy of pulse oximetry is dependent on multiple factors including range of oxygenation, probe position, motion and ambient light interference, and low perfusion, among others. In the presence of fetal hemoglobin, a normally clinically acceptable level of SpO2 may not translate to adequate oxygen delivery to the tissue because of its high affinity to oxygen.
