It is important to note that clinical interpretation and intervention based on SpO2 values can be significantly altered by the oximeter software and settings. Users of early generation oximeters relied on visual documentation of a stable plethysmographic waveform to identify periods of motion associated with artificial falls in SpO2 that immediately returned to baseline indicating lapses in signal integrity. More recent new generation oximeters have implemented noise reduction filters with vast improvements in signal quality but potentially at the expense of missed hypoxemia and bradycardia, with the number of missed events dependent on the individual manufacturer. Alarm settings can vary by NICU, but a high oximeter alarm of 95% to 96% is commonly used for infants receiving supplemental oxygen to comply with the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommended oxygen saturation target of 90% to 95%20 and avoid excessive oxygen exposure. Low alarm thresholds of 87% to 89%, combined with a plan to increase FiO2 in small increments, can be used to reduce periods of hypoxemia while avoiding periods of “hyperoxia overshoot.” Alarm delays range from 0 to 15 seconds depending on the manufacturer and individual NICU guidelines to reduce nuisance alarms and allow for spontaneous recovery (thereby preventing unnecessary supplemental oxygen exposure) with the cost of increasing response time. The longest delay of 15 seconds has been shown to reduce the number of alarms by as much as 67%.21 In contrast, increasing the averaging time from 2 to 16 seconds decreased the number of alarms by ∼50% but also doubled the alarm duration with overall no effect on the proportion of time in alarm conditions.

Averaging time is probably the most misunderstood parameter on the pulse oximeter display. Conceptually, a longer averaging time will minimize oscillations in the SpO2 waveform and reduce nuisance alarms by averaging the current data point with previous values within a specified window (2–16 seconds). However, prolonged averaging times (>10 seconds) can distort the SpO2 waveform by eliminating true short events, reducing actual event severity (nadir), and merging closely occurring events into fewer events but of longer duration,22 which is concerning as longer events are more likely to be treated with supplemental oxygen. Although there is no official standard, the commonly used averaging time of 8 seconds has been shown to reduce alarms due to short (<20 seconds) self-resolving hypoxemia events while minimizing the creation of falsely prolonged events.22

SpO2 values are displayed on the monitor and updated approximately every second. Many oximeters also provide histogram distributions of the percent time the infant spent in user-defined oxygen saturation ranges. This can provide the clinician with the overall time spent in hyper/ hypoxia but cannot distinguish multiple prolonged events from one prolonged event. Recent improvements in commercial software (Trace, Masimo) can inform the clinician with the number, duration, and time of each hypoxemic event. Future research expanding on models encompassing the entire oxygen saturation waveform, as opposed to falls below an arbitrarily chosen threshold, is sorely needed to identify subtle, high-risk patterns of oxygenation linked to poor outcomes. For example, preliminary data using wavelet models have revealed that lower frequency spectral components by 3 weeks of life were associated with the future progression of severe retinopathy of prematurity.23 These types of time series models can inform the next generation of pulse oximetry by providing an early warning of patients that can most benefit from interventional therapeutics.

Lastly, smartphone vital sign monitoring has become prevalent and pulse oximetry has been no exception. Pulse oximetry-based home baby monitors are popular among parents but are not regulated by the US Food and Drug Administration. Concerning findings have revealed large inconsistencies in hypoxemia and bradycardia detection on smartphone-based oximeters when compared to standard hospital bedside monitors (Masimo, Radical 7).24 In fact, this study reported that two marketed home monitors had sensitivities of 0% to 88.8% and 0% for hypoxemia and bradycardia, respectively; caution should be exercised when discussing these home monitors with patient families.

### Transcutaneous Monitoring of Oxygen

Transcutaneous oxygen tension (PtcO2) provides an estimate of the concentration of oxygen dissolved in the plasma and is based on the principle of oxygen diffusion through the skin. The electrode consists of a platinum cathode and silver reference anode encased in an electrolyte solution that is then separated from the skin by a membrane permeable to oxygen. The electrode is heated, which arterializes the blood in the capillaries underneath the skin and breaks down the stratum corneum barrier, allowing diffusion across the skin surface. The oxygen from the skin sensor reacts with the platinumsilver chloride sensor to create an electrical current, which is converted to partial pressure measurements of oxygen.

Agreement between PtcO2 measured at the skin surface and arterial PaO2 is influenced by multiple factors, including decreased solubility of oxygen in blood owing to heating of the skin, oxygen consumption in the heated skin and inside the electrode, air bubbles under the sensor, insecure seal with the skin, and excessive contact gel. The sensor must be placed in a well-perfused area and properly heated before reliable values can be attained, which may take as long as 15 minutes. A goal temperature of 44.0° C has been suggested, as lower temperatures will underestimate arterial values,25 and the sensor location should be altered every 2 to 4 hours to correct for transient electrode drift and avoid heat-related


## PDF page 636 | printed page 627

skin complications. However, even shorter durations of 2 hours have been associated with hyperpigmented macules and prolonged erythema in preterm infants with fragile skin. Multiple studies have shown a linear relationship between PtcO2 and PaO2, but accuracy may differ at low and high levels of PaO2, with about 15% of hypoxemic and hyperoxemic events missed by PtcO2 monitors25 and overall sensitivity ranging from 68% to 100% for hypoxemia (<50 mm Hg) and 71% to 92% for hyperoxemia (>80 mm Hg).25 Given this wide variability in sensitivity, PtcO2 should be used in conjunction with intermittent blood gas sampling to confirm levels of oxygenation and minimize unnecessary supplemental oxygen exposure.

Although PtcO2 monitoring offers the advantages of continuous oxygenation monitoring and increased stability during motion, it is limited by a slow response time and a reduced period in which reliable data can be acquired.25 In contrast to pulse oximetry, which can detect immediate arterial changes at the sensor site of the percentage of oxygen-bound heme, PtcO2 monitoring must account for a 16- to 30-second time delay, the time needed for oxygen to diffuse through the capillaries and across the sensor membrane. During SpO2 probe placement, oxygen saturation measurements can be immediately acquired after detection of an adequate plethysmograph waveform with no need for relocation of the probe. In contrast, a delay of approximately 15 minutes needed to heat the transcutaneous probe compounded with multiple site locations to reduce the risk of burns can lead to a large percentage of the monitoring period without measurements of oxygenation. Given these limitations, pulse oximetry is considered the most widely accepted modality for continuous measures of oxygenation in the neonatal intensive care setting.

### Near-Infrared Spectroscopy

In contrast to pulse oximetry, which measures arterial oxygenation, near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) measures oxygen uptake in the tissue. This technology has been used in a variety of organ systems, with a particular interest in cerebral oxygenation in the preterm infant population. NIRS relies on the presence of chromophores, compounds whose absorption of NIR light is dependent on oxygen status, in the tissue. These chromophores include cytochrome aa3, myoglobin, and the most often studied, hemoglobin. Using light absorption properties of oxyhemoglobin (HbO2) and deoxyhemoglobin (HHb) in the IR range (700–1300 nm), NIRS measures the difference between the oxygen delivered and the oxygen extracted by the tissue. This measurement is also known as regional oxygen saturation (rSO2), where

rSO2 = HbO2/ (HbO2 + HHb)

Cerebral NIRS entails a probe placed on one temple of the infant’s head with a laser or LED probe as a source of NIR wavelength transmission. The lasers/LEDs are pulsed in sequential order where multiple photodetectors, attached to the opposite temple, collect the transmitted light photons

that are not absorbed in the tissue. An additional reference signal is used to correct for light reflected from the skin, laser drift, and skin coloration. By measuring the difference between the amount of light transmitted through the deep tissue and the surface path, NIRS values can estimate the amount of spectral absorption that occurs in the tissue bed. Spatial resolution is currently limited to approximately 1 cm2 with several layers of tissue, including skin, skull surface vasculature, and gray matter in one two-dimensional sample. The current primary target area is restricted to the surface of the cortex, because access to deeper brain structures would require lasers of increased intensity and risk of damage to brain tissue. Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) values have been shown to correlate with cerebral venous saturation with improved precision with increased tissue homogeneity.26 However, overall comparability and reproducibility of different NIRS devices remain poor. This may be because of manufacturer-specific variations in design that include the source of monochromatic light, the number and specific wavelengths used, the frequency of light cycling, and the frequency at which the signals are updated for digital display. Modifications in sensor geometry27 and adjustments for the variability in arterial blood pressure28 may have promise in improving precision.

An international standard has been recently issued by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) that should improve differences between manufacturers.29 Nevertheless, interpretation of absolute measurements of rSO2 is still the subject of ongoing research. Average cerebral oxygen saturation values of 77.9% ± 8.5% have been recorded in healthy term newborns30 with a normative range of 55% to 85% in extremely preterm infants,31 but rSO2 can be influenced by gestational age,32 body position,33 and age at the time of study.32,34 There has been some suggestion that alterations in neonatal cerebral oxygenation may be associated with clinical outcomes such as intraventricular hemorrhage, cognitive impairment, and mortality, whereas others have shown no relationship with any clinical characteristics.32 This is further complicated by improvements in oxygen saturation stability and time in target not always translating into improved cerebral oxygen tissue saturation.35 Given these findings, the role of NIRS in identifying etiologies of brain injury has yet to be determined, and more extensive research is needed before NIRS can be routinely used in the clinical neonatal setting. In extremely preterm infants, treatment guided by cerebral oximetry monitoring for the first 72 hours after birth was not associated with a lower incidence of death or severe brain injury at 36 weeks’ postmenstrual age than usual care.

### Carbon Dioxide

The presence of hypocarbia, hypercarbia, and fluctuations between states has been implicated with a wide range of neonatal morbidities, including chronic lung disease, intraventricular hemorrhage, and neurodevelopmental impairment,36,37 although optimal ranges require further investigation.38 For this reason, maintenance of normocarbia and avoidance


## PDF page 637

of extreme levels of arterial CO2 are imperative in preterm infants. As discussed, an arterial blood gas is the gold standard for assessing gas exchange, but it is intermittent, invasive, and may cause complications. During periods of respiratory instability in which oscillations in Paco2 are known to occur,39 arterial sampling or indwelling catheters may not be adequate. Under these conditions, continuous measurements of end-tidal or transcutaneous CO2 monitoring have become increasingly popular in the intensive care unit.

### End-Tidal Carbon Dioxide Monitoring

End-tidal CO2 monitoring originally used mass spectroscopy to estimate CO2 from samples of exhaled gas. Because of improvements in technology allowing for portable devices, IR spectroscopy is now the method of choice. IR spectroscopy is based on the principle that CO2 molecules absorb light in the IR wavelength of 4.26 μm. Light is transmitted through the sample using an IR emitter with light absorption measured with photodetectors. The amount of light absorbed in the given IR spectrum is then proportional to the concentration of CO2.

Capnography sensor designs fall into two categories: sidestream and mainstream. Sidestream systems require constant aspiration of expired gas, which may result in underestimation of CO2 readings in preterm infants with low tidal volumes. This incidence may be reduced with the development of microstream technology, which uses a refined spectrum of discrete wavelengths, allowing for extremely small sample volumes (15 μL) and a correspondingly lower sample rate of 50 mL/min.40 The advantage of the sidestream system is that it can be used on both spontaneously breathing and intubated patients. During intubation, sampling of gas at the distal end of the endotracheal tube is recommended to improve accuracy, although both proximal and distal measurements of the end-tidal pressure of carbon dioxide (Petco2) have been shown to provide acceptable estimates of Paco2 in relatively healthy infants with diminished performance in infants with more severe respiratory disease.41 Accuracy may be affected by water vapor or secretions occluding the adapter or condensation on the photo detector. This is eliminated by vertical positioning or the use of Nafion tubing, a semipermeable polymer that allows water to pass through and evaporate. Mainstream systems rely on gas passing through a wide chamber, or cuvette, placed in line with the patient circuit. As opposed to a remote device with sidestream systems, a miniature IR optical system is placed directly over the chamber. This allows for nearinstantaneous measurements in less than 500 ms. However, it is limited to intubated patients or patients with a closed circuit, that is, a sealed nasal/oral mask. Erroneous values caused by water condensation are reduced by slight heating of the cuvette. Additional factors that can contribute to measurement error for both sidestream and mainstream systems include temperature dependence, miscalibration, drift, noise, and pressure effects from the sampling system.

In addition to instrumental design, the accuracy of end-tidal CO2 monitoring is dependent on patient

characteristics. Petco2 has been shown to accurately estimate alveolar CO2 in healthy newborns,42 but the agreement is poor and negatively influenced by the presence and severity of pulmonary disease43 and inadequate gas exchange caused by atelectasis, V/Q mismatch, and chronic lung disease in bronchopulmonary dysplasia.44 Neonates have small tidal volumes and high respiratory rates, which often result in wide variations in end-tidal CO2 values and underestimation of true alveolar gas, also making it a prohibitive modality for estimating CO2 during high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV). Microstream capnography through a double-lumen endotracheal tube with specially designed software for HFOV has been introduced.45 Despite its limitations, the ability to detect extreme low and high CO2 levels may be of use for trending or screening patients for abnormal arterial CO2 values. End-tidal CO2 monitoring may also be used to guide respiratory support in the delivery room.46

Disposable colorimetric end-tidal CO2 detectors are an efficient method of verifying correct endotracheal tube placement in the newborn.47 When placed between the ventilator and endotracheal tube, the pH-sensitive chemical indicator (metacresol purple) changes from purple to yellow when exposed to expired CO2. The minimum and maximum CO2 concentrations needed to establish a color change are 0.54% (0.5 kPa) and 2% to 5% (2–5 kPa), respectively. Because neonatal extubation failure can have devastating consequences, calorimetric detectors can play a significant role in the intensive care unit. However, this device cannot detect hypocarbia, hypercarbia, right mainstem bronchus intubation, or oropharyngeal placement in spontaneous breathing patients.

### Transcutaneous Monitoring of Carbon Dioxide

Transcutaneous carbon dioxide tension measurements are based on the principle of CO2 diffusion through the skin. The sensor consists of a pH-sensitive glass electrode with an adjacent silver chloride reference anode covered by a hydrophobic membrane permeable to carbon dioxide and separated by a sodium bicarbonate electrolyte solution. Changes in pH are measured as carbon dioxide from the skin diffuses through the electrode membrane. These changes are then converted to corresponding Paco2 values.

Data assessing the relationship between Paco2 and transcutaneously measured partial pressure of CO2 (Ptcco2) in preterm infants have shown a wide variation in both slope and intercept values.48,49 Additional data by Martin et al. demonstrated a progressive increase in the difference between tcPco2 and Paco2 as Paco2 increased (tcPco2 − Paco2, 5 ± 4 mm Hg and 9 ± 6 mm Hg in normocapnia and hypercapnia, respectively).50 These data suggest that as Paco2 increases, there may be an imbalance between CO2 production and removal. This can be attributed to multiple factors, including metabolic events in the skin, circulatory disturbances that permit gas to accumulate in the tissues, the anaerobic heating coefficient of blood, and increased CO2 tension with higher electrode temperature.

The use of heated Ptcco2 electrodes entails a risk of skin damage caused by burns that require repeated repositioning of the sensor. ### Respiratory Monitoring

Respiratory instability in the preterm infant can be attributed to immaturity of the central nervous system and a highly compliant chest wall, resulting in both central and obstructive apnea. During normal respiration, the diaphragm contracts, expanding the thorax in conjunction with activation of accessory muscles that stabilize the rib cage and maintain upper airway patency. Because of the highly compliant chest wall of the preterm infant, any loss of accessory muscle tone, including intercostals stabilizing the rib cage or hypoglossus maintaining upper airway patency, may result in instability and retraction of the rib cage in response to negative pressure generated by the diaphragm during inspiration. As a result, asynchronous or paradoxical chest wall movements will occur with partial airway obstruction, which is a common respiratory pattern in the preterm infant, particularly during rapid eye movement sleep. During extreme occasions, total airway obstruction may occur, presenting as asynchronous chest wall and abdominal efforts and no corresponding airflow. Respiratory pauses may also arise because of decreased central respiratory drive, as can occur during periods of periodic breathing and spontaneous central apnea. Therefore ideal respiratory monitoring should have the ability to detect both central and obstructive apnea.

### Flow Sensors

The pneumotachometer is considered the gold standard for measuring flow and volume and is most often used during mechanical ventilation and calculations of respiratory mechanics. There are two types of pneumotachometers: fixed orifice and laminar flow. The fixed orifice design consists of a fixed orifice placed within the tubular attachment placed in the airway. The differential pressure is measured across the fixed orifice, which is proportional to the square of the flow rate. This mathematical relationship can then be used to calculate a given flow. The laminar flow design consists of a simple compartment containing a resistive element, usually

consisting of a mesh screen or capillary network. The pressure drop across the resistive element is linearly related to the flow passing through the compartment and can be calibrated accordingly. The range in which there is a linear relationship between pressure and flow will be dependent on the design of the device, including the length, width, and type of resistive element used. To maintain precision, all flow must pass through the device, which may be problematic during mechanical ventilation in preterm infants with a high occurrence of endotracheal tube leaks. During spontaneous respiration, the pneumotachometer must be incorporated into a nasal/oral mask. To minimize the effect of the mask on the respiratory pattern, the mask design should include minimal dead space, the ability to flush the mask to reduce CO2 retention, and low resistance to minimize work of breathing.

Pneumotachometer use in the clinical setting has been limited to pulmonary function measurements in spontaneously breathing patients, incorporated into a sealed nasal/ oral mask, or tidal volume measurements when attached to the endotracheal tube in mechanically ventilated patients. During these periods, the device may add a significant resistive load, especially in severely ill ELBW infants. As a result, many companies have replaced the pneumotachometer with the hot-wire anemometer for volume measurements during mechanical ventilation. The hot-wire anemometer includes a heated element placed in the airway circuit. As flow passes, the sensor is cooled. The system delivers an electrical current to maintain the default sensor temperature. The amount of current needed to maintain the sensor temperature can be calibrated to a given flow. If bidirectional flow is desired, a second wire can be placed in the system. Accurate measurements of flow may be compromised if secretions accumulate on the heated element. However, because of its high-frequency response, proven accuracy, and minimal resistive load, the hot-wire anemometer is a promising modality for measurements of respiration in the preterm infant, including periods of high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV).55

Although the pneumotachometer and hot-wire anemometer give quantifiable measurements of flow and volume, additional devices, such as thermistor/thermocouple sensors and end-tidal CO2, can display qualitative estimates. The relationship between peak-to-peak amplitude of the thermistor signal and actual measures of flow has been shown to be nonlinear and frequency dependent.56 There is also minimal correlation between Petco2 and actual measures of volume. Therefore the implementation of thermistor or Petco2 monitoring is limited to the sleep lab, where, used in conjunction with chest wall motion sensors, it can be used to identify the presence or absence of flow associated with central and obstructive apnea.

### Other Respiratory Monitoring Devices

Despite concerns regarding the accuracy of impedance-based apnea monitoring,57 impedance technology continues to be the most widely used modality for measuring respiration in


## PDF page 639

the hospital setting. With two electrodes placed on either side of the chest above and below the insertion of the diaphragm, impedance monitoring measures changes in electrical impedance across the thorax during a breath. Specific placement of electrodes for optimal signal quality can vary between infants. This modality is based on the principle that air has a much higher level of impedance than tissue. During inspiration, there is a decrease in conductivity (and corresponding increase in impedance), owing to both an increase in gas volume of the chest in relation to the fluid volume and increased length of the conductance path with chest wall expansion. Using a high-frequency current of greater than 25 kHz, the same electrodes used for measuring ECG can be used for detection of respiratory efforts. The ECG waveform is filtered out by manufacturer-based signal processing algorithms, thus eliminating this potential source of noise artifact. However, changes in thoracic blood volume may be falsely identified as a breath. In addition, proprietary algorithms cannot distinguish obstructive efforts from normal respiration with no monitor alarm during obstructive apnea as air moves from one compartment to the other.

Impedance-based apnea detection is both poorly sensitive and predictive in preterm infants,57 but there are advancements in machine learning methods and application of impedance technology. For example, recent developments using hidden Markov-based models have identified robust algorithms that can identify or predict apnea with accompanying bradycardia and/or hypoxemia58,59 and may be a first step toward personalized risk assessment for severe clinical events during hospitalization and after NICU discharge. Ongoing advances in impedance technology, notably electrical impedance tomography (EIT), also show great promise in identifying continuous high-resolution images of gas distribution throughout the lung. Small alternating currents applied sequentially through 8 to 32 electrodes placed circumferentially around the thorax are reconstructed into one image. Sequential images are compared to a baseline, and variations over a given time interval represent alterations in ventilation distribution across the region. EIT is currently used as a noninvasive and radiation-free imaging tool providing data on lung collapse, overdistension, and air distribution in mechanically ventilated patients60 but may have a future role in bedside impedance monitoring by identifying obstructive apnea in spontaneously breathing infants.

Respiratory inductance plethysmography (RIP) has been used extensively in both clinical research and pulmonary function lab settings. It is currently not used at the bedside but could be a promising alternative for respiratory monitoring. As with impedance, it is a noninvasive method of measuring respiration with two bands wrapped around the chest and abdomen, respectively. Each band contains a sinusoidal inductance coil with a small AC current that travels through the coil, as opposed to through the chest wall, as occurs with impedance. RIP relies on the principle that a current applied through a loop of wire generates a magnetic field (Faraday’s law) and that a change in the area enclosed by the loop generates an opposing current directly proportional to the change in area (Lenz’s

law). Thus, as the chest wall expands, the coil in the band elongates, altering the magnetic properties, or inductance, of the band. The strength of this modality is the representation of respiration as a two-dimensional model. Thus obstructive apnea will present as asynchronous, 180-degree out-of-phase movements between the rib cage and abdomen as air flows from one compartment to the other. With the addition of a software algorithm to calibrate the rib cage and abdominal waveforms, a semiquantitative volume waveform can be acquired, giving RIP the ability to identify obstructive apnea without the need for an oral/nasal flow sensor (Fig. 37.5).

A small cohort study of moderately preterm infants has shown that transcutaneous diaphragm electromyogram (dEMG) activity is feasible in the delivery room as a useful indicator of respiratory rate, heart rate, and diaphragm activity. Heart rate (dEMG) measures showed high to moderate agreement with ECG and pulse oximeter values, respectively, with modest agreement between respiratory rate (dEMG) and direct measures of airflow.61 Neural measures of electrical diaphragmatic activity (Edi) using an orogastric catheter provide another EMG-based alternative to respiratory monitoring and are part of the standard procedure during noninvasive ventilation with neurally adjusted ventilatory assist support (NIV-NAVA).62 Further investigations of the addition of respiratory efforts, as denoted by EMG amplitude, could lead to a better understanding of respiratory physiology and optimization of respiratory support.

Overall, the current technology for respiratory monitoring contains many obstacles for newborn infants, including cumbersome sensors and wiring that compromise clinical care, skin integrity, and overall infant comfort. Ongoing developments in wireless and inexpensive polyvinylidenefluoride sensors with complementary metal-oxide semiconductors integrated circuitry use both pyroelectric and piezoelectric properties and are small enough to be incorporated into a nasal cannula or patient mattress.63 Acoustic sensors placed on the neck region, carotid vessel complex, and nasal region and contactless ultrawideband pulse radar sensors are also being investigated as alternative modes for measuring respiration. Preliminary data suggest that these prototypes can detect respiration in an ideal, experimental environment, but many challenges need to be overcome before they can be implemented in the NICU setting.

### Future Directions

The need for advanced diagnostic systems, including cardiorespiratory monitors, in neonatal care continues to expand. This growth should incorporate the development of safe and effective devices for use in the NICU and a collaborative research and testing effort among the biomedical engineering disciplines. Areas in which improvements are needed include the development of “smart alarms” for cardiorespiratory monitoring, education of personnel pertaining to the use of equipment, automated signal quality assessment, wireless technology, and electronic storage of longitudinal waveforms. As physicians continue to be bombarded with physiologic data from bedside monitors, current clinical practice uses only a fraction of the information available for patient care. For instance, pulse oximetry waveform extrapolation is limited to simple values of baseline oxygen saturation and time in various target ranges. Future exploitation of these various waveforms may include identification of subtle pathologic heart rate cross-correlation factors6 and SpO2 waveform patterns,64 maintaining normocapnia,65 and the use of automated feedback controllers66 to avoid or alert caregivers of high-risk patterns associated with adverse outcomes. Key Points

• Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring plays a crucial

role in stabilizing oxygenation and ventilation in preterm infants. • Neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) protocols of oxygen

and carbon dioxide monitoring must include a practical balance between accuracy and noninvasive acquisition.

The major challenge for development and application of high-risk predictive models to the clinical setting requires large-scale centralized and automated storage of waveforms and development of integrated systems incorporating multiple physiologic parameters from electronic patient database records while protecting patient confidentiality. Current trials are attempting to meet this challenge by reducing this vast amount of data into a comprehensible parameter that is useful for clinical practice.

title: Diagnostic Imaging of the Neonate

paragraphs.text: 38 Diagnostic Imaging of the Neonate
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Diagnostic imaging is integral to the evaluation of neonates with medical and surgical conditions. Understanding the advantages and shortcomings of imaging modalities, as well as the most recent practice patterns, facilitates the selection of appropriate imaging. This chapter begins with an introduction to the benefits, risks, and limitations of relevant imaging modalities. The remainder of the chapter reviews the imaging approach to common neonatal diseases according to organ system. This discussion highlights the imaging appearance of normal anatomy and common neonatal pathologies.
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: Digital radiography is the most common imaging technique used in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU), with many infants having multiple radiographs during their stay. These images, largely of the chest and abdomen, provide critical information about life-support device placement, acute lifethreatening conditions such as tension pneumothorax and bowel perforation, and disease response to medical and surgical interventions. To generate these important diagnostic images, digital radiography—along with fluoroscopy and computed tomography (CT)—uses low doses of ionizing radiation.
paragraphs.heading: Digital Radiography, Fluoroscopy, and Computed Tomography

paragraphs.text: Substantial scientific data show that high-energy photons from ionizing radiation can damage DNA when delivered at high doses. These effects occur at many multiples of the doses received in diagnostic medical imaging and natural background exposure. Although children are more radiosenstive than adults (i.e., the cancer risk per unit dose of radiation is higher) and have longer lifetimes over which to express a radiation-induced genetic mutation, adaptive DNA repair mechanisms appear to function well in children exposed to low doses of radiation.1 It is known that delivering doses at increments rather than all at once allows tissues
paragraphs.heading: Digital Radiography, Fluoroscopy, and Computed Tomography

paragraphs.text: to recover and that the risk from multiple serial exams is not cumulative.2 As ionizing radiation is among the potential iatrogenic harms to which neonates and their parents and caregivers may be exposed, it is important to understand how dose is measured, as well as how dose is optimized in neonatal radiographic, fluoroscopic, and CT imaging.
paragraphs.heading: Digital Radiography, Fluoroscopy, and Computed Tomography

paragraphs.text: The average annual effective dose of natural background ionizing radiation in the United States is 3 milliSeiverts (mSv), with a range from 1 to 20 mSv. At these background doses, there is no direct evidence of harm.3 Estimation of the exposure to medical radiation in the NICU has been reported using modern digital radiographic techniques. These studies report effective dose ranges from 0.012 to 0.016 mSv per radiograph.4,5 Even the highest reported total radiation doses during a NICU stay are less than the annual natural background effective dose. In order to help caregivers better understand dose metrics, use of a relative risk descriptor comparing medical radiation dose to natural background dose is helpful. Because of the complexity of scientific dose metrics, the background equivalent radiation time (BERT) was designed to educate the general public about radiation dose without complex concepts or terminology. Based on the BERT relative risk descriptor, a single portable radiograph of the chest would be the equivalent of about 1 day of natural background radiation (Table 38.1).6
paragraphs.heading: Digital Radiography, Fluoroscopy, and Computed Tomography

paragraphs.text: Another concern that arises in the NICU is the significance of scatter or secondary radiation in the vicinity of a radiographic exposure.7 Scatter radiation occurs when the beam intercepts an object—most frequently the patient’s body—and causes the x-rays to be scattered. The radiation dose from scatter is a very small fraction of the dose received from the primary x-ray beam. An important principle of dose reduction is the inverse square law, a property of physics stating that, if one doubles the distance from the primary radiation source, the dose is reduced by a factor of four. To minimize the scatter radiation dose to caregivers, parents, and neighboring patients in the NICU, these individuals should be positioned at least 1 meter from the irradiated field; at this distance, the primary scatter radiation is estimated to represent approximately 0.1% to 0.2% of the
paragraphs.heading: Digital Radiography, Fluoroscopy, and Computed Tomography

paragraphs.text: incident radiation. If health care personnel are required to be within 1 meter of the radiation field, they should wear a lead apron.
paragraphs.heading: Digital Radiography, Fluoroscopy, and Computed Tomography

paragraphs.text: Commonly performed fluoroscopy procedures in the newborn, such as an upper gastrointestinal (UGI) series, contrast enema, or voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG), can be performed at doses between 0.5 and 2.0 mSv. Although performed far less frequently, CT is also performed at low radiation doses; most head and body CT scans can be performed at a dose less than 2 mSv. Current epidemiological evidence supporting future cancer risk or mortality from medical imaging using low-dose radiation (below 100 mSv ) is inconclusive.8 In the absence of data confirming a causal relationship between low-dose radiation exposure and cancer, parents and providers should be reassured that the benefits of a medically necessary exam far exceed any potential future cancer risk.9 Even so, current recommendations advise performing only medically necessary exams and limiting radiation exposure to doses that are as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA).10 Such steps include using patient size–based tube current and tube voltage, paying attention to patient positioning, artifact removal, and beam collimation.
paragraphs.heading: Digital Radiography, Fluoroscopy, and Computed Tomography

paragraphs.text: Since the first patient scan in 1971, CT use has increased rapidly because of this modality’s excellent diagnostic accuracy, availability, short acquisition time, and cost-effectiveness. With this expansion in application, CT scientists have adapted the technology for child-size protocols that automatically adjust exposure based on patient size and reduce dose by using features such as iterative reconstruction.11 As hypothetical predicted cancer risks from CT are extremely low, the “anticipated benefits to the patient are highly likely to outweigh any small potential risks.”8
paragraphs.heading: Digital Radiography, Fluoroscopy, and Computed Tomography

paragraphs.text: Infants requiring a CT scan of the brain or body are typically scanned without sedation, as image acquisition times are usually less than 5 seconds. Intravenous iodinated contrast media (ICM) may be administered to evaluate for cardiovascular abnormalities, neoplasm, or infectious disease. In the absence of known renal failure, neonates show no increased risk for renal toxicity after receiving ICM.12 A rare reported side effect of the administration of ICM is transient hypothyroidism. Risk factors that increase the likelihood of transient hypothyroidism include low birth weight, prematurity, and the presence of cardiac or other conditions requiring care in neonatal or pediatric intensive care units. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) recently issued a recommendation to monitor infants and toddlers under the age of 3 years for hypothyroidism or a temporary decrease in thyroid hormone levels following exposure to ICM.13 The American College of Radiology (ACR) reviewed the research studies cited by the FDA and determined the “risk of clinically-relevant hypothyroidism related to ICM to be quite low in the pediatric population under three months of age, and minimal to absent in children three months of age and older.” The ACR suggests that the decision to perform thyroid function testing following intravascular contrast material exposure should be on a “patient-by-patient basis following the review of that patient’s specific risk factors” and “universal testing in all young children is not warranted nor supported by the literature at this time.”14
paragraphs.heading: Digital Radiography, Fluoroscopy, and Computed Tomography

paragraphs.text: Once a mainstay of patient radiation protection, gonadal shielding for radiography, fluoroscopy, and CT has been reexamined by the scientific community. In light of the most current scientific literature, the American Association of Physicists in Medicine (AAPM), ACR, Health Physics Society, Radiologic Society of North America, and Image Gently and Image Wisely recommend discontinuation of the use of patient gonadal shielding as a routine practice.15 Use of these shields during diagnostic imaging may obscure anatomic information, compromise the diagnostic efficacy of the exam, and result in a second exposure. Further, shields that are detected by automatic exposure controls of an imaging system can result in an increase in the patient’s radiation dose: “Because of these tangible risks and minimal to nonexistent benefit associate with fetal and gonadal shielding, the AAPM recommends that the use of such shielding should be discontinued.”15 Because patient shielding has been used for more than 70 years, this recent shift in practice may result in questions from health care providers and parents. The AAPM has prepared a list of frequently asked questions to help health care providers address common concerns about the discontinuation of lead shielding (Box 38.1).2
paragraphs.heading: Digital Radiography, Fluoroscopy, and Computed Tomography

paragraphs.text: Following radiography, sonography is the most common imaging examination performed in the neonate. Ultrasound
paragraphs.heading: Ultrasound

paragraphs.text: is particularly suitable for newborns because of its low cost, accessibility, portability, lack of ionizing radiation, and absence of known health risks. Technologists capture both static and cine images characterizing flow dynamics with color and spectral Doppler without the need for sedation. High-quality sonographic images are far more dependent on operator skill and experience than any other imaging modality. Knowledge of both normal and abnormal anatomy, identification of optimal viewing windows, and appropriate selection of ultrasound probes of varying frequencies are essential for obtaining diagnostic images. Small, handheld ultrasound devices now offer the opportunity for rapid, real-time, acute point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) diagnostic imaging to be performed and interpreted by bedside clinicians.16 Because sound waves travel poorly through air and calcified structures, sonographic imaging is limited if obscured by gas-filled bowel, aerated lung, or overlying bone. Other disadvantages of ultrasound are the relatively
paragraphs.heading: Ultrasound

paragraphs.text: low spatial resolution and limited field of view relative to CT and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
paragraphs.heading: Ultrasound

paragraphs.text: Although ultrasound remains the screening modality of choice in the prenatal period, MRI has become a valuable adjunct to identify at-risk infants who may benefit from in utero intervention, as well as to prepare for optimal perinatal management. In the postnatal period, MRI can provide vital detailed information that ultrasound and CT cannot—particularly in the diagnosis of traumatic or anoxic brain injury, vascular malformations, and congenital anomalies. Intravenous gadolinium-based contrast agents (GBCAs) may be used without risk of renal toxicity in infants without known renal failure.12 Gadolinium deposition has been identified in the brain tissue of patients receiving multiple GBCA doses over their lifetimes. Although there are no known adverse clinical consequences associated with gadolinium deposition, additional research is warranted, and it is “prudent to consider the clinical benefit of the diagnostic information or treatment result that MRI or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) may provide against the unknown potential risk of gadolinium deposition in the brain for each individual patient.”17 Despite scan times that may exceed 30 minutes, the majority of infants under 3 months of age can be scanned without sedation using the “feed and swaddle” technique.18,19 Careful attention must be taken to ensure that monitors and leads are not only MR safe but also free of white noise emissions that can degrade image quality. Infant hypothermia during MRI is common if not proactively managed.20 In the MRI suite, infants should be swaddled with blankets and wear a cap and, if possible, arrive in an MRI-compatible isolette. The most significant barrier to MRI use is the need to travel to the radiology department MRI suite, which frequently is not in close proximity to the NICU. Dedicated infant-sized MR scanners designed to be housed in the NICU may offer a solution to the risks of transport and minimize the disruption of care for critically ill neonates.21,22 A recent study suggests that in-NICU MRI has the potential to be a valuable clinical tool. Specifically, in a cohort with conventional 3T MRI for comparison, in-NICU MRI provided images with similar diagnostic yields.22
paragraphs.heading: Magnetic Resonance Imaging

paragraphs.text: Nuclear medicine contributes to the care of newborns with congenital anomalies, infection, and neoplasm. The radiopharmaceuticals used are nonallergenic and show no toxic effects. The radiation dose for most exams is between 0.6 and 5.5 mSv, in the range of CT imaging. Although most studies require that the patient remain still for a relatively long period of time, most neonates can be imaged without sedation. As with CT and ultrasound, these exams require
paragraphs.heading: Scintigraphy

paragraphs.text: patient transport to the nuclear medicine suite of the radiology department.
paragraphs.heading: Scintigraphy

paragraphs.text: POCUS is an emerging imaging modality in neonatology. Bedside providers perform POCUS to answer a focused clinical question, often in a clinical situation requiring rapid assessment. POCUS is intended to complement the physical exam and is not meant to replace the comprehensive exams performed by cardiologists and radiologists. Similar to conventional ultrasonography, the quality of the study and the information obtained are operator dependent. Neonatal POCUS can be used for both procedural and diagnostic applications, and the level of required training varies based on the indication.23 Significant limitations to the broad adaptation of neonatal POCUS in the United States are the limited training opportunities and the lack of consensus regarding the credentialing process.24–26 The credentialing process for clinician-performed ultrasound is more formalized in some other countries, such as through the Australasian Society for Ultrasound in Medicine in Australia.
paragraphs.heading: Point-of-Care Ultrasound

paragraphs.text: Cardiac POCUS, also referred to as targeted neonatal echocardiography (TNE), can provide immediate information about the patient’s cardiac physiology to inform medical decision-making.27 Bedside providers trained in cardiac POCUS can use ultrasound for various cardiac indications, including determining the quality of myocardial function, identifying a hemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), visualizing ultrasonographic signs of pulmonary hypertension, assessing volume status, and detecting cardiac tamponade or pericardial effusion.25,28 Cardiac POCUS is particularly useful for serial monitoring of a patient’s condition and evaluating response to intervention.28 At this time in the United States, there is no national consensus on the extent of training one needs to be considered competent in cardiac bedside ultrasound. Required training and credentialing are typically decided at an institutional level; however, postfellowship training programs in advanced hemodynamics and TNE are available for interested providers.
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac

paragraphs.text: Although air does not allow the transmission of ultrasound waves, the artifacts seen on lung ultrasound allow it to serve as a valuable imaging tool.29 Lung pathologies identifiable by clinician-performed lung ultrasound include pneumothorax, pleural effusion, transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTN), respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), and meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS).30 The ultrasound findings used to diagnose a pneumothorax are the absence of lung sliding, presence of a lung point, absence
paragraphs.heading: Chest

paragraphs.text: of B lines, and seeing a stratosphere or barcode sign.31 In one study, lung ultrasound was superior to clinical evaluation and faster than obtaining conventional radiography,31 thus allowing clinicians to intervene earlier in potentially life-threatening situations.
paragraphs.heading: Chest

paragraphs.text: POCUS can be utilized to visualize intraventricular hemorrhages (IVHs). The usefulness of clinician-performed cranial ultrasound may be limited in detecting subtle changes, but it can guide clinical management when interpreted during an acute patient decompensation.29
paragraphs.heading: Neuroimaging

paragraphs.text: Abdominal indications for POCUS include assessing for free fluid in the abdomen. Trained providers can identify the largest area of fluid and verify that structures, such as the epigastric vessels, are outside the targeted area before performing ultrasound-guided paracentesis.32 POCUS can also be used to visualize the bladder, assess urinary retention, measure bladder volume, and provide direct ultrasound guidance during suprapubic aspiration.
paragraphs.heading: Abdomen

paragraphs.text: POCUS has been shown to be accurate in confirming the position of umbilical catheters and peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs).33,34 Randomized studies have demonstrated that bedside ultrasound results in a decrease in the time needed for catheter placement, line manipulations, and number of radiographs required.33,35 POCUS has good agreement with conventional radiography for both umbilical and PICC lines.34 Similar to central venous lines, POCUS improved overall success rates and decreased the number of attempts required for peripheral arterial lines in randomized controlled trials of anesthesiology providers.36,37
paragraphs.heading: Vascular Access

paragraphs.text: Bedside ultrasound can be used during lumbar punctures using a static or dynamic approach. The static method uses ultrasound to identify the anatomical structures before the procedure, usually marking the appropriate entrance site with a sterile pen.32 The dynamic approach uses ultrasound to guide the needle into the cerebrospinal fluid space.32 POCUS is emerging as a useful adjuvant tool for diagnostic and interventional support in neonatology. Standardization of training and credentialing is urgently needed in the United States.
paragraphs.heading: Lumbar Punctures

paragraphs.text: Respiratory distress is the most common indication for imaging in the newborn. The chest radiograph plays an important role in the assessment of cardiopulmonary
paragraphs.heading: Chest

paragraphs.text: pathology in the neonate and young infant and is usually the initial examination of choice. Portable chest radiographs are obtained in the anteroposterior (AP) view with the infant lying supine. The arms should be extended away from the body or above the head, and the thighs should be immobilized. The chin should be visible on the upper margin of the exposure with the head in a neutral position without lateral rotation or neck flexion. With proper positioning, the radiograph should demonstrate symmetry of the clavicles and ribs and a midline appearance of the superior mediastinum. It is important to ensure proper patient positioning because a rotation-distorted image may obscure or mimic cardiac and pulmonary pathology. Further, leads and electrodes may also compromise image quality by obscuring regions of critical importance such as tube and line placement or small air leaks.
paragraphs.heading: Chest

paragraphs.text: Additional imaging modalities can be used to evaluate specific neonatal chest abnormalities. Sonography is useful in the assessment of diaphragmatic motion, pleural fluid, and catheter complications. Cross-sectional imaging with CT or MRI is useful for surgical and medical treatment planning for more complex thoracic conditions. Specifically, CT is the study of choice to evaluate parenchymal and mediastinal lesions. Both CT and MRI are useful in the evaluation of complex congenital heart conditions.
paragraphs.heading: Chest

paragraphs.text: Familiarity with the normal appearance of the newborn chest radiograph improves recognition of pathologic changes. Normal lungs appear primarily radiolucent and symmetric in volume. The pulmonary vessels are seen as branching, linear shadows that taper in size as they extend from the hilum to the lung periphery. Normal vessels decrease in size and number in the lateral half of the lung and are not visualized in the lung periphery. Normally collapsed, the pleural space is visualized only when it is distended from fluid, air, or pleural thickening. The heart borders should be distinct, and the diaphragm should be outlined clearly by aerated lung. The normal cardiac diameter on an AP radiograph should be less than 60% of the thoracic diameter. The normal thymus is visible in most newborns. Extremely variable in size and shape, it is composed of two asymmetric lobes and may therefore have an asymmetric appearance in chest radiography (Fig. 38.1). The “wavy” undulations of the lateral borders often silhouette a portion of the heart and can give the appearance of cardiomegaly (Fig. 38.2).
paragraphs.heading: Evaluating a Normal Chest

paragraphs.text: The positions of the endotracheal tube, enteric tube, and various arterial and venous catheters should be evaluated on all neonatal radiographs, as malpositioning may lead to complications. The endotracheal tube tip should overlie in the trachea between the medial ends of the clavicles and the carina. To prevent unplanned extubation, the position of the endotracheal tube can be digitally annotated on the
paragraphs.heading: Catheters, Tubes, and Lines

paragraphs.text: radiograph at the time of the exposure (Fig. 38.3). This way, the location of the tube is documented at the time of the radiograph in the event that the tube moves after the exposure. Intubation of the right mainstem bronchus is the most common site of tube malposition. The enteric tube should terminate in the stomach body, beyond the gastroesophageal junction.
paragraphs.heading: Catheters, Tubes, and Lines

paragraphs.text: Umbilical catheters can be easily identified by their characteristic paths. The umbilical venous catheter (UVC) courses superiorly and gradually posteriorly within the umbilical vein to intersect the left portal vein, continuing through the ductus venosus, left or middle hepatic vein, and then into the inferior vena cava (IVC). Its tip should be directed superiorly, ending at the right atrial (RA)/IVC junction. Malposition of the UVC within the liver is the most common complication and may result in portal vein thrombosis or portal hypertension. The umbilical arterial catheter (UAC) first extends inferiorly and posteriorly to the junction of the umbilical artery and internal iliac artery. The catheter then turns superiorly to course through the common iliac artery and aorta. The tip of the UAC should
paragraphs.heading: Catheters, Tubes, and Lines

paragraphs.text: also be directed superiorly, lying below the ductus arteriosus and above or below the visceral arteries. The UAC therefore may be placed in a high position, ending between T6 and T10, or in a low position, ending between L3 and L5. Malposition of the UAC may result in thrombosis of the aortic branches and possible ischemic injury.
paragraphs.heading: Catheters, Tubes, and Lines

paragraphs.text: The position of percutaneously placed catheters, including PICC lines and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) catheters, must also be documented. The tip of an upper extremity PICC line should lie within the superior vena cava (SVC) or at the RA/SVC junction. A lower extremity PICC line should end between the 9th and 12th ribs. An ECMO circuit may use a venous and an arterial catheter or a dual-lumen venous catheter. The venous catheter is inserted through the right internal jugular vein and ends in the RA. The arterial catheter is inserted into the common carotid artery and ends near the origin of the innominate artery. Complications of all vascular catheters include malposition, thrombosis, perforation, or infection.
paragraphs.heading: Catheters, Tubes, and Lines

paragraphs.text: RDS from surfactant deficiency is the most common cause of respiratory distress and a leading cause of morbidity in the premature infant. The typical radiographic appearance of RDS reflects generalized alveolar collapse and shows a finely granular or ground-glass pattern with diminished lung volumes. The severity of radiographic disease is variable and usually correlates with the severity of clinical disease. Mild radiographic disease is characterized by a finely granular pattern that allows visualization of normal vessels (Fig. 38.4), whereas severe disease
paragraphs.heading: Respiratory Disease: Medically Treated Respiratory Distress Syndrome

paragraphs.text: results in loss of defined heart borders and diaphragm, which is rarely seen today with current therapies (Fig. 38.5). Peripheral air bronchograms may be seen with severe disease because of air in the bronchi visualized against a background of alveolar collapse. The distribution of disease is usually diffuse and symmetric; however, patchy or asymmetric disease may be seen. The radiographic changes associated with RDS are often seen immediately after birth but can also develop over the first 6 to 12 hours of life. The radiographic abnormalities related to uncomplicated RDS should resolve by the time the neonate is 3 to 4 days old or sooner if surfactant therapy is given. Severe RDS on the initial radiograph in the first few hours of life has been proposed as being predictive of continuous positive airway pressure failure in extremely low birth weight infants.38 New diffuse worsening of bilateral opacities in the lungs may be seen with pulmonary edema or pulmonary hemorrhage. Sudden increase in focal opacity usually indicates atelectasis.
paragraphs.heading: Respiratory Disease: Medically Treated Respiratory Distress Syndrome

paragraphs.text: Chest radiography can be used to help assess the effectiveness of surfactant replacement therapy in infants with RDS. Typically, improvement in the appearance of the lungs is rapid and uniform after surfactant administration. In 80% to 90% of neonates treated with surfactant, improvement occurs in one or both lungs. When there is a partial response, the improvement may be asymmetric or even restricted to one lung. Explanations for asymmetric radiographic improvement following surfactant therapy include (1) maldistribution of surfactant, (2) insufficient surfactant, and (3) regional differences in lung aeration before surfactant treatment. The absence of radiographic improvement after surfactant administration is a poor prognostic sign and suggests a diagnosis other than surfactant deficiency. Surfactant-related
paragraphs.heading: Respiratory Disease: Medically Treated Respiratory Distress Syndrome

paragraphs.text: pulmonary hemorrhage may mimic RDS with focal or diffuse alveolar parenchymal disease.
paragraphs.heading: Respiratory Disease: Medically Treated Respiratory Distress Syndrome

paragraphs.text: A variety of air leaks can result from the high distending pressures of mechanical ventilation that may be required in the treatment of RDS. Alveolar rupture from overdistention results in pulmonary interstitial emphysema (PIE). The radiographic appearance of PIE includes small, rounded or linear lucencies representing interstitial air coursing along the bronchovascular sheaths (Fig. 38.6). These meandering radiolucencies may be diffuse or localized. Larger focal air collections, referred to as pseudocysts or pneumatoceles, may also form in the interstitium of the lung. Pulmonary interstitial emphysema can dissect into the mediastinum or the pleural space, resulting in a pneumomediastinum or pneumothorax. Radiographic signs of pneumomediastinum include (1) lateral displacement of the mediastinal pleura, (2) continuous diaphragm sign, and (3) superior elevation of the thymus, which is referred to as the spinnaker sail sign or angel wings (Fig. 38.7). Radiographic findings of pneumothorax include (1) increased lucency, (2) identification of the visceral pleural line (Fig. 38.8), (3) increased sharpness of the adjacent mediastinal border or hemidiaphragm, and (4) visualization of a deep costophrenic sulcus. Pneumothoraces may be seen bilaterally (Fig. 38.9). Lateral decubitus or cross-table lateral radiographs can be useful in the detection of small pneumothoraces. Large pneumothoraces can produce tension, resulting in contralateral shift of mediastinal structures and depression or eversion of the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm. Pneumopericardium, a life-threatening emergency, may be associated with air leaks in other locations. Neonatal pneumopericardium appears as a “halo sign,” a continuous band of air that conforms to the cardiac contour and does not extend beyond the level of the great vessels. (Fig. 38.10)
paragraphs.heading: Respiratory Disease: Medically Treated Respiratory Distress Syndrome

paragraphs.text: Neonatal pneumonias may be acquired in utero, during delivery, or after birth. Infection typically disseminates widely throughout the lungs because of incomplete formation of the interlobar fissures at this age. Diffuse granular or ground-glass opacities are often seen and are indistinguishable from RDS. Alternatively, coarse nodularity or a streaky, hazy appearance of the lungs may be seen. The presence of pleural fluid should raise the suspicion of bacterial infection, because effusions are uncommon in RDS or viral pneumonia.
paragraphs.heading: Neonatal Pneumonia

paragraphs.text: TTN is associated with retained lung fluid that may be associated with precipitous delivery or cesarean section. Typically a clinical diagnosis, TTN has a varied and nonspecific appearance. The radiograph may appear normal or show streaky, perihilar opacities and hyperinflation. Small pleural effusions may also be seen. A normal heart size with TTN
paragraphs.heading: Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn

paragraphs.text: helps distinguish retained fluid from pulmonary edema or heart failure. The radiographic and clinical findings of TTN have a benign course, usually resolving within the first 24 to 48 hours of life.
paragraphs.heading: Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn

paragraphs.text: Fetal aspiration of meconium causes obstruction of small airways with associated atelectasis and air trapping. Radiographic findings of MAS are seen within the first few hours of birth and include coarse, patchy, or nodular opacities and segmental hyperinflation (Fig. 38.11). The distribution of disease is bilateral and often asymmetric, and pleural effusion may be present. Complications include chemical pneumonitis, surfactant inactivation, pulmonary hypertension, and air-leak phenomena such as pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum.
paragraphs.heading: Meconium Aspiration Syndrome

paragraphs.text: In intubated patients, pulmonary hemorrhage is usually established by detecting blood in the endotracheal tube. The radiographic appearance of pulmonary hemorrhage is variable and nonspecific; small amounts of hemorrhage may not be visible, but more extensive hemorrhage results in focal or diffuse ground-glass opacities. Findings may mimic pneumonia or pulmonary edema. The radiographic changes from a single episode of pulmonary hemorrhage are usually transient, resolving within 24 to 48 hours.
paragraphs.heading: Pulmonary Hemorrhage

paragraphs.text: Chronic lung disease in the premature infant, which is referred to as bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), is most often seen in very low birth weight infants. BPD is also seen in higher birth weight infants following prolonged mechanical ventilation for conditions including neonatal
paragraphs.heading: Chronic Respiratory Disease of Prematurity

paragraphs.text: pneumonia, meconium aspiration, and congenital cardiac disorders. Pathologically, BPD is considered to be part of the group of alveolar growth abnormalities and can be recognized on imaging. Because BPD is the result of injury and repair of the immature developing lung, the pathologic and radiologic findings are affected by changes in therapy and the degree of prematurity of the infant. Chest radiograph findings of the later stages of BPD include hyperinflated lungs; asymmetric, coarse, patchy opacities; and bubbly cystic emphysematous changes (Fig. 38.12). Studies have related the cystic bubbly radiographic changes to a greater need for oxygen therapy.39 A large study with a cohort of more than 8000 infants showed that bubbly/cystic changes at 28 days were more predictive of home oxygen therapy than gestational age, birth weight, chorioamnionitis, or any other factor.40 Those without the bubbly/cystic changes had only a 2% rate of home oxygen.
paragraphs.heading: Chronic Respiratory Disease of Prematurity

paragraphs.text: Chest CT can provide detailed evaluation of the lungs for air-trapping, cysts, mosaic perfusion, and opacities, which can range from linear bands and small triangular opacities against the pleura to large confluent opacities. CT performed during tidal breathing and after removal of airway pressure support can document tracheobronchomalacia, which is present in 10% to 48% of neonates undergoing bronchoscopy.41
paragraphs.heading: Chronic Respiratory Disease of Prematurity

paragraphs.text: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is a complex life-threatening lesion caused by defective fusion of the pleuroperitoneal membranes during embryologic development. Patent pleuroperitoneal canals located posterolaterally are known as the foramina of Bochdalek. Bowel and solid organs may herniate through the foramen into the hemithorax, most commonly on the left side. At birth, the
paragraphs.heading: Respiratory Disease: Surgically Treated Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia

paragraphs.text: herniated bowel loops may be fluid filled, making radiographic diagnosis difficult. Eventually, gas-filled bowel loops are seen in the thorax with a paucity of bowel loops in the abdomen (Fig. 38.13). The ipsilateral lung is almost universally hypoplastic, and there is usually contralateral shift of the mediastinum, resulting in contralateral lung hypoplasia. However, partial aeration of the ipsilateral lung with a smaller hernia may also occur and may be difficult to distinguish from complete eventration (Fig. 38.14). In such cases, ultrasound can be used to evaluate for continuity of the hemidiaphragm. Prenatal sonography and fetal MRI (Fig. 38.15) allow early diagnosis and may predict neonatal survival by evaluating the degree of pulmonary hypoplasia and defining associated anomalies.
paragraphs.heading: Respiratory Disease: Surgically Treated Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia

paragraphs.text: Congenital lung malformations include congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM), congenital lobar overinflation (CLO), bronchial atresia, and bronchopulmonary sequestration (BPS). Most congenital lung malformations are hybrid lesions and share a common embryological origin with in utero airway obstruction and potential persistent embryological vascular supply. CPAMs are a group of congenital, hamartomatous cystic and noncystic lung masses characterized by overgrowth of the primary bronchioles, arrested alveolar development, and proximal communication with a defective bronchial tree.
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Lung Malformations

paragraphs.text: According to the classification system of Stocker et al.,42 there are five types of CPAMs based on the presumed site of maldevelopment. Type 0 is acinar dysplasia of tracheal or bronchial origin and is incompatible with life. Type 1, the most common, has a single or multiple large cysts (>2 cm) of bronchial or bronchiolar origin. Type 2 has a single or multiple small cysts (≤2 cm) of bronchiolar origin. Type 3 is predominantly solid with microcysts (<0.5 cm) of bronchiolar-alveolar duct origin. Finally, type 4,
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Lung Malformations

paragraphs.text: characterized by large air-filled cysts, has a distal acinar origin and is indistinguishable from pleuropulmonary blastoma on imaging.
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Lung Malformations

paragraphs.text: BPSs are lesions containing bronchial and pulmonary tissue that does not communicate with the tracheobronchial tree or pulmonary arteries. They can be extralobar
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Lung Malformations

paragraphs.text: (extrapleural) or intralobar (intrapleural), and supradiaphragmatic or infradiaphragmatic. These lesions will appear mostly solid, and a systemic feeding vessel is frequently identified. Ultrasound or MRI can confirm or exclude the presence of a systemic vessel arising from the aorta in the setting of a “hybrid” lesion.
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Lung Malformations

paragraphs.text: Prenatal sonography and fetal MRI classify CPAMs mainly based on the presence of macrocysts, microcysts, or solid tissue. At birth, chest radiography and CT may show a range of findings from large single or multiple air-filled cystic structures to solid lesions that resemble consolidation (Fig. 38.16A and B). Because of the association of CPAMs with sequestration, precise vascular mapping is essential. Ultrasound may be useful in identifying an abnormal vascular systemic supply typical of sequestration (see Fig. 38.16C). However, CT angiography with two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) reconstructions provides the most accurate assessment of the lung parenchymal and vascular anatomy of these lesions. For example, there are
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Lung Malformations

paragraphs.text: characteristic thoracic CT findings for combined bronchial atresia–CPAM congenital lung lesions. CT imaging shows a solitary, well-circumscribed solid and multicystic mass; a nonenhancing nodule reflects the bronchial atresia component, and an adjacent cystic mass represents the CPAM component.43
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Lung Malformations

paragraphs.text: CLO is a condition characterized by progressive overinflation of one or more pulmonary lobes. CLO most commonly affects the left upper lobe, followed by the right middle lobe and right upper lobe. At birth, the involved lobe may be radiographically opaque because of retained lung fluid. When the fluid clears, imaging demonstrates progressively increased volume, hyperlucency, and attenuated vascular markings of the involved lobe with compression of the remaining ipsilateral lung and mediastinal shift (Fig. 38.17). CT more precisely characterizes these findings and can distinguish multilobar involvement. CT is also helpful in excluding causes of extrinsic bronchial compression such as vascular anomalies or mediastinal.
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Lobar Overinflation

paragraphs.text: The pairing of the terms esophageal atresia and tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) describes a disorder in formation and separation of the primitive foregut and esophagus. A spectrum of malformations is noted, ranging from esophageal atresia (with or without a proximal or distal TEF) to a TEF without esophageal atresia. The most common type, involving proximal esophageal atresia with a distal TEF, accounts for more than 80% of cases. With this type, a blind-ending, air-filled proximal esophageal pouch is noted on a chest radiograph (Fig. 38.18). The presence of a distal fistula is supported by air in the gastrointestinal tract. An esophagram can be performed to evaluate for a fistulous tract or stricture. TEF is associated with multisystem abnormalities in approximately one-third of cases, including vertebral, cardiac, renal, and limb anomalies, as well as other
paragraphs.heading: Esophageal Atresia and Tracheoesophageal Fistula

paragraphs.text: gastrointestinal tract atresias. All infants with a tracheoesophageal abnormality should undergo additional imaging evaluation to assess for associated anomalies.
paragraphs.heading: Esophageal Atresia and Tracheoesophageal Fistula

paragraphs.text: Cardiac disease in infants is usually congenital in origin. Chest radiography rarely leads to a specific diagnosis and is primarily used to exclude pulmonary conditions as a cause
paragraphs.heading: Heart

paragraphs.text: of respiratory distress. Cardiac echocardiography remains the primary imaging tool for the diagnosis of congenital heart disease. Although POCUS is increasingly used at the bedside, it should not be used as a screening tool for congenital heart disease. Rather, POCUS offers valuable physiological and hemodynamic information to assist in real-time decision-making.16 Cardiac echocardiography may incompletely define extracardiac vasculature and associated airway involvement. Computed tomography angiography (CTA) and cardiac MRI/MRA complement echocardiography by illustrating not only vital extracardiac structures but also complex spatial relationships, anatomy, and function inadequately defined with echocardiography. MRI/MRA is the recommended modality for ventricular function, flow measurements, shunt quantification, valvular disease and cardiac masses, and postoperative evaluation (Fig. 38.19). CTA is recommended for evaluation of the coronary arteries, vascular rings, and associated pulmonary or airway anomaly.44
paragraphs.heading: Heart

paragraphs.text: High spatial and temporal resolution in cardiac CTA together with fast imaging times allow delineation of the cardiac anatomy, usually without the need for sedation. CT and CTA are particularly useful in evaluation of aortic arch anomalies (coarctation of the aorta, interrupted aortic arch, and vascular ring or sling) (Fig. 38.20A and B). Prospectively electrocardiogram-gated volumetric scanning with iterative reconstruction performed with a 320-multiple detector computed tomography (MDCT) scanner has several benefits in cardiovascular imaging of neonates and infants, including low radiation dose, improved image quality compared to retrospective gating, high diagnostic accuracy, and ability to perform freebreathing studies.45
paragraphs.heading: Heart

paragraphs.text: Plain-film abdominal radiography is a frequently performed examination in the high-risk neonate suspected of having intra-abdominal pathology. The exam is obtained in the AP projection with the infant supine. If there is concern for free air, a cross-table lateral view (with the infant supine) or a lateral decubitus view (with the infant turned on either their right or left side) will identify smaller amounts of air than the AP view. Air is seen in the stomach within minutes of birth, within most of the small bowel by 3 hours, and within most of the large bowel by 8 to 9 hours. Gas-filled normal bowel loops should appear polygonal in shape. Gas-filled loops of bowel that are conspicuously located in the central abdomen suggest the presence of ascites. A paucity of bowel gas may relate to fluid-filled bowel or bowel obstruction.
paragraphs.heading: Evaluation of the Normal Abdominal Radiograph

paragraphs.text: Intestinal obstruction is the most common abdominal emergency in the newborn period. Neonatal obstruction is typically characterized as high, occurring proximal to the distal ileum, or low, involving the distal ileum or colon. The clinical presentation of infants with high and low intestinal obstruction may overlap with symptoms of abdominal distention, vomiting, and poor feeding. Low obstructions are often characterized by failure to pass meconium. Abdominal radiographs are the initial imaging examination of choice to distinguish between high and low intestinal obstructions. Radiographs in infants with high intestinal obstruction
paragraphs.heading: Gastrointestinal Tract

paragraphs.text: typically show few dilated bowel loops (Fig. 38.21), whereas radiographs in infants with low obstruction show many dilated bowel loops (Fig. 38.22). When bowel obstruction is present, the dilated bowel loops become elongated and are stacked in a parallel configuration. The distinction between high and low intestinal obstruction dictates the type of imaging that the infant may need. With a high obstruction, the upper gastrointestinal (UGI) series is the examination
paragraphs.heading: Gastrointestinal Tract

paragraphs.text: of choice. Infants with a suspected low obstruction are typically evaluated with a water-soluble contrast enema. As with all radiologic examinations, proper positioning is important because even a small degree of patient rotation may distort anatomic landmarks.
paragraphs.heading: Gastrointestinal Tract

paragraphs.text: Midgut malrotation is the most critical etiology of upper intestinal obstruction. Most infants with malrotation present with bilious vomiting; up to 75% of patients present in
paragraphs.heading: High Intestinal Obstruction

paragraphs.text: the first month of life. Bilious vomiting in an infant should be considered a potential surgical emergency, and, in the absence of another defined cause, evaluation for midgut malrotation should be performed. The abdominal radiographic findings may be normal in infants with malrotation. A high obstruction pattern may be seen in the setting of abnormal peritoneal attachments (Ladd bands) or midgut volvulus. Dilatation of multiple bowel loops may indicate volvulus-induced ischemia. The diagnostic examination of choice is the UGI. The location of the duodenum seen on this study is predictive of the mesenteric attachment. Normally, the third portion of the duodenum (D3) courses posteriorly in the retroperitoneum, crossing the midline to reach the duodenal-jejunal junction (DJJ). This junction is normally located to the left of midline and at the level of the pyloric channel. An abnormal course of the duodenum and abnormal location of the DJJ are diagnostic of midgut malrotation (Fig. 38.23A). A spiral or corkscrew appearance of the duodenum and jejunum indicates midgut volvulus (Fig. 38.23B). The wrapping of the superior mesenteric artery around the superior mesenteric vein, known as the “whirlpool sign,” is specific for the diagnosis of midgut volvulus.
paragraphs.heading: High Intestinal Obstruction

paragraphs.text: Cross-sectional imaging with sonography or CT has been proposed as an alternative method to diagnose midgut malrotation by identifying the anatomic location of D3 and its relationship to the superior mesenteric vessels. However, a normal retroperitoneal position of D3 does not exclude malrotation, and the relationship of the mesenteric vessels is highly variable and unreliable.46 Because of the lack of sensitivity or specificity of cross-sectional imaging, UGI remains the gold standard for diagnosing midgut malrotation.
paragraphs.heading: High Intestinal Obstruction

paragraphs.text: Duodenal atresia is the most common cause of high intestinal obstruction in the newborn. It occurs more commonly
paragraphs.heading: High Intestinal Obstruction

paragraphs.text: than duodenal stenosis or web and results from congenital failure of recanalization of the duodenum during embryologic development. Because the majority of cases occur distal to the ampulla, infants often present with bilious vomiting.
