Ileal Atresia

Ileal atresia may be caused by a vascular accident similar to jejunal atresia or may result from other gastrointestinal anomalies such as meconium ileus. Abdominal radiographs in neonates with ileal atresia usually show a low intestinal obstruction pattern. Contrast enema demonstrates an unused microcolon and may be diagnostic if reflux of contrast into the distal ileum demonstrates the level of the atresia.

### Anorectal Malformation

Anorectal malformations (ARMs) represent a spectrum of abnormalities ranging from a rectoperineal fistula to very complex malformations such as a persistent cloaca and cloacal exstrophy. A persistent cloaca represents a fusion of the rectum, vagina, and urinary tract to create a common channel (or cloaca). This common channel may end in the perineum with one or more perineal openings. The type of cloaca is categorized by the length of the common channel that can be measured endoscopically. The length of the common channel can vary from 1 to 10 cm, and the longer the common channel (>3 cm), the higher the chance for poor bowel control, neurogenic bladder, and reproductive abnormalities.

### Necrotizing Enterocolitis

Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), seen predominantly in premature infants, is the most common acquired gastrointestinal emergency in the NICU. Infants usually present with abdominal distention, abdominal tenderness, feeding disturbance, and guaiac-positive stools. Abdominal radiography plays an important role in the diagnosis of NEC. Early radiographic findings of NEC are nonspecific and include bowel dilation and rounded or elongated loops. Focal or asymmetric distribution of fixed bowel dilation may be seen. As the disease progresses, intramural gas in the bowel wall, specific for pneumatosis intestinalis, develops.

Radiographically, pneumatosis intestinalis appears as a “bubbly” pattern or as curvilinear lucencies (Fig. 38.29). This somewhat mottled radiolucency can be difficult to differentiate from stool. Pneumatosis is most commonly seen in the right lower quadrant. Intramural gas may extend into the veins of the bowel wall and then into the portal venous system. Portal venous gas is seen in the porta hepatis as branching, linear lucencies overlying the liver (Fig. 38.30) and is typically a later finding in more severe cases of NEC. Like intramural gas, this finding may be transient and may not correlate with the severity of clinical disease.

### Biliary Atresia

A frequent clinical challenge is to differentiate biliary atresia from idiopathic neonatal hepatitis (INH), as both present with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. The principal difference between the two entities is that there is patency of the biliary tree in infants with INH. Sonography is the primary imaging examination for neonatal jaundice, as it can identify alternative etiologies such as choledochal cyst, biliary sludge, and cholelithiasis. The infant should be fasted for at least 3 hours to optimize visualization of a full gallbladder. The gallbladder in infants with biliary atresia might be small, measuring less than 15 to 19 mm when measurements are obtained in the fasted state.52 A normal gallbladder should measure 15 to 30 mm in infants younger than 1 year and should have a thin, defined wall.53,54 The gallbladder is not identified in approximately 80% of patients and is usually small, with an abnormal shape and abnormal wall in the remainder.55 In addition to an absent or abnormal, small, and irregular

gallbladder, other ultrasound findings may be present such as nonvisualization/absence of the common bile duct, presence of microcysts or macrocysts near the porta hepatis, increased hepatic artery diameter (>1.5 mm), peripheral arterialization, and polysplenia. A fibrous remnant of the obliterated biliary duct along the right portal vein may appear as a “triangular cord sign” when this tubular echogenic thickening measures greater than 3 to 4 mm. Although difficult to identify in the neonate, the triangular cord sign in combination with a gallbladder abnormality is reported to be 84% sensitive and 100% specific for biliary atresia.52

Hepatobiliary scintigraphy is a highly sensitive examination used to diagnose biliary atresia.56 The infant is pretreated with phenobarbital to enhance hepatocellular function and improve specificity. Gastrointestinal excretion of the administered isotope excludes biliary atresia, whereas lack of excretion of isotope by 24 hours is highly suggestive of the condition. Cholangiogram is the gold standard for the diagnosis of biliary atresia with findings showing absence of a gallbladder lumen, presence of an atretric gallbladder, or absence of contrast in the biliary ductal system and small bowel.

### Choledochal Cyst

A choledochal cyst is a congenital cystic dilation of the extrahepatic or intrahepatic biliary tree and is a rare cause of neonatal cholestatic jaundice. Biliary atresia should always be ruled out in these infants given the association of these entities and similar clinical presentations.53 Choledochal cysts are classified on the basis of their location, morphology, and the number of cysts. The Todani classification categorizes cysts based on the number, configuration, and location (intra- or extrahepatic) of the ductal dilation.57 Ultrasound is the initial imaging method used to evaluate the size and location of the cyst and to evaluate for additional cystic changes of the biliary tree. The sonographic and cross-sectional imaging appearance includes a focal, rounded, thinwalled cyst (Fig. 38.35A); fusiform dilation of the common bile duct; or cystic segments of the intrahepatic biliary tree (Fig. 38.35B). Magnetic resonance cholangiography is now the gold standard for the evaluation of choledochal cysts, as these images confirm the biliary origin of the cyst and assist with preoperative planning.

### Cholelithiasis

Approximately 10% of all cases of gallstones in children occur in the first 6 months of life. Neonatal cholelithiasis is associated with total parenteral nutrition, furosemide therapy, dehydration, infection, hemolytic anemia, and shortgut syndrome. Neonates who undergo parenteral nutrition are at greatest risk, and gallstones have been reported in up to 40% of such infants. The typical sonographic appearance of a gallstone is a rounded, mobile, echogenic focus within the gallbladder.

### Hepatic Calcifications

Isolated hepatic calcifications are relatively common in the fetal liver during prenatal sonography and may persist in the neonatal period. Neonatal calcifications may be solitary or multiple and are usually idiopathic. Intrauterine infections such as cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, rubella, herpes, syphilis, and varicella can result in both hepatic calcifications and ascites. Hepatic calcifications can also be seen in congenital malformations and aneuploidy. Subcapsular calcifications may be caused by emboli from the portal or hepatic veins. These may result from umbilical venous catheter complications. Perihepatic calcifications may be secondary to meconium peritonitis.

### Liver Tumors

The most symptomatic hepatic tumor in the neonatal period, infantile hepatic hemangioendothelioma (IHHE), is diagnosed in the first 6 months of life over 80% of patients. Prenatal and postnatal images show very similar findings, making the prenatal diagnosis highly accurate. At sonography, IHHE appears as a complex lesion with solid and complex fluid components and dilated hepatic vasculature; some contain flow in large anechoic vascular spaces and others can show a peripheral ring of vascular flow. IHHE is best evaluated with MRI, where flow voids may be seen in a heterogeneous lesion that enhances centripetally following gadolinium administration. Hepatoblastoma may also present in the newborn period as a soft tissue mass, frequently originating in the right hepatic lobe, which demonstrates heterogeneous enhancement (Fig. 38.36A and B).

### Urinary Tract

Sonography is the initial imaging examination used in the evaluation of urinary tract abnormalities both prior to and

following birth. Fetal MR may prove helpful in better characterization of genitourinary abnormalities, specifically in cases of bladder outlet obstruction and severe oligo-/anhydramnios58 due to its large field of view, higher image resolution, and better visualization of the renal parenchyma. Postnatal MR urography may be used to evaluate complex renal and urinary tract anatomy and suspected urinary tract obstruction; gadolinium-enhanced MR urography allows for functional evaluation that includes an estimation of differential renal function,59 although in many centers a mercaptoacetyltriglycine (MAG3) nuclear medicine study is performed in place of the functional MR urography.

Sonography is the imaging examination of choice for the initial evaluation of suspected urinary tract abnormalities in infants. The neonatal kidney typically demonstrates increased parenchymal echogenicity because of the relatively high number of glomeruli and the increased cellularity. In contrast to a child or adult kidney, the renal parenchyma is often isoechoic or hyperechoic relative to the liver and spleen. The increased parenchymal echogenicity persists until age 3 to 4 months. The neonatal kidney also demonstrates conspicuously hypoechoic pyramids because of the larger medullary volume present. This finding may persist until 1 year of age and should not be confused with a dilated collecting system.

### Multicystic Dysplastic Kidney

MCDK results from an insult in early embryologic development that leads to pelvic infundibular atresia. Infants with MCDK usually present with a unilateral palpable flank mass. The sonographic criteria for diagnosing an MCDK include multiple noncommunicating cysts of variable size and absence of renal parenchyma or collecting system (Fig. 38.40). Rarely, the MCDK appears as a single large cyst. Up to 50% of patients have a coexistent contralateral renal abnormality such as UPJ obstruction or vesicoureteral reflux. The natural history of an MCDK is a gradual decrease in the number and size of the cysts over several months or years as the cyst fluid resorbs.

### Nephrocalcinosis

Nephrocalcinosis refers to the deposition of calcium in the renal parenchyma, most commonly in the medullary pyramids. Most cases of medullary nephrocalcinosis in neonates are the result of increased calcium excretion related to furosemide therapy. This entity may also be seen in association with hypervitaminosis D and distal renal tubular acidosis. Nephrocalcinosis associated with furosemide therapy gradually resolves after the medication is stopped. Sonography is used to diagnose and monitor the evolution of the disease. Initial findings include increased echogenicity without acoustic shadowing in the normally hypoechoic renal pyramids (Fig. 38.42). Medullary nephrocalcinosis is typically seen diffusely throughout both kidneys. In the first few days of life, the normal neonatal kidney may also demonstrate transient increased echogenicity of the medullary pyramids. This finding is usually diffuse and bilateral and resolves within 10 days.

Conditions associated with adrenal hemorrhage include perinatal asphyxia, sepsis, coagulation disorders, hypotension, and surgery. Although unilateral involvement is more common, clinical manifestations are typically seen only when there is diffuse, bilateral gland involvement, resulting in adrenal cortical insufficiency.

Sonography is the examination of choice to evaluate for suspected adrenal hemorrhage. The sonographic appearance of adrenal hemorrhage is that of an oval or triangular solid mass of variable echotexture. There may be focal or diffuse involvement of one or both adrenal limbs. Adrenal calcifications may develop weeks to months after the hemorrhage. Large adrenal hemorrhages may be difficult to differentiate from a tumor, particularly if calcification is already present. In such cases, follow-up sonographic images show a gradual decrease in size over 1 to 2 weeks (Fig. 38.43).

### Neuroblastoma

Neuroblastoma is the most common neonatal neoplasm and may present in the prenatal or neonatal period. Although perinatal neuroblastoma most often arises from the adrenal gland, a primary lesion can arise from any site in the sympathetic chain. Sonography is usually the initial imaging examination of choice and demonstrates a solid or cystic suprarenal mass that may contain calcifications. CT or MRI offers more precise characterization of the organ of origin and is required for staging (Fig. 38.44). MRI can be useful to assess intraspinal extension. Iodine 123 (123I)-metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) is the first-line functional imaging agent used with uptake seen in 90% of neuroblastomas. 123I-MIBG identifies both the primary tumor and sites of metastatic disease. The addition of single-photon emission CT to 123I-MIBG improves characterization of uptake.63

### Brain

Sonography is the primary means of evaluating cranial and neck pathology in the newborn. The most frequent indication for cranial ultrasound is to evaluate for preterm brain injury in premature infants. Sonography is performed at the bedside through the anterior fontanelle with a highfrequency sector transducer.66 Imaging through the anterior fontanelle provides coronal and sagittal images of the near and far-field brain anatomy. Near-field images assess graywhite matter differentiation, extra-axial fluid compartment, meninges, and dural venous sinuses. Far-field images depict ventricles and cisterns and sulcal/gyral morphology. Imaging through the mastoid fontanelle best characterizes the

anatomy of the tentorium, brainstem, and occipital horns and improves detection of findings in the posterior fossa, such as cerebellar hemorrhage. Color, power, and spectral Doppler ultrasound techniques offer effective evaluation of morphology and flow characteristics of large intracranial arteries and veins for sinovenous thrombosis and vascular malformations. Newer scanners and transducers offer novel advanced imaging techniques such as microvessel imaging that may contribute functional insights impacting diagnostic and therapeutic decision-making.67 Evaluation of parenchymal, subarachnoid, and subdural abnormalities is limited on sonographic examination, and they are better characterized with cross-sectional imaging. CT is rarely used and should be limited for emergencies such as evaluation of intracranial hemorrhage and masses with increased intracranial pressure. MRI is used to optimally characterize congenital anomalies, infectious, and neoplastic processes. MRI is more sensitive for detection of cerebellar hemorrhage, even when mastoid views are performed on cranial ultrasound.68 MRI is also the gold standard for evaluation of preterm white matter brain injury but is performed less frequently in light of risks related to transport, need for sedation, and high cost. Although MRI provides optimal anatomic detail, the value of routine MRI screening of preterm infants at term-equivalent or discharge is questioned because findings do not correlate with long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes.69

Germinal matrix hemorrhage–intraventricular hemorrhage (GMH-IVH) is seen primarily in premature infants. Infants at highest risk are those with a gestational age of less than 32 weeks or a birth weight of less than 1500 g. Most hemorrhages occur by the first week of life. The site of origin for GMH-IVH is the caudothalamic groove, an area bordered by the ventricular surface of the caudate nucleus and the thalamus. The traditional classification system for GMH is based on the presence of subependymal hemorrhage and IVH, ventriculomegaly, and parenchymal abnormalities. Grade 1 is subependymal hemorrhage only; grade 2 is subependymal hemorrhage and IVH occupying 10% to 50% of the ventricular area; grade 3 is subependymal hemorrhage and IVH occupying at least 50% of the ventricular area; and grade 4 is periventricular hemorrhagic infarction. Periventricular infarcts are thought to be caused by compression of the periventricular veins by the subependymal hemorrhage. Not all IVH results from a GMH; choroid plexus hemorrhage and isolated hemorrhagic venous infarct are alternative etiologies for IVH in the preterm infant.

At sonography, a grade 1 hemorrhage appears as a subependymal echogenic focus inferolateral to the frontal horn of the lateral ventricle (Fig. 38.45). If the subependymal hemorrhage is large, it may efface the ipsilateral lateral ventricle. In grade 2 hemorrhage, blood is seen as echogenic material within the nondilated lateral ventricle (Fig. 38.46). In grade 3 hemorrhage, the IVH expands the ventricle, resulting in ventriculomegaly (Fig. 38.47). Grade 4 hemorrhage is characterized by additional echogenic periventricular abnormalities representing hemorrhagic venous infarct (Fig. 38.48).

Ventriculomegaly is a frequent sequela of intraventricular GMH that results from obliterative arachnoiditis or intraventricular obstruction from clot or debris. The ventriculomegaly may develop soon after the GMH or may be delayed by several weeks. Typically, the trigones and occipital horns of the lateral ventricles dilate before the frontal horns, and the lateral ventricles may dilate alone or to a greater degree than the third and fourth ventricles. The frontotemporal horn ratio has been demonstrated to be a useful twodimensional quantitative biomarker of vetriculomegaly in preterm infants and may help standardize ventricular measurements.70

### Periventricular Leukomalacia

Periventricular leukomalacia (PVL) represents infarction of deep white matter adjacent to the trigones and frontal horns of the lateral ventricles in premature infants. Infants with PVL may also have IVH. Cranial ultrasound performed soon after the infarction is most often normal. The earliest sonographic abnormality is increased periventricular echogenicity (Fig. 38.49). With progression of disease, cavitation may occur, resulting in parenchymal cystic areas (Fig. 38.50). These areas may communicate with the ipsilateral lateral ventricle, resulting in cyst wall collapse and ex vacuo dilatation of the subjacent ventricle. MRI is the most sensitive imaging modality for the assessment of PVL. Peritrigonal areas of hyperintensity are seen on T2-weighted images. The corpus callosum is often thinned or atrophic. In addition, irregularity of the lateral ventricular contour and asymmetric ventricular enlargement may be noted.

### Hypoxic Ischemic Encephalopathy in Term Infants

Hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy is a condition that may result in severe neurologic deficit. Cranial ultrasound may appear normal or show diffuse cerebral edema (Fig. 38.51A). MR with special techniques such as diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) plays a central role in early diagnosis and prompt intervention. DWI may show cytotoxic edema of hypoxic injury during the acute phase before signal intensity changes are evident on conventional T1- or T2-weighted images. Cytotoxic edema appears as high signal restricted diffusion on DWI and low signal on corresponding diffusion coefficient mapping (Fig. 38.51B). Diffusion restriction on DWI predicts a poor outcome.

### Lenticulostriate Vasculopathy

Lenticulostriate vasculopathy (LSV) describes the sonographic appearance of echogenic vessels in regions of the basal ganglia and thalamus. Since it was first described in 1988, LSV has been reported in 0.3% to 32% of populations studied. The incidence of LSV has been reported at 15% in neonates <32 weeks of gestational age.71 In the absence of other intracranial pathology, infants with isolated LSV show normal neurodevelopment, and no further imaging is needed. LSV was originally described in newborns with congenital TORCH infections (i.e., toxoplasmosis, other, rubella, cytomegalovirus, and herpes). ### Skeletal

### Intrauterine Infection

Intrauterine infection may involve the skeletal system. Congenital rubella and cytomegalovirus infection result in metaphyseal lesions with vertical striations that resemble a celery stalk. Congenital syphilis may cause both periostitis as well as single or multifocal metaphyseal lesions, which vary from radiolucent transverse metaphyseal bands to focal destruction and fragmentation of bone (Fig. 38.54).

### Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) may be seen in infants with breech presentation in the third trimester, a family history of dysplasia, or other orthopedic problems such as clubfoot and metatarsus adductus. Sonography is the examination of choice for screening infants with known risk factors or an abnormal exam up until 6 months of age. This screening dynamic ultrasound exam is optimally performed after 4 weeks of age when hip maturation improves exam specificity. After the child is 4 to 5 months old, ossification of the femoral epiphysis begins to obscure sonographic landmarks, and radiography becomes more reliable for detection of DDH. After 6 months of age, an AP radiograph of the pelvis with the hips in neutral position is recommended for both diagnosis and follow-up of treated DDH. ### Congenital and Developmental Anomalies

Skeletal radiography plays a primary role in the evaluation of congenital and developmental abnormalities of the axial skeleton and extremities. Imaging of a specific site is performed when there is a localized concern, such as craniosynostosis, congenital spinal deformity, radial ray abnormality, or scapular nondescent. When a skeletal dysplasia is suspected, a skeletal survey should be performed. This survey includes lateral views of the skull and spine, as well as AP views of the upper and lower extremities, pelvis, chest, and abdomen.

### Future Directions

Diagnostic imaging in neonates will continue to grow with advances in hardware and software technology. The increasing use of fetal MRI will facilitate earlier diagnosis and treatment of infants with conditions affecting the brain, spine, heart, chest, and abdomen. MRI evaluation of the newborn will grow with the use of faster sequences and functional imaging. High-quality neonatal body MRI will be possible with completely free-breathing body MRI protocols, obviating the need for breath-suspension, sedation, and general anesthesia. title: Anesthesia in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: 39 Anesthesia in the Neonate
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: The administration of anesthesia to the neonatal patient requires knowledge and understanding of neonatal anatomy and pathophysiology in addition to the ability to understand how the pharmacology of standard anesthetic drugs is altered in preterm and term neonates. Perioperative surgical anesthetic risk in children increases with decreasing age, making neonatal patients some of the most vulnerable patients anesthesiologists provide anesthetic care for. Anesthesia for these oftentimes critical patients is best performed by specialty-trained pediatric anesthesiologists, as anesthesia-related morbidity is reduced in children anesthetized by pediatric anesthesiologists compared with children cared for by non-pediatric anesthesiologists.1 The American College of Surgeons has developed standards recommending that children under the age of 2 years have anesthesia administered by a pediatric specialty-trained anesthesiologist.2
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: The goals of neonatal anesthesia are similar to those in adults but require different skills, knowledge, and care. The differences between adults and children are most profound in neonates, particularly premature infants. Advances in neonatology and the almost routine survival of infants weighing greater than 1000 g have led to new challenges for pediatric anesthesiologists. Successful anesthetic management in a neonate requires meticulous attention to detail and a thorough understanding of neonatal physiology and development, pharmacology, and pathophysiology. The neonatal period is characterized by immaturity of organ systems, homeostasis, and metabolic pathways. It is a time of major developmental changes, and the effects of anesthesia on that development are not well characterized. Knowledge of the anatomic and physiologic differences among neonates, children, and adults is critical to careful anesthetic administration and management. Maturity of organ systems and metabolic processes varies significantly not only between adults and neonates but also between preterm and term neonates.
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: Personnel, equipment, and the operating room environment need to be specifically adapted for neonates. Monitors, anesthesia delivery systems, mechanical ventilators,
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: and environmental controls all need to be appropriate for use with neonates.
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: It is important to emphasize the perioperative nature of anesthetic management. Anesthesia care does not start and end at the door to the operative suite, and this is as critical in neonates as in older children and adults. Preoperative medical status and current medical management strategies can affect intraoperative care. Transport to the operating room can be one of the most critical aspects of an operation in a premature neonate. The postoperative period requires close monitoring and management of ventilation, fluid balance, and an environment tailored to the special needs of neonates. Assessment and control of postoperative pain require methods and tools specific to neonates.
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: Surgery in neonates is accompanied by a humoral stress response that, left untreated, leads to increased complications and mortality, as shown in the landmark study by Anand and colleagues in 1987.3 This response is diminished by adequate anesthesia (Fig. 39.1, Table 39.1), resulting in improved surgical outcomes. Consequently, over the subsequent decades, adequate anesthesia for all surgical procedures in neonates has been accepted as both a clinical and an ethical imperative.
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: It is also now generally accepted that neonates are capable of sensing pain and discomfort. We have no recallable memories before 3 to 4 years of age (termed infantile amnesia), but neonates do possess consciousness and a sense of self and can form implicit memories—that is, changes in behavior based on prior experience that do not require intentional recall. Plasticity is an inherent characteristic of the developing nervous system, and early pain experiences can lead to exaggerated responses to later painful stimuli or stress, as well as impaired neurodevelopmental outcome.4,5 Activation of brain regions in response to graded moderate pain stimuli is significantly different in school-aged children and adolescents with neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) experience compared with controls, as measured by functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).6 Based on such evidence, the goals of anesthesia in neonates are not restricted to prevention of the stress response to surgery but also include effective management of pain and discomfort.7,8
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: The safety of modern anesthetics in this vulnerable population continues to be an area of concern, as numerous animal studies have shown neuronal apoptosis and neurocognitive deficits as a result of exposure to virtually all commonly used modern anesthetic agents.9,10 These animal studies, including some in nonhuman primates, have demonstrated abnormal neuroapoptosis and, in some, long-term cognitive deficits, including delayed learning, impaired memory formation and retention, altered motor development, and altered behavioral development. Development of the nervous system is complex, involving neuronal proliferation, migration, differentiation, and “pruning” accomplished by
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: apoptosis. This development is in part dependent on the balance of excitatory and inhibitory stimuli and neurotransmitters. Given the complexity of the process, as well as the obvious physiologic and developmental differences inherent in the application of animal studies to humans, the overall impact of these studies is not completely certain. Concerns have been raised with respect to the animal data regarding dosing and the time course of exposure. A clinically appropriate dose is the minimum necessary to induce anesthesia in the species. In some species, and with some agents, this dose also results in significant mortality, increasing the difficulty of interpreting the significance. Synaptogenesis in rats occurs postnatally over the first 2 weeks of life. An analogous period in humans would range from the third trimester of pregnancy through the first 3 years of life. Whether the child might be susceptible to anesthetic toxicity during this entire period is unknown. Studies in nonhuman primates are assumed to be more translatable to humans. Infant macaques exposed to multiple sevoflurane or isoflurane anesthetics exhibited increased anxiety behaviors and motor reflex deficits.11,12 Finally, most of the animal studies of apoptosis involve anesthesia without surgery. Because neurodevelopment is related to the balance of stimulatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters, there is some indication that the absence of surgical stress may alter the neurodevelopmental response to anesthetics.
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: Prior to 2015, human studies of the long-term effects of anesthetic exposure on the developing brain were largely retrospective and observational, employed varying study designs, and used a wide range of tools to assess neurodevelopmental outcomes. The results were inconsistent and at times conflicting. Exposure to multiple anesthetics during infancy and early childhood was often associated with
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: poorer neurodevelopmental outcomes, whereas a single anesthetic exposure varied between no adverse outcomes to some degree of neurodevelopmental impairment.
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: These concerns led the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), as a result of their ongoing initiative, to study the risk of anesthetic exposure on brain development, to publish a warning in 2016 against repeated or lengthy use of general anesthetics and sedation drugs during surgeries and procedures in children younger than 3 years of age or in pregnant women.13
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: More recent prospective studies with more robust methodology and longer-term follow-up reveal that a single brief anesthetic in early life may have no effect on longterm neurocognitive development. The General Anaesthesia Compared to Spinal Anaesthesia (GAS) study, a prospective randomized controlled trial comparing sevoflurane general anesthesia to awake regional anesthesia (spinal or caudal) for herniorrhaphy in infancy, did not reveal any difference in neurodevelopmental outcome at both 2- and 5-year follow-up.14
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: The Pediatric Anesthesia and Neurodevelopment Assessment (PANDA) study, a prospective sibling-matched cohort study, compared neurocognitive outcomes in infants receiving a short inhaled general anesthetic for herniorrhaphy to a biological sibling with no anesthetic exposure. Follow-up neuropsychological assessment of sibling pairs at ages varying from 8 to 15 years old showed no difference in neurocognitive outcomes.15 The Mayo Anesthesia Safety in Kids (MASK) study, a matched cohort study of almost 1000 children that underwent neuropsychological testing between the ages of 8 and 12 years old or 15 and 19 years old, found that exposure to general anesthesia during childhood was not associated with deficits in cognition.16 In addition, three large retrospective matched cohorts with greater than 59,000 children combined did not find sufficient data to conclude that young age at initial exposure or multiple anesthetic exposures contributed to adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes.17–19
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: No one can question the overwhelming benefit of anesthesia in the setting in which a surgical procedure, or any noxious procedure with significant stress, is required. The detrimental effects of surgical stress have been well shown. Similarly, the benefits of early repair of some surgical problems, such as congenital heart defects or neonatal hernia with risk of incarceration, have been shown, although such repair may lead to anesthesia at a younger, and potentially more susceptible, age. When deciding to proceed with an anesthetic, the benefit versus the risk of delay in surgical procedures, particularly if performed in premature infants, should be carefully considered. Reassuringly, current human studies suggest that a short anesthetic exposure during early development is safe.
paragraphs.heading: Safety and Challenges of Neonatal Anesthesia

paragraphs.text: The presence of certain comorbidities along with intrinsic surgical risk play a role in estimating perioperative risk of
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: morbidity and mortality for all pediatric patients. A retrospective multivariate analysis of over 350,000 surgical cases determined that the presence of the following risk factors in the setting of higher risk surgical procedures was associated with risk for 30-day mortality:20 • Weight <5 kg • American Society of Anesthesiology (ASA) status III or
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: higher • Preoperative sepsis • Inotropic support • Ventilator dependence prior to surgery
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: Similar findings were found in the Neonate-Children Study of Anaesthesia Practice in Europe (NECTARINE) study.21 These comorbidities are present in many neonatal patients along with the need for some higher-risk surgical procedures. Understanding the risks undertaken with both the anesthetic and the surgical procedure for a given patient allows for an informed discussion with both families and the neonatology team.
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: The preoperative evaluation should include the neonate’s current physical condition, including significant illness, the degree of transition from fetal to newborn physiology, maturity, and the presence of any congenital anomalies. Particular attention should be paid to cardiorespiratory status, required ventilatory or hemodynamic support, blood chemistries, and nutritional support.
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: A full maternal history including the course of pregnancy, labor, and delivery provides important details. A family history of anesthetic difficulties, most importantly a history of malignant hyperthermia or pseudocholinesterase deficiency, must be obtained as these conditions alter the choice of medications that can be used to perform a safe anesthetic. Maternal diseases such as diabetes, systemic lupus erythematosus, and preeclampsia have implications for the neonate. Congenital infections, oligohydramnios, intrauterine growth restriction, and maternal drug and alcohol use are also important considerations.
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: Gestational age, birth weight, and postnatal age affect anesthetic care. Birth weight does not accurately reflect maturity unless the infant is appropriate for gestational age, which is defined as being within 2 standard deviations of the mean for gestational age. Infants who are small for gestational age are more mature than their birth weight would indicate. Infants who are large for gestational age are often children of diabetic mothers, and they are at increased risk of hypoglycemia in the first 48 hours after birth. A history of birth asphyxia or neonatal resuscitation and Apgar scores can provide information about the health status of the neonate.
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: Medical history should include complete details of the present illness and treatment. Medications and administration times, details of vascular access, and respiratory parameters including ventilator type and settings all are crucial details, especially in sicker infants. Infants on highfrequency oscillatory ventilation may need to be switched to conventional ventilation and observed for several hours to facilitate movement to an operating room. If the infant
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: is on some other modality, such as inhaled nitric oxide or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, arrangements may also need to be made, and transport to the operating room would require more resources and assistance.
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: The time of the last oral feed should be noted to assure that appropriate nil per os (NPO, nothing by mouth) guidelines have been met. Attenuation of airway reflexes with induction of anesthesia places the infant at risk for aspiration of acidic gastric contents, which can lead to serious inflammatory pneumonitis. These guidelines are summarized in Table 39.222 and are meant to ensure that the volume and composition of gastric contents are as minimal as possible. However, attempts should be made to avoid longer than necessary NPO times to prevent interruptions in vital nutrition and avoid dehydration. The intake of clear fluids up to 2 hours prior to the induction of anesthesia is actually encouraged, as it can help to avoid fluctuations in blood glucose levels, avoids neonatal distress due to hunger, and improves parental satisfaction. In neonates, dehydration and hypoglycemia occur much more quickly than in older patients, and this risk is even greater in an infant without an intravenous line if NPO times are prolonged.
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: Gastric emptying is delayed with stress, anxiety, and illness. Infants with diseases such as pyloric stenosis, duodenal atresia, malrotation, or other obstructive lesions are often already NPO leading up to surgery, and they need an intravenous line to maintain appropriate hydration. Despite the NPO status, there usually are significant gastric contents, and rapid-sequence induction and intubation are required if there is any concern for obstruction. Emptying the stomach via nasogastric drainage is undependable and usually inadequate. Gastric feeds even in intubated infants also should be discontinued at an appropriate time because the infant may need to be reintubated during surgery, and a full stomach would increase the risk for aspiration.
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: Physical examination should include an assessment of vital signs noting trends or recent changes. Careful attention should be paid to evaluation of the cardiorespiratory system. Many neonates requiring surgery are ill and are at risk for hemodynamic or respiratory instability.
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: The presence of any congenital anomalies must be noted, as they may have an impact on anesthetic care. Often, a group of defects suggests a well-recognized and characterized syndrome. A number of common syndromes with their anesthetic implications are listed in Table 39.3.
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: Difficult intubation is a common problem in infants with congenital defects, and the airway must be carefully assessed. The presence of micrognathia or retrognathia can be an indicator of a difficult airway. Intraoral, facial or neck masses may make a neonate difficult to both mask ventilate and intubate. Limitations in neck mobility can also affect airway management. Because of the tendency for rapid oxygen desaturation in infants, difficulties with intubation can be extremely serious. In infants who are already intubated, tube size and position should be evaluated. The pressure at which a leak occurs around the tube should be documented. The quantity and consistency of secretions and need for
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: frequent suctioning should be ascertained. The small tubes required in premature infants can easily be blocked by tenacious secretions and are easily dislodged. If there is any question about adequacy of intubation, the infant should be electively reintubated before surgery; emergently replacing an endotracheal tube under the drapes after beginning an operation is not a benign procedure.
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: Preoperative evaluation of the pulmonary system in the neonate should include a review of recent chest x-rays, notation of current ventilation or oxygen therapies (including ventilator settings), and a physical exam noting work of breathing, stridor, or adventitious lung sounds. History related to length of intubation, prior modes of ventilation, and current issues related to apneas, desaturations, and bradycardia should be obtained. The pulmonary circulation in a neonate is hyperreactive; multiple stressors including surgical stimulation can initiate episodes of pulmonary hypertension, resulting in decreased cardiac output and oxygen desaturation. Any history of such spells requires increased vigilance to avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, and acidosis, which increase pulmonary resistance. Infants with bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) are at risk of pulmonary hypertension and susceptible to excessive pulmonary vasoconstriction in response to hypoxia, hypothermia, or acidosis. Because of their chronic lung disease, these infants may have some degree of right heart dysfunction, and decreases in myocardial function related to anesthetics may result in acute right heart failure. Patients with severe BPD may benefit from an echocardiogram to evaluate for evidence of pulmonary hypertension prior to undergoing anesthesia. Other problems in BPD include airway hyperreactivity, increased airway secretions, electrolyte abnormalities because of diuretic therapy, and frequently tracheomalacia.23
paragraphs.heading: Preoperative Evaluation and Preparation

paragraphs.text: Evaluation of cardiac status should investigate for congenital heart disease, as well as identify patients who might be at higher risk of intraoperative hemodynamic instability due to the need for preoperative inotropic support. Major congenital anomalies requiring operative intervention within the first days to weeks of life, including omphalocele, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, tracheoesophageal fistula, duodenal atresia, and imperforate anus, are often more highly associated with congenital heart disease.24 Echocardiograms are frequently performed for these patients prior to surgery and anesthesia. Right-to-left shunts affect the oxygenation of the infant, whereas left-to-right shunts typically result in volume overload. Volume status needs to be
