of surgical procedures, but most still require recovery and monitoring in an intensive care setting. Neuromuscular blockade should be reversed, as previously discussed. Hypothermia can prolong neuromuscular blockade, precluding extubation if temperature control has not been adequate, and infants with hypothermia may need to be actively warmed. Transport from the operating room involves the same considerations of temperature maintenance and airway management that have previously been discussed.

The infant should resume regular rhythmic respiration; to achieve this, ventilation may have to be decreased toward the end of the anesthetic to allow the PCO2 to increase to mildly hypercapnic levels. Volume status must be adequate, and plasma hemoglobin should be close to normal. Flexion

title: Care of Periviable Micropreemies- The Japanese Perspective

paragraphs.text: 40 Care of Periviable Micropreemies: The Japanese Perspective
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: One of the most rapidly changing areas of perinatal care over the last several decades is the care of preterm infants at a limit of viability, defined as preterm infants born before 24 weeks of gestation.1 Only limited centers or countries have been providing comprehensive and intensive treatment for these infants due to poor outcomes. On the other hand, the Japanese academia involved in perinatal medicine has been attempting to treat and care for these periviable preterm infants for almost the last 25 years.2 Because of this effort, the overall outcomes of these infants have been improving constantly. In order to achieve progress in the care of periviable preterm infants, aggressive intervention is the first priority. Then, the accumulation of experiences and the sharing of these experiences become crucial. Many practices applied to periviable preterm infants have not been established through well-designed clinical trials because most clinical trials have excluded periviable preterm infants. Sharing information is important for further improvement in the care of periviable preterm infants. Therefore, in this chapter, Japanese experiences and challenges in the care of periviable preterm infants are introduced, especially with regard to care in the acute phase.3
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: After 1990, when the Maternal Health Act lowered the upper limit of interventional abortion from 24 to 22 weeks of pregnancy, some perinatal centers in Japan started to resuscitate infants born before 24 weeks of gestation. Of course, before the amendment, several periviable preterm infants who survived to discharge in limited perinatal centers were
paragraphs.heading: Background

paragraphs.text: reported, and these actual real-world data became a catalyst for the amendment.4 Since then, an increased number of survivors has been reported, and the outcomes of periviable infants have gradually been improving. Although there are still many challenges in the care of periviable preterm infants at present, the practices adopted at different clinical sites should be shared and through these processes, standardized care based on scientific knowledge can be utilized to address these challenges on a global level. Furthermore, sharing information is also crucial to ensure collaboration among several stakeholders.5
paragraphs.heading: Background

paragraphs.text: The neonatal database operated by the Neonatal Research Network of Japan has been collecting outcomes among very preterm infants since 2003 to evaluate the current situation in the care of preterm infants and to improve their outcomes through quality improvement.6 According to this database, the most recent survival rates in infants born at 22 and 23 weeks of gestation are around 60% and 80%, respectively (Fig. 40.1).7 Mortality rates are higher compared to those of infants with a higher gestational age; however, an overall improvement can be seen. Furthermore, the incidence of cerebral palsy at 3 years of age among survivors has not been increasing but rather decreasing (Fig. 40.2).7 Conversely, the high incidence of developmental delay among survivors, which ranges between 50% and 60%, is becoming an important issue in periviable preterm infants, and it remains at a critical level.8–10 These results mean that the intensive care of periviable preterm infants can improve their survival rates without increasing the incidence of neurological deficits. At the same time, however, it is necessary to note that the incidence of neurological impairment is still clearly higher
paragraphs.heading: Outcomes

paragraphs.text: than that among older preterm infants, with an almost 10 times higher incidence of cerebral palsy than among preterm infants born at 31 weeks of gestation (Fig. 40.3).
paragraphs.heading: Outcomes

paragraphs.text: In order to improve the outcomes among periviable preterm infants, a continuous and multidisciplinary approach in perinatal centers is very important. Box 40.1 shows key practices necessary for perinatal centers responsible for the care of periviable preterm infants, as well as the current, unique challenges in Japan. Although most procedures and practices have not been supported by clinical trials based on robust scientific evidence, a certain degree of standardization of practices derived from experience is necessary to execute medical care for periviable preterm infants born in a clinical setting, which is a challenge but a necessary step for future harmonization and standardization of care. None of the practices described in this chapter has officially been established as a standard
paragraphs.heading: Care for the Improvement of Outcomes Among Preterm Infants

paragraphs.text: of care and might be changed in the future. Nevertheless, the latest and most widely used practices in Japan are described.
paragraphs.heading: Care for the Improvement of Outcomes Among Preterm Infants

paragraphs.text: If the early ultrasound determination of pregnancy is not performed, it should be considered that the estimation of weeks of pregnancy is not accurate. Even though the ultrasound examination is performed at the early stages of pregnancy, there is still a 5-day variation in the time of pregnancy. When the mortality in periviable preterm infants was calculated based on the gestational week and day, a continuous improvement in mortality was seen with an increment in gestational day (Fig. 40.4).7 A 1-day prolongation of pregnancy before 24 weeks of pregnancy could increase the survival rate of periviable preterm infants by 5%, from 65% down to 15%. Therefore the determination of gestational age is crucial during the periviable period. Before consulting parents, neonatologists should confirm the accuracy of

paragraphs.heading: Outcomes in Periviable Preterm Infants

paragraphs.text: A meta-analysis published in 2020 showed that a cesarean delivery for singleton preterm infants born before 28 weeks of gestation significantly reduced mortality; however, it could not show any beneficial effects on combined mortality or severe brain injury among them (Table 40.2).17 Furthermore, only a limited number of infants born before 24 weeks of gestation were included in the study; therefore the basic approach toward selecting a delivery mode should be based on spontaneous delivery. Many perinatal centers, however, prefer to select cesarean section for several reasons, including less traumatic delivery for periviable infants, scheduling time,
paragraphs.heading: Selection of Delivery Mode

paragraphs.text: and staff availability. Fig. 40.5 shows the cesarean delivery rate by gestational age from 2003 to 2019 in Japan. Infants born at 22 and 23 weeks of gestation were delivered by cesarean section at the rates of 30% and 60%, respectively. However, infants born after 24 weeks of gestation were at almost 80%. This suggests that periviable preterm infants were less likely to be delivered by cesarean section, probably due to the high mortality. Outcomes of mothers were prioritized over infants, but the cesarean rate for periviable preterm infants showed a constantly increasing trend (Fig. 40.6). This could be explained by the improvement in mortality among periviable preterm infants. An increased cesarean rate in very preterm infants was also reported in the United States.18 These trends might mean that the improved outcome in periviable preterm infants is achieved at the cost of an extra burden on mothers from another perspective. Therefore the strict criteria for cesarean delivery must be maintained.
paragraphs.heading: Selection of Delivery Mode

paragraphs.text: Without any aggressive resuscitation from birth, periviable preterm infants cannot survive.19 In this sense, quick and appropriate resuscitation is mandatory. Although tracheal intubation at birth can be associated with the later development of chronic lung disease in most vulnerable lungs, the effectiveness of resuscitation by tracheal intubation far exceeds that of noninvasive methods. Furthermore,
paragraphs.heading: At Birth

paragraphs.text: resuscitation with continuous positive air pressure (i.e., noninvasive resuscitation) did not show a clear advantage over tracheal intubation in preventing bronchopulmonary dysplasia.20 Damage to the lung due to tracheal intubation at birth among periviable preterm infants is not a conclusive
paragraphs.heading: At Birth

paragraphs.text: etiology for lung injury; therefore prompt tracheal intubation followed by positive pressure ventilation with a mask and bag is our recommendation (Fig. 10.7).21 Fig. 40.8 shows the intubation rate at birth in Japan among very preterm infants. The intubation rate of infants born at 22 weeks of gestation was less than that at 23 weeks of gestation, probably because of the withholding of aggressive resuscitation due to poor general condition at birth. Eventually, only 8 out of 1158 infants (0.7%) survived to discharge without intubation during their stay in the NICU.7 No intubation at birth should be considered an exception in periviable preterm infants.
paragraphs.heading: At Birth

paragraphs.text: Placental transfusion for preterm infants has improved short-term outcomes, including death and morbidities, as well as long-term outcomes, including neurodevelopment.22,23 Although there are insufficient numbers of periviable preterm infants in clinical trials, one-time umbilical cord milking after cord cutting is currently applied to some of these infants in Japan.24
paragraphs.heading: At Birth

paragraphs.text: Insensible water loss from the skin in periviable preterm infants is significantly higher than in older preterm infants.
paragraphs.heading: Fluid Balance

paragraphs.text: Direct measurement of insensible water loss in preterm infants born at 22 and 23 weeks of gestation on the first day of life under 80% relative humidity was reported at around 80 mL/kg/day.25 Similarly, estimated insensible water loss from daily urine output and body weight in periviable preterm infants was around 60 mL/kg/day under almost 100% relative humidity on the first day of life.26 Therefore the fluid intake of periviable preterm infants should be adjusted according to their daily insensible water loss and urine volume. Moreover, fluid intake during the first week of life should be less than the sum of insensible water loss and urine output, because fluid overload has been associated with an increased risk of patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC).27 An increase in environmental humidity, as close to 100% as possible, is the best strategy for fluid management in periviable preterm infants. Even under these circumstances, periviable preterm infants may show a body weight loss of over 20% during the first week of life.26
paragraphs.heading: Fluid Balance

paragraphs.text: The incidence of NEC is also highly dependent on the gestational age (Fig. 40.9).7 The incidence of NEC or intestinal
paragraphs.heading: Necrotizing Enterocolitis Prevention

paragraphs.text: perforation in preterm infants born at 22, 23, and 24 weeks of gestation is around 12%, 11%, and 10%, respectively. NEC is well known to have a high mortality rate; therefore improvement in the survival rate in periviable preterm infants is greatly related to the prevention of NEC. Currently, our main approach to preventing NEC is associated with the use of probiotics and the unstudied use of glycerin enema, 2 mg/kg of the 25% solution 2 or 3 times a day. Although the benefit of probiotics used to prevent NEC in preterm infants is controversial, most NICUs adopt this strategy.3,28,29 Probiotic use was also reported to have the advantage of accelerating enteral feeding in very low birth weight infants.30 Therefore probiotic use is recommended for periviable preterm infants as nutritional care.
paragraphs.heading: Necrotizing Enterocolitis Prevention

paragraphs.text: Survival of periviable infants has become realistic since the introduction of surfactant and antenatal glucocorticoids.31–33 Furthermore, several respiratory modes have become available and are being selected for periviable preterm infants.34 During the acute phase, however, invasive ventilation after surfactant installation is almost inevitable. Box 40.2 shows the choice of initial respiratory modes.

paragraphs.text: dardized procedures for the resuscitation of periviable preterm infants, but respiratory and circulatory stabilization immediately after birth should be prioritized. Without intensive support with positive pressure ventilation, the establishment of effective respiration among periviable preterm infants is not possible. The first step in postnatal stabilization is initiated by positive airway pressure with a bag and mask. When the heart rate increases above 100 beats per minute, tracheal intubation could be attempted. The initial fraction of inspired oxygen (IFiO2) should be between 0.3 and 0.6. Temperature control in infants is also critical for successful resuscitation. After the intratracheal tube is secured, the infant should be transferred to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) for further procedures. (Data from Kusuda S, Nakanishi H, Oei JL. paragraphs.text: The concept of a respiratory strategy is based on maximum oxygenation with less likelihood of damage to vulnerable lungs; however, without positive pressure ventilation, severe apneic attacks could deteriorate not only respiratory conditions but also the infant’s general condition and lead to a vicious cycle. Although no standardized practice guidelines have been established, a noninvasive respiratory strategy cannot be applied to periviable preterm infants. Using available respiratory strategies, each hospital has its own strategy for respiratory care.35 A short intubation period was reported to be associated with the reduced incidence of bronchopulmonary dysplasia in very preterm infants.36 Despite this evidence, most periviable preterm infants were reported to be managed under mechanical ventilation.37 From a clinical point of view, therefore, periviable preterm infants should be managed with mechanical ventilation, which seems a much safer and more feasible method to ensure their survival.
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 40.9 Incidence of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) and intestinal

paragraphs.text: Although all practices are essential for better outcomes in periviable preterm infants, circulatory care is especially crucial to support their survival. Respiratory care is mainly dependent on the lung maturation of preterm infants. If their lungs are not ready for gas exchange due to anatomical immaturity, no treatment can be effective to improve the respiratory condition. Even surfactant installation might not be successful if the lungs are not sufficiently matured to allow breathing at alveolar levels. On the other hand, there are many organized approaches to support the circulatory condition in periviable preterm infants. Furthermore, the Japanese approach to circulatory care in periviable preterm infants is unique in the following two features: hemodynamic management by functional echocardiography by neonatologists and timely use of hydrocortisone based on echocardiographic assessment.38 A main focus of this chapter is related to circulatory management in periviable preterm infants in Japan.
paragraphs.heading: Circulatory Care: Role of Functional Echocardiography

paragraphs.text: The concept of point-of-care functional echocardiography by neonatologists is familiar and has been well accepted in such areas as Australia, New Zealand, Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, European countries, and Japan since the 2000s.39–45 The noninvasive nature of echocardiography is advantageous because it allows neonatologists to assess cardiovascular function
paragraphs.heading: Circulatory Care: Role of Functional Echocardiography

paragraphs.text: under physiological and pathological conditions repeatedly and provides neonatologists with targeted interventions. Furthermore, functional echocardiography can be performed by all neonatologists after a certain period of training, and its use is not restricted to cardiac specialists.46 Cardiac output depends on four elements, including preload, cardiac contractility, afterload, and heart rate; besides heart rate, the other three parameters can be measured by functional echocardiography in a short examination time. In addition to cardiac functions, the severity of symptomatic PDA can also be evaluated by repeated functional echocardiography.
paragraphs.heading: Circulatory Care: Role of Functional Echocardiography

paragraphs.text: Box 40.3 shows the conditions evaluated and parameters measured by functional echocardiography in the NICU, and Table 40.3 provides their reference ranges.38 When neonatologists have been trained to perform functional echocardiography, all necessary parameters can be measured within 10 minutes. The most prominent benefit of neonatologists who perform echocardiography is repeatability. As often as three times a day, circulatory status can be evaluated and adjusted from moment to moment. This repeated evaluation is especially required during the transitional circulation from fetus to neonate. This process takes place in all infants; however, the ability to adapt in periviable preterm infants is so limited that some form of tailor-made adjustment is desirable.45 In fact, 95% of high-performance NICUs in Japan use functional echocardiography for the circulatory management of extremely low birth weight infants in acute phases.47
paragraphs.heading: Circulatory Care: Role of Functional Echocardiography

paragraphs.text: Although cardiac output in periviable preterm infants can be evaluated in terms of three factors measurable by functional echocardiography, the immaturity of their myocardial
paragraphs.heading: Myocardial Function

paragraphs.text: function should always be considered. This unique feature is sometimes critical to anticipating the response to pharmaceutical drugs.48 Myocardial contraction is solely dependent on the rapid increase in the intracellular Ca2++ concentration. A calcium-induced calcium release (CICR) system in the mature myocardium can enhance the Ca++ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and make a rapid increase in concentration possible.49 In contrast, the CICR system in periviable preterm infants is not well developed, and the supply of Ca++ to the myofibrils relies mainly on direct extracellular calcium influx, resulting in a limited increase in intracellular Ca2++.49 In addition, the myocardium structure is also not well developed, which reduces its contractile ability as well as its diastolic expanding capacity compared to those in older preterm infants. Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging of the fetal heart shows the development of cardiomyocyte maturation and alignment.50 Maturation of the sheet structure of the heart occurs late in gestation, and it evolves further after birth. These findings indicate that periviable preterm infants are less adaptable to preload and afterload, which leads to a relatively flat response to the Frank-Starling law (Fig. 40.10).
paragraphs.heading: Myocardial Function

paragraphs.text: Heart rate is regulated by the sympathetic and parasympathetic nerve systems. Heart rate variability analysis in preterm infants shows a low parasympathetic tone, which results in maintaining higher heart rates.51 Therefore periviable preterm infants have a limited ability to increase cardiac output by further increasing the heart rate.
paragraphs.heading: Myocardial Function

paragraphs.text: Factors affecting cardiac output are shown in Fig. 40.11. As mentioned above, the ability to change the heart rate and
paragraphs.heading: Cardiac Output

paragraphs.text: myocardial function in periviable preterm infants is limited. Maintaining adequate preload and myocardial contractility and avoiding over-afterload are required for the care of periviable preterm infants. In order to adjust these parameters, repeated functional echocardiography by neonatologists is inevitable.
paragraphs.heading: LA

paragraphs.text: Circulating blood volume can also be assessed using echography (Box 40.3). Figs. 40.12 and 40.13 show the actual assessment of blood volume using inferior vena cava (IVC)/descending aorta (dAo) ratio and the left atrium (LA)/aortic root (Ao) ratio.52 The reference range of these parameters in periviable preterm infants has not yet been confirmed; however, repeated measurement of their values is much more useful rather than a single measurement. Again, less invasive point-of-care echography by neonatologists can demonstrate its usefulness.
paragraphs.heading: LA

paragraphs.text: Cardiac contractility is assessed by the left ventricular volume change between the diastolic and systolic phases. The difference is directly collated with cardiac output per one stroke volume. In functional echocardiography, the left ventricular internal diameter is substituted for its internal volume. Therefore the ejection fraction is calculated using these two parameters and can be easily evaluated repeatedly, without a heavy burden on infants. Fig. 40.14 shows a series of functional echocardiography in a periviable infant with low cardiac output indicated by low ejection fraction. The first attempt to improve cardiac contractility using catecholamines failed. Periviable preterm infants with impaired myocardial performance may not be responsive to catecholamines. In this
paragraphs.heading: LA

paragraphs.text: case, glucocorticoids can increase the responsiveness of catecholamine receptors.53 Hydrocortisone should be actively used for periviable preterm infants with cardiac dysfunction.38
paragraphs.heading: LA

paragraphs.text: Afterload is the backpressure to the left ventricle during myocardial contraction. The peripheral resistance of systemic circulation is a principal component in determining the degree of afterload. If the peripheral resistance overrides the myocardial contractility, left ventricular ejection capacity is impaired; however, blood pressure does not decrease but rather increases, followed by reduced peripheral perfusion. This means that blood pressure is not an adequate parameter for organ blood flow.51 In clinical practice, the left ventricular end-systolic wall stress (ESWS) calculated by echocardiography is used to evaluate afterload combined with rate-corrected mean velocity of fiber shortening (mVcfc).45 The ESWSmVcfc relation, also known as the stress-velocity relationship, shows an inverse correlation with a tendency of steepness in slope in preterm infants (Fig. 40.15).45,55,56 Therefore a so-called afterload mismatch in which cardiac output deteriorates severely in the face of increased afterload compared with cardiac contractility is not uncommon in periviable preterm infants.
paragraphs.heading: LA

paragraphs.text: As already mentioned, blood pressure is not a suitable indicator of organ blood flow. When afterload increases, a vasodilator should be used to decrease the peripheral resistance, which may decrease blood pressure and increase cardiac output consequently. Fig. 40.16 shows a case of cardiac dysfunction due to increased peripheral resistance,

The infant was treated with pulmonary surfactant due to severe respiratory distress syndrome. On day 0, the patient showed a low blood pressure of 27/20 mm Hg with decreased urine output. The infant’s functional echocardiography revealed poor movement of the left ventricle. The left ventricular diastolic dimension (LVDd) and left ventricular systolic dimension (LVDs) were 8.7 mm and 7.4 mm, respectively, with a low left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 37.9%. The infant’s cardiac function was not recovered by catecholamines and hydrocortisone; however, when the vasodilator milrinone was administered, the left ventricular contractility improved rapidly, indicating the excess afterload.47 This condition is not usually associated with low blood pressure but rather with increased blood pressure. In essence, a hemodynamically significant PDA is judged by the volume of shunt flow, which affects parameters such as the LA/Ao ratio and left pulmonary artery end-diastolic velocity (LPAedv) (Fig. 40.17). paragraphs.text: activity of the fetus; conversely, excessive exposure is harmful to many organs, especially the developing brain. Therefore two mechanisms operate to protect the fetus from excessive cortisol exposure. The first is based on the suppression of 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (3β-HSD), which is a key enzyme for cortisol production in the adrenal cortex. The progesterone necessary to produce cortisol is supplied through the placenta, thus the ability to produce cortisol is limited. The other mechanism is the conversion of cortisol from the mother through the placenta to an inactive form of cortisol, cortisone, by 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (11β-HSD) type 2. After preterm birth, cortisol must be produced by preterm infants, but the activity of 3β-HSD remains suppressed, and the supply of progesterone from the placenta is stopped. When stress exceeds a certain level, cortisol production becomes insufficient in preterm infants, resulting in relative adrenal insufficiency. paragraphs.text: placental supply of progesterone is completely and suddenly interrupted. This condition reduces the ability to produce sufficient cortisol under stress in preterm infants. Consequently, some preterm infants might display adrenal insufficiency. This phenomenon occurs not only during the acute phase but also in the postacute phase, usually after 2 weeks of age. The former is known as adrenal insufficiency and refractory hypotension in preterm infants, and the latter is known as late-onset circulatory collapse (LCC).61,62 A study reported that LCC was associated with relative adrenal insufficiency under stress due to the immaturity of 3β-HSD enzyme activity.63 Both types of adrenal insufficiency showed a sufficient response to a physiological dose of hydrocortisone, 1 to 2 mg/kg.64 Because the maturation of 3β-HSD is dependent on gestational weeks, the incidence of LCC is higher in periviable preterm infants (Fig. 40.19).7 The incidence in periviable infants was found to be approximately 30% in infants born at 22 weeks of age and 25% at 23 weeks of age, meaning that more than onequarter of infants might suffer from circulatory collapse even 2 weeks after birth. LCC not only is a life-threatening form of hypotension but is also strongly associated with cerebral palsy with PVL in very preterm infants.65,66 Therefore the management of LCC is critical for the care of periviable preterm infants. Fig. 40.20 shows typical changes in arterial blood flow patterns in an infant with LCC. At present, the diagnosis of LCC is solely dependent on clinical findings, with no specific biomarker.67 The ruling out of sepsis or hypovolemic shock is essential before the diagnosis. Sepsis should be ruled out through other inflammatory markers, such as C-reactive protein and white cell

paragraphs.text: Circulatory management in periviable preterm infants using functional echocardiography is summarized in Fig. 40.21. From fetal to neonatal development, circulatory adaptation is an especially large burden and a challenge to survival in periviable preterm infants. Therefore we believe noninvasive and repeatable functional echocardiography by neonatologists is a mandatory procedure in NICUs to improve outcomes in periviable preterm infants.

figures.caption: • Fig. 40.7 Recommended algorithm of resuscitation for periviable preterm infants. There are no standardized procedures for the resuscitation of periviable preterm infants, but respiratory and circulatory stabilization immediately after birth should be prioritized. Without intensive support with positive pressure ventilation, the establishment of effective respiration among periviable preterm infants is not possible. The first step in postnatal stabilization is initiated by positive airway pressure with a bag and mask. When the heart rate increases above 100 beats per minute, tracheal intubation could be attempted. The initial fraction of inspired oxygen (IFiO2) should be between 0.3 and 0.6. Temperature control in infants is also critical for successful resuscitation. After the intratracheal tube is secured, the infant should be transferred to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) for further procedures. (Data from Kusuda S, Nakanishi H, Oei JL. Practical procedures for the delivery room resuscitation of micropreemies. Semin Fetal Neonatal Med. 2022;27:101349.)

figures.caption: • Fig. 40.10 Frank-Starling law: A heart with normal myocardial function can increase its output in response to an increased preload when all other factors remain constant (blue line). In contrast, an immature myocardial muscle can respond to a lesser degree due to the underdevelopment of muscle fibers (red line). Furthermore, if preload is exceeded or afterload is high, it may cause a limited response to preload (right portion of red line), resulting in congestive heart failure. The range within which periviable preterm infants can adapt their cardiac output depending on preload is limited, and the adjustment of preload using functional echocardiography is critical.

figures.caption: • Fig. 40.18 Enzymatic pathway of the fetal adrenal gland. Cortisol is essential for maintaining the vital activity of the fetus; conversely, excessive exposure is harmful to many organs, especially the developing brain. Therefore two mechanisms operate to protect the fetus from excessive cortisol exposure. The first is based on the suppression of 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (3β-HSD), which is a key enzyme for cortisol production in the adrenal cortex. The progesterone necessary to produce cortisol is supplied through the placenta, thus the ability to produce cortisol is limited. The other mechanism is the conversion of cortisol from the mother through the placenta to an inactive form of cortisol, cortisone, by 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (11β-HSD) type 2. After preterm birth, cortisol must be produced by preterm infants, but the activity of 3β-HSD remains suppressed, and the supply of progesterone from the placenta is stopped. When stress exceeds a certain level, cortisol production becomes insufficient in preterm infants, resulting in relative adrenal insufficiency. LDL, Low-density lipoprotein; DHA, dehydroepiandrosterone; DHAS, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate. (Adapted from Masumoto K, Kusuda S. Catecholamines can be used at doses of 1 to 10 μg/kg/min of dopamine and 1 to 10 μg/kg/min of dobutamine; however, the effectiveness of catecholamines in periviable preterm infants should be considered limited. 40 Care of Periviable Micropreemies: The Japanese Perspective

### SATOSHI KUSUDA, KENICHI MASUMOTO, AND HIDEHIKO NAKANISHI

### Introduction

One of the most rapidly changing areas of perinatal care over the last several decades is the care of preterm infants at a limit of viability, defined as preterm infants born before 24 weeks of gestation.1 Only limited centers or countries have been providing comprehensive and intensive treatment for these infants due to poor outcomes. On the other hand, the Japanese academia involved in perinatal medicine has been attempting to treat and care for these periviable preterm infants for almost the last 25 years.2 Because of this effort, the overall outcomes of these infants have been improving constantly. In order to achieve progress in the care of periviable preterm infants, aggressive intervention is the first priority. Then, the accumulation of experiences and the sharing of these experiences become crucial. Many practices applied to periviable preterm infants have not been established through well-designed clinical trials because most clinical trials have excluded periviable preterm infants. Sharing information is important for further improvement in the care of periviable preterm infants. Therefore, in this chapter, Japanese experiences and challenges in the care of periviable preterm infants are introduced, especially with regard to care in the acute phase.3

### Background

After 1990, when the Maternal Health Act lowered the upper limit of interventional abortion from 24 to 22 weeks of pregnancy, some perinatal centers in Japan started to resuscitate infants born before 24 weeks of gestation. Of course, before the amendment, several periviable preterm infants who survived to discharge in limited perinatal centers were

reported, and these actual real-world data became a catalyst for the amendment.4 Since then, an increased number of survivors has been reported, and the outcomes of periviable infants have gradually been improving. Although there are still many challenges in the care of periviable preterm infants at present, the practices adopted at different clinical sites should be shared and through these processes, standardized care based on scientific knowledge can be utilized to address these challenges on a global level. Furthermore, sharing information is also crucial to ensure collaboration among several stakeholders.5

### Outcomes

The neonatal database operated by the Neonatal Research Network of Japan has been collecting outcomes among very preterm infants since 2003 to evaluate the current situation in the care of preterm infants and to improve their outcomes through quality improvement.6 According to this database, the most recent survival rates in infants born at 22 and 23 weeks of gestation are around 60% and 80%, respectively (Fig. 40.1).7 Mortality rates are higher compared to those of infants with a higher gestational age; however, an overall improvement can be seen. Furthermore, the incidence of cerebral palsy at 3 years of age among survivors has not been increasing but rather decreasing (Fig. 40.2).7 Conversely, the high incidence of developmental delay among survivors, which ranges between 50% and 60%, is becoming an important issue in periviable preterm infants, and it remains at a critical level.8–10 These results mean that the intensive care of periviable preterm infants can improve their survival rates without increasing the incidence of neurological deficits. At the same time, however, it is necessary to note that the incidence of neurological impairment is still clearly higher

### Care for the Improvement of Outcomes Among Preterm Infants

In order to improve the outcomes among periviable preterm infants, a continuous and multidisciplinary approach in perinatal centers is very important. Box 40.1 shows key practices necessary for perinatal centers responsible for the care of periviable preterm infants, as well as the current, unique challenges in Japan. Although most procedures and practices have not been supported by clinical trials based on robust scientific evidence, a certain degree of standardization of practices derived from experience is necessary to execute medical care for periviable preterm infants born in a clinical setting, which is a challenge but a necessary step for future harmonization and standardization of care. None of the practices described in this chapter has officially been established as a standard

### Before Delivery

### Confirmation of Weeks of Pregnancy

If the early ultrasound determination of pregnancy is not performed, it should be considered that the estimation of weeks of pregnancy is not accurate. Even though the ultrasound examination is performed at the early stages of pregnancy, there is still a 5-day variation in the time of pregnancy. ### Antenatal Corticosteroid Use

Table 40.1 shows the international guidelines for antenatal glucocorticoid use for preterm delivery.11–15 Most guidelines recommend the routine use of antenatal glucocorticoids after 24 weeks of pregnancy, with consideration at 22 and 23 weeks of gestation. However, if the recent improvement in the survival rate of periviable preterm infants is considered, the antenatal corticosteroid should be used after 22 weeks of pregnancy unless consent is not obtained.16

### Selection of Delivery Mode

A meta-analysis published in 2020 showed that a cesarean delivery for singleton preterm infants born before 28 weeks of gestation significantly reduced mortality; however, it could not show any beneficial effects on combined mortality or severe brain injury among them (Table 40.2).17 Furthermore, only a limited number of infants born before 24 weeks of gestation were included in the study; therefore the basic approach toward selecting a delivery mode should be based on spontaneous delivery. Many perinatal centers, however, prefer to select cesarean section for several reasons, including less traumatic delivery for periviable infants, scheduling time,

and staff availability. Fig. 40.5 shows the cesarean delivery rate by gestational age from 2003 to 2019 in Japan. Infants born at 22 and 23 weeks of gestation were delivered by cesarean section at the rates of 30% and 60%, respectively. However, infants born after 24 weeks of gestation were at almost 80%. This suggests that periviable preterm infants were less likely to be delivered by cesarean section, probably due to the high mortality. Outcomes of mothers were prioritized over infants, but the cesarean rate for periviable preterm infants showed a constantly increasing trend (Fig. 40.6). This could be explained by the improvement in mortality among periviable preterm infants. An increased cesarean rate in very preterm infants was also reported in the United States.18 These trends might mean that the improved outcome in periviable preterm infants is achieved at the cost of an extra burden on mothers from another perspective. Therefore the strict criteria for cesarean delivery must be maintained.

Although tracheal intubation at birth can be associated with the later development of chronic lung disease in most vulnerable lungs, the effectiveness of resuscitation by tracheal intubation far exceeds that of noninvasive methods. Although no standardized practice guidelines have been established, a noninvasive respiratory strategy cannot be applied to periviable preterm infants. ### Circulatory Care: Role of Functional Echocardiography

Although all practices are essential for better outcomes in periviable preterm infants, circulatory care is especially crucial to support their survival. Respiratory care is mainly dependent on the lung maturation of preterm infants. If their lungs are not ready for gas exchange due to anatomical immaturity, no treatment can be effective to improve the respiratory condition. Even surfactant installation might not be successful if the lungs are not sufficiently matured to allow breathing at alveolar levels. On the other hand, there are many organized approaches to support the circulatory condition in periviable preterm infants. Furthermore, the Japanese approach to circulatory care in periviable preterm infants is unique in the following two features: hemodynamic management by functional echocardiography by neonatologists and timely use of hydrocortisone based on echocardiographic assessment.38 A main focus of this chapter is related to circulatory management in periviable preterm infants in Japan.

The concept of point-of-care functional echocardiography by neonatologists is familiar and has been well accepted in such areas as Australia, New Zealand, Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, European countries, and Japan since the 2000s.39–45 The noninvasive nature of echocardiography is advantageous because it allows neonatologists to assess cardiovascular function

This unique feature is sometimes critical to anticipating the response to pharmaceutical drugs.48 Myocardial contraction is solely dependent on the rapid increase in the intracellular Ca2++ concentration. A calcium-induced calcium release (CICR) system in the mature myocardium can enhance the Ca++ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and make a rapid increase in concentration possible.49 In contrast, the CICR system in periviable preterm infants is not well developed, and the supply of Ca++ to the myofibrils relies mainly on direct extracellular calcium influx, resulting in a limited increase in intracellular Ca2++.49 In addition, the myocardium structure is also not well developed, which reduces its contractile ability as well as its diastolic expanding capacity compared to those in older preterm infants. Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging of the fetal heart shows the development of cardiomyocyte maturation and alignment.50 Maturation of the sheet structure of the heart occurs late in gestation, and it evolves further after birth. These findings indicate that periviable preterm infants are less adaptable to preload and afterload, which leads to a relatively flat response to the Frank-Starling law (Fig. 40.10).

Heart rate is regulated by the sympathetic and parasympathetic nerve systems. Heart rate variability analysis in preterm infants shows a low parasympathetic tone, which results in maintaining higher heart rates.51 Therefore periviable preterm infants have a limited ability to increase cardiac output by further increasing the heart rate.

Afterload is the backpressure to the left ventricle during myocardial contraction. The peripheral resistance of systemic circulation is a principal component in determining the degree of afterload. If the peripheral resistance overrides the myocardial contractility, left ventricular ejection capacity is impaired; however, blood pressure does not decrease but rather increases, followed by reduced peripheral perfusion. This means that blood pressure is not an adequate parameter for organ blood flow.51 In clinical practice, the left ventricular end-systolic wall stress (ESWS) calculated by echocardiography is used to evaluate afterload combined with rate-corrected mean velocity of fiber shortening (mVcfc).45 The ESWSmVcfc relation, also known as the stress-velocity relationship, shows an inverse correlation with a tendency of steepness in slope in preterm infants (Fig. 40.15).45,55,56 Therefore a so-called afterload mismatch in which cardiac output deteriorates severely in the face of increased afterload compared with cardiac contractility is not uncommon in periviable preterm infants.

As already mentioned, blood pressure is not a suitable indicator of organ blood flow. When afterload increases, a vasodilator should be used to decrease the peripheral resistance, which may decrease blood pressure and increase cardiac output consequently. ### • Fig. 40.18 Enzymatic pathway of the fetal adrenal gland. Cortisol is essential for maintaining the vital

activity of the fetus; conversely, excessive exposure is harmful to many organs, especially the developing brain. Therefore two mechanisms operate to protect the fetus from excessive cortisol exposure. The first is based on the suppression of 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (3β-HSD), which is a key enzyme for cortisol production in the adrenal cortex. The progesterone necessary to produce cortisol is supplied through the placenta, thus the ability to produce cortisol is limited. The other mechanism is the conversion of cortisol from the mother through the placenta to an inactive form of cortisol, cortisone, by 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (11β-HSD) type 2. After preterm birth, cortisol must be produced by preterm infants, but the activity of 3β-HSD remains suppressed, and the supply of progesterone from the placenta is stopped. When stress exceeds a certain level, cortisol production becomes insufficient in preterm infants, resulting in relative adrenal insufficiency. Consequently, some preterm infants might display adrenal insufficiency. This phenomenon occurs not only during the acute phase but also in the postacute phase, usually after 2 weeks of age. The former is known as adrenal insufficiency and refractory hypotension in preterm infants, and the latter is known as late-onset circulatory collapse (LCC).61,62 A study reported that LCC was associated with relative adrenal insufficiency under stress due to the immaturity of 3β-HSD enzyme activity.63 Both types of adrenal insufficiency showed a sufficient response to a physiological dose of hydrocortisone, 1 to 2 mg/kg.64 Because the maturation of 3β-HSD is dependent on gestational weeks, the incidence of LCC is higher in periviable preterm infants (Fig. 40.19).7 The incidence in periviable infants was found to be approximately 30% in infants born at 22 weeks of age and 25% at 23 weeks of age, meaning that more than onequarter of infants might suffer from circulatory collapse even 2 weeks after birth. LCC not only is a life-threatening form of hypotension but is also strongly associated with cerebral palsy with PVL in very preterm infants.65,66 Therefore the management of LCC is critical for the care of periviable preterm infants. Fig. 40.20 shows typical changes in arterial blood flow patterns in an infant with LCC. At present, the diagnosis of LCC is solely dependent on clinical findings, with no specific biomarker.67 The ruling out of sepsis or hypovolemic shock is essential before the diagnosis. • Fig. 40.7 Recommended algorithm of resuscitation for periviable preterm infants. There are no standardized procedures for the resuscitation of periviable preterm infants, but respiratory and circulatory stabilization immediately after birth should be prioritized. Without intensive support with positive pressure ventilation, the establishment of effective respiration among periviable preterm infants is not possible. The first step in postnatal stabilization is initiated by positive airway pressure with a bag and mask. When the heart rate increases above 100 beats per minute, tracheal intubation could be attempted. The initial fraction of inspired oxygen (IFiO2) should be between 0.3 and 0.6. Temperature control in infants is also critical for successful resuscitation. After the intratracheal tube is secured, the infant should be transferred to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) for further procedures. (Data from Kusuda S, Nakanishi H, Oei JL. title: The Late Preterm Infant

paragraphs.text: 41 The Late Preterm Infant
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Births between 34 and 36 6/7 weeks’ gestation (referred to herein as late preterm births) account for a significant proportion of preterm births in North America and elsewhere. These infants are larger than usual premature infants, and they are generally passed off as mature infants, but they often manifest signs of physiologic immaturity or delayed transition in the neonatal period. Several studies have documented the high incidence of neonatal complications leading to neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admissions in these infants. They have a higher incidence of transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTN), respiratory distress syndrome (RDS),1 persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), respiratory failure,2 jaundice, temperature regulation problems, hypoglycemia,3 and feeding difficulties than term infants.4
paragraphs.heading: HOPE ELIZABETH ARNOLD, KIMBERLY V. PARSONS, AND LUCKY JAIN

paragraphs.text: Concern about higher morbidity in late preterm infants has led to numerous publications with largely the same conclusions: late preterm infants are more prone to problems related to delayed transition and overall immaturity, and they should be treated differently from their more mature term counterparts.5–7 These observations have led to greater attention being paid to tracking short-term morbidity, health care costs, hospital stays, and issues such as rehospitalization. Nearly three out of four preterm births occur at late preterm gestational ages.6 The significant contribution of late preterm births is a worldwide phenomenon, although reported rates seem to be quite variable. An international review article published in 2019 on late preterm birth prevalence in 29 high-income countries including several European countries, the United States, Canada, and Japan, ranged from 3% to 6% in 2010.8 In Brazil, a country known to have one of the highest preterm birth rates in the world, the first national birth survey estimated the late preterm birth rate to be 8.5% in 2011.9
paragraphs.heading: HOPE ELIZABETH ARNOLD, KIMBERLY V. PARSONS, AND LUCKY JAIN

paragraphs.text: Preterm infants have been aptly and clearly classified for many decades. The World Health Assembly in 1948 described preterm infants as those weighing less than 2500
paragraphs.heading: Definition

paragraphs.text: g or being less than 37 weeks’ gestation. In 1950, the World Health Organization revised this definition, identifying all infants born before 37 completed weeks’ gestation (259th day), counting from the first day of the last menstrual period, as preterm infants.10 The American Academy of Pediatrics (APP) and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) agree with this definition.11
paragraphs.heading: Definition

paragraphs.text: Preterm, term, and post-term have been clearly defined according to the week and day of gestation by the World Health Organization, the American Academy of Pediatrics, and the American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology, with further delineation of late preterm and early term infants.
paragraphs.heading: Definition

paragraphs.text: To clarify and to place a greater emphasis on the fact that these slightly premature infants have a greater risk of morbidity and mortality than term infants, an expert panel at a workshop convened by the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development of the National Institutes of Health in July 2005 recommended that births between 34 completed weeks (34 weeks or day 239) and less than 37 completed weeks (36 6/7 weeks or day 259) of gestation be referred to as late preterm infants (Fig. 41.1).12 Several factors led to this definition; 34 weeks is considered a maturational milestone in obstetric practice, after which surfactant is usually present in the lungs, and historically has been used as a cutoff for giving antenatal steroids.
paragraphs.heading: Definition

paragraphs.text: In the United States there were 3,613,647 live births in 2020, of which 10.09%, or approximately 365,000, were preterm.6 Late preterm infants, at 6.3%, constituted 73% of all preterm births (Fig. 41.2). Preterm births had been steadily declining since 2007, reaching a nadir of 9.57% in 2014, but the rate increased between 2014 and 2019 (up to 10.23%). Increased awareness of the contribution of late preterm births to the total preterm birth rate and the increased risk to the infant previously lead to a significant reduction in such deliveries (Fig. 41.3).13 The decrease seen between 2007 and 2014 may be attributed to national

The late preterm birth rate was 9.54% for non-Hispanic Black infants, 7.32% for Hispanic infants, and 6.9% for non-Hispanic White infants, showing a slow increase in all races between 2014 and 2019 with a small decrease from 2019 to 2020 (Fig. 41.4).
