### Disposition and Hospice

Not infrequently, neonates survive longer than anticipated based on prenatal findings. Ideally, this possibility should be included in prenatal discussions, but some families may not be able to engage in such a level of planning until after delivery and survival through the immediate postpartum transition. If an infant is relatively clinically stable after day one or two of life, discharge from the NICU may be appropriate simultaneous with the mother’s discharge, depending on the family’s goals and the infant’s clinical status. The multiple disposition options include discharge home with hospice supports, use of inpatient hospice facilities, or the infant remaining an inpatient through the EOL.

For some families, transition from the hospital to the home environment is highly desirable. Discharge criteria for these infants are frequently different than for the traditional NICU discharge candidate. In some instances, discharge with unresolved respiratory or feeding issues may be appropriate, including discharge with nasogastric feedings or up to 2 L/min of supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula. Discussions about the utilization of these supports as comfort measures, rather than as a means of life prolongation, should occur prior to discharge. In these situations, the medical team should work to identify and establish in-home support, typically in the form of hospice care. Hospice represents a group of services, including nursing, social work, chaplaincy, and more. Typically, hospice nursing staff will visit the home as frequently as needed, usually once or twice a week. It is important to note that hospice care does not include private-duty nursing or staff who come into a home and work a traditional nursing shift. The hospice agency can offer significant support for symptom management and psychosocial support to the family through the infant’s medical journey and after the EOL. It is also worth noting that, given the high degree of uncertainty about a prognosis in many of these circumstances, some infants may do well after discharge and go on to live months or even years, graduating from hospice and transitioning to a different, more traditional level of pediatric and subspecialty care.

Depending on institutional standards and team comfort, continued admission in the NICU or hospital for EOL care may also be appropriate. Efforts should be made to continue partnering with parents and family to engage in meaningful plans of care to support families through the EOL process regardless of the time frame.

Finally, discharge to an inpatient hospice facility or a hospice house may also offer an alternative to remaining in the hospital but avoiding an EOL in a family’s home. This may be a good option for families not wishing to discharge home for a variety of reasons but who do not wish to remain in the hospital. Specific resources vary by area.

### Follow-Up After Discharge

Regardless of the inpatient medical journey, when a baby is discharged from the initial hospitalization a clear follow-up plan should be established. For infants discharged with hospice support, a hospice attending of record should be identified. This may be a local pediatrician, the medical director of the hospice agency, or occasionally a subspecialist closely involved in the patient’s care. Regardless of hospice involvement, engaging in routine pediatric care may be a meaningful experience for some families. Additionally, subspecialty involvement may be indicated for complex symptom management and evolving decision making.

### Psychosocial Support for Teams and Family

One of the primary roles of PPC is to provide ongoing psychosocial support for patient families throughout these challenging circumstances. Doing so requires an emphasis on continuity, serving as stewards of the patient’s story and striving for optimal communication and goal-concordant care, in addition to holding space for emotion processing and neutral safe spaces. This, particularly, requires interdisciplinary collaboration with mutual respect. Many PPC teams include medical clinicians such as doctors and nurses, but equally as important are the roles of social workers, psychologists, child life specialists, chaplains, and more. It is important to surround the family with this intensive support throughout their journey prenatally, during the child’s life, and after death.

Although formal PPC practitioners may vary from institution to institution, there is a significant role for palliative care champions at all levels. These are individuals who can advocate for the principles and practices outlined in this chapter, as well as the involvement of formal PPC when available. These individuals may participate in additional training, either within the institution or externally, and help perpetuate good PPC practices and normalize the involvement of PPC into standards of care.

In addition to supporting patients and families, it frequently is the role of palliative care providers and champions to provide additional support to team members involved in the intensive and complicated work of planning for and executing exceptional PPC. Institutions should strive to offer opportunities for debriefings after patient deaths and other difficult circumstances. Additionally, palliative care


## PDF page 767

education and implementation must be accompanied by discussions of resiliency and mindfulness. PPC inevitably takes a toll on all who are involved the work; long-term impacts such as burnout should be mitigated as much as possible and given appropriate and thorough consideration at each level.

### Symptom Management

The remainder of this chapter focuses on symptom management. Neonatologists are frequently skilled at symptom management in the neonate, and much of this knowledge can be translated into the palliative care realm. Particularly important is considering the underlying cause of the symptom and, if possible, addressing this cause as a primary means of alleviating the symptom. Identifying potential causes for symptoms is also paramount in determining the appropriate intervention or medication for treatment. The most significant difference is the primary focus of the treatment, which, typically in palliative care or comfort-focused settings, is the alleviation of suffering rather than resolving or treating the underlying issue or cause.

In addition to the choice of medication, the dose, route of administration, and potential adverse effects require additional attention in circumstances such as technology removal or end of life. Some families express a desire to remove lines and tubes, creating a more natural state for their child’s EOL. Consistent and convenient routes of administration such as central lines or peripheral intravenous lines may be removed (or may not be replaced if lost) based on each family’s wishes. The benefit of maintaining secure access for symptom control should be discussed with families, and preferences should be elucidated. Most frequently, this is a concern when there is significant concern for pain, seizures, and dystonia. Alternative dosing routes (e.g., oral, buccal, enteral, intranasal) should also be considered to continue symptom control without the need to maintain or establish intravenous access.

### Pain

Pain is among the most concerning symptoms during intensive care and particularly in the context of palliative care or comfort-focused care. Although previously misunderstood, it is now well accepted that inadequate treatment of pain in the neonate is unethical, especially in the EOL setting.18 Exposure to analgesic and anxiolytic medications in infants who die in intensive care units has increased significantly over the past 15 years.19 However, there remain concerns that pain is still inconsistently treated, including in the EOL period.20 This may be related, in part, to concerns about hastening death through pain medication administration. However, evidence demonstrates that infants with adequate pain control live longer than those with uncontrolled pain and agitation.21 Multiple studies have shown that morphine administration is not likely to hasten patient death.22,23 Yet, concerns remain among practitioners and institutions.

Ethically, this is addressed by the principle of double effect, which focuses on the intent of an action rather than the outcome.24 This can be applied to the administration of pain medication at frequency and dosing higher than typically utilized outside of EOL care. If the intention of the action is to alleviate pain and suffering, any associated sequelae, even if anticipated or expected, are considered ethically permissible.

Treating pain requires consistent and objective evaluation of the pain using a consistent scale or method. No individual pain scale has been found to be superior to others.25,26 However, it is important to note that these criteria may be loosened or forgone in the EOL setting dependent on treatment goals and families’ preferences. Families may not want frequent medical assessments that would typically occur in routine pain assessments, and these wishes should be respected. Caregivers and bedside staff can be educated to look for signs of pain and distress in the neonate (e.g., grimacing, agitation), and treatment can be alternatively based on these signs. Additional factors may impact pain assessment and treatment during comfort care; for example, some families may accept some discomfort to be able to spend time with their infant while he or she is awake and alert. Alternatively, many families feel that optimized pain control, even at the expense of wakeful periods, is preferable.

### Nonpharmacologic Treatment of Pain and Suffering

First steps to alleviate pain and suffering should always include nonpharmacological interventions that occasionally are sufficient in the neonatal population. Nonpharmacologic treatments should be continued as adjunctive therapies if additional medications and interventions are added to the comfort plan of care. Many simple interventions reduce pain in neonates in the ICU, including skin-to-skin/ kangaroo care, holding, swaddling, breastfeeding, exposure to the odor of maternal breast milk, non-nutritive sucking (including pacifier use), and massage.27–29 Although not specifically described in the PPC setting in the literature, these are simple, non-invasive interventions that may offer significant benefit with minimal or no risk. Additionally, these are interventions that can frequently be performed by parents or caregivers, allowing families to be actively engaged with their child and minimize the need for medical personnel, which may be desirable to some families.

### Opioids

In conjunction with the nonpharmacologic interventions discussed above, opioids are consistently utilized in the NICU setting when minimizing pain is a primary objective. Opioids are a class of medication used worldwide for the treatment of pain in a multitude of circumstances. Within the central nervous system, opioids bind to the mu, kappa, delta, and sigma receptors and can act as partial or


## PDF page 768 | printed page 759

complete agonists, antagonists, and mixed agonist-antagonists. As a class, opioids can cause respiratory depression, more frequently with fentanyl than morphine, and sedation. Although becoming more controversial for the treatment of many causes of pain, opioids remain a mainstay of pain alleviation in the EOL setting. For the purposes of this discussion, the concerns about opioid misuse and abuse are not addressed.

Morphine and fentanyl are the most utilized opioids in the NICU setting. Morphine is used in almost all patient populations in palliative care and remains an excellent choice in the EOL setting due to its multiple routes of administration and being relatively inexpensive and widely available. Additionally, it can also alleviate dyspnea, another symptom of significant concern in the EOL periods. Important side effects to consider include hyperalgesia, myoclonic movements, or pruritus, which can increase distress in the EOL period.30 These side effects are more likely to occur with the use of continuous morphine infusion. Hyperalgesia should be suspected with persistent pain, despite multiple escalations in opioid dosing. In the event of hyperalgesia, opioid rotation, frequently to hydromorphone, as well as the addition of clonidine as an adjuvant medication, should be considered.31

Fentanyl is significantly more potent than morphine (approximately 100 times), with a shorter onset of action and shorter half-life, making this a favorable choice for rapid titration to achieve pain control. Fentanyl is available in intravenous and intranasal routes, with the latter emerging as a safe and effective means of treating pain in the newborn population.32 Pertinent sequelae to consider with fentanyl use include chest wall rigidity, typically seen with large bolus doses that are rapidly administered,33 and increased frequency of apneas, associated with bolus rather than continuous administration.34

### Non-Opioid Pain Medications

A variety of medications and drug classes can be used in conjunction with or as alternatives to opioids. A frequently utilized medication in this population is acetaminophen, which can be administered orally or rectally as an antipyretic or for mild to moderate pain. This drug is typically widely available and relatively inexpensive. Intravenous paracetamol (the prodrug of acetaminophen) is an effective opioid adjunct for the management of neonatal pain.35 Data on the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen and naproxen) at the EOL in the newborn population remain lacking but these are generally not utilized.

Much of what is known about neonatal pain control comes from the world of postoperative and procedure research. Both dexmedetomidine and propofol have become widely utilized in these contexts and are gaining popularity in the PPC population. Additionally, clonidine and ketamine are also being considered and used more frequently. These are good alternatives if there are concerns

about respiratory depression from opioid use; however, specific recommendations cannot be made at this time due to a lack of robust literature in the PPC domain. Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-2 adrenoreceptor agonist and is only available intravenously. Its half-life is approximately 2 hours. Another medication in this class is clonidine, which can be used as an opioid adjuvant in cases of hyperalgesia as described above. Propofol offers additional routes of administration (intravenous and intranasal) and has noted variability in patient response.36 Ketamine has multiple desirable properties in addition to pain control, including anxiolysis and amnesia. Typically, it is administered intravenously, although there is emerging evidence of its efficacy when administered intranasally.37,38 Again, none of these medications has significant research demonstrating their utility for PPC, but they may be utilized based on individual experience, unique patient characteristics, and involvement of specialists such as pain management teams or anesthesiology.

Benzodiazepines, most frequently midazolam and lorazepam, can be used in conjunction with opioids to improve pain control, but they should not be utilized as a single agent. This class of medications can also alleviate agitation and anxiety, although validated means of measuring these symptoms are not readily available for the neonatal population. As many as 10% of neonates receiving benzodiazepines can develop myoclonic jerking, a distressing symptom for caregivers.39 This may be related to neurological immaturity or ischemic injury. If myoclonic jerking occurs, transition to another medication should take place. Benzodiazepines can be administered in a variety of routes, making them desirable in the EOL setting, particularly if families choose to not have intravenous access maintained throughout the dying process.

As mentioned previously, the cause of symptoms is an important consideration in medication selection. If there is concern for neuropathic pain, gabapentin may be beneficial. Gabapentin is a gamma-aminobutyric acid analog that is thought to inhibit pain via voltagedependent calcium ion channels in the central nervous system; it has been shown to reduce opioid and sedative medication use.40 This medication can be particularly useful in infants with neuro-irritability, chronic pain, and suspected viscera hyperalgesia. Gabapentin may also be a useful adjunct to morphine.41 There are few side effects of concern with gabapentin, and dosing can be rapidly increased. Another medication with potential neuroreceptor activity is the opioid methadone, although its extremely long half-life makes it unable to be titrated more quickly than every few days, making its utility in the acute EOL period limited.

### Dyspnea

Dyspnea is a significant concern for many families facing the end of their child’s life. This may be expressed as a worry about “suffocation,” “air hunger,” or any description


## PDF page 769

of distress related to the inability to breathe. Patients at risk for dyspnea in the NICU include those who were previously dependent on ventilatory support, especially those who have been managed on positive pressure or a fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) of >0.40 for a lengthy period. It is important to clarify that, when treating dyspnea in the EOL setting, the goal is comfort rather than cure. This may feel counterintuitive to many NICU providers, as typically the treatment for dyspnea is to increase respiratory support; however, when the goal is comfort, increasing support will not aid in achieving this goal and may increase suffering. Opioid medications remain the mainstay of treatment for dyspnea in the dying newborn. Specific to the concern of dyspnea, intranasal fentanyl and sublingual morphine are helpful options. The utilization of opioids as previously discussed is also an acceptable method of dyspnea management. Prompt relief of air hunger is desirable due to the ongoing stress witnessing it can cause to family members.

### Anxiety and Agitation

Although there are no standardized or validated tools for monitoring anxiety and agitation at the EOL, these are distressing symptoms for families to observe and should be assessed frequently and treated accordingly. Like pain, initial interventions for the management of anxiety and agitation should include nonpharmacologic interventions and adjusting environmental factors. Additionally, anxiety and agitation may be diminished by achieving adequate pain control and minimizing noxious or invasive interventions. Medical devices, such as endotracheal tubes, suctioning, and monitors, may contribute to agitation, and there should be discussion of reducing noxious stimuli. External stimuli should be similarly reduced when possible, such as eliminating or reducing laboratory testing (heel pricks, phlebotomy, or arterial sticks), imaging studies, bright lights, and noise exposure.

Benzodiazepines are the class of medications most frequently utilized to treat anxiety and agitation in neonatal patients. They reduce anxiety and effect muscle relaxation through the central nervous system, thereby reducing agitation, and thus reducing the augmentation or potentiation of pain. Barbiturates have been used historically to treat agitation and seizures in neonates. Phenobarbital has a long half-life and is difficult to titrate quickly, making it less desirable for acute symptom management purposes. Pentobarbital can be given orally or intravenously; it demonstrates more profound effects than phenobarbital and is shorter acting. Finally, barbiturates have been demonstrated to be effective as a sole agent for sedation in some patients where tolerance to opioid and benzodiazepines has developed due to long-term utilization.42,43 The barbiturate pentobarbital has historical use in euthanasia, which may contribute to practitioner or family distress. However, education about the indication for its use as an anxiolytic agent rather than for euthanasia should be provided, and

continued communication throughout its utilization may alleviate this concern.

### Seizures

Although all uncontrolled symptoms can be difficult to witness in a dying neonate, seizures are particularly distressing for families, due to the physical manifestations of convulsing serving as visible evidence of suffering and the interruption of other importance experiences such as holding. Dying patients are at risk for seizures regardless of a known seizure disorder due to hypoxia and other factors. Therefore anticipation of this should be included in EOL planning, and treatment should be readily accessible. If a patient is known to have an underlying seizure disorder, any established anticonvulsant medications should be continued. As previously mentioned, some benzodiazepines, including lorazepam and midazolam, are frequently used as pain adjuncts and anxiolytics at the EOL. Midazolam has also been studied in the palliative care setting.44 Their multitude of uses, including seizure control, makes benzodiazepines useful for NICU patients experiencing EOL.

### Delirium

The concern for delirium in NICU patients is a relatively new concern, yet it has quickly become identified as an important symptom to address. The Cornell Assessment of Pediatric Delirium can be used in the neonatal population and is tied to developmental anchor points that can be utilized in infants.45 Similar to pain and agitation, delirium and pain also overlap significantly.46 Therefore adequate treatment of pain and additional symptoms should be simultaneously pursued while treating delirium. Consultation with pediatric psychiatry may also be helpful. Patients at risk for delirium in the NICU include older infants (e.g., 2 to months of age or older) with a long history of requiring assisted ventilation and surgical patients demonstrating symptoms despite the use of opioids and benzodiazepines.47–49 There is some evidence indicating effective treatment of neonatal delirium with haloperidol or atypical antipsychotics such as risperidone or quetiapine.47,49–51 Weaning continuous infusions of benzodiazepines and opioids or decreasing dosing may also be effective.

### Sialorrhea

Part of the anticipated death process involves increased difficulty with managing one’s own secretions. This can be exacerbated in NICU patients if there are additional neurologic, musculoskeletal, or respiratory concerns. If not managed adequately and without appropriate education, this can be very distressing to families. Although deep suctioning can be traumatic, oral and pharyngeal suctioning may help alleviate some secretions. The use of atropine drops and transdermal scopolamine is well accepted in older patients52,53 but has yet to be described in the neonatal population.

### Myoclonus

In addition to a potential side effect from opioid use, myoclonic jerking may occur in the neonate because of hypoxic ischemic brain damage or an immature central nervous system. Management should be focused on reversing the underlying cause, if possible. If the jerking is not determined to be the side effect of a medication, discussion with the family and reassurance may be helpful. Neuromuscular blocking agents should not be utilized to mask myoclonus, and they do not have an accepted place in pediatric EOL care.

### Anticipatory Guidance for End of Life

Family members and loved ones of a dying neonate should be informed about the natural dying process and anticipated changes, including changes in respiratory patterns, color change of the skin, vital sign lability, cooling and mottling of the extremities, and any other known anticipated changes. If possible, a general timeline or range should also be discussed, such as the anticipation that a fully ventilator-dependent infant will live for minutes to hours after a palliative extubation or that a patient with anticipated cardiopulmonary failure related to congenital differences may live for hours to days. Open and clear communication about what to expect as part of the dying process should be frequent and fluid, as each individual child has a unique course and every collection of loved ones and family members will have different values and needs.

Key Points

• A variety of neonatal intensive care unit patients benefit

from palliative care, not only those at end of life, but patients and families facing significant uncertainty for the future and complex medical decision making. • Delivery of perinatal palliative care should include an

interdisciplinary approach addressing the physical, psychological, social, spiritual, and cultural considerations of a patient’s care. A central theme of this care should be delineating and aligning with the family’s goals of care.

### What the Future Looks Like

PPC continues to be a growing and expanding field. Neonatologists and other clinicians caring for the neonatal population will undoubtedly encounter circumstances necessitating palliative care at an increasing incidence, particularly as technology and science continue to advance. In addition to the increasing number of PPC programs and providers, it is hoped that the future will also offer an increase in research on these topics and continued evolution of the practices discussed in this chapter.54

Multiple organizational decrees have recommended the inclusion of PPC into their standards for obstetrical and neonatal care, including the 2019 American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology outline of the importance of PPC.9

Similarly, the 2013 American Academy of Pediatrics guidelines on hospice and palliative care indicated that palliative care support should be available to patients and families throughout the spectrum of life, including prenatally.55 The National Association of Neonatal Nurses and the National Perinatal Association have both issued position statements endorsing the importance of PPC.56,57 This national recognition represents the importance of this facet of perinatal care and indicates that the inclusion of these practices will continue to expand and grow in the coming years and decades.

title: Principles of Drug Use in the Fetus and Neonate

paragraphs.text: 45 Principles of Drug Use in the Fetus and Neonate
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: The use of medications during pregnancy, prescription and over the counter, is a common and increasing occurrence. Multiple studies have demonstrated that approximately 90% of pregnant women take at least one medication during their pregnancy.1 The average number of medications used during pregnancy has increased by 68%, from 2.5 to 4.2, over the past 30 years, and the use of four or more medications has increased from 23% to 50% of pregnant women.1 When interviewed, patients, physicians, and pharmacists all cite safety of the mother and fetus as a top priority when making decisions about medication use.2 Unfortunately, safety data for the vast majority of medications are limited.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Drug Disposition

paragraphs.text: Most of the drugs administered to the mother reach the fetus; the extent of fetal exposure depends on maternal drug disposition and placental drug transfer. The result of maternal drug disposition is the steady-state concentration of the drug in the maternal circulation, which ultimately determines the amount of the drug available for distribution to the fetal compartment. The steady-state concentration is impacted in varying degrees by maternal absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion of drug, all of which are altered during pregnancy.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Drug Disposition

paragraphs.text: Drug absorption is affected by a number of factors, including gastric emptying time and intestinal motility, which can significantly change during pregnancy. Gastric emptying time is unchanged in most pregnant women, although intestinal motility is decreased during pregnancy. This results in a reduced rate of absorption of many medications with a potential increase in the extent of absorption because of the prolonged transit time through the intestinal tract. Intestinal metabolizing enzymes are also altered during pregnancy, which can result in either an increase or decrease in drug absorption. Together, these factors impact the oral bioavailability of a drug and ultimately the maternal steady-state concentration.
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Pharmacokinetics

paragraphs.text: Steady-state concentration may also be altered by physiologic changes that occur during pregnancy and that influence drug distribution (Tables 45.1 and 45.2). Maternal total body water, extracellular fluid, and plasma volume all increase gradually during pregnancy by about 32%, 36%, and 50%, respectively (see Table 45.2). Maternal cardiac output also increases by about 40% to 50% as a result of increases in both heart rate and stroke volume. The increase in body water is the primary reason for the observed decreases in peak drug concentrations with standard dosing of water-soluble drugs. When the drug dose is kept constant in the presence of increasing body water, the drug’s apparent volume of distribution (Vd) increases, and steady-state drug concentrations decrease. Such a decrease in steady-state concentrations may alter the therapeutic effect of the drug in the mother and influence the amount of drug available for diffusion across the placenta. Similarly, the increase in cardiac output affects drug transfer by limiting the time a drug resides in the villous space of the placenta and is available for transfer to the fetus.
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Pharmacokinetics

paragraphs.text: Coincident with the changes in body water distribution and cardiac output, the amount of maternal fat increases in a relatively constant proportion to the increase in body weight (see Table 45.2). The result is an increase in Vd for lipophilic drugs and the potential for accumulation within the adipose tissue. Minimal changes in drug efficacy are expected under these circumstances; however, the adipose tissue can act as a reservoir and slowly release the drug into systemic circulation. An increased half-life and prolonged drug effects may be observed.
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Pharmacokinetics

paragraphs.text: Complicating the picture even further is the fluctuation in serum proteins during gestation. Both albumin and α1acid glycoprotein are decreased during pregnancy, resulting in an increase in the free (active) fraction of various highly protein-bound drugs. For example, the free fraction of tacrolimus may increase as much as 91% during mid and late pregnancy.3 This unbound drug is not only the active moiety but also the form that is available for metabolism and elimination by the mother and transfer to the fetus.
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Pharmacokinetics

paragraphs.text: Changes in hepatic metabolism during pregnancy affect the normal rate and extent of drug transformation and, ultimately, renal elimination. During pregnancy, hepatic blood flow may increase, leading to increased drug metabolism in the liver; however, this is controversial. Less debated is the alteration in the activity of hepatic enzymes during pregnancy. Enzymes from the cytochrome P450 (CYP) family and those responsible for glucuronidation reactions (uridine 5′-diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase [UGT]) exhibit changes in activity as a result of pregnancy, which can potentially affect maternal and fetal drug exposure (Table 45.3). For example, labetalol is a commonly used antihypertensive agent in pregnant women, and it is extensively metabolized by UGT enzymes that have increased activity during pregnancy. Therefore, as expected, the clearance of labetalol after oral administration is increased during the second and third trimesters by as much as 30%, and the half-life is significantly shorter in the pregnant patient compared with the nonpregnant patient.4 The consequence for the mother is an increase in total daily dose to maintain the same steady-state concentration and well-controlled blood pressure, which is critical for both mother and fetus.
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Pharmacokinetics

paragraphs.text: Alterations in renal elimination during pregnancy also impact mother and fetus. These changes result from the increase in renal blood flow by 10% to 40% and the increase in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) by about 40%.5 As a result, there is enhanced elimination of drugs that are typically excreted unchanged in the urine (e.g., penicillin, digoxin). Active renal transporters (OCT2, P-gp, OAT1) also exhibit increased activity during pregnancy, further enhancing elimination of some medications (metformin, digoxin).6 The net result is a lower steady-state concentration that may or may not be clinically significant for the mother but will likely result in less drug exposure to the fetus.
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Pharmacokinetics

paragraphs.text: In addition to maternal pharmacokinetics, the placenta also plays a major role in determining fetal drug exposure. From the fourth week of gestation until term, the surface area of the placenta increases dramatically to accommodate the increasing needs of the maturing fetus. The surface area of the villi, which represents the real area for exchange, is
paragraphs.heading: Placental Handling of Drug

paragraphs.text: about 3.4 m2 at 28 weeks’ gestation, compared with about 12.6 m2 at term. In contrast, the thickness of the placental membrane decreases with advancing gestation. During late gestation (about 32 weeks), the tissue barrier separating the maternal and fetal circulations may be less than 2 mm, and the areas become specialized in the transport functions of the placenta (i.e., rapid diffusion of substances) rather than the metabolic ones. By term, the placenta has only a single cell layer of fetal chorionic tissue separating the fetal capillary endothelium from the maternal blood. This separation, with its loose intercellular connections, presents little hindrance to small molecule transfer. Both the decreasing membrane thickness and increasing surface area with advancing gestation favor the greater transfer of drugs as gestation progresses.
paragraphs.heading: Placental Handling of Drug

paragraphs.text: Very little specific information defines the mechanisms of the processes and extent of drug transfer across the placenta. A number of interdependent variables influence the rate and extent of drug transfer across the placenta from the maternal to the fetal compartment. Most investigators and clinicians believe that the vast majority of compounds found in the maternal circulation will cross the placenta and enter the fetal compartment. Therefore the fundamental questions are about the rate and extent of this activity. Unfortunately, even today, this information is only partially available for just a few chemical entities. Similarly, the mechanisms by which drugs are transferred across the placenta are not always clear, and more than one type of transfer may be involved.
paragraphs.heading: Placental Handling of Drug

paragraphs.text: The possible modes of drug transfer across the placenta are listed in order of importance in Box 45.1. For most drugs and other compounds, it is presumed that the primary mode of transfer is by simple, passive, nonionic diffusion, which requires no energy. Pinocytosis and phagocytosis require energy and likely occur much too slowly to have any
paragraphs.heading: Placental Handling of Drug

paragraphs.text: significant impact on drug transfer, whereas facilitated and active transport play a role for some drugs.
paragraphs.heading: Placental Handling of Drug

paragraphs.text: Corticosteroids are an example of a drug class that undergoes facilitated diffusion. No energy is required to transfer steroids across the placenta, but the steroid must form a complex with a specific carrier on the placenta to be transferred from maternal to fetal circulation. Active transport occurs in a similar way, but energy is required for active transport to take place. Metformin is thought to undergo active transport via the placental OCT3 transporter, resulting in fetal concentrations that are 70% to greater than 100% of maternal concentrations.6,8 Another important aspect of active transport involves the efflux of drugs back into maternal circulation subsequent to binding with a carrier on the placenta. Digoxin is one such drug that binds to the carrier protein P-gp.6 P-gp is expressed on the maternal side of the placental-trophoblastic layer, where it mediates active efflux from the fetal compartment. This efflux is unidirectional from the fetal to maternal circulation and is probably responsible for the removal of a number of highly lipid-soluble compounds and drugs from the fetal compartment. P-gp expression is highest during the first trimester and declines over the course of the pregnancy, potentially protecting the developing fetus during its most vulnerable stages.9
paragraphs.heading: Placental Handling of Drug

paragraphs.text: As stated, most drugs are transported across the placenta by simple diffusion, and the factors that influence this process have been more extensively evaluated than those affecting the other transport mechanisms discussed. Simple diffusion is described by the Fick equation as follows:
paragraphs.heading: Placental Handling of Drug

paragraphs.text: Rate of diffusion = K A (Cm−Cf) /d
paragraphs.heading: Placental Handling of Drug

paragraphs.text: where K is the diffusion constant of the drug, which is dependent on the drug’s physicochemical characteristics; A is the surface area of the membrane to be traversed; Cm and Cf are the concentrations of the drug in maternal and fetal blood, respectively; and d is the thickness of the membrane to be traversed. Thus Cm − Cf represents the concentration gradient across the placenta, which is primarily regulated by the surface area (A) and thickness (d) of the placenta. As previously mentioned, changes in these characteristics as pregnancy progresses allow for easier transfer of drugs from maternal to fetal circulation.
paragraphs.heading: Placental Handling of Drug

paragraphs.text: The important physicochemical characteristics that influence passive drug transfer across membranes (i.e., placenta), as represented by K in the Fick equation, are outlined in Box 45.2. The characteristics that facilitate placental transfer include high lipid solubility, the unionized form under physiologic and pathophysiologic conditions, low molecular weight (<500 daltons), and low protein binding. Very few clinically important drugs meet all these “ideal” characteristics, which explains the high degree of variability reported in various studies of placental transfer. There are also a very limited number of medications, like heparin and insulin (molecular weights >1000 daltons), with any one characteristic that renders the drug 100% impermeable.
paragraphs.heading: Placental Handling of Drug

paragraphs.text: Other factors important to drug transfer across the placenta include differences between the maternal and fetal osmotic pressures and pH, as well as changes in uterine or placental blood flow. Under normal circumstances, the maternal osmotic pressure is higher than that in the fetal
paragraphs.heading: Placental Handling of Drug

paragraphs.text: compartment, and a pH difference of 0.1 to 0.15 unit exists between the fetal and maternal blood (i.e., fetal umbilical blood is −0.1 unit of pH lower than maternal blood). If alterations in either the osmotic pressures or pH occur, drug transfer will be affected. With regard to changes in blood flow, the placental flow increases from 50 mL/min at 10 weeks to 600 mL/min at term, whereas uterine blood flow approaches 150 mL/kg/min of newborn body weight at term.10 Depending on the physicochemical characteristics of the drug, blood flow may have an important influence on the rate and amount of drug transfer.
paragraphs.heading: Placental Handling of Drug

paragraphs.text: The degree to which the placenta metabolizes a drug, if at all, also influences the amount that is estimated to cross the placenta and the amount of active drug that reaches the fetus. Many CYP mixed-function oxidase enzymes have been isolated from the human placenta.11 The placenta also possesses some capacity to catalyze phase II conjugation reactions, which enhance the water solubility of the affected drugs and ultimately drug transfer.
paragraphs.heading: Placental Handling of Drug

paragraphs.text: The number of different substrates biotransformed by enzymes located in the placenta is large, but the actual content of CYP enzymes in placental tissue is low, and the activity appears to be much lower than that determined in the fetal or adult liver. Thus the actual contribution of placental enzyme activity to the biotransformation of administered drugs is believed to be inconsequential and of limited clinical significance for most drugs administered maternally. Nevertheless, the differential placental metabolism of certain corticosteroids (e.g., prednisolone, in contrast to betamethasone)12 and the resulting poor clinical outcomes with prednisolone compared with betamethasone in enhancing fetal lung maturation suggest a significant effect of placental metabolism in certain clinical scenarios.
paragraphs.heading: Placental Handling of Drug

paragraphs.text: Contrary to the popular belief that the fetus resides in a privileged and protected environment, it is clear that it is exposed to virtually every chemical entity to which the mother is exposed. Thus the absorption of most drugs into the fetal circulation is both rapid and complete. Most of this absorption is believed to occur through passive nonionic diffusion down the concentration gradients between maternal and fetal blood (which oppose each other in the placental villi), where they are separated by only a single layer of cells. However, as described earlier, a number of energy-dependent placental transporters have been characterized and are responsible for drug influx and efflux.11 In addition, the fetus may undergo continued drug exposure after its elimination because of the recirculation of amniotic fluid through the fetal gastrointestinal tract.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Pharmacokinetics

paragraphs.text: Investigators have recently taken the first steps in the development of a fetal pharmacokinetic model that could be used to predict fetal drug exposure and toxicity in the future.13 Although this model is still under development and validation, we continue to have little knowledge of a drug’s fate or potential activity once it is within fetal
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Pharmacokinetics

paragraphs.text: circulation. It will likely be distributed to the fetal organs in a manner similar to that observed after birth. However, it is not known whether there are any unusual fetal barriers to drug distribution analogous to those of the blood–brain barrier or the anterior chamber of the eye. In fact, it is not even known whether these barriers actually exist during fetal life. Additionally, a drug may have an increased affinity for a specific fetal tissue that is not the typical target tissue. For example, tetracycline has a high affinity for fetal teeth and warfarin for fetal bones.14 Protein binding will also affect drug distribution. The fetus has lower levels of serum proteins, and the proteins that are present have a lower affinity for binding drugs. The serum protein levels increase with gestational age, but free drug levels remain high secondary to the binding affinity of fetal proteins.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Pharmacokinetics

paragraphs.text: Once a drug has reached various organs, it is often not known whether it has any effect at all. It is clear that both receptor number and receptor affinity change during development. Likewise, receptor–effector coupling undergoes a programmed maturation. Thus, even though a drug may interact with specific receptors, there may be no discernible pharmacologic effect because the effector mechanisms have not yet been developed.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Pharmacokinetics

paragraphs.text: There is no question that the mean residence time for drugs in the fetus is longer than that observed in older children and adults because of the immaturity of drug clearance mechanisms. For drugs undergoing significant hepatic metabolism, there are many unknown factors. Although most hepatic metabolic pathways are less active in the fetus than in adults, this is not universally true. Moreover, in the fetus, the adrenal gland has a significant complement of drug-metabolizing enzymes that, although active during fetal and neonatal life, disappear by 6 months of postnatal age. Thus the true ability of the fetus to metabolize drugs is largely unknown, but it at least partially depends on the particular drug under consideration, the gestational age of the fetus, and its drug metabolism phenotype.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Pharmacokinetics

paragraphs.text: As noted, multiple enzyme systems are involved in xenobiotic metabolism within the body. Of the phase I or oxidative enzymes, CYP predominates. The human fetal liver contains many different CYP forms (Table 45.4), although they are present in fewer numbers and with less density than in the adult liver. The liver of the human fetus does exhibit
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Pharmacokinetics

paragraphs.text: some CYP450 activity, but the overall functional capacity of fetal CYP activity is very low, and its metabolic capacity is qualitatively and quantitatively very different from the activity observed in the adult liver. For example, nevirapine is metabolized by the adult liver via CYP 3A4, 2B6, and 2D6 but in the fetus only negligible metabolism of the drug occurs, and it does not impact overall fetal drug exposure.15
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Pharmacokinetics

paragraphs.text: The enzyme activity observed in the fetus is primarily caused by CYP3A7 expression, which is minimally expressed in the adult liver. CYP3A7 may serve as a detoxifying enzyme and protect the fetus from steroids and retinoic acid derivatives. Other enzymes expressed also serve protective roles for the fetus, such as CYP2E1, which is involved in fetal alcohol metabolism.14 Although our understanding of the expression of CYP forms by the fetus is growing exponentially, the extent of our understanding of their function remains limited. Nevertheless, the available data clearly indicate that the overall functional capacity of the fetal liver to effectively metabolize xenobiotics is far less than that of the adult liver.16
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Pharmacokinetics

paragraphs.text: Even more limited is the ability of the fetus to clear drugs that are entirely eliminated by renal excretion. The ontogeny of glomerular filtration and tubular secretion has been well studied, and renal elimination is not a significant mechanism of drug excretion for the fetus. Furthermore, any drug that is renally excreted by the fetus is eliminated into the amniotic fluid, which the fetus may swallow, leading to redistribution of the drug and the need for elimination again.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Pharmacokinetics

paragraphs.text: As discussed, most of the pharmacologic agents present in the maternal circulation cross the placenta and enter the fetal circulation and are therefore potentially harmful to the fetus. The adverse effects of in utero exposure to drugs can vary from reversible effects such as altered thyroid or renal function to irreversible effects such as fetal death, intrauterine growth restriction, structural malformations, and mental retardation.17,18 Unfortunately, the details of drug interaction with the maternal-placental-fetal unit for most drugs are extremely complex and not well studied. In a review of 172 medications approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) from 2000 to 2010, the teratogenic risk was undetermined for 97.7% of the medications.7 This lack of knowledge not only places the fetus at risk but may also cause prescribers to inadequately treat pregnant women for fear of a drug’s teratogenic potential.1
paragraphs.heading: Exposure of the Fetus to Drugs

paragraphs.text: A number of drugs are possible teratogens in humans; however, at present only a few (<30) have been positively identified as such.14 Preclinical testing during drug development is typically performed using a rodent model; however, not all human teratogens are teratogens in different animal species, and further postmarketing phase IV epidemiologic evaluations for teratogenic effects are vitally important. It has been estimated that to establish that a given drug changes the naturally occurring frequency of a congenital
paragraphs.heading: Exposure of the Fetus to Drugs

paragraphs.text: deformity by 1%, a sequential trial involving about 35,000 patients would be required. In the case of abnormalities that occur quite often in the population, physicians may not be alerted to the direct causal relationship between exposure of the fetus to the drug and the resulting adverse effect. Therefore, for most medications, it remains virtually impossible to prove teratogenicity, and prescribers must often rely on international pregnancy drug registries, the experience and reports of others, or animal studies to guide drug therapy during pregnancy.
paragraphs.heading: Exposure of the Fetus to Drugs

paragraphs.text: The teratogenic effects of thalidomide, discovered in the 1960s, illustrate the totally unpredictable nature of drug toxicity in the fetus during the first trimester. Thalidomide doses that induced analgesia with no demonstrable undesirable side effects in the mother produced major structural defects in the fetus.19 The discovery that thalidomide caused congenital malformations was made possible because this drug was widely used, induced dramatic and rare congenital defects, and had a high probability (estimated at 20%–35%) of producing a teratogenic effect after exposure from the third to the eighth week after conception. Unfortunately, these three criteria are rarely met when one is attempting to assess the teratogenicity of other drugs.
paragraphs.heading: Exposure of the Fetus to Drugs

paragraphs.text: In the absence of any clear data for a particular drug’s teratogenic potential, other factors can be taken into consideration to help predict the risk of drug exposure to the fetus. The timing of drug exposure is frequently a critical determinant of the effect of a drug on the fetus. During the first week of gestation, the most common adverse effect of drugs is the termination of pregnancy, which may occur before the woman even knows that she is pregnant. Exposure of the preimplantation embryo to embryotoxic drugs may retard development, perhaps by decreasing cell numbers in the blastocyst, or it may even produce malformations. In the second to the eighth week of gestation, drugs may produce dramatic and catastrophic structural malformations, such as the neural tube defects associated with valproic acid and carbamazepine. Other adverse effects during this period of organogenesis may include fetal waste, transplacental carcinogenesis (diethylstilbestrol), and intrauterine growth restriction. From the third to the ninth month of gestation, the effects of drugs on a fetus are widely varied and relatively specific to the drug administered. For example, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) may cause oligohydramnios, tetracycline is associated with staining of the teeth and bones, and paroxetine may slightly increase the risk for cardiac malformations.17
paragraphs.heading: Exposure of the Fetus to Drugs

paragraphs.text: In addition to the drug itself and timing of administration, the drug dose, maternal disease state, and number of medications administered are also important factors impacting teratogenicity. Epilepsy is one disease state in which these factors must be considered. Many antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) are associated with an increased risk of congenital malformations as well as adverse cognitive outcomes of the child. However, uncontrolled epilepsy can also be harmful to the fetus. Prolonged seizures have been
paragraphs.heading: Exposure of the Fetus to Drugs

paragraphs.text: associated with fetal loss, and frequent tonic-clonic seizures are associated with poorer cognitive development of the child.20 It has been suggested that the teratogenic effects of AEDs are more common in women on multiple anticonvulsant medications and those on higher doses.20 For these reasons, it is ideal to optimize an epileptic woman’s drug regimen before conception with the fewest drugs possible at the lowest effective doses. According to the FDA and the American Epilepsy Society, valproate should specifically be avoided as part of this optimization unless other treatments have failed.21 Frequent monitoring throughout pregnancy is also required, as the state of pregnancy can significantly impact the pharmacokinetics of AEDs, possibly impacting both seizure control and fetal well-being.
paragraphs.heading: Exposure of the Fetus to Drugs

paragraphs.text: The decision of whether to give a drug during pregnancy is difficult. If a mother is not healthy, the baby may not be healthy. If drug therapy can improve the mother’s health, it seems it should also benefit the fetus. However, limited or incomplete knowledge of fetal outcomes for most drugs complicates the picture. Available information on the potential adverse effects for some of the commonly prescribed known or suspected teratogens is listed in Table 45.5.17
paragraphs.heading: Exposure of the Fetus to Drugs

paragraphs.text: At birth, a term infant in North America typically receives three medications: an ophthalmic antimicrobial agent, vitamin K, and the hepatitis B vaccine. Sick and premature infants receive an increasing number of drugs, with the constant introduction of new drugs or old drugs with new indications into the neonatal therapeutic armamentarium. The appropriate and safe use of these drugs requires a thorough understanding of their various pharmacologic profiles. Fig. 45.1 illustrates many of the interrelationships of the absorption, distribution, binding, biotransformation, and excretion of a drug and its concentration at the locus of action.22 To produce its characteristic effect, a drug must be present in sufficient concentrations at its sites of action or receptor sites. The concentration of the drug at the receptor site depends not only on the amount of drug administered but also on the interrelationships listed in the preceding and shown in Fig. 45.1. Those factors that have been evaluated in the newborn infant differ substantially from those in the adult and even in the young infant beyond the neonatal period.22
paragraphs.heading: Neonatal Drug Disposition

paragraphs.text: Drug absorption is the passage of a drug from its site of administration into the circulation. In neonates who can tolerate gastric feedings, the oral route of drug administration is the most common because of its convenience and safety. The absorption of a drug or substance through the gastrointestinal system may be defined as the net movement of a drug from the gastrointestinal lumen into the systemic circulation draining this organ. This process entails the movement of drugs across the gastrointestinal epithelium,

paragraphs.text: which behaves like a semipermeable lipid membrane and constitutes the main barrier to absorption. The various processes operating to induce the transepithelial membrane movement of drug molecules include simple diffusion through lipid membranes or aqueous pores of the membrane; filtration through aqueous channels or membrane pores; carrier-mediated transport, such as active transport or facilitated diffusion; and vesicular transport, such as pinocytosis. Of these, the most important is the process of simple diffusion because most drugs administered orally are absorbed through this process.
paragraphs.heading: Selected Therapeutic Agents With Known or Suspected Teratogenic Potential

paragraphs.text: The rate and extent of gastrointestinal drug absorption are partly determined by the physical and chemical characteristics of the drug. Polarity, nonlipid solubility, and a large molecular size tend to decrease absorption. In contrast, nonpolarity, lipid solubility, and a small molecular size increase absorption. The degree of ionization, determined by the pKa of the drug and the pH of the solution in which it exists, is an important determinant in drug absorption. The gastrointestinal epithelium is more permeable to the nonionized form because this portion is usually lipid soluble and favors absorption. The degree of drug ionization changes as the pH increases from the stomach through the distal portion of the gut.
paragraphs.heading: Selected Therapeutic Agents With Known or Suspected Teratogenic Potential

paragraphs.text: Ionization also changes with the substantial changes in gastric pH observed during the neonatal period. Gastric acid production is generally low at birth, and the gastric pH is usually 6 to 8. In the first few hours of life, a burst of acid secretion occurs, decreasing the pH to values of 1 to 3.
paragraphs.heading: Selected Therapeutic Agents With Known or Suspected Teratogenic Potential

paragraphs.text: Acid secretion then returns to a low level, and the gastric pH remains near neutral for the first 10 days of life.23 The gastric pH then tends to fall and approaches adult values by 2 years of age. Clinically, the result of any decrease in pH is the increased absorption of weak acids (e.g., furosemide, phenobarbital) because they are more likely to be in the unionized, lipid-soluble state. Conversely, an increase in pH enhances the absorption of weak bases (e.g., morphine, erythromycin) and limits the absorption of weak acids. Thus a neonate transitioning from intravenous to enteral morphine may not require the standard threefold increase in dose used in older children. Instead, the administration of an oral dose that is two times that of the intravenous dose is typically sufficient.
paragraphs.heading: Selected Therapeutic Agents With Known or Suspected Teratogenic Potential

paragraphs.text: The slow gastric emptying time and intestinal motility in the newborn may also affect drug absorption. The primary site for drug absorption is the proximal bowel, which has the greatest absorptive surface area. With slower motility and emptying, it takes longer for a drug to reach this site of absorption, and the rate at which absorption can occur may be limited. Conversely, a slow transit time or slow intestinal motility may facilitate the absorption of some drugs, such as iron, which is primarily absorbed in the duodenum.
paragraphs.heading: Selected Therapeutic Agents With Known or Suspected Teratogenic Potential

paragraphs.text: The colonization of the gastrointestinal tract by bacteria is another process that influences intestinal drug absorption. Intestinal flora are involved in the metabolism of bile salts and selected drugs, as well as intestinal motility. The gut flora vary with age, type of drug delivery, and type of feeding. Concurrent drug therapy also plays a role, particularly
paragraphs.heading: Selected Therapeutic Agents With Known or Suspected Teratogenic Potential

paragraphs.text: because antibiotics, which decrease intestinal flora, are some of the most commonly administered medications to neonates. Although the actual characterization of the colonization of intestinal flora relative to age is limited, data suggest that all full-term, formula-fed, vaginally delivered infants are colonized with anaerobic bacteria by 4 to 6 days of postnatal life. By 5 to 12 months of age, an adult pattern of microbial reduction products appears to be established.
paragraphs.heading: Selected Therapeutic Agents With Known or Suspected Teratogenic Potential

paragraphs.text: Additional factors such as pancreatic and biliary function and the activity of intestinal drug-metabolizing enzymes and efflux transports can also alter absorption. As expected, this function and activity are not fully developed in the neonate, further contributing to the differences in absorption observed between neonates and older children or adults.23
paragraphs.heading: Selected Therapeutic Agents With Known or Suspected Teratogenic Potential

paragraphs.text: Overall, the differences in the neonatal gastrointestinal tract likely impact the rate of drug absorption but not the extent. The gastrointestinal absorption of drugs is relatively slow in the neonate, which can prolong the time to reach the steady-state concentration but not the actual concentration achieved. Thus the clinical significance of altered absorption in the neonate is likely minor for the majority of medications.
paragraphs.heading: Selected Therapeutic Agents With Known or Suspected Teratogenic Potential

paragraphs.text: Distribution of a drug into the extravascular tissues is largely influenced by body composition, which is much different in a neonate compared with an older infant or adult. Total body water is about 80% of body weight in a term infant and is an even greater percentage of body weight in preterm neonates. In comparison, an adult has a total body water percentage of approximately 60%.24 The extracellular water compartment of a neonate is also larger, whereas the fat content is lower. At 28 weeks’ gestation, body fat is only 1% to 3% of body weight, and at term, it is 15% to 28%.14 In addition, the fat that is found in neonates is about 50% water, compared with 25% water in an adult. The end result of these differences is a larger Vd for hydrophilic drugs, whereas lipophilic drugs may not distribute as extensively as expected. In the case of water-soluble medications, a lower peak serum concentration, higher milligram-per-kilogram doses, and delayed excretion are often observed. For example, the Vd for acyclovir in neonates has been reported to be as high as 10.8 L/kg, compared with 0.7 L/kg in adults. To achieve therapeutic concentrations of acyclovir in term neonates, a dose of 20 mg/kg every 6 hours is required, compared with 10 mg/kg every 8 hours in older children and adults.25
paragraphs.heading: Drug Distribution in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: Protein binding also plays an important role in neonatal drug distribution. The unbound or free concentration of a drug in plasma is considered to be the pharmacologically active fraction of the drug. For some drugs, the binding to plasma proteins is decreased in the newborn compared with that in the adult (Table 45.6).23 Reasons for this deficiency include decreased albumin concentrations in the neonate as well as qualitative differences in neonatal albumin. Albumin is the primary drug-binding protein in both neonates and
paragraphs.heading: Drug Distribution in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: adults, but the albumin found in neonates has less affinity for drugs compared with adult albumin. Competitive binding to albumin by many endogenous substrates, such as hormones, may also decrease protein binding. Hyperbilirubinemia may accentuate this competition because bilirubin is able to displace some drugs, such as phenytoin, from the albumin-binding site. This activity contrasts with the well-known drug–protein binding interaction with bilirubin, in which drugs such as sulfonamides or their excipients may displace bilirubin from its binding site. Regardless of cause, the decrease in protein binding observed in neonates leads to an increase in free or active drug. This outcome suggests that a more intense pharmacologic response may be obtained in the newborn infant than the adult for the same total drug concentration. Clinically, decreased protein binding in the neonate does not typically affect initial dosing, but it is important to consider this factor in the application of adult therapeutic plasma concentrations to the neonatal patient.
paragraphs.heading: Drug Distribution in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: Many drugs are lipophilic and require conversion to more water-soluble metabolites for efficient elimination from the body. These metabolic processes most often occur via drug uptake into the liver and are traditionally categorized as either phase I or II reactions. In a phase I reaction, a more polar compound is formed through oxidation, reduction, or hydrolysis of the parent molecule. Phase II metabolism involves conjugation with endogenous substrates such as sulfate, acetate, and glucuronic acid. Drugs may be conjugated directly or made more amenable to conjugation after the introduction of a functional group by phase I metabolism (e.g., hydroxylation). Typically, the metabolites formed by either type of reaction are inactive; however, some drugs can be transformed into active metabolites (e.g., theophylline to caffeine). It is well recognized that the neonate may have limited uptake of drugs into the liver and is deficient in many of the enzymes responsible for phases I and II drug metabolism.22,23
paragraphs.heading: Drug Metabolism in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: Phase I metabolism is mediated primarily by the CYP enzymes. These enzymes are present in several tissues throughout the body, including the intestine, lung, kidney, and adrenal glands, but are most highly concentrated in the liver. Numerous isoforms have been identified; the primary enzymes involved in drug metabolism are listed in Table 45.7. Considerable individuality is evident with respect to substrate specificity, polymorphic expression, and susceptibility to induction and inhibition.
paragraphs.heading: Drug Metabolism in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: The general pattern of development of CYP enzymes is illustrated in Fig. 45.2. In the fetal liver, studies have shown that CYP3A7 is by far the most significant CYP enzyme in terms of protein expression and activity. CYP3A7 concentrations decline during the neonatal period as CYP3A4 concentrations increase.23 CYP3A4 is the most abundant CYP enzyme in adults, accounting for 30% to 40% of hepatic CYP and as much as 70% of the content of CYP
paragraphs.heading: Drug Metabolism in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: in the intestine. Most other CYP enzymes develop rapidly in the neonatal period. Whether they are triggered by the loss of a maternal repressing factor or stimulated by transcription factors intrinsic to newborns, concentrations of CYP2D6 and CYP2E1 increase within hours of birth, followed closely by the CYP2C and CYP3A4 enzymes.22 By 1 month of age, hepatic concentrations are about 25% to 30% of those in adults. The notable exception is CYP1A2, which develops more slowly, reaching less than 5% of adult concentrations in the first month.22 It is generally assumed that premature babies exhibit greater impairment in drug metabolism than full-term infants; this response has been documented in several studies involving drugs metabolized by a wide range of CYP enzymes.26,27 It may result from the greater degree of immaturity of these enzymes at birth, a delay of the postnatal surge in CYP concentration observed in full-term babies, or a combination of these two factors.
paragraphs.heading: Drug Metabolism in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: The pharmacokinetics of many drugs in neonates is consistent with the pattern of development of the CYP enzymes shown in Fig. 45.2. Caffeine, which is administered for the treatment of neonatal apnea, exhibits an extremely prolonged half-life of several days in neonates compared with 4 to 6 hours in adults.26 This result is caused by the delayed development of the CYP1A2 enzyme, which is responsible for the demethylation of caffeine in the primary metabolic pathway. The structurally related bronchodilator theophylline also exhibits reduced clearance and a prolonged half-life in neonates. However, the effect is not as dramatic as that observed with caffeine because theophylline is partially oxidized by other CYP enzymes, such as CYP2E1, in addition to CYP1A2. For drugs metabolized primarily by CYP2D6 or CYP2C, it seems reasonable to expect drug clearance
paragraphs.heading: Drug Metabolism in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: to be low at birth but to increase rapidly during the first month of life. Recommended age-based dosing for phenytoin, which is a substrate for CYP2C9, supports this view. At birth, the phenytoin dose is 4 to 8 mg/kg every 24 hours, but therapeutic doses can be as high as 8 mg/kg every 8 hours after the first week of life as metabolism and clearance mature.
paragraphs.heading: Drug Metabolism in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: The clearance of drugs metabolized by CYP3A4 may be reduced less in neonates than substrates for other CYP enzymes if CYP3A7 is capable of contributing to the metabolic process. CYP3A4 and CYP3A7 show more than 85% amino acid sequence homology and have partially overlapping affinities for both endogenous and exogenous substrates.28 The catalytic activity of CYP3A4 toward drugs such as midazolam, carbamazepine, and nifedipine is greater than that of CYP3A7, whereas the latter appears relatively active in metabolizing erythromycin.28 However, even if catalytic activity is low, CYP3A7 may contribute to the overall clearance of a drug at birth, owing to the high concentrations present. This activity may account for the observation that the elimination of CYP3A substrates such as carbamazepine29 and the reverse transcriptase inhibitor nevirapine30 during the first week of life is relatively similar to that observed in adults.
paragraphs.heading: Drug Metabolism in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: The metabolism of phase II drugs is mediated by a number of different enzymes, the most important of which are N-acetyltransferase (acetylation), sulfotransferase (sulfation), and UGT (glucuronidation). Acetylation and glucuronidation are not completely developed at birth, whereas sulfation appears to be reasonably well developed relative to other pathways of drug metabolism. Glucuronidation is an important route of metabolism for many drugs (acetaminophen, morphine, zidovudine) as well as endogenous compounds such as bilirubin.23 Although UGT activity is generally presumed to be immature at birth, establishing a clear pattern for its development is complicated by the existence of numerous isoforms of the enzyme with broad and overlapping substrate specificity. UGT1A1, which is involved in the glucuronidation of bilirubin and raltegravir, is virtually absent in the fetus and develops slowly over several months after birth. Raltegravir, an antiretroviral often used to prevent transmission of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) from mother to baby, exhibits reduced clearance in neonates and incomplete elimination in some.31 A somewhat similar pattern of development exists for UGT1A6, which is responsible for the glucuronidation of acetaminophen. UGT2B7 catalyzes the formation of morphine-3-glucuronide and morphine-6-glucuronide. Its activity is decreased in newborns and increases to adult levels by 2 to 6 months of age, thus morphine clearance in neonates remains well below that of older children.23 For some medications, such as acetaminophen, increased sulfation partially compensates for the reduced glucuronidation in neonates. The proportion of a dose of acetaminophen excreted as a sulfate conjugate is higher in neonates than in older children or adults. Similar to observations with drugs metabolized by CYP, glucuronidation in premature
paragraphs.heading: Drug Metabolism in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: infants is impaired to a greater extent than it is in full-term infants.32
paragraphs.heading: Drug Metabolism in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: Conclusions based on studies of drug metabolism in the term and preterm neonate must be interpreted with caution because of the small numbers of subjects in many investigations and the potentially confounding effects of genetics and disease states on metabolism. Nevertheless, the available data suggest the following tentative conclusions: 1. The rate of drug metabolism is generally low at birth in
paragraphs.heading: Drug Metabolism in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: full-term babies and even lower in premature infants, regardless of the specific route of metabolism. Decreased clearance and a prolonged drug half-life require drug administration with longer dosing intervals. 2. Many of the enzymes responsible for metabolism exhibit
paragraphs.heading: Drug Metabolism in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: significant development during the first month of life. Dosing regimens appropriate during the first few days of postnatal life may not be appropriate 3 to 4 weeks after birth because dose requirements may increase, and dosing intervals decrease. 3. The development of individual drug-metabolizing
paragraphs.heading: Drug Metabolism in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: enzymes varies widely among neonates and may be delayed in premature infants. Predicting clearance is difficult, and dosing regimens must be individualized for patients based on the careful observation of the patient’s response and tolerance; monitoring of plasma drug concentrations may be useful for selected drugs.
paragraphs.heading: Drug Metabolism in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: The kidneys are the most important organs for drug elimination for most agents. In the newborn, the most frequently used drugs, such as antimicrobial agents and caffeine in the premature neonate, are excreted by way of the kidney. Renal elimination of these drugs reflects and depends on neonatal renal function, which is characterized by a low GFR, low effective renal blood flow, and low tubular function (secretion and reabsorption) compared with that in the adult. The neonatal GFR is about 50% of the adult value and is greatly influenced by gestational age at birth. A term neonate has a GFR of 2 to 4 mL/min/1.73 m2, whereas the GFR at less than 34 weeks of gestation is about 0.7 to 0.8 mL/min/1.73 m2. The most rapid changes in renal function occur during the first week of life, but adult values are not reached until 6 to 12 months after birth in term neonates.23,24 As expected, it takes even longer for the GFR to reach adult values in preterm infants secondary to the smaller number of glomeruli present.24 Medications administered to the neonate can also cause a decrease in GFR and ultimately reduce the elimination of concurrent drugs. For example, indomethacin inhibits prostaglandin synthesis, which leads to an increase in renal vascular resistance and thus a reduction in renal blood flow. The consequence of this is a decreased clearance of other medications, such as gentamicin, that are dependent on glomerular filtration for elimination.
paragraphs.heading: Renal Excretion of Drugs

paragraphs.text: Effective renal blood flow may influence the rate at which drugs are presented to and eliminated by the kidneys. Available data suggest that there is low effective renal blood flow
paragraphs.heading: Renal Excretion of Drugs

paragraphs.text: during the first 2 days of life (34–99 mL/min/1.73 m2), which increases to 54 to 166 mL/min/1.73 m2 by 14 to 21 days and further increases to adult values of about 600 mL/min/1.73 m2 by age 1 to 2 years. These data are probably not applicable to premature infants with very low birth weight, particularly those who weigh less than 750 g at birth. It is assumed, pending definitive data, that the GFR and renal blood flow in these infants are substantially lower than those in bigger premature infants, such as those who weigh more than 1000 g at birth. Nevertheless, renal function in these patients is highly variable, as reflected in the highly variable body clearance of a number of commonly administered drugs.
paragraphs.heading: Renal Excretion of Drugs

paragraphs.text: Tubular secretion and reabsorption are also variable and immature in neonates, initially present at only 20% to 30% of the activity observed in adults.24 Tubular secretion approaches adult values by 7 to 12 months of age in term neonates, whereas reabsorption maturation is more gradual and continues through adolescence.23 In premature neonates, tubular function is even more limited. Drugs that require tubular secretion for elimination (e.g., furosemide, morphine) typically exhibit decreased clearance during the neonatal period.
paragraphs.heading: Renal Excretion of Drugs

paragraphs.text: The pharmacokinetic behavior of drugs eliminated through the neonatal kidneys exhibits characteristics similar to those underlying hepatic biotransformation. For instance, the half-lives of many antimicrobials, such as ampicillin (Fig. 45.3), show marked interindividual variability at birth, which narrows somewhat with advancing age. The plasma half-life also shortens progressively after birth, achieving adult rates of elimination within 1 month. Studies of the pharmacokinetics of ceftazidime, famotidine, and meropenem have shown direct correlations between plasma drug clearance and the maturational changes in renal function.17,24 The drug-dependent variability in the elimination process partially reflects the major renal mechanisms of drug excretion. Those drugs that undergo substantial elimination by glomerular filtration (e.g., aminoglycosides) may
paragraphs.heading: Renal Excretion of Drugs

paragraphs.text: be excreted more rapidly than those requiring substantial tubular excretion (e.g., penicillins).
paragraphs.heading: Renal Excretion of Drugs

paragraphs.text: As with hepatic metabolism, the renal excretion of certain drugs may be as efficient as that in adults. However, usually drug excretion by way of the neonatal kidneys is deficient relative to that in an adult. Pathophysiologic insults further compromise the inherent deficiency in drug elimination, complicating individual drug dosage regimens. Hypoxemia decreases the already slow glomerular and tubular functions in neonates, leading to the slower renal excretion of drugs, as shown with amikacin. Intrauterine growth restriction leads to a decrease in the number of nephrons and renal mass, leading to a prolonged half-life of drugs such as vancomycin.33 Moreover, very small infants, who receive the most drugs in the neonatal population, exhibit the worst functional deficiency in drug elimination.
paragraphs.heading: Renal Excretion of Drugs

paragraphs.text: Age-related (gestational and postnatal) changes have been considered in the dosage regimen recommendations for antibiotics and other drugs used in the treatment of infants. Drug doses, particularly for those agents excreted by the kidneys, are dynamically changing as functions of gestational and postnatal ages. For example, more than 70% of meropenem is excreted unchanged in the urine. It has a reported clearance of 0.253 to 0.389 L/h in preterm neonates compared with 0.414 to 0.753 L/h in term neonates, and the half-life of meropenem is 3.8 hours in preterm infants compared with 1 hour in adults.24 These differences have led to specific FDA-recommended dosing that varies with gestational and postnatal age. In general, the total daily dose of a drug is directly related to the postconceptional age, and the fetal maturity is inversely related to dose interval. Thus, as an infant matures, the total daily dose increases, and the dose interval decreases. However, the neonate is often unpredictable, and rigorous monitoring of drug efficacy and patient tolerability are required regardless of gestational and postnatal age.
