A known complication of Citrobacter koseri and Enterobacter sakazakii meningitis in neonates and young infants is the formation of brain abscesses, so it is important to obtain brain imaging whenever these species are isolated from the CSF.62,63 Although L. monocytogenes is a relatively uncommon cause of neonatal meningitis, it can lead to significant morbidity and mortality because of its association with rhombencephalitis. It has been estimated to cause 5% to 20% of neonatal meningitis cases.64 Nosocomial pathogens for late-onset meningitis include CoNS, Candida, and resistant gram-negative organisms, particularly Pseudomonas.61
paragraphs.heading: Meningitis

paragraphs.text: The clinical presentation of neonatal meningitis is often nonspecific and is similar to that of neonatal sepsis. The most common finding is temperature instability, which occurs in approximately 60% of infants with meningitis. Common neurologic signs include irritability, poor feeding, respiratory distress, apneas, lethargy, hypo- or hypertonia, seizures, and abnormal pupillary response. Most infants present with a full, but not bulging, fontanelle without meningeal signs.
paragraphs.heading: Meningitis

paragraphs.text: Neonates with suspected bacterial meningitis should undergo a complete sepsis evaluation—including blood culture, CBC with differential, urine culture if greater than 6 days of age, and lumbar puncture for CSF Gram stain and culture, with cell count and differential, glucose, and
paragraphs.heading: Meningitis

paragraphs.text: protein in order of priority. For clinically stable infants, the lumbar puncture should be performed before administration of antibiotics.
paragraphs.heading: Meningitis

paragraphs.text: CSF studies need to be interpreted based on the infant’s GA, postnatal age, and birth weight (see Table 50.3), as well as prior antibiotic administration. A CSF WBC count of greater than 20 to 30 cells/μL is consistent with meningeal inflammation. However, neonatal meningitis has been shown to occur with normal CSF parameters, and there is some overlap in CSF WBC values between neonates with and without meningitis.65 If CSF findings are not definitive in an infant whose clinical picture is otherwise suspicious for meningitis, a repeat lumbar puncture obtained 24 to 48 hours later will still show pleocytosis if true meningeal inflammation is present even with the use of antibiotics. CSF protein and glucose values are highly variable in neonates with and without meningitis. CSF Gram stain may be helpful in providing an early presumptive etiologic diagnosis, although a negative Gram stain certainly does not exclude the diagnosis. If the lumbar puncture is traumatic, it is not recommended to adjust the CSF white blood cell count based on the red blood cell counts, as this does not improve the diagnostic utility for neonates.66 Ultrasound to guide lumbar puncture may reduce the incidence of traumatic taps.67 Multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) against common newborn pathogens has been utilized as a diagnostic tool in situations where the CSF is uninterpretable or has been obtained after antibiotic
paragraphs.heading: Meningitis

paragraphs.text: therapy. Automated systems are now US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved and may reduce antibiotic exposure.68
paragraphs.heading: Meningitis

paragraphs.text: Empiric therapy for early-onset meningitis includes ampicillin and an aminoglycoside. If infection with a gram-negative organism is suspected, the regimen may be expanded to include a third-generation cephalosporin in addition to ampicillin due to concerns about the high degree of ampicillin resistance in neonatal E. coli strains and poor CNS penetration of gentamicin. Aminoglycosides are not used as monotherapy because of their poor CNS penetration. When a pathogen has been identified, therapy should be tailored according to the causative organism and susceptibility testing.
paragraphs.heading: Meningitis

paragraphs.text: GBS meningitis is treated initially with ampicillin (or penicillin) plus an aminoglycoside. GBS has thus far been shown to be uniformly susceptible to penicillins, but resistance to clindamycin and erythromycin is reported.46,54 Combination therapy (e.g., penicillin and gentamicin) is used because synergy in killing activity is seen in vitro, and animal studies have shown improved outcomes with combination therapy versus penicillin alone.69 When the patient shows clinical improvement and the CSF is sterilized, therapy can be narrowed to ampicillin or penicillin monotherapy to continue for 14 days after the first negative culture. GBS ventriculitis should be treated for 4 weeks at least. Providers should refer to the latest edition of the AAP Red Book for dosages, intervals, and duration of therapy (Table 50.4).54
paragraphs.heading: Meningitis

paragraphs.text: In general, both ampicillin and penicillin are dosed more frequently in infants >7 days old than in younger infants due to pharmacokinetic differences in drug clearance. Although not all patients with GBS meningitis require a lumbar puncture at the end of therapy to confirm treatment response, it should be considered in patients with a complicated clinical course, including seizures, abnormal neuroimaging, prolonged positive CSF cultures, or slow clinical response to therapy.
paragraphs.heading: Meningitis

paragraphs.text: Gram-negative meningitis is treated with a third-generation cephalosporin for at least 21 days or for 14 days after the first negative CSF culture if that is longer. An aminoglycoside is added until CSF sterilization, which usually takes longer for meningitis caused by gram-negative organisms than for GBS meningitis. A fourth-generation cephalosporin (cefepime) or a carbapenem (meropenem) in combination with an aminoglycoside may be considered for infection with members of the Enterobacteriaceae family with inducible beta-lactamase resistance (e.g., Citrobacter, Enterobacter, Serratia) and for Pseudomonas. Studies have shown that recommended meningitic doses of meropenem may be toxic at lower GAs and may produce seizures.70 A lumbar puncture may be considered before discontinuation of antibiotics at the end of the entire treatment duration.
paragraphs.heading: Meningitis

paragraphs.text: L. monocytogenes and Enterococcus species are not susceptible to cephalosporins and should be treated with ampicillin and an aminoglycoside until CSF sterilization, followed by ampicillin monotherapy for 14 days after first negative culture. Vancomycin should be avoided, if possible, in patients with infection by L. monocytogenes, as treatment failures have been reported. Meningitis with CoNS is seen in preterm infants and is often associated with the presence of a foreign body in the CNS. Most of these organisms are resistant to penicillin, and treatment
paragraphs.heading: Meningitis

paragraphs.text: with vancomycin is often required. The duration of treatment is generally 14 to 21 days after CSF sterilization, with removal of any foreign body. Adjunctive use of corticosteroids has not shown improvement in the outcome for neonatal bacterial meningitis other than tuberculosis meningitis.71
paragraphs.heading: Meningitis

paragraphs.text: Mortality from neonatal meningitis has decreased dramatically over the past several decades, although substantial neurologic morbidity continues to be seen among affected patients. Mortality rates were estimated at almost 50% in the 1970s and have decreased to current estimates of 10% to 15%, with higher mortality rates among preterm infants and those in developing countries.61,72 Studies estimate that, among survivors, 21% to 38% will have mild deficits and 24% to 29% will have severe neurologic sequelae.61,73 Neurologic sequelae include developmental delay, seizures, hydrocephalus, cerebral palsy, blindness, and hearing loss. Predictors of poor neurologic outcomes include seizures lasting >72 hours, presence of coma, hypotension requiring the use of inotropes, leukopenia (<5.0/mm3), and abnormal electroencephalogram findings.61,74 All neonates with a diagnosis of meningitis should receive audiologic testing prior to discharge and ongoing audiologic monitoring until school age.
paragraphs.heading: Meningitis

paragraphs.text: Pneumonia is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in neonates, especially in developing countries, where it is a leading cause of death for all children under 5 years of age.75 The incidence of lower respiratory tract infection in developed countries is estimated at less than 1% among fullterm infants but may be as high as 10% in low birth weight infants. In developed countries, the morbidity and mortality from neonatal pneumonia depend largely on the GA of
paragraphs.heading: Pneumonia

paragraphs.text: the patient, severity of disease, and underlying medical conditions, especially chronic lung disease. Neonatal pneumonia is also categorized into two patterns of disease according to timing and route of acquisition. EOS more commonly presents as pneumonia than LOS. Early-onset pneumonia is usually acquired within the first 3 days of life via vertical transmission, including aspiration of infected amniotic fluid and transplacental transmission. Early-onset pneumonia, which occurs in the setting of maternal infection, is usually referred to as congenital pneumonia and presents at birth or within the first 48 hours of age. Late-onset pneumonia occurs after the first week of life, and infection arises from pathogenic organisms in the infant’s environment. The risk for late-onset pneumonia is highest among infants who require mechanical ventilation. Although ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is not clearly defined in neonates, experts recommend a minimum of 48 hours of mechanical ventilation along with other clinical signs of respiratory decompensation to diagnose neonatal VAP. Other risk factors include extreme prematurity, prolonged hospitalization, and previous bloodstream infection.76 Neonatal autopsy studies found that intrauterine and early-onset pneumonia occurred in 10% to 38% of stillborns and 20% to 63% of live-born babies who subsequently died.77
paragraphs.heading: Pneumonia

paragraphs.text: The most common cause of early-onset pneumonia in developed countries is GBS. Other common causes include S. pneumoniae, nontypable Haemophilus influenzae, S. aureus, E. coli, Klebsiella, and atypical organisms. Ureaplasma urealyticum has been linked to the development of chronic lung disease in colonized infants. A recent randomized placebo-controlled trial showed that azithromycin was effective in treating Ureaplasma infection and in preventing bronchopulmonary dysplasia in those babies who are colonized after birth.78 Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia can occur in the first week of life but more typically presents between 2 and 4 weeks of age, given its long incubation. C. trachomatis pneumonia and ophthalmia neonatorum are discussed in more detail elsewhere. Although syphilis, L. monocytogenes, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis can be transmitted across the placenta, these pathogens are uncommon causes of neonatal pneumonia.
paragraphs.heading: Pneumonia

paragraphs.text: Definitive culture data are often lacking for cases of lateonset, community-acquired neonatal pneumonia, some of which are polymicrobial in nature. S. pneumoniae is considered a predominant causative pathogen in this population. Other important pathogens include S. aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, nontypable H. influenza, and gram-negative enteric organisms. S. aureus, streptococci, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Citrobacter, Enterobacter, Serratia, and Pseudomonas, all of which have been shown to have the potential to cause extensive lung injury, including abscess formation, empyema, and pneumatoceles. Although it generally causes self-limiting illness in older children and adults, Bordetella pertussis infection in young infants can lead to respiratory failure and death. Pertussis can present as apneas in preterm neonates. The infantile pertussis cases in the early 2000s had doubled from the previous baseline of 60 per 100,000 infants
paragraphs.heading: Pneumonia

paragraphs.text: to 120 per 100,000.79 The CDC updated their vaccination guidelines in 2013 to include a recommendation that all pregnant women get a dose of the tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis (Tdap) vaccine during each pregnancy. Receipt of the Tdap vaccine during pregnancy allows for increased maternal pertussis antibody transfer to the neonate. This provides added protection for infants from birth to the time of infant pertussis vaccination at 2 months.79 Since 2015, the infantile pertussis rates have come down and stayed around 60 per 100,000 infants.79
paragraphs.heading: Pneumonia

paragraphs.text: The clinical presentation of early-onset pneumonia often includes respiratory distress and tachycardia within the first few hours of life. Other associated signs are apnea, lethargy, poor feeding, temperature instability, abdominal distention, poor perfusion, and metabolic acidosis. None of these signs is specific for pneumonia, and any infant with these symptoms should undergo a complete sepsis evaluation. Copious or purulent tracheal secretions may also be present. Increasing frequency of suctioning of the endotracheal tube along with increased FiO2 requirements may be the only signs of a bacterial lung infection in mechanically ventilated neonates.
paragraphs.heading: Pneumonia

paragraphs.text: The diagnosis of neonatal pneumonia can be difficult. The differential diagnosis of clinical respiratory distress is broad and includes many noninfectious causes such as transient tachypnea of the newborn, respiratory distress syndrome, meconium aspiration, pulmonary hemorrhage, pneumothorax, hypoglycemia, and metabolic acidosis. Anatomic abnormalities that can cause respiratory distress include primary pulmonary hypoplasia, tracheoesophageal fistula, choanal atresia, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, and congenital heart disease, among many others. Causative pathogens are rarely obtained and identified from the lower respiratory tract. Blood cultures should be obtained from any neonate with suspected pneumonia because it is often a manifestation of systemic infection. Chest radiographs can be helpful in making the clinical diagnosis, although there is significant radiologic overlap between pneumonia and other respiratory disorders of the newborn. In pneumonia, radiographs often reveal bilateral alveolar densities with air bronchograms or irregular, patchy pulmonary infiltrates. Pleural effusions are seen in up to two-thirds of pneumonia cases and are almost never seen in uncomplicated respiratory distress syndrome. The chest radiograph may appear normal in up to 15% of pneumonia cases. Tracheal aspirate Gram stain and culture results are valuable if obtained immediately following intubation. If an infant has been intubated for several days, the endotracheal tube will invariably become colonized and has limited specificity.86 Nonbronchoscopic bronchoalveolar lavage has been studied as an alternative to tracheal aspirates in obtaining lower respiratory samples in mechanically ventilated infants.80
paragraphs.heading: Pneumonia

paragraphs.text: Like most early-onset newborn infections, empiric antibiotic treatment includes ampicillin and an aminoglycoside. Therapy can then be tailored to susceptibility results if a causative organism is identified. Empiric antibiotic therapy for late-onset pneumonia will depend on local bacterial resistance patterns in both the hospital and the community.
paragraphs.heading: Pneumonia

paragraphs.text: Vancomycin and a third-generation cephalosporin such as cefotaxime are commonly used as empiric therapy to provide coverage against newborn pathogens, as well as CoNS and MRSA. If Pseudomonas is suspected, an aminoglycoside plus an antipseudomonal beta-lactam, such as ceftazidime, cefepime, or piperacillin-tazobactam, should be given. Recommended duration of therapy for uncomplicated pneumonia is 5 to 7 days and longer for preterm infants or mechanically ventilated infants.76 Ventilator-associated pneumonia prevention bundles are being used in NICUs and include earlier extubation, hand washing, and closedcircuit suctioning.
paragraphs.heading: Pneumonia

paragraphs.text: The incidence of bacteriuria in term newborns is estimated to be 0.1% to 1%. The incidence is higher in preterm infants and is thought to be around 2%. In the neonatal period, urinary tract infection (UTI) is more common among males than females. Over the first 6 months of life, the incidence of UTI in males decreases, whereas in females it increases. By 1 year of age or older, girls are more likely than boys to have UTIs.81 Uncircumcised males are at higher risk for UTI than are circumcised males. This is due to enhanced bacterial adherence to the foreskin and increased bacterial colonization in the urogenital tract.82 It is rare for a UTI to occur in the first 3 days of life; therefore urine cultures are not recommended as part of the routine EOS evaluation.
paragraphs.heading: Urinary Tract Infections

paragraphs.text: Infection of the urinary tract in neonates is thought to be acquired either through hematogenous spread or by ascending infection, often associated with anatomic abnormalities. Hematogenous spread is thought to be the cause for many young infants with UTI, because bacteremia with the same organism is seen in approximately one-third of neonates with urinary tract infection.81 Preterm infants are at higher risk for UTI with concordant bacteremia. Associated meningitis is also seen in 1% to 2% of these cases.83 Urinary tract abnormalities are seen in approximately 20% to 50% of infants with UTIs.81,84 The most common abnormality seen is vesicoureteral reflux (VUR). VUR is associated with younger age at UTI presentation and is fourfold higher in infants with Klebsiella UTIs than E. coli UTIs.85 Other abnormalities that may increase the risk for UTI include ectopic ureter, duplicated collecting system, renal dysplasia, and causes of obstruction, such as posterior urethral valves and ureteropelvic junction obstruction. An additional risk factor for UTI is the presence of an indwelling urinary catheter.
paragraphs.heading: Urinary Tract Infections

paragraphs.text: The most common causative pathogen for neonatal UTI is E. coli, which has been isolated in approximately 80% of cases in some large series.81,84 E. coli has several virulence factors that confer an increased ability to cause UTI. Uropathogenic E. coli, the causative organism in most UTIs, can invade and replicate within uroepithelial cells. Adhesins on the bacterial surface allow for increased adhesion to urogenital tract cells, and fimbriae are important in promoting persistence of infection. Other common causative organisms
paragraphs.heading: Urinary Tract Infections

paragraphs.text: include other Enterobacteriaceae: Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Proteus, Citrobacter, Salmonella, and Serratia. Gram-positive organisms are isolated much less frequently than gramnegative organisms, although Enterococcus faecalis and S. aureus are also known to cause UTI in newborns. CoNS are more common in preterm infants, and there is 18% concordance with positive blood cultures.86
paragraphs.heading: Urinary Tract Infections

paragraphs.text: The signs of neonatal UTI are nonspecific and may include fever, lethargy, failure to thrive, poor feeding, abdominal distention, vomiting, tachypnea, and cyanosis. The clinical presentation of preterm infants is similar to that of term infants, although term infants present more commonly with a fever as compared to preterm infants, who usually have poor feeding or respiratory symptoms. Neonatal UTIs are associated with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and the AAP recommends that all infants with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia be screened for UTI. Infants with high unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that cannot be otherwise explained should also be screened for UTI; E. coli is the most common pathogen isolated in these cases.87,88 Definitive diagnosis must be made by urine culture with specimens obtained by catheterization or suprapubic bladder aspiration. Samples collected into a bag are not useful because they are frequently contaminated. Any growth of a urinary pathogen from bladder aspirate is considered significant. Catheterization cultures with greater than 50,000 CFU/mL are considered positive. Urinalysis, although not a substitute for urine culture, should be obtained, as recent studies have shown improved sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing UTIs in febrile infants ≤60 days old, especially those with ≥50,000 CFU/mL, and particularly for UTIs with associated bacteremia.89 Blood cultures should be obtained for all infants with suspected UTI, as one-third with UTIs will have bacteremia with the same organism. Clinicians should have a very low threshold for performing a lumbar puncture in neonates with UTI, because the risk for concomitant meningitis is 1% to 2%.83
paragraphs.heading: Urinary Tract Infections

paragraphs.text: Empiric antibiotic treatment for neonatal UTI includes ampicillin and an aminoglycoside. Hospitalized infants with late-onset infections should be given vancomycin and a cephalosporin to provide coverage for hospital-associated infections with CoNS, MRSA, and resistant strains of enteric organisms. If the infant has had a prior infection, antibiotics should be chosen based on the susceptibility results from the prior episode. If the infection is caused by a highly resistant pathogen or if there is a known anatomical abnormality, a urine culture may be repeated 2 to 3 days after start of treatment to confirm sterilization of the urine. If cultures remain positive despite adequate therapy, the infant should be further evaluated for a potential reservoir of infection with a renal ultrasonography. The duration of therapy is generally 7 to 10 days for uncomplicated bacterial UTI in a newborn.54 Indwelling catheters should be removed promptly, as they serve as a nidus of bacterial growth. Neonates and newborns with delayed clinical response, prematurity, bacteremia, or presence of anatomic abnormalities are usually given intravenous antibiotics for
paragraphs.heading: Urinary Tract Infections

paragraphs.text: the entire course. Older infants with uncomplicated disease may be switched to oral antibiotics after demonstration of clinical improvement.
paragraphs.heading: Urinary Tract Infections

paragraphs.text: All neonates with UTIs should undergo imaging evaluation because of the high prevalence of urinary tract abnormalities. If prenatal ultrasound data are not available, a renal ultrasound should be performed after the infant has clinically stabilized. Ultrasound can detect structural abnormalities, although it cannot detect VUR or renal scarring. A voiding cystourethrogram is performed to detect VUR, and this is usually done 3 to 6 weeks after completion of antibiotic treatment. Long-term outcomes of UTIs can include renal scarring with subsequent hypertension and chronic kidney disease. If renal damage is suggested by ultrasound, renal cortical scintigraphy can be performed to better assess for renal scarring.81
paragraphs.heading: Urinary Tract Infections

paragraphs.text: Osteomyelitis and septic arthritis are uncommon infections in neonates and can be difficult to diagnose in this population. In neonates, the most common route for infection to the bone or joint is by hematogenous spread. There are important differences in the pathophysiology of musculoskeletal infections in neonates compared with older children and adults. In infants, metaphyses are susceptible to hematogenous seeding of infection because of the sluggish blood flow within metaphyseal blood vessels, which make hairpin turns before emptying into venous sinusoids. In addition, the lining of the venous sinusoids has reduced macrophage activity.90 In infants, secondary ossification centers have not yet formed, and their cartilaginous epiphyses are supplied with blood directly from transphyseal vessels from the bone metaphysis up until 8 to 18 months of life. Therefore osteomyelitis in infants commonly leads to epiphyseal damage and joint infections. This contiguous infection rarely occurs in older children and adults with osteomyelitis, because the epiphyses and metaphyses have separate blood supplies. Similarly, anatomic differences in the blood supply to the spinal column render neonates more susceptible to discitis than to vertebral body osteomyelitis.91
paragraphs.heading: Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

paragraphs.text: In preterm neonates, the femur and the tibia are the most common bones (50%) involved in neonatal osteomyelitis, followed by the humerus and the fibula. The most common causative organisms are S. aureus, E. coli, and GBS.91 Less common pathogens include Kingella kingae, group A Streptococcus, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, other enteric gramnegative bacilli, and Candida. The signs and symptoms of osteomyelitis and joint infections in neonates are often subtle and similar to signs of sepsis. Infants may present with irritability, poor feeding, or fever. Some will show positional preference, lack of use of the involved extremity (pseudoparalysis), joint or limb swelling, or pain with passive motion, as with diaper changes. Infections are often multifocal. If left untreated, septic arthritis of the hip can lead to spontaneous drainage along the internal obturator muscle, resulting in a lower abdominal mass just above the inguinal canal.
paragraphs.heading: Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

paragraphs.text: Osteomyelitis in term neonates differs slightly from preterm neonates. Neonates with late-onset GBS disease often present with osteomyelitis of the proximal humerus, especially those with a history of shoulder dystocia. The skull is the second most common site of osteomyelitis in previously healthy term infants. These infants have a history of iatrogenic injury, cephalohematoma, or fetal scalp electrodes. Calcaneal or heel osteomyelitis is a rare disease following heel punctures for blood sampling and usually is due to CoNS or S. aureus.91
paragraphs.heading: Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

paragraphs.text: Imaging studies should be obtained for any patient with suspected osteomyelitis or septic arthritis. The radiologic investigation usually starts with plain radiographs, although they cannot detect changes of osteomyelitis in a large percentage of cases. Findings can include deep soft tissue swelling, widening of the joint space or joint dislocation, osteoporosis, periosteal new bone formation, and bony destruction.92 Soft tissue swelling is the earliest finding and can be detected as early as 48 hours after the onset of infection. Bony changes, however, are not apparent until 7 to 10 days after onset of infection. Ultrasound can detect subperiosteal collections and joint effusions, so it is very useful in cases of suspected septic arthritis. Bone scintigraphy is more sensitive than plain films for detecting osteomyelitis early on, and it is useful for detecting multiple foci of infection.92 Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can detect bony changes within 24 to 48 hours after the onset of symptoms and is the diagnostic tool of choice for osteomyelitis. MRI should include a combination of T1-weighted images and short tau inversion recovery (STIR) images in the coronal or sagittal plane, axial fat-suppressed T2-weighted images, and postgadolinium fat-suppressed T1-weighted images in the axial and longitudinal planes.93 MRI provides excellent anatomic detail without exposing infants to ionizing radiation and also provides better information on growth plate involvement compared with bone scintigraphy. However, careful interpretation of bone scans and MRI is necessary to distinguish physiologic from pathologic increased uptake due to increased vascularity of the metaphyseal region in neonates.
paragraphs.heading: Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

paragraphs.text: Fluid collections in soft tissue or bone should be aspirated and sent for Gram stain and culture, and patients with joint involvement should have synovial fluid sent for Gram stain and culture. Blood cultures yield the causative organism in approximately 50% of cases.94 Lumbar puncture should be performed on ill-appearing infants or those with positive blood cultures.
paragraphs.heading: Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

paragraphs.text: Recommended empiric antibiotic treatment includes vancomycin for broad gram-positive coverage and an aminoglycoside or third-generation cephalosporin for gramnegative coverage. Therapy can be narrowed when the causative organism has been isolated. Most patients with osteomyelitis can be managed with conservative, or nonsurgical, treatment. Hip and shoulder joint infections and bony abscesses require surgical drainage, as do some infected cephalohematomas. Knee, ankle, and elbow joints usually need aspiration. The total duration of therapy is 4 to 6 weeks for
paragraphs.heading: Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

paragraphs.text: uncomplicated cases. Therapy should be 8 weeks for osteomyelitis caused by MRSA and 6 to 12 months for infants with fungal disease caused by Candida.95,96 Pediatric infectious disease and pediatric orthopedic specialists should be involved in the care of these infants.
paragraphs.heading: Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

paragraphs.text: Significant morbidity may be associated with neonatal musculoskeletal infections, and prompt diagnosis and treatment are needed to minimize complications. Septic arthritis of the hip is associated with serious long-term sequelae. Complications include growth plate damage, avascular necrosis, limb length discrepancies, and angular joint deformities, among many others.97 These patients should be followed for the development of long-term complications, as many will require surgical intervention.
paragraphs.heading: Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

paragraphs.text: Ophthalmia neonatorum is conjunctivitis occurring in the first month of life. Bacterial causes include S. aureus, nontypable H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, enteric gram-negative bacilli, GBS, N. gonorrhoeae, and C. trachomatis. The differential also includes viral causes, particularly herpes simplex virus, and noninfectious causes, such as chemical conjunctivitis. Conjunctivitis in neonates is managed aggressively because of the high risk for associated systemic illness and complications. Prophylactic administration of ophthalmic antibiotic agents shortly after birth greatly reduces the risk of gonococcal conjunctivitis but not chlamydial disease, as topical ophthalmic ointments do not prevent nasopharyngeal colonization, which is the primary route of chlamydial infection.
paragraphs.heading: Ophthalmia Neonatorum

paragraphs.text: The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that eye prophylaxis be provided to all newborns.98 Regimens with equal efficacy include 0.5% erythromycin ointment, 1% tetracycline ointment, and silver nitrate solution, although the latter two are not commercially available in the United States. Chemical conjunctivitis is usually seen soon after birth and improves over 48 hours.
paragraphs.heading: Ophthalmia Neonatorum

paragraphs.text: The clinical presentation of bacterial conjunctivitis in neonates is similar to that in older patients. Typical signs include purulent ocular discharge, erythema and edema of the eyelids, and injection of the conjunctivae. Gonococcal infection in the newborn is typically acquired during delivery, with perinatal transmission occurring in 30% to 40% of cases of active maternal cervical infection.99 Infants usually show signs of infection 2 to 5 days after birth, with profuse, purulent ocular discharge and swelling of the eyelids. Untreated infection can spread into the subconjunctival connective tissue and cornea, leading to ulceration, scarring, and visual loss. In addition to conjunctivitis, infection of other mucosal surfaces can occur, and scalp abscess may be associated with the use of fetal monitoring electrodes. Disseminated infection can lead to septic arthritis or, less commonly, bacteremia or meningitis.
paragraphs.heading: Ophthalmia Neonatorum

paragraphs.text: C. trachomatis is usually transmitted to the neonate during vaginal delivery, and approximately 20% of infants born to mothers with active cervical infection will develop
paragraphs.heading: Ophthalmia Neonatorum

paragraphs.text: conjunctivitis.100 Chlamydial conjunctivitis is also known as inclusion conjunctivitis. The serovariants of C. trachomatis causing infection in neonates (D–K) reflect the primary serotypes causing genital disease in adults. The onset of conjunctivitis is often 5 to 14 days after birth. Findings may range from mild eyelid swelling with minimal watery discharge to mucopurulent discharge, significant swelling, and red, thickened conjunctivae. If the exudate adheres to the conjunctivae, a pseudomembrane may form. Bloody discharge may also be noted with intense inflammation. Without treatment, infection may lead to corneal and conjunctival scarring or progression toward pneumonia 2 to 8 weeks after birth. Approximately half of the infants with chlamydia pneumonia have a history of conjunctivitis.
paragraphs.heading: Ophthalmia Neonatorum

paragraphs.text: All newborns who develop conjunctivitis after the first days of life should have laboratory testing performed to determine the etiology, because there is significant overlap in clinical presentation among the causative pathogens. If gonococcal infection is suspected, CSF and blood cultures are obtained to determine if dissemination occurred.54 Purulent ocular discharge is sent for Gram stain and culture. Culture on selective media (e.g., Thayer-Martin) is needed to evaluate for gonococcal infection. Additionally, conjunctival specimens should be sent for C. trachomatis testing. These are obtained from an everted eyelid using a Dacron-tipped swab. C. trachomatis is an obligate intracellular organism, so specimens must contain conjunctival epithelial cells; ocular exudates are not adequate specimens for testing. Culture of the organism is the gold standard for diagnosis of C. trachomatis infection in infants. Nucleic acid amplification tests may also be considered because they have been found to have high specificity and sensitivity, although none has been approved by the FDA for use on conjunctival specimens, for which direct fluorescent antibody tests are preferred.101 In infants with signs of pneumonia, testing for C. trachomatis can be sent from nasopharyngeal specimens.
paragraphs.heading: Ophthalmia Neonatorum

paragraphs.text: Systemic antibiotics are required to treat conjunctivitis resulting from N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. For other causes of bacterial conjunctivitis, topical antibiotic ointment or solution given for 7 to 10 days provides adequate therapy. Infants with gonococcal eye disease should be hospitalized and monitored for response to treatment, as well as for signs of disseminated disease. Recommended treatment for gonococcal conjunctivitis is a single dose of intramuscular or intravenous ceftriaxone. If the infant is receiving intravenous calcium, cefotaxime should be used instead of ceftriaxone because precipitation can occur. Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin from albumin, so levels should be monitored in these infants. If there is concurrent concern for gonococcal scalp abscess or disseminated infection, treatment should be continued for 7 days or 14 days if meningitis is suspected. The eyes should also be irrigated frequently with sterile saline until the discharge has resolved. Recommended treatment for either chlamydial conjunctivitis or pneumonia is oral erythromycin base or succinate for 14 days or azithromycin for 3 days.54 Data are limited on the effectivenes and optimal dosing of azithromycin in neonatal ophthalmia. Providers
paragraphs.heading: Ophthalmia Neonatorum

paragraphs.text: should be aware that oral erythromycin is associated with an increased incidence of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, and these infants should be followed for such.
paragraphs.heading: Ophthalmia Neonatorum

paragraphs.text: A diagnosis of neonatal ophthalmia should prompt testing for sexually transmitted infections in the mother and her partner(s). Infants born to mothers with untreated gonorrhea should receive prophylactic intravenous or intramuscular ceftriaxone after birth. These infants do not need any prophylactic ophthalmic ointment. Infants born to mothers with untreated Chlamydia infection do not need prophylactic systemic treatment but should be followed closely for signs of ophthalmia.
paragraphs.heading: Ophthalmia Neonatorum

paragraphs.text: Omphalitis is an infection of the umbilicus or surrounding tissues. Newborns are predisposed to umbilical infections following colonization of the umbilicus by a wide array of microorganisms shortly after birth as devitalized tissues of the cord stump provide for excellent bacterial growth. Bacteria can reach the bloodstream through patent vessels of the newly cut cord and lead to systemic infection and severe complications. The incidence of omphalitis in developed countries is low and is estimated to be less than 1%.102 Although complete data are lacking from developing countries, the incidence is expected to be much higher. The risk may be six times greater for infants delivered at home than for hospital births. Other risk factors for omphalitis include low birth weight, prolonged rupture of membranes, umbilical catheterization, and improper cord care. Postnatal application of substances to the cord presumed to aid in faster separation is often an inciting factor in omphalitis. Immune deficiencies such as leukocyte adhesion defect often present with omphalitis in the neonatal period.
paragraphs.heading: Omphalitis

paragraphs.text: Organisms that colonize the umbilicus or surrounding skin can produce omphalitis. Common pathogens include S. aureus, group A streptococci, GBS, and gram-negative bacilli, including E. coli, Klebsiella, and Pseudomonas. Polymicrobial infections are common in omphalitis. Anaerobic bacteria can contribute to infection, especially in infants born to mothers with chorioamnionitis.
paragraphs.heading: Omphalitis

paragraphs.text: The clinical presentation of omphalitis is usually around 3 to 5 days in preterm neonates and 5 to 9 days for term neonates, and it starts with periumbilical erythema followed by purulent drainage from the umbilical stump (or from the navel after the cord has separated), with surrounding induration and tenderness. The drainage may be foul smelling, which is suggestive of infection with anaerobic bacteria. Infants with more severe infection will display systemic signs of illness, including fever, lethargy, poor feeding, and irritability. Involvement of the abdominal wall, black eschar, or extensive edema should prompt consideration for necrotizing fasciitis as a complication. Other complications of omphalitis include peritonitis, intra-abdominal abscess, suppurative thrombophlebitis of portal or umbilical veins, and umbilical hernia with bowel ischemia. Delayed treatment of neonatal omphalitis is associated with a high case fatality rate.
paragraphs.heading: Omphalitis

paragraphs.text: Omphalitis is a clinically apparent diagnosis but can be confused with patent urachus or funisitis. Purulent discharge should be sent for Gram stain and culture. Blood and CSF cultures should be obtained from infants with signs of systemic illness, including fever, lethargy, and irritability. Prompt treatment with broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotics must be started if there is clinical suspicion of omphalitis due to the high mortality rate associated with this disease. Typically, an antistaphylococcal penicillin and an aminoglycoside are given to provide gram-positive and gram-negative coverage. If the community prevalence of MRSA is high, vancomycin should be used instead of antistaphylococcal penicillin. The addition of clindamycin or metronidazole may be considered if there is suspicion of anaerobic involvement, especially for infants with foul-smelling discharge or if there is a history of maternal chorioamnionitis. For uncomplicated cases, duration of treatment is typically 10 days. A switch to oral therapy for completion of the course of treatment may be considered, depending on the patient’s age, culture results, and clinical response.103
paragraphs.heading: Omphalitis

paragraphs.text: Prevention of omphalitis involves both clean delivery services and hygienic cord care. It is generally agreed upon that the umbilical cord should be cut with clean hands using a sterile blade or scissors. This helps to prevent both omphalitis and neonatal tetanus. However, optimal care of the cord stump after the cord has been cut is an area of active research and some debate. Since 1998, the WHO has recommended dry cord care in high-resource settings. In low-resource settings where delivery might not be in a hospital, there is benefit of applying 4% chlorhexidine to the cord to reduce omphalitis and neonatal mortality.104 However, the benefit of chlorhexidine in the hospital setting in such countries remains debated and is still a topic of active research.105,106 A 2004 Cochrane review of 21 studies, most of them performed in high-income countries, showed no difference in risk for omphalitis among cords treated with antiseptics (such as alcohol, iodine, and chlorhexidine) compared with dry cord care or placebo.107
paragraphs.heading: Omphalitis

paragraphs.text: Group B Streptococcus (GBS), or Streptococcus agalactiae, is the most common cause of EOS in term neonates (>50%) in the United States. The GBS serotype corresponds to its capsular polysaccharide. Serotype Ia, Ib, II, III, IV, and V account for >95% of EOS cases and >97% of LOS cases in the United States. Serotype III is strongly linked to meningitis and accounts for a significant proportion of LOS cases.9 GBS is the second most common cause of EOS in preterm neonates less than 37 weeks′ GA (13%–20%) after E. coli. For all GAs combined, the incidence varies from cohort to cohort. The most recent National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD) database (2015–2017) lists it as second most common at 30.2% behind E. coli (36.6.%), whereas a CDC surveillance cohort from 2005 to 2014 ranked it as the most common (35.8%).11,12 The primary risk factor for early-onset
paragraphs.heading: Group B Streptococcus

paragraphs.text: GBS disease in the neonate is maternal GBS colonization of the genitourinary or gastrointestinal tract leading to intrapartum vertical acquisition of GBS during passage through the birth canal. The introduction of universal screening for maternal GBS colonization and the use of intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis have led to an 80% reduction in the burden of early-onset GBS disease, yet has had no impact on late-onset disease.46 The incidence of GBS LOS remained at ∼1 per 1000 live births in preterm infants and ∼0.2 per 1000 live births in term infants from 2006 to 2015, despite widespread adoption of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) intrapartum prophylaxis recommendations.9
paragraphs.heading: Group B Streptococcus

paragraphs.text: Following several clinical trials and observational studies, which demonstrated that early-onset GBS disease in neonates could be decreased by administering intravenous antibiotics during labor to women at risk for transmitting GBS, the CDC has recommended GBS screening for pregnant women for the prevention of neonatal GBS disease. The most updated guidelines have endorsed the AAP and ACOG recommendations of screening and intrapartum prophylaxis. The ACOG no longer recommends a “riskbased” prevention strategy but recommends that all pregnant women, regardless of planned mode of birth, should undergo antepartum GBS testing between 36 0/7 and 37 6/7 weeks’ pregnancy, unless intrapartum prophylaxis is indicated for a history of GBS bacteriuria during pregnancy or previous infant with GBS disease.46,108
paragraphs.heading: Group B Streptococcus

paragraphs.text: Women with GBS colonization who have cesarean delivery performed before the onset of labor or rupture of membranes do not require intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. The guidelines also contain recommendations for management of women with unknown GBS status at the onset of labor, expanded recommendations for laboratory identification of GBS, a change in the recommended dose of penicillin G prophylaxis, and recommendations for women with penicillin allergy. Algorithms are included to assist in the management of women with preterm labor, women with preterm PROM, and newborns at risk for early-onset GBS disease. Intravenous penicillin remains the drug of choice for GBS prophylaxis, with ampicillin as an acceptable alternative. In women with a strong history of penicillin allergy, either vancomycin or clindamycin can be used (only if the GBS isolate is susceptible to clindamycin).
paragraphs.heading: Group B Streptococcus

paragraphs.text: Before the initiation of active prevention with intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis, the estimated incidence of invasive neonatal GBS disease in the United States was 1.8 cases per 1000 live births (1.5/1000 for early onset and 0.35/1000 for late onset). Following implementation of the CDC guidelines in the mid-1990s, the incidence of earlyonset disease decreased by 80% to 0.3 to 0.4 cases per 1000 live births after 2002.12,109
paragraphs.heading: Group B Streptococcus

paragraphs.text: Despite the dramatic decrease in the incidence of newborn GBS disease, it remains the leading infectious cause of morbidity and mortality among newborns in the United States.27 Rates of maternal GBS colonization have remained unchanged since the 1970s.110 The use of intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis has had no effect on the incidence rate of
paragraphs.heading: Group B Streptococcus

paragraphs.text: late-onset GBS disease, which has remained approximately 0.30 cases per 1000 live births (Fig. 50.1), increasing to almost 4 per 1000 live births in VLBW infants.18 Continued monitoring is needed to evaluate for potential adverse consequences of intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis, including the emergence of drug resistance and a possible increase in the incidence of non-GBS neonatal pathogens. Clinical trials are underway to evaluate administration of GBS serotype–specific polysaccharide-protein conjugate vaccines in pregnant women, which is one of the priority areas of the WHO. Maternal vaccination has the potential to provide a simpler strategy for prevention, without the concerns about antibiotic resistance and emergence of non-GBS pathogens associated with intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis.111
paragraphs.heading: Group B Streptococcus

paragraphs.text: Early-onset GBS disease most commonly presents within the first day of life. Invasive early-onset disease may lead to bacteremia, pneumonia, meningitis, or bone or joint involvement. Late-onset GBS disease occurs after the first week of life, and patients commonly present with bacteremia and meningitis.109 Recommended definitive antibiotic therapy for GBS disease is penicillin G, given its narrow spectrum and excellent in vitro activity. GBS is consistently susceptible to penicillin, ampicillin, first- and second-generation cephalosporins, and vancomycin. Approximately 30% of GBS isolates are resistant to erythromycin, and approximately 20% are resistant to clindamycin. Dosing of ampicillin or penicillin G for GBS disease depends on GA and postnatal age, so providers should refer to the latest
paragraphs.heading: Group B Streptococcus

paragraphs.text: AAP Red Book for updated dosing recommendations (Table 50.4).54 The duration of therapy depends on the location of disease involvement. Therapy should be continued for 10 days for bacteremia without a focus, 14 days for uncomplicated meningitis, 21 to 28 days for septic arthritis, and 4 to 6 weeks for osteomyelitis.54
paragraphs.heading: Group B Streptococcus

paragraphs.text: The widespread use of intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis has led to a substantial decrease in mortality associated with all causes of early-onset neonatal sepsis. In the period just before implementation of intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (1985–1991), mortality from EOS was 24.9 per 100,000 cases. In the years following implementation of intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (1995–1999), mortality rates had decreased to 15.6 per 100,000 cases.46 As with all pathogens causing neonatal sepsis, mortality from GBS disease is higher among preterm and low birth weight infants. Data published in 2020 showed mortality rates from earlyonset GBS disease of 20% in preterm infants and <2% in term infants. Intrapartum prophylaxis is the only intervention that reduces mortality from GBS EOS. Late-onset GBS mortality that is not prevented by intrapartum prophylaxis occurs in up to 20% of preterm infants <28 weeks’ GA and 1% to 2% of term infants.18
paragraphs.heading: Group B Streptococcus

paragraphs.text: S. aureus is a facultative anaerobic gram-positive coccus, and it is frequently found as a commensal organism in the respiratory tract and on the skin. Although it is not always pathogenic, it is a common cause of infection, leading to diseases that range from mild to severe and life threatening. In neonates, S. aureus is more often seen as a cause of late-onset infection and does not commonly occur within the first 72 hours of life. It is a common cause of hospital-acquired infection among neonates in the intensive care unit. Bloodstream infections are often associated with umbilical or central venous catheters. Other frequent manifestations include pneumonia, conjunctivitis, and skin and soft tissue infections. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) can present as generalized erythematous blistering skin disease in neonates due to the production of exfoliative exotoxins. SSSS is a mild disease in older children but can be fatal in neonates due to lack of protective exotoxin antibodies.
paragraphs.heading: Staphylococcus aureus

paragraphs.text: The spread of drug-resistant S. aureus is a continuing problem that affects patients of all ages. There are increasing reports of MRSA outbreaks in NICUs across the United States. Data from the Emerging Infections Program network report on MRSA show that African Americans have nearly twice the rate of invasive disease than Caucasians (29.9 vs. 17.7 per 100,000 population).112 The incidence of MRSA infections in NICUs has increased, stressing the importance of continued efforts at infection control and prevention.113
paragraphs.heading: Staphylococcus aureus

paragraphs.text: Community-acquired S. aureus infections among previously healthy neonates have a wide variety of clinical manifestations. These include pustulosis, cellulitis, and skin abscess, as well as invasive disease with bacteremia, UTI,
paragraphs.heading: Staphylococcus aureus

paragraphs.text: pneumonia, and musculoskeletal infections. Symptoms often begin after the first week of life. Neonatal infection may be associated with recent or current maternal infection, such as mastitis, cellulitis, abscess, or cesarean wound infection. As with hospital-acquired infection, drug resistance is increasing among community-acquired S. aureus isolates, with rates of MRSA among neonates reflecting the increasing rates among the general population in the community.114
paragraphs.heading: Staphylococcus aureus

paragraphs.text: Initial diagnostic evaluation and empiric antibiotic therapy depend on the location and severity of illness at presentation along with local methicillin-resistance rates. In any infant with systemic signs of illness or in whom invasive disease is suspected, a full sepsis evaluation with blood, urine, and CSF cultures should be obtained. Empiric S. aureus coverage with nafcillin should be given until final susceptibility results are available. Completion of therapy with nafcillin alone is appropriate for infections caused by methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA). Vancomycin is the preferred therapy for MRSA infections in neonates and might be considered as the first choice prior to susceptibility results in NICUs with high MRSA prevalence or in a critically systemically ill neonate. Clindamycin or linezolid may provide an alternative to vancomycin therapy. However, clindamycin is bacteriostatic rather than bactericidal against S. aureus, so it should not be used to treat bacteremia or severe infections. Rifampin is occasionally used for MSSA or CoNS bloodstream infections, which are more difficult to clear using conventional antibiotic therapy such as nafcillin, although adult studies have shown no benefit.115 For bloodstream infections associated with central venous or umbilical catheters, the catheter should be removed if possible and antibiotics administered for at least 14 days, given the high virulence of S. aureus and its propensity to colonize foreign material and create biofilms.54
paragraphs.heading: Staphylococcus aureus

paragraphs.text: There is little evidence available to guide clinicians in the treatment and evaluation of otherwise healthy, fullterm neonates with mild, localized S. aureus skin infections. Localized pustulosis can be treated with topical antibiotics such as mupirocin, whereas localized disease in premature or very-low-birth-weight infants is treated with intravenous medication.95 A more thorough evaluation (including blood and CSF cultures) and parenteral antibiotics should be given to infants with systemic symptoms, premature or low birth weight infants, or infants with more widespread infection. Empiric treatment options for staphylococcal skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs) include vancomycin, clindamycin, and linezolid. Infants initially started on parenteral therapy who have shown clinical improvement and have negative blood and CSF cultures can often be switched to oral therapy. Oral antibiotic options for staphylococcal SSTIs include cephalexin, clindamycin, linezolid, and amoxicillin-clavulanate. A total duration of 7 to 14 days of therapy is recommended.
paragraphs.heading: Staphylococcus aureus

paragraphs.text: The CDC recommends active surveillance testing for S. aureus colonization in NICUs when there is increased incidence of S. aureus infection and for MRSA colonization
paragraphs.heading: Staphylococcus aureus

paragraphs.text: when there is increased evidence of ongoing health care– associated transmission within the unit.116 Considerations of decolonization remain a controversial issue and a topic of current research. The safety and efficacy of intranasal mupirocin have not been established in patients younger than 12 years. Proven techniques to prevent MRSA outbreaks and transmission include hand washing, contact precautions for all MRSA-positive patients, and cohorting of MRSA-positive patients.
paragraphs.heading: Staphylococcus aureus

paragraphs.text: Syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum, a thin, motile spirochete. Syphilis is generally acquired through sexual contact, in which the spirochete enters through breaches in squamous or columnar epithelium. Transmission of congenital syphilis is most frequently transplacental, although infection is rarely acquired by contact with genital lesions during delivery. The incidence of congenital syphilis parallels that of primary and secondary disease in women. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, the incidence of acquired and congenital syphilis increased dramatically in the United States. Decreasing incidence was seen in the late 1990s, but since 2001 the rates of primary and secondary syphilis have increased again. The rates of congenital syphilis have consistently increased since 2012 (Fig. 50.2). In 2019, there were 48.5 cases per 100,000 live births, representing a 477% increase relative to 2012 (8.4 cases per 100,000 live births). This increase mirrors the increase in rates of primary and secondary syphilis in women 15 to 44 years of age.117 Maternal risk factors for syphilis during pregnancy include sex with multiple partners, sex in conjunction with drug use or transactional sex, late or no prenatal care, substance abuse, incarceration, and homelessness.
paragraphs.heading: Syphilis

paragraphs.text: Transmission can occur at any time during pregnancy transplacentally and at any stage of maternal disease or from contact with infected maternal secretions during delivery. Rates of transmission are higher during primary and secondary maternal syphilis (60%–100%) than with later stages of disease (40% with early latent and <8% with late latent). Risk of transmission also increases with increasing GA.
paragraphs.heading: Syphilis

paragraphs.text: Transmission does not happen via breast milk but can happen through an infected breast lesion. Intrauterine infection may result in spontaneous abortion, hydrops fetalis, stillbirth, or neonatal sepsis. Infection also increases the risk for preterm birth, low birth weight, and perinatal death. Clinical manifestations in infected infants within the first 1 to 2 months of age include hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, rash, mucocutaneous lesions, copious nasal secretions (snuffles), pneumonia, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and skeletal involvement (osteochondritis, periostitis, and osteitis). The nasal secretions and skin lesions in untreated infants are highly infectious. Infected infants may also be completely asymptomatic.
paragraphs.heading: Syphilis

paragraphs.text: Treatment of early-stage infection can prevent late manifestations of infection. Left untreated, late-stage findings usually appear after 2 years of age and include CNS, skeletal, dental, ocular, and skin involvement. Several of these findings may not occur until many years later. The Hutchinson triad refers to interstitial keratitis, eighth cranial nerve deafness, and notched central incisors (Hutchinson teeth). Other manifestations include frontal bossing, saddle nose deformity, and anterior bowing of the shins.
paragraphs.heading: Syphilis

paragraphs.text: All women should be screened for syphilis with serologic testing early in pregnancy and again at delivery.118 Initial screening should be done with a nontreponemal test, such as rapid plasma reagin (RPR) and Venereal Diseases Research Laboratory (VDRL) screening. The result of a positive nontreponemal test should be confirmed with a treponemal antibody test, such as fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS), T. pallidum enzyme immunoassay (TP-EIA), microhemagglutination test for antibodies to T. pallidum (MHA-TP), or T. pallidum particle agglutination (TP-PA). Any woman treated for syphilis during pregnancy should have follow-up testing with a nontreponemal titer to assess response to therapy. Increasingly, clinical laboratories are utilizing a “reverse algorithm” for serologic testing of syphilis where a positive screen with a treponemal test is confirmed with a nontreponemal test such VDRL or RPR.119 Penicillin is the only recommended treatment for pregnant women. Admission for desensitization to penicillin is recommended for women with penicillin allergies.
paragraphs.heading: Syphilis

paragraphs.text: Low-titer, false-positive nontreponemal test results do sometimes occur during pregnancy. A false-positive nontreponemal test result is confirmed if a woman has a reactive nontreponemal test but a consistently negative treponemal test result. Subsequent evaluation of the infant should be based on the infant’s RPR or VDRL titer results as compared with the mother’s.
paragraphs.heading: Syphilis

paragraphs.text: The physician should refer to the latest edition of the AAP Red Book for testing and treatment algorithms for congenital syphilis.54 An infant should be fully evaluated for congenital syphilis if the maternal RPR/VDRL titer has increased fourfold at the time of delivery, the infant’s RPR/VDRL titer is fourfold greater than the mother’s, if the mother was untreated or treated at <4 weeks before delivery, or the infant has an abnormal exam. If an infant is born to a mother adequately treated for syphilis with penicillin before
paragraphs.heading: Syphilis

paragraphs.text: the pregnancy with a stable low titer and normal physical examination, the infant does not require further evaluation or treatment. If the mother was adequately treated with penicillin during pregnancy more than 4 weeks before delivery, the infant has a normal examination, and the infant’s RPR/ VDRL is the same as or less than fourfold the maternal titer, then the infant may be treated with penicillin without further evaluation.
paragraphs.heading: Syphilis

paragraphs.text: Full evaluation for congenital syphilis includes RPR/ VDRL, CBC, and CSF examination for cell count, protein, and quantitative VDRL. Other tests should be done as clinically indicated, including long bone radiographs, eye examination, liver function tests, neuroimaging, hearing tests, and chest radiographs. A definite or highly probable diagnosis of congenital syphilis is based on the presence of any of the following: physical, laboratory, or radiographic evidence of active infection; a positive CSF VDRL; an infant RPR/ VDRL titer fourfold or greater than that of the mother; or a positive specific treponemal stain of the placenta or umbilical cord.
paragraphs.heading: Syphilis

paragraphs.text: The recommended treatment for definite, highly probable, or possible congenital syphilis is intravenous penicillin G. The dose is based on chronologic rather than GA. The recommended dose is 50,000 U/kg every 12 hours if 1 week of age or younger, and then every 8 hours if older than 1 week, for a total duration of 10 days. If more than 1 day of therapy is missed, the entire course should be restarted. If intravenous access cannot be obtained, procaine penicillin G as a daily intramuscular injection for 10 days can be considered. Those infants in whom congenital syphilis is less likely or unlikely (infant has negative tests or mother was treated adequately more than 4 weeks prior to delivery) can receive just a one-time intramuscular dose of penicillin G.54
paragraphs.heading: Syphilis

paragraphs.text: Pediatric infectious disease specialists should be consulted for infants diagnosed with congenital syphilis. All infants with reactive RPR/VDRL or those who were born to mothers who were seroreactive at delivery require careful followup during the first year of life. Nontreponemal tests should be performed every 2 to 3 months until the test becomes nonreactive or the titer has decreased at least fourfold. If the infant was adequately treated in the neonatal period, the nontreponemal titer should be nonreactive by 6 months of age. Infants with increasing or persistently stable titers 6 to 12 months after treatment should be re-evaluated (including CSF VDRL) and treated with a 10-day course of intravenous penicillin G. Infants diagnosed with congenital neurosyphilis should have a repeat clinical evaluation with CSF examination every 6 months until the CSF is normal. If the CSF VDRL is positive 6 months after the initial treatment course, the infant should be retreated with another 10-day course of penicillin.54
paragraphs.heading: Syphilis

paragraphs.text: Listeriosis is caused by L. monocytogenes, a non–spore-forming, short, gram-positive bacillus. It is an intracellular pathogen that is able to survive and multiply within host phagocytic
paragraphs.heading: Listeriosis

paragraphs.text: cells. Listeriosis primarily affects older adults, pregnant women, neonates, and immunocompromised hosts. Listeria is found in soil and decaying vegetable matter. It is also found in the intestinal tracts of several mammals, birds, fish, and crustaceans. In adults, most infections are thought to arise from oral ingestion of contaminated material, leading to intestinal mucosal penetration and systemic infection. Recent foods that have been implicated in listeriosis outbreaks in the United States include deli meats, soft and raw cheeses, raw milk, enoki mushrooms, and packaged salads.120 Impaired cell-mediated immunity and macrophage function are associated with increased susceptibility to infection with Listeria.121 In pregnant women, Listeria is able to cross the placenta during maternal bacteremia due to cellcell interactions between the Listeria internalin molecules and E-cadherin molecules on the syncytiotrophoblasts122 and infect the fetus. Infection in pregnant women can lead to spontaneous abortion, stillbirth, preterm labor, or neonatal infection.
paragraphs.heading: Listeriosis

paragraphs.text: In a systematic review of peer-reviewed literature, the WHO estimated that listeriosis resulted in 23,150 illnesses worldwide in 2010, leading to 5463 deaths. In this review of listeriosis cases, 20.7% were perinatal infections, with septicemia occurring in 30.7% of infected neonates.123
paragraphs.heading: Listeriosis

paragraphs.text: Among all organisms causing neonatal sepsis, L. monocytogenes is a relatively uncommon cause. Listeria infection in neonates is classified as early onset (≤72 hours of age) or late onset (>72 hours of age). The signs and symptoms of listeriosis in neonates are indistinguishable from the signs and symptoms of other postnatal bacterial infections. Early-onset disease is most often acquired by transplacental transmission, and affected infants are symptomatic soon after birth. Meconium passage in utero is often associated with intrauterine Listeria infection. Common manifestations of early-onset infection include neonatal sepsis and pneumonia. Newborns can present with an erythematous rash with small pale papules characterized by granulomas, known as granulomatosis infantisepticum. Late-onset infection may be acquired by vertical transmission from a colonized mother during passage through the birth canal or by transmission from other colonized or infected caregivers. Symptoms usually arise after the first week or two of life. The most common manifestation of late-onset listeriosis is meningitis, often with insidious onset. The case fatality rate from Listeria EOS is 14% to 56% and from LOS it is ∼25%.
paragraphs.heading: Listeriosis

paragraphs.text: As for any neonate with suspected sepsis, blood and CSF cultures should be obtained. In addition, isolation of L. monocytogenes from cultures of amniotic fluid or placental tissue may support the diagnosis of early-onset disease. The FDA-approved meningitis multiplex PCR panel includes Listeria as one of the tested pathogens.68 Recommended empiric antibiotic treatment for neonatal sepsis includes ampicillin and an aminoglycoside. This regimen provides important coverage for listeriosis, as cephalosporins have no activity against L. monocytogenes. When infection with Listeria has been confirmed, the antibiotic of choice is ampicillin.
paragraphs.heading: Listeriosis

paragraphs.text: The addition of gentamicin is recommended to provide synergy. After the patient demonstrates clinical improvement, gentamicin can be discontinued and ampicillin given alone to complete the remainder of treatment. For all cases of Listeria meningitis, a repeat lumbar puncture should be performed 1 to 2 days after the start of treatment to confirm sterilization of the CSF. Treatment duration of 14 days is recommended for uncomplicated bacteremia. For meningitis, treatment should be continued for 21 to 28 days. Longer courses are needed for parenchymal brain infection or endocarditis.54 Iron supplements should be discontinued during the treatment, as iron enhances the pathogenicity of Listeria. All patients with Listeria meningitis should have neuroimaging obtained near the anticipated end of treatment to determine whether there is parenchymal involvement and whether the patient may require a more prolonged course of treatment.
paragraphs.heading: Listeriosis

paragraphs.text: Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by M. tuberculosis, an acid-fast bacilli. Although perinatal TB is rare in the United States, the burden of TB, especially worldwide, among women of childbearing age is quite high.124 The risk for perinatal TB is much higher in areas with a high prevalence of both TB and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection among young women. Perinatal TB includes both congenital and neonatal TB. Mother-to-child transmission of congenital TB may occur in utero by hematogenous dissemination via the umbilical vein or by intrapartum aspiration of infected amniotic fluid or genital secretions. TB during pregnancy is also associated with an increased risk for preterm labor, low birth weight, and fetal and perinatal death. Clinical manifestations of congenital TB are often nonspecific and include respiratory distress, lethargy, irritability, fever, low birth weight, hepatosplenomegaly, and poor feeding.
paragraphs.heading: Tuberculosis

paragraphs.text: Neonatal TB, which is somewhat more common than congenital TB, is transmitted through the inhalation or ingestion of respiratory droplets or through ingestion of infected breast milk. Even more rarely, mothers may have endometrial TB, and this can result in late-onset neonatal infection which is more difficult to diagnose because the mother may not have pulmonary symptoms. Infants born to mothers who travel to the United States from an endemic area who have atypical respiratory disease should be considered for TB infection. Clinical manifestations include failure to thrive, fever, vomiting, cough, and tachypnea. Because perinatal disease is very rare, there are little data on mortality rates and outcomes. Without prompt evaluation and treatment, mortality rates are quite high and are estimated at 50%.125
paragraphs.heading: Tuberculosis

paragraphs.text: Any neonate with suspected TB disease should undergo a complete evaluation for both TB and bacterial sepsis as they cannot be distinguished based on presentation. A tuberculin skin test (TST) should be placed, although newborns may have a nonreactive TST in the presence of active disease. Interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) also have low
paragraphs.heading: Tuberculosis

paragraphs.text: sensitivity but should be obtained as part of the workup. A chest radiograph should be obtained. Mycobacterial stains and cultures should be obtained from three consecutive, early-morning gastric aspirates to evaluate for pulmonary TB. Mycobacterial stains and cultures can also be obtained from other sites if extrapulmonary TB is suspected. CSF obtained for evaluation of routine bacterial meningitis should also be sent for mycobacterial stains and cultures.
paragraphs.heading: Tuberculosis

paragraphs.text: Regardless of the initial TST result and while other studies are pending, the infant should be promptly started on anti-TB therapy with isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and either ethambutol or an aminoglycoside such as amikacin, kanamycin, or streptomycin. The infant’s mother should undergo a full evaluation for pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB (including uterine infection). The placenta should be examined for the presence of granulomas and sent for mycobacterial stains and culture. If the infant’s physical examination and diagnostic work-up are consistent with TB, a full treatment regimen should be administered. This should consist of 2 months of the described four-drug regimen, followed by at least 4 months of isoniazid and rifampin. If TB meningitis is confirmed, corticosteroids should be added.54
paragraphs.heading: Tuberculosis

paragraphs.text: Management of the asymptomatic newborn whose mother or another household contact has TB will depend on whether the contact has latent TB infection or active disease. If the mother has a positive TST or IGRA, has a normal chest radiograph, and is asymptomatic, then no separation between mother and baby is required. The infant needs no special evaluation or therapy. The mother is a candidate for latent TB infection treatment after the initial postpartum period. Breastfeeding is not contraindicated.
paragraphs.heading: Tuberculosis

paragraphs.text: If the mother (or household contact) has a positive TST/ IGRA along with clinical symptoms or an abnormal chest radiograph consistent with active TB disease, the infant and mother should be separated until the mother has been fully evaluated, including testing for HIV. The infant should be evaluated for congenital TB, and all household contacts should be evaluated for TB infection. If the mother is diagnosed with active TB, separation from the infant is only required until the mother is on anti-TB treatment and the infant is receiving isoniazid. Continued separation is necessary if the mother has suspected multidrug-resistant TB or has poor adherence to therapy. The mother may breastfeed if she has been on therapy for at least 2 weeks and is not considered contagious. If congenital TB is excluded, the infant should be given isoniazid until 3 or 4 months of age, when a repeat TST is performed. If the TST is positive, repeat evaluation for TB disease is required. If the TST is negative, the infant should receive a total of 9 months of isoniazid.54
paragraphs.heading: Tuberculosis

paragraphs.text: Infant botulism is caused by Clostridium botulinum, a heterogeneous group of ubiquitous, spore-forming, obligate anaerobic, gram-positive bacilli. The spores are found across
paragraphs.heading: Botulism

paragraphs.text: the globe in soil, water, agricultural products, and honey. When appropriate environmental conditions are present, the spores germinate and grow into toxin-producing bacteria. Eight serologically distinct types of C. botulinum toxin have been described. Toxin types A, B, E, and rarely F and G cause disease in humans. After entry into the body, the toxin disperses widely throughout the body and binds to a specific receptor on peripheral cholinergic synapses of ganglia and neuromuscular junctions.126 Binding of the toxin leads to irreversible disruption of acetylcholine release by the presynaptic nerve terminal, which in turn leads to a severe neuroparalytic syndrome. Different types of botulism infection are classified according to the mode of acquisition. Foodborne botulism occurs after ingestion of preformed botulinum toxin in contaminated food. Infant botulism occurs after ingestion of the spores, which then colonize the host’s gastrointestinal tract and release toxin produced in vivo.
paragraphs.heading: Botulism

paragraphs.text: Infant botulism was first recognized as a distinct entity in 1976. On average, 100 to 150 cases of botulism are reported each year in the United States. Of these, approximately 75% are cases of infant botulism.127 The incidence is highest in California (which accounts for over 50% of cases), Texas, and Pennsylvania. Although infant botulism has long been associated with the ingestion of raw honey, most cases likely result from ingestion of environmental dust containing C. botulinum spores. The spores have been isolated from several types of environmental samples, including yard soil and vacuum dust.
paragraphs.heading: Botulism

paragraphs.text: Clinical manifestations of infant botulism range from mild disease to sudden death, and onset may be insidious or fulminant. The diagnosis must be considered in any infant presenting with hypotonia, constipation, and poor feeding. In the United States, the median age of affected infants is approximately 17 weeks, ranging from 1 to 60 weeks of age.127 Presenting symptoms often include lethargy, poor feeding, drooling, constipation, and progressive, symmetric weakness. The weakness may involve descending or global hypotonia. Patients are typically afebrile. Early in the course, the physical examination may be normal. As the infection progresses, cranial nerve palsies, poor head control, and weak cry develop. Loss of gag, swallow, and suck reflexes can lead to airway compromise. Initially, deep tendon reflexes may be normal, although these become diminished or absent as the descending, symmetric, flaccid paralysis progresses.
paragraphs.heading: Botulism

paragraphs.text: Because confirmatory stool studies and electrophysiologic studies can be nonspecific and may require several days to obtain results, a presumptive diagnosis should be made based on clinical presentation, and therapy should be administered as soon as possible. For assistance with management of any suspected case of infant botulism in the United States, the California Department of Health Services Infant Botulism Treatment and Prevention Program may be contacted (www.infantbotulism.org; 510-231-7600) for discussions with on-call physicians.
paragraphs.heading: Botulism

paragraphs.text: The diagnosis is supported by isolation of C. botulinum spores from the stool and confirmed by identification of the botulinum toxin in the stool. Stool sample collection is often difficult because most patients are constipated, and it takes several days to obtain results from these stool studies (which must be sent out to reference laboratories at state health departments or the CDC). While stool study results are pending, electromyography (EMG) may be performed. EMG findings that are consistent with infant botulism include short-duration, low-amplitude motor unit potentials, as well as abnormal incremental response to repetitive nerve stimulation.128
paragraphs.heading: Botulism

paragraphs.text: Treatment includes supportive care and very close monitoring for signs of respiratory failure. All suspected cases should receive Botulism Immune Globulin Intravenous (BIG-IV, or BabyBIG) as early as possible. BIG-IV is a human-derived botulinum antitoxin, and it has been shown to be a safe and effective treatment for infant botulism. A randomized, placebo-controlled trial showed that patients who received BIG-IV had reduced duration of hospital stay, intensive care, mechanical ventilation, and tube or intravenous feedings. BIG-IV was not associated with any serious adverse events.129 Antibiotics are not recommended for infant botulism because lysis of C. botulinum organisms within the gastrointestinal lumen could increase the amount of toxin available for absorption.130
paragraphs.heading: Botulism

paragraphs.text: Recovery often requires several weeks, although most patients are expected to achieve complete recovery. Botulinum toxin does not cross the blood-brain barrier and thus does not affect the CNS. The case fatality rate for infant botulism is currently less than 1%.127
paragraphs.heading: Botulism

paragraphs.text: Tetanus is acquired through exposure to the spores of Clostridium tetani, a slender, anaerobic, gram-positive bacillus. Neonatal tetanus is very rare in developed countries because of widespread hygienic birth conditions and maternal immunization, although it remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in developing countries. When the spores germinate, the bacteria produce the tetanospasmin toxin (also known as tetanus toxin). The toxin reaches the spinal cord and brainstem and binds tightly and irreversibly to receptors at the neuromuscular synapse. Its effects occur through disinhibition of neurons that modulate excitatory impulses from the motor cortex. This results in increased muscle tone, spasms, and autonomic instability.
paragraphs.heading: Tetanus

paragraphs.text: C. tetani is present in the soil and can be found in human and animal feces.
