Because it is impossible to eliminate the bacteria or its spores from the environment, control of the disease relies on widespread immunization and proper wound care. The WHO reported that neonatal tetanus resulted in approximately 34,019 deaths in 2015, representing a 96% reduction in deaths since the late 1980s.131 Neonatal tetanus remains a problem in several countries because of inadequate maternal immunization coverage and unhygienic birth practices leading to infection of the umbilical stump.
paragraphs.heading: Tetanus

paragraphs.text: Disease onset typically occurs at 1 week of age, with incubation periods ranging from 1 day to 1 month. Clinical manifestations include irritability, poor suck, fever, rigidity, muscle spasms, and seizures. Spasms are exacerbated by stimulation. On examination, infants usually have hyperreflexia and extreme flexion of the toes. Although trismus is commonly seen in generalized tetanus in adults, it is seen less often in infants. Other signs include tachycardia, tachypnea, and apnea. Laryngospasm may lead to aspiration pneumonia, and pulmonary processes are a frequent cause of death in neonatal tetanus.
paragraphs.heading: Tetanus

paragraphs.text: The diagnosis is based strictly on clinical presentation. Treatment is largely supportive. Intramuscular human tetanus immune globulin is given to neutralize unbound toxin, and metronidazole is given to reduce the number of toxin-producing bacteria. Airway management and maintaining adequate ventilation are essential, although, unfortunately, critical care services are often not available in resource-poor settings where most neonatal tetanus occurs. Benzodiazepines and baclofen can be given to help
paragraphs.heading: Tetanus

paragraphs.text: Key Points
paragraphs.heading: Tetanus

paragraphs.text: • Newborns are extremely susceptible to infection, and the
paragraphs.heading: Tetanus

paragraphs.text: presenting signs and symptoms of sepsis are nonspecific. • Group B Streptococcus (GBS) and E. coli are the two
paragraphs.heading: Tetanus

paragraphs.text: most common causes of early-onset sepsis (EOS). GBS EOS has been decreasing since the adoption of universal screening of pregnant women and intrapartum prophylaxis, but E. coli is on the rise. Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis has no impact on GBS late-onset sepsis. • Ampicillin and gentamicin remain the drugs of choice
paragraphs.heading: Tetanus

paragraphs.text: for empiric antibiotic therapy for neonates with suspected EOS. Resistance to both drugs is rising, and
paragraphs.heading: Tetanus

paragraphs.text: control muscle spasms. Because stimulation can precipitate spasms and seizures, efforts should be made to reduce environmental stimulation as much as possible. Magnesium sulfate and beta-blockers can help control autonomic dysfunction.
paragraphs.heading: References

paragraphs.text: Since the introduction of mechanical ventilation and benzodiazepines in the 1960s and 1970s, the morbidity and mortality of tetanus patients of all ages have significantly decreased. If modern critical care services are available, mortality rates may be less than 20%. If basic medications and high-quality nursing care are provided, mortality rates can be reduced to under 50%. Survivors may have full recovery or varying degrees of neurologic sequelae, ranging from minor deficits to cerebral palsy.

# 50. Postnatal Bacterial Infections
> Source attribution: [Source credits](../../SOURCE_CREDITS.md).


## PDF page 862 | printed page 857

50 Postnatal Bacterial Infections

### DEVASHIS MUKHERJEE AND RITA M. RYAN

### Neonatal Sepsis

Neonates are extremely susceptible to bacterial infection, and sepsis is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in this population. Neonatal sepsis usually presents in a nonspecific manner with clinical signs including, but not limited to, fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea or hyperventilation, and an abnormally high or low white blood cell count. Prior definitions of systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) are no longer utilized commonly, and there are ongoing efforts to extrapolate adult sepsis scores (sepsis-3 and sequential organ failure assessment [SOFA]) to the neonatal population.1 Although this chapter focuses on bacterial infections, it is important to also consider viral, fungal, and parasitic causes in the differential diagnosis of newborns with similar signs and symptoms.

### Epidemiology and Microbiology

Neonatal sepsis is categorized according to the infant’s postnatal age at onset of disease. Although the definitions for early-onset sepsis (EOS) and late-onset sepsis (LOS) vary, most reports define EOS as occurring at or before 72 hours of life and LOS occurring between 72 hours and at least 30 days of life.2 Certain reports include infections up to 90 days of life in the LOS category. The categories reflect the different etiologies and pathophysiologic changes associated with timing of disease onset.

In EOS, infants acquire infection either (1) in utero by vertical transmission through amniotic fluid or after premature rupture of membranes (PROM), or (2) intrapartum through acquisition of bacterial flora from the mother’s genitourinary tract. Examples of bacteria that cross the placenta to cause fetal infection are Treponema pallidum and Listeria monocytogenes. Exposure of the neonate to maternal vaginal microbiota during delivery is essential for healthy development during the newborn period, providing the primary source for normal gut colonization, initiating host immune maturation, and metabolism.3 Common perinatal interventions such as cesarean section, antibiotic use, and formula feeding alter the infant microbiome and might have implications in future immune pathologies. Vaginal dysbiosis, even in the absence of specific pathogens isolated from the

genital tract, is a risk factor for preterm PROM and is associated with early-onset neonatal sepsis.4,5

Factors that increase the risk for EOS can be divided into those that are maternal and those that are neonatal. Maternal intrapartum conditions that increase the risk of infection include maternal group B β-hemolytic streptococci (group B Streptococcus [GBS]) colonization, GBS bacteriuria, diagnosis of intra-amniotic infection (IAI), prolonged rupture of membranes, or inadequate intrapartum antibiotic administration before delivery. IAI is suspected when maternal intrapartum temperature is greater than 39°C or the temperature is between 38°C and 39°C and one additional risk factor of maternal leukocytosis, purulent cervical drainage, or fetal tachycardia is present. Newborn conditions that are associated with EOS are prematurity, low birth weight, congenital anomalies, and complicated or instrumentassisted delivery.4,6 The immune systems of preterm infants have a smaller pool of monocytes and neutrophils, impaired ability of these cells to kill pathogens, and lower production of cytokine, which limits T-cell activation and reduces the ability to fight bacteria, compared to term infants.7

The epidemiology of neonatal sepsis has changed significantly over the past several decades and continues to change. The seminal study by Boyer and Gotoff8 demonstrated significantly decreased GBS colonization and infection after GBS-colonized mothers were given intrapartum antimicrobial prophylaxis (IAP) with ampicillin. Universal antenatal screening for GBS colonization with IAP for women colonized with GBS has significantly reduced the rate of earlyonset GBS sepsis from 0.37 to 0.23 per 1000 live births from 2006 to 2015 based on Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Active Bacterial Core surveillance data.9,10 The overall incidence of all-cause bacterial EOS in the United States is estimated to be between 0.77 and 1.08 per 1000 live births based on latest epidemiologic data from the CDC and the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development’s Neonatal Research Network (NRN).11,12 The highest rates occur among preterm and low birth weight infants.13 There are no differences between rates of EOS based on race or assigned sex at birth.11,14 For those infants with a birth weight less than 1500 g, the rate is 13.9 per 1000 live births; for those with a birth weight between 1500 and 2500 g, the rate is 1.88.11,14 Mortality

857


## PDF page 863

rates are also inversely proportional to gestational age (GA). Although the case fatality rate among full-term infants has dramatically decreased over the past several decades to 2.5% to 3%, the mortality rates for extremely low birth weight (ELBW) infants remain high at 40% to 70%.11–14 The mortality rate among all infants from Escherichia coli is almost four to five times that from GBS EOS in both NRN and CDC cohorts (23%–32% vs. 6%–7%); this difference narrows in very low birth weight (VLBW) infants with high mortality rates for both GBS and E. coli in this vulnerable population.11,12 The majority of deaths from EOS occur within 72 hours of age. The most common pathogens isolated in EOS are GBS and E. coli.13,15

Although GBS has been the most common pathogen in term infants as well as all GA infants combined for several decades, E. coli is rapidly overtaking GBS as the number one cause for EOS. E. coli is the most common pathogen in preterm EOS (51%), and data from the NRN cohort (2015– 2017) suggest that E. coli is more common than GBS in all infants combined (37% vs. 30%). Haemophilus species and Staphylococcus aureus isolates are the third and fourth most commonly isolated species in VLBW infants, respectively, whereas Enterococcus and viridans group streptococci were isolated most commonly in term infants after GBS and E. coli. Listeria monocytogenes, once ranked as the third most common pathogen in EOS, is not commonly implicated in any of the recent cohort studies. Other pathogens in both preterm and term infants include group A streptococci and other enteric gram-negative organisms, including Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Citrobacter, Acinetobacter, and Pseudomonas.

In LOS, acquisition of infection is predominantly through the infant’s environment. The infant becomes colonized with pathogenic bacteria ubiquitous in their physical environment, including part of the flora of their caregivers. The gut microbiome is often involved in the pathogenesis of LOS. Although the agent can vary, the causative organism is usually found to be abundant in the infant’s gastrointestinal tract.16 Extreme prematurity is one of the greatest risk factors for LOS, and 16% of VLBW infants with EOS will go on to have LOS further along in their neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) course.14 A 2010 NRN report on morbidity and mortality rates for extremely preterm infants showed that LOS is a frequent complication for these patients. Among 9575 infants born between 22 and 28 weeks’ gestation, 36% developed LOS.17 More recent Vermont Oxford Network (VON) data indicate lower rates of LOS (8.9%) in VLBW infants, with rates of 32% in infants born at ≤23 weeks’ GA.18 LOS rates have been decreasing over time with better infection control practices, although the rates of late-onset GBS disease and LOS in VLBW infants both remain very high.19,20

As overall care and survival rates for premature and low birth weight infants continue to improve, long hospital stays and indwelling vascular catheters remain additional infectious risk factors for these infants.6 The two most common bacterial causes of LOS in this population of infants include coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS) and S. aureus. GBS and E. coli are also commonly implicated in LOS.

E. coli is frequently a cause of urosepsis in young infants. Although screening for maternal GBS colonization and intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis have markedly decreased the incidence of early-onset GBS, it has not reduced the incidence of late-onset GBS disease in either term or preterm infants.21 Late-onset GBS disease is estimated at 0.28 to 0.31 per 1000 infants in the United States, with 50% of these caused by serotype III.22 As with EOS, preterm infants have twice as high mortality rates from late-onset GBS disease as compared to full term infants (7.8% vs. 3.4%).9

Improved surgical care and survival for neonates with congenital heart disease have led to prolonged hospitalizations with associated risk for sepsis in these infants. CoNS, S. aureus, E. coli, and candidiasis are common causes of bloodstream infections in this population and are associated with increased mortality risk. The use of histamine-2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors, as well as gastrointestinal tract pathology, has been associated with an increased risk for lateonset gram-negative bacilli bloodstream infections.23 Efforts are underway to reduce the incidence of LOS, including comprehensive central catheter-care bundles and aggressive enteral feeding programs with earlier catheter removal.24,25 In low- and middle-income countries, the microbiology of LOS is shifted toward a gram-negative bacilli predominance, with Enterobacterales being the most common isolate.26

### Clinical Presentation

The clinical signs of sepsis in a neonate are varied and often nonspecific. Prompt detection requires that clinicians maintain a high index of suspicion. Familiarity with known epidemiologic risk factors is crucial in determining the likelihood of infection and deciding on the empiric antibiotic regimen. Clinical signs and symptoms can mimic noninfectious etiologies. These include, but are not limited to, temperature instability, lethargy or irritability, hypotonia, tachycardia, respiratory distress, cyanosis, apnea, feeding difficulties, poor perfusion, bleeding problems, and abdominal distention.27 Tachycardia and respiratory distress are the two most common presenting features of neonatal sepsis, but subtle signs such as poor feeding could be the only initiating presenting symptom. Metabolic changes may include hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia, acidosis, and hyperbilirubinemia, with acidosis being the most common of all of these. Meningitis can present with predominantly central nervous system (CNS) signs and symptoms such as lethargy, hypo- or hypertonia, and seizures. Noninfectious etiologies that can mimic newborn sepsis are numerous and include respiratory distress syndrome, cardiogenic pulmonary edema, metabolic acidosis, meconium aspiration syndrome, and electrolyte, endocrine, or metabolic disturbances.

### Diagnosis

Because signs and symptoms are nonspecific, the clinical diagnosis of neonatal sepsis is extremely challenging. A definitive diagnosis requires the isolation of a pathogen


## PDF page 864 | printed page 859

from a normally sterile body site, including blood, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and urine. Isolation of bacteria from blood using aerobic or anaerobic culture is considered the gold standard for the diagnosis of sepsis.28 A blood culture collection volume of at least 1 mL is recommended, as this can reliably detect 1 to 10 colony-forming units per milliliter (CFU/mL) using modern techniques such as antimicrobial neutralization elements to neutralize beta-lactams and gentamicin, as well as automated bacterial CO2 production detectors.29 This is especially important in infants with a low level of bacteremia or those who received intrapartum antibiotics. Although volumes as low as 0.5 mL can detect bacterial growth, GBS, especially, requires volumes of at least 1 mL for accurate detection.30 The CDC recommends chlorhexidine instead of betadine for skin prep prior to blood collection in late preterm and term infants.

A lumbar puncture should also be considered in any infant with suspected sepsis. (See Table 50.1 for normal values for CSF cell counts, protein, and glucose according to GA, postnatal age, and birth weight.) If the infant is critically ill with respiratory or hemodynamic instability, the procedure can be deferred until the patient is more stable. The incidence of culture-confirmed meningitis in the absence of culture-confirmed bacteremia is one to two per 100,000 live births.12 In VLBW infants, the incidence of meningitis is almost 17-fold higher than in term infants (0.7 per 1000 live births), but these are also infants who are sicker and usually mechanically ventilated.31 The neonatologist should carefully weigh the risks of performing a lumbar puncture in a critically ill neonate against the duration and choice of antibiotic therapy when meningitis is suspected. Studies have shown poor correlation between results of blood and CSF cultures, so blood culture results alone should not be used to determine which patients should receive a lumbar puncture.

For suspected EOS, a urine culture is not part of the recommended work-up in infants who are ≤72 hours old. In newborns, urinary tract infections (UTIs) are primarily caused by renal seeding during bacteremia; thus urine cultures are of low yield in EOS. But, in older infants greater than 72 hours of age, UTIs increasingly result from ascending infection, so urine cultures should be part of the evaluation of LOS.32 Suprapubic aspiration or sterile catheterization are the preferred procedures to obtain cultures; a urine bag should not be used to obtain a reliable urine culture.

To date, no single blood cell index has been shown to be sensitive enough to safely exclude sepsis. A complete blood count (CBC) with differential should be obtained in all neonates suspected of sepsis. A CBC obtained 6 to 12 hours after birth is more reflective of a pathologic inflammatory response compared with a CBC obtained at birth.33 Studies have shown that leukopenia, low absolute neutrophil count (ANC), and a high ratio of immature (I) to total (T) neutrophils (I:T ratio >0.2) were associated with EOS. LOS has been associated with both high and low white blood cell (WBC) count, high ANC, and high I:T ratio.34 I:T ratios are ideally measured by manual inspection of blood sample.

Newer automated counters have recently been studied, but these are have not been validated in neonates for measuring I:T ratios. Thrombocytopenia is also a frequent finding in both EOS and LOS. No individual value in the CBC is predictive of sepsis. However, one multicenter study showed that a WBC count <1000/μL, ANC <1000, and I:T ratio >0.25 had a positive likelihood ratio of 3 in predicting EOS in infants <34 weeks old.34 Abnormal WBC and platelet counts can be seen often in the setting of maternal preeclampsia, chronic abruption, and PROM and hence must be interpreted with caution.35

C-reactive protein (CRP) and procalcitonin are two acute-phase reactants that have been studied extensively in


## PDF page 865

neonatal sepsis. In healthy neonates, both CRP and procalcitonin increase physiologically after birth, peaking at 24 hours of age. Both markers are also inversely proportional to birth weight and GA but are not affected by sex.36 CRP levels increase within 6 to 8 hours after infection and peak after 24 hours.37 The sensitivity of CRP for neonatal sepsis is lowest early in infection and then increases over the next 10 to 12 hours after the onset of infection.27 Serial determinations may be useful for identifying infants who do not have a bacterial infection or for monitoring response to treatment for infected infants.38 The positive and negative predictive values of CRP in neonatal sepsis is very variable.27,39 Preterm infants have lower CRP values and response, which affect its predictive value. Recent studies point toward poor predictive value of CRP in both early- and late-onset neonatal sepsis, and use of this marker to solely decide initiation or cessation of antimicrobial therapy is not encouraged.39a

Procalcitonin concentrations peak as early as 6 to 8 hours following infection, although there is a physiologic increase within the first 24 hours after birth. Increased levels can be seen with noninfectious causes such as respiratory distress syndrome. Thus procalcitonin appears to have better sensitivity but less specificity than CRP for identifying neonatal sepsis.40 The NeoPIns trial showed that in infants greater than 34 weeks’ GA with suspected EOS, procalcitoninguided antibiotic therapy led to shorter duration of treatment.41 Serial abnormal values of CRP and/or procalcitonin should be not be used to guide antibiotic duration in the absence of a positive culture until larger trials are performed.

Specific cytokines have also been evaluated for potential roles in the diagnosis of neonatal sepsis. Serum concentrations of interleukin (IL)-1β, IL-6, and IL-8; tumor necrosis factor-α; soluble interleukin-2 receptor (sIL-2R); and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor all increase in newborns with bacterial infection.39 Several have been shown to rise early in the course of infection, often before clinical findings become apparent.40 Although cytokine and cytometry assays may be helpful in diagnosis or in guiding decisions regarding therapy, their use is not widely employed related to issues of cost, the need for specialized equipment, and the processing time.39,42

A new focus on screening for sepsis involves predictive monitoring of heart rate variability and decelerations using computer algorithm–based heart rate observation (HeRO) scores. This approach has been used by NICUs in the United States as an early warning sign for neonatal sepsis. ELBW infants who underwent predictive monitoring had significantly increased survival from LOS as compared to infants with routine cardiorespiratory monitoring.43

### Risk Stratification for Early-Onset Sepsis

The 2010 CDC guidelines for management of EOS in late preterm and term neonates based on categorical risk factor assessment have been revised after widespread acceptance of the multivariate risk assessment–based sepsis calculator (https://neonatalsepsiscalculator.kaiserpermanente.org) in the United States.44,45 The American Academy of Pediatrics

(AAP) clinical reports published in 2018 and 2019 on management of infants with suspected EOS or at risk for GBS disease are considered to be the current standards of care for EOS in late preterm and term infants and have since been endorsed by the CDC.44,46,47 The multivariate risk assessment tool incorporates previous probability of infection based on local or national EOS rates and maternal characteristics (fever, GBS status, intrapartum antibiotics, duration of ROM), along with postnatal physical examination findings in the newborn which classify the clinical presentation into well-appearing, equivocal, and clinical illness categories (Table 50.1). Widespread implementation of the sepsis calculator has led to a dramatic decrease in empiric antibiotic usage for EOS without increasing cases of missed EOS as compared to conventional management strategies.48 This tool, however, is only validated in infants who are ≥35 weeks’ GA, requires prior knowledge of local EOS incidence, and requires more frequent clinical monitoring. A third type of risk assessment based on clinical condition only requires more intense serial assessments and institution-based criteria for empiric antibiotic therapy. These three choices available to institutions for the evaluation of infants at >35 weeks’ gestation with suspected EOS are summarized in Table 50.2.

There has also been a paradigm shift in the management of preterm neonates when it comes to “choosing wisely” and deciding on empiric antibiotic therapy.49 Current acceptable practice is to risk stratify preterm infants for EOS. Low-risk infants include those born preterm due to obstetric indications such as pre-eclampsia and those without any onset of labor and no rupture of membranes or signs of maternal fever or fetal distress. These infants can be followed clinically with or without obtaining a blood culture and starting empiric antibiotics. Preterm infants who do not fall in these categories, such as those with preterm premature prolonged rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis, preterm labor, or nonreassuring fetal status, should be started on empiric antibiotics pending blood culture results.

### Management

Ampicillin and an aminoglycoside are recommended as empiric therapy for possible EOS. This combination provides coverage against GBS and E. coli, the most common causative pathogens; however, up to 80% of E. coli isolates from infants with EOS are reported to be ampicillin resistant. Overall, 8% of EOS pathogens are resistant to both ampicillin and gentamicin, presenting more commonly in VLBW infants.50 Given the fact that over 90% of EOS pathogens will be susceptible to the current regimen, these two antibiotics remain the drugs of choice for EOS in term and preterm infants. Empiric use of third-generation cephalosporins is not recommended because of concerns for development of resistance and the increased risk for invasive candidiasis with prolonged administration.51 If gramnegative meningitis is suspected, then it is recommended to add cefotaxime or ceftazidime to the empiric regimen,

Empiric therapy for LOS usually consists of nafcillin and an aminoglycoside or third-generation cephalosporin, providing coverage for the most common LOS pathogens, CoNS, S. aureus, and gram-negative organisms. For preterm infants or infants with complex medical problems necessitating surgeries or prolonged indwelling central catheters, infants with a prior history of methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) colonization or infection, or infants who are in centers with high local MRSA rates, vancomycin should be given in lieu of nafcillin. When a pathogen has been identified, therapy should be tailored to the species and antimicrobial susceptibilities. Duration will be determined by the site of infection and the patient’s clinical response. There is little evidence from randomized, controlled trials on the appropriate duration of treatment for culture-proven sepsis, especially in preterm and low birth weight infants. Bacteremia without a focus of infection is usually treated for 10 days.32 It is reasonable to expect that early preterm infants (<32 weeks’ GA) may require slightly longer treatment courses of 10 to 14 days.53 In addition, gram-negative bacteremia tends to be treated with longer courses of 10 to 14 days. In general, uncomplicated GBS meningitis is treated for 21 days. Longer courses are needed for other focal complications of GBS infection (see Specific Pathogens section). For gram-negative bacterial meningitis, treatment is for 21 days or 2 weeks beyond the first negative CSF culture, whichever is longer.54

Consultation with pediatric infectious disease specialists is strongly recommended in these less common scenarios. Prolonged courses of antibiotics such as vancomycin and aminoglycosides, which are renally excreted, require continuous pharmacokinetic monitoring of trough and peak levels to modify dosing appropriately.

In well-appearing infants without clinical or hematologic evidence for infection, standard practice is to discontinue antibiotics if cultures are negative after 36 to 48 hours. Management decisions are much more challenging for infants for whom sepsis is highly suspected but cultures are negative, which is often the case for preterm infants or when sufficient volume of blood is not obtained for culture. CSF culture data may be lacking in infants who are not clinically stable enough to tolerate a lumbar puncture. Noninfectious conditions mimicking sepsis can also complicate the clinical picture. Studies have shown potential harm associated with longer duration (>5 days) of empiric antibiotics, including increased risk for necrotizing enterocolitis, candidemia, and mortality among premature infants.32,55 There is also concern that early antibiotic exposure may permanently alter the microbiome and predispose to obesity.56 There is little available evidence on when it is safe to discontinue antimicrobials in such cases, and clinicians must consider each patient’s clinical course, as well as the risks associated with longer courses of antibiotics.57 The CDC has led efforts to reduce antibiotic exposure in a campaign entitled “Choosing Wisely.”49 These efforts have championed the use of sepsis risk calculators and early stopping rules.

### Prevention

As mentioned, universal antenatal screening for GBS colonization and intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for the prevention of early-onset GBS disease have been highly successful, although this approach has not influenced the incidence of late-onset GBS.10 Details of the latest recommendations for antenatal GBS screening and intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis are included in a later section. Efforts to produce GBS vaccines for pregnant women are underway. Preventive efforts to reduce the risk of LOS have focused on infection control in the postnatal environment. Successful measures include hand hygiene, proper management of central venous catheters, appropriate use of antibiotics, and limited use of histamine-2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors.23,58 Human milk feeding started within 72 hours of birth has been shown to reduce the incidence of LOS. The roles of probiotic prophylaxis in prevention of LOS require further study. There is conflicting data as to whether probiotic supplementation reduces the risk of LOS in preterm infants, although it has been shown to reduce the incidence of necrotizing enterocolitis.59,60 Immune replacement therapies such as intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) have failed to show any benefit in reducing LOS. Routine skin decontamination with chlorhexidine also is not recommended, as it reduces commensal bacteria and can alter skin pH.

### Bacterial Infections by Organ System

### Meningitis

Bacterial meningitis is more common in the first month of life than at any other age.61 The incidence of neonatal bacterial meningitis varies across the globe. Although the incidence is estimated to be 0.3 per 1000 live births in developed countries, neonatal meningitis is much higher (0.8–6.1 per 1000 live births) in developing nations.61 As with neonatal sepsis, neonatal meningitis can be categorized into two patterns of disease: early onset and late onset. Earlyonset meningitis is highly correlated with the same maternal and intrapartum risk factors as EOS. Late-onset meningitis occurs after the first week of life and reflects community or nosocomial transmission. Among infants with bacteremia, as many as 25% of them will also have meningitis.32

The causative pathogens for neonatal meningitis are similar to those for neonatal sepsis, with GBS and E. coli being predominant. GBS has been the most common cause of early-onset neonatal meningitis in term infants for several decades now and is the causative agent in up to 40% of infants with early-onset meningitis. Gram-negative enteric bacilli cause 30% to 40% of cases of neonatal meningitis, and E. coli accounts for approximately 50% of the gramnegative isolates.11,14,61 E. coli is now recognized as the most common cause of early-onset meningitis among VLBW (<1500 g birth weight) infants. The majority of E. coli strains causing meningitis contain the K1 polysaccharide capsular antigen, which assists the organism in evading host defenses. Other important gram-negative organisms include Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Citrobacter, and Serratia species. A known complication of Citrobacter koseri and Enterobacter sakazakii meningitis in neonates and young infants is the formation of brain abscesses, so it is important to obtain brain imaging whenever these species are isolated from the CSF.62,63 Although L. monocytogenes is a relatively uncommon cause of neonatal meningitis, it can lead to significant morbidity and mortality because of its association with rhombencephalitis. It has been estimated to cause 5% to 20% of neonatal meningitis cases.64 Nosocomial pathogens for late-onset meningitis include CoNS, Candida, and resistant gram-negative organisms, particularly Pseudomonas.61

The clinical presentation of neonatal meningitis is often nonspecific and is similar to that of neonatal sepsis. The most common finding is temperature instability, which occurs in approximately 60% of infants with meningitis. Common neurologic signs include irritability, poor feeding, respiratory distress, apneas, lethargy, hypo- or hypertonia, seizures, and abnormal pupillary response. Most infants present with a full, but not bulging, fontanelle without meningeal signs.

Neonates with suspected bacterial meningitis should undergo a complete sepsis evaluation—including blood culture, CBC with differential, urine culture if greater than 6 days of age, and lumbar puncture for CSF Gram stain and culture, with cell count and differential, glucose, and

protein in order of priority. For clinically stable infants, the lumbar puncture should be performed before administration of antibiotics.

CSF studies need to be interpreted based on the infant’s GA, postnatal age, and birth weight (see Table 50.3), as well as prior antibiotic administration. A CSF WBC count of greater than 20 to 30 cells/μL is consistent with meningeal inflammation. However, neonatal meningitis has been shown to occur with normal CSF parameters, and there is some overlap in CSF WBC values between neonates with and without meningitis.65 If CSF findings are not definitive in an infant whose clinical picture is otherwise suspicious for meningitis, a repeat lumbar puncture obtained 24 to 48 hours later will still show pleocytosis if true meningeal inflammation is present even with the use of antibiotics. CSF protein and glucose values are highly variable in neonates with and without meningitis. CSF Gram stain may be helpful in providing an early presumptive etiologic diagnosis, although a negative Gram stain certainly does not exclude the diagnosis. If the lumbar puncture is traumatic, it is not recommended to adjust the CSF white blood cell count based on the red blood cell counts, as this does not improve the diagnostic utility for neonates.66 Ultrasound to guide lumbar puncture may reduce the incidence of traumatic taps.67 Multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) against common newborn pathogens has been utilized as a diagnostic tool in situations where the CSF is uninterpretable or has been obtained after antibiotic

Empiric therapy for early-onset meningitis includes ampicillin and an aminoglycoside. If infection with a gram-negative organism is suspected, the regimen may be expanded to include a third-generation cephalosporin in addition to ampicillin due to concerns about the high degree of ampicillin resistance in neonatal E. coli strains and poor CNS penetration of gentamicin. Mortality from neonatal meningitis has decreased dramatically over the past several decades, although substantial neurologic morbidity continues to be seen among affected patients. Mortality rates were estimated at almost 50% in the 1970s and have decreased to current estimates of 10% to 15%, with higher mortality rates among preterm infants and those in developing countries.61,72 Studies estimate that, among survivors, 21% to 38% will have mild deficits and 24% to 29% will have severe neurologic sequelae.61,73 Neurologic sequelae include developmental delay, seizures, hydrocephalus, cerebral palsy, blindness, and hearing loss. Predictors of poor neurologic outcomes include seizures lasting >72 hours, presence of coma, hypotension requiring the use of inotropes, leukopenia (<5.0/mm3), and abnormal electroencephalogram findings.61,74 All neonates with a diagnosis of meningitis should receive audiologic testing prior to discharge and ongoing audiologic monitoring until school age.

### Pneumonia

Pneumonia is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in neonates, especially in developing countries, where it is a leading cause of death for all children under 5 years of age.75 The incidence of lower respiratory tract infection in developed countries is estimated at less than 1% among fullterm infants but may be as high as 10% in low birth weight infants. In developed countries, the morbidity and mortality from neonatal pneumonia depend largely on the GA of


## PDF page 870 | printed page 865

the patient, severity of disease, and underlying medical conditions, especially chronic lung disease. Neonatal pneumonia is also categorized into two patterns of disease according to timing and route of acquisition. EOS more commonly presents as pneumonia than LOS. Early-onset pneumonia is usually acquired within the first 3 days of life via vertical transmission, including aspiration of infected amniotic fluid and transplacental transmission. Early-onset pneumonia, which occurs in the setting of maternal infection, is usually referred to as congenital pneumonia and presents at birth or within the first 48 hours of age. Late-onset pneumonia occurs after the first week of life, and infection arises from pathogenic organisms in the infant’s environment. The risk for late-onset pneumonia is highest among infants who require mechanical ventilation. Although ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is not clearly defined in neonates, experts recommend a minimum of 48 hours of mechanical ventilation along with other clinical signs of respiratory decompensation to diagnose neonatal VAP. Other risk factors include extreme prematurity, prolonged hospitalization, and previous bloodstream infection.76 Neonatal autopsy studies found that intrauterine and early-onset pneumonia occurred in 10% to 38% of stillborns and 20% to 63% of live-born babies who subsequently died.77

The most common cause of early-onset pneumonia in developed countries is GBS. Other common causes include S. pneumoniae, nontypable Haemophilus influenzae, S. aureus, E. coli, Klebsiella, and atypical organisms. Ureaplasma urealyticum has been linked to the development of chronic lung disease in colonized infants. A recent randomized placebo-controlled trial showed that azithromycin was effective in treating Ureaplasma infection and in preventing bronchopulmonary dysplasia in those babies who are colonized after birth.78 Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia can occur in the first week of life but more typically presents between 2 and 4 weeks of age, given its long incubation. C. trachomatis pneumonia and ophthalmia neonatorum are discussed in more detail elsewhere. Although syphilis, L. monocytogenes, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis can be transmitted across the placenta, these pathogens are uncommon causes of neonatal pneumonia.

Definitive culture data are often lacking for cases of lateonset, community-acquired neonatal pneumonia, some of which are polymicrobial in nature. S. pneumoniae is considered a predominant causative pathogen in this population. Other important pathogens include S. aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, nontypable H. influenza, and gram-negative enteric organisms. S. aureus, streptococci, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Citrobacter, Enterobacter, Serratia, and Pseudomonas, all of which have been shown to have the potential to cause extensive lung injury, including abscess formation, empyema, and pneumatoceles. Although it generally causes self-limiting illness in older children and adults, Bordetella pertussis infection in young infants can lead to respiratory failure and death. Pertussis can present as apneas in preterm neonates. The infantile pertussis cases in the early 2000s had doubled from the previous baseline of 60 per 100,000 infants

to 120 per 100,000.79 The CDC updated their vaccination guidelines in 2013 to include a recommendation that all pregnant women get a dose of the tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis (Tdap) vaccine during each pregnancy. Receipt of the Tdap vaccine during pregnancy allows for increased maternal pertussis antibody transfer to the neonate. This provides added protection for infants from birth to the time of infant pertussis vaccination at 2 months.79 Since 2015, the infantile pertussis rates have come down and stayed around 60 per 100,000 infants.79

The clinical presentation of early-onset pneumonia often includes respiratory distress and tachycardia within the first few hours of life. Other associated signs are apnea, lethargy, poor feeding, temperature instability, abdominal distention, poor perfusion, and metabolic acidosis. None of these signs is specific for pneumonia, and any infant with these symptoms should undergo a complete sepsis evaluation. Copious or purulent tracheal secretions may also be present. Increasing frequency of suctioning of the endotracheal tube along with increased FiO2 requirements may be the only signs of a bacterial lung infection in mechanically ventilated neonates.

The diagnosis of neonatal pneumonia can be difficult. The differential diagnosis of clinical respiratory distress is broad and includes many noninfectious causes such as transient tachypnea of the newborn, respiratory distress syndrome, meconium aspiration, pulmonary hemorrhage, pneumothorax, hypoglycemia, and metabolic acidosis. Anatomic abnormalities that can cause respiratory distress include primary pulmonary hypoplasia, tracheoesophageal fistula, choanal atresia, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, and congenital heart disease, among many others. Causative pathogens are rarely obtained and identified from the lower respiratory tract. Blood cultures should be obtained from any neonate with suspected pneumonia because it is often a manifestation of systemic infection. Chest radiographs can be helpful in making the clinical diagnosis, although there is significant radiologic overlap between pneumonia and other respiratory disorders of the newborn. In pneumonia, radiographs often reveal bilateral alveolar densities with air bronchograms or irregular, patchy pulmonary infiltrates. Pleural effusions are seen in up to two-thirds of pneumonia cases and are almost never seen in uncomplicated respiratory distress syndrome. The chest radiograph may appear normal in up to 15% of pneumonia cases. Tracheal aspirate Gram stain and culture results are valuable if obtained immediately following intubation. If an infant has been intubated for several days, the endotracheal tube will invariably become colonized and has limited specificity.86 Nonbronchoscopic bronchoalveolar lavage has been studied as an alternative to tracheal aspirates in obtaining lower respiratory samples in mechanically ventilated infants.80

Like most early-onset newborn infections, empiric antibiotic treatment includes ampicillin and an aminoglycoside. Therapy can then be tailored to susceptibility results if a causative organism is identified. Empiric antibiotic therapy for late-onset pneumonia will depend on local bacterial resistance patterns in both the hospital and the community.

Vancomycin and a third-generation cephalosporin such as cefotaxime are commonly used as empiric therapy to provide coverage against newborn pathogens, as well as CoNS and MRSA. If Pseudomonas is suspected, an aminoglycoside plus an antipseudomonal beta-lactam, such as ceftazidime, cefepime, or piperacillin-tazobactam, should be given. Recommended duration of therapy for uncomplicated pneumonia is 5 to 7 days and longer for preterm infants or mechanically ventilated infants.76 Ventilator-associated pneumonia prevention bundles are being used in NICUs and include earlier extubation, hand washing, and closedcircuit suctioning.

### Urinary Tract Infections

The incidence of bacteriuria in term newborns is estimated to be 0.1% to 1%. The incidence is higher in preterm infants and is thought to be around 2%. In the neonatal period, urinary tract infection (UTI) is more common among males than females. Over the first 6 months of life, the incidence of UTI in males decreases, whereas in females it increases. By 1 year of age or older, girls are more likely than boys to have UTIs.81 Uncircumcised males are at higher risk for UTI than are circumcised males. This is due to enhanced bacterial adherence to the foreskin and increased bacterial colonization in the urogenital tract.82 It is rare for a UTI to occur in the first 3 days of life; therefore urine cultures are not recommended as part of the routine EOS evaluation.

Infection of the urinary tract in neonates is thought to be acquired either through hematogenous spread or by ascending infection, often associated with anatomic abnormalities. Hematogenous spread is thought to be the cause for many young infants with UTI, because bacteremia with the same organism is seen in approximately one-third of neonates with urinary tract infection.81 Preterm infants are at higher risk for UTI with concordant bacteremia. Associated meningitis is also seen in 1% to 2% of these cases.83 Urinary tract abnormalities are seen in approximately 20% to 50% of infants with UTIs.81,84 The most common abnormality seen is vesicoureteral reflux (VUR). VUR is associated with younger age at UTI presentation and is fourfold higher in infants with Klebsiella UTIs than E. coli UTIs.85 Other abnormalities that may increase the risk for UTI include ectopic ureter, duplicated collecting system, renal dysplasia, and causes of obstruction, such as posterior urethral valves and ureteropelvic junction obstruction. An additional risk factor for UTI is the presence of an indwelling urinary catheter.

The most common causative pathogen for neonatal UTI is E. coli, which has been isolated in approximately 80% of cases in some large series.81,84 E. coli has several virulence factors that confer an increased ability to cause UTI. Uropathogenic E. coli, the causative organism in most UTIs, can invade and replicate within uroepithelial cells. Adhesins on the bacterial surface allow for increased adhesion to urogenital tract cells, and fimbriae are important in promoting persistence of infection. Other common causative organisms

include other Enterobacteriaceae: Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Proteus, Citrobacter, Salmonella, and Serratia. Gram-positive organisms are isolated much less frequently than gramnegative organisms, although Enterococcus faecalis and S. aureus are also known to cause UTI in newborns. CoNS are more common in preterm infants, and there is 18% concordance with positive blood cultures.86

The signs of neonatal UTI are nonspecific and may include fever, lethargy, failure to thrive, poor feeding, abdominal distention, vomiting, tachypnea, and cyanosis. The clinical presentation of preterm infants is similar to that of term infants, although term infants present more commonly with a fever as compared to preterm infants, who usually have poor feeding or respiratory symptoms. Neonatal UTIs are associated with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and the AAP recommends that all infants with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia be screened for UTI. Infants with high unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that cannot be otherwise explained should also be screened for UTI; E. coli is the most common pathogen isolated in these cases.87,88 Definitive diagnosis must be made by urine culture with specimens obtained by catheterization or suprapubic bladder aspiration. Samples collected into a bag are not useful because they are frequently contaminated. Any growth of a urinary pathogen from bladder aspirate is considered significant. Catheterization cultures with greater than 50,000 CFU/mL are considered positive. Urinalysis, although not a substitute for urine culture, should be obtained, as recent studies have shown improved sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing UTIs in febrile infants ≤60 days old, especially those with ≥50,000 CFU/mL, and particularly for UTIs with associated bacteremia.89 Blood cultures should be obtained for all infants with suspected UTI, as one-third with UTIs will have bacteremia with the same organism. Clinicians should have a very low threshold for performing a lumbar puncture in neonates with UTI, because the risk for concomitant meningitis is 1% to 2%.83

Empiric antibiotic treatment for neonatal UTI includes ampicillin and an aminoglycoside. Hospitalized infants with late-onset infections should be given vancomycin and a cephalosporin to provide coverage for hospital-associated infections with CoNS, MRSA, and resistant strains of enteric organisms. If the infant has had a prior infection, antibiotics should be chosen based on the susceptibility results from the prior episode. If the infection is caused by a highly resistant pathogen or if there is a known anatomical abnormality, a urine culture may be repeated 2 to 3 days after start of treatment to confirm sterilization of the urine. If cultures remain positive despite adequate therapy, the infant should be further evaluated for a potential reservoir of infection with a renal ultrasonography. The duration of therapy is generally 7 to 10 days for uncomplicated bacterial UTI in a newborn.54 Indwelling catheters should be removed promptly, as they serve as a nidus of bacterial growth. Neonates and newborns with delayed clinical response, prematurity, bacteremia, or presence of anatomic abnormalities are usually given intravenous antibiotics for


## PDF page 872 | printed page 867

the entire course. Older infants with uncomplicated disease may be switched to oral antibiotics after demonstration of clinical improvement.

All neonates with UTIs should undergo imaging evaluation because of the high prevalence of urinary tract abnormalities. If prenatal ultrasound data are not available, a renal ultrasound should be performed after the infant has clinically stabilized. Ultrasound can detect structural abnormalities, although it cannot detect VUR or renal scarring. A voiding cystourethrogram is performed to detect VUR, and this is usually done 3 to 6 weeks after completion of antibiotic treatment. Long-term outcomes of UTIs can include renal scarring with subsequent hypertension and chronic kidney disease. If renal damage is suggested by ultrasound, renal cortical scintigraphy can be performed to better assess for renal scarring.81

### Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis

Osteomyelitis and septic arthritis are uncommon infections in neonates and can be difficult to diagnose in this population. In neonates, the most common route for infection to the bone or joint is by hematogenous spread. There are important differences in the pathophysiology of musculoskeletal infections in neonates compared with older children and adults. In infants, metaphyses are susceptible to hematogenous seeding of infection because of the sluggish blood flow within metaphyseal blood vessels, which make hairpin turns before emptying into venous sinusoids. In addition, the lining of the venous sinusoids has reduced macrophage activity.90 In infants, secondary ossification centers have not yet formed, and their cartilaginous epiphyses are supplied with blood directly from transphyseal vessels from the bone metaphysis up until 8 to 18 months of life. Therefore osteomyelitis in infants commonly leads to epiphyseal damage and joint infections. This contiguous infection rarely occurs in older children and adults with osteomyelitis, because the epiphyses and metaphyses have separate blood supplies. Similarly, anatomic differences in the blood supply to the spinal column render neonates more susceptible to discitis than to vertebral body osteomyelitis.91

In preterm neonates, the femur and the tibia are the most common bones (50%) involved in neonatal osteomyelitis, followed by the humerus and the fibula. The most common causative organisms are S. aureus, E. coli, and GBS.91 Less common pathogens include Kingella kingae, group A Streptococcus, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, other enteric gramnegative bacilli, and Candida. The signs and symptoms of osteomyelitis and joint infections in neonates are often subtle and similar to signs of sepsis. Infants may present with irritability, poor feeding, or fever. Some will show positional preference, lack of use of the involved extremity (pseudoparalysis), joint or limb swelling, or pain with passive motion, as with diaper changes. Infections are often multifocal. If left untreated, septic arthritis of the hip can lead to spontaneous drainage along the internal obturator muscle, resulting in a lower abdominal mass just above the inguinal canal.

Osteomyelitis in term neonates differs slightly from preterm neonates. Neonates with late-onset GBS disease often present with osteomyelitis of the proximal humerus, especially those with a history of shoulder dystocia. The skull is the second most common site of osteomyelitis in previously healthy term infants. These infants have a history of iatrogenic injury, cephalohematoma, or fetal scalp electrodes. Calcaneal or heel osteomyelitis is a rare disease following heel punctures for blood sampling and usually is due to CoNS or S. aureus.91

Imaging studies should be obtained for any patient with suspected osteomyelitis or septic arthritis. The radiologic investigation usually starts with plain radiographs, although they cannot detect changes of osteomyelitis in a large percentage of cases. Findings can include deep soft tissue swelling, widening of the joint space or joint dislocation, osteoporosis, periosteal new bone formation, and bony destruction.92 Soft tissue swelling is the earliest finding and can be detected as early as 48 hours after the onset of infection. Bony changes, however, are not apparent until 7 to 10 days after onset of infection. Ultrasound can detect subperiosteal collections and joint effusions, so it is very useful in cases of suspected septic arthritis. Bone scintigraphy is more sensitive than plain films for detecting osteomyelitis early on, and it is useful for detecting multiple foci of infection.92 Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can detect bony changes within 24 to 48 hours after the onset of symptoms and is the diagnostic tool of choice for osteomyelitis. MRI should include a combination of T1-weighted images and short tau inversion recovery (STIR) images in the coronal or sagittal plane, axial fat-suppressed T2-weighted images, and postgadolinium fat-suppressed T1-weighted images in the axial and longitudinal planes.93 MRI provides excellent anatomic detail without exposing infants to ionizing radiation and also provides better information on growth plate involvement compared with bone scintigraphy. However, careful interpretation of bone scans and MRI is necessary to distinguish physiologic from pathologic increased uptake due to increased vascularity of the metaphyseal region in neonates.

Fluid collections in soft tissue or bone should be aspirated and sent for Gram stain and culture, and patients with joint involvement should have synovial fluid sent for Gram stain and culture. Blood cultures yield the causative organism in approximately 50% of cases.94 Lumbar puncture should be performed on ill-appearing infants or those with positive blood cultures.

Recommended empiric antibiotic treatment includes vancomycin for broad gram-positive coverage and an aminoglycoside or third-generation cephalosporin for gramnegative coverage. Therapy can be narrowed when the causative organism has been isolated. Most patients with osteomyelitis can be managed with conservative, or nonsurgical, treatment. Hip and shoulder joint infections and bony abscesses require surgical drainage, as do some infected cephalohematomas. Knee, ankle, and elbow joints usually need aspiration. The total duration of therapy is 4 to 6 weeks for


## PDF page 873

uncomplicated cases. Therapy should be 8 weeks for osteomyelitis caused by MRSA and 6 to 12 months for infants with fungal disease caused by Candida.95,96 Pediatric infectious disease and pediatric orthopedic specialists should be involved in the care of these infants.

Significant morbidity may be associated with neonatal musculoskeletal infections, and prompt diagnosis and treatment are needed to minimize complications. Septic arthritis of the hip is associated with serious long-term sequelae. Complications include growth plate damage, avascular necrosis, limb length discrepancies, and angular joint deformities, among many others.97 These patients should be followed for the development of long-term complications, as many will require surgical intervention.

### Ophthalmia Neonatorum

Ophthalmia neonatorum is conjunctivitis occurring in the first month of life. Bacterial causes include S. aureus, nontypable H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, enteric gram-negative bacilli, GBS, N. gonorrhoeae, and C. trachomatis. The differential also includes viral causes, particularly herpes simplex virus, and noninfectious causes, such as chemical conjunctivitis. Conjunctivitis in neonates is managed aggressively because of the high risk for associated systemic illness and complications. Prophylactic administration of ophthalmic antibiotic agents shortly after birth greatly reduces the risk of gonococcal conjunctivitis but not chlamydial disease, as topical ophthalmic ointments do not prevent nasopharyngeal colonization, which is the primary route of chlamydial infection.

The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that eye prophylaxis be provided to all newborns.98 Regimens with equal efficacy include 0.5% erythromycin ointment, 1% tetracycline ointment, and silver nitrate solution, although the latter two are not commercially available in the United States. Chemical conjunctivitis is usually seen soon after birth and improves over 48 hours.

The clinical presentation of bacterial conjunctivitis in neonates is similar to that in older patients. Typical signs include purulent ocular discharge, erythema and edema of the eyelids, and injection of the conjunctivae. Gonococcal infection in the newborn is typically acquired during delivery, with perinatal transmission occurring in 30% to 40% of cases of active maternal cervical infection.99 Infants usually show signs of infection 2 to 5 days after birth, with profuse, purulent ocular discharge and swelling of the eyelids. Untreated infection can spread into the subconjunctival connective tissue and cornea, leading to ulceration, scarring, and visual loss. In addition to conjunctivitis, infection of other mucosal surfaces can occur, and scalp abscess may be associated with the use of fetal monitoring electrodes. Disseminated infection can lead to septic arthritis or, less commonly, bacteremia or meningitis.

C. trachomatis is usually transmitted to the neonate during vaginal delivery, and approximately 20% of infants born to mothers with active cervical infection will develop

conjunctivitis.100 Chlamydial conjunctivitis is also known as inclusion conjunctivitis. The serovariants of C. trachomatis causing infection in neonates (D–K) reflect the primary serotypes causing genital disease in adults. The onset of conjunctivitis is often 5 to 14 days after birth. Findings may range from mild eyelid swelling with minimal watery discharge to mucopurulent discharge, significant swelling, and red, thickened conjunctivae. If the exudate adheres to the conjunctivae, a pseudomembrane may form. Bloody discharge may also be noted with intense inflammation. Without treatment, infection may lead to corneal and conjunctival scarring or progression toward pneumonia 2 to 8 weeks after birth. Approximately half of the infants with chlamydia pneumonia have a history of conjunctivitis.

All newborns who develop conjunctivitis after the first days of life should have laboratory testing performed to determine the etiology, because there is significant overlap in clinical presentation among the causative pathogens. If gonococcal infection is suspected, CSF and blood cultures are obtained to determine if dissemination occurred.54 Purulent ocular discharge is sent for Gram stain and culture. Culture on selective media (e.g., Thayer-Martin) is needed to evaluate for gonococcal infection. Additionally, conjunctival specimens should be sent for C. trachomatis testing. These are obtained from an everted eyelid using a Dacron-tipped swab. C. trachomatis is an obligate intracellular organism, so specimens must contain conjunctival epithelial cells; ocular exudates are not adequate specimens for testing. Culture of the organism is the gold standard for diagnosis of C. trachomatis infection in infants. Nucleic acid amplification tests may also be considered because they have been found to have high specificity and sensitivity, although none has been approved by the FDA for use on conjunctival specimens, for which direct fluorescent antibody tests are preferred.101 In infants with signs of pneumonia, testing for C. trachomatis can be sent from nasopharyngeal specimens.

Systemic antibiotics are required to treat conjunctivitis resulting from N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. For other causes of bacterial conjunctivitis, topical antibiotic ointment or solution given for 7 to 10 days provides adequate therapy. Infants with gonococcal eye disease should be hospitalized and monitored for response to treatment, as well as for signs of disseminated disease. Recommended treatment for gonococcal conjunctivitis is a single dose of intramuscular or intravenous ceftriaxone. If the infant is receiving intravenous calcium, cefotaxime should be used instead of ceftriaxone because precipitation can occur. Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin from albumin, so levels should be monitored in these infants. If there is concurrent concern for gonococcal scalp abscess or disseminated infection, treatment should be continued for 7 days or 14 days if meningitis is suspected. The eyes should also be irrigated frequently with sterile saline until the discharge has resolved. Recommended treatment for either chlamydial conjunctivitis or pneumonia is oral erythromycin base or succinate for 14 days or azithromycin for 3 days.54 Data are limited on the effectivenes and optimal dosing of azithromycin in neonatal ophthalmia. Providers

should be aware that oral erythromycin is associated with an increased incidence of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, and these infants should be followed for such.

A diagnosis of neonatal ophthalmia should prompt testing for sexually transmitted infections in the mother and her partner(s). Infants born to mothers with untreated gonorrhea should receive prophylactic intravenous or intramuscular ceftriaxone after birth. These infants do not need any prophylactic ophthalmic ointment. Infants born to mothers with untreated Chlamydia infection do not need prophylactic systemic treatment but should be followed closely for signs of ophthalmia.

### Omphalitis

Omphalitis is an infection of the umbilicus or surrounding tissues. Newborns are predisposed to umbilical infections following colonization of the umbilicus by a wide array of microorganisms shortly after birth as devitalized tissues of the cord stump provide for excellent bacterial growth. Bacteria can reach the bloodstream through patent vessels of the newly cut cord and lead to systemic infection and severe complications. The incidence of omphalitis in developed countries is low and is estimated to be less than 1%.102 Although complete data are lacking from developing countries, the incidence is expected to be much higher. The risk may be six times greater for infants delivered at home than for hospital births. Other risk factors for omphalitis include low birth weight, prolonged rupture of membranes, umbilical catheterization, and improper cord care. Postnatal application of substances to the cord presumed to aid in faster separation is often an inciting factor in omphalitis. Immune deficiencies such as leukocyte adhesion defect often present with omphalitis in the neonatal period.

Organisms that colonize the umbilicus or surrounding skin can produce omphalitis. Common pathogens include S. aureus, group A streptococci, GBS, and gram-negative bacilli, including E. coli, Klebsiella, and Pseudomonas. Polymicrobial infections are common in omphalitis. Anaerobic bacteria can contribute to infection, especially in infants born to mothers with chorioamnionitis.

The clinical presentation of omphalitis is usually around 3 to 5 days in preterm neonates and 5 to 9 days for term neonates, and it starts with periumbilical erythema followed by purulent drainage from the umbilical stump (or from the navel after the cord has separated), with surrounding induration and tenderness. The drainage may be foul smelling, which is suggestive of infection with anaerobic bacteria. Infants with more severe infection will display systemic signs of illness, including fever, lethargy, poor feeding, and irritability. Involvement of the abdominal wall, black eschar, or extensive edema should prompt consideration for necrotizing fasciitis as a complication. Other complications of omphalitis include peritonitis, intra-abdominal abscess, suppurative thrombophlebitis of portal or umbilical veins, and umbilical hernia with bowel ischemia. Delayed treatment of neonatal omphalitis is associated with a high case fatality rate.

Omphalitis is a clinically apparent diagnosis but can be confused with patent urachus or funisitis. Purulent discharge should be sent for Gram stain and culture. Blood and CSF cultures should be obtained from infants with signs of systemic illness, including fever, lethargy, and irritability. Prompt treatment with broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotics must be started if there is clinical suspicion of omphalitis due to the high mortality rate associated with this disease. Typically, an antistaphylococcal penicillin and an aminoglycoside are given to provide gram-positive and gram-negative coverage. If the community prevalence of MRSA is high, vancomycin should be used instead of antistaphylococcal penicillin. The addition of clindamycin or metronidazole may be considered if there is suspicion of anaerobic involvement, especially for infants with foul-smelling discharge or if there is a history of maternal chorioamnionitis. For uncomplicated cases, duration of treatment is typically 10 days. A switch to oral therapy for completion of the course of treatment may be considered, depending on the patient’s age, culture results, and clinical response.103

Prevention of omphalitis involves both clean delivery services and hygienic cord care. It is generally agreed upon that the umbilical cord should be cut with clean hands using a sterile blade or scissors. This helps to prevent both omphalitis and neonatal tetanus. However, optimal care of the cord stump after the cord has been cut is an area of active research and some debate. Since 1998, the WHO has recommended dry cord care in high-resource settings. In low-resource settings where delivery might not be in a hospital, there is benefit of applying 4% chlorhexidine to the cord to reduce omphalitis and neonatal mortality.104 However, the benefit of chlorhexidine in the hospital setting in such countries remains debated and is still a topic of active research.105,106 A 2004 Cochrane review of 21 studies, most of them performed in high-income countries, showed no difference in risk for omphalitis among cords treated with antiseptics (such as alcohol, iodine, and chlorhexidine) compared with dry cord care or placebo.107

### Specific Pathogens

### Group B Streptococcus

Group B Streptococcus (GBS), or Streptococcus agalactiae, is the most common cause of EOS in term neonates (>50%) in the United States. The GBS serotype corresponds to its capsular polysaccharide. Serotype Ia, Ib, II, III, IV, and V account for >95% of EOS cases and >97% of LOS cases in the United States. Serotype III is strongly linked to meningitis and accounts for a significant proportion of LOS cases.9 GBS is the second most common cause of EOS in preterm neonates less than 37 weeks′ GA (13%–20%) after E. coli. For all GAs combined, the incidence varies from cohort to cohort. The most recent National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD) database (2015–2017) lists it as second most common at 30.2% behind E. coli (36.6.%), whereas a CDC surveillance cohort from 2005 to 2014 ranked it as the most common (35.8%).11,12 The primary risk factor for early-onset


## PDF page 875

GBS disease in the neonate is maternal GBS colonization of the genitourinary or gastrointestinal tract leading to intrapartum vertical acquisition of GBS during passage through the birth canal. The introduction of universal screening for maternal GBS colonization and the use of intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis have led to an 80% reduction in the burden of early-onset GBS disease, yet has had no impact on late-onset disease.46 The incidence of GBS LOS remained at ∼1 per 1000 live births in preterm infants and ∼0.2 per 1000 live births in term infants from 2006 to 2015, despite widespread adoption of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) intrapartum prophylaxis recommendations.9

Following several clinical trials and observational studies, which demonstrated that early-onset GBS disease in neonates could be decreased by administering intravenous antibiotics during labor to women at risk for transmitting GBS, the CDC has recommended GBS screening for pregnant women for the prevention of neonatal GBS disease. The most updated guidelines have endorsed the AAP and ACOG recommendations of screening and intrapartum prophylaxis. The ACOG no longer recommends a “riskbased” prevention strategy but recommends that all pregnant women, regardless of planned mode of birth, should undergo antepartum GBS testing between 36 0/7 and 37 6/7 weeks’ pregnancy, unless intrapartum prophylaxis is indicated for a history of GBS bacteriuria during pregnancy or previous infant with GBS disease.46,108

Women with GBS colonization who have cesarean delivery performed before the onset of labor or rupture of membranes do not require intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. The guidelines also contain recommendations for management of women with unknown GBS status at the onset of labor, expanded recommendations for laboratory identification of GBS, a change in the recommended dose of penicillin G prophylaxis, and recommendations for women with penicillin allergy. Algorithms are included to assist in the management of women with preterm labor, women with preterm PROM, and newborns at risk for early-onset GBS disease. Intravenous penicillin remains the drug of choice for GBS prophylaxis, with ampicillin as an acceptable alternative. In women with a strong history of penicillin allergy, either vancomycin or clindamycin can be used (only if the GBS isolate is susceptible to clindamycin).

Before the initiation of active prevention with intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis, the estimated incidence of invasive neonatal GBS disease in the United States was 1.8 cases per 1000 live births (1.5/1000 for early onset and 0.35/1000 for late onset). Following implementation of the CDC guidelines in the mid-1990s, the incidence of earlyonset disease decreased by 80% to 0.3 to 0.4 cases per 1000 live births after 2002.12,109

Despite the dramatic decrease in the incidence of newborn GBS disease, it remains the leading infectious cause of morbidity and mortality among newborns in the United States.27 Rates of maternal GBS colonization have remained unchanged since the 1970s.110 The use of intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis has had no effect on the incidence rate of

late-onset GBS disease, which has remained approximately 0.30 cases per 1000 live births (Fig. 50.1), increasing to almost 4 per 1000 live births in VLBW infants.18 Continued monitoring is needed to evaluate for potential adverse consequences of intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis, including the emergence of drug resistance and a possible increase in the incidence of non-GBS neonatal pathogens. Clinical trials are underway to evaluate administration of GBS serotype–specific polysaccharide-protein conjugate vaccines in pregnant women, which is one of the priority areas of the WHO. Maternal vaccination has the potential to provide a simpler strategy for prevention, without the concerns about antibiotic resistance and emergence of non-GBS pathogens associated with intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis.111

Early-onset GBS disease most commonly presents within the first day of life. Invasive early-onset disease may lead to bacteremia, pneumonia, meningitis, or bone or joint involvement. Late-onset GBS disease occurs after the first week of life, and patients commonly present with bacteremia and meningitis.109 Recommended definitive antibiotic therapy for GBS disease is penicillin G, given its narrow spectrum and excellent in vitro activity. GBS is consistently susceptible to penicillin, ampicillin, first- and second-generation cephalosporins, and vancomycin. Approximately 30% of GBS isolates are resistant to erythromycin, and approximately 20% are resistant to clindamycin.
