### Neuroimaging of White Matter Injury

### Neonatal Sonography

Neonatal sonography is the one major bedside technique to image the neonatal brain. Unlike IVH, damage to the white matter can have different appearances, and depending on the timing of the injury, the imaging characteristics can be nonspecific, generally with an increase in echogenicity in the acute phase of the injury (Fig. 54.9). In clinical practice, at least in the older preterm infant, the condition of white matter is judged by its echogenic potential as compared with that of the choroid plexus. Generally, the echogenicity found in early PVL is similar in intensity to that of the choroid plexus. The echogenicity is bilateral but slightly

asymmetric in appearance, can be sharply delineated, and may have nodular components. This has to be differentiated from normal peritrigonal flaring, which is perfectly symmetric and with a radial appearance. Evolution of such hyperechogenicity can be twofold: either complete disappearance or evolution into cysts and/or ventricular dilatation. Cyst formation in analog to neuropathology is a process typical for the second week (10–40 days) after the insult. DeVries et al.61 postulated an ultrasound-based classification for PVL of four grades. Increasing grades are associated with increasing neurodevelopmental handicap. Grade I is defined as transient (>7 days) periventricular densities without cyst formation. If cysts develop and are few in number, localized primarily in frontal and frontoparietal white matter, this is classified as grade II. When they are widespread and extend into the parieto-occipital region, they are referred to as grade III; these may grow and gradually disappear, leaving an irregularly dilated lateral ventricle. Grade IV cysts are present all the way into the subcortical area, resembling porencephaly (Table 54.1). In a pooled analysis based on data from 15 published studies, 11% of infants with small, 35% of those with medium, and 60% of those with large ultrasound-defined white matter echolucencies had an intelligence or developmental index less than 70, which outlines the importance of potentially associated microstructural alterations in cortical development after white matter injury. More recently, these classifications have been extended to include overall brain injury in the preterm infant as well as defined algorithms for timing of screening.62,63

Ultrasound can be viewed as the ideal mode of imaging to detect cystic PVL but has very limited value for detecting diffuse white matter injury and the processes leading to encephalopathy of prematurity, as shown in studies comparing neonatal sonography with MRI.64 MRI has been found to be less sensitive for pathologies such as lenticulostriate vasculopathy or calcifications.65

### Conventional Magnetic Resonance Imaging

Conventional T1- and T2-weighted imaging can show signal abnormalities in the periventricular white matter that are different from the cystic lesions detected by ultrasound. The typical conventional MR imaging pattern in the subacute phase consists of punctate periventricular areas of T1 signal hyperintensities and T2 signal hypointensities (Fig. 54.10). The precise neuropathologic correlate of these signal abnormalities is not completely known but may be caused by either some hemorrhagic components of the lesions and/or the cellular reaction of glial cells and macrophages, which are known to contain lipid droplets (see Models of Encephalopathy of Prematurity) accounting for the high signal intensity in T1-weighted MR images. Some differentiation is possible with the addition of susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI), a method useful for detecting intravascular venous deoxygenated blood as well as extravascular blood products. ### Diffusion Magnetic Resonance Imaging

Diffusion-weighted MR imaging (DWI) or diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) measures the self-diffusion of water. The two primary pieces of information available from DWI studies—water apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) and diffusion anisotropy measures—change dramatically during development, reflecting underlying changes in tissue water content and cytoarchitecture (see Chapter 53).

Parameters of DWI also change in response to brain injury. The ADC decreases in acute injury, and possible mechanisms leading to this decrease are decrease in extracellular fluid due to cellular swelling (cytotoxic edema), swelling of mitochondria and reduction of cytoplasmic diffusion, axonal swelling, and other mechanisms such as membrane changes owing to fatty acid peroxidation.

Early assessment of periventricular white matter in preterm infants with DWI can reveal bilateral periventricular diffusion restriction similar to the typical distribution of PVL when ultrasound and conventional MRI show no or nonspecific abnormalities (Fig. 54.14).78 A reduced ADC in an otherwise normal preterm brain is considered an early indicator of white matter damage (just as a reduced ADC is seen shortly after the onset of an acute cerebral ischemic lesion in adults). The typical histologic changes in the acute phase of PVL outlined previously are characterized by some of the same mechanisms leading to restriction of water diffusivity. These changes are responsible for the diffusion changes described earlier in that they considerably change the microstructure of white matter and therefore change water diffusivity.

Further quantitative measures of diffusion at term among premature infants with perinatal white matter lesions (both T2 hyperintensities as well as T1 hyperintensities [punctate lesions]), when compared to preterm infants without white matter injury, showed lower anisotropy values in the area of the previous

injury (i.e., central periventricular white matter) but also in the underlying posterior limb of the internal capsule (Fig. 54.17).80 The lower anisotropy in the injured cerebral white matter suggests that white matter fiber tracts were destroyed or their subsequent development was impaired. Whether this effect involves axon bundles per se, their packing density, or their encasement by premyelinating oligodendroglia is unknown. The lower anisotropy in the internal capsule further suggests a disturbance in the development of the descending corticospinal tracts.

Fiber tracking is another technique applied to the developing brain to study quantitative assessment of specific pathway maturation in white matter.81 Berman et al.82 were able to show significant differences in the maturational changes in fractional anisotropy and transverse diffusion between the motor and the somatosensory pathways in premature infants between 30 and 40 weeks’ gestational age. This approach further allowed the measurement of diffusion changes across multiple levels of the functional tract and therefore the assessment of myelination progress over a given white matter fiber tract.

The subsequent neurologic deficits after cerebral white matter injury are grouped together under the term of cerebral palsy. Structural correlates of cerebral palsy have been assessed using DTI in the newborn period, adding to prognostication of cerebral palsy in the newborn period. Tractspecific evaluation of children with cerebral palsy after PVL identified most frequently alterations in white matter fiber tract development in the retrolenticular part of the internal capsule, posterior thalamic radiation, superior corona radiate, and in commissural fibers of the corpus callosum. In another study, regional measurements in the primary site of white matter lesions showed increased Dav values and decreased fractional anisotropy values, suggesting primary degeneration, whereas the corticospinal tract ipsilateral showed secondary degeneration with increased Dav and decreased fractional anisotropy; contralateral contraction stress test (CST) showed increased Dav but an increase in fractional anisotropy, suggesting reorganization of sensorimotor tracts.83

The clinical relevance of injury and related modifications of white matter architecture detected in this fashion is not yet known, and long-term follow-up studies of prematurely born children are underway. Linking functional outcome to structural white matter development assessed by diffusionbased imaging, applying either a diffusion tensor model or more advanced models such as neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI)84 and functional imaging, is being studied.81,85

Given the diffuse character of neuropathologic features of encephalopathy of prematurity described earlier, the overall wiring of the brain, which is assumed to occur mostly during the second part of pregnancy, is most affected. ### Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging— Functional Connectivity

The process of establishing permanent functional connectivity is influenced by several factors, such as neuron survival, competition for trophic factors, electrical activity of axons, and afferent inputs.19 Functional connectivity can be studied even in the newborn period by resting state functional MRI (fMRI) and analysis of the regional time course of blood-oxygenation-level-dependent (BOLD) fluctuations. fMRI uses deoxygenated hemoglobin as an endogenous contrast agent to produce a BOLD signal. By using these BOLD signals in neonates, it is possible to identify networks with synchronous neuronal activity in sleeping neonates to study resting-state functional connectivity. Studies indicate that aberrant functional connectivity relevant to cognitive outcome is observed in preterm infants89 with specific disruption of connectivity in fronto-paralimbic/ limbic and posterior default mode network regions,90 which might underlie the behavioral and social cognition difficulties reported in the preterm population. ### Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy

One of the essential contributors to the progress in both noninvasive detection of tissue metabolism and in vivo biochemistry has been magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS), which gives specific chemical information on the biochemistry of numerous intracellular metabolites.93 The biochemical characteristics of white matter damage in preterm infants have been studied in vivo using MRS.94 Similar to the high diagnostic value of MRS in term asphyxia, MRS in acute phases of immature white matter injury can detect indicators of anaerobic glycolysis with increased intracerebral lactate. Data suggest that white matter damage in the preterm infant studied around term gestational age resulted in high Lac/Cr and high myo-inositol/Cr ratios,95 and N-acetylaspartate (NAA) as a marker of neuroaxonal integrity was reduced in the damaged periventricular white matter; these reductions were also found more recently in preterm infants with cerebellar injury.96 As outlined in Chapter 53, astrocytes further play a variety of complex nutritive and supportive roles in relation to neuronal metabolic homeostasis. For example, astrocytes take up glutamate and convert it to glutamine. This removal of glutamate from the extracellular space protects surrounding cells from excitotoxicity from glutamate. injury, indicating impaired cerebral cortical development.103 In moderately preterm infants without signs of white matter injury, cortical development was similar to that of full-term infants.106 When assessing cerebellar volume at term, there was a significant reduction in cerebellar volume of preterm infants when compared with term infants.107 Unilateral cerebral white matter lesions resulted in contralateral reduction of cerebellar volume, indicating the trophic interplay owing to loss of cerebrocerebellar connectivity.108 When assessing overall volumetric data at term equivalent age in preterm infants without overt cerebral white matter injury, it has shown limited predictability for neurodevelopmental outcome,109,110 with a large effect of environmental factors indicating the potential for growth plasticity post-term.

Long-term follow-up studies of preterm infants have confirmed the permanent character of these disruptive/adaptive changes in brain development, and many of them are related to functional deficits.111–113 Evaluations of 8-year-old preterm infants with volumetric brain assessment showed persistence of cortical gray matter reduction in preterm infants accompanied with a reduction in the volume of hippocampus, which correlated with cognitive scores indicating longterm functional consequences.114 Studying a larger cohort of preterm subjects at the same age, Nosarti115 noted widespread alterations in both gray and white matter volumes throughout the brain. Of note, several gray matter regions, including the middle temporal gyrus, superior temporal

gyrus, sensorimotor region, and precentral and postcentral gyri, were linearly related to gestational age for the preterm group. Furthermore, decreases in both gray and white matter volumes in the middle temporal gyrus were associated with cognitive impairment in the preterm group. With the development of whole brain connectivity analysis, specific long-term effects of prematurity and associated brain injury have been defined, affecting not only sensorimotor connectivity116 but also, more importantly, the prefrontal and the limbic cortico-basal ganglia-thalamocortical loops, tightly linked to performance in executive function and social behavior.117 New mathematical modeling techniques such as graph model theory have further allowed us to look at the efficiency of brain networks in ex-preterm infants, indicating that their network efficiency can be altered both globally and regionally.90 Neuroimaging has defined new biomarkers of later neurofunctional outcomes and has become a useful adjunct to clinical practice.113

Human brain development is characterized by several interrelated steps. Neuronal and radial glial proliferation and migration are early events in brain development that are followed by a series of organizational events that result in the complex circuitry of axons and dendrites characteristic of the human brain. The immature cortex is characterized by a radial organization seen both in rodents and humans. The preterm cortex at term equivalent age reveals a persisting fetal radial organization that can be characterized by DTI-based analysis (higher fractional anisotropy) and is associated with decreased cortical folding, which is more pronounced in preterm infants with signs of white matter injury.118 Elaboration of dendritic and axonal ramifications and attainment of proper alignment and orientation is most likely one of the driving forces for the folding of the cerebral cortex during development.119 Several authors have investigated the influence of preterm birth on primary cortical folding. Dubois et al.120,121 observed a trend toward lower cortical surface areas and smaller cortical and white matter volumes but equivalent sulcation in female preterm infants when compared with male preterm subjects. Furthermore, preterm neonates with intrauterine growth restriction had a more pronounced reduction of volume in relation to surface area and increased sulcation with resultant changes in cortical thickness, which correlated with impaired behavioral functions. Infants with early white matter lesions at birth showed a trend toward increased sulcation in the overlaying cortex. Prematurity itself also changed the maturational profile of cortical sulcation.122 Early alteration of white matter connectivity and ensuing disruption to the white matter circuits and to the subcortical plate may therefore alter subsequent density, survival, and organization of cortical neurons. In severe cases, secondary polymicrogyria after primarily early white matter injury has been described (Fig. 54.19).123 Neuropathology of the cerebral cortex in preterm infants has revealed cortical dysplasia in cortical areas overlaying white matter destruction.124 These abnormalities of cortical development are found secondary to disturbances of afferent input to and efferent output from areas of the cortex

Many studies confirm the potential long-term effect of the earlier described brain abnormalities, making the encephalopathy of prematurity one of the major concerns in neonatology.64

Key Points

### • The origin of perinatal brain damage is multifactorial. • Encephalopathy of prematurity is based on a combina-

tion of destructive and developmental disturbances.

### • MRI provides in vivo brain macro-, microstructural, and

metabolic biomarkers of injury.

### • MRI-based biomarkers at term equivalent age have high

negative predictive value for neurodevelopmental outcome but limited positive predictive power.

### • Advanced quantitative neuroimaging tools provide

evidence for long-term lateration of brain structure and function associated with encephalopathy of prematurity.

title: Intracranial Hemorrhage and Stroke in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: 55 Intracranial Hemorrhage and Stroke in the Neonate
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Germinal matrix hemorrhage-intraventricular hemorrhage (GMH-IVH) continues to be a common form of brain injury in very preterm infants. Despite major advances in neonatology, GMH-IVH remains associated with high rates of neurodevelopmental impairment (NDI), especially when complicated by progressive posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation (PHVD) and periventricular hemorrhagic infarction (PVHI). Cranial ultrasonography (cUS) is the most widely used neuroimaging modality since the early 1980s for the diagnosis of GMH-IVH. Serial cUS scanning allows early detection and accurate grading of the hemorrhage and monitoring of its complications, especially PHVD. Data are accumulating to suggest that PHVD should be treated before the onset of clinical symptoms. cUS is less sensitive than magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in identifying hemorrhages in the temporal and occipital regions, coexisting subtle white matter injuries, and small cerebellar hemorrhages (CBHs). Infarction within the territory of a major artery or a branch arising from it around the time of birth is referred to as perinatal stroke. Perinatal arterial ischemic stroke (PAIS) is a form of arterial stroke that usually presents with focal clonic seizures in the first few days after birth. Cerebral sinovenous thrombosis (CSVT) is classified as a venous type of stroke, which may present with IVH with or without unilateral thalamic hemorrhage in a term neonate. The first part of this chapter focuses on GMH-IVH and PHVD in the preterm infant as well as extra-axial hemorrhages in the term infant, whereas the second part focuses on perinatal stroke, mainly PAIS and CSVT.
paragraphs.heading: Summary

paragraphs.text: GMH-IVH is the most common form of intracranial hemorrhage in the neonatal population and mainly occurs in
paragraphs.heading: Incidence

paragraphs.text: very preterm infants.1 The first studies, using computed tomography (CT) scans, were performed in the late 1970s and showed an incidence reaching almost 50% in infants with a birth weight of less than 1500 g.2 Later studies using cUS showed a steady decline in the rates of GMH- IVH in the following decades until the last decade, when it plateaued at around 25%. The decrease in the incidence of GMH-IVH is mainly attributed to improved perinatal and neonatal care practices, increased use of antenatal corticosteroids, and the postnatal use of surfactant.3
paragraphs.heading: Incidence

paragraphs.text: Although there are numerous reports on the incidence of GMH-IVH in very preterm infants, there is considerable heterogeneity in the literature, which is largely because of gestational age (GA) differences in these studies. In a recent meta-analysis of 37 studies on 87,993 infants, Lai et al.4 provided GA-based pooled estimates and reported any grade GMH-IVH of around 45% for GA less than 25 weeks, 34% for GA less than 28 weeks, and 17% for GA 28 to 31 weeks. The Vermont Oxford Network (VON) database 2020 report on 47,324 very preterm infants demonstrated that the incidence of severe GMH-IVH (grade 3 or grade 4 according to Papile2) remains at 7.8%.5 The VON database also underscores the close association between the degree of prematurity and risk for GMH-IVH, with around a sevenfold higher risk (50% vs. 7%) in extremely preterm infants less than 27 weeks’ GA compared with those who were born at 27 to 32 weeks’ GA.5
paragraphs.heading: Incidence

paragraphs.text: Accurate timing of GMH-IVH is possible only when serial cUS scans are performed. Recently, Inder et al.6 published a comprehensive review of the application of cUS in preterm infants, outlining the need for more frequent serial cUS to improve the accurate detection of GMH-IVH and its complications. Diagnosis of a hemorrhage of antenatal onset can only be made when the first cUS is performed on the day of admission within the first few hours after delivery.6 cUS studies showed that more than 90% of GMH-IVH occurs within the first 3 days of life and of
paragraphs.heading: Screening Method and Timing of Hemorrhage

paragraphs.text: those, around half occur within the first 6 hours and twothirds within the first 24 hours of postnatal life. The lesion reaches its maximal extent by 3 to 5 days after initial detection. Only around 10% of cases occur beyond the first week, in contrast to preterm white matter injuries wherein late onset is not uncommon.6
paragraphs.heading: Screening Method and Timing of Hemorrhage

paragraphs.text: GMH-IVH typically originates from the subependymal germinal matrix, which is a highly cellular and vascular region of the developing brain between 23 and 32 weeks of gestation.7 It is described as an “immature vascular rete” because the vessels within this structure are primitive and cannot be classified as arterioles, venules, or capillaries. During the fetal period, the germinal matrix serves as a source of neural precursors that will migrate to the cerebral cortex and thalamus, as well as glial precursors that will produce astrocytes and oligodendroglia. The germinal matrix regresses gradually, with the complete involution of the structure by 34 to 36 weeks of gestation.8
paragraphs.heading: Neuropathology

paragraphs.text: The germinal matrix is mainly supplied by a branch of the anterior cerebral artery known as the Heubner artery. The rest of the blood supply is received from the anterior choroidal artery and the terminal branches of the lateral striate arteries. Venous drainage occurs through fan-shaped medullary veins through which blood flows into the germinal matrix and subsequently into the terminal vein, which is located below the germinal matrix. The anatomic distribution of parenchymal hemorrhages associated with GMH- IVH suggests venous infarction owing to obstruction of these medullary veins. Using susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI), it was demonstrated that preterm infants with GMH-IVH have higher variability in their vascular anatomy showing a narrower curvature of the terminal portion of subependymal veins, which may be a predisposing factor for GMH-IVH in preterm infants.9
paragraphs.heading: Neuropathology

paragraphs.text: The germinal matrix is most abundant over the head and body of the caudate nucleus; thus hemorrhage most commonly originates from the caudothalamic germinal matrix site. However, in the autopsy series and in recent MRI studies, using SWI, small hemorrhages were also detected in the temporal and occipital germinal matrix sites. The size of the GMH changes with the maturity of the infant, that is, larger GMHs occur in less mature infants. The site also varies with maturity, with occurrence over the body of the caudate nucleus in the less mature infant and over the head of the caudate nucleus in the more mature infant. In around half of the preterm infants with GMH-IVH, choroid plexus hemorrhage may also exist, whereas in more mature term infants the choroid plexus may be the primary region of hemorrhage caused by full regression of the germinal matrix by term. When the GMH is followed longitudinally with cUS, a subependymal cyst is commonly seen as a sequel after several weeks. This cyst is often still present at term
paragraphs.heading: Germinal Matrix Hemorrhage

paragraphs.text: equivalent age (TEA) and can be better visualized with cUS than with brain MRI.
paragraphs.heading: Germinal Matrix Hemorrhage

paragraphs.text: GMH can cause disruption of the subependymal ventricular lining and spill over into the lateral ventricles to become an IVH. The quantity of IVH can vary considerably and, if large, can lead to acute distension of the lateral ventricles.10 The blood can fill part of or the entire ventricular system, spreading through the foramen of Monro, the third ventricle, the aqueduct of Sylvius, the fourth ventricle, and the foramina of Luschka and Magendie to collect eventually around the brainstem and in the posterior fossa. Clot formation can lead to outflow obstruction at any level, but most commonly at the level of the aqueduct of Sylvius or more diffusely at the level of the arachnoid villi. More gradual progressive ventricular dilatation occurs, especially in those with a large GMH- IVH, which is known as PHVD.10 This can be a transient or persistent event. In a small proportion, it can be rapidly progressive and noncommunicating, usually because of obstruction at the level of the aqueduct of Sylvius or the outlet of the foramina of Luschka and Magendie. Unilateral outflow obstruction at the level of the foramen of Monro can lead to unilateral hydrocephalus (Fig. 55.1). In infants with communicating progressive PHVD, the increase in ventricular size is more gradual and is considered to be caused by obliterative arachnoiditis resulting from blood collecting in the subarachnoid spaces of the posterior fossa, leading to an imbalance between cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) production and reabsorption. Other than these obstructive mechanisms and impaired reabsorption of the CSF, Karimy et al.11 demonstrated in a rat model that GMH-IVH causes a Toll-like receptor-4 and nuclear factor-κB-dependent inflammatory response in the choroid plexus epithelium that is associated with a threefold increase in CSF secretion. These data uncover a previously unrecognized contribution of CSF hypersecretion to the pathogenesis of PHVD.
paragraphs.heading: Intraventricular Hemorrhage and Ventricular Dilatation

paragraphs.text: In around 15% of infants with GMH-IVH, a characteristic ipsilateral periventricular parenchymal hemorrhage is also seen, which is referred to as PVHI.
paragraphs.heading: Parenchymal Hemorrhage

paragraphs.text: This phenomenon was previously referred to as grade 4 hemorrhage by Papile et al.2 and thought to be an extension of an ipsilateral large IVH; however, the extension of blood into the parenchyma from the ventricle is now considered unlikely because the ventricular ependymal lining was shown to remain intact in most infants with PVHI. It is now clearly documented that a unilateral periventricular parenchymal lesion accompanying GMH-IVH is caused by hemorrhagic infarction because of periventricular venous stasis followed by congestion and ischemia.12 The incidence of PVHI increases with decreasing GA.5 PVHI is unilateral in 90% of the cases, associated with an ipsilateral grade 3 IVH in more than 80% of the cases, and is most commonly located in the parietal lobe.13
paragraphs.heading: Parenchymal Hemorrhage

paragraphs.text: Largest PVHI size is usually reached in the first postnatal week.13,14 In rare cases, an atypical presentation either in the fetal period or late neonatal onset is also possible. Testing for thrombophilia, especially factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene mutation, as well as collagen gene mutations including COL4A1 and COL4A2 is recommended in these infants.15
paragraphs.heading: Parenchymal Hemorrhage

paragraphs.text: Bassan et al.14 developed a scoring system using cUS by assigning each subject a severity score based on the extent of echogenicity, laterality (unilateral or bilateral), and the presence or absence of a midline shift. The investigators found that higher severity scores were significantly associated with mortality and motor disability. Dudink et al.16 sought to refine the PVHI patterns by relating subtypes to affected veins and evaluated the effects of these anatomic subtypes on the outcome and found that all infants with complete terminal vein infarction developed hemiplegia. The appearance of the PVHI has also changed since the early 1990s. It is possible that advances in perinatal and neonatal care over the past decades are associated with the change in the appearance of the unilateral parenchymal hemorrhage seen over time.13 Instead of a unilateral globular lesion merging with the ventricle and evolving into a single porencephalic cyst in the chronic phase, a smaller, triangular parenchymal lesion can be seen, with the tip of the triangle toward the lateral ventricle. There may be partial or even no communication of the parenchymal hemorrhage with the lateral ventricle. Several weeks later, these lesions evolve into small cystic lesions that are separate from or partially in communication with the lateral ventricle (Figs. 55.2 and 55.3).13 These small cystic lesions not communicating with the ventricle are sometimes mistakenly classified as unilateral cystic periventricular leukomalacia; however, one should keep in mind that these are cystic transformations of PVHI.10
paragraphs.heading: Parenchymal Hemorrhage

paragraphs.text: The incidence of CBH in preterm infants varies widely, primarily because of differences in GA and various neuroimaging techniques used. Similar to GMH-IVH, the incidence of CBH increases with decreasing GA and is reported in up to 9% in very preterm infants less than 32 weeks in cUS studies using the mastoid fontanelle.17 However, MRI is more sensitive than cUS in detecting CBH, and the reported incidence is up to 19% using MRI.17 Gano et al.18 reported a considerably higher incidence of 37% in very preterm infants who were scanned with high-resolution 3T-MRI using the SWI sequence. Based on the size and extent, CBHs can be broadly divided into three categories: punctate CBHs (<4 mm), which are generally detected only on MRI; limited CBHs (>4 mm but <1/3 of the cerebellar hemisphere); and large CBHs (>1/3 of the cerebellar hemisphere).19 It is important to note that cUS through the mastoid window is more successful in making the diagnosis but is still inferior to MRI (Fig. 55.4).10 GMH-IVH has also been shown to be associated with a reduction in cerebellar volume. This is attributed to (1) direct toxicity of blood products, especially hemosiderin, negatively affecting the proliferation of the external granular layer of the cerebellum; and (2) crossed cerebellar diaschisis caused by the loss of cerebral cortical input in the context of supratentorial hemorrhagic brain injury.
paragraphs.heading: Cerebellar Hemorrhage and Dysmaturation

paragraphs.text: The pathogenesis of GMH-IVH is multifactorial, and the contributing factors can be better understood when reviewed under three major categories: vascular, intravascular, and extravascular factors.1 Vascular factors are those caused by insufficient capillary integrity because of being an immature vascular network with a simple endothelial lining
paragraphs.heading: Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: and a paucity of tight junction proteins. Recently, variant subependymal venous anatomy has also been shown to be a contributing factor.9 Intravascular factors are caused by either an increase in cerebral venous pressure in the context of prolonged labor, dystocia, respiratory distress, and head
paragraphs.heading: Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: positioning or a decrease in blood flow because of systemic hypotension or fluctuations in blood pressure in a pressurepassive circulation. Fluctuations in cerebral blood flow can also cause hemorrhagic injury and are generally caused by hypercarbia, rapid volume expansion, hypoglycemia, or a
paragraphs.heading: Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: rapid decline in hemoglobin. Finally, extravascular factors are a result of deficient extracellular and vascular matrix support such as pericytes.1
paragraphs.heading: Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: Prenatal, intrapartum, and postnatal factors contribute to the pathogenesis of GMH-IVH at different stages. Among them, male gender, the degree of prematurity, lack of antenatal steroids, clinical chorioamnionitis, delivery room resuscitation, prolonged mechanical ventilation, and requirement of inotropes were consistently shown to be associated with GMH-IVH. These will be discussed in detail below.
paragraphs.heading: Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: Histologic chorioamnionitis and clinical chorioamnionitis are two distinct entities. Histologic chorioamnionitis has been shown by some to increase the risk of GMH-IVH, but not by others.20 In a recent prospective multicenter cohort study, Bierstone et al.20 evaluated 350 very preterm infants less than 32 weeks’ gestation of whom 145 (41.4%) had histologic chorioamnionitis on placental pathologic examination. The authors found that histologic chorioamnionitis was not associated with GMH-IVH, nor was it associated with worse cognitive and motor outcomes assessed by the Bayley-III test at 18 to 24 months corrected. However, a multicenter study from the Canadian Neonatal Network21 showed that clinical chorioamnionitis is associated with an increased risk of early-onset neonatal sepsis (odds ratio [OR] 5.54; 95% confidence interval [CI] 2.87–10.69) and severe IVH (OR 1.62; 95% CI 1.17–2.24). The association remained significant even after adjusting for illness severity. In a population-based prospective cohort of 2085 singleton infants, adverse outcomes were found to be a function of the degree of prematurity and complications leading to preterm birth. Among these, fetal growth restriction did not lead to increased neonatal brain injury on cUS but was associated with increased mortality. Of note, pre-eclampsia has been associated with a reduced risk of GMH-IVH. The protective effect appears to be a result of enhanced in utero maturation of the fetus.
paragraphs.heading: Prenatal Factors

paragraphs.text: The administration of antenatal steroids has been consistently shown to be a protective factor against the development of GMH-IVH. The effect may be caused by a direct maturational effect on the developing brain, but other factors may also be involved, such as reduction in respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) and decreased need for inotropes. In line with the previous literature, a 2020 meta-analysis of 12 studies on 8475 preterm infants showed the probable association between antenatal corticosteroids and reduced risk of GMH-IVH (risk ratio [RR] 0.58; 95% CI 0.45–0.75).3
paragraphs.heading: Prenatal Factors

paragraphs.text: Data are controversial on the association between the mode of delivery and GMH-IVH. Prolonged labor rather than the vaginal birth itself has been hypothesized to be the major contributor to the development of GMH-IVH. A recent
paragraphs.heading: Intrapartum Factors

paragraphs.text: study by the German Neonatal Network studied 2203 preterm infants with a birth weight less than 1500 g and GA between 220/7 and 366/7 weeks. Infants were stratified into three categories according to the mode of delivery: (1) planned cesarean section (C/S, n = 1381), (2) vaginal delivery (n = 632), and (3) emergency C/S (n = 190). GMH-IVH was more common in the vaginal delivery (26.6%) and emergency C/S group (31.1%) as compared with planned C/S (17.2%), respectively. In the multivariable model, vaginal delivery (OR 1.7; 95% CI 1.3–2.2, P ≤ .001) and emergency cesarean section (OR 1.9; 95% CI 1.3–2.7, P ≤ .001) were independently associated with increased GMH-IVH risk. The authors concluded that elective C/S is associated with a reduced risk of GMH-IVH in preterm infants less than 30 weeks’ gestational when presenting with preterm labor.22 However, in a large cohort of 20,231 preterm infants less than 34 weeks, C/S was not found to be associated with a reduced risk of GMH-IVH after adjusting for confounding factors (adjusted OR 0.99; 95% CI 0.84–1.17).23
paragraphs.heading: Intrapartum Factors

paragraphs.text: Perinatal hypoxic-ischemic events, such as low Apgar scores, metabolic acidosis, use of bicarbonate, and significant delivery room resuscitation, have been associated with the development of GMH-IVH.8,24 A cohort study of preterm infants born with a birth weight of less than 1000 g and GA less than 30 weeks assessed 8685 infants of whom 1333 (15%) received resuscitation in the delivery room. Infants who received resuscitation had higher odds of grades 3 to 4 GMH-IVH (OR, 1.47; 95% CI 1.23–1.74).24
paragraphs.heading: Intrapartum Factors

paragraphs.text: There is an inverse correlation between hemoglobin concentration and cerebral blood flow in neonates, and this observation led to studies on the timing of cord clamping in the delivery room. Although several retrospective studies reported that delayed cord clamping (DCC) was associated with a reduction in GMH-IVH, a large randomized controlled trial by the Australian Placental Transfusion Study Collaborative Group25 did not show an association between DCC and a reduced risk of GMH-IVH. In this trial, investigators randomly assigned preterm infants less than 30 weeks of gestation to either immediate cord clamping (ICC) of the umbilical cord (≤10 seconds after delivery) or DCC (≥60 seconds after delivery). The primary composite outcome was death or major morbidity, defined as severe brain injury on postnatal cUS, severe retinopathy of prematurity, necrotizing enterocolitis, or late-onset sepsis by 36 weeks’ postmenstrual age. Of the 1566 infants who were randomized, there was no significant difference in the incidence of the primary outcome between infants assigned to DCC (37%) and those assigned to ICC (37.2%) (RR 1.00; 95% CI 0.88–1.13; P = .96). There were also no significant differences between the groups in rates of GMH- IVH or late cerebral abnormality on cUS. In a prematurely terminated randomized controlled trial, Katheria et al.26 compared umbilical cord milking (UCM) with DCC and found no significant difference in mortality; however, severe
paragraphs.heading: Intrapartum Factors

paragraphs.text: GMH-IVH was significantly higher in the UCM group than in the DCC group (8% vs. 3%, respectively; risk difference, 5%; 95% CI 1%–9%; P = .02). In the subgroup analysis, among infants born between 23 and 27 weeks’ gestation, severe GMH-IVH was significantly higher with UCM than with DCC (22% vs. 6%, respectively; risk difference 16%; 95% CI 6%–26%; P = .002). Recently, Jasani et al.27 conducted a network meta-analysis comparing different cord management strategies for preterm infants. The investigators assessed a total of 56 studies on 6852 preterm infants and showed that DCC was associated with lower odds of GMH-IVH (25 trials, 3316 participants; 17.8% vs. 15.4%; OR 0.73; 95% CI 0.54–0.97) compared with ICC. Of note, compared with ICC, UCM was also associated with lower odds of GMH-IVH (10 trials, 645 participants; 22.5% vs. 16.2%; OR 0.58; 95% CI 0.38–0.84). There was no significant difference between UCM and DCC for any outcome, and the investigators concluded that further studies directly comparing DCC and UCM are warranted.
paragraphs.heading: Intrapartum Factors

paragraphs.text: Infants who are born outside of a tertiary care center and require neonatal transport are more likely to develop GMH- IVH. A large US database of 67,596 preterm infants showed that the transport group had more GMH-IVH compared with the inborn group (27.4% vs. 13.4%; adjusted OR 1.75; 95% CI 1.64–1.86; P < .001). Severe GMH-IVH was also higher in the transport group compared with the inborn group (44.1% vs. 32.9%; adjusted OR 1.44; 95% CI 1.22–1.70, P = .001).28 A recent observational study by the Neonatal Research Network of Japan studied 15,842 very low birth weight preterm infants and showed a higher incidence of severe GMH-IVH (8.2% vs. 4.1%; OR 3.45; 95% CI 1.16–10.3) in outborn infants.29
paragraphs.heading: Intrapartum Factors

paragraphs.text: Also of note, there seems to be an association between being born at off-peak hours (12 am to 7 am) and neonatal morbidities. In a retrospective population-based cohort study on 47,617 very preterm infants, 9317 (19.6%) infants were born during off-peak hours. After adjusting for maternal, infant, and hospital characteristics, off-peak hour delivery was associated with increased odds of severe GMH-IVH among survivors (OR 1.39; 95% CI 1.23–1.57) and the composite outcomes of death or severe GMH-IVH (OR 1.16; 95% CI 1.07–1.25).30
paragraphs.heading: Intrapartum Factors

paragraphs.text: Respiratory disturbances, and RDS in particular, have been recognized as important risk factors in the development of GMH-IVH. This association is most likely not causal but owing to the complications that occur during mechanical ventilation, such as hypocarbia, hypercarbia, hypoxemia, acidosis, increased need for tracheal suctioning, and pneumothorax. These factors may result in fluctuations in cerebral blood flow and elevated central venous pressure. In a meta-analysis of 22 studies on 1065 preterm infants, there was moderate-quality evidence to show that volume
paragraphs.heading: Postnatal Factors

paragraphs.text: targeted ventilation (VTV) resulted in a reduction in the primary outcome of death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia at 36 weeks’ gestation and the secondary outcome of grade 3 or 4 GMH-IVH (RR 0.53; 95% CI 0.37–0.77; number needed to treat [NNT] 11; 95% CI 7–25) as well as the combined outcome of periventricular leukomalacia with or without grade 3 or 4 GMH-IVH (RR 0.47; 95% CI 0.27– 0.80; NNT 11; 95% CI 7–33).31 Also of note, delivering high tidal volumes (>6 mL/kg) during the positive pressure ventilation in the delivery room was shown to increase the rate of GMH-IVH and severe GMH-IVH in a prospective observational study.32
paragraphs.heading: Postnatal Factors

paragraphs.text: Although in some studies, an increased risk of severe GMH-IVH and periventricular leukomalacia was found with the use of high-frequency oscillatory ventilation when compared with conventional ventilation, a 2015 metaanalysis did not show significant differences between the groups. The authors concluded that it is highly likely that many factors, both related to the respiratory intervention itself as well as the individual patient characteristics, interact in complex ways.33 It seems reasonable to choose noninvasive ventilation and less-invasive intervention strategies over invasive mechanical ventilation whenever possible in preterm infants. Because of improvements in ventilatory techniques, including increased use of nasal continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), hypercarbia and severe acidosis have become less common. In a multicenter randomized controlled trial, 211 preterm infants between 23 and 27 weeks of gestation were randomly assigned to receive surfactant either via a thin endotracheal catheter during CPAP-assisted spontaneous breathing or after endotracheal intubation during mechanical ventilation. A significant reduction in severe GMH-IVH (10.3% vs. 22.1%; P = .02) was seen in infants receiving surfactant via a thin endotracheal catheter during CPAP.34
paragraphs.heading: Postnatal Factors

paragraphs.text: The immature brain is considered vulnerable to fluctuations in blood pressure owing to limitations in the autoregulation of cerebral blood flow. Impaired autoregulation renders the cerebral circulation “pressure-passive” and, hence, unprotected from any wide swings in blood pressure. Abrupt increases, decreases, and fluctuations in cerebral blood flow, as well as increases in cerebral venous pressure, result in injury to the vulnerable germinal matrix capillaries. This applies especially to sick preterm infants. Earlier studies using near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) showed that NIRS can be used at the bedside to identify premature infants with impaired cerebrovascular autoregulation, that this impairment is relatively common in such infants, and that the presence of this impairment is associated with a high likelihood of occurrence of severe GMH-IVH. Alderliesten et al.35 continuously monitored 30 very preterm infants less than 32 weeks’ gestation for the first 72 hours after birth with NIRS in a case-control study. The authors showed cerebral hyperperfusion in infants with severe GMH-IVH alongside impaired autoregulation and
paragraphs.heading: Postnatal Factors

paragraphs.text: concluded that continuous assessment of regional cerebral oxygenation and arterial blood pressure may identify preterm infants at risk for GMH-IVH and prompt consideration of preventive measures. However, contradicting results were reported by Noori et al.36 in a prospective observational study of 22 extremely preterm infants born less than 27 weeks of gestation. Using targeted echocardiography and NIRS, the investigators found that patients with GMH-IVH tended to have reduced left ventricular output, lower left ventricle stroke volume, cerebral regional oxygen saturation, and higher cerebral fractional oxygen extraction during the first 12 hours of the study. By 28 hours, these variables were similar in infants with or without GMH- IVH, and the middle cerebral artery mean flow velocity was higher in the GMH-IVH group. Cardiac function and cerebral blood flow remained stable in infants who did not develop GMH-IVH within the first 3 postnatal days. The authors concluded that in very preterm infants developing GMH-IVH, lower systemic perfusion and cerebral blood flow followed by an increase in these variables precede the development of GMH-IVH. Recently, the early NIRS multicenter prospective study recruited very preterm infants with a birth weight of less than 1250 g from six tertiary neonatal intensive care units in the United States. Mean arterial blood pressure and cerebral oxygen saturation were continuously monitored until 96 hours of age. Of 103 infants with a mean GA of 26 weeks, infants with adverse outcomes had a lower mean cerebral tissue oxygenation. Infants with adverse outcomes were also more likely to have findings of impaired cerebral autoregulation. The authors concluded that early NIRS monitoring may detect periods of lower cerebral oxygenation and altered cerebral autoregulation, identifying preterm infants at risk for mortality or hemorrhagic injury.37
paragraphs.heading: Postnatal Factors

paragraphs.text: There is controversy over whether mutations of hemostatic genes predispose preterm infants to GMH-IVH. The factor V Leiden mutation, which renders factor V resistant to cleavage by activated protein C, and the prothrombin G20210A mutation, which was found to be associated with raised plasma concentrations of prothrombin, were suggested to play a role in the development of GMH-IVH. The Gene Targets for Intraventricular Hemorrhage Study Group investigated 224 preterm infants in a prospective study and was unable to confirm previously reported associations of hemostasis gene variants and development of severe IVH (grades 3 and 4 according to Papile et al.2) except for an increased prevalence for the methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase 1298A>C variant.38
paragraphs.heading: Genetic Factors

paragraphs.text: Antenatal porencephaly was reported to be associated with a mutation in the collagen gene (COL4A1) that encodes basement membrane protein in a case series.39 Collagen mutations can have a wide range of presentations, including familial porencephaly, hemorrhagic stroke, IVH with parenchymal involvement, as well as extensive supratentorial lesions in combination with cerebellar injury. This
paragraphs.heading: Genetic Factors

paragraphs.text: diagnosis can be made antenatally and should be considered in the presence of a supratentorial parenchymal hemorrhage associated with a CBH. It is also important to remember that an atypical presentation of PVHI in preterm infants tends to occur more often in the presence of thrombophilia, and further testing, especially for factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene mutations, is recommended in these infants.15
paragraphs.heading: Genetic Factors

paragraphs.text: The majority of GMH-IVH in preterm infants occurs within the first 3 days of postnatal life. Of those, almost half occur within the first 6 hours and approximately two-thirds within the first 24 hours. By postnatal 7 days, around 95% of IVH will have occurred, with only a small percentage appearing beyond day 7.1 Three clinical syndromes can be recognized in preterm infants: the first is known as catastrophic deterioration and is characterized by a sudden deterioration in the infant’s clinical state, such as an increase in oxygen requirement or ventilatory settings, deterioration in hemodynamic status, decline in blood pressure, and/or acidosis. More often, however, a drop in hematocrit is seen without a clear change in the infant’s condition. The saltatory syndrome is more common and gradual in onset, presenting with a change in spontaneous general movements. The third and most frequent presentation is the silent or asymptomatic type, which is detected by routine cUS screening without any obvious clinical signs.1
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: With cUS readily available in modern neonatal units, most high-risk preterm infants have a routine screening soon after admission or within the first few days after birth. In 1978 Papile et al.2 described the neuroimaging findings of 46 very low birth weight infants on CT scans and described four separate grades of hemorrhage as follows: grade 1—subependymal hemorrhage; grade 2—IVH without ventricular dilatation; grade 3—IVH with ventricular dilatation; and grade 4—IVH with parenchymal hemorrhage. This initial classification has been modified by Volpe using cUS scans into three grades and includes a separate notation for the presence of periventricular hemorrhagic infarction (PVHI). In this classification, grade 1 indicates hemorrhage confined to the germinal matrix or minimal intraventricular extension occupying less than 10% of the ventricular area on the parasagittal view, grade 2 indicates IVH occupying 10% to 50% of the ventricular area, and grade 3 represents IVH in greater than 50% of the ventricular area, usually associated with acute ventricular dilatation.1 In a recent consensus article by Mohammad et al.10 these classification systems were revisited with an aim to achieve homogeneity between different disciplines. In this consensus viewpoint, grade 1 represents hemorrhage confined to the germinal matrix region; in grade 2, hemorrhage spills over into the ventricle without causing acute ventricular distension, whereas in grade 3, acute ventricular distension accompanies IVH with an anterior horn width (AHW) measurement of greater than 6 mm. Similar to the Volpe classification, PVHI was defined as
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: a separate notation in this consensus article (Table 55.1). This type of lesion is classically triangular or fan-shaped, with the apex at the outer border of the lateral ventricle, and in some cases the lesion is globular. The globular type of lesion evolves over 2 to 3 weeks into a porencephalic cyst (Fig. 55.5).
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: cUS is a noninvasive bedside technique that uses the anterior fontanelle and, increasingly, also the posterior, mastoid, and temporal fontanelle as acoustic windows. The posterior fontanelle improves the detection of small IVHs that accumulate in the posterior horn of the lateral ventricle. The mastoid window allows detection of CBHs with a diameter of greater than 4 mm.17 Good correlations of sonographic
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: GMH-IVH signs with autopsy findings have been reported for the more severe hemorrhages. With the increased use of MRI, it has become apparent that GMHs at sites other than at the level of the caudate nucleus, such as the roof of the temporal horn, are not always identified using cUS. With cUS, it is also not always possible to be certain about the presence or absence of a small associated IVH. Immediate access to cUS in contrast to MRI, and the fact that the examination can be repeated as often as indicated, still makes cUS the first method of choice.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: The timing of the examination depends on the questions raised. An examination within hours after delivery helps in timing the lesion as antenatal or postnatal. A single scan at the end of the first week shows 95% of all hemorrhages as well as their maximum extent. Further serial cUS examinations are required in infants with any degree of hemorrhage to detect the occurrence of posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation (PHVD), which occurs in around a quarter of infants, and the occurrence of associated white matter injury.1 Several groups recommended different schedules for the performance of cUS scans in preterm infants. In 2020, the American Academy of Pediatrics published a statement on routine neuroimaging of the preterm brain and recommended cUS screening of all preterm infants less than 30 weeks with an initial scan within the first 7 days and repeat scans at 4 to 6 weeks of life and around term or discharge from the hospital.40 However, literature on neuroimaging of the preterm brain shows that these infrequent screening protocols may limit the opportunities for the initiation of neurologic interventions. To address this issue, a joint group of experts published a review article emphasizing more frequent serial cUS to improve the timely recognition of GMH-IVH and associated complications. This review recommends more frequent serial cUS, especially in the most immature infants less than 28 weeks’ gestation, to allow full elucidation of the nature and timing of brain injury and subsequent complications.6 Of note, the authors also recommend obtaining a routine TEA-MRI) in preterm infants
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: born less than 28 weeks’ gestation and in infants between 28 and 32 weeks’ gestation presenting with significant clinical risk factors and ultrasonographic findings. The details of the proposed cUS schedule are presented in Table 55.2.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Clinical management of neonates who present with GMH- IVH is mainly supportive, and the mainstay of the treatment is the preservation of cerebral perfusion, early detection of complications, and minimization of further brain injury.1 Minimal handling, prevention of fluctuations in blood pressure and CO2 levels, prevention of asynchrony between the infant and the ventilator, and optimization of any coagulopathy may be warranted in an attempt to prevent extension of the initial hemorrhage. A blood transfusion may be needed in case of a large GMH-IVH associated with a significant drop in hemoglobin. Continuous electroencephalographic monitoring, mostly done with amplitude-integrated electroencephalography, may be helpful in the detection of electrographic only seizures. The use of fibrinolytic therapy in an attempt to resolve the initial clot has been disappointing and can even result in rebleeding.41
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: Serial cUS scans are indicated to diagnose and monitor PHVD, the most common complication of GMH-IVH, in a timely manner.6 Ventricular dilatation seen on cUS usually precedes the development of clinical symptoms by several weeks. The clinical signs are a bulging fontanelle, split sutures, and a rapid increase in head circumference greater than 2 cm per week. The sunsetting phenomenon of the eyes is a late finding.1,42 PHVD is transient in approximately half of the infants and is persistent or rapidly progressive in the remaining cases. Once it is recognized that the ventricles have begun to enlarge, the baseline size should be measured using cUS. The most widely adopted measurement is that
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: described by Levene and Starte.43 This “ventricular index” (VI) is the longest horizontal distance between the midline and the lateral border of the ventricle measured in a coronal view in the plane of the third ventricle. Another useful measurement is the depth of the frontal horn, or in other words the longest oblique distance, taken just in front of the thalamic notch, the so-called AHW, with a height of greater than 3 mm being used to define ventriculomegaly and one greater than 6 mm representing two standard deviations (SD) above the normal. Measuring the occipital horn, the so-called thalamo-occipital distance (TOD), in a sagittal plane can also be useful because there can be a discrepancy between the anterior and posterior horn widths (see Fig. 55.1). Any measurement greater than 24 mm also suggests severe PHVD.42 Levene’s VI graph has a GA range of 27 to 40 weeks. Because extremely preterm infants less than 27 weeks’ gestation are commonly admitted to neonatal intensive care units today, new reference values for the VI, AHW, and TOD were studied and published in a prospective cohort study of 625 neonates with a median GA of 33.4 weeks (range, 24.7–42.6 weeks).44 These new reference curves are also implemented on intervention charts described by El-Dib et al. (Fig. 55.6).42 Alternative measures are the frontal and occipital horn ratio (FOHR) and the frontal and temporal horn ratio (FTHR), both of which show a strong correlation with ventricular volumes.45
paragraphs.heading: Management

In the long term, pressureinduced destruction of neuronal tissue can lead to motor and cognitive impairments.8 Short-term adverse effects on the developing brain have been confirmed using somatosensory and visual evoked potentials, Doppler estimates of cerebral blood flow velocity, and NIRS.46 In a study of nine infants with PHVD, NIRS was used, and a significant increase in cerebral blood flow was measured (15.6%) following a ventricular tap, but without a corresponding change in cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (1.02 ± 0.41 mL O2/100 g/min).46 CSF levels of IL-8, interferon (IFN)-γ, and soluble Fas were noted to be raised in infants with PHVD and especially so in those with associated white matter injury.47 Other CSF biomarkers were found to be increased in infants with PHVD, including amyloid precursor protein (APP), soluble APP-α, and L1 cell adhesion molecule.48

paragraphs.text: Accumulating evidence shows that early drainage of CSF alters the natural history and outcome of PHVD. Brouwer et al.49 evaluated the differential impact of GMH-IVH and PHVD on the brain and CSF volumes and diffusion variables in preterm-born infants at TEA. The majority of the infants in this cohort were treated with early interventions. The authors showed that PHVD was independently associated with volumes of deep gray matter (β −1.4 cc; 95% CI −2.3 to −0.5), cerebellum (β −2.7 cc; 95% CI −3.8 to −1.6), ventricles (β +12.7 cc; 95% CI 7.9–17.4), and extracerebral CSF (β −11.2 cc; 95% CI −19.2 to −3.3), and with apparent diffusion constant (ADC) values in occipital, parietooccipital, and parietal white matter (β +0.066 to 0.119 × 10−3 mm2/s) on TEA-MRI (P < .05). No associations were found between GMH-IVH grades 2 and 3 and brain and CSF volumes or ADC values. In summary, PHVD was negatively related to deep gray matter and cerebellar volumes and positively to white matter ADC values on TEA-MRI, despite early intervention for PHVD in the majority of the infants. A recent observational study from Canada and the Netherlands showed results favoring earlier intervention for PHVD. In this study, outcomes were compared at 18 to 24 months between infants with and without intervention in preterm infants undergoing either an early approach in Dutch centers or a late approach in the Canadian center. It is important to note that the common practice in the Dutch centers was to intervene early based on the cUS measurements of the ventricles, whereas intervention decisions were based on the clinical findings of PHVD rather than the cUS measurements in the Canadian center. The study showed that infants undergoing earlier intervention for progressive PHVD, even when eventually requiring a ventriculoperitoneal shunt (VPS), had cognitive and motor outcomes similar to those without intervention, all being within the normal range. In contrast, later intervention was associated with an increased risk of adverse outcomes.50

paragraphs.text: The initial phase I trial of the drainage, irrigation, and fibrinolytic therapy (DRIFT) study showed a reduced need for VPS insertion of 26% compared with around 60% in previous multicenter studies. The authors concluded that reducing pressure, free iron, and pro-inflammatory and
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 55.6 A practical clinical tool to monitor commonly used ventricular measures and proposed risk stratification and management of infants with

paragraphs.text: profibrotic cytokines may reduce periventricular brain damage and hydrocephalus.51 A subsequent randomized controlled trial randomly assigned 70 preterm infants with progressive PHVD who had GAs of 24 to 34 weeks to either (1) DRIFT or (2) tapping of CSF by the ventricular reservoir to control excessive expansion and signs of pressure (standard treatment). The composite outcome of death and VPS was not significantly different (44% vs. 50%, respectively). Of note, 12 (35%) of 34 infants who received DRIFT had secondary IVH compared with 3 (8%) of 36 in the standard group. Secondary IVH was associated with an increased risk for subsequent VPS surgery and more blood transfusions.52 However, when assessed at 2 years corrected age in a follow-up study, of 39 infants assigned to DRIFT, 21 (54%) died or were severely disabled versus 27 of 38 (71%) in the standard group (adjusted OR 0.25; 95% CI 0.08–0.82). Among the survivors, 11 of 35 (31%) in the DRIFT group had severe cognitive disability versus 19 of 32 (59%) in the standard group (adjusted OR 0.17; 95% CI 0.05–0.57). The authors concluded that despite an increase in secondary IVH, DRIFT reduced severe cognitive disability in survivors and overall death or severe disability.53 Recently, the DRIFT investigators further assessed if the cognitive advantage of DRIFT seen at 2 years persisted until 10 years of age. Among survivors, 28 in the DRIFT group and 24 in the standard treatment group were assessed, and the mean cognitive score was 69.3 ± 30.1 in the DRIFT group and 53.7 ± 35.7 in the standard treatment group (unadjusted P = .1; adjusted P = .01, after adjustment for the prespecified variables of gender, birth weight, and IVH grade). Survival without severe cognitive disability was 66% in the DRIFT group and 35% in the standard treatment group (unadjusted P = .019; adjusted P = .003).54 In summary, DRIFT was the first intervention for PHVD to objectively demonstrate sustained cognitive improvement in preterm infants with PHVD.

paragraphs.text: Although LPs have not been shown to be effective in a meta-analysis to prevent PHVD, the treatment of PHVD interventions typically starts with LPs to decompress the ventricles as the initial step. It has been hypothesized that the physical removal of CSF that contains blood components and protein might mitigate the neuroinflammatory and neurotoxic reactions, decrease deposition of extracellular matrix proteins, and re-establish normal CSF drainage.55 Several retrospective studies in the past two decades have shown the various beneficial effects of intervening earlier based on cUS measurements.50 The ELVIS (Early versus Late Ventricular Intervention Study) trial56 was a multicenter study to address when and how best to intervene in preterm infants with progressive PHVD. In this prospective randomized controlled trial, a total of 126 preterm infants of less than 34 weeks’ GA with progressive PHVD were included between 2006 and 2016. Infants were eligible when they had a GMH-IVH grade 3, with or without PVHI. Recruited infants were randomly allocated to either low-threshold (LT) group (intervention when an increase in VI above the 97th percentile line showing an
paragraphs.heading: • Fig. 55.6 A practical clinical tool to monitor commonly used ventricular measures and proposed risk stratification and management of infants with

paragraphs.text: increase toward the 97th percentile + 4 mm line, but before crossing the 97th percentile + 4 mm line; and an increase in AHW >6 mm and toward 10 mm and/or TOD >25 mm), or high-threshold (HT) group (intervention when the VI crossed the 97th percentile + 4 mm line and the AHW was >10 mm). Interventions started with lumbar punctures (LP) with a maximum number of 3, and if necessary, this was followed by tapping from a ventricular reservoir, aiming for VI less than 97th percentile line in both study arms within the next 7 to 10 days. Once or twice daily, 10 mL/kg were removed based on cUS measurements. Reservoir taps were continued until ventricular stabilization was documented. An infant with an ongoing requirement of reservoir taps when weight reached 2000 to 2500 g was challenged, and when ongoing punctures were needed, a VPS was inserted because of the requirement of permanent CSF diversion.

paragraphs.text: The two noteworthy aspects of the ELVIS trial were that in both arms, interventions were solely based on cUS criteria and commenced while the infants were asymptomatic, and that the aim was to effectively reduce the ventricular size to less than 97th percentile in both study arms, whereas the prior studies focused on preventing further ventricular dilatation. Although no further reduction in the need for a VPS in the LT group was found, the need for VPS placement in both study arms was the lowest reported in the literature (19% and 23% in the LT and HT groups, respectively). In the LT group, the number of infants who received temporizing interventions with LPs or ventricular reservoirs was significantly higher than in the HT group. In a subsequent nested substudy, brain injury scores and brain volumes were compared between the groups on TEA-MRIs.57 Among the survivors, MRIs were obtained in 88 infants with an equal number of infants in each study arm. The most significant finding was the smaller ventricular volumes in the LT group. FOHR was lower in the LT group, and infants in the LT arm had lower global brain abnormality scores. After excluding infants with PVHI, the combination of the white matter and gray matter volumes was higher in the LT group, which shows the negative effect of enlarged ventricles on further brain injury. Infants in the HT group also more commonly demonstrated a delay in myelination and more often had thinning of the corpus callosum. Neurodevelopmental outcomes of the ELVIS trial at 2 years corrected age were also recently published.58 In 92% of the surviving infants, outcomes were assessed, and the composite adverse outcome was defined as death, CP, or cognitive/ motor score less than −2 SD on the Bayley Scales of Infant Development, second edition, or the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, third edition. Although there was no difference between the LT (35%) and HT (51%) groups with respect to the composite outcome, in the post hoc analysis the LT intervention was associated with a decreased risk of an adverse outcome after correcting for GA, the severity of GMH-IVH, and CBH (adjusted OR 0.24; 95% CI 0.07–0.87; P = .03). These observations support the hypothesis that draining CSF earlier based on

paragraphs.text: LPs are followed by temporizing neurosurgical interventions if stabilization or regression of ventricular size does not occur. The American Academy of Neurological Surgeons reported that both a ventricular reservoir and ventriculosubgaleal shunt are acceptable options with similar complication rates. A recent meta-analysis by Lai et al.59 showed that a ventricular access device was the most commonly used temporizing neurosurgical intervention. The pooled rate for conversion to VPS was 60.5% (95% CI 54.9–65.8), moderate-severe NDI 34.8% (95% CI 27.4–42.9), infection 8.2% (95% CI 6.7–10.1), revision 14.6% (95% CI 10.4–20.1), and death 12.9% (95% CI 10.2–16.4). The investigators also found that older age at temporizing neurosurgical procedures was a predictor of conversion to VPS (P < .001) and moderate to severe NDI (P < .01).

paragraphs.text: Neuroendoscopic lavage (NEL) is a surgical intervention that washes away hemorrhagic intraventricular CSF and removes remnants of blood clots. Irrigation is continued until anatomic landmarks are clearly visualized. This method seems to be more effective than intermittent punctures from a VAD to remove the hemorrhagic CSF.60 However, it is an invasive technique and requires considerable expertise. In a preliminary study, Park et al.61 performed a combination of ventricular drainage with intermittent administration of urokinase to actively dissolve blood clots via a single catheter (6000 IU/mL) for 14 days. Every day, 20 to 25 mL of hemorrhagic CSF was drained. The investigators started this intervention within 3 weeks of GMH-IVH onset and were able to show that this therapy was associated with fewer VPS placements (14%) and better neurodevelopmental outcomes, with no secondary hemorrhages following the procedure.

paragraphs.text: In 2020, an international group of PHVD researchers published a medical progress article on the effective management of PHVD. The authors stated that combining the evidence from preclinical data showing the ability of early interventions to reverse brain injury, and from clinical data demonstrating improved neurodevelopmental outcomes in centers and trials using ventricular measurements as criteria for interventions, it appears prudent to adopt this evidence into clinical practice.42 Waiting for clinical signs can lead to late intervention and the potential for further brain injury. The investigators developed a practical tool to define risk zones based on the reference charts by Brouwer et al.44 to help the clinician plot ventricular measurements over time to assess risk progress. In this tool, the low-risk infants should be monitored closely and assessed by cUS at least twice weekly until the ventricles are stable for 2 weeks and then every 1 to 2 weeks until 34 weeks’ postmenstrual age. Infants in the moderate-risk group benefit from neurosurgical consultation and 2 to 3 LPs, aiming for the removal of 10 mL/kg of CSF. LPs can be started as soon as infants meet the criteria for measurements of ventricular size. cUS should be performed before and, preferably, also following the LP to assess the effect. Infants who reach the high-risk group

paragraphs.text: may also benefit from 2 to 3 LPs done acutely, while actively planning potential neurosurgical interventions. Temporizing neurosurgical interventions include ventricular reservoir or ventricular subgaleal shunt (likely after the infant’s weight is >700 g) based on center preference. Interventions might also include a VPS, based on such factors as center preferences, age, weight, clinical condition, CSF protein, and red cell count. The authors also recommended a TEA-MRI in all risk groups to better assess the extent of the injury and for better prognostication.
