title: Respiratory Distress Syndrome in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: 65 Respiratory Distress Syndrome in the Neonate
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Enormous strides have been made in understanding the pathophysiology of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) and the role of surfactant in its cause and treatment (see Chapter 63). Nevertheless, RDS, formerly referred to as hyaline membrane disease, remains a dominant clinical problem among preterm neonates despite the introduction of pharmacologic acceleration of pulmonary maturity using antenatal corticosteroids and the development of surfactant replacement therapy in the 1990s.1,2 The incidence of complications in the survivors of RDS remains significant and continues to be differentially represented between infants of varying ancestries.3,4 These include intracranial hemorrhage, late-onset sepsis, necrotizing enterocolitis, severe retinopathy of prematurity, and bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD). It is often impossible to determine whether these disorders may result as the sequelae of RDS, its treatment, or the underlying prematurity. In this section, the clinical features and evaluation of infants with RDS are discussed, and therapeutic approaches other than assisted ventilation (see Chapter 66) are outlined. Other recommendations and details can be found in the recent consensus guidelines for RDS.5,5a
paragraphs.heading: MEGAN LAGOSKI, AARON HAMVAS, AND JENNIFER A. WAMBACH

paragraphs.text: RDS is one of the most common causes of morbidity and mortality in preterm neonates, although lack of a precise definition among infants with very low birth weight necessitates cautious interpretation of statistics regarding incidence, mortality, and outcome.6,7 The diagnosis can be established pathologically or by biochemical documentation of surfactant deficiency; nonetheless, most series refer only to a combination of clinical and radiographic features. Without biochemical evidence of surfactant deficiency, it is difficult to clinically diagnose RDS in infants with extremely low birth weight. The term respiratory insufficiency of prematurity had been used in some centers for infants who require oxygen and ventilator support in the absence of typical radiographic evidence of RDS. The term
paragraphs.heading: Incidence

paragraphs.text: respiratory instability of prematurity has been proposed to describe very low birth weight infants who require some respiratory support but may have additional contributing factors such as inconsistent central respiratory drive or poor inspiratory effort.6
paragraphs.heading: Incidence

paragraphs.text: RDS occurs throughout the world and has a slight male predominance.8 The greatest risk factors appear to be early gestational age and low birth weight; however, European descent, late preterm delivery (35–36 weeks), or elective delivery in the absence of labor are also prominent risk factors.8,9 Given the associated adverse respiratory outcomes of late preterm and early term births, initiatives to delay elective deliveries until 39 weeks’ gestation have been successful in reducing pulmonary and nonpulmonary morbidity in these infants.10 Infants born to mothers with diabetes also have an increased risk for RDS.11
paragraphs.heading: Incidence

paragraphs.text: The incidence of RDS is inversely proportional to gestational age: nearly all infants born at 22 to 24 weeks’ gestation have RDS, decreasing to approximately 25% in infants with birth weights between 1251 and 1500 g.12,13 Even infants of 34 weeks’ gestation and greater, especially males of European descent, have a discernible risk of RDS that decreases from ∼10% at 34 weeks to less than 1% at 37 weeks (Fig. 65.1).8
paragraphs.heading: Incidence

paragraphs.text: The lungs of infants who succumb from RDS have a characteristic uniformly ruddy and airless appearance, macroscopically resembling hepatic tissue. On microscopic examination, the striking feature is diffuse atelectasis such that only a few widely dilated alveoli are readily distinguishable (Fig. 65.2). An eosinophilic membrane lines the visible airspaces that usually constitute terminal bronchioles and alveolar ducts. This characteristic membrane (from which the term hyaline membrane disease is derived) consists of a fibrinous matrix of materials derived from the blood and contains cellular debris derived from injured epithelium. The recovery phase is characterized by
paragraphs.heading: Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: regeneration of alveolar cells, including the type II cells, with a resultant increase in surfactant activity. The development of RDS begins with impaired or delayed surfactant synthesis and secretion followed by a series of events that may progressively increase the severity of the disease for several days in the absence of exogenous surfactant
paragraphs.heading: Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: replacement (Fig. 65.3). Surfactant synthesis is a dynamic process that depends on factors such as pH, temperature, and perfusion and may be compromised by cold stress, hypovolemia, hypoxemia, and acidosis. Other unfavorable factors, such as exposure to high inspired oxygen concentration and the effects of volutrauma or atelectrauma from assisted ventilation, can trigger the release of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines and further damage the alveolar epithelial lining, resulting in reduced surfactant synthesis and function. The leakage of proteins such as fibrin in the intra-alveolar space further aggravates surfactant deficiency by promoting surfactant inactivation. Deficiency of surfactant and the accompanying decrease in lung compliance lead to alveolar hypoventilation and ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) imbalance. Severe hypoxemia and systemic hypoperfusion result in decreased oxygen delivery with subsequent lactic acidosis secondary to anaerobic metabolism. Hypoxemia and acidosis also result in pulmonary hypoperfusion secondary to pulmonary vasoconstriction, and the result is a further aggravation of hypoxemia because of right-to-left shunting at the level of the ductus arteriosus, the foramen ovale, and within the lung itself.
paragraphs.heading: Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: The relative roles of surfactant deficiency and pulmonary hypoperfusion in the overall clinical picture of RDS vary somewhat with each patient. The natural history of RDS
paragraphs.heading: Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: is now almost invariably altered by a combination of antenatal corticosteroid administration, exogenous surfactant therapy, assisted ventilation, and in some cases, intrauterine inflammation.
paragraphs.heading: Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: A genetic contribution to the risk of RDS has been suggested in twin studies where the concordance for RDS in monozygotic twins is greater than that for dizygotic twins and with isolated reports of recurrence in families.14–16 With the application of molecular techniques, the contribution of genetic variations (single nucleotide variants, pathogenic variants) to the pathogenesis of respiratory disorders in newborns is emerging.17,18
paragraphs.heading: Heritability of Respiratory Distress Syndrome

paragraphs.text: Pathogenic variants in genes encoding surfactant protein-B (SP-B, SFTPB), surfactant protein-C (SP-C, SFTPC), the ATP binding cassette subfamily A, member 3 (ABCA3, ABCA3), and the thyroid transcription factor (TTF-1, NKX2-1) represent rare monogenic causes of RDS.19–22 Inherited SP-B deficiency is a recessive disorder that presents as severe respiratory failure in the immediate newborn period and is unresponsive to standard neonatal intensive care interventions. With a disease frequency of
paragraphs.heading: Heritability of Respiratory Distress Syndrome

paragraphs.text: approximately 1 per 1 to 5 million live births, the absence of SP-B, the presence of incompletely processed proSP-C, and a generalized disruption of surfactant metabolism cause surfactant dysfunction and the clinical syndrome. Dominantly expressed pathogenic variants in SFTPC are present in significantly less than 0.1% of the population (gnomAD [gnomad.broadinstitute.org; accessed May 2022]) and typically result in interstitial lung disease in infants older than 1 month of age, although an “RDS-like” neonatal presentation has been described.18,23,24 The accumulation of misfolded proSP-C within cellular secretory pathways results in activation of cell stress responses, apoptosis, perturbed proteostasis and autophagy, and impaired surfactant function.25,26 Biallelic (recessive) pathogenic variants in ABCA3 result in progressive neonatal respiratory failure or chronic respiratory insufficiency and interstitial lung disease in infants older than 1 month of age and children.22,27 While most ABCA3 variants are private (unique to individuals and families), loss-of-function variants and the most common pathogenic variant p.E292V are present in ∼0.5% of individuals (gnomAD) suggesting a disease incidence of ∼1 in 90,000 births, although this is likely an underestimate. Accumulating experience suggests that ABCA3 deficiency is the most common of these disorders of surfactant homeostasis. Data from humans and mice suggest that ABCA3 mediates surfactant phospholipid transport
paragraphs.heading: Heritability of Respiratory Distress Syndrome

paragraphs.text: (primarily phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylglycerol) into lamellar bodies, and thus dysfunction of phospholipid transport into the lamellar body leads to reduced surfactant function.28–30 Dominantly expressed pathogenic variants in NKX2-1 were first identified in the context of benign hereditary chorea, but since then, they have also been recognized in lethal and nonlethal neonatal RDS as well as interstitial lung disease in older children.19,31,32 A triad of neurologic disease, characterized by hypotonia, developmental delay and movement disorders, congenital hypothyroidism, and RDS has been termed the brain-thyroid-lung syndrome, but any single organ presentation or combination thereof may be the initial and only manifestation of the syndrome. Pathogenic variants in NKX2-1 are rare, and the frequency of disease is unknown. Disruption in structural lung development and/or decreased expression of surfactant-associated genes are the postulated mechanisms of disease.
paragraphs.heading: Heritability of Respiratory Distress Syndrome

paragraphs.text: Large-scale cohort-based resequencing efforts have demonstrated an over-representation of heterozygous (monoallelic), predicted deleterious variants in ABCA3 in newborns 34 weeks and greater with RDS, suggesting that these variants are modifiers for the risk or severity of respiratory disease in developmentally susceptible newborns.17,18,24,33 These efforts have not identified an unequivocal contribution of rare or common variants in the surfactant protein-B or -C genes to RDS in newborns, suggesting that if these genes play a role in RDS, it is likely to be through interactions with variants in other lung-associated genes. Exome and genome sequencing are increasingly being used in the neonatal intensive care unit and will yield additional insights into candidate genes that not only account for the heritability of RDS but provide insight into systemic disorders with prominent respiratory manifestations.34–38
paragraphs.heading: Heritability of Respiratory Distress Syndrome

paragraphs.text: In the early 1970s, Liggins, while studying the effects of steroids on premature labor in lambs, noticed the lack of RDS and increased survival in preterm animals prenatally exposed to steroids. The effects of various catecholamines as well as aminophylline and thyroid hormone have been studied; however, the most successful method to induce fetal lung maturation is prenatal corticosteroid administration (see Chapter 63).39
paragraphs.heading: Prevention: Pharmacologic Acceleration of Pulmonary Maturation

paragraphs.text: If premature delivery of an infant appears probable or necessary, lung maturity can be hastened pharmacologically. Accelerated lung maturation occurs with physiologic stress levels of corticosteroids via receptor-mediated induction of specific developmentally regulated proteins, including those associated with surfactant synthesis. Steroids, when administered to the mother at least 24 to 48 hours before delivery, decrease the incidence and severity of RDS.40 Corticosteroids appear to be most effective before 34 weeks’ gestation and when administered at least 24 hours and no longer than 7 days before delivery. Because corticosteroid therapy for
paragraphs.heading: Prevention: Pharmacologic Acceleration of Pulmonary Maturation

paragraphs.text: less than 24 hours is still associated with significant reductions in neonatal mortality, RDS, and intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), without increasing the risk of infection to the mother or fetus, antenatal steroids should always be considered unless immediate delivery is anticipated.41 Data regarding the risks and benefits of antenatal corticosteroid administration for late preterm infants born at 34 to 36 weeks’ gestation are more equivocal. The clear short-term benefits of a reduction in respiratory complications may be outweighed by more uncertain impacts on longer-term neurodevelopmental outcomes, but further data are required to come to a more certain conclusion.42–44
paragraphs.heading: Prevention: Pharmacologic Acceleration of Pulmonary Maturation

paragraphs.text: Less clear are the effects of repeated courses of antenatal corticosteroids on the short- and long-term outcomes of preterm infants. Early retrospective studies suggested decreased fetal growth and adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes, but subsequent analyses have suggested short-term benefits without long-term harm on childhood outcomes.45 Further, the use of a rescue course of corticosteroids in the setting of premature rupture of membranes remains controversial.41,46
paragraphs.heading: Prevention: Pharmacologic Acceleration of Pulmonary Maturation

paragraphs.text: Although preterm infants as early as 23 weeks’ estimated gestation may benefit from antenatal corticosteroid exposure, their use before 23 weeks’ gestation also remains controversial. Regardless, the topic of prenatal corticosteroids is an important component of the joint neonatal-obstetrical counseling and approach to these anticipated early gestation deliveries.47–49
paragraphs.heading: Prevention: Pharmacologic Acceleration of Pulmonary Maturation

paragraphs.text: In the 1990s, the observation that thyroid hormone could augment lung development and surfactant production in vitro prompted trials of antenatally administered thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH). However, these trials failed to demonstrate a benefit and also raised concerns for adverse consequences on neurodevelopment, thereby significantly dampening enthusiasm for this therapy.50
paragraphs.heading: Prevention: Pharmacologic Acceleration of Pulmonary Maturation

paragraphs.text: The classic clinical presentation of RDS includes grunting respirations, retractions, nasal flaring, cyanosis, and increased oxygen requirement, together with diagnostic radiographic findings and onset of symptoms shortly after birth. The respiratory rate is usually regular and increased well above the normal range of 30 to 60 breaths/min. These infants usually show progression of respiratory symptoms and require supplemental oxygen. The presence of apneic episodes at this early stage is an ominous sign that could reflect thermal instability or sepsis, but more often is a sign of hypoxemia and respiratory failure. This characteristic picture is modified in many infants with low birth weight as a result of the early administration of exogenous surfactant and immediate noninvasive or invasive assisted ventilation.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Features

paragraphs.text: Retractions are prominent and are the result of the compliant rib cage collapsing on inspiration as the infant generates high negative intrathoracic pressures to expand the poorly compliant lungs. The typical expiratory grunt is an early feature and may subsequently disappear. Grunting results from partial closure of the glottis during expiration and in this way acts to trap alveolar air and maintain functional residual
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Features

paragraphs.text: capacity (FRC). Although these signs are characteristic for neonatal RDS, they can result from a wide variety of nonpulmonary causes, such as hypothermia, hypoglycemia, anemia, polycythemia, or sepsis; furthermore, such nonpulmonary conditions can complicate the clinical course of RDS.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Features

paragraphs.text: Cyanosis is a consequence of V/Q mismatch in RDS and is typically relieved by administering ventilatory support and supplemental oxygen. Impaired cardiac output resulting from respiratory effort that is asynchronous with the ventilator may further impede oxygen delivery and lead to poor peripheral perfusion or cyanosis. The consistency of the arterial waveform with invasive blood pressure monitoring or the pulse signal with oxygen saturation monitoring can provide information about the effectiveness of cardiac output. Acrocyanosis of the hands and feet is a common finding in healthy infants and should not be confused with central cyanosis, which always must be investigated.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Features

paragraphs.text: During auscultation of the chest, breath sounds are widely transmitted and cannot be relied upon to reflect pathologic conditions. Nonhomogeneous aeration plus elevated endogenously or exogenously generated intrathoracic pressures can cause pulmonary air leaks. Thus unilaterally decreased breath sounds (with mediastinal shift to the opposite side) or bilaterally decreased air entry could indicate pneumothorax, and immediate transillumination should be performed. Chest radiography is also needed to confirm endotracheal tube placement and if air entry sounds are asymmetric. The murmur of a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is most often audible during the recovery phase of RDS, when pulmonary vascular resistance has fallen below systemic levels and there is left-to-right shunting. Distant, muffled heart sounds should alert one to the possibility of pneumopericardium or pericardial effusion. Percussion of the chest is of no diagnostic value in preterm infants.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Features

paragraphs.text: A constant feature of RDS is the early onset of clinical signs of the disease. Most infants present with signs and symptoms either in the delivery room or within the first 6 hours after birth. The uncomplicated clinical course is characterized by a progressive worsening of symptoms, with a peak severity by days 2 to 3 and onset of recovery by 72 hours. Surfactant therapy often shortens this course as it reconstitutes the surfactant pool and prevents atelectasis until endogenous surfactant production is sufficient. When the disease process is severe enough to require assisted ventilation or is complicated by the development of air leak, significant shunting through a PDA, concomitant infection, or early signs of BPD, recovery can be delayed for days, weeks, or months (see Fig. 65.3). In the most affected preterm patients, the transition from the recovery phase of RDS to chronic lung disease is clinically imperceptible.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Features

paragraphs.text: The diagnosis of RDS is based on a combination of the previously described clinical features, evidence of prematurity, exclusion of other causes of respiratory distress, and characteristic radiographic appearance (see Chapter
paragraphs.heading: Radiographic Findings

paragraphs.text: 38). The typical radiographic features consist of a diffuse reticulogranular pattern, giving the classic ground-glass appearance, in both lung fields with low lung volumes and superimposed air bronchograms (Fig. 65.4). Although the radiologic appearance of RDS is typically symmetric and homogeneous, asymmetry has also been described.
paragraphs.heading: Radiographic Findings

paragraphs.text: The reticulogranular pattern is primarily caused by alveolar atelectasis, although there may be some component of pulmonary edema. The prominent air bronchograms represent aerated bronchioles superimposed on a background of nonaerated alveoli. An area of localized air bronchograms may be normal in the left lower lobe overlying the cardiac silhouette, but in RDS they are widely distributed, particularly in the upper lobes. In the most severe cases, a complete opacification of the lungs can be observed, with total loss of the cardiac borders. Heart size is typically normal or slightly increased. Cardiomegaly may herald the development of congestive cardiac failure from a hemodynamically significant PDA. After the administration of exogenous surfactant therapy, the chest radiograph usually shows improved aeration of the lungs bilaterally; however, asymmetric clearing of the lungs may occur, especially if surfactant therapy has been administered preferentially to one side.
paragraphs.heading: Radiographic Findings

paragraphs.text: The radiographic appearance of RDS, typical or atypical, cannot be reliably differentiated from that of neonatal pneumonia, which is most commonly caused by group B streptococcal or gram-negative (e.g., Escherichia coli) infection. The overlapping clinical features of RDS and infection have resulted in the widespread use of empiric antibiotics in the initial management of infants with RDS (see Antibiotics section below).51,52
paragraphs.heading: Radiographic Findings

paragraphs.text: Infants with RDS reportedly have a larger thymic silhouette than infants of comparable size without RDS, sometimes giving the impression of cardiomegaly. Echocardiographic evaluation of selected infants with RDS may be of value in the diagnosis of a hemodynamically significant PDA, to quantitate elevations in pulmonary artery pressure, to assess cardiac function, and to exclude congenital heart disease (e.g., obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous return) (see Chapter 76).
paragraphs.heading: Radiographic Findings

paragraphs.text: Therapy for RDS includes careful application of general supportive measures supplemented by respiratory support and selective use of surfactant therapy. Close and detailed supervision of small infants requires a dedicated, trained staff experienced and attuned to problems specific to the preterm neonate and skillful in the unique technical procedures involved, such as continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) administration, endotracheal intubation, surfactant administration, titration of invasive and noninvasive respiratory support, assessment of neonatal blood gases, and meticulous fluid management. Other supportive measures include transfusion of packed red blood cells to increase oxygen-carrying capacity (see Chapter 84).
paragraphs.heading: Treatment

paragraphs.text: Delivery of distending pressure to maintain airway and alveolar expansion through invasive and noninvasive means is the mainstay of treatment for RDS (see Chapter 66). The most common approaches of invasive mechanical ventilation via an endotracheal tube use a time-cycled, flow-triggered, volumeor pressure-targeted mode with each synchronized breath or with pressure support for spontaneous breaths between mandatory breaths. Alternatively, high-frequency jet ventilation or high-frequency oscillatory ventilation is used either as a primary means of ventilation or as rescue when conventional mechanical ventilation has failed. Neurally adjusted ventilatory assist (NAVA) is another mode of ventilation that synchronizes ventilated breaths with electrical activity of the diaphragm rather than inspiratory air flow, and it has been shown to be effective in minimizing supplemental oxygen needs and inspiratory pressures and improving patient-ventilator synchrony (see Chapter 66 and Chapter 68).53
paragraphs.heading: Positive-Pressure Ventilation

paragraphs.text: There has been much enthusiasm for noninvasive methods of ventilation, especially nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) via a variety of interfaces. The benefits of CPAP include maintenance of a constant airway opening pressure, establishment and maintenance of FRC, reduction of pharyngeal or laryngeal obstruction, and improvement of oxygenation. When compared to invasive mechanical ventilation, nCPAP reduces volutrauma, atelectrauma, airway damage, and risk of secondary infections, and enhances mucociliary transport.54
paragraphs.heading: Positive-Pressure Ventilation

paragraphs.text: Early studies demonstrated reduced need for mechanical ventilation among preterm infants treated with surfactant and nCPAP, even those born as early as 24 weeks’ gestation. These trials demonstrate that a subset of extremely preterm infants, especially those exposed to antenatal corticosteroids, can be stabilized with nCPAP shortly after birth and may avoid intubation, ventilation, and surfactant replacement altogether.55,56
paragraphs.heading: Positive-Pressure Ventilation

paragraphs.text: Although some extremely preterm infants can be treated with nCPAP, many infants fail this strategy because of persistent and severe apnea, desaturation, bradycardia, or respiratory acidosis. Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation (NIPPV) combines nCPAP with intermittent ventilator breaths and can be administered through short binasal prongs.
paragraphs.heading: Positive-Pressure Ventilation

paragraphs.text: Some studies have found increased success at avoiding intubation with the use of NIPPV.57 The nasal interface for delivery of CPAP and NIPPV is important to consider and likely influences the success of these interventions. The downside of NIPPV is the lack of synchronization; however, noninvasive NAVA provides synchronization and may decrease the frequency and severity of apneic events, decrease the need for invasive ventilation, and facilitate extubation.58,59 Although not as widely used, nasal high-frequency ventilation is another noninvasive method that may be superior to CPAP alone.60
paragraphs.heading: Positive-Pressure Ventilation

paragraphs.text: Caffeine is a common treatment for preterm infants, especially those less than 32 weeks’ gestation, that decreases the risk of extubation failure, reduces the frequency of apnea, reduces the severity of BPD, and has reassuring longterm safety data.61–63
paragraphs.heading: Positive-Pressure Ventilation

paragraphs.text: However, despite increased use of less invasive ventilation strategies to avoid intubation and mechanical ventilation among extremely preterm infants, the frequency of need for supplemental oxygen at 36 weeks’ corrected gestational age has not decreased and pulmonary function during childhood has not significantly improved.64
paragraphs.heading: Positive-Pressure Ventilation

paragraphs.text: First introduced in 1990, no intervention in the past 30 years has had more impact on the care of newborns with RDS than surfactant replacement therapy. A thorough history of the development of surfactant replacement therapy can be found in Chapter 63.65 The discovery that surfactant deficiency was key in the pathophysiology of RDS led to the development of synthetic and animal-derived surfactant preparations which contain extracts of bovine or porcine lungs. Despite differences in chemical composition, extraction methods, dosage amount, and frequency (Table 65.1), endotracheal administration of exogenous surfactant decreases mortality because of RDS and the risk of pneumothorax, whether as part of prevention (delivery room administration), early treatment (within first few hours of life), or rescue (administration for established RDS).66–69 Given the increased use of antenatal corticosteroids and success of postdelivery stabilization on nCPAP, selective administration of surfactant to infants requiring intubation is now a preferred alternative to prophylactic surfactant administration.55,70
paragraphs.heading: Surfactant Therapy

paragraphs.text: Despite the general improvements in mortality and other complications caused by RDS, the incidence of BPD has not changed.64 This could be a consequence of the enhanced survival of very preterm infants, but is more likely because of the fact that BPD is not completely a direct consequence of RDS as many preterm infants develop BPD without significant antecedent RDS.
paragraphs.heading: Surfactant Therapy

paragraphs.text: Some infants do not exhibit the anticipated favorable response to surfactant therapy, which may be because of the degree of initial illness or surfactant inactivation via inflammation, oxidant injury, hemorrhage, or proteinaceous edema fluid in the alveolar space. In addition, data from the early surfactant trials suggested slightly higher pulmonary hemorrhage rates in the smallest and most immature infants; however, these findings have not been consistently
paragraphs.heading: Surfactant Therapy

paragraphs.text: identified in the literature and controversy still exists. In fact, treatment with surfactant has been shown to lower oxygen requirement in neonates with pulmonary hemorrhage.71
paragraphs.heading: Surfactant Therapy

paragraphs.text: The most well-studied and only FDA-approved method of giving surfactant is via the endotracheal tube. As mechanical ventilation is known to increase the risk of injury to the lungs, the INSURE technique (INtubate, SURfactant, Extubate) gained popularity because it has demonstrated a decreased need for reintubation and mechanical ventilation.72 A meta-analysis demonstrated no significant difference in composite outcomes of BPD or death or other associated morbidities, but suggested INSURE was favorable compared to noninvasive respiratory support alone.73 Because even short periods of invasive ventilation can induce lung injury and intubation attempts can damage the airway, multiple studies have examined alternative noninvasive methods of surfactant administration including aerosolization or nebulization, nasopharyngeal or pharyngeal instillation, laryngeal mask administration, and intratracheal administration via a thin catheter. A comparison of the most studied methods is included in Table 65.2.
paragraphs.heading: Modes of Surfactant Administration

paragraphs.text: Less-invasive surfactant administration (LISA) or minimally invasive surfactant therapy (MIST) combine the benefits of early surfactant administration while continuing nCPAP and avoiding intubation among preterm infants. These methods involve either placement of a small gastric catheter into the trachea via Magill forceps or insertion of a semirigid vascular catheter under direct laryngoscopy. Meta-analyses and systematic reviews demonstrate decreased risk of BPD or death at 36 weeks’ corrected gestational age, among other morbidities, when compared with INSURE or no surfactant therapy.74–76 However, some of these outcomes should be interpreted with caution as a limited number of patients at the most immature gestational ages were included.
paragraphs.heading: Modes of Surfactant Administration

paragraphs.text: Laryngeal mask airways (LMA) provide the advantage of not requiring direct laryngoscopy, which requires a skilled clinician, and insertion can result in hypoxemia, bradycardia, increased intracranial pressure, and pain. Multiple randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have evaluated surfactant administration via LMA. Although one study demonstrated superiority of LMA to avoid intubation compared to CPAP or INSURE technique, this loses significance when pooled with other studies, and no significant differences in morbidities or mortality were identified.77,78
paragraphs.heading: Modes of Surfactant Administration

paragraphs.text: Inhalation of aerosolized surfactants is, in fact, the only truly noninvasive method of administering surfactant. Most studies are small, but pooled data suggest that the risk of intubation within 72 hours is lower among infants who received nebulized surfactant without significant differences in morbidities or mortality.79 However, the optimal dose of nebulized surfactant needed to provide adequate effect has not yet been determined.
paragraphs.heading: Modes of Surfactant Administration

paragraphs.text: The threshold for treatment of premature neonates with RDS with surfactant is continually under debate as more emphasis is being placed on noninvasive modes of respiratory support. As such, less invasive routes of surfactant administration via thin catheter or laryngeal mask airway are gaining support.74–78 The recent RDS NeXT (RDS Neonatal Expert Taskforce) workshop created a consensus statement based on survey and modified Delphi method. Consensus is that surfactant is most effective if administered within 1–2 hours after birth for invasively ventilated neonates with RDS.5a The fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) at which surfactant should be considered is less clear but ranges from 0.3 for an invasively ventilated neonate to more than 0.4 for a noninvasively ventilated neonate. The route of surfactant administration should be determined based on the provider’s experience, skill level, available equipment, and institutional practice.

paragraphs.text: Surfactant has also been used as a vehicle because of its lipid interface and ease of widespread distribution in the lungs. As early systemic postnatal steroids have been shown to reduce the incidence and severity of BPD, but with adverse neurodevelopmental implications, a combination of budesonide and surfactant has been investigated. Although the number of studies is limited, data suggest this combination is safe, may lessen the amount of time needed for invasive ventilation, and may decrease the risk of BPD or death at 36 weeks’ corrected gestational age without affecting growth or neurodevelopment.80–82

paragraphs.text: Although no adverse immunologic consequences of foreign tissue protein administration have been reported in the recipients of natural surfactant therapy, concerns for transmitted disease have prompted the desire to develop synthetic, non–animal-based products. Preparations that contain synthetic peptides that mimic the biophysical properties of SP-B or SP-C continue to be investigated but have not found their way into general use.83 SP-A and SP-D, although not essential for surface-lowering activity, could play a significant role in the lung’s innate immune response and modulation of inflammation. It is not yet known whether the use of purified SP-A or recombinant SP-D has
paragraphs.heading: Other Use of Surfactant

paragraphs.text: a therapeutic role in neonatal lung disease, although clinical trials are ongoing. The combination of a new generation of surfactants along with gentler ventilation strategies could hold promise for improving pulmonary outcomes for preterm infants in the future.
paragraphs.heading: Other Use of Surfactant

paragraphs.text: Inhaled nitric oxide (iNO), currently approved for treatment of hypoxic respiratory failure in near-term and fullterm infants, has been proposed as a potential intervention in preterm infants at risk for developing BPD or with RDS that is complicated by pulmonary hypertension (see Chapter 73). Although individual trials have exhibited variable results in survival without BPD, meta-analyses and randomized clinical trials have failed to clearly demonstrate improved respiratory or neurodevelopmental outcomes associated with routine use of iNO in preterm infants.84,85 However, when pulmonary hypertension accompanies RDS, or with decreased vascular surface area and pulmonary hypoplasia resulting from oligohydramnios and prolonged rupture of membranes, early use of iNO may improve oxygenation and survival.86,87 An echocardiogram is recommended to confirm clinical suspicion of pulmonary hypertension in preterm infants.88,89
paragraphs.heading: Inhaled Nitric Oxide Therapy

paragraphs.text: The ability to accurately monitor gas exchange is essential in all cases of neonatal respiratory disease (see Chapter 37 and Chapter 64). In its most basic form, this involves intermittent arterial sampling, usually via an indwelling umbilical arterial catheter or, less commonly, a peripheral (e.g., radial or posterior tibial) arterial line. Infants with RDS requiring a significantly increased inspired oxygen concentration or assisted ventilation should have blood gases sampled as often as their clinical condition dictates. A strategy of “permissive hypercapnia” has been used in attempts to reduce lung injury in preterm infants. In general, PaCO2 is maintained in the 45 to 55 mm Hg range with a pH of at least 7.25, although in the most immature infants these ranges have been relaxed to minimize the degree of ventilatory support in an effort to decrease ventilation-associated morbidities.90
paragraphs.heading: Assessment of Blood Gas Status

paragraphs.text: Pulse oximetry is an indirect measure of the percentage of oxygen-saturated arterial hemoglobin and is the standard of care for noninvasive and continuous monitoring. It typically uses a microprocessor-based pulse oximeter consisting of a light-emitting probe attached to a distal extremity of the infant. Oxygen saturation is computed from the light absorption characteristics of the pulsatile flow (containing both oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin) as it passes beneath the probe. The monitor readings closely correlate with saturation measurements obtained from arterial samples. However, for infants with moderate or severe RDS,
paragraphs.heading: Noninvasive Monitoring

paragraphs.text: noninvasive measurement remains an important adjunct rather than a substitute for arterial blood gas sampling. One should bear in mind that a normal arterial oxygen tension or saturation does not ensure adequate tissue oxygen delivery, because oxygen delivery is dependent on cardiac output and oxygen content of the blood. Hence, interpretation of gas exchange should always be correlated with a thorough clinical assessment.
paragraphs.heading: Noninvasive Monitoring

paragraphs.text: The major disadvantage of pulse oximetry is that changes in saturation are small on the flat portion of the hemoglobin dissociation curve at PaO2 values greater than approximately 60 mm Hg (depending on the fetal hemoglobin content, acidosis, temperature, and other factors affecting position of the hemoglobin dissociation curve). More recently, it has been suggested that pulse oximetry may be less accurate and occult hypoxemia may occur slightly more frequently in children of African descent.91,92
paragraphs.heading: Noninvasive Monitoring

paragraphs.text: There is continuing debate as to the most appropriate target oxygen saturation ranges in the early neonatal period with several large trials demonstrating the tradeoff of significant decreases in severe retinopathy of prematurity with lower saturations between 85% and 89% but a lower incidence of necrotizing enterocolitis and mortality with saturations between 90% and 95%.93–95 Therefore values of O2 saturations in the upper 80s to low to mid 90s seem to be a reasonable goal. Significant variability in even resting oxygen saturations in some infants provides a significant challenge to administer the appropriate amount of oxygen to remain within these constraints, but automated oxygen titration systems that are under development show promise.96
paragraphs.heading: Noninvasive Monitoring

paragraphs.text: A major effect of pulse oximetry has been the ability to rapidly optimize respiratory care and drastically reduce the time required to determine optimum inspired oxygen concentrations, levels of CPAP, and ventilator settings. Other benefits include the ability to assess responses to all procedures, including surfactant instillation, as well as excessive handling. Complications such as pneumothorax, endotracheal tube dislodgement, disconnection from oxygen supply, or ventilator malfunction are rapidly recognized so that immediate corrective treatment can be performed. Episodes of hypoxemia or desaturation can occur spontaneously or accompany feedings and have complex etiologies, as discussed in Chapter 68. Noninvasive monitoring of oxygenation allows such episodes to be identified and their relationship to apnea and bradycardia recorded.
paragraphs.heading: Noninvasive Monitoring

paragraphs.text: Although not used as universally as pulse oximetry, noninvasive methods for monitoring carbon dioxide levels can also provide an important adjunct to blood gas monitoring (see Chapter 37). Capnography has become the standard of care in resuscitation situations for accurately and rapidly demonstrating that the endotracheal tube is in the airway. Quantitative end-tidal CO2 monitoring, though routinely used during anesthesia, is useful for following trends but
paragraphs.heading: Noninvasive Monitoring

paragraphs.text: is not always reliable in preterm infants. Transcutaneous PCO2 monitoring is also very useful for monitoring trends, especially when trying to optimize the ventilatory settings when initiating conventional or high-frequency ventilation. The possible association of PaCO2 levels of less than 30 mm Hg with periventricular leukomalacia in preterm infants demonstrates the need for careful CO2 monitoring.97
paragraphs.heading: Noninvasive Monitoring

paragraphs.text: NIRS provides a noninvasive assessment of cerebral oxygenation that can be used for following trends in cerebral hemodynamics. Although the algorithms are becoming more refined to account for noncerebral tissue (e.g., scalp, skull), early studies have suggested that cerebral hypoxia is associated with low electrical activity and intracranial hemorrhage, but the impact on longer term neurodevelopmental outcomes has not been determined.98,99
paragraphs.heading: Noninvasive Monitoring

paragraphs.text: There is enthusiasm for wireless sensor technology under development that can monitor multiple domains such as blood pressure and temperature in addition to the standard ECG and respiratory waveforms.100
paragraphs.heading: Noninvasive Monitoring

paragraphs.text: Umbilical artery catheterization should be performed by an experienced clinician and under strict surgical sterile technique. Once the umbilical arteries have been identified by their anatomic characteristics, one of the vessels is dilated with the use of an iris forceps. The catheter is then gently advanced to a predetermined length estimated to place its tip at a high (T6–T8) or low (L3–L4) position. Several methods have been developed to estimate the length of catheter to be inserted to achieve proper placement; however, radiologic or ultrasound confirmation of catheter position is still imperative.
paragraphs.heading: Arterial Sampling

paragraphs.text: Although umbilical artery catheters still form the basic means of arterial sampling in infants with RDS, the list of catheter-related complications is formidable. The most common visible problem from an umbilical arterial line is blanching or cyanosis of part or all of a distal extremity or the buttock area, resulting either from vasospasm or a thrombotic or embolic incident. This complication may be reduced by high placement of the umbilical artery catheter tip at the level of T6-T8 as opposed to lower placement at L3-L4 just above the aortic bifurcation.
paragraphs.heading: Arterial Sampling

paragraphs.text: Tyson and associates observed frequent thromboatheromatous complications resulting from umbilical artery catheters in neonates at autopsy.101 Small amounts of heparin added to the continuous infusion appear to reduce the risk of arterial thrombi. Hypertension can result if a renal artery is involved. A rare complication of indwelling arterial umbilical catheters is aneurysmal dilation with dissection of the abdominal aorta, which can be diagnosed by careful ultrasound examination. Retrograde blood flow into the proximal aorta can occur during flushing of radial and umbilical artery lines and result in transient blood pressure elevation; therefore routine flushing should be performed with a small volume over a period of several seconds.
paragraphs.heading: Arterial Sampling

paragraphs.text: The risk of catheter-associated bloodstream infection increases significantly the longer the catheter remains in place; thus limiting the number of days umbilical catheters remain in place reduces the risk of infection and catheterassociated thrombosis.102 All these complications illustrate the importance of applying careful techniques for the insertion and removal of indwelling arterial catheters and the need for less hazardous methods of monitoring blood gases.
paragraphs.heading: Arterial Sampling

paragraphs.text: Peripheral arterial catheters, most commonly placed in the radial artery, can also be used for arterial blood sampling. The Allen test should be performed before the insertion of a radial artery line to establish the presence of adequate collateral circulation to the fingers. Similar to umbilical artery catheters, the most common complication of peripheral arterial catheters is blanching or cyanosis of part or all of a distal extremity, resulting from vasospasm or a thromboembolic event.
paragraphs.heading: Arterial Sampling

paragraphs.text: A change in acid-base balance should prompt a rapid determination of the type of imbalance, respiratory or metabolic, and a thorough evaluation of the cause (see Chapter 96). Acidosis, respiratory or metabolic, especially when coupled with hypoxia, can cause pulmonary arterial vasoconstriction and V/Q abnormalities, decreased cardiac output, or both. Metabolic acidosis out of proportion to the degree of respiratory distress might signify hypoperfusion, sepsis, or IVH. Although sodium bicarbonate was historically used to correct metabolic acidosis, its routine use has not been shown to improve morbidity or mortality among preterm infants and may be associated with increased risk for adverse neonatal outcomes.103 Treatment of metabolic acidosis depends on the underlying etiology (e.g., lactic acidosis, renal tubular acidosis), and therapy should be targeted accordingly.
paragraphs.heading: Acid-Base Therapy

paragraphs.text: Respiratory acidosis requires measures to increase minute ventilation, often requiring assisted ventilation, and serial blood gases should be performed to titrate respiratory support. Administration of sodium bicarbonate to infants with respiratory acidosis is not indicated and could further increase the PCO2.
paragraphs.heading: Acid-Base Therapy

paragraphs.text: Comprehensive management of patients with RDS includes a close evaluation and monitoring of the cardiovascular system. An in-depth understanding of the physical and physiologic interactions between the cardiovascular and pulmonary systems in the mechanically ventilated patient is paramount. For example, after surfactant administration, with the improvement in the mechanical properties of the lungs, an unrecognized overdistension of the lungs by excessive mechanical ventilation support can decrease systemic venous return to the heart and result in decreased cardiac output. Radiographically, a typical squeezed-heart silhouette and flattened diaphragm are found. These findings may also be present in an infant receiving high-frequency ventilation with high mean airway pressure. A thorough clinical evaluation should include sequential assessment of vital
paragraphs.heading: Cardiovascular Management

paragraphs.text: signs, peripheral pulses, capillary refill, and urine output as surrogate markers of adequate cardiac output.
paragraphs.heading: Cardiovascular Management

paragraphs.text: Myocardial dysfunction secondary to ischemia or hypoperfusion may be present and could lead to decreased peripheral perfusion with lactic acidemia and metabolic acidosis. Systemic hypotension is common in the early stages of RDS; thus continuous monitoring of systemic blood pressure by means of an indwelling arterial catheter is of utmost importance in neonates with moderate to severe RDS. Noninvasive intermittent monitoring of systemic blood pressure should be reserved for the mildly affected neonate. Judicious use of crystalloids for intravascular expansion and vasopressor support are often indicated. In patients with persistent hypotension not responsive to fluid therapy or pressors (e.g., dopamine), serum cortisol levels should be measured and treatment with stress doses of hydrocortisone should be considered.
paragraphs.heading: Cardiovascular Management

paragraphs.text: Failure of the ductus arteriosus to close is a common complication in preterm infants with RDS and has been linked to worsening respiratory distress and acidosis. Clinically, the presence of a hemodynamically significant PDA is heralded by a widened pulse pressure, an active precordium, and bounding peripheral pulses. A heart murmur on the left subclavicular area and the back is often present. On the chest radiograph, cardiomegaly might signal the presence of a hemodynamically significant PDA with congestive heart failure. With clinical suspicion, a confirmatory echocardiogram, which should demonstrate evidence of pulmonary overcirculation, such as left atrial enlargement, is usually obtained. The decision whether to proceed with pharmacologic closure of the ductus arteriosus with a prostaglandin synthesis inhibitor such as indomethacin or ibuprofen remains controversial. Fluid restriction, vasopressors, and a loop diuretic (e.g., furosemide) may be indicated for the medical management of a hemodynamically significant PDA with congestive heart failure (see Chapter 75).
paragraphs.heading: Cardiovascular Management

paragraphs.text: Neonatal pneumonia (most commonly caused by group B streptococci or gram-negative organisms) can be indistinguishable
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: Key Points
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: • Antenatal corticosteroids enhance surfactant production
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: as well as lung parenchymal maturation and reduce comorbidities such as intraventricular hemorrhage. • Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) results from a
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: developmental deficiency of pulmonary surfactant production that may be aggravated by maternal diabetes and perinatal hypoxia-ischemia.
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: from RDS both clinically and radiographically. Such infection usually is acquired around the time of delivery, either through ascending infection or passage through a colonized genital tract. Prenatal features suggestive of neonatal infection include maternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes, and clinical evidence of chorioamnionitis. The suspicion for bacterial infection is raised by a history of maternal genital colonization with group B streptococcus in an inadequately treated mother.
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: The potentially fulminant course of neonatal pneumonia, especially in preterm infants, and the difficulty in distinguishing it from RDS have led to the widespread practice that infants with significant respiratory distress receive empiric antibiotics.51,52 A more judicious approach to empiric antibiotic use for term and late preterm neonates at risk for earlyonset sepsis has been recommended with development of a sepsis risk calculator.104 Early empiric antibiotic administration can also be limited for preterm infants less than 36 weeks’ gestation who are deemed to be low risk for early-onset sepsis as defined by cesarean delivery without labor or membrane rupture before delivery and no intrapartum concerns for intrauterine infection or nonreassuring fetal status.105
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: In the neonate, persistent hypotension, metabolic acidosis, early onset of apnea, neutropenia, or neutrophilia accompanied by an increase in immature neutrophils (left shift) are clinical findings suggestive of systemic infection. Nonetheless, the absence of these features does not definitively exclude the diagnosis of sepsis or pneumonia. Ampicillin combined with an aminoglycoside is the most commonly prescribed antibiotic regimen and may be discontinued after 36 hours based on blood culture results and clinical course of the neonate.106,107 Prolonged empiric antibiotic exposure for preterm neonates is associated with increased risks of necrotizing enterocolitis and mortality.108,109
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: Despite substantial improvements in the treatment of RDS, prevention of preterm birth is still the ultimate goal and will have significant impact on the prevention of RDS. In the meantime, understanding the interactions of the intrauterine environment and genetic determinants of lung development with the pathogenesis of RDS is essential to develop mechanism-specific interventions.
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: • RDS, pulmonary immaturity, and the complications of
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: their management remain common causes of acute and longer-term morbidity. • Various techniques of surfactant replacement, respiratory
paragraphs.heading: Antibiotics

paragraphs.text: support including continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), and other supportive therapy are the mainstays of treatment.

65 Respiratory Distress Syndrome in the Neonate

### MEGAN LAGOSKI, AARON HAMVAS, AND JENNIFER A. WAMBACH

Enormous strides have been made in understanding the pathophysiology of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) and the role of surfactant in its cause and treatment (see Chapter 63). Nevertheless, RDS, formerly referred to as hyaline membrane disease, remains a dominant clinical problem among preterm neonates despite the introduction of pharmacologic acceleration of pulmonary maturity using antenatal corticosteroids and the development of surfactant replacement therapy in the 1990s.1,2 The incidence of complications in the survivors of RDS remains significant and continues to be differentially represented between infants of varying ancestries.3,4 These include intracranial hemorrhage, late-onset sepsis, necrotizing enterocolitis, severe retinopathy of prematurity, and bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD). It is often impossible to determine whether these disorders may result as the sequelae of RDS, its treatment, or the underlying prematurity. In this section, the clinical features and evaluation of infants with RDS are discussed, and therapeutic approaches other than assisted ventilation (see Chapter 66) are outlined. Other recommendations and details can be found in the recent consensus guidelines for RDS.5,5a

### Incidence

RDS is one of the most common causes of morbidity and mortality in preterm neonates, although lack of a precise definition among infants with very low birth weight necessitates cautious interpretation of statistics regarding incidence, mortality, and outcome.6,7 The diagnosis can be established pathologically or by biochemical documentation of surfactant deficiency; nonetheless, most series refer only to a combination of clinical and radiographic features. Without biochemical evidence of surfactant deficiency, it is difficult to clinically diagnose RDS in infants with extremely low birth weight. The term respiratory insufficiency of prematurity had been used in some centers for infants who require oxygen and ventilator support in the absence of typical radiographic evidence of RDS. The term

1226

respiratory instability of prematurity has been proposed to describe very low birth weight infants who require some respiratory support but may have additional contributing factors such as inconsistent central respiratory drive or poor inspiratory effort.6

RDS occurs throughout the world and has a slight male predominance.8 The greatest risk factors appear to be early gestational age and low birth weight; however, European descent, late preterm delivery (35–36 weeks), or elective delivery in the absence of labor are also prominent risk factors.8,9 Given the associated adverse respiratory outcomes of late preterm and early term births, initiatives to delay elective deliveries until 39 weeks’ gestation have been successful in reducing pulmonary and nonpulmonary morbidity in these infants.10 Infants born to mothers with diabetes also have an increased risk for RDS.11

The incidence of RDS is inversely proportional to gestational age: nearly all infants born at 22 to 24 weeks’ gestation have RDS, decreasing to approximately 25% in infants with birth weights between 1251 and 1500 g.12,13 Even infants of 34 weeks’ gestation and greater, especially males of European descent, have a discernible risk of RDS that decreases from ∼10% at 34 weeks to less than 1% at 37 weeks (Fig. 65.1).8

### Pathophysiology

The lungs of infants who succumb from RDS have a characteristic uniformly ruddy and airless appearance, macroscopically resembling hepatic tissue. On microscopic examination, the striking feature is diffuse atelectasis such that only a few widely dilated alveoli are readily distinguishable (Fig. 65.2). An eosinophilic membrane lines the visible airspaces that usually constitute terminal bronchioles and alveolar ducts. This characteristic membrane (from which the term hyaline membrane disease is derived) consists of a fibrinous matrix of materials derived from the blood and contains cellular debris derived from injured epithelium. Surfactant synthesis is a dynamic process that depends on factors such as pH, temperature, and perfusion and may be compromised by cold stress, hypovolemia, hypoxemia, and acidosis. Other unfavorable factors, such as exposure to high inspired oxygen concentration and the effects of volutrauma or atelectrauma from assisted ventilation, can trigger the release of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines and further damage the alveolar epithelial lining, resulting in reduced surfactant synthesis and function. The leakage of proteins such as fibrin in the intra-alveolar space further aggravates surfactant deficiency by promoting surfactant inactivation. Deficiency of surfactant and the accompanying decrease in lung compliance lead to alveolar hypoventilation and ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) imbalance. Severe hypoxemia and systemic hypoperfusion result in decreased oxygen delivery with subsequent lactic acidosis secondary to anaerobic metabolism. Hypoxemia and acidosis also result in pulmonary hypoperfusion secondary to pulmonary vasoconstriction, and the result is a further aggravation of hypoxemia because of right-to-left shunting at the level of the ductus arteriosus, the foramen ovale, and within the lung itself.

The relative roles of surfactant deficiency and pulmonary hypoperfusion in the overall clinical picture of RDS vary somewhat with each patient. The natural history of RDS

### Heritability of Respiratory Distress Syndrome

A genetic contribution to the risk of RDS has been suggested in twin studies where the concordance for RDS in monozygotic twins is greater than that for dizygotic twins and with isolated reports of recurrence in families.14–16 With the application of molecular techniques, the contribution of genetic variations (single nucleotide variants, pathogenic variants) to the pathogenesis of respiratory disorders in newborns is emerging.17,18

Pathogenic variants in genes encoding surfactant protein-B (SP-B, SFTPB), surfactant protein-C (SP-C, SFTPC), the ATP binding cassette subfamily A, member 3 (ABCA3, ABCA3), and the thyroid transcription factor (TTF-1, NKX2-1) represent rare monogenic causes of RDS.19–22 Inherited SP-B deficiency is a recessive disorder that presents as severe respiratory failure in the immediate newborn period and is unresponsive to standard neonatal intensive care interventions. Large-scale cohort-based resequencing efforts have demonstrated an over-representation of heterozygous (monoallelic), predicted deleterious variants in ABCA3 in newborns 34 weeks and greater with RDS, suggesting that these variants are modifiers for the risk or severity of respiratory disease in developmentally susceptible newborns.17,18,24,33 These efforts have not identified an unequivocal contribution of rare or common variants in the surfactant protein-B or -C genes to RDS in newborns, suggesting that if these genes play a role in RDS, it is likely to be through interactions with variants in other lung-associated genes. Exome and genome sequencing are increasingly being used in the neonatal intensive care unit and will yield additional insights into candidate genes that not only account for the heritability of RDS but provide insight into systemic disorders with prominent respiratory manifestations.34–38

### Prevention: Pharmacologic Acceleration of Pulmonary Maturation

In the early 1970s, Liggins, while studying the effects of steroids on premature labor in lambs, noticed the lack of RDS and increased survival in preterm animals prenatally exposed to steroids. The effects of various catecholamines as well as aminophylline and thyroid hormone have been studied; however, the most successful method to induce fetal lung maturation is prenatal corticosteroid administration (see Chapter 63).39

If premature delivery of an infant appears probable or necessary, lung maturity can be hastened pharmacologically. Accelerated lung maturation occurs with physiologic stress levels of corticosteroids via receptor-mediated induction of specific developmentally regulated proteins, including those associated with surfactant synthesis. Steroids, when administered to the mother at least 24 to 48 hours before delivery, decrease the incidence and severity of RDS.40 Corticosteroids appear to be most effective before 34 weeks’ gestation and when administered at least 24 hours and no longer than 7 days before delivery. Because corticosteroid therapy for

less than 24 hours is still associated with significant reductions in neonatal mortality, RDS, and intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), without increasing the risk of infection to the mother or fetus, antenatal steroids should always be considered unless immediate delivery is anticipated.41 Data regarding the risks and benefits of antenatal corticosteroid administration for late preterm infants born at 34 to 36 weeks’ gestation are more equivocal. The clear short-term benefits of a reduction in respiratory complications may be outweighed by more uncertain impacts on longer-term neurodevelopmental outcomes, but further data are required to come to a more certain conclusion.42–44

Less clear are the effects of repeated courses of antenatal corticosteroids on the short- and long-term outcomes of preterm infants. Early retrospective studies suggested decreased fetal growth and adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes, but subsequent analyses have suggested short-term benefits without long-term harm on childhood outcomes.45 Further, the use of a rescue course of corticosteroids in the setting of premature rupture of membranes remains controversial.41,46

Although preterm infants as early as 23 weeks’ estimated gestation may benefit from antenatal corticosteroid exposure, their use before 23 weeks’ gestation also remains controversial. Regardless, the topic of prenatal corticosteroids is an important component of the joint neonatal-obstetrical counseling and approach to these anticipated early gestation deliveries.47–49

In the 1990s, the observation that thyroid hormone could augment lung development and surfactant production in vitro prompted trials of antenatally administered thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH). However, these trials failed to demonstrate a benefit and also raised concerns for adverse consequences on neurodevelopment, thereby significantly dampening enthusiasm for this therapy.50

### Clinical Features

The classic clinical presentation of RDS includes grunting respirations, retractions, nasal flaring, cyanosis, and increased oxygen requirement, together with diagnostic radiographic findings and onset of symptoms shortly after birth. The respiratory rate is usually regular and increased well above the normal range of 30 to 60 breaths/min. These infants usually show progression of respiratory symptoms and require supplemental oxygen. The presence of apneic episodes at this early stage is an ominous sign that could reflect thermal instability or sepsis, but more often is a sign of hypoxemia and respiratory failure. This characteristic picture is modified in many infants with low birth weight as a result of the early administration of exogenous surfactant and immediate noninvasive or invasive assisted ventilation.

Retractions are prominent and are the result of the compliant rib cage collapsing on inspiration as the infant generates high negative intrathoracic pressures to expand the poorly compliant lungs. The typical expiratory grunt is an early feature and may subsequently disappear. Grunting results from partial closure of the glottis during expiration and in this way acts to trap alveolar air and maintain functional residual


## PDF page 1232

capacity (FRC). Although these signs are characteristic for neonatal RDS, they can result from a wide variety of nonpulmonary causes, such as hypothermia, hypoglycemia, anemia, polycythemia, or sepsis; furthermore, such nonpulmonary conditions can complicate the clinical course of RDS.

Cyanosis is a consequence of V/Q mismatch in RDS and is typically relieved by administering ventilatory support and supplemental oxygen. Impaired cardiac output resulting from respiratory effort that is asynchronous with the ventilator may further impede oxygen delivery and lead to poor peripheral perfusion or cyanosis. The consistency of the arterial waveform with invasive blood pressure monitoring or the pulse signal with oxygen saturation monitoring can provide information about the effectiveness of cardiac output. Acrocyanosis of the hands and feet is a common finding in healthy infants and should not be confused with central cyanosis, which always must be investigated.

During auscultation of the chest, breath sounds are widely transmitted and cannot be relied upon to reflect pathologic conditions. Nonhomogeneous aeration plus elevated endogenously or exogenously generated intrathoracic pressures can cause pulmonary air leaks. Thus unilaterally decreased breath sounds (with mediastinal shift to the opposite side) or bilaterally decreased air entry could indicate pneumothorax, and immediate transillumination should be performed. Chest radiography is also needed to confirm endotracheal tube placement and if air entry sounds are asymmetric. The murmur of a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is most often audible during the recovery phase of RDS, when pulmonary vascular resistance has fallen below systemic levels and there is left-to-right shunting. Distant, muffled heart sounds should alert one to the possibility of pneumopericardium or pericardial effusion. Percussion of the chest is of no diagnostic value in preterm infants.

A constant feature of RDS is the early onset of clinical signs of the disease. Most infants present with signs and symptoms either in the delivery room or within the first 6 hours after birth. The uncomplicated clinical course is characterized by a progressive worsening of symptoms, with a peak severity by days 2 to 3 and onset of recovery by 72 hours. Surfactant therapy often shortens this course as it reconstitutes the surfactant pool and prevents atelectasis until endogenous surfactant production is sufficient. When the disease process is severe enough to require assisted ventilation or is complicated by the development of air leak, significant shunting through a PDA, concomitant infection, or early signs of BPD, recovery can be delayed for days, weeks, or months (see Fig. 65.3). In the most affected preterm patients, the transition from the recovery phase of RDS to chronic lung disease is clinically imperceptible.

### Radiographic Findings

The diagnosis of RDS is based on a combination of the previously described clinical features, evidence of prematurity, exclusion of other causes of respiratory distress, and characteristic radiographic appearance (see Chapter

• Fig. 65.4 Typical radiographic appearance of respiratory distress syndrome with reticulogranular infiltrates and air bronchograms.

38). The typical radiographic features consist of a diffuse reticulogranular pattern, giving the classic ground-glass appearance, in both lung fields with low lung volumes and superimposed air bronchograms (Fig. 65.4). Although the radiologic appearance of RDS is typically symmetric and homogeneous, asymmetry has also been described.

The reticulogranular pattern is primarily caused by alveolar atelectasis, although there may be some component of pulmonary edema. The prominent air bronchograms represent aerated bronchioles superimposed on a background of nonaerated alveoli. An area of localized air bronchograms may be normal in the left lower lobe overlying the cardiac silhouette, but in RDS they are widely distributed, particularly in the upper lobes. In the most severe cases, a complete opacification of the lungs can be observed, with total loss of the cardiac borders. Heart size is typically normal or slightly increased. Cardiomegaly may herald the development of congestive cardiac failure from a hemodynamically significant PDA. After the administration of exogenous surfactant therapy, the chest radiograph usually shows improved aeration of the lungs bilaterally; however, asymmetric clearing of the lungs may occur, especially if surfactant therapy has been administered preferentially to one side.

The radiographic appearance of RDS, typical or atypical, cannot be reliably differentiated from that of neonatal pneumonia, which is most commonly caused by group B streptococcal or gram-negative (e.g., Escherichia coli) infection. The overlapping clinical features of RDS and infection have resulted in the widespread use of empiric antibiotics in the initial management of infants with RDS (see Antibiotics section below).51,52

Infants with RDS reportedly have a larger thymic silhouette than infants of comparable size without RDS, sometimes giving the impression of cardiomegaly. Echocardiographic evaluation of selected infants with RDS may be of value in the diagnosis of a hemodynamically significant PDA, to quantitate elevations in pulmonary artery pressure, to assess cardiac function, and to exclude congenital heart disease (e.g., obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous return) (see Chapter 76).

### Treatment

Therapy for RDS includes careful application of general supportive measures supplemented by respiratory support and selective use of surfactant therapy. Close and detailed supervision of small infants requires a dedicated, trained staff experienced and attuned to problems specific to the preterm neonate and skillful in the unique technical procedures involved, such as continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) administration, endotracheal intubation, surfactant administration, titration of invasive and noninvasive respiratory support, assessment of neonatal blood gases, and meticulous fluid management. Other supportive measures include transfusion of packed red blood cells to increase oxygen-carrying capacity (see Chapter 84).

### Positive-Pressure Ventilation

Delivery of distending pressure to maintain airway and alveolar expansion through invasive and noninvasive means is the mainstay of treatment for RDS (see Chapter 66). The most common approaches of invasive mechanical ventilation via an endotracheal tube use a time-cycled, flow-triggered, volumeor pressure-targeted mode with each synchronized breath or with pressure support for spontaneous breaths between mandatory breaths. Alternatively, high-frequency jet ventilation or high-frequency oscillatory ventilation is used either as a primary means of ventilation or as rescue when conventional mechanical ventilation has failed. Neurally adjusted ventilatory assist (NAVA) is another mode of ventilation that synchronizes ventilated breaths with electrical activity of the diaphragm rather than inspiratory air flow, and it has been shown to be effective in minimizing supplemental oxygen needs and inspiratory pressures and improving patient-ventilator synchrony (see Chapter 66 and Chapter 68).53

There has been much enthusiasm for noninvasive methods of ventilation, especially nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) via a variety of interfaces. The benefits of CPAP include maintenance of a constant airway opening pressure, establishment and maintenance of FRC, reduction of pharyngeal or laryngeal obstruction, and improvement of oxygenation. When compared to invasive mechanical ventilation, nCPAP reduces volutrauma, atelectrauma, airway damage, and risk of secondary infections, and enhances mucociliary transport.54

Early studies demonstrated reduced need for mechanical ventilation among preterm infants treated with surfactant and nCPAP, even those born as early as 24 weeks’ gestation. These trials demonstrate that a subset of extremely preterm infants, especially those exposed to antenatal corticosteroids, can be stabilized with nCPAP shortly after birth and may avoid intubation, ventilation, and surfactant replacement altogether.55,56

Although some extremely preterm infants can be treated with nCPAP, many infants fail this strategy because of persistent and severe apnea, desaturation, bradycardia, or respiratory acidosis. Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation (NIPPV) combines nCPAP with intermittent ventilator breaths and can be administered through short binasal prongs.

Some studies have found increased success at avoiding intubation with the use of NIPPV.57 The nasal interface for delivery of CPAP and NIPPV is important to consider and likely influences the success of these interventions. The downside of NIPPV is the lack of synchronization; however, noninvasive NAVA provides synchronization and may decrease the frequency and severity of apneic events, decrease the need for invasive ventilation, and facilitate extubation.58,59 Although not as widely used, nasal high-frequency ventilation is another noninvasive method that may be superior to CPAP alone.60

Caffeine is a common treatment for preterm infants, especially those less than 32 weeks’ gestation, that decreases the risk of extubation failure, reduces the frequency of apnea, reduces the severity of BPD, and has reassuring longterm safety data.61–63

However, despite increased use of less invasive ventilation strategies to avoid intubation and mechanical ventilation among extremely preterm infants, the frequency of need for supplemental oxygen at 36 weeks’ corrected gestational age has not decreased and pulmonary function during childhood has not significantly improved.64

### Surfactant Therapy

First introduced in 1990, no intervention in the past 30 years has had more impact on the care of newborns with RDS than surfactant replacement therapy. A thorough history of the development of surfactant replacement therapy can be found in Chapter 63.65 The discovery that surfactant deficiency was key in the pathophysiology of RDS led to the development of synthetic and animal-derived surfactant preparations which contain extracts of bovine or porcine lungs. Despite differences in chemical composition, extraction methods, dosage amount, and frequency (Table 65.1), endotracheal administration of exogenous surfactant decreases mortality because of RDS and the risk of pneumothorax, whether as part of prevention (delivery room administration), early treatment (within first few hours of life), or rescue (administration for established RDS).66–69 Given the increased use of antenatal corticosteroids and success of postdelivery stabilization on nCPAP, selective administration of surfactant to infants requiring intubation is now a preferred alternative to prophylactic surfactant administration.55,70

Despite the general improvements in mortality and other complications caused by RDS, the incidence of BPD has not changed.64 This could be a consequence of the enhanced survival of very preterm infants, but is more likely because of the fact that BPD is not completely a direct consequence of RDS as many preterm infants develop BPD without significant antecedent RDS.

Some infants do not exhibit the anticipated favorable response to surfactant therapy, which may be because of the degree of initial illness or surfactant inactivation via inflammation, oxidant injury, hemorrhage, or proteinaceous edema fluid in the alveolar space. In addition, data from the early surfactant trials suggested slightly higher pulmonary hemorrhage rates in the smallest and most immature infants; however, these findings have not been consistently

### Modes of Surfactant Administration

The most well-studied and only FDA-approved method of giving surfactant is via the endotracheal tube. As mechanical ventilation is known to increase the risk of injury to the lungs, the INSURE technique (INtubate, SURfactant, Extubate) gained popularity because it has demonstrated a decreased need for reintubation and mechanical ventilation.72 A meta-analysis demonstrated no significant difference in composite outcomes of BPD or death or other associated morbidities, but suggested INSURE was favorable compared to noninvasive respiratory support alone.73 Because even short periods of invasive ventilation can induce lung injury and intubation attempts can damage the airway, multiple studies have examined alternative noninvasive methods of surfactant administration including aerosolization or nebulization, nasopharyngeal or pharyngeal instillation, laryngeal mask administration, and intratracheal administration via a thin catheter. A comparison of the most studied methods is included in Table 65.2.

Less-invasive surfactant administration (LISA) or minimally invasive surfactant therapy (MIST) combine the benefits of early surfactant administration while continuing nCPAP and avoiding intubation among preterm infants. These methods involve either placement of a small gastric catheter into the trachea via Magill forceps or insertion of a semirigid vascular catheter under direct laryngoscopy. Meta-analyses and systematic reviews demonstrate decreased risk of BPD or death at 36 weeks’ corrected gestational age, among other morbidities, when compared with INSURE or no surfactant therapy.74–76 However, some of these outcomes should be interpreted with caution as a limited number of patients at the most immature gestational ages were included.

Multiple randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have evaluated surfactant administration via LMA.
