Inhalation of aerosolized surfactants is, in fact, the only truly noninvasive method of administering surfactant. Most studies are small, but pooled data suggest that the risk of intubation within 72 hours is lower among infants who received nebulized surfactant without significant differences in morbidities or mortality.79 However, the optimal dose of nebulized surfactant needed to provide adequate effect has not yet been determined.

The threshold for treatment of premature neonates with RDS with surfactant is continually under debate as more emphasis is being placed on noninvasive modes of respiratory support. As such, less invasive routes of surfactant administration via thin catheter or laryngeal mask airway are gaining support.74–78 The recent RDS NeXT (RDS Neonatal Expert Taskforce) workshop created a consensus statement based on survey and modified Delphi method. Consensus is that surfactant is most effective if administered within 1–2 hours after birth for invasively ventilated neonates with RDS.5a The fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) at which surfactant should be considered is less clear but ranges from 0.3 for an invasively ventilated neonate to more than 0.4 for a noninvasively ventilated neonate. The route of surfactant administration should be determined based on the provider’s experience, skill level, available equipment, and institutional practice.

### Other Use of Surfactant

Surfactant has also been used as a vehicle because of its lipid interface and ease of widespread distribution in the lungs. ### Inhaled Nitric Oxide Therapy

Inhaled nitric oxide (iNO), currently approved for treatment of hypoxic respiratory failure in near-term and fullterm infants, has been proposed as a potential intervention in preterm infants at risk for developing BPD or with RDS that is complicated by pulmonary hypertension (see Chapter 73). Although individual trials have exhibited variable results in survival without BPD, meta-analyses and randomized clinical trials have failed to clearly demonstrate improved respiratory or neurodevelopmental outcomes associated with routine use of iNO in preterm infants.84,85 However, when pulmonary hypertension accompanies RDS, or with decreased vascular surface area and pulmonary hypoplasia resulting from oligohydramnios and prolonged rupture of membranes, early use of iNO may improve oxygenation and survival.86,87 An echocardiogram is recommended to confirm clinical suspicion of pulmonary hypertension in preterm infants.88,89

### Assessment of Blood Gas Status

The ability to accurately monitor gas exchange is essential in all cases of neonatal respiratory disease (see Chapter 37 and Chapter 64). In its most basic form, this involves intermittent arterial sampling, usually via an indwelling umbilical arterial catheter or, less commonly, a peripheral (e.g., radial or posterior tibial) arterial line. Infants with RDS requiring a significantly increased inspired oxygen concentration or assisted ventilation should have blood gases sampled as often as their clinical condition dictates. A strategy of “permissive hypercapnia” has been used in attempts to reduce lung injury in preterm infants. In general, PaCO2 is maintained in the 45 to 55 mm Hg range with a pH of at least 7.25, although in the most immature infants these ranges have been relaxed to minimize the degree of ventilatory support in an effort to decrease ventilation-associated morbidities.90

### Noninvasive Monitoring

Pulse oximetry is an indirect measure of the percentage of oxygen-saturated arterial hemoglobin and is the standard of care for noninvasive and continuous monitoring. It typically uses a microprocessor-based pulse oximeter consisting of a light-emitting probe attached to a distal extremity of the infant. Oxygen saturation is computed from the light absorption characteristics of the pulsatile flow (containing both oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin) as it passes beneath the probe. The monitor readings closely correlate with saturation measurements obtained from arterial samples. However, for infants with moderate or severe RDS,

noninvasive measurement remains an important adjunct rather than a substitute for arterial blood gas sampling. One should bear in mind that a normal arterial oxygen tension or saturation does not ensure adequate tissue oxygen delivery, because oxygen delivery is dependent on cardiac output and oxygen content of the blood. Hence, interpretation of gas exchange should always be correlated with a thorough clinical assessment.

The major disadvantage of pulse oximetry is that changes in saturation are small on the flat portion of the hemoglobin dissociation curve at PaO2 values greater than approximately 60 mm Hg (depending on the fetal hemoglobin content, acidosis, temperature, and other factors affecting position of the hemoglobin dissociation curve). More recently, it has been suggested that pulse oximetry may be less accurate and occult hypoxemia may occur slightly more frequently in children of African descent.91,92

There is continuing debate as to the most appropriate target oxygen saturation ranges in the early neonatal period with several large trials demonstrating the tradeoff of significant decreases in severe retinopathy of prematurity with lower saturations between 85% and 89% but a lower incidence of necrotizing enterocolitis and mortality with saturations between 90% and 95%.93–95 Therefore values of O2 saturations in the upper 80s to low to mid 90s seem to be a reasonable goal. Significant variability in even resting oxygen saturations in some infants provides a significant challenge to administer the appropriate amount of oxygen to remain within these constraints, but automated oxygen titration systems that are under development show promise.96

A major effect of pulse oximetry has been the ability to rapidly optimize respiratory care and drastically reduce the time required to determine optimum inspired oxygen concentrations, levels of CPAP, and ventilator settings. Other benefits include the ability to assess responses to all procedures, including surfactant instillation, as well as excessive handling. Complications such as pneumothorax, endotracheal tube dislodgement, disconnection from oxygen supply, or ventilator malfunction are rapidly recognized so that immediate corrective treatment can be performed. Episodes of hypoxemia or desaturation can occur spontaneously or accompany feedings and have complex etiologies, as discussed in Chapter 68. Noninvasive monitoring of oxygenation allows such episodes to be identified and their relationship to apnea and bradycardia recorded.

Noninvasive Carbon Dioxide Monitoring

Although not used as universally as pulse oximetry, noninvasive methods for monitoring carbon dioxide levels can also provide an important adjunct to blood gas monitoring (see Chapter 37). Capnography has become the standard of care in resuscitation situations for accurately and rapidly demonstrating that the endotracheal tube is in the airway. Quantitative end-tidal CO2 monitoring, though routinely used during anesthesia, is useful for following trends but

Transcutaneous PCO2 monitoring is also very useful for monitoring trends, especially when trying to optimize the ventilatory settings when initiating conventional or high-frequency ventilation. The possible association of PaCO2 levels of less than 30 mm Hg with periventricular leukomalacia in preterm infants demonstrates the need for careful CO2 monitoring.97

Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (NIRS)

NIRS provides a noninvasive assessment of cerebral oxygenation that can be used for following trends in cerebral hemodynamics. Although the algorithms are becoming more refined to account for noncerebral tissue (e.g., scalp, skull), early studies have suggested that cerebral hypoxia is associated with low electrical activity and intracranial hemorrhage, but the impact on longer term neurodevelopmental outcomes has not been determined.98,99

Emerging Wireless Technology

There is enthusiasm for wireless sensor technology under development that can monitor multiple domains such as blood pressure and temperature in addition to the standard ECG and respiratory waveforms.100

### Arterial Sampling

Umbilical artery catheterization should be performed by an experienced clinician and under strict surgical sterile technique. Once the umbilical arteries have been identified by their anatomic characteristics, one of the vessels is dilated with the use of an iris forceps. The catheter is then gently advanced to a predetermined length estimated to place its tip at a high (T6–T8) or low (L3–L4) position. Several methods have been developed to estimate the length of catheter to be inserted to achieve proper placement; however, radiologic or ultrasound confirmation of catheter position is still imperative.

Although umbilical artery catheters still form the basic means of arterial sampling in infants with RDS, the list of catheter-related complications is formidable. The most common visible problem from an umbilical arterial line is blanching or cyanosis of part or all of a distal extremity or the buttock area, resulting either from vasospasm or a thrombotic or embolic incident. This complication may be reduced by high placement of the umbilical artery catheter tip at the level of T6-T8 as opposed to lower placement at L3-L4 just above the aortic bifurcation.

Tyson and associates observed frequent thromboatheromatous complications resulting from umbilical artery catheters in neonates at autopsy.101 Small amounts of heparin added to the continuous infusion appear to reduce the risk of arterial thrombi. Hypertension can result if a renal artery is involved. A rare complication of indwelling arterial umbilical catheters is aneurysmal dilation with dissection of the abdominal aorta, which can be diagnosed by careful ultrasound examination. Retrograde blood flow into the proximal aorta can occur during flushing of radial and umbilical artery lines and result in transient blood pressure elevation; therefore routine flushing should be performed with a small volume over a period of several seconds.

The risk of catheter-associated bloodstream infection increases significantly the longer the catheter remains in place; thus limiting the number of days umbilical catheters remain in place reduces the risk of infection and catheterassociated thrombosis.102 All these complications illustrate the importance of applying careful techniques for the insertion and removal of indwelling arterial catheters and the need for less hazardous methods of monitoring blood gases.

Peripheral arterial catheters, most commonly placed in the radial artery, can also be used for arterial blood sampling. The Allen test should be performed before the insertion of a radial artery line to establish the presence of adequate collateral circulation to the fingers. Similar to umbilical artery catheters, the most common complication of peripheral arterial catheters is blanching or cyanosis of part or all of a distal extremity, resulting from vasospasm or a thromboembolic event.

### Acid-Base Therapy

A change in acid-base balance should prompt a rapid determination of the type of imbalance, respiratory or metabolic, and a thorough evaluation of the cause (see Chapter 96). Acidosis, respiratory or metabolic, especially when coupled with hypoxia, can cause pulmonary arterial vasoconstriction and V/Q abnormalities, decreased cardiac output, or both. Metabolic acidosis out of proportion to the degree of respiratory distress might signify hypoperfusion, sepsis, or IVH. Although sodium bicarbonate was historically used to correct metabolic acidosis, its routine use has not been shown to improve morbidity or mortality among preterm infants and may be associated with increased risk for adverse neonatal outcomes.103 Treatment of metabolic acidosis depends on the underlying etiology (e.g., lactic acidosis, renal tubular acidosis), and therapy should be targeted accordingly.

Respiratory acidosis requires measures to increase minute ventilation, often requiring assisted ventilation, and serial blood gases should be performed to titrate respiratory support. Administration of sodium bicarbonate to infants with respiratory acidosis is not indicated and could further increase the PCO2.

### Cardiovascular Management

Comprehensive management of patients with RDS includes a close evaluation and monitoring of the cardiovascular system. An in-depth understanding of the physical and physiologic interactions between the cardiovascular and pulmonary systems in the mechanically ventilated patient is paramount. For example, after surfactant administration, with the improvement in the mechanical properties of the lungs, an unrecognized overdistension of the lungs by excessive mechanical ventilation support can decrease systemic venous return to the heart and result in decreased cardiac output. Radiographically, a typical squeezed-heart silhouette and flattened diaphragm are found. These findings may also be present in an infant receiving high-frequency ventilation with high mean airway pressure. A thorough clinical evaluation should include sequential assessment of vital


## PDF page 1238

signs, peripheral pulses, capillary refill, and urine output as surrogate markers of adequate cardiac output.

Myocardial dysfunction secondary to ischemia or hypoperfusion may be present and could lead to decreased peripheral perfusion with lactic acidemia and metabolic acidosis. Systemic hypotension is common in the early stages of RDS; thus continuous monitoring of systemic blood pressure by means of an indwelling arterial catheter is of utmost importance in neonates with moderate to severe RDS. Noninvasive intermittent monitoring of systemic blood pressure should be reserved for the mildly affected neonate. Judicious use of crystalloids for intravascular expansion and vasopressor support are often indicated. In patients with persistent hypotension not responsive to fluid therapy or pressors (e.g., dopamine), serum cortisol levels should be measured and treatment with stress doses of hydrocortisone should be considered.

Failure of the ductus arteriosus to close is a common complication in preterm infants with RDS and has been linked to worsening respiratory distress and acidosis. Clinically, the presence of a hemodynamically significant PDA is heralded by a widened pulse pressure, an active precordium, and bounding peripheral pulses. A heart murmur on the left subclavicular area and the back is often present. On the chest radiograph, cardiomegaly might signal the presence of a hemodynamically significant PDA with congestive heart failure. With clinical suspicion, a confirmatory echocardiogram, which should demonstrate evidence of pulmonary overcirculation, such as left atrial enlargement, is usually obtained. The decision whether to proceed with pharmacologic closure of the ductus arteriosus with a prostaglandin synthesis inhibitor such as indomethacin or ibuprofen remains controversial. Fluid restriction, vasopressors, and a loop diuretic (e.g., furosemide) may be indicated for the medical management of a hemodynamically significant PDA with congestive heart failure (see Chapter 75).

### Antibiotics

Neonatal pneumonia (most commonly caused by group B streptococci or gram-negative organisms) can be indistinguishable

from RDS both clinically and radiographically. Such infection usually is acquired around the time of delivery, either through ascending infection or passage through a colonized genital tract. Prenatal features suggestive of neonatal infection include maternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes, and clinical evidence of chorioamnionitis. The suspicion for bacterial infection is raised by a history of maternal genital colonization with group B streptococcus in an inadequately treated mother.

The potentially fulminant course of neonatal pneumonia, especially in preterm infants, and the difficulty in distinguishing it from RDS have led to the widespread practice that infants with significant respiratory distress receive empiric antibiotics.51,52 A more judicious approach to empiric antibiotic use for term and late preterm neonates at risk for earlyonset sepsis has been recommended with development of a sepsis risk calculator.104 Early empiric antibiotic administration can also be limited for preterm infants less than 36 weeks’ gestation who are deemed to be low risk for early-onset sepsis as defined by cesarean delivery without labor or membrane rupture before delivery and no intrapartum concerns for intrauterine infection or nonreassuring fetal status.105

In the neonate, persistent hypotension, metabolic acidosis, early onset of apnea, neutropenia, or neutrophilia accompanied by an increase in immature neutrophils (left shift) are clinical findings suggestive of systemic infection. Nonetheless, the absence of these features does not definitively exclude the diagnosis of sepsis or pneumonia. Ampicillin combined with an aminoglycoside is the most commonly prescribed antibiotic regimen and may be discontinued after 36 hours based on blood culture results and clinical course of the neonate.106,107 Prolonged empiric antibiotic exposure for preterm neonates is associated with increased risks of necrotizing enterocolitis and mortality.108,109

Despite substantial improvements in the treatment of RDS, prevention of preterm birth is still the ultimate goal and will have significant impact on the prevention of RDS. In the meantime, understanding the interactions of the intrauterine environment and genetic determinants of lung development with the pathogenesis of RDS is essential to develop mechanism-specific interventions.

title: Assisted Ventilation and Its Complications

paragraphs.text: 66 Assisted Ventilation and Its Complications
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Mechanical ventilation has been used to treat neonatal respiratory failure for more than a half century. The earliest applications began as modifications of adult ventilators, treating babies of modest size and prematurity by today’s standards. Most devices were timecycled, pressure-limited ventilators. Landmark advances in respiratory care occurred in the 1970s. Antenatal corticosteroids were shown to enhance fetal lung maturity, and transcutaneous oxygen monitoring (TcPo2) taught us much about the vulnerability of the preterm infant. The 1980s brought pulse oximetry and high-frequency ventilation (HFV), which greatly expanded the therapeutic armamentarium. The surfactant replacement era began in the 1990s and was accompanied contemporaneously by patient-triggered ventilation, real-time pulmonary graphics, and a host of pharmacologic agents. Finally, in the new millennium, the microprocessor was incorporated into neonatal ventilators to greatly expand capabilities, monitoring, safety, and efficacy. This technological revolution has extended survival to infants born extremely prematurely as well as those with severe pulmonary disease that was heretofore lethal.
paragraphs.heading: STEVEN M. DONN, GRETCHEN E. STEPANOVICH, AND MOHAMMAD A. ATTAR

paragraphs.text: Mechanical ventilation can now be provided in many permutations. Clinicians can alter target variables, waveforms, cycling mechanisms, and modes simply by adjusting a dial. This has led to the development of disease-specific strategies to deal with the wide spectrum of neonatal respiratory failure. Similar to the speed of change in the computer industry, advances have been rapid and are often introduced into clinical practice without much of an evidence base, causing further confusion and consternation. This chapter reviews the classification and principles of both noninvasive ventilation and mechanical ventilation, with an emphasis on nomenclature and terminology.
paragraphs.heading: STEVEN M. DONN, GRETCHEN E. STEPANOVICH, AND MOHAMMAD A. ATTAR

paragraphs.text: Although mechanical ventilation has been the primary treatment for significant respiratory failure in most
paragraphs.heading: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure and Noninvasive Ventilation

paragraphs.text: preterm babies, there continues to be a concern that it is a major contributor to lung injury. This has led to a growing interest in noninvasive forms of respiratory support in the belief that this will reduce the need for mechanical ventilation and its associated complications. The noninvasive neonatal respiratory support modalities fall into two broad groups: a single level of pressure, such as by continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC), or bilevel positive airway pressure in the form of nasal small pressure difference (bi-level CPAP [BiPAP] or synchronized bilevel CPAP [SiPAP]) or in the form of nasal intermittent positive-pressure ventilation (NIPPV). NIPPV uses a higher pressure difference than BiPAP or SiPAP and can be synchronized or nonsynchronized.
paragraphs.heading: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure and Noninvasive Ventilation

paragraphs.text: When used to treat respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), CPAP prevents collapse of the alveoli at end-expiration, maintaining some degree of alveolar inflation. It thus decreases the work of breathing in accordance with Laplace’s law, in which the pressure required to overcome the collapsing forces generated by surface tension is reduced because the radius of curvature is greater when the alveolus is partially inflated. In this way, CPAP helps to maintain functional residual capacity (FRC) and to facilitate gas exchange. In addition, CPAP helps to maintain upper airway stability by stenting the airway and decreasing obstruction. It may also augment stretch receptors and decrease diaphragmatic fatigue and thus be useful in treating apnea of prematurity, and it has been shown to conserve surfactant at the air-liquid interface within the lung.
paragraphs.heading: Physiology of Continuous Positive Airway Pressure

paragraphs.text: CPAP is a form of continuous distending pressure (CDP), which is defined as the maintenance of increased
paragraphs.heading: Nasal Continuous Positive Airway Pressure

paragraphs.text: transpulmonary pressure during the expiratory phase of respiration. When positive pressure is applied to the airways of spontaneously breathing infants, it is called CPAP, whereas distending pressure applied to a mechanically ventilated infant is called positive end expiratory pressure (PEEP). Thus both CPAP and PEEP are types of CDP (although not technically a form of ventilation) that provide low-pressure distension of the lungs and prevent the collapse of alveoli at the end of expiration. CDP helps to maintain FRC and thus facilitates gas exchange throughout the respiratory cycle. In addition, CPAP supports the breathing of premature infants in a number of other ways, including abolition of upper airway occlusion and decreasing upper airway resistance, enhancement of diaphragmatic tone and activity, improvement in lung compliance, and decrease in lower airway resistance, increase in tidal volume delivery by improving pulmonary compliance, conservation of surfactant at the alveolar surface, and reducing alveolar edema.1
paragraphs.heading: Nasal Continuous Positive Airway Pressure

paragraphs.text: CPAP may be administered invasively through an indwelling endotracheal tube, or it may be provided noninvasively using a variety of different nasal interfaces. This is referred to as nasal CPAP (NCPAP). Although single nasal prongs cut from endotracheal tubes were once used for this purpose, there are now many models made specifically for neonates. Although not without leaks, CPAP interfaces are intended to create and maintain at least a moderate seal to ensure delivery of the desired pressure to the airways.
paragraphs.heading: Nasal Continuous Positive Airway Pressure

paragraphs.text: Short binasal prongs are available in several designs; they have two short tubes that fit snugly in the nares to generate a seal. They may be more effective at preventing the need for reintubation than single nasal prongs,2 though the degree of pressure applied to the nose can result in injuries including erythema or skin breakdown at the tip or bridge of the nose, nasal septum, and upper lip, as well as changes in the shape of the nose or nostrils.3 Similar in concept, the RAM cannula has two large-bore nasal prongs that are intended to occlude 60% to 80% of the nares; studies have reported a 25% to 37% loss in pressure with the use of the RAM cannula compared to other interfaces, so a higher pressure may be needed to achieve the same CDP.4,5 However, it may be useful as a different mechanism of pressure delivery in the setting of facial or nasal injury. NCPAP masks, designed using data from three-dimensional facial scanning, may also be used and can result in excellent fit and seal; studies have shown nasal masks to be at least as effective and result in less facial injury than prongs (Fig. 66.1).6
paragraphs.heading: Nasal Continuous Positive Airway Pressure

paragraphs.text: The clinical use of NCPAP in the neonate falls into one of several groups: (1) early use in resuscitation, (2) management of RDS, (3) post-extubation care, (4) treatment of apnea, and (5) management of mild upper airway obstruction (Box 66.1).
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Indications for Continuous Positive Airway Pressure in Newborns

paragraphs.text: The gas mixture delivered by CPAP is derived from either continuous or variable flow (Box 66.2). Continuous-flow CPAP consists of gas flow generated at a source and directed against the resistance of the expiratory limb of the circuit. Ventilator-derived CPAP and bubble or underwater CPAP are examples of continuous-flow devices, whereas infant flow drivers (flow-driven CPAP) and Benveniste valve CPAP are examples of variable-flow devices.
paragraphs.heading: Methods of Generating Continuous Positive Airway Pressure

paragraphs.text: Flow-driven CPAP is a prototype of variable-flow CPAP. It uses a dedicated flow driver and gas generator with a fluidicflip mechanism to deliver variable-flow CPAP. The principle is the Bernoulli effect, which directs gas flow toward each nostril, and the Coanda effect, which causes the inspiratory flow to flip and leave the generator chamber via the expiratory limb during exhalation. This assists spontaneous breathing and reduces the work of breathing by lowering expiratory resistance and maintaining stable airway pressure. Flow-driven CPAP can be delivered using binasal prongs or a nasal mask.
paragraphs.heading: Methods of Generating Continuous Positive Airway Pressure

paragraphs.text: Underwater bubble continuous positive airway pressure (BCPAP) is a continuous-flow system used since the early 1970s (although initially described by von Reuss in 1914). In this method, the blended gas is heated and humidified and then delivered to the infant through a secured lowresistance interface. The distal end of the expiratory tubing is immersed in water and the CPAP pressure generated is equal to the depth of immersion of the CPAP limb. It has also been proposed that chest vibrations produced by the bubbling may contribute to gas exchange. BCPAP is an effective and inexpensive option to provide respiratory support to premature babies.1
paragraphs.heading: Methods of Generating Continuous Positive Airway Pressure

paragraphs.text: Ventilator-derived CPAP is another conventional way to administer continuous-flow CPAP. The CPAP is increased or decreased by varying the ventilator’s expiratory orifice diameter. The exhalation valve works in conjunction with other controls, such as flow control and pressure transducers, to maintain the CPAP at the desired level.
paragraphs.heading: Methods of Generating Continuous Positive Airway Pressure

paragraphs.text: As premature birth results in surfactant-deficient lungs that are still in the saccular or canalicular stages of development and coupled with a very compliant chest wall, most infants born prematurely need some form of respiratory support soon after birth. Although routine intubation and prophylactic surfactant was once the standard of care, Subramaniam et al. published a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials involving 3123 very low birth weight infants at risk for
paragraphs.heading: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure Immediately After Birth

paragraphs.text: RDS which compared CPAP commenced in the immediate postnatal period to support with mechanical ventilation. They found early CPAP use decreased the need for mechanical ventilation and surfactant treatment and reduced the incidence of BPD at 36 weeks as well as the combined outcome of BPD or death.7 CPAP is now considered to be the optimal first modality of respiratory support in the delivery room.8
paragraphs.heading: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure Immediately After Birth

paragraphs.text: When CPAP is indicated immediately following delivery, the initial pressure applied is typically 5 to 6 cm H2O, though this recommendation is by convention and expert consensus because there are little data to support the optimum initial CPAP to help establish and maintain FRC.8 Although a
paragraphs.heading: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure Immediately After Birth

paragraphs.text: meta-analysis of studies investigating prophylactic intubation and surfactant administration versus CPAP use in the delivery room supports a trial of CPAP, the targeted pressures and interfaces used varied between the studies, resulting in different pressures delivered to the airways and therefore limited conclusions.7 Determination of the ideal starting CPAP is necessary to minimize CPAP failure and to avoid or reduce exposure to positive pressure while also limiting the risk of air leaks. Interestingly, animal studies have supported higher early levels (8–12 cm H2O), yielding improved lung aeration and response to surfactant administration.10 A multicenter randomized controlled trial is currently investigating the application of higher (6–8 cm H2O) versus lower (3–5 cm H2O) initial CPAP, with the primary outcome the need for intubation and mechanical ventilation; results of this study may shape delivery room CPAP strategies (NCT04111770).11
paragraphs.heading: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure Immediately After Birth

paragraphs.text: Another strategy proposed to optimize an infants’ respiratory status during neonatal resuscitation is “sustained inflation.” Sustained inflation (SI) uses pressures of 20 to 30 cm H2O for 5 to 25 seconds during resuscitation to recruit lung airspaces immediately after delivery and to establish FRC. Thus far, studies have shown mixed results of this attempted lung recruitment strategy, with neither a decrease in the rates of death nor BPD.12
paragraphs.heading: Sustained Inflation at Neonatal Resuscitation

paragraphs.text: Higher flow rates delivered via nasal cannula were able to be introduced following the advent of heated, humidified flow
paragraphs.heading: High-Flow Nasal Cannula

paragraphs.text: systems. The flow of gas in excess of 1 L per min, and up to 8 L per min, through a small nasal cannula might provide some degree of CPAP. The physiologic benefits of HFNC are attributed to the washout of the nasopharyngeal dead space, possible reduction of the inspiratory resistance, and provision of a degree of CPAP.13 However, a major problem is that the CPAP level is usually not measurable in clinical practice and has been shown to be highly variable, depending on the degree of leak at the nose and/or mouth. The cannula tips should not be more than 50% of the internal diameter of the nares to allow optimal washout of the dead space.14 This leak around the nasal cannula affects the measured CPAP according to an in vitro study.15 In a study of preterm infants, a flow of 2 L per min generated 9.8 cm H2O pressure (measured by an esophageal balloon) when a nasal cannula (0.3-cm outer diameter) was used, emphasizing the potential risk of the inappropriate size of the nasal cannula.16 Utilization of this technique has increased in many units as a result of the simpler patient interface compared to CPAP, and because the use of HFNC appears to be associated with less nasal trauma.17
paragraphs.heading: High-Flow Nasal Cannula

paragraphs.text: HFNC in preterm infants has been used as a primary modality of support shortly after birth, post-extubation, and for apnea. In a large randomized, controlled noninferiority trial, early (after birth) use of HFNC for primary support for RDS in infants older than 27 weeks was associated with more frequent treatment failures compared to CPAP.18 Furthermore, a meta-analysis (2022) of 10 randomized controlled trials revealed greater treatment failure using HFNC compared to CPAP, although this did not result in a greater rate of reintubation, because CPAP as a rescue therapy was often permitted. Moreover, secondary analysis of these data demonstrated a lower rate of nasal injury associated with the use of HFNC. HFNC may therefore be a reasonable early form of respiratory support to consider in premature infants who do not require invasive therapy.19
paragraphs.heading: High-Flow Nasal Cannula

paragraphs.text: Methods of noninvasive ventilation include NIPPV, synchronized nasal intermittent positive-pressure ventilation (SNIPPV), SiPAP, and neurally adjusted ventilatory assist (NAVA). In all of these modalities, ventilator inflations augment NCPAP, whereas PEEP, peak inspiratory pressure (PIP), respiratory rate, and inspiratory time can all be manipulated. Terminology used to describe NIPPV is not standardized and may be confusing. SiPAP, a form of NIPPV, is also termed biphasic or bilevel NCPAP.20 The proposed mechanisms of action of NIPPV include benefits provided by CPAP, such as avoidance of alveolar collapse and end-inspiration, maintenance of FRC, and increase in tidal volume, improvement in gas exchange, and overall decreased work of breathing.21
paragraphs.heading: Noninvasive Nasal Ventilation

paragraphs.text: NIPPV has been compared to NCPAP for multiple applications: primary support for premature infants with RDS,
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Indications for Nasal Intermittent Positive- Pressure Ventilation

paragraphs.text: prevention of reintubation following extubation, and for treatment of apnea. Interpretation of the results of these studies has been challenging because of the heterogeneity of the devices used and the primary outcomes studied. There have been several meta-analyses to navigate this heterogeneity and direct appropriate conclusions. One such meta-analysis concluded NIPPV to be superior to CPAP in reducing extubation failure and the need for reintubation,22 whereas another concluded that NIPPV was not associated with fewer events attributable to apnea of prematurity than CPAP alone.23 Compared to nonsynchronized NIPPV and NCPAP, superiority has been demonstrated by synchronous NIPPV in terms of decreasing the need for invasive mechanical ventilation in premature infants with RDS, increasing the rate of extubation success, and improving apnea of prematurity. However, at present, the technology to provide SNIPPV is only available in Europe.21
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Indications for Nasal Intermittent Positive- Pressure Ventilation

paragraphs.text: Other forms of NIPPV have been introduced to overcome the limited pneumatic synchrony of noninvasive support caused by air leaks at the patient interface. The noninvasive neurally adjusted ventilator assist (NIV-NAVA) uses a trigger that incorporates electrical activity of the diaphragm (Edi) by placing a probe at the gastroesophageal junction to trigger and proportionally pressure-assist each breath depending on the level of the measured diaphragmatic activity (see Box 66.3). PEEP is provided as in traditional NIPPV. If an infant has “apnea” (with the duration of lack of respiratory effort defined by the clinician, ordered as the “apnea time”), a set back-up PIP and rate take effect. To
paragraphs.heading: New Modes of Nasal Intermittent Positive-Pressure Ventilation

paragraphs.text: that end, CPAP can be provided with a NAVA level of 0 with a back-up rate available should the infant have apnea. One study revealed this strategy to reduce the number of clinically significant bradycardia and desaturation events in premature infants with apnea of prematurity.24 Contraindications to the use of NAVA include total lack of respiratory drive or inability to place the NAVA catheter (such as in an infant with esophageal atresia).
paragraphs.heading: New Modes of Nasal Intermittent Positive-Pressure Ventilation

paragraphs.text: Data from clinical studies using NIV-NAVA are limited, but compared to NIPPV, NAVA appears to have the following advantages: improved infant-ventilator synchrony with decreased wasted infant respiratory effort, decreased auto-triggering, and decreased delivered PIP compared to the clinician-anticipated PIP need. NIV-NAVA may therefore be a more efficient modality of respiratory support than unsynchronized NIPPV. As appropriate gas exchange may occur at lower peak airway pressures, NAVA use has been proposed to result in decreased cumulative lung barotrauma.25,26 However, several small RCTs comparing NIV- NAVA to NCPAP as a primary form of respiratory support or following extubation have not shown a difference in the short-term outcomes.21 Currently, NIV-NAVA is the only form of synchronized NIPPV available in the United States.
paragraphs.heading: New Modes of Nasal Intermittent Positive-Pressure Ventilation

paragraphs.text: The use of high-frequency ventilators with a nasal interface (noninvasive high-frequency ventilation [NIHFV]) theoretically eliminates the need for synchrony by delivering high-frequency, small tidal volume ventilation. There are ventilators dedicated to NIHFV, although high-frequency ventilators intended for invasive use may have similar efficacy.27 A meta-analysis of eight small RCTs published in 2019 suggested that NIHFV may increase carbon dioxide elimination and decrease the risk of reintubation, although the studies were inadequately powered to make conclusions on other outcomes such as the incidence of intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), BPD, or death.28 Two RCTs are currently underway to further investigate the use of NIHFV, both as a primary mode of support (NCT03099694) and following extubation (NCT03181958).
paragraphs.heading: New Modes of Nasal Intermittent Positive-Pressure Ventilation

paragraphs.text: Intubation with surfactant administration, followed by extubation (INSURE, INtubation-SURfactant-Extubation) is a method of surfactant administration for premature infants supported with CPAP. It is typically indicated in infants demonstrating normal spontaneous respiratory effort with an FiO2 greater than 0.3 without other indications for invasive mechanical ventilation. A meta-analysis of studies involving INSURE failure and the need for subsequent mechanical ventilation found extremely low birth weight, lower gestational age (especially <26 weeks), and RDS severity to be factors increasing the risk of subsequent need for intubation and mechanical ventilation.29
paragraphs.heading: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure and Surfactant Administration

paragraphs.text: Less invasive surfactant administration (LISA) describes administering surfactant to spontaneously breathing premature infants through a small catheter or feeding tube,
paragraphs.heading: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure and Surfactant Administration

paragraphs.text: without traditional endotracheal intubation, and thus avoidance of invasive positive pressure ventilation. Several studies have investigated whether INSURE or LISA change important long-term outcomes compared to CPAP with or without rescue intubation and mechanical ventilation; multiple meta-analyses demonstrated a reduction in death and/or BPD in premature infants who had received LISA. Recent data demonstrate a reduced incidence of BPD in survivors when CPAP was supported by minimally invasive surfactant therapy.29a Other less invasive forms of surfactant administration currently being studied include administration via laryngeal mask airway (LMA) directly into the pharynx, and via nebulization.30 Although nebulization seems appealing as a truly noninvasive method of surfactant administration, it has been met with many practical challenges, including difficulties with aerosolizing surfactant, long administration times, and poor surfactant delivery, with inadequate and uneven distribution into the airways and distal lung tissue.8,31
paragraphs.heading: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure and Surfactant Administration

paragraphs.text: Despite its widespread use, there are a number of potential complications from CPAP.32 Nasal prongs rarely fit tightly into the nares, resulting in gas leak and the inability to maintain a stable baseline pressure. The set CPAP level is rarely maintained in the pharynx. The best way to reduce nasal leak is to ensure that the prongs are of sufficient size to snugly fit the nostrils without making them blanch. A chin strap can be used to reduce leaks around the mouth, but the setup is cumbersome and not simple to use in practice (Fig. 66.2).
paragraphs.heading: Practical Problems and Complications of Nasal Continuous Positive Airway Pressure

paragraphs.text: Nasal trauma is a common problem with NCPAP, especially in very premature infants. Proposed interventions include alternating binasal prongs with a nasal mask and using a nasal barrier dressing.33 Excessive CPAP may contribute to lung overinflation and increase the risk of air leaks. CPAP can increase intrathoracic pressure and decrease venous return and cardiac output. If set too high, CPAP may actually lead to impaired gas exchange and resultant carbon dioxide retention. Gastric distension is a commonly encountered problem and may be at least partially alleviated by the placement of an orogastric tube to vent the gastric air.
paragraphs.heading: Practical Problems and Complications of Nasal Continuous Positive Airway Pressure

paragraphs.text: Neonates can be extubated to any form of noninvasive respiratory support, but it can be challenging to choose which will optimize extubation success and minimize the likelihood of reintubation. A meta-analysis published in 2020 compared multiple methods for post-extubation non-invasive pulmonary support, with the primary outcome of need for reintubation and mechanical ventilation. Synchronized NIPPV resulted in the greatest likelihood of extubation success, whereas the use of continuous flow CPAP had the greatest risk of need for reintubation; BiPAP, variable flow CPAP, and HFNC had comparable, intermediate efficacies.
paragraphs.heading: Post-Extubation Respiratory Support

paragraphs.text: Secondary analyses were notable for post-extubation HFNC to be the least likely support to result in air leak or nasal trauma, and S-NIPPV use to be associated with the lowest rate of BPD.34 Although traditional S-NIPPV is not available in the United States, NIV-NAVA may be used for this purpose; an RCT published in 2020 found post-extubation NIV-NAVA to be superior to NIPPV in need for reintubation within 120 hours following extubation.26
paragraphs.heading: Post-Extubation Respiratory Support

paragraphs.text: Discontinuation of CPAP can be done in several ways, including abrupt discontinuation of respiratory support, a gradual pressure wean, a stepdown strategy with transition to HFNC or low-flow nasal cannula, and “interval” training, in which CPAP is held for longer periods of time each day. A meta-analysis published in 2020 found gradual weaning to be the most effective way to keep an infant off CPAP altogether although, on average, CPAP was discontinued at a later post-menstrual age. The stepdown strategy kept infants off CPAP but resulted in a longer duration of oxygen therapy, and in one study where infants received 1.0 FiO2 at 0.2 LPM, there was an increased incidence of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP).35
paragraphs.heading: Discontinuing Continuous Positive Airway Pressure

paragraphs.text: Prompted by animal studies showing improved lung growth induced by CPAP usage, an RCT published in 2020 compared infants with an average corrected gestational age of 32 weeks who were clinically ready for CPAP cessation to either have CPAP discontinued or continued for an additional 2 weeks. Pulmonary function tests were performed at the time of randomization, after the 2-week period, and before discharge. The infants randomized to the extended
paragraphs.heading: Discontinuing Continuous Positive Airway Pressure

paragraphs.text: treatment arm had a significantly greater increase in FRC after 2 weeks, as well as the time of discharge.36 Considering the potential benefit of CPAP for lung growth, some NICUs now continue CPAP through a minimum prespecified post-menstrual age, typically between 32 and 34 weeks.
paragraphs.heading: Discontinuing Continuous Positive Airway Pressure

paragraphs.text: The use of CPAP immediately after birth with selective surfactant treatment has generally replaced the practice of prophylactic surfactant replacement in preterm infants. This change in practice was influenced by evidence from multiple randomized trials that used CPAP for initial stabilization and demonstrated a decreased risk of death or BPD compared to prophylactic surfactant therapy.7,37 Initial support with CPAP in spontaneously breathing infants has been further supported by strategies of surfactant administration that minimize exposure to intubation and mechanical ventilation, including INSURE and LISA. Furthermore, there has been an increase in the use of other noninvasive forms of pulmonary support such as NIPPV or NAVA, in an attempt to limit mechanical ventilation duration and to decrease the risk of lung injury. In a large, multicenter epidemiologic study in the United States comparing four discrete 3-year epochs (2003–2005, 2006–2008, 2009–2001, 2012–2014), the rate of ICD-9 coded RDS increased over the time period studied. From beginning to end, there was an increase in the use of noninvasive respiratory support, especially within the first 24 hours of life, and a concomitant decrease in all-cause mortality as well as the combined outcome of BPD and/or death.38 Furthermore, a single-center study from the Netherlands reported a significant decrease in the combined rate of death or neurodevelopmental
paragraphs.heading: Long-Term Outcomes

paragraphs.text: impairment at 24 months following the institution of a policy to limit mechanical ventilation and to liberalize the use of respiratory stimulants.39 Therefore, at this time, the most prudent strategy for respiratory support in premature infants appears to be a trial of NCPAP in the delivery room, with intubation reserved for infants with apnea or inadequate ventilation/oxygenation despite noninvasive support, selective surfactant use (administered noninvasively when possible), early use of NIPPV, and gradual de-escalation of support following improvement in RDS.
paragraphs.heading: Long-Term Outcomes

paragraphs.text: Mechanical ventilation is intended to take over or assist the work of breathing in babies who are unable to support effective pulmonary gas exchange on their own. The causes for respiratory insufficiency may be pulmonary, such as RDS or meconium aspiration syndrome; extrapulmonary, such as airway obstruction or compression; or neurologic, such as central apnea or neuromuscular disease. Respiratory failure may also accompany other systemic derangements, including sepsis or shock.
paragraphs.heading: Indications for Assisted Ventilation

paragraphs.text: Indications for assisted ventilation may be thought of as absolute and relative (Box 66.4). Absolute indications include entities encountered in the delivery room, such as the failure to establish spontaneous breathing despite positive-pressure mask ventilation, persistent bradycardia despite positive-pressure ventilation by mask, or the presence of major anomalies such as diaphragmatic hernia or severe hydrops fetalis, where there is a high likelihood of immediate respiratory failure. In the neonatal intensive care unit, sudden respiratory or cardiac collapse with apnea and bradycardia unresponsive to mask ventilation and massive pulmonary hemorrhage are two examples of absolute indications.40
paragraphs.heading: Indications for Assisted Ventilation

paragraphs.text: Relative indications may be based on clinical judgment, such as intubating very preterm babies for early surfactant administration, or they may be based on an objective assessment of impaired gas exchange as evidenced by abnormal
paragraphs.heading: Indications for Assisted Ventilation

paragraphs.text: blood gases. Various recommendations exist to define respiratory failure severe enough to warrant assisted ventilation. In general, the easiest of these is the so-called “50-50 rule,” whereby hypoxemia is defined as a failure to maintain an arterial oxygen tension of 50 mm Hg with a fraction of inspired oxygen of 0.5 or greater, and hypercapnia is defined as an arterial carbon dioxide tension greater than 50 mm Hg. Some have suggested that the arterial carbon dioxide tension criterion should be coupled with a pH value such as less than 7.25. Additional relative indications for assisted ventilation include the stabilization of infants who are at risk for sudden deterioration, such as preterm infants with apnea unresponsive to CPAP or methylxanthines; severe systemic illness, such as sepsis; the need to maintain airway patency, such as meconium aspiration syndrome or tracheobronchomalacia; the need to maintain control of carbon dioxide elimination, such as in persistent pulmonary hypertension; or following severe hypoxic-ischemic brain injury; or for the management of drug-induced respiratory depression, such as maternal magnesium sulfate therapy, general anesthetics, or analgesics.
paragraphs.heading: Indications for Assisted Ventilation

paragraphs.text: The two major factors responsible for oxygenating the blood are the fraction of inspired oxygen and the pressure to which the lung is exposed (Box 66.5). The role of inspired oxygen can be understood from the alveolar gas equation (see Chapter 71). Oxygenation is also proportional to mean airway pressure (mean Paw), which is the average pressure applied to the lungs during the respiratory cycle and is represented by the area under the curve for the pressure versus time waveform. Inflation of the lung recruits more airspaces and exposes more of the pulmonary surface area to alveolar gas. Thus those factors that increase mean airway pressure will, up to a certain point, improve oxygenation (Fig. 66.3).41
paragraphs.heading: Oxygenation

paragraphs.text: The most direct impact comes from PEEP because it is applied throughout the respiratory cycle. PEEP is the baseline pressure, the lowest level to which airway pressure falls. It is used to take advantage of Laplace’s law by maintaining some degree of alveolar inflation at end-expiration, thus reducing the pressure necessary to further inflate the alveolus during inspiration. There is a 1:1 relationship between PEEP and mean Paw; for every 1 cm H2O increase in PEEP,
paragraphs.heading: Oxygenation

paragraphs.text: there is a 1 cm H2O increase in mean Paw. Excessive PEEP is potentially harmful. It may over-distend the alveoli, increasing the risk of air leaks; it may impede venous return and cardiac output; and it may decrease the amplitude, leading to carbon dioxide retention (see Complications of Continuous Positive Airway Pressure).42
paragraphs.heading: Oxygenation

paragraphs.text: PIP will also increase the mean Paw, but this will be proportional to the inspiratory time (TI) or duration of positive pressure. PIP is the driving pressure and also establishes the upper limit of the amplitude. Excessive PIP poses many of the same risks as excessive PEEP, including hyperinflation (over-distension) of the lung, leading to excessive stretch of the alveolar units (baro- or volutrauma); high intrathoracic pressure with decreased venous return and cardiac output; and air leaks. Additionally, if PIP and/or PEEP is/are inadequate, there may be alveolar atelectasis and resultant damage to the lung from cyclic opening and closing of lung units, a process referred to as atelectrauma.43
paragraphs.heading: Oxygenation

paragraphs.text: Mean Paw is also affected by TI and the duration of positive pressure. As TI increases, the mean Paw will also increase if all other parameters are held constant. Similarly, on machines where the inspiratory:expiratory (I:E) ratio is adjusted, mean Paw will increase as the inspiratory phase is lengthened or the expiratory phase is shortened. If the TI is too long, however, there is an increased risk of gas trapping, inadvertent PEEP, and air leak. If it is too short, there may be inadequate lung expansion, air hunger, and patientventilator asynchrony, leading to inefficient gas exchange.
paragraphs.heading: Oxygenation

paragraphs.text: Changes in the ventilator rate will have a slight effect on mean Paw. At faster rates, the mean Paw will rise, because there are more breaths delivered per minute, and the cumulative area under the curve per unit of time increases. Rapid rates may result in incomplete emptying of the lung, with gas trapping, inadvertent PEEP, and lung hyperinflation.
paragraphs.heading: Oxygenation

paragraphs.text: Finally, circuit gas flow will also impact mean Paw. If the TI is held constant, more volume (and hence higher pressure) will be delivered as flow is increased. If the flow is set too high, turbulence, incomplete emptying of the lung, inadvertent PEEP, and hyperinflation may occur.44 If the
paragraphs.heading: Oxygenation

paragraphs.text: flow is set too low, air hunger and asynchrony will result. The injurious effects of improper airway flow have been referred to as rheotrauma.45
paragraphs.heading: Oxygenation

paragraphs.text: Ventilation refers to carbon dioxide removal. Its two primary determinants are tidal volume and frequency (Box 66.6).46 Tidal volume is determined by the amplitude of the mechanical breath, or the difference between the peak (PIP) and baseline (PEEP) pressures. During conventional ventilation, carbon dioxide removal is the product of tidal volume and frequency. Clinically, this is usually expressed as the minute volume, or mL/kg/min, of exhaled gas. It is also important to consider the contribution of spontaneous breathing to minute ventilation (which is not always measured), and that pulmonary blood flow is also a key element in carbon dioxide removal and oxygen absorption. During HFV, carbon dioxide removal is the product of frequency and approximately the square of the tidal volume.47 Thus small changes in amplitude may have a profound effect on arterial carbon dioxide tension (see later).
paragraphs.heading: Ventilation

paragraphs.text: Control of ventilation during patient-triggered ventilation requires an understanding of the physiology of gas exchange. Most newborns will have intact chemoreceptors and will seek to maintain normocapnia. This is accomplished by adjustments in minute ventilation. Thus, if the clinician sets the amplitude too low, the baby will compensate by increasing the spontaneous (and hence, triggered) breathing rate. Conversely, if the amplitude is set too high, the infant’s hypercapnic drive will be abolished and the baby will “ride” the ventilator rate.48
paragraphs.heading: Ventilation

paragraphs.text: Carbon dioxide tension is affected by minute ventilation, which in turn is the product of tidal volume and frequency during conventional mechanical (tidal) ventilation (CMV). Of these two parameters, adjustment in tidal volume (by adjusting the amplitude) has a more predictable effect on minute ventilation.42
paragraphs.heading: Ventilation

paragraphs.text: The use of mechanical ventilators requires an understanding of the respiratory time constant. The respiratory time
paragraphs.heading: Time Constant

paragraphs.text: constant refers to the time required to allow pressure and volume equilibration of the lung. Mathematically, the time constant is the product of compliance and resistance. When the lung is stiff (low compliance) and has limited expansibility, such as occurs during RDS, it takes less time to fill and empty than it does at higher compliance. This pattern is clinically illustrated by observing the spontaneous breathing pattern of an infant with RDS not requiring assisted ventilation. Early on, when compliance is poor, the baby will breathe rapidly and take shallow breaths. As the disease process remits, compliance improves, and the baby breathes more slowly and takes deeper breaths.
paragraphs.heading: Time Constant

paragraphs.text: If expiratory time is set at one time constant, approximately 63% of the change in pressure or volume will occur; if it is lengthened to three time constants, changeover will increase to 95%, and at a five time constant-length, it will approach 99%. Thus setting the expiratory time at less than three to five times the length of the time constant will increase the risk of gas trapping and potentially inadvertent PEEP and alveolar rupture.49
paragraphs.heading: Time Constant

paragraphs.text: Over the past two decades, newer mechanical ventilation devices have been introduced into neonatal practice, and these devices are based on sound physiologic principles. The proliferation of devices and techniques has caused confusion about nomenclature and classification, which are frequently device-specific. In a general sense, mechanical ventilators can be divided into two groups: those that deliver physiologic tidal volumes, often referred to as conventional mechanical ventilators, and those that deliver tidal volumes that are less than physiologic dead space, referred to as highfrequency devices, which will be discussed below.
paragraphs.heading: Classification of Mechanical Ventilators

paragraphs.text: Among conventional mechanical ventilators, it is advisable to use a simple hierarchical classification to describe devices according to the variables they use (Fig. 66.4). These variables fall into two categories, those that control the type of ventilation (called ventilatory modalities) and those that determine the breath type (called ventilatory modes).46 Chatburn, El-Khatib, and Mireles-Cabodevila proposed a taxonomy for mechanical ventilation. This system uses the defining of the control variable, breath sequence, targeting
paragraphs.heading: Classification of Mechanical Ventilators

paragraphs.text: scheme, and mode classification to describe what is happening. This scheme, if widely adopted, could eliminate the widespread inconsistencies in nomenclature and terminology that presently exist among different devices and manufacturers.50
paragraphs.heading: Classification of Mechanical Ventilators

paragraphs.text: At any one time, the ventilator can control only a single variable—time, pressure, or volume. However, the same ventilatory device can operate using different control variables at different times. Ventilatory modalities can target either pressure or volume as the primary variable. Because volume is the integral of flow, volume- and flow-controlled ventilation are actually the same. When pressure is controlled, volume will fluctuate according to the compliance of the lungs, and conversely, when volume is controlled, pressure will fluctuate as a function of compliance.46,50
paragraphs.heading: Control Variables (Ventilatory Modalities)

paragraphs.text: The mechanical breaths delivered by the ventilator have four phases, and more than one variable can be used to design the type of breath to suit the underlying lung mechanics and/or pathophysiology. The first of these is the variable that initiates or triggers inspiration (trigger). The second is the variable that is used to limit the inspiratory gas flow (limit). The third is the variable that changes inspiration to expiration and vice versa (cycle). The final is the variable that maintains the baseline pressure during expiration (PEEP).46
paragraphs.heading: Phase Variables (Ventilatory Modes)

paragraphs.text: A number of variables can be used to trigger a breath. In the past, most neonatal ventilators used time to start inspiration. The clinician programmed either a set inspiratory time or ventilator rate and inspiratory:expiratory ratio, and the exhalation valve would open and close according to the lapse of time. Other triggering variables have been introduced, allowing for the synchronization of the onset of mechanical inflations to spontaneous breathing. The clinician can set a threshold flow or pressure, above which the ventilator initiates a mechanical breath. These variables are used as a surrogate for spontaneous effort and include pressure or flow, with time as a backup. Most present ventilators use flow-triggering devices for newborns because this
paragraphs.heading: Phase Variables (Ventilatory Modes)

paragraphs.text: requires significantly less effort to trigger than pressure and is thus associated with less work of breathing.45
paragraphs.heading: Phase Variables (Ventilatory Modes)

paragraphs.text: The limit variable restricts the inspiratory flow to a preset value. Traditionally, pressure has been used as a limit variable, but volume and flow are other variables that can limit inspiratory flow. True volume limitation is difficult to achieve because cuffed endotracheal tubes are seldom used in newborns, and there is almost always some degree of volume loss around the endotracheal tube.
paragraphs.heading: Phase Variables (Ventilatory Modes)

paragraphs.text: The cycling mechanism is the variable used to end inspiration. Most neonatal ventilators, including high-frequency ventilators, are time-cycled, but changes in airway flow may also be used to end the inspiratory phase.51,52 Termination of inspiration occurs when decelerating inspiratory flow has reached a preset percentage of peak inspiratory flow. At this point, the exhalation valve opens and expiration begins. Flow cycling more accurately mimics the physiologic breathing pattern and allows for the mechanical breath to be fully synchronized to the spontaneous breath during both inspiration and expiration and to be controlled by the baby. Changes in transthoracic electrical impedance that occur during spontaneous respiration can also be used to generate a trigger signal.53 Thus triggering during both active inspiration and active expiration can achieve total synchronous breathing between the baby and the ventilator.
paragraphs.heading: Phase Variables (Ventilatory Modes)

paragraphs.text: An addition to neonatal ventilation has been NAVA. This modality uses the electrical activity of the diaphragm to trigger, cycle, and control the level of support (see Box 66.3).54 Although there is a paucity of clinical data, the method appears promising but will require further investigation.
paragraphs.heading: Phase Variables (Ventilatory Modes)

paragraphs.text: Using different phase variables, which are interchangeable, a variety of ventilatory modes can be generated that are applicable to both pressure- and volume-controlled modalities. The commonly used ventilatory modes are intermittent mandatory ventilation (IMV), synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation (SIMV), assist/control (A/C) ventilation, and pressure support ventilation (PSV).55 Fig. 66.5 is a graphic comparison of IMV and SIMV demonstrating the effects of asynchronous ventilation.
paragraphs.heading: Modes of Ventilation

paragraphs.text: IMV delivers mechanical breaths at a rate set by the clinician. Inflations are provided at regular intervals and are not influenced by spontaneous breathing. The baby may breathe spontaneously with, between, or even against the mechanical breath, supported only by PEEP, and patient-ventilator asynchrony can be a major problem, resulting in a wide variability in delivered tidal volume. In the past, efforts to reduce asynchrony have included increasing the rate to override the spontaneous drive and “capture” the baby, generous use of sedatives, and in some instances, the administration of skeletal muscle relaxants. Virtually all forms of synchronized ventilation have been shown to be superior to IMV,
paragraphs.heading: Intermittent Mandatory Ventilation

paragraphs.text: and the latter should only be used when there is a complete cessation of spontaneous breathing.
paragraphs.heading: Intermittent Mandatory Ventilation

paragraphs.text: SIMV is a mode in which the onset of mechanical breaths is synchronized to the onset of spontaneous breaths if the patient begins to breathe within a timing window. As a result, mechanical breaths are not delivered as regularly as in IMV but vary slightly according to the baby’s own breathing pattern. In between the mechanical breaths, the baby may breathe spontaneously, but again, the spontaneous breaths are supported only by PEEP unless pressure support is used (see later). In time-cycled SIMV, synchrony between mechanical and spontaneous breath occurs only during inspiration, because the inspiratory time for both mechanical and spontaneous breaths may be different. This discrepancy can be offset by using flow cycling, where synchrony occurs during both inspiration and expiration.
paragraphs.heading: Synchronized Intermittent Mandatory Ventilation

paragraphs.text: In the A/C mode, the ventilator delivers a mechanical breath each time the patient’s inspiratory effort exceeds the preset threshold (trigger) criterion. When the patient triggers the ventilator to deliver a mechanical breath, the breath is said to be assisted. This mode also provides the safety of a guaranteed minimal mechanical breath rate (the control rate, set by the operator) in case no patient effort occurs or none is detected. A/C breaths can be time-cycled or flow-cycled. During A/C ventilation, as long as the baby breathes above the control rate, lowering the control rate will have no effect on the total respiratory rate, and thus the reduction of pressure should be the primary weaning strategy (see later).52,56
paragraphs.heading: Assist/Control Ventilation

paragraphs.text: PSV was developed to help intubated patients overcome the imposed work of breathing created by the narrow lumen (high resistance) endotracheal tube, circuit dead space, and demand valve (if one is being used). It is, however, a spontaneous breath mode. Spontaneous breaths that exceed the trigger threshold result in the delivery of additional inspiratory pressure to a limit set by the clinician. These breaths are flow-cycled, but for safety purposes, they may be time limited. Most commonly, PSV is used in conjunction with SIMV to support spontaneous breathing between SIMV breaths with something more substantial than PEEP (Fig. 66.6). If the pressure limit of the PSV breath is adjusted to provide a full tidal volume breath, it is referred to as PSmax. If the pressure applied is just enough to overcome the imposed work of breathing, it is referred to as PSmin. PSV is still a relatively new neonatal mode, but it is gaining acceptance.57,58 It is most commonly used as a weaning strategy with a low rate SIMV.59
paragraphs.heading: Pressure Support Ventilation

paragraphs.text: Proportional assist ventilation (PAV) is a fully adaptive modality that attempts to provide a breath in total synchrony with patient breathing. The ventilator will also
paragraphs.heading: Proportional Assist Ventilation

paragraphs.text: adapt the inspiratory flow to provide a breath waveform that matches what the patient is attempting to do. To achieve this, the ventilator continuously measures the respiratory effort of the baby, proportionally adjusting pressure and flow. Unfortunately, there remains a paucity of clinical data.
paragraphs.heading: Proportional Assist Ventilation

paragraphs.text: Pressure-targeted modalities are characterized by limiting the amount of pressure that can be delivered during inspiration. The clinician sets the maximum pressure, and the ventilator will not exceed this level. The volume of gas delivered to the baby will vary according to lung compliance and the degree of synchronization between the baby and the ventilator. If compliance is low, less volume will be delivered than if compliance is high.60–62 In IMV, tidal volume will fluctuate depending on whether the baby is breathing with the ventilator or against it.
paragraphs.heading: Pressure-Targeted Modalities

paragraphs.text: There are three main pressure-targeted modalities: pressure-limited ventilation (PLV), pressure control ventilation (PCV), and PSV, which is also a mode. All three are pressure-limited. Some devices allow both PLV and PCV to be time- or flow- cycled. Traditional PSV is flow-cycled but time limited. Inspiratory flow during PLV is continuous and is set by the clinician. During both PCV and PSV, inspiratory flow is variable and is related to lung mechanics and patient effort. It accelerates rapidly early in inspiration then decelerates quickly, producing a characteristic waveform.63 Some devices allow modulation of the accelerating portion by offering an adjustable rise time. This enables “fine tuning” of flow to avoid pressure overshoot or flow
paragraphs.heading: Pressure-Targeted Modalities

paragraphs.text: starvation and helps to achieve optimal hysteresis of the pressure-volume loop.
paragraphs.heading: Pressure-Targeted Modalities

paragraphs.text: PLV has been used to treat neonatal respiratory failure for a half century. It was developed from adult ventilators by adding continuous flow to the bias circuit to allow the baby to have a fresh source of gas from which to breathe between mechanical inflations. It is relatively easy to use and was presumed to be safe because the delivered inspiratory pressure could be limited, thus reducing the risks associated with barotrauma. Although the inspiratory pressure is very consistent on a breath-to-breath basis, the delivered tidal volume will fluctuate, as noted above. In the post-surfactant era, lung compliance may vary considerably following the administration of surfactant, and unless the clinician is vigilant, the subsequent increase in tidal volume can lead to overexpansion and volutrauma.
paragraphs.heading: Pressure-Targeted Modalities

paragraphs.text: PCV was more recently introduced into neonatal ventilators. It differs from PLV primarily in the manner in which flow is regulated. PCV produces a waveform that accelerates rapidly and then quickly decelerates. A rapid rise in flow early in inspiration leads to earlier pressurization of the ventilator circuit, and delivery of gas to the baby occurs early in inspiration. Intuitively, this should be beneficial in disease states characterized by homogeneity and the need for a higher opening pressure, such as in early RDS. Variable flow should be advantageous when resistance is high, such as when a small endotracheal tube is used. The relative novelty of PCV has thus far precluded adequate direct comparison to PLV.
paragraphs.heading: Pressure-Targeted Modalities

paragraphs.text: Both PLV and PCV are used as mandatory modes (IMV, SIMV, or A/C). PSV is solely a spontaneous mode; that is, it is applied only to the spontaneous breaths the baby takes between mandatory mechanical inflations to support spontaneous breathing and overcome the imposed work of breathing created by the narrow lumen endotracheal tube, circuit dead space, and the demand valve (if one is used). Because it is patient-triggered and flow-cycled, it is completely synchronized to the baby’s own breathing; thus the baby controls the rate and the inspiratory time. The clinician sets the pressure level to augment spontaneous breathing. PSV can be used in conjunction with SIMV or, in patients with reliable respiratory drive, it may be used as a primary mode.64 There is an evolving body of evidence that PSV is both safe and efficacious.42,65–68 Still to-be-determined is
paragraphs.heading: Pressure-Targeted Modalities

paragraphs.text: the best way to apply PSV as a weaning tool. Table 66.1 compares the characteristics of pressure-targeted modalities.
paragraphs.heading: Pressure-Targeted Modalities

paragraphs.text: Broadly speaking, volume-targeted ventilation can be provided in several ways. Volume-controlled ventilation (VCV) targets a set tidal volume, which is delivered irrespective of lung compliance or the pressure required to deliver it (pressure may be limited for safety reasons). Hybrid ventilators are essentially pressure-targeted but aim to deliver the tidal volume within a set range using computer-controlled feedback mechanisms. Finally, standard pressure-targeted ventilation can function in a quasi–volume-targeted capacity if strict and vigilant attention is paid to volume delivery.69
paragraphs.heading: Volume-Targeted Modalities

paragraphs.text: The first ventilator designed specifically for volume-targeted ventilation in infants was the Bourns LS 104-150 of the 1970s, which was modified from an adult ventilator. Because of a multiplicity of problems, including a high trigger sensitivity, long response times, lack of continuous flow during spontaneous breathing, limited rate capability, poor circuit design, and the inability to measure small tidal volumes, this device (and VCV) fell out of favor in the early 1980s. Technologic advances in the 1990s enabled the reintroduction of VCV to neonatal and pediatric patient populations. The new ventilators incorporate sophisticated devices to trigger, deliver, and accurately measure the tiny tidal volumes required by infants weighing as little as 500 g.
paragraphs.heading: Volume-Targeted Modalities

paragraphs.text: VCV for newborns differs from “adult” volume-cycled ventilation, where inspiration is terminated and the machine is cycled into expiration when the specific target tidal volume has been delivered. However, the use of uncuffed endotracheal tubes in newborns results in some degree of gas leak around the tube and precludes the ability to cycle based on a true delivered tidal volume. Thus volume cycling is a misnomer in neonatal ventilation, and the terms volumecontrolled, volume-targeted, or volume-limited better describe this modality. Many current ventilators provide the option of using a leak compensation algorithm to at least partially offset this problem.
paragraphs.heading: Volume-Targeted Modalities

paragraphs.text: During VCV, there is also a discrepancy between the volume of gas leaving the ventilator and that reaching the proximal airway, which results from compression of gas within
paragraphs.heading: Volume-Targeted Modalities

paragraphs.text: the ventilator circuit. This is referred to as the compressible volume loss, which is greatest when pulmonary compliance is lowest. The use of semi-rigid circuits may help to offset this. Compressible volume is also affected by humidification. It is therefore critical that the delivered tidal volume is measured as close to the proximal airway as possible (i.e., at the patient wye piece).
paragraphs.heading: Volume-Targeted Modalities

paragraphs.text: The principal feature of VCV is that it delivers the set tidal volume irrespective of the underlying lung compliance by automatically adjusting the PIP (Fig. 66.7). Another important feature of VCV that differentiates it from PLV is the way that gas is delivered during the inspiratory phase.62,70 In traditional VCV, a square flow waveform is generated, and peak volume and pressure delivery are achieved at the end of inspiration (Fig. 66.8). These may be thought of as “back end” loaded breaths. In comparison, in PLV the gas flow pattern accelerates rapidly, then decelerates, resulting in the achievement of peak pressure and volume delivery early in inspiration. This produces a “front end” loaded breath. Because these are very different, certain disease states might be more amenable to one form than the other.
paragraphs.heading: Volume-Targeted Modalities

paragraphs.text: Detractors of VCV have argued that, unlike the limited pressure used in PLV, VCV may use a high inflation pressure to deliver the preset volume in cases of decreased compliance. This anxiety in the past arose because of the perceived risks of barotrauma and its consequences associated with high PIP. However, it has since become clear that it is not necessarily the high pressure but rather the excessive tidal volume (volutrauma) that causes lung injury,71 and thus attention to controlling tidal volume delivery has become an essential part of neonatal ventilation. It should also be realized that high peak pressure associated with fixed-flow delivery in VCV is a reflection of proximal airway pressure rather than alveolar pressure. When the compliance of the patient’s lungs improves (increases), the ventilator generates
paragraphs.heading: Volume-Targeted Modalities

paragraphs.text: less pressure to deliver the same tidal volume, thus leading to an automatic reduction of the PIP. It is also a misconception that PLV of infants is superior to VCV because it maintains a constant airway pressure in the presence of leaks around uncuffed endotracheal tubes. The reasoning seems to be that constant pressure implies that the delivered volume remains constant, but this is not true, because leaks around the uncuffed endotracheal tube also occur with PLV. Some VCV devices provide a way to compensate for leaks by adding additional flow to the circuit to automatically maintain a stable baseline pressure.
paragraphs.heading: Volume-Targeted Modalities

paragraphs.text: Like PLV, VCV can be provided as IMV, SIMV, and A/C ventilation. It may also be combined with PSV during SIMV and even A/C in some devices.72
paragraphs.heading: Volume-Targeted Modalities

paragraphs.text: Some newer devices use a blended approach to volume targeting. They are primarily pressure-targeted ventilators but involve computerized servo-controlled ventilation, wherein a ventilator algorithm adjusts the rise and fall of pressure to produce tidal volume delivery within a set range. These include volume guarantee (VG), pressure-regulated volume control (PRVC), and volume-assured pressure support (VAPS). These hybrid forms try to achieve the same goal, the optimization of tidal volume delivery, although each has a different mechanism. Clinicians must familiarize themselves with the specific features of individual machines to maximize safety and efficacy.
paragraphs.heading: Volume-Targeted Modalities

paragraphs.text: VG ventilation is a commonly used form of volume targeting.73 It is a dual-loop, synchronized, pressure-targeted modality of ventilation with microprocessor-based adjustments in pressure to ensure adequate tidal volume delivery. The operator chooses a target tidal volume and selects a pressure limit up to which the inspiratory pressure (the working pressure) may be adjusted. The machine uses the exhaled tidal volume of the previous breath as a reference to adjust the working pressure up or down over the next breath to achieve the target volume. The autofeedback mechanism is an improvement in design but has some limitations. For example, if adjustments to PIP are made in small increments to avoid overcompensation and are based on the exhaled tidal volumes, the delivered tidal volume may not compensate for large breath-to-breath fluctuations in the presence of large leaks.
