Usually a combination of multiple parameters such as activated clotting time (ACT), antifactor Xa assay, and partial thromboplastin times (PTTs), among others, are used.151
paragraphs.heading: Basic Techniques

paragraphs.text: When the infant is placed on ECMO, ventilation and airway oxygen support are reduced to avoid further ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI) while maintaining functional residual capacity (FRC) and allowing for pulmonary
paragraphs.heading: Basic Techniques

paragraphs.text: hygiene. Wide practice variation exists with regard to ventilator settings used for “lung rest” during bypass support, and more research is needed to provide evidence-based best-practice guidance for rest settings during ECMO. A retrospective cohort study using the ELSO database found that the use of conventional ventilation compared to highfrequency ventilation and the use of a mid-PEEP (7–9 cmH2O) or high-PEEP (10–12 cmH2O) strategy compared to a low-PEEP strategy (4–6 cmH2O) were associated with a shorter time on ECMO.154 Currently, ELSO recommends using a PIP of 15 to 10 cmH2O, PEEP of 5 to 10 cmH2O and lower with air leak, a rate of 12 to 20 breaths per minute, inspiratory time of 0.5 to 1 seconds, and fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) of 0.21 to 0.3.151 As lung function improves and pulmonary hypertension abates, the mixed venous saturation and PaO2 improve, and weaning from ECMO support can commence. When the infant has reached minimal ECMO support and is able to be adequately supported with acceptable ventilator settings, the patient can be decannulated. Upon removal of the cannulas, the vessels are often ligated; however, in shorter ECMO runs (typically <7 days), a surgeon may consider vessel reconstruction. Although studies have demonstrated that reconstructing the right common carotid does not pose an increased risk of embolic events and neurodevelopmental impairment, there is no consensus on the utility of carotid reconstruction.155-157
paragraphs.heading: Basic Techniques

paragraphs.text: Although VV ECMO is the predominant mode of ECMO for respiratory support reported in the ELSO database, VA ECMO support continues to be the most frequently used mode for neonatal respiratory ECMO. In 2020, only 11% of neonatal respiratory ECMO cases were VV.150 The reason for this is likely multifactorial and includes size constraints, recent lack of VV cannulas, and EMCO team comfort with VV ECMO. Advantages of VV bypass include avoidance of carotid artery cannulation, which is highly desirable, and maintenance of normal pulmonary blood flow. The major disadvantage is that, unlike VA bypass, VV ECMO does not provide cardiac support. The severity of cardiac dysfunction in ECMO-sick patients is highly variable, and often the heart function will improve when adequate oxygen content is restored on VV ECMO. Survival on VV ECMO is no worse than VA, and in some reports may even be better than VA ECMO. However, these retrospective studies are limited by selection bias, as VA patients tend to be smaller and sicker when going on ECMO.158 Only 10% to 12% of VV cases require conversion from VV to VA support should the patient’s cardiac output prove to be subpar.150 Therefore VV bypass should always be the first consideration in infants whose primary diagnosis is pulmonary disease.
paragraphs.heading: Basic Techniques

paragraphs.text: The cumulative experience of many ECMO centers has resulted in the establishment of guidelines that are currently used to decide whether ECMO support is appropriate.151
paragraphs.heading: Criteria for Patient Selection

paragraphs.text: These are described in Box 67.5, and other clarifications follow.
paragraphs.heading: Criteria for Patient Selection

paragraphs.text: Preterm newborns with respiratory failure carry a higher risk for intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) compared with term infants at baseline, and this risk is heightened with systemic anticoagulation required during ECMO support. Furthermore, changes in cerebral blood flow patterns associated with cardiopulmonary bypass can also place the immature brain at increased risk for bleeding.
paragraphs.heading: Criteria for Patient Selection

paragraphs.text: In the early ECMO trials, premature infants less than 35 weeks’ gestation had an 89% incidence of spontaneous ICH associated with heparinization.159 Subsequent studies (all retrospective) revisiting this issue reported improvement in outcome but confirmed increased rates of ICH in preterm infants. When compared to term infants, late preterm infants had higher mortality and increased morbidities, including ICH.160 A study comparing ECMO outcome at 34 weeks’ gestation to that of preterms between 29 and 33 weeks’ gestation, reported survival was greater at 34 weeks’ gestation (58%) compared to 48% survival in the <34-week cohort. The rate of ICH peaked at 44% at 31 weeks and decreased incrementally to 17% by 34 weeks.161 Although it is generally accepted that ECMO should be used for those infants of 34 weeks’ gestation or greater, an earlier gestational age could be considered for ECMO after discussion with the team and the family with the understanding of associated risks.
paragraphs.heading: Criteria for Patient Selection

paragraphs.text: Severe IVH and uncontrollable bleeding are also contraindications for ECMO. Severe IVH (grades III and IV) are likely to expand when the infant is anticoagulated for ECMO and worsen long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes.
paragraphs.heading: Criteria for Patient Selection

paragraphs.text: Infants in severe respiratory failure must have an echocardiogram to rule out congenital heart disease as the underlying cause for refractory hypoxemia. In some instances, the degree of hypoxemia is not easily explained based on the heart lesion alone (e.g., in a newborn with an atrioventricular canal complicated by meconium aspiration or sepsis). In such an instance, ECMO can provide cardiovascular support to stabilize the patient until the reversible component of the lung disease is no longer an issue. Similarly, an infant with suspected cyanotic congenital heart disease
paragraphs.heading: Criteria for Patient Selection

paragraphs.text: may present with profound cyanosis and cardiogenic shock despite the use of prostaglandins and inotropes. Preoperative ECMO can stabilize such infants who are believed to have reparable cardiac defects but who are deemed to be poor surgical candidates by virtue of their clinical instability.
paragraphs.heading: Criteria for Patient Selection

paragraphs.text: ECMO is an invasive procedure used for infants with hypoxic respiratory failure unresponsive to optimal conventional therapy. In the early days of ECMO (1975–1995), infants with an 80% mortality risk based on retrospective data at the time were considered candidates for ECMO. Over the past 30 years, however, much has changed in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) management of infants with hypoxic respiratory failure, including ventilator management and adjuvant therapies for pulmonary hypertension, as well as the choices of optimal blood gas parameters. Hyperventilation, alkali therapy, and muscle paralysis are no longer recommended, as serious side effects are associated with each of these interventions. It is therefore difficult to know what might constitute an 80% mortality risk in the ECMO-sick newborn today. Box 67.6 offers guidelines utilized by ECMO intensivists for deciding when bypass is likely needed. One of the most difficult decisions faced by neonatologists who are not in an ECMO center is when to refer a newborn in respiratory failure to an ECMO center. Because of the volatile nature of PPHN, the risk of sudden cardiorespiratory decompensation and death remains high in any infant not responding favorably to conventional supportive measures. Likewise, transporting these unstable babies is problematic, with one series reporting 25% mortality among ECMO transports before inhaled NO was available.162,163
paragraphs.heading: Criteria for Patient Selection

paragraphs.text: It is essential that ECMO referrals be made as expeditiously as possible and preferably before the baby reaches ECMO-eligible criteria. Early and frequent telephone contact with an ECMO physician to discuss the details of each case can help establish transport criteria agreeable to both parties. Expert opinion has stated that, when the oxygenation index is greater than 25, a non-ECMO center should
paragraphs.heading: Criteria for Patient Selection

paragraphs.text: at least be in discussion with an ECMO center to determine the optimal time to transport the infant.
paragraphs.heading: Criteria for Patient Selection

paragraphs.text: CDH is the most common indication for neonates with hypoxic respiratory failure to receive ECMO support. ECMO gives these infants time for their pulmonary hypertension and/or cardiac dysfunction to improve, but only about half of the infants with CDH placed on ECMO survive.150,164 There has been wide variability across centers as to when to use ECMO in the CDH population, which infants are candidates, when the CDH should be repaired, and the mode of ECMO that should be used. Recently, ELSO provided a guideline for the use of ECMO in the CDH population which is summarized below.
paragraphs.heading: The Dilemma of Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia

paragraphs.text: ECMO is reserved for patients with CDH who are failing optimal medical treatment, including a strategy of pressure-limited (gentle) ventilation to minimize ventilatorassociated lung injury and optimizing the medical management of their pulmonary hypertension. The initiation criteria should be the same as for neonates without CDH. Consensus indications based on recent expert opinion are summarized in Box 67.7. Contraindications are similar to those for patients without CDH. In addition, infants with
paragraphs.heading: The Dilemma of Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia

paragraphs.text: CDH+ (co-existing additional major anomalies, chromosomal aberrations, or syndromes) have a significantly lower survival than infants with isolated CDH, and it may be reasonable not to offer ECMO to those patients.67 The survival among CDH infants treated with ECMO over the last 5 years is 56%, which has not changed much over time and reflects the highest mortality among neonatal etiologies of respiratory failure reported in the ELSO Registry.150 In 1991, survival in this cohort was 64%. The reason for this decline is not entirely clear, but it is thought that potentially those infants requiring ECMO are sicker with higher mortality and lengths of ECMO runs.165
paragraphs.heading: The Dilemma of Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia

paragraphs.text: Which mode of ECMO to use for CDH patients and when to repair the CDH remain topics of controversy. Proponents of VV ECMO comment on the improved delivery of oxygen to the lungs and decreased neurologic complications. Studies have demonstrated that CDH patients can be successfully managed on VV ECMO; however, no survival benefit has been shown.164
paragraphs.heading: The Dilemma of Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia

paragraphs.text: The optimum timing for repair of the hernia in ECMOsick patients remains unclear, however, because of variability among centers and lack of convincing data on how best to proceed. The current guidelines recommend it for infants who can be decannulated or weaned off ECMO, but there may be benefit to delaying repair until after the infant is off ECMO. For patients with a severe CDH phenotype, very early repair while on ECMO may afford a survival advantage because non-repairs will be avoided, complication rates may be lower than with late repair, and early correction of the mechanical contributors to pulmonary and vascular pathophysiology may facilitate weaning off support.30 What is important is that the decision takes into consideration the challenges associated with operating on ECMO and potential issues from delaying repair until the infant is near to being and hopefully able to be decannulated.
paragraphs.heading: The Dilemma of Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia

paragraphs.text: The true impact of ECMO on survival and long-term outcome in newborns with CDH is difficult to ascertain. Infants with CDH who receive ECMO support appear to have a higher risk and greater severity of neurologic morbidity compared to those who have not received ECMO or those who received ECMO for other causes of hypoxemic respiratory failure.166–168 Among neonatal ECMO patients who survived to hospital discharge, patients with CDH had a 74% 5-year survival compared to 98% survival in patients with MAS.169 Most deaths in the CDH cohort were caused by chronic lung disease.170 It is difficult to differentiate whether these outcomes are associated with the underlying disease process or their need for ECMO support. All survivors should have multidisciplinary follow-up that includes neurodevelopmental assessments.
paragraphs.heading: The Dilemma of Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia

paragraphs.text: More than 33,000 infants have been treated for respiratory failure in more than 400 ECMO centers worldwide for an overall survival to discharge of 73%.150 The outcome
paragraphs.heading: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Follow-Up

paragraphs.text: of these children compares favorably with that of term and near-term infants surviving severe respiratory compromise and PPHN with conventional management.
paragraphs.heading: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Follow-Up

paragraphs.text: A valid criticism of early ECMO follow-up studies was the lack of proper control data—that is, the outcome of infants with severe respiratory compromise who were managed during the ECMO era with conventional treatment alone. Such control data are essential for distinguishing morbid outcome caused by the underlying disease process and NICU management of respiratory failure, or both, from the morbidity that is secondary to the ECMO procedure itself.
paragraphs.heading: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Follow-Up

paragraphs.text: Single-center, early outcome studies found that patients treated with ECMO had higher survival, less chronic lung disease, and less reactive airway disease when compared to the neonates managed with conventional medical therapy. There were no differences between neurodevelopmental outcomes at 8 and 20 months of age.171 In another study at 12 to 30 months of age, the mean developmental scores of ECMO survivors were similar to those for infants who survived without ECMO. Neuroimaging abnormalities or diagnosis of bronchopulmonary dysplasia each independently predicted adverse neurodevelopmental outcome regardless of treatment strategies used in the NICU.172 The UK Collaborative ECMO Trial Group found that there was no difference in cognitive function, with 76% of the children having a cognitive level within normal range, and there were similar rates of learning difficulties between the groups, notably difficulties with spatial and processing tasks at 7 years of age. Similar to the other early studies, children who were treated conventionally continued to have higher respiratory morbidities, including wheezing and inhaler use. Conventionally treated children also had more behavioral problems, typically hyperactivity. These results are equivalent to one additional child surviving without severe disability for every four to five children referred for ECMO.173
paragraphs.heading: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Follow-Up

paragraphs.text: The majority of more recent long-term neurodevelopmental follow-up of ECMO survivors has been reported from a nationwide prospective follow-up program in The Netherlands. The severity of critical illness and the underlying disease that resulted in cardiorespiratory failure and the need for ECMO are the primary determinants of adverse long-term outcomes.174 About 25% of neonatal ECMO survivors will have neuropsychologic deficits that may have potential impact on academic performance in later life. After serial longitudinal cognitive testing at 2, 5, and 8 years, the Dutch group found that intelligence was stable over time; however, more of the survivors required special education supports compared to a normal Dutch reference cohort. Increased behavior and attention issues were also cited. There were also problems with visual and spatial information processing and attention/concentration issues.167 The group also reported that a small cohort of the adolescent ECMO survivors were at risk of verbal, visualspatial, and working memory problems.175 Motor delays also become apparent with time. At 5, 8, and 12 years of age, motor function was normal in 74%, 75%, and 41%,
paragraphs.heading: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Follow-Up

paragraphs.text: respectively. The significant decline in motor scores at 12 years was most pronounced in children with chronic lung disease and CDH. Exercise capacity (based on the Bruce treadmill protocol) also worsened significantly over time.176 The significance in such decline in motor performance and exercise capacity is troublesome and points to a serious need for long-term follow-up of these children not only throughout their pediatric years but also into adulthood. In the United States, unfortunately, we do not have neurodevelopmental follow-up to compare to the UK and Netherlands programs. In 2016, a survey assessment of a cohort of 142 adult (>18 years, born before 1994) survivors of neonatal ECMO in the United States was published. Although this self-reported outcome was largely favorable, this study represented only a small fraction (<2%) of neonatal ECMO survivors who have reached adulthood.177 Finding these patients, particularly those not receiving routine medical care, will prove formidable.
paragraphs.heading: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Follow-Up

paragraphs.text: Thoracic cage and skeletal abnormalities are a rare group of conditions that can cause respiratory distress by restriction of thoracic volume. They include a number of entities incompatible with life or life limiting. In this group of diseases are those with hypoplasia of the ribs and thorax, including asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy (Jeune syndrome), thanatophoric dysplasia, achondrogenesis, homozygous achondroplasia, osteogenesis imperfecta type II, Ellis-van Creveld syndrome (chondroectodermal dysplasia), hypophosphatasia, spondylothoracic dysostosis, and cerebrocostomandibular syndrome.178
paragraphs.heading: Rib Cage Abnormalities

paragraphs.text: Respiratory distress caused by structural abnormalities of the chest wall should be readily apparent. However, marked narrowing of the thorax can result in what appears to be a distended abdomen, and the respiratory problem can be erroneously attributed to an intra-abdominal pathologic condition. The presence of other associated anomalies (for example, short-limbed dwarfism), together with close observation of respiratory excursions, examination of the bony thorax, and measurement of the circumference of the chest, establishes the diagnosis even before a review is made of the thoracic and skeletal radiographs.
paragraphs.heading: Rib Cage Abnormalities

paragraphs.text: With structural abnormalities of the chest wall, asphyxia and respiratory distress are present from birth. The infants are cyanotic and tachypneic and demonstrate severe retractions and, characteristically, a virtually immobile chest. Diaphragmatic excursions are prominent; thus respiration appears entirely abdominal. Pulmonary hypoplasia accompanies the thoracic dystrophy, and radiographically the lungs can appear airless.
paragraphs.heading: Rib Cage Abnormalities

paragraphs.text: Infants with asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy, thanatophoric dwarfism, achondrogenesis, homozygous achondroplasia, or Ellis-van Creveld syndrome have thoracic radiographs with a squared-off appearance, and the posterior rib arcs all appear to be the same length. The clavicles
paragraphs.heading: Rib Cage Abnormalities

paragraphs.text: appear very high, and the diaphragms are low (Fig. 67.11). The transverse diameter of the thorax can appear diminished in comparison with the vertical diameter. On a lateral view, the ribs are very short and can appear clubbed anteriorly. The anteroposterior diameter of the thorax is decreased. The lungs may be poorly aerated, infiltrates are often present, and the heart might appear enlarged. Differentiating among the various syndromes of thoracic cage and skeletal abnormalities usually is accomplished by means of a skeletal survey. Multiple fractures and bone demineralization are characteristic of osteogenesis imperfecta and hypophosphatasia. Definitive diagnosis is made with the help of radiologists and geneticists, and there is growing knowledge of the genetic mutations involved in the various skeletal dysplasias.178
paragraphs.heading: Rib Cage Abnormalities

paragraphs.text: Jeune syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive skeletal dysplasia with multiorgan involvement. The genetic etiologies are very heterogeneous and result from autosomal mutations in one of at least 17 genes, including DYNC2H1, DYNC2LI1, TTC21B, IFT140, and IFT80 genes, among others. These genes encode proteins involved in the formation or function of cilia, which play a role in the signaling pathways important for the growth, proliferation, and differentiation of cells during the formation and maintenance of cartilage and bone.178 The hallmarks of asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy are extreme constriction and narrowing of the thorax and pulmonary hypoplasia, short ribs, and variable shortening of the limbs with abnormalities of the bones of the pelvis and extremities. The thorax is relatively immobile, and the ribs are horizontally directed and short with bulbous ends. In addition to the thoracic abnormalities, the infants have trident iliac bones with a double-notch appearance of the acetabulum. Associated anomalies include polydactyly and deformed teeth. Renal abnormalities may be present, and renal failure can occur later in life.
paragraphs.heading: Asphyxiating Thoracic Dystrophy (Jeune Syndrome)

paragraphs.text: These infants usually present with respiratory distress and recurrent respiratory infections during the neonatal period. It has been reported that 60% to 80% of cases are
paragraphs.heading: Asphyxiating Thoracic Dystrophy (Jeune Syndrome)

paragraphs.text: fatal in early childhood, but if they survive the early years, the patients’ respiratory problems tend to decrease with age, and a subset of children affected by this disorder can have long-term survival.179
paragraphs.heading: Asphyxiating Thoracic Dystrophy (Jeune Syndrome)

paragraphs.text: Thanatophoric dysplasia (see Chapter 29) is the most common form of lethal skeletal dysplasia. It is caused by de novo mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) gene and is an autosomal dominant condition.180 Appearance at birth is characteristic and includes striking micromelia in association with a normal trunk, a large head with frontal bossing, and a narrow thorax. The radiographic findings include severely flattened vertebral bodies with markedly widened intervertebral disk spaces, small iliac rings, and flaring of the metaphyses of the long bones. There is a high incidence of polyhydramnios, and the infants often present in the breech position.
paragraphs.heading: Thanatophoric Dysplasia

paragraphs.text: Infants present at birth with severe pulmonary insufficiency, requiring mechanical ventilation and intensive neonatal care. Immediate and accurate diagnosis is important in guiding medical decisions about continuation of support. The majority of infants die in the neonatal period, but a recent report from Japan has described survival beyond the neonatal period with ventilator management.181
paragraphs.heading: Thanatophoric Dysplasia

paragraphs.text: Phrenic nerve injury with paralysis of the diaphragm is an unusual cause of neonatal respiratory distress. It is usually associated with birth trauma and presents in association with an ipsilateral brachial plexus injury. When occurring on the right, Horner syndrome can coexist; however, injury can also occur after cardiovascular or thoracic surgeries or following invasive procedures. The injuries are observed in infants who are large for gestational age, especially following shoulder dystocia or difficult breech extractions. Fractures of the humerus or clavicle are often observed. The nerve roots of C3 to C5 are stretched, with lateral hyperextension and traction on the neck. Recovery depends on the degree of injury; avulsion results in permanent injury, and diaphragmatic eventration secondary to muscle atrophy ensues. Lesser injury or edema of the nerve roots results in a spectrum of respiratory symptoms that can include cyanosis, weak cry, tachypnea, or apnea. On radiographic examination, the involved hemidiaphragm is elevated, and atelectasis is usually observed on that side. The heart and mediastinum are shifted away from the affected side (Fig. 67.12). Ultrasonographic or fluoroscopic evaluation should be diagnostic and reveal paradoxic movement of the diaphragm with elevation during inspiration and descent with expiration. Congenital eventration of the diaphragm also results in an elevated hemidiaphragm with paradoxical movement. Secondary pneumonia is the major source of morbidity and mortality. Treatment of phrenic nerve palsy initially is supportive
paragraphs.heading: Phrenic Nerve Injury

paragraphs.text: and, in the absence of avulsion, spontaneous resolution is to be expected. Surgical plication of the diaphragm might be required for selected infants with avulsion.182,183
paragraphs.heading: Phrenic Nerve Injury

paragraphs.text: Key Points
paragraphs.heading: Phrenic Nerve Injury

paragraphs.text: • Not all respiratory distress after birth is due to respiratory
paragraphs.heading: Phrenic Nerve Injury

paragraphs.text: distress syndrome. • The degree of respiratory distress due to these other causes
paragraphs.heading: Phrenic Nerve Injury

paragraphs.text: is dependent on the timing of the insult and the degree to which it causes pulmonary hypoplasia and decreased pulmonary vascular growth.
paragraphs.heading: Phrenic Nerve Injury

# 67. Spectrum of Neonatal Respiratory Disorders
> Source attribution: [Source credits](../../SOURCE_CREDITS.md).

67 Spectrum of Neonatal Respiratory Disorders

### MOIRA A. CROWLEY

Multiple pathophysiologic mechanisms can present with pulmonary manifestations in term and preterm infants. The clinical picture is most commonly dominated by respiratory distress, which presents as tachypnea, grunting, flaring, retractions, cyanosis, and hypoxemia. However, apnea and hypoventilation are also common. In preterm infants, these manifestations are commonly associated with respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), as discussed in Chapter 65. Nonpulmonary etiologies of respiratory distress include thermal instability, circulatory problems, cardiac disease, neuromuscular disorders, sepsis, anemia or polycythemia, and methemoglobinemia (Box 67.1). This chapter presents an overview of the many other respiratory disorders that can affect preterm and term infants. It also discusses treatment strategies for these respiratory disorders including extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) for severe cardiorespiratory failure resulting from some of these diagnoses.

### Developmental Diseases

### Pulmonary Underdevelopment: Pulmonary Agenesis, Aplasia, and Hypoplasia

Abnormal lung development varies from mild hypoplasia to agenesis of a single lobe or whole lung. Agenesis of the lung is a rare congenital anomaly defined as the total absence of pulmonary parenchyma, its supporting vasculature, and bronchi after the bifurcation.1 Complete agenesis of the lung is usually unilateral (90%), although dysgenesis of the other lung has been reported.2 Pulmonary aplasia is a subset of pulmonary agenesis, defined by the presence of a blindending, rudimentary bronchus without associated lung parenchyma or pulmonary vasculature.3 It has been hypothesized that pulmonary agenesis is vascular in origin, most likely resulting from a disruption of the dorsal aortic arch blood flow during the fourth week of gestation. Although lung agenesis can be an isolated finding, in as many as 50% to 76% cases it is associated with other congenital malformations, including urogenital, vertebral, cardiac, and

gastrointestinal, as well as malformations of the first and second branchial arch derivatives and radial ray defects.4 As a result, pulmonary agenesis has been considered a subset of the VACTERL (vertebral, anal atresia, cardiac defect, tracheo-esophageal fistula, renal anomalies, limb anomalies) sequence and, when involving the ipsilateral branchial arch or radial ray malformations, Goldenhar syndrome.2

Diagnosis is confirmed on antenatal ultrasound by the presence of mediastinal shift in the absence of a diaphragmatic hernia or lung mass. Antenatal echocardiogram reveals total absence of the pulmonary artery or one of its branches on the affected side. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) examination can confirm the diagnosis, evaluate the size of the remaining lung, and evaluate the presence of other congenital malformations. After delivery, diagnosis of infants with unilateral pulmonary agenesis can be suspected by decreased breath sounds and displacement of the mediastinum to the affected side. Some breath sounds, however, may be audible over the affected side if a portion of normal lung, which usually has undergone compensatory hypertrophy, has herniated across the midline into the affected hemithorax. The radiographic appearance of a radiopaque hemithorax helps confirm the diagnosis, and accompanying vertebral defects are not uncommon (Fig. 67.1). Treatment is largely supportive, and the prognosis depends on the presence or absence of other anomalies; those with isolated pulmonary agenesis have better survival.4

Pulmonary hypoplasia is the result of deficient or incomplete development of the lung parenchyma leading to decreased number of distal airways, alveoli, and associated pulmonary vessels. It can be classified as either primary, caused by intrinsic failure of normal lung development, or secondary, caused by a multitude of different pathologic processes that interfere with normal lung development. The pathophysiology of secondary pulmonary hypoplasia includes (1) oligohydramnios secondary to renal malformations, prolonged early amniotic fluid leak, placental abnormalities, or intrauterine growth restriction; (2) spaceoccupying lesions compressing the lungs and preventing normal growth as seen with congenital diaphragmatic

Diagnosis of pulmonary hypoplasia is made pathologically by measuring the lung-to-body ratio; however, this truly only captures those with lethal pulmonary hypoplasia. Methods to diagnose pulmonary hypoplasia antenatally in those fetuses at risk for developing pulmonary hypoplasia because of associated findings have been reported and include the use of prenatal ultrasound techniques and fetal MRI. Ultrasound measurement techniques include thoracic circumference (TC) corrected for gestational age or femur length, TC:abdominal circumference ratio, and thoracic:heart area. These techniques, however, measure the thoracic wall rather than lung parenchyma itself and have inadequate positive and negative predictive values to be a reliable tool for predicting pulmonary hypoplasia in isolation. More recently, measurement of lung volume using three-dimensional ultrasound has been reported, but, even in the most experienced hands, 8% to 48% of cases did not have a calculable lung volume on at least one side.5 MRI has shown promise in predicting pulmonary hypoplasia, especially in the setting of CDH, but seems to be no better for other causes of pulmonary hypoplasia.5 Pathologic examination of the hypoplastic lung can show a low ratio of lung to body weight, low DNA content, or decreased radial alveolar count. Peripheral bronchioles are decreased in number, as are the pulmonary arterioles, which often exhibit hypertrophy of medial smooth muscle, a predisposition to persistent pulmonary hypertension.

Secondary pulmonary hypoplasia is most commonly encountered in oligohydramnios and CDH. Survival of

infants with pulmonary hypoplasia depends on the degree to which lung growth is restricted and the underlying cause of hypoplasia. It is not uncommon for these patients to present with severe respiratory distress associated with bilateral pneumothoraces, as well as hypoxia from both fixed and reactive pulmonary hypertension. Pulmonary hypoplasia is present in up to 33% of patients with oligohydramnios and can be associated with a high mortality rate (55%–100%) depending on the severity of hypoplasia6 (see Chapter 23). Patients with pulmonary hypoplasia secondary to prolonged premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) starting in the second trimester have been shown to have a better prognosis than initially expected. Survival and intact survival are dependent upon gestational age at the time of rupture and the gestational age of the infant at delivery, with longer latency periods portending a higher survival rate.7 In some retrospective studies, survival rates were as high as near 90%.7,8 The improved survival in recent times is thought to be secondary to improved obstetrical (prenatal steroids) and modern neonatal therapies. However, among survivors, over half have severe morbidities, with 10% to 63% having bronchopulmonary dysplasia.7 Both human and animal studies have shown that some of these infants who present with early severe respiratory failure consistent with pulmonary hypoplasia may benefit from inhaled nitric oxide (iNO).9,10 Supportive therapy with gentle ventilation is the mainstay of therapy. Serial amnioinfusion has been proposed as a potential therapy to mitigate the effects of oligohydramnios/anhydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia caused by both PPROM and renal abnormalities. When used in the setting of PPROM, there is no improved survival.11 When used for renal dysplasia, there have been a few case reports of long-term success, but overall survival remains low.12 At this time, no randomized controlled trials exist to prove its efficacy in either case.

### Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia

CDH results from a developmental defect during the formation of the diaphragm that permits abdominal contents to herniate into the thoracic cavity, leading to varying degrees of pulmonary hypoplasia, lung compression, and pulmonary hypertension. In some cases, the herniated viscera are covered with a membranous sac. Defects of the diaphragm are classified according to the anatomic region of the diaphragm that is defective. The most common defect involves the posterolateral diaphragm (Bochdalek) and accounts for 70% of diaphragmatic hernias. Anterior diaphragm defects (Morgagni) account for 25% to 30% of diaphragmatic hernias, and central diaphragmatic defects are rare, occurring in 2% to 5% of cases.13 The incidence of CDH is one in 2000 to 3000 live births, and it occurs most commonly on the left side (85%), whereas bilateral hernias are rare (1%) and usually fatal. In CDH, there are fewer alveoli that have thickened septae, resulting in markedly diminished

alveolar airspace and gas-exchange surface area. Vascular development parallels that of the airways, thus there also are reduced number of vessels, adventitial thickening, medial muscle hyperplasia, and peripheral extension of the muscular layer into the smaller intra-acinary arterioles, resulting in a fixed increase in pulmonary vascular resistance. Both lungs are affected, the ipsilateral one more than the contralateral one. After delivery, these morphologic changes compromise effective gas exchange, resulting in respiratory failure and pulmonary hypertension.

The pathogenesis of CDH is not fully understood. Traditionally, it was thought that the pulmonary hypoplasia associated with CDH was caused by compression of the lungs by the herniated abdominal viscera during early development. However, as our understanding of the pathophysiology has grown, it has been demonstrated that pulmonary development has already been disturbed prior to diaphragm development and before compression from abdominal organs can occur. Thus the dual hit hypothesis has emerged to explain the severe pulmonary hypoplasia often seen in this condition.14 The first insult affects both lungs before diaphragm development is complete. The second insult affects the growth of the ipsilateral lung because of compression of that lung by the herniated viscera. The origin of the diaphragmatic defect lies in the disruption of the mesenchymal substrata of the pleuroperitoneal folds, which form the scaffold for the eventual migration of muscular precursor cells into the nascent diaphragm. In human embryology, this would point to a defect as early as 4 to 5 weeks’ gestation, long before the formation of the “muscular” diaphragm.15

The pathogenesis of CDH and associated pulmonary hypoplasia is slowly being unraveled in part due to animal models, which have confirmed that developmental regulation of the lung and diaphragm are controlled by some of the same genes. The nitrofen mouse model has proposed that CDH is a result of a disturbance in the retinoic acid pathway. A defect in the retinoid signaling pathway, specifically, inhibition of retinal dehydrogenase-2 (Raldh2), has been proposed as the likely etiology of the embryonic disruption resulting in CDH. Lower retinol levels have been found in infants with CDH compared to non-CDH.15 However, despite convincing animal data, the use of nitrofen and retinol has not been linked to human CDH.13

The retinoic acid pathway is not the only pathway thought to be involved in the pathogenesis of CDH. Lung development requires the interplay of several growth factor and signaling pathways, and disruption along any of these pathways has been shown to lead to CDH through animal models. Recent advances in genetic diagnostic modalities along with the use of knockout mice have shed more light on specific genes that may be involved in the pathogenesis of CDH. Several genes, including Wilms tumor 1 (Wt-1) and members of the sonic hedgehog (Shh) pathway (Shh, Gli2, Gli3), have been implicated in CDH. Wt-1-, Gli2-, and Gli3-null mice have all been shown to have diaphragmatic defects.

Shh has been demonstrated to be downregulated in human hypoplastic lungs of CDH patients. Another growth factor– related gene, platelet-derived growth factor (PDGFRα), was demonstrated to play a role in posterolateral diaphragm and lung development, but the mice knockouts demonstrate features of Fryns syndrome; thus PDGFRα may be involved in nonisolated CDH. As advances are made in molecular genetics, more candidate genes are being discovered.16

CDH either is an isolated defect or can be associated with other congenital anomalies, including cardiac, urogenital, chromosomal, and musculoskeletal. Most reports estimate that 40% to 60% of patients with CDH have non-hernia– related anomalies, designated CDH+.17 Overall, a genetic etiology for CDH is identified in about 30% of affected infants, most often in the CDH+ group, but this percentage is increasing as access to and improvements in genetic testing evolve.18 Genetic abnormalities that have been associated with CDH include aneuploidy, copy number variants, and single gene mutations (see Box 67.2). Genetic evaluation should be a standard element of CDH evaluation. As our understanding of the pathophysiology of CDH improves, this can lead to novel therapeutic approaches. Genetic evaluation can also provide information regarding recurrence risk and aide in prenatal consultation and prognosticating.

For all the reasons aforementioned, it is important to adequately evaluate for associated malformations in patients with CDH as well as performing genetic testing antenatally, if not then postnatally. About half of CDH cases are diagnosed antenatally. Antenatal diagnosis has been associated with a poor prognosis, but the data suggest that infants with a prenatal diagnosis have a better chance of survival if they are born in a tertiary center with reported survival rates of isolated, operative CDH cases approaching 70% to 90%.19 Several antenatal parameters have been evaluated for their ability to predict survival and morbidity in cases of isolated CDH. Most of these predictors rely on the indirect

assessment of the size of the contralateral lung as a proxy for pulmonary hypoplasia. Methods used include lung area to head circumference ratio (LHR) between 22 and 28 weeks’ gestation, the presence of the liver in the chest (which has been thought to be most predictive), and estimated fetal lung volume by MRI.20–24 Because it has been reported that the LHR increases exponentially with gestational age, some experts have advocated that the LHR should be corrected for gestational age and have used an observed:expected (O/E) LHR based on the LHR in the CDH patient compared with what is considered normal for that gestational age.25 When using the O/E LHR in conjunction with liver position, survival has been predicted as26: • Fetuses with O/E LHR less than 15% have extreme pul-

monary hypoplasia, with virtually no survivors. • Fetuses with O/E LHR between 15% and 25% have

severe pulmonary hypoplasia, with a predicted survival of 20%. (Those with liver completely down in the abdomen fare better than those with liver herniated up into the chest.) • Fetuses with O/E LHR between 36% and 45% and liver

in the chest have moderate pulmonary hypoplasia, with expected survival between 30% and 60%. • Fetuses with O/E LHR between 36% and 45% with liver

down and those with an O/E LHR greater than 45% have mild hypoplasia and are likely to survive (>75%). More recently, authors have focused on the use of MRI to evaluate total lung volume (TLV), observed to expected (O/E) TLV, and the percentage of liver herniated into the chest (%LH) to predict survival and/or need for ECMO support. When using O/E TLV, thresholds of <25%, 25% to 35%, and >35% were predictive of 0% to 25%, 25% to 69%, and 75% to 89% survival, respectively.27 Also, when combining O/E TLV and %LH, severe CDH defined as an O/E TLV <32% and %LH >21% carried a 50% mortality; mild CDH, which included those with an O/E TLV >32% and %LH <21%, had only an 8% risk of mortality.28

The ability of these parameters to predict survival has not been consistent. This is mostly secondary to the small number of patients in each series, challenges in measurement consistency among operators, lack of correlation with actual and functional lung volume and pulmonary vasculature size, inconsistent measures for survival or morbidity, and differences in postnatal management and survival. Nevertheless, these tools give clinicians some data to use when counseling families faced with the diagnosis of CDH.

The clinical presentation of patients with CDH can vary from asymptomatic in mild cases to severe respiratory failure at birth. Diagnosis should be suspected in previously undiagnosed patients by the presence of severe respiratory distress, cyanosis, scaphoid abdomen, and failure to improve with ventilation. Physical examination reveals the absence of breath sounds on the affected side with displacement of heart sounds to the contralateral side, and occasionally bowel sounds can be heard over the thorax. When the diagnosis has been made or is suspected, patients should be immediately intubated and an orogastric tube placed

to evacuate the stomach. Aggressive ventilatory strategies should be avoided (see later). Chest radiograph shows the presence of bowel loops in the affected chest cavity with shifting of the heart to the contralateral side (Fig. 67.2). If the stomach is included in the hernia, the tip of the orogastric tube will be seen within the thorax. The presence of liver in the chest is suspected by deviation of the umbilical venous line. Late presentation of Bochdalek hernia occurs in less than 3% of cases.29 These patients can be asymptomatic at birth and usually present later in life with respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms. High index of suspicion is needed in these cases to prevent unwarranted and potentially dangerous interventions such as the insertion of a chest tube for suspected pleural effusion or pneumothorax. Diagnosis can be made after nasogastric tube insertion, contrast upper gastrointestinal study, or chest computed tomography (CT) scan. Prognosis for cases with late presentation is excellent once the correct diagnosis is made.

Improved survival has been reported using a consistent approach in the management of CDH that can be facilitated by the development of multidisciplinary standardized treatment guidelines, including input from neonatology, pediatric surgery, ECMO specialists, and respiratory therapy (Box 67.3). Predetermined criteria for the use of ECMO and an underlying protect-the-lung strategy are essential components of caring for these infants and can be as important as the specific medical interventions chosen.30 Whereas animal studies have suggested lung immaturity and surfactant deficiency in models of CDH, the use of antenatal steroids and surfactant replacement has not been shown to be beneficial.31 A systematic review of strategies associated with improved survival among infants with CDH in 13 centers that cared for at least 20 patients and reported a survival rate of 75% or more described multiple successful treatment strategies associated with this improved survival.19 Although these centers used different mechanical ventilation strategies, most of these targeted the use of gentle ventilation or permissive hypercapnia. The basic elements of this treatment strategy are: 1. Ventilation of the patient with low peak inspiratory pres-

sures (PIPs) to minimize lung injury; the goal of PIP is usually less than 25 cm H2O.

• Accept preductal saturations ≥85%, PaCO2 ≤65 mm Hg,

2. Accepting preductal saturations of ≥85%, regardless of

postductal saturation, and higher PaCO2 levels of ≤65 to 70 with a pH of at least 7.2 to 7.25 as long as there is evidence of adequate tissue perfusion and oxygenation. 3. Instituting high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV) or high-frequency positive pressure ventilation when the preset limit has failed to achieve adequate ventilation, although HFOV was used by some as the primary mode of ventilation. 4. Even though iNO might produce short-term benefits,

the routine use of iNO is not supported by current data and might actually be associated with a worse outcome, especially in the setting of LV dysfunction. Other pulmonary vasodilators have been used with some success (see Chapter 73). 5. Using ECMO as rescue therapy with variable indications

and improvement of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN). Surgical repair is delayed until the pulmonary hypertension is resolved or significantly improved such that, if need be, support may be escalated postoperatively if necessary. The procedure often involves either a primary closure of the diaphragmatic defect or, if too large, the use of a prosthetic patch. Recently, centers are reporting on thoracoscopic closure, but no trials comparing the methods exist.

Postnatal survival rate at tertiary centers has improved with reported rates of 70% to 90%.19 However, the survival data might underestimate hidden mortality secondary to the termination, stillborn, and referral pattern for outborn patients. With improvement in survival, there has been a focus on improving long-term morbidity of survivors. Infants born with CDH have multiple long-term morbidities affecting the pulmonary, gastrointestinal, neurologic, and skeletal systems. Respiratory complications include pulmonary vascular abnormalities presumably causing pulmonary hypertension, a higher incidence of obstructive airway disease, and a restrictive lung function pattern that

continues into adulthood.32 Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), sometimes in combination with failure to thrive, is a well-recognized complication in patients with CDH, and several patients require antireflux surgery. It is unknown whether GERD has an effect on pulmonary function in this population. Pulmonary hypoplasia and PPHN predispose children born with CDH to a high risk for hypoxemia, which may result in neurodevelopmental delay. It has been reported that infants with CDH are at higher risk to have neuromotor delay, hypotonia, and delayed language skills.33 There is also a high percentage of these infants with sensorineural hearing loss.34 Chest wall deformities and scoliosis are more common among CDH patients, although deformities are mild and surgery is rarely required.35 These data emphasize the need for a multidisciplinary team approach in the postoperative management and follow-up of all survivors of CDH. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) section on surgery has provided a suggested schedule for follow-up for these children.36

The mainstay of CDH treatment and outcomes is dependent on postnatal care. Fetal therapies—namely, fetoscopic endotracheal occlusion (FETO)—in the most severe cases (where survival was <25% given prenatal predictors) have shown some promise in early reports for improving survival in those cases, including improved lung growth in utero, less pulmonary hypertension, and overall improved survival when compared to expectant management. However, some of these successes have come at a cost of increased preterm delivery, although with improved techniques, the rate of preterm birth is declining.37,38 The Tracheal Occlusion To Accelerate Lung Growth (TOTAL) trial, a large, international, multicenter, randomized control study, was recently conducted to better study the use of FETO to improve the outcomes of severe and moderately severe CDH patients.39,40 FETO was performed at 27 to 29 weeks’ gestation with balloon retrieval at 34 weeks’ gestation. The patients in each arm were managed by a standard guideline. Those infants with severe CDH treated with FETO had a higher survival to discharge when compared to those who received expectant care (40% vs. 15%). However, as in prior trials, this increased survival also came with increased risks of preterm, premature rupture of membranes and preterm birth. The survival of 15% in the expectant care group was similar to the anticipated survival of 18% based on the quotient of the O/E LHR at randomization. Although these results are promising, this intervention should remain in the hands of those who are experienced and should continue to monitor outcomes of these babies. The results did not demonstrate a benefit of FETO done at 30 to 32 weeks’ gestation on survival for moderately severe CDH fetuses with an increased risk of preterm delivery.

### Alveolar Capillary Dysplasia

Alveolar capillary dysplasia with misalignment of pulmonary veins (ACD/MPV) is a rare, often fatal pulmonary disease that presents in the newborn period, usually within the first 48

hours of life, with severe hypoxemia and PPHN unresponsive to treatment.41 The true incidence of the disease is unknown and likely higher than what is reported, because the diagnosis is made by pathology, and if there is no autopsy or antemortem lung biopsy, then the diagnosis cannot be confirmed. Histologically, ACD/MPV is characterized by a paucity of capillaries proximal to the alveolar epithelium, anomalous distended pulmonary veins within the bronchovascular bundle (rather than within the interlobular septae), and immature alveolar development with medial thickening of small pulmonary arteries and muscularization of the arterioles, as well as, in approximately one-third of cases, lymphangiectasis. These characteristic findings are diffuse in 85% of patients and patchy in the remainder. Although the mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis of ACD/MPV and its associated pulmonary hypertension are not fully understood, it has been suggested that it is related to a failure of fetal lung vascularization with capillary hypoplasia and discontinuity of these capillaries and pulmonary veins impairing pulmonary blood flow, as well as a component of reactive pulmonary vasoconstriction mediated by hypoxia.42,43 The role of prominent right-to-left intrapulmonary vascular shunt pathways has been identified and implicated in the severe hypoxia seen in these patients.44 Extrapulmonary findings are present in 50% to 80% of cases, most commonly affecting the gastrointestinal, genitourinary, and cardiovascular systems.45 Although the disease is mostly sporadic, reports of multiple affected siblings in subsets of families suggest an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.46,47 Mutations of the FOXF1 gene located on chromosome 16q24.1 have been identified in 70% to 90% of patients with ACD/MPV, and, more recently, there is evidence that genomic imprinting plays a role in the development of ACD/MPV.48 Sending genetic testing may allow for the diagnosis to be made when a pathologic diagnosis is unable to be performed or for prenatal diagnosis in high-risk families.49,50 However, not all cases of ACD/MPV have a FOXF1 mutation.

Most patients with ACD/MPV present within the first few hours of life. These infants are usually born at term and have appropriate size and normal Apgar scores. Although these babies might be asymptomatic at delivery, respiratory distress, cyanosis, and hypoxemia progress quickly to respiratory failure in more than half of these patients within hours after delivery. A small percentage of these patients do not present with symptoms until 2 to 6 weeks of life. Treatment is always unsatisfactory. Although a transient response to iNO might be observed, PPHN is not responsive to medical treatment, and the disease progression is that of a fulminant course and rapid progression to death, although there are reports of survival beyond the neonatal period. A high index of suspicion and diagnostic lung biopsy are required to avoid the use of more invasive and futile treatments, including ECMO.

### Congenital Pulmonary Lymphangiectasia

Congenital pulmonary lymphangiectasia (CPL) is a pulmonary disorder first described by Virchow in 1856, characterized by dilation of lymphatic vessels in multiple areas of


## PDF page 1279 | printed page 1277

the lungs. Most cases of CPL are sporadic, with a predilection for male involvement (2:1). However, familial presentations have been described, suggesting an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. The incidence is difficult to estimate, as few cases are reported in the literature. CPL is classified as primary or secondary. Primary CPL refers to developmental abnormalities of lymphatics that either are localized to just the lung parenchyma or are a part of a more generalized lymphatic developmental defect or part of a genetic syndrome (most commonly Noonan, Down, and Turner). Patients with generalized lymphangiectasia tend to have less severe pulmonary involvement. Secondary cases of CPL are often associated with cardiac malformations with obstructed pulmonary venous return, including obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous return, hypoplastic left heart syndrome, and cor triatriatum. The characteristic pathologic finding of CPL is pulmonary lymphatic dilation in the subpleural, interlobar, perivascular, and peribronchial lymphatics. It may be associated with nonimmune hydrops fetalis and congenital chylothorax.51

The etiology of CPL is not clear but is thought to be secondary to a failure of regression of lymphatics that normally occurs between 16 and 20 weeks’ gestation. Multiple genes have been found to be involved in lymphatic development, including Forkhead box C2 (FOXC2), SYR box 18 (SOX18), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)-3 and -C, as well as genes involved in the Ras–mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling pathway associated with Noonan syndrome.52,53 Patients with CPL usually present with intractable respiratory failure, cyanosis, and hypoxia associated with bilateral chylothorax in the first few hours of life, although diagnosis can be delayed for several weeks in cases of unilobar involvement. Nonimmune hydrops is also a well-recognized presentation in patients with CPL. Examination of the pleural fluid shows characteristic findings of chylothorax, including a lymphocytosis and elevated triglycerides, although elevated triglycerides might be absent in nonfed infants (see later). Chest radiograph reveals hyperinflation of the lung with bilateral interstitial infiltrates and bilateral pleural effusions. High-resolution CT demonstrates diffuse thickening of the peribronchovascular interstitium and the septa surrounding the lobules. Definitive diagnosis is made by lung biopsy showing the characteristic features: increased fibrous tissue with dilation of cystic lymphatic spaces and collapsed alveoli, although differentiation from lymphangiomatosis can be difficult.51

Treatment is mostly supportive. Intubation and mechanical ventilation, drainage of pleural and peritoneal effusions, and correction of hypoxia, acidosis, and shock might be needed in the delivery room for stabilization. Persistent chylothorax might require chest tube placement. Nutritional therapy with medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs) and total parenteral nutrition has been successful in the treatment of CPL. Case reports of using octreotide and antiplasmin to treat CPL as well as intestinal lymphangiectasia have been reported with success.51 Pleurodesis with sclerosing agents has been used to treat persistent chylothoraces associated

with the disease. Reports of using lymphangiogram with ethiodized oil as a successful treatment modality have been reported.54 Propranolol has also been reported to be a successful treatment for a preterm patient with diffuse lymphangietasia.55 The prognosis appears to depend on the severity of symptoms in the immediate newborn period. Although traditionally thought to be fatal, there are reports of survival in some patients presenting with respiratory failure, chylothorax, and hydrops fetalis in the immediate neonatal period. Later presentation carries a better prognosis with the possibility of spontaneous resolution, although respiratory morbidity might be common.

### Chylothorax

Chylothorax is the accumulation of lymphatic fluid (chyle) in the pleural cavity. It is the most common cause of pleural effusion in neonates and can be primary (congenital) or secondary (acquired). It is a rare entity, with a reported incidence of 1:10,000 to 1:24,000 births with a male predominance.56 Congenital chylothorax accounts for less than 10% of all chylothoraces. The majority of fetal hydrothoraces may be associated with abnormalities of the lymphatic system, congenital malformations such as congenital heart disease or mediastinal malignancies, or chromosomal abnormalities such as trisomy 21, Noonan syndrome, or Turner syndrome. Secondary chylothoraces are most commonly associated with trauma during thoracic surgery but can also be the result of increased superior vena caval pressure caused by venous thrombosis.

Clinical presentation is that of respiratory distress secondary to lung compression, pulmonary hypoplasia, or symptoms of the underlying pulmonary or cardiac disease. Many cases of congenital chylothorax are diagnosed by prenatal ultrasound, and antenatal management consists of thoracentesis, thoracoamniotic shunt placement, or pleurodesis to try to prevent the development of pulmonary hypoplasia.56 However, even with prenatal treatment, these infants can still present with significant respiratory distress at birth as fluid reaccumulates, requiring postnatal treatment.

Physical examination is significant for decreased breath sounds on the affected side with shifting of the cardiac apex to the contralateral side. Chest radiograph shows a pleural effusion, compression of the lung on the affected side, and displacement of the heart to the opposite side. However, not all effusions are unilateral. Diagnosis is established by analysis of the pleural fluid. In neonates with established feedings, chylothorax appears milky in color; however, in nonfed neonates, it is clear. Büttiker and colleagues proposed the following criteria for establishing the diagnosis of chylothorax: absolute cell count of greater than 1000/μL with a lymphocyte fraction of greater than 80% and triglyceride levels greater than 1.1 mmol/L.57

Optimal treatment for chylothoraces has not been defined but is mostly supportive while awaiting healing of the lymphatic vessels and resolution of the effusion. Initial support including mechanical ventilation, drainage of the


## PDF page 1280

chylothorax, and nutritional support using total parenteral nutrition is essential. When feedings are initiated, formulas containing a high percentage of MCTs are recommended because lymphatics are not needed for MCT absorption. In most cases, spontaneous resolution occurs within 4 to 6 weeks. If the chylothorax persists, other measures may be taken to encourage resolution. The efficacy of such interventions is mostly demonstrated in small, uncontrolled studies. Pharmacologic management with somatostatins, particularly octreotide, has been successful, as well as propranolol and sildenafil. Finally, more invasive management strategies may need to be used, including pleurodesis, ligation of the thoracic duct, and pleuroperitoneal shunt.58–61 Emerging therapeutic modalities that provide an ability to provide minimally invasive lymphatic interventions such as embolization of the thoracic duct and interstitial lymphatic embolization are increasing our ability to treat complex cases and may be the future for these babies.62,63

### Congenital Cystic Pulmonary Malformations

Congenital cystic lung disease encompasses a broad spectrum of rare, but clinically significant, developmental abnormalities that include congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM; previously known as congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation [CCAM]), bronchopulmonary sequestration (BPS), bronchogenic cyst (BC), and congenital lobar emphysema (CLE). These lesions can be identified on prenatal ultrasound, but the classification of the lesion should wait until postnatal examination and histology are available. These lesions should be followed

### Congenital Pulmonary Airway Malformation

Congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM) constitutes multiple different hamartomatous lesions arising from the abnormal branching of the immature bronchial tree. This entity was first described by Ch’in and Tang in 1949,65 and since then the term has been evolving as our understanding of the entity improves. Currently, the Stoker classification system is used to describe the different pathologic entities of this class of lung lesions. When initially described in 1977, there were three subtypes: I, II, and III.66 More recently, Stocker described two new types, 0 and 4, and revised his original classification system as described further below. The original term congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation (CCAM) is not used as only three types (1, 2, and 3) are adenomatoid and only types 1, 2, and 4 are cystic.67 However, the term CCAM may still appear in the literature.

CPAM is the most common congenital cystic lung disease, occurring in one in 11,000 to 30,000 (although a recent report states an incidence of one in 2000 to 8000) live births and affecting more males.64,68 Both lungs are affected equally, and the disease is most commonly unilobar with predilection for the lower lung lobes. Unlike BPS, it is connected to the tracheobronchial tree and has a pulmonary blood supply (Table 67.1). CPAM develops during the pseudoglandular phase (7–17 weeks’ gestation) of fetal lung development. In addition to the classification system described in the preceding, some have suggested classifying the lesions, at least during the prenatal period, as microcystic versus macrocystic based on the gross anatomy and

Type 0 CPAM is the rarest form; it arises from the trachea or bronchus and contains multiple small cysts. These infants also have other associated lesions, including cardiovascular anomalies, renal hypoplasia, and focal dermal hypoplasia. The lung itself is hypoplastic, weighing only 30% to 50% of the expected weight. Microscopically, the tissue consists almost entirely of irregular bronchial-like structures lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium surrounded by thick cartilage plates and bundles of smooth muscle fibers. Usually all lobes of the lung are involved; thus this diagnosis is usually lethal.67

Type 1 CPAM is the most common form, representing 60% to 70% of all CPAMs; however, more recent reports have demonstrated a decreased incidence of type 1 CPAMs.70,71 These lesions consist of large cysts (2–10 cm) surrounded by multiple small cysts that arise from the distal bronchus or proximal bronchiole and are rarely associated with other congenital malformations. These CPAMs can be large and can have significant mass effect in utero, which can lead to fetal hydrops and pulmonary hypoplasia. However, many of these cysts collapse as pregnancy progresses, allowing normal lung growth of the unaffected lobes. Radiographically, they appear as either a single or multiple airfilled or air/fluid-filled cysts in one or (much less frequently) multiple lobes. Depending on size, there can be flattening of the diaphragm, mediastinal shift, and compression of adjacent lung. Often, due to their size and effect on adjacent lung tissue, infants are symptomatic shortly after birth and require excision. Overall, these lesions have a good prognosis. However, a number of reports describe the occurrence of a bronchioloalveolar carcinoma, especially when the CPAM is not fully resected, with a malignant transformation risk of 1%.72

Type 2 CPAM accounts for 15% of all CPAMs and is the second most frequent type of CPAM. These malformations are of bronchiolar origin and consist of multiple small cysts (0.5–2 cm) and are often (about 60%) associated with other congenital anomalies, including renal agenesis/dysplasia, cardiovascular anomalies, CDH, and extralobar sequestrations (ELSs).67 Radiographically, they are characterized by multiple small cysts that may not even be visible on chest x-ray. Prognosis is usually related to the severity of the associated anomalies.

Type 3 CPAM accounts for 5% to 10% of all CPAMs. These are of bronchiolar/alveolar duct origin and are almost exclusively seen in males. These lesions were the original congenital adenomatoid malformation described by Ch’in and Tang in 1949.65 They consist of multiple smaller cysts (rarely >0.2 cm) and appear as a solid mass that is associated with a significant risk of hydrops and polyhydramnios resulting from caval obstruction and cardiac compression secondary to mediastinal shift. This also leads to pulmonary

hypoplasia, because, unlike type 1 CPAMs, this lesion does not regress with progression of pregnancy. The extent of the pulmonary hypoplasia is the primary determinant of survival.

Finally, type 4 CPAM accounts for approximately 10% of CPAMs and is of distal acinar origin. The lesion primarily consists of large (up to 10 cm), air-filled, thin-walled cysts usually located at the lung periphery. This lesion can be asymptomatic at birth and presents from the neonatal period to 4 years of age. Often, this will be an incidental finding on an x-ray that was taken for other reasons, such as acute respiratory distress related to a tension pneumothorax or pneumonia. This lesion can be confused with pleuropulmonary blastema; therefore blastemas must be looked for histologically. Surgical resection of the lobe is accompanied by an excellent prognosis.67

In addition to the pathologic classification system, a classification system based on prenatal imaging has also been used to classify these lesions. The vast majority of these lesions are diagnosed on antenatal ultrasound. Most lesions have distinguishing features, such as location, appearance, and vascular supply. However, distinguishing CPAMs from other cystic lung lesions can be difficult. Adzick et al.69 proposed the classification of antenatal cystic lung lesions based on their appearance on ultrasound as either macrocystic (cysts ≥5 mm) or microcystic (cysts <5 mm). This classification system has been used to better counsel families and guide antenatal monitoring for possible intervention.73

Understanding of the natural history of CPAMs continues to evolve. Up to 15% of these lesions appear to “disappear” in the prenatal period, usually after 28 weeks’ gestation when the growth of these lesions tends to plateau; however, in most cases, postnatal CT scan or fetal MRI will show persistence of the anomaly (Fig. 67.3). The unpredictability of the in utero growth of these lesions requires careful follow-up. Midgestation, these lesions can grow quite rapidly, which can cause mediastinal shift, pulmonary hypoplasia, and impaired venous return leading to hydrops. It has been well established that the diagnosis of fetal hydrops associated with CPAM portends a poor prognosis, with mortality near 100%.74,75 In 2002, it was hypothesized that the volume of the lesion would predict whether hydrops would develop in the fetus. The CPAM volume ratio (CVR) was developed as a prognostic tool and is calculated by measuring the three dimensions of the lung lesion and dividing by the head circumference. A CVR ≥1.6 at initial diagnosis was found to reliably predict a subgroup of fetuses at increased risk for developing fetal hydrops and is now used to evaluate which infants might benefit from in utero interventions.76 Fetal surgery using thoracoamniotic shunting or cyst aspiration has been successful for macrocystic lesions, with survival rates in hydropic fetuses of 50% and 69%, respectively.77 The use of betamethasone for large microcystic lesions has been shown to be efficacious to decrease the size of the CPAM and resolve hydrops.78 For those who do not respond to betamethasone, open fetal surgery is an option, with a survival rate of 52%.75,76,79 The ex utero

### Bronchopulmonary Sequestrations

BPSs are microscopic cystic masses of nonfunctioning lung tissue thought to arise from the primitive foregut. These structures do not communicate to the bronchial tree, and their blood supply arises from the systemic circulation. Two forms are recognized—intralobar sequestration (ILS) and extralobar sequestration (ELS)—and are differentiated by their venous drainage and relationship to the surrounding pleura. ILS occurs when the accessory bud arises before establishment of the pleura and is contained within the normal lung, and venous drainage is via the pulmonary vasculature to the left atrium. If the accessory lung bud arises after the pleura are established, it has its own pleural covering and is completely separated from the normal lung and is classified as an ELS. Venous drainage for ELS is systemic, and some large lesions are at risk for high-output heart failure. The majority of BPSs are located in the lower, usually left, lobe. However, a small portion (<10%) of ELSs are located infradiaphragmatic.64 Their anatomical location is dependent on the level of the foregut at which they arise.

On antenatal ultrasound, sequestrations appear as welldefined, solid, echogenic masses very similar to type 3 CPAM. A distinguishing feature of BPS is the documentation of systemic blood supply by color Doppler. If unclear, ultrafast MRI can establish the blood supply, define the lesion, and identify other associated malformations. It is difficult to distinguish ELS from ILS on prenatal ultrasound unless it is surrounded by a pleural effusion or is located below the diaphragm, which can only be features of an ELS. Intra-abdominal ELS appears as a suprarenal solid mass and should be differentiated from other suprarenal masses, including neuroblastoma and mesoblastic nephroma.68 Antenatal or postnatal echocardiography can show associated cardiac malformation. BPS appears on chest radiograph as a posterior thoracic mass mostly on the left. Chest CT scan or even MRI might be needed to further delineate systemic blood supply.

Like CPAMs, sequestrations (extralobar more so than intralobar) can be associated with multiple congenital malformations, including CDH, congenital heart disease, and vertebral anomalies. A feature unique to BPS is high-output cardiac failure due to the redundant circulation of the sequestration and occasionally massive left-toleft shunt. Like a CPAM, BPS can also cause fetal hydrops, either from the mass effect or from a tension hydrothorax that is the result of either fluid or lymph secretion from the BPS or from high-output cardiac failure. If there is significant in utero compromise of the fetus, fetal intervention may be necessary in the form of a thoracoamniotic shunt

### Bronchogenic Cyst

A bronchogenic cyst (BC) is a single cyst lined by respiratory epithelium and covered with elements of the tracheobronchial tree, including cartilage and smooth muscle. BCs originate from an abnormal budding of the ventral surface of the primitive foregut between the 26th and 40th day of fetal life, a budding that does not undergo further branching, resulting in a blind cyst that may or may not communicate with the airways. These cysts are mostly found in the mediastinum near the carina but can occur within the lung parenchyma, pleura, or diaphragm.88

In the neonatal period, most patients with BCs are asymptomatic, and diagnosis is usually made on prenatal ultrasound and fetal MRI or incidentally on a chest radiograph after birth. On chest radiograph, BCs can appear as radiopaque areas if they are fluid filled, but if connected to the airway, an air-fluid level may be seen. A CT scan is the study of choice before undergoing surgery and provides a thorough characterization of the lesion and its relation to mediastinal structures.

Symptoms, if present, are secondary to mass effects on the airways, gastrointestinal tract, or cardiovascular system. Even though major airway obstruction is uncommon, subcarinal lesions can present with severe obstruction. On the other hand, obstruction of smaller airways can cause air trapping, overdistension, and a clinical picture mimicking CLE. Cases not diagnosed in the neonatal period usually present in older children or adults with pneumonia, hemoptysis, pneumothorax, dysphagia, or signs of caval obstruction.

Treatment of all cases of BCs is complete surgical excision. In symptomatic patients, this is performed after immediate clinical stabilization. Simple aspiration should be considered as a temporizing measure in patients with severe compromise, but complete resection is subsequently required. In asymptomatic newborns, surgery can be done electively at a few months of age. Patients who undergo resection of a BC have an excellent outcome. Only a few patients develop lifethreatening complications before surgery and have a poorer

outcome. There are no long-term complications related to the resection of a BC.89

### Congenital Lobar Emphysema

CLE is a rare anomaly of the lung that is characterized by postnatal overdistension of one or more segments or lobes of the lung. The mechanism underlying CLE is that of intrinsic or extrinsic obstruction of the airways resulting in air trapping, overdistension, and subsequent emphysema. Multiple mechanisms have been described to explain the development of CLE, including dysplastic bronchial cartilage, inspissated mucus, aberrant cardiopulmonary vasculature, and infection. In half of the cases, no underlying pathology is identified. The left upper lobe is most frequently affected, followed by the right middle lobe and the right upper lobe. The lower lobes are rarely involved. CLE is three times more common in males.90,91

Patients usually present in the neonatal period with respiratory distress (80% within the first month of life); however, later presentations have been described. The severity of the clinical picture depends on the size of the CLE and the degree of compression of the normal lung. Physical examination might be indistinguishable from that of a pneumothorax with decreased air entry, bulging of the affected hemithorax, and, in severe cases, shifting of the apical heartbeat to the contralateral side. However, these children are often hemodynamically stable, thus differentiating it from a tension pneumothorax.

CLE can be detected at midgestation using a combination of ultrasonography and ultrafast fetal MRI, but most are not diagnosed prenatally. Differentiation from CPAM can be difficult on prenatal imaging.64,73,91 Diagnosis is usually made by chest radiograph, which may show an early opaque mass due to delayed clearance of lung fluid followed by a hyperlucent, overexpanded area of lung with atelectasis of the adjacent lobes of the lung, depression of the diaphragm, and mediastinal shift to the opposite side (Fig. 67.4). The distinction of CLE from pneumothorax is essential to prevent attempted aspiration and potential
