risk for poor lung function in later life.46 Adults diagnosed with BPD as infants consistently exhibit significantly lower FEV1 and FEF25%–75%, confirming a clinically important and substantial airflow obstruction in their third and fourth decade of life compared with non-BPD preterm and term infants.60 In a population-based cohort study, very low birth weight (VLBW) infants had worse lung function (FEV1, FEV1/FVC, DLCO), reduced exercise capacity, and altered cardiac structure and function as adults.61 Several studies have found a similar correlation between preterm birth and reduced exercise capacity,62,63 with females at higher risk than males.64 Low FEV1 by early adulthood is a significant risk factor for COPD development.65 Critical constraints to tidal volume expansion may lead to reduced exercise tolerance, severe dyspnea, and leg discomfort in adults born preterm.66 Respiratory limitations to exercise in adults born preterm are similar to those in patients with COPD. Emphysema, a form of COPD, has been reported among young adult survivors of moderate and severe BPD.67 The nature of lung disease in adults of former preterm infants is mostly a combination of airflow obstruction, failure of normal development, and lung destruction.68 These adults can present with shortness of breath and hypoxemia but also can be asymptomatic, making early diagnosis difficult. Eliciting appropriate prenatal and postnatal history, including birth weight, gestational age, neonatal course, postnatal hospitalizations, respiratory symptoms and treatments in childhood, lung imaging, and longitudinal lung function assessments, will facilitate identifying children born preterm at higher risk for early-onset COPD in adulthood.

### Prevention

Recent studies have demonstrated that early-life lung function may track through the lifespan, and poor lung functional trajectories from childhood to old age are an important risk factor for developing COPD in adults (Fig. 71.3).51,69 Early life risk factors such as maternal cigarette smoking, air pollution, and childhood asthma play a

Routine screening for pulmonary function and the development of lung biomarkers should facilitate early diagnosis and treatment. Suppose the burden of premature airflow obstruction and the risk of early-onset COPD can be prevented. Convincing mothers to quit smoking before pregnancy or during pregnancy as early as possible is a significant challenge. However, the long-term implications of maternal tobacco smoke for the developing fetus are huge, with social and economic consequences. Novel methods of reducing exposure of pregnant mothers to air pollution are warranted both at the individual and the community level, because the problem is particularly more acute in rapidly industrializing developing countries. Globally, addressing nutritional issues in pregnancy may decrease FGR and infants born with low birth weight. All of the above interventions will not only facilitate lung growth but also may reduce the long-term impact on lung function in these infants.

### Research Gaps

Management of adults born preterm is an emerging challenge, implied by the evolving nature of long-term consequences and the complexity of multisystem involvement in these individuals. Studies focusing on lung function must characterize the patterns of airway obstruction both in the presence and absence of BPD and the nature of COPD seen in these adults born preterm. The debate on whether “catch-up” growth occurs in adolescence or rather that lung function tracks throughout life, especially in adults born preterm, is uncertain.68 Longitudinal studies on peak lung function and lung function tracking through a lifetime are essential to analyze the nature of the lung disease in preterm adults and its relationships to COPD. The effects of maternal smoking and air pollution on lung structure and function in the developing fetus may further help define COPD

Tools such as predictive analytics may help assess the risk of COPD in adults born preterm based on lung function testing and antenatal and postnatal factors.

### Summary

Neonatologists now sometimes care for preterm infants not only in the intensive care setting but also in multidisciplinary teams in outpatient follow-up clinics. title: Cardiac Embryology

paragraphs.text: 72 Cardiac Embryology
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Congenital heart defects (CHDs) affect about 1% of all live births around the world, with variations in reporting depending on birth rates and access to medical care.1 The care of children with CHDs has increasingly become a neonatal specialty, aided by prenatal detection. The fetal diagnosis of critical CHDs decreases postsurgical morbidity and mortality, and reparative or palliative cardiovascular surgery is commonplace in the first months of life.2 This success has led to a larger population of adults with CHDs and an expansion of a subspecialty for the care of these individuals. In parallel with these clinical advances, there has been exciting progress in understanding the cellular and molecular basis of normal and abnormal cardiogenesis and the relationship of heart defects to other congenital defects. The global incidence of CHDs has not decreased and has in fact increased as prenatal detection becomes more common worldwide.1 Yet, our knowledge of the pathogenesis of CHDs is far from complete. Understanding normal and abnormal cardiac embryology is critical to understanding the pathology underlying CHDs and ultimately their prevention.
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: The mature heart is the product of gene expression driven by endogenous and exogenous influences. The developing heart manifests its morphologic and physiologic plasticity under environmental stimuli. A detailed understanding of the factors that drive normal cardiogenesis is necessary for understanding the causes and consequences of abnormal development. Errors in cardiac morphogenesis involved with septation, valve formation, and proper patterning of the great vessels are responsible for most forms of CHDs. Normal heart development requires precise timing for coordination of the complex three-dimensional contortions of tissues, but, paradoxically, these tissues also have a remarkable capacity for modifications that compensate for mistakes. These adjustments allow abnormal heart structures and resultant functions to be compatible with life up to and even after birth, but they complicate identification of the primary causes of cardiac anomalies. This chapter focuses on clinically relevant aspects of cardiac embryology and how disruptions of this process may lead to CHDs.
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: The following description of human heart development, especially the earlier events, is synthesized from information provided by studies of animal models and human embryonic and fetal tissues. A timetable of selected events in human heart development is presented in Fig. 72.1,3 which depicts the major transitions in early mammalian heart development.
paragraphs.heading: Overview of Normal Heart Development

paragraphs.text: The primordia of the heart are formed by bilaterally symmetric heart fields derived from the lateral plate mesoderm. These primordia migrate through the primitive streak, between the ectoderm and endoderm layers, to become symmetric mesoderm regions on either side of the primitive streak. During body folding, the primary heart fields fuse to form a tubular structure comprised of an inner layer of endocardium, a thick layer of extracellular matrix, and an outer layer of myocardium. This apparently “simple” tube begins to contract rhythmically and grows differentially so that dilations (primordia of the heart chambers) and constrictions (primordia of the partitions between chambers) appear along its length. Later additions from the second heart field to the distal ends of the tubular heart form the outflow tract and the sinus venosus. Dextral looping of the tube brings the venous caudal portion to a more dorsal position and to the left of the arterial cranial portion as septation of the tubular heart begins. The epicardium arises from tissue dorsal to the heart at the level of the atrioventricular (AV) junction and spreads over the outer surface of the myocardium as a layer of squamous epithelial cells and associated connective tissue during the early phase of septation. This layer is key to coronary vessel and fibroblast development in the heart.
paragraphs.heading: Overview of Normal Heart Development

paragraphs.text: The atrial chamber divides into two chambers by the growth of the septum primum, which forms perforations to create the foramen secundum. A second atrial septum subsequently grows to the right of the primary atrial septum and forms a one-way valve (right-to-left blood flow) between the two atria in the fetus. This avenue of blood flow, the foramen ovale, is permanently closed shortly after birth to functionally complete atrial septation. Ventricular septation is not complete at the time the primary atrial septum is formed. The ventricular septum results from the
paragraphs.heading: Overview of Normal Heart Development

paragraphs.text: growth and remodeling of trabecular sheets, continues with expansion of the ventricular chambers, and ends with the fusion of several tissues, including endocardial cushions from several sources and the muscular septum, to form the membranous and muscular interventricular septum. The outflow tract septation is the result of growth and fusion of spiraling ridges that eventually divide the truncus into aortic and pulmonary tracts. The venous and arterial vessels (aortic arches) undergo partial incorporation into cardiac chambers, differential degeneration, fusion, and growth to attain the mature structures.
paragraphs.heading: Overview of Normal Heart Development

paragraphs.text: The human heart has completed the major morphogenetic processes 8 weeks after fertilization. What follows is the completion of maturation of structures, growth, accumulation of cellular junctions at the intercalated discs, biochemical and metabolic adjustments, and compensation for the abrupt changes in patterns of blood flow at birth, such
paragraphs.heading: Overview of Normal Heart Development

paragraphs.text: as permanent closure of the foramen ovale of the atrial septum and closure and fibrosis of the ductus arteriosus and ductus venosus.
paragraphs.heading: Overview of Normal Heart Development

paragraphs.text: The tissue regions giving rise to the heart have been mapped by the application of dyes, particles, and radiolabels at stages when the vertebrate embryo is comprised of two layers: the epiblast (or primitive ectoderm) and the hypoblast (or primitive endoderm). The process of gastrulation, the movement of precardiac epiblast cells through the primitive streak, appears to be important in specification (Fig. 72.2A).4 These cells migrate laterally to form the left and

paragraphs.text: right heart fields (see Fig. 72.2B), which then create the horseshoe-shaped first and second heart fields around the end of the primitive streak, the primitive node. The second heart fields are adjacent to and influenced by cardiac neural crest cells, which are implicated in many genetic syndromes, including RASopathies (mutations of the Ras-MAPK pathway) such as 22q11 deletion syndromes.

paragraphs.text: The origin of cells in the embryonic heart determines their ultimate destination (Fig. 72.3).5 Disruptions in the early migration of these cells cause specific congenital malformations in the four-chambered heart. The first heart field, which makes the primitive heart tube, forms the left ventricle and the atria. The right ventricle, valves, parts of the atria, and outflow tracts are made from the second heart field and cardiac neural crest cells, all of which must migrate to the first heart field to expand the primitive heart tube. Understanding the cell lineages makes it easier to understand the origins of congenital heart disease and how malformations can be tied together.

paragraphs.text: Within each side of the first heart fields primitive endocardial tubes form, come together, and fuse as the lateral body portions fold to create the primitive heart tube. The
paragraphs.heading: The Tubular and Looping Heart

paragraphs.text: Aorta
paragraphs.heading: The Tubular and Looping Heart

paragraphs.text: Pulmonary arteries
paragraphs.heading: SVC

paragraphs.text: LCx

paragraphs.text: Conduction system
paragraphs.heading: LAD

paragraphs.text: most caudal cells of the right and left heart fields will form the most ventral portion of the primitive heart tube (asterisks in Fig. 72.2). The inflow portion of the heart quickly gains pacemaker activity and initiates slow, unidirectional contractions along the tube. Concurrent with this process, endocardial and myocardial cells, which form the layers of the developing heart, emerge from a common precursor.6 The myocardium secretes a thick layer of acellular extracellular matrix, also known as cardiac jelly, which creates a distinct layer between the myocardium and the endocardium (Fig. 72.4). This tissue progression requires cell differentiation, sorting, and polarization. Evidence supports both negative and positive influences from the surrounding neural tissue and endoderm on these processes.
paragraphs.heading: LAD

paragraphs.text: The primitive heart tube undergoes three connected steps—looping, convergence, and wedging—all of which are crucial to normal cardiac septation. Looping is the first obvious structural left-right lateralization in the developing embryo (Fig. 72.5).7 The heart tube elongates and folds into an “S” shape to the right. The direction of looping will determine the ultimate ventricular positions. Looping to the right will give the normal dextro, or “D,” looping. If the primitive tube loops to the left, this will result in levo, or “L,” looping, with the left ventricle on the right side and the right ventricle on the left side (Fig. 72.6).8 The left-right handedness of looping is directed by monocilia in the primitive node many stages before looping starts. These
paragraphs.heading: LAD

paragraphs.text: cilia are angled 40° posterior and rotate in a clockwise direction, resulting in a leftward laminar flow of fluid containing key signaling molecules. Mutations in genes responsible for ciliary ultrastructure result in syndromes such as Kartagener syndrome.9 Importantly, the primitive atrium is not involved in this portion of looping, so atrial position is not severely disturbed by abnormal looping. Atrial positions are affected by situs abnormalities as seen in heterotaxy syndromes. Left-right embryologic abnormalities have a wide range of known genetic causes in which mutations interfere with early breaking of left-right symmetry, abnormal signal transduction or gene expression in the lateral plate mesoderm, and abnormal morphogenesis of internal organs.10
paragraphs.heading: LAD

paragraphs.text: Convergence is the process of proper orientation of the inflow and outflow tracts (Fig. 72.7). The inflow tract rises cranially behind the outflow tract such that the inflow and outflow tracts are aligned, with the outflow tract ventral to the inflow tract. Abnormalities can lead to irregularities in atrial and ventricular septa and outflow tracts. Convergence and looping are dependent on lengthening of the polar ends of the heart tube, which is achieved by the addition of cells from the second heart field. The original primitive heart tube will grow to become the left ventricle and portions of the AV canal, and additions from the second heat field will direct formation of the outflow tracts, right ventricle, and atria. As cardiac neural crest cells influence the second heart field, it becomes easier to understand how neural crest
paragraphs.heading: LAD

paragraphs.text: cell–associated diseases such as 22q11 deletion syndromes and velocardiofacial syndromes result in abnormalities of these cardiovascular structures.
paragraphs.heading: A A A

paragraphs.text: Occurring in parallel with convergence and septation (see Fig. 72.7) is wedging (Fig. 72.8). Here, the outflow tract rotates counterclockwise approximately 45°, resulting in the future aorta residing behind the future pulmonary artery (see Fig. 72.8d–e). The aortic portion shortens, and the future site of the aortic valve “wedges” between the future tricuspid and mitral valves. This separates the mitral valve from the septum, which is why the mitral valve has no connections to the septal wall. If convergence and wedging do not occur correctly, then the outflow tract, the ventricular septum, and the AV endocardial cushion tissue do not meet. This results in conotruncal defects such as double inlet left ventricle, double outlet right ventricle, and tetralogy of Fallot.11
paragraphs.heading: A A A

paragraphs.text: The vertebrate heart tube normally loops to the right side of the embryo. Sidedness appears to be influenced by factors acting at a time when the heart is not recognizable as
paragraphs.heading: A A A

paragraphs.text: a distinct organ structure.13 Transplantation studies using the early chicken embryo suggest that left and right sidedness are already determined in the precardiac mesoderm stages. Sidedness can also be regulated in part by retinoids. Retinoic acid–soaked bead implants in chicken embryos or application of all-trans retinoic acid in mouse embryos cause transposition of the great arteries.14 Abnormalities in the direction of cardiac looping also occur in humans.15 These abnormalities are linked to an autosomal recessive gene defect that has been detected in the Amish population and another gene defect in the X chromosome (Xq24-q27.1)
paragraphs.heading: A A A

paragraphs.text: in the general population.16 Interestingly, abnormalities in genes associated with left-right asymmetry may also be responsible for apparently isolated cases of CHDs. Mutations in the laterality CFC1 gene have manifested as transposition of the great arteries in humans without other obvious laterality defects.
paragraphs.heading: A A A

paragraphs.text: Two mouse mutants have abnormalities in sidedness. The iv/iv mutant mouse develops L-looping and dextrocardia 50% of the time.17 A large percentage of these mice have a combination of cardiac defects, including persistent sinus venosus, atrial and ventricular septal defects, common AV canal, double outlet right ventricle, tetralogy of Fallot, and transposition of the great arteries. This gene has been mapped to mouse chromosome 12, which is homologous to human chromosome 14. The inv/inv mutant mouse develops situs inversus close to 100% of the time.18 Mutation screens using the zebrafish have uncovered a number of genes involved in laterality specification and indicate that there are organ-specific laterality regulators.19 Identification of the genes involved in these human, mouse, and zebrafish mutations could provide valuable insight into the mechanisms of normal dextral looping of the heart.20
paragraphs.heading: A A A

paragraphs.text: Septation of the heart begins with swelling of the extracellular matrix between the endocardium and the myocardium at specific regions of the heart tube. These regions include the AV junction, the outflow tract, the leading edge of the primary atrial septum, and the ridge of the interventricular septum. As chamber differentiation proceeds, endocardial cushions grow into the lumen of the tubular heart and act as primitive valves to promote unidirectional blood flow. These simple mounds of extracellular matrix lined by a single layer of endocardial cells eventually mature into valves with thinned valve leaflets. A complex set of inductive events has been elucidated by studying cushion formation of the AV junction and the outflow tract.21 These events include signaling between the specialized myocardium and a subset of competent endocardial cells through growth factors (e.g., transforming growth factor-β [TGF-β], vascular endothelial growth factor [VEGF], bone morphogenetic proteins [BMPs]) and extracellular matrix molecules. Various proteases and homeobox genes are also involved.
paragraphs.heading: Septation Endocardial Development: Formation of Cushion Tissue

paragraphs.text: The subsequent cascade of events includes release and migration of cells from the endocardial epithelium (termed endothelial-mesenchymal transition [EMT]) into the previously acellular cardiac jelly and proliferation, death, and differentiation of these endocardial mesenchyme cells within a complex matrix. The cushions are also populated by cardiac neural crest cells. The cushions eventually give rise to, or at least greatly influence, the subsequent development of septa and valves of the heart. Because a number of factors, cell types, and tissues are involved in this process at multiple levels and at different stages, there are many sites where mistakes can occur. It is therefore not surprising that septation
paragraphs.heading: Septation Endocardial Development: Formation of Cushion Tissue

paragraphs.text: defects are so common. The differentiation of resilient valves requires remodeling of the extracellular matrix. It has been revealed that steps in cardiac valve differentiation and maturation share mechanisms with those of cartilage, tendon, and bone development.22
paragraphs.heading: Septation Endocardial Development: Formation of Cushion Tissue

paragraphs.text: In the primitive atrium, a ring of tissue, the septum primum, grows toward the endocardial cushions near the AV junction (Fig. 72.9). Through apoptosis, fenestrations form in this tissue, creating the osteum secundum. The osteum primum, between the tip of this outgrowth of the septum primum and the endocardial cushion, closes as the tissue advances. The atrial roof folds inward, and the septum secundum begins to grow down on the right of the septum primum and continues in a crescent shape to form to the right of the base of the septum primum. This makes the septum primum a flap over the foramen ovale, allowing only right-to-left flow across the atria.
paragraphs.heading: Septation Endocardial Development: Formation of Cushion Tissue

paragraphs.text: Ventricular and outflow tract septation occur in tandem, and aberrations in one may have structural consequences for the other. The myocardium from the outer curvature of the ventricle invaginates, growing cranially. AV canal endocardial cushions grow toward the myocardium, completing the ventricular septum. Outflow tract endocardial cushions form ridges that spiral along the conotruncus (Fig. 72.10). These ridges grow together to divide the conotruncus into
paragraphs.heading: Septation Endocardial Development: Formation of Cushion Tissue

paragraphs.text: the trunks of the aorta and pulmonary artery. The AV canal and outflow tract endocardial cushions join, completing ventricular septation.
paragraphs.heading: Septation Endocardial Development: Formation of Cushion Tissue

paragraphs.text: Endocardial cushions act as primitive valves and include the precursor cells of mature valves. During endothelial mesenchymal transition (EMT), TGF-β and Notch signaling induces endothelial cells to adopt an invasive phenotype, and cells invade the previously acellular cardiac jelly. These cells adopt a mesenchymal phenotype to create fibrous tissue and collagen (Fig. 72.11). As the cushions grow, they delaminate from the myocardium, forming thin strands (chordae tendineae) that attach to outgrowths of myocardium (papillary muscles). The tricuspid valve attaches to papillary muscles on the interventricular
paragraphs.heading: Septation Endocardial Development: Formation of Cushion Tissue

paragraphs.text: septum, as well as the free wall of the right ventricle. The mitral valve, however, has attachments only to the apex and the free wall of the left ventricle. Septal attachments do not form because the aortic valve displaces the primitive mitral valve from the septum during wedging. These early valve differences help identify ventricles during fetal and neonatal echocardiography.
paragraphs.heading: Septation Endocardial Development: Formation of Cushion Tissue

paragraphs.text: Semilunar valve formation is similar to that of the AV valves; however, the apical surfaces of the valve leaflets develop depressions, eventually molding the leaflets into cusps (see Fig. 72.11). The arterial surfaces of the cusps become a more condensed fibrous tissue. Rather than chordae tendineae and papillary muscles, the leaflets extend attachments into the vessel walls to anchor them.
paragraphs.heading: Septation Endocardial Development: Formation of Cushion Tissue

paragraphs.text: The atrial septum, ventricular septum, and all valves are formed from the second heart field–derived endocardial cushions. Therefore valve and septal defects are commonly found together. Classically, the common AV canal has been known as “the endocardial defect,” as it includes malformations of both AV valves, the atrial septum, and the ventricular septum. However, not all of these defects must be present for the defects to be endocardial cushion defects. In fact, many of the valve and septal defects seen clinically are variations of endocardial cushion defects.
paragraphs.heading: Septation Endocardial Development: Formation of Cushion Tissue

paragraphs.text: A subset of neural crest cells that originate and migrate from the dorsal region of the neural tube contributes significantly to the development of the heart and associated vessels (Fig. 72.12).23,24 The role of the neural crest has been
paragraphs.heading: Neural Crest Contributions to Cardiogenesis

paragraphs.text: determined by the study of avian embryos using immunohistochemical neural crest markers, transplantation (quail-chicken chimeras), ablation, and genetic manipulation of mice. The neural crest cells from the cranial and trunk regions of the neural tube migrate through the third, fourth, and sixth aortic arches (Fig. 72.13) to contribute to the walls of the aortic arch arteries, including the proximal aorta, the stems of the proximal coronary arteries, and the sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation of the heart (including the cardiac ganglia). A subset enters the heart within the endocardium and is involved in septation of the aortic and pulmonary trunk. A subset also appears to enter the heart and regulates the formation and maturation of the cardiac conduction system.25 Removal or disruption of neural crest cells causes cardiac inflow anomalies, including double inlet left ventricle, tricuspid atresia,
paragraphs.heading: Neural Crest Contributions to Cardiogenesis

paragraphs.text: and straddling tricuspid valve; cardiac outflow anomalies, including persistent truncus arteriosus; and abnormalities in the aortic arch arteries, including interruption of the aorta, double aortic arch, variable absence of the carotid arteries, and left aortic arch. In contrast, the systemic and pulmonary venous structures are not as affected by disruption of cardiac neural crests.
paragraphs.heading: Neural Crest Contributions to Cardiogenesis

paragraphs.text: A more global role for the cardiac neural crest is now recognized after the findings that removal or disturbance of cardiac neural crest cells can influence the function and proliferation of cardiomyocytes before neural crest cells migrate into the heart.26 Findings point to a role for cardiac neural crest–derived cells in influencing the mesenchyme of the secondary or anterior heart-forming field that produces late-forming cardiac structures, including the outflow tract.27,28 Because disturbances of neural crest development have the potential to cause cardiovascular anomalies, factors controlling normal neural crest cell development are receiving much attention. 22q11 deletion and related syndromes that include craniofacial and outflow tract abnormalities are believed to result from disruption of neural crest cell development.29
paragraphs.heading: Neural Crest Contributions to Cardiogenesis

paragraphs.text: The CHDs most commonly found in 22q11 deletion syndromes include conotruncal defects such as tetralogy of Fallot, pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect, truncus arteriosus, interrupted aortic arch, isolated aortic arch anomalies, and ventricular septal defects.30 Consider that 22q11 deletion syndromes are associated with abnormalities in cardiac neural crest cells and the second heart field. Fig. 72.13 displays the derivatives of neural crest cells. Understanding the origins and derivatives of the neural crest cells helps explain how these cardiac neural crest cell abnormalities lead to these specific CHDs.
paragraphs.heading: Neural Crest Contributions to Cardiogenesis

paragraphs.text: The search for the “DiGeorge syndrome gene” was confounded by the number of candidate genes in the
paragraphs.heading: Neural Crest Contributions to Cardiogenesis

paragraphs.text: DiGeorge critical region and by the differences between the phenotypes of mice and humans mutated in homologous genes. It is also puzzling that individuals without the deletion can closely resemble those with the DiGeorge region missing. TBX1 and CRKL are currently described
paragraphs.heading: Neural Crest Contributions to Cardiogenesis

paragraphs.text: as the best candidate genes within the most common 22q11 deletion. However, researchers continue to propose that there is no single affected gene responsible for the defects associated with DiGeorge or the 22q11 deletion syndrome. Rather, a combination of affected genes within that region, as well as those outside that region, appears to regulate the same critical cellular processes. Data suggest that many of the mutations identified in individuals with a range of craniofacial and cardiac syndromes that include 22q11 deletion syndrome are in genes associated with the extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) pathway.31,32 These genes include upstream genes such as TBX1 and CRKL and downstream genes such as SRF. A broader hypothesis is emerging that anything that dysregulates the activity of the ERK pathway up or down in developing neural crest cells results in craniofacial and cardiac syndromes.
paragraphs.heading: Neural Crest Contributions to Cardiogenesis

paragraphs.text: Primordia of the pulse-generating system function early in the caudal region of the tubular heart and allow unidirectional blood flow, but subsequent events in the development of the cardiac conduction system (CCS) are not well understood. Investigations of CCS embryogenesis in a variety of species, including the mouse, chicken, and zebrafish, have contributed to this understanding.33 Classic histologic analyses are limited in the information they provide because the early CCS cannot be readily distinguished histologically or even structurally from the surrounding myocardium. Biochemical markers have been detected that transiently stain portions of the CCS and have been used to follow these tissues during the three-dimensionally complex morphogenesis of the heart. The rabbit model is unique in that there is a marker for it, NF-150, an antibody against neurofilament proteins, that delineates its CCS throughout development and into the adult. These markers show that some of the tissues that give rise to the CCS can be distinguished from other cardiomyocytes as early as the tubular heart stages, because they have a different pattern of gene expression and cell proliferation.
paragraphs.heading: Development of the Cardiac Conduction System

paragraphs.text: Lineage tracing of myocardial cells provided clues to the origin of the CCS. The clonal relationship between CCS cells and working cardiomyocytes suggests that these specialized myocardia can be recruited from unspecialized myocardial cells. Evidence from avian systems supports the hypothesis that the vasculature can be the source of factors that initiate such recruitment, with endothelin-1 being a strong candidate for signaling.34
paragraphs.heading: Development of the Cardiac Conduction System

paragraphs.text: Less is known about the physiology of the developing CCS primarily because of technical barriers to resolution. These barriers are being overcome by advances in biomedical engineering technologies, such as optical mapping using voltagesensitive fluorescent dyes and optical coherence tomography, that allow the capture of images of the tiny beating heart at high spatiotemporal resolution. The tubular heart has a peristaltic-type contraction pattern resulting from a pulse-generating focus of cells and a slow distribution of action potentials
paragraphs.heading: Development of the Cardiac Conduction System

paragraphs.text: radiating evenly from that region in all directions.35 In the septating heart, alternating regions of relatively slow and fast conduction allow pumping of blood in one direction, with the endocardial cushions acting as primitive valves. Slow regions, such as the sinus venosus, AV junction, and outflow tract, cause a delay of the impulse conduction between chambers.36 The ventricular conduction system achieves its mature morphology simultaneously with the appearance of the mature sequence of activation.37 Subsequent differentiation allows for increasing speed of action potential conduction through the fascicular portion of this system and compensation for the growth of the heart. Maturation of the fibrous ring that separates the atrial from ventricular muscle and the connective tissue sheath around the conduction system also follows, serving as an insulative barrier to inappropriate conduction to neighboring working myocardium.
paragraphs.heading: Development of the Cardiac Conduction System

paragraphs.text: The epicardium is a relatively late-forming cardiac tissue that does not appear until septation is under way. It provides the bulk of the non-cardiomyocyte cellular components, including smooth muscle cells, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells. The progression of epicardial development has been studied in detail using avian and mouse models. The epicardium, the outer layer of the heart, forms by the growth of epithelial tissue from the dorsal mesothelium of the sinus venosus region. This single-cell layer spreads in a stereotyped pattern over the myocardium. The squamous epithelium of the primitive epicardium and the myocardium are initially juxtaposed, but rapid accumulation and differentiation of connective tissue components between these layers ensue to thicken the epicardium. The cells within the epicardium invade the myocardium and the endocardium, giving rise to valve cells, fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells, and other components of the coronary vasculature.38 The controversy regarding the origin of the coronary endothelial cells is understandable because of the apparently conflicting findings from lineage tracing studies. Using retroviral lineage tracing, precursor cells labeled in the proepicardium were found to give rise to endothelial cells as well as smooth muscle cells.24 However, Cre-lox lineage tracing using what appeared to be epicardial-specific promoters identified only a small subset of labeled coronary endothelial cells.39,40 Other investigators using a novel lineage tracing approach showed evidence that endothelial cells come from the endocardial lining of the sinus venosus.41 More recently, it was proposed that coronary endothelial cells within the myocardium originate from endocardial cells within the ventricles.42 Another investigation using another lineage tracing method now proposes that the bulk of coronary endothelial cells come from the cells within the epicardium (subepicardial cells) that originate from the endocardium lining the atrium or sinus venosus.43 These findings are not necessarily in conflict; the endothelium lining the myriad of vessels within the myocardium is likely to come from several sources, depending on location within the heart and the types of vessel (see Fig. 72.12).
paragraphs.heading: Epicardium

paragraphs.text: The epicardium is also the tissue in which cardiac ganglia develop, nerves travel, and fat cells accumulate. Evidence suggests that the embryonic epicardium may also include cells that can contribute a subset of cardiomyocytes.39,40 This interesting tissue and its interaction with the myocardium are the focus of much current research.
paragraphs.heading: Epicardium

paragraphs.text: Although it is known that the adult vertebrate heart has an extensive lymphatic network, the lymphatic vasculature of the embryonic heart is still under active investigation. Cardiac lymphatics develop shortly after formation of the coronary vasculature, which is around the eighth week of gestation in humans. Lymphatic vessels start around the mediastinal lymphatics and grow from the base to the apex, following the vasculature.44,45 The vessels connect to form capillaries without a muscular wall, later connecting to the main lymphatic network. By the fourth month of gestation, the lymphatics have covered most of the surface of the heart, and then they grow into the myocardium (Fig. 72.14). The reader is referred to the review by Gancz et al.46 for a more
paragraphs.heading: Lymphatics

paragraphs.text: thorough explanation of cardiac lymphatic formation and function.
paragraphs.heading: Lymphatics

paragraphs.text: Differential control of cell division and cell death can in part account for the enormous differences in morphologic features of the various regions of the heart. For example, the cells of the thin-walled atria divide less than the cells of the thick-walled ventricle. The central structures of the fascicular CCS slow their proliferation rate early compared with surrounding myocardium.47 Apoptosis—programmed cell death—is a developmentally controlled strategy in the morphogenesis of many structures. It occurs during pruning of the nervous system and sculpting of digits of the hands and feet, and it occurs at many sites throughout cardiogenesis.48 Endocardial cushion mesenchyme cells, which include cardiac neural crest cells, undergo a high level of apoptosis during septation. A high frequency of apoptosis of cardiomyocytes occurs coincident with outflow tract morphogenesis. Experimental manipulation to increase or decrease cell death at this stage results in conotruncal abnormalities.49 Thus regulated apoptosis of outflow tract cardiomyocytes is critical for the normal docking of the great arteries with the ventricles. Environmental and genetic factors that alter the level of apoptosis at these critical stages and sites in the developing heart may contribute to CHDs.
paragraphs.heading: Cell Division and Cell Death

paragraphs.text: The more common genetic disorders that affect heart development are T21, T18, T13, and 22q11 deletions. All of the syndromes below can usually be detected by routine prenatal testing that would include first-trimester fetal ultrasounds, cell-free DNA screening (noninvasive prenatal test [NIPT]), or pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP- A). Karyotyping of chromosomes from cells collected by amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling often follow to confirm the diagnosis.
paragraphs.heading: Human Genetics

paragraphs.text: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is most commonly associated with the presence of three copies of chromosome 21 or, in rare cases, a translocation of an extra piece of chromosome 21. This and other trisomies are caused by improper cell division either during meiosis or, less commonly, early in embryonic development. T21 mosaicism, in which only a subset of cells has the trisomy, may also be present. Features seen in individuals with trisomy 21 include craniofacial features and neurodevelopmental disorders, and 50% will have some type of CHD. The more common CHDs detected in T21 infants include AV septal defect (a defect of endocardial cushions), ventricular septal defect, persistent ductus arteriosus, and tetralogy of Fallot.50,51 Infants with T21 are also more likely to have persistent pulmonary hypertension, both with and without CHD.52,53
paragraphs.heading: Human Genetics

paragraphs.text: Trisomy 18, or Edwards syndrome, is characterized by slow prenatal growth resulting in low birth weight, small craniofacial features, anomalies of the extremities, and CHDs. The prognosis is grim, with many individuals succumbing
paragraphs.heading: Human Genetics

paragraphs.text: to prenatal death or death soon after birth. CHDs seen in T18 include ventricular septal defect, persistent/patent ductus arteriosus, pulmonary stenosis, coarctation of the aorta, and abnormal heart valves.54,55
paragraphs.heading: Human Genetics

paragraphs.text: Trisomy 13, or Patau syndrome, is characterized by prenatal death or death soon after birth, slow growth and low birth weight, craniofacial anomalies, holoprosencephaly, exophthalmos, or omphalocele, as well as other anomalies throughout the body. CHDs are detected in 80% of newborns with trisomy 13 and include the range of CHDs found in trisomy 18. Ventricular septal defects are the most common.56 Surgery to correct CHDs in individuals with trisomy 13 or 18 is much more common now than 20 or even 10 years ago, although it still carries significant risks for morbidity and mortality.57
paragraphs.heading: Human Genetics

paragraphs.text: The 22q11 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge/velocardiofacial syndrome) has been discussed briefly above in the context of cardiac neural crest cells because it is considered a neurocristopathy, or a disease caused by disturbances in the generation, migration, or differentiation of neural crest cells. It is also categorized as a RASopathy because it results in abnormalities in signaling of the RAS pathway. Most of these patients have a microdeletion of the region 22q11.2 that contains many genes (30–40) including TBX1. Clinical and mouse studies have shown that TBX1 codes for a key transcription factor. Its absence prevents the expression of
paragraphs.heading: Human Genetics

paragraphs.heading: Human Genetics

paragraphs.text: • The majority of cardiac development is complete by 8
paragraphs.heading: Human Genetics

paragraphs.text: weeks’ human gestation. • The primary heart field is responsible for the left ven-
paragraphs.heading: Human Genetics

paragraphs.text: tricle and portions of the atria, whereas the second heart field and cardiac neural crest cells are responsible for parts of the atria, valve, outflow tract, and right ventricle formation.
paragraphs.heading: Human Genetics

paragraphs.text: genes, leading to multiple malformations.58 Phenotypes of these patients vary widely from mild to severe and typically include neurodevelopmental, craniofacial, and a wide range of cardiac anomalies. A large proportion of individuals with this syndrome (75%) have CHDs that include conotruncal defects such as truncus arteriosus, interrupted aortic arch B, and tetralogy of Fallot.59
paragraphs.heading: References

paragraphs.text: Cardiomyopathies are intrinsic disorders of heart muscle that are generally classified morphologically as hypertrophic, dilated, restrictive, and arrhythmogenic.60,61 A genetic basis can be identified in a majority of these lesions, usually a mutation in a sarcomeric or structural gene that results in contractile abnormalities. Hundreds of mutations in dozens of genes have been identified as causative in familial and sporadic forms of cardiomyopathy.60 The ultimate cardiac phenotype can develop at any age but occasionally presents in the neonatal period.62 Left ventricular noncompaction is an increasingly recognized (particularly in neonates) form of cardiomyopathy characterized by dense trabeculation of the normally smooth-walled left ventricular cavity. This is a poorly understood defect that may be caused by abnormalities in the Notch signaling pathway or mutations in various sarcomeric genes.62,63 Ongoing genetic studies are focused not only on the identification of genetic abnormalities leading to cardiomyopathy but also on investigating the factors that lead to clinical disease progression.

Some of the myocardial cells lining these regions release factors that activate a subset of the overlaying endocardium, resulting in select endocardial cells that invade the cardiac jelly and assume a mesenchymal phenotype. This process is known as endothelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). These cells proliferate, migrate, and differentiate. In AV valves, the portion of the cushions adjacent to the underlying myocardium differentiates onto a fibroblastic phenotype. Fenestrations develop and coalesce beneath this layer, resulting in delamination of the tissue from the developing cushion. Fenestrations also develop in the residual mesenchymal tissue strands, and these will develop into the tendinous cords of the AV valves. Semilunar valves form similarly, but instead of delaminating they form conical depressions facing the myocardium in a process referred to as excavation. 72 Cardiac Embryology

### STEPHANIE M. FORD AND MICHIKO WATANABE

### Introduction

Congenital heart defects (CHDs) affect about 1% of all live births around the world, with variations in reporting depending on birth rates and access to medical care.1 The care of children with CHDs has increasingly become a neonatal specialty, aided by prenatal detection. The fetal diagnosis of critical CHDs decreases postsurgical morbidity and mortality, and reparative or palliative cardiovascular surgery is commonplace in the first months of life.2 This success has led to a larger population of adults with CHDs and an expansion of a subspecialty for the care of these individuals. In parallel with these clinical advances, there has been exciting progress in understanding the cellular and molecular basis of normal and abnormal cardiogenesis and the relationship of heart defects to other congenital defects. The global incidence of CHDs has not decreased and has in fact increased as prenatal detection becomes more common worldwide.1 Yet, our knowledge of the pathogenesis of CHDs is far from complete. Understanding normal and abnormal cardiac embryology is critical to understanding the pathology underlying CHDs and ultimately their prevention.

The mature heart is the product of gene expression driven by endogenous and exogenous influences. The developing heart manifests its morphologic and physiologic plasticity under environmental stimuli. A detailed understanding of the factors that drive normal cardiogenesis is necessary for understanding the causes and consequences of abnormal development. Errors in cardiac morphogenesis involved with septation, valve formation, and proper patterning of the great vessels are responsible for most forms of CHDs. Normal heart development requires precise timing for coordination of the complex three-dimensional contortions of tissues, but, paradoxically, these tissues also have a remarkable capacity for modifications that compensate for mistakes. These adjustments allow abnormal heart structures and resultant functions to be compatible with life up to and even after birth, but they complicate identification of the primary causes of cardiac anomalies. This chapter focuses on clinically relevant aspects of cardiac embryology and how disruptions of this process may lead to CHDs.

1358

### Overview of Normal Heart Development

The following description of human heart development, especially the earlier events, is synthesized from information provided by studies of animal models and human embryonic and fetal tissues. A timetable of selected events in human heart development is presented in Fig. 72.1,3 which depicts the major transitions in early mammalian heart development.

The primordia of the heart are formed by bilaterally symmetric heart fields derived from the lateral plate mesoderm. These primordia migrate through the primitive streak, between the ectoderm and endoderm layers, to become symmetric mesoderm regions on either side of the primitive streak. During body folding, the primary heart fields fuse to form a tubular structure comprised of an inner layer of endocardium, a thick layer of extracellular matrix, and an outer layer of myocardium. This apparently “simple” tube begins to contract rhythmically and grows differentially so that dilations (primordia of the heart chambers) and constrictions (primordia of the partitions between chambers) appear along its length. Later additions from the second heart field to the distal ends of the tubular heart form the outflow tract and the sinus venosus. Dextral looping of the tube brings the venous caudal portion to a more dorsal position and to the left of the arterial cranial portion as septation of the tubular heart begins. The epicardium arises from tissue dorsal to the heart at the level of the atrioventricular (AV) junction and spreads over the outer surface of the myocardium as a layer of squamous epithelial cells and associated connective tissue during the early phase of septation. This layer is key to coronary vessel and fibroblast development in the heart.

The atrial chamber divides into two chambers by the growth of the septum primum, which forms perforations to create the foramen secundum. A second atrial septum subsequently grows to the right of the primary atrial septum and forms a one-way valve (right-to-left blood flow) between the two atria in the fetus. This avenue of blood flow, the foramen ovale, is permanently closed shortly after birth to functionally complete atrial septation. Ventricular septation is not complete at the time the primary atrial septum is formed. The ventricular septum results from the

growth and remodeling of trabecular sheets, continues with expansion of the ventricular chambers, and ends with the fusion of several tissues, including endocardial cushions from several sources and the muscular septum, to form the membranous and muscular interventricular septum. The outflow tract septation is the result of growth and fusion of spiraling ridges that eventually divide the truncus into aortic and pulmonary tracts. The venous and arterial vessels (aortic arches) undergo partial incorporation into cardiac chambers, differential degeneration, fusion, and growth to attain the mature structures.

The human heart has completed the major morphogenetic processes 8 weeks after fertilization. What follows is the completion of maturation of structures, growth, accumulation of cellular junctions at the intercalated discs, biochemical and metabolic adjustments, and compensation for the abrupt changes in patterns of blood flow at birth, such

as permanent closure of the foramen ovale of the atrial septum and closure and fibrosis of the ductus arteriosus and ductus venosus.

### Septation Endocardial Development: Formation of Cushion Tissue

Septation of the heart begins with swelling of the extracellular matrix between the endocardium and the myocardium at specific regions of the heart tube. These regions include the AV junction, the outflow tract, the leading edge of the primary atrial septum, and the ridge of the interventricular septum. As chamber differentiation proceeds, endocardial cushions grow into the lumen of the tubular heart and act as primitive valves to promote unidirectional blood flow. These simple mounds of extracellular matrix lined by a single layer of endocardial cells eventually mature into valves with thinned valve leaflets. A complex set of inductive events has been elucidated by studying cushion formation of the AV junction and the outflow tract.21 These events include signaling between the specialized myocardium and a subset of competent endocardial cells through growth factors (e.g., transforming growth factor-β [TGF-β], vascular endothelial growth factor [VEGF], bone morphogenetic proteins [BMPs]) and extracellular matrix molecules. Various proteases and homeobox genes are also involved.

The subsequent cascade of events includes release and migration of cells from the endocardial epithelium (termed endothelial-mesenchymal transition [EMT]) into the previously acellular cardiac jelly and proliferation, death, and differentiation of these endocardial mesenchyme cells within a complex matrix. The cushions are also populated by cardiac neural crest cells. The cushions eventually give rise to, or at least greatly influence, the subsequent development of septa and valves of the heart. Because a number of factors, cell types, and tissues are involved in this process at multiple levels and at different stages, there are many sites where mistakes can occur. It is therefore not surprising that septation

defects are so common. The differentiation of resilient valves requires remodeling of the extracellular matrix. It has been revealed that steps in cardiac valve differentiation and maturation share mechanisms with those of cartilage, tendon, and bone development.22

In the primitive atrium, a ring of tissue, the septum primum, grows toward the endocardial cushions near the AV junction (Fig. 72.9). Through apoptosis, fenestrations form in this tissue, creating the osteum secundum. The osteum primum, between the tip of this outgrowth of the septum primum and the endocardial cushion, closes as the tissue advances. The atrial roof folds inward, and the septum secundum begins to grow down on the right of the septum primum and continues in a crescent shape to form to the right of the base of the septum primum. This makes the septum primum a flap over the foramen ovale, allowing only right-to-left flow across the atria.

Ventricular and outflow tract septation occur in tandem, and aberrations in one may have structural consequences for the other. The myocardium from the outer curvature of the ventricle invaginates, growing cranially. AV canal endocardial cushions grow toward the myocardium, completing the ventricular septum. Outflow tract endocardial cushions form ridges that spiral along the conotruncus (Fig. 72.10). These ridges grow together to divide the conotruncus into

### Development of the Cardiac Conduction System

Primordia of the pulse-generating system function early in the caudal region of the tubular heart and allow unidirectional blood flow, but subsequent events in the development of the cardiac conduction system (CCS) are not well understood. Investigations of CCS embryogenesis in a variety of species, including the mouse, chicken, and zebrafish, have contributed to this understanding.33 Classic histologic analyses are limited in the information they provide because the early CCS cannot be readily distinguished histologically or even structurally from the surrounding myocardium. Biochemical markers have been detected that transiently stain portions of the CCS and have been used to follow these tissues during the three-dimensionally complex morphogenesis of the heart. The rabbit model is unique in that there is a marker for it, NF-150, an antibody against neurofilament proteins, that delineates its CCS throughout development and into the adult. These markers show that some of the tissues that give rise to the CCS can be distinguished from other cardiomyocytes as early as the tubular heart stages, because they have a different pattern of gene expression and cell proliferation.

Lineage tracing of myocardial cells provided clues to the origin of the CCS. The clonal relationship between CCS cells and working cardiomyocytes suggests that these specialized myocardia can be recruited from unspecialized myocardial cells. Evidence from avian systems supports the hypothesis that the vasculature can be the source of factors that initiate such recruitment, with endothelin-1 being a strong candidate for signaling.34

Less is known about the physiology of the developing CCS primarily because of technical barriers to resolution. These barriers are being overcome by advances in biomedical engineering technologies, such as optical mapping using voltagesensitive fluorescent dyes and optical coherence tomography, that allow the capture of images of the tiny beating heart at high spatiotemporal resolution. The tubular heart has a peristaltic-type contraction pattern resulting from a pulse-generating focus of cells and a slow distribution of action potentials

radiating evenly from that region in all directions.35 In the septating heart, alternating regions of relatively slow and fast conduction allow pumping of blood in one direction, with the endocardial cushions acting as primitive valves. Slow regions, such as the sinus venosus, AV junction, and outflow tract, cause a delay of the impulse conduction between chambers.36 The ventricular conduction system achieves its mature morphology simultaneously with the appearance of the mature sequence of activation.37 Subsequent differentiation allows for increasing speed of action potential conduction through the fascicular portion of this system and compensation for the growth of the heart. Maturation of the fibrous ring that separates the atrial from ventricular muscle and the connective tissue sheath around the conduction system also follows, serving as an insulative barrier to inappropriate conduction to neighboring working myocardium.

### Epicardium

The epicardium is a relatively late-forming cardiac tissue that does not appear until septation is under way. It provides the bulk of the non-cardiomyocyte cellular components, including smooth muscle cells, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells. The progression of epicardial development has been studied in detail using avian and mouse models. The epicardium, the outer layer of the heart, forms by the growth of epithelial tissue from the dorsal mesothelium of the sinus venosus region. This single-cell layer spreads in a stereotyped pattern over the myocardium. The squamous epithelium of the primitive epicardium and the myocardium are initially juxtaposed, but rapid accumulation and differentiation of connective tissue components between these layers ensue to thicken the epicardium. The cells within the epicardium invade the myocardium and the endocardium, giving rise to valve cells, fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells, and other components of the coronary vasculature.38 The controversy regarding the origin of the coronary endothelial cells is understandable because of the apparently conflicting findings from lineage tracing studies. Using retroviral lineage tracing, precursor cells labeled in the proepicardium were found to give rise to endothelial cells as well as smooth muscle cells.24 However, Cre-lox lineage tracing using what appeared to be epicardial-specific promoters identified only a small subset of labeled coronary endothelial cells.39,40 Other investigators using a novel lineage tracing approach showed evidence that endothelial cells come from the endocardial lining of the sinus venosus.41 More recently, it was proposed that coronary endothelial cells within the myocardium originate from endocardial cells within the ventricles.42 Another investigation using another lineage tracing method now proposes that the bulk of coronary endothelial cells come from the cells within the epicardium (subepicardial cells) that originate from the endocardium lining the atrium or sinus venosus.43 These findings are not necessarily in conflict; the endothelium lining the myriad of vessels within the myocardium is likely to come from several sources, depending on location within the heart and the types of vessel (see Fig. 72.12).

### Lymphatics

Although it is known that the adult vertebrate heart has an extensive lymphatic network, the lymphatic vasculature of the embryonic heart is still under active investigation. Cardiac lymphatics develop shortly after formation of the coronary vasculature, which is around the eighth week of gestation in humans. Lymphatic vessels start around the mediastinal lymphatics and grow from the base to the apex, following the vasculature.44,45 The vessels connect to form capillaries without a muscular wall, later connecting to the main lymphatic network. By the fourth month of gestation, the lymphatics have covered most of the surface of the heart, and then they grow into the myocardium (Fig. 72.14). ### Cell Division and Cell Death

Differential control of cell division and cell death can in part account for the enormous differences in morphologic features of the various regions of the heart. For example, the cells of the thin-walled atria divide less than the cells of the thick-walled ventricle. The central structures of the fascicular CCS slow their proliferation rate early compared with surrounding myocardium.47 Apoptosis—programmed cell death—is a developmentally controlled strategy in the morphogenesis of many structures. It occurs during pruning of the nervous system and sculpting of digits of the hands and feet, and it occurs at many sites throughout cardiogenesis.48 Endocardial cushion mesenchyme cells, which include cardiac neural crest cells, undergo a high level of apoptosis during septation. A high frequency of apoptosis of cardiomyocytes occurs coincident with outflow tract morphogenesis. Experimental manipulation to increase or decrease cell death at this stage results in conotruncal abnormalities.49 Thus regulated apoptosis of outflow tract cardiomyocytes is critical for the normal docking of the great arteries with the ventricles. Environmental and genetic factors that alter the level of apoptosis at these critical stages and sites in the developing heart may contribute to CHDs.

### Human Genetics

The more common genetic disorders that affect heart development are T21, T18, T13, and 22q11 deletions. All of the syndromes below can usually be detected by routine prenatal testing that would include first-trimester fetal ultrasounds, cell-free DNA screening (noninvasive prenatal test [NIPT]), or pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP- A). Karyotyping of chromosomes from cells collected by amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling often follow to confirm the diagnosis.

Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is most commonly associated with the presence of three copies of chromosome 21 or, in rare cases, a translocation of an extra piece of chromosome 21. This and other trisomies are caused by improper cell division either during meiosis or, less commonly, early in embryonic development. T21 mosaicism, in which only a subset of cells has the trisomy, may also be present. Features seen in individuals with trisomy 21 include craniofacial features and neurodevelopmental disorders, and 50% will have some type of CHD. The more common CHDs detected in T21 infants include AV septal defect (a defect of endocardial cushions), ventricular septal defect, persistent ductus arteriosus, and tetralogy of Fallot.50,51 Infants with T21 are also more likely to have persistent pulmonary hypertension, both with and without CHD.52,53

Trisomy 18, or Edwards syndrome, is characterized by slow prenatal growth resulting in low birth weight, small craniofacial features, anomalies of the extremities, and CHDs. The prognosis is grim, with many individuals succumbing

Trisomy 13, or Patau syndrome, is characterized by prenatal death or death soon after birth, slow growth and low birth weight, craniofacial anomalies, holoprosencephaly, exophthalmos, or omphalocele, as well as other anomalies throughout the body. CHDs are detected in 80% of newborns with trisomy 13 and include the range of CHDs found in trisomy 18. Ventricular septal defects are the most common.56 Surgery to correct CHDs in individuals with trisomy 13 or 18 is much more common now than 20 or even 10 years ago, although it still carries significant risks for morbidity and mortality.57

The 22q11 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge/velocardiofacial syndrome) has been discussed briefly above in the context of cardiac neural crest cells because it is considered a neurocristopathy, or a disease caused by disturbances in the generation, migration, or differentiation of neural crest cells. It is also categorized as a RASopathy because it results in abnormalities in signaling of the RAS pathway. Most of these patients have a microdeletion of the region 22q11.2 that contains many genes (30–40) including TBX1.
