Premature atrial beats are common (present in 1%–3% of pregnancies) and are generally well tolerated unless a sustained tachycardia develops. The risk of fetal tachycardia when premature atrial contractions have been seen is approximately 0.5% to 1%, although couplets and blocked atrial bigeminy may increase this risk. Medical treatment is not recommended for either isolated premature atrial contractions or blocked atrial bigeminy; however, interval auscultation of the fetal heart rate weekly by the obstetrician is recommended for frequent premature atrial or ventricular contractions until resolution of the arrhythmia is documented.2

Fetal tachycardia is generally defined as fetal heart rates greater than 180 bpm. The majority of fetal tachycardias are supraventricular in origin, and ventricular tachycardias are very rare. Management of fetal supraventricular tachycardia is targeted to those at risk for heart failure. Intermittent tachycardia is generally well tolerated by the fetus, with the risk for hydrops increasing proportionally with increased time spent in the abnormal rhythm. Therapy is generally felt to be indicated for sustained tachycardias—those that occur most of the time or greater than 50% of the time while monitored. Most of these tachyarrhythmias can be treated through maternal administration of antiarrhythmic medications with transplacental delivery to the fetus.24 However, the influence of certain medications, such as amiodarone, on the developing fetus and fetal myocardium must be taken into account. Ventricular tachycardia is very rare in the fetus. It may be associated with myocardial disease or observed in the presence of cardiac tumors. Rarely,

Psychological distress may persist for months after birth. There is a need for research to determine the most effective techniques for counseling and family support, as well as investigating potential modifiable variables of maternal stress that may alter the impact.30

Prenatal diagnosis does allow for sustained education and guidance between diagnosis and delivery. Little research has been done on the most effective methods for prenatal counseling and family support. Some important elements to address during prenatal counseling would include findings and limitations, results given in close proximity to the time of testing (preferably the same day), natural history in utero, prognosis for the remainder of the pregnancy and beyond as able, possible associations with genetic anomalies, alleviating parental guilt, and a potential range of management options.2 The practitioner must utilize good communication skills and empathy. The level of parental understanding must be assessed continuously during counseling with the knowledge that understanding may be limited by grief, and multiple counseling sessions may be required.2

### Impact of Prenatal Diagnosis

The goal of early detection of a pathologic state is to alter long-term outcome in a favorable way. Early studies of the impact of fetal diagnosis on postnatal outcome were not satisfying. However, subsequent publications suggest an improvement in postnatal mortality and morbidity. One study looking at the impact of prenatal diagnosis in hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) showed that preoperative status and first-stage mortality were affected by prenatal diagnosis, with a total survival of 75% in those who elected to undergo surgery. All of the patients who were diagnosed prenatally survived, whereas only 65% of the patients who were diagnosed postnatally survived. In addition, patients diagnosed prenatally had a lower incidence of preoperative acidosis, tricuspid regurgitation, and ventricular dysfunction, and they were also less likely to need preoperative inotropic medications or bicarbonate. Preoperative risk factors that correlated with early mortality included postnatal diagnosis, more severe acidosis, need for bicarbonate or inotropes, and ventricular dysfunction.31 Another study on prenatal diagnosis of CHD evaluated the neurologic outcomes in fetuses with HLHS. Although the overall mortality did not differ in the prenatal versus postnatal groups, prenatal diagnosis was associated with fewer adverse neurologic events when compared with those with postnatal diagnosis.32 Similarly, diagnosis, metabolic acidosis level, preoperative mortality, length of stay, and postoperative mortality were all significantly better in patients with a prenatal diagnosis of TGA compared with the group diagnosed postnatally.33

However, although these data are encouraging, further studies are needed to evaluate the CHD outcomes in the

setting of prenatal diagnosis. Certain populations continue to have poor outcomes despite prenatal diagnosis, including those with HLHS with intact or restrictive atrial septum, right atrial and left atrial isomerisms (heterotaxy), and pulmonary atresia with intact septum with right-ventricular–dependent coronary circulation. Further studies into markers of outcome in these patients and improved survival may depend on fetal intervention.34–36

Specific findings on fetal echocardiogram allow for comprehensive delivery planning to prevent hemodynamic compromise in high-risk CHD. Disease-specific delivery room recommendations are currently well accepted in clinical practice.2,37,38 Level-of-care recommendations should include follow-up, possible need for transport to a tertiary care center, likelihood of neonatal intervention (catheterbased or surgical), or, in rare cases, the need for emergent intervention in the delivery. ### Limitations of Fetal Echocardiograms

Advances in ultrasound technology have greatly improved the sensitivity of fetal echocardiograms over the past 20 to 25 years, and it is currently expected that fetal echocardiograms can diagnose even complex CHD in specific detail. However, despite the advances in technology over time, data indicate that only 48% to 60% of congenital heart defects are detected prenatally.39 Detection rates are poorest in rural communities.40 In addition, recent research has demonstrated significantly discrepant prenatal detection rates—specifically, TGA and HLHS—with lower socioeconomic quartile, Hispanic ethnicity, and public insurance, in addition to rural residence, being associated with lower and later prenatal detection rates.41 This suggests that better access to care, screening mechanisms, and indications for fetal echocardiogram are needed, particularly in underserved communities.

It is important to recognize the limitations of fetal echocardiography both in diagnosing certain types of CHD and in detecting associated lesions. A recent study reviewing fetal echocardiograms from 2008 to 2017 demonstrated a diagnostic discrepancy rate as high as 13.5% in fetuses with major CHD, mostly minor and moderate in severity, indicating that we can still do better at elucidating the finer details of anatomy and physiology when CHD is present.42 Ultrasound and fetal echocardiography are intrinsically more sensitive for some types of CHD than others. Even in the most optimal of situations, fetal echocardiography is less sensitive to detect abnormalities of smaller structures. Thus diagnoses such as partial anomalous pulmonary venous return (PAPVR), small ventricular septal defects, and minor valve abnormalities, including bicuspid aortic valve, cannot be ruled out on fetal echocardiograms. ### Fetal Therapies

The first attempt at performing a fetal cardiac intervention was in 1987, when attempts were made to pace the fetal heart to prevent progression of hydrops fetalis. The first attempt at fetal aortic valve intervention was made more than 30 years ago by attempting to dilate the aortic valve in a fetus with severe aortic stenosis. This attempt was successful, and the infant eventually underwent a biventricular repair.17,18,36,45–47 Currently, there is a growing body of evidence in support of fetal cardiac intervention. Several techniques have been attempted for fetal balloon interventions. Ideally, fetal cardiac interventional procedures are performed percutaneously to limit maternal risks. The least invasive technique involves maternal sedation with percutaneous access to the fetus. More invasive methods, which increase maternal risk, have the benefit of better fetal position.17,18,36,45–47 The goal after fetal intervention is to allow the fetus to spend as much time in utero as possible to promote remodeling and allow the fetal lung to complete maturity. The underlying hypothesis in support of many fetal interventions is that the left ventricle undergoes severe myocardial injury or fibroblast damage, compromising the pressure-generating capability of the ventricle

prenatally.17,18,36,45–47 If the underlying cause of the injury, such as is the case in severe aortic stenosis, can be resolved, the left ventricle has the potential to remodel, allowing for improvement in contractile function and, it is hoped, a biventricular repair.

As in all procedures, appropriate selection of patients is of utmost importance. The goal is to offer the appropriate procedure to the right patient. Criteria for selection for fetal aortic valve balloon dilation currently include a large left ventricle with persistent patency of the aortic valve, a normal-appearing mitral valve, reversed flow in the aortic arch, and a left-to-right shunt at the atrial level.17,18,36,45–47

The most promising group for fetal intervention may be patients with HLHS with intact or restrictive atrial septum. Postnatal mortality is extremely high in this group of patients, with reported rates of 48% to 80%. Intact atrial septum can be found in up to 6% of patients with HLHS, with the majority of their mortality reported during the first few weeks of life. This suggests that mortality risk may be associated with intrapulmonary arterial or venous changes.17,18

### Novel Approaches to Prenatal Diagnosis of Congenital Heart Disease

Just as in fetal intervention, advances in the diagnostic realm are being made. Promising results have been seen with the performance of fetal echocardiograms during the first trimester. A study evaluating the feasibility and accuracy of first-trimester echocardiography identified fetuses with ventricular septal defects, TGA, and HLHS. The sensitivity of these early echocardiograms compared with the standard study performed at 18 to 22 weeks’ gestation was calculated as 60.0% and the specificity was 98.7%, with a positive predictive value of 75.0% and a negative predictive value that reached 97.4%.48 Earlier detection of significant heart defects allows for more timely counseling and decision making.

Newer indices of ventricular performance, including the Tei index (also known as the myocardial performance index), are currently being evaluated in the fetus. The Tei index has been used widely as a measure of global (combined systolic and diastolic) myocardial function in adults and children. It has also been shown to be useful in the assessment of fetal cardiac function.39

Three-dimensional fetal echocardiography also shows promise in increasing both the efficiency of fetal echocardiography and the accuracy of diagnosis. However, poor frame rates and false-positive results continue to be an issue.

### Summary

In summary, the field of fetal cardiology has experienced rapid growth in the last 45 years. Advances in image quality allow for the diagnosis of a wide array of cardiac pathologies. Such imaging also allows for well-coordinated post-delivery

title: Patent Ductus Arteriosus

paragraphs.text: 75 Patent Ductus Arteriosus
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: In utero, the ductus arteriosus provides a connection between the pulmonary artery and descending aorta, which carries deoxygenated blood returning to the right heart toward the placenta for reoxygenation. Although essential to normal fetal physiology, it typically constricts, closes, and becomes a fibrous remnant after birth. Failure of those processes, resulting in persistent ductal patency into childhood or adulthood, has been recognized as pathologic for many years. More than 60 years ago, Burnard reported that the murmur of a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) was heard more frequently and for longer after birth in preterm infants and typically was associated with respiratory distress.1 Subsequently, prolonged ductal patency in preterm infants was linked to more severe respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), prolonged assisted ventilation, pulmonary hemorrhage, bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), renal impairment, intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), periventricular leukomalacia (PVL), cerebral palsy, and death.2 The plausible hypothesis that these morbidities might be caused by excessive pulmonary blood flow or systemic ischemia resulting from a large leftto-right shunt through the ductus led many practitioners to adopt strategies for closing the ductus, either in anticipation of or after confirmation of prolonged patency. In randomized trials, however, those interventions consistently failed to produce benefits other than ductal closure, and concerns arose regarding potential adverse effects. Although consensus on many aspects of management is lacking, the current approach consists of identifying pathologic persistent ductal patency, evaluating hemodynamic consequences, and minimizing deleterious effects.
paragraphs.heading: WILLIAM E. BENITZ AND SHAZIA BHOMBAL

paragraphs.text: The ductus arteriosus is derived from the distal portion of the embryonic sixth brachial arch and is approximately the diameter of the descending aorta in utero. In a normal term infant, the ductus arteriosus constricts soon after birth, stimulated by the rapid postnatal increase in arterial oxygen tension. The muscularis of the ductus is uniquely responsive to oxygen, reacting to an increase in ambient oxygen with sustained contraction. The mechanisms of this response
paragraphs.heading: Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: are not fully understood, but the cytochrome P450 system (CYP450), endothelin-1 (ET-1), and intracellular oxidation-reduction (redox) balance appear to be important.3 Glucocorticoids may be essential in maturation of the ductal oxygen-sensing apparatus, because antenatal glucocorticoid treatment increases expression of genes for calcium and potassium channels implicated in the oxygen response and with decreased risk of persistent ductal patency. This direct response is augmented by a rapid decline in circulating levels of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), a potent, very rapidly metabolized smooth muscle relaxant that has a major role in keeping the ductus arteriosus open in the fetus. The placenta is the primary source of fetal PGE2, so circulating levels fall precipitously upon umbilical cord clamping. Maximal effects of PGE2 withdrawal seem to require antenatal priming of ductal muscle by rising levels of PGE2 late in gestation. Dynamic functional closure initiates at the pulmonary end of the ductus arteriosus and usually is complete within the first 4 days after birth, but anatomic obliteration is not achieved until after 1 week of age.
paragraphs.heading: Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: In otherwise normal infants born at or near term, it is unusual for the ductus arteriosus to fail to close within the first 4 days. With decreasing gestational age at birth, both the age at spontaneous closure and the proportion of infants with a PDA at any postnatal age progressively increase.4,5 Before interventions to close the PDA in preterm infants were widely adopted, ductal closure nearly always occurred spontaneously if given sufficient time, sometimes as late as 4 to 6 months of age. However, those observations date from an era before adoption of antenatal steroid treatment and availability of exogenous surfactant, when very low birth weight (VLBW) infants rarely survived and extremely low birth weight (ELBW) infants essentially never survived. In many randomized trials, numerous control subjects were treated to achieve ductal closure, typically late in or after the first week after birth, obscuring the natural course of spontaneous ductal closure as well as risk factors that might predict failure of that process. High rates of spontaneous closure have been observed in control subjects in trials in which open treatment was used rarely or not at all, however. Observational data from centers that avoid interventions to close the ductus, where only 6% were treated to close
paragraphs.heading: Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: PDA, show that 90% of nearly 1200 otherwise unselected VLBW infants achieved ductal closure without treatment (80% before discharge).4–9 Spontaneous ductal closure is particularly likely in babies born at greater than 28 weeks’ gestation, weighing greater than 1000 g at birth, or without RDS. In addition to birth at an earlier gestational age, prolongation of ductal patency is associated with exposure to chorioamnionitis10 or gestational hypertension,11 or to higher fluid intake during the first 2 days after birth (but not on subsequent days),12 but whether these factors have a causal role in maintenance of a PDA remains uncertain.
paragraphs.heading: Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: The mechanisms underlying delay or failure of ductal closure in preterm infants have not been fully elucidated.13 Birth before term may simply come before the ductus is prepared, functionally or structurally, to respond to signals that normally induce closure. For example, lamb studies have demonstrated that the intensity of ductal constriction in response to oxygen is gestational-age dependent. Genes essential to ductal responses, including K+ and Ca2+ channels involved in muscle contraction and phosphodiesterases that degrade cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) and cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), mediators of the vasodilator responses to nitric oxide (NO) and PGE2, are developmentally upregulated in the ductus arteriosus of the fetus approaching term. Lack of preconditioning by PGE2 in late gestation may make the ductus less sensitive to withdrawal of that vasorelaxant. Inadequate glucocorticoid production, common in extremely preterm infants, may compromise oxygen-sensing pathways, particularly in infants not exposed to maternal antenatal steroids. Cytokines produced by a fetal inflammatory response, a frequent correlate of preterm birth, may directly impede ductal responses.14 These potential mechanisms correspond to the clinical observations that presence of a PDA is strongly associated with extreme immaturity, lack of exposure to antenatal steroids, and signs of fetal inflammation or infection.
paragraphs.heading: Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: Before birth, the pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) is high, so approximately 75% of the right ventricular output flows right-to-left through the ductus arteriosus. With the first breath, lung inflation and oxygenation produce a rapid decline in PVR, a decrease in pulmonary arterial pressures, and a large increase in pulmonary blood flow. Removal of the low-resistance placenta from the systemic circulation leads to increased systemic vascular resistance, and ductal flow quickly reverses direction to left-to-right. If ductal closure occurs in the first few days, the imbalance in distribution of the total cardiac output, with increased pulmonary blood flow relative to systemic blood flow, is well tolerated. If the ductus arteriosus remains open, however, the continued decline in PVR over the first several days and weeks results in progressively increasing left-to-right shunting through the PDA, with excessive pulmonary blood flow, increased volume work for the left heart, and the potential for systemic ischemia.
paragraphs.heading: Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: Term infants can often tolerate large left-to-right shunts with high pulmonary-to-systemic blood flow ratios (Q̇ P/ Q̇ S) without developing pulmonary edema. In preterm infants, surfactant deficiency, low serum oncotic pressures, and compromised capillary integrity (e.g., that which accompanies bacteremia) lower the threshold for development of pulmonary edema. Accumulation of alveolar and interstitial fluid increases the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient and reduces lung compliance. A large left-to-right shunt increases volume work for the left heart, leading to atrial and ventricular enlargement and myocardial dysfunction. The combination of left heart dysfunction and diversion of aortic flow into the lungs (a “ductal steal”) may compromise systemic cardiac output, with consequent risk of end-organ ischemia. Low diastolic pressures may impair coronary artery perfusion, producing signs of myocardial ischemia, including ST segment depression and elevated serum troponin levels. Increasing ductal left-to-right shunting may be associated with Doppler ultrasound evidence of decreased, absent, or reversal of diastolic flow in the middle cerebral, superior mesenteric, and renal arteries, as well as the descending aorta. Impaired cerebral blood flow has been associated with PDA in several studies, implicating but not proving a causal role for PDA in development of IVH and, possibly, PVL. Similarly, bowel or kidney ischemia resulting from compromised mesenteric or renal arterial flow may be associated with NEC or impaired renal function. Reversal of aortic diastolic flow in term infants with surgical congenital heart disease has been associated with NEC, but empiric data have not demonstrated a direct correlation between estimates of severity of the ductal steal and the risk of ischemic complications in preterm infants with PDA.
paragraphs.heading: Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: Recognition of a persistent PDA in a preterm infant typically begins with auscultation of the characteristic coarse systolic murmur, heard best along the left sternal border. The continuous “machinery murmur” typical of PDA in an older child is rarely present. Infants with a very large PDA and high Q̇ P/Q̇ S ratio may have no audible murmur. Increasing murmur intensity may reflect increasing flow velocity through a narrowing ductus rather than increasing shunt volume. Hemodynamic effects of the large leftto-right shunt may be evident in an increased precordial impulse (owing to the increased left ventricular stroke volume) and in arterial pulses that are prominent, bounding, or palpable where they are not normally, such as in the palms (resulting from diastolic runoff into the low-pressure pulmonary circulation). In preterm infants greater than 1000 g, systemic arterial diastolic blood pressures are reduced and pulse pressures may be increased. Among babies less than 1000 g, reduction in both systolic and diastolic pressures without widened pulse pressures are more typical. These findings are nonspecific, insensitive, and correlate poorly with echocardiographic findings. Similar physical findings may be present in infants with an aortopulmonary window,
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: large arteriovenous malformation, hemitruncus, or certain other cardiac defects, or they may simply reflect a relatively hyperdynamic state of another cause. Often, a hemodynamically significant PDA (hsPDA) is suspected only because of signs of excessive pulmonary perfusion, such as an increasing Paco2 and/or alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient, decreasing lung compliance, or inability to wean the infant from supplemental oxygen, distending airway pressure, or positive pressure ventilation. Pulmonary hemorrhage is an infrequent complication often attributed to increased pulmonary flow from a PDA.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Patent ductus arteriosus is most readily confirmed by color Doppler echocardiography, which documents anatomic patency and the direction and velocity of ductal blood flow throughout the cardiac cycle (Fig. 75.1). Ductal shunt patterns and systemic to diastolic flow ratios also may aid in identifying an hsPDA, with early demonstration of a pulsatile pattern with a high systolic-to-diastolic ratio predicting a large PDA at 1 month, compared with a restrictive pattern with a low systolic-to-diastolic ratio (Fig. 75.2).15 Echocardiography also allows characterization of the hemodynamic consequences of the ductal shunt, including assessment of degree of pulmonary overflow and systemic hypoperfusion (Table 75.1).16 Findings that correlate with a large shunt include a large ductal diameter, evidence for increased pulmonary flow, such as an increased left atrial to aortic root diameter (LA:Ao) ratio, left heart distention, ratio of early passive to late atrial contractile transmitral filling (E wave to A wave ratio), left ventricular isovolumic relaxation time (IVRT), and signs of systemic hypoperfusion, such as absent or reversed diastolic flow in cerebral, renal, or mesenteric arteries or descending aorta (Fig. 75.3).17,18 The utility of individual markers is low, but composite scores appear to
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: increase diagnostic utility. Preliminary results suggest that high composite scores may predict development of chronic lung disease.16,17,19 Schena et al. used a scoring system for shunt severity to report association of prolonged patent ductus with BPD.20 These results need to be confirmed and extended to other adverse outcomes potentially attributable to PDA, but they represent essential first steps toward establishing the role of such measures in identifying candidates for enrollment in management trials and ultimately for targeted interventions.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Measurement of regional tissue oxygen saturations (rSpo2) or fractional tissue oxygen extraction (FTOE) by near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) has been proposed for evaluation of the peripheral hemodynamic consequences of ductal patency. PDA, whether hemodynamically significant by echocardiographic criteria or not, correlates with lower renal rSpo2 and increased renal FTOE; cerebral rSpo2 is reduced only if arterial oxygen saturations are, and cerebral FTOE is not increased by PDA or hsPDA (Table 75.2).21 Paired comparisons show increases in cerebral rSpo2 and decreases in FTOE following medical or surgical closure of the ductus arteriosus,22 but similar effects on renal rSpo2 were not observed. Larger ductal diameters and other echocardiographic measures of hemodynamic significance are not consistently related to NIRS indicators of reduced tissue perfusion.22–24 Although these observations show promise, the utility of NIRS measurements for diagnosis or severity assessment of PDA, identification of infants with PDA for selective treatment, or prediction of long-term consequences has not been evaluated.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Serum biomarkers are potential tools for evaluation of hemodynamic significance of PDA, guiding treatment of PDA, or predicting adverse outcomes.25 Plasma levels of B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) or NT-pro-BNP, an inactive byproduct of BNP production, are elevated in infants with significant PDA, correlate with echocardiographic

paragraphs.text: echocardiography. There have been no studies evaluating these markers as criteria for intervention to close the ductus arteriosus.
paragraphs.heading: systolic diastolic

paragraphs.text: Chest radiographs may demonstrate an enlarged cardiac silhouette, prominent pulmonary vascular markings, or evidence of pulmonary edema. Although these signs may suggest the diagnosis, they are nonspecific and insensitive.
paragraphs.heading: systolic diastolic

paragraphs.text: Because PDA in preterm infants is strongly associated with adverse outcomes, surgical and medical strategies for closing the ductus arteriosus were widely adopted soon after they became available. Surgical ligation in preterm infants with RDS was first reported in 1968, and the first case series appeared in 1972. Medical induction of ductal closure with indomethacin was described in 1976. The conviction that ductal closure was beneficial became so pervasive that the landmark National Collaborative Study of indomethacin in preterm infants with PDA had no nontreatment arm: all three regimens mandated ductal closure by either indomethacin or ligation. These reports were followed by numerous descriptions of successful surgical or medical closure of the ductus, which heavily influenced practice for many years, but the utility of routine intervention to achieve ductal closure late in the first or during the second week of life has come into question.
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: The seminal reports that nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs, now called cyclo-oxygenase inhibitors) induce constriction and closure of the ductus arteriosus have been followed by more than 60 randomized, placebocontrolled trials of cyclo-oxygenase inhibitors in preterm infants.28–33 Indomethacin and ibuprofen are equally effective in reducing rates of persistent PDA, resulting in lower rates of ductal ligation. These agents may be less effective in achievement of ductal closure in the most immature
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: preterm infants; however, in a randomized trial in infants less than 27 weeks’ gestation, timing of ductal closure did not differ between the oral ibuprofen and placebo groups.34 Observational data from the 1970s suggested that indomethacin might be less likely to induce ductal closure in infants greater than 10 to 14 days of age, but contemporary experiences indicate that efficacy is not lost with increasing age, at least over the first 3 to 4 weeks35,36 and perhaps much longer.37 Repeated courses of indomethacin or ibuprofen may be effective in infants who do not respond to the first or second course.38 Acetaminophen is gaining favor as an equally effective alternative for PDA closure with fewer adverse effects,39 but its role in optimal management of preterm infants with PDA remains to be established.
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: Neither individual trials nor meta-analyses have identified improvements in long-term outcomes with these treatments.28 In early randomized trials, indomethacin prophylaxis started before 12 hours of age decreased rates of any IVH and of grade III/IV IVH. These effects are not achieved with later treatment2 nor with ibuprofen,40 do not appear to be mediated by PDA closure, and may not obtain in the current era, because baseline rates of IVH are now much lower.41 Reduction in IVH did not correlate with improved long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes. Compared with placebo-treated controls, infants given low-dose indomethacin prophylaxis had better vocabulary skills and a lower probability of an IQ less than 70 at age 4.5 years, but their mothers were more likely to describe them as having significant problems on the daily living domain of the Vineland scale at age 8. No effects on many other neurodevelopmental outcome measures were evident. Although indomethacin reduces cerebral, mesenteric, and renal arterial blood flow and is associated with diminished cerebral oxygen levels, reduced creatinine clearance, and oliguria, meta-analyses of randomized trials indicate that these hemodynamic changes do not increase mortality or potential complications, including BPD, NEC, bowel perforation, retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), or neurodevelopmental impairment.28 A randomized trial in preterm infants aged less than 28 weeks with moderate to large PDAs who were receiving respiratory support after the first week found that early routine treatment did not reduce PDA ligations or the presence of a PDA at discharge and did not improve any prespecified secondary outcomes. However, early treatment delayed full feeding and was associated with higher rates of late-onset sepsis and death in infants born at ≥26 weeks of gestation.42 The effect of prophylactic indomethacin on BPD risk remains unclear, with recent data from contemporary cohorts indicating either a decrease or no increase in BPD incidence.43,44 Co-administration of indomethacin with a glucocorticosteroid increases the risk of bowel perforation, however. Ibuprofen has less impact on cerebral and renal blood flow and minimal if any effect on mesenteric perfusion, so it is less likely than indomethacin to cause significant oliguria and may be less likely to be associated with NEC.45 In vitro studies suggest that ibuprofen may displace bilirubin from its binding site on albumin. Medical PDA
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: prophylaxis reduces severe pulmonary hemorrhage during the first week but not over the entire hospital course.46
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: Although many case series of surgical ligation have appeared, the three randomized trials that assessed the impact of this intervention demonstrated no consistent improvements in mortality or long-term morbidities.2 Ligation is a reliable method for closing the ductus arteriosus, but it is not without hazard. In up to one-third of infants, ligation precipitates severe left ventricular dysfunction and cardiorespiratory decompensation, requiring major increases in intensive care support in the immediate postoperative period. The risk of this complication decreases with postnatal age, so later ligations (at >4 weeks of age) are better tolerated than earlier surgeries. Infants who develop postoperative hypotension refractory to catecholamine infusion have lower postoperative serum cortisol levels than those who do not become hypotensive or respond to catecholamine treatment.47 Some have reported that milrinone infusion reduces postoperative hemodynamic instability,48 but others have not found this treatment to be beneficial.49 Other surgical complications include chylothorax, pneumothorax, phrenic or recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, and scoliosis.50 Paralysis of the left vocal cord, which occurs in up to 67% of ELBW infants following ductal ligation,51 is associated with prolongation of assisted ventilation and oxygen supplementation, a higher probability of BPD, feeding difficulties, tube feeding, longer neonatal hospitalization, and vocal and respiratory impairments in adulthood.52 Infants who undergo early ductal ligation are at increased risk for BPD and have higher rates of neurodevelopmental impairment; these adverse outcomes may result from the indication for surgery rather than the surgery itself.
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: Transcatheter ductus closure (TCC), the newest treatment option, has been demonstrated to be safe and effective.53 Devices have been FDA-approved for use in infants as small as 700 g. Adverse effects appear to be limited to rare device displacement or embolization, which have mostly been manageable by another catheter-based intervention. Although a few early reports described ischemic limb injury following arterial access, such events have been very rare since adoption of the femoral vein as the preferred access site. Post-procedure circulatory decompensation is much less common than with surgical ligation. It is not yet known if a more favorable adverse effect profile will lead to favorable effects on longterm outcomes, because there have been no controlled trials of this treatment. Consequently, the indications and optimal timing for this procedure are not yet clearly defined.
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: Current evidence indicates that routine, early treatment to achieve ductal closure does not improve long-term outcomes.2 Although some individual trials have found statistically significant effects on scattered outcomes, meta-analyses have found only reduction in IVH or IVH > grade II and increased ROP ≥ stage 3 to be significant in pooled data.28 Rates of untoward outcomes do not correlate with differences in rates of ductal closure among trials. Elimination of trials that frequently provided open treatment of infants in the “control” arm does not change these conclusions.28 Because
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: most clinical trials addressed treatment early in the postnatal course, the effects of prolonged exposure to a moderate or large left-to-right shunt in ELBW infants remain unknown. Recent post hoc analyses from Clyman and colleagues have found that increased rates of BPD or of death or BPD are associated with prolonged PDA only for infants who require ongoing intubation for positive pressure ventilation, and that prolongation of PDA exposure beyond a threshold duration of 10 to 14 days does not further augment the incidence of those outcomes.54–56 Consequently, the indications (if any) for, potential benefits from, and optimal timing of later ductal closure remain indeterminate. Similarly, these global observations do not imply that there cannot be some infants for whom ductal closure would be beneficial, particularly within groups that are not well represented in those older studies (e.g., those <26 weeks’ gestation).
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: Better strategies for assessment of the magnitude of ductal shunting, based on echocardiographic findings such as those listed in Table 75.1 or scores based on those measurements with or without additional clinical or biomarker variables,17,19 promise to help identify infants who may be candidates for ductal closure,16,17 but benefits of treatment for infants selected using such criteria remain to be demonstrated. Until such information is available, practice will be guided by consensus, belief, and individualized clinical judgment. The perceived balance between benefits (reduced IVH and early pulmonary hemorrhage) and disadvantages (more severe respiratory disease, intestinal perforation with concomitant glucocorticoid use) will guide the choice between the use and avoidance of indomethacin prophylaxis. High rates of spontaneous closure in infants greater than 1000 g, and their demonstrated ability to tolerate longer periods of ductal shunting, support a permissive approach to PDA management. Infants weighing less than 1000 g who develop hypotension or overt congestive heart failure may be deemed to require ductal closure, but the criteria for that decision remain uncertain.
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: Experience with less aggressive strategies for management of PDA continues to accumulate. Although earlier studies mostly described effects of moderate reductions in the proportion of infants with PDA who received treatment, there are now several reports of cohorts and randomized trials in which treatment was rarely used. Although some cohort studies suggest an increase in adverse outcomes with adoption of conservative PDA management practices, randomized trials consistently fail to demonstrate differences in outcomes between groups managed with or without active PDA closure. Elimination of cyclo-oxygenase inhibitor treatment in 139 infants less than 30 weeks’ gestation who required ventilation and surfactant replacement was associated with lower rates of chronic lung disease (8% vs. 18%– 28%) and NEC (0% vs. 4%–6%) and comparable rates of IVH (7% vs. 6%–7%) and mortality (13% vs. 12%), versus network benchmarks, and ligation was used in fewer than 5%.57 Adoption of a conservative treatment approach in 72 VLBW infants (<1500 g) was followed by a significant reduction in the rate of oxygen use or ventilation at
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: 36 weeks’ postmenstrual age (from 49% in prior treatment eras to 18%) among those diagnosed with PDA, despite treatment of PDA with ibuprofen in only 7% of cases and no use of ligation, without any increase in rates of NEC, IVH/PVL, or death.7 Among 132 infants 23 to 26 weeks’ gestation who required ventilation and had an hsPDA at least 2 mm in diameter, transition from mandatory PDA closure to nonintervention eliminated indomethacin use and ligation (compared to baseline rates of 58% and 82%, respectively). BPD declined from 58% to 38% (P = .006), without changes in other morbidities or mortality.58 In 321 infants weighing less than 1500 g monitored by serial echocardiography, fewer than 5% were treated for PDA, and rates of chronic lung disease, severe IVH, PVL, NEC, and severe ROP compared favorably to contemporaneous Vermont Oxford Network benchmarks.4 After adoption of a noninterventional strategy at one center, mortality among infants less than 26 weeks, BPD in those 26 to 29 weeks’ gestation, and BPD or death in both groups significantly declined.9 These experiences do not prove that permissive management strategies for preterm infants with PDA result in improved outcomes, because better outcomes may result from contemporaneous changes in other practices, but they do indicate that permissive approaches to PDA management do not substantially worsen outcomes. Available data do not exclude possible effects of nontreatment that have not been studied, such as late development of pulmonary hypertension or pulmonary veno-occlusive disease, so vigilance for unexpected sequelae of practice changes is necessary.
paragraphs.heading: Management

paragraphs.text: Growing awareness that aggressive intervention to achieve ductal closure may not be beneficial should not lead to an assumption that a persistently patent ductus arteriosus can simply be ignored. As with other large shunts, the hemodynamic and secondary pulmonary, cerebral, or visceral effects may require active management.50 Factors that may delay ductal closure, such as late-onset bacterial infection or excessive fluid administration (>150 mL/kg/day), should be avoided. Furosemide apparently does not compromise ductal closure in response to indomethacin59 but may prolong ductal patency in untreated infants. Circulatory imbalance, while the ductus arteriosus remains patent, may be managed by measures that increase PVR (permissive hypercapnia, increased distending airway pressure, or maintenance of a higher hematocrit) or that avoid or correct circumstances that may lower PVR (metabolic alkalosis, excessive supplemental oxygen, NO). Reduced systemic blood flow may be improved by agents that decrease systemic afterload (captopril, milrinone) or exacerbated by those that increase systemic vascular resistance (systemic vasopressor agents), which may increase diversion of cardiac output to the pulmonary circulation. Compromised systemic cardiac output may also be helped by measures that increase PVR, reducing ductal steal (Q̇ P/Q̇ S), and by increasing total cardiac output if Q̇ P/Q̇ S remains constant. Ensuring adequacy of preload may require invasive monitoring of central venous pressures or frequent assessment with functional echocardiography. # 75. Patent Ductus Arteriosus
> Source attribution: [Source credits](../../SOURCE_CREDITS.md).


## PDF page 1401 | printed page 1401

75 Patent Ductus Arteriosus

### WILLIAM E. BENITZ AND SHAZIA BHOMBAL

In utero, the ductus arteriosus provides a connection between the pulmonary artery and descending aorta, which carries deoxygenated blood returning to the right heart toward the placenta for reoxygenation. Although essential to normal fetal physiology, it typically constricts, closes, and becomes a fibrous remnant after birth. Failure of those processes, resulting in persistent ductal patency into childhood or adulthood, has been recognized as pathologic for many years. More than 60 years ago, Burnard reported that the murmur of a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) was heard more frequently and for longer after birth in preterm infants and typically was associated with respiratory distress.1 Subsequently, prolonged ductal patency in preterm infants was linked to more severe respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), prolonged assisted ventilation, pulmonary hemorrhage, bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), renal impairment, intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), periventricular leukomalacia (PVL), cerebral palsy, and death.2 The plausible hypothesis that these morbidities might be caused by excessive pulmonary blood flow or systemic ischemia resulting from a large leftto-right shunt through the ductus led many practitioners to adopt strategies for closing the ductus, either in anticipation of or after confirmation of prolonged patency. In randomized trials, however, those interventions consistently failed to produce benefits other than ductal closure, and concerns arose regarding potential adverse effects. Although consensus on many aspects of management is lacking, the current approach consists of identifying pathologic persistent ductal patency, evaluating hemodynamic consequences, and minimizing deleterious effects.

### Pathogenesis

The ductus arteriosus is derived from the distal portion of the embryonic sixth brachial arch and is approximately the diameter of the descending aorta in utero. In a normal term infant, the ductus arteriosus constricts soon after birth, stimulated by the rapid postnatal increase in arterial oxygen tension. The muscularis of the ductus is uniquely responsive to oxygen, reacting to an increase in ambient oxygen with sustained contraction. The mechanisms of this response

are not fully understood, but the cytochrome P450 system (CYP450), endothelin-1 (ET-1), and intracellular oxidation-reduction (redox) balance appear to be important.3 Glucocorticoids may be essential in maturation of the ductal oxygen-sensing apparatus, because antenatal glucocorticoid treatment increases expression of genes for calcium and potassium channels implicated in the oxygen response and with decreased risk of persistent ductal patency. This direct response is augmented by a rapid decline in circulating levels of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), a potent, very rapidly metabolized smooth muscle relaxant that has a major role in keeping the ductus arteriosus open in the fetus. The placenta is the primary source of fetal PGE2, so circulating levels fall precipitously upon umbilical cord clamping. Maximal effects of PGE2 withdrawal seem to require antenatal priming of ductal muscle by rising levels of PGE2 late in gestation. Dynamic functional closure initiates at the pulmonary end of the ductus arteriosus and usually is complete within the first 4 days after birth, but anatomic obliteration is not achieved until after 1 week of age.

In otherwise normal infants born at or near term, it is unusual for the ductus arteriosus to fail to close within the first 4 days. With decreasing gestational age at birth, both the age at spontaneous closure and the proportion of infants with a PDA at any postnatal age progressively increase.4,5 Before interventions to close the PDA in preterm infants were widely adopted, ductal closure nearly always occurred spontaneously if given sufficient time, sometimes as late as 4 to 6 months of age. However, those observations date from an era before adoption of antenatal steroid treatment and availability of exogenous surfactant, when very low birth weight (VLBW) infants rarely survived and extremely low birth weight (ELBW) infants essentially never survived. In many randomized trials, numerous control subjects were treated to achieve ductal closure, typically late in or after the first week after birth, obscuring the natural course of spontaneous ductal closure as well as risk factors that might predict failure of that process. High rates of spontaneous closure have been observed in control subjects in trials in which open treatment was used rarely or not at all, however. Observational data from centers that avoid interventions to close the ductus, where only 6% were treated to close

1401


## PDF page 1402

PDA, show that 90% of nearly 1200 otherwise unselected VLBW infants achieved ductal closure without treatment (80% before discharge).4–9 Spontaneous ductal closure is particularly likely in babies born at greater than 28 weeks’ gestation, weighing greater than 1000 g at birth, or without RDS. In addition to birth at an earlier gestational age, prolongation of ductal patency is associated with exposure to chorioamnionitis10 or gestational hypertension,11 or to higher fluid intake during the first 2 days after birth (but not on subsequent days),12 but whether these factors have a causal role in maintenance of a PDA remains uncertain.

The mechanisms underlying delay or failure of ductal closure in preterm infants have not been fully elucidated.13 Birth before term may simply come before the ductus is prepared, functionally or structurally, to respond to signals that normally induce closure. For example, lamb studies have demonstrated that the intensity of ductal constriction in response to oxygen is gestational-age dependent. Genes essential to ductal responses, including K+ and Ca2+ channels involved in muscle contraction and phosphodiesterases that degrade cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) and cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), mediators of the vasodilator responses to nitric oxide (NO) and PGE2, are developmentally upregulated in the ductus arteriosus of the fetus approaching term. Lack of preconditioning by PGE2 in late gestation may make the ductus less sensitive to withdrawal of that vasorelaxant. Inadequate glucocorticoid production, common in extremely preterm infants, may compromise oxygen-sensing pathways, particularly in infants not exposed to maternal antenatal steroids. Cytokines produced by a fetal inflammatory response, a frequent correlate of preterm birth, may directly impede ductal responses.14 These potential mechanisms correspond to the clinical observations that presence of a PDA is strongly associated with extreme immaturity, lack of exposure to antenatal steroids, and signs of fetal inflammation or infection.

### Pathophysiology

Before birth, the pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) is high, so approximately 75% of the right ventricular output flows right-to-left through the ductus arteriosus. With the first breath, lung inflation and oxygenation produce a rapid decline in PVR, a decrease in pulmonary arterial pressures, and a large increase in pulmonary blood flow. Removal of the low-resistance placenta from the systemic circulation leads to increased systemic vascular resistance, and ductal flow quickly reverses direction to left-to-right. If ductal closure occurs in the first few days, the imbalance in distribution of the total cardiac output, with increased pulmonary blood flow relative to systemic blood flow, is well tolerated. If the ductus arteriosus remains open, however, the continued decline in PVR over the first several days and weeks results in progressively increasing left-to-right shunting through the PDA, with excessive pulmonary blood flow, increased volume work for the left heart, and the potential for systemic ischemia.

Term infants can often tolerate large left-to-right shunts with high pulmonary-to-systemic blood flow ratios (Q̇ P/ Q̇ S) without developing pulmonary edema. In preterm infants, surfactant deficiency, low serum oncotic pressures, and compromised capillary integrity (e.g., that which accompanies bacteremia) lower the threshold for development of pulmonary edema. Accumulation of alveolar and interstitial fluid increases the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient and reduces lung compliance. A large left-to-right shunt increases volume work for the left heart, leading to atrial and ventricular enlargement and myocardial dysfunction. The combination of left heart dysfunction and diversion of aortic flow into the lungs (a “ductal steal”) may compromise systemic cardiac output, with consequent risk of end-organ ischemia. Low diastolic pressures may impair coronary artery perfusion, producing signs of myocardial ischemia, including ST segment depression and elevated serum troponin levels. Increasing ductal left-to-right shunting may be associated with Doppler ultrasound evidence of decreased, absent, or reversal of diastolic flow in the middle cerebral, superior mesenteric, and renal arteries, as well as the descending aorta. Impaired cerebral blood flow has been associated with PDA in several studies, implicating but not proving a causal role for PDA in development of IVH and, possibly, PVL. Similarly, bowel or kidney ischemia resulting from compromised mesenteric or renal arterial flow may be associated with NEC or impaired renal function. Reversal of aortic diastolic flow in term infants with surgical congenital heart disease has been associated with NEC, but empiric data have not demonstrated a direct correlation between estimates of severity of the ductal steal and the risk of ischemic complications in preterm infants with PDA.

### Clinical Presentation

Recognition of a persistent PDA in a preterm infant typically begins with auscultation of the characteristic coarse systolic murmur, heard best along the left sternal border. The continuous “machinery murmur” typical of PDA in an older child is rarely present. Infants with a very large PDA and high Q̇ P/Q̇ S ratio may have no audible murmur. Increasing murmur intensity may reflect increasing flow velocity through a narrowing ductus rather than increasing shunt volume. Hemodynamic effects of the large leftto-right shunt may be evident in an increased precordial impulse (owing to the increased left ventricular stroke volume) and in arterial pulses that are prominent, bounding, or palpable where they are not normally, such as in the palms (resulting from diastolic runoff into the low-pressure pulmonary circulation). In preterm infants greater than 1000 g, systemic arterial diastolic blood pressures are reduced and pulse pressures may be increased. Among babies less than 1000 g, reduction in both systolic and diastolic pressures without widened pulse pressures are more typical. These findings are nonspecific, insensitive, and correlate poorly with echocardiographic findings. Similar physical findings may be present in infants with an aortopulmonary window,

large arteriovenous malformation, hemitruncus, or certain other cardiac defects, or they may simply reflect a relatively hyperdynamic state of another cause. Often, a hemodynamically significant PDA (hsPDA) is suspected only because of signs of excessive pulmonary perfusion, such as an increasing Paco2 and/or alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient, decreasing lung compliance, or inability to wean the infant from supplemental oxygen, distending airway pressure, or positive pressure ventilation. Pulmonary hemorrhage is an infrequent complication often attributed to increased pulmonary flow from a PDA.

### Diagnostic Evaluation

Patent ductus arteriosus is most readily confirmed by color Doppler echocardiography, which documents anatomic patency and the direction and velocity of ductal blood flow throughout the cardiac cycle (Fig. 75.1). Ductal shunt patterns and systemic to diastolic flow ratios also may aid in identifying an hsPDA, with early demonstration of a pulsatile pattern with a high systolic-to-diastolic ratio predicting a large PDA at 1 month, compared with a restrictive pattern with a low systolic-to-diastolic ratio (Fig. 75.2).15 Echocardiography also allows characterization of the hemodynamic consequences of the ductal shunt, including assessment of degree of pulmonary overflow and systemic hypoperfusion (Table 75.1).16 Findings that correlate with a large shunt include a large ductal diameter, evidence for increased pulmonary flow, such as an increased left atrial to aortic root diameter (LA:Ao) ratio, left heart distention, ratio of early passive to late atrial contractile transmitral filling (E wave to A wave ratio), left ventricular isovolumic relaxation time (IVRT), and signs of systemic hypoperfusion, such as absent or reversed diastolic flow in cerebral, renal, or mesenteric arteries or descending aorta (Fig. 75.3).17,18 The utility of individual markers is low, but composite scores appear to

### Management

Because PDA in preterm infants is strongly associated with adverse outcomes, surgical and medical strategies for closing the ductus arteriosus were widely adopted soon after they became available. Surgical ligation in preterm infants with RDS was first reported in 1968, and the first case series appeared in 1972. Medical induction of ductal closure with indomethacin was described in 1976. The conviction that ductal closure was beneficial became so pervasive that the landmark National Collaborative Study of indomethacin in preterm infants with PDA had no nontreatment arm: all three regimens mandated ductal closure by either indomethacin or ligation. These reports were followed by numerous descriptions of successful surgical or medical closure of the ductus, which heavily influenced practice for many years, but the utility of routine intervention to achieve ductal closure late in the first or during the second week of life has come into question.

The seminal reports that nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs, now called cyclo-oxygenase inhibitors) induce constriction and closure of the ductus arteriosus have been followed by more than 60 randomized, placebocontrolled trials of cyclo-oxygenase inhibitors in preterm infants.28–33 Indomethacin and ibuprofen are equally effective in reducing rates of persistent PDA, resulting in lower rates of ductal ligation. Neither individual trials nor meta-analyses have identified improvements in long-term outcomes with these treatments.28 In early randomized trials, indomethacin prophylaxis started before 12 hours of age decreased rates of any IVH and of grade III/IV IVH. These effects are not achieved with later treatment2 nor with ibuprofen,40 do not appear to be mediated by PDA closure, and may not obtain in the current era, because baseline rates of IVH are now much lower.41 Reduction in IVH did not correlate with improved long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes. Compared with placebo-treated controls, infants given low-dose indomethacin prophylaxis had better vocabulary skills and a lower probability of an IQ less than 70 at age 4.5 years, but their mothers were more likely to describe them as having significant problems on the daily living domain of the Vineland scale at age 8. No effects on many other neurodevelopmental outcome measures were evident. Although indomethacin reduces cerebral, mesenteric, and renal arterial blood flow and is associated with diminished cerebral oxygen levels, reduced creatinine clearance, and oliguria, meta-analyses of randomized trials indicate that these hemodynamic changes do not increase mortality or potential complications, including BPD, NEC, bowel perforation, retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), or neurodevelopmental impairment.28 A randomized trial in preterm infants aged less than 28 weeks with moderate to large PDAs who were receiving respiratory support after the first week found that early routine treatment did not reduce PDA ligations or the presence of a PDA at discharge and did not improve any prespecified secondary outcomes. However, early treatment delayed full feeding and was associated with higher rates of late-onset sepsis and death in infants born at ≥26 weeks of gestation.42 The effect of prophylactic indomethacin on BPD risk remains unclear, with recent data from contemporary cohorts indicating either a decrease or no increase in BPD incidence.43,44 Co-administration of indomethacin with a glucocorticosteroid increases the risk of bowel perforation, however. Ibuprofen has less impact on cerebral and renal blood flow and minimal if any effect on mesenteric perfusion, so it is less likely than indomethacin to cause significant oliguria and may be less likely to be associated with NEC.45 In vitro studies suggest that ibuprofen may displace bilirubin from its binding site on albumin. Medical PDA

prophylaxis reduces severe pulmonary hemorrhage during the first week but not over the entire hospital course.46

Although many case series of surgical ligation have appeared, the three randomized trials that assessed the impact of this intervention demonstrated no consistent improvements in mortality or long-term morbidities.2 Ligation is a reliable method for closing the ductus arteriosus, but it is not without hazard. In up to one-third of infants, ligation precipitates severe left ventricular dysfunction and cardiorespiratory decompensation, requiring major increases in intensive care support in the immediate postoperative period. The risk of this complication decreases with postnatal age, so later ligations (at >4 weeks of age) are better tolerated than earlier surgeries. Infants who develop postoperative hypotension refractory to catecholamine infusion have lower postoperative serum cortisol levels than those who do not become hypotensive or respond to catecholamine treatment.47 Some have reported that milrinone infusion reduces postoperative hemodynamic instability,48 but others have not found this treatment to be beneficial.49 Other surgical complications include chylothorax, pneumothorax, phrenic or recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, and scoliosis.50 Paralysis of the left vocal cord, which occurs in up to 67% of ELBW infants following ductal ligation,51 is associated with prolongation of assisted ventilation and oxygen supplementation, a higher probability of BPD, feeding difficulties, tube feeding, longer neonatal hospitalization, and vocal and respiratory impairments in adulthood.52 Infants who undergo early ductal ligation are at increased risk for BPD and have higher rates of neurodevelopmental impairment; these adverse outcomes may result from the indication for surgery rather than the surgery itself.

Transcatheter ductus closure (TCC), the newest treatment option, has been demonstrated to be safe and effective.53 Devices have been FDA-approved for use in infants as small as 700 g. Adverse effects appear to be limited to rare device displacement or embolization, which have mostly been manageable by another catheter-based intervention. Although a few early reports described ischemic limb injury following arterial access, such events have been very rare since adoption of the femoral vein as the preferred access site. Post-procedure circulatory decompensation is much less common than with surgical ligation. It is not yet known if a more favorable adverse effect profile will lead to favorable effects on longterm outcomes, because there have been no controlled trials of this treatment. Consequently, the indications and optimal timing for this procedure are not yet clearly defined.

Current evidence indicates that routine, early treatment to achieve ductal closure does not improve long-term outcomes.2 Although some individual trials have found statistically significant effects on scattered outcomes, meta-analyses have found only reduction in IVH or IVH > grade II and increased ROP ≥ stage 3 to be significant in pooled data.28 Rates of untoward outcomes do not correlate with differences in rates of ductal closure among trials. Elimination of trials that frequently provided open treatment of infants in the “control” arm does not change these conclusions.28 Because


## PDF page 1407 | printed page 1407

most clinical trials addressed treatment early in the postnatal course, the effects of prolonged exposure to a moderate or large left-to-right shunt in ELBW infants remain unknown. Recent post hoc analyses from Clyman and colleagues have found that increased rates of BPD or of death or BPD are associated with prolonged PDA only for infants who require ongoing intubation for positive pressure ventilation, and that prolongation of PDA exposure beyond a threshold duration of 10 to 14 days does not further augment the incidence of those outcomes.54–56 Consequently, the indications (if any) for, potential benefits from, and optimal timing of later ductal closure remain indeterminate. Similarly, these global observations do not imply that there cannot be some infants for whom ductal closure would be beneficial, particularly within groups that are not well represented in those older studies (e.g., those <26 weeks’ gestation).

Better strategies for assessment of the magnitude of ductal shunting, based on echocardiographic findings such as those listed in Table 75.1 or scores based on those measurements with or without additional clinical or biomarker variables,17,19 promise to help identify infants who may be candidates for ductal closure,16,17 but benefits of treatment for infants selected using such criteria remain to be demonstrated. Until such information is available, practice will be guided by consensus, belief, and individualized clinical judgment. The perceived balance between benefits (reduced IVH and early pulmonary hemorrhage) and disadvantages (more severe respiratory disease, intestinal perforation with concomitant glucocorticoid use) will guide the choice between the use and avoidance of indomethacin prophylaxis. High rates of spontaneous closure in infants greater than 1000 g, and their demonstrated ability to tolerate longer periods of ductal shunting, support a permissive approach to PDA management. Infants weighing less than 1000 g who develop hypotension or overt congestive heart failure may be deemed to require ductal closure, but the criteria for that decision remain uncertain.

Experience with less aggressive strategies for management of PDA continues to accumulate. Although earlier studies mostly described effects of moderate reductions in the proportion of infants with PDA who received treatment, there are now several reports of cohorts and randomized trials in which treatment was rarely used. Although some cohort studies suggest an increase in adverse outcomes with adoption of conservative PDA management practices, randomized trials consistently fail to demonstrate differences in outcomes between groups managed with or without active PDA closure. Elimination of cyclo-oxygenase inhibitor treatment in 139 infants less than 30 weeks’ gestation who required ventilation and surfactant replacement was associated with lower rates of chronic lung disease (8% vs. 18%– 28%) and NEC (0% vs. 4%–6%) and comparable rates of IVH (7% vs. 6%–7%) and mortality (13% vs. 12%), versus network benchmarks, and ligation was used in fewer than 5%.57 Adoption of a conservative treatment approach in 72 VLBW infants (<1500 g) was followed by a significant reduction in the rate of oxygen use or ventilation at

36 weeks’ postmenstrual age (from 49% in prior treatment eras to 18%) among those diagnosed with PDA, despite treatment of PDA with ibuprofen in only 7% of cases and no use of ligation, without any increase in rates of NEC, IVH/PVL, or death.7 Among 132 infants 23 to 26 weeks’ gestation who required ventilation and had an hsPDA at least 2 mm in diameter, transition from mandatory PDA closure to nonintervention eliminated indomethacin use and ligation (compared to baseline rates of 58% and 82%, respectively). BPD declined from 58% to 38% (P = .006), without changes in other morbidities or mortality.58 In 321 infants weighing less than 1500 g monitored by serial echocardiography, fewer than 5% were treated for PDA, and rates of chronic lung disease, severe IVH, PVL, NEC, and severe ROP compared favorably to contemporaneous Vermont Oxford Network benchmarks.4 After adoption of a noninterventional strategy at one center, mortality among infants less than 26 weeks, BPD in those 26 to 29 weeks’ gestation, and BPD or death in both groups significantly declined.9 These experiences do not prove that permissive management strategies for preterm infants with PDA result in improved outcomes, because better outcomes may result from contemporaneous changes in other practices, but they do indicate that permissive approaches to PDA management do not substantially worsen outcomes. Available data do not exclude possible effects of nontreatment that have not been studied, such as late development of pulmonary hypertension or pulmonary veno-occlusive disease, so vigilance for unexpected sequelae of practice changes is necessary.

Growing awareness that aggressive intervention to achieve ductal closure may not be beneficial should not lead to an assumption that a persistently patent ductus arteriosus can simply be ignored. As with other large shunts, the hemodynamic and secondary pulmonary, cerebral, or visceral effects may require active management.50 Factors that may delay ductal closure, such as late-onset bacterial infection or excessive fluid administration (>150 mL/kg/day), should be avoided. Furosemide apparently does not compromise ductal closure in response to indomethacin59 but may prolong ductal patency in untreated infants. Circulatory imbalance, while the ductus arteriosus remains patent, may be managed by measures that increase PVR (permissive hypercapnia, increased distending airway pressure, or maintenance of a higher hematocrit) or that avoid or correct circumstances that may lower PVR (metabolic alkalosis, excessive supplemental oxygen, NO). Reduced systemic blood flow may be improved by agents that decrease systemic afterload (captopril, milrinone) or exacerbated by those that increase systemic vascular resistance (systemic vasopressor agents), which may increase diversion of cardiac output to the pulmonary circulation. Compromised systemic cardiac output may also be helped by measures that increase PVR, reducing ductal steal (Q̇ P/Q̇ S), and by increasing total cardiac output if Q̇ P/Q̇ S remains constant. Ensuring adequacy of preload may require invasive monitoring of central venous pressures or frequent assessment with functional echocardiography. Hydrocortisone and/or cardiotonic agents may be useful in

### • Delayed closure of the ductus arteriosus is common in

extremely premature neonates and is associated with a variety of untoward outcomes, but there is a lack of evidence for improvement in outcomes with treatment for closure.

title: Congenital Defects of the Cardiovascular System

paragraphs.text: 76 Congenital Defects of the Cardiovascular System
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Congenital heart defects are the most common type of birth defects worldwide. The following chapter provides an overview of the anatomy, physiology, clinical presentation, diagnostic evaluation, and management strategies for a wide range of congenital heart disease in neonates and infants. Although the information herein is detailed, it is important to keep in mind that many different anatomic and physiologic variants are encountered in practice, often altering clinical management. The chapter is generally organized based on the predominant pathophysiology—cyanotic, obstructive, or shunting—for a given congenital heart defect. There can be considerable overlap between these physiologies, particularly in complex forms of congenital heart disease involving multiple defects. Defect physiology can also change considerably over time, particularly in the immediate postnatal transitional period around ductal closure. Prompt recognition and diagnosis of hemodynamically significant congenital heart defects can greatly impact effective management and outcomes in affected newborns and infants.
paragraphs.heading: Summary

paragraphs.text: In dextro-transposition of the great arteries (D-TGA), the aorta arises from the right ventricle, which receives systemic venous deoxygenated blood, and the pulmonary artery arises from the left ventricle, which receives pulmonary venous oxygenated blood. The blood flow in these patients is in parallel with the deoxygenated blood entering the aorta and recirculating to the body, while the richly oxygenated pulmonary venous return is recirculated to the lungs. In the absence of any shunting across connections between the systemic and pulmonary circulations to allow mixing of the deoxygenated and oxygenated blood, it results in systemic hypoxia and is often lethal. In D-TGA, three levels where
paragraphs.heading: Dextro-Transposition of the Great Arteries Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: mixing can occur are atrial level defect (patent foramen ovale [PFO] or atrial septal defect [ASD]), patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), or ventricular septal defect (VSD). The most effective site of mixing is at the atrial level through a PFO or ASD, with the other forms (PDA and VSD) being less reliable. It is therefore extremely important at birth to make sure that there is an adequately sized atrial level communication.
paragraphs.heading: Dextro-Transposition of the Great Arteries Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: Associated defects have a dramatic effect on the presentation and pathophysiology of newborn infants with D-TGA. At a minimum, an atrial level defect with balanced bidirectional shunting is essential for survival. The presence of a PDA also allows for additional shunting from the aorta (deoxygenated blood) to the pulmonary artery (oxygenated blood), resulting in increased pulmonary venous return and added left-to-right shunting at the atrial level. An associated VSD occurs in about 25% of infants with D-TGA. Its presence contributes to mixing of the oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood, but, as previously stated, atrial level mixing is the most reliable. Coarctation of the aorta or aortic arch interruption can also occur in association with D-TGA, particularly in cases with a subpulmonary VSD.1
paragraphs.heading: Associated Defects

paragraphs.text: D-TGA is the most common cyanotic heart defect identified in the first week of life, and the diagnosis should be considered in any cyanotic neonate. Fetal diagnosis is common, and factors such as hypermobility of the atrial septum and reversal of diastolic flow in the PDA on fetal echocardiography can potentially predict the need for urgent balloon atrial septostomy.2 Even with prenatal diagnosis, however, profound hypoxia caused by a highly restrictive atrial level defect can lead to rapid deterioration and death within the first hours of life. Respiratory symptoms in this disorder are absent or limited to hyperpnea or tachypnea. The patient’s second heart sound is loud and single because of the anterior position of the aorta and
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: the posterior position of the pulmonary artery. A holosystolic murmur, when present, suggests an associated VSD; a systolic ejection murmur is auscultated in the setting of pulmonary stenosis (PS). In the absence of these associated defects, murmurs are generally not heard. The peripheral pulses are normal unless coarctation of the aorta is present. Persistent ductal patency or high pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) will affect the clinical findings of an associated VSD or coarctation of the aorta with potential for reverse differential cyanosis showing preductal saturation in the upper extremities lower than postductal saturation in the lower extremities.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: The electrocardiogram (ECG) is usually normal or may demonstrate right ventricular (RV) hypertrophy after a few weeks of life. Similarly, the classic egg-shaped heart with increased pulmonary vascularity on the chest radiograph might not be seen in the newborn period. Echocardiography defines the diagnosis, associated defects, and coronary artery anatomy, which are central to surgical planning.3 Cardiac catheterization is usually reserved for neonates requiring balloon atrial septostomy, and it is occasionally useful for further delineating other anatomic details, although it is rarely necessary to evaluate the coronary arteries (Fig. 76.1). Dual-source computed tomography angiography (CTA) can also be used for delineating coronary artery origin and course, as well as other associated intra- and extracardiac anomalies.4
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Maintaining patency of the ductus arteriosus with intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion in newborn infants with D-TGA often improves arterial oxygenation by increasing shunting from the oxygen-rich pulmonary artery to the deoxygenated aorta. Aortic to pulmonary artery shunting at the ductal level may increase pulmonary venous return, distending the left atrium and facilitating left-to-right
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: atrial shunting of fully oxygenated blood. If the prostaglandin E1 infusion does not result in adequate systemic oxygenation, the atrial level defect is enlarged by balloon atrial septostomy performed either at the bedside or in the cardiac catheterization lab under echocardiographic guidance.
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: Historically, the surgical interventions for D-TGA were the atrial switch operations, Senning (1959) and Mustard (1964). In these procedures, deoxygenated blood from the vena cavae is baffled to the morphologic left ventricle and then to the pulmonary artery, while the oxygenated pulmonary venous blood is directed to the morphologic right ventricle and the aorta. This results in physiologic circulation. However, the Senning and Mustard procedures are associated with a number of long-term complications, including RV dysfunction, systemic venous baffle obstruction and leaks, and atrial arrhythmias, as well as increased right atrial volumes and decreased right atrial emptying fractions.5
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: Drs. Adib Jatene and Magdi Yacoub pioneered the anatomic repair of D-TGA via the arterial switch operation, which requires transection of the aorta and main pulmonary artery, reconnection to establish ventriculoarterial concordance (systemic left ventricle to the aorta and pulmonic right ventricle to the main pulmonary artery), and reimplantation of the coronary arteries to the neoaortic root. Other associated intracardiac defects are generally repaired at the time of the initial surgery. The arterial switch operation is optimally performed in the first week of life for infants with D-TGA. If there is a prolonged delay, the risk of left ventricular (LV) deconditioning and resultant inability to function adequately as the systemic ventricle increases. Long-term follow-up data on patients who have undergone the arterial switch operation are quite favorable.7 Risk factors for early mortality include prematurity, low birth weight, and RV hypoplasia. Abnormal coronary artery anatomy (particularly in cases with an intramural course), a risk factor in earlier experiences, can now be managed effectively, although with potentially higher hospital morbidity.6 Long-term follow-up studies demonstrate excellent ventricular function, normal rhythm, and low incidence of obstruction at the aortic and coronary suture lines. Narrowing in the supravalvar pulmonary area and branch pulmonary arteries may require subsequent surgeries or catheter interventions. Neoaortic root dilation and neoaortic valve regurgitation are found in some children, but these rarely require further intervention in childhood. Progressive neoaortic regurgitation requiring neoaortic valve replacement remains a long-term complication in adulthood.7 Follow-up data in children 16 years of age with D-TGA from the Boston Circulatory Arrest Study suggest that adolescents with D-TGA who have undergone the arterial switch operation are at increased
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: neurodevelopmental risk and may benefit (along with other children born with congenital heart disease) from ongoing surveillance to identify emerging difficulties.8
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: In 1888, Etienne Fallot described the association of a large VSD, infundibular (subvalvar) and valvar PS, RV hypertrophy, and a large aorta overriding the ventricular septum—the tetralogy which bears his name.
