As such, the rationale for deciding between initial palliation versus complete neonatal repair is multifactorial and includes the anatomic details of the lesion, patient size, comorbidities, and, perhaps most importantly, institutional preference.
paragraphs.heading: Primary Neonatal Repair Versus Palliation and Management of Tetralogy of Fallot

paragraphs.text: As with right-heart obstructive lesions, left-heart obstructive lesions encompass a broad spectrum of morphologic
paragraphs.heading: Left-Heart Obstructive Lesions

paragraphs.text: defects affecting single or multiple left heart components— including the mitral valve apparatus, components of the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT), the ascending aorta, and the aortic arch. The resulting physiology, and thus management, is largely dependent on the severity of obstruction, level of obstruction, and the number of obstructive lesions involved. For example, mild isolated aortic valve stenosis is relatively hemodynamically insignificant early in life and may not require intervention until much later, if at all. On the opposite end of the spectrum, HLHS is a multi-level lesion resulting in a diminutive LV and ductal-dependent systemic blood flow requiring neonatal intervention and single ventricle palliation.
paragraphs.heading: Left-Heart Obstructive Lesions

paragraphs.text: Congenital left ventricular outflow tract obstruction (LVOTO) is a classification of lesions that includes the subaortic, aortic valve, and supravalvar areas of the heart. By far the most common condition that occurs in isolation is valvar aortic stenosis (70% of all LVOTO lesions) with subvalvar (10%–20%), supravalvar (5%–10%), or mixed (8%) representing the remainder.21,34 Although most cases of valvar aortic stenosis do not become clinically significant before adolescence, a small percentage of patients present with critical aortic valve stenosis that requires neonatal intervention.21 Isolated subvalvar and supravalvar aortic stenosis rarely present with severe obstruction in the neonatal period and tend to progress with time. However, if these conditions are part of a multilevel obstructive process (e.g., Shone complex), early neonatal intervention may be required.
paragraphs.heading: Left-Heart Obstructive Lesions

paragraphs.text: Aortic coarctation, aortic arch hypoplasia, and interrupted aortic arch (IAA) are congenital anomalies that result in left-sided obstruction above the level of aortic valve and supravalvar areas. Classic coarctation results in a discrete narrowing at the aortic isthmus—the area between the left subclavian artery and ductus arteriosus (or ligamentum arteriosum). Coarctation of the aorta can also be associated with transverse arch hypoplasia, resulting in diffuse narrowing along multiple arch segments beginning after the takeoff of the right brachiocephalic artery. Interrupted aorta results in dissociation between segments of the aortic arch and is classified based on the location of interruption. Type A occurs when the interruption occurs after the left subclavian artery, type B is an interruption between the left common carotid artery and left subclavian artery, and type C is an interruption between the innominate artery and left common carotid artery.
paragraphs.heading: Left-Heart Obstructive Lesions

paragraphs.text: Clinical presentation, timing of intervention, and technique of repair are dependent on the location, extent, and severity of the stenosis. For example, mild discrete narrowing of the isthmus may be asymptomatic until adolescence, often only identified after a murmur is detected or during the work-up for hypertension. Conversely, severe aortic coarctation and IAA are ductal-dependent lesions that—if not detected with fetal imaging—will present following ductal closure during the neonatal period.
paragraphs.heading: Left-Heart Obstructive Lesions

paragraphs.text: Aortic arch lesions are often discovered on prenatal ultrasound and with early postnatal screening. However, many cases are still missed even when standard prenatal care is
paragraphs.heading: Left-Heart Obstructive Lesions

paragraphs.text: provided. Although it is possible to detect mild aortic coarctation prenatally, severe arch lesions (e.g., severe coarctation and IAA) are more easily detected, and it is usually recommended that these infants be delivered at centers where neonatal and surgical treatment can be provided. For cases in which prenatal detection has not occurred, postnatal symptoms develop with the advent of ductus arteriosus closure. These symptoms include poor feeding, respiratory distress, and eventually shock-like appearance because of low cardiac output. The postnatal diagnosis is typically confirmed using surface echocardiogram, which typically shows isthmus hypoplasia (periductal area), a posterior shelf causing flow acceleration on Doppler interrogation, varying degrees of transverse arch hypoplasia, or complete arch interruption. The severity and even presence of coarctation of the aorta can often not be fully appreciated in the setting of a moderateor large-sized PDA, so it is helpful to get echocardiographic confirmation just before or immediately after starting PGE1 infusion when the duct is small or absent. However, in cases of severe low cardiac output, the initiation of prostaglandins should not be withheld to allow time to obtain the echocardiogram. Occasionally, it is uncertain whether ductal closure will result in significant neonatal coarctation. In this scenario, the patient is placed on an “arch watch” to closely monitor hemodynamic, anatomic, and laboratory parameters (e.g., serum lactate) while the PDA is allowed to close. If PDA closure results in pathologic changes suggestive of coarctation, PGE1 is immediately restarted and surgical correction is indicated.
paragraphs.heading: Left-Heart Obstructive Lesions

paragraphs.text: Patients born with severe or critical obstruction on the left side of the heart can often be asymptomatic in the immediate newborn period while the ductus arteriosus remains patent. The oxygen saturation might be normal or just mildly low during the screening pulse oximetry, especially if only checked in the upper extremity. These patients may appear well clinically and be discharged to home after an unremarkable observation period in the newborn nursery. However, as the ductus arteriosus closes, systemic cardiac output decreases and the neonate will progress to having cardiogenic shock and end organ dysfunction if not treated in expedited fashion. Although the incidence of undiagnosed postnatal presentation has significantly dropped with contemporary prenatal and postnatal CHD screening, studies have shown that the prenatal detection rate for isolated arch obstruction still hovers around 20% to 30%.35 Consequently, there continues to be a significant number of patients who will present postnatally every year, and neonatologists will need continued vigilance for these patients that present postnatally.
paragraphs.heading: Left-Heart Obstructive Lesions

paragraphs.text: It follows then that management of neonates with critical left-sided obstruction is aimed at initial stabilization and resuscitation to correct acidosis and protect end-organ perfusion. PGE1 infusion is used to maintain a PDA, and in some cases mechanical ventilation and inotropic support is necessary for critically ill neonates. Once the infant has been adequately resuscitated, then the patient can go on to have an intervention to correct the underlying obstructive
paragraphs.heading: Left-Heart Obstructive Lesions

paragraphs.text: process, whether that be a transcatheter intervention or a definitive surgical repair.
paragraphs.heading: Left-Heart Obstructive Lesions

paragraphs.text: Balloon aortic valvuloplasty (BAV) is performed in the newborn period in patients who present with critical or severe valvar aortic stenosis. The first reported BAV was reported in 1983 by Lababidi, and the procedure has been markedly improved upon over the last few decades, predominantly related to the availability of compliant balloons with very small crossing profiles (down to 3 French).36–38 Recommendations for limiting the balloon diameter-to-annulus ratio to 80% to 100% has greatly improved the procedural results, in which relief of obstruction is obtained without causing severe degrees of valvar regurgitation.37,38 However, BAV itself can be technically challenging with a much higher risk profile in the neonatal population and should only be performed by experienced operators with surgical backup nearby. Aortic valvuloplasty is most commonly performed via a retrograde approach from the femoral artery but can also be performed via the femoral vein if an atrial communication is present. In smaller patients, the procedure can be performed via a surgical cut-down or direct percutaneous access to the common carotid artery.39 A smaller balloon diameter-to-annulus ratio can be performed first, with progressively larger balloons if a significant residual pressure gradient remains. Outcomes are better for tricuspid and bicuspid aortic valve morphologies with unicuspid valve morphologies having the poorest response. Multiple studies have defined a successful neonatal BAV as a reduced aortic valve gradient ≤35 mm Hg with no worsening aortic valve insufficiency.38,40,41
paragraphs.heading: Transcatheter Strategies for Left-Heart Obstructive Lesions Balloon Aortic Valvuloplasty

paragraphs.text: Transcatheter therapies for neonatal coarctation are typically performed when definitive surgical repair is deferred because of patient comorbidities. The most common reason for intervention is a patient presenting in shock because of ductal closure in whom the ductus arteriosus cannot be opened or cannot be opened enough to allow for effective resuscitation and resolution of end organ dysfunction.42 In these situations, the coarctation is treated with balloon angioplasty during which a balloon is inflated across the lesion to provide temporary relief of the obstruction and resuscitation of end organs until eventual surgical correction can be performed. The most common acute complication associated with balloon angioplasty is femoral arterial injury. Long-term complications of balloon coarctation angioplasty that does not subsequently need surgical repair include pseudoaneurysm formation and recurrent coarctation. Recurrent coarctation of the aorta following surgery is often treated in the catheterization laboratory with balloon angioplasty and/or implantation of a stent.43,44 Implantation of a stent across a neonatal coarctation lesion is rarely
paragraphs.heading: Transcatheter Treatment of Coarctation

paragraphs.text: performed, and usually only when palliative angioplasty alone does not open the obstructed area adequately. The use of primary stenting in the neonatal period is limited by the size of the introducer sheath required to implant the stent via the femoral artery. This limitation can be overcome by using a hybrid surgical approach via a cut-down on the carotid artery or percutaneously via direct carotid access. Work is currently underway to develop bioresorbable stents that could be implanted in the neonatal period, dissolve over a period of 6 to 18 months, and then be stented again with larger stents, potentially obviating the need for surgical repair.45
paragraphs.heading: Transcatheter Treatment of Coarctation

paragraphs.text: Transcatheter balloon valvuloplasty is considered the primary treatment strategy among neonates with isolated valvar aortic stenosis,46,47 with surgical aortic valve repair reserved for patients with moderate or worse aortic insufficiency, concomitant cardiac defects, recurrent aortic stenosis, or failed transcatheter intervention.21 However, primary surgical valvuloplasty is gaining favor at some centers with the belief that it may provide a more durable long-term outcome when compared to catheter-based interventions.48–51 When looking at outcomes, early mortality is comparable between surgical and transcatheter interventions, but with morbidity being less for the transcatheter method. It is generally accepted that balloon valvuloplasty results in a greater decrease in aortic valve gradient, but an increased risk of aortic insufficiency compared to surgical valvotomy.47 However, the 10-year event-free survival is higher after surgery compared to transcatheter valvuloplasty. This suggests the risk of aortic valve re-intervention may be decreased if a primary surgical approach is used.34,49,50
paragraphs.heading: Operative Strategies for Left-Heart Obstructive Lesions Surgical Aortic Valve Repair

paragraphs.text: Surgical aortic valve repair is performed via a median sternotomy on cardiopulmonary bypass with aortic crossclamping, allowing direct visualization of the aortic valve. In the newborn with isolated aortic valve stenosis, the most common anatomic construct is a bicuspid or unicuspid valve with fused commissures. In this setting, surgical valvotomy, consisting of a controlled commissurotomy, can effectively increase the valve orifice without significant insufficiency. Additional leaflet debulking, including excision of myxomatous nodularities and shaving or thinning of thickened dysplastic leaflets, may help increase the effective valve orifice area.34
paragraphs.heading: Operative Strategies for Left-Heart Obstructive Lesions Surgical Aortic Valve Repair

paragraphs.text: For neonates with aortic valves that cannot be repaired, or in infants with combined valvar and subvalvar obstruction, aortic valve replacement is necessary. Unfortunately, replacement options are limited and suboptimal, because there are no bioprosthetic valves manufactured small enough to fit a neonate. If a small enough valve existed, it would quickly become flow restricting without the ability to keep pace
paragraphs.heading: Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement

paragraphs.text: with the rapid somatic growth of an infant. For these neonates, the entire aortic root and valve need to be replaced, either with a cryopreserved human cadaveric homograft or the patient’s own pulmonary valve as an autograft (Ross procedure). The disadvantage of a homograft includes the known risk of early calcification especially in the neonate, leading to valve dysfunction, the lack of growth potential, and the increased risk of repeat coronary artery reimplantation. Therefore the Ross procedure has become the aortic valve/root replacement option of choice in neonates.52,53 The principles of the operation include reconstructing the LVOT and replacing the aortic valve with the child’s own living tissue—a pulmonary root autograft (rim of right ventricular muscle, valve, and the main pulmonary artery), reimplantation of the coronary arteries, and replacement of the pulmonary valve with a pulmonary valve homograft. In theory, this operation exchanges aortic valve disease for pulmonary valve disease with the reasoning that repeat interventions on the aortic valve carry increasing risk, whereas repeat interventions on the pulmonary valve are not only less frequent but also less risky.
paragraphs.heading: Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement

paragraphs.text: Significant neonatal coarctation can present as a discrete “juxtaductal” lesion, or as long segment, diffuse tubular hypoplasia. Barring additional intracardiac pathology, the size of the proximal arch typically dictates the surgical approach. If the proximal arch is an adequate size, coarctation repair can be conducted though a thoracotomy approach. Alternatively, if the proximal arch is significantly hypoplastic, arch reconstruction via a median sternotomy is necessary. Although the type of surgical approach differs between discrete coarctation and diffuse hypoplasia (described below), in both instances neonatal surgery is indicated in situations of ductal dependency or significant systolic blood pressure gradient measured between upper and lower extremities. Similarly, the diagnosis of IAA is an indication for neonatal repair.
paragraphs.heading: Surgical Repair of Coarctation

paragraphs.text: A juxtaductal coarctation manifests as a discrete area of aortic narrowing at the junction of the ductus arteriosus to the aortic isthmus. It occurs within the first few days or weeks of life as the constrictive process that normally closes the PDA extends into the adjacent aortic tissue, leading to the clinical manifestations previously described. In this setting, the typical operation is a coarctectomy and extended end-to-end aortic anastomosis. This operation is performed via a thoracotomy without cardiopulmonary bypass. The principles of the operation include division of the PDA, complete resection of the coarctation segment of the aorta and any adjacent ductal tissue (coarctectomy), and mobilization of the proximal and distal segments of the aorta. Subsequently, the proximal incision is extended onto the underside of the aortic arch to the level of the proximal arch and the distal incision is extended posteriorly down the descending aorta. This allows for a large, tension-free anastomosis to be created between the descending aorta and
paragraphs.heading: Surgical Repair of Coarctation

paragraphs.text: the proximal aortic arch—hence the term extended endto-end anastomosis. The benefits of this operation include complete relief of obstruction and durable repair that can grow with the patient at very low risk. The potential downsides of the operation include the inability to address any transverse aortic arch hypoplasia as well as a circumferential aortic suture line that may develop resistant scar tissue, leading to recurrent stenosis at this site.
paragraphs.heading: Surgical Repair of Coarctation

paragraphs.text: Coarctation with associated arch hypoplasia and IAA require a significantly more invasive operation than isolated coarctation. The operation is performed via a median sternotomy on cardiopulmonary bypass, to allow complete mobilization of the aortic arch and proximal descending aorta. Additionally, deep hypothermia with antegrade cerebral perfusion is required for arch reconstruction. The typical reconstruction for IAA is an arch advancement operation. After ligation and resection of the PDA, the distal aorta is mobilized and anastomosed to the underside of the proximal arch as it transitions into the ascending aorta. A similar arch advancement technique can be performed for patients with diffuse arch hypoplasia. An alternative strategy is patch augmentation of the aortic arch. This involves division of the PDA, resection of ductal tissue, and patching the undersurface of the aortic arch from distal ascending aorta to mid-descending thoracic aorta. Patch augmentation leaves a posterior wall of native aortic tissue that allows growth of the reconstructed aorta.
paragraphs.heading: Surgical Repair of Coarctation

paragraphs.text: Admixture lesions (see Table 79.1) are congenital heart defects in which blood from the systemic and pulmonary veins mix within the heart via a single or multiple defects (predominantly at the atrial level). The obligate mixing of systemic venous return with pulmonary venous return make admixture lesions a form of cyanotic heart disease. However, the degree of cyanosis is variable and can range from very mild desaturation undetectable on clinical exam, to clinically significant desaturation resulting in visible cyanosis. As blood is completely mixed within the heart, arterial saturation is dependent on the size of the intracardiac shunt, amount of PBF, and the presence of preferential streaming of saturated or desaturated blood to the aorta. Variations in the size and location of the outflow tracts determine where the “mixed” blood is ejected. Admixture lesions occur in single ventricle defects (e.g., tricuspid atresia and HLHS), and biventricular defects (e.g., total anomalous systemic venous return and truncus arteriosus). As such, there is no uniform management approach for admixture lesions and the specific anatomy and physiology dictate the optimal intervention. However, there are some basic principles that can be applied in the management of these neonates.
paragraphs.heading: Admixture Lesions

paragraphs.text: Patients with admixture lesions and unrestricted PBF develop pulmonary overcirculation, which can result in respiratory distress/failure, difficulty feeding, failure to thrive, and potentially necrotizing enterocolitis. If left unabated, excessive PBF can lead to changes in the pulmonary
paragraphs.heading: Admixture Lesions

paragraphs.text: arterioles, causing irreversible elevation of the pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR). This is of particular importance for single ventricle patients because elevated PVR can make the patient ineligible for eventual Fontan palliation. To prevent these problems from developing, patients with admixture lesions and excessive PBF require interventions to limit or control the amount of flow to the lungs, often as part of a series of staged palliation surgeries for functional single ventricle anatomy and physiology. Alternatively, patients with a restrictive or absent atrial communication may have diminished cardiac output, pulmonary venous congestion, and/or progressive cyanosis because complete atrial mixing is required for these conditions to be compatible with life. If the atrial communication is absent or inadequate, then creation or enlargement of the atrial communication is necessary for survival. Pulmonary artery banding (PAB) as a method to restrict PBF and methods to increase mixing at the atrial level will be discussed in the sections below. In addition, interventional, surgical, and hybrid approaches to some of the admixture lesions that are commonly performed during the neonatal period will be discussed.
paragraphs.heading: Admixture Lesions

paragraphs.text: PAB to limit PBF has been used for decades as a palliative approach to children with large left-to-right shunts and single ventricle defects with pulmonary overcirculation. However, as outcomes for primary repair have improved over recent years, the tendency to palliate neonates with PABs has decreased and more infants are undergoing complete repair early on. Nevertheless, PAB to restrict PBF before complete repair remains the optimal strategy in certain situations. The most common indication for PAB is as the first-stage procedure in the management of certain single ventricle physiologies, such as tricuspid atresia or double-inlet left ventricle. Other indications include anatomic defects that continue to carry a higher risk of suboptimal early repair, such as multiple apical VSDs, or patients with otherwise repairable anomalies but significant associated comorbidities, such as prematurity or intracerebral hemorrhage. In these situations, a pulmonary artery band can be an effective palliative technique to control PBF.
paragraphs.heading: Restricting Pulmonary Blood Flow: Pulmonary Artery Banding

paragraphs.text: The procedure can be performed via a thoracotomy but is most often performed through a midline sternotomy, and without the need for a cardiopulmonary bypass. Technical aspects include creating a space between the aorta and the main pulmonary artery through which a nondistensible band of prosthetic material is passed as a ring around the main pulmonary artery. The band is located between the valve and the origin of the branch pulmonary arteries. The band is then tightened to the desired effect again based on the underlying anatomy, physiology, and planned next stage. In general, the goals of a pulmonary artery band are to improve the balance of systemic to pulmonary artery circulation and to protect the distal pulmonary vasculature from unrestricted pressure and flow. Achievement of balanced
paragraphs.heading: Restricting Pulmonary Blood Flow: Pulmonary Artery Banding

paragraphs.text: flow is guided by the changes in systemic oxygen saturation with tightening, and the pressure restriction is demonstrated by reduction in the pulmonary artery pressure distal to the band. In patients without a main pulmonary artery, such as truncus arteriosus, and those in which complete neonatal repair is not possible, separate banding of the left and right branch pulmonary arteries is possible. Recovery from PAB is short and uncomplicated, and patients are often easier to manage once the degree of PBF is appropriately restricted.
paragraphs.heading: Restricting Pulmonary Blood Flow: Pulmonary Artery Banding

paragraphs.text: Admixture lesions and patients with transposition physiology are dependent on adequate intracardiac mixing of blood at the atrial level to both maintain adequate oxygen saturations and allow adequate cardiac output. Although other levels of mixing might be present (e.g., VSD or PDA), adequate atrial-level mixing of systemic and pulmonary venous blood is the most effective in almost all situations. When inadequate mixing occurs in patients with admixture lesions, disproportionate streaming of the deoxygenated blood to the systemic circulation results in severe cyanosis. To demonstrate this, consider HLHS, in which the left-sided structures are not adequate to support a full cardiac output. To provide the systemic circulation with adequate quantities of oxygenated blood, there must be unrestricted flow from the left atrium to the aorta (left atrium→right atrium→right ventricle→pulmonary artery→ductus arteriosus→aorta). Thus unrestricted atrial communication is necessary for both adequate oxygenation and maintenance of cardiac output. Furthermore, without unrestrictive atrial communication, left atrial hypertension develops because of the inability of pulmonary venous return to unload. This leads to pulmonary venous hypertension and subsequent pulmonary edema with pulmonary artery hypertension. This can be devastating for patients with single ventricle admixture lesions. Although D-TGA is not technically an admixture lesion because systemic cardiac output is not dependent on
paragraphs.heading: Procedures to Increase Mixing of Blood at the Atrial Level

paragraphs.text: atrial level shunting, an unrestrictive atrial communication is equally important because inadequate mixing results in severe hypoxemia, as only deoxygenated systemic venous return is circulated to the systemic arterial system.
paragraphs.heading: Procedures to Increase Mixing of Blood at the Atrial Level

paragraphs.text: In summary, all admixture lesions and conditions with transposition physiology typically require adequate mixing at the atrial level for survival in the neonatal period. In some cases, this involves the creation of an atrial-level communication, and in other cases, enlargement of an existing albeit restrictive communication. In this section, current approaches available to provide unrestrictive atrial-level communication for both admixture lesions and conditions with transposition physiology are described (Table 79.4).
paragraphs.heading: Procedures to Increase Mixing of Blood at the Atrial Level

paragraphs.text: Balloon atrial septostomy (BAS) is the standard method for enlarging an existing atrial communication when there is inadequate mixing. The most common indication is D-TGA with restrictive atrial septum, which occurs in one-third of neonates with this condition.54 The BAS procedure has been performed for more than 50 years and remains the standard approach in most cases because of the relative safety and efficacy when performed by experienced operators.
paragraphs.heading: Balloon Atrial Septostomy

paragraphs.text: The standard BAS procedure can be done in either the catheterization laboratory or bedside in the neonatal intensive care unit. Procedural guidance is typically provided by fluoroscopy, echocardiography, or a combination of both. Performing the procedure in the catheterization laboratory allows additional procedures to be performed (i.e., coronary angiography) and allows easy access to additional catheterization equipment should the procedure be technically difficult. Bedside BAS under echocardiographic guidance has been shown to be a safe and more cost-effective approach in patients with D-TGA.55 The procedure can be performed via femoral venous access or by taking over the existing umbilical vein catheter, which can then be replaced following the procedure. The septostomy catheter is advanced under fluoroscopic and/ or echocardiographic guidance until it is seen in the left
paragraphs.heading: Balloon Atrial Septostomy

paragraphs.text: atrium across an existing PFO/ASD (Fig. 79.4A–B). The balloon is inflated in the left atrium and a quick, forceful, yet controlled, “jerk” is performed to pull the inflated balloon through the existing communication. The septum tears during this process, resulting in a larger atrial communication and hopefully unrestricted atrial shunting. In the event of a thick septum that does not tear, repeat BAS is not advised and a different approach must be sought for the patient as noted below.
paragraphs.heading: Balloon Atrial Septostomy

paragraphs.text: If the patient is profoundly hypoxemic before or during the procedure, this can exacerbate the already elevated PVR and lead to worsening pulmonary hypertension. In this setting, PBF can become severely reduced, which decreases the amount of oxygenated blood returning to the left atrium. This leads to a vicious cycle of worsening hypoxemia, which can reach critically low levels. If hypoxemia persists before, during, or even after a successful BAS, the treatment team should have a low threshold to start inhaled nitric oxide to help decrease PVR and increase PBF, which typically results in improved systemic oxygenation.
paragraphs.heading: Balloon Atrial Septostomy

paragraphs.text: As discussed above, BAS may not be effective if the atrial septum is thick or intact. If there is an existing communication between the atria, this can be crossed and made larger using transcatheter interventions. If no atrial communication exists, the atrial septum may be crossed using the radiofrequency wire (described in the RVOT perforation section), a radioperforation transseptal needle, or with a standard transseptal needle.56–58 Once the thick or intact septum is perforated, a guidewire can then be passed through the perforation and positioned into a left-sided pulmonary
paragraphs.heading: Other Atrial Septostomy Techniques

paragraphs.text: vein. At this point, there are multiple options that the operator can choose for opening the atrial septum, including static balloon septoplasty, cutting balloon septoplasty, blade atrial septostomy, and atrial septal stenting. Balloon septoplasty is a procedure where a balloon (with or without cutting microsurgical blades) is inflated across the ASD. This approach may not be effective long term, because the ASD can become restrictive over time. A Park blade septostomy catheter, which contains a retractable blade at its distal end (Fig. 79.5), can be carefully pulled across the atrial septum to enlarge the defect. Although a blade septostomy may create a much larger defect compared to balloon septoplasty, the blade catheters can be too large for small patients and its use in the current era is very limited.
paragraphs.heading: Other Atrial Septostomy Techniques

paragraphs.text: In very small patients with thick and/or intact atrial septa, an atrial communication is best created by atrial septal stenting.58 After perforating, crossing the atrial septum, and gaining stable wire position, a long sheath is passed into the left atrium. A premounted stent (typically 6–8 mm in diameter) is advanced through the delivery sheath and over the guidewire until half of it is seen in the left atrium using fluoroscopy and transesophageal echocardiography guidance. The delivery sheath is slowly retracted, and the stent positioning is adjusted to center the stent on the atrial septum. Once the stent positioning is confirmed, the stent is deployed (Fig. 79.6A–C). Adequacy of stent size is evaluated by echocardiogram, with particular attention given to the decrease in mean Doppler gradient across the septum. The implanted stent is resected with the atrial septectomy procedure during a subsequent planned surgical operation.
paragraphs.heading: Other Atrial Septostomy Techniques

paragraphs.text: In newborns that are not candidates for percutaneous transcatheter strategies to open the atrial septum, a surgical atrial septectomy can be performed. The operation is performed through a median sternotomy on cardiopulmonary bypass. The goal of the operation is complete excision of the atrial septum creating a reliable and durable opening. Surgical atrial septectomy in the neonate is almost exclusively performed on patients with single ventricle anatomy and physiology.57
paragraphs.heading: Atrial Septectomy

paragraphs.text: Tricuspid atresia is a single ventricle lesion in which there is an absent tricuspid valve with a subsequent lack of direct communication between the right atrium and RV. The result is that all systemic venous return to the right atrium must pass through an ASD as an obligate right-to-left shunt before being delivered to the systemic LV. There is variable RV hypoplasia determined by the presence and size of a VSD; however, in all cases, the RV is rudimentary and is not sufficient to support biventricular physiology.
paragraphs.heading: Specific Admixture Lesions Tricuspid Atresia

paragraphs.text: Tricuspid atresia has traditionally been classified based on the relationship of the great arteries, presence of a VSD, and the amount of PBF. Type I tricuspid atresia has normally related great vessels (i.e., the pulmonary artery arises from the rudimentary RV and aorta arises from the LV) and accounts for ∼70% of all cases. Type I is further subdivided into Ia: no VSD and pulmonary atresia, Ib: small VSD with pulmonary stenosis, and Ic: large VSD and no pulmonary
paragraphs.heading: Specific Admixture Lesions Tricuspid Atresia

paragraphs.text: stenosis. Type II tricuspid atresia is associated with D-TGA (i.e., the aorta arises from the rudimentary RV and pulmonary artery arises from the LV) and accounts for ∼25% of cases. Similarly, type II tricuspid atresia is subdivided into three categories, IIa: no VSD and pulmonary atresia, IIb: VSD with pulmonary or subpulmonary stenosis, and IIc: VSD with no pulmonary stenosis. Type III tricuspid atresia is associated with L-transposition of the great arteries, only accounts for ∼5% of cases, and is outside the scope of this chapter.59
paragraphs.heading: Specific Admixture Lesions Tricuspid Atresia

paragraphs.text: Pulmonary blood flow, and thus clinical presentation and treatment strategy, is determined by the size of the VSD, relationship of the great arteries, and presence of pulmonary valve atresia or stenosis. For example, neonates with diminished PBF (type Ia, IIa) will become severely cyanotic with ductal closure. For these patients, initial intervention is either an mBTT shunt or PDA stent. At the other end of the spectrum are neonates with excessive PBF (types Ic, IIc). These patients typically present with signs of CHF secondary to pulmonary overcirculation and require a pulmonary artery band for initial palliation. In the middle are neonates with type Ib and IIb who often have a balanced circulation. These patients may not need any intervention before undergoing their bidirectional cavopulmonary connection (i.e., Glenn procedure).
paragraphs.heading: Specific Admixture Lesions Tricuspid Atresia

paragraphs.text: HLHS comprises a spectrum of congenital heart lesions in which the LV is underdeveloped and not able to support the systemic circulation. Although there are a number of anatomic variants that fall within the spectrum of HLHS, the primary driver of pathophysiology is that the RV must be used to pump blood to the systemic circulation and blood flow to the pulmonary circulation must be achieved by another route. As mentioned above, systemic cardiac output is dependent on adequate atrial level mixing and a widely PDA. The latter is initially achieved by starting an infusion of PGE1. If the atrial communication is not large enough, a BAS can be performed. However, once the neonate is stabilized and receiving nutritional support, the treatment team will then decide which stage 1 palliation approach the patient will receive.
paragraphs.heading: Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome

paragraphs.text: Most patients with HLHS undergo a series of staged palliative operations, ultimately culminating with the Fontan operation. However, primary cardiac transplantation or transplant after any stage remains an option for some children with HLHS. The objectives for any stage 1 palliative intervention for HLHS are to achieve (1) unobstructed systemic outflow, (2) unrestricted pulmonary venous egress, (3) balanced PBF, and (4) unobstructed coronary artery perfusion.60
paragraphs.heading: Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome

paragraphs.text: The basic principles of the Norwood operation include (1) amalgamating the ascending aorta and proximal pulmonary artery (Damus-Kaye-Stansel [DKS] anastomosis) along with aortic arch reconstruction—these steps provide unobstructed systemic outflow, (2) performing an atrial septectomy to provide unimpeded pulmonary venous blood
paragraphs.heading: Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome

paragraphs.text: flow to the right atrium, and (3) providing systemic to pulmonary artery blood flow, either through an mBTT shunt or via an RV to pulmonary artery (RV-PA) conduit—also termed a Sano modification. Both Norwood with mBTT shunt and Norwood with RV-PA conduit are used in contemporary practice, and there are advantages and disadvantages to both.61 Most congenital heart centers will perform both operations, but typically have a preference for one over the other for standard patients with HLHS. Although the early and mid-term results vary between the two approaches, both offer patients similar long-term outcomes and the
paragraphs.heading: Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome

paragraphs.text: ability to progress through all three stages of palliation and eventual Fontan operation.62
paragraphs.heading: Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome

paragraphs.text: Despite the relative success of the Norwood operation, there was concern that the need for cardiopulmonary bypass along with deep hypothermic circulatory arrest or antegrade cerebral perfusion during the neonatal period might be associated with poor long-term outcomes. It was in this context that the hybrid approach emerged as an alternative strategy to the Norwood operation for the
paragraphs.heading: Hybrid Stage I Palliation

paragraphs.text: management of HLHS and other complex neonatal heart anomalies beginning in the early 1990s.63,64 The term hybrid refers to procedures performed during which a combination of surgical and interventional methods are used, with the primary advantage being the avoidance of cardiopulmonary bypass and altered cerebral perfusion. Because published medium-term results of the hybrid procedure demonstrated outcomes comparable to surgical palliation, this alternative approach was adopted by many more institutions.65 The hybrid stage 1 procedure is performed via midline sternotomy without the use of cardiopulmonary bypass and typically includes three steps: (1) bilateral branch pulmonary artery bands that protect the lungs from persistent high pressure and flow, while balancing the pulmonary versus systemic circulations, (2) a stent in the PDA to assure unobstructed systemic blood flow, and (3) BAS, or rarely stenting, to assure unrestricted flow from the left atrium to the right atrium (Fig. 79.7). This hybrid stage 1 palliation has been used successfully in patients with standard risk factors, those with a high-risk profile, as a tool for salvage, as a bridge to heart transplantation, and as a bridge to a two-ventricle repair. All forms of HLHS have been successfully palliated with a hybrid stage 1 procedure including aortic atresia/mitral atresia with a diminutive ascending aorta. Moreover, neither patient size nor prematurity has proven to be a contraindication to using this strategy nor has significant associated comorbidities. That is why the hybrid stage 1 is used in many centers for their high-risk patients with known poor outcomes with more traditional surgical approaches.
paragraphs.heading: Hybrid Stage I Palliation

paragraphs.text: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR) is an embryologic failure of fusion of the confluence of the
paragraphs.heading: Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Return

paragraphs.text: pulmonary veins to the adjacent left atrium. The pulmonary venous return finds its way back to the right atrium via a communicating vein in one of four ways (1) supracardiac—is the most common, whereby the confluence of the pulmonary veins drain into an ascending vertical vein that connects to the innominate vein then the superior vena cava; (2) infracardiac—has a descending vertical vein draining into the portal vein or inferior vena cava; (3) cardiac—has a direct communication from the confluence to the coronary sinus; and (4) mixed—is the least common and has some combination of the previous three. In TAPVR all systemic venous and pulmonary venous return is via the right atrium. As such, TAPVR is an admixture lesion, where mixing takes place in the right atrium and cardiac output is dependent on the presence of a right-to-left shunt at the atrial level.
paragraphs.heading: Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Return

paragraphs.text: In unobstructed TAPVR with an unrestrictive ASD, cyanosis is usually mild and complete repair can wait until 3 to 6 months of age. Newborns with obstructed TAPVR present with both profound cyanosis and cardiogenic shock. Obstruction of pulmonary venous return most commonly occurs in patients with infracardiac TAPVR, in which the descending vertical vein narrows as it crosses the diaphragm before connecting to the IVC. Another potential obstruction can occur within the liver when the vertical vein empties into the portal venous system. In this anatomic situation, when the ductus venosus closes, egress of blood into the hepatic veins and right atrium becomes restrictive and both portal and pulmonary venous congestion develop. Both obstruction of the vertical vein and a closing ductus venosus can be treated by endovascular stenting to provide temporary relief of the obstruction if discovered early enough, allowing time for the patient to be stabilized before surgery.98 However, if obstruction occurs before the diagnosis is made or if the anatomy is not amenable to interventional therapies, then these newborns will become critically ill and often end up on extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Once on ECMO, the diagnosis of TAPVR is more difficult to make by echocardiography. Therefore the medical teams must maintain a high index of suspicion for TAPVR, and advanced imaging with cardiac CT or cardiac catheterization is sometimes necessary to confirm the diagnosis.
paragraphs.heading: Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Return

paragraphs.text: Surgical repair of TAPVR is done via a median sternotomy on cardiopulmonary bypass. The principles of the operation include direct anastomosis of the anterior wall of the confluence of the pulmonary veins to the posterior wall of the adjacent left atrium as well as ligation of the communicating vein. Typically, a PFO or small ASD is left to help the management of potential postoperative pulmonary hypertensive events.
paragraphs.heading: Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Return

paragraphs.text: Truncus arteriosus is a conotruncal heart defect in which a common arterial trunk arises from the base of the heart and gives rise to the systemic, pulmonary, and coronary arterial circulation. A common classification for truncus
paragraphs.heading: Truncus Arteriosus

paragraphs.text: arteriosus, the Collett and Edwards system, is based on the origin of the pulmonary arteries from the common trunk.66 The pulmonary arteries are usually well-developed without central stenosis and may arise from a discrete main pulmonary artery segment that bifurcates into branch pulmonary arteries (type I). Alternatively, the branch pulmonary arteries may arise independently with separate orifices, either spaced close together from the posterior aspect of the common trunk (type II) or widely spaced and arising from the lateral aspect of the common trunk (type III).
paragraphs.heading: Truncus Arteriosus

paragraphs.text: Almost all cases of truncus are associated with an unrestrictive, subarterial VSD that results from a deficiency in the formation of the infundibular septum. Rather than two separate semilunar valves, a single truncal valve forms from the fusion of the aortic and pulmonary valves because of a lack in development of the conotruncal septum. The truncal valve commonly has three or four leaflets but may have as few as two or as many as six leaflets.
paragraphs.heading: Truncus Arteriosus

paragraphs.text: The common truncal valve overrides the VSD, and thus allows blood from the RV and LV to pass through the VSD into the common arterial trunk, where the blood mixes before circulating to the pulmonary, systemic, and coronary arterial systems. As such, truncus arteriosus is an admixture lesion and results in at least mild cyanosis. The distribution of blood flow, and thus oxygen saturation, is determined by the systemic vascular resistance (SVR) and PVR. Early after birth, the PVR is still relatively elevated and limits excessive PBF, resulting in systemic oxygen saturations between 75% and 85%. As PVR drops after birth, PBF increases, and oxygen saturations can increase to as high as the low 90s%. The pulmonary arterial diastolic runoff results in excessive PBF and retrograde flow in the abdominal aorta. This combination leads to severe overcirculation and diastolic steal from coronary and renal vasculature. Surgical repair is indicated relatively early to avoid these complications.
paragraphs.heading: Truncus Arteriosus

paragraphs.text: The operation is performed through a median sternotomy on cardiopulmonary bypass, and complete repair of truncus arteriosus involves separating the pulmonary arteries from the common arterial trunk, diverting blood from the LV through the truncal valve by closing the VSD, establishing RV-PA continuity with a valved conduit, and truncal valve repair, if necessary. Survival after neonatal truncal valve repair has significantly improved in recent years, with a 1-year survival of greater than 90%. The long-term prognosis is largely dependent on the durability of the truncal valve. Truncal valve insufficiency is both a risk factor for death after the initial operation and a risk factor for increased reintervention.67
paragraphs.heading: Truncus Arteriosus

paragraphs.text: Simple transposition of the great arteries, also termed dextro or D-TGA, is one of the most common causes of newborn cyanosis.21,68 Despite the relatively common prevalence, D-TGA is diagnosed prenatally in less than 50% of patients.68 D-TGA is defined by atrioventricular concordance with ventriculoarterial discordance. That is,
paragraphs.heading: Transposition of the Great Arteries

paragraphs.text: the aorta arises anteriorly from the morphologic RV and the pulmonary artery arises posteriorly from the morphologic LV. In contrast to the normal in-series circulation, D-TGA anatomy results in a parallel circulation, whereby deoxygenated systemic venous return is recirculated from the RV to the aorta and systemic circulation. Conversely, oxygenated blood returning from the lungs is recirculated from the LV to the pulmonary artery and to the pulmonary circulation. Without a source of mixing between the pulmonary and systemic circulations, there is inadequate tissue oxygen delivery. The result is profound desaturation, tissue hypoxia, metabolic acidosis, and ultimately cardiovascular collapse. Mixing between oxygenated and deoxygenated blood is dependent on a communication between the two parallel circulations and can take place at the level of the great arteries (PDA), atrial level (ASD), or ventricular level (VSD). Although the existence of the PDA and VSD may temporize the patient in the postnatal period, the presence of adequate atrial level mixing is the most consequential to ensuring adequate systemic oxygenation.
paragraphs.heading: Transposition of the Great Arteries

paragraphs.text: Management of neonates with D-TGA has become fairly standardized in the current era. Initial management is aimed at medical stabilization, correction of metabolic derangements, respiratory support, and vasoactive therapies, if necessary. Patients should be started on PGE1 infusion to maintain ductal patency regardless of the status of other intracardiac shunts until the status of the atrial level shunt is confirmed. If there is any concern that the atrial communication is not adequate at that moment or will not remain adequate for the duration until definitive surgery can be performed, then neonates with D-TGA should undergo a BAS. Once an adequate atrial communication is confirmed or created following BAS, it is reasonable to attempt to wean the PGE1 infusion and start enteral feeds before surgical repair. However, any change in clinical status should prompt rapid re-initiation of PGE1 and cessation of feeding.
paragraphs.heading: Transposition of the Great Arteries

paragraphs.text: The arterial switch operation (ASO) is the standard surgery offered to patients with D-TGA and has excellent early survival as well as long-term outcomes.21,68 The ASO is typically performed during the first week of life after stabilization after birth and the initial fall in PVR (48–72 hours). The operation is performed via a median sternotomy and on cardiopulmonary bypass. After initial dissection and standard cardioplegic arrest, the aorta is transected and the coronary ostia are mobilized from the aorta as coronary “buttons.” These coronary buttons include native aortic wall tissue to allow coronary reimplantation in the neo-aorta. Next, the main pulmonary artery is transected and the coronary buttons are translocated to the pulmonary root—which becomes the neo-aorta. Subsequently, the main pulmonary artery is brought anterior to the aorta (LeCompte maneuver) and aortic continuity is reestablished by direct anastomosis between the ascending aorta and neo-aortic root. Finally, the neo-pulmonary root is reconstructed with the autologous pericardium, pulmonary artery continuity is created by anastomosing the main pulmonary artery to the reconstructed neo-pulmonary root, and the ASD is closed.
paragraphs.heading: Transposition of the Great Arteries

paragraphs.text: Some heart conditions or combinations of conditions cannot be easily placed into one of the major physiologic groups detailed above or deserve special attention on their own. The following section contains miscellaneous procedures that do not fall into one of the rubrics above. A list of commonly performed surgeries in the current era is found in Table 79.4.
paragraphs.heading: Miscellaneous Procedures

paragraphs.text: Isolated branch pulmonary artery stenosis outside of the commonly encountered peripheral pulmonic stenosis (PPS) is rarely observed in the neonatal period. The most common cause is due to constriction of the proximal left pulmonary artery following ductus arteriosus closure. In severe cases, the left pulmonary artery can become completely obstructed or isolated if not treated early. Moderate lesions can typically be treated via balloon angioplasty, but severe lesions often require stent implantation for a sustained result. Although there are stents which can be placed in the neonate, many of them cannot be dilated to the size of an adult pulmonary artery. As a result, these stents are placed as a palliative step when future surgical intervention is anticipated. At the time of surgical intervention, these small stents can either be surgically removed or transected, allowing for enlargement of the vessel. Studies have demonstrated that some of these stents may be fractured with high-pressure balloons or “unzipped,” but this is highly dependent on the type of stent used.69,70 Similar to neonatal stenting of aortic coarctation, bioresorbable stents may prove to be a useful therapeutic option in this patient population.71
paragraphs.heading: Pulmonary Artery Stenosis

paragraphs.text: A PDA is commonly encountered in premature neonates. Hemodynamically significant PDAs are encountered more commonly the more gestationally premature the infant is at the time of birth. Large PDAs can result in significant left-to-right shunting, with medical consequences including respiratory failure, renal insufficiency, and feeding intolerance. The management of the hemodynamically significant PDA in the neonatal period, particularly the premature and extremely premature population, is controversial and very institutional and provider dependent. Long-standing methods for PDA closure include medical therapy with prostaglandin inhibitors and surgical ligation. Medical closure of PDA is covered extensively in other chapters, so it will not be addressed in this section. Surgical closure has been the gold standard for over 60 years but has recently fallen out of favor because of short- and long-term data showing poorer outcomes with those premature infants who received ligation. When necessary, PDA ligation is performed via posterolateral thoracotomy, and typically a clip is placed on the PDA, versus suture ligation and division. Surgical PDA
paragraphs.heading: Treatment of Patent Ductus Arteriosus (see also Chapter 75)

paragraphs.text: ligation is essentially 100% effective and is typically performed safely when done by experienced operators. However, the procedure is not without risk, and complications include vocal cord paralysis, pneumothorax, diaphragm paralysis, and post-ligation cardiac syndrome. Much of the morbidity and mortality of PDA surgical ligation are related to the preoperative clinical status of the neonate, and therefore the timing of when patients are referred for surgical ligation is crucial.
paragraphs.heading: Treatment of Patent Ductus Arteriosus (see also Chapter 75)

paragraphs.text: Over the past 10 years, many institutions have started pursuing transcatheter approaches for neonatal PDA closure using off-label devices approved for other vascular occlusion indications. Transcatheter PDA closure in older infants and children with stainless steel coils and nitinolbased devices has been performed since the 1970s with great success. As a result, PDA surgical ligation outside of the neonatal population is almost never performed. The unique neonatal ductal anatomy and small patient size has limited the occlusion of neonatal PDAs with traditional FDA-approved devices. However, the development of smaller interventional devices and delivery catheters has now allowed for safe transcatheter occlusion of the ductus arteriosus in premature neonates.72–74 Multiple off-label devices have been used over the years, but a single device is now FDA approved for PDA closure in premature infants— the Amplatzer Piccolo Occluder (Abbott, Santa Clara, CA), which was approved in January of 2019. Because a learning curve for this procedure exists and widespread experience is still growing, a thoughtful and intentional approach by each institution must be taken so that premature PDA device closure can be performed safely and effectively.72–75 Premature PDA device closure is most safely performed with femoral venous access only and with both fluoroscopic and echocardiographic guidance, although some centers are moving to 100% echocardiographic guidance and eliminating the need for a catheterization laboratory. Although the procedure and device have been demonstrated to be safe and effective, there are adverse events associated with the procedure, notably device obstruction of the left branch pulmonary artery or descending thoracic aorta. This is usually discovered before the device is released by angiography or transthoracic echocardiogram, at which time the device can be safely removed and another size or device can be tried or the patient can be referred for surgical ligation. Further research and cumulative experience with both approved (on-label) and off-label devices are expected to demonstrate transcatheter PDA closure to be safe and effective for many premature infants.
paragraphs.heading: Treatment of Patent Ductus Arteriosus (see also Chapter 75)

paragraphs.text: Isolated pulmonary vein stenosis is a rare anomaly in the neonate, is associated with poor outcomes, and is commonly seen in conjunction with other defects. Stenosis of multiple pulmonary veins is associated with pulmonary venous hypoplasia and poorer prognosis, and it is more common in infants born extremely premature, especially
paragraphs.heading: Pulmonary Vein Stenosis

paragraphs.text: those with coexisting intracardiac shunt lesion.76 This condition can be congenital or acquired after a pulmonary vein repair operation. Interventional experience with this condition is growing, with multiple case series describing balloon angioplasty (both conventional and cutting balloons) and stent implantation for this lesion.77,78 The process of progressive pulmonary vein stenosis is poorly understood but appears inflammatory in nature, and there is a growing body of literature regarding the use of both drug-eluting stents and systemically administered antiproliferative agents to reduce or halt the inflammatory process leading to restenosis.79
paragraphs.heading: Pulmonary Vein Stenosis

paragraphs.text: Neonates with CHD often require indwelling central venous catheters and arterial monitoring lines for prolonged periods. This is the reason there is a high prevalence of venous and arterial occlusion in the CHD population, especially in those with functional single ventricle heart conditions. The importance of obtaining umbilical venous and arterial access immediately after birth cannot be emphasized enough. Studies have shown that single ventricle patients who have umbilical venous lines placed instead of femoral lines have had significantly lower complication rate of vascular thrombosis and occlusion.80 Furthermore, these patients require multiple catheterization procedures in their lifetime, and occluded femoral veins or arteries complicate these procedures considerably and can make some future interventions impossible to perform. If nonumbilical access is required, it is our practice to use the smallest catheter necessary for medical management. Use of single lumen instead of double lumen results in less vascular occlusion. Tunneling central lines is associated with less thrombosis and a decreased rate of central line–associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI). Placement of catheters in the upper extremities or neck vessels is not recommended in single ventricle patients before the Fontan operation. If catheters are necessary in these positions, anticoagulation should be administered immediately after placement, and the line should be removed as soon as it is safely possible to reduce the risk of vascular stenosis or occlusion. Finally, when other alternative sites of access have been exhausted, transhepatic lines can be placed in the catheterization laboratory and have been shown to be a feasible and safe alternative in infants with otherwise limited access.81
paragraphs.heading: Central Line Placement

paragraphs.text: Pericardiocentesis or pericardial drain placement can be safely performed in the neonate. The procedure is typically guided by transthoracic echocardiogram but can be performed by landmark alone in emergency cases when the patient is suffering from cardiac tamponade. There are multiple causes for tamponade in the neonate, but one of the most common causes is associated with indwelling central venous catheters. It is not known whether the mechanism
paragraphs.heading: Pericardiocentesis

paragraphs.text: of tamponade is perforation or simple diffusion across a very thin atrial wall, but analysis of the effusion often shows similar fluid composition to the infusate.82
paragraphs.heading: Pericardiocentesis

paragraphs.text: Fetal intervention (see Chapter 12) has been the subject of much interest over the past 15 years. Its use is attractive in some of the congenital cardiac defects with poor outcomes secondary to valvar obstructions, which can lead to ventricular hypoplasia. There are currently three catheterbased interventions that have been performed in fetuses with CHD: balloon valvuloplasty in aortic valve stenosis (thought to lead to HLHS), balloon valvuloplasty in pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum (with impending hypoplastic right ventricle), and ASD creation or enlargement in HLHS with restrictive atrial septum. Fetal cardiac interventions are not performed as standard of care at all heart centers and are typically only performed at centers with experienced teams made up of high-risk obstetrics (maternal-fetal medicine), fetal cardiology, and interventional cardiology. As such, it is common for centers that do not offer the procedure to refer patients to one of the experienced centers. There is a noninsignificant risk to the fetus and potentially the mother, so candidates for fetal cardiac intervention must be carefully screened and vetted before the decision to proceed is made. Accurate diagnosis must be made early enough in gestation to allow for potential reversal of disease progression following the intervention. Lastly, information regarding the natural history of these defects is not completely understood, making it difficult to predict which fetus will develop ventricular hypoplasia and should undergo these high-risk fetal interventions.83 The mortality associated with these procedures is improving as experience is gained. Nevertheless, it is still not clear-cut that early fetal intervention will consistently alter disease progression beyond the watchful waiting and treating the high-risk neonate with established strategies.84
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Cardiac Intervention

paragraphs.text: One of the most feared complications of systemic to pulmonary artery shunts is complete or near-complete shunt occlusion in patients solely dependent on the shunt for pulmonary blood flow. When severe cyanosis develops secondary to shunt obstruction, the two treatment strategies include surgical revision or transcatheter intervention. If possible, this is best dealt with in the catheterization laboratory to avoid another midline sternotomy. In the event of complete occlusion, patients sometimes need to be stabilized on ECMO to provide adequate oxygenation and then can be transported to the catheterization laboratory. Transcatheter interventions include simple balloon dilation, thrombus evacuation, or stent implantation within the shunt (Fig. 79.8A–B).85 Interventions for modified Blalock-Taussig shunt obstructions are usually approached from the femoral artery. RV-PA (Sano) shunts are typically approached from the femoral vein.86 For
paragraphs.heading: Shunt Obstruction

paragraphs.text: partial or near occlusion, these procedures carry a high risk, as crossing the already obstructed shunt further decreases the diminutive pulmonary blood flow and can lead to severe cyanosis and cardiac arrest. Nevertheless, when performed by experienced operators, the success rate is encouraging and surgical revision is rarely required.
paragraphs.heading: Shunt Obstruction

paragraphs.text: Heart transplantation in the neonate continues to be reserved for those babies with congenital cardiac anomalies or cardiomyopathies that are not amenable to repair. Even high-risk single ventricle conditions such as HLHS are rarely treated primarily with heart transplantation. The reasons for this are many, as highlighted in the 2017 report of the International Society for Heart and Lung Transplantation.87 The number of infant (<1 year old) heart transplantations performed in North America and Europe combined has been stable for years at only about 120 per year. Not only is this a reflection of the limited indications for transplantation, but more importantly it reflects the severely limited donor pool of this rare resource. Patient survival is about 75% at 8 years and 50% at 22 years, which is somewhat better than reported results for older children.88 Reasons for the improved survival rate include the immaturity of the immune system leading to decreased antibody-mediated rejection. In addition, neonatal transplant patients have been shown to have less graft vasculopathy89 and require less immune suppression.90 However, there are the lifelong challenges with immunosuppression and the balance of rejection and infection that lead to a continuous risk hazard of significant morbidities. The continuous risk of developing a malignancy is 10% at 10 years, primarily lymphomas as well as the continuous risk of life-threatening infections. The
paragraphs.heading: Neonatal Heart Transplantation

paragraphs.text: continuous risk of graft failure secondary to cardiac allograft vasculopathy is 50% at 15 years. Unfortunately, despite the ability to perform re-transplantations for graft failure, both patient and graft survival is less compared to primary transplantation. Therefore, when considering a lifelong management strategy for newborn CHD, transplantation needs to be reserved for those without other options. Nonetheless, in neonates that require transplantation, there are ongoing efforts to expand the donor supply by considering donation from anencephalic donors as well as those with marginal function and prolonged ischemic time. Also, the ability to successfully perform ABO-incompatible heart transplantation is unique in the neonate by taking advantage of their somewhat naïve immunologic response to antigens.91 A list of relative and absolute contraindications to infant cardiac transplantation is shown in Table 79.5.
paragraphs.heading: Neonatal Heart Transplantation

paragraphs.text: In infants with a known prenatal diagnosis of ductal-dependent CHD, prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) infusion should be initiated shortly after birth and after intravenous access is obtained. For infants in whom ductal-dependent CHD is suspected based on cyanosis or shocklike clinical picture, PGE1 infusion should also be initiated immediately and continued until further testing, usually an echocardiogram, can be performed to either confirm or negate the diagnosis. In these undiagnosed clinical situations, prompt initiation of PGE1 is critical and can be lifesaving. PGE1 can be infused through virtually any vascular access that can be obtained, including the intraosseous route. The standard dose for maintenance of ductal patency is 0.03 μg/
paragraphs.heading: Prostaglandin E1

paragraphs.text: kg per min. For infants with suspected ductal-dependent CHD who present with severe cyanosis or shock, an initial dose of 0.1 μg/kg per min is often a recommended starting dose to open the ductus arteriosus. This dose can be increased in certain situations to 0.2 μg/kg per min if the ductus arteriosus remains closed at the 0.1 μg/kg per min dose. Conversely, the dose can often be decreased back to a maintenance dose of 0.03 μg/kg per min once the ductus arteriosus is reopened and the infant has begun to stabilize clinically. The short-term side effects of PGE1 include apnea/hypopnea, skin flushing, and fever, and these tend to be dose-dependent effects.92 If side effects are occurring and causing management issues, the dose can be titrated down to as low as 0.01 μg/kg per min as long as the ductus arteriosus remains patent and an adequate size at that level. There is no limit to how long PGE1 can be infused, and sometimes it is necessary to maintain an infant on PGE1 for prolonged periods, especially for those infants with significant medical comorbidities or extreme prematurity. As stated in the sections above, the alternative for prolonged PGE1 infusion is implanting a ductal stent to maintain patency and therefore
paragraphs.heading: Prostaglandin E1

paragraphs.text: avoid the long-term effects of PGE1, including periosteal hyperostosis or gastric outlet obstruction.
paragraphs.heading: Prostaglandin E1

paragraphs.text: Most patients with mild and moderate forms of CHD do not require special consideration regarding oxygen therapy and ventilation strategies. They can typically be managed following standard neonatal strategies appropriate for age and size. Patients with single ventricle physiology and some with two ventricles who will require a PDA for ductal-dependent CHD require more specific management strategies to maintain pH levels within tighter ranges and judicious use of delivered oxygen. The cardiac output and systemic oxygenation of neonates with single ventricle heart conditions who have systemic and pulmonary circulations connected by the PDA are extremely dependent on the balance of vascular resistances in both circulations. As the PVR drops over the first week, keeping an appropriate balance of circulations becomes more difficult and close attention to arterial blood gas parameters becomes
paragraphs.heading: Oxygen and Ventilation

paragraphs.text: increasingly important. The most exemplary situation when ventilation and supplemental oxygen therapy can affect the balance between the systemic and the pulmonary vascular beds is in the care of infants with HLHS.93 Preoperatively, systemic output is dependent on right-toleft flow across the PDA, which is typically maintained by PGE1. When PVR is high, blood flow through the PDA is right-to-left in systole as well as during a portion of diastole. As such, oxygen saturations will be relatively low because of relatively reduced amounts of pulmonary blood flow and systemic perfusion will be adequately maintained. As the PVR falls during the first day to week of life, blood flow remains right-to-left in systole across the PDA but becomes left-to-right in all of diastole, resulting in rising oxygen saturations with increasing pulmonary blood flow. If the PVR falls significantly and measures are not taken to counterbalance this change in physiology, systemic perfusion can become inadequate and end organ injury (acute renal insufficiency, necrotizing enterocolitis) can result. This condition, termed “pulmonary overcirculation/systemic hypoperfusion,” can happen after even a very short period of time in the preoperative period. As such, regular checks of arterial blood gases (preferably) or capillary gases can provide significant insight into the balance of circulations. Elevation in arterial lactate levels can precede clinical instability and end organ injury, so it is recommended to follow and trend these levels serially. In general, pH should be maintained between 7.34 and 7.40, and alkalosis should be avoided. The pCO2 and serum bicarbonate levels are less reliable to follow, especially when the neonate is receiving diuretics caused by the contraction alkalosis these medications can cause. If pH is maintained in this range, most patients will not overcirculate to a significant degree. In nonintubated neonates, relative overcirculation can lead to hyperventilation, and respiratory rates in the 80s to 90s are not uncommon. In these situations, the neonate may blow off considerable amounts of CO2 leading to alkalosis and worsening pulmonary overcirculation. When these situations arise, it is sometimes necessary to intubate and assume control of the ventilation by dropping rate and minute ventilation until pH is back into the desired range.
paragraphs.heading: Oxygen and Ventilation

paragraphs.text: Oxygen, particularly alveolar or delivered oxygen, is a potent pulmonary vasodilator. The administration of supplemental oxygen can lead to dramatic drops in PVR and increasing pulmonary blood flow. In general, supplemental oxygen should be avoided in single ventricle patients, especially HLHS, unless there is significant lung disease leading to suspected pulmonary venous desaturation, in which saturations are consistently less than 70%. On the contrary, in patients with high saturations from pulmonary overcirculation, it is sometimes necessary to provide subambient levels of oxygen, which raises the PVR and “discourages” pulmonary blood flow. Subambient oxygen can be administered by bleeding in nitrogen gas into a ventilation tent or through the endotracheal tube in an intubated infant. An FiO2 of 18% to 20% can be effective at raising PVR, but
paragraphs.heading: Oxygen and Ventilation

paragraphs.text: close monitoring of oxygen saturations and PaO2 is necessary if this therapy is pursued.
paragraphs.heading: Oxygen and Ventilation

paragraphs.text: Infants with cyanotic CHD often have deficient oxygen delivery to vital tissue and organs because of the high levels of fetal hemoglobin, which holds on tightly to oxygen, and their inability to fully saturate hemoglobin molecules. Therefore it is important to maximize the oxygen-carrying capacity in these patients, and studies have shown that increasing the hemoglobin to greater than 13 g per dL or hematocrit to greater than 40% is ideal. This can be accomplished in the short term by transfusing packed red blood cells (15–20 cc/kg) or, over a longer period of time, some institutions have achieved higher levels by administering weekly erythropoietin injections.94 The exposure to many different blood donors can lead to antigen sensitization and make future matches for cardiac transplantation difficult. Furthermore, excessive use of packed red blood cell transfusions has been linked to transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI), prolonged length of intensive care unit (ICU) stay, increased risk of infection, and higher mortality. Therefore neonatal transfusions should be used only when absolutely necessary for optimizing clinical status. Platelet transfusions are uncommon in the preoperative state in neonatal patients with CHD. The presence of thrombocytopenia in neonatal CHD is likely related to perinatal insults, such as infection of intracranial bleeds, and unlikely related to the cardiac diagnosis. Usual replacement practices should be followed by the neonatology team in these cases. Similarly, the need for fresh-frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate, or other factor replacement is rare in the preoperative state for neonates with CHD. Postoperatively, however, the need for platelets and plasma is common and usually directed by the cardiothoracic ICU team or cardiac intensivists to address postoperative bleeding and to optimize oxygen delivery.
paragraphs.heading: Blood Products

paragraphs.text: Preload, or the overall volume status of neonates, is often very difficult to assess because of the tendency for capillary leak and the third-spacing of fluid. For neonates with CHD, especially those with fetal hydrops or those who develop edema shortly after birth, trying to assess and optimize preload can be extremely difficult. However, preventing fluid overload when hypotension is present and withholding fluid when the neonate appears edematous from third-spacing in the presence of end organ hypoperfusion are management decisions that have potential for tremendous impact on the overall course of neonates requiring complex operations. Profound fluid overload has been correlated with increased duration of mechanical ventilation, prolonged ICU times, and delayed recovery of kidney function. These situations can develop even in the absence of concomitant conditions such as atrioventricular
paragraphs.heading: Preload

paragraphs.text: or semilunar valve dysfunction, hypoalbuminemia, anemia, and sepsis, which can all make assessments and treatment decisions that much more complex and difficult. Therefore it is crucial that the management teams pay close attention to daily weights, input/output totals, clinical exam findings such as liver span and fullness of fontanelle, electrolytes, and renal function (BUN and creatinine) on a daily if not per-shift basis. Teams must take the entirety of information into account to decide if fluid restriction or resuscitation is required.
paragraphs.heading: Preload

paragraphs.text: There are specific times when fluid management techniques may differ from simply attempting to achieve euvolemia. In the postoperative period, edema is extremely common because of fluid received in the operating room, capillary leak syndrome associated with cardiopulmonary bypass, and the need for perioperative blood products. In an attempt to combat this fluid overload, crystalloid or colloid administration should be used judiciously while maximizing the cardiac output with the use of inotropic and vasoactive agents. Often, medication drips or hyperalimentation can be concentrated or even discontinued if not immediately critical. Urine output can be maximized by maintaining good cardiac output and the aggressive use of diuretics. First-line diuretic therapy is generally a loop diuretic such as furosemide or bumetanide, often used in combination with a thiazide diuretic such as chlorothiazide for potentiation of effect. Hypokalemia is common with higher doses of loop diuretics, and patients may require either potassium supplementation or a potassium-sparing diuretic such as spironolactone (which also has beneficial ventricular remodeling properties) to avoid the hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis associated with long-term diuretic therapy.
paragraphs.heading: Preload

paragraphs.text: Besides the postoperative period, it is common for patients with lesions resulting in pulmonary overcirculation (left-to-right shunts) to become fluid overloaded and need diuretic therapy. Although the PVR is still somewhat elevated and may temporarily protect the patient from overcirculation, certain lesions, such as a large PDA, unrestrictive VSDs, certain forms of truncus arteriosus, and large aortopulmonary collaterals will result in excessive pulmonary blood flow, and diuretics will almost certainly be required before neonatal surgical repair.
paragraphs.heading: Preload

paragraphs.text: In other situations, it may be beneficial to keep the patient relatively fluid-loaded, but not overloaded. For example, in patients with RVOT obstruction, such as tetralogy of Fallot, subpulmonary obstruction is somewhat dynamic and a preloaded right ventricle can help to keep these patients from having hypercyanotic spells. A volumeloaded right ventricle will physically stretch or distend the subpulmonary area, thereby decreasing the amount of dynamic collapse that leads to limited pulmonary blood flow and cyanosis. Similarly, patients with certain forms of cardiomyopathy will have stiff, noncompliant ventricles with significant diastolic dysfunction. These patients also need to have adequate preload to maintain ventricular filling and stroke volume.
paragraphs.heading: Preload

paragraphs.text: Afterload refers to the cumulative pressure against which the systemic ventricle must work to eject blood during systole. Although systemic blood pressure makes up the most significant portion of the afterload, the condition of the ventricle (wall stress and preload) must also be considered. For example, in a healthy heart with normal systolic and diastolic ventricular function, increasing afterload can be overcome by the ventricle by increasing ventricular wall stress and contractility. If the high afterload is chronic, myocardial hypertrophy will develop to assist the ventricle in overcoming this stress.
