However, in a dysfunctional ventricle, the capacity to overcome acute and chronically elevated afterload is not as robust. In this situation, high afterload leads to higher systolic pressures and wall stress, which then leads to rising filling pressures and atrial hypertension. Although fluid resuscitation may allow for maintained cardiac output over a short period of time, fluid overload may ensue and other measures are required to assist the diseased ventricle. Oral afterload reducing agents are typically antihypertensive medications that lower SVR and systemic blood pressure. Although medications like angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE-Is) and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) do provide long-term ventricular remodeling effects, in the short term they only affect afterload by the blood pressure-lowering effects. For critically ill neonates, these medications are rarely used. The medication most commonly used for this situation is milrinone, which has afterload reducing, inotropic, and lusitropic (ventricular relaxing) properties. The net effect of milrinone is to have improved ventricular filling, improved stroke volume, and lower afterload for an overall increase in cardiac output. Dobutamine has similar effects but usually results in a significantly elevated heart rate. For neonates that have a much higher resting heart rate, the tachycardia of dobutamine makes it less desirable compared to milrinone. Nitroprusside infusion is rarely used in neonates because it is a potent vasodilator and afterload reducing agent but lacks the inotropic and lusitropic properties of milrinone. The relatively low blood pressure of most neonates does not lend itself to treatment by this drug on a regular basis.
paragraphs.heading: Afterload

paragraphs.text: To reduce afterload in the subpulmonary ventricle, any agent that selectively decreases PVR can be considered in neonates. Oxygen and inhaled nitric oxide are potent pulmonary vasodilators and reduce pulmonary afterload very well. Other agents (sildenafil or bosentan) used to treat pulmonary hypertension can be considered for use under the guidance of pediatric pulmonary hypertension experts.95
paragraphs.heading: Afterload

paragraphs.text: Agents that increase inotropy and cardiac contractility can improve cardiac output. A commonly used oral agent to increase contractility is digoxin, which has been shown to be safe in the neonate with left ventricular volume overload
paragraphs.heading: Contractility

paragraphs.text: and systolic dysfunction.96 However, this oral medication is rarely used in the neonatal period solely for the purpose of treating ventricular systolic dysfunction or heart failure, unless added to a regimen that includes afterload reducing agents and diuretics, because it is typically a secondary or tertiary agent.
paragraphs.heading: Contractility

paragraphs.text: Intravenous inotropic support is more commonly encountered in the neonatal period to treat perinatal, preoperative, and postoperative systolic dysfunction.97 Dopamine and dobutamine have similar inotropic effects, although dopamine is usually preferred because of its greater effect in premature infants and because it causes less tachycardia and systemic vasodilation than dobutamine. Epinephrine is used in low doses for its inotropic effect, although counterintuitive effects of increasing myocardial oxygen demand through increased heart rate and SVR can limit its use. As discussed in the afterload section, milrinone is commonly used in the postoperative period because of its improved inotropy, lusitropy, and afterload reducing effects.
paragraphs.heading: Contractility

paragraphs.text: Hypercyanotic spells or “TET spells” are acute episodes that can develop in patients with tetralogy of Fallot when there is dynamic subpulmonary obstruction of the RVOT. When acute worsening of RVOT obstruction develops, there is a significant decrease in pulmonary blood flow and subsequent shunting of blood right-to-left at the ventricular level leading to severe hypoxia and cyanosis. The infundibulum of the right ventricle is thought to be reactive to circulating catecholamines, which increase with increasing patient agitation, resulting in increased gradient across the RV outflow tract forcing deoxygenated blood across the VSD into the aorta, resulting in cyanosis. Other factors such as decreased right ventricular filling owing to relative hypovolemia and lack of preload or tachycardia may further predispose these patients to hypercyanotic episodes. The treatment for hypercyanotic episodes is to find ways to decrease the subpulmonary obstruction, encourage more pulmonary blood flow, and increase the relative degree of left to right shunting at the ventricular level. If these maneuvers are followed, hypercyanotic spells can often be treated quickly before the infant is hypoxic for an unsafe amount of time. Some of these maneuvers and the physiologic rationale for their use are illustrated in Table 79.6.
paragraphs.heading: Treatment of Hypercyanotic Spells

paragraphs.text: The field of CHD is constantly changing and innovation is typically the rule and not the exception. The past 25 years have seen a tremendous improvement in the medical, surgical, and interventional therapies for neonates and children with CHD. The FDA approval of the Amplatzer Piccolo Duct Occluder is an example of the medical device industry beginning to focus more on smaller niche fields. Similarly, although not as relevant for neonatal management, the
paragraphs.heading: What the Future Holds

paragraphs.text: field of CHD has seen two new transcatheter pulmonary valves approved for use in the United States for the treatment of symptomatic chronic severe pulmonary regurgitation as seen after repair of tetralogy of Fallot and pulmonary stenosis. The expectation is that there will be more devices approved for PDA closure in premature infants, including Medtronic’s microvascular plug and the Micro Plug Set (KA Medical, Minneapolis, MN). Although transcatheter valves and stents are not currently for use via the typical transcatheter route in neonates and infants, the miniaturization of this technology is underway so that more infants will be candidates for hybrid implants in the near future.
paragraphs.heading: What the Future Holds

paragraphs.text: Biodegradable materials and devices remain one of the most important focuses of research and are at the forefront of innovation in pediatrics because of the ideal potential to allow placement or implantation of a device that would eventually resorb or degrade and not inhibit the growth of the vessel or heart structure in which it has been placed or inhibit access to a particular area of the heart. Catheters are also being made smaller and more versatile to avoid some vascular complications that have gone on for decades using adult-sized equipment in children.
paragraphs.heading: What the Future Holds

### Introduction

Congenital heart disease (CHD) is the most common birth defect and is frequently encountered by providers in newborn nurseries and neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) during the immediate postnatal period. Despite the frequency that these conditions are encountered, nearly 75% of neonates born with CHD will not require an interventional or surgical procedure before 1 year of life.1 For these patients, the clinical course is often straightforward and team discussions

1470

are primarily focused on the anticipated follow-up and postdischarge planning. Conversely, only approximately 15% of infants born with CHD have critical heart problems that require interventions within the first few days or weeks of life.1–4 For these neonates, a well-integrated and multidisciplinary team approach is paramount to achieve optimal outcomes. Many of the important management principles routinely followed by neonatologists can be applied to critically ill newborn cardiac patients, including thermal regulation, prematurity issues, nutritional strategies, and ventilator support. However, there are many cardiac-specific management strategies, procedures, and surgeries performed on these patients in the neonatal period that require the neonatology team to have a deepened understanding so that care can be seamlessly integrated.

This chapter focuses on the cardiac-specific medical management strategies, catheter-based interventions, and congenital heart surgeries that are performed during the neonatal period on newborns with more complex heart conditions. The objective of this chapter is to describe the management strategies and procedures typically performed based on the prevailing anatomic or physiologic deficit faced by the infant during the neonatal period. Since many of these conditions have similar underlying physiologies and early goals for palliation or treatment, the strategies used can be applied to many different disease conditions. We will also discuss situations in which early intervention would not alter clinical outcomes and for which the best course of management may be cardiac transplantation or palliative comfort measures. For patients requiring intervention in the neonatal period, the focus within this chapter is to describe the indications for the procedure, include brief description of the technique, and delineate some risks involved. The intention here is not to be a procedural textbook chapter describing interventional and surgical techniques in great detail, but to give the neonatologist sufficient framework to understand the procedures performed. Similarly, preoperative management strategies will be discussed as they relate to certain conditions, but postoperative management is outside the scope of this chapter and will not be addressed.


## PDF page 1471 | printed page 1471

### Classification of Congenital Heart Disease

There are many different ways to classify different forms of CHD. Typical schemes include cyanotic versus acyanotic, left-to-right versus right-to-left shunt lesions, obstructive lesions, ductal dependent for pulmonary blood flow versus ductal dependent for systemic blood, biventricular versus univentricular anatomy, and many others. In reality, the many forms of CHD have overlapping anatomies and physiologies, making it difficult to organize management in the scope of a single chapter.

Cyanotic congenital heart conditions represent a broad class of anatomic and physiologic derangements that result in patients with decreased systemic oxygenation following birth, including (1) obstruction to pulmonary blood flow with an intracardiac shunt such as an atrial septal defect (ASD) or ventricular septal defect (VSD) (e.g., critical pulmonary stenosis or tetralogy of Fallot), (2) admixture lesions in which there is a common site for mixing of systemic and pulmonary venous blood (atria or ventricles) which is pumped to both circulations (e.g., hypoplastic left heart syndrome [HLHS]), (3) transposition physiology in which systemic venous blood is pumped to the systemic circulation (e.g., D-transposition of great arteries [D-TGA]), and (4) pure right-to-left shunting (e.g., pulmonary AV malformations). Although this classification is helpful for understanding the physiologic mechanisms of cyanosis, it is less useful when discussing management strategies, because the various conditions require vastly different initial approaches.

It is much more helpful for the neonatologist to consider the conditions based on the site of anatomic obstruction or restriction to blood flow, ductal dependency, or the underlying presenting physiology (Table 79.1). For example, critical CHD can be classified as (1) right-heart obstructive lesions—ductal-dependent pulmonary blood flow, (2) leftheart obstructive lesions—ductal-dependent systemic blood flow, (3) admixture and single ventricle defects, and (4) defects with parallel circulation (e.g., transposition physiology). Although not all forms of CHD requiring neonatal intervention are captured with this grouping, it is a useful scheme that allows for a systematic approach to thinking about how to manage neonates with critical CHD.

### Right-Heart Obstructive Lesions

Right-heart obstructive lesions include a broad morphologic spectrum of defects with obstruction to the right ventricular inflow, the subpulmonary outflow tract, or both. On one end of the spectrum is isolated pulmonary valve stenosis, an anatomically straightforward defect resulting in single-level obstruction at the pulmonary valve. Conversely, tricuspid atresia is an anatomically complex lesion resulting in single ventricle physiology. Furthermore, the specific defects within the broader group of right-heart obstructive lesions exist on an anatomic continuum. For example, isolated pulmonary valve stenosis may be limited to mild valve dysplasia causing a minor right ventricular outflow tract

(RVOT) gradient, without the need for early intervention. Alternatively, critical pulmonary valve stenosis is a ductaldependent lesion requiring neonatal intervention.

Irrespective of the specific defect, however, neonates with critical right-heart obstruction require (1) an obligate intracardiac communication (e.g., ASD, VSD) to deliver blood to the sub-aortic ventricle (typically the left ventricle), and (2) an arterial-to-pulmonary vascular communication— commonly via a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) or less frequently in the form of major aorto-pulmonary artery collaterals (MAPCAs). In critical right-heart obstruction, the absence of an adequate intracardiac communication or lack of systemic-to-pulmonary artery communication will result in cardiovascular collapse without emergent intervention. As such, the primary objective in early management of these neonates is to establish a stable source of PBF by relieving right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (RVOTO), by creating a durable systemic-to-pulmonary artery connection, and in some cases, both interventions are necessary.

### Procedures to Increase or Maintain Pulmonary Blood Flow

The first management strategy in a patient with critical right heart obstruction is to maintain a PDA, which is best accomplished by starting a prostaglandin (PGE1) infusion immediately after birth or as soon as the critical lesion is identified. PGE1 is a safe and effective means to maintain ductal patency for a relatively short period until a more durable source can be established. Once a surgical or catheter-based intervention is performed, the PGE1 infusion can be discontinued. Advancements in catheter-based device technologies have led to an increasing number of transcatheter options for neonates with critical CHD. Many of these options for maintaining and/or increasing pulmonary blood flow will be discussed in the sections below.

### Transcatheter Strategies for Right-Heart Obstructive Lesions

Transcatheter interventions to establish PBF through the RVOT include simple balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty (BPV), RVOT perforation, and RVOT stent placement. PDA stent placement is an increasingly used strategy for establishing systemic-to-pulmonary artery blood flow in patients with or without a patent RVOT (Table 79.2). Of note, it is not uncommon for strategies to be used in combination. For example, in neonates with membranous pulmonary atresia, perforation of the atretic pulmonary valve and balloon valvuloplasty may be followed by PDA stenting to allow time for the relatively hypoplastic and stiff RV to grow and relax until antegrade PBF through the RVOT is sufficient to provide adequate systemic oxygenation.

### Right Ventricular Outflow Tract Stenting

Severe obstruction of the RVOT can be seen in patients with tetralogy of Fallot and double outlet right ventricle leading to severe cyanosis. Some patients will undergo a complete surgical repair in the neonatal period depending on the patient’s weight, size of branch pulmonary arteries, and extracardiac medical issues. Certain centers will perform aortopulmonary shunts (see below) for cyanotic patients with small branch pulmonary arteries and bring them back for complete surgical repair at 4 to 6 months of age. BPV is typically not effective in this anatomy given the severe obstruction across the RVOT. Over the past 10 years, centers have started palliating these patients by implanting stents across the RVOT.14,15 During the procedure, the RVOT and main pulmonary artery are imaged using angiography. The RVOT is then crossed with a catheter and wire position is established to guide the procedure. A stent is selected based on

the size of the RVOT. The stent is advanced over the wire and typically through a long introducer sheath until it is positioned across the RVOT. The stent is deployed within the RVOT and follow-up angiography is then performed to assess the adequacy of antegrade flow through the implanted stent. Multiple stents may need to be placed depending on the anatomy of the RVOT. Most patients maintained on prostaglandins can be weaned off the medication following stent implantation within the RVOT. In premature or small neonates or those with vascular access issues, hybrid per-ventricular stenting of the RVOT, whereby the pediatric heart surgeon places the sheath directly into the right ventricle via a small sub-xiphoid incision, allows effective palliation in this challenging population.16 In either approach, these stents are removed at the time of surgical repair, which is ultimately delayed, allowing for growth in both the patient and branch pulmonary arteries.17

### Systemic Artery to Pulmonary Artery Shunts

The ability to augment PBF by a surgically created shunt between the aorta, or one of its branches, and the central pulmonary arteries dates back to 1945 with the introduction of the Blalock-Taussig-Thomas (BTT) shunt. The classic BTT shunt was performed using the divided subclavian artery as an end-to-side anastomosis to the pulmonary artery.20 Following the BTT shunt, additional shunt techniques were introduced, including the Potts shunt, Waterson shunt, Mee (or Melbourne) shunt, and modified BTT (mBTT) shunt.21–24

Today, the most common palliative neonatal surgical shunt is the mBTT. The mBTT shunt provides a durable

source of PBF in the neonatal period and allows for delayed complete biventricular repair later in life when the surgery will be better tolerated. An mBTT shunt is created by placing a polytetrafluoroethylene (e.g., Gore-Tex) tube graft from the innominate or subclavian artery to the branch PAs. Regulation of flow through the mBTT shunt is determined, in part, by the diameter and length of the shunt and location of the proximal anastomosis (i.e., a shunt of the innominate artery will provide increased flow compared to a shunt off the subclavian artery). For most neonates, a 3- to 4-mm Gore-Tex graft is selected. An mBTT shunt is most commonly performed through a median sternotomy; however, classically, it was performed via a posterolateral thoracotomy (an approach still preferred by some institutions today).21

A central shunt is an anastomosis between the ascending aorta and the main pulmonary artery. A central shunt can be performed by a direct anastomosis between the two vessels (Mee or Melbourne shunt) or by using a Gore-Tex interposition graft (Laks-type central shunt).25 Central shunts are commonly used in patients with PA/VSD and MAPCAs with diminutive branch pulmonary arteries. The strategy is to rehabilitate or grow the native pulmonary arteries by providing relatively unrestrictive degree of flow through a shorter and larger shunt.26

### Surgical Correction of Right-Heart Obstructive Lesions

An alternative to surgical palliation in patients with severe or critical right-heart obstruction is to perform a “complete” neonatal repair. The technique for surgical repair is largely dependent on the specific anatomy of the cardiac lesion, and a detailed discussion of surgical techniques for individual lesions is outside the scope of this chapter. However, the principles for complete repair of right-heart obstructive lesions involve relieving the RVOTO and closure of intracardiac septal defects (i.e., ASD, VSD), thus resulting in a septated heart with normal biventricular physiology.

The operation is performed via a median sternotomy on cardiopulmonary bypass. Relief of RVOTO is dependent on the level of the obstruction, that is, valvar, supravalvar, or subvalvar. In most cases, resection of hypertrophied muscle (septomarginal trabeculations) below the level of the pulmonary infundibulum is performed to relieve subpulmonary obstruction. If the pulmonary valve is adequate (or near adequate) size, a valve-sparing approach may be used, which may include no pulmonary valve intervention, a pulmonary valvotomy, or gentle intraoperative pulmonary valve dilation. Alternatively, if there is significant valvar or annular hypoplasia, it is necessary to perform a more

### Primary Neonatal Repair Versus Palliation and Management of Tetralogy of Fallot

Advancements in surgical technique, CPB strategies, myocardial and cerebral protection, and intensive care management have made it possible to achieve excellent outcomes among smaller and younger neonates, even in the setting of more complex cardiac defects.27 It is reasonable therefore that management for CHD has tended to favor complete primary repair over palliative interventions for biventricular circulation whenever possible.27 Despite these advancements, however, there are specific instances in which the merits of early complete repair versus initial palliation followed by delayed repair remain debatable.

The treatment of neonates with critical tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is the paradigm lesion illustrating the “primary repair versus palliation” dichotomy. Although the surgical history for treatment of TOF dates back more than 75 years, the optimal management strategy for neonates with symptomatic TOF remains undefined.27 For the majority of infants with TOF, the management is straightforward. That is, most patients without critical pulmonary stenosis have a well-balanced circulation without significant cyanosis. These children typically do well in early infancy and undergo complete repair between 3 and 9 months of age. Given an expected early mortality of less than 1% and excellent long-term outcomes, there is little debate as to the management of these “ideal” TOF patients.27–29

Alternatively, symptomatic neonates with TOF present with hypercyanotic episodes (“TET spells”), profound ongoing

cyanosis, and ductal-dependent pulmonary blood flow. These neonates represent patients at the most extreme end of the spectrum with regard to RVOTO. Unlike the “ideal” TOF patient where complete TOF repair between 3 and 9 months has become the standard of care, the optimal management strategy for neonates with critical TOF is debatable. After initial stabilization, interventional options for these neonates include primary neonatal repair or initial palliation followed by complete repair at 6 to 9 months. As discussed above, palliation may be performed surgically by creating an mBTT shunt, or patients may undergo transcatheter palliation, either by placement of a ductal stent or stent placement in the RVOT.

Proponents of primary neonatal repair note that the operative mortality at experienced centers remains low and suggest that early intervention results in fewer surgical reinterventions, a shorter duration of chronic hypoxemia, and the avoidance of shunt-associated complications (if an mBTT shunt is the palliative method selected).27–30 Conversely, advocates for initial palliation note that primary repair is less likely to preserve the pulmonary valve (i.e., increased rate of TAP), is associated with more frequent postoperative comorbidities, and may be associated with increased rates of all reinterventions.30 Furthermore, although single-center studies have demonstrated excellent results following neonatal repair, aggregate data suggest early mortality after neonatal repair is approximately 4% to 8%.27

When considering palliation for neonates with TOF, early mortality after mBTT shunt is reported between 4% and 6.2%.31,32 Additionally, recent studies comparing outcomes after mBTT shunt and PDA stenting have demonstrated similar early survival between the two groups. It should be noted, however, that although there were a significant portion of patients with TOF in these studies, the population was comprised of a heterogeneous group of infants with ductal-dependent pulmonary blood flow.33 In comparison, centers that have adopted RVOT stenting as their primary strategy for palliation of symptomatic neonates with TOF report an early mortality between 0% and 4.9%.29,31 The accumulated data with respect to RVOT stenting are limited in terms of volume and follow-up; however, the early reports suggest promising outcomes.

Although excellent outcomes after neonatal repair have been described for a number of lesions and across a number of centers, many institutions achieve comparable results using a palliative approach (either surgical or transcatheter).27 For many lesions, including TOF, the data do not provide evidence-based guidelines for the management of neonates with critical CHD. As such, the rationale for deciding between initial palliation versus complete neonatal repair is multifactorial and includes the anatomic details of the lesion, patient size, comorbidities, and, perhaps most importantly, institutional preference.

### Left-Heart Obstructive Lesions

As with right-heart obstructive lesions, left-heart obstructive lesions encompass a broad spectrum of morphologic

defects affecting single or multiple left heart components— including the mitral valve apparatus, components of the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT), the ascending aorta, and the aortic arch. The resulting physiology, and thus management, is largely dependent on the severity of obstruction, level of obstruction, and the number of obstructive lesions involved. For example, mild isolated aortic valve stenosis is relatively hemodynamically insignificant early in life and may not require intervention until much later, if at all. On the opposite end of the spectrum, HLHS is a multi-level lesion resulting in a diminutive LV and ductal-dependent systemic blood flow requiring neonatal intervention and single ventricle palliation.

Congenital left ventricular outflow tract obstruction (LVOTO) is a classification of lesions that includes the subaortic, aortic valve, and supravalvar areas of the heart. By far the most common condition that occurs in isolation is valvar aortic stenosis (70% of all LVOTO lesions) with subvalvar (10%–20%), supravalvar (5%–10%), or mixed (8%) representing the remainder.21,34 Although most cases of valvar aortic stenosis do not become clinically significant before adolescence, a small percentage of patients present with critical aortic valve stenosis that requires neonatal intervention.21 Isolated subvalvar and supravalvar aortic stenosis rarely present with severe obstruction in the neonatal period and tend to progress with time. However, if these conditions are part of a multilevel obstructive process (e.g., Shone complex), early neonatal intervention may be required.

Aortic coarctation, aortic arch hypoplasia, and interrupted aortic arch (IAA) are congenital anomalies that result in left-sided obstruction above the level of aortic valve and supravalvar areas. Classic coarctation results in a discrete narrowing at the aortic isthmus—the area between the left subclavian artery and ductus arteriosus (or ligamentum arteriosum). Coarctation of the aorta can also be associated with transverse arch hypoplasia, resulting in diffuse narrowing along multiple arch segments beginning after the takeoff of the right brachiocephalic artery. Interrupted aorta results in dissociation between segments of the aortic arch and is classified based on the location of interruption. Type A occurs when the interruption occurs after the left subclavian artery, type B is an interruption between the left common carotid artery and left subclavian artery, and type C is an interruption between the innominate artery and left common carotid artery.

Clinical presentation, timing of intervention, and technique of repair are dependent on the location, extent, and severity of the stenosis. For example, mild discrete narrowing of the isthmus may be asymptomatic until adolescence, often only identified after a murmur is detected or during the work-up for hypertension. Conversely, severe aortic coarctation and IAA are ductal-dependent lesions that—if not detected with fetal imaging—will present following ductal closure during the neonatal period.

Aortic arch lesions are often discovered on prenatal ultrasound and with early postnatal screening. However, many cases are still missed even when standard prenatal care is

Although it is possible to detect mild aortic coarctation prenatally, severe arch lesions (e.g., severe coarctation and IAA) are more easily detected, and it is usually recommended that these infants be delivered at centers where neonatal and surgical treatment can be provided. For cases in which prenatal detection has not occurred, postnatal symptoms develop with the advent of ductus arteriosus closure. These symptoms include poor feeding, respiratory distress, and eventually shock-like appearance because of low cardiac output. The postnatal diagnosis is typically confirmed using surface echocardiogram, which typically shows isthmus hypoplasia (periductal area), a posterior shelf causing flow acceleration on Doppler interrogation, varying degrees of transverse arch hypoplasia, or complete arch interruption. The severity and even presence of coarctation of the aorta can often not be fully appreciated in the setting of a moderateor large-sized PDA, so it is helpful to get echocardiographic confirmation just before or immediately after starting PGE1 infusion when the duct is small or absent. However, in cases of severe low cardiac output, the initiation of prostaglandins should not be withheld to allow time to obtain the echocardiogram. Occasionally, it is uncertain whether ductal closure will result in significant neonatal coarctation. In this scenario, the patient is placed on an “arch watch” to closely monitor hemodynamic, anatomic, and laboratory parameters (e.g., serum lactate) while the PDA is allowed to close. If PDA closure results in pathologic changes suggestive of coarctation, PGE1 is immediately restarted and surgical correction is indicated.

Patients born with severe or critical obstruction on the left side of the heart can often be asymptomatic in the immediate newborn period while the ductus arteriosus remains patent. The oxygen saturation might be normal or just mildly low during the screening pulse oximetry, especially if only checked in the upper extremity. These patients may appear well clinically and be discharged to home after an unremarkable observation period in the newborn nursery. However, as the ductus arteriosus closes, systemic cardiac output decreases and the neonate will progress to having cardiogenic shock and end organ dysfunction if not treated in expedited fashion. Although the incidence of undiagnosed postnatal presentation has significantly dropped with contemporary prenatal and postnatal CHD screening, studies have shown that the prenatal detection rate for isolated arch obstruction still hovers around 20% to 30%.35 Consequently, there continues to be a significant number of patients who will present postnatally every year, and neonatologists will need continued vigilance for these patients that present postnatally.

It follows then that management of neonates with critical left-sided obstruction is aimed at initial stabilization and resuscitation to correct acidosis and protect end-organ perfusion. PGE1 infusion is used to maintain a PDA, and in some cases mechanical ventilation and inotropic support is necessary for critically ill neonates. Once the infant has been adequately resuscitated, then the patient can go on to have an intervention to correct the underlying obstructive

process, whether that be a transcatheter intervention or a definitive surgical repair.

### Transcatheter Strategies for Left-Heart Obstructive Lesions Balloon Aortic Valvuloplasty

Balloon aortic valvuloplasty (BAV) is performed in the newborn period in patients who present with critical or severe valvar aortic stenosis. The first reported BAV was reported in 1983 by Lababidi, and the procedure has been markedly improved upon over the last few decades, predominantly related to the availability of compliant balloons with very small crossing profiles (down to 3 French).36–38 Recommendations for limiting the balloon diameter-to-annulus ratio to 80% to 100% has greatly improved the procedural results, in which relief of obstruction is obtained without causing severe degrees of valvar regurgitation.37,38 However, BAV itself can be technically challenging with a much higher risk profile in the neonatal population and should only be performed by experienced operators with surgical backup nearby. Aortic valvuloplasty is most commonly performed via a retrograde approach from the femoral artery but can also be performed via the femoral vein if an atrial communication is present. In smaller patients, the procedure can be performed via a surgical cut-down or direct percutaneous access to the common carotid artery.39 A smaller balloon diameter-to-annulus ratio can be performed first, with progressively larger balloons if a significant residual pressure gradient remains. Outcomes are better for tricuspid and bicuspid aortic valve morphologies with unicuspid valve morphologies having the poorest response. Multiple studies have defined a successful neonatal BAV as a reduced aortic valve gradient ≤35 mm Hg with no worsening aortic valve insufficiency.38,40,41

### Transcatheter Treatment of Coarctation

Transcatheter therapies for neonatal coarctation are typically performed when definitive surgical repair is deferred because of patient comorbidities. The most common reason for intervention is a patient presenting in shock because of ductal closure in whom the ductus arteriosus cannot be opened or cannot be opened enough to allow for effective resuscitation and resolution of end organ dysfunction.42 In these situations, the coarctation is treated with balloon angioplasty during which a balloon is inflated across the lesion to provide temporary relief of the obstruction and resuscitation of end organs until eventual surgical correction can be performed. The most common acute complication associated with balloon angioplasty is femoral arterial injury. Long-term complications of balloon coarctation angioplasty that does not subsequently need surgical repair include pseudoaneurysm formation and recurrent coarctation. Recurrent coarctation of the aorta following surgery is often treated in the catheterization laboratory with balloon angioplasty and/or implantation of a stent.43,44 Implantation of a stent across a neonatal coarctation lesion is rarely

The use of primary stenting in the neonatal period is limited by the size of the introducer sheath required to implant the stent via the femoral artery. This limitation can be overcome by using a hybrid surgical approach via a cut-down on the carotid artery or percutaneously via direct carotid access. Work is currently underway to develop bioresorbable stents that could be implanted in the neonatal period, dissolve over a period of 6 to 18 months, and then be stented again with larger stents, potentially obviating the need for surgical repair.45

### Operative Strategies for Left-Heart Obstructive Lesions Surgical Aortic Valve Repair

Transcatheter balloon valvuloplasty is considered the primary treatment strategy among neonates with isolated valvar aortic stenosis,46,47 with surgical aortic valve repair reserved for patients with moderate or worse aortic insufficiency, concomitant cardiac defects, recurrent aortic stenosis, or failed transcatheter intervention.21 However, primary surgical valvuloplasty is gaining favor at some centers with the belief that it may provide a more durable long-term outcome when compared to catheter-based interventions.48–51 When looking at outcomes, early mortality is comparable between surgical and transcatheter interventions, but with morbidity being less for the transcatheter method. It is generally accepted that balloon valvuloplasty results in a greater decrease in aortic valve gradient, but an increased risk of aortic insufficiency compared to surgical valvotomy.47 However, the 10-year event-free survival is higher after surgery compared to transcatheter valvuloplasty. This suggests the risk of aortic valve re-intervention may be decreased if a primary surgical approach is used.34,49,50

Surgical aortic valve repair is performed via a median sternotomy on cardiopulmonary bypass with aortic crossclamping, allowing direct visualization of the aortic valve. In the newborn with isolated aortic valve stenosis, the most common anatomic construct is a bicuspid or unicuspid valve with fused commissures. In this setting, surgical valvotomy, consisting of a controlled commissurotomy, can effectively increase the valve orifice without significant insufficiency. Additional leaflet debulking, including excision of myxomatous nodularities and shaving or thinning of thickened dysplastic leaflets, may help increase the effective valve orifice area.34

### Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement

For neonates with aortic valves that cannot be repaired, or in infants with combined valvar and subvalvar obstruction, aortic valve replacement is necessary. Unfortunately, replacement options are limited and suboptimal, because there are no bioprosthetic valves manufactured small enough to fit a neonate. If a small enough valve existed, it would quickly become flow restricting without the ability to keep pace

with the rapid somatic growth of an infant. For these neonates, the entire aortic root and valve need to be replaced, either with a cryopreserved human cadaveric homograft or the patient’s own pulmonary valve as an autograft (Ross procedure). The disadvantage of a homograft includes the known risk of early calcification especially in the neonate, leading to valve dysfunction, the lack of growth potential, and the increased risk of repeat coronary artery reimplantation. Therefore the Ross procedure has become the aortic valve/root replacement option of choice in neonates.52,53 The principles of the operation include reconstructing the LVOT and replacing the aortic valve with the child’s own living tissue—a pulmonary root autograft (rim of right ventricular muscle, valve, and the main pulmonary artery), reimplantation of the coronary arteries, and replacement of the pulmonary valve with a pulmonary valve homograft. In theory, this operation exchanges aortic valve disease for pulmonary valve disease with the reasoning that repeat interventions on the aortic valve carry increasing risk, whereas repeat interventions on the pulmonary valve are not only less frequent but also less risky.

### Surgical Repair of Coarctation

Significant neonatal coarctation can present as a discrete “juxtaductal” lesion, or as long segment, diffuse tubular hypoplasia. Barring additional intracardiac pathology, the size of the proximal arch typically dictates the surgical approach. If the proximal arch is an adequate size, coarctation repair can be conducted though a thoracotomy approach. Alternatively, if the proximal arch is significantly hypoplastic, arch reconstruction via a median sternotomy is necessary. Although the type of surgical approach differs between discrete coarctation and diffuse hypoplasia (described below), in both instances neonatal surgery is indicated in situations of ductal dependency or significant systolic blood pressure gradient measured between upper and lower extremities. Similarly, the diagnosis of IAA is an indication for neonatal repair.

A juxtaductal coarctation manifests as a discrete area of aortic narrowing at the junction of the ductus arteriosus to the aortic isthmus. It occurs within the first few days or weeks of life as the constrictive process that normally closes the PDA extends into the adjacent aortic tissue, leading to the clinical manifestations previously described. In this setting, the typical operation is a coarctectomy and extended end-to-end aortic anastomosis. This operation is performed via a thoracotomy without cardiopulmonary bypass. The principles of the operation include division of the PDA, complete resection of the coarctation segment of the aorta and any adjacent ductal tissue (coarctectomy), and mobilization of the proximal and distal segments of the aorta. Subsequently, the proximal incision is extended onto the underside of the aortic arch to the level of the proximal arch and the distal incision is extended posteriorly down the descending aorta. This allows for a large, tension-free anastomosis to be created between the descending aorta and

the proximal aortic arch—hence the term extended endto-end anastomosis. The benefits of this operation include complete relief of obstruction and durable repair that can grow with the patient at very low risk. The potential downsides of the operation include the inability to address any transverse aortic arch hypoplasia as well as a circumferential aortic suture line that may develop resistant scar tissue, leading to recurrent stenosis at this site.

Coarctation with associated arch hypoplasia and IAA require a significantly more invasive operation than isolated coarctation. The operation is performed via a median sternotomy on cardiopulmonary bypass, to allow complete mobilization of the aortic arch and proximal descending aorta. Additionally, deep hypothermia with antegrade cerebral perfusion is required for arch reconstruction. The typical reconstruction for IAA is an arch advancement operation. After ligation and resection of the PDA, the distal aorta is mobilized and anastomosed to the underside of the proximal arch as it transitions into the ascending aorta. A similar arch advancement technique can be performed for patients with diffuse arch hypoplasia. An alternative strategy is patch augmentation of the aortic arch. This involves division of the PDA, resection of ductal tissue, and patching the undersurface of the aortic arch from distal ascending aorta to mid-descending thoracic aorta. Patch augmentation leaves a posterior wall of native aortic tissue that allows growth of the reconstructed aorta.

### Admixture Lesions

Admixture lesions (see Table 79.1) are congenital heart defects in which blood from the systemic and pulmonary veins mix within the heart via a single or multiple defects (predominantly at the atrial level). The obligate mixing of systemic venous return with pulmonary venous return make admixture lesions a form of cyanotic heart disease. However, the degree of cyanosis is variable and can range from very mild desaturation undetectable on clinical exam, to clinically significant desaturation resulting in visible cyanosis. As blood is completely mixed within the heart, arterial saturation is dependent on the size of the intracardiac shunt, amount of PBF, and the presence of preferential streaming of saturated or desaturated blood to the aorta. Variations in the size and location of the outflow tracts determine where the “mixed” blood is ejected. Admixture lesions occur in single ventricle defects (e.g., tricuspid atresia and HLHS), and biventricular defects (e.g., total anomalous systemic venous return and truncus arteriosus). As such, there is no uniform management approach for admixture lesions and the specific anatomy and physiology dictate the optimal intervention. However, there are some basic principles that can be applied in the management of these neonates.

Patients with admixture lesions and unrestricted PBF develop pulmonary overcirculation, which can result in respiratory distress/failure, difficulty feeding, failure to thrive, and potentially necrotizing enterocolitis. If left unabated, excessive PBF can lead to changes in the pulmonary

arterioles, causing irreversible elevation of the pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR). This is of particular importance for single ventricle patients because elevated PVR can make the patient ineligible for eventual Fontan palliation. To prevent these problems from developing, patients with admixture lesions and excessive PBF require interventions to limit or control the amount of flow to the lungs, often as part of a series of staged palliation surgeries for functional single ventricle anatomy and physiology. Alternatively, patients with a restrictive or absent atrial communication may have diminished cardiac output, pulmonary venous congestion, and/or progressive cyanosis because complete atrial mixing is required for these conditions to be compatible with life. If the atrial communication is absent or inadequate, then creation or enlargement of the atrial communication is necessary for survival. Pulmonary artery banding (PAB) as a method to restrict PBF and methods to increase mixing at the atrial level will be discussed in the sections below. In addition, interventional, surgical, and hybrid approaches to some of the admixture lesions that are commonly performed during the neonatal period will be discussed.

### Restricting Pulmonary Blood Flow: Pulmonary Artery Banding

PAB to limit PBF has been used for decades as a palliative approach to children with large left-to-right shunts and single ventricle defects with pulmonary overcirculation. However, as outcomes for primary repair have improved over recent years, the tendency to palliate neonates with PABs has decreased and more infants are undergoing complete repair early on. Nevertheless, PAB to restrict PBF before complete repair remains the optimal strategy in certain situations. The most common indication for PAB is as the first-stage procedure in the management of certain single ventricle physiologies, such as tricuspid atresia or double-inlet left ventricle. Other indications include anatomic defects that continue to carry a higher risk of suboptimal early repair, such as multiple apical VSDs, or patients with otherwise repairable anomalies but significant associated comorbidities, such as prematurity or intracerebral hemorrhage. In these situations, a pulmonary artery band can be an effective palliative technique to control PBF.

The procedure can be performed via a thoracotomy but is most often performed through a midline sternotomy, and without the need for a cardiopulmonary bypass. Technical aspects include creating a space between the aorta and the main pulmonary artery through which a nondistensible band of prosthetic material is passed as a ring around the main pulmonary artery. The band is located between the valve and the origin of the branch pulmonary arteries. The band is then tightened to the desired effect again based on the underlying anatomy, physiology, and planned next stage. In general, the goals of a pulmonary artery band are to improve the balance of systemic to pulmonary artery circulation and to protect the distal pulmonary vasculature from unrestricted pressure and flow. Achievement of balanced

In patients without a main pulmonary artery, such as truncus arteriosus, and those in which complete neonatal repair is not possible, separate banding of the left and right branch pulmonary arteries is possible. Recovery from PAB is short and uncomplicated, and patients are often easier to manage once the degree of PBF is appropriately restricted.

### Procedures to Increase Mixing of Blood at the Atrial Level

Admixture lesions and patients with transposition physiology are dependent on adequate intracardiac mixing of blood at the atrial level to both maintain adequate oxygen saturations and allow adequate cardiac output. Although other levels of mixing might be present (e.g., VSD or PDA), adequate atrial-level mixing of systemic and pulmonary venous blood is the most effective in almost all situations. When inadequate mixing occurs in patients with admixture lesions, disproportionate streaming of the deoxygenated blood to the systemic circulation results in severe cyanosis. To demonstrate this, consider HLHS, in which the left-sided structures are not adequate to support a full cardiac output. To provide the systemic circulation with adequate quantities of oxygenated blood, there must be unrestricted flow from the left atrium to the aorta (left atrium→right atrium→right ventricle→pulmonary artery→ductus arteriosus→aorta). Thus unrestricted atrial communication is necessary for both adequate oxygenation and maintenance of cardiac output. Furthermore, without unrestrictive atrial communication, left atrial hypertension develops because of the inability of pulmonary venous return to unload. This leads to pulmonary venous hypertension and subsequent pulmonary edema with pulmonary artery hypertension. This can be devastating for patients with single ventricle admixture lesions. ### Balloon Atrial Septostomy

Balloon atrial septostomy (BAS) is the standard method for enlarging an existing atrial communication when there is inadequate mixing. The most common indication is D-TGA with restrictive atrial septum, which occurs in one-third of neonates with this condition.54 The BAS procedure has been performed for more than 50 years and remains the standard approach in most cases because of the relative safety and efficacy when performed by experienced operators.

The standard BAS procedure can be done in either the catheterization laboratory or bedside in the neonatal intensive care unit. Procedural guidance is typically provided by fluoroscopy, echocardiography, or a combination of both. Performing the procedure in the catheterization laboratory allows additional procedures to be performed (i.e., coronary angiography) and allows easy access to additional catheterization equipment should the procedure be technically difficult. Bedside BAS under echocardiographic guidance has been shown to be a safe and more cost-effective approach in patients with D-TGA.55 The procedure can be performed via femoral venous access or by taking over the existing umbilical vein catheter, which can then be replaced following the procedure. If hypoxemia persists before, during, or even after a successful BAS, the treatment team should have a low threshold to start inhaled nitric oxide to help decrease PVR and increase PBF, which typically results in improved systemic oxygenation.

### Other Atrial Septostomy Techniques

As discussed above, BAS may not be effective if the atrial septum is thick or intact. If there is an existing communication between the atria, this can be crossed and made larger using transcatheter interventions. If no atrial communication exists, the atrial septum may be crossed using the radiofrequency wire (described in the RVOT perforation section), a radioperforation transseptal needle, or with a standard transseptal needle.56–58 Once the thick or intact septum is perforated, a guidewire can then be passed through the perforation and positioned into a left-sided pulmonary

Atrial Septal Stenting

In very small patients with thick and/or intact atrial septa, an atrial communication is best created by atrial septal stenting.58 After perforating, crossing the atrial septum, and gaining stable wire position, a long sheath is passed into the left atrium. A premounted stent (typically 6–8 mm in diameter) is advanced through the delivery sheath and over the guidewire until half of it is seen in the left atrium using fluoroscopy and transesophageal echocardiography guidance. The delivery sheath is slowly retracted, and the stent positioning is adjusted to center the stent on the atrial septum. Once the stent positioning is confirmed, the stent is deployed (Fig. 79.6A–C). Adequacy of stent size is evaluated by echocardiogram, with particular attention given to the decrease in mean Doppler gradient across the septum. The implanted stent is resected with the atrial septectomy procedure during a subsequent planned surgical operation.

### Atrial Septectomy

In newborns that are not candidates for percutaneous transcatheter strategies to open the atrial septum, a surgical atrial septectomy can be performed. The operation is performed through a median sternotomy on cardiopulmonary bypass. The goal of the operation is complete excision of the atrial septum creating a reliable and durable opening. Surgical atrial septectomy in the neonate is almost exclusively performed on patients with single ventricle anatomy and physiology.57

### Specific Admixture Lesions Tricuspid Atresia

Tricuspid atresia is a single ventricle lesion in which there is an absent tricuspid valve with a subsequent lack of direct communication between the right atrium and RV. The result is that all systemic venous return to the right atrium must pass through an ASD as an obligate right-to-left shunt before being delivered to the systemic LV. There is variable RV hypoplasia determined by the presence and size of a VSD; however, in all cases, the RV is rudimentary and is not sufficient to support biventricular physiology.

Tricuspid atresia has traditionally been classified based on the relationship of the great arteries, presence of a VSD, and the amount of PBF. Type I tricuspid atresia has normally related great vessels (i.e., the pulmonary artery arises from the rudimentary RV and aorta arises from the LV) and accounts for ∼70% of all cases. Type I is further subdivided into Ia: no VSD and pulmonary atresia, Ib: small VSD with pulmonary stenosis, and Ic: large VSD and no pulmonary

stenosis. Type II tricuspid atresia is associated with D-TGA (i.e., the aorta arises from the rudimentary RV and pulmonary artery arises from the LV) and accounts for ∼25% of cases. Similarly, type II tricuspid atresia is subdivided into three categories, IIa: no VSD and pulmonary atresia, IIb: VSD with pulmonary or subpulmonary stenosis, and IIc: VSD with no pulmonary stenosis. Type III tricuspid atresia is associated with L-transposition of the great arteries, only accounts for ∼5% of cases, and is outside the scope of this chapter.59

Pulmonary blood flow, and thus clinical presentation and treatment strategy, is determined by the size of the VSD, relationship of the great arteries, and presence of pulmonary valve atresia or stenosis. For example, neonates with diminished PBF (type Ia, IIa) will become severely cyanotic with ductal closure. For these patients, initial intervention is either an mBTT shunt or PDA stent. At the other end of the spectrum are neonates with excessive PBF (types Ic, IIc). These patients typically present with signs of CHF secondary to pulmonary overcirculation and require a pulmonary artery band for initial palliation. In the middle are neonates with type Ib and IIb who often have a balanced circulation. These patients may not need any intervention before undergoing their bidirectional cavopulmonary connection (i.e., Glenn procedure).

### Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome

HLHS comprises a spectrum of congenital heart lesions in which the LV is underdeveloped and not able to support the systemic circulation. Although there are a number of anatomic variants that fall within the spectrum of HLHS, the primary driver of pathophysiology is that the RV must be used to pump blood to the systemic circulation and blood flow to the pulmonary circulation must be achieved by another route. As mentioned above, systemic cardiac output is dependent on adequate atrial level mixing and a widely PDA. The latter is initially achieved by starting an infusion of PGE1. If the atrial communication is not large enough, a BAS can be performed. However, once the neonate is stabilized and receiving nutritional support, the treatment team will then decide which stage 1 palliation approach the patient will receive.

Most patients with HLHS undergo a series of staged palliative operations, ultimately culminating with the Fontan operation. However, primary cardiac transplantation or transplant after any stage remains an option for some children with HLHS. The objectives for any stage 1 palliative intervention for HLHS are to achieve (1) unobstructed systemic outflow, (2) unrestricted pulmonary venous egress, (3) balanced PBF, and (4) unobstructed coronary artery perfusion.60

The basic principles of the Norwood operation include (1) amalgamating the ascending aorta and proximal pulmonary artery (Damus-Kaye-Stansel [DKS] anastomosis) along with aortic arch reconstruction—these steps provide unobstructed systemic outflow, (2) performing an atrial septectomy to provide unimpeded pulmonary venous blood

### Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Return

Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR) is an embryologic failure of fusion of the confluence of the

pulmonary veins to the adjacent left atrium. The pulmonary venous return finds its way back to the right atrium via a communicating vein in one of four ways (1) supracardiac—is the most common, whereby the confluence of the pulmonary veins drain into an ascending vertical vein that connects to the innominate vein then the superior vena cava; (2) infracardiac—has a descending vertical vein draining into the portal vein or inferior vena cava; (3) cardiac—has a direct communication from the confluence to the coronary sinus; and (4) mixed—is the least common and has some combination of the previous three. In TAPVR all systemic venous and pulmonary venous return is via the right atrium. As such, TAPVR is an admixture lesion, where mixing takes place in the right atrium and cardiac output is dependent on the presence of a right-to-left shunt at the atrial level.

In unobstructed TAPVR with an unrestrictive ASD, cyanosis is usually mild and complete repair can wait until 3 to 6 months of age. Newborns with obstructed TAPVR present with both profound cyanosis and cardiogenic shock. Obstruction of pulmonary venous return most commonly occurs in patients with infracardiac TAPVR, in which the descending vertical vein narrows as it crosses the diaphragm before connecting to the IVC. Another potential obstruction can occur within the liver when the vertical vein empties into the portal venous system. In this anatomic situation, when the ductus venosus closes, egress of blood into the hepatic veins and right atrium becomes restrictive and both portal and pulmonary venous congestion develop. Both obstruction of the vertical vein and a closing ductus venosus can be treated by endovascular stenting to provide temporary relief of the obstruction if discovered early enough, allowing time for the patient to be stabilized before surgery.98 However, if obstruction occurs before the diagnosis is made or if the anatomy is not amenable to interventional therapies, then these newborns will become critically ill and often end up on extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Once on ECMO, the diagnosis of TAPVR is more difficult to make by echocardiography. Therefore the medical teams must maintain a high index of suspicion for TAPVR, and advanced imaging with cardiac CT or cardiac catheterization is sometimes necessary to confirm the diagnosis.

Surgical repair of TAPVR is done via a median sternotomy on cardiopulmonary bypass. The principles of the operation include direct anastomosis of the anterior wall of the confluence of the pulmonary veins to the posterior wall of the adjacent left atrium as well as ligation of the communicating vein. Typically, a PFO or small ASD is left to help the management of potential postoperative pulmonary hypertensive events.

Alternatively, the branch pulmonary arteries may arise independently with separate orifices, either spaced close together from the posterior aspect of the common trunk (type II) or widely spaced and arising from the lateral aspect of the common trunk (type III).

Almost all cases of truncus are associated with an unrestrictive, subarterial VSD that results from a deficiency in the formation of the infundibular septum. Rather than two separate semilunar valves, a single truncal valve forms from the fusion of the aortic and pulmonary valves because of a lack in development of the conotruncal septum. The truncal valve commonly has three or four leaflets but may have as few as two or as many as six leaflets.

The common truncal valve overrides the VSD, and thus allows blood from the RV and LV to pass through the VSD into the common arterial trunk, where the blood mixes before circulating to the pulmonary, systemic, and coronary arterial systems. As such, truncus arteriosus is an admixture lesion and results in at least mild cyanosis. The distribution of blood flow, and thus oxygen saturation, is determined by the systemic vascular resistance (SVR) and PVR. Early after birth, the PVR is still relatively elevated and limits excessive PBF, resulting in systemic oxygen saturations between 75% and 85%. As PVR drops after birth, PBF increases, and oxygen saturations can increase to as high as the low 90s%. The pulmonary arterial diastolic runoff results in excessive PBF and retrograde flow in the abdominal aorta. This combination leads to severe overcirculation and diastolic steal from coronary and renal vasculature. Surgical repair is indicated relatively early to avoid these complications.

The operation is performed through a median sternotomy on cardiopulmonary bypass, and complete repair of truncus arteriosus involves separating the pulmonary arteries from the common arterial trunk, diverting blood from the LV through the truncal valve by closing the VSD, establishing RV-PA continuity with a valved conduit, and truncal valve repair, if necessary. Survival after neonatal truncal valve repair has significantly improved in recent years, with a 1-year survival of greater than 90%. The long-term prognosis is largely dependent on the durability of the truncal valve. Truncal valve insufficiency is both a risk factor for death after the initial operation and a risk factor for increased reintervention.67

### Parallel Circulation

### Transposition of the Great Arteries

Simple transposition of the great arteries, also termed dextro or D-TGA, is one of the most common causes of newborn cyanosis.21,68 Despite the relatively common prevalence, D-TGA is diagnosed prenatally in less than 50% of patients.68 D-TGA is defined by atrioventricular concordance with ventriculoarterial discordance. That is,

the aorta arises anteriorly from the morphologic RV and the pulmonary artery arises posteriorly from the morphologic LV. In contrast to the normal in-series circulation, D-TGA anatomy results in a parallel circulation, whereby deoxygenated systemic venous return is recirculated from the RV to the aorta and systemic circulation. Conversely, oxygenated blood returning from the lungs is recirculated from the LV to the pulmonary artery and to the pulmonary circulation. Without a source of mixing between the pulmonary and systemic circulations, there is inadequate tissue oxygen delivery. The result is profound desaturation, tissue hypoxia, metabolic acidosis, and ultimately cardiovascular collapse. Mixing between oxygenated and deoxygenated blood is dependent on a communication between the two parallel circulations and can take place at the level of the great arteries (PDA), atrial level (ASD), or ventricular level (VSD). Although the existence of the PDA and VSD may temporize the patient in the postnatal period, the presence of adequate atrial level mixing is the most consequential to ensuring adequate systemic oxygenation.

Management of neonates with D-TGA has become fairly standardized in the current era. Initial management is aimed at medical stabilization, correction of metabolic derangements, respiratory support, and vasoactive therapies, if necessary. Patients should be started on PGE1 infusion to maintain ductal patency regardless of the status of other intracardiac shunts until the status of the atrial level shunt is confirmed. If there is any concern that the atrial communication is not adequate at that moment or will not remain adequate for the duration until definitive surgery can be performed, then neonates with D-TGA should undergo a BAS. Once an adequate atrial communication is confirmed or created following BAS, it is reasonable to attempt to wean the PGE1 infusion and start enteral feeds before surgical repair. However, any change in clinical status should prompt rapid re-initiation of PGE1 and cessation of feeding.

The arterial switch operation (ASO) is the standard surgery offered to patients with D-TGA and has excellent early survival as well as long-term outcomes.21,68 The ASO is typically performed during the first week of life after stabilization after birth and the initial fall in PVR (48–72 hours). The operation is performed via a median sternotomy and on cardiopulmonary bypass. After initial dissection and standard cardioplegic arrest, the aorta is transected and the coronary ostia are mobilized from the aorta as coronary “buttons.” These coronary buttons include native aortic wall tissue to allow coronary reimplantation in the neo-aorta. Next, the main pulmonary artery is transected and the coronary buttons are translocated to the pulmonary root—which becomes the neo-aorta. Subsequently, the main pulmonary artery is brought anterior to the aorta (LeCompte maneuver) and aortic continuity is reestablished by direct anastomosis between the ascending aorta and neo-aortic root. Finally, the neo-pulmonary root is reconstructed with the autologous pericardium, pulmonary artery continuity is created by anastomosing the main pulmonary artery to the reconstructed neo-pulmonary root, and the ASD is closed.

### Miscellaneous Procedures

Some heart conditions or combinations of conditions cannot be easily placed into one of the major physiologic groups detailed above or deserve special attention on their own. The following section contains miscellaneous procedures that do not fall into one of the rubrics above. A list of commonly performed surgeries in the current era is found in Table 79.4.

### Pulmonary Artery Stenosis

Isolated branch pulmonary artery stenosis outside of the commonly encountered peripheral pulmonic stenosis (PPS) is rarely observed in the neonatal period. The most common cause is due to constriction of the proximal left pulmonary artery following ductus arteriosus closure. In severe cases, the left pulmonary artery can become completely obstructed or isolated if not treated early. Moderate lesions can typically be treated via balloon angioplasty, but severe lesions often require stent implantation for a sustained result. Although there are stents which can be placed in the neonate, many of them cannot be dilated to the size of an adult pulmonary artery. As a result, these stents are placed as a palliative step when future surgical intervention is anticipated. At the time of surgical intervention, these small stents can either be surgically removed or transected, allowing for enlargement of the vessel. Studies have demonstrated that some of these stents may be fractured with high-pressure balloons or “unzipped,” but this is highly dependent on the type of stent used.69,70 Similar to neonatal stenting of aortic coarctation, bioresorbable stents may prove to be a useful therapeutic option in this patient population.71

### Treatment of Patent Ductus Arteriosus (see also Chapter 75)

A PDA is commonly encountered in premature neonates. Hemodynamically significant PDAs are encountered more commonly the more gestationally premature the infant is at the time of birth. Large PDAs can result in significant left-to-right shunting, with medical consequences including respiratory failure, renal insufficiency, and feeding intolerance. The management of the hemodynamically significant PDA in the neonatal period, particularly the premature and extremely premature population, is controversial and very institutional and provider dependent. Long-standing methods for PDA closure include medical therapy with prostaglandin inhibitors and surgical ligation. Medical closure of PDA is covered extensively in other chapters, so it will not be addressed in this section. Surgical closure has been the gold standard for over 60 years but has recently fallen out of favor because of short- and long-term data showing poorer outcomes with those premature infants who received ligation. When necessary, PDA ligation is performed via posterolateral thoracotomy, and typically a clip is placed on the PDA, versus suture ligation and division. Surgical PDA

ligation is essentially 100% effective and is typically performed safely when done by experienced operators. However, the procedure is not without risk, and complications include vocal cord paralysis, pneumothorax, diaphragm paralysis, and post-ligation cardiac syndrome. Much of the morbidity and mortality of PDA surgical ligation are related to the preoperative clinical status of the neonate, and therefore the timing of when patients are referred for surgical ligation is crucial.

Over the past 10 years, many institutions have started pursuing transcatheter approaches for neonatal PDA closure using off-label devices approved for other vascular occlusion indications. Transcatheter PDA closure in older infants and children with stainless steel coils and nitinolbased devices has been performed since the 1970s with great success. As a result, PDA surgical ligation outside of the neonatal population is almost never performed. The unique neonatal ductal anatomy and small patient size has limited the occlusion of neonatal PDAs with traditional FDA-approved devices. However, the development of smaller interventional devices and delivery catheters has now allowed for safe transcatheter occlusion of the ductus arteriosus in premature neonates.72–74 Multiple off-label devices have been used over the years, but a single device is now FDA approved for PDA closure in premature infants— the Amplatzer Piccolo Occluder (Abbott, Santa Clara, CA), which was approved in January of 2019. Because a learning curve for this procedure exists and widespread experience is still growing, a thoughtful and intentional approach by each institution must be taken so that premature PDA device closure can be performed safely and effectively.72–75 Premature PDA device closure is most safely performed with femoral venous access only and with both fluoroscopic and echocardiographic guidance, although some centers are moving to 100% echocardiographic guidance and eliminating the need for a catheterization laboratory. Although the procedure and device have been demonstrated to be safe and effective, there are adverse events associated with the procedure, notably device obstruction of the left branch pulmonary artery or descending thoracic aorta. This is usually discovered before the device is released by angiography or transthoracic echocardiogram, at which time the device can be safely removed and another size or device can be tried or the patient can be referred for surgical ligation. Further research and cumulative experience with both approved (on-label) and off-label devices are expected to demonstrate transcatheter PDA closure to be safe and effective for many premature infants.

Isolated pulmonary vein stenosis is a rare anomaly in the neonate, is associated with poor outcomes, and is commonly seen in conjunction with other defects. ### Central Line Placement

Neonates with CHD often require indwelling central venous catheters and arterial monitoring lines for prolonged periods. This is the reason there is a high prevalence of venous and arterial occlusion in the CHD population, especially in those with functional single ventricle heart conditions. The importance of obtaining umbilical venous and arterial access immediately after birth cannot be emphasized enough. Studies have shown that single ventricle patients who have umbilical venous lines placed instead of femoral lines have had significantly lower complication rate of vascular thrombosis and occlusion.80 Furthermore, these patients require multiple catheterization procedures in their lifetime, and occluded femoral veins or arteries complicate these procedures considerably and can make some future interventions impossible to perform. If nonumbilical access is required, it is our practice to use the smallest catheter necessary for medical management. Use of single lumen instead of double lumen results in less vascular occlusion. Tunneling central lines is associated with less thrombosis and a decreased rate of central line–associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI). Placement of catheters in the upper extremities or neck vessels is not recommended in single ventricle patients before the Fontan operation. If catheters are necessary in these positions, anticoagulation should be administered immediately after placement, and the line should be removed as soon as it is safely possible to reduce the risk of vascular stenosis or occlusion. Finally, when other alternative sites of access have been exhausted, transhepatic lines can be placed in the catheterization laboratory and have been shown to be a feasible and safe alternative in infants with otherwise limited access.81

### Pericardiocentesis

Pericardiocentesis or pericardial drain placement can be safely performed in the neonate. The procedure is typically guided by transthoracic echocardiogram but can be performed by landmark alone in emergency cases when the patient is suffering from cardiac tamponade. There are multiple causes for tamponade in the neonate, but one of the most common causes is associated with indwelling central venous catheters. It is not known whether the mechanism

of tamponade is perforation or simple diffusion across a very thin atrial wall, but analysis of the effusion often shows similar fluid composition to the infusate.82

### Fetal Cardiac Intervention

Fetal intervention (see Chapter 12) has been the subject of much interest over the past 15 years. Its use is attractive in some of the congenital cardiac defects with poor outcomes secondary to valvar obstructions, which can lead to ventricular hypoplasia. There are currently three catheterbased interventions that have been performed in fetuses with CHD: balloon valvuloplasty in aortic valve stenosis (thought to lead to HLHS), balloon valvuloplasty in pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum (with impending hypoplastic right ventricle), and ASD creation or enlargement in HLHS with restrictive atrial septum. Fetal cardiac interventions are not performed as standard of care at all heart centers and are typically only performed at centers with experienced teams made up of high-risk obstetrics (maternal-fetal medicine), fetal cardiology, and interventional cardiology. As such, it is common for centers that do not offer the procedure to refer patients to one of the experienced centers. There is a noninsignificant risk to the fetus and potentially the mother, so candidates for fetal cardiac intervention must be carefully screened and vetted before the decision to proceed is made. Accurate diagnosis must be made early enough in gestation to allow for potential reversal of disease progression following the intervention. Lastly, information regarding the natural history of these defects is not completely understood, making it difficult to predict which fetus will develop ventricular hypoplasia and should undergo these high-risk fetal interventions.83 The mortality associated with these procedures is improving as experience is gained. Nevertheless, it is still not clear-cut that early fetal intervention will consistently alter disease progression beyond the watchful waiting and treating the high-risk neonate with established strategies.84

### Shunt Obstruction

One of the most feared complications of systemic to pulmonary artery shunts is complete or near-complete shunt occlusion in patients solely dependent on the shunt for pulmonary blood flow. When severe cyanosis develops secondary to shunt obstruction, the two treatment strategies include surgical revision or transcatheter intervention. If possible, this is best dealt with in the catheterization laboratory to avoid another midline sternotomy. In the event of complete occlusion, patients sometimes need to be stabilized on ECMO to provide adequate oxygenation and then can be transported to the catheterization laboratory. Transcatheter interventions include simple balloon dilation, thrombus evacuation, or stent implantation within the shunt (Fig. 79.8A–B).85 Interventions for modified Blalock-Taussig shunt obstructions are usually approached from the femoral artery. RV-PA (Sano) shunts are typically approached from the femoral vein.86 For

### Neonatal Heart Transplantation

Heart transplantation in the neonate continues to be reserved for those babies with congenital cardiac anomalies or cardiomyopathies that are not amenable to repair. Even high-risk single ventricle conditions such as HLHS are rarely treated primarily with heart transplantation. The reasons for this are many, as highlighted in the 2017 report of the International Society for Heart and Lung Transplantation.87 The number of infant (<1 year old) heart transplantations performed in North America and Europe combined has been stable for years at only about 120 per year. Not only is this a reflection of the limited indications for transplantation, but more importantly it reflects the severely limited donor pool of this rare resource. Patient survival is about 75% at 8 years and 50% at 22 years, which is somewhat better than reported results for older children.88 Reasons for the improved survival rate include the immaturity of the immune system leading to decreased antibody-mediated rejection. In addition, neonatal transplant patients have been shown to have less graft vasculopathy89 and require less immune suppression.90 However, there are the lifelong challenges with immunosuppression and the balance of rejection and infection that lead to a continuous risk hazard of significant morbidities. The continuous risk of developing a malignancy is 10% at 10 years, primarily lymphomas as well as the continuous risk of life-threatening infections. The

continuous risk of graft failure secondary to cardiac allograft vasculopathy is 50% at 15 years. Unfortunately, despite the ability to perform re-transplantations for graft failure, both patient and graft survival is less compared to primary transplantation. Therefore, when considering a lifelong management strategy for newborn CHD, transplantation needs to be reserved for those without other options. Nonetheless, in neonates that require transplantation, there are ongoing efforts to expand the donor supply by considering donation from anencephalic donors as well as those with marginal function and prolonged ischemic time. Also, the ability to successfully perform ABO-incompatible heart transplantation is unique in the neonate by taking advantage of their somewhat naïve immunologic response to antigens.91 A list of relative and absolute contraindications to infant cardiac transplantation is shown in Table 79.5.

There is no limit to how long PGE1 can be infused, and sometimes it is necessary to maintain an infant on PGE1 for prolonged periods, especially for those infants with significant medical comorbidities or extreme prematurity.
