which is documented by two to three CBCs per week for 6 weeks, to cycle neutrophil counts approximately every 21 days plus or minus 3 days. Autosomal dominant ELA2 mutations are the most common and severe. Sporadic inheritance is also described. Supportive care for fevers and infections and possible use of G-CSF to modulate the nadir are common management strategies.6

Congenital Neutropenia With Extra Hematopoietic Abnormalities

The most common congenital neutropenias with extra hematopoietic defects in neutropenia registries are HAX-1 mutations, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS), and the glucose-6-phosphatase complex disorders. Many rare congenital neutropenia syndromes have been described clinically, and some have associated genetic defects identified. Deficits in neutrophil function as well as a myriad of dysmorphic defects are associated with these syndromes, although it is important to realize that not all defects are present in the neonatal period and not all defects appear in a particular patient. The reader is referred to an excellent review of congenital neutropenia by Donadieu and co-workers for more details.6

Shwachman-Diamond Syndrome. Once believed rare, but now accounting for about one-fourth of patients in neutropenia registries, SDS is characterized by pancreatic exocrine dysfunction, failure to thrive, neutropenia of varying degrees, neutrophil chemotactic dysfunction, and many other dysmorphic features presenting at various times over the life of the patient. Bony abnormalities, rash, cytopenias, mental retardation, and failure to thrive are among the most common features. SDS is often included as part of the differential diagnoses with Pearson syndrome and cystic fibrosis. Hematologic manifestations include intermittent neutropenia, cytopenias, aplastic anemia, myelodysplastic syndrome (mutations in chromosome 7), and leukemic transformation. Autosomal recessive inheritance is described, often with defects in the SBDS gene on 7q11 with resultant defect in ribosomal function affecting multiple organ systems.26 Diagnostic testing may include radiographic demonstration of skeletal abnormalities, evidence of pancreatic insufficiency (decreased fecal elastase and low serum trypsinogen), as well as hematologic changes. Finding of typical mutation is diagnostic. Supportive care with pancreatic enzyme replacement, G-CSF for neutropenia or severe infection, antibiotics, and antifungals are recommended. Monitoring for malignant transformation is important. HSC transplantation is indicated for severe cytopenia, myelodysplastic syndrome, or acute myeloid leukemia.23

Glucose-6-Phosphatase Complex Disorders: Glycogen

Storage Disease Type 1b and G6PC3. Hepatic glycogen can be dephosphorylated by G-6-P to produce glucose as an energy source. Two of the three proteins that comprise the G-6-P complex on the endoplasmic reticulum are associated with congenital neutropenia: the translocase SLC37A4 and the catalytic protein G6PC3. G6PC3 disorders are characterized by severe, permanent neutropenia with myeloid arrest, thin skin, genitourinary abnormalities, cardiac disease, and myopathy.6

GSD1b is characterized by hypoglycemia at birth, lactic acidemia, hepatomegaly with hepatic glycogen accumulation, Crohn-like colitis, neutropenia, and variable neutrophil dysfunction. Diagnosis is based on constellation of symptoms and genetic testing. Patients respond to G-CSF, although in GSD1b, patients may develop worsening splenomegaly. acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) has been reported in GSD1b.23

### Congenital Neutropenia With Defective Immune System

As part of the innate immune system, neutrophils participate in the development of the adaptive immune system, and there are some shared receptors and proteins among lymphocytes and neutrophils. Neutropenia may be an early presenting feature of a more global and lethal immunologic defect, with or without autoimmune phenomena. Recent publications highlight the need to consider PIDDs in the differential diagnosis when evaluating infants with neutropenia.27 Young age at presentation, failure to thrive, lymphopenia, eczema, and serious infections should be signals that a comprehensive evaluation of innate and adaptive immunity should be undertaken.

X-Linked Neutropenia/Myelodysplasia

An X-linked mutation of the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS) gene protein presents with neutropenia but without the classic WAS phenotype.

Cartilage-Hair Hypoplasia. Cartilage-hair hypoplasia is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by shortlimbed dwarfism, fine hair, hyperextensible digits, increased susceptibility to infection, lymphopenia, impaired cellular immunity, and chronic neutropenia. This autosomal recessive disease is caused by mutations in RMRP, a noncoding RNA gene involved in mitochondrial DNA replication, ribosome biogenesis, and ribosomal RNA processing.6

Dyskeratosis Congenita. Dyskeratosis congenita is characterized by neutropenia (and other cytopenias), abnormal skin pigmentation, nail dystrophy, and mucosal leukoplakia. Other features include immunodeficiency, fragile bones, tooth decay, short stature, alopecia or premature graying, gonadal hypoplasia, urethral abnormalities, pulmonary fibrosis, liver cirrhosis, esophageal strictures, mental retardation, and a predisposition to cancers of the skin, gastrointestinal tract, and other sites.

### Leukemoid Reaction

Newborns sometimes mount an exaggerated response to infection. As in older children, the circulating neutrophil count increases, and a left shift occurs (band forms, myelocytes, and metamyelocytes increase in the peripheral circulation). A significant increase in early neutrophil precursors in the peripheral blood, as well as an increase in the WBC count (generally exceeding 50,000/μL), is considered a leukemoid reaction. A normal newborn in the first 2 days of life displays neutrophilia. Immature myeloid forms and even blasts can be seen in the first day or two, and these are especially common in premature infants. A leukemoid reaction associated with severe infection in the newborn often is accompanied by neutrophil cytoplasmic vacuoles and toxic granulations. A rare, autosomal dominant hereditary neutrophilia has been described.

Down Syndrome Hematologic Abnormalities and Transient Abnormal Myelopoiesis

Hematologic abnormalities are common in Down syndrome (Table 82.3). The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends ordering a CBC for newborns with Down syndrome to screen for hematologic problems. About 10% of infants who have Down syndrome develop a transient clonal myeloproliferative disorder now called transient abnormal myelopoiesis (TAM). This process also sometimes occurs in a phenotypically normal child with trisomy 21 mosaicism, including an isolated clone of trisomy 21 bone marrow cells. TAM is characterized by a leukoerythroblastic picture with megakaryoblasts in the peripheral blood, variable thrombocytopenia, and hepatosplenomegaly.28 Abnormalities of all three hematopoietic cell lineages have been described. ### Adhesion Disorders: Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency Types I and II

Leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD) includes a rare group of autosomal recessive disorders characterized by persistent leukocytosis, delayed separation of the umbilical cord, and recurrent infections. LAD-I is characterized by the impairment of the respiratory burst generation of complementopsonized microorganisms and is associated with defects in neutrophil adhesion and chemotaxis (Fig. 82.2). The clinical picture varies depending on the relative deficiency of CD18, the β2 subunit of integrin. LAD should be suspected in any infant who has unusually severe bacterial infections accompanied by normal to increased blood leukocyte counts. There is a striking absence of pus at the site of infection because neutrophils do not migrate from the vasculature to sites of inflammation within tissues. Diagnosis is made by flow cytometry analysis demonstrating a deficiency of CD18 or CD11b/CD18. Carriers can be identified by the expression of about 50% of normal CD18 on circulating neutrophils. Chediak-Higashi Syndrome and Griscelli Syndrome Type 2

Chediak-Higashi syndrome, caused by a defective CHS1 gene, is an autosomal recessive syndrome featuring oculocutaneous albinism, nystagmus, photophobia, neurodegeneration, neutropenia, giant red inclusions in leukocytes, natural killer (NK) cell dysfunction, recurrent infection, and progression to lymphoproliferative and hemophagocytic disorders. Griscelli syndrome type 2 shares many of these features but lacks the leucocyte inclusions.6

### Neonatal Immune Deficiencies

It is important for neonatologists to understand primary immune deficiencies, as failure to recognize them early can result in delayed treatment and worse outcomes for these patients. Severe combined immune deficiency (SCID) newborn screen (NBS) using the T-cell receptor excision circle (TREC) assay has allowed early detection of T-cell lymphopenia in newborns. By November 2018, 48 states plus Puerto Rico were screening all infants for SCID, as were an increasing number of nations and jurisdictions.36 Affected infants are reliably detected and promptly referred to centers that provide immune system restoring treatments. Bone marrow transplantation (BMT) has success rates that vary from 50% to 100%.37 Patients with SCID transplanted within the first 31⁄2 months of life have a superior outcome. Population-based screening has determined the incidence of SCID to be 1 in 65,000 births, higher than previous estimates.36 An infant with recurrent infections and an ALC less than 3000/μL should warrant immediate referral and further testing of immune system.38 Absence of a thymic shadow on x-ray is another hint of SCID. Family history is important as well. SCID patients are at risk to succumb to opportunistic life-threatening infections (bacterial, fungal, viral, and mycobacterial). They are also at risk of developing graft versus host disease (GVHD) secondary to maternally derived T cells as well as transfusions with nonirradiated blood products. IVIG has a role if B-cell function is impaired.

Primary immune deficiencies can be classified based on immune cells involved (T cells, B cells, NK cells). The

majority have an alteration in more than one cellular compartment (combined immune deficiencies). Table 82.4 summarizes the most common immune deficiencies and defects involved.37 Below is a brief review of the most recognized diseases.

### Humoral Immune Defects Transient Hypogammaglobulinemia of Infancy

This is caused by a delay in maturation of immunoglobulin production and presents with prolonged hypogammaglobulinemia but is rarely symptomatic. It resolves by 3 to 4 years of age.37

### X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia

This is the most common of the agammaglobulinemias. It is caused by pathogenic variants in the BTK gene, resulting in impaired B cells differentiation and maturation.39 These patients are protected by maternal antibodies in the first months of life. Recurrent infections with encapsulated bacteria or viruses occur later. There is a lack of IgA conjunctivitis; otitis may occur earlier. The mainstay of treatment is IVIG.37

### Hyper Immunoglobulin M Syndrome

This is caused by defects in a CD40 ligand/CD40 interaction. It results in very low levels of IgG, IgA, and IgE but normal or elevated levels of IgM. The immunoglobulin class switch is impaired. Patients can present early in infancy and have neutropenia as well as typical infections characteristic for combined immune deficiencies. BMT is treatment of choice. IVIG infusions are given as well.37

### Combined Immune Deficiencies Severe Combined Immunodeficiency

Common γ Chain Deficiency (X-Linked SCID)

This condition should be considered a pediatric emergency that is fatal if untreated. Patients present within the first few months of life with recurrent sinopulmonary and skin infections and diarrhea. The pathogens include bacterial, fungal, viral, and mycobacterial organisms. GVHD from maternally acquired T cells can occur.37 These patients sometimes present with a complete absence of functional lymphocytes. B cells are preserved, but immunoglobulin production is severely reduced, if not absent.40 X-SCID is caused by mutations in the interleukin-2 receptor gamma (IL2RG) gene. The treatment is BMT.

Adenosine Deaminase Deficiency

Adenosine deaminase deficiency is the most common autosomal recessive SCID. Lack of ADA activity allows toxic metabolites to accumulate in immune cells. ADA deficiency is responsible for a severe immunodeficiency affecting all lymphoid lineages (T–B–NK–SCID). In addition to complications listed under X-linked SCID, these patients also have ribcage anomalies and osteochondral dysplasia.37 Most patients die early in life unless treated by enzyme replacement therapy (ERT), HSCT, or gene therapy.40

### IRAK 4 Mutation

Defective expression of the interleukin-1 receptor-associated kinase 4 (IRAK-4) gene results in impaired innate immunity caused by defective IRAK-4. ### Dendritic Cell Disorders: Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis

Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH), the most common disorder of dendritic cells, is defined by accumulation of dendritic cells similar to Langerhans cells in various organs. The disease may be unifocal or multiorgan in involvement. Any organ can be affected, most commonly skeleton, skin, and pituitary. BRAF mutations have been identified in more than half of LCH cases. Diagnosis is made by biopsy of involved tissues and demonstration of Birbeck granules, as well as positivity for S-100, CD1a, and Langerin (CD207). LCH can occur in the perinatal period. The incidence of LCH in neonates is 15.3 per million41 and is more frequent in persons of Hispanic origin. ### Congenital Self-Healing Reticulohistiocytosis With Spontaneous Regression

This variant of LCH typically appears at birth or in the neonatal period as multiple crusted papular skin lesions. ### Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) is a condition characterized by persistent fever, cytopenias, splenomegaly, hypertriglyceridemia and/or hypofibrinogenemia, elevated serum ferritin, hemophagocytosis, low NK cell activity, and elevation in the soluble IL-2 receptor (sCD25/sIL-2R). HLH in the neonatal period is extremely rare. The incidence of neonatal HLH is not confirmed and may range from 1 in 50,000 to 150,000.45 Familial HLH, a form of primary HLH, is an autosomal recessive disorder that most often presents in infancy. Familial HLH has five subtypes described based on genes involved: one to five correspond to defects in HPLH1, PRF1, UNC13D, STX11, and STXBP2 genes, respectively.46 Demonstration of a genetic defect is diagnostic but often lags behind fulfillment of clinical criteria and the need to initiate treatment. Management of primary HLH consists of immunomodulatory therapy followed by HSC transplantation. SCID-associated HLH in neonates has been described. Neonates can also succumb to herpes simplex virus–associated HLH; therefore prompt initiation of acyclovir is needed.47

title: Neoplasms in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: 83 Neoplasms in the Neonate
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: The annual incidence of cancer in the first year of life, 236 per million infants, is the highest for all of childhood (<15 years of age) according to the National Cancer Institute’s Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) statistics for the years 1992–2014. This represents 10% of all childhood malignancies. The first year of life is the only period in childhood when the incidence of cancer is not higher in males than females.1,2 Neonatal tumors comprise 2% of all childhood malignancies.3 The majority of neonatal tumors are solid and can be picked up by a perinatal ultrasound. Teratoma, a germ cell tumor (GCT) presenting most often on prenatal ultrasound in the sacrococcygeal area, is the most common neoplasm in infancy but is usually surgically excised as a nonmalignant (i.e., noncancerous) tumor. Fig. 83.1 provides a graphic summary of infant cancer incidence by common types.
paragraphs.heading: Infant Cancer

paragraphs.text: In adults, cancer is thought to occur after a long interplay between environmental triggers and genetic predisposition. In infancy, especially in the neonatal period, the normal, genetically programmed protections against unregulated growth of cells fail very early. Consequently, embryonal tumors such as neuroblastoma, Wilms tumor, medulloblastoma, hepatoblastoma, and retinoblastoma are more common during this time period when compared with older ages.
paragraphs.heading: Infant Cancer

paragraphs.text: It is thought that about 10% of childhood cancers are associated with a known cancer predisposition gene.4 In neonates, cancer predisposition syndromes can manifest in three ways. First among these is the identification of a tumor that has a level of association with germline cancer predisposition genes. One example of this is adrenal cortical carcinoma, which when found in the perinatal period has a probability of association with TP53 gene mutations of up to 80%.5,6 Similarly, 100% of bilateral retinoblastomas are associated with a germline RB1 gene mutation, regardless of family history. Other tumors that occur in this period with known associations with germ line mutations include rhabdoid tumors (60% have SMARCB1 mutation), pleuropulmonary blastoma (70% have DICER1 mutation), and medulloblastoma with desmoplastic or extensive nodularity subtypes (50% have SUFU mutation).
paragraphs.heading: Infant Cancer

paragraphs.text: The second way that a cancer predisposition may manifest during infancy is through the association with an identified syndrome with developmental defects that conveys a higher risk of cancer. An example of this would be Beckwith-Wiedemann, an overgrowth syndrome presenting with hemihypertrophy, macroglossia, omphalocele, and neonatal hypoglycemia. These patients have abnormal imprinting in the 11p15 telomeric region and are at risk for hepatoblastoma, adrenal cortical carcinoma, and Wilms tumor. Similarly, children with WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary abnormalities, mental retardation) have an 11q13 deletion and carry a 50% risk for Wilms tumor in infancy. Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome is caused by the PHOX2B gene mutation, and children with this abnormality have a 3% risk of neuroblastoma during infancy. Trisomy 21, Down syndrome, has a 4% to 10% risk of transient abnormal myelopoiesis as well as a risk of acute megakaryoblastic leukemia during infancy.
paragraphs.heading: Infant Cancer

paragraphs.text: Finally, a known familial cancer predisposition syndrome may be present, either elicited through a careful family history or known from prior genetic testing, and so the practitioner should be on alert for possible tumor development. Examples of these include familial RB1 gene mutations, which manifest as retinoblastoma, TP53 mutations, or Li- Fraumeni syndrome, for which adrenal cortical carcinoma is the most common tumor of infancy, and ALK gene mutations, which are associated with familial neuroblastoma. In this setting, consultation with an experienced geneticist is crucial and may have occurred before birth or should be undertaken shortly thereafter. Unique screening protocols are available for many inherited syndromes, because each one confers a risk for distinct tumors at different developmental stages in the patient’s life.4
paragraphs.heading: Infant Cancer

paragraphs.text: Historically, the 5-year overall survival rate for all neonates affected by cancer (age <1 month) is 60.3%. Neonates with extracranial solid tumors had the highest 5-year overall survival (71.2%), followed by leukemia (39.1%) and central nervous system (CNS) tumors (15%). Except for neuroblastoma, all of the neonatal tumors are known to have significantly inferior outcomes compared with those that can be achieved in older patients.7 The inferior survival rates for similar histologic tumors are likely attributable both to differences in the tumor biology and to altered drug
paragraphs.heading: Infant Cancer

paragraphs.text: metabolism and increased toxic effects of therapy during infancy.8–10 Treatment protocols for infant cancers include elimination or reduction of radiation therapy and age- and weight-based decreases in chemotherapy doses.
paragraphs.heading: Infant Cancer

paragraphs.text: Neuroblastoma, an embryonal tumor of neural crest origin arising anywhere along the sympathetic chain, is the leading malignant tumor of the perinatal period and the most common extracranial solid tumor in childhood. About half of infant neuroblastomas are diagnosed within the first 4 months of life, with many being detected as an adrenal mass in utero. The survival of infants with neuroblastoma detected before birth is better than that of those diagnosed after birth.11 Other common sites of presentation are cervical and thoracic sympathetic ganglia. Neurologic signs and symptoms of spinal cord compression prompt urgent diagnosis and management with steroids and chemotherapy in about 20% of neonatal neuroblastomas. Many neuroblastoma tumors secrete catecholamines. Urine homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid levels are commonly used diagnostic tests. Mass infant screening programs using these urine tests in Japan, Quebec, and Europe have increased the detection of good-prognosis tumors but have failed to change the mortality rate from high-risk neuroblastoma.12,13 Familial neuroblastoma with germline mutations in PHOX2B or ALK accounts for 1% of childhood neuroblastoma.14
paragraphs.heading: Neuroblastoma

paragraphs.text: The most important prognostic variables for infant neuroblastoma are the patient’s age at diagnosis, the stage of the tumor, DNA index, and MYCN amplification. Tumor hyperdiploidy (DNA index >1) is a favorable prognostic indicator, whereas MYCN amplification is associated with a more aggressive disease.15 Infants with neuroblastoma have a better prognosis than older children, with an overall 5-year survival rate of about 88% (versus 45% for those >1 year at diagnosis). Infants with localized tumors have a 5-year survival rate of 95%. Expectant observation of babies younger than 6 months of age with small adrenal masses has reduced surgical morbidity and mortality while maintaining excellent event-free survival rates.14 Either observation or surgery, with or without
paragraphs.heading: Neuroblastoma

paragraphs.text: administration of low-dose chemotherapy, is recommended for lower-risk neuroblastoma in infants. High-dose chemotherapy with peripheral blood stem cell rescue, radiation therapy, cisretinoic acid, and immunotherapy are all established treatment modalities for infants with high-risk, MYCN-amplified disease.
paragraphs.heading: Neuroblastoma

paragraphs.text: A unique stage of neuroblastoma is stage 4S, or MS. Patients in this category must be less than 1 year of age, have a localized primary tumor with disease dissemination to skin and liver, and have less than 10% of their bone marrow involved with negative meta-iodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) uptake in bone marrow. The skin lesions that arise in infants with 4S neuroblastoma are raised and bluish in color and should be included in the differential diagnosis of the infant with a blueberry muffin rash. Stage 4S accounts for 7% to 10% of the cases of neuroblastoma.14 This subgroup of infants has the unique, poorly understood characteristic of spontaneous tumor regression in both the primary tumor and the metastatic lesions and in most settings can be observed. However, in neonates, massive hepatomegaly from rapidly progressing disease can be life threatening. Therefore, in the presence of hepatomegaly, early intervention with chemotherapy is recommended for neonates rather than using an observation approach.16,17
paragraphs.heading: Neuroblastoma

paragraphs.text: Leukemia is the second most common cancer in infancy; however, it is still rare. Infant leukemias tend to present toward the second half of the first year of life. The estimated incidence rates per 1 million infants in the United States yearly with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is 160 per million, acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is 70 per million, and juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML) is 1.2 per million.18 Neonatal or congenital leukemia, estimated to occur in 1 to 5 per million infants, is diagnosed within the first month of life and carries a particularly grave prognosis. AML is more common than ALL in neonatal leukemia. Rearrangements of the mixed lineage leukemia (MLL) gene at chromosome 11q23, MLL-r, are common in congenital and infant ALL and AML. The MLL gene has more recently been described as the histone lysine methyltransferase 2A (KMT2A) gene, discussed in later sections. Prenatal MLL-r events promote rapid development of additional mutations or “hits” resulting in early leukemia presentation. If a monozygotic twin is diagnosed with leukemia in the first year of life, intrauterine transfer of the mutation results in an almost 100% concordance for the other twin, with a brief lag time of weeks until the other twin’s leukemia diagnosis.19
paragraphs.heading: Leukemia

paragraphs.text: There are many genetic syndromes associated with increased leukemia risk. Bone marrow failure syndromes, primary and secondary immunodeficiencies, defects in DNA repair, and genetic defects impacting tumor suppressor genes are associated with leukemogenesis as well as oncogenesis (a term used to describe the development of a tumor or tumors). Down syndrome (ALL, AML), Noonan syndrome (JMML, AML), and neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1; ALL, AML, JMML) have strong associations with leukemia and are associated with early leukemia presentations.
paragraphs.heading: Leukemia

paragraphs.text: The differential diagnosis for congenital leukemia includes transient abnormal myelopoiesis of Down syndrome, leukemoid reaction, congenital infections, hypoxia or hemolysis, hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, and stage 4S neuroblastoma. Langerhans cell histiocytosis can also present in infants with pancytopenia, organomegaly, and cutaneous extramedullary hematopoiesis.
paragraphs.heading: Leukemia

paragraphs.text: A number of clinical features that are associated with a poorer prognosis are common in neonates and infants with ALL; these include large tumor cell burden (hyperleukocytosis), massive hepatosplenomegaly, involvement of the CNS, leukemic skin infiltrates (leukemia cutis), and hypogammaglobulinemia. The leukemic blasts in infant ALL often are CD10 negative, express myeloid antigens, and have cytogenetic abnormalities involving the KMT2A gene, which carries a worse prognosis. Strategies to intensify therapy have improved survival for infants with ALL, but not for the ones with KMT2A rearrangement.20 A small percentage of these leukemias are biphenotypic (i.e., they possess characteristics of both ALL and AML). Neonates experience significant toxicities from both chemotherapy and CNS irradiation, which may translate into significant late effects that limit quality of life in survivors. The especially poor prognosis for infant ALL is owing to the high incidence of bone marrow and extramedullary relapse and the difficulty in treating relapsed disease. Infants less than 90 days of age at diagnosis have worse outcomes.20 Progressively more intensive chemotherapeutic regimens and bone marrow transplantation have been used in these patients, but the event-free survival rate at 5 years is only in the 30% range.19 A study of 30 infants with ALL using immunotherapy along with traditional chemotherapy showed significantly improved 1-year event-free survival, but longer follow-up and more patients will be needed to show definitive long-term survival in this very hard to treat population.21
paragraphs.heading: Infant Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia

paragraphs.text: Neonates with AML have similarly poor remission and disease-free survival rates, indistinguishable from those for older children. Distinctive features of AML in the infant include very high incidences of cutaneous involvement (leukemia cutis) and CNS disease, hepatosplenomegaly, hyperleukocytosis, and an unusually high number of cases with blasts of the monoblastic or myelomonocytic type. Leukostasis, a complication of severe hyperleukocytosis more commonly seen in AML than in ALL, is characterized by white blood cell plugs in the microvasculature, causing CNS events such as stroke, as well as respiratory and cardiac failure. Cytogenetic abnormalities in the blasts are exceptionally common and usually involve KMT2A gene rearrangements, such as t(11;19)(q23;p13) and t(9;11)(p21;q23). Infants with Down syndrome who are diagnosed with AML have a superior survival rate compared with those without Down syndrome and AML, because they tend to develop the acute megakaryoblastic leukemia subset
paragraphs.heading: Infant Acute Myeloid Leukemia

paragraphs.text: of AML (AMKL or M7) and frequently have a very high response rate to therapy. Approximately one-third of infants who experience transient abnormal myelopoiesis will develop AMKL. Most other infants with AMKL have a t(1;22) (p13;q13) aberration, which confers a poor prognosis.19
paragraphs.heading: Infant Acute Myeloid Leukemia

paragraphs.text: JMML (formerly known as juvenile chronic myelogenous leukemia) is classified as a myeloproliferative neoplasm/myelodysplastic syndrome that accounts for less than 1% of pediatric leukemias. Ten percent of cases are diagnosed before 3 months of age, and the majority are diagnosed by 2 years of age. Clinical manifestations include splenomegaly, rash, lymphadenopathy, failure to thrive, leukoerythroblastosis, monocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and elevated fetal hemoglobin. The abnormal growth of JMML cells has been linked to a dysregulated transduction signal through the pathway that involves the cytokine growth factor, granulocyte-monocyte colony stimulating factor (GM-CSF), the GM-CSF receptor neurofibromin, and Ras.
paragraphs.heading: Juvenile Myelomonocytic Leukemia

paragraphs.text: About 10% of children with JMML have NF1. NF1activating mutations and RAS family oncogene mutations are seen in the leukemic cells of JMML patients. Patients with Noonan syndrome, a disorder associated with gainof-function mutations in PTPN11, the gene encoding the protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP-2, are also at an increased risk for developing JMML. SHP-2 mutations are present in the leukemia cells of one-third of JMML cases. Mutations of the E3 ubiquitin ligase CBL are now identified in up to another 10% of cases. Monosomy 7 is also seen in a subset of JMML.22 Patients diagnosed before 3 years of age and those with Noonan syndrome have a better prognosis. Although a variety of therapies have been used to treat JMML, allogeneic bone marrow transplantation is the only curative treatment.23
paragraphs.heading: Juvenile Myelomonocytic Leukemia

paragraphs.text: Most infant GCTs are diagnosed before the age of 2 months. GCTs comprise a wide range of benign and malignant tumors. They originate from preinvasive precursors that transform into overt tumors during infancy, adolescence, or young adulthood. Whereas 90% of GCTs diagnosed during adult life are gonadal, two-thirds of neonatal and childhood GCTs are extragonadal, with sacrococcygeal teratoma being the most prevalent.24 Serum markers used to help in diagnosis of malignant GCTs are α-fetoprotein (AFP) and β-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-HCG). It is important to note that normal serum AFP levels are high at birth and decrease to adult values only by 8 to 12 months of age.24 See Table 83.1 for age-adjusted AFP values. Elevated AFP or β-HCG levels can alert a clinician to the presence of malignant components in a tumor that may not have been evident in the portions of the tumor sampled by pathology.
paragraphs.heading: Teratomas and Other Germ Cell Tumors

paragraphs.text: Most neonatal GCTs, irrespective of location, are benign. The term teratoma describes both benign and malignant tumors composed of haphazardly intermixed tissues that originate from pluripotent stem cells and that are foreign
paragraphs.heading: Teratomas and Other Germ Cell Tumors

paragraphs.text: to the anatomic site in which they arise. Traditionally, tissue components from all three embryonic germ layers—endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm—should be represented in a teratoma. However, it is now generally accepted that tumors that are foreign to the site where they arise and consist of more than one embryonic layer can be classified as teratomas. Teratomas can include only mature tissue, can be a mix of mature and immature tissue, and can include a malignant component, which is primarily a yolk sac tumor in the neonatal period.20
paragraphs.heading: Teratomas and Other Germ Cell Tumors

paragraphs.text: Sacrococcygeal teratomas are frequently detected prenatally or at birth as a mass in the region of the sacrum or buttocks, sometimes accompanied by obstruction of the rectum or urinary tract. Vertebral anomalies can be seen in patients with sacrococcygeal teratomas. The mainstay of therapy for GCTs is surgical resection. Typically, teratomas have an excellent outcome. Immature teratomas have a prognosis comparable to mature teratomas, provided the tumor can be totally excised. In the case of sacrococcygeal teratomas, prematurity, perioperative hemorrhage, and other postoperative events result in a 10% to 20% risk for mortality. If a fully resected, sacrococcygeal teratoma is found to have malignant components, the patient can be observed and does not require chemotherapy.25 Endodermal sinus (yolk sac) tumors of the infant testis have a better prognosis than
paragraphs.heading: Teratomas and Other Germ Cell Tumors

paragraphs.text: those at later ages and other locations, including the ovary. In the rare incidence that a malignant GCT cannot be safely resected or in the presence of metastatic disease, biopsy followed by neoadjuvant chemotherapy is recommended before complete surgical resection.26
paragraphs.heading: Teratomas and Other Germ Cell Tumors

paragraphs.text: Infant soft tissue sarcomas account for about 7% of infant cancers and are the fifth most common malignancy in the first year of life. About one-third of these are rhabdomyosarcomas. Rare non-rhabdomyosarcoma tumors of soft tissue that have an increased incidence in infancy include infantile fibrosarcoma (25%), malignant rhabdoid tumor (15%), and infantile hemangiopericytoma (4%). Although the prognoses for infantile fibrosarcoma and infantile hemangiopericytoma are excellent, in general, infantile soft tissue sarcomas have a worse outcome than those in older children. Radiation therapy is less likely to be used in infants, and vulnerability to acute and late effects of chemotherapy requires dose reductions and careful monitoring for toxicity.9 Neonatal soft tissue sarcomas can have the appearance of a vascular tumor on scans; therefore it is important to obtain a histologic diagnosis if there is any doubt.10
paragraphs.heading: Soft Tissue Sarcomas

paragraphs.text: Rhabdomyosarcoma is a tumor of striated muscle that accounts for about half of infant soft tissue sarcomas. One to 2% of all rhabdomyosarcomas present at birth; 5% to 10% are diagnosed in the first year of life.10 Neonatal rhabdomyosarcoma commonly occurs in the genitourinary area or trunk rather than appearing as masses in the head and neck region, as in older infants, or as masses in either the head and neck or extremities, as in older children. The prognosis depends on both the histologic type (embryonal or alveolar in best to worst order of prognosis) and the extent of tumor resection. Embryonal RMS accounts for 70% of cases. Both radiation therapy and chemotherapy are important adjuvants to surgical resection. Infants receive modified chemotherapy dosing because of poor tolerance historically, and they are less likely to receive radiation as part of local tumor therapy.9 Survival rates for neonates and infants with rhabdomyosarcoma are inferior to those of children 1 to 9 years of age, with estimated event-free survival ranging from 41% to 53% compared with 72%, an outcome that may in part be because of those modifications in therapy.10
paragraphs.heading: Rhabdomyosarcoma

paragraphs.text: Infantile fibrosarcoma is a spindle-cell tumor of the soft tissues. It usually presents before the age of 2 years. Surgery is the mainstay of therapy, which, coupled with a good response to chemotherapy, invariably results in an excellent prognosis. A novel chromosomal translocation, t(12;15) (p13;q25), which gives rise to an ETV6-NTRK3 fusion transcript, is present in these tumors as well as in congenital mesoblastic nephroma.9 Recently TRK inhibitors have been shown to be an effective targeted therapy with a favorable toxicity profile for infantile fibrosarcoma in the relapse setting.6
paragraphs.heading: Infantile Fibrosarcoma

paragraphs.text: The incidence of neonatal brain tumors is low, accounting for less than 1% of pediatric CNS malignancies. The histologic types of neonatal brain tumors differ from those found in older children and include teratomas, astrocytomas, embryonal tumors, gangliogliomas, etc. Teratomas are the most common of these tumors. Neonatal brain tumors can be diagnosed using antenatal ultrasonography, which may identify macrocephaly, hydrocephaly, or other changes suggestive of the presence of an intracranial tumor. Postnatal infants with brain tumors may present with increased head circumference, signs of increased intracranial pressure, bulging fontanelles, hypotonia, irritability, seizures, and neurologic deficits. Magnetic resonance imaging is the imaging modality of choice for postnatal diagnosis.27 For infants with suspected germ-cell tumors, checking the AFP and β-hCG values may help in diagnosis. Treatment is restricted to surgical resection and chemotherapy, if indicated. Radiation therapy should not be

83 Neoplasms in the Neonate

### KRISTEN VANHEYST, JOHN LETTERIO, AND RACHEL EGLER

### Infant Cancer

The annual incidence of cancer in the first year of life, 236 per million infants, is the highest for all of childhood (<15 years of age) according to the National Cancer Institute’s Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) statistics for the years 1992–2014. This represents 10% of all childhood malignancies. The first year of life is the only period in childhood when the incidence of cancer is not higher in males than females.1,2 Neonatal tumors comprise 2% of all childhood malignancies.3 The majority of neonatal tumors are solid and can be picked up by a perinatal ultrasound. Teratoma, a germ cell tumor (GCT) presenting most often on prenatal ultrasound in the sacrococcygeal area, is the most common neoplasm in infancy but is usually surgically excised as a nonmalignant (i.e., noncancerous) tumor. Fig. 83.1 provides a graphic summary of infant cancer incidence by common types.

In adults, cancer is thought to occur after a long interplay between environmental triggers and genetic predisposition. In infancy, especially in the neonatal period, the normal, genetically programmed protections against unregulated growth of cells fail very early. Consequently, embryonal tumors such as neuroblastoma, Wilms tumor, medulloblastoma, hepatoblastoma, and retinoblastoma are more common during this time period when compared with older ages.

It is thought that about 10% of childhood cancers are associated with a known cancer predisposition gene.4 In neonates, cancer predisposition syndromes can manifest in three ways. First among these is the identification of a tumor that has a level of association with germline cancer predisposition genes. One example of this is adrenal cortical carcinoma, which when found in the perinatal period has a probability of association with TP53 gene mutations of up to 80%.5,6 Similarly, 100% of bilateral retinoblastomas are associated with a germline RB1 gene mutation, regardless of family history. Other tumors that occur in this period with known associations with germ line mutations include rhabdoid tumors (60% have SMARCB1 mutation), pleuropulmonary blastoma (70% have DICER1 mutation), and medulloblastoma with desmoplastic or extensive nodularity subtypes (50% have SUFU mutation).

1566

The second way that a cancer predisposition may manifest during infancy is through the association with an identified syndrome with developmental defects that conveys a higher risk of cancer. An example of this would be Beckwith-Wiedemann, an overgrowth syndrome presenting with hemihypertrophy, macroglossia, omphalocele, and neonatal hypoglycemia. These patients have abnormal imprinting in the 11p15 telomeric region and are at risk for hepatoblastoma, adrenal cortical carcinoma, and Wilms tumor. Similarly, children with WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary abnormalities, mental retardation) have an 11q13 deletion and carry a 50% risk for Wilms tumor in infancy. Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome is caused by the PHOX2B gene mutation, and children with this abnormality have a 3% risk of neuroblastoma during infancy. Trisomy 21, Down syndrome, has a 4% to 10% risk of transient abnormal myelopoiesis as well as a risk of acute megakaryoblastic leukemia during infancy.

Finally, a known familial cancer predisposition syndrome may be present, either elicited through a careful family history or known from prior genetic testing, and so the practitioner should be on alert for possible tumor development. Examples of these include familial RB1 gene mutations, which manifest as retinoblastoma, TP53 mutations, or Li- Fraumeni syndrome, for which adrenal cortical carcinoma is the most common tumor of infancy, and ALK gene mutations, which are associated with familial neuroblastoma. In this setting, consultation with an experienced geneticist is crucial and may have occurred before birth or should be undertaken shortly thereafter. Unique screening protocols are available for many inherited syndromes, because each one confers a risk for distinct tumors at different developmental stages in the patient’s life.4

Historically, the 5-year overall survival rate for all neonates affected by cancer (age <1 month) is 60.3%. Neonates with extracranial solid tumors had the highest 5-year overall survival (71.2%), followed by leukemia (39.1%) and central nervous system (CNS) tumors (15%). Except for neuroblastoma, all of the neonatal tumors are known to have significantly inferior outcomes compared with those that can be achieved in older patients.7 The inferior survival rates for similar histologic tumors are likely attributable both to differences in the tumor biology and to altered drug

### Neuroblastoma

Neuroblastoma, an embryonal tumor of neural crest origin arising anywhere along the sympathetic chain, is the leading malignant tumor of the perinatal period and the most common extracranial solid tumor in childhood. About half of infant neuroblastomas are diagnosed within the first 4 months of life, with many being detected as an adrenal mass in utero. The survival of infants with neuroblastoma detected before birth is better than that of those diagnosed after birth.11 Other common sites of presentation are cervical and thoracic sympathetic ganglia. Neurologic signs and symptoms of spinal cord compression prompt urgent diagnosis and management with steroids and chemotherapy in about 20% of neonatal neuroblastomas. Many neuroblastoma tumors secrete catecholamines. Urine homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid levels are commonly used diagnostic tests. Mass infant screening programs using these urine tests in Japan, Quebec, and Europe have increased the detection of good-prognosis tumors but have failed to change the mortality rate from high-risk neuroblastoma.12,13 Familial neuroblastoma with germline mutations in PHOX2B or ALK accounts for 1% of childhood neuroblastoma.14

The most important prognostic variables for infant neuroblastoma are the patient’s age at diagnosis, the stage of the tumor, DNA index, and MYCN amplification. Tumor hyperdiploidy (DNA index >1) is a favorable prognostic indicator, whereas MYCN amplification is associated with a more aggressive disease.15 Infants with neuroblastoma have a better prognosis than older children, with an overall 5-year survival rate of about 88% (versus 45% for those >1 year at diagnosis). Infants with localized tumors have a 5-year survival rate of 95%. Expectant observation of babies younger than 6 months of age with small adrenal masses has reduced surgical morbidity and mortality while maintaining excellent event-free survival rates.14 Either observation or surgery, with or without

administration of low-dose chemotherapy, is recommended for lower-risk neuroblastoma in infants. High-dose chemotherapy with peripheral blood stem cell rescue, radiation therapy, cisretinoic acid, and immunotherapy are all established treatment modalities for infants with high-risk, MYCN-amplified disease.

A unique stage of neuroblastoma is stage 4S, or MS. Patients in this category must be less than 1 year of age, have a localized primary tumor with disease dissemination to skin and liver, and have less than 10% of their bone marrow involved with negative meta-iodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) uptake in bone marrow. The skin lesions that arise in infants with 4S neuroblastoma are raised and bluish in color and should be included in the differential diagnosis of the infant with a blueberry muffin rash. Stage 4S accounts for 7% to 10% of the cases of neuroblastoma.14 This subgroup of infants has the unique, poorly understood characteristic of spontaneous tumor regression in both the primary tumor and the metastatic lesions and in most settings can be observed. However, in neonates, massive hepatomegaly from rapidly progressing disease can be life threatening. Therefore, in the presence of hepatomegaly, early intervention with chemotherapy is recommended for neonates rather than using an observation approach.16,17

### Leukemia

Leukemia is the second most common cancer in infancy; however, it is still rare. Infant leukemias tend to present toward the second half of the first year of life. The estimated incidence rates per 1 million infants in the United States yearly with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is 160 per million, acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is 70 per million, and juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML) is 1.2 per million.18 Neonatal or congenital leukemia, estimated to occur in 1 to 5 per million infants, is diagnosed within the first month of life and carries a particularly grave prognosis. AML is more common than ALL in neonatal leukemia. Rearrangements of the mixed lineage leukemia (MLL) gene at chromosome 11q23, MLL-r, are common in congenital and infant ALL and AML. The MLL gene has more recently been described as the histone lysine methyltransferase 2A (KMT2A) gene, discussed in later sections. Prenatal MLL-r events promote rapid development of additional mutations or “hits” resulting in early leukemia presentation. If a monozygotic twin is diagnosed with leukemia in the first year of life, intrauterine transfer of the mutation results in an almost 100% concordance for the other twin, with a brief lag time of weeks until the other twin’s leukemia diagnosis.19

There are many genetic syndromes associated with increased leukemia risk. Bone marrow failure syndromes, primary and secondary immunodeficiencies, defects in DNA repair, and genetic defects impacting tumor suppressor genes are associated with leukemogenesis as well as oncogenesis (a term used to describe the development of a tumor or tumors). Down syndrome (ALL, AML), Noonan syndrome (JMML, AML), and neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1; ALL, AML, JMML) have strong associations with leukemia and are associated with early leukemia presentations.


## PDF page 1567

The differential diagnosis for congenital leukemia includes transient abnormal myelopoiesis of Down syndrome, leukemoid reaction, congenital infections, hypoxia or hemolysis, hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, and stage 4S neuroblastoma. Langerhans cell histiocytosis can also present in infants with pancytopenia, organomegaly, and cutaneous extramedullary hematopoiesis.

### Infant Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia

A number of clinical features that are associated with a poorer prognosis are common in neonates and infants with ALL; these include large tumor cell burden (hyperleukocytosis), massive hepatosplenomegaly, involvement of the CNS, leukemic skin infiltrates (leukemia cutis), and hypogammaglobulinemia. The leukemic blasts in infant ALL often are CD10 negative, express myeloid antigens, and have cytogenetic abnormalities involving the KMT2A gene, which carries a worse prognosis. Strategies to intensify therapy have improved survival for infants with ALL, but not for the ones with KMT2A rearrangement.20 A small percentage of these leukemias are biphenotypic (i.e., they possess characteristics of both ALL and AML). Neonates experience significant toxicities from both chemotherapy and CNS irradiation, which may translate into significant late effects that limit quality of life in survivors. The especially poor prognosis for infant ALL is owing to the high incidence of bone marrow and extramedullary relapse and the difficulty in treating relapsed disease. Infants less than 90 days of age at diagnosis have worse outcomes.20 Progressively more intensive chemotherapeutic regimens and bone marrow transplantation have been used in these patients, but the event-free survival rate at 5 years is only in the 30% range.19 A study of 30 infants with ALL using immunotherapy along with traditional chemotherapy showed significantly improved 1-year event-free survival, but longer follow-up and more patients will be needed to show definitive long-term survival in this very hard to treat population.21

### Infant Acute Myeloid Leukemia

Neonates with AML have similarly poor remission and disease-free survival rates, indistinguishable from those for older children. Distinctive features of AML in the infant include very high incidences of cutaneous involvement (leukemia cutis) and CNS disease, hepatosplenomegaly, hyperleukocytosis, and an unusually high number of cases with blasts of the monoblastic or myelomonocytic type. Leukostasis, a complication of severe hyperleukocytosis more commonly seen in AML than in ALL, is characterized by white blood cell plugs in the microvasculature, causing CNS events such as stroke, as well as respiratory and cardiac failure. Cytogenetic abnormalities in the blasts are exceptionally common and usually involve KMT2A gene rearrangements, such as t(11;19)(q23;p13) and t(9;11)(p21;q23). Infants with Down syndrome who are diagnosed with AML have a superior survival rate compared with those without Down syndrome and AML, because they tend to develop the acute megakaryoblastic leukemia subset

of AML (AMKL or M7) and frequently have a very high response rate to therapy. Approximately one-third of infants who experience transient abnormal myelopoiesis will develop AMKL. Most other infants with AMKL have a t(1;22) (p13;q13) aberration, which confers a poor prognosis.19

### Juvenile Myelomonocytic Leukemia

JMML (formerly known as juvenile chronic myelogenous leukemia) is classified as a myeloproliferative neoplasm/myelodysplastic syndrome that accounts for less than 1% of pediatric leukemias. Ten percent of cases are diagnosed before 3 months of age, and the majority are diagnosed by 2 years of age. Clinical manifestations include splenomegaly, rash, lymphadenopathy, failure to thrive, leukoerythroblastosis, monocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and elevated fetal hemoglobin. The abnormal growth of JMML cells has been linked to a dysregulated transduction signal through the pathway that involves the cytokine growth factor, granulocyte-monocyte colony stimulating factor (GM-CSF), the GM-CSF receptor neurofibromin, and Ras.

About 10% of children with JMML have NF1. NF1activating mutations and RAS family oncogene mutations are seen in the leukemic cells of JMML patients. Patients with Noonan syndrome, a disorder associated with gainof-function mutations in PTPN11, the gene encoding the protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP-2, are also at an increased risk for developing JMML. SHP-2 mutations are present in the leukemia cells of one-third of JMML cases. Mutations of the E3 ubiquitin ligase CBL are now identified in up to another 10% of cases. Monosomy 7 is also seen in a subset of JMML.22 Patients diagnosed before 3 years of age and those with Noonan syndrome have a better prognosis. Although a variety of therapies have been used to treat JMML, allogeneic bone marrow transplantation is the only curative treatment.23

### Teratomas and Other Germ Cell Tumors

Most infant GCTs are diagnosed before the age of 2 months. GCTs comprise a wide range of benign and malignant tumors. They originate from preinvasive precursors that transform into overt tumors during infancy, adolescence, or young adulthood. Whereas 90% of GCTs diagnosed during adult life are gonadal, two-thirds of neonatal and childhood GCTs are extragonadal, with sacrococcygeal teratoma being the most prevalent.24 Serum markers used to help in diagnosis of malignant GCTs are α-fetoprotein (AFP) and β-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-HCG). It is important to note that normal serum AFP levels are high at birth and decrease to adult values only by 8 to 12 months of age.24 See Table 83.1 for age-adjusted AFP values. Elevated AFP or β-HCG levels can alert a clinician to the presence of malignant components in a tumor that may not have been evident in the portions of the tumor sampled by pathology.

Most neonatal GCTs, irrespective of location, are benign. The term teratoma describes both benign and malignant tumors composed of haphazardly intermixed tissues that originate from pluripotent stem cells and that are foreign

Teratomas can include only mature tissue, can be a mix of mature and immature tissue, and can include a malignant component, which is primarily a yolk sac tumor in the neonatal period.20

Sacrococcygeal teratomas are frequently detected prenatally or at birth as a mass in the region of the sacrum or buttocks, sometimes accompanied by obstruction of the rectum or urinary tract. Vertebral anomalies can be seen in patients with sacrococcygeal teratomas. The mainstay of therapy for GCTs is surgical resection. Typically, teratomas have an excellent outcome. Immature teratomas have a prognosis comparable to mature teratomas, provided the tumor can be totally excised. In the case of sacrococcygeal teratomas, prematurity, perioperative hemorrhage, and other postoperative events result in a 10% to 20% risk for mortality. ### Soft Tissue Sarcomas

Infant soft tissue sarcomas account for about 7% of infant cancers and are the fifth most common malignancy in the first year of life. About one-third of these are rhabdomyosarcomas. Rare non-rhabdomyosarcoma tumors of soft tissue that have an increased incidence in infancy include infantile fibrosarcoma (25%), malignant rhabdoid tumor (15%), and infantile hemangiopericytoma (4%). Although the prognoses for infantile fibrosarcoma and infantile hemangiopericytoma are excellent, in general, infantile soft tissue sarcomas have a worse outcome than those in older children. Radiation therapy is less likely to be used in infants, and vulnerability to acute and late effects of chemotherapy requires dose reductions and careful monitoring for toxicity.9 Neonatal soft tissue sarcomas can have the appearance of a vascular tumor on scans; therefore it is important to obtain a histologic diagnosis if there is any doubt.10


## PDF page 1569

### Rhabdomyosarcoma

Rhabdomyosarcoma is a tumor of striated muscle that accounts for about half of infant soft tissue sarcomas. One to 2% of all rhabdomyosarcomas present at birth; 5% to 10% are diagnosed in the first year of life.10 Neonatal rhabdomyosarcoma commonly occurs in the genitourinary area or trunk rather than appearing as masses in the head and neck region, as in older infants, or as masses in either the head and neck or extremities, as in older children. The prognosis depends on both the histologic type (embryonal or alveolar in best to worst order of prognosis) and the extent of tumor resection. Embryonal RMS accounts for 70% of cases. Both radiation therapy and chemotherapy are important adjuvants to surgical resection. Infants receive modified chemotherapy dosing because of poor tolerance historically, and they are less likely to receive radiation as part of local tumor therapy.9 Survival rates for neonates and infants with rhabdomyosarcoma are inferior to those of children 1 to 9 years of age, with estimated event-free survival ranging from 41% to 53% compared with 72%, an outcome that may in part be because of those modifications in therapy.10

### Infantile Fibrosarcoma

Infantile fibrosarcoma is a spindle-cell tumor of the soft tissues. It usually presents before the age of 2 years. Surgery is the mainstay of therapy, which, coupled with a good response to chemotherapy, invariably results in an excellent prognosis. A novel chromosomal translocation, t(12;15) (p13;q25), which gives rise to an ETV6-NTRK3 fusion transcript, is present in these tumors as well as in congenital mesoblastic nephroma.9 Recently TRK inhibitors have been shown to be an effective targeted therapy with a favorable toxicity profile for infantile fibrosarcoma in the relapse setting.6

### Neonatal Brain Tumors

The incidence of neonatal brain tumors is low, accounting for less than 1% of pediatric CNS malignancies. The histologic types of neonatal brain tumors differ from those found in older children and include teratomas, astrocytomas, embryonal tumors, gangliogliomas, etc. Teratomas are the most common of these tumors. Neonatal brain tumors can be diagnosed using antenatal ultrasonography, which may identify macrocephaly, hydrocephaly, or other changes suggestive of the presence of an intracranial tumor. Postnatal infants with brain tumors may present with increased head circumference, signs of increased intracranial pressure, bulging fontanelles, hypotonia, irritability, seizures, and neurologic deficits. Magnetic resonance imaging is the imaging modality of choice for postnatal diagnosis.27 For infants with suspected germ-cell tumors, checking the AFP and β-hCG values may help in diagnosis. Treatment is restricted to surgical resection and chemotherapy, if indicated. Radiation therapy should not be

used in infants because of the long-term side effects such as developmental retardation, neuroendocrine abnormalities, the risk of secondary CNS malignancies, and premature death.27 Survival in neonates with CNS tumors is poor because of the inability to perform aggressive resection, avoidance of radiation, and high-grade pathology. Also, these patients have a very high incidence of endocrine, neurologic, and cognitive deficits later in life.27

paragraphs.heading: ABBREVIATIONS

paragraphs.text: Neonates constitute one of the most heavily transfused patient groups in the hospital. In a Canadian study, over 40% of very low birth weight (VLBW) infants and greater than 90% of extremely low birth weight infants (ELBW; birth weight of less than 1000 g) received at least one red blood cell (RBC) transfusion during their initial hospitalization.1 Neonatal transfusion practices differ substantially from adult and pediatric transfusion practices because of unique differences in neonatal physiology. Neonates have small blood volumes when compared with older children and adults but high blood volume per body weight. Their immature organ system function predisposes them to metabolic derangements from blood products and additive solutions and to the infectious and immunomodulatory hazards of transfusion such as transfusion-transmitted cytomegalovirus (TT-CMV) infection and transfusion-associated graftversus-host disease (TA-GVHD). Neonates undergo rapid growth but have a limited capacity to expand their blood volume. In addition, passive transfer of maternal antibodies to the immunologically naïve newborn creates unique compatibility scenarios not commonly encountered in children or adults. Their responses to stresses, including hypothermia, hypovolemia, hypoxia, and acidosis, are dependent on gestational age, birth weight, and co-morbidities. These considerations necessitate special approaches to transfusion therapy in the neonate.2
paragraphs.heading: Special Considerations for Transfusion Therapy in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: Advances in donor recruitment, blood screening, and processing have decreased the risks associated with blood transfusion. As part of patient blood management, current transfusion considerations and guidelines focus on reducing both transfusion number and donor exposures while striving to minimize iatrogenic blood losses. Nevertheless, hematologic, immunologic, infectious, cardiovascular, and metabolic complications can occur. Many of these risks exist for transfusion recipients of any age, whereas others pose a greater threat to the neonatal recipient. These potential risks affect the choice and processing of blood products. Parents must be advised of the risks, benefits, and alternatives to transfusion, and informed consent should be documented in the medical record along with the indications for, and results of, the prescribed transfusion.
paragraphs.heading: Risks of Transfusion Therapy

paragraphs.text: Neonates, especially extremely premature infants, are more susceptible to metabolic alterations caused by the immaturity of many of their organ systems. Glucose imbalances, hyperkalemia, and hypocalcemia are the most common metabolic derangements related to transfusion, owing to the inability of the infant to efficiently metabolize and/or excrete elements intrinsic to blood and blood components,
paragraphs.heading: Metabolic Complications

paragraphs.text: including anticoagulants, preservative solutions, and other solutes that accumulate during refrigerated storage.
paragraphs.heading: Metabolic Complications

paragraphs.text: Hypoglycemia (see Chapter 90) can result from the combination of decreased glucose infusion rates during transfusion and impaired glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis within the liver of the preterm neonate. Continuous glucose infusion rates of greater than 3 to 4 mg/kg/min are often required in preterm infants; if maintenance fluids are suspended during transfusion, glucose infusion rates can decrease to approximately 0.2 mg/kg/min for citrate-phosphate-dextrose-adenine (CPDA-1) preserved RBCs and 0.5 mg/kg/min for the RBC additive Adsol (AS-1) preserved RBCs. In neonatal intensive care units, holding feeds during blood transfusions, particularly for premature infants, has become a common practice to decrease the risk of neonatal enterocolitis (NEC) and generally does not result in adverse nutritional outcomes.3 Reported incidences of hypoglycemia in neonates either during or after exchange transfusions range from 1.4% to 3.6%. Hypoglycemia occurring after exchange transfusion is believed to be caused by intraprocedural hyperglycemia (from the dextrose in blood additive solutions), which causes rebound hypoglycemia from insulin secretion.4 Preventive measures for transfusion-associated hypoglycemia include recognizing those infants at risk for developing glucose homeostatic imbalances, continuing the infusion of maintenance fluids rich in dextrose (albeit at a slower rate) to maintain an adequate glucose infusion rate during simple transfusions, and close monitoring of blood glucose during both small and large volume transfusions. To minimize the risk of RBC hemolysis and/or agglutination, dextrose-rich fluids should be infused in a separate intravenous line from the blood transfusion.5
paragraphs.heading: Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: The risk of transfusion-induced hyperkalemia is directly related to the magnitude of the K+ load delivered with RBC transfusion, which depends on the age, plasma volume, and plasma concentration of K+ of the unit, and the rate at which K+ is delivered (potassium infusion rate). Potassium infusion rates greater than 0.01 mEq/kg/min may pose a potential risk of transfusion-associated hyperkalemia and have been shown to result in cardiac arrhythmia/arrest in neonates.6 As stored RBCs age, intracellular potassium leaks out into the plasma and raises the extracellular potassium level within the component. Units of RBCs in extendedstorage media (AS-1, AS-3, AS-5) have a hematocrit (Hct) of approximately 60%, and RBCs stored in CPDA-1 have an Hct of approximately 70%. Furthermore, some pediatric transfusion centers centrifuge RBC aliquots before transfusions for neonates to further reduce the plasma component to 20% (e.g., RBC unit: Hct >80%). Such an approach helps reduce the content of potassium, mannitol, and RBC microvesicles in irradiated RBC aliquots stored up to 21 days.7 After 42 days of storage, K+ levels in the plasma of an AS-1-preserved RBC unit approximate to 0.05 mEq/mL.
paragraphs.heading: Hyperkalemia

paragraphs.text: Therefore infusing 15 mL/kg over 3 hours would yield a potassium dose of 0.33 mEq/kg and a potassium infusion rate of 0.002 mEq/kg/min (e.g., 1-kg infant receiving 15 mL RBC and 6 mL plasma). Conversely, after 35 days of storage of CPDA-1-preserved RBCs, potassium levels in the plasma approximate to 0.08 mEq/mL. Transfusing 15 mL/ kg of the CPDA-1-stored product over 3 hours would yield a potassium dose of 0.36 mEq/kg (e.g., 1-kg infant receiving 15 mL RBC and 4.5 mL plasma) at a potassium infusion rate of 0.002 mEq/kg/min. Given that daily potassium requirement is approximately 2 to 3 mEq/kg, simple RBC transfusions infused slowly over 2 to 4 hours (2 to 5 mL/ kg/h) do not pose a threat for hyperkalemia (Table 84.1).
paragraphs.heading: Hyperkalemia

paragraphs.text: It has been shown in multiple studies that transfusing dedicated RBC units to their expiration dates does not cause hyperkalemia even in extremely preterm infants. Therefore the routine practice of washing older RBCs is unnecessary for most small-volume RBC transfusions (10 to 20 mL/kg) in infants, including those with birth weights less than 1.5 kg.4 Irradiation of RBC components damages the erythrocyte membranes, causing K+ leakage and a linear increase in plasma potassium concentration over time. Irradiation substantially increases plasma K+ compared with nonirradiated RBC components, both within the first 24 hours after irradiation (twofold increase) and for the life of the RBC component. The difference was detectable as early as 2 hours after irradiation.8
paragraphs.heading: Hyperkalemia

paragraphs.text: Large-volume RBC transfusions (>25 mL/kg), particularly if infused rapidly, may pose a significant risk to the neonate. There have been reports of hyperkalemia-induced
paragraphs.heading: Hyperkalemia

paragraphs.text: electrocardiac abnormalities and cardiac arrest when RBC transfusions (fresh and old) have been administered via rapid infusion (10 to 20 mL/kg over 10 to 15 minutes) to neonates with concurrent low cardiac output states when the RBCs were irradiated more than 24 hours before infusion and/or when they were given via central line directly into the inferior vena cava.6 Whenever possible, fresh RBC units should be issued for large-volume RBC transfusions. When fresh RBC units are unavailable, they should be volume reduced or washed and transfused as soon as possible after washing to minimize K+ reaccumulation. Previously irradiated and stored (≥24 hours) units may have plasma K+ levels unsafe for large-volume transfusion to neonates, especially if administered rapidly. Therefore they should be issued immediately post-irradiation or volume-reduced or washed to remove extracellular K+ that accumulates after processing.2 In emergent circumstances of unexpected massive bleeding, when neither fresh nor washed nor volumereduced RBC units are available, the infusion rate should not exceed 0.5 mL/kg/min.
paragraphs.heading: Hyperkalemia

paragraphs.text: Special considerations should be taken when RBCs need to be transfused rapidly and should be coordinated with the transfusion center so that proper preparation can be performed to avoid hyperkalemia. Measures to reduce the risk of transfusion-associated hyperkalemia leading to cardiac arrest include anticipating and replacing blood loss before significant hemodynamic compromise occurs, using largerbore (>23-gauge) peripheral intravenous catheters rather than central venous access, checking and correcting electrolyte abnormalities frequently, and using fresher RBCs for
paragraphs.heading: Hyperkalemia

paragraphs.text: massive transfusion.6 For patients on extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), pre-bypass ultrafiltration helps normalize the electrolyte balance of the circuit prime and may reduce the risk of hyperkalemia-related cardiac arrest.9 In Japan, where universal irradiation of cellular blood products is performed, a study used a potassium filter with high adsorption efficacy for neonatal RBC transfusions. The authors noted that potassium reduction is accompanied by an increase in sodium, which may occasionally be clinically significant.10
paragraphs.heading: Hyperkalemia

paragraphs.text: Infants, especially premature infants, are particularly susceptible to hypocalcemia (see Chapter 91) within the first week of life. Because of the immaturity in neonatal liver and kidney function, and small skeletal muscle mass, transfusion of citrate-enriched blood can result in hypocalcemia from citrate toxicity. The amount of citrate infused into a neonate during a small-volume transfusion (10 to 15 mL/kg) is very unlikely to cause hypocalcemia; however, the citrate load during an exchange transfusion can reach very high levels and lead to symptomatic hypocalcemia. In a retrospective review of neonatal exchange transfusions, symptomatic hypocalcemia was one of the most common side effects, along with bleeding associated with thrombocytopenia, catheter-related complications, apnea, bradycardia, and other metabolic disturbances. Adverse events were generally higher among ill neonates (i.e., presence of co-morbidities besides indication for exchange) when compared to healthy peers, and complication frequency increased with decreasing birth weights.11 Because clinical manifestations of hypocalcemia are often subtle and/or variable in premature infants, many recommend monitoring ionized calcium levels and/or QT intervals throughout exchange transfusion procedures, in addition to minimizing potentiating factors such as hypomagnesemia, hyperkalemia, alkalosis, and hypothermia in high-risk (ill) patients. Insufficient evidence is currently available in the literature to support or reject the continual use of prophylactic intravenous calcium infusions in neonates receiving exchange transfusions.12
paragraphs.heading: Hypocalcemia

paragraphs.text: The toxicity associated with the use of the plasticizer di- (2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) in blood storage bags has been debated in the transfusion medicine community for over 50 years. (See also Chapter 13.) DEHP is added to polyvinylchloride plastic storage blood bags to increase bag flexibility, RBC survival, and oxygen permeability for platelet storage. DEHP also stabilizes RBC membranes, which prevents hemolysis and alteration during refrigerated storage. Because of its desirable structural properties, it is also widely used in medical plastics as well as in food storage and household products. Critically ill neonates exposed to endotracheal tubes, orogastric tubes, intravenous tubing, and blood products can have DEHP exposures that exceed safe levels by 3 to 5 orders of magnitude.13
paragraphs.heading: Effect of Plasticizers

paragraphs.text: However, there is evidence that DEHP exerts detrimental effects on the endocrine system by acting as an androgen antagonist and an estrogen agonist. While DEHP is broken down in the gastrointestinal tract to some extent, transfusions bypass this protection. At particular risk for toxicity are neonates receiving high-volume transfusions, such as neonatal RBC exchange, during ECMO, and during massive transfusion. Health concerns have prompted European authorities to start restricting its use according to European Regulation 2017/745, and efforts are underway to identify suitable alternatives.14
paragraphs.heading: Effect of Plasticizers

paragraphs.text: Transfusion reactions are less common in neonates than in older children or adults. Nevertheless, neonates undergoing transfusions should be closely monitored for symptoms and signs of a reaction. Often, potential reactions are noted by a change in vital signs or a rash early in the course of a transfusion, but they may occur at any point. The Joint Commission recommends that vital signs be measured at baseline (pre-transfusion), within 15 minutes of initiation, and within 60 minutes after the end of the transfusion.15 Hospital policies are based on these guidelines but may differ with respect to each other. In addition to vital signs, it is important to also assess the patient for cutaneous changes (e.g., rash, hives), respiratory distress, discomfort, or pain.
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: When an acute transfusion reaction occurs, it is crucial to discontinue the transfusion immediately, maintain intravenous access, and verify that the correct unit was transfused while treating the patient’s symptoms. Notifying the transfusion service for further laboratory evaluation of the reaction is essential to properly categorize the reaction so that the patient can be managed appropriately.9 Because a single blood donation often results in several different blood products, untransfused co-components may need to be quarantined until the investigation is complete.
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: Acute hemolytic transfusion reactions occur when RBCs are transfused to a recipient with preformed antibodies to antigens expressed on the transfused RBCs. Almost all acute hemolytic transfusion reaction fatalities are the result of transfusion of ABO-incompatible blood because of clerical errors and misidentification; however, nonimmune causes of acute hemolysis may also occur. These include hemolysis from shear and/or heat stress imposed on erythrocytes by extracorporeal circuits, infusion devices, filters, blood warmers, or phototherapy light exposure. These reactions are characterized by fever, chills, diaphoresis, abdominal pain, hypotension, and hemoglobinuria with potential progression to disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and acute renal failure. When a hemolytic transfusion reaction is suspected, the transfusion should be immediately stopped, blood cultures from both the patient and blood component(s) should be obtained, and the transfusion service should be notified. A clerical check of all labels,
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: inspection of the blood component(s), post-transfusion hemolysis check, and direct antiglobulin test (DAT) should be completed by the transfusion service. The patient’s hemoglobin/Hct, serum bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase, and urobilinogen should be monitored, and intravenous fluids should be administered to offset hypotension and ensure adequate urine output. Mannitol may be administered to force diuresis, but osmotic diuresis in neonates is controversial because of concerns about alterations in cerebral microcirculation and risk of intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH). Although infants less than 4 months old have an absence of native A and B hemagglutinins and other RBC alloantibodies, maternal IgG antibodies can cross the placenta, causing hemolysis of transfused RBCs and therefore should be considered when transfusing infants.
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: Delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions (DHTRs) occur 3 to 10 days following RBC transfusion and manifest as unexplained anemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and abdominal pain. As with acute hemolytic reactions, the diagnosis is confirmed by a positive DAT, identification of a new RBC antibody, hyperbilirubinemia, and a reduction in hemoglobin.9 DHTRs are extremely rare in neonates because of the immaturity of the immune system. Even though there have been case reports of anti-E and anti-Kell formation in infants as young as 18 days of life, the majority of reports have supported the infrequency of RBC alloimmunization and DHTRs in infants less than 4 months of age. A cohort study of 1641 neonates and children up to the age of 3 years found no alloimmunization cases within the first 6 months of life. The authors conclude that after initial testing, repeat antibody screening and cross-matching during the first 4 months of life can be safely omitted.16
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: Febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reactions (FNHTRs) are characterized by fever, chills, and diaphoresis. These reactions are believed to result from the release of pyrogenic cytokines by leukocytes within the plasma during storage. The incidence of FNHTRs has decreased dramatically since the implementation of pre-storage leukoreduction of RBCs and platelet products in 1999. Whereas FNHTRs occurred in approximately 10% of transfusions in the past, the incidence since the introduction of leukoreduction is now 0.1% to 3% (approximately 0.2% for prestorage leukoreduction) for all products.17 When FNHTR is suspected, the transfusion should be stopped and more serious reactions must be ruled out. A sample of blood from the patient may be sent for DAT, plasma hemoglobin quantification, serum lactate dehydrogenase, and bilirubin level to ensure that the patient is not experiencing a hemolytic transfusion reaction. The transfusion service may repeat the crossmatch between the RBC unit and a post-transfusion patient sample to ensure that there is no new unexpected incompatibility. Bacterial contamination should be assessed via cultures of the transfused product and the patient’s blood; empiric antibiotic therapy may be warranted. Most FNHTRs respond to antipyretics, and meperidine may be used for rigors.9
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: Allergic transfusion reactions (ATRs) are marked by urticaria and itching but can include flushing, bronchospasm, and anaphylaxis in severe cases. For mild or localized cases, transfusion can be continued once symptoms have subsided; however, severe allergic reactions (anaphylactoid or anaphylactic reactions) may require treatment with corticosteroids and/or epinephrine. The same blood unit should never be restarted in severe cases, even after symptoms have abated. Leukoreduction does not decrease the incidence of ATRs as it has for FNHTRs.9 Premedication with antihistamines with or without steroids is recommended for ATRs. Because these reactions are caused by an antibody response in a sensitized recipient to soluble plasma proteins within the blood product, washed RBCs and platelets may be used for severe or recurrent ATRs nonresponsive to medication. Severe ATRs leading to anaphylaxis can be caused by the development of anti-IgA antibodies in recipients who are IgA-deficient.
