In these instances, IgA-deficient plasma products may be obtained but require the use of rare donor registries. In patients of Asian descent, haptoglobin deficiency may also be associated with severe ATRs.17
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: The use of platelets in additive solution (PAS) resulted in decreased incidence of ATRs and FNHTRs in one adult study, presumably because of decrease in donor plasma content in the blood products.18 A retrospective study in Japan of two different PAS formulations showed prevention of ATRs in children without other adverse events. The ages ranged from 0 to 19 years but the proportion of neonates was not specified.19
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: TA-GVHD occurs when an immunosuppressed or immunodeficient patient receives cellular blood products that contain immunologically competent lymphocytes. The transfused donor lymphocytes are able to proliferate and engraft within the immunologic incompetent recipient because the recipient is unable to detect and reject foreign cells.9 The degree of similarity between human leukocyte antigens (HLA) of donor and recipient also increases the likelihood of developing TA-GVHD. As an example, in the setting of directed donation from a first-degree relative, donor lymphocyte homozygosity for an HLA haplotype for which the recipient is haploidentical predisposes to recipient tolerance, donor lymphocyte engraftment, and alloreaction leading to TA-GVHD.17
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: The clinical signs and symptoms of TA-GVHD include fever; generalized, erythematous rash that may progress to desquamation; watery diarrhea; mild hepatitis to fulminant liver failure; respiratory distress; and pancytopenia, which is unusually severe because hematopoietic progenitor cells are preferentially affected. Onset is usually from 5 to 10 days following transfusion of lymphocyte-replete cellular blood components in older children and adults; however, there may be a longer latency period before the onset of clinical manifestations of TA-GVHD and a longer course of disease before death in neonates.9 Prolonged latency of clinical
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: manifestations and death is believed to result from thymic and/or extrathymic semi-tolerance for allogeneic cytotoxic T lymphocytes.
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: Neonates at “high risk” for TA-GVHD include those with impaired cellular immunity, such as severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) or Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, those receiving intrauterine transfusions and/or neonatal exchange transfusion, and those receiving cellular blood components from family members or those who are genetically similar to the recipient. Extremely premature neonates are also considered by many to be at significant risk for TA-GVHD.17
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: No effective therapy is available to treat TA-GVHD except for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and owing to bone marrow hypoplasia, the mortality rate is 90% in the pediatric population. Fortunately, this complication can be prevented by pretransfusion gamma or X-ray irradiation of cellular blood components at a dose of 2.5 Gy, which effectively abolishes lymphocyte proliferation.20 The shelf life of irradiated RBCs is 28 days; however, no data currently exist on the safety in the neonatal population of gamma-irradiated or X-ray-treated RBCs that are stored for this amount of time. Because potassium and free hemoglobin increase after irradiation and storage of RBCs, it is preferable to irradiate cellular blood products immediately before issue for neonates, who may not be able to tolerate high potassium loads.8 There exists no “standard of care” regarding irradiation of blood products for otherwise nonhigh-risk infants. Many transfusion services irradiate all cellular blood products given to preterm infants born weighing 1.0 to 1.2 kg or less, whereas some irradiate all cellular blood products (i.e., RBCs, platelets, granulocytes) for infants less than 4 months of age, citing the lack of clinical studies on the incidence of TA-GVHD in the neonatal population and the concern for failure to recognize an infant with an undiagnosed congenital immunodeficiency. When an infant requires irradiated blood components, all cellular blood components for that infant should be irradiated; however, it is not necessary to irradiate acellular blood components, such as fresh frozen plasma (FFP) and cryoprecipitate. The known and presumed indications for irradiation of blood components for neonates are listed in Box 84.1. Although leukoreduction decreases the risk of TA-GVHD, it is not considered sufficient to prevent the complication.21
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) is an uncommon, potentially fatal acute immune-related transfusion reaction that typically occurs within 4 to 6 hours of transfusion and presents with respiratory distress caused by noncardiogenic pulmonary edema (normal central venous pressure and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure), hypotension, fever, and severe hypoxemia.9 Differentiation from transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO), an acute, nonimmune transfusion reaction that presents with respiratory distress, cardiogenic pulmonary edema, and hypertension caused by volume overload, is important because
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: treatments differ. Furthermore, transient leukopenia, which is commonly seen with TRALI but is absent in TACO, can aid in differentiation of these reactions. Symptoms of TRALI usually improve within 48 to 96 hours; however, three-fourths of patients require aggressive respiratory support. Treatment is mainly supportive, including fluid and/ or vasopressor support in the face of hypotension. Whereas aggressive diuresis is often required in TACO, this should be avoided in TRALI.9
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: Although the exact mechanism of TRALI remains uncertain, it is generally believed to be caused by the passive transmission of HLA and/or neutrophil antibodies directed against recipient leukocyte antigens. These antibodies activate and sequester recipient neutrophils within the endothelium of the lungs, ultimately leading to the production of vasoactive mediators and capillary leak. Plasma products (such as FFP, plasma frozen within 24 hours of phlebotomy [FP24], and apheresis platelets) account for the majority of severe TRALI cases, and multiparous women are the most commonly implicated donors.22 Because of these findings, various preventative measures have been adopted in the United States and elsewhere. These include the use of maleonly, high-volume plasma products (FFP, FP24, platelets), or the selection of donor products from donors who have a low likelihood of being alloimmunized via pregnancy or prior transfusions or who are negative on HLA antibody screen.23 TRALI has been well-documented in the pediatric population, and a case report described possible TRALI in the setting of a designated blood transfusion between mother and infant.24
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: T-antigen activation is a phenomenon that can cause immune-mediated hemolysis in neonates, ranging from minor to fulminant and fatal. Removal of N-acetyl neuraminic (sialic) acid residues from the O-linked
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: oligosaccharides on glycophorins (A, B, and C) on RBC membranes by neuraminidase-producing bacteria, particularly Clostridium bacteroides and Streptococcus pneumoniae, results in exposure of the normally masked Thomsen-Friedenreich (T) cryptantigen on the RBC surface of the neonate. Transfusion of adult blood products containing plasma with naturally occurring anti-T antibodies into neonates with T-antigen activation can produce intravascular hemolysis following transfusion or unexplained failure to achieve an expected post-transfusion hemoglobin increment.25 The incidence of T-antigen activation has been reported in 5% to 35% of infants with NEC.26 The rate of T-antigen activation is higher in infants with more severe disease (e.g., multiple cultures positive for Clostridia, presence of intestinal perforation, need for surgical intervention).
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: The picture is complicated by the fact that T-antigen activation may be detected in the laboratory without any evidence of clinical hemolysis, making broad-based screening impractical and arguing against a direct causal link. T-antigen activation may instead correlate with the amount of circulating bacterial toxin and serve as a surrogate marker for disease severity. In a retrospective report, laboratory evidence of T-antigen activation was detected by lectin agglutination testing in 9% of 43 Taiwanese infants with stage II/III NEC but did not result in hemolysis, regardless of whether washed or unwashed RBC units were administered or contribute to an increase in NEC-related mortality.27 A more recent publication reported that transfusion-associated hemolysis is often not seen in T-antigen activated infants when transfused with donor anti-T-containing plasma. The authors concluded that the use of plasma-containing blood products is not contraindicated in NEC patients with coagulopathy or requiring hemostatic factors, even if T-antigen activation is present.26
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: Routine cross-matching techniques may not detect the polyagglutination owing to T-antigen activation when monoclonal ABO antiserum is used. Minor cross-matching of neonatal T-antigen activated RBCs with donor anti-Tcontaining serum may show agglutination, but this is not performed routinely. Infants with discrepancies in forward and reverse blood typing and those with evidence of hemolysis on smear should be suspected of T-antigen activation. The diagnosis is confirmed by specific agglutination tests using peanut lectin Arachis hypogea and Glycine soja.
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: Reports of severe hemolysis in the setting of T-antigen have nevertheless led to cautious practice guidelines. For example, the American Society for Apheresis recommends avoiding plasma-containing blood components and instead suggests using albumin when plasma exchange is performed in S. pneumoniae-associated hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). The optimal strategy for transfusion support in T-antigen activation has not been established, and there is debate in the literature about the benefit of providing blood products with low levels of anti-T. RBCs stored in additive solutions already contain smaller amounts of plasma, which mitigates hemolysis risk. Washing these products is therefore unlikely to significantly benefit the patient but does
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: negatively impact the RBCs because of cell loss. Manipulations of platelets to decrease anti-T content (for example, by volume reducing or washing) reduce their potency, result in pre-transfusion activation, and may introduce contamination. Attempting to find low anti-T titer plasma from a blood center may be difficult and may possibly delay an important transfusion. Nevertheless, if a patient with T-antigen activation receives a transfusion, their hemoglobin should be closely monitored and the possible increased need for RBC support should be anticipated.25
paragraphs.heading: Immunologic Complications Transfusion Reactions

paragraphs.text: Transfusion-associated dyspnea (TAD) is defined as acute respiratory distress occurring within 24 hours of cessation of transfusion. Diagnosis requires ruling out other types of transfusion reactions associated with respiratory symptoms such as ATR, TACO, and TRALI.9 In some cases, TAD may represent allergic reactions without the full complement of cutaneous and hemodynamic manifestations.
paragraphs.heading: Transfusion-Associated Dyspnea

paragraphs.text: Septic transfusion reactions generally present with fever, hypotension, shock, and acute decompensation. Platelets are most frequently implicated because their storage at room temperature can foster growth of bacterial contaminants. Based on the inoculum of the pathogen, the onset of symptoms may occur earlier or later in the transfusion. However, the diagnosis can be challenging because similar manifestations may also present as part of other transfusion reactions or as a result of the patient’s underlying disease.28
paragraphs.heading: Transfusion-Related Sepsis

paragraphs.text: If a septic transfusion reaction is suspected, the transfusion should be stopped immediately. It is important to maintain venous access by running normal saline through the intravenous line. The remaining blood bag should be sent to the transfusion service for visual inspection, clerical check, possible culture, and quarantine (along with any co-components from the same donation). If the clinical suspicion for sepsis is high, empiric antibiotic therapy should be started immediately. Cultures of the patient and/or blood product may not demonstrate immediate growth.
paragraphs.heading: Transfusion-Related Sepsis

paragraphs.text: NEC is a devastating gastrointestinal emergency that primarily afflicts premature infants but can occur in at-risk term gestation infants as well. Severity and treatment can range from full recovery with conservative medical management to intestinal perforation and bowel necrosis requiring surgical intervention. NEC-related morbidity and mortality remains quite high, with up to 30% of affected infants succumbing to the disease, many with an acute presentation followed by rapid deterioration and death. For a full description of clinical presentations, pathophysiology, diagnosis, and treatment of NEC, refer to Chapter 89.
paragraphs.heading: Transfusion-Related Necrotizing Enterocolitis

paragraphs.text: Although the exact mechanism of NEC is not completely elucidated, ischemic insult to the gastrointestinal tract has been proposed as one major contributor to NEC. Some hypothesize that even subtle reductions in blood flow and subsequent reperfusion occurring in response to hypoxia may contribute to bowel injury. This phenomenon may be exacerbated by abnormalities associated with stored RBCs, including reduced erythrocyte deformability, increased erythrocyte adhesion/aggregation, and decreased nitric oxide stores. This last effect may predispose to vasoconstriction and further ischemic insult owing to transfused RBCs acting as a nitric oxide sink within the intestinal microvasculature. Microbial imbalance, immature intestinal development, and possible genetic factors may also contribute.29 Proposed, but unproven, pathologic mechanisms for transfusion-associated NEC include transfusion immunologic injury to the intestine similar to that observed in TRALI and/or transfusion-related ischemia/reperfusion injury as described previously.
paragraphs.heading: Transfusion-Related Necrotizing Enterocolitis

paragraphs.text: Retrospective studies have demonstrated a temporal association between RBC transfusion and neonatal NEC, with 25% to 38% of NEC cases occurring within 48 hours of RBC transfusion. In addition, the risk of transfusionassociated NEC increases with decreasing gestational age of the infant.30 However, other studies suggest that RBC transfusions may be an epiphenomenon with respect to NEC rather than a contributor to the pathogenesis of disease. In a meta-analysis of the published literature on transfusions and NEC, increased RBC transfusions were associated with lower rates of NEC; the direction of effect of RBC transfusions on NEC in randomized trials was opposite to that seen in observational studies.31 Keir and colleagues performed a separate systematic review and did not find an association between transfusions and NEC.32 One prospective study of 598 VLBW infants found that severe anemia (hemoglobin <8 g/dL), but not RBC transfusion, was associated with an increased risk of NEC.33 This was corroborated by a mouse model of phlebotomy-induced anemia which demonstrated that anemia alone appears to alter immune function and foster inflammatory cytokine secretion and intestinal injury, factors which increase the risk for NEC.29 Thus prevention of severe anemia may be more important than avoidance of RBC transfusion alone. The temporal relationship observed between RBC transfusion and neonatal NEC may represent reverse causation, whereby clinical instability from evolving NEC leads to RBC transfusion before the formal diagnosis of NEC.
paragraphs.heading: Transfusion-Related Necrotizing Enterocolitis

paragraphs.text: Previous retrospective studies have raised concern for another risk of transfusions among VLBW neonates based on an association between RBC transfusion and the development of, and progression to, severe IVH. (See also Chapter 55.) An analysis of 155 VLBW neonates with normal head ultrasounds during the first week of life indicated an
paragraphs.heading: Transfusion-Related Intraventricular Hemorrhage

paragraphs.text: association between RBC transfusion and the risk of developing a severe IVH within the first month, independent of hemoglobin level, initial pH, sepsis, ventilation, coagulation studies, or severe thrombocytopenia. During the first 72 hours of life, 67% of neonates who later developed severe IVH were noted to have received one or more RBC transfusions compared to 31% who did not develop IVH (P < .001).34 Additionally, each subsequent RBC transfusion during the first week was determined to double the risk of a severe IVH (each transfusion increased relative risk 2.02; 95% CI 1.54 to 3.33).
paragraphs.heading: Transfusion-Related Intraventricular Hemorrhage

paragraphs.text: These associations do not necessarily indicate a cause-andeffect relationship because of inherent limitations in retrospective studies such as failure to recognize confounding variables and susceptibility to bias. Furthermore, no difference in risk of IVH (all grades, or ≥ grade III) was seen in those infants randomized to liberal versus restrictive transfusion practices in either the multi-institutional Canadian Premature Infants in Need of Transfusion (PINT) study35 or the Bell study.36 A meta-analysis similarly did not identify increased rates of IVH in association with transfusions.32 Additional studies are needed to determine if early RBC transfusion plays any pathogenic role in IVH development or extension.
paragraphs.heading: Transfusion-Related Intraventricular Hemorrhage

paragraphs.text: Many infectious agents can be transmitted by blood or blood component transfusion (Table 84.2). These include viruses, bacteria, protozoa, and other pathogens. Current transfusion-transmitted disease testing for allogeneic blood donation in the United States includes hepatitis B virus surface antigen (HBsAg), hepatitis B virus core antibody (anti-HBc), anti-hepatitis C virus antibody (anti-HCV), antibody to human immunodeficiency virus HIV-1 and HIV-2, antibody to human T-lymphotropic virus (HTLV-I and HTLV-II), serology for syphilis and Trypanosoma cruzi, and nucleic acid testing (NAT) for HIV-1, HIV-2, HCV, HBV, West Nile virus (WNV), and Babesia (in states with higher prevalence).37
paragraphs.heading: Infectious Complications

paragraphs.text: The prevalence of human cytomegalovirus (CMV) ranges from 30% to 70% in blood donors based on demographic differences within areas of the United States and increases with age. This DNA virus remains latent within the leukocytes of immune persons and can be transmitted by transfusion of cellular blood components into seronegative recipients. There is wide variation in clinical sequelae from primary CMV infection, ranging from asymptomatic serologic conversion to significant morbidity and mortality from CMV-related pneumonia, cytopenias, and hepatic dysfunction. Premature, seronegative neonates weighing less than 1250 g, fetuses receiving intrauterine transfusions, severely immunocompromised individuals, and recipients of hematopoietic stem cell and solid-organ transplants are at increased risk for post-transfusion CMV-related morbidity and mortality.2
paragraphs.heading: Cytomegalovirus Infection

paragraphs.text: Because the prevalence of CMV seropositivity among blood donors limits the availability of seronegative components, supplementary strategies can be used to minimize the risk of transfusion transmitted CMV (TT-CMV) infection in high-risk infants. Use of fourth-generation leukoreduction filters at the time of collection of cellular products has been recommended for recipients at risk for TT-CMV. The Association for the Advancement of Blood and Biotherapies (AABB) states that “leukoreduced” blood products must contain fewer than 5 × 106 total white blood cells (WBCs) per unit. European standards maintain a more stringent definition of leukoreduced as less than 1 × 106 total WBCs per unit.15
paragraphs.heading: Cytomegalovirus Infection

paragraphs.text: Leukocyte reduction has been shown to be effective in preventing CMV infection in neonates, among other groups; however, whether leukocyte reduction is as efficacious as the use of CMV-seronegative blood has been disputed. A prospective observational study of 23 allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients in CMV-negative donorpatient paired individuals were transfused a total of 1847 leukoreduced cellular blood products from CMV “untested” donors and demonstrated no CMV DNA within the blood or CMV-associated clinical complications in the patients greater than 100 days post-transplant, despite anti-CMV IgG seroconversion in 17 of 23 patients.38 These reports support the notion that leukoreduced blood products are “CMV safe,” and some experts have argued that leukocytereduction alone is sufficient. However, no formal consensus on the debate of equivalency has been developed,39 leading many to advise against the elimination of “dual inventories” of blood products for CMV-seronegative and seropositive units. Nonetheless, variable strategies for preventing TT- CMV currently exist depending on the number of highrisk patients treated at a given center, the regional donor demographics, and product availability. A prospective multicenter birth cohort study revealed that transfusion of leukoreduced, CMV-seronegative blood products effectively prevented transmission of CMV to VLBW infants. In fact, acquisition of CMV in the patient population was primarily through maternal breast milk.40 Cell-free CMV remains a concern with current blood component processing as it can bypass all filters. Given the fact that no hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients developed TT-CMV even when low levels of CMV DNA were identified in the donations tested, the residual threat of TT-CMV after leukocyte reduction appears to be very low.41
paragraphs.heading: Cytomegalovirus Infection

paragraphs.text: Post-transfusion hepatitis A infection is an infrequent complication of transfusion because of the short period of viremia and the lack of an asymptomatic carrier state associated with the virus. The risk of hepatitis A transmission increases when the transfused product is derived from a pool of products, such as cryoprecipitate and plasma-derived clotting factors. Because they rely on solvent/detergent disruption of lipid membranes, purification processes used to treat derivatives of human plasma are ineffective against nonenveloped viruses such as hepatitis A.37 The virus has demonstrated varying susceptibility to pathogen reduction technologies.
paragraphs.heading: Hepatitis A Virus

paragraphs.text: Acute infection with HBV is symptomatic in about 50% of adults, and 5% to 10% of those infected become chronic carriers.37 In contrast, HBV infection acquired in infancy and early childhood is often asymptomatic, yet 70% of those infected become chronic carriers. Elimination of paid blood donors, uniform screening of blood donations for HBsAg, and routine immunization for hepatitis B improved the safety of the donor pool. Initiation of donor HBV NAT has further reduced the estimated incidence of TT-HBV to
paragraphs.heading: Hepatitis B Virus

paragraphs.text: levels close to HIV and HCV (about 1 in 1,000,000 units transfused) by shortening the window period (time interval between infection and laboratory test positivity when viral markers are too low for detection).42
paragraphs.heading: Hepatitis B Virus

paragraphs.text: HCV is a well-known cause of transfusion-associated hepatitis. Since the advent of NAT for HCV in the late 1990s, the incidence of transfusion-transmitted HCV has decreased to 1 in 1.9 million within the United States. This is because of shorter window periods from time of acute infection to laboratory markers of infection (8 days) within the donor population.37
paragraphs.heading: Hepatitis C Virus

paragraphs.text: Acute HCV infection is often asymptomatic, but the likelihood of developing chronic hepatitis exceeds 60%. Approximately one-third of those with untreated chronic hepatitis will develop hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis within two decades; those with cirrhosis have a 1% to 5% risk of hepatocellular carcinoma 20 years after cirrhosis is diagnosed. Long-term outcome is dependent upon the route of transmission, age when infected, gender, and coexisting morbidities. A retrospective study of 31 adults with transfusion-associated HCV acquired at birth (35 years earlier) described a milder disease with slower progression to hepatic fibrosis in perinatally acquired HCV than those who acquire HCV in early adulthood.43 In a look-back study involving previously transfused infants and children, 88% of those with silent infection (positive anti-HCV enzyme immunoassay) had persistent HCV viremia at 10 years post transfusion. This is in contrast to previously reported pediatric HCV clearance rates of 45% and 42% at 19.5 and 35 years post-transfusion, respectively, which indicated that pediatric patients, unlike adults, may clear HCV over time.43 The current standard treatment of chronic HCV infection in children ages 3 or older is pegylated-interferon-alpha and ribavirin. However, because of adverse effects (e.g., constitutional symptoms, bone marrow suppression, neuropsychiatric complications, hypothyroidism, and inhibited growth), therapy is often held until later in life. In adults, these medications have been largely supplanted by direct-acting antivirals (DAA) because of improved side effect profile and sustained virologic response. Practice guidelines for DAA use in children are available.44
paragraphs.heading: Hepatitis C Virus

paragraphs.text: The retroviruses HIV-1 and HIV-2 are the agents responsible for acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). In the United States, the vast majority of AIDS cases are related to HIV-1. Virtually all transfusion-transmitted HIV infections occurred before 1985, when serologic screening for HIV was initiated, and numerous effective methods of viral inactivation for plasma-derived clotting factor concentrates subsequently became available. Today, the risk of HIV transmission from blood transfusion is less than 1 in 2.1 million because of improved donor history screening and the advent of NAT testing in the late 1990s, which decreased the estimated window period to about 9 days.37
paragraphs.heading: HIV-1 and HIV-2

paragraphs.text: WNV, a mosquito-borne, single-stranded RNA virus of the Flaviviridae family, has become a major public health concern since its first detection in the United States in 1999. The first cases of transfusion-transmitted WNV occurred in 2002, with growing numbers of cases through 2004. Infection results in neuroinvasive disease (meningo-encephalitis, spastic paralysis) in roughly 20% of individuals, with more severe sequelae in the older adult and immunocompromised. Donors with WNV virus are commonly asymptomatic, meaning that the donor health questionnaire may fail to identify donors at risk. Despite implementation of pooled blood donor sample WNV NAT testing (which is converted to more sensitive individual donation testing when local disease activity exceeds preset thresholds) in 2003, sporadic cases of transfusion-transmitted WNV in immunosuppressed patients show that rare breakthrough transmissions may still occur in the United States.37
paragraphs.heading: West Nile Virus

paragraphs.text: Zika virus (ZIKV) is a flavivirus first discovered in the Zika Forest in Uganda in 1947. For many years, the virus caused sporadic outbreaks in Africa before gradually moving east. Several Pacific Islands were affected in 2013 to 2014. In 2016 the virus appeared in South America and rapidly spread. The virus is transmitted by the Aedes mosquito and therefore shows more activity during the summer months.
paragraphs.heading: Zika Virus

paragraphs.text: Unlike other flaviviruses, ZIKV has been associated with microcephaly and other fetal abnormalities when placental transmission occurs in an acutely infected pregnant woman and is currently under intense study.45 Of concern for blood supply safety, about 80% of infected patients are asymptomatic, resulting in great risk of a viremic blood donation and transmission to a susceptible donor before the advent of a suitable method of laboratory detection. Blood collections were temporarily halted in areas with local virus transmission (e.g., Puerto Rico) at the onset of the outbreak. In the fall of 2016, NAT screening of all donations in the United States was implemented under an investigational new drug protocol. During a period of about 2 months, 5 of 466,834 donations tested for ZIKV RNA were found to be positive.46 The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) cleared the first approved ZIKV detection test based on viral RNA in the plasma of blood donors in October 2017. To date, there have been no confirmed transfusiontransmission cases of ZIKV in the United States. However, cases of ZIKV transmission through platelet transfusions have been documented in Brazil. In 2021 the FDA determined that ZIKV no longer had sufficient incidence or prevalence to affect the potential donor population in the United States and permitted blood collectors to discontinue testing.47
paragraphs.heading: Zika Virus

paragraphs.text: The betacoronavirus (SARS-CoV-2) which causes the associated disease COVID-19 has undoubtedly had a negative
paragraphs.heading: COVID-19

paragraphs.text: impact on blood collection efforts because of social distancing measures and staffing shortages. Given its primary method of transmission via respiratory pathway, no cases of transfusion-transmitted infections have been documented. Asymptomatic individuals have at most very low viremia detectable in the blood. 48
paragraphs.heading: COVID-19

paragraphs.text: Transmission of babesiosis and malaria has been reported in neonates within endemic areas such as the northeast United States and Africa, respectively.49 Healthy patients transfused with Babesia microti–contaminated blood often do not get sick; however, transfusion-transmitted Babesia can be a significant cause of transfusion-related morbidity and mortality, especially for premature infants. Neonatologists in endemic areas should have a high index of suspicion for babesiosis in premature infants exposed to blood transfusions. At this time, blood products collected in United States regions with high prevalence of the disease (e.g., Minnesota, Wisconsin, Massachusetts, New York state, and Connecticut) are tested for Babesia by a NAT. However, implementation of nationwide testing has not been mandated because of cost-effectiveness considerations.37
paragraphs.heading: Emerging Pathogens

paragraphs.text: Continuous attention is being paid to emerging infections such as chikungunya, dengue fever, Ebola, T. cruzi, variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, and malaria, among others. Despite extensive donor screening and laboratory testing, these infections can still be transmitted through blood products. Pathogen reduction (PR)/inactivation offers the advantage of eliminating the risk of infection by any nucleic acid–containing agent, which includes viruses, bacteria, protozoa, and fungi (prions excluded). However, current pathogen reduction/techniques using nucleic acid–inactivating agents are still under investigation, because no single technique has proven to be effective for all blood components.
paragraphs.heading: Emerging Pathogens

paragraphs.text: Current screening approaches are reactive in nature and depend on pathogen identification, characterization of infectious markers, and development of detection assays. Although this iterative approach has greatly increased the safety of the blood supply, it requires significant resources and time to implement for each emerging pathogen.
paragraphs.heading: Pathogen Reduction

paragraphs.text: PR is an all-encompassing term for a variety of methods (e.g., photochemical activation or solvent detergent treatment) that may be applied to blood products following collection to confer broad protection against multiple infectious agents by countering proliferation and contamination.42 Many of these technologies target DNA or cell membranes and are effective across different classes of pathogens (e.g., viruses, bacteria, and parasites), offering the ability to interdict agents that are known to be transfusion-transmissible as well as emerging pathogens that pose uncertain risks to the blood supply.
paragraphs.heading: Pathogen Reduction

paragraphs.text: The appeal of pathogen reduction is that it is a proactive approach to blood safety that inactivates pathogens instead of only screening for their presence. Although developed to complement current testing, PR could ultimately prove to be an alternative to testing. If widely effective, PR could reduce the number of donor deferrals because of disease risk factors. Because PR inactivates white blood cells, it may provide additional benefits such as TA-GVHD prevention without the need for irradiation and alloimmunization reduction.50
paragraphs.heading: Pathogen Reduction

paragraphs.text: Two different methodologies of photochemical activation that have been more extensively studied will be briefly described, but others are at various stages of development. Thus far, these technologies have been applied only to platelets and plasma. Platelets are of primary concern because their storage at 20 to 24°C heightens their risk of contamination. No photochemical activation process is currently in clinical use for RBCs because of the obstacles associated with light absorption by hemoglobin.
paragraphs.heading: Pathogen Reduction

paragraphs.text: The only photochemical activation platform approved by the FDA at the time of this writing is the INTERCEPT system (Cerus, Concord, CA). This technique uses amotosalen, a compound which can intercalate between DNA bases. In the presence of activation by UVA light, this molecule irreversibly crosslinks with the DNA, thus preventing DNA transcription and cellular reproduction. After INTERCEPT treatment, an adsorption step removes excess amotosalen, resulting in minimal residual amounts in the transfused blood product.51
paragraphs.heading: INTERCEPT and Mirasol Systems

paragraphs.text: INTERCEPT is widely used for platelets and plasma and is approved in the United States and European Union for this purpose.52 The technology is effective against viruses, bacteria, and protozoans. However, breakthrough transmission has been reported with hepatitis A virus (HAV), hepatitis E virus (HEV), parvovirus B19, poliovirus, and certain spore-forming and/or fast-growing bacteria.53 There have also been cases of severe septic reactions with Acinetobacter baumannii complex and other bacteria because of processing or environmental contamination after INTERCEPT treatment.54
paragraphs.heading: INTERCEPT and Mirasol Systems

paragraphs.text: The Mirasol (Terumo BCT, Lakewood, CO) system uses riboflavin as a photosensitizer compound with ultraviolet B (UVB) light. Riboflavin readily traverses lipid membranes and then intercalates nonspecifically with nucleic acids. Upon exposure to UVB light, intercalated riboflavin-modified guanine residues promote the generation of oxygen radicals. Because riboflavin and its byproducts are naturally occurring, no additional steps for removal following treatment are believed to be necessary. Mirasol has shown efficacy against a wide variety of pathogens that pose a risk of transfusion transmission.55
paragraphs.heading: INTERCEPT and Mirasol Systems

paragraphs.text: A Cochrane review that evaluated 10 randomized controlled trials (RCT) (9 with INTERCEPT, 1 with Mirasol) showed no difference in clinically significant bleeding
paragraphs.heading: INTERCEPT and Mirasol Systems

paragraphs.text: or severe bleeding between recipients of pathogen-reduced platelets compared to control platelets. When evaluated, allcause mortality, product utilization, and adverse events were also not increased.56 Clinical trials performed with INTER- CEPT-treated plasma have shown no difference in clinical efficacy when compared to standard FFP.57
paragraphs.heading: INTERCEPT and Mirasol Systems

paragraphs.text: There is relative paucity of neonatal and pediatric safety data. A European prospective hemovigilance study of INTERCEPT-treated platelets following 19,175 transfusions in 2441 patients demonstrated a low incidence of acute transfusion reactions and a safety profile in line with conventional platelet components. Forty-six of the patients were neonates (<28 days of age) who received a range of 1 to 9 platelet transfusions, and 242 were children (<18 years of age) who received a range of 1 to 66 transfusions. Similar rates of adverse events occurred in children compared to adults. No events were reported in the neonates.58 In another study, Mirasol platelets were transfused to 2458 patients, including 99 neonates (age range not specified) and 379 children (<15 years of age). A historic cohort of 132 neonates was used for comparison. Overall, adverse event rate was similar in all patient groups, but neonates did have higher transfusion requirements when receiving PR platelets.59
paragraphs.heading: INTERCEPT and Mirasol Systems

paragraphs.text: Collection of autologous umbilical cord blood was first reported in 1979. Depending on the gestational age of the infant, the umbilical cord contains 75 to 120 mL of fetal blood, which could serve as an alternative source of RBCs for transfusion. It has been shown that collection of placental blood in both vaginal and cesarean deliveries is possible and that the RBC component is able to be stored for short periods of time (21 to 28 days) in additive solutions (e.g., AS-3). However, problems with obtaining sufficient volumes, clotting or hemolysis within the stored unit, and bacterial contamination are frequently reported, particularly in those who are most likely to benefit from autologous RBC transfusions (e.g., ELBW neonates).60 In most of the reports to date, autologous RBC transfusions have been shown to replace only a minority of allogeneic RBC transfusions needed by the infants, and the cost of collecting and storing autologous umbilical cord blood for subsequent RBC transfusion did not justify the limited benefits. For example, Khodabux and colleagues reported that of the 176 attempted autologous umbilical cord blood collections performed in neonates with gestational age less than 32 weeks, 101 (57%) yielded 15 mL/kg or greater, and only 64 (36%) yielded satisfactory units for transfusion.61 Furthermore, only 17% of umbilical cord blood collections were available for autologous RBC transfusions in infants with birth weights less than 1000 g. Of those infants who received autologous RBCs, their allogeneic RBC transfusion requirements were reduced by only 15%.61 As better techniques
paragraphs.heading: Autologous Red Blood Cell Transfusions

paragraphs.text: are developed for harvesting, storing, and administering autologous RBCs from the umbilical cord, the benefits of using autologous RBC transfusions may outweigh the cost and risks as a means to reducing the need of allogeneic RBC transfusion in VLBW infants. Reports have demonstrated improved techniques for the processes described above and the feasibility of using this autologous blood for thalassemia, autoimmune disease, cancer, renal failure, diabetes, infectious diseases, and other causes of anemia.60 However, additional large RCTs are needed to validate the safety and efficacy of this process before it can become routine neonatal intensive care unit practice.62
paragraphs.heading: Autologous Red Blood Cell Transfusions

paragraphs.text: Delayed clamping of the umbilical cord of premature infants has been reported as a successful variation of autologous transfusion. (See also Chapter 34.) A 2021 systematic review of 56 studies enrolling 6852 preterm infants found that delayed cord clamping was associated with lower odds of mortality, IVH and need for RBC transfusion compared to immediate cord clamping.63
paragraphs.heading: Delayed Cord Clamping and Cord Stripping

paragraphs.text: One limitation with delayed cord clamping is the required delay of 30 seconds or more in neonatal resuscitation during a VLBW delivery. As an alternative, “milking” or “stripping” the cord has been proposed. This is done by holding the placental end of the umbilical cord and gently moving blood within the umbilical vessels toward the neonate. This “stripping” is performed one to four times before clamping and cutting the cord. A Cochrane review in 2012 showed that delayed cord clamping up to 180 seconds or umbilical cord milking versus immediate cord clamping resulted in 39% fewer transfusions for anemia, 41% fewer patients with IVH, and 38% fewer patients with NEC.64 The aforementioned 2021 systematic review found that umbilical cord clamping was beneficial compared to immediate cord clamping with respect to odds of IVH and need for RBC transfusion. There was no significant difference for any assessed outcome between umbilical cord milking and delayed cord clamping.63 The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists currently recommends a delay in umbilical cord clamping in vigorous term and preterm infants for at least 30 to 60 seconds after birth.65
paragraphs.heading: Delayed Cord Clamping and Cord Stripping

paragraphs.text: Concern over transfusion-associated infections has encouraged directed-donor blood programs, including those that allow biologic parents to serve as directed donors for their neonates. No data exist to support the contention that directed-donor programs increase safety. Indeed, a retrospective review at a pediatric institution found that parental donors had higher rates of infectious-disease-testing positivity than community donors.66 Furthermore, paternal blood products are a poor choice in neonates with immune-mediated hemolysis (such as hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn, or HDFN) or neonatal alloimmune
paragraphs.heading: Parental Blood Donation

paragraphs.text: thrombocytopenia (NAIT). In these cases, transfused paternal cells express the antigens to which the mother has been sensitized and are passively transferred via the placenta to the neonate. Maternal plasma may contain alloantibodies directed against paternal RBC, leukocyte, platelet, and HLA antigens. Transfusion of any blood component containing maternal plasma exposes the infant to these antibodies, with the potential to cause significant hemolytic, thrombocytopenic, or pulmonary reactions. Given these concerns, when parental-directed donation is considered for an infant, the following recommendation should be reviewed with families and the provider: • All parental cellular blood components must be irradiated
paragraphs.heading: Parental Blood Donation

paragraphs.text: before transfusion to the neonate to prevent TA-GVHD. • If maternal RBCs or platelets are transfused, they should
paragraphs.heading: Parental Blood Donation

paragraphs.text: be given as washed/plasma reduced and irradiated. • Fathers are not recommended as RBC donors for their
paragraphs.heading: Parental Blood Donation

paragraphs.text: newborns. • Fathers should not donate granulocytes or platelets to
paragraphs.heading: Parental Blood Donation

paragraphs.text: their infants unless maternal serum is shown to lack lymphocytotoxic antibodies.
paragraphs.heading: Parental Blood Donation

paragraphs.text: In the first few days of life, full-term infants have an elevated hemoglobin concentration (14 to 20 gm/dL); however, because of physiologic decreases in erythropoietin (EPO) levels and rapidly expanding blood volumes, hemoglobin concentration decreases to a nadir of 10 to 12 gm/ dL at approximately 2 to 3 months of age before beginning to rise. This is referred to as the physiologic anemia of infancy or “physiologic nadir.” In preterm infants, this anemia is more significant, with mean nadirs of 8 gm/dL in VLBW infants (birth weight: 1000 to 1500 g) and 7 gm/ dL in ELBW infants (birth weight: <1000 g). This is the result of lower hemoglobin concentrations at birth, frequent blood sampling, low total blood volume (TBV) to blood
paragraphs.heading: Red Blood Cell Transfusion

paragraphs.text: sampling ratio, increased risk for other co-morbidities, and diminished capacity of the premature infant to increase EPO. Normal ranges of hemoglobin and Hct have been established for full-term and premature infants, yet guidelines for RBC transfusion therapy vary; however, many take into consideration postnatal age and cardiorespiratory support when setting thresholds for transfusion.67 In general, infants with significant cardiac or respiratory disease receive more aggressive RBC transfusion therapy. Recommended guidelines for replacement transfusion therapy in neonates are given in Table 84.3. Several studies have attempted to address high versus low threshold transfusion guidelines based on level of respiratory support in ELBW and VLBW infants. The multi-institutional Canadian PINT study35 (enrolling 451 ELBW preterm infants) demonstrated no advantage for liberal transfusion practices. However, the Bell study36 (enrolling 100 preterm infants) suggested that restrictive transfusion was associated with more apneic episodes, intraparenchymal brain hemorrhage, and periventricular leukomalacia. The disparate results may be a result of a greater hemoglobin difference in the restrictive/liberal transfusion groups (Bell study: 2.7 gm/dL versus PINT: 1.1 gm/dL) and a higher overall hemoglobin value in the liberal transfusion group in the Bell study compared to the PINT study.
paragraphs.heading: Red Blood Cell Transfusion

paragraphs.text: Interestingly, long-term developmental assessments of subgroups from both studies continued to show divergent results. Those individuals in the liberal transfusion group from the Bell cohort performed poorer than those in the restrictive group on visual memory, reading, and associative verbal fluency measures at school age, in accord with decreased intracranial volumes which were especially significant in females from the liberal transfusion cohort.68 Previously enrolled infants from the PINT study who were followed up at 18 to 21 months’ corrected age showed a statistically significant advantage of the liberal transfusion group on post-hoc analysis of cognitive delay defined as Mental Development Index (MDI) score less than 85; however, there was no significant difference in cerebral palsy,
paragraphs.heading: Red Blood Cell Transfusion

paragraphs.text: severe cognitive delay (MDI <70), severe hearing or visual impairment, or death.69
paragraphs.heading: Red Blood Cell Transfusion

paragraphs.text: Two more recent studies have sought to clarify previously conflicting results. The Transfusion of Prematures (TOP) trial randomized 1824 ELBW infants to a restrictive (7 to 11 g/dL) versus liberal (10 to 13 g/dL) transfusion strategy and found no significant differences in death or neurodevelopmental outcomes at 22 to 26 months corrected age.70 Concordant results were found in the Effects of Transfusion Thresholds on Neurocognitive Outcome of Extremely Low- Birth-Weight Infants (ETTNO) trial which randomized 1013 ELBW infants to restrictive versus liberal Hct transfusion thresholds and found no difference in death or disability at 24 months corrected age. The thresholds depended on the postnatal age and whether the health state was critical or noncritical.71 Taken together, these studies suggest that a restrictive transfusion threshold does not appear to put VLBW and ELBW infants at greater risk of poor neurodevelopmental outcomes; however, absolute thresholds for transfusion need to be individualized with consideration given to postnatal age, clinical status, and level of respiratory support.
paragraphs.heading: Red Blood Cell Transfusion

paragraphs.text: Most RBC transfusions in newborns are administered to either replace blood loss or treat anemia of prematurity. Blood loss can result from hemorrhage or phlebotomy. Iatrogenic losses from phlebotomy can be considerable but can be minimized by judicious testing strategies, sampling from indwelling catheters, using microtainers for laboratory assays, and implementing point-of-care testing.
paragraphs.heading: Red Blood Cell Transfusion

paragraphs.text: The use of recombinant human EPO has been proposed to decrease neonatal transfusion burden, donor exposure, and anemia of prematurity, as well as other co-morbidities. A 2020 Cochrane review assessing the effectiveness and safety of early (<8 days of life) initiation of erythropoiesisstimulating agents (ESAs) showed minimal benefits with regard to donor blood exposure, number of RBC transfusions, and volume of transfusions (mL/kg) in 3643 premature infants.72 There was some protective effect of ESAs on NEC (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.91) and IVH (RR 0.6, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.85). Although ESAs lowered the risk of neurodevelopmental impairment at 18 to 22 months’ corrected age (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.8), the results were mixed and the quality of evidence was low. A multi-center, randomized, double-blind trial of early, high-dose EPO administered to infants delivered between 24 and 0/7 weeks to 27 and 6/7 weeks through 32 weeks’ postmenstrual age showed no mortality or protection from severe neurodevelopmental impairment at 2 years of age.73 However, the treatment group received fewer transfusions (3.5 vs. 5.2, RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.75), lesser transfusion volume (47.6 mL vs. 76.3 mL, mean difference −25.66, 95% CI −33.26 to −18.07) and fewer donor exposures (1.6 vs. 2.4, RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.77). There were also a significant number who remained transfusion free in the treatment arm (43 in placebo vs. 117 in the treatment arm, P < .001).74 The greatest differences in transfusions were generally seen in infants born at later gestational ages. Meta-analysis of late ESA use
paragraphs.heading: Red Blood Cell Transfusion

paragraphs.text: (>8 days of life) involving 1651 preterm infants showed a significant decrease in the number of infants who required transfusion (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.79) and in the total number of transfusions received (mean difference −0.22, 95% CI −0.38 to 0.06); however, there were no differences in the total volume/kg transfused or decrease in the number of donor exposures as many infants received transfusions before ESA administration.75 There was no effect on incidence of co-morbidities aside from a nonsignificant trend toward increased risk of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) with ESA administration. When comparing early versus late initiation of ESAs, there were no significant reductions in the frequency of transfusion and the number of transfusions; however, there was a statistically significant increased risk of ROP in the early initiation group (RR 1.4, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.86).75 Therefore early ESA use may decrease donor exposures and transfusion volume; however, it is unclear how clinically meaningful those differences are, and there is currently no conclusive evidence that either early or late ESA use offers any clear morbidity and/or mortality benefit, though there may be a signal for increasing ROP.
paragraphs.heading: Red Blood Cell Transfusion

paragraphs.text: Before RBC transfusion, a blood sample is obtained for ABO and Rh determination (blood group and type) and to screen for antibodies against blood group antigens. Because antibodies identified in the neonate’s blood are most often of maternal origin, maternal blood can often serve as the source of serum/plasma for the antibody screen. A newborn’s ABO group is assigned solely on the testing of the patient’s RBCs for the A and B antigens (forward typing), because the isohemagglutinins anti-A and anti-B are not present in the serum at birth. The use of cord blood specimens for infant blood type determination is discouraged because of possible contamination with Wharton jelly and concerns about proper identification of the specimen.
paragraphs.heading: Pretransfusion Testing

paragraphs.text: If the newborn’s antibody screen is negative, ABO- and Rh-specific RBCs may be transfused, and the antibody screen does not need to be repeated during the remainder of the infant’s hospitalization until the infant reaches 4 months of age. If the screening identifies passively acquired maternal blood group antibodies, as in Rh HDFN, then O-negative RBCs should be transfused until repeat testing is negative for antibodies reacting against the ABO- or Rh-specific units. When antibodies to other RBC antigens other than RhD are detected, RBCs selected for transfusion should also be negative for the identified antibody or compatible by crossmatch. In cases when reconstituted whole blood is needed for large-volume transfusion procedures (i.e., exchange transfusions, cardiopulmonary bypass, ECMO), the neonate may be given plasma that is ABO-compatible with the neonate’s RBCs but receive RBCs that are compatible with maternal serum. This may result in disparate ABO group of the RBC and plasma units. An alternative used by some transfusion centers entails the use of low isohemagglutinin titer, group-O whole blood, if available.2 Infants whose Rh-negative mothers were treated with Rh
paragraphs.heading: Pretransfusion Testing

paragraphs.text: immune globulin (RhIG) during pregnancy often have a positive DAT because of circulating anti-D antibody from the RhIG. The clinician must distinguish this situation from Rh HDFN.
paragraphs.heading: Pretransfusion Testing

paragraphs.text: In infants older than 4 months of age, repeat testing for blood group, Rh-type, and antibody screening is performed within 72 hours of each RBC transfusion if the patient has received a transfusion during the last 3 months or if the history is uncertain or unavailable. Reverse ABO blood group testing, which detects anti-A and anti-B antibodies, is frequently deferred for the first 4 to 6 months of life, because this testing is often weak or nonreactive in babies less than 1 year of age.
paragraphs.heading: Pretransfusion Testing

paragraphs.text: Viability and functional activity of RBCs require that they be preserved in additive solutions that support their metabolic demands. All anticoagulant/preservative (AP) solutions contain citrate, phosphate, and dextrose (CPD), which function as an anticoagulant, a buffer, and a source of RBC metabolic energy, respectively. The addition of mannitol and adenine to existing additive solutions has increased the shelf life of RBCs from 21 days (CPD) to 35 days (CPDA-1) and to 42 days for newer AP solutions (Adsol [AS-1], Nutricel [AS-3], Optisol [AS-5]) by stabilizing the RBC membrane and maintaining 2,3-diphosphoglycerate and adenosine triphosphate within erythrocytes. Studies have shown that extended-storage preservative solutions are as safe and efficacious as CPDA-1 RBCs in increasing the Hct for neonates receiving small-volume (10 to 15 mL/kg) RBC transfusions.2 However, there are no clinical studies that have confirmed or refuted the effect of an AP on metabolic abnormalities in massive transfusion (>20 mL/kg) for the neonate. Therefore some experts recommend avoiding RBCs stored in extended-storage media (AS-1, AS-3, AS-5) for large-volume transfusions.
paragraphs.heading: Red Blood Cell Preparations

paragraphs.text: Data are mixed regarding the utility of washing RBCs for neonates. Meta-analysis based on limited evidence suggests that there is no evidence of benefit.76 However, modern studies evaluating specific effects on cytokine responses in preterm infants (<29 weeks) suggest that washing may modulate the pro-inflammatory response to transfusion, yet the effect on clinical outcomes remains unknown.77
paragraphs.heading: Red Blood Cell Preparations

paragraphs.text: The highest relative blood volumes (mL/kg) are found in neonates. Adult blood volumes on a per-kilogram basis are achieved by 3 months of age (Table 84.4). A typical replacement transfusion is 10 to 15 mL of RBCs per kilogram. Because infants are so small, many pediatric transfusion centers dispense small aliquots from one RBC unit (300 to 350 mL) to one or several neonates who require multiple transfusions to decrease donor exposure and to conserve RBC inventory. This practice requires sterile connecting devices to assure that the original RBC unit remains a closed system and transfer packs or syringe sets that permit multiple aliquots to be removed. Studies have shown that
paragraphs.heading: Red Blood Cell Dose and Administration

paragraphs.text: CPDA-1 and AS-3-preserved split RBC packs effectively limit donor exposures and are safe for use in neonatal smallvolume transfusions after 35 days of storage.
paragraphs.heading: Red Blood Cell Dose and Administration

paragraphs.text: A few small studies have compared the consequences of RBCs on clinical outcomes; however, only one prospective study has been conducted in premature infants to evaluate whether fresh RBCs (≤7 days) decreased morbidity and mortality in VLBW infants compared with standard RBCs. In the Age of Red Blood Cells in Premature Infants (ARIPI) trial conducted in Canada, 188 infants provided with fresh RBC transfusions (mean age of transfused RBCs 5.1 days, SD 2.0 days) did not demonstrate an improvement in a composite outcome measure of major neonatal morbidities (NEC, IVH, bronchopulmonary dysplasia [BPD], and ROP) or death at 30 and 90 days compared with the 189 infants who received standard RBC products (mean age of transfused RBCs 14.6 days, SD 8.3 days) despite having 60% more donor exposures.78 Although an unblinded RCT suggested an advantage in clinical outcomes in neonates with congenital heart disease receiving reconstituted fresh whole blood defined as less than 48 hours old when dispensed for cardiopulmonary bypass pump priming and postoperative transfusion support,79 the role of fresh RBCs for routine transfusion support in premature infants has not shown a clear benefit. ARIPI has subsequently been criticized for insufficient separation of mean RBC storage time between its two cohorts (<2 weeks) and for inadequately addressing the issue of storage lesion in the oldest additive solution units (35 to 42 days). However, based on the results of this and other RCTs in older children and adults, such as ABC PICU,80 RECESS,81 and TOTAL,82 guidelines for neonatal transfusion do not recommend limiting the age of transfused RBCs to less than 10 days.83
paragraphs.heading: Red Blood Cell Dose and Administration

paragraphs.text: Because RBC units are stored at 4 to 6°C, hypothermia can develop after massive transfusion unless the blood products are first warmed to body temperature. Inline blood warmers should be used for RBC exchange transfusions, and radiant heaters should be avoided because they can result in hemolysis of the RBC component. When phototherapy is in progress, the blood component and tubing should be positioned so as to minimize exposure to phototherapy light, which may also cause hemolysis.2
paragraphs.heading: Red Blood Cell Dose and Administration

paragraphs.text: As with older children and adults, platelet transfusions are administered to neonates therapeutically or prophylactically to prevent the hemorrhagic complications of thrombocytopenia. Neonates have different risks of bleeding given the same degree of thrombocytopenia. For example, thrombocytopenic neonates with NAIT have a high risk of major bleeding, whereas those with sepsis, NEC, or intrauterine growth restriction have an intermediate and low risk of major hemorrhage, respectively. Differences in platelet function or concurrent coagulopathy are likely causes for these discrepancies. A historic RCT addressing whether platelet transfusions reduce major bleeding in neonates found no benefit of maintaining a normal platelet count (platelets >150,000/μL) in preterm neonates compared with those maintained at greater than 50,000/μL. However, this study did not address bleeding risk or transfusion benefit for neonates with platelet counts less than 50,000/μL.84 A more recent RCT, the Platelet Transfusion Thresholds in Premature Neonates (PlaNet-2) study, compared prophylactic platelet transfusion thresholds of 25,000/μL and 50,000/μL in terms of mortality and major bleeding complications in 660 premature infants (less than 34 weeks). Infants randomized to the higher transfusion threshold had higher occurrence of a new major bleeding episode or death than infants randomized to the lower threshold (26% vs. 19%, P = .02).85
paragraphs.heading: Platelet Transfusion Indications

paragraphs.text: Subsequent secondary analysis demonstrated that a threshold of 25,000/μL was safe for all preterm neonates regardless of their baseline risk of bleeding or death.86 Another recent RCT examined the effect of platelet transfusion on time to patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) closure in 44 thrombocytopenic preterm (<35 weeks’ gestation) neonates randomized to either a liberal transfusion group (platelet count >100,000/μL) or standard transfusion group (platelet count >20,000/μL). Not only was there no difference in PDA closure time, but the liberal transfusion group also had a significantly higher rate of IVH compared to the standard transfusion group (40.9% vs. 9.1%, P = .034).87
paragraphs.heading: Platelet Transfusion Indications

paragraphs.text: Historically, neonatal platelet transfusion threshold policies varied widely88 and were largely based on expert panel recommendations garnered from clinical experience because of the absence of high-quality evidence. Because of the concern for IVH in the sick neonate, many physicians traditionally adopted an aggressive platelet threshold for transfusion (e.g., platelet count >100,000/μL in high-risk patients). However, in a cross-sectional observational study of neonatal outcomes with severe thrombocytopenia, Stanworth and colleagues failed to show a clear relationship between nadir platelet count/degree of thrombocytopenia and major hemorrhage (intraventricular, pulmonary, intra-abdominal, hematuria). In the 169 neonates studied with severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count nadir <60,000/μL), 154 (91%) did not experience major hemorrhage. Of the 15 (9%) that experienced major
paragraphs.heading: Platelet Transfusion Indications

paragraphs.text: hemorrhage, 12 patients (80%) had a platelet count nadir before the hemorrhage of greater than 20,000/μL,89 and follow-up analysis revealed that thrombocytopenia alone was not a strong indicator of bleeding risk, whereas gestational age (<34 weeks), early onset of postnatal thrombocytopenia (<10 days after birth), and coexistence of NEC were strong clinical risk factors for bleeding in this population.90 Retrospective studies have also failed to establish a link between the severity of thrombocytopenia and risk of IVH91 across both liberal and restrictive transfusion practices.92 A retrospective study of VLBW infants demonstrated that a restrictive platelet transfusion protocol using platelet count thresholds of 25,000/μL in clinically stable neonates and 50,000/μL in clinically unstable neonates, extremely premature neonates within the first week of life, or neonates at high risk of major bleeding was not associated with an increased risk for IVH compared with a more aggressive transfusion protocol.92 Before publication of the two RCTs supporting a transfusion threshold of 20,000 to 25,000/μL, a 2016 retrospective review found that a majority of neonatal platelet transfusions in the United States were administered for pretransfusion platelet counts of ≥50,000/μL in VLBW infants despite evidence that platelet transfusion had little appreciable impact on the risk of IVH after adjustment for underlying clinical variables.93
paragraphs.heading: Platelet Transfusion Indications

paragraphs.text: In light of the recent RCT findings demonstrating increased harm associated with maintaining higher platelet counts, a platelet count of 25,000/μL appears to be a reasonable transfusion threshold for preterm infants who are not bleeding, over 7 days old, and not undergoing an invasive procedure in the following 24 hours.2,94 For neonates who do not meet the criteria above, transfusion decisions should be based on clinical judgment and individual patient characteristics and risk of bleeding. Current recommended thresholds for neonatal platelet transfusion are listed in Box 84.2. Platelet transfusions are also indicated to treat hemorrhage associated with acquired (i.e., ECMO,
paragraphs.heading: Platelet Transfusion Indications

paragraphs.text: cardiopulmonary bypass, uremia) or congenital qualitative platelet abnormalities (i.e., Glanzmann thrombasthenia, Bernard-Soulier syndrome), even if the platelet count is within the normal range.
paragraphs.heading: Platelet Transfusion Indications

paragraphs.text: Platelets express intrinsic ABO antigens but not Rh antigens. In patients with limited blood volumes, they should be ABO-group specific whenever possible because of reports of intravascular hemolysis following transfusion of ABOincompatible platelets in infants and children. Platelets do not routinely require cross-matching unless they contain over 2 mL of contaminating RBCs.95 Although Rh matching does not affect post-transfusion platelet survival, RBCs are present in small amounts of whole blood–derived platelet concentrates (and even smaller amounts in apheresis platelets) and can potentially cause Rh sensitization in an Rh-negative recipient. However, actual alloimmunization rates in children and adults following exposure to Rh-positive platelet transfusion have been extremely low (<2%).96 Depending on clinical circumstances or institutional policy, administration of RhIG may be considered for Rh-negative neonates, especially females, within 72 hours of exposure to Rh-positive RBCs through a platelet transfusion. The recommended immune globulin dose is 120 IU per mL of RBCs transfused if administered intramuscularly or 90 IU per mL of RBCs if administered intravenously.28
paragraphs.heading: Pretransfusion Testing

paragraphs.text: A standard unit of platelets, prepared from a single donation of whole blood, contains at least 5.5 × 1010 platelets in 50 to 70 mL of plasma. Apheresis platelets, often called singledonor platelets, contain a minimum of 3 × 1011 platelets in approximately 250 mL (range: 200 to 400 mL) of plasma, the equivalent of an estimated 6 units of whole blood– derived platelets. There are two ways to calculate platelet doses in neonates, based on mL/kg or based on equivalent units/kg. An equivalent unit (EU) is the volume of a platelet aliquot that has a minimum platelet content of 5.5 × 1010. Because one apheresis unit contains at least 3 × 1011 platelets, the content of an apheresis platelet unit is equivalent to approximately 6 units of whole blood–derived platelets. The standard dose based on this method is 1 EU per 5 to 10 kg with a minimum dose of 1 EU. EU-based dosing offers the advantage of reducing platelet content variability in the transfused product because a minimum platelet content will be administered regardless of its volume. This may be clinically significant in sick neonates with thrombocytopenia.
paragraphs.heading: Component Definition and Dosing

paragraphs.text: Platelet components may be volume reduced to 15 to 20 mL for patients requiring significant volume restrictions, but this is associated with significant platelet loss of 15% to 35% and may affect platelet function adversely. Rapid decreases in pH have also been observed for aliquots stored in syringes after volume reduction; for this reason, infusion of these products is recommended within 4 to 6 hours of processing to avoid induction or exacerbation of acidosis in transfusion recipients.97 Platelets are stored at 20 to 24°C
paragraphs.heading: Component Definition and Dosing

paragraphs.text: under constant agitation and have a shelf life of up to 7 days after collection, depending on bacterial contamination mitigation strategy. Transfusion of 10 to 15 mL/kg of platelets for neonates, or 1 EU per 5 to 10 kg for children over 5 to 10 kg, should yield a platelet increment of 50,000 to 100,000/μL if no predisposing risk factors for refractoriness exist. It is important to account for device-related dead space (10 to 30 mL) when issuing the product, as this can be considerable in relation to the overall platelet dose. The expected rise in the platelet count after transfusion may not be met because of destructive thrombocytopenia occurring with splenomegaly, fever, sepsis, DIC, bleeding, or antibiotic therapy. Immune-mediated causes of platelet refractoriness, such as alloantibodies to platelet-specific antigens (e.g., HPA-1a, 5b) in NAIT and autoantibodies to common platelet antigens in idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, require consideration in this population so that appropriate management can be initiated.2
paragraphs.heading: Component Definition and Dosing

paragraphs.text: Neonates, particularly those with VLBWs, are susceptible to overwhelming bacterial infection. Many factors contribute to this risk, including disruption of mucosal barriers, hypogammaglobulinemia, and qualitative neutrophil defects. Furthermore, preterm neonates may become neutropenic during sepsis because of a reduced capacity to increase myeloid progenitor cell proliferation with infections. Transfusion of granulocytes has been used in the treatment of neonatal sepsis; however, the efficacy of such transfusions is controversial. Meta-analysis of the safety and efficacy of granulocyte infusion adjunctive to antimicrobial therapy in the treatment of septic neutropenic neonates failed to show that granulocyte infusions reduce mortality or morbidity, although a reduction in the latter approached statistical significance.98 The Resolving Infection in Neutropenia with Granulocytes (RING) randomized clinical trial compared standard antimicrobial therapy alone against daily granulocyte transfusion from donors stimulated with granulocyte colony stimulating factor (GCSF) and dexamethasone in addition to standard therapy and found no difference in survival or microbial response in the granulocyte arm,99 although secondary analyses indicated that higher doses of granulocytes achieved through GCSF stimulation were associated with better outcomes than lower doses.100 Although children (defined as <18 years of age) were included in this study, they comprised only a minority of the total number of subjects (6/49 in control arm, 4/48 in granulocyte arm).99 In spite of the conflicting evidence, granulocyte transfusion may be considered in neonates with qualitative neutrophil defects with severe (or progressive) bacterial or fungal infection who have not responded to appropriate aggressive antimicrobial treatment.
paragraphs.heading: Granulocyte Transfusion

paragraphs.text: Granulocyte concentrates for neonatal transfusion are prepared by automated leukapheresis of healthy stimulated (dexamethasone ± GCSF) donors and contain 1 to 2 × 109 neutrophils per kilogram in a volume of 10 to 15 mL/kg.
paragraphs.heading: Granulocyte Transfusion

paragraphs.text: Treatment should be continued daily until clinical improvement or neutrophil count recovery (absolute neutrophil count >3000/μL in first week of life; >1500/μL thereafter). All granulocytes should be gamma or x-ray irradiated to prevent TA-GVHD, and leukodepletion is obviously contraindicated. Although CMV-seronegative granulocytes may be preferred for naive recipients to prevent transfusion-transmitted infection, practical considerations must be taken into account because such products may not always be available on short notice. Because granulocyte concentrates have a significant amount of RBCs (Hct: 15% to 20%), the component must be ABO/Rh and cross-match compatible with the intended neonatal recipient. Because granulocytes must be transfused within 24 hours of collection, FDA-mandated testing for blood products will not be completed before the product is released for administration. Overall, the risks and benefits of transfusing an untested or CMV-positive blood product must be weighed by the medical team and the parents of the infant and documented accordingly in the medical record.2
paragraphs.heading: Granulocyte Transfusion

paragraphs.text: There are unique risks to granulocyte transfusion. They include varying degrees of pulmonary reactions from mild transient respiratory distress to severe pulmonary edema, hypoxia, and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), as well as a high incidence of febrile transfusion reactions. Pulmonary complications have been reported in 4% of transfused infants, and severe pulmonary reactions resembling TRALI have been reported.98 Mild to moderate reactions occur in 25% to 50% and severe reactions in about 1% of all granulocyte transfusions.99 Administration of amphotericin B should not occur within 6 hours of granulocyte transfusion because of suspected increased risk of severe pulmonary reactions. Polycythemia secondary to granulocyte transfusion is an infrequently reported complication but may be especially relevant in neonates, owing to the large volume of RBCs within the granulocyte product relative to the patient’s blood volume. Given the relatively high RBC volume in granulocyte concentrates (Hct 15% to 20%), a significant increase in the patient’s Hct may be observed when granulocytes are given at doses of 15 to 20 mL/kg for several days in a row.101
paragraphs.heading: Granulocyte Transfusion

paragraphs.text: Although granulocyte colony-stimulating factor and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor have been used successfully to stimulate neutrophil numbers, and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) has been attempted to augment traditional antimicrobial therapy to support septic neonates, data on efficacy are inconclusive.102,103 Because of the lack of clear consensus on their impact on improving host defense mechanisms and improving outcomes, these adjuncts to standard antimicrobial and antifungal therapy require further investigation.
paragraphs.heading: Granulocyte Transfusion

paragraphs.text: Plasma can be prepared by either whole blood separation or by apheresis. When the plasma product is frozen to −18°C or colder within 8 hours of collection, it is labeled as FFP
paragraphs.heading: Fresh Frozen Plasma Transfusion

paragraphs.text: (approximately 250 to 300 mL) and can be stored at this temperature for up to 1 year.2 FP24 has a similar shelf life and is considered essentially bioequivalent to FFP with the exception of factor VIII activity, which is typically 15% to 30% lower.104 To conserve plasma inventory and limit donor exposures for infants who receive only fractions of an adult-sized unit, plasma can be separated into multiple satellite bags and frozen as aliquots. Once thawed, plasma components can be further subdivided into aliquots for multiple neonates via sterile connecting devices, stored at 1°C to 6°C for up to 5 days, and transfused as “thawed plasma.”2 Although thawed plasma has approximately 40% factor V and VIII (heat labile factors) activity, effective hemostasis is maintained at this level, making thawed plasma clinically similar to FFP and FP24.
paragraphs.heading: Fresh Frozen Plasma Transfusion

paragraphs.text: Plasma is used primarily to treat acquired coagulation factor deficiencies as a result of DIC, liver failure, exposure to extracorporeal circuits,105 and vitamin K deficiency from malabsorption, biliary disease, warfarin therapy, or dilutional coagulopathy from massive transfusion. It can also be used for specific factor replacement in congenital factor deficiencies when specific factor concentrates or recombinant products are not manufactured or unavailable (e.g., factor V).2 Additionally, it may be combined with RBCs to form reconstituted whole blood for neonatal exchange or extracorporeal circuit (cardiopulmonary bypass or ECMO) priming.94 However, the optimal role of plasma in neonatal transfusion practice has not been established through evidence-based studies, and a majority of plasma transfusions in patients of all ages appear to be given for prophylactic purposes.106 Recent transfusion guidelines do not recommend routine use of plasma for correction of coagulopathy in neonates without clinically significant bleeds. In contrast, plasma may be of use in neonates with significant bleeding, including those requiring massive transfusion or at high risk for bleeding because of an invasive procedure or significant coagulopathy as evidenced by markedly prolonged prothrombin time (PT) or activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT). Plasma is not indicated for volume expansion, enhancement of wound healing, or as first-line treatment for congenital factor deficiencies when either a virally inactivated, plasma-derived factor concentrate or recombinant factor is available.
paragraphs.heading: Fresh Frozen Plasma Transfusion

paragraphs.text: Plasma transfusions should be ABO-compatible with the neonate’s RBCs to avoid passive transfer of isohemagglutinins from ABO-incompatible plasma, which may result in hemolysis.2 Because the freezing process renders the frozenthawed plasma component free of viable leukocytes, plasma products are not screened for CMV antibody, nor are leukoreduction and irradiation necessary for the prevention of CMV reactivation and TA-GVHD, respectively. However, passive administration of antibody to CMV in plasma may cause CMV IgG testing to become positive in the transfused neonate. This does not represent CMV infection, and the antibody disappears in a time course consistent with the 21-day half-life of gamma-globulin.38
paragraphs.heading: Fresh Frozen Plasma Transfusion

paragraphs.text: Plasma is typically dosed at 10 to 15 mL/kg. Assuming that 1 mL of plasma equates to 1 U of factor activity (definition of 100% activity), one can predict the amount of replacement of most factors following plasma transfusion.
