Medical expenses in children who have undergone surgical intervention for NEC continue to be higher for 1 to 2 years.52 Outpatient follow-up of infants who have had NEC is vital because of the significant long-term consequences of this disease. Standardized multidisciplinary approaches with particular attention to nutrition and rehabilitation should be utilized.

### Pathophysiology of Necrotizing Enterocolitis

As previously mentioned, we would like to preface this section with the disclaimer that we do not have a good definition of NEC. Therefore the information provided is what is currently available that relates to a form of intestinal injury referred to as NEC that involves a multifactorial pathway, and these may represent more discrete entities.

NEC pathogenesis has historically been attributed to the multifactorial nature of its development. Several risk factors, such as formula feeding, prematurity, ischemia, dysmotility, dysbiosis, and compromised intestinal host response, have led to one common pathway.43,53,54 What we refer to as NEC represents more than one disease (or endotype). Each of these diseases is being shown to have a different pathophysiology. Considering this, we need to evaluate NEC not as one disease but as various diseases with

different pathophysiologies, such as is done in cancer and diabetes. The classic form of NEC is associated with prematurity, with 90% of cases developing prior to 37 weeks’ corrected gestational age, implying that NEC is specific to the developing underdeveloped gut. It occurs at 2 to 6 weeks of age, with the highest incidence of the disease occurring at 28 to 32 weeks of corrected gestational age. Although many factors predispose preterm infants to NEC, prematurity, formula feeding, impaired mucosal defenses, altered immune response and mucosal development, and intestinal dysbiosis are major contributing factors for NEC development.55–57 A concerted effort elucidates the factors associated with prematurity that predispose this already vulnerable population to NEC. Those factors are categorized and described below.

### Altered Host Defense, Inflammatory Mediators, and Immune Response

The ability of premature infants to respond to and control infection is significantly different from full-term newborns. This complicated and interconnected system is comprised of • Physical barriers that prevent intrusion of infectious

agents (skin, mucous membranes, epithelium of the intestine with the mucous layer, and biomedical factors) • Innate and adaptive immune systems (including cellular

and humoral components) Human and animal studies indicate that the abovementioned barriers are deficient in premature infants compared to term infants and adults.58,59 This deficiency can be quantitative, qualitative, or both for different elements of the host defense. The ability of gastric parietal cells to secrete acid is also diminished in premature infants. Coordination of contractile activity in the developing gut corresponds with gestational age. The mature pattern of peristalsis is not developed until around 36 weeks of gestational age.

There is a lack of data on gestational development of a tight junctional barrier, but this barrier is thought to be deficient in premature infants.60 The defense mechanisms of the intestinal epithelial layer itself are underdeveloped in preterm infants. This includes decreased numbers of Paneth cells. Paneth cells produce several peptides (lysozyme, defensins, and secretory phospholipase A2) that play essential roles in protecting the intestinal epithelium from bacterial invasion and shaping the microbiome. The ability of goblet cells to secrete mucin is also increasing throughout gestation and achieves maturity at term.61 The mucous layer protects the intestinal epithelium from interacting with pathogenic microorganisms while creating an environment for the growth of commensal microorganisms.62

Of particular interest is an excessive proinflammatory phenotype of macrophages observed in patients with NEC compared to healthy term infants. Studies explain this phenomenon by upregulation of Smad7 in macrophages of patients with NEC, which inhibits transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β).63–65 The latter factor downregulates the proinflammatory response of macrophages. Intraepithelial lymphocytes (IELs) can be an essential communication


## PDF page 1656

channel between intestinal content and the adaptive immune system. The predominant type of IELs in the intestine of preterm infants is γδ cells.66 They play an essential role in mucosal defense and are significantly decreased in intestinal samples obtained from infants with NEC.

Another imbalance in the cellular component of the immune system of infants with NEC is a shift in T-cell differentiation with an increase in CD4+ Th17 lymphocytes and a decrease in counter-inflammatory Treg cells.67 Interleukin-17 (IL-17), a product of CD4+ Th17 lymphocytes, leads to increased apoptosis of enterocytes and negatively affects intestinal epithelial tight junctions and the proliferation of enterocytes.54 The CD4+ Th17/Treg disbalance was also shown to result in apoptosis of Lgr5+ intestinal stem cells in the mouse model.68 The B-cell arm of the adaptive immune system serves as antigen-presenting cells and produces immunoglobulins. Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is of particular significance, as animal studies have shown that secretory IgA (sIgA) shapes intestinal microbiota and regulates the maturation of intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) and development of the intestinal barrier function.69–71 Short- and long-term benefits of exposure to maternal sIgA have also been shown. sIgA in human breast milk is considered one of the components contributing to the protective effect of this mode of nutrition, especially in preterm infants. A review of studies that evaluated the potential benefit of immunoglobulins in preterm infants did not show a reduction in NEC incidence.72 It is important to point out that only studies of intravenous immunoglobulins were reviewed.

Intestinal epithelium, to some extent, can be viewed as a teeter-totter, with the microbiome on one side and the hyperactivated immune system on the other. Pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) of intestinal microbiota bind and activate a series of pattern recognition receptors (PRRs). TLR-4 receptors and their activation are one of the cornerstones in NEC pathogenesis.56,67 These receptors participate in normal gut development in humans and mice.73 This explains the higher level of expression of these receptors in the developing gut. In premature infants, TLR-4 expression remains elevated after birth and peaks at the same time of highest risk for NEC.57,74 The TLR-4 receptors located on IECs are activated by lipopolysaccharide (LPS), abundant in cell walls of gram-negative bacteria that colonize the gut.75 This activation leads to several adverse effects: increased apoptosis, impaired regeneration of IECs, and proinflammatory cytokine response. Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress resulted from TLR-4 activation in animal studies.76 All of the above features are essential elements of NEC. Human breast milk significantly reduces TLR-4 signaling in neonatal mice via activation of the EGF receptor, which may explain its protective action against NEC.77 TLR-9, however, seems to counterbalance the proinflammatory response of TLR-4 activation.74 Further studies on TLRs are being done.

NOD receptors are a family of intracellular receptors present in monocytes, Paneth cells, and IECs.78 Peptidoglycan from the bacterial wall of gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria serve as a ligand for NOD receptors. NOD2 receptors mediate the production of defensins by Paneth cells.79 NOD2 activation was shown to inhibit TLR-4 in IECs and decrease apoptosis while improving mucosal intestinal injury repair.80 NOD2 provides a way of communication between intestinal commensal bacteria and the innate immune system. One population-based study from Germany showed that VLBW infants with two or more NOD2 variant alleles were at higher risk of developing surgical NEC.81 Refer to Table 89.2 for the roles of cytokines and chemokines in the pathogenesis of NEC.

Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and the development of intestinal microvasculature also appear to be involved in the pathogenesis of NEC. One study demonstrated that VEGF level is decreased in intestinal tissue obtained from infants with NEC.82 An animal study also demonstrated the importance of VEGF and its receptor signaling for maintaining the integrity of intestinal microvasculature in the postnatal period.83 Interestingly, the peak incidence of NEC occurs at the same corrected gestational age as retinopathy of prematurity (ROP). This coincidence is intriguing, and whether this relates to the VEGF system requires additional research.

### Dysbiosis

Sterility of the fetus in utero had been a well-accepted notion; however, we now know that microorganisms colonize the fetal gut before birth.84 Culture and non–culturebased studies have revealed the presence of microorganisms in the amniotic fluid, placenta, and meconium. Known factors that affect gut colonization in infants are preterm birth, mode of delivery, the use of antibiotics, and breast milk versus formula feeding. The resemblance between fetal and neonatal bacterial colonization on one side and bacterial flora of the maternal oral cavity and placenta on the other side strongly points to the hematogenous transfer of bacteria during gestation.85–87 The microbiome of a developing gut can modify health outcomes of both term and preterm infants for years to come. The intestinal microbial environment plays a crucial role in the development of NEC. Bacterial colonization of the intestine has been revealed as a requirement in developing NEC as bacterial endotoxin identified in the blood of infants with NEC.88,89 The study of gut colonization in preterm infants showed that shifts in predominant bacterial classes are well orchestrated and abrupt: from bacilli to Gammaproteobacteria and then to Clostridia.90 The proportion of anaerobes approached that of older children by 33 to 36 weeks of postconceptual age. Factors such as gestational age at sample collection, mode of delivery, and antibiotic treatment affected only the pace of colonization but not the actual sequence of bacterial classes.91,92

Studies comparing stool microbiome of preterm infants who developed NEC with matched controls found an increase in Gammaproteobacteria and a decrease in Clostridia and Negativicutes in those infants who developed NEC.6,91–93 A systematic review and meta-analysis of sequencing data from 14 studies showed that preterm infants that developed NEC had increased relative abundance of Gammaproteobacteria and decreased relative abundance of Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes. Increased relative abundance of Gammaproteobacteria prior to the development of NEC emerged as a critical element of a dysbiotic shift observed in this pathology. This provides an abundance of LPS—a ligand of the TLR-4 receptor. TLR-4 activation, as discussed earlier, is a crucial step in the pathogenesis of

NEC. Further studies using a metagenomic and multi-omic systems biology approach are needed.

### Enteral Feedings

Most NEC cases occur in infants who have received partial or full enteral nutrition. The disease usually develops days to weeks after initiation of enteral feedings; therefore this form of alimentation was regarded as an important risk factor for the classic form of NEC for decades. Delaying initiation and slow advancement of enteral feedings were used to avoid this dreaded disease; however, several studies have shown that these methods did not prevent or decrease NEC incidence.94,95 Results from animal and adult human studies provide compelling evidence that these practices have a negative impact on the gastrointestinal tract, including mucosal atrophy, bacterial translocation, sepsis, and dysregulation in the secretion of trophic hormones. Neonatal studies suggest that more extended nil per os (NPO) status in preterm infants is associated with an increased risk for NEC and an increase in intestinal inflammation.96,97 In 2022, a Cochrane review dedicated to this question found no evidence that delaying initiation of enteral feeding beyond 4 days of life affects the risk of NEC development.98 This review included 1551 infants from 14 RCTs. Delayed introduction of progressive feeds has also been associated with fewer days on full feeds and increased morbidities such as ROP, bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), and intestinal inflammation.97,99 When enteral nutrition is initiated, the controversy shifts toward determining the optimal rate of volume advancement. A Cochrane review published in 2021 included 13 RCTs with 4033 infants. Slow advancement was defined as a daily increment of 15 to 20 mL/ kg of enteral feeding volume and faster advancement as a daily increment of 30 to 40 mL/kg. No difference in NEC risk and all-cause mortality was found between the groups. Advancing at a slower rate may slightly increase the risk for infection.100 The recently published Speed of Increasing milk Feeds Trial (SIFT) randomized more than 2800 infants to 18 mL/kg/d versus 30 mL/kg/d feeding advancements.94 There was no significant difference in survival or morbidities between both groups.101

### Role of Human Milk

Breast milk provided by the mother (mother’s own milk [MoM]) is considered the gold standard of nutrition for an infant of any gestational age. Human milk has been accepted for over 30 years as being associated with a decreased incidence of NEC.102–104 Further, it is dose dependent, with an 83% reduction in NEC if the infant feeds more than 50% of MoM in the first 14 days.105 Meinzen-Derr et al.106 showed that the likelihood of NEC or death after 2 weeks decreased by a factor of 0.83 for each 10% increase in the proportion of human milk in the total intake. Another study showed


## PDF page 1658

that the administration of exclusive breast milk for less than 7 days in the first month of life increased the risk of NEC fourfold in VLBW infants.107

Breast milk contains multiple bioactive components that collectively confer protective benefits to the growing premature infant. These benefits include augmentation of the infant’s immune system, anti-inflammatory effects, strengthening the mucosal barrier, and enriching beneficial bacterial flora of the gut. Breast milk components include EGF, heparin-binding EGF-like growth factor, platelet-activating factor acetylhydrolase (PAF-AH), sIgA, lactoferrin, human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs), nitrates, glutamine, and IL-10, among others. Freezing, thawing, and pasteurization of breast milk affect the content of these components and will likely decrease its protective effect.

In many cases, however, mothers of preterm infants do not produce sufficient breast milk, especially in the immediate postnatal period, and alternative feeding is required. Human donor breast milk (HDM) emerged as an alternative for the nutrition of preterm infants when MoM is unavailable. A 2019 Cochrane review of 12 trials (1871 infants) concluded that formula-fed infants had a twofold greater risk for NEC development compared with infants who received HDM.108 However, as with most meta-analyses, the outcomes can be misleading because they are only as good as the studies that comprise the review. Currently, there are no adequately powered randomized prospective studies of human milk versus formula that evaluate NEC as an outcome. Furthermore, in a recent review, the protective effect of DHM versus formula to prevent surgical NEC was not demonstrated.109 The Donor Milk for Improved Neurodevelopmental Outcomes (DoMINO) group studied neurodevelopmental outcomes of infants randomized to HDM versus formula and did not find significant benefit at 18 months in a study of 363 infants.110

Fortification of human milk products (MoM and HDM) is necessary to meet the nutritional needs of the preterm infant. Studies suggest that feeding only human milk and human milk–based fortifier provides better protection against NEC when compared to feeding bovine products. The occurrence of NEC reportedly decreased from 17% to 5% and surgical NEC from 12% to 1%. However, the studies used in this analysis were not powered to detect NEC occurrence as a primary outcome. In a multicenter RCT, Cristofalo et al.111 showed that infants fed an exclusive human milk diet had decreased incidence of NEC when compared to those fed with preterm formula (3% vs. 21%). However, the control group also received infant formula, which is currently not the standard of care in present neonatal intensive care units (NICUs). Hair et al.112 found that an exclusive human milk diet (MoM and HDM+ human milk–based fortifier) significantly reduced the incidence of NEC, late-onset sepsis, ROP, BPD, and mortality when compared with

a bovine-based diet. In one of the largest, nonindustry RCTs, O’Connor et al.,110,113 of the OptiMoM Feeding group, compared premature infants <1250 g randomized to human milk-based fortifier versus bovine milk–based fortifier and found no statistically significant advantage in morbidity, mortality, growth, or 18-month neurodevelopmental outcomes. The most recent Cochrane review comparing human-based fortifier versus bovine-based fortifier revealed that further studies are needed to conclude that human-based fortifier reduces morbidity, mortality, feeding intolerance, and improves growth.114 The use of a human milk–based fortifier does not come without potential disadvantages. Eibensteiner et al.115 reported poor weight gain, longer duration of parenteral nutrition, and delayed achievement of full enteral feeds. In a recent review of six randomized studies, an exclusive human milk diet was associated with lower weight gain compared to bovine milk–derived fortification.116 Human milk–based fortifier requires it to be added at a 1:1 ratio with human milk to reach adequate caloric density, which results in a dilution of MoM. As previously discussed, MoM has a dose-dependent protective effect that may be diminished by the dilution caused by human milk–based fortification.

### Role of Blood Transfusions

Premature infants are at higher risk of needing packed red blood cell (pRBC) transfusions, with some studies estimating that about 90% of infants with birth weight below 1500 g receive at least one.117 This intervention has long been under scrutiny for its potential role in NEC pathogenesis with a proposed mechanism like that of transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI), prompting the term transfusionrelated acute gut injury (TRAGI) or transfusion-associated NEC (TANEC).118 Distinguishing whether transfusions predispose preterm infants to NEC or whether NEC is related to a deteriorating pretransfusion status remains difficult. Transfusion guidelines are not uniform, and changes in an infant’s clinical status frequently trigger laboratory evaluations with subsequent pRBC transfusions.

Earlier studies found associations between pRBC transfusion and NEC development. This association was reinforced by a systematic review of 12 retrospective studies, although only part of those studies was included in calculating odds ratios. Only five out of the 12 included studies reported unadjusted infants’ exposure to transfusion in the previous 48 hours and NEC, and only four studies reported adjusted estimates of such exposure. Several mechanisms were proposed to explain the role of transfusions in the development of NEC: (1) reperfusion injury due to transfusion; (2) immunologic reactions and injury of intestinal mucosa triggered by cytokines, fragmented RBCs, and free hemoglobin; and (3) transient mesenteric ischemia after blood transfusion. A prospective observational study found a significant elevation of proinflammatory cytokines,


## PDF page 1659 | printed page 1661

including IL-1β, IL-8, interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), IL-17, monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), interferon gamma-induced protein 10 (IP-10), and intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1), at different time points following blood transfusion in preterm infants less than 32 weeks of gestation.

Alternatively, evidence has also accumulated about the lack of association between pRBC transfusions and NEC. Moreover, some studies have found that blood transfusions are associated with a lower risk for NEC.119–121 In the secondary analysis of a prospective multicenter study, Patel and colleagues122 revealed that severe anemia (Hb <8 g/dL), but not blood transfusion, was associated with the development of NEC. In one meta-analysis, the authors found that RCT data conflicted with the results of observational studies. The RCTs show that blood transfusions are associated with a lower risk for NEC, and the observational studies show that transfusions are associated with NEC.123 Two large RCTs studying liberal versus restrictive transfusion thresholds (ETTNO and ToP) on VLBW infants did not reveal significant differences in morbidity, including NEC, between both groups.124,125 These results further put into question whether the transfusions themselves are associated with the development of NEC or with the severity of anemia.

Administration of enteral feedings during blood transfusion is another daunting issue. A small case-control study found that implementing a policy for withholding enteral feedings during pRBC transfusion was associated with reducing NEC incidence.126 Another small study looked at trends of mesenteric tissue oxygenation during and after pRBC transfusions relative to feeding status.127 This study found that infants who received enteral alimentation during pRBC transfusions had negative trends in postprandial mesenteric tissue oxygenation for up to 15 hours after the transfusion compared to infants who were not fed. There was no difference in mesenteric oxygenation during the transfusion between the groups. The authors suggested relative postprandial ischemia after transfusion in infants who were fed. It is important to note that most infants who were fed during transfusion were getting formula feedings (six out of eight), and many infants whose feeds were held during transfusion were receiving breast milk feedings (seven out of nine).127 This difference could have had a significant impact on the difference in the NEC incidence. A systematic review recently evaluated the evidence for withholding enteral feedings during pRBC transfusions.128 This review showed that withholding enteral feedings during pRBC transfusions significantly reduced the incidence of TANEC (risk ratio [RR] = 0.47; 95% CI, 0.28–0.80; P = .005). No RCTs were included in this review because there were none. Conclusions were drawn by comparing rates of TANEC before and after implementation of the practice to withhold feedings in the peri-transfusion period. The authors stated that the quality of the generated evidence was moderate. A

small RCT revealed no difference in splanchnic oxygenation when feeds were withheld, restricted, or continued during transfusion.129 In summary, controlled and adequately powered studies are needed to generate better evidence to determine the association between withholding enteral feedings during pRBC transfusions and NEC. One might also simply conclude that the lack of evidence to support the existence of TANEC should be adequate not to preclude feedings during transfusions.

### Preventive Strategies

Developing preventive strategies to reduce the incidence of classic NEC is very important because of the limited ability to diagnose the early stages of the disease and treat it. Below is a discussion of several of the most critical aspects of NEC prevention. Readers should keep in mind that: • Only evidence-based measures should be employed. • Rather than any separate intervention, a combination of

measures has the highest potential for decreasing NEC incidence in the NICU setting. Standardized evidence-based feeding protocols have been shown to decrease NEC incidence and improve other vital outcomes such as shortening the time to achieve full enteral feeds and decreasing the incidence of late-onset sepsis and mortality.130–132 The advantages of maternal breast milk and donor breast milk over formula products have been discussed earlier. This evidence should be incorporated into feeding guidelines for VLBW and ELBW infants. The advent of human milk–based fortifier and several studies showing a reduction in the incidence of NEC have prompted centers to adopt human milk–based fortifier to prevent NEC. However, there have been conflicting results from a large RCT and insufficient evidence to support routine recommendation. Human milk–based human fortifiers have also been associated with poor weight gain and a longer duration of parenteral nutrition.115 Currently, a randomized trial is being done to further compare human milk–based fortifiers versus bovine milk fortifiers (NCT03797517).

Understanding the role that dysbiosis plays in NEC development leads to developing new strategies to avoid alteration of the developing intestinal microbiome. Antibiotics are among the most used medications in the NICU. Most VLBW and ELBW infants receive broad-spectrum antibiotics in the NICU. These medications alter the intestinal microbiome in neonates.133,134 Prolonged use of broadspectrum antibiotics in culture-negative infants is associated with worse outcomes, including increased risk of NEC, lateonset sepsis, and higher mortality.134,135 One study found an almost threefold increase in NEC risk when infants were exposed to antibiotics for more than 10 days.136 Therefore antibiotic stewardship is a necessary part of the medical culture in the NICU.


## PDF page 1660

Antireflux medications (H2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors) have also been overused in the NICU. These medications are mainly prescribed not to treat the symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux (GER) per se but rather with the hope to decrease the number of apneas and episodes of bradycardia and desaturation in preterm infants. A large study showed that only about 3% of these events follow an episode of GER.137,138 Therefore the prescription of antireflux medications is clinically unsubstantiated in most infants. Additionally, it is shown that prescription of antireflux medications leads to undesired effects, such as alteration of the microbiome, bacterial overgrowth, impaired bactericidal properties of gastric secretions, delayed gastric emptying, and impaired chemotactic response.139 Indeed, an extensive systematic review has shown a strong association between antireflux medications and NEC in preterm infants.140 Therefore routine use of these medications should be avoided in premature infants.

Perhaps the most controversial topic in NEC prevention is the use of probiotics. This seems to be a logical step given the importance of dysbiosis in the pathogenesis of NEC. Probiotics are live bacteria that confer health benefits on the host when administered in adequate amounts. Multiple studies and meta-analyses were performed to study whether probiotics reduce NEC in preterm infants. The latest Cochrane review results showed a statistically significant reduction in NEC incidence and mortality in infants who received enteral probiotics.141 However, the trials included in this review were highly variable in their inclusion criteria, baseline risk of NEC in control groups and, most importantly, timing, dose, formulation of probiotics, and feeding regimen. In addition, few of the trials included extremely premature (<26 weeks’ gestational age) and ELBW (<1000 g) infants. This necessitates caution with regard to interpreting the results.

The largest randomized, adequately powered, doubleblinded, placebo-controlled trial that showed a statistically significant reduction of NEC in VLBW infants was published in 2013.159 This trial was conducted in 10 centers across Australia and New Zealand. It used a combination of three bacteria in the intervention group: Bifidobacterium infantis, Streptococcus thermophilus, and Bifidobacterium lactis. There were no differences in primary outcomes between the groups (late-onset sepsis and all-cause mortality). NEC incidence was a secondary outcome. NEC incidence was reduced from 4.4% in the control group to 2% in the intervention group (RR = 0.46; 95% CI, 0.23–0.93; P = .03). As seen in previous studies, babies with birth weights of less than 1000 g did not show a benefit. The results of that trial were marred by the fact that, in 2014, the manufacturer recalled the product (Solgar ABC Dophilus) used in the intervention group. The recall was based on a report by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention that revealed contamination of the product by a fungus, Rhizopus oryzae, which caused a lethal infection in a premature infant. This incident raises a safety concern for using live bacteria

in preparations that are not considered pharmaceuticalgrade quality in preterm infants whose immune systems are compromised.

A large study that evaluated the effect of the probiotic bacterium Bifidobacterium breve BBG-001 on NEC and sepsis was published in 2016.142 This study was randomized, double blinded, and adequately powered to detect differences in the primary outcomes of NEC (Bell stage 2 or 3), late-onset culture-positive sepsis, and death before discharge. There was no statistically significant reduction of NEC in the intervention group. No differences in other primary outcomes were observed between the groups, as well. This study also revealed that about half of the infants in the control group were colonized with the bacterium used for intervention by the end of the trial, raising concern about potential cross-contaminations in the control groups of probiotic studies.

The American Academy of Pediatrics recently published a clinical report on the use of probiotics in preterm infants that echoes these concerns.143 Most recent trials have not shown a reduction in NEC for those at the highest risk of the disease. Furthermore, a pharmaceutical-grade product has not been established in the United States, further questioning long-term safety concerns. The Canadian Pediatric Society also called for caution in using probiotics in infants with a birth weight of <1000 g, citing the lack of high-quality evidence.144 The European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology Hepatology and Nutrition noted incomplete evidence regarding the optimal length of treatment and starting time.145 Two National Institutes of Health–funded trials are currently studying pharmaceutical-grade products (NCT01954017 and NCT03978000), but they have yet to publish their results.

In conclusion, although probiotics remain a promising preventative strategy for NEC, we should not recommend them for routine use in NICUs at this time. Strong evidence supporting specific probiotics that are pharmaceutical grade for NEC prevention is lacking, especially in ELBW infants at the highest risk for developing this devastating disease. The following issues should be addressed: 1. Probiotic formulations must be manufactured under

strict pharmaceutical regulations by country-specific agencies to ensure the safety and quality of these agents. 2. Each probiotic strain or a combination of strains must be

assessed separately by an adequately powered, randomized, blinded, and placebo-controlled trial before any recommendation for their widespread use can be made.

### Food Protein Intolerance Enterocolitis Syndrome

Food protein intolerance enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES) has typically been found in infants outside of the neonatal period presenting with bloody stools, flank discoloration, and abdominal distention, which improve after cow milk protein is excluded from their diets.146–148 However, FPIES can also present in the neonatal period. Many of these infants have relapsed after a cow milk protein challenge, and these infants have been diagnosed as having FPIES. This is a non–IgE-mediated disease. Neonates with a disease process like that seen in older children with FPIES were described in a series of preterm neonates, where five atypical cases initially diagnosed as NEC were more consistent with FPIES.149 The authors suggested that FPIES may be underdiagnosed in this population.

At this juncture, diagnostic biomarkers for FPIES have not yet been developed. Infants and children with FPIES tend to have normal CRP, leukocytosis, lymphocytosis, and thrombocytosis. In contrast, infants with NEC tend to have high CRP levels, low leukocytes, and thrombocytopenia.150 FPIES in infants may also have an eosinophil predominance with hemoccult-positive stools and hypoalbuminemia. Management of FPIES includes removal of the offending antigen by eliminating it from the diet. With NEC, the patient is usually made NPO for several days, requires parenteral nutrition for extended periods, and is given antibiotics. Therefore it is crucial to differentiate the two entities.

### Ischemic Intestinal Necrosis

One condition often confused with NEC is ischemic intestinal necrosis due to congenital heart disease. The risk of intestinal necrosis is approximately 10 to 100 times that of the term neonatal population without congenital heart disease.17,109,151 Bubberman and colleagues151 compared preterm infants who developed NEC and those with congenital heart disease with intestinal necrosis. They found differences

in age of onset and peak CRP levels. They also reveal that the anatomic site of the disease differed, as the colon was significantly more often involved in infants with congenital heart disease than in preterm infants without congenital heart disease. Mortality was statistically different (22% vs. 11%; P = .47). Several congenital cardiac diseases have been related to ischemic intestinal necrosis. The most common entities are hypoplastic left heart syndrome, aortic arch obstruction, univentricular heart disease, truncus arteriosus, and aortopulmonary window accounting for ischemic intestinal necrosis.160,161

### Congenital Gastrointestinal Anomalies That May Mimic Necrotizing Enterocolitis

Intestinal obstruction due to volvulus, intussusception, and meconium ileus due to cystic fibrosis may present with signs and symptoms of NEC, including radiographic features such as pneumatosis intestinalis. Hirschsprung disease may develop inflammatory enterocolitis, leading to significant morbidity and mortality. This can present with rectal bleeding, vomiting, loose stools, and abdominal distention, making it sometimes difficult to differentiate it from classic NEC.152

### Spontaneous Intestinal Perforation

The first studies that articulated that SIP may be a distinct diagnosis from NEC were published more than 40 years ago.71,153,162 One of the main differentiating characteristics is that SIP is often an isolated perforation in the terminal ileum in an antimesenteric position.122 The remaining bowel appears grossly normal. Histologic investigation of SIP reveals an area of hemorrhagic necrosis without the typical coagulation necrosis seen largely in NEC.154

The pathophysiology of SIP remains poorly understood; yet, it is clearly a different disease from NEC.155 SIP is typified by an isolated perforation with minimal surrounding necrosis or neutrophil infiltrate. The onset of SIP is usually earlier than that of the more classic form of NEC. SIP appears to be also related to the combined use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents, such as indomethacin and ibuprofen, and postnatal corticosteroids.156 However, Berrington and Embleton13 reported that there might be a significant overlap between the two diseases occurring in the first 14 days after birth. There is developing evidence suggesting that the timing of antenatal corticosteroids in relation to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents, particularly proximity to delivery, is associated with SIP.157,158 Further studies are needed.

NEC shows radiologic features, including pneumatosis intestinalis and portal venous gas, that do not precede SIP. SIP typically presents with a rapid onset of abdominal distention but without predisposing radiological findings except for free air on radiograph. Despite these differences, both NEC and SIP are treated similarly with the placement of a peritoneal drain.41 Because of this, there are many cases


## PDF page 1662

where it is unclear whether the bowel experienced significant necrosis as seen with NEC compared to a simple perforation as seen with SIP because no laparotomy was performed. It is therefore unclear which disease process caused the perforation. Contamination of our datasets for NEC and SIP is likely to occur, and often SIP is reported as NEC.

title: Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: 90 Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism in the Neonate
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: The fetus depends entirely on the mother for its nutritional needs, of which glucose is the principal energy substrate that fuels fetal growth and metabolism. At birth, separation from the maternal glucose supply requires metabolic adjustments for the independent existence of the neonate. Perturbations in the neonate’s glucose homeostasis during this transition to the extrauterine environment because of the mother’s metabolism or intrinsic fetal and placental problems are common. An understanding of the normal physiologic adaptation of the maternal-fetal nutritional relationship during pregnancy and of fetal glucose homeostasis and glucose metabolism during the transition to extrauterine life serves as a framework for evaluating disordered glucose metabolism in the neonate.
paragraphs.heading: MEENA GARG AND SHERIN U. DEVASKAR

paragraphs.text: The primary role of the placenta is to transport nutrients such as glucose, amino acids, and oxygen to the fetus. Glucose accounts for about 80% of fetal energy consumption. The remaining 20% of fetal energy needs are provided by lactate, amino acids, and other substrates. The placental syncytiotrophoblast forms the key cell layer that mediates nutrient and substrate transport between mother and fetus (Fig. 90.1). However, there is no significant transfer of maternal peptide hormones such as insulin from the mother to the fetus. The fetal endocrine and paracrine responses are mediated by the transport of nutrients such as glucose and amino acids.
paragraphs.heading: Placental Transport of Nutrients: Maternal- Fetal Relationship

paragraphs.text: The fetus depends entirely on maternal glucose, because there is minimal fetal gluconeogenesis.1,2 Glucose is transported to the fetus along a downward concentration gradient via facilitated transport mediated by glucose transporters (GLUTs) encoded by the SCL2A family of genes.3 A higher concentration of GLUT1 is present on the maternal side of the syncytiotrophoblastic (SC) cell membrane than the fetal
paragraphs.heading: Glucose

paragraphs.text: side of the SC basal membrane, suggesting a rate-limiting step in glucose transport. In normal pregnancies, the plasma glucose concentration of the fetus is about 70% to 80% of that of the mother. The wide range of maternal glucose concentrations observed during pregnancy does not saturate maternal-fetal glucose transfer, thus fetal glucose uptake can become excessive as the maternal glucose concentration rises in diabetes. When fetal glucose uptake exceeds the fetal requirements of energy production and growth, the excess glucose is stored as glycogen and triglycerides. Glucose transfer by the placenta is also affected by the placental surface area, glucose metabolism, and blood flow.
paragraphs.heading: Glucose

paragraphs.text: The non-esterified fatty acids (NEFAs) are transferred from the placenta to the fetus by diffusion and are facilitated by membrane transporters. NEFAs are a critical source of energy and are an essential component of cell membranes, tissue development (white adipose tissue), and organogenesis (brain).2 A progressive shortening of chain length from C16 to C8 is associated with an increased transfer rate. Protein binding appears to slow the rate of transfer. Several fatty acid transport proteins (FATP 1 to 4, and 6) that are present in SC membranes in placenta are involved in the cellular uptake of long-chain fatty acids.3 In addition, a significant amount of nonessential fatty acids appears to be synthesized de novo by the fetus in utero. Maternal adipose tissue and dietary intake are the primary sources of transplacental long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LCPUFAs) to the fetus.4 The cord blood levels of LCPUFAs are higher than in maternal blood, suggesting placental bio-magnification in addition to the dietary intake.
paragraphs.heading: Fatty Acids

paragraphs.text: Amino acids are transported to the fetus against a concentration gradient by a carrier-mediated transport process. Amino acids may be transported through the placenta either unchanged or after placental metabolism and processing;
paragraphs.heading: Amino Acids

paragraphs.text: for example, leucine can be transferred intact or as its keto analogue α-keto-isocaproic acid. The syncytiotrophoblast is usually considered the main transport mediating epithelium of the term placenta (see Fig. 90.1). Amino acids are transported by means of energy-dependent processes through selective amino acid transport systems.
paragraphs.heading: SC

paragraphs.text: β-Hydroxybutyrate and possibly acetoacetate, the major ketone bodies, are transported along a concentration gradient.5,6 The concentration of β-hydroxybutyrate in fetal blood is significantly less than that in maternal plasma (≈50%); however, a linear correlation between the maternal and fetal concentrations has been reported.
paragraphs.heading: Other Fetal Substrates

paragraphs.text: There is a linear correlation between maternal and fetal glycerol levels, with the fetal level in most instances being somewhat lower than the simultaneously determined maternal plasma level.2
paragraphs.heading: Glycerol

paragraphs.text: Data on the maternal-fetal lactate relationship in human studies are conflicting. Experimental data in sheep demonstrated placental production and fetal use of lactate, but data in human studies showed higher levels of lactate in fetal than in maternal blood. In the few studies in which
paragraphs.heading: Lactate

paragraphs.text: umbilical artery and vein samples were obtained simultaneously, the data could be interpreted as net fetal production and placental clearance of lactate.
paragraphs.heading: Lactate

paragraphs.text: The placenta is impervious to insulin. At eight weeks of gestation, insulin is detectable in fetal plasma synthesized from the fetal pancreatic tissue. Insulin-like growth factors (IGF I and II) are highly expressed in all fetal tissues. IGF I in the fetus is nutrient-sensitive and corresponds with fetal growth independent of growth hormone. Fetal insulin is therefore a growth-promoting hormone of the fetus. Pancreatic insulin response is minimal in the euglycemic fetal environment of normal pregnancy. In maternal diabetes, hyperglycemic conditions enhance fetal pancreatic B-cell sensitivity with a more significant insulin response. High fetal insulin concentration correlates positively with fetal weight, whereas fetal growth maintains its typical trajectory in the absence of GH. Like insulin, the placenta is also impermeable to human growth hormone (GH). The fetal pituitary synthesizes GH after nine weeks of gestation. At term, fetal plasma GH levels are higher than maternal plasma levels. Fetal hyperglycemia does not suppress GH levels and shows a paradoxical rise, unlike that seen in adults. Insulin serves more as a fetal growth hormone rather than growth hormone itself.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Hormones Mediating Growth

paragraphs.text: Studies in humans and animals under normal conditions demonstrate that the fetus does not produce glucose and that maternal glucose is the only source of fetal glucose. The fetal energy metabolism and the synthesis of other metabolic substrates entirely depend on a continuous supply of glucose from the mother. Fluctuations in maternal blood glucose result in parallel changes in fetal glucose concentration.2 The fetal liver contains the full complement of enzymes required for the synthesis and breakdown of glycogen. Hepatic glycogen content is low early in gestation; a slow, continuous increase occurs between 15 and 20 weeks; and a rapid accumulation of glycogen in the liver occurs late in gestation. In the mammalian species studied, the gluconeogenic capacity is not expressed in utero under unperturbed circumstances, and the contribution of gluconeogenesis from lactate, pyruvate, or alanine to glucose is quantitatively negligible.1,7 The hepatic gluconeogenic enzymes are present in the fetal liver and kidney, although their concentrations are much lower than those in adults. Animal data suggest that the rate-limiting enzyme may be phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK) that appears only after birth.8 Although such data in the human fetus are not available, nonhuman primates studies show mitochondrial PEPCK and PEPCK-C gene expression increase most significantly after birth, whereas glucose-6-phosphatasealpha (G6Pase-a) and its target gene FOXO1 expression are higher during early gestation (Fig. 90.2).8
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Glucose Metabolism

paragraphs.text: After separation from the umbilical circulation at birth and cessation of maternal glucose and other nutrient supply, the newborn infant mobilizes its own depots to meet energy requirements. This initial drop in glucose concentration may be an essential step in activating physiologic processes necessary for postnatal survival, such as promoting glucose production by gluconeogenesis, stimulation of appetite, adaptation to fast/feed cycles, and enhancement of oxidative fat metabolism. Acute surge in the levels of circulating epinephrine, norepinephrine, and glucagon and a fall in the levels of insulin coincides with clamping of the umbilical cord. These hormones concomitantly mobilize
paragraphs.heading: Glucose Metabolism After Birth— Transitional Neonatal Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: hepatic glycogen and stimulate gluconeogenesis, resulting in a steady rate of glucose production and maintenance of the plasma glucose concentration. Studies using tracer stable isotopic methods suggest that gluconeogenesis may contribute to 30% to 70% of glucose produced after birth.
paragraphs.heading: Glucose Metabolism After Birth— Transitional Neonatal Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: At term, the mean plasma glucose concentration is 9 mg/ dL lower than the average maternal glucose level of 70 to 90 mg/dL. Immediately after birth, the plasma glucose concentration drops by 25 to 30 mg/dL, reaching about 50 to 66 mg/dL by 1 to 2 hours of postnatal age. The plasma glucose concentration in healthy full-term neonates rises over the next 24 to 48 hours and is then maintained at a steady level of 70 to 100 mg/dL.9 This transitional neonatal hypoglycemia in the normally grown term infants is associated with suppressed ketogenesis (ketones and free fatty acids) because of incomplete suppression of insulin during hypoglycemia. Harris et al. performed observational continuous glucose monitoring and intermittent heel-stick plasma glucose measurement from birth to 120 hours in 67 healthy term appropriately grown singleton infants.10 The mean glucose concentration increased in the first 18 hours and then stabilized at 59 + 11 mg/dL until 48 hours of age. The 10th percentile for plasma glucose was 47 mg/dL in the first 48 hours, and 39% of infants had more than one episode below this threshold. The next higher plateau occurred at the fourth day of life with a mean glucose value of 89 + 13 mg/dL suggesting a metabolic transition to adult glucose concentrations by four days of age. It is important to be vigilant in identifying infants with risk factors for persistent hypoglycemia beyond this transitional period of 2 to 3 days.
paragraphs.heading: Glucose Metabolism After Birth— Transitional Neonatal Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: Full-term newborn infants can tolerate fasting without a significant change in the blood glucose concentration. Fasting up to 9 hours after a meal did not cause a decrease in the plasma glucose concentration. After 4 to 6 hours post feeding state, steady state plasma glucose concentration is maintained with interactions between insulin and counter regulatory hormones (glucagon, cortisol, GH, epinephrine, and norepinephrine). Prolonged fasting state triggers increased utilization of free fatty acids (FFAs) and ketone bodies, with decrease in hepatic glycogenesis and increase in gluconeogenesis in response to increase in circulating glucagon and decrease in insulin concentrations.1
paragraphs.heading: Glucose Metabolism After Birth— Transitional Neonatal Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: During hypoglycemia, endogenous hepatic glucose production (EHGP) is derived from gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. The rates of endogenous glucose production in both full-term and preterm infants are significantly higher than in adults. In preterm infants, gluconeogenesis is attributed to account for 72% of EHGP. On average, the neonate produces glucose at rates between 4 and 6 mg/kg/ min. The higher rates of glucose production in the neonate reflect the higher ratio of brain to body weight, the brain being the major glucose-utilizing organ. In the first few days after birth, the rate of glucose production during fasting in full-term infants has been reported to decrease slightly. As the infant grows, the rate of glucose production expressed per unit of body weight decreases, so by adolescence, it approaches the rate seen in adults.
paragraphs.heading: Glucose Metabolism After Birth— Transitional Neonatal Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: EHGP depends on (1) adequate glycogen stores, (2) sufficient supplies of endogenous gluconeogenic precursors, (3) normally functioning hepatic gluconeogenic and glycogenolytic systems, and (4) a normal endocrine system for modulating these processes. At birth, the neonate has glycogen stores that are greater than those in the adult. However, because of twofold greater basal glucose use, the stores begin to decline within 2 to 3 hours after birth. Muscle and cardiac carbohydrate levels fall more slowly. During asphyxia, the energy requirements are met by anaerobic glycolysis, an inefficient mechanism that results in a limited amount of energy and a decrease in glycogen stores. In premature infants, both total carbohydrate and fat content are reduced, and depletion of liver carbohydrates occurs. Endogenous gluconeogenic substrate availability is probably not a limiting factor, because the concentration of plasma amino acids is high at birth as a consequence of active placental transport. Similarly, other gluconeogenic precursors, such as lactate, pyruvate, and glycerol, are also increased. Nevertheless, active gluconeogenesis has been demonstrated in the human newborn soon after birth.7 Finally, EHGP is normally regulated; that is, it decreases in response to glucose as well as insulin infusion in both full-term and preterm healthy neonates.11 However, in extremely immature infants and in sick or stressed neonates, exogenous glucose infusion may not completely suppress endogenous glucose production.
paragraphs.heading: Glucose Metabolism After Birth— Transitional Neonatal Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: The fall in blood glucose that normally occurs after birth is accompanied by an increased level of GH, a relatively low concentration of immunoreactive insulin, and an increase in plasma glucagon. The neonate shows an attenuated but significant insulin response to a variety of stimuli. After the oral administration of glucose, the normal neonate lags in an insulin response with a delayed peak similar to that seen in adults with chemical diabetes. The premature infant, on the other hand, has a minimal and variable insulin response, but the insulin concentrations are markedly increased by the intravenous administration of glucose plus amino acids. The physiologic role of increased GH levels has not been defined; GH values are high during the first 48 to 72 hours and gradually decline but are still elevated at 8 weeks of age. In addition, the newborn shows a paradoxic rise in GH after glucose infusion. Plasma glucagon values at birth are similar to or slightly higher than maternal levels. Glucagon and GH are not suppressed during hyperglycemia. In healthy newborns, intravenous and oral alanine feedings raise plasma glucagon and glucose levels.
paragraphs.heading: Glucose Metabolism After Birth— Transitional Neonatal Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: Adaptation to prolonged starvation in adult humans is facilitated by the ability of the brain to derive much of its energy from the oxidation of ketone bodies, which decreases the need for gluconeogenesis and spares muscle protein. The enzymes involved in ketone body utilization pathways are present in the brain tissue of human fetuses and newborns. Additionally, this has been shown to be true by measurements of arteriovenous differences across the brain.
paragraphs.heading: Glucose Metabolism After Birth— Transitional Neonatal Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: The transition from an intrauterine environment to independent extrauterine life is also characterized by intense lipid mobilization, as shown by a rapid increase in plasma
paragraphs.heading: Glucose Metabolism After Birth— Transitional Neonatal Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: glycerol and FFAs. In addition, there is a shift in the sources of energy for oxidative metabolism, as evidenced by a decline in the respiratory quotient. An increased contribution of fat to oxidative metabolism is reflected in a drop in the respiratory quotient from near 1.0 at birth to a level between 0.8 and 0.85 within a few hours after birth. Evidence of significant lipolysis in the neonate has been obtained by using isotopic tracers to measure glycerol kinetics. These studies showed that lipolysis in the neonate occurs at rates almost threefold greater than those in adults and that the major metabolic fate of glycerol released as a result of lipolysis is conversion to glucose. Free fatty acids are used by the heart and muscle in the absence of readily available glucose, producing ketone bodies that readily cross the blood-brain barrier to be used as fuel sources for the brain. Therefore the hypoglycemic neonate may remain asymptomatic because of the ability in utilizing alternate nutrients (ketones and lactate). However, neonatal hypoglycemia caused by hyperinsulinism leads to reduced concentrations of free fatty acids and ketone bodies, depriving the brain of an alternative energy source of ketones for fueling cerebral metabolism. This results in neuroglycopenic symptoms with severe neurologic injury and dysfunction.12 This situation constitutes a metabolic emergency.
paragraphs.heading: Glucose Metabolism After Birth— Transitional Neonatal Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: Factors frequently overlooked in the interpretation of glucose concentration are the type of sample and the method of analysis. Whole blood includes red blood cells which therefore display a glucose concentration lower than that of plasma. Plasma glucose values are higher than those of whole blood by about 14%; the difference may be greater at very low glucose values (<30 mg/dL). Whole-blood glucose content also varies in accordance with the hematocrit. Neonatal red blood cells contain high concentrations of glycolytic intermediates; therefore whole blood must be deproteinized before analysis. Capillary blood samples should be collected from a warm heel and kept on ice, because the rate of in vitro glycolysis is increased in red blood cells at room temperature; whole-blood glucose values may drop 15 to 20 mg/dL/h if the sample is allowed to stand at room temperature. The most frequently used method for glucose determination in the laboratory is an automatic analysis technique with glucose oxidase or a commercial glucose oxidase immobilized electrode. Plasma or serum glucose concentrations are determined, and the results are very accurate.
paragraphs.heading: Measurement of Glucose

paragraphs.text: In most newborn nurseries and intensive care settings, the rapid point-of-care assessment of whole-blood glucose concentrations is performed by a glucose oxidase and peroxidase chromogen test strip method, either alone or with a reflectance colorimeter. However, all test strip methods show significant variations in glucose concentrations compared with laboratory methods, particularly in the low glucose range (<45 mg/dL). Devices and operator techniques vary, with confounding influences of incubation time and the hematocrit values. There should not be sole reliance
paragraphs.heading: Measurement of Glucose

paragraphs.text: on test strip devices, and tests resulting in borderline values (<40–45 mg/dL) should be repeated by using standard laboratory methods.
paragraphs.heading: Measurement of Glucose

paragraphs.text: Continuous glucose monitoring using a subcutaneously placed micro-dialysis sensor has been validated in small studies in neonates.10 The feasibility, safety, and usefulness of these techniques have been examined in babies with low birth weight.13,14 However, similar to point-of-care devices, these methods cannot measure glucose levels less than 45 mg/dL with confidence. Thus far, continuous glucose monitoring has been used mostly for research studies, and its use in clinical settings is still limited.
paragraphs.heading: Measurement of Glucose

paragraphs.text: Neonatal hypoglycemia occurs in 5% to 15% of all neonates with the potential of harm in the form of brain injury, yet the thresholds in defining and treating neonatal hypoglycemia remain much debated. Additionally, the critical value of glucose concentration that causes long-term neurologic injury is unknown.15,16 The statistical definition of hypoglycemia is a glucose concentration that falls below the 5th to 10th percentile in epidemiologic datasets generated for blood glucose concentrations from large numbers of infants. Two pediatric organizations, American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and Pediatric Endocrine Society (PES), suggest different glucose value ranges using two different approaches. AAP recommends screening for hypoglycemia in all asymptomatic at-risk infants. These include late preterm infants 34−36+6/7 weeks’ gestation and term infants born to mothers with diabetes and small for gestational age or large for gestational age babies. The AAP algorithm recommends intervention at glucose concentrations between
paragraphs.heading: Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: 25 and 40 mg/dL in the first 4 hours of life. Between 4 and 24 hours after birth, the lowest level requiring action is less than 45 mg/dL to ensure a margin of safety (Fig. 90.3). Early initiation of feedings and use of an oral glucose gel, when indicated, is the first line of therapy toward maintaining the postnatal age-related glucose value in the acceptable range. PES17 established mean glucose concentrations of 55 to 65 mg/dL in the first 48 hours of life based on ensuring safety using neuroendocrine and metabolic characteristics of transitional hyperinsulinemia which is accompanied by low ketones and limited glycogenolysis. By 72 hours of age glucose concentrations are to reach greater than 70 mg/dL (see Fig. 90.3).
paragraphs.heading: Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: The definition of hypoglycemia for preterm infants should not be any different from that for full-term infants. Additionally, hypoglycemia in the neonate should be described as transient or persistent, and in either or both cases, as symptomatic or asymptomatic. Such a description has implications for both clinical management and long-term consequences. Transient hypoglycemia implies low glucose values that resolve within 2 to 3 days of life. In contrast, persistent and recurrent hypoglycemia implies a form that requires prolonged management (glucose infusions for several days at high rates of infusion) and perhaps pharmacologic intervention. Several of these hypoglycemia syndromes may present during the newborn period only to continue throughout infancy and childhood.
paragraphs.heading: Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: The clinical manifestations of hypoglycemia are nonspecific and similar to those of many disorders in newborn infants (Box 90.1). It is difficult to distinguish between symptomatic and asymptomatic infants, particularly when the symptoms are subtle and can be generic to many other conditions, not just hypoglycemia. The clinical signs and
paragraphs.heading: Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: symptoms of hypoglycemia should improve with correction of the low glucose concentration. In addition, careful attention should be paid in ensuring that other associated disorders (e.g., sepsis, asphyxia) are not overlooked.
paragraphs.heading: Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: Neuroglycopenia is known to cause seizures and permanent brain damage.18 The critical glucose concentration at which there is an inadequate supply of glucose for the brain has been suggested to be less than 47 mg/dL. This limit was based on observations of altered somatosensory-evoked potentials and lower scores for subsequent mental and motor development when blood glucose concentrations presented below this threshold. However, many of the extensive observational cohort studies of hypoglycemic neonates do not support this observation. Using a lower than traditional blood glucose threshold of less than 36 mg/dL in 689 asymptomatic and otherwise healthy neonates born at or greater than 35 weeks of gestation and weighing greater than 2000 g failed to demonstrate any adverse outcomes at 18 months of age.19 In contrast, another study from the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences of 1400 10-year-old fourth graders with transient neonatal hypoglycemia (glucose <45 mg/dL) reported an association with decreased literacy and mathematics proficiency at fourth-grade achievement testing when compared to age- and size-matched controls.20
paragraphs.heading: Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: McKinlay et al. reported no association between adverse neurodevelopmental outcome at two years and neonatal hypoglycemia (blood glucose <47 mg/dL) in 404 infants with birth weights less than 2500 g or greater than 4500 g and less than 37 weeks of gestational age.14 The glucose was monitored continuously in this cohort, and abnormal neurodevelopmental outcomes showed a U-shaped relationship with adverse cognitive outcomes associated with time spent outside the range of 54 to 72 mg/dL in the first 48 hours of life.14 In summary, the inadequate blood supply to the brain or neuroglycopenia probably occurs within a range of glucose values. The harmful effect of blood glucose may be at low, as well as unstable, or high blood glucose values.
paragraphs.heading: Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: Although the long-term prognosis and clinical management differ for neonatal transient hypoglycemia compared
paragraphs.heading: Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: to that of genetic or persistent hypoglycemia (Box 90.2), it is difficult to differentiate between the two types during the early neonatal transitional period. Therefore, although AAP guidelines focus on the first 24 to 48 hours of life in highrisk asymptomatic infants, it is essential to heed the PES guidelines in greater than 72-hour-old infants by ensuring blood glucose values are maintained at greater than 70 mg/ dL (see Fig. 90.3).
paragraphs.heading: Hypoglycemia

paragraphs.text: As discussed, the fetus is entirely dependent on the mother for the supply of glucose, and fetal glucose concentration
paragraphs.heading: Transient Hypoglycemia Caused by Changes in Maternal Metabolism Intrapartum Glucose Administration

paragraphs.text: closely mimics that of the mother.2 An increase in maternal glucose concentration as a result of exogenous glucose infusion causes an increase in fetal glucose concentration, which in turn causes an increase in fetal insulin levels. Studies in animals have shown that fetal hyperinsulinism, caused by either direct infusion of insulin to the fetus or fetal hyperglycemia, results in an increased metabolic rate in the fetus, fetal hypoxemia, and metabolic acidosis. The acute administration of glucose during the intrapartum period—for example, to prevent hypotension during the conduction of anesthesia, results in increased glucose, insulin, and lactate levels in the cord blood obtained at delivery. Fetal hyperinsulinism leads to hyperinsulinemia and hypoglycemia in the neonate. Similar observations have been reported in a diabetic pregnancy. Therefore caution should be exercised in the administration of glucose to the mother during labor and delivery. Blood glucose concentrations in the mother should not be allowed to exceed those observed in the normal physiologic range.
paragraphs.heading: Transient Hypoglycemia Caused by Changes in Maternal Metabolism Intrapartum Glucose Administration

paragraphs.text: Poor glycemic control during pregnancy has increased risk of diabetic embryopathy and congenital malformations. Oral antihyperglycemic agent metformin alone or with insulin is used most commonly for glycemic control to decrease macrosomia, respiratory distress, and neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admissions.21 Glyburide is another oral antidiabetic drug with good efficacy, but it crosses the placenta and has a higher incidence of large-for-gestational-age (LGA) infants and neonatal hypoglycemia. Older antidiabetic drugs such as tolbutamide and chlorpropamide cross the placenta and produce pancreatic beta-cell hyperplasia and increased insulin release.
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Pharmacologic Treatment

paragraphs.text: Benzothiadiazide diuretics may cause neonatal hypoglycemia by stimulation of fetal beta cells or secondary to an elevation in maternal glucose levels. Salicylates may cause hypoglycemia by uncoupling mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Pharmacologic Treatment

paragraphs.text: Oral beta-sympathomimetic tocolytic drugs such as terbutaline and ritodrine may cause sustained hypoglycemia and elevated cord blood insulin concentrations in infants delivered within 2 days after termination of tocolytic therapy. These agents may cause neonatal hypoglycemia through maternal hyperglycemia and fetal hyperglycemia and hyperinsulinemia. Fortunately, more recently, these tocolytics are not in routine use, with magnesium sulfate taking precedence.
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Pharmacologic Treatment

paragraphs.text: Beta-adrenergic blocking agents such as propranolol cross the mammalian placenta, affecting the fetus. These drugs are used during pregnancy for the treatment of hypertension, hyperthyroidism, cardiac arrhythmia, and other conditions. They may interfere with the effects of the normal surge in catecholamine levels at birth. In animal studies, propranolol impairs fetal growth and may cause neonatal hypoglycemia and impair the thermogenic response to cold exposure.
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Pharmacologic Treatment

paragraphs.text: There is increasing prevalence of diabetes during pregnancy. Estimates from IDF (International Diabetes Federation)
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes in Pregnancy: The Infant of a Diabetic Mother

paragraphs.text: data of gestational hyperglycemia shows that 85% were because of gestational diabetic mother (GDM), 7.5% caused by pre-existing diabetes, and 7.4% by other types of diabetes first detected during pregnancy.22 The worldwide increase in obesity and diabetes at younger ages raises the concern for fetal programming. Small changes in the fetal metabolic environment can result in epigenetic modifications and gene expression lasting a lifetime and modifying the phenotype. Intermittent hyperglycemia in the mother results in fetal hyperglycemia and hyperinsulinemia arising from hypertrophied fetal pancreatic islets and beta cells. The circulating insulin in the fetal compartment is mostly of fetal origin because of lack of transplacental transfer. Increased intracellular glucose concentration by upregulated glucose transporters enhances mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. The resulting increase in reactive oxygen species production plays an important role in diabetic embryopathy. Research studies and animal experiments show that aberrations in intracellular conditions result in oxidative stress, nitrosative stress, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and hexosamine stress.23 These changes induce apoptosis and alterations in genetic and epigenetic systems, resulting in dysmorphogenesis.23 Chronically higher fetal metabolic rate and oxygen consumption lead to relative hypoxemia, which in turn results in upregulation of proangiogenic factors, such as leptin, vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), or fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF2), and matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) such as MMP14 and MMP15.24 Fetal hypoxia caused by increased glycation of hemoglobin and reduced 2,3 DPG concentration, in addition to hyperglycemia and hyperinsulinemia, leads to increased erythropoietin and increased red blood cell mass resulting in polycythemia. In addition, hyperinsulinemia suppresses surfactant production in the lung and thus predisposes the infant to respiratory distress syndrome after birth. An excessive accumulation of glycogen in the liver, adipose tissue, and other tissues has also been observed in infants of diabetic mothers (IDMs). The sequence of these metabolic events is outlined in Fig. 90.4.
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes in Pregnancy: The Infant of a Diabetic Mother

paragraphs.text: Although the excessive transport of glucose from the mother to the fetus is primarily responsible for fetal metabolic and physiologic perturbations in the IDM, nonglucose metabolites (fatty acids, amino acids, and micronutrients) play an important role as well. The increased concentration of these nutrients in the fetal circulation stimulates fetal insulin secretion, which in turn stimulates excessive fetal growth. Despite advances in early recognition and perinatal care in the mother, GDM continues to result in neonatal morbidities involving major organ systems (Table 90.1).
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes in Pregnancy: The Infant of a Diabetic Mother

paragraphs.text: After birth, the newborn IDM is unable to produce sufficient circulating glucose and alternative fuels. Even infants of mothers with rigorous management (i.e., those who have maintained normoglycemia throughout gestation) develop significantly lower blood glucose concentrations than those of normal infants. In addition, they do not mobilize fatty acids from adipose tissue, resulting in lower circulating levels of FFAs, while a normal increase in plasma glycerol occurs.
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes in Pregnancy: The Infant of a Diabetic Mother

paragraphs.text: This metabolic picture suggests persistent insulin action and the lack of a counter-regulatory hormonal response and is characterized by a lack of an increase in circulating glucagon and catecholamine concentration in IDMs during hypoglycemia. The combination of hyperinsulinism and insufficient counter-regulation results in decreased hepatic glucose production, increased peripheral glucose uptake, and impaired lipolysis. When measured by the stable isotope tracer method, IDMs produce glucose at significantly lower rates than normal infants do. In addition, their basal metabolic rates or rates of oxygen consumption have been reported to be lower than those of normal infants.
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes in Pregnancy: The Infant of a Diabetic Mother

paragraphs.text: Data from several studies showed that with rigorous management throughout pregnancy, IDMs do not become hypoglycemic and maintain normal rates of glucose production and basal metabolism.
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes in Pregnancy: The Infant of a Diabetic Mother

paragraphs.text: Clinical studies have validated the risk of congenital anomalies to be proportional to the maternal glycohemoglobin (HbA1C) in the first trimester.22 The risk is as high as 23% to 25% when HbA1C is greater than 9.2%, compared to 1% to 2% when it is less than 7.1% in the first trimester. The overall reported risk of major malformation is 5% to 6% with somewhat higher risk in GDM needing insulin therapy.22 The congenital anomalies may involve many systems (Box 90.3) with cardiovascular and central nervous system being involved in two-thirds of the cases.
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes in Pregnancy: The Infant of a Diabetic Mother

paragraphs.text: Macrosomia. At birth, these infants are obese, plethoric, and LGA and show evidence of excessive fat as well as visceromegaly in the form of a large liver, spleen, and heart (Fig. 90.5). Because the growth of the brain and possibly the kidney is not dependent on insulin, these two organs are normal in size. Careful management of maternal metabolism tends to reduce the incidence of macrosomia but does not prevent it entirely.
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes in Pregnancy: The Infant of a Diabetic Mother

paragraphs.text: Congenital Anomalies. The incidence of congenital malformations is increased two- to threefold in infants of insulin-dependent diabetic mothers compared with the normal population. The frequency of congenital anomalies is, however, not increased in infants of GDM or in those of diabetic fathers. Chronic hyperglycemia in the diabetic embryo, causing accumulation of advanced glycosylation end-products (AGE) and glycated protein and oxidative stress, have been suggested to induce malformations.23 A number of congenital anomalies, including facial, skeletal, and neural tube defects, were induced in the diabetic environment created in a RAGE (receptor for AGE) knock-out mouse model.23 Dysmorphology of the cardiovascular system and genitourinary system has been reported. Caudal agenesis or dysplasia syndrome (Fig. 90.6) is seen with markedly increased frequency, especially in IDMs. This syndrome consists of agenesis or hypoplasia of the femora in conjunction with agenesis of the lower vertebrae and sacrum. Data from animal models show a complex process of genetic and
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes in Pregnancy: The Infant of a Diabetic Mother

paragraphs.text: epigenetic processes enhancing apoptosis and resulting in diabetic embryopathy with multiple structural defects. The frequency of congenital anomalies is significantly increased in mothers with poor metabolic control, as evidenced by increased hemoglobin A1C levels early in gestation, and a significant decrease in congenital malformations has been reported with rigorous metabolic regulation in the periconceptional period.
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes in Pregnancy: The Infant of a Diabetic Mother

paragraphs.text: Hypoglycemia. Immediately after birth, there is a significant decrease in plasma glucose concentration, reaching a nadir between 30 and 90 minutes and followed by a spontaneous recovery in most infants. However, in some infants, the plasma glucose concentration remains persistently low (i.e., <45 mg/dL), necessitating intervention. Most of these infants are asymptomatic. Irrespective of symptoms, the current recommendation is to correct the hypoglycemia with an appropriate glucose infusion. It should be underscored that hypoglycemia in the newborn does not necessarily reflect the magnitude of antepartum metabolic control of the mother and may simply be the consequence of hyperglycemia during labor and delivery.
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes in Pregnancy: The Infant of a Diabetic Mother

paragraphs.text: Hypocalcemia and Hypomagnesemia. Alterations in calcium and magnesium homeostasis occur in about 50% of infants born to insulin-dependent diabetic mothers. Unlike hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia becomes apparent between 48 and 72 hours after birth. Plasma calcium concentrations of lower than 7 mg/dL (hypocalcemia) is frequently related to the severity and duration of maternal diabetes. In addition, it
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes in Pregnancy: The Infant of a Diabetic Mother

paragraphs.text: may be potentiated by prematurity and asphyxia. The mechanisms of hypocalcemia are probable failure of the IDM to mount an appropriate parathyroid hormone (PTH) response, persistently high levels of calcitonin, and possible alterations in vitamin D metabolism. Hypomagnesemia (<1.5 mg/dL) has also been frequently observed. It is usually transient, and its pathophysiologic significance remains uncertain.
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes in Pregnancy: The Infant of a Diabetic Mother

paragraphs.text: Both hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia manifest as jitteriness and may require supplemental calcium therapy. However, in most infants, they are transient events that improve spontaneously.
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes in Pregnancy: The Infant of a Diabetic Mother

paragraphs.text: The management strategies for other clinical problems, such as polycythemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and renal vein thrombosis that occur with slightly higher frequency in IDMs are similar to those in otherwise normal infants.
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes in Pregnancy: The Infant of a Diabetic Mother

paragraphs.text: Septal Hypertrophy of the Heart. Septal hypertrophy and cardiomegaly are specific phenotypic consequences of diabetes in pregnancy and may be manifested with heart failure in the neonate (Fig. 90.7). In addition, data in asymptomatic infants of gestationally diabetic mothers have shown alterations in diastolic function and decreased passive compliance of the ventricular myocardium. By serially evaluating cardiac growth in utero in the fetuses of diabetic mothers, it has been shown that despite good metabolic control, cardiac hypertrophy developed in late gestation (34–40 weeks). Although IDMs with septal hypertrophy
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes in Pregnancy: The Infant of a Diabetic Mother

paragraphs.text: may present with obstructive left heart failure, they may also be asymptomatic. Follow-up data show that cardiomyopathy in an IDM is a transient disease and usually disappears spontaneously within 6 months after birth. Otherwise minor functional changes, such as impaired diastolic filling, have been reported in infants of gestational diabetic mothers and are usually not clinically significant.
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes in Pregnancy: The Infant of a Diabetic Mother

paragraphs.text: Strict metabolic control, improved fetal surveillance, early delivery, and neonatal intensive care have led to improved survival among IDMs. Preconceptional and early postconceptional metabolic control may decrease the incidence of congenital malformations. Improving maternal compliance, preventing ketoacidosis, and recognizing and treating pregnancy-induced hypertension and pyelonephritis are particularly important. Attempts should be made to maintain maternal fasting plasma glucose values at less than 80 mg/ dL and 2-hour postprandial plasma glucose values at less than 120 mg/dL.
paragraphs.heading: Diabetes in Pregnancy: The Infant of a Diabetic Mother

paragraphs.text: With appropriate ambulatory support, hospitalization is not required for most mothers. Indications for hospitalization include pregnancy-induced hypertension, acute or chronic polyhydramnios, infections, and poor metabolic control.
