paragraphs.text: iv. Thyroglobulin synthetic defect v. Peripheral tissue resistance to thyroid hormone 2. Central hypothyroidism a. Genetic mutation or deletion (see Table 92.1) i. Isolated deficiency of TSH alpha-subunit ii. Abnormality of hypothalamic-pituitary develop-
paragraphs.heading: Etiology and Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: ment, with multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies b. Midline congenital defect (septo-optic dysplasia,
paragraphs.heading: Etiology and Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: holoprosencephaly, ectopic posterior pituitary gland, cleft lip, single central incisor) c. Acquired birth injury (usually hypothalamic TRH
paragraphs.heading: Etiology and Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: deficiency; birth injury, hemorrhage, hydrocephalus, meningitis, trauma, nonaccidental injury)
paragraphs.heading: Etiology and Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: The relative incidences of each type of congenital hypothyroidism vary widely in different geographic locations, but overall, congenital hypothyroidism occurs in 1:2000 to 4000 newborns. Although a gender difference is noted in the incidence of congenital hypothyroidism, where the femaleto-male ratio is about 2:1 (in North America), it is less pronounced than in thyroid disorders during childhood and adult life.27 In iodine-sufficient regions, defective embryogenesis of the thyroid gland accounts for 80% to 90% of nonendemic congenital hypothyroidism. Failure in the anatomic development of the thyroid gland may be complete or partial. Residual thyroid tissue in the normal position or an ectopic location is detected in the majority (∼2/3) of infants and children with hypothyroidism. Ectopic thyroid is usually composed of a remnant of undescended thyroid tissue that is typically situated in the midline. Undescended thyroid is located at the base of the tongue in about half of the cases, between the tongue and the hyoid bone in about one-fourth, and between the hyoid bone and the normal location in the remaining one-fourth. Ectopic tissue is often capable of undergoing compensatory hypertrophy when hormone production becomes inadequate and thus may be found as a midline mass. Most cases of thyroid dysgenesis are sporadic, but there is evidence of a familial or genetic component in certain patients. Loss-of-function mutations of the TSH receptor gene lead to hypoplasia of the thyroid gland and TSH elevation (see Table 92.1).28,29 Mutations in transcription factors (e.g., PAX8, FOXE1, NKX2-1, NKX2-5) may be responsible for some cases of congenital hypothyroidism.
paragraphs.heading: Defective Embryogenesis of the Thyroid

paragraphs.text: Genetically determined errors of T4 synthesis or metabolism involve a deficiency of one or more enzymes necessary at various stages of the biosynthetic and metabolic pathways. These occur in approximately 10% of cases of congenital hypothyroidism. Impaired secretion of T4 and T3 results in hypersecretion of TSH, usually leading to compensatory hyperplasia of the thyroid. The familial forms of congenital hypothyroidism are usually referred to as familial
paragraphs.heading: Familial Dyshormonogenesis

paragraphs.text: dyshormonogenesis. Hypothyroidism, goiter, or both may be present in the newborn and infant, depending on the degree and time of onset of the hormonal deficiency.
paragraphs.heading: Familial Dyshormonogenesis

paragraphs.text: Hypothyroidism caused by a defect in the trapping of iodide is because of a mutation in SLC5A5, the sodiumiodide symporter. SLC5A5 mutations are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Infants will typically have a normal-size or enlarged thyroid gland as determined by ultrasonography and elevated serum thyroglobulin levels. Patients with iodide trapping defects can be confused with athyreosis because of the failure of administered radioiodine to be concentrated in the neck; however, there will also be a lack of another physiologic iodine uptake (i.e., in the salivary glands, gastric mucosa, nasopharynx). The severity of hypothyroidism is variable and may depend on the amount of dietary iodine present.29
paragraphs.heading: Familial Dyshormonogenesis

paragraphs.text: There are specific types of defects in the oxidation or organification of iodide. Among them, thyroid peroxidase enzyme deficiency (because of mutations in the thyroperoxidase gene) is the most frequent cause of dyshormonogenesis. Thyroperoxidase mutations are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and can result in severe hypothyroidism with large goiter. Another form of congenital hypothyroidism results from impairment of the normal generation of hydrogen peroxide because of mutations in DUOX1 and DUOX2. Hydrogen peroxide is a substrate for thyroid peroxidase in the oxidation of iodide. DUOX gene mutations demonstrate variable phenotypes ranging from mild or transient hypothyroidism to severe hypothyroidism with large goiters capable of airway obstruction. DUOX2 mutations are the most common form of congenital hypothyroidism in certain populations (Japanese and Chinese).30
paragraphs.heading: Familial Dyshormonogenesis

paragraphs.text: In Pendred syndrome, patients have congenital sensorineural hearing loss and goiter, which typically develops later in childhood or adolescence. The incidence of this disorder is estimated to be about 1.5 to 3 per 100,000 schoolchildren. Affected individuals are either euthyroid or have mild hypothyroidism. Many will have an abnormal radioiodide discharge from the thyroid after perchlorate administration, indicative of defective iodide organification. Pendred syndrome is caused by a biallelic inactivating mutation of the SLC26A4 gene, located on chromosome 7 (7q31). The SLC26A4 gene encodes the protein pendrin, which is expressed in the apical membrane of the thyroid and facilitates passive iodide efflux into the lumen. Pendrin is also expressed in the inner ear and is important for maintaining normal acid-base homeostasis of the endolymphatic fluid. The thyroid phenotype in Pendred syndrome is affected by nutritional iodide intake. With adequate dietary iodide, about 90% of patients remain clinically and biochemically euthyroid; in the other 10%, TSH is elevated and goiter is present.31
paragraphs.heading: Familial Dyshormonogenesis

paragraphs.text: Patients with iodothyronine defects (DEHAL1 gene) do not technically have dyshormonogenesis, as the primary cause of their hypothyroidism is a rapid turnover of thyroid iodine and wasting of iodotyrosines into the urine.
paragraphs.heading: Familial Dyshormonogenesis

paragraphs.text: The defect may be generalized, or it may be limited to intrathyroidal or peripheral deiodination. The onset of goiter and hypothyroidism in these patients is variable and may be because of dietary iodine intake and the presence of partial activity of protein. Patients have been reported to have been rendered euthyroid with supplemental iodide.29
paragraphs.heading: Familial Dyshormonogenesis

paragraphs.text: Defects in thyroglobulin synthesis can result in moderate to severe congenital hypothyroidism with goiter. These patients will have low or absent TG levels and abnormal iodoproteins in their sera. Mutations in the TG gene (8q24, stopping synthesis or causing conformational changes in the molecule) have been reported in these patients.29
paragraphs.heading: Familial Dyshormonogenesis

paragraphs.text: Finally, there are rare defects described in the transport of thyroid hormone to the intracellular space at target organs. MCT8 is one such transporter in which defects result in the X-linked Allen-Herndon-Dudley syndrome. T3 transport into neurons is impaired, resulting in intellectual disability. The biochemical profile has been described with TSH and T3 elevations, and reductions in T4.32
paragraphs.heading: Familial Dyshormonogenesis

paragraphs.text: Resistance to thyroid hormone is because of mutations in thyroid hormone receptors, primarily point mutations in the thyroid hormone receptor-β. It is rare, with an incidence of about 1:40,000. Patients have high serum T4, fT4, and T3 with normal or mildly elevated serum TSH. In childhood, there may be a development of tachycardia, failure to thrive, and attention deficit disorder. The severity of hormone resistance varies among tissues because of differences in relative expression of the two thyroid hormone receptors (β and α), with some tissues such as cardiac exhibiting a more hyperthyroid state because of predominant expression of the α isoform of the thyroid hormone receptor.33
paragraphs.heading: Defects in TSH or Thyroid Hormone Action

paragraphs.text: A lack of responsiveness of the thyroid gland to TSH has been reported in some children with congenital hypothyroidism without goiter. Serum TSH was elevated, and exogenous TSH stimulation caused no increased radioiodine uptake or serum iodothyronine levels. Loss-of-function germline mutations of both alleles of the gene for the TSH receptor have been reported to cause this resistance to the action of TSH and the resultant hypothyroidism. The mutations are located in the extracellular, TSH-binding domain of the TSH receptor. The TSH receptor is coupled to the protein that binds to guanine nucleotide, or G-protein. In these mutations, the TSH receptor does not activate G-protein, and the effector adenylate cyclase (cAMP) signaling pathway remains inactive (GNAS mutations).33
paragraphs.heading: Defects in TSH or Thyroid Hormone Action

paragraphs.text: Endemic goiter and cretinism are still prevalent in large geographic areas where dietary iodine is deficient. Iodide deficiency results in decreased thyroid hormone production in both the mother and fetus. Iodine deficiency also causes preferential production of T3 relative to T4. Reduced maternal T4 levels early in gestation may deprive the developing
paragraphs.heading: Iodine Deficiency

paragraphs.text: fetal brain of T4, which is likely the essential iodothyronine for early brain maturation. Severe iodine deficiency that remains untreated can result in two severe types of endemic cretinism: myxedematous cretinism with metabolic symptoms of hypothyroidism and neurologic cretinism with dominant neurologic disorders (severe mental deficiency, deaf-mutism, and motor spasticity).34
paragraphs.heading: Iodine Deficiency

paragraphs.text: Significant progress has been made to reduce iodine deficiency through programs of universal salt iodization. About 70% of households worldwide have access to iodized salt, but thirty countries have a mild or moderate iodine deficiency. There are recent data that U.S. women are mildly iodine-deficient. Iodine deficiency has re-emerged in parts of the developed world and may be related to initiatives to lower population sodium consumption. Iodine supplementation before or during pregnancy improves thyroid function in the mother and newborn. The recommended daily iodine intake for all pregnant women is 250 μg.35
paragraphs.heading: Iodine Deficiency

paragraphs.text: Secondary (pituitary) and tertiary (hypothalamic) hypothyroidism are less common forms of thyroid hormone deficiency in neonates. In the United States, the combined incidence of secondary and tertiary hypothyroidism is about 1 in 80,000 to 100,000 births. Infants with central hypothyroidism can be detected through neonatal thyroid screening programs when T4 measurements are included with TSH. However, when TSH alone is measured, infants with central hypothyroidism may have normal or mildly elevated TSH levels and are missed until they are older. A low T4 by direct dialysis is the confirmatory test that determines the need for starting treatment when the diagnosis is suspected on the basis of initial tests.
paragraphs.heading: Central Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: Overall, the prevalence of central congenital hypothyroidism is reported to be higher than previously thought (1 in 13,000–30,000).36 Autosomal recessive disorders that cause severe hypothyroidism as a result of congenital central hypothyroidism have been reported. Mutations have been identified in the β-subunit of TSH, the TRH gene, and the TRH receptor gene. Multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies may suggest a genetic defect in the signaling cascade leading to fetal pituitary formation, such as PROP1, LHX3, or POU1F1. When present, pituitary aplasia may be associated with anencephaly or other severe malformations of the brain.
paragraphs.heading: Central Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: Midline facial, cranial, or intracranial defects may also indicate the possibility of hypopituitarism. Septo-optic dysplasia, often associated with pituitary hormone deficiencies, can be manifested as secondary or (more commonly) tertiary hypothyroidism. A genetic mutation in HESX1 has been described in septo-optic dysplasia. Clinical symptoms include hypopituitarism, such as neonatal hypoglycemia (from growth hormone and ACTH deficiencies), polyuria (from antidiuretic hormone deficiency), or a small phallus in boys (from gonadotropin and/or growth hormone deficiencies). Often these are accompanied by blindness, congenital
paragraphs.heading: Central Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: nystagmus, or midline defects of the brain. These findings should alert the physician to suspect septo-optic dysplasia.
paragraphs.heading: Central Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: The incidence of true congenital hypothyroidism (including dyshormonogenesis) is greatly increased in Down syndrome. Obvious congenital hypothyroidism occurs in about 2% of those with Down syndrome, and thyroid hormone replacement should be implemented in those individuals, followed by prudent and selective reassessment of the need for replacement at an older age (typically >3 years of age). Many additional children with Down syndrome have mildly elevated TSH (5 to 15 mU/L). The underlying etiology of this observation is unclear, although thyroid-stimulating hormone bioactivity appears to be normal. It has been suggested that this may be reflective of a nonpathologic shift in the normal range of TSH, although this notion, as well as whether these individuals warrant intervention, is unclear. In a single randomized controlled study of infants and toddlers with Down syndrome, early replacement therapy resulted in modest growth and developmental benefits. However, these differences did not clearly persist in the follow-up of this population at age 10 years.37
paragraphs.heading: Other Conditions Associated With Congenital Hypothyroidism or Abnormal Thyroid Function Testing in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: Screening programs that measure T4 also identify infants with thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) deficiency. TBG deficiency has no clinical importance and therefore requires no intervention, but leads to abnormal laboratory tests. T4 concentrations are low, in the context of normal TSH and fT4 concentrations. Diagnosis can be confirmed by low TBG concentration on specific radioimmunoassay. This condition is discussed in greater detail elsewhere in this chapter.
paragraphs.heading: Other Conditions Associated With Congenital Hypothyroidism or Abnormal Thyroid Function Testing in the Neonate

paragraphs.text: Every state in the United States and every province in Canada has legislatively mandated the screening of newborns for congenital hypothyroidism. CH guidelines screening programs have also been established in Western Europe, parts of Eastern Europe, Japan, Australia, and parts of Asia, South America, and Central America. However, many countries still do not have a nationwide program for neonatal thyroid screening, despite clear evidence that early detection and treatment of congenital hypothyroidism prevents neurodevelopmental disability.27
paragraphs.heading: Neonatal Screening for Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: Most programs currently use the filter paper spot technique. Capillary blood specimens from a heel stick are typically obtained at 24 to 48 hours of age, and some programs routinely obtain a second sample at 1 to 3 weeks of age. Most programs throughout the world screen for primary hypothyroidism with the measurement of TSH only. In some US states and some Canadian provinces, initial screening primarily measures T4 with a reflex to test TSH in those
paragraphs.heading: Neonatal Screening for Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: samples that fall below the lowest 10th percentile. These methods effectively screen for congenital hypothyroidism for the following reasons: (1) they are easily incorporated into the existing metabolic-genetic screening programs (e.g., phenylketonuria screening); (2) primary T4 with confirmatory TSH screening (T4 + TSH) also rapidly identifies those infants with central hypothyroidism or TBG deficiency; (3) selectivity is high because TSH measurements discriminate between affected and nonaffected infants, with a low recall rate (0.3%–1%); (4) cases of mild congenital hypothyroidism are identified by primary TSH screening, and most cases are also identified by T4 + TSH screening.
paragraphs.heading: Neonatal Screening for Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: Both methods of screening (primary TSH and primary T4 with reflex to TSH) appear to be capable of detecting almost all infants with primary congenital hypothyroidism, which carries a high risk for mental retardation if not detected early and treated adequately. Although a TSH level of greater than 40 mU/L is highly suggestive of congenital hypothyroidism, some affected infants have TSH values between 25 and 40 mU/L. These infants require prompt serum confirmation testing because many will be shown to have primary congenital hypothyroidism. Additionally, infants with high hematocrit may have falsely lower TSH values, which may therefore falsely reassure against hypothyroidism. The practice of early hospital discharge (before 48 hours of age) has led to a higher rate of indeterminate results. Infants screened before 48 hours of age require a recheck of the newborn screen by the primary care physician at 2 weeks. Infants who are preterm, of low and very low birth weight, ill, the result of multiple gestations (particularly same sex), or have had samples collection done within the first 24 hours of life should have a second specimen collected and analyzed at 2 weeks of age or 2 weeks after initial sample collection. These infants may be categorized incorrectly based on initial screening because of multiple factors.
paragraphs.heading: Neonatal Screening for Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: Even in athyreotic infants, classic clinical features of congenital hypothyroidism are usually absent at birth, resultant from maternal T4 crossing the placenta, with umbilical cord levels of T4 reaching 25% to 50% of those of normal newborns. Length and weight at birth are generally normal, and manifestations appear gradually over several weeks in infants who do not receive thyroid hormone replacement. These manifestations include lethargy, inactivity, hypotonia, periorbital edema, large anterior and posterior fontanelles, feeding difficulty including needing to be awakened to feed, respiratory distress, pallor, prolonged jaundice, perioral cyanosis, mottled skin, poor or hoarse crying, constipation, and hypothermia. Respiratory distress associated with myxedema of the airway is characterized by noisy breathing, nasal stuffiness, and intermittent cyanosis, especially in the perioral area. After the first week of life, prolonged physiologic jaundice may be an indication of hypothyroidism. In primary hypothyroidism, indirect hyperbilirubinemia
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Manifestations of Congenital Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: predominates, whereas, in central hypothyroidism, there is a mixture of indirect and direct hyperbilirubinemia. Serum creatinine may be elevated. In patients with a functional remnant of thyroid tissue and those with familial dyshormonogenesis, clinical manifestations may be delayed several months or years, depending on the functional state of the thyroid.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Manifestations of Congenital Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: Classic features of congenital hypothyroidism in the infant usually become apparent after about 6 weeks of age (Fig. 92.4). They include typical facies, characterized by a depressed nasal bridge, a relatively narrow forehead, puffy eyelids, dry and cold skin, long and abundant coarse hair, large tongue, abdominal distention, umbilical hernia, hyporeflexia, bradycardia, hypotension with narrow pulse pressure, anemia, and widely patent cranial sutures.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Manifestations of Congenital Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: Lingual thyroid tissue can occasionally be seen in infants and children as a discrete round mass at the base of the tongue (Fig. 92.5). The base of the tongue must be firmly depressed to visualize the lingual thyroid. Because ectopic thyroid tissue may function normally at birth, the ectopic gland of a child may not be detected by newborn screening and may present during childhood or adolescence with a lingual mass associated with speech and feeding problems. In some instances, the sublingual thyroid is palpable as a round midline mass deep under the mandible or is visualized by ultrasonography.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Manifestations of Congenital Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: Neonatal goiters may be extremely large, asymmetric, and confused with hygroma or other cervical masses (see Fig. 92.6). Alternatively, the goiter may be quite small and escape notice. The thyroid can be palpated in infants by placing them in the prone position, gently hyperextending the neck, identifying the thyroid cartilage, and palpating inferiorly and laterally for the thyroid isthmus and lobes. The normal size of each thyroid lobe is about equal to the volume of the distal segment of the patient’s thumb.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Manifestations of Congenital Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: In infants with central hypothyroidism, there is no thyroid enlargement. The onset of symptoms tends to be gradual because some T4 production continues. As a result, the prognosis for mental development remains good. However, signs of other pituitary hormone deficiencies, congenital midbrain defects, or both are typically present. These signs may include neonatal hypoglycemia, a small penis, hypospadias, undescended testes, wandering nystagmus, cleft lip or palate, and combined direct and indirect hyperbilirubinemia. Growth failure gradually becomes evident in these patients. Infants with congenital hypothyroidism are at higher (roughly four-fold) risk to have certain co-morbid congenital malformations, including cardiac (such as septal defects), gastrointestinal, skeletal, renal, or urologic anomalies, and a careful clinical evaluation of these infants should be done.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Manifestations of Congenital Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: When the diagnosis of congenital hypothyroidism is suspected, thyroid function tests should be performed (see Box 92.2). It is advisable to assess fT4 and TSH, and in selected
paragraphs.heading: Laboratory Manifestations

paragraphs.text: patients, TG levels. The initial measurement of T3, rT3, fT3, and T3U is not currently indicated. Elevated serum TSH value is the most sensitive and specific test to confirm the diagnosis of primary hypothyroidism. The normal value for TSH in cord blood is higher than that at any other age (see
paragraphs.heading: Laboratory Manifestations

paragraphs.text: The typical laboratory findings for primary hypothyroidism are an elevated TSH, with T4 and fT4 values in the low or low-normal range. Occasionally, TG may be used as an adjunct to distinguish between etiologies of primary hypothyroidism if imaging is equivocal. A low or undetectable TG concentration with TSH elevation confirms a dysgenetic or absent thyroid gland, whereas a high TG with TSH elevation suggests an organification defect. In central hypothyroidism, TSH can be normal, mildly high, or low; T4 is low or low/normal; and fT4 is low or low/normal. Confirmation of suspected central hypothyroidism requires interrogation of the remainder of pituitary function and anomalies in pituitary anatomy.
paragraphs.heading: Laboratory Manifestations

paragraphs.text: In infants with acute or chronic illness, the euthyroid sick syndrome or nonthyroidal illness syndrome may be present and affect thyroid function test results but does not result in functional hypothyroidism. Typical laboratory findings in nonthyroidal illness are low or normal serum T4, normal fT4 by direct dialysis, and normal TSH. Total T3 can be very low, and rT3 is elevated.
paragraphs.heading: Laboratory Manifestations

paragraphs.text: Another testing that could be considered depending on the clinical scenario includes thyroid autoantibodies in neonates born to a mother with autoimmune thyroid disease. This testing could aid in the differentiation of permanent versus transient hypothyroidism in the child. Measurement of urinary iodine concentration could be considered with suspicion of either iodine excess or deficiency. Finally, genetic testing may be sought in cases where hypothyroidism is familial or in the context of a suspected syndrome.
paragraphs.heading: Laboratory Manifestations

paragraphs.text: For the majority of patients with clear biochemical testing, ultrasonography may not be necessary. However, in patients with equivocal results, those suspected to have transient hypothyroidism, or those with a goiter, ultrasound can provide helpful data that could potentially alter the course of therapy. An enlarged, lingual, or dysgenetic thyroid may be identifiable by ultrasound; however, it is highly user-dependent and also limited in its ability to detect lingual and sublingual ectopy. If an ectopic thyroid is detected, typically additional imaging (i.e., radionucleotide uptake scan) is generally not necessary. Goiters found on ultrasonography may suggest dyshormonogenesis in an infant with laboratory findings consistent with congenital hypothyroidism.
paragraphs.heading: Utilization and Interpretation of Imaging Results

paragraphs.text: The use of 123I or 99mTc-pertechnetate is recommended, when practical, to distinguish dysgenesis from ectopia, as well as to detect a large gland or one with high levels of uptake. Tracer uptake is decreased or absent in hypoplastic
paragraphs.heading: Utilization and Interpretation of Imaging Results

paragraphs.text: or aplastic thyroid glands. A decrease in uptake may also be indicative of maternal blocking antibodies or acute iodine excess (including from iodine-containing contrast agents or cleansing agents applied to open body cavities). Avid or high uptake is suggestive of iodine deficiency, or certain forms of dyshormonogenesis with defects downstream of iodine uptake or trapping (e.g., defects in thyroid peroxidase, dual oxidase 2, thyroglobulin, pendrin, or dehalogenase).
paragraphs.heading: Utilization and Interpretation of Imaging Results

paragraphs.text: A perchlorate discharge test, which assesses the discharge of 123I following the administration of perchlorate, may aid in the diagnosis of an organification defect. When rapid oxidation and organification of inorganic iodide fails to take place in the thyroid (i.e., a lack of conversion to iodine), an anion such as perchlorate can competitively inhibit the iodide accumulation, leading to a net loss of iodide from the gland. 123I-iodide uptake is measured at 2 hours, immediately after which sodium or potassium perchlorate is given orally in doses of 10 mg/kg of body weight. Thyroid uptake is measured every 15 to 30 minutes for 2 hours. If the uptake decreases by more than 10% of the initial value, a defect in iodide oxidation or organification is confirmed.
paragraphs.heading: Utilization and Interpretation of Imaging Results

paragraphs.text: Imaging should never delay the initiation of treatment in infants with suspected congenital hypothyroidism. Scintigraphy can be performed within 7 days of starting levothyroxine. Patients can also be treated for a few years, with a definitive study undertaken at a later date. Ultimately, the findings of imaging studies can help to further guide diagnostic evaluation (i.e., molecular genetic testing) to confirm the presence of true congenital hypothyroidism and the underlying etiology.
paragraphs.heading: Utilization and Interpretation of Imaging Results

paragraphs.text: Retardation of bone maturation is present in about half of the newborns with primary hypothyroidism and may suggest the fetal age at which a deficiency developed in the delivery of thyroid hormone to responsive tissues. This assessment has been reported as a predictive indicator of persistent developmental delays, even in the setting of early intervention. Retardation of bone maturation in neonates is best assessed by radiographs of the knee and can be used as an additional proxy of intrauterine disease severity and onset. Ossification of the cartilage of the epiphyses is also disturbed in hypothyroidism, and normally begins from the center of the cartilage and extends peripherally in an orderly manner. In hypothyroidism, calcification of epiphyseal centers starts from multiple irregular foci scattered within the developing cartilage. The irregular calcification pattern appears on the radiograph as stippled or fragmented ossification centers and is referred to as epiphyseal dysgenesis, a finding that is highly characteristic of hypothyroidism (see Fig. 92.1). Stippled epiphyses may also occur in thyroid hormone resistance, as well as in multiple epiphyseal dysplasias, although thyroid function is normal in this familial disease.
paragraphs.heading: Utilization and Interpretation of Imaging Results

paragraphs.text: Errors in diagnosis of congenital hypothyroidism usually result from a failure of the newborn screening program (no
paragraphs.heading: Differential Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: specimen collected or a laboratory error), from a clinical failure to suspect the condition, or from the misdiagnosis of other disorders such as hypothyroidism. These errors typically arise when the diagnosis is based on a few suggestive clinical features and laboratory data are incorrectly interpreted. It is necessary to perform newborn screening even in sick newborns so that clear-cut abnormalities cannot be missed. Repeated screening is then indicated as the illness resolves.
paragraphs.heading: Differential Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: During the early neonatal period, respiratory difficulty, pallor, and cyanosis in hypothyroid infants must be differentiated from other common causes of respiratory distress and from congenital heart disease. Lethargy, inactivity, hypotonia, and feeding difficulty may be mistaken for manifestations of sepsis or brain damage from a variety of causes. Prolonged jaundice in hypothyroidism may be confused with icterus caused by hemolytic anemia, septicemia, or hepatic disease. The coarse facial features, macroglossia, and dry skin of hypothyroidism can mislead one to suspect Hurler syndrome, chondrodystrophy, or Down syndrome. A large goiter must not be confused with a hygroma, cyst, or tumor of the neck. A lingual thyroid, when visible or obstructing the airway, may be mistaken for a tumor of the pharyngeal area (see Fig. 92.5). Although epiphyseal dysgenesis may resemble osteochondritis deformans in its radiographic appearance, the latter does not occur during the neonatal period.
paragraphs.heading: Differential Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: The prevalence of transient neonatal hypothyroidism differs by geographic location, related to variability in iodine intake. In areas with an adequate iodine supply, most infants with transient hypothyroidism were born to mothers who received goitrogens during pregnancy. Some cases result from placental transmission of maternal blocking antibodies or from exposure of the fetus or newborn to high doses of iodine (e.g., amiodarone, iodine-containing contrast, or topical absorption of iodine-containing antiseptic compounds).38
paragraphs.heading: Transient Disorders of Thyroid Function

paragraphs.text: Transient neonatal thyroid dysfunction must be distinguished from permanent disorders of thyroid function. The results of neonatal screening tests from these patients may mimic those found in permanent hypothyroidism and may lead to an erroneous diagnosis and prolonged treatment. About 24% to 36% of children diagnosed with congenital hypothyroidism by newborn screening are later determined to have transient hypothyroidism.
paragraphs.heading: Transient Disorders of Thyroid Function

paragraphs.text: In mothers with Graves disease, the transplacental passage of antithyroid drugs may cause transient hypothyroidism with goiter in the neonate. These drugs are rapidly cleared from the neonate within days.
paragraphs.heading: Transient Disorders of Thyroid Function

paragraphs.text: Transplacental transfer of maternal inhibiting TSHreceptor antibodies (TRAb) can rarely result in transient neonatal primary hypothyroidism (1:180,000 newborns). These antibodies may persist in the infant’s circulation for up to 6 months, although 3 months is more typical. No
paragraphs.heading: Transient Disorders of Thyroid Function

paragraphs.text: goiter is present, and absent or decreased uptake is seen on thyroid scintigraphy, although thyroid tissue can be seen on an ultrasonogram.
paragraphs.heading: Transient Disorders of Thyroid Function

paragraphs.text: Neonates with large hepatic hemangiomas are at risk for consumptive hypothyroidism because of excessive production of type 3 deiodinase. High-dose levothyroxine may be required. Once these anomalies are treated or self-resolve, hypothyroidism should improve.39
paragraphs.heading: Transient Disorders of Thyroid Function

paragraphs.text: Premature neonates have many aberrations in thyroid status, including a delay and blunting of their postnatal TSH surge. In some very preterm infants (<31 weeks), T4 concentrations do not rise and may fall within the first 1 to 2 weeks, termed transient hypothyroxinemia of prematurity. fT4 levels tend to be less affected, and the laboratory profile reflects abnormal protein binding or decreased TBG levels (affecting infants <30 weeks of gestation). Many other factors are thought to affect thyroid status in premature neonates, including immaturity of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. Iatrogenic iodine overload may cause transient hypothyroidism even in term infants, but premature infants appear to be more susceptible to iodine-induced transient hypothyroidism. Radiocontrast agents or the excessive application of iodine-containing antiseptics to mucous membranes (e.g., omphalocele) or intact skin can be sources of excessive iodine exposure. In addition, given the prevalent neonatal morbidities in premature infants, laboratory anomalies consistent with euthyroid sick syndrome are common. It is recommended that thyroid screening in preterm infants be repeated at 2 weeks of age or 2 weeks after the initial screening was done.
paragraphs.heading: Transient Disorders of Thyroid Function

paragraphs.text: The incidence of transient primary hypothyroidism is higher in geographic areas where the dietary supply of iodine is insufficient. Premature infants are more susceptible, with incidence increasing with decreasing gestational age. Low urinary iodine concentration suggests this as the causative factor, and iodine supplementation may successfully correct hypothyroidism and goiter in these infants.
paragraphs.heading: Transient Disorders of Thyroid Function

paragraphs.text: Heterozygous or homozygous DUOX2 mutations, impacting enzymes involved in iodine oxidation, may result in transient primary hypothyroidism in the neonate.
paragraphs.heading: Transient Disorders of Thyroid Function

paragraphs.text: Neonates whose mothers had uncontrolled hyperthyroidism during pregnancy may also be transiently centrally hypothyroid.
paragraphs.heading: Transient Disorders of Thyroid Function

paragraphs.text: Finally, if the mother was taking anti-thyroid drugs during pregnancy, namely propylthiouracil or methimazole, both are known to cross the placenta and result in transient neonatal hypothyroidism.
paragraphs.heading: Transient Disorders of Thyroid Function

paragraphs.text: Acutely ill patients, including neonates, commonly have alterations in thyroid function testing. The current hypothesis is that these alterations occur as an adaptive response to decrease basal metabolic rates in severely ill patients. The syndrome has been recognized in sick infants and children, with both acute and/or chronic illness.40
paragraphs.heading: Euthyroid Sick Syndrome

paragraphs.text: In the neonatal period, preterm infants with respiratory distress syndrome are the most frequently encountered patients with the euthyroid sick syndrome. An alteration in T4 metabolism favors the production of rT3 over T3. The prevalence and severity of euthyroid sick syndrome increase with decreasing gestational age. The consistent finding is a low serum T3 level, often accompanied by an increase in the rT3 level. Serum T4, TBG, and TSH may both be low or normal, whereas fT4 is generally normal. Abnormal thyroid function gradually reverts to normal function as the patient’s primary illness improves. During recovery, TSH may be transiently elevated (up to 15 mU/L). Treatment with thyroid hormone is not indicated in these patients. However, preterm infants at risk should be monitored by serial determinations of fT4 and TSH, and T4 treatment should be considered if there is a progressive increase in serum TSH and a decrease in fT4.
paragraphs.heading: Euthyroid Sick Syndrome

paragraphs.text: Transplacental transfer of maternal T4 during gestation initially offers some protection for brain development in the hypothyroid neonate. Serum T4 concentrations at term in athyreotic babies are 25% to 50% of those found in normal neonates. However, the half-life of serum T4, including T4 acquired from the mother, is short in infants (3–4 days) compared with adults (about 6 days), and within 1 to 2 weeks the infant’s serum T4 level will have dropped significantly. A delay in the initiation of thyroid hormone therapy can result in a decrease in IQ score, and replacement is recommended within the first 2 weeks of life. Thyroid hormone replacement therapy for neonatal congenital hypothyroidism must be started as soon as the blood is collected for serum confirmation tests. Therefore all hypothyroid infants, with or without goiter, should be rendered euthyroid as promptly as possible with replacement therapy. Those with mild TSH elevation and normal fT4 may be monitored with serial TSH and fT4 tests and not treated for up to 4 weeks. However, if TSH remains elevated, thyroid hormone therapy should be started. In rare instances in which the diagnosis of a congenital hypothyroidism cannot be established expeditiously because of confounding laboratory results, the safest course is to fully treat the infant, with consideration of withdrawal of therapy at an older age.
paragraphs.heading: Treatment of Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: Asymptomatic infants and those with minimal clinical manifestations of congenital hypothyroidism can be given sodium-l-thyroxine, 10 to 15 μg/kg/day (administered orally once per day), beginning as soon as the diagnosis is established. The higher end of this dosing spectrum is recommended for more severely affected infants to more rapidly correct hypothyroidism. There is no evidence that sole or combination therapy with l-T3 is superior to therapy with l-T4 alone and therefore is not recommended. The bioavailability of brand l-T4 may be different than generic; however, either may be used. Importantly, when brands (even between generic manufacturers) are changed, repeat thyroid function testing should be done 4 to 6 weeks later.
paragraphs.heading: Treatment of Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: The pill should be crushed and suspended in a small amount of formula, breast milk, or water (not the whole bottle). Human breast milk does not contain enough T4 to alter thyroid hormone levels in the infant, and therefore breastfeeding can continue with the appropriate replacement of l-T4. This mixture can be provided by way of a cross-cut nipple and followed later by feeding. The crushed tablet can also be mixed into a smaller amount (∼1/2–1 ounce) of formula and fed, with the remainder of the formula fed from the same bottle in an attempt to administer as much as possible of the crushed tablet remnants which may have adhered to the sides of the bottle. Administration can be either before or with feedings, although the routine should be the same with every dose. Although absorption of levothyroxine is reduced when given with feeds, the dose can be titrated to normalize thyroid function from serum, and the dose may therefore need to be slightly higher than if it were given fasting. However, separation from intake of soy, iron, antacids (aluminum hydroxide), simethicone, or calcium is advised because these can reduce absorption to a greater degree. There are commercial liquid formulations of levothyroxine available in the United States, although data regarding their use in congenital hypothyroidism are scarce. Compounded preparations are not recommended at all because of inconsistent concentrations and dosing.
paragraphs.heading: Treatment of Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: TSH and fT4 values should be initially rechecked 1 to 2 weeks after initiation of therapy, and then at 2-week intervals until normalization of TSH. Because the initiated dose of levothyroxine is generous with the goal of the rapid normalization of thyroid function, it is not infrequent that the dose of thyroid hormone will require reduction. This is typically done if fT4 is high (age normative range), TSH suppression occurs, or clinical symptoms of thyrotoxicosis develop. For infants with primary congenital hypothyroidism, the target for TSH concentrations should be in the normal range (ideally lower half of normal range) for age during thyroid hormone replacement therapy, with fT4 levels in the upper half of normal for age. For infants with central hypothyroidism, dose adjustments are driven by fT4. Age-appropriate levels in children differ from those in adults (see Fig. 92.2). Caution should be taken when interpreting TSH levels following initiation of treatment, because often infants with congenital hypothyroidism show a laboratory pattern consistent with some degree of thyroid hormone resistance. This is evident when TSH levels remain elevated despite fT4 levels in the normal or high range and may be the result of intrauterine hypothyroidism and abnormal development of pituitary-thyroid feedback. This can be transient but also may persist. In these situations, therapy decisions may need to be driven by fT4 rather than primarily by TSH.
paragraphs.heading: Treatment of Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: During the first years of life, patients should be monitored frequently—at least every 2 months during the first 6 months of life, every 3 to 4 months during the next 2 years, and then twice a year—to assess clinical progress and adjust levothyroxine to maintain fT4 and TSH in the target range. Thyroid hormone requirement based on weight (μg/kg/day) will gradually decrease from a dose of 8 to 10 μg/kg/day at age
paragraphs.heading: Treatment of Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: 3 to 6 months to 2 to 3 μg/kg/day in adolescents. In adults, the thyroid hormone requirement is approximately 1.7 μg/ kg/day.27 In children with transient hypothyroidism, treatment initiation, and duration are determined by the underlying etiology. Maternal blocking antibodies, as previously discussed, are typically cleared by the infant between 6 weeks and 6 months of age. During this time, replacement therapy is implemented, with consideration of discontinuation at the end of this time frame, although withdrawal of therapy can also be delayed until 2 or 3 years of age out of abundance of caution. Iodine excess occasionally requires replacement therapy, although the understanding that normal thyroid function recovers after a few weeks drives the duration of treatment. Iodine deficiency requires replacement. Consumptive hypothyroidism in the context of hemangiomas may endure for months to a year until involution, and during this time, high doses of levothyroxine are required.38
paragraphs.heading: Treatment of Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: Given altered thyroid hormone physiology in preterm infants, the diagnosis of hypothyroidism and the determination of appropriate therapy can be difficult. In infants with neonatal transient hypothyroxinemia, a transient process characterized by low fT4 or total T4 levels with low or normal TSH values, the efficacy of thyroid hormone therapy has also not been established, although data are mixed.40 An association between hypothyroxinemia in preterm infants and neurodevelopmental problems and intellectual disability has been documented; however, these were observational studies that did not establish causality. If primary or central hypothyroidism is suspected or confirmed, replacement therapy should be initiated and trialed off later. When initiating replacement therapy in preterm infants, the same starting dose of T4 (10–15 μg/kg/day) is recommended to promptly increase T4 to normal. The dose may need to be decreased, as previously described, once free or total T4 values reach the desired normal level.
paragraphs.heading: Treatment of Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: In treatment of infants with severe myxedema with fluid retention, possible complications should be kept in mind. Cardiac insufficiency caused by pericardial effusions or overloading of the myxedematous heart through too rapid a mobilization of the myxedema fluid into the circulation is well known in the adult. This complication in older children and adults is prevented by administering a small dose of thyroid hormone at first and gradually increasing the dosage. However, infants generally tolerate a rapid restoration to the euthyroid state better than adults, and a prompt restoration of T4 to a normal value is important for the preservation of brain development and maturation. Nevertheless, excessive thyroid hormone therapy must be avoided, and the dose must be adjusted judiciously (starting at ∼50% of the target dose, increasing gradually after 2 weeks) if there is evidence of severe myxedema, particularly of the heart. Aspiration of feeds can occur in cases of severe myxedema resulting from impairment in swallowing (caused by myxedema of the pharyngeal area), compounded by an increased appetite as the euthyroid state is restored. Therefore, when myxedema is severe, the infant should be fed carefully and slowly during the early phase of treatment.
paragraphs.heading: Treatment of Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: Congenital hypothyroidism caused by the maternal ingestion of goitrogens is a self-limited condition. The blocking effect of antithyroid drugs usually disappears several days after birth. Therefore, if the goiter is small, TSH is not elevated, and the patient is euthyroid, no treatment is required. However, if the patient is hypothyroid and TSH is elevated or if the goiter is large, it is safer to treat the infant until the age of 3 years, as described previously. In nursing mothers with Graves disease, both propylthiouracil and methimazole are secreted in breast milk in small concentrations. However, studies of breastfed infants of mothers taking these medications have demonstrated normal thyroid function and intellectual development.41
paragraphs.heading: Treatment of Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: Prenatal diagnosis and intrauterine treatment of congenital hypothyroidism have been successful in only a few cases. Optimal methods for monitoring fetal thyroid state still need to be established. Imaging studies alone are not sufficient to determine appropriate therapy because a goiter can result from either hypo- or hyperthyroid states. Measurement of accurate TSH levels (compared to gestational age norms) is done by cordocentesis, but this increases the risk of fetal loss and should therefore only be done when intervention is contemplated. In utero treatment with intra-amniotic l-thyroxine injection is effective for reducing fetal goiter size, which may be considered for a fetus with progressive hydramnios, a risk for premature delivery, and/or concerns for tracheal obstruction. However, there are no clear recommendations for dosing regimens or outcome data to show neurodevelopmental benefits from therapy because the number of cases treated in utero is small. Prenatal diagnosis and treatment of congenital hypothyroidism await further developments.
paragraphs.heading: Treatment of Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: Shortly after adequate substitution therapy is instituted, clinical manifestations of hypothyroidism resolve. If growth restriction was present before treatment, accelerated linear growth occurs. After a period of catch-up growth, an optimal rate of growth is maintained. Goiter or a hypertrophied ectopic thyroid gradually shrinks in size when the patient is properly treated. If there was a delay in skeletal maturation at diagnosis, treatment is associated with acceleration in bone maturation after a latent period of a few months, with subsequent osseous development that parallels chronologic age. Overtreatment should be avoided because this can result in rapid epiphyseal closure and craniosynostosis.
paragraphs.heading: Prognosis for Congenital Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: The age of initiation of thyroid hormone therapy is a major determinant of neurodevelopmental outcomes. Comparisons of an earlier age of treatment (day of life 12–30) versus later age (>30 days of life) found that infants started at the earlier age averaged more than 15 IQ points higher. The initial starting dose of levothyroxine is also important. The majority of studies have found that children started on doses of 10 to 15 μg/kg/day had the best IQ outcome. The severity of hypothyroidism was also thought to contribute to poor outcomes in prior studies, although studies do not consistently support this finding. Last, good compliance
paragraphs.heading: Prognosis for Congenital Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: with thyroid hormone therapy during infancy and childhood is vital; recurrent episodes in childhood of insufficiently managed TSH are associated with school delay.
paragraphs.heading: Prognosis for Congenital Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: Overall, if infants are treated early and with sufficient dosing, the neurologic function is generally normal. However, there are additional neurologic sequelae for which patients are at risk, even in the context of normal IQ. Residual defects may include visual-spatial processing, sensorimotor defects, attention problems, speech deficits, and selective memory. There are only minor differences in intelligence, school achievement, and neuropsychological test scores in affected congenital hypothyroidism adults treated early with thyroid hormone compared with control groups of classmates and siblings. Poor attention can also be seen in patients who have been overtreated. Overall, the intellectual and neurologic prognosis for patients with congenital hypothyroidism has greatly improved since the advent of newborn screening. We may still expect further improvement in the future because thyroid hormone treatment regimens used today are more aggressive in targeting the early correction of TSH than the regimens used 30+ years ago.
paragraphs.heading: Prognosis for Congenital Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: Sensorineural hearing loss has also been reported with greater frequency in individuals with congenital hypothyroidism, although it seems to be concentrated in those with athyreosis rather than those with ectopia. As previously discussed, hearing can also be associated with congenital hypothyroidism in the case of Pendred syndrome, and these patients will have a normally placed gland on imaging. The prevalence of hearing loss seems to have been higher before widespread newborn screening programs, but the risk still remains higher than in the general population after early detection. Therefore routine hearing screening should be done in these individuals.27
paragraphs.heading: Prognosis for Congenital Hypothyroidism

paragraphs.text: Maternal Graves disease is the most common cause of neonatal hyperthyroidism, and it results from transplacental transfer of stimulating TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb) from the mother to fetus in the second half of gestation when the fetal TSH receptors become physiologically responsive to TSH and TRAb. The disease can occur in the neonate of a mother known to have active Graves disease and in mothers with a history of Graves disease previously treated with thyroidectomy or radioiodine ablation. Neonatal Graves disease occurs in 1% to 5% of at-risk pregnant mothers. There is an increased likelihood of neonatal Graves hyperthyroidism if there is higher maternal stimulatory TRAb concentration during the third trimester. The highest risk occurs when maternal TSI is greater than 5 index units (above three times the upper limit of normal for the assay).24
paragraphs.heading: Etiology and Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: Clinical manifestations of fetal hyperthyroidism can be seen in utero. If a pregnant woman has uncontrolled
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Manifestations

paragraphs.text: hyperthyroidism or elevated TRAb greater than three times the upper limit of normal, serial fetal ultrasounds should be performed.24 Ultrasound can detect fetal tachycardia, rapid bone maturation, and goiter, which indicate a fetal hyperthyroid state. Postnatally, hyperthyroidism may become apparent within the first 24 hours of life. Infants may be born prematurely from such a mother. Clinical features that may be seen include hyperkinesis, diarrhea, poor weight gain, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, craniosynostosis, tachycardia, exophthalmos, and goiter. Although a goiter is inevitably present in neonatal thyrotoxicosis, its size varies considerably; it may be small and escape notice on a cursory examination, or it may be large enough to cause tracheal compression. Exophthalmos is usually mild when present. In severe neonatal thyrotoxicosis, hyperthermia, arrhythmia, and high-output cardiac failure may occur. If the condition remains untreated, death may result. In most cases, the course of neonatal hyperthyroidism is self-limited because of the gradual depletion of transplacentally acquired stimulating TRAb. The signs and symptoms subside spontaneously after 3 weeks to 6 months; rapid resolution of symptoms occurs when the initial titer of serum-stimulating TRAb in the neonate is lower. However, the goiter may persist for some time after all signs of hyperthyroidism disappear. The thyroid gradually returns to its normal size. In rare instances, neonatal thyrotoxicosis may not be a transient disorder and may persist for years, usually indicating the presence of activating mutations of the TSH receptor.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Manifestations

paragraphs.text: In the infant born to a mother who received antithyroid medications for the treatment of Graves disease during the latter part of pregnancy, the onset of clinical manifestations may be modified by the transplacental acquisition of the antithyroid agent as well as stimulating TRAb. At birth, the infant may be euthyroid or even hypothyroid, and the presence of a goiter may be the only abnormal feature. Because the plasma half-life of antithyroid agents is short compared with the half-life of stimulating TRAb, the typical manifestations of neonatal thyrotoxicosis may appear several days to 2 weeks after birth. Although neonatal Graves disease is a disease mediated by monoclonal antibodies, polyclonal antibodies are sometimes produced by the mother and cause atypical disease in the infant. Hyperthyroidism may not develop until 1 to 2 months of age if a high-affinity TSH-binding/inhibiting immunoglobulin (TBII) in low concentrations initially predominates; once it is metabolized, a second population of stimulating TRAb prevails to cause late-onset hyperthyroidism.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Manifestations

paragraphs.text: Maternal history of Graves disease before or during pregnancy is important to identify infants at risk for neonatal Graves disease. Information concerning both prior and current treatment of maternal hyperthyroidism and maternal TRAb levels must also be obtained. If maternal TRAb levels from the second or third trimester are negative, no specific
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis and Differential Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: neonatal follow-up is necessary; if unavailable or positive, consider the newborn as “at risk” for the development of hyperthyroidism. Determine levels of TSH-receptor antibodies in cord blood, or as soon as possible thereafter, so that newborns with negative antibodies can be discharged from follow-up. In “at risk” infants, perform fT4 and TSH levels at days 3 to 5 of life, repeat at days 10 to 14 of life, and follow clinically until 2 to 3 months of life.42 The infant should be examined sequentially for signs of thyrotoxicosis, and the neck should be palpated carefully to detect a goiter. Most cases of neonatal Graves are diagnosed in 2 weeks, but there are rare cases of later presentation.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis and Differential Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: In the euthyroid or hypothyroid neonate born to a mother who received antithyroid medication during the latter part of pregnancy, it is almost impossible to predict whether thyrotoxicosis will ensue. Therefore serial examinations of the infant must be undertaken during the first 2 weeks of life. Although neonatal thyrotoxicosis can be confused with various neurologic disorders, narcotic withdrawal in the infant of an addicted mother, congenital heart disease, or sepsis, a positive maternal history of Graves disease and the presence of goiter should readily alert the physician to the correct diagnosis. In normal neonates and infants, the thyroid gland is difficult to palpate. Therefore an easily palpable thyroid in such an infant should generally be regarded as a goiter.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis and Differential Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: More rarely, neonatal hyperthyroidism may result from defects in the TSH receptor or the downstream mediators, and unlike neonatal Graves disease, these forms of hyperthyroidism are persistent and are not mediated by TRAb. These germline mutations demonstrate autosomal dominant inheritance (see Table 92.1) and occur in the transmembrane domains of the receptor or affect receptor coupling to stimulatory G protein, which leads to constitutive activation of the adenylate cyclase.43 Because of disease severity and frequent relapse, definitive therapy with surgery or radioactive iodine is eventually indicated when the patient is older.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnosis and Differential Diagnosis

paragraphs.text: Prenatal therapy is possible with the use of oral maternal antithyroid drugs and adjustment of the dose to normalize fetal TSH and cardiac function. If fetal hypothyroidism results from maternal overtreatment with antithyroid drugs, serial fetal ultrasound can be helpful to determine if subsequent dose reduction of the antithyroid drug is sufficient. Invasive examinations such as cordocentesis or amniotic fluid sampling should only be used when the diagnosis is unclear or intra-amniotic thyroxine injection is required to treat a persistent fetal hypothyroid state secondary to ATD administration.
paragraphs.heading: Treatment

paragraphs.text: The treatment of thyrotoxicosis in a neonate is similar to treatment in an older child and involves the use of antithyroid drugs. Care should be exercised not to induce hypothyroidism with excessive medication. Methimazole (MTZ) can be given in doses of 0.2 to 0.5 mg/kg/day divided into two
paragraphs.heading: Treatment

paragraphs.text: doses. Propylthiouracil (PTU) is no longer recommended for use in children because of its association with liver failure.44 Iodine (Lugol solution) can also be given in more severe cases. Lugol solution can be given at a dose of one drop three times daily. Although iodine rapidly inhibits the release of T4 from the thyroid, its effects tend to disappear after several weeks. Iodine should be given at least 1 hour after methimazole to avoid exacerbating hyperthyroidism acutely. Most symptoms of hyperthyroidism are closely related to increased adrenergic response. Therefore beta-adrenergic blocking drugs can alleviate many of the potentially life-threatening manifestations of neonatal thyrotoxicosis. In contrast to antithyroid drugs, these agents can rapidly diminish the severity of thyrotoxicosis, and their effects are evident within a few hours. Propranolol, together with iodine and MTZ, may be used in the treatment of severe neonatal thyrotoxicosis. Propranolol is given orally in a dose of 2 mg/kg/day divided into two doses. In critically ill newborns, a short course of pharmacologic glucocorticoids which inhibits thyroid hormone secretion and impairs the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 may be needed to help stabilize the infant (prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day in 1–2 divided doses).42
paragraphs.heading: Treatment

paragraphs.text: Circulating T4 has a half-life of 3 to 4 days in neonates and about 6 days in adults. Therefore little or no clinical response to antithyroid drugs can be expected during the first few days of therapy. The TSH response to a hypothyroid state induced by the excessive treatment of thyrotoxicosis may be diminished for several months or longer in these infants. Therefore lack of TSH elevation cannot be relied on to indicate the excessive treatment of thyrotoxicosis. It is recommended that thyroid function be measured weekly until fT4 concentrations are stable and then every 2 weeks. MTZ should be decreased and eventually discontinued when fT4 concentrations have normalized. Monitoring of TRAb titers may facilitate decision-making about when to discontinue therapy as well. Depending on the initial TRAb titers, neonatal Graves typically resolves by 6 months of age; treatment duration usually last about 1 to 2 months.
paragraphs.heading: Treatment

paragraphs.text: The hypothyroid infant born to a mother who received antithyroid medications during pregnancy should be managed as described in the section on congenital hypothyroidism. If the infant has already received thyroid hormone, such therapy should be decreased as soon as thyrotoxic manifestations occur, and the appropriate management of hyperthyroidism must be initiated.
paragraphs.heading: Treatment

paragraphs.text: Most infants diagnosed promptly and treated appropriately for neonatal Graves will improve quickly. However, it has been reported that some patients on long-term follow-up are found to have lower IQs. Craniosynostosis, hyperactivity, and other behavioral problems have also been seen.45 There have also been cases described associating neonatal Graves and/or poorly controlled maternal hyperthyroidism with the development of central hypothyroidism in the infant. It seems as if fetal or neonatal exposure to high thyroid
paragraphs.heading: Prognosis

paragraphs.text: hormone concentrations can impair neurodevelopment and specifically the maturation of the hypothalamic-pituitarythyroid axis. These findings highlight the importance of close monitoring of both maternal and neonatal thyroid function and drug management.
paragraphs.heading: Prognosis

paragraphs.text: Genetic disorders resulting in either increased or decreased levels of T4-binding proteins have been reported. Affected individuals are healthy and asymptomatic because a change in the level of T4-binding proteins does not lead to an alteration of fT4. The disorders are usually discovered fortuitously by the measurement of T4, which reveals unexpectedly high or low values. Therefore the only clinical significance of these conditions lies in the abnormal T4 level, possibly leading to an erroneous diagnosis. The TSH levels are normal in these individuals.
paragraphs.heading: Familial Abnormalities of Thyroxine- Binding Proteins

paragraphs.text: TBG is one of the major serum transport proteins for thyroid hormone. TBG is encoded by 1 gene copy on the long arm of the X chromosome (Xp22.2). Inherited TBG defects typically follow an X-linked pattern. Complete TBG deficiency occurs in 1/15,000 newborns and partial deficiency in 1/4000 newborns. Males with complete deficiency have undetectable TBG and heterozygous females typically have half the normal TBG concentration. Mutations that cause TBG excess result in TBG concentrations 2 to 4× the normal level in affected males. Inherited TBG excess is more rare and occurs in 1:25,000 newborns. Carrier females have levels slightly above half of affected males. TBG excess and deficiency are usually diagnosed incidentally with lab work demonstrating abnormal T4 and/or T3 with normal free T4.46
paragraphs.heading: Thyroxine-Binding Globulin Defects

paragraphs.text: Families with increased levels of TTR have been reported and specific gene mutations identified. Serum T4 is elevated, but fT4 is normal. Only a small amount of T4 is bound to TTR; therefore T4 level is only significantly elevated in variants with much higher binding affinity for thyroid hormone.46
paragraphs.heading: Increased Transthyretin

paragraphs.text: Familial dysalbuminemic hyperthyroxinemia is caused by the gain of function mutations in the human serum albumin gene resulting in enhanced binding of T4 by abnormal serum albumin. Its prevalence can be as high as 1:50 individuals among Hispanics, and in non-Hispanic Whites it is estimated to be 1:1000. Affected individuals typically have elevated T4 or T3, depending on the specific mutation. Free T4 concentration measured by direct dialysis is normal, but if analog methods are used, there may be interference from abnormal albumin, resulting in falsely elevated levels.46

# 92. Thyroid Disorders in the Neonate
> Source attribution: [Source credits](../../SOURCE_CREDITS.md).


## PDF page 1724 | printed page 1728

92 Thyroid Disorders in the

Neonate

### IRIS GUTMARK-LITTLE AND JANET CHUANG

Thyroid hormone is critical for growth and maturation of thyroid-dependent tissues, including the brain. Many physiologic factors influence fetal and neonatal thyroid function, including fetal-maternal relationships and the dynamic alteration of thyroid function with birth. Understanding the action of thyroid hormones, the synthesis and transport of these hormones, and mechanisms regulating thyroid function is important in the evaluation and management of thyroid disorders. Thyroid hormone abbreviations are defined in Box 92.1. This chapter will review thyroid physiology and embryology and then discuss the evaluation, diagnosis, and treatment of thyroid disorders seen in neonates.

### Physiologic Action of Thyroid Hormones

### Functions of the Thyroid Gland

The principal functions of the thyroid gland are to synthesize, store, and release the thyroid hormones thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) into circulation. The major secretory product of the thyroid is T4. Thyroidal secretion of T3 accounts for only about 20% of its production. The remaining 80% is derived from peripheral deiodination of T4. Therefore T4 acts as a prohormone for T3 because T4 has negligible intrinsic metabolic activity in most tissues. Most of the physiologic effects of thyroid hormone are mediated by T3 through its interaction with the nuclear thyroid hormone receptors that influence gene expression by binding thyroid response elements on DNA.

### Neurologic Effects

Prenatal and postnatal maturation of the brain, retina, and cochlea is thyroid hormone dependent. Thyroid hormone modulates the expression of thyroid hormone–responsive target genes at precise times during development, controlled by an interplay of deiodinases, thyroid receptor expression, transporters, cofactors, and transcription factors. T3 promotes the neural differentiation of embryonic

1728

stem cells at the dendritic level, and both T3 and T4 impact cerebral vascular development, neuronal migration, and myelination.

As normal levels of thyroid hormone are essential for fetal brain development, congenital thyroid hormone deficiency results in severe mental retardation if not treated. This effect is prevented by thyroid hormone replacement early in life. Early detection of congenital hypothyroidism occurs through newborn screening, which was initiated in the 1970s. Intellectual development is normal in children with congenital hypothyroidism who are treated early and aggressively.1,2 The degree of mental retardation is related to the severity and duration of the hypothyroid state of the infant. The central nervous system is most susceptible to a lack of thyroid hormone during developmental stages in the first several years of life as it undergoes rapid growth and maturation.

### Basal Metabolic Rate

Thyroid hormone stimulates basal metabolic rate primarily by increasing ATP production for metabolic processes and by maintaining ion gradients (Na/K+ and Ca2+) that consumes ATP. Thyroid hormone is a key driver of thermogenesis. It uncouples oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria and reduces the activity of shuttle molecules that transfer reducing equivalents into the mitochondria. Thyroid hormone also increases sensitivity to catecholamine effect which is required for the maintenance of core body temperature. Clinically, the calorigenic action of thyroid hormone affects circulation by increasing heart rate, stroke volume, and cardiac output. The pulse pressure is widened mainly by a decrease in the diastolic pressure and by some elevation in the systolic pressure. Circulation time is also reduced.

### Lipid, Carbohydrate, and Calcium Metabolism

Thyroid hormone stimulates the expression of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptors and in hypothyroidism, the

number of hepatic LDL receptors is reduced, leading to the decreased clearance of circulating LDL. Hypothyroidism results in increased serum total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol, apolipoprotein B, and lipoprotein (a). Carbohydrate metabolism is impacted by thyroid hormone through stimulation of gluconeogenesis, reduction in insulin sensitivity, and increase in insulin metabolism. Calcium balance is also influenced by thyroid hormones. In hyperthyroidism, calcium balance tends to be negative. Urinary and fecal calcium excretion is enhanced. Demineralization of bone also occurs through an increase in osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. The efflux of calcium from the bones leads to higher plasma ionized calcium and phosphate and lower circulating 1,25(OH)2D3, which in turn results in decreased calcium absorption from the intestine.

### Liver and Renal Function

Hypothyroidism leads to decreased biliary output and cholestasis; the glucuronic acid conjugation mechanism of the liver may also be impaired. In infants, congenital hypothyroidism is associated with either conjugated or unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and can present as prolonged neonatal jaundice. Renal function is influenced by thyroid hormone through pre-renal effects on the cardiovascular system/renal blood flow and through direct effects on the glomerular filtration rate. Hypothyroidism causes
