### Micropenis

A micropenis is caused by a deficiency in the factors needed for normal penile growth to occur after 14 weeks of gestation, when formation of the urethra is complete. Important hormonal mediators of penile growth are testosterone, DHT, and growth hormone. The major causes of micropenis include hypopituitarism (LH deficiency, GH deficiency, or both: 30%), primary hypogonadism (25%), disorders of androgen action (pAIS 2%), and idiopathic causes (43%). Other rarer causes include 5-alphareductase-deficiency, Klinefelter syndrome, and other X chromosome aneuploidies. Hypogonadism and associated micropenis may also be a part of a syndromic spectrum such as Prader-Willi, Bardet-Biedl, Laurence-Moon, and Russel Silver syndrome.15 The association of a micropenis with early neonatal hypoglycemia (GH and ACTHcortisol deficiencies), cryptorchidism (LH deficiency–see Fig. 93.8), persistent neonatal jaundice (hypothyroidism, GH, and ACTH-cortisol deficiency), or cleft palate should immediately raise the possibility of congenital hypopituitarism (e.g., in septo-optic dysplasia). Micropenis in the presence of other genital abnormalities such as hypospadias should raise suspicion for a diagnosis of DSD. Complete absence of the penis (aphallia) may rarely occur.

The diagnostic evaluation of a micropenis includes the assessment of GH, LH, FSH, and testosterone status. Karyotype may be considered if there is associated cryptorchidism or additional concerns with the appearance of the genitalia. An hCG stimulation test may be performed if testosterone levels are low to assess for biosynthetic defects. A course of testosterone therapy to assess penile responsiveness may be administered to exclude significant androgen insensitivity. The overall efficacy of testosterone therapy in improving patient psychosocial outcomes and final adult SPL is not clear, and there is a lack of consensus regarding timing of administration and dose.

### Cryptorchidism

Cryptorchidism is present when one or both testes have failed to descend completely into the scrotum, reaching a final position 4 cm or more below the pubic crest in fullterm males weighing more than 2.5 kg. Testicular descent occurs between 7 months’ gestation and several months postnatally and therefore most of the affected newborns are found to be normal when they are reevaluated. The incidence of cryptorchidism at birth is 1% to 8% in full-term males, 30% in premature males. However, the postnatal completion of testicular descent in full-term cryptorchid males is observed in 50% in the first months of life. Rates of cryptorchidism are 3% by 3 months and 1% by 1 year. Seventy-three percent of premature, cryptorchid males will have completed testicular descent by 3 months. Spontaneous descent beyond 9 months of age is rare. Overall, 75% of full-term and 90% of premature cryptorchid newborns have full testicular descent by the age of 9 months without therapeutic intervention.75 In addition to prematurity, other factors associated with an increased incidence of cryptorchidism are low birth weight, birth by cesarean delivery, and maternal obesity.

Testicular descent is a complex process involving hormonal, mechanical, and genetic factors.76 These include the presence and normal function of the gubernaculum, attachment of the epididymis to the testis, rising abdominal pressure, the genitofemoral nerve, the production and action of AMH, testosterone and DHT, and possibly LH and FSH. Cryptorchidism frequently occurs with disorders of the hypothalamic-pituitary-testicular hormone axis, with dysgenetic testes, and with anatomic defects of the epididymis and the abdominal wall. Cryptorchidism is seen with a higher incidence in patients with umbilical hernia (6%), gastroschisis (15%), omphalocele (33%), and Eagle-Barrett (prune-belly) syndrome (100%), in which abnormal intraabdominal pressure may contribute. It is also seen more frequently in individuals with meningomyelocele (25%), particularly when the defect is above L2, and in those with cerebral palsy (41%). Cryptorchidism is associated with lower levels of LH and testosterone during the mini puberty of infancy that occurs between 1 and 3 months’ postnatal age and it is also seen in association with hypopituitarism, primary hypogonadism, Prader-Willi syndrome, and androgen


## PDF page 1782

insensitivity syndrome. Cryptorchidism has been associated with persistent müllerian duct syndrome, suggesting a role for AMH in this process.58 An association is also seen with trisomies 13 and 18 and with Aarskog, Noonan, Robinow, Smith-Lemli-Opitz, and other syndromes. Familial cases are reported and cryptorchidism is found in 6.2% of brothers and 1.5% to 4% of fathers of affected patients. The relative risk of developing cryptorchidism increases 4- to 6-fold for males with an affected first-degree relative.76

Associated anomalies include an inguinal hernia in many patients, abnormal epididymal formation in 36% to 66%, and hypospadias in about 3%. There are major upper urinary tract anomalies in about 3% of patients, but routine invasive diagnostic studies are not warranted. Complications of cryptorchidism include progressive histologic deterioration of the testes with changes beginning after 6 months of age. Spermatogenesis is impaired, with a decrease in the number of germ cells after the first year of life and resultant reduced fertility potential. There is also a 4- to 10-fold increased risk of malignancy in both the undescended and contralateral testis (in unilateral cases). Other complications include trauma to the testis that is in a relatively fixed position, testicular torsion, symptomatic inguinal hernia, and psychological concerns related to altered body image. An associated inguinal hernia may require repair in early infancy if it is large enough to permit the abdominal contents to enter or if the patient is symptomatic.

If both testes are nonpalpable, the differential diagnosis includes a 46,XX infant with CAH or other severe virilizing disorder, anorchia (which occurs in 1% of bilaterally cryptorchid patients), intra-abdominal testes, which can be either normal (as in persistent müllerian duct syndrome) or dysgenetic (as in mixed gonadal dysgenesis or testicular dysgenesis). The evaluation of the infant with nonpalpable testes should include a karyotype and a 17-OHP. To evaluate the function of the testicles, other hormonal studies might include measuring AMH or, inhibin B and LH, FSH, and testosterone. An hCG stimulation test can also provide important information regarding Leydig cell function if testosterone level is low. A pelvic ultrasound is an easy first step to evaluate internal genitalia if there are concerns related to a possible DSD. Magnetic resonance imaging and laparoscopy have been useful in locating intra-abdominal testes, but explorative laparotomy is definitive in cases that are not otherwise resolved. The presence of wolffian structures indicates functional AMH at an early time in genital duct development and can suggest degeneration of testes later in utero because of torsion or a vascular incident; however, dysgenetic testes may also be present. Parental counseling should be undertaken in anticipation of this likelihood.

### Clitoromegaly

Clitoromegaly is defined as the appearance of clitoral enlargement regardless of cause. The clitoris may be prominent (protruding from between the labia majora), swollen, widened, or elongated. A prominent clitoral hood or postnatal edema may be mistaken for clitoromegaly. An inverse relationship between clitoral size and gestational age or birth weight has not been consistently observed, and thus the clitoris may appear to be more prominent in small for gestational age and premature infants.17 The causes of clitoromegaly are listed in Box 93.4. The clitoris must be measured to determine whether the paired corpora cavernosa are abnormally enlarged and to rule out the presence of a tumor. Most commonly, clitoromegaly is a benign finding and both the corpora cavernosa are of normal size and there is no evidence of a tumor. In this case, no further diagnostic evaluation is necessary. If the corpora cavernosa are enlarged (>6.5 mm), a DSD is more likely. Further evaluation should include other signs of androgenization or incomplete masculinization (posterior labial fusion, ventral placement of the urethra, or hypospadias), determination of presence and location of the gonads, identification of internal genitalia (müllerian structures), and measurement of androgens and 17-OH progesterone levels. A karyotype may also be warranted.

title: Inborn Errors of Metabolism

paragraphs.text: 94 Inborn Errors of Metabolism
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Among physicians caring for a sick newborn infant, the primary dilemmas are to know when to consider the possibility of a metabolic disorder, what to do to determine most efficiently whether a child has a metabolic disease, and how to best treat the patient until a diagnosis is established.1,2 A listing of clinical and laboratory findings characteristic of inborn errors of metabolism is presented, and the differential diagnoses for these findings and recommendations for further diagnostic testing to reach a diagnosis are provided, along with detailed information about specific diseases.3–5
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: Two approaches to providing medical care for neonates with inborn errors of metabolism are (1) prospective care of the apparently healthy newborn infant, and (2) reactive care of the clinically ill newborn infant. Prospective care seeks to identify neonates who have a specific metabolic disorder before clinical manifestations of that disorder develop. The aim of the prospective approach is to prevent the morbidity or mortality that often occurs in the period before recognition, diagnosis, and initiation of therapy for what might be a preventable or treatable disease. The reactive approach aims to arrest or minimize the sequelae of the disease state after the affected child shows recognizable symptoms or signs or becomes ill.
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: This chapter outlines several common misconceptions about inborn errors of metabolism, addresses prospective recognition of inborn errors (including newborn screening programs), and discusses reactive recognition and care of the critically ill newborn infant.
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: Metabolic diseases of infancy are oftentimes a difficult group of conditions for many physicians and other medical professionals caring for newborns to address. Several misconceptions contribute to this difficulty. These misconceptions are presented below in an exaggerated way to emphasize that, on reflection, most physicians would acknowledge that these ideas are not necessarily true. However, experience suggests that, in the intense atmosphere surrounding a critically ill
paragraphs.heading: Common Misconceptions

paragraphs.text: neonate, these misconceptions often influence the care of the child with an inborn error of metabolism.
paragraphs.heading: Common Misconceptions

paragraphs.text: Inherited metabolic diseases are rarely a cause of disease in the neonate and should therefore be considered diagnostically as a last resort.
paragraphs.heading: Misconception 1

paragraphs.text: Although individual metabolic diseases are relatively rare, inherited metabolic diseases collectively represent a more common cause of disease in the neonatal period. The estimated incidence in the general population of specific inherited metabolic diseases varies, ranging from one case per 10,000 live births for phenylketonuria (PKU) to one case per 200,000 for homocystinuria. The overall incidence of metabolic disease is approximately one case per 2000 persons. Newborn screening programs alone have found an incidence of approximately one in 4000 for a subset of these diseases. Not all of the nearly 100 inherited metabolic disorders that are identifiable in the neonatal period are screened for on antenatal screening. There is good reason to believe that this estimate of the incidence of metabolic disease in neonates is an underestimate, because many metabolic diseases go underdiagnosed and many diseases are yet to be identified in these patients.
paragraphs.heading: Misconception 1

paragraphs.text: The possibility of a genetic metabolic disease should be considered only when there is a family history of the disease.
paragraphs.heading: Misconception 2

paragraphs.text: Most neonates with an inborn error of metabolism do not have a similarly affected sibling or other relative. The reason for this pattern follows the rules of Mendelian inheritance. Most inborn errors of metabolism are inherited as autosomal recessive traits, for which the odds are 3:1 in each pregnancy that two heterozygous (carrier) parents will have an unaffected child. The trend toward smaller family sizes in developed countries make it less likely to see two affected offspring (homozygous or compound heterozygotes) from a pair of carrier parents. For example, in a family of two siblings, the odds are about 6% that both siblings will have the disease if both parents are carriers for an inborn error of metabolism. In a family of three children, the odds are
paragraphs.heading: Misconception 2

paragraphs.text: about 14% that two of the three siblings will be affected and about 2% that all three siblings will be affected.
paragraphs.heading: Misconception 2

paragraphs.text: There often is no forewarning of an affected male neonate with an X-linked disorder, because he may have one or more healthy older sisters; heterozygous females do not necessarily express many X-linked disorders. Also, some X-linked disorders are the result of new mutations (in onethird of cases with no family history), and the birth of a sick newborn could not be anticipated. Similarly, because some autosomal dominant disorders are also the result of new mutations or there are variable degrees of expressivity from family member to family member (some with very mild to no symptoms in some relatives vs. a severe presentation in others), a positive family history would not necessarily be expected.
paragraphs.heading: Misconception 2

paragraphs.text: It is difficult to know when to suspect that a sick newborn infant may have a metabolic disorder, because presentation of such disorders often mimics that of sepsis in the newborn infant.
paragraphs.heading: Misconception 3

paragraphs.text: The clinical manifestations of many metabolic diseases are in fact similar to the presentation of many neonatal infections. In fact, the presentation is so similar, it is often difficult to distinguish a septic neonate from a newborn in a metabolic crisis. The “sepsis work-up” is a broadly focused approach to identifying an underlying infection. However, a metabolic evaluation should also be included as part of the evaluation for suspected sepsis. It is also important to note that a neonate with a metabolic disease may be at greater risk of sepsis than other newborn infants, and the presence of documented sepsis does not exclude the possibility of an underlying metabolic disorder. Galactosemia is a well-documented example of a metabolic disease that predisposes an infant to serious infection (specifically Escherichia coli sepsis).
paragraphs.heading: Misconception 3

paragraphs.text: It is difficult to diagnose a metabolic disease.
paragraphs.heading: Misconception 4

paragraphs.text: The examination of patients with suspected metabolic disease must be staged, progressing from broad screening tests that should be available in all settings where care is provided to sick neonates to highly specialized tests that may be available in only a handful of centers. The idea of a staged evaluation is perhaps best illustrated by congenital hyperammonemia. The ability to diagnose hyperammonemia should be possible in most settings by measuring an ammonia level. However, the subsequent delineation of a specific cause of the hyperammonemia and the subsequent care of the patient are best reserved for a few specialized centers where metabolic genetics specialists are available. The primary responsibility of the physician initially caring for the sick newborn is to recognize the possibility of hyperammonemia and to measure the blood ammonia level in a timely manner before the patient suffers irreversible damage, in addition to providing or referring them for appropriate
paragraphs.heading: Misconception 4

paragraphs.text: treatment (this may require referral to a more specialized center with experts in metabolic diseases).
paragraphs.heading: Misconception 4

paragraphs.text: Metabolic test results take forever to return.
paragraphs.heading: Misconception 5

paragraphs.text: Some metabolic tests do not produce immediate results and may take several days for results to become available. It is important to stage the evaluation. It is generally best to begin with relatively broad-based screening tests that come back quickly (such as an ammonia level, blood gas, renal function panel, or lactate). These more immediately available tests can then be followed by more specific diagnostic studies that usually take longer to be completed. The aim is to use the screening studies to obtain preliminary indications on which to base further evaluations and to initiate appropriate care before a final diagnosis is confirmed.
paragraphs.heading: Misconception 5

paragraphs.text: Relatively few metabolic diseases can be treated, so why spend a great deal of effort looking for something that you cannot fix?
paragraphs.heading: Misconception 6

paragraphs.text: A large number of metabolic disorders can be treated, often successfully. As time goes on, technology advances and clinical trials expand with the latest treatments available. Subsequently, new and often times more effective treatments have become available for disorders that previously had nothing to be offered. The approach to the differential diagnosis should give greater consideration to detecting potentially treatable entities. The initial screening studies should permit identification of classes of disease for which there are therapies. For example, the congenital hyperammonemias are a group of disorders for which generic general therapy (i.e., ammonia scavengers) is available; therapy can be further modified after a more specific diagnosis is made. It is also important to establish a diagnosis for the sake of the parents, who seek to understand why they have a sick baby, and for the purpose of formal genetic counseling to allow future preventative testing.
paragraphs.heading: Misconception 6

paragraphs.text: There are two types of prospective care. The first type is the screening of a high-risk segment of the population—the siblings or other at-risk relatives of patients known to have a particular metabolic disorder. The second type is screening of the entire population or specific subset of newborn infants.
paragraphs.heading: Prospective Approaches

paragraphs.text: Neonates at high risk for metabolic disorders are the siblings or other at-risk relatives of patients with a known metabolic disorder. These infants include those at risk for diseases for which there is no prenatal diagnosis. Postnatal
paragraphs.heading: The Newborn Infant at High Risk for a Particular Metabolic Disorder

paragraphs.text: confirmation is required for a positive or a negative prenatal test result in at-risk patients. This is especially important to avoid the rare false-negative prenatal test result that could lead to failure to treat an affected patient. Finally, siblings of an infant with an inborn error of metabolism that may have a variable age of onset are also at risk for developing disease and should also undergo evaluation and testing.
paragraphs.heading: The Newborn Infant at High Risk for a Particular Metabolic Disorder

paragraphs.text: Management of pregnancies and neonates at high risk requires a coordinated effort among the obstetrician, metabolic geneticist, neonatologist, and/or pediatrician. The first decision is to determine where the at-risk baby will be delivered. If the baby will not be delivered at a center at which a metabolic expert is available, the indications for transfer after birth must be developed before birth. Regardless of where the baby is delivered, a detailed plan must be prepared and made available to all personnel caring for the newborn. The plan should include specific details of what tests will be needed to identify the disease, how the tests will be performed, where the samples for testing are to be sent after they are obtained, and who will follow up on the test results and inform the family.
paragraphs.heading: The Newborn Infant at High Risk for a Particular Metabolic Disorder

paragraphs.text: Newborn screening combines a number of significant medical and legal issues. These issues will become progressively more complex and diverse as an increasing number of inborn errors of metabolism become amenable to newborn screening and as the responsibilities of the physician in follow-up of such testing becomes greater.6–8 Although there is ongoing discussion and some debate about which medical conditions should be screened and how they are to be screened, there is a consensus about the goals of mass newborn screening. The US Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) has an appointed Advisory Committee of Heritable Disorders in Newborns and Children (ACHDNC) who periodically issues reports that update their Recommended Uniform Screening Panel (RUSP) list. This list currently includes 35 specific “core” and 26 secondary conditions that are recommended to be included on the newborn screening panel in every state. The goal of this panel is to encourage newborn screening to be uniform and comprehensive throughout the United States but is not required by law. This list was last updated in July of 2018 (https://www.hrsa.gov/advisory-committees/heritable-disor ders/rusp/index.html).9 This panel is based on the principles outlined below but is always evolving based on the most up to date data.
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: Historically, the requirements of an acceptable mass screening program for a particular disease include the following: • The availability of a reliable screening test with a low
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: false-negative rate • A test that is simple and inexpensive, because exponen-
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: tially more negative tests will be performed for each case identified • A rapid screening test that can provide results quickly
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: enough to permit effective intervention
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: • A definitive follow-up test that is available for unambigu-
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: ous identification of true-positive results and elimination of false-positive results • A disorder of a sufficiently deleterious nature that, if
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: untreated, would result in significant morbidity or death • An effective therapy that significantly alters the natural
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: history of the disease Relatively few metabolic disorders satisfy all of these requirements. These criteria have been demonstrated, in a strict sense, only for biotinidase deficiency and PKU. On the other hand, neonates with classic galactosemia or maple syrup urine disease (MSUD), for example, might become very sick within the first few days of life before the results of newborn screening tests are available, thereby compromising the benefit of the screening program. More recently, disorders such as X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD) and Krabbe disease have been added to newborn screening panels in some states. There is debate regarding the addition of these disorders in particular to newborn screening programs. In the case of X-linked ALD, the testing detects a large number of carrier females who, in most cases, will not be symptomatic or could have milder symptoms later in adulthood (i.e., adrenomyeloneuropathy [AMN] or adrenal insufficiency). Even males who are identified by newborn screening may or may not ever develop severe symptoms of ALD, as there is variable expressivity, even in the same family. However, some patients develop symptoms of classic ALD as young children, and early identification can lead to the availability of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) as a cure to be initiated with notation of the initial ALD-associated changes on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). On the other hand, some males may never develop ALD but might develop adrenal insufficiency or AMN later in life.10 Therefore it may not be clear in the neonatal period if the child will require treatment in the future and when in life this will occur. This leads to a situation where there is a potential diagnosis of adult-onset disorders in patients under the age of 18 years without their consent for testing. This is an area of concern ethically in the field of medical genetics, because testing minors for adult-onset disorders is not considered to be appropriate.
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: In the case of Krabbe disease, another devastating neurodegenerative disease that may begin in the first months of life and progress rapidly, the availability of HSCT is an option to greatly slow progression of a disease that would otherwise be fatal in infancy. However, the treatment must be initiated as early as possible (within the first weeks of life), and it is not a cure. Patients who have been treated still have progression of disease, just at a slower pace. Also, there are overwhelmingly high numbers of false-positive cases due to the presence of pseudodeficiency alleles, the detection of many carriers, and cutoff reference range values on screening set high enough to not miss the affected patients. Most families who have had their babies identified as at increased risk for Krabbe disease on newborn screening often express negative views on the screening for this disorder as it caused
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: them undue stress, even to the point of posttraumatic stress disorder in some cases. However, for the few families who had affected children diagnosed early enough to have the option of treatment with HSCT, their children are still with them a few years after they would have certainly passed away without intervention. As time goes on as the patients treated are followed longitudinally, it will become more clear if newborn screening for Krabbe disease should be universally offered by all states (see below regarding the RUSP in place in the United States).9,11
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: A few principles apply to all screening programs. First, all screening tests are subject to false-positive results because of normal biologic variation, genetic heterogeneity, and human error. Accordingly, all positive screening results must be confirmed by definitive analysis. It is important that all patients who require therapy receive it and, conversely, that patients who do not require therapy not be treated.
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: Second, all positive results must be considered medical emergencies. Many positive results turn out to be falsely positive, but the concept underlying newborn screening is that identification of the few affected patients is crucial. In addition to the potential tragedy of a missed diagnosis of the individual neonate, lack of attention that permits delayed care of a single affected patient can seriously jeopardize the public’s confidence in and the cost-benefit structure of a statewide screening program and can compromise the continuation of such programs.
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: Third, the disorders that are part of newborn screening may exhibit variable clinical expression even within families. Thus the siblings of a patient identified by a screening program should be biochemically evaluated for the same disorder, because they could be affected, although they appear free of symptoms at the time.
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: Fourth, all patients should be referred to an experienced specialist for definitive diagnosis. These disorders are characterized by clinical and genetic heterogeneity, which can significantly affect care of the patient and genetic counseling for the family.
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: There is considerable variation in the screening programs among different states in the United States and in various nations. This variability depends on several factors (https://www.hrsa.gov/advisory-committees/heritable-disor ders/rusp/index.html)9: 1. The frequency of the disorder in the state’s population 2. The availability of treatments and follow-up for each
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: condition in the region 3. The financial costs of screening and the funding sources
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: for the newborn screening program in the state or territory 4. Laws in the state or territory
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: All states and US territories screen for PKU. Until relatively recently, most states performed newborn screening for just three to six metabolic disorders (including PKU, homocystinuria, MSUD, and galactosemia), one endocrine disorder (congenital hypothyroidism), and the
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: hemoglobinopathies. However, with the availability of tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS), many more disorders have been added to newborn screening panels in the United States since the early 2000s, as discussed further below. Newborn screening is now more standardized from state to state, with most including fatty acid oxidation disorders, organic acidemias, some urea cycle disorders, and biotinidase deficiency. More recently, specific lysosomal storage disorders have been added to some state newborn screening panels.11 Several states are also screening for spinal muscular atrophy (see Chapter 58) and X-linked ALD (as noted above). The requirements and procedures for screening for hemoglobinopathies and congenital hypothyroidism are discussed in Chapters 81 and 92, respectively.
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: Most state screening programs originally focused primarily on the classic inborn errors of metabolism. The testing programs employed separate tests for each disease of interest which limited the scope of screening.6,7,12 These earlier assays could not be easily adapted to screen for other groups of disorders, such as disorders of organic acid metabolism and fatty acid oxidation. The other limitation in expanding newborn screening was that the standard methods being used to diagnose the organic acidemias and fatty acid oxidation disorders—gas chromatography, or combined gas chromatography and mass spectrometry (GC/MS)—could not be upgraded to large-scale newborn screening programs because they required tedious sample preparation and long analysis times.
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: Since the 1990s, intensive efforts have been made to expand the scope of newborn screening using MS/MS, which circumvents the limitations of the bacterial inhibition assay, gas chromatography, and GC/MS methods.6–8 In brief, MS/MS permits analysis of a broad range of metabolites in hundreds of blood samples per day. Most states have adopted the MS/MS approach to newborn screening as part of their program. The process of expanding the scope of newborn screening programs is still continuing as new and improved technologies become available and as new treatments for previously untreatable disease are discovered (making the usefulness of newborn screening important in these patients).8
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: Newborn screening by MS/MS starts, as did the traditional screening programs, by collecting a small blood sample via heel stick and applying it to a standardized filter paper card. The period for appropriate postpartum collection is 24 to 72 hours. Samples collected from either premature infants or sick newborns are potentially more difficult to interpret and are subject to greater false-positive and false-negative rates. The blood samples are shipped to a centralized laboratory where a standardized amount of the specimen card is punched out. The metabolites of interest are then extracted from the punch, subjected to specific chemical modifications to make them compatible for subsequent MS/MS analysis, and automatically introduced into and analyzed by the MS/MS system.
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: As opposed to traditional screening protocols that required different analytic approaches for each disorder, the current MS/MS techniques permit analysis of a large number of metabolites belonging to a particular category of disease— hence, many disorders—in each sample. Hundreds of samples can be prepared for analysis, analyzed, and interpreted each day with highly sensitive, accurate, and concurrent identification of multiple metabolites. Computer software permits pattern recognition using several related metabolites, thereby improving the reliability of the testing. In summary, the MS/MS technology is ideally suited for newborn screening of many samples for many possible disorders.
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: As with traditional newborn screening programs, the current MS/MS screening programs must determine the normal range for the different metabolites they analyze in their system. More importantly, the programs must set cutoffs above or below in order to identify a case as at-risk. This is a difficult, ongoing task. Programs that set their cutoffs too high have an unacceptable false-negative rate; conversely, programs that set their cutoffs too low have an unacceptable false-positive rate.
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: Experience has now demonstrated that MS/MS programs can detect PKU, MSUD, and homocystinuria as well as or better than the traditional screening approaches.6,8 Nevertheless, the practitioner must still be aware that the MS/MS-based screening programs still have false-positive and false-negative results, as did their older counterparts, although at lower rates. The practitioner must still determine whether a particular result is truly positive or falsely positive as expeditiously as possible. Expanded newborn screening programs have found that approximately 1 in 4000 newborns have an identifiable inborn error of metabolism.
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: Most states in the United States have adopted MS/MS screening to analyze disorders of amino acid metabolism (including several urea cycle disorders), organic acid metabolism, and fatty acid oxidation. However, they are still screening for several other disorders using test-specific methods (e.g., biotinidase deficiency, Pompe disease, galactosemia).8 The amino acid disorders and urea cycle disorders are detected by analyzing for increased blood concentrations of specific amino acids or combinations of amino acids. Many programs do not screen for disorders that are associated with reduced concentrations of specific amino acids, such as using a low serine concentration to screen for serine biosynthesis disorders or low citrulline to assess for proximal urea cycle disorders (ornithine transcarbamylase [OTC], carbamoyl phosphate synthetase-1 [CPS1], and N-acetylglutamate synthetase [NAGS] deficiency). However, in recent years at least eight states have added screening for the proximal urea cycle disorders via measurement of low citrulline alone or as a ratio with other biochemical markers.13,14 Specifically, more recently, following up a low citrulline with a glutamine-to-glutamate ratio will more reliably identify affected individuals while distinguishing them from healthy newborns.15
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: Similarly, the organic acidemias and fatty acid oxidation disorders are detected by analyzing for increased blood concentrations of specific acylcarnitines, which are the esters formed between carnitine and the acids that characteristically accumulate in the various organic acidemias and fatty acid oxidation disorders. Many programs evaluate samples for combinations of particular acylcarnitines to increase the reliability of their results. Screening for the plasma membrane carnitine uptake defect (also known as carnitine uptake deficiency) is an exception to the rule of looking for increased concentrations of characteristic metabolites, because it is based on identification of a reduced (rather than increased) concentration of free carnitine.
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: As noted above, significant progress has been achieved in developing and introducing newborn screening for two additional categories of inborn errors of metabolism: lysosomal storage disorders and peroxisomal disorders. Two lysosomal disorders, Hurler syndrome (aka mucopolysaccharidosis type I [MPS I])11 and Pompe disease (aka glycogen storage disease type II),16 and one peroxisomal disorder, X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD) as noted above,17 have been added to the federal RUSP.9,8 Screening for each of these disorders is currently available or approved for implementation in several states. The infantile form of Hurler disease typically manifests in the first year of life, whereas Pompe disease typically manifests in the first 6 months of life. Effective treatment is now available for Hurler syndrome (HSCT)18 and Pompe disease (enzyme replacement therapy),19,20 if it is started prior to the onset of irreversible clinical manifestations.
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: Similarly, HSCT significantly improves the prognosis for X-ALD, a peroxisomal disorder that does not manifest clinically until 2 years or older. Here, too, follow-up studies have shown that the outcome is best for patients who have received HSCT prior to the onset of subclinical evidence of neurologic damage.21 The screening protocol for X-ALD also identifies patients who have Zellweger spectrum disorder, a generalized defect in peroxisomal assembly and function that ultimately leads to defective peroxisomal very long-chain fatty acid oxidation. Unfortunately, there is no proven effective therapy for this group of peroxisomal disorders.22
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: It should be noted that there is ongoing concern regarding screening for these lysosomal and peroxisomal disorders, as it is possible to detect later-onset forms of these diseases with the screening tests for which there are limitations in our ability to predict if, or when, the patient will develop significant clinical manifestations. For example, in the case of X-ALD, some patients identified by newborn screening and then confirmed to have an ABCD1 gene mutation may never develop clinically significant disease, but we are unable to predict this during the neonatal period, leaving many years of uncertainty and worry ahead for the family and the patient’s physicians.10,17 This concern may also apply to other disorders detected by newborn screening, but the concern for the lysosomal storage disorders and peroxisomal disorders is heightened by the fact that the recommended
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: treatment for these disorders is more invasive (and expensive) than that required for most other disorders detected by newborn screening. It is anticipated that newborn screening for currently tested and additional lysosomal storage disorders, as well as peroxisomal disorders, will become available in more states in the near future. Similarly, it is expected that additional inborn errors of metabolism will be incorporated into newborn screening programs as screening technology improves, more therapeutic options are developed and assessed, and better genotype/phenotype correlations are established.
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: The confirmatory studies listed in Table 94.1 are readily available or orderable in most clinical settings and are discussed in detail later (see Specialized Biochemical Testing). The confirmatory studies cited include tests that have a relatively rapid turnaround time, generally 1 to 2 weeks, and could lead to rapid confirmation or elimination of a possible diagnosis. Additional, more refined studies, including specific enzyme analysis, whole cell studies, or genetic mutational analysis, are often required to definitively establish a specific diagnosis, but these generally have a longer turnaround time.
paragraphs.heading: Newborn Screening Programs

paragraphs.text: The abnormal laboratory findings listed in Table 94.1 permit the diagnosis of more than 30 genetic disorders, including amino acid disorders, fatty acid oxidation disorders, organic acidemias, urea cycle disorders, and several unrelated enzymatic defects. The list of metabolites provided in Table 94.1 is not comprehensive. Many other metabolites have been identified or can theoretically be identified, but they are not listed because of the rarity or uncertain clinical phenotype of the associated disorder. paragraphs.text: through with appropriate follow-up evaluation. The physician should then assess the newborn’s clinical status and arrange to see the family as expeditiously as possible.
paragraphs.heading: Inborn Errors of Metabolism That Can Be Ascertained by Newborn Screening Programs*—cont’d

paragraphs.text: The primary physician should either see the patient or refer the patient to a metabolic specialist for further evaluation and care. It is often best that the primary physician see the patient as soon as possible to assess the patient’s status, discuss the newborn screening results with the family, and then work with the metabolic specialist to develop an expeditious plan for evaluation. Confirmatory testing should be initiated as soon as possible.
paragraphs.heading: Inborn Errors of Metabolism That Can Be Ascertained by Newborn Screening Programs*—cont’d

paragraphs.text: The decisions about if or when to initiate treatment and how to treat are based on the nature of the laboratory abnormality found, the quantitative degree of the abnormality, the prior experience of the program with false positives for that metabolite, and the patient’s clinical status. In general, starting a treatment immediately after the initial confirmatory studies are initiated is both safe and unlikely to compromise the ability to establish a diagnosis. However, this option is predicated on the ability of the physician to make certain that the diagnostic samples are collected properly, sent to the appropriate laboratory, and received in satisfactory condition by the laboratory. Failure to do this before starting treatment might significantly delay the time required to establish a diagnosis and initiate appropriate treatment.
paragraphs.heading: Inborn Errors of Metabolism That Can Be Ascertained by Newborn Screening Programs*—cont’d

paragraphs.text: Many of the disorders identified are treated, at least in part, by some form of dietary restriction. A family’s desire to continue breastfeeding while the diagnostic studies are in progress should be carefully considered in all cases. However, depending on the disorder under consideration and the patient’s clinical status, the default position should be in favor of pausing breastfeeding until a provisional diagnosis has been established. During that time, the mother can continue to express breast milk via a breast pump and store it for later use. It is generally a matter of few days before the results of the initial confirmatory studies are available, when a more definitive decision can be made about the advisability of continuation of breastfeeding. Similar reasoning should be exercised about starting vitamin or cofactor supplementation.
paragraphs.heading: Inborn Errors of Metabolism That Can Be Ascertained by Newborn Screening Programs*—cont’d

paragraphs.text: The impact of the expanded newborn screening programs is still being determined. There have clearly been many instances when the programs have led to the early recognition of an as-yet-unaffected newborn, followed by the introduction of appropriate treatment. In some cases, this has meant that a newborn with one of the organic acidemias or urea cycle defects that can manifest with an acute neurologic intoxication syndrome in the first few days of life does not suffer an insult that produces severe, irreversible neurologic damage. In other cases, the newborn screening result becomes available after a newborn is already ill, but the result provides a rapid diagnosis for the illness and leads to earlier introduction of appropriate therapy, thereby improving the patient’s outcome. However, it is not yet clear whether early recognition and institution of appropriate treatment changes the
paragraphs.heading: Inborn Errors of Metabolism That Can Be Ascertained by Newborn Screening Programs*—cont’d

paragraphs.text: long-term prognosis for many of these diseases, such as recurrent hyperammonemic crises in the urea cycle defects or renal failure in methylmalonic acidemia.
paragraphs.heading: Inborn Errors of Metabolism That Can Be Ascertained by Newborn Screening Programs*—cont’d

paragraphs.text: There may also be negative consequences to these expanded newborn screening programs. For example, the screening programs could produce undesirable effects on the family of a child with a false-positive result, including increased hospitalization of the child, parental stress, and parent-child dysfunction.23
paragraphs.heading: Inborn Errors of Metabolism That Can Be Ascertained by Newborn Screening Programs*—cont’d

paragraphs.text: In addition to the current MS/MS newborn screening programs for amino acid and acylcarnitine analysis, new methods for evaluating other groups of inborn errors of metabolism, including the lysosomal storage disorders and peroxisomal disorders, are being utilized in many states and are under development in others. It seems reasonable to anticipate that many of these methods will be introduced for additional disorders over the next several years, further expanding the responsibility and role of the pediatrician and neonatologist in caring for children with metabolic disorders.
paragraphs.heading: Inborn Errors of Metabolism That Can Be Ascertained by Newborn Screening Programs*—cont’d

paragraphs.text: Separate summaries of several disorders that were part of the traditional screening programs and that are now evaluated by MS/MS programs (e.g., homocystinuria, MSUD, PKU) are provided next because they are useful paradigms for understanding the benefit of the newborn screening programs and how they work.24 A summary is also provided for medium-chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency, because it is the most common of the fatty acid oxidation disorders that are now evaluated by MS/MS programs, and it is one of the paradigms for this group of disorders. Summaries are also provided for biotinidase deficiency and galactosemia, which are disorders that are primarily evaluated by methodologies other than MS/MS. Other disorders that are now part of expanded newborn screening programs are discussed elsewhere in this chapter, including fatty acid β-oxidation disorders (see Hypoglycemia), nonketotic hyperglycinemia (see Metabolic Seizures), organic acidemias (see Metabolic Acidosis), tyrosinemia type I (see Hepatic Dysfunction), urea cycle defects (see Hyperammonemia), and, most recently, specific lysosomal disorders and peroxisomal disorders.
paragraphs.heading: Inborn Errors of Metabolism That Can Be Ascertained by Newborn Screening Programs*—cont’d

paragraphs.text: Biotinidase is an enzyme necessary for recycling biotin, a vitamin cofactor required for four critical intracellular carboxylation reactions: acetyl-coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA) carboxylase, 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase, propionyl-CoA carboxylase, and pyruvate carboxylase. Hence, biotinidase deficiency is one cause of multiple carboxylase deficiency (the other cause is holocarboxylase synthetase deficiency).24,25 These carboxylase reactions are involved in fatty acid biosynthesis, branched-chain amino acid metabolism, and gluconeogenesis.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: Biotinidase deficiency is characterized by a variable clinical presentation but can lead to severe metabolic decompensation in the newborn period; features include ketoacidosis,
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: hypotonia, seizures, and coma. Some infants also have significant dermatologic findings (including rash and alopecia) and immunodeficiency. If untreated, older children could have visual problems, hearing loss, and developmental delay. This disorder can be treated successfully with biotin supplementation (5–10 mg/d PO). Some residual neurologic deficits could persist if treatment does not begin before the onset of symptoms. Newborn screening allows for early diagnosis and initiation of treatment, which reduces morbidity.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: Serum biotinidase enzyme activity is the gold standard for newborn screening of biotinidase deficiency.24,25 The disorder can also be detected using MS/MS to measure the blood concentration of C5-OH (3-hydroxyisovalerylcarnitine), the acylcarnitine that is formed due to the secondary deficiency of 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase. However, the sensitivity of the MS/MS approach is unknown, and it might not provide a reliable method for newborn screening. A positive screening result should be confirmed by quantitative serum biotinidase analysis and by performing plasma carnitine analysis and urine organic acid analysis, looking for the characteristic plasma acylcarnitine pattern and organic aciduria that is present in a small percentage of affected patients.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: Care must be exercised in collecting and processing the serum specimen used for biotinidase enzyme analysis. It is best to obtain a concurrent control from an unrelated individual to establish that the sample has been processed properly (i.e., eliminate the chance of a false-positive result) and was not exposed to environmental factors during transport that could affect the results (such as excess heat or cold).
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: Classic galactosemia is the consequence of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT) deficiency. Classic galactosemia can manifest in the newborn period with lethargy, poor feeding, jaundice, cataracts, and in some cases, E. coli sepsis.24,26 If unrecognized, this disorder can lead to early death or a chronic course characterized by cirrhosis, cataracts, seizures, and intellectual disability. The mainstay of therapy for classic galactosemia is strict dietary galactose restriction.24,26 Dietary galactose restriction should be started as early as possible (preferably within the first few days after birth) to have the best chance of precluding the development of the severe illness described above as well as long-term intellectual disabilities. However, even children treated early often exhibit learning disabilities and verbal dyspraxia. Affected girls frequently develop premature ovarian failure (∼80%).26,27 This observation serves as a caution to those caring for children with galactosemia that longterm follow-up is mandatory and further improvements in treatment are required over time as new recommendations and information become available.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: There are two other forms of galactosemia to be considered: uridine diphosphate galactose-4′-epimerase deficiency and galactokinase deficiency. In most cases, epimerase deficiency is a benign condition that does not require treatment. The rarer, systemic form of epimerase deficiency produces a clinical picture similar to classic galactosemia. Galactokinase
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: deficiency is also rare and produces nuclear cataracts but none of the other manifestations of classic galactosemia. Early recognition and treatment of this disorder via dietary galactose restriction are generally successful.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: One approach to newborn screening for galactosemia measures GALT enzyme activity in red blood cells. This assay can detect GALT deficiency without impact of prior dietary intake of galactose; however, it does not evaluate either epimerase activity or galactokinase activity. Therefore newborns with either epimerase deficiency or galactokinase deficiency are not ascertained by this approach to newborn screening. Another approach to newborn screening for galactosemia is to measure total galactose and galactose- 1-phosphate (the substrate for GALT). This allows for evaluation for all three enzyme deficiencies associated with the galactosemias. However, recent galactose intake (in the form of breast milk or formula) may affect these results, leading to a false-positive results; conversely, patients not receiving a lactose-containing diet may have false-negative results.1 Because of the rapid onset of symptoms in classic galactosemia and the presence of galactose in breast milk and many cow milk–based formulas, screening programs for galactosemia must provide rapid results. However, the screening results are not always available before the affected neonate becomes ill; initial evaluation of a sick newborn should therefore include testing for the presence of urinary-reducing substances, as this would be positive in galactosemia (see Specialized Biochemical Testing). A newborn identified by newborn screen as possibly having classic galactosemia should have definitive biochemical testing by measuring whole blood or erythrocyte GALT activity and erythrocyte galactose-1-phosphate. In addition, genetic analysis for the common GALT mutations is often helpful in interpreting the results of the GALT activity measurements and making treatment decisions. Following initiation of these studies, galactose should be withdrawn from the diet, pending results of the laboratory investigations, by replacing breast milk or cow milk–based formula with a soy-based formula.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: Widespread neonatal testing of erythrocyte GALT activity in various populations has revealed considerable genetic heterogeneity of this enzyme deficiency.26 Some individuals have a partial enzyme deficiency that does not result in significant impairment of galactose metabolism or any discernible clinical disorder; there is no evidence of a need for dietary treatment of these cases. In other cases with partial enzyme activity, erythrocyte galactose-1-phosphate concentrations are increased, and minimal symptoms can develop. These cases can be managed with restriction of dietary galactose intake.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: Several inborn errors of metabolism produce homocystinuria.24,28,29 The most common of these disorders is caused by cystathionine β-synthase deficiency, an autosomal recessive disorder. Cystathionine β-synthase is a pyridoxine (vitamin B6)-dependent enzyme. Rare disorders that also lead to homocystinuria include defects in folate or
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: cobalamin metabolism. Screening programs for homocystinuria are based on detection of elevated blood levels of methionine, a precursor of cystathionine. Hypermethioninemia is characteristic of cystathionine β-synthase deficiency but may not be associated with other causes of homocystinuria. In fact, patients who have homocystinuria due to a defect in cobalamin metabolism may actually have low methionine levels. Therefore only some cobalamin disorders are detected by newborn screening for hypermethioninemia, whereas others are detected by their abnormal acylcarnitine profile. For example, cobalamin C disease will exhibit both methylmalonic acidemia and homocystinuria. These patients are ascertained by an elevated propionylcarnitine (C3), which is related to the methylmalonic acidemia associated with their disease. In the case of a related disorder, patients with cobalamin E disease exhibit homocystinuria/homocystinemia, megaloblastic anemia, and low methionine but are missed by newborn screening.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: Other false-positive and false-negative results occur in screening programs for homocystinuria.29,24 False-positive results are generally the consequence of artifacts (e.g., poor quality of sample), but they may also result from nongenetic causes of hypermethioninemia, such as parenteral administration of amino acids, generalized liver disease, hepatic immaturity, or, rarely, from a genetic cause such as hereditary tyrosinemia, galactosemia, or citrin deficiency (see Hepatic Dysfunction). False-negative results are produced by the milder variants of cystathionine β-synthase deficiency, especially the pyridoxine-responsive form, which might not exhibit hypermethioninemia in the neonatal period or the cobalamin metabolism disorders mentioned above that do not result in elevated methionine but still are associated with homocystinuria.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: The diagnosis of homocystinuria should be confirmed in patients with a positive newborn screening test by measuring total plasma homocysteine, plasma amino acids, and plasma methylmalonic acid. The diagnosis of cystathionine β-synthase deficiency can be confirmed by measuring the enzyme activity in cultured skin fibroblasts or by genetic testing.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: Cystathionine β-synthase deficiency rarely manifests in the neonatal period, but it can cause lethargy, poor feeding, and thromboembolic phenomena when it does.24,28,29 If untreated, the disorder can lead to musculoskeletal anomalies suggestive of a marfanoid habitus, ectopia lentis, thromboembolic vascular disease, behavioral or psychiatric problems, and intellectual disabilities. Patients with pyridoxine-responsive defects tend to have milder disease than do patients with pyridoxine-nonresponsive defects. All patients should undergo a pyridoxine challenge test to determine whether they are pyridoxine responsive.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: Patients with pyridoxine-responsive forms of homocystinuria might require only daily vitamin B6 supplementation and mild methionine restriction, whereas nonresponders may require a stricter, low-methionine diet with cysteine supplementation (cysteine is the product of
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: the cystathionine β-synthase reaction and may therefore be deficient in patients with classic homocystinuria). Patients might also benefit from folate, vitamin B12, and betaine supplementation, as these substances augment the remethylation of homocysteine to methionine, thereby reducing the toxic effects of excessive homocysteine. The outcome for vitamin B6–responsive patients appears to be good, but the outcome for nonresponders has often been less satisfactory because of the irreversible damage caused by the presenting episode, the therapeutic inadequacy of the present dietary and medical management, or both.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: MCAD deficiency is the most common inherited disorder of fatty acid oxidation, with an incidence of approximately 1 in 15,000.30,31 It has a highly variable clinical presentation, even within families. Patients are rarely symptomatic in the newborn period because newborns feed very frequently. Most patients present between 3 and 24 months of age, but others remain asymptomatic until they are much older, even into adulthood. However, MCAD deficiency has been associated with sudden, unexplained infant deaths (SIDS) and life-threatening hypoglycemia in neonates, especially when feeding poorly.31
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: The typical presentation is that of an infant who has unexplained progressive vomiting, hepatomegaly, lethargy leading to coma, and seizures associated with an infectious illness or a period of prolonged fasting. The characteristic laboratory finding is nonketotic or hypoketotic hypoglycemia; signs of liver dysfunction may also be present. Older patients could have a more indolent course that is associated with failure to thrive, developmental delay, or chronic muscle weakness. A significant proportion of patients are asymptomatic. MCAD deficiency may be diagnosed in an “unaffected” older sibling after his or her younger sibling comes to medical attention for an acute metabolic crisis or a positive newborn screening result for MCAD deficiency.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: The diagnosis of MCAD deficiency is confirmed by plasma carnitine analysis with an acylcarnitine profile, urine organic acid analysis, and urine acylglycine analysis.24,31 The plasma total and free carnitine concentration can vary with the phase of the illness. The plasma acylcarnitine profile typically shows increased amounts of C6, C8, and C10 acylcarnitines with an elevated C8:C10 ratio. However, patients with secondary carnitine deficiency could have a relative increase, but not an absolute increase, in these acylcarnitines. Urine organic acid analysis generally shows a typical medium-chain dicarboxylic aciduria (C6–C10) in symptomatic patients, but it could be normal in asymptomatic patients. Urinary acylglycine analysis can be useful in detecting the characteristic metabolite (suberylglycine) in asymptomatic patients.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: Genetic testing is useful for confirming the diagnosis. It used to be thought that at least 90% of patients carried at least one copy of the same abnormal allele, the A985G mutation, but the frequency of this particular allele is lower
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: in patients identified by newborn screening programs compared with those who present symptomatically.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: Patients with MCAD deficiency should receive frequent feedings and avoid fasting. Infants younger than 6 months require feeding every 3 to 4 hours. The older infant or child may be allowed to fast for progressively longer periods of time as they get older but not for more than 12 hours.31 The potential metabolic stress of nocturnal fasting might be reduced for toddlers by providing them with uncooked cornstarch or other complex carbohydrate as a source of slow-release glucose immediately before going to bed for the night. Dietary fat restriction is no longer recommended, but oral carnitine supplementation may be indicated for patients with secondary carnitine deficiency, as they can become deficient in free carnitine. Levocarnitine (l-carnitine) supplementation should be monitored with periodic plasma carnitine analysis. Patients should be evaluated and admission to the hospital considered for patients with anorexia or vomiting associated with an acute infectious illness or other potential metabolic stressor. Acute metabolic crises should be treated with intravenous glucose and l-carnitine. The prognosis for patients who are identified and treated before the onset of irreversible neurologic damage due to severe or recurrent hypoglycemia and its sequelae is generally excellent.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: Several genetic disorders produce hyperphenylalaninemia. Classic PKU and the milder hyperphenylalaninemia are caused by defects in phenylalanine hydroxylase. Variant PKU is caused by one of several defects in tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) metabolism.24,32 Several nongenetic factors also produce hyperphenylalaninemia in the newborn, but this hyperphenylalaninemia disappears in the first year of life (and usually in the first weeks of life). The most common causes of transient hyperphenylalaninemia are prematurity and high protein intake just prior to the blood draw. Newborn screening programs identify infants with genetic and nongenetic hyperphenylalaninemia. It is imperative that patients identified by the screening program receive a rapid, accurate, and definitive diagnosis, because the clinical implications and therapies for the various forms of hyperphenylalaninemia are different, and early initiation of appropriate treatment minimizes morbidity.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: All genetic forms of hyperphenylalaninemia are caused by defects that directly or indirectly affect the activity of the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase. This enzyme catalyzes the conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine and requires BH4 as a cofactor. Classic PKU and hyperphenylalaninemia are caused by allelic defects of phenylalanine hydroxylase itself, whereas variant PKU is caused by defects of BH4 biosynthesis or reutilization. BH4 is also a cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase and tryptophan hydroxylase, which are enzymes involved in neurotransmitter biosynthesis. Approximately 98% of patients with hyperphenylalaninemia have a defect
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: in phenylalanine hydroxylase, whereas 2% have a defect in BH4 metabolism.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: Patients with milder deficiencies of phenylalanine hydroxylase (i.e., patients with hyperphenylalaninemia) usually do not require dietary treatment. However, patients with more severe deficiencies (that is, patients with classic PKU) require lifelong phenylalanine restriction. Treatment should start within the first month of life to avoid irreversible neurologic damage. Early treatment is generally effective in preventing the long-term neurologic sequelae of this disease; however, standard treatment may not prevent subtle intellectual and behavioral disabilities in some individuals.24,32 Dietary restriction of phenylalanine should be lifelong, although some newer treatments noted below may reduce the need for dietary restriction in part or completely. Women with PKU who fail to maintain the appropriate diet are at risk for having neurologically impaired offspring (maternal PKU syndrome; see Maternal Diseases Affecting the Fetus).
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: It has been demonstrated that some patients with milder forms of classic PKU respond to oral supplementation with a synthetic form of BH4 known as sapropterin. They appear to tolerate a higher dietary protein intake while maintaining acceptable serum phenylalanine concentrations. However, many patients still require some degree of dietary phenylalanine restriction with or without a specialized metabolic formula.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: Defects of BH4 metabolism cause defective neurotransmitter synthesis as well as hyperphenylalaninemia and lead to a more generalized neurologic syndrome known as variant PKU, characterized by convulsions, abnormal tone and posture, abnormal movements (i.e., dystonia), hyperthermia, hypersalivation and swallowing difficulties, drowsiness, irritability, and developmental delay. Standard dietary management and/or use of sapriopterin correct the hyperphenylalaninemia that these patients have but do not improve the neurologic problems related to their neurotransmitter deficiencies. Only a small percentage of patients with hyperphenylalaninemia have BH4-related defects, and these patients must be identified early to initiate appropriate therapy. Various approaches are being used to treat these patients with some success, depending on the specific biopterin defect present.24,32
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: Newborn screening for hyperphenylalaninemia is based on measuring the concentration of phenylalanine in the blood while the newborn infant is receiving breast milk or a standard formula (i.e., a phenylalanine-containing diet).7,24 Blood samples are generally obtained for newborn screening between 24 and 48 hours of age. The results for samples collected before 24 hours of age may not be reliable, and a follow-up sample should be obtained for screening purposes if collected before the 24-hour mark.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: The rate of false-negative results is less a problem with MS/MS screening than the earlier approaches, partly because it is possible to measure the concentrations of
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: phenylalanine and tyrosine (the product of the phenylalanine hydroxylase reaction) concurrently. Those who have a positive screening result require prompt attention, including plasma amino acid analysis. If the plasma phenylalanine concentration and the plasma phenylalanine-totyrosine ratio are increased, the patient should be placed on a low phenylalanine diet. Therefore breastfeeding may need to be stopped and replaced by a phenylalanine-free/ tyrosine-enriched metabolic formula. The mother may wish to express breast milk via pump so that later, when the phenylalanine levels are under control and the patient can have a small amount of intact protein containing phenylalanine again, a small measured amount of breast milk can be provided as part of the prepared metabolic formula recipe. In all cases of confirmed hyperphenylalaninemia, the patient should be evaluated by a metabolic disorders specialist to rule out a defect in BH4 metabolism.
paragraphs.heading: Screening for Specific Disorders

paragraphs.text: On the whole, newborn infants with inborn errors of metabolism have relatively few clinical presentations. The most common are listed in Table 94.3, along with differential diagnoses of the categories of metabolic disorders that may be associated with each presentation. A more detailed discussion of each presentation follows.
paragraphs.heading: Phenotypes

paragraphs.text: Several inborn errors of metabolism can manifest prenatally, affecting the pregnant mother and/or the developing fetus. These inborn errors can be grouped into three categories: maternal diseases affecting the fetus, fetal diseases affecting the mother, and fetal diseases affecting the fetus.33,34
paragraphs.heading: Prenatal Onset

paragraphs.text: The prototype of a maternal disease affecting the fetus is maternal PKU.35 A pregnant woman who has poorly controlled PKU is at increased risk for miscarriage. She also has an increased risk of having a child with major birth anomalies, including intrauterine growth restriction, microcephaly, intellectual disabilities, and congenital heart defects, as well as a broad range of minor anomalies. The risk of birth defects is proportional to the mother’s serum phenylalanine concentration. There is no safe level below which the fetus is not at risk. Women with PKU should be placed on a strict low phenylalanine diet before conception and remain on a phenylalanine-restricted diet throughout pregnancy with a goal to keep phenylalanine levels between 120 and 360 μmol/L with at least weekly monitoring throughout pregnancy. Some patients also do well on sapropterin—approximately 50% of patients with
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Diseases Affecting the Fetus

paragraphs.text: PKU respond to this cofactor with at least a 20% reduction of their phenylalanine level from baseline. This can help responsive patients to maintain phenylalanine levels within the goal range more easily.36 However, maternal PKU syndrome remains a significant problem for many women with PKU.
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Diseases Affecting the Fetus

paragraphs.text: As a rule, the majority of inborn errors of metabolism of the fetus are not thought to affect the pregnant mother. However, reports began to appear in the 1990s describing mothers who, while carrying a fetus, had experienced acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP) who subsequently were identified to have a long-chain fatty acid oxidation defect after giving birth. AFLP is the most extreme end of a clinical spectrum of maternal complications of pregnancy that includes HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and a low platelet count) and AFLP. The HELLP syndrome and AFLP are potentially serious complications of pregnancy (see Chapter 16).
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Diseases Affecting the Mother

paragraphs.text: Clinical, biochemical, and histologic evidence of hepatic dysfunction mark both disorders. Patients with HELLP syndrome commonly develop epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, headache, proteinuria, low platelets, elevated serum liver enzymes, and occasionally disseminated intravascular coagulation. AFLP is less common than HELLP syndrome and shows a greater degree of hepatic dysfunction. It often produces a severe coagulopathy, hypoglycemia, and fulminant hepatic failure. Microvesicular fatty deposits in the liver characterize both disorders. Both disorders can have life-threatening consequences for the fetus and mother. Women with either of these disorders improve remarkably after delivery, suggesting that the fetus is causing a toxic effect on the mother that resembles symptoms that are often seen in patients with inborn errors of fatty acid oxidation.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Diseases Affecting the Mother

paragraphs.text: Further, there is convincing evidence that a specific defect of fatty acid oxidation, long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCHAD) deficiency, in the fetus is associated with the HELLP syndrome and AFLP spectrum in the mother.37,38 LCHAD is part of a trifunctional multimeric enzyme complex that performs the three terminal steps in long-chain fatty acid β-oxidation: long-chain 2,3-enoyl- CoA hydratase, LCHAD, and long-chain 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase. LCHAD can be seen as an isolated deficiency or as part of trifunctional protein (TFP) deficiency that affects all three enzyme activities. Both disorders are inherited as autosomal recessive traits.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Diseases Affecting the Mother

paragraphs.text: Isolated LCHAD deficiency is marked by relative genetic homogeneity. More than 50% of the mutant alleles found in patients who have this disease carry the same mutation: a G1528C change in the gene that encodes for the α-subunit of LCHAD. Other mutations in the same gene that predispose a heterozygous mother to AFLP have also been identified. A relatively large number of at-risk pregnancies have now been identified and
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Diseases Affecting the Mother

paragraphs.text: reviewed after the birth of a child with LCHAD deficiency.37,38 These studies show that a woman who is heterozygous for LCHAD deficiency is at risk for developing HELLP syndrome or AFLP during a pregnancy in which she is carrying a fetus who is homozygous for the same deficiency. Thus a heterozygous mother is only at risk if her fetus inherits a second LCHAD mutation from the father. The fetus, in turn, is at risk for significant postnatal problems associated with its enzyme deficiency. The diagnosis and care of a child with LCHAD deficiency is discussed later under Hypoglycemia. Rarely, other inborn errors of long-chain fatty acid β-oxidation can also produce AFLP.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Diseases Affecting the Mother

paragraphs.text: The current recommendation is to evaluate all pregnant women who develop AFLP to determine if they carry a mutation associated with LCHAD deficiency or related fatty acid oxidation disorders by biochemical and genetic testing. This recommendation should also be considered
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Diseases Affecting the Mother

paragraphs.text: for women who develop recurrent and/or severe HELLP syndrome.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Diseases Affecting the Mother

paragraphs.text: The fetus does not generally suffer prenatal consequences of its own inborn error of metabolism, because the abnormal metabolites that it produces are removed by the maternal circulation or, conversely, metabolic deficiencies produced by the inborn error are replenished by the maternal circulation. There are, however, several groups of disorders that include significant exceptions: amino acid disorders, congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDGs), fatty acid β-oxidation disorders, lysosomal storage disorders, mitochondrial disorders, and peroxisomal disorders (see Dysmorphic Syndromes).
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Diseases Affecting the Fetus

paragraphs.text: Although most of the clinical disorders that affect the developing fetus are discussed later, the disorders that can lead to congenital ascites or hydrops fetalis are discussed
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Diseases Affecting the Fetus

paragraphs.text: here. A major group of inborn errors of metabolism that lead to hydrops fetalis includes the lysosomal storage disorders, such as β-glucuronidase deficiency and Morquio syndrome (mucopolysaccharidoses); Farber disease and GM1-gangliosidosis (spingolipidoses); galactosialidosis and sialidosis (oligosaccharidoses); and free sialic storage disease (a lysosomal transport defect).33,39 Other disorders that can also lead to hydrops fetalis are CDGs (specifically type Ia), glycogen storage diseases (specifically type IV), Niemann- Pick disease type C, and transaldolase deficiency,33,34 as well as several inborn errors of red cell glycolytic enzymes (see Chapter 81).
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Diseases Affecting the Fetus

paragraphs.text: Newborn infants have a limited number of responses to an illness such as an inborn error of metabolism.1,2 These responses generally include cardiorespiratory, feeding, and neurologic difficulties. The neurologic difficulties, such as altered consciousness (encephalopathy), altered tone, or seizures, are discussed in detail elsewhere in this book (see Chapters 55–58). As noted in these chapters, these neurologic difficulties are most commonly caused by infection, brain malformations, or hypoxemic-ischemic encephalopathy and less commonly by inborn errors of metabolism. Although it is important to evaluate a patient for these common problems, it is also important to remember that inborn errors of metabolism can also produce brain malformations and/or can mimic the clinical picture of hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.40
