Glycosuria may also be seen in infants with congenital renal diseases such as renal dysplasia, in which there is significant tubular dysfunction. Glycosuria in an infant with severe, watery diarrhea should raise the suspicion of congenital intestinal glucose-galactose malabsorption syndrome.
paragraphs.heading: Glycosuria

paragraphs.text: AKI is a common condition in the NICU, ranging from mild renal dysfunction to complete anuric kidney failure. AKI is characterized by a sudden decline in kidney function over hours to days, resulting in derangements in fluid, electrolyte, and acid–base balance. There has been difficulty in establishing a standardized definition of AKI in neonates because of a number of factors, including maturational difference in kidney function at different gestational ages, the overall low GFR of neonates, and the fact that serum Cr reflects maternal Cr for days to a week after birth. The neonatal modified KDIGO (Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes) criteria has recently become widely accepted as a consensus definition for neonatal AKI.21 These criteria define neonatal AKI in infants under 120 days of age as an increase in serum Cr ≥0.3 mg/dL or 50% or more from the
paragraphs.heading: Acute Kidney Injury

paragraphs.text: previous lowest value and/or urine output less than 0.5 mL/ kg/h. The three stages of neonatal AKI are defined by relative changes in serum Cr from baseline and/or reduction in urine output (Table 97.4). Biomarkers including neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL), urinary interleukin-18, and cystatin C show promise in the earlier detection of neonatal AKI, potentially identifying earlier stages of kidney injury, which occur before the elevation of serum creatinine.22
paragraphs.heading: Acute Kidney Injury

paragraphs.text: Neonatal AKI is a common occurrence, occurring in 30% of critically ill neonates recently evaluated in a large multicenter retrospective cohort study.23 The incidence of AKI varied by gestational age group, occurring in 48% of infants 22 to 29 weeks’ gestation, 18% of infants 29 to 36 weeks’ gestation, and 37% of infants ≥36 weeks’ gestation.23
paragraphs.heading: Acute Kidney Injury

paragraphs.text: Neonates are at particularly high risk of developing AKI because of their intrinsically low GFR in the first week of life, immaturity of renal tubules, increased susceptibility of the kidney to impaired perfusion, high exposure to nephrotoxic agents including indomethacin and aminoglycosides, and frequent use of umbilical access catheters with potential for thrombosis.21 Within the NICU population, certain groups at heightened risk of developing AKI include term and near-term neonates with perinatal asphyxia, very low birth weight and extremely low birth weight infants, and infants requiring cardiac surgery or ECMO support.
paragraphs.heading: Acute Kidney Injury

paragraphs.text: Clinical signs of AKI may include oliguria, systemic hypertension, cardiac arrhythmia, evidence of fluid overload or volume depletion, decreased activity, seizure, vomiting, and anorexia. Laboratory findings may include elevated serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and a prolonged half-life for medications excreted by the kidney (e.g., aminoglycosides, vancomycin, theophylline). The causes of neonatal AKI are multiple and can be divided into prerenal, renal, and postrenal categories (Box 97.2).
paragraphs.heading: Acute Kidney Injury

paragraphs.text: Functional or prerenal AKI is the most common type of AKI in the neonate and may account for up to 85% of all cases. Prerenal AKI is caused by inadequate renal perfusion,
paragraphs.heading: Functional (Prerenal) Acute Kidney Injury

paragraphs.text: which, if promptly treated, is followed by improvements in renal function and urine output. The most common causes of prerenal AKI are hypotension, volume depletion, hemorrhage, septic shock, necrotizing enterocolitis, patent ductus arteriosus, and congestive heart failure. The administration of medications that reduce RBF, such as indomethacin or ibuprofen, ACE inhibitors, and phenylephrine eye drops, can also result in prerenal AKI.
paragraphs.heading: Functional (Prerenal) Acute Kidney Injury

paragraphs.text: The most common cause of intrinsic AKI in neonates is ATN. Risk factors for ATN include a prolonged prerenal state, perinatal asphyxia, sepsis, neonatal cardiac surgery, need for ECMO support, and nephrotoxic drug administration (acyclovir, aminoglycoside antibiotics, amphotericin B, ACE inhibitors, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), radiocontrast agents, and vancomycin). The pathophysiology of ATN is complex and appears to involve interrelationships among renal tubular cellular injury, hypoxia, and altered glomerular filtration and hemodynamics. Other causes of intrinsic AKI in the newborn include renal dysplasia, autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD), and renal arterial or venous thrombosis. Glomerulonephritis, although a common cause of AKI in older children and adolescents, is very uncommon in the neonatal population.
paragraphs.heading: Intrinsic (Renal) Acute Kidney Injury

paragraphs.text: Obstructive AKI in the neonate may be related to a variety of congenital urinary tract conditions, including PUV, bilateral ureteropelvic or ureterovesical junction obstruction,
paragraphs.heading: Obstructive (Postrenal) Acute Kidney Injury

paragraphs.text: and neurogenic bladder. Rarer causes of obstructive AKI include intrinsic obstruction of the urinary tract by urolithiasis or fungal balls or extrinsic compression by a congenital tumor such as a sacrococcygeal teratoma. Although relief of urinary tract obstruction may yield improvement in urine output and GFR, many infants will develop CKD because of variable degrees of associated renal dysplasia.
paragraphs.heading: Obstructive (Postrenal) Acute Kidney Injury

paragraphs.text: A careful history should focus on prenatal ultrasound abnormalities, perinatal asphyxia, the pre- or postnatal administration of potentially nephrotoxic drugs, and the presence of other conditions such as sepsis, PDA, cardiac dysfunction, or hypotension. The physical examination should focus on signs of volume depletion or volume overload, the abdomen, genitalia, and a search for other congenital anomalies or signs of the oligohydramnios (Potter) sequence. Focused laboratory evaluation should include electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, and creatinine (Cr). Serum cystatin C may be superior to serum Cr in assessing kidney function, although this test is not yet available in all laboratories.19 Urine should be sent for urinalysis, as well as sodium and creatinine determination, to calculate fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) (Table 97.5):
paragraphs.heading: Evaluation

paragraphs.text: FENa (%) = (UNa×PCr)/(PNa×UCr)×100%
paragraphs.heading: Evaluation

paragraphs.text: where U = urinary, P = plasma
paragraphs.heading: Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Neonates with a FENa value of more than 3.0% generally have intrinsic AKI, whereas those with a FENa value of less than 2.5% have prerenal AKI, although this parameter may not apply to preterm neonates who may have a baseline FENa as high as 6% at birth. Elevation of biomarkers such as urine NGAL may be useful in early identification of intrinsic AKI, before detection of a rise in serum creatinine.22 Kidney and bladder ultrasound is helpful in the identification of congenital abnormalities of the kidney and urinary tract, urinary tract obstruction, and vascular thrombosis.
paragraphs.heading: Evaluation

paragraphs.text: The prevention of AKI in newborn infants requires maintenance of adequate kidney perfusion, careful fluid and electrolyte management, and prompt diagnosis and treatment of hemodynamic or respiratory abnormalities. Nephrotoxic medications such as acyclovir, aminoglycoside antibiotics, amphotericin B, ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, radiocontrast agents, and vancomycin should be avoided in neonates at high risk for AKI. Nephrotoxic medication monitoring programs have recently proven successful in reducing the incidence of nephrotoxic medication-associated AKI and duration of AKI in neonates.24 Theophylline may be considered as a preventative agent in neonates with perinatal asphyxia; a recent meta-analysis showed it to be associated with a lower incidence of AKI.25 Although treatment with caffeine has been associated with a decreased incidence of AKI in several studies of neonates less than 33 weeks’
paragraphs.heading: Prevention of Acute Kidney Injury

paragraphs.text: gestational age, it is not yet recommended as a preventative approach.26,27
paragraphs.heading: Prevention of Acute Kidney Injury

paragraphs.text: In the case of established oliguric AKI, a urinary catheter should be placed to exclude LUTO. If there is no improvement in urine output after bladder drainage is established, a fluid challenge of 10 to 20 mL/kg should be administered over 1 to 2 hours to exclude prerenal AKI. Consideration should be given to use of vasopressor support such as dopamine to ensure that the infant has a mean arterial pressure adequate to provide renal perfusion. A lack of improvement in urine output and serum creatinine following adequate bladder drainage, fluid resuscitation, and establishment of an adequate mean arterial pressure suggests intrinsic AKI.
paragraphs.heading: Medical Management

paragraphs.text: The goal of medical management of intrinsic AKI is to provide supportive care until there is spontaneous improvement in kidney function. After adequate resuscitation, intake should be restricted to insensible losses (500 mL/m2/ day, or 30 mL/kg/day) plus urine output and other measured losses (see Chapter 96) to prevent symptomatic fluid overload. Daily to twice daily weights and careful intake and output measurements are essential to follow volume status. Nephrotoxic drugs should be discontinued to reduce the risk of additional kidney injury. Medications should be adjusted by dose, interval, or both according to the degree of kidney dysfunction. Potassium and phosphorus should be restricted in those neonates with hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, oliguria, and/or rapidly worsening kidney function. Metabolic acidosis may require treatment with intravenous or oral sodium bicarbonate. Loop diuretics may prove helpful in augmenting the urinary flow rate but should be withheld if there is no response or in the case of anuria.
paragraphs.heading: Medical Management

paragraphs.text: Renal replacement therapy (RRT) should be considered if conservative medical management fails to maintain acceptable fluid and electrolyte levels in an infant with AKI. Indications for the initiation of RRT include hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, acidosis, hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia,
paragraphs.heading: Renal Replacement Therapy

paragraphs.text: uremic symptoms, greater than 10% fluid overload, and the inability to provide adequate nutrition because of the need for fluid restriction (Box 97.3).28 The two purposes of RRT are ultrafiltration (removal of water) and dialysis (removal of solutes). In general, RRT is restricted to neonates greater than 1.5-2 kg in size given the limited ability to place and maintain dialysis access. Prompt initiation of RRT is critical, because mortality has been directly correlated with the degree of fluid overload at time of initiation of RRT.29
paragraphs.heading: Renal Replacement Therapy

paragraphs.text: Peritoneal dialysis (PD) is the most commonly used form of RRT in the neonatal population. For this procedure, dialysate is repeatedly infused into and drained out of the peritoneal cavity through a surgically placed catheter, accomplishing both fluid and solute removal. Cycle length, volume of dialysate infused (“dwell volume”), and the osmolar concentration of the dialysate can be varied to accomplish the goals of therapy. Advantages of PD include its simplicity, preservation of vascular access, lack of need for anticoagulation, and tolerance of the procedure even in hemodynamically unstable infants. Contraindications to PD include recent abdominal surgery, necrotizing enterocolitis, pleuroperitoneal leakage, and ventriculoperitoneal shunting. Ideally, initiation of PD should be delayed for 2 weeks following catheter placement to reduce the risk of peri-catheter leakage and infection. In anuric infants, support with CRRT or modified aquapheresis (see below) may be necessary to allow complete healing of the PD catheter exit site.
paragraphs.heading: Renal Replacement Therapy

paragraphs.text: Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is becoming a more frequently used modality in neonates
paragraphs.heading: Renal Replacement Therapy

paragraphs.text: and infants with AKI. For this procedure, the patient’s blood is continuously circulated through a pump-driven extracorporeal circuit containing a highly permeable hemofilter. CRRT can be used independently or in conjunction with ECMO. The chief advantage of CRRT is the ability to carefully control fluid removal, which makes this modality especially useful in the neonate with hemodynamic instability. The main disadvantages are the need to achieve and maintain central vascular access and the need for continuous anticoagulation.
paragraphs.heading: Renal Replacement Therapy

paragraphs.text: Most standard CRRT machines are approved for use in patients greater than 20 kg and have relatively large extracorporeal circuits. Several machines with very low blood volume circuits (CARPEDIEM and Aquadex FlexFlow) have been introduced to provide CRRT to the neonatal population.30,31 Catheters smaller than those used for standard hemodialysis may be used with these machines, expanding the use of CRRT in the neonatal population.32
paragraphs.heading: Renal Replacement Therapy

paragraphs.text: Hemodialysis is a less commonly used but technically feasible mode of RRT in the neonatal population. Hemodialysis involves intermittent 3- to 4-hour treatments in which fluid and solutes are rapidly removed from the infant using an extracorporeal circuit, with clearance achieved by the use of countercurrent dialysate. The chief advantage of hemodialysis is the ability to rapidly remove solutes and fluid. The main disadvantages are the requirement for central vascular access, and the hemodynamic instability and osmolar shifts that may occur with rapid solute and fluid shifts.
paragraphs.heading: Renal Replacement Therapy

paragraphs.text: Providing adequate RRT to an infant in the NICU may be limited by the challenges in placing and/or maintaining intravascular or PD access in the very small premature neonate. If dialysis access cannot be established, care of the infant with AKI is limited to maximal supportive medical management, with meticulous attention to fluid, electrolyte, and acid–base balance.
paragraphs.heading: Renal Replacement Therapy

paragraphs.text: Research has demonstrated that AKI is not just a marker of severity of illness in neonates but is also independently associated with poor outcomes. A large multicenter retrospective study demonstrated that the presence of AKI was independently associated with increased mortality in neonates (10% vs. 1%), as well as increased length of hospital stay (median 23 vs. 19 days).23 In addition, infants with higher stages of AKI had higher mortality rates and lengths of hospitalization when compared to infants with lower stages of AKI.23
paragraphs.heading: Prognosis

paragraphs.text: In the past, AKI was thought of as a completely reversible condition, with the idea that the return of serum creatinine to baseline indicated no further renal risk. However, observational studies have demonstrated high rates of CKD in survivors of neonatal AKI.33 The risk of CKD in survivors of neonatal AKI may be compounded by the independent risks of prematurity and low birth weight, both of which are associated with CKD because of associated inadequate nephron development.2,3 Outpatient nephrology follow-up care is
paragraphs.heading: Prognosis

paragraphs.text: important for all neonates with an identified episode of significant AKI to monitor for proteinuria, hypertension, and rise in serum creatinine over time indicating development of CKD. Special attention should be given to those infants with a history of AKI stages 2 and 3, treatment with dialysis, significant prematurity, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), or underlying urinary tract anomalies. Early identification of CKD allows implementation of strategies to slow the loss of GFR, including healthy lifestyle, careful management of BP, reduction of proteinuria, hydration, and avoidance of nephrotoxin exposure.
paragraphs.heading: Prognosis

paragraphs.text: The incidence of hypertension in neonates is estimated to be approximately 1% to 2%.34 Hypertension is most often seen in infants with a concurrent condition such as chronic lung disease, kidney disease, or a history of umbilical arterial catheterization. The definition of neonatal hypertension is sustained blood pressure above the 95th percentile for infants of similar size, gestational age, and postnatal age. Identification of elevated blood pressure in neonates can be difficult because of variations in blood pressure measurement techniques, normal changes in blood pressure with gestational age and weight, and other factors that affect blood pressure readings, including level of wakefulness, feeding, crying, and pain.
paragraphs.heading: Hypertension Incidence and Definition

paragraphs.text: Useful data on normal infant blood pressures were published by Zubrow and colleagues, who prospectively measured blood pressure in nearly 700 infants, showing that blood pressure increased with gestational age, postconceptual age, and birth weight.35 Based on these data and synthesis of several other studies, a practical table of systolic, diastolic, and mean arterial blood pressure values was created and may be useful in defining normal and elevated blood pressures in neonates greater than 2 weeks of age from 26 to 44 weeks’ postconceptual age (Table 97.6).34
paragraphs.heading: Hypertension Incidence and Definition

paragraphs.text: The many causes of neonatal hypertension are outlined in Box 97.4 and differ significantly from the most common causes of hypertension in older children and adults. Historically, renovascular hypertension has been considered the most frequent cause of neonatal hypertension. Causes include renal arterial thromboembolism related to umbilical artery catheterization, congenital renal artery stenosis, fibromuscular dysplasia, mid-aortic coarctation, and renovascular compression by tumors.
paragraphs.heading: Causes

paragraphs.text: AKI has been increasingly recognized as being associated with hypertension, as shown in the AWAKEN study.36 Other kidney disorders including ARPKD and obstructive uropathy may also cause neonatal hypertension. BPD is the most common cause of nonrenal hypertension in neonates. Although the mechanism by which BPD is associated with hypertension is not clearly defined, the severity of the blood pressure elevation appears to correlate with the severity of the lung disease.37 Less common causes of neonatal hypertension include
paragraphs.heading: Causes

paragraphs.text: endocrine disorders, coarctation of the aorta, intraventricular hemorrhage, history of abdominal wall closure, tumors, treatment with ECMO, seizures, pain, and drug withdrawal. Medications such as corticosteroids, vasopressors, caffeine, theophylline, and bronchodilators have been associated with elevated blood pressures in neonates. Interestingly, one study showed that nearly half of neonatal hypertension has no specific identifiable cause.38
paragraphs.heading: Causes

paragraphs.text: The majority of neonates with hypertension are asymptomatic, as elevated blood pressures are typically noted on routine monitoring. If present, symptoms of neonatal hypertension are often nonspecific, including poor feeding, irritability, and lethargy. Marked blood pressure elevation may lead to cardiopulmonary symptoms, including tachypnea, cyanosis, apnea, impaired perfusion, vasomotor instability, congestive heart failure, and hepatosplenomegaly. Neurologic symptoms such as tremors, hypertonicity, hypotonicity, opisthotonos, asymmetric reflexes, hemiparesis, seizures, apnea, or coma may also occur. The renal effects of hypertension may include AKI and sodium wasting related to pressure natriuresis.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: The first step is to determine whether the elevated blood pressure persists when the infant is quiet and relaxed. A standardized protocol for accurate blood pressure measurement in neonates is shown in Box 97.5.34 Blood pressures are preferably measured in the upper arm, because leg blood pressure measurements tend to overestimate the true blood pressure. History should focus on prenatal medication exposures, presence or history of an umbilical artery catheter, and treatment with medications that raise blood pressure. Blood pressure trends since birth should be reviewed to establish the onset and severity of hypertension. A complete physical examination includes
paragraphs.heading: Evaluation

paragraphs.text: four-extremity blood pressure measurements to diagnose or rule out aortic coarctation. The infant should be examined carefully for signs of volume overload, including peripheral edema, cardiac gallop, or rales. The abdomen should be carefully inspected for presence of abdominal or flank masses or renal bruits. Ambiguous genitalia in a hypertensive infant should raise the suspicion of congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Initial laboratory studies should include a urinalysis and determinations of serum electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, serum creatinine, and serum calcium. Other diagnostic studies, including renin, aldosterone, cortisol, thyroid function tests, and catecholamines,
paragraphs.heading: Evaluation

paragraphs.text: can be considered based on the clinical scenario and results of screening studies.
paragraphs.heading: Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Ultrasonography of the kidneys with a Doppler flow study of the aorta and renal arteries should be performed to exclude a renal arterial or aortic thrombus or structural anomalies of the urinary tract. Absence of a defined thrombus does not, however, rule out renovascular hypertension as the majority of thrombi are very small and not detectable by ultrasonography. Computed tomography, magnetic resonance angiography, and angiography may be considered in more difficult cases, although their use may be limited in the very small infant. Echocardiography should be performed to exclude aortic coarctation and evaluate the left ventricular mass.
paragraphs.heading: Evaluation

paragraphs.text: The first approach to the treatment of neonatal hypertension is to correct all iatrogenic causes of blood pressure elevation, including improper measurement technique, vasopressor administration, volume overload, narcotic withdrawal, or inadequately controlled pain. If blood pressures remain elevated above the 99th percentile, experts advocate antihypertensive treatment with an intravenous or oral antihypertensive agent to prevent adverse effects on the kidneys, heart, and central nervous system (Tables 97.7 and 97.8).
paragraphs.heading: Treatment

paragraphs.text: Neonates with signs and symptoms of a hypertensive emergency such as cardiopulmonary failure, acute neurologic dysfunction, and AKI are best treated with a continuous intravenous infusion of an antihypertensive agent such as nicardipine, esmolol, or labetalol. Careful monitoring using an arterial line is recommended. The chief advantage of a continuous infusion is the ability to quickly increase or decrease the rate of infusion to achieve the desired blood pressure. The goal of therapy is a gradual decrease in blood pressure to minimize injury to the brain, heart, and kidneys. Blood pressure should not be lowered below the 95th percentile for at least 24 to 48 hours to avoid the possibility of cerebral and optic disc ischemia.
paragraphs.heading: Treatment

paragraphs.text: Oral antihypertensive agents are best used in infants with less severe hypertension or in those whose acute hypertension has been controlled with intravenous infusions and who are ready to switch to chronic oral therapy. Calcium channel blockers, such as isradipine and amlodipine, are first-choice agents. ACE inhibitors such as captopril may be useful, but many clinicians avoid use in infants less than 44 weeks’ postconceptional age because of concern for impairment of the final stages of renal maturation. If ACE inhibitors are used, careful attention to urine output and the levels of serum creatinine and potassium is recommended, because neonates may be extremely sensitive to the reduction in RBF associated with the administration of these agents. Diuretics such as chlorothiazide may be useful agents in infants with chronic lung disease. Intermittent administration of intravenous agents, such as hydralazine or labetalol, may be considered in hypertensive infants with mild to moderate hypertension in whom oral agents cannot be used because of gastrointestinal dysfunction.
paragraphs.heading: Treatment

paragraphs.text: If present, the umbilical artery catheter should be removed as soon as possible. If a large thrombus is identified, systemic heparinization may be considered to prevent extension of the clot. If the hypertension cannot be controlled medically or massive aortic thrombosis results in major complications, thrombolysis with urokinase, streptokinase, or tissue plasminogen activator may be considered. If severe hypertension persists, surgical thrombectomy or nephrectomy may be contemplated.
paragraphs.heading: Treatment

paragraphs.text: Infants with neonatal hypertension should have regular outpatient nephrology follow-up and blood pressure monitoring. Most neonates with hypertension associated with umbilical artery catheters, BPD, or of unknown cause experience improvement in their blood pressures and do not typically require antihypertensive medications beyond 6 to 12 months of age. Infants may require periodic increases in their antihypertensive medications following discharge from the hospital because of rapid growth, but antihypertensive agents may often be weaned by maintaining a stable medication dose as the infant grows in size. On the other hand, infants with hypertension related to a secondary cause
paragraphs.heading: Prognosis

paragraphs.text: such as kidney disease will most likely have hypertension that persists into childhood.
paragraphs.heading: Prognosis

paragraphs.text: Long-term studies of children and adolescents with a history of neonatal hypertension are needed. There is growing evidence that neonates born before completion of nephrogenesis at 34 to 36 weeks’ gestation may be at increased risk for development of hypertension and CKD in adolescence or adulthood.2,3
paragraphs.heading: Prognosis

paragraphs.text: Nephrocalcinosis, defined as calcium salt deposition in the renal interstitium, is a well-known complication in the neonatal population, occurring in 7% to 41% of hospitalized premature infants.39 Infants at highest risk appear to be those with lower gestational age and birth weight, often in combination with severe respiratory disease. Nephrocalcinosis is usually discovered incidentally on abdominal imaging studies, although infants with nephrocalcinosis may present with microscopic or gross hematuria, granular material in the diaper, or urinary tract infection.
paragraphs.heading: Nephrocalcinosis

paragraphs.text: Neonatal nephrocalcinosis is multifactorial in etiology and develops as the consequence of an imbalance between stone-promoting and stone-inhibiting factors.39 The immature renal tubules of the preterm infant are more susceptible to crystal formation and aggregation. Furthermore, the low GFR of the preterm infant results in a low tubular fluid flow rate that promotes crystal formation. Hypercalciuria (excessive urinary calcium excretion) is a common risk factor and may result from chronic treatment with loop diuretics, increased calcium intake from TPN, or vitamin D supplementation. Subcutaneous fat necrosis following birth trauma or therapeutic hypothermia is a rare but serious cause of hypercalciuria.40 Other risk factors for nephrocalcinosis include hypocitraturia (low urinary citrate excretion); this is a common finding in patients with persistent metabolic acidosis, which often occurs in ill preterm infants. Less common genetic conditions in which there is an increased risk of nephrocalcinosis include primary hyperoxaluria, distal renal tubular acidosis (RTA), Bartter syndrome, Williams syndrome, and idiopathic infantile hypercalcemia.
paragraphs.heading: Nephrocalcinosis

paragraphs.text: Routine ultrasonographic screening should be considered for all infants who receive long-term loop diuretics for chronic lung or heart disease. In those with documented nephrocalcinosis, loop diuretics should be discontinued, if possible. Thiazide diuretics, such as chlorothiazide, may be substituted because they tend to reduce urinary calcium excretion, although serum calcium must be monitored closely to avoid hypercalcemia. Agents that may increase urinary calcium excretion, including glucocorticoids, xanthine derivatives, and any sodium-containing supplements should be minimized or discontinued if possible. Administration of calcium and phosphorus in TPN as well as vitamin D supplementation should be reduced if excessive. A high urinary flow rate should be maintained to reduce the probability of urinary crystallization. Metabolic acidosis, if
paragraphs.heading: Nephrocalcinosis

paragraphs.text: present, should be treated with potassium citrate. The goal of therapy should be the maintenance of the spot urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio at less than 0.8 for infants less than 7 months of age.39
paragraphs.heading: Nephrocalcinosis

paragraphs.text: The usual outcome for infants with neonatal nephrocalcinosis without an underlying genetic defect is spontaneous resolution over the first 2 years of life. Serial renal ultrasonography is needed to confirm resolution of nephrocalcinosis. There is concern that neonatal nephrocalcinosis may increase risk for impairment in kidney function later in life, particularly in premature infants who are inherently at increased risk of CKD. Although results are conflicting regarding the long-term impact of nephrocalcinosis, there have been several studies raising concern that nephrocalcinosis may be an additional risk factor for impaired kidney growth and function in former preterm infants.41,42 Longterm nephrology follow-up care of premature infants with nephrocalcinosis is recommended.
paragraphs.heading: Nephrocalcinosis

paragraphs.text: Thromboembolic complications are rare but serious events in the NICU. The neonatal kidney is particularly vulnerable to thrombosis because of its relatively low blood flow, small vessel diameter, enhanced renal vasoconstriction, and intervening events including hypoxia, volume depletion, hypotension, and infection that disturb the delicate balance between procoagulant and anticoagulant factors. Both venous and arterial thrombosis may occur in the neonate, although renal venous thromboses (RVTs) are more common. Risk factors for RVT include prematurity, maternal diabetes mellitus, congenital heart disease, polycythemia, hypertonic dehydration, acute blood loss, perinatal asphyxia, in utero death of a twin, sepsis, respiratory distress syndrome, and prolonged central venous cannulation.43 A subset of neonates with RVT have an inherited thrombophilia, including deficiencies of protein C, protein S or antithrombin, factor V Leiden mutation, or the prothrombin gene mutation.
paragraphs.heading: Renal Vascular Thrombosis

paragraphs.text: Thrombosis begins in the small renal veins and propagates toward the main renal vein, ultimately reaching the inferior vena cava. Thrombosis is usually unilateral (70%) but may be bilateral or extend into the inferior vena cava and is associated with adrenal infarction in a minority of patients.
paragraphs.heading: Renal Vascular Thrombosis

paragraphs.text: The classic clinical triad of symptoms in RVT includes a flank mass, macroscopic hematuria, and thrombocytopenia, although all elements of the triad are present in fewer than 25% of infants with RVT. Additional signs may include oliguric AKI, hypertension, vomiting, lethargy, anorexia, fever, and shock. Ultrasonography in the acute phase reveals enlarged and echogenic kidneys with loss of corticomedullary differentiation. A Doppler study may reveal resistance or absence of blood flow in the main renal vein and collateral vessels. Uptake may be absent or severely diminished on a radionuclide scan. Ultrasonography following the acute phase may show gradual decrease in kidney size with renal atrophy.
paragraphs.heading: Renal Vascular Thrombosis

paragraphs.text: Initial evaluation after identification of a thrombosis should include baseline testing, including a CBC, prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), and fibrinogen concentration. Maternal blood may be tested for lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibody. Testing for an inherited prothrombotic state should be conducted in neonates with clinically significant thrombosis but is best deferred until after resolution of the acute event.
paragraphs.heading: Renal Vascular Thrombosis

paragraphs.text: There are no evidence-based guidelines for management of neonatal RVT, although expert opinion guidelines suggest the need for a multidisciplinary team including neonatology, nephrology, radiology, and hematology. If the thrombosis appears to be catheter-associated, the catheter should be removed. Supportive medical treatment consists of correction of fluid and electrolyte imbalances as well as supportive treatment of AKI, possibly including dialysis. Anticoagulation (unfractionated heparin or low molecular weight heparin) may be used to prevent the extension of thrombosis, although the benefits of anticoagulation should be weighed against the risks of hemorrhagic events, including intraventricular hemorrhage. Thrombolytic therapies such as recombinant tissue plasminogen activator or urokinase should be reserved for cases of critical compromise of kidney function, as seen in bilateral renal vein thrombosis. Surgical thrombectomy is considered in patients with thrombosis of the inferior vena cava, and nephrectomy may be necessary in infants with severe refractory hypertension.
paragraphs.heading: Renal Vascular Thrombosis

paragraphs.text: Although the perinatal mortality rate in infants with RVT has decreased progressively during the past decades, the prognosis for the affected kidney is poor, with progressive atrophy in up to 70% of kidneys.43 Long-term complications include hypertension in 20% of patients, CKD, and end-stage kidney disease in the minority of patients with a history of bilateral thrombosis.
paragraphs.heading: Renal Vascular Thrombosis

paragraphs.text: CAKUT are seen in 4 to 60/10,000 births and account for 20% to 30% of congenital anomalies.8 CAKUT is of great clinical importance, because it is the underlying etiology in up to 50% of children and adolescents with CKD. CAKUT represent a broad spectrum of conditions, ranging from clinically silent transient hydronephrosis to anuric kidney failure requiring dialysis in first week of life (Box 97.6; see also Table 97.1). The challenge to the obstetrician and neonatal providers is distinguishing clinically important conditions from minor anomalies. Most infants with CAKUT are diagnosed on prenatal imaging, which identifies the correct diagnosis in 60% to 85% of cases, especially with imaging performed in the third trimester.8
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Anomalies of Kidney and Urinary Tract

paragraphs.text: Our understanding of the genetic basis of CAKUT has expanded dramatically in the past 2 decades, with the identification of mutations in a number of genes including HNF- 1B and PAX2, transcription factors critical to normal fetal kidney development (see Table 97.1).5 There is substantial
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Anomalies of Kidney and Urinary Tract

paragraphs.text: genotype-phenotype heterogeneity among patients with the same identified gene, which suggests an effect of other genetic, epigenetic, and environmental factors in the development of CAKUT. The following section will review some of the most common CAKUT that present in neonates and infants.
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Anomalies of Kidney and Urinary Tract

paragraphs.text: Unilateral renal agenesis (URA; congenital absence of the kidney) occurs in 1 of 2000 births and is one of the most common forms of CAKUT.44 URA occurs when the ureteric bud fails to induce proper differentiation of the metanephric mesenchyme, an event that may be related to both genetic and environmental factors. URA may occur in healthy infants and is more common in males and on the left side. Birth registry data suggest that about 30% of infants with URA have extra-renal anomalies, including cardiac in 60% and skeletal in 30%.44 URA may be seen in infants with a variety of syndromes including VACTERL association (i.e., vertebral abnormalities, anal atresia, cardiac abnormalities, tracheoesophageal fistula or esophageal atresia, renal agenesis and dysplasia, and limb defects), caudal
paragraphs.heading: Renal Agenesis

paragraphs.text: regression syndrome, and branchio-oto-renal (BOR) syndrome. Approximately 30% of girls with URA have an associated Müllerian anomaly, which is usually clinically silent until puberty when girls may present with amenorrhea or dysmenorrhea.45 In males, congenital absence of the vas deferens along with URA has been reported.46
paragraphs.heading: Renal Agenesis

paragraphs.text: In patients with URA, it is important to carefully assess the health of the remaining solitary kidney; the presence of small kidney size, renal cysts, an echogenic appearance, or hydronephrosis suggests significant kidney disease. If this is the case, early involvement of a nephrologist and/or urologist is recommended. If the solitary kidney appears healthy, serial ultrasounds should demonstrate appropriate compensatory hypertrophy, with the kidney growing beyond the 95th percentile for age over time. In some patients, compensatory hypertrophy may be evident as early as 20 weeks’ gestation.47 The presence of hypertrophy in a solitary kidney is an important clinical indicator in terms of prognosis for good long-term kidney function. Most clinicians now reserve VCUG for patients with URA who have moderate to severe hydronephrosis, bladder abnormality, or develop a febrile urinary tract infection. Long-term nephrology follow-up is recommended for children with URA to screen for complications of reduced nephron number, including renal dysfunction, proteinuria, and hypertension.48
paragraphs.heading: Renal Agenesis

paragraphs.text: Bilateral renal agenesis (BRA) occurs in 1 of 4000 to 10,000 births.44 This diagnosis is generally made on early prenatal ultrasonography with the absence of kidneys, bladder, and anhydramnios. Historically, this diagnosis was incompatible with life, although with recent fetal interventions such as serial amnioinfusions, intensive ventilatory support after birth, and neonatal dialysis, the prognosis has improved somewhat, although with significant lifelong health burden.
paragraphs.heading: Renal Agenesis

paragraphs.text: MCDK is one of the most common forms of CAKUT, occurring in 1 in 1000 to 4300 live births.49 MCDK is a nonfunctional kidney composed of multiple large cysts and no normal renal parenchyma (Fig. 97.4). With the widespread use of prenatal ultrasonography, MCDK is usually detected prenatally. MCDK has a male predominance and occurs twice as often on the left side as the right side. The pathogenesis likely involves abnormal interaction between the ureteric bud and the mesonephric mesenchyme, leading to failure of normal kidney development.49 MCDK often occurs sporadically but can be seen in infants with a number of congenital syndromes. Mutations in a number of renal developmental genes have been identified in patients with MCDK (see Table 97.1). About 20% of children with unilateral MCDK will have VUR into the contralateral kidney, which is usually low grade and is often clinically insignificant.
paragraphs.heading: Multicystic Dysplastic Kidney

paragraphs.text: Management of the patient with MCDK is conservative because of the benign natural history of this condition. It is important to confirm the health of the single functioning contralateral kidney, ruling out dysplasia and obstruction. Although a screening VCUG was previously recommended
paragraphs.heading: Multicystic Dysplastic Kidney

paragraphs.text: for all infants with MCDK to rule contralateral VUR, most providers now reserve this testing for patients with significant hydronephrosis, signs of dysplasia, or those who develop a febrile urinary tract infection. The majority of MCDK undergo partial or complete spontaneous involution over time; in some patients involution occurs prenatally, but in most there is gradual involution with nearly 60% of MCDK fully involuted by 10 years of age.49 The contralateral kidney generally develops compensatory hypertrophy, allowing preservation of normal renal function. Although it has been common practice to follow patients with MCDK with frequent serial ultrasonography to assure compensatory hypertrophy and involution of the MCDK, there are now questions about the need for this approach.50 Many clinicians suggest that it is more important to focus on longterm monitoring of patients with MCDK for development of hypertension, urinary tract infection, or signs of CKD.51 Surgical removal is reserved for the minority of children in whom the MCDK grows larger over time.
paragraphs.heading: Multicystic Dysplastic Kidney

paragraphs.text: Renal dysplasia is characterized by abnormal renal development in the fetus, leading to replacement of the renal parenchyma by cartilage and disorganized epithelial structures. The pathogenesis of renal dysplasia may involve mutations in developmental genes (see Table 97.1), urinary tract obstruction, or in utero toxin/medication exposure.8 Renal dysplasia may occur as an isolated finding but also occurs in infants with obstructive uropathy or congenital disorders including VACTERL association; CHARGE syndrome; BOR syndrome; Jeune syndrome; and trisomies 13, 18, and 21. Most forms of “polycystic kidneys” that are reported prenatally or in association with syndromes, in fact, represent cystic dysplasia. The function of dysplastic kidneys is quite variable; some infants may have well preserved kidney function into adulthood and others may exhibit signs of renal insufficiency as early as the first few days of life.
paragraphs.heading: Renal Dysplasia

paragraphs.text: Concentration and acidification defects may also be present, but hematuria, proteinuria, and hypertension are unusual findings. Many children with bilateral renal dysplasia develop progressive CKD during childhood and adolescence because of increasing demands of growth that exceed the capability of the dysplastic kidneys.
paragraphs.heading: Renal Dysplasia

paragraphs.text: Hydronephrosis, defined as dilation of the upper urinary tract (Fig. 97.5), is one of the most common congenital findings detected by prenatal ultrasonography and is seen in 1% to 2% of pregnancies.52 Hydronephrosis may be seen in a wide spectrum of conditions, ranging from transient physiologic hydronephrosis to high grade VUR or urinary tract obstruction (Box 97.7). The challenge for the provider is predicting which infants are at risk of significant urinary tract disease while avoiding unnecessary testing and caregiver anxiety in those likely to have a benign condition. In general, the likelihood of clinically important urinary tract disease is directly correlated to the severity of antenatal hydronephrosis. In addition, the presence of bilateral hydronephrosis, progression of dilation, ureteral dilatation, renal parenchymal disease, bladder abnormalities, or oligohydramnios raises concern for significant CAKUT.
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Hydronephrosis

paragraphs.text: Several systems have been used over the years to grade congenital hydronephrosis. In 2014, a multidisciplinary consensus devised the Urinary Tract Dilation (UTD) Classification System which grades hydronephrosis both antenatally and postnatally, using three categories (UTD1, UTD2 and UTD3).52 This system is dependent on the measurement of the maximal anterior–posterior renal pelvis dilation (APRPD) as well as several other features of the renal parenchyma, ureters, bladder and the presence or absence of oligohydramnios. Normal APRPD is less than 4 mm at 16 to 27 weeks’ gestation, less than 7 mm after 28 weeks, and less than 10 mm at 2 days of life.52 Some providers feel that APRPD greater than 10 mm in the second trimester or greater than 15 mm in the third trimester is associated with a higher risk of clinically significant CAKUT.
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Hydronephrosis

paragraphs.text: The postnatal management of infants with congenital hydronephrosis is dependent on the degree of dilation seen on third-trimester ultrasound and the clinical suspicion for significant CAKUT or urinary tract obstruction. If there is a history of mild (UTD1) antenatal hydronephrosis, the initial postnatal ultrasound should be delayed at least 48 hours of age and may even be delayed until one month of age. Ultrasounds may be falsely reassuring if obtained in the first 2 days of life before good urine output is established.
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Hydronephrosis

paragraphs.text: On the other hand, a different approach is recommended for infants with moderate to severe hydronephrosis (UTD2 and 3) and/or concern for significant CAKUT (thick-walled bladder, bilateral and/or severe hydronephrosis, renal cystic
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Hydronephrosis

paragraphs.text: dysplasia, oligohydramnios, or dilated ureters). In these patients, a renal ultrasound should be performed promptly after birth and evaluation by a pediatric urologist and/or nephrologist should be promptly arranged. Most providers recommend VCUG to rule out high grade VUR and/ or bladder outlet obstruction. Further testing with nuclear scanning may be recommended by urology consultants. Antibiotic prophylaxis may be considered, although this remains controversial in the absence of VUR.
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Hydronephrosis

paragraphs.text: At least 80% of all prenatally detected mild isolated hydronephrosis is transient or physiologic and resolves spontaneously over the first 2 years of life. The risk of underlying urinary tract pathology is very low. Transient hydronephrosis may be caused by a delay in the maturation of the ureter, which leads to transient urinary flow obstruction.
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Hydronephrosis

paragraphs.text: Ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction is the most common cause of moderate to severe congenital hydronephrosis. UPJ obstruction is believed to result from incomplete recanalization of the proximal ureter or abnormal development of the ureteral musculature. UPJ obstruction is more common in boys and may be associated with other congenital anomalies or syndromes. The diagnosis is confirmed by an obstructive pattern observed on a diureticenhanced radionuclide scan, which is typically deferred until 4 to 6 weeks of age owing to limitation in testing
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Hydronephrosis

paragraphs.text: related to low newborn GFRs. Antibiotic prophylaxis may be considered to prevent urinary tract infection, although this practice is variable amongst providers. A conservative approach is recommended in most patients, with serial ultrasonography to trend the degree of hydronephrosis and radionuclide scans to assess differential renal function. Some patients will have spontaneous resolution of hydronephrosis over time, but those who develop worsening hydronephrosis or reduced differential renal function may benefit from surgical correction. Early and ongoing consultation with an experienced pediatric urologist is recommended.
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Hydronephrosis

paragraphs.text: Ureterovesical junction (UVJ) obstruction is characterized by significant congenital hydronephrosis in conjunction with a dilated ureter. It may be unilateral or bilateral and is usually not associated with other congenital malformations. UVJ obstruction is believed to be related to the deficient development of the distal ureter or the presence of a ureterocele, an outpouching of the ureter into the bladder lumen. The diagnosis is confirmed by a radionuclide scan and VCUG. UVJ obstruction resolves spontaneously in the majority of patients, although a subset of patients require temporary or permanent surgical intervention, so early urologic consultation is recommended.
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Hydronephrosis

paragraphs.text: VUR is a condition seen in 1% to 2% of children; it may be an isolated condition or associated with CAKUT including PUV, EBS, and renal dysplasia (see below). VUR is defined as the backward movement of urine from the bladder to the upper urinary tract during voiding. VUR is believed to be related to ectopic insertion of the ureter into the bladder wall, resulting in a shorter intravesicular ureter, which acts as an incompetent valve during urination. VUR is diagnosed by VCUG and is graded from I to V, with grade I indicating the mildest form and grade V the most severe form. The degree of hydronephrosis correlates poorly with the grade of VUR and postnatal ultrasound is considered a poor screening test for the presence or absence of VUR. Although the exact genetic basis of this condition has not been determined, there appears to be a genetic component, because the incidence of VUR increased in first-degree relatives, including siblings. Table 97.1 lists a number of mutations which have been associated with VUR. VUR usually resolves over time as the intravesical segment of the ureter elongates with growth.
paragraphs.heading: Vesicoureteral Reflux

paragraphs.text: The primary risk for infants with VUR is development of febrile urinary tract infections (UTIs). Although in the past, most infants with hydronephrosis underwent a VCUG, this testing is now reserved for infants with suspected bladder outlet obstruction, severe hydronephrosis or following the first febrile UTI. Antibiotic prophylaxis may be useful for those with higher grade (III, IV, V) VUR. Infants with VUR should be followed by a nephrologist or urologist and may need surgical correction if VUR does not resolve
paragraphs.heading: Vesicoureteral Reflux

paragraphs.text: spontaneously or if repeated febrile UTIs occur despite antibiotic prophylaxis. Long-term concerns include development of hypertension, renal scarring, and progressive CKD because of associated renal dysplasia or infection-related scarring (“reflux nephropathy”).
paragraphs.heading: Vesicoureteral Reflux

paragraphs.text: PUV represent the most common cause of LUTO, with an incidence of 1 in 5000 to 8000 live male births. A posterior urethral valve is a congenital membrane that fails to involute during fetal development and obstructs or partially obstructs the posterior urethra, variably affecting normal development of the bladder and upper urinary tract. Findings on prenatal ultrasound may include moderate to severe hydronephrosis; dilated ureters; a thickened, trabeculated bladder; dilated proximal urethra; and oligohydramnios. The antenatal presentation may include a palpable, distended bladder, poor urinary stream, and signs and symptoms of renal and pulmonary insufficiency. The VCUG is diagnostic for PUV and reveals associated VUR in 30% of patients.
paragraphs.heading: Posterior Urethral Valves

paragraphs.text: There are now several treatment options for fetuses identified to have severe LUTO. These options include vesicoamniotic shunting and fetal cystoscopy with valve ablation;53,54 both interventions have the purpose of preserving amniotic fluid volume to allow fetal lung development and optimizing kidney function and development. Criterion for prenatal intervention include normal karyotype, no other anatomic abnormality, ultrasound findings of bladder obstruction, oligohydramnios or anhydramnios, and “favorable” urine studies. The benefits of prenatal intervention for LUTO are promising, but because of the inherent risks involved, such interventions must be limited to centers with extensive expertise in prenatal intervention.
paragraphs.heading: Posterior Urethral Valves

paragraphs.text: Postnatal treatment is centered on securing adequate drainage of the urinary tract, initially by placement of a bladder catheter and later by primary ablation of the valves. Vesicostomy may be required in infants who show persistent obstruction and impaired urinary drainage despite ablation. Upper tract diversion is less commonly required but may be considered in patients with markedly dilated, tortuous ureters and worsening renal function despite adequate bladder drainage. The long-term outcome for infants with PUV depends on the degree of associated renal dysplasia; ongoing care with both a pediatric nephrologist and a urologist is recommended.
paragraphs.heading: Posterior Urethral Valves

paragraphs.text: EBS (“prune belly” syndrome) is characterized by a triad of genitourinary abnormalities (markedly enlarged, poorly contractile bladder, megaureters, and renal dysplasia), deficiency of abdominal wall musculature, and cryptorchidism (Fig. 97.7). Not all patients display all three components, and the severity of findings may be variable. The estimated incidence is 1 in 29,000 to 40,000 live births, with more than 95% of the cases occurring in boys. Although most
paragraphs.heading: Eagle-Barrett Syndrome

paragraphs.text: cases occur sporadically, familial clustering of cases and recent identification of mutations in a number of genes that regulate genitourinary muscle development suggest that at least some cases of EBS may have a genetic component.55 Cardiac, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, and orthopedic anomalies are present in 60% of EBS patients, some of which may be attributable to oligohydramnios sequence. Treatment in the neonatal period involves optimization of urinary tract drainage, management of renal dysfunction, and antibiotic prophylaxis. Management later in childhood may include the surgical repair of reflux, orchiopexy, reconstruction of the abdominal wall, and dialysis and/or kidney transplantation.
paragraphs.heading: Eagle-Barrett Syndrome

paragraphs.text: Congenital disorders of the bladder include classic bladder exstrophy (exstrophy-epispadias complex) and a more severe disorder called cloacal exstrophy.56 These disorders occur because of the failure of the cloacal membrane to be reinforced by ingrowth of mesoderm during fetal development. The cloacal membrane is therefore subject to premature rupture, and depending on the extent and timing of rupture, either classic bladder exstrophy or cloacal exstrophy develops.
paragraphs.heading: Disorders of the Bladder

paragraphs.text: Bladder exstrophy is a rare congenital malformation resulting in a lower abdominal wall defect exposing an open bladder and urethra, a wide diastasis of the pubic symphysis, and an epispadic urethral opening. The incidence of bladder exstrophy is estimated to be 1 in 10,000 births with a male predisposition. Bladder exstrophy can be detected prenatally, with absence of bladder filling, low-set umbilicus,
paragraphs.heading: Disorders of the Bladder

paragraphs.text: widened pubic rami, small genitalia, and a lower abdominal mass that increases in size through pregnancy. At birth, the examination reveals an exposed bladder and posterior urethra on the anterior abdominal wall, with urine dripping from the ureteric orifices on the bladder surface. Bilateral inguinal hernias are usually present and pubic bones can be felt on both sides of the bladder. In boys, the penis appears shorter and the epispadic urethra covers the dorsum of the penis. In females, the clitoris is completely split next to the open urethra. Abnormalities of the kidneys are seen in a minority of patients. Treatment involves urologic closure of the bladder often with pelvic osteotomy by orthopedic surgery.
paragraphs.heading: Disorders of the Bladder

paragraphs.text: Cloacal exstrophy represents a more severe abdominal wall defect, which is one of the rarest urologic anomalies with an incidence of 1 in 200,000 to 400,000 births. It is commonly referred to as the omphalocele, exstrophy, imperforate anus, and spinal abnormalities (OEIS) complex. The examination shows ileocecal and bladder exstrophy with an associated omphalocele, imperforate anus, complete phallic separation, undescended testes in males, vaginal duplication in females, and pubic diastasis. Abnormalities of the upper urinary tract are present in approximately 50% of patients and can be associated with progressive CKD. Infants with cloacal exstrophy require immediate evaluation in a tertiary center with renal ultrasound, spinal and hip imaging, and preparation for early closure of the omphalocele, creation of a colostomy or ileostomy, and initial surgical closure of the bladder. Patients require long-term follow-up with a multidisciplinary team that includes a pediatric urologist, pediatric orthopedic surgeon, pediatric nephrologist (if renal dysplasia is present), and appropriate support team.
paragraphs.heading: Disorders of the Bladder

paragraphs.text: Oligohydramnios/anhydramnios may occur in cases of bilateral renal agenesis (BRA), severe bilateral renal dysplasia, or severe LUTO (see also Chapters 14 and 23). Lack of amniotic fluid early in gestation is detrimental to fetal pulmonary function, and it results in pulmonary hypoplasia and features of Potter sequence. Recently serial amnioinfusions have shown promise in treatment of cases of early pregnancy renal anhydramnios (EPRA) because of congenital BRA.54 There is currently an ongoing National Institutes of Health (NIH)-sponsored clinical trial, Renal Anhydramnios Fetal Therapy (RAFT), to further evaluate this intervention in select fetal therapy centers. Ethical considerations regarding amnioinfusions to patients with BRA who will be dependent on lifelong dialysis and transplant support are considerable.57 As discussed above, in select patients with LUTO/ PUV, vesicoamniotic shunting and fetal cystoscopy with valve ablation may be a prenatal treatment option.53
paragraphs.heading: Disorders of the Bladder

paragraphs.text: Inherited renal disorders include a spectrum of abnormalities involving the glomeruli or renal tubules. Monogenic
paragraphs.heading: Inherited Renal Disorders

paragraphs.text: diseases (those with single gene defects) that may present in the newborn period include congenital nephrotic syndrome, polycystic kidney diseases, and several disorders of tubular transport.
paragraphs.heading: Inherited Renal Disorders

paragraphs.text: Congenital nephrotic syndrome (CNS) is a rare condition defined as the development of nephrotic syndrome within the first 3 months of life.58 A prenatal diagnosis of CNS should be suspected in mothers with a high serum or amniotic fluid α-fetoprotein concentration, which results from massive fetal urinary protein losses. Placental edema, ascites, or fetal hydrops on prenatal ultrasonography should also raise suspicion of this disorder. Infants with CNS typically have full-blown nephrotic syndrome at birth or shortly afterward, with massive proteinuria, profound hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia, and generalized edema. Infants with congenital nephrotic syndrome are often delivered prematurely and may be small for gestational age. The placenta is large, weighing greater than 25% of the infant’s birth weight.
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Nephrotic Syndrome

paragraphs.text: CNS is most commonly caused by mutations in genes encoding proteins in the glomerular epithelial cell (podocyte), a cell critical in the prevention of urinary protein loss. The most common mutation is in NPHS1, a gene that encodes an important slit diaphragm protein called nephrin. Mutations in nephrin are most common in the Finnish population; thus infants with CNS because of nephrin mutations are said to have Finnish-type nephrotic syndrome. Other genetic mutations have been associated with CNS, including mutations in NPHS2 (podocin), LAMB2 (laminin β-2 gene), PLCE1 (phospholipase C epsilon gene) and WT-1 (Wilms tumor suppressor gene). Pathogenic variants in WT-1 can result in isolated kidney disease or developmental syndromes, including Denys-Drash and Frasier syndrome, both characterized by nephrotic syndrome, genital anomalies, pseudohermaphroditism, and risk for tumor development.
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Nephrotic Syndrome

paragraphs.text: The evaluation and treatment of congenital nephrotic syndrome is complex. The clinician should first exclude nongenetic causes such as syphilis, HIV, CMV, hepatitis B, congenital rubella, toxoplasmosis, membranous nephropathy from maternal anti-NEP (neutral endopeptidase) antibodies, and maternal systemic lupus erythematosus, all of which have been associated with treatable forms of congenital nephrotic syndrome. If genetic CNS is suspected, testing by whole exome sequencing or next generation sequencing is recommended to establish an accurate diagnosis. Corticosteroids and immunosuppressive agents, used in treatment of nephrotic syndrome in older children, are not recommended. Current treatment includes intravenous albumin infusions, diuretics, aggressive nutritional support, thyroid hormone replacement, preventative anticoagulation, and prompt treatment of infectious and thromboembolic complications. Bilateral nephrectomy is typically required for the management of
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Nephrotic Syndrome

paragraphs.text: massive protein loss, followed by PD support and early kidney transplantation.
paragraphs.heading: Congenital Nephrotic Syndrome

paragraphs.text: ARPKD is a rare inherited disorder characterized by enlarged cystic kidneys and a developmental bile duct disorder called congenital hepatic fibrosis.59 ARPKD occurs in approximately 1 in 20,000 live births. Prenatal ultrasonography shows enlarged, echogenic kidneys and oligohydramnios. The newborn infant with ARPKD may present with palpable abdominal masses, severe hypertension, and renal insufficiency. Respiratory failure related to pulmonary hypoplasia and abdominal distention from the massively enlarged kidneys is common. Although the majority of patients with ARPKD present in the newborn period, there is significant phenotypic heterogeneity, and presentations later in childhood may occur.
paragraphs.heading: Polycystic Kidney Disease

paragraphs.text: ARPKD is caused by mutations in PKHD1, a gene that encodes fibrocystin/polyductin, a large protein localized in the primary cilia of the kidney tubular cells, liver bile duct epithelia, and pancreas. The genetic defect leads to fusiform dilatation of the renal collecting ducts, causing enlarged echogenic kidneys without visible macrocysts. Virtually all infants with ARPKD have histologic evidence of congenital hepatic fibrosis at birth, although clinical evidence of hepatic involvement is present in only 40% of affected newborns.
paragraphs.heading: Polycystic Kidney Disease

paragraphs.text: The diagnosis of ARPKD is typically made based on characteristic clinical features, including enlarged echogenic kidneys, history of oligohydramnios, and hypertension. However, other cystic disorders, including diffuse cystic dysplasia, HNF-1B-related kidney disease, and ADPKD can be clinically indistinguishable from ARPKD in the newborn period. Although initial management is similar for all of the disorders, establishing a definitive diagnosis may be helpful for offering prognosis, surveillance for associated conditions, and future family planning. Therefore it is recommended to offer genetic testing via next generation sequencing cystic kidney disease panel.60
paragraphs.heading: Polycystic Kidney Disease

paragraphs.text: The management of the neonate with ARPKD is largely supportive.61 Mechanical ventilation, including oscillator support, is critical in neonates with respiratory failure because of pulmonary hypoplasia or respiratory embarrassment from abdominal distension. Infants with hypertension may require the administration of multiple antihypertensive agents to achieve blood pressure control. Patients may require correction of electrolyte imbalances, notably hyponatremia. Optimizing nutrition may be challenging owing to massively enlarged kidneys causing feeding difficulties. Unilateral nephrectomies have not been shown to improve the respiratory status but may improve feeding issues. Hepatic complications, such as portal hypertension, are typically absent in the newborn period, and synthetic function is intact.
paragraphs.heading: Polycystic Kidney Disease

paragraphs.text: Neonatal survival for patients with ARPKD is estimated to be about 70%. Most mortality results from inability to achieve adequate oxygenation and ventilation despite
paragraphs.heading: Polycystic Kidney Disease

paragraphs.text: aggressive ventilatory support. Long-term survival has improved, and approximately 80% of neonatal survivors are alive at 10 years of life. Morbidity is significant, however, and complications include CKD, growth failure, hepatic complications (portal hypertension, bleeding varices, and ascending cholangitis), and chronic lung disease.59 Progression to end-stage kidney disease requiring dialysis or kidney transplantation occurs in 50% of patients in the first decade of life. With improving long-term survival, portal hypertension has emerged as an important cause of morbidity and mortality, and subsequent liver transplantation may be necessary.
paragraphs.heading: Polycystic Kidney Disease

paragraphs.text: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) caused by mutations in PKD1 and PKD2 genes may also present in the neonatal period. Clinical presentation ranges from asymptomatic cysts on renal ultrasonography to severe neonatal manifestations similar to that of ARPKD. Because the two conditions can be very similar, a careful family history and genetic testing is recommended to establish the correct diagnosis.60 Although ADPKD is a systemic disease that commonly affects the liver, gastrointestinal tract, and cerebral vessels in adults, such extra-renal manifestations are rarely seen until adulthood.
paragraphs.heading: Polycystic Kidney Disease

paragraphs.text: Neonatal Bartter syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive hypokalemic tubulopathy with an incidence of 1 in 50,000 to 100,000 live births. Newborn infants with neonatal Bartter syndrome typically present with profound salt wasting, polyuria, hypokalemia, and hypercalciuria (see also Chapter 96).
paragraphs.heading: Neonatal Bartter Syndrome

paragraphs.text: RTA is caused by a defect in the reabsorption of bicarbonate or in the secretion of hydrogen ions that is not related to a decrease in GFR. RTA should be suspected in infants with persistent hyperchloremic (i.e., nonanion gap) metabolic acidosis. There are three forms of RTA: proximal (type II), distal (type I), and hyperkalemic (type IV). RTA may be sporadic or inherited as a classic Mendelian trait. RTA is discussed in detail in Chapter 96.
paragraphs.heading: Renal Tubular Acidosis

paragraphs.text: Renal tumors in the newborn infant are uncommon, accounting for approximately 5% to 7% of all neonatal tumors.62 Because only 15% of renal tumors are detected antenatally, the most common neonatal clinical presentation is abdominal distension or a palpable mass. Other symptoms may include hypertension, hematuria, lethargy,
paragraphs.heading: Tumors of the Kidney

paragraphs.text: Key Points
paragraphs.heading: Tumors of the Kidney

paragraphs.text: • Acute kidney injury (AKI) occurs in 30% of critically ill
paragraphs.heading: Tumors of the Kidney

paragraphs.text: neonates and is independently associated with increased mortality and length of hospital stay.
paragraphs.heading: Tumors of the Kidney

paragraphs.text: pallor and feeding intolerance. The most common types of renal tumors seen in the neonate are congenital mesoblastic nephroma, (nephroblastoma), multilocular cystic nephroma, and Wilms tumor.62
paragraphs.heading: Tumors of the Kidney

paragraphs.text: Congenital mesoblastic nephroma (nephroblastoma) is the most common renal tumor in the first year of life, accounting for 54% to 66% of tumors.62 The clinical presentation is usually a unilateral abdominal mass, although congestive heart failure and hypertension are less common manifestations. Seventy percent of affected pregnancies are associated with polyhydramnios; premature delivery and hydrops have been reported. Nephrectomy is curative, with the exception of infrequent local recurrences and rare pulmonary metastases.
paragraphs.heading: Tumors of the Kidney

paragraphs.text: Multilocular cystic nephroma is a benign renal tumor that consists of large cysts separated by fibrous septae. This tumor arises from metanephric blastema and has features of immature blastema, tubules, and skeletal muscle on histopathologic examination. The prognosis is excellent with nephrectomy alone.
paragraphs.heading: Tumors of the Kidney

paragraphs.text: Wilms tumor accounts for 20% of all renal tumors diagnosed in the neonatal population. The clinical presentation is similar to that of congenital mesoblastic nephroma. Most Wilms tumors occur sporadically, but 10% are associated with congenital syndromes that predispose to tumorigenesis, including WAGR (Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, range of developmental delays) syndrome, Denys-Drash syndrome, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, and Golabi-Behmel syndrome.62
paragraphs.heading: Tumors of the Kidney

paragraphs.text: Malignant rhabdoid tumor of the kidney (MRTK) is a rare but very aggressive renal tumor, often presenting with metastatic disease. It is treated with nephrectomy, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy and has a poor outcome. Clear cell sarcoma of the kidney (CCTK) is the least common neonatal renal tumor, accounting for only 3% of renal tumors in this age group. Treatment is similar to that of MRTK, with nephrectomy, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy; patient outcome is less dismal than with neonatal MRTK.
paragraphs.heading: Tumors of the Kidney

paragraphs.text: Definitive therapy for a localized renal mass begins with surgical exploration, and in most cases the primary treatment is nephrectomy. Infants with congenital mesoblastic nephromas and multilocular cystic nephromas require no postoperative therapy. Infants with malignant tumors such as Wilms tumor are treated according to well-established oncologic protocols. The prognosis for most infants with neonatal renal tumors is good, although an infant with aggressive Wilms tumor, atypical congenital mesoblastic nephroma, MRTK, or CCTK may have a poor prognosis.

# 97. The Kidney and Urinary Tract of the Neonate
> Source attribution: [Source credits](../../SOURCE_CREDITS.md).


## PDF page 1960 | printed page 1966

97 The Kidney and Urinary

Tract of the Neonate

### BETH A. VOGT

In the past 30 years, the field of clinical neonatal nephrology has expanded significantly in concert with major advances and changes in the care and survival of neonates, particularly premature neonates. The widespread use of prenatal ultrasonography has expanded early identification of congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT), many of which are caused by mutations in key developmental genes. Because of the wide spectrum of CAKUT, the new challenge for providers is to determine which infants with a history of abnormal antenatal imaging need evaluation and intervention and which have benign conditions that will be of little clinical significance. Acute kidney injury (AKI) has been increasingly recognized as a common and important condition in the hospitalized neonate which is associated with increased length of hospitalization, mortality, and risk for later development of chronic kidney disease (CKD). Neonatal hypertension remains an important complication of umbilical artery catheters, but there is now increased recognition of hypertension associated with bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) support, or idiopathic causes.

The goals of this chapter are to review the anatomic and functional development of the kidney, outline the recommended approach to the evaluation of the neonate with suspected renal disease, and provide an overview of the common nephrologic and urologic problems seen in preterm and term neonates.

### Kidney and Urinary Tract Development

The development of the kidney and urinary tract is a carefully coordinated process that involves the regulated activation and inactivation of hundreds of genes that encode transcription factors, growth factors and receptors, structural proteins, adhesion molecules, and other regulatory proteins.1 Genetic, environmental, and epigenetic factors that interrupt this complex process can lead to a spectrum of congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT), described later in this chapter.

1966

### Development of the Kidney

Human kidney development begins in the first trimester of pregnancy. There are three stages of development: the pronephros, mesonephros, and metanephros (illustrated in Fig. 97.1). The pronephros develops in the cervical region and disappears by the end of the fourth week of gestation. As the pronephros regresses, the mesonephros appears caudally to it, and, by the end of the eighth week of gestation, most portions of the mesonephros disappear.

The metanephros, which ultimately becomes the definitive kidney, begins forming at 5 weeks of gestation. A subset of cells from the metanephric mesenchyme secretes glial-like derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF), a signal that initiates budding of the ureteric bud (UB) from the mesonephric duct. The UB then invades the metanephric mesenchyme and induces cells to undergo mesenchymal-epithelial transformation to begin formation of fetal kidney. Branching morphogenesis occurs, dependent on back and forth signaling between the UB and the metanephric mesenchyme. The metanephros develops through a series of transitional stages and ultimately develops into the glomeruli and tubules which comprise the upper part of the nephron. The UB forms the lower part of the nephron (collecting ducts), as well as the renal pelvis and ureters.

The metanephric kidney becomes functional during the second half of pregnancy. Fetal urine becomes a major contributor to amniotic fluid at 16 to 20 weeks of gestation. Nephrogenesis, the formation of new nephron units, is complete at 34 weeks of gestation, when each kidney contains its definitive complement of approximately 800,000 to 1.2 million nephrons.1 Infants of mothers with nutritional deficiency, placental insufficiency, or those born before completion of nephrogenesis can be born with a suboptimal number of nephrons and be at risk for future development of CKD or hypertension.2,3

### Development of the Bladder and Urethra

The bladder and urethra are formed during the second and third months of gestation, which is illustrated in Fig. 97.2.

### Renal Blood Flow

Absolute renal blood flow (RBF) and the percentage of cardiac output directed to the kidneys increase steadily with advancing gestational age. The kidneys of a human fetus receive approximately 3% to 5% of the cardiac output. The relatively low RBF of the fetus is related to high renovascular resistance caused by the increased activity of the reninangiotensin-aldosterone and sympathetic nervous systems. The RBF increases dramatically postnatally, reaching 10% of the cardiac output at 1 week of life, and achieves adult values of 25% of the cardiac output by 2 years of age. This rise in RBF is caused primarily by decreasing renovascular resistance and increasing cardiac output and perfusion pressure.

### Glomerular Filtration

### Concentration and Dilution of Urine

Newborn infants have a limited capacity to concentrate their urine, with maximal urinary osmolality of 800 mOsm/ kg in a term infant compared to that of a 2-year-old, which approximates adult values of 1400 mOsm/kg. In contrast, the term newborn infant has full ability to maximally dilute its urine in response to a water load, achieving adult values of 50 mOsm/kg. Preterm infants are unable to fully dilute their urine but can achieve urine osmolality of 70 mOsm/ kg. However, the response of premature infants to an acute water load may be limited because of their low GFR and the decreased activity of sodium transporters in the diluting segment of the nephron. The excessive administration of water may place the newborn infant at a high risk for dilutional hyponatremia and hypervolemia. Urinary diluting and concentrating capacity in term and preterm infants are discussed in more detail in Chapter 96.
