### Eye Findings in Chromosomal Syndromes

Chromosomal anomalies involve significant alteration of genetic materials with multiple genes being affected simultaneously. However, genes that control the development and function of the eye are spread on multiple chromosomes. Therefore it is not surprising that the majority of chromosomal anomalies involve the eye in some form. Following is a selection of eye features that are important, given the frequency or severity.

### Trisomy 21

Ocular findings associated with Down syndrome are extensive. Because of this, children with Down syndrome should be examined by an ophthalmologist during infancy and periodically after that. From front to back, the eye findings are as follows: significant refractive errors, amblyopia, nystagmus, strabismus, nasolacrimal duct obstruction, epicanthus, telecanthus, upward slant of palpebral fissures, blepharitis, keratoconus, glaucoma, iris nodules (Brushfield spots), cataract, and optic nerve swelling. Caution should be exercised when using dilating drops in these children, because they can have an exaggerated systemic reaction to atropine, and atlanto-axial instability can induce a risk in case of neck hyperextension.

### Trisomy 13

Ocular findings are present in 90% of Patau syndrome subjects.52 Intraocular cartilage found at histopathology is virtually pathognomonic for trisomy 13.52 Typical inferonasal iris coloboma with sectoral cataract in the same location is highly suggestive of this syndrome. Other eye features in this syndrome are microphthalmia, cyclopia, short/slanted palpebral fissures, ptosis, hypertelorism, corneal opacities, luxation of the lens, coloboma of the lens, persistent tunica vasculosalentis, persistent fetal vasculature (formerly known as persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous), typical coloboma of the choroid, and retinal dysplasia.52

### Trisomy 18

The most common eye anomalies in Edwards syndrome include epicanthus, hypertelorism, and hypoplastic supraorbital ridges. Ankyloblepharon filiforme adnatum (strands joining the upper and lower lids together) is very suggestive of trisomy 18. Less frequently, strabismus, cyclopia, colobomatous microphthalmia, microcornea, corneal opacities, congenital glaucoma, posterior subcapsular cataract, and retinal depigmentation are present in this syndrome.

### 11p Abnormalities

The PAX6 gene on the short arm of chromosome 11 is the master regulator of the development of the eye. Any defect in the PAX6

gene can therefore result in a range of ocular dysgenesis conditions, the most common of which is aniridia. The adjacent WT1 gene on the 11p13 locus may be simultaneously affected by the mutation affecting PAX6, which results in WAGR syndrome (aniridia, Wilms tumor, genitourinary abnormalities, and mental retardation).32 PAX6 mutation can be sporadic (occurring de novo), autosomal dominant, or autosomal recessive. Autosomal dominant mutations are the most common (85%), with complete penetrance and variable expressivity, clinically presenting as variable degrees of aniridia among members of the same family. Sporadic mutations are less common (13%–33%) and are associated with WAGR syndrome. Ophthalmic examination of family members is therefore extremely important. Genetic testing of a child with aniridia, especially if no other family members are affected, is essential. Periodic long-term evaluation for Wilms tumor with abdominal ultrasound is a must for those with sporadic mutations.

### 13q Abnormalities

The most important possible finding that requires a comprehensive retinal examination is retinoblastoma. The retinoblastoma gene is a tumor suppressor gene that is lost in 13q deletion. That creates a situation in which cells throughout the body have only one copy of the tumor suppressor gene and are vulnerable to lose that copy and start developing tumors, among them retinoblastoma, which tends to be bilateral and start at a young age. Other ocular abnormalities are almost always present and severe, including microphthalmia, iris and choroidal colobomas, ptosis, cataracts, and down-slanting palpebral apertures and epicanthus.

### Turner Syndrome

Strabismus, ptosis, congenital cataracts, and occasionally corneal nebulae and blue sclerae in the neonatal period have been described as being associated with Turner syndrome.

### Eye Findings in Craniofacial Syndromes

Eye abnormalities can be associated with congenital anomalies of the face, skull, or head in both craniosynostotic and nonsynostotic forms.

### Craniosynostosis Syndromes

There is well-defined eye involvement in craniosynostosis syndromes that requires careful follow-up and management. Proptosis is secondary to maldeveloped, small orbits and can further be complicated by lagophthalmos, exposure keratopathy, or globe subluxation. Globe subluxation, when the globe protrudes anteriorly to the eyelids, is an ocular emergency that needs to be treated by the caregiver or medical personnel immediately to avoid optic nerve ischemic damage with permanent vision loss. One approach for globe subluxation is to place a finger on the visible conjunctiva in the interpalpebral area and apply firm pressure until the globe

is behind the eyelids. This approach avoids damage to the cornea. Lagophthalmos with exposure keratopathy and a possible corneal scar is another cause of vision loss requiring an aggressive approach consisting of frequent lubrication, moist chamber, taping the eyelids closed at night, and tarsorrhaphy. The definitive treatment of lagophthalmos is orbital expansion. The optic nerve can develop edema or atrophy. Edema is secondary to increased intracranial pressure, secondary to difficult expansion of the cranium, and less often because of compressive optic neuropathy in a tight optic canal. Optic atrophy is the end result of longstanding optic nerve edema. Strabismus is a common occurrence in craniosynostosis, with V pattern exotropia and inferior oblique overaction seen as characteristic types.

Because of comparable cranial and orbital anomalies, eye findings can be similar in the other craniosynostosis syndromes such as Crouzon syndrome, Apert syndrome,53 Saethre-Chotzen syndrome, and Pfeiffer syndrome.

### Hemifacial Microsomia

Ocular manifestations can range from clinical anophthalmia to minor fissure asymmetry. Goldenhar syndrome is probably a variant of this group, with characteristic limbal dermoids and orbital lipodermoids. Limbal dermoids are reported more frequently than lipodermoids and are occasionally bilateral. Another common finding is an upper eyelid coloboma, almost always on the more affected side. Less frequent findings are Duane syndrome and microphthalmia.54

### Terminal Transverse Defects With Orofacial Malformations and Oromandibular-Limb Hypogenesis

These are a heterogeneous collection of syndromes with a wide variety of facial and limb anomalies; they include Möbius syndrome. The minimal findings of this syndrome are abduction weakness (cranial nerve 6 palsy) and facial nerve palsy, with frequent limb and tongue anomalies.

### Pierre Robin Sequence

The Pierre Robin sequence is characterized by micrognathia, glossoptosis, and cleft palate. Pierre Robin sequence can occur in isolation or be part of a syndrome. About 10% of patients with Pierre Robin sequence have Stickler syndrome as well, with the additional features of high myopia, propensity for retinal detachment, cataracts, deafness, and arthritis.55

### Waardenburg Syndrome

Waardenburg syndrome is transmitted as an autosomal dominant trait and has been divided into four types based on clinical attributes. The most common is Waardenburg syndrome type 1. It is associated with lateral displacement of the medial canthi (i.e., telecanthus), abnormal position of the lacrimal puncta, coalescing of eyebrows (i.e., synophrys),

white forelock, heterochromia irides, retinal pigmentary changes, and sensorineural deafness.

### Cornelia de Lange Syndrome

The typical facial appearance in infants with Cornelia de Lange syndrome is a low hairline, synophrys, long eyelashes, and a small upturned nose. Eye disorders, which are less frequently encountered, include hypertelorism and downslanting palpebral fissures, dacryostenosis, strabismus, nystagmus, ptosis, severe myopia, and pupillary abnormalities.56

### CHARGE Association

This heterogeneous group of anomalies (colobomas, (heart defects, choanal (atresia, (restricted growth, (genital hypoplasia, and (ear malformations) presents with typical coloboma of the optic nerve, choroid, or iris in the inferior nasal direction. Other eye involvements have been described: microphthalmia, refractive errors, and vertical strabismus.1

### Deformation Syndromes

Congenital deformations resulting from intrauterine restraints are common and may involve craniofacial structures. Congenital torticollis is one of the deformation syndromes that can have ophthalmic implications, because it may be confused with superior oblique palsy with compensatory head posture.

### Eye Findings in Neurocutaneous Disorders (Phakomatoses)

Eye findings are important manifestations in phakomatoses, which are a group of disorders featuring discrete hamartomas in multiple organ systems including the skin and the brain. Four disorders have been designated as classic phakomatoses with other conditions sometime included as well. From the four classic phakomatoses—neurofibromatosis, tuberous sclerosis, encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis, and retinal angiomatosis— only the first three are active in infancy or early childhood.

### Neurofibromatosis

Neurofibromatosis (NF) is described in two types. Both NF type 1 and 2 are autosomal dominant genetic conditions with high penetrance and high spontaneous mutation rates. NF1 (von Recklinghausen disease) is characterized by melanocytic and glial cell lesions distributed in the brain, skin, and eye. The occurrence of these lesions is highly age dependent, with some features that present early in life with stabilization or regression, and other features that start late with subsequent progression throughout life. Overall, NF1 is rarely diagnosed in neonates. Early ophthalmic manifestations of NF1 are plexiform neurofibroma of the upper eyelid, glaucoma, optic nerve glioma, and sphenoid dysplasia. Neuroimaging should be obtained in patients with ocular pulsations, neurofibromas of the eyelid,

Progressive enlargement of the globe or buphthalmos is seen if glaucoma with high intraocular pressure is present before 2 years of life. Optic nerve glioma, although rare with a rate of up to 5%, is an important cause of morbidity and mortality in NF1. Iris Lisch nodules that are often sought to help in early diagnosis are rarely seen in infants and in only a 25% minority by 2 years with presence in 90% by puberty.57 Despite this, Lisch nodules are valuable features as they have a tendency to be present before the hallmark lesion of NF1, nodular neurofibromas of the skin. NF2 is less common than NF1 and has the hallmark lesion of bilateral eighth nerve tumors, hence the name of central NF. Early-onset posterior subcapsular or wedge-shape cataracts have been described in NF2.

### Encephalofacial Angiomatosis (Sturge-Weber Syndrome)

As the name implies, this condition encompasses angiomas of the facial skin with ipsilateral leptomeningeal vascular malformation. There is no apparent hereditary pattern. Ocular complications of Sturge-Weber syndrome include glaucoma, which affects 30% to 75% of patients, and chorioretinal angioma. Glaucoma can present in two types, one of them resembling congenital glaucoma, with enlargement of the globe, high myopia, and amblyopia. The associated choroidal angioma is usually indistinct and difficult to visualize without indirect ophthalmoscopy. If present, it may lead to macular edema and decreased visual acuity.

### Tuberous Sclerosis (Bourneville Disease)

Hamartomas of the brain that cause seizures and mental retardation associated with hamartomas in the eyes, kidney, heart, lungs, and skin are the hallmarks of this autosomal condition. The spontaneous rate of mutation is very high, similar to that with NF. Retinal lesions, called astrocytic hamartomas (or phakomas), have one of two distinct appearances. Phakoma type 1 is seen at a very young age and has the appearance of gray-white nodules with a smooth, flat surface and indistinct borders. Consequently, these lesions are difficult to visualize, and special techniques are used on indirect ophthalmoscopy to avoid missing the early lesions.

### Ocular Trauma

Two types of eye trauma are seen only in this age group: birth trauma and shaken baby syndrome. Accidental contusions and lacerations may occur as well but are much less common in infancy than later in life because of decreased mobility.

### Birth Trauma

Birth trauma to the eyes is associated with the duration of labor and difficulty of delivery. Lid petechiae and

hemorrhages, observed more often with face presentations than with vertex presentations, usually resolve rapidly without treatment. Subconjunctival hemorrhages are also common and require no treatment. Such findings, however, should increase the suspicion of associated intraocular injuries.

Retinal hemorrhages are common after delivery, occurring in 78% of newborns after vacuum delivery, 30% after normal vaginal delivery or with forceps assists, and only 8% after cesarean delivery.58 These retinal hemorrhages are usually small, multiple, and scattered throughout the retina; they may persist for months and must be considered in the differential diagnosis of suspected nonaccidental trauma (shaken baby syndrome).58 Bleeding into the orbital contents (retrobulbar hemorrhage) can result from birth trauma. This bleeding produces a unilateral proptosis that tends to increase gradually in size during the first 3 or 4 hours after birth. Ecchymosis of the lids can be associated findings immediately or 1 to 2 days later. The differential diagnosis includes dermoid cysts, teratomas, and other congenital tumors of the orbit. The hematoma usually absorbs spontaneously over 1 to 2 weeks. It is important during this time to ensure that the cornea is not dry from exposure or abraded and that the retinal circulation is not compromised. A detailed fundoscopic exam is indicated, and if it shows impairment of arterial or venous circulation, immediate surgical decompression of the orbit is required. Forceps deliveries, particularly when associated with improper application, can produce bruises and lacerations of the lid or globe. A forceps mark or lid laceration requires a careful and complete examination of the orbit and globe for associated injuries. Forceps application can produce a rupture in the cornea’s endothelial basement membrane (Descemet membrane). Seen with magnification, these ruptures appear as vertical lines in the posterior portion of the cornea. They can lead to rapid corneal edema (hydrops) because of compromised water pump mechanism of the endothelium, with a cloudy appearance that must be differentiated from other congenital corneal opacities. Children with Descemet membrane ruptures can develop astigmatism and dense amblyopia. Traumatic forceps delivery has been known to cause a variety of other ocular injuries, including Purtscher retinopathy, choroid ruptures, and traumatic optic neuropathy. Ocular injury in the newborn has also been reported as a result of fetal monitors, surgical instruments, phototherapy lights, prenatal maternal injury, and amniocentesis.

### Shaken Baby Syndrome

Forceful, repeated back and forth movement of the head can result in devastating and blinding ocular injuries. Characteristic hemorrhages involve preretinal, intraretinal, and subretinal spaces; are numerous; and extend in the far periphery of the fundus.

The retina can even be folded in a circumferential manner along the vascular arcades surrounding the macula, another finding highly suggestive of shaken baby syndrome. Retinal hemorrhages may resolve without sequelae, but involvement of the optic nerve, macula, or occipital cortex can produce profound lifelong visual loss.59 The extent and type of retinal hemorrhages that occur in shaken baby syndrome can be pathognomonic of the syndrome and may support the legal prosecution of the offender (see Fig. 99.23).59 Accidental head trauma and cardiopulmonary resuscitation in infants do not result in the type and extent of retinal hemorrhage seen in shaken baby syndrome.59

### Neonatal Ocular Infections

### Neonatal Conjunctivitis (Ophthalmia Neonatorum)

Neonatal conjunctivitis represents inflammation or infection of the conjunctiva in the neonatal period. What makes an otherwise benign condition a public health concern requiring prophylaxis at birth in all neonates is the possibility of long-term vision loss and systemic associated conditions. Neonatal conjunctivitis is the most common infection in the first month of life with incidence from 1% to 24%.60 The four categories of neonatal conjunctivitis are chemical, bacterial, chlamydial, and viral. Conjunctival injection, chemosis, discharge, and eyelid edema can occur with all subtypes of neonatal conjunctivitis. Clinical history, most importantly prenatal history, and clinical elements such as character of the discharge, presence of chemosis and membranes, or skin vesicles can suggest the specific etiology and direct laboratory testing.

Chemical conjunctivitis occurs 1 to 2 days after instillation of silver nitrate 1% or other antibiotics for prophylaxis at birth. Typical chemical conjunctivitis is bilateral and has a low amount of purulence; the Gram stain shows no organisms, and it resolves spontaneously within 2 days. Alternative treatments for neonatal prophylaxis other than silver nitrate 1% include erythromycin ointment 0.5%, povidone iodine 2.5%, and tetracycline ointment 1%.

Chlamydial conjunctivitis is now a common infection in the neonatal period with higher rates in absent prenatal care. The infection is typically acquired from the mother as the child passes through the birth canal, although it can occur after cesarean section. This type of conjunctivitis develops typically in the second week of life with unilateral or bilateral mucopurulent discharge with possible pseudomembranes. Evolution is chronic with disappearance of discharge after weeks or months, but with the possibility of scarring of the conjunctiva or cornea and possibility of systemic spread and complications. The usual cultures and

Gram staining are unhelpful in the diagnosis of chlamydia because it is an obligate intracellular organism. Cell culture is the gold standard because of high specificity but is expensive. Diagnosis can be made more conveniently by Giemsa staining of a conjunctival scraping or by a variety of commercially available antibody or PCR tests. Chlamydial conjunctivitis is treated with erythromycin ointment three times a day for 2 to 3 weeks. Systemic antibiotics are necessary because chlamydia can cause pneumonia, otitis, or nasal congestion.60

Neisseria gonorrhoeae is an acute, severe, purulent conjunctivitis with an incubation period of 2 to 5 days. If N. gonorrhoeae is the cause of the conjunctivitis, immediate treatment with systemic and topical antibiotics is necessary. In cases of infection with organisms resistant to penicillin, a third-generation cephalosporin is indicated.

Ophthalmia neonatorum also can result from other common pathogens such as staphylococci, pneumococci, streptococci, or gram-negative bacteria. These bacterial infections usually appear several days after birth. Most respond well to topical antibiotics or ointment.

Older infants with chronic or recurrent mucous or purulent discharge usually have a blocked nasolacrimal duct as the underlying cause. The duct frequently opens spontaneously during the first year of life. Treatment with topical antibiotics and massage of the lacrimal sac can help resolve the problem.

### Ocular Manifestations of Intrauterine Infections

A number of intrauterine infections have important ophthalmic manifestations. These congenital infections are known by the acronym TORCH. These infections include toxoplasmosis, “other infections,” rubella, cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex. The “other” designation is used for syphilis and varicella, as well as lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus. Some infections result from maternal infections that either cross the placental barrier or are transmitted during passage through the birth canal. Congenital toxoplasmosis manifests with necrotizing retinochoroiditis with associated vitritis and retinal vasculitis. These lesions result in chorioretinal scars characterized by white areas of exposed sclera circumscribed by well-defined darkly pigmented borders. Retinochoroiditis in toxoplasmosis is a recurrent condition; new lesions develop topically at the border of a scar, although it can develop in areas devoid of scar or in the other eye. Serologic confirmation of congenital infection is done by elevated IgM and IgA titers.61 Syphilis can affect most structures of the eye ranging from eyelid skin rash, orbital inflammation, interstitial keratitis, and various types of intraocular inflammation to cranial nerve involvement and central visual pathway involvement, including optic nerve atrophy and pupillomotor disturbances. The interstitial keratitis associated with congenital syphilis is a late finding, not apparent until after the age of 5 years.


## PDF page 2051

Treatment with penicillin in the neonatal period does not prevent later development of interstitial keratitis. The most common eye finding in lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus infection is generalized chorioretinal scars.61 Neonatal herpes infection is most often acquired during passage through the birth canal and can cause typical herpetic eye disease such as blepharoconjunctivitis, keratitis, iritis, or chorioretinitis. Ocular involvement with either congenital cytomegalovirus disease or varicella is unusual but can result in chorioretinitis, keratitis, or cataract. Timely treatment with systemic and topical antiviral agents (acyclovir IV 45 mg/kg/day plus vidarabine 3% ointment 5×/day for 14–21 days) is very important to avoid dissemination to the CNS and resultant encephalitis. Ocular involvement in congenital rubella is common, including microphthalmia, corneal haze, cataract, glaucoma, uveitis, and retinopathy. The characteristic “salt and pepper” retinopathy is the most common occurrence, but cataract is responsible for the greatest visual loss. The incidence of children with congenital human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is decreasing dramatically with the advent of new drugs. Chorioretinitis secondary to various other infectious agents including herpes, CMV, and toxoplasma were described in this population.

### Preseptal and Orbital Cellulitis

The diagnosis of infective orbital cellulitis requires urgent evaluation and treatment to prevent rapid worsening with cavernous sinus thrombosis, cerebral abscess, osteomyelitis, and septicemia. Orbital cellulitis is the most common cause of proptosis in older children but is fortunately rare in neonates. Bacterial spread from paranasal sinuses is the main etiology with hematogenous or direct inoculation very infrequent at this age. The disease is characterized by the rapid onset of progressive proptosis, often with erythema of the lids, chemosis of the conjunctiva, limited motility, and systemic signs of toxicity and hyperpyrexia. Rapid loss of vision caused by compression of the orbital structures can occur and persist as a sequela if compression is not reversed in a timely manner. Afferent pupillary defect is a sign of compression in this setting. Diagnosis is made by clinical appearance and radiologic evaluation of the orbits and sinuses. Treatment includes admission to a hospital, CT scan of the orbits, intravenous administration of antibiotics, application of warm compresses, and surgical drainage of persistent orbital abscesses if necessary.62 At this early age, the subperiosteal fluid collection in the orbit has high likelihood of being devoid of bacteria and resolves with intravenous antibiotics only.62

In preseptal cellulitis, the infection is limited to the lids and does not extend past the orbital septum to involve the orbital contents. It is usually caused by streptococcal and staphylococcal bacteria. In older children, it can be treated on an outpatient basis with oral antibiotics, but in

infants, admission to the hospital for intravenous antibiotics is indicated. Widespread vaccination has dramatically decreased Haemophilus-associated orbital and preseptal cellulitis.

### Other Ocular Tumors in Infants

### Lymphatic Malformation (Lymphangioma)

Lymphatic malformations are slowly progressive, diffuse, soft tumors composed of thin-walled vascular channels that can involve the orbit, conjunctiva, and lids. They may be present at birth or develop during the first several years of life and cease growing by early adulthood. An upper respiratory tract infection and spontaneous hemorrhage may increase the size of the lesion and cause rapid proptosis. The tumors can also cause ptosis, strabismus, or anisometropia. Amblyopia is common and must be aggressively treated. MRI can be exceedingly helpful in diagnosing a lymphatic malformation. The lesion itself is difficult to treat because it does not regress spontaneously or respond to radiation or corticosteroid therapy. Surgery is rarely used, because results are not always satisfactory. Reports on using percutaneous sclerotherapy using interventional radiology techniques show promise in this difficult-to-treat tumor.63

### Teratoma

Teratoma is a primary orbital tumor composed of the three embryonic cell layers. It can differentiate into a variety of tissues containing cartilage, connective tissue, skin, hair, and sebaceous glands, or into endodermal epithelium. Bone is a common component and can be identified by CT. Orbital teratomas that are present at birth produce a striking massive proptosis. Treatment is early excision of the teratoma. Malignant transformation can occur but is rare in the orbit.

### Rhabdomyosarcoma

Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common malignant tumor of the orbit in children although is rare in infants. Rhabdomyosarcoma develops in the orbit more often than elsewhere in the body. Orbital involvement produces proptosis that develops over a few weeks. Diagnosis is made by biopsy. Treatment involves chemotherapy and radiation therapy.

### Ocular Manifestations of Maternal Substance Abuse

An increasing number of infants are born bearing the physical, mental, and social consequences of maternal drug and alcohol abuse. Miller and colleagues described many of the ocular findings of fetal alcohol syndrome, including refractive errors, strabismus, anterior segment abnormalities,


## PDF page 2052 | printed page 2061

cataract, ptosis, long eyelashes, telecanthus, and optic nerve hypoplasia.64

Maternal ingestion of cocaine can result in optic nerve abnormalities, delayed visual maturation, and prolonged eyelid edema.65

Key Points

### • Ocular problems are very common in the neonatal

period, so a thorough examination with at least a simple pen light should be performed on every child.

### • Ocular findings can be the precursor of systemic find-

ings, and some specific ocular findings can lead to definitive diagnosis for many vague systemic findings. Ophthalmology consultation should be initiated for such guidance and possible ocular involvement.

title: Retinopathy of Prematurity

paragraphs.text: 100 Retinopathy of Prematurity
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) was first described ∼70 years ago as retrolental fibroplasia. The introduction of closed incubators with high levels of unmonitored supplemental oxygen enabled the survival of more premature infants. Still, doing so caused inhibition of retinal blood vessel growth followed by pathologic vasoproliferation, traction, and eventually retinal detachment. At examination, a fibrous membrane behind the crystalline lens was seen representing the end stage of the disease.1 Supplemental oxygen increased the risk of blindness but also improved survival. When oxygen use was curtailed in the 1950s, the incidence of ROP decreased, but mortality and morbidity increased.1 In modern times, the improved quality of neonatal care has reduced mortality in immature babies worldwide. However, when resources to control oxygen and to screen for and treat sight-threatening ROP are lacking, more surviving infants will become blind from ROP. It was estimated that in 2010 approximately 32,300 preterm infants became blind or visually impaired from ROP, with the highest numbers in the East, Southeast Asia, and Pacific region.2
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: In countries with advanced neonatal care, most cases of ROP now occur among infants who are born extremely preterm with a gestational age (GA) <28 weeks. Determining the current incidence of ROP in population-based studies, even among more developed countries, is challenging because there is considerable variability in study design, in GA of the included premature infants, and in survival rates.3 Improved neonatal care increases survival of very immature infants at high risk for ROP and lowers ROP risk in more mature infants. Worldwide, the incidence of ROP is also influenced by the fact that even more mature infants at very low risk for ROP with more advanced neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) care are at much higher risk in regions with uncontrolled oxygen delivery and less intensive neonatal care.4
paragraphs.heading: Incidence

paragraphs.text: In a national cohort of infants born at GA <31 weeks in Sweden from 2008 to 2017, 32% had some degree of ROP; 6% had severe ROP and were treated. The overall
paragraphs.heading: Incidence

paragraphs.text: incidence of ROP was similar over the years, but the frequency of treatment increased with time, concomitant with increased survival of infants of GA <24 weeks and increased oxygen saturation target levels.5 In a large US cohort, the ROP rate as well as ROP treatment declined from 2008 to 2018.6 Unchanged ROP rates but increased frequency of treatment between 2010 and 2019 were reported in a large Chinese cohort.7
paragraphs.heading: Incidence

paragraphs.text: The lower the GA at birth, the less complete is the retinal development at birth. In a very simplified model, a first phase of ROP is characterized by cessation of normal retinal blood vessel growth due to retinal hyperoxia from supplemental oxygen which inhibits the production of the angiogenic protein vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). The first visible sign of ROP on an ocular fundus examination is a sharp demarcation line separating the central vascularized and the peripheral avascular retina. In most cases, vascular growth resumes, and the second neovascular phase does not occur; however, even in cases with mild, spontaneously regressing ROP, impaired photoreceptor function may remain.
paragraphs.heading: Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: In severe cases, a second phase with pathologic neovascularization at the ridge and into the vitreous is triggered by markedly elevated levels of VEGF secreted when the increasingly metabolically active yet poorly vascularized retina becomes hypoxic. Without timely treatment, the most severe cases lead to fibrous scar formation, retinal detachment, and blindness.8
paragraphs.heading: Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: In reality, the pathogenesis of ROP is much more complex and poorly understood. Many factors are involved, some of which will be presented in the following discussion on risk factors.
paragraphs.heading: Pathogenesis

paragraphs.text: Low GA and low birth weight, reflecting the degree of immaturity and vulnerability to insult of the neurovascular tissues of the retina at birth, are the main risk factors for ROP.9 In a Swedish study of 7249 infants, treatment of severe ROP had been performed in 49.4% of those with
paragraphs.heading: Risk Factors Low Gestational Age and Birth Weight

paragraphs.text: GA 21 to 22 weeks, 7.5% with GA 26 weeks, and 0.3% of infants with GA 29 weeks.5
paragraphs.heading: Risk Factors Low Gestational Age and Birth Weight

paragraphs.text: In normal intrauterine retinal vascularization, the blood vessels begin to grow from the optic nerve head toward the periphery at about 13 weeks of gestation. Development proceeds toward the physiologically hypoxic periphery stimulated by hypoxia-regulated angiogenic growth factors such as VEGF, following a template being laid by retinal astrocytes. After birth, energy needs are increased, and higher oxygenation is needed to sustain life. This relative hyperoxia, even from room air and exacerbated by supplemental oxygen given to sustain life, suppresses VEGF and is an important driver for the arrest of vascular growth in phase 1 in both animal models and human studies. In 1952, Patz first demonstrated the clinical association between oxygen and ROP.10 In 1954, Ashton established the concepts of oxygen toxicity (phase 1) followed by hypoxia-mediated vasoproliferation (phase 2) in ROP in a kitten model.11
paragraphs.heading: Supplemental Oxygen

paragraphs.text: It is clear that unmonitored high oxygen supplementation contributes to the first phase of ROP, even in more mature infants, but the best level that balances the risk of ROP with high oxygen saturation versus the morbidity and mortality that occur with insufficient oxygenation is not known. This is partly due to the fact that oxygen saturation target levels and not infant oxygen saturation have been evaluated in the studies on which current recommendations are based.12 In a meta-analysis of five clinical trials of infants born at GA <28 weeks, a lower oxygen saturation target range of 85% to 89% compared to 91% to 95% was associated with a lower risk of needing ROP treatment but a higher risk of death and necrotizing enterocolitis.12 Not only hyperoxia but also desaturations are common in very preterm infants. They contribute to oxygen saturation fluctuations that appear to be detrimental to the developing retinal vasculature and associated with increased ROP risk.13 In fact, infants with severe ROP have been reported to have lower mean achieved oxygen saturation than those with no or mild ROP.14
paragraphs.heading: Supplemental Oxygen

paragraphs.text: Phase 2 of ROP is characterized by retinal hypoxia. Theoretically, oxygen treatment in phase 2 could suppress high levels of hypoxia-stimulated growth factors such as VEGF that cause proliferative disease. This premise has been examined in several studies. Individually, these studies did not show a benefit from higher oxygen in phase 2. Chen et al.15 performed a meta-analysis of 10 publications to assess, at the two phases of ROP, the association between severe ROP and high or low target oxygen saturation. They found that low oxygen saturation targets (70%–96%) in the first several postnatal weeks were associated with reduced risk. High oxygen saturation targets (94%–99%) at or after 32 weeks’ postmenstrual age were associated with decreased risk for progression to severe ROP, and control of oxygen in the first phase was more important than the higher oxygen saturation in the second phase.15
paragraphs.heading: Supplemental Oxygen

paragraphs.text: The optimal oxygen saturation levels after extremely preterm birth are still undefined.16 Studies have suggested
paragraphs.heading: Supplemental Oxygen

paragraphs.text: that oxygen saturation (SpO2) target ranges of 85% to 89% versus 91% to 95% decrease the incidence of severe ROP but increase mortality.17 However, a systematic review and meta-analysis of those results found that the quality of evidence was moderate or low for the mortality rate outcomes.18 Other target ranges, such as 88% to 92%, have not been investigated. Increased rates of severe ROP have been reported after implementation of higher oxygen saturation targets after these trials.19
paragraphs.heading: Supplemental Oxygen

paragraphs.text: Oxygenation is dependent on the type of hemoglobin (Hb) present in erythrocytes. During gestation, fetal Hb with high affinity to oxygen dominates, but a switch to adult Hb with lower oxygen affinity occurs after birth at term. Most extremely preterm infants receive multiple transfusions with adult erythrocytes. An association between ROP and lower levels of fetal Hb during the first postnatal week, as well as at postmenstrual age 31 and 34 weeks, corresponding to the time period of phase 2 ROP, has been reported.20,21
paragraphs.heading: Blood Transfusions and Low Levels of Fetal Hemoglobin

paragraphs.text: After very preterm birth, the nutrient supply from the mother and factors essential for growth, immune defense, and other functions are lost. They are replaced by parenteral nutrition with solutions developed for adults, together with increasing enteral feedings with the mother’s own milk, donor milk, or preterm formula, or combinations of these. The inability to assimilate enough nutrients after birth contributes to subnormal levels of factors essential for growth and development, resulting in a high rate of growth restriction.22
paragraphs.heading: Low Insulin-Like Growth Factor 1 and Poor Weight Gain

paragraphs.text: Circulating insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) is an indicator of the nutritional status of an individual and becomes reduced with starvation, infection, and stress.23 IGF-1 acts as a permissive factor for VEGF-dependent vascular endothelial cell growth and survival24 and is critical for normal growth and development of many tissues including brain and blood vessels. There is a strong association between early postnatal low serum IGF-1 concentrations and later ROP, as well as other prematurity-related morbidities.25
paragraphs.heading: Low Insulin-Like Growth Factor 1 and Poor Weight Gain

paragraphs.text: Neonatal hyperglycemia is common after extremely preterm birth and is an independent risk factor for ROP.26 High neonatal plasma glucose levels have been associated with both lower IGF-1 levels and increased ROP severity. In a model of ROP in mice with additional streptozotocin-induced low insulin and hyperglycemia, supplementation with IGF-1 resulted in improved retinal revascularization and decreased pathologic neovascularization, indicating a possible role for IGF-1 in ROP prevention.27
paragraphs.heading: Hyperglycemia and Insulin Use

paragraphs.text: Increasing nutrition alone also does not influence weight gain (normalized for GA) or IGF-1 levels in extremely low birth weight infants who appear to be unable to assimilate enough nutrients to increase circulating IGF-1.28 Exogenous
paragraphs.heading: Hyperglycemia and Insulin Use

paragraphs.text: IGF-1 can improve growth in experimental states of undernutrition. In rats fed half of their needed calories, exogenous IGF-1 improved weight gain.29 As postnatal weight gain predicts ROP risk,30 this suggests that both increased nutrition and adequate IGF-1 levels are required for postnatal growth and for a reduction in ROP risk.
paragraphs.heading: Hyperglycemia and Insulin Use

paragraphs.text: After birth, more energy is needed to sustain life than in utero. The immaturity of oral and gastrointestinal functions makes the extremely preterm infant dependent on parenteral nutrition for varying periods of time after birth. The duration of parenteral nutrition has been identified as one risk factor for ROP.31
paragraphs.heading: Inadequate Nutrition

paragraphs.text: Fresh maternal milk contains not only macro- and micronutrients but also bioactive components involved in immune defense, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory defense, and gut microbiome establishment, as well as food tolerability and metabolism. These factors are lacking in preterm formula, and many of them are lacking in processed donor milk.32 Provision of any amount of maternal milk, but not pasteurized donor milk, is associated with a lower incidence of both any ROP and severe ROP.33,34
paragraphs.heading: Inadequate Nutrition

paragraphs.text: The omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid (LCP- UFA), docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), and the omega-6 LCPUFA arachidonic acid (AA) are structural and functional components of membranes in neurovascular and other tissues and are selectively transferred from the mother during gestation.35 Animal studies have shown that a lack of omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids increases susceptibility for retinopathy.36 Most studies on LCPUFA and ROP and other prematurity-related disorders have focused on omega-3 LCPUFA and not omega-6 LCPUFA. A few studies providing omega-3 LCPUFA-rich fish oil instead of soybean-based oil in parenteral nutrition have reported decreased rates of proliferative ROP with fish oil.37,38 However, fish oil reduces AA levels,39 and low levels of AA have been associated with an increased risk of any ROP and severe ROP.40 Enteral supplementation with both AA and DHA lowered the risk of severe ROP by 50%.41 Higher mean daily serum levels of DHA during the first 28 postnatal days were associated with a reduced risk of severe ROP but only in infants with sufficiently high AA levels, indicating the importance of a proper balance between these fatty acids.42
paragraphs.heading: Inadequate Nutrition

paragraphs.text: The International Classification of Retinopathy of Prematurity was developed in the 1980s and was revisited in 2005.43 A third edition was published in 2021.44 Disease severity at the vascular/avascular junction is expressed as stages 1
paragraphs.heading: Classification

paragraphs.text: through 5. A demarcation line in stage 1 and a ridge in stage 2 separate the vascular and avascular parts of the retina. Stage 3 is characterized by abnormal blood vessel growth on the ridge into the vitreous. This extraretinal neovascularization may regress spontaneously or progress to cause partial (stage 4) or total (stage 5) retinal detachment. With stage 5 ROP, blindness is irreversible. The retina is divided into three zones (Fig. 100.1). The extent of the disease is described by the number of 30° sectors (“clock hours”) affected. Increased venous dilation and arterial tortuosity reflect severe disease and are classified as “plus disease” (or “preplus disease” if it is not normal but is not pronounced enough to meet the criteria for plus disease). Aggressive posterior ROP, a central form of ROP with plus disease and rapid progression through ill-defined stages, was defined in the 2005 classification. In the latest classification, the name has changed to aggressive ROP, as similar progression has been seen with more peripheral ROP.44 The Early Treatment for Retinopathy of Prematurity (ETROP) study reclassified ROP into type 1 (requiring treatment) and type 2 (to be followed).45
paragraphs.heading: Classification

paragraphs.text: Infants at risk for severe ROP undergo repeated retinal examinations with indirect ophthalmoscopy or widefield photography through dilated pupils. Because ROP risk is dependent on the quality of neonatal care, screening guidelines have to be adjusted to regional conditions. National guidelines differ in inclusion criteria regarding GA and birth weight. Starting at about 31 weeks’ postmenstrual age, at the
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Course and Screening

paragraphs.text: earliest, eye examinations are performed every 2 weeks to twice a week, depending on findings, to detect those needing treatment. The sequential development of the stages of ROP is monitored until ROP has regressed or progressed to type 1 disease, a certain combination of stages, zones, and/or plus disease for which treatment was found to be efficient in reducing blindness in the ETROP study.45 Rates of progression are variable, and the worst prognosis is associated with onset of severe disease in zone I (most central) that can rapidly progress to type 1 disease with high risk of retinal detachment. Onset in zone II, or a slower evolution of the disorder, leads more often to resolution. ROP with an onset in zone III has a good prognosis for recovery.46 Fig. 100.2 presents a flow chart showing the sequential course of ROP, including regression and progression to treatment in the worse eye of infants screened for ROP during a 10-year period in Sweden.5 After the neonatal period, extremely preterm infants have increased risk of reduced visual acuity, refractive errors, strabismus, and amblyopia which are strongly associated with ROP treatment.47 In addition, after treatment for type 1 ROP, retinal abnormalities such as persistent avascular retina with lattice-like changes and retinal tears may cause later retinal detachment at any age.48 Even eyes not meeting the treatment criteria in infancy may have similar changes and develop retinal detachment later in life.49 Therefore ROP should be considered a life-long disease, and treated children should be followed. Retinal fluorescein angiography can be used to visualize the pathology better because sometimes it could be difficult to see the
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Course and Screening

paragraphs.text: extent and the severity of the pathology with simple direct visualization (Fig. 100.3).
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Course and Screening

paragraphs.text: The eye examinations are often painful and stressful, and the dilating eye drops may have adverse effects. Less than 10% of screened infants need ROP treatment,5 and algorithms to predict the risk of needing treatment for ROP have been developed to identify infants with high risk and those for whom examinations are unnecessary. Because poor postnatal weight gain was identified as a risk factor for severe ROP, a number of prediction models based on weight gain have been developed and validated.50,51 However, after implementation of higher oxygen saturation targets, the predictive ability of weight gain was lost in one study.52 In addition, information on body weight is not always available to ophthalmologists, and prediction tools based on birth characteristics alone or together with information on status and age when ROP was first diagnosed have been developed and validated.53,54 Prediction tools have hitherto been used mainly to judge when to safely end screening and not to exclude infants from eye examinations.
paragraphs.heading: Prediction

paragraphs.text: Oxygen control is a main factor in ROP prevention. Introduction of an educational program for care providers and
paragraphs.heading: Prevention

paragraphs.text: a detailed policy for O2 monitoring and administration to minimize repeated episodes of hyperoxia after desaturations was shown to reduce ROP and the need for ROP treatment.55 Automation of oxygen titration appears promising so far, with a reduction in severe blood oxygen saturation (SpO2) deviations and the need for manual fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) adjustments compared with manual control.56
paragraphs.heading: Prevention

paragraphs.text: The mother’s own breast milk compensates for some of the losses of nutrients and bioactive factors after preterm birth, although it requires fortification.32 Programs to promote early provision of maternal milk instead of pasteurized donor milk or preterm formula are a cheap and safe intervention for ROP prevention.33 Maternal milk also contains the LCPUFAs DHA and AA, but not enough for the extremely preterm infant’s needs. In 2021, a randomized controlled study reported a 50% reduction in severe ROP after enteral supplementation with AA (100 mg/kg/d) and DHA (50 mg/kg/d) from the first days of life to 40 weeks’ postmenstrual age.41 Further studies are needed.
paragraphs.heading: Prevention

paragraphs.text: Loss of fetal Hb due to excessive blood sampling in extremely preterm infants is a risk factor for ROP.20 Development of methods to analyze small volumes of blood may decrease anemia and the need for transfusions of adult red blood cells. Studies on the feasibility of allogenic transfusion of red blood cells from umbilical cord with high levels of fetal Hb are ongoing.57,58 Because persistently low serum
paragraphs.heading: Prevention

paragraphs.text: IGF-I concentrations in preterm infants are associated with ROP and other morbidities59 and because supplemental IGF-I seems to improve food utilization in undernutrition,29 supplementation with exogenous IGF-I has been suggested as therapy to improve growth and reduce ROP and other morbidities. A phase II trial of supplementation of IGF-1 and the IGF binding protein IGFBP3 (NCT010100784) performed in 120 preterm infants showed no effects on ROP outcome but a reduced incidence of bronchopulmonary dysplasia.60 A phase III study is now under way, with ROP as the secondary endpoint.
paragraphs.heading: Prevention

paragraphs.text: The standard treatment of sight-threatening ROP is laser therapy to ablate the entire peripheral avascular retina, which is overproducing angiogenic factors such as VEGF, resulting in pathologic neovascularization on the ridge (Fig. 100.4). The criteria for laser treatment established by the ETROP multicenter trial first published in 2003 are shown in Box 100.1.45 Ablative treatment of nonvascularized retina helps prevent blindness but does not address the underlying cause of ROP or other co-morbidities—the failure of normal neural and vascular growth. Furthermore, the peripheral retina is destroyed to save central vision (see Fig. 100.3). Intravitreal injections of agents that block VEGF—mainly
paragraphs.heading: Treatment of Type 1 Retinopathy of Prematurity

paragraphs.text: bevacizumab, which is a full humanized antibody against VEGF, or ranibizumab, a fragment of a full antibody—are increasingly being used instead of or as a complement to laser therapy.61 Laser therapy is time consuming and usually performed under general anesthesia by highly skilled retinal surgeons, whereas anti-VEGF injections are more easily administered using local anesthesia. A review published in 2022 compared several aspects of anti-VEGF and laser treatments.61 Superior effects of anti-VEGF compared to laser in preventing retinal detachment primarily in zone I have been reported in a few studies, whereas similar effects of the two treatment modalities have been seen in zone II disease. Recurrences and longer times from treatment to recurrence, as well as more retinal vascular abnormalities detected with fluorescein angiography, have been seen in eyes treated with anti-VEGF compared to laser-treated eyes. A matter of concern with anti-VEGF treatment is leakage of the drug into the systemic blood circulation, where circulating VEGF is suppressed for weeks to months with unknown effects on the development of immature organs such as gut and brain.62 More research is needed regarding the choice of drug, dosage, and long-term effects of these drugs. Results of a systematic review and meta-analysis from 2021 indicated an increased risk of cognitive impairment and lower cognitive and language composite scores after bevacizumab therapy compared to laser therapy for severe ROP.63 Surgery
paragraphs.heading: Treatment of Type 1 Retinopathy of Prematurity

paragraphs.text: for partial retinal detachment (stage 4) may yield some form of vision, but total retinal detachment (stage 5) surgery yields very poor results.64
paragraphs.heading: Treatment of Type 1 Retinopathy of Prematurity

paragraphs.text: At-risk premature infants need to be examined by a trained clinician with indirect ophthalmoscopy or with widefield photography to detect ROP before it reaches the well-established clinical criteria for treatment to prevent progression of the disease. Ophthalmic and pediatric societies periodically publish recommendations for the screening guidelines, which may vary among countries (Box 100.2). In the United States, infants at risk are suggested to be those weighing ≤1500 g or born at ≤30 weeks’ gestation.65 In addition, screening is recommended for more mature preterm infants with birth weight between 1500 and 2000 g or a GA >30 weeks who have had an unstable medical course. The infants should be examined initially by 31 weeks’ postmenstrual age or 4 weeks’ chronologic age and then repeatedly until the retina is fully vascularized. Intervals between examinations are scheduled according to severity of disease, ranging from 2 to 3 weeks to less than 1 week as stated in the national guidelines.65
paragraphs.heading: Recommendations for Examination Schedule

paragraphs.text: Neonatologists and ophthalmologists must work closely together to ensure an efficient tracking system for timely examination of these infants and to be certain that followup examinations occur at the best times both in the hospital and after discharge or transfer. The goal is to ensure that no infants who reach the criteria for ROP treatment are missed in an attempt to minimize life-long vision loss.
paragraphs.heading: Recommendations for Examination Schedule

paragraphs.text: After the acute process has resolved, continued followup is dictated by the worst degree of ROP that occurred in
paragraphs.heading: Recommendations for Examination Schedule

paragraphs.text: the acute course. For infants who have had laser or anti- VEGF for ROP, close observation of the retina and assessment for refractive errors, strabismus, amblyopia, or late retinal detachments through childhood are also important.66 One should also bear in mind that infants with severe ROP have increased risk of brain lesions and that their visual impairment may not be solely retinal in origin. Cerebral visual impairment is associated with reduced visual acuity and visual fields, strabismus, nystagmus, and optic atrophy. In addition, varying degrees of visual perceptual deficits may make visual problems more severe than indicated by visual acuity.67 Questionnaires regarding visual perceptual problems provide a simple method to identify children who might benefit from further neuropsychiatric investigation.68 Research must continue in order to learn more about the basic mechanisms involved in the control of neurovascular development. # 100. Retinopathy of Prematurity
> Source attribution: [Source credits](../../SOURCE_CREDITS.md).


## PDF page 2055 | printed page 2064

100 Retinopathy of Prematurity

### YE SUN, ANN HELLSTRÖM, AND LOIS E.H. SMITH

### Introduction

Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) was first described ∼70 years ago as retrolental fibroplasia. The introduction of closed incubators with high levels of unmonitored supplemental oxygen enabled the survival of more premature infants. Still, doing so caused inhibition of retinal blood vessel growth followed by pathologic vasoproliferation, traction, and eventually retinal detachment. At examination, a fibrous membrane behind the crystalline lens was seen representing the end stage of the disease.1 Supplemental oxygen increased the risk of blindness but also improved survival. When oxygen use was curtailed in the 1950s, the incidence of ROP decreased, but mortality and morbidity increased.1 In modern times, the improved quality of neonatal care has reduced mortality in immature babies worldwide. However, when resources to control oxygen and to screen for and treat sight-threatening ROP are lacking, more surviving infants will become blind from ROP. It was estimated that in 2010 approximately 32,300 preterm infants became blind or visually impaired from ROP, with the highest numbers in the East, Southeast Asia, and Pacific region.2

### Incidence

In countries with advanced neonatal care, most cases of ROP now occur among infants who are born extremely preterm with a gestational age (GA) <28 weeks. Determining the current incidence of ROP in population-based studies, even among more developed countries, is challenging because there is considerable variability in study design, in GA of the included premature infants, and in survival rates.3 Improved neonatal care increases survival of very immature infants at high risk for ROP and lowers ROP risk in more mature infants. Worldwide, the incidence of ROP is also influenced by the fact that even more mature infants at very low risk for ROP with more advanced neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) care are at much higher risk in regions with uncontrolled oxygen delivery and less intensive neonatal care.4

In a national cohort of infants born at GA <31 weeks in Sweden from 2008 to 2017, 32% had some degree of ROP; 6% had severe ROP and were treated. The overall

2064

incidence of ROP was similar over the years, but the frequency of treatment increased with time, concomitant with increased survival of infants of GA <24 weeks and increased oxygen saturation target levels.5 In a large US cohort, the ROP rate as well as ROP treatment declined from 2008 to 2018.6 Unchanged ROP rates but increased frequency of treatment between 2010 and 2019 were reported in a large Chinese cohort.7

### Pathogenesis

The lower the GA at birth, the less complete is the retinal development at birth. In a very simplified model, a first phase of ROP is characterized by cessation of normal retinal blood vessel growth due to retinal hyperoxia from supplemental oxygen which inhibits the production of the angiogenic protein vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). The first visible sign of ROP on an ocular fundus examination is a sharp demarcation line separating the central vascularized and the peripheral avascular retina. In most cases, vascular growth resumes, and the second neovascular phase does not occur; however, even in cases with mild, spontaneously regressing ROP, impaired photoreceptor function may remain.

In severe cases, a second phase with pathologic neovascularization at the ridge and into the vitreous is triggered by markedly elevated levels of VEGF secreted when the increasingly metabolically active yet poorly vascularized retina becomes hypoxic. Without timely treatment, the most severe cases lead to fibrous scar formation, retinal detachment, and blindness.8

In reality, the pathogenesis of ROP is much more complex and poorly understood. Many factors are involved, some of which will be presented in the following discussion on risk factors.

### Risk Factors Low Gestational Age and Birth Weight

Low GA and low birth weight, reflecting the degree of immaturity and vulnerability to insult of the neurovascular tissues of the retina at birth, are the main risk factors for ROP.9 In a Swedish study of 7249 infants, treatment of severe ROP had been performed in 49.4% of those with


## PDF page 2056 | printed page 2065

GA 21 to 22 weeks, 7.5% with GA 26 weeks, and 0.3% of infants with GA 29 weeks.5

### Supplemental Oxygen

In normal intrauterine retinal vascularization, the blood vessels begin to grow from the optic nerve head toward the periphery at about 13 weeks of gestation. Development proceeds toward the physiologically hypoxic periphery stimulated by hypoxia-regulated angiogenic growth factors such as VEGF, following a template being laid by retinal astrocytes. After birth, energy needs are increased, and higher oxygenation is needed to sustain life. This relative hyperoxia, even from room air and exacerbated by supplemental oxygen given to sustain life, suppresses VEGF and is an important driver for the arrest of vascular growth in phase 1 in both animal models and human studies. In 1952, Patz first demonstrated the clinical association between oxygen and ROP.10 In 1954, Ashton established the concepts of oxygen toxicity (phase 1) followed by hypoxia-mediated vasoproliferation (phase 2) in ROP in a kitten model.11

It is clear that unmonitored high oxygen supplementation contributes to the first phase of ROP, even in more mature infants, but the best level that balances the risk of ROP with high oxygen saturation versus the morbidity and mortality that occur with insufficient oxygenation is not known. This is partly due to the fact that oxygen saturation target levels and not infant oxygen saturation have been evaluated in the studies on which current recommendations are based.12 In a meta-analysis of five clinical trials of infants born at GA <28 weeks, a lower oxygen saturation target range of 85% to 89% compared to 91% to 95% was associated with a lower risk of needing ROP treatment but a higher risk of death and necrotizing enterocolitis.12 Not only hyperoxia but also desaturations are common in very preterm infants. They contribute to oxygen saturation fluctuations that appear to be detrimental to the developing retinal vasculature and associated with increased ROP risk.13 In fact, infants with severe ROP have been reported to have lower mean achieved oxygen saturation than those with no or mild ROP.14

Phase 2 of ROP is characterized by retinal hypoxia. Theoretically, oxygen treatment in phase 2 could suppress high levels of hypoxia-stimulated growth factors such as VEGF that cause proliferative disease. This premise has been examined in several studies. Individually, these studies did not show a benefit from higher oxygen in phase 2. Chen et al.15 performed a meta-analysis of 10 publications to assess, at the two phases of ROP, the association between severe ROP and high or low target oxygen saturation. They found that low oxygen saturation targets (70%–96%) in the first several postnatal weeks were associated with reduced risk. High oxygen saturation targets (94%–99%) at or after 32 weeks’ postmenstrual age were associated with decreased risk for progression to severe ROP, and control of oxygen in the first phase was more important than the higher oxygen saturation in the second phase.15

The optimal oxygen saturation levels after extremely preterm birth are still undefined.16 Studies have suggested

that oxygen saturation (SpO2) target ranges of 85% to 89% versus 91% to 95% decrease the incidence of severe ROP but increase mortality.17 However, a systematic review and meta-analysis of those results found that the quality of evidence was moderate or low for the mortality rate outcomes.18 Other target ranges, such as 88% to 92%, have not been investigated. Increased rates of severe ROP have been reported after implementation of higher oxygen saturation targets after these trials.19

### Blood Transfusions and Low Levels of Fetal Hemoglobin

Oxygenation is dependent on the type of hemoglobin (Hb) present in erythrocytes. During gestation, fetal Hb with high affinity to oxygen dominates, but a switch to adult Hb with lower oxygen affinity occurs after birth at term. Most extremely preterm infants receive multiple transfusions with adult erythrocytes. An association between ROP and lower levels of fetal Hb during the first postnatal week, as well as at postmenstrual age 31 and 34 weeks, corresponding to the time period of phase 2 ROP, has been reported.20,21

### Low Insulin-Like Growth Factor 1 and Poor Weight Gain

After very preterm birth, the nutrient supply from the mother and factors essential for growth, immune defense, and other functions are lost. They are replaced by parenteral nutrition with solutions developed for adults, together with increasing enteral feedings with the mother’s own milk, donor milk, or preterm formula, or combinations of these. The inability to assimilate enough nutrients after birth contributes to subnormal levels of factors essential for growth and development, resulting in a high rate of growth restriction.22

Circulating insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) is an indicator of the nutritional status of an individual and becomes reduced with starvation, infection, and stress.23 IGF-1 acts as a permissive factor for VEGF-dependent vascular endothelial cell growth and survival24 and is critical for normal growth and development of many tissues including brain and blood vessels. There is a strong association between early postnatal low serum IGF-1 concentrations and later ROP, as well as other prematurity-related morbidities.25

### Hyperglycemia and Insulin Use

Neonatal hyperglycemia is common after extremely preterm birth and is an independent risk factor for ROP.26 High neonatal plasma glucose levels have been associated with both lower IGF-1 levels and increased ROP severity. In a model of ROP in mice with additional streptozotocin-induced low insulin and hyperglycemia, supplementation with IGF-1 resulted in improved retinal revascularization and decreased pathologic neovascularization, indicating a possible role for IGF-1 in ROP prevention.27

Increasing nutrition alone also does not influence weight gain (normalized for GA) or IGF-1 levels in extremely low birth weight infants who appear to be unable to assimilate enough nutrients to increase circulating IGF-1.28 Exogenous


## PDF page 2057

IGF-1 can improve growth in experimental states of undernutrition. In rats fed half of their needed calories, exogenous IGF-1 improved weight gain.29 As postnatal weight gain predicts ROP risk,30 this suggests that both increased nutrition and adequate IGF-1 levels are required for postnatal growth and for a reduction in ROP risk.

### Inadequate Nutrition

Parenteral Nutrition

After birth, more energy is needed to sustain life than in utero. The immaturity of oral and gastrointestinal functions makes the extremely preterm infant dependent on parenteral nutrition for varying periods of time after birth. The duration of parenteral nutrition has been identified as one risk factor for ROP.31

Lack of Breast Milk

Fresh maternal milk contains not only macro- and micronutrients but also bioactive components involved in immune defense, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory defense, and gut microbiome establishment, as well as food tolerability and metabolism. These factors are lacking in preterm formula, and many of them are lacking in processed donor milk.32 Provision of any amount of maternal milk, but not pasteurized donor milk, is associated with a lower incidence of both any ROP and severe ROP.33,34

Lack of Long-Chain Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids

The omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid (LCP- UFA), docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), and the omega-6 LCPUFA arachidonic acid (AA) are structural and functional components of membranes in neurovascular and other tissues and are selectively transferred from the mother during gestation.35 Animal studies have shown that a lack of omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids increases susceptibility for retinopathy.36 Most studies on LCPUFA and ROP and other prematurity-related disorders have focused on omega-3 LCPUFA and not omega-6 LCPUFA. A few studies providing omega-3 LCPUFA-rich fish oil instead of soybean-based oil in parenteral nutrition have reported decreased rates of proliferative ROP with fish oil.37,38 However, fish oil reduces AA levels,39 and low levels of AA have been associated with an increased risk of any ROP and severe ROP.40 Enteral supplementation with both AA and DHA lowered the risk of severe ROP by 50%.41 Higher mean daily serum levels of DHA during the first 28 postnatal days were associated with a reduced risk of severe ROP but only in infants with sufficiently high AA levels, indicating the importance of a proper balance between these fatty acids.42

Stage 3 is characterized by abnormal blood vessel growth on the ridge into the vitreous. This extraretinal neovascularization may regress spontaneously or progress to cause partial (stage 4) or total (stage 5) retinal detachment. With stage 5 ROP, blindness is irreversible. Aggressive posterior ROP, a central form of ROP with plus disease and rapid progression through ill-defined stages, was defined in the 2005 classification. ### Prediction

The eye examinations are often painful and stressful, and the dilating eye drops may have adverse effects. Less than 10% of screened infants need ROP treatment,5 and algorithms to predict the risk of needing treatment for ROP have been developed to identify infants with high risk and those for whom examinations are unnecessary. Because poor postnatal weight gain was identified as a risk factor for severe ROP, a number of prediction models based on weight gain have been developed and validated.50,51 However, after implementation of higher oxygen saturation targets, the predictive ability of weight gain was lost in one study.52 In addition, information on body weight is not always available to ophthalmologists, and prediction tools based on birth characteristics alone or together with information on status and age when ROP was first diagnosed have been developed and validated.53,54 Prediction tools have hitherto been used mainly to judge when to safely end screening and not to exclude infants from eye examinations.

### Recommendations for Examination Schedule

At-risk premature infants need to be examined by a trained clinician with indirect ophthalmoscopy or with widefield photography to detect ROP before it reaches the well-established clinical criteria for treatment to prevent progression of the disease. Ophthalmic and pediatric societies periodically publish recommendations for the screening guidelines, which may vary among countries (Box 100.2). In the United States, infants at risk are suggested to be those weighing ≤1500 g or born at ≤30 weeks’ gestation.65 In addition, screening is recommended for more mature preterm infants with birth weight between 1500 and 2000 g or a GA >30 weeks who have had an unstable medical course. The infants should be examined initially by 31 weeks’ postmenstrual age or 4 weeks’ chronologic age and then repeatedly until the retina is fully vascularized. Intervals between examinations are scheduled according to severity of disease, ranging from 2 to 3 weeks to less than 1 week as stated in the national guidelines.65

Neonatologists and ophthalmologists must work closely together to ensure an efficient tracking system for timely examination of these infants and to be certain that followup examinations occur at the best times both in the hospital and after discharge or transfer. The goal is to ensure that no infants who reach the criteria for ROP treatment are missed in an attempt to minimize life-long vision loss.
